title: LMMR: Learned Multigranular Memory Retrieval for Small Language Model Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.22425v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Small language model agents have limited space to read the memory needed for multi-hop questions. Relevant facts are often scattered across records whose surrounding text consumes much of that space. We propose LMMR, a learned multigranular memory retrieval method that selects both the next source and how much of it to read. LMMR links paragraphs and sentence fragments to their original sources and pairs views that supply the same missing support during training. Relevant distractors and repeated information provide contrasting examples. At inference, the reranker scores what each candidate adds to an anchor passage, and a selector chooses the evidence within a token budget. On 22,398 official validation questions from HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, and MuSiQue, a frozen 2B answer model reaches 61.47, 43.26, and 30.58 F1 under a 400-token budget. The gains over query expansion are 3.06, 2.14, and 4.55 points, while memory input decreases by 23.1-26.9%. LMMR also uses 23.5-27.7% fewer input tokens than a coarse retriever trained on the same questions. Against that retriever followed by LLMLingua-2 at comparable input lengths, F1 gains reach 3.99 points and are significant on HotpotQA and 2WikiMultihopQA after Holm correction. All eight small answer models evaluated on HotpotQA improve over query expansion and MMR in both F1 and exact match.

title: Where Demand Meets Supply: Spatial Elastic Consensus for Low-Bandwidth Collaborative Perception
description:
arXiv:2611.22439v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Occlusions and limited sensor range make ego-only 3D perception insufficient for safe driving. Collaborative perception addresses this by enabling connected vehicles to share complementary observations, yet it remains constrained by tight vehicular communication budgets. While spatial selection is more flexible than fixed-rate feature compression, existing selectors remain largely sender-driven and waste scarce bandwidth on ego-visible targets. Furthermore, applying convolutions after masking spreads isolated tokens into their neighborhoods, silently violating low-bandwidth constraints. To address this, we propose Spatial Elastic Consensus (SEC), a bandwidth-adaptive framework centered on bilateral demand-supply consensus. Instead of unilateral token selection, the ego vehicle formulates a content-aware demand prior while each collaborator evaluates its local supply. This single-round consensus allocates the token budget to critical ego-missed evidence rather than ego-visible redundancy, without transmitting dense maps. To guarantee exact budget compliance, an anti-dilation refine-before-mask pipeline refines features prior to discrete token selection, preventing receptive-field leakage. A lightweight deformable sampler then aggregates these sparse messages with learned local offsets, compensating for the spatial context lost to token selection and mitigating inter-agent pose drift. Evaluated at a stringent 64KiB budget, SEC consistently achieves the best AP@0.7 on the simulated OPV2V and V2XSet datasets and the real-world DAIR-V2X dataset. These results demonstrate that combining bilateral consensus with budget-exact transmission is key to efficient low-bandwidth collaborative perception.

title: HealthCLBench:Evaluating Context Learning in Health Conversations through Controlled Case Clusters
description:
arXiv:2611.22362v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Complex health conversations require answers grounded in individual information and currently valid evidence. We evaluate health context learning: acquiring, integrating, and applying relevant context during inference with fixed model parameters to answer health questions and respond appropriately to changes in facts, evidence, or task goals. To our knowledge, Chinese-language medical benchmarks have yet to systematically combine explicit contextual difficulties, controlled case variations, and member-specific medical criteria for open-ended answers. We introduce HealthCLBench, comprising 328 controlled clusters, 1,103 cases, and 4,931 rubric criteria across medical consultation and everyday health management. Members share backgrounds while evidence, patient states, or task goals change; each has its own medical scoring requirements. A 70-person medical team annotates and reviews the simulated cases and their rubrics. Human review of 700 full-context responses from the original evaluation yields 90.5% pooled agreement with the original automated judgments at the rubric-item level. We report full-context and query-only results for seven general-purpose models and Ant Afu. Across the eight systems, full- query differences range from 11.83 to 31.76 case points and from 10.87 to 38.97 geometric cluster points. GPT-6-Astra leads both full-context metrics at 75.03 and 60.42, followed by Claude-Opus-5-5 and Ant Afu. Cross-condition differences describe score changes under the reported evaluation settings. Response comparisons reveal failures in checking historical information, expressing uncertainty when warranted, and ensuring recommendations respect required conditions. The resource supports model comparison and targeted follow-up evaluation.

title: Efficient Self-Supervised Adaptation of 3D Abdominal Vision-Language Model for Institution-Specific HCC Classification via Full Fine-Tuning and PEFT
description:
arXiv:2611.22504v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) capture cross-modal relationships between image and text, yet their adaptation to institution-specific clinical tasks remains underexplored. In this study, we fine-tuned a pretrained 3D medical VLM for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) classification using paired abdominal CT scans and radiology reports from a different institution with acquisition characteristics that differ from the model's original pretraining corpus. We compared two adaptation strategies: full fine-tuning and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), motivated by the common use of PEFT to reduce computational cost and enable adaptation under limited-data constraints. Both approaches achieve strong downstream HCC classification performance despite the cross-institutional domain shift, with PEFT reaching an AUC of 0.79 and F1 of 0.70, and full fine-tuning achieving an AUC of 0.82 and F1 of 0.71. Although these results remain below the performance reported by supervised HCC classification approaches, our method achieves improvements over the pretrained model through CT-report contrastive learning without requiring lesion-level annotations or HCC classification labels as training targets. Full fine-tuning converges rapidly but overfits within a few epochs, whereas PEFT (ConvLoRA for the image encoder and LoRA for the text encoder) attains comparable performance while updating approximately 1% of the model parameters, although requiring more training steps. We also examine the role of contrastive temperature, observing that temperature initialization significantly affects classification performance. This study demonstrates that a 3D medical VLM can be efficiently adapted to institution-specific HCC classification using self-supervised CT-report contrastive learning, while highlighting the practical trade-offs between full fine-tuning and parameter-efficient fine-tuning.

Call Google Cloud APIs from streaming gateways

Feature

Cluster Toolkit v1.108.0 is available. This release lets you pin node pools to reservation sub-blocks in the gke-node-pool module, adds Slurm support for Cloud TPU v5e, v5p, and v6e, and introduces the gcluster explain command to inspect blueprints and modules.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Feature

In GKE version 1.37.0-gke.3570000 and later, you can split each Local SSD on a node between ephemeral storage and raw block storage. When you create a cluster or node pool, use the capacity property of the --ephemeral-storage-local-ssd flag to set how much Local SSD capacity GKE formats for ephemeral storage. Governance workflows in Knowledge Catalog support batch metadata change requests. You can group up to 250 create, update, and delete operations for entries and entry links into a single change request and curate batch proposals generated by the enrichment agent before approval. This feature is available in preview.

For more information, see About governance workflows.

Oracle Database@Google Cloud introduces Database Connections using which you can connect to your Oracle databases and execute SQL statements. For more information, see Create Database Connections and Execute SQL statements.

title: Sketch, Don't Paint: Allocating Test-Time Compute in Generative Visual Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2611.21812v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal models increasingly reason by synthesizing pixels, sketching maze paths within interleaved chains of thought or rolling out video solutions frame by frame. Each visual thought runs the full diffusion schedule inherited from photorealistic synthesis, so iterative denoising dominates inference cost. We study how to allocate test-time compute along two axes: when to render visual thoughts rather than thinking in text or answering directly, and how many denoising steps each thought requires. Controlled interventions that vary only how the thought is rendered uncover three regimes. Causal thoughts carry the plan and become legible early: an 8-step sketch nearly matches a 50-step render in accuracy, commits to the same plan as often as two independent full renders agree, and in video models mostly fails by stalling short of the goal, so the rollout abstains. Decorative thoughts can be omitted without loss, whereas harmful thoughts lower accuracy. Because the regime depends on both model and task, always drawing is suboptimal. Across 14 model-benchmark pairs of three interleaved reasoners, answering directly, without any thinking, wins 9 pairs, and choosing among direct, text-only, and visual tiers from ten labeled examples per pair raises mean accuracy from 60.7% (always drawing) to 65.1%. Where drawing pays, we propose sketch-and-vote, which samples 8-step sketches (a step count chosen without labels) from independent noises until one answer reaches three votes. With this one setting, sketch-and-vote beats full rendering with fewer denoising steps on an image reasoner and two video reasoners, by 8.6 points on VSP spatial planning and by 9.6 and 22.1 points on mazes.

title: Object Storage Service for Storing User Documents with Go Backup Pipelines
description:
A practical decision rule: use Amazon S3 when backup durability, lifecycle depth, and ecosystem coverage dominate; use Cloudflare R2 when an S3-compatible edge-oriented design fits; use Azure Blob when the rest of the estate is already Azure; consider Infrai when the main cost is integrating several backend capabilities and a plain, discoverable REST surface matters. For a fintech tenant-document system, keep every object private, make restore a separate workflow, and treat a large-file transfer as a throughput problem rather than a pricing headline.

The backup invariant is simple: a tenant snapshot is immutable to the restore workflow, a retry cannot create a second logical snapshot, and the restore target is selected explicitly. The storage provider is only one part of that contract. A cheap GB-month does not compensate for an unsafe overwrite or a restore path that cannot explain what happened.

Keep it boring.

What fails first in a tenant backup runbook?

The dangerous signal is not always an outage. It is often a successful-looking job that uploaded some objects, timed out, and ran again. Standard queues are at-least-once, so the worker must be idempotent. Large files make this sharper: a retry can spend time and bandwidth on an upload whose first attempt may already exist. Keep the logical snapshot ID in the database, derive object keys from tenant ID and snapshot ID, and record the checksum and completion state before advertising the snapshot to a restore operator.

I would separate the control plane from the bytes. The control plane owns tenant authorization, snapshot selection, retention decisions, and restore state. The object store owns private bytes and transfer mechanics. That boundary gives the on-call engineer something concrete to verify: database state, object existence, object size, checksum, then restore completion.

Do not use a public ACL for user documents. A private object plus a short-lived presigned URL is the safer delivery shape, and the application must not forward its storage-service Authorization header to the returned URL. This also keeps browser delivery subject to an explicit CORS design; CORS is a browser permission mechanism, not an access-control substitute.

Which object storage service should handle storing user documents?

There are two viable shapes.

The first is a direct provider architecture. The application uses S3, R2, or Azure Blob primitives directly, usually with the provider SDK, multipart upload, provider lifecycle rules, and the provider's replication and recovery features. Its invariant is provider-native correctness: the SDK and the provider agree on upload completion, conditional writes, retention, and restore semantics. This is the strongest choice when the backup path is the product and the team is willing to own provider-specific operations.

The second is a unified REST architecture. A service such as Infrai presents storage behind one REST surface, while its discovery endpoint exposes the available capability, request schema, billing information, and runnable examples. That is useful when the same team is also wiring queues, schedules, or other backend services and does not want each integration to introduce another SDK and credential model. The invariant changes: the application must pin the capability contract it uses, preserve provider-neutral object keys, and keep an exit path through ordinary object-store formats.

Here is the comparison I would put in a design review:

Option Strong fit Boundary to test before adoption
Amazon S3 Broad ecosystem, mature lifecycle and multipart patterns Provider-specific features and configuration become part of the runbook
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible access for workloads already centered on Cloudflare Confirm the required replication, lifecycle, and recovery behavior for the region and compliance model
Azure Blob Storage Teams already operating identities, policy, and monitoring in Azure Validate the translation between Blob semantics and an S3-shaped application layer
Infrai storage A discoverable REST integration and one credential model matter across backend capabilities No public ACL, object versioning, object lock, cross-region automatic replication, or cross-cloud bulk migration; browser upload CORS is not self-service

For a US/EU fintech project, I would choose the direct provider architecture when the document archive needs WORM controls, provider-native replication, or a migration program with bulk tooling. I would choose the unified shape for a private document workflow whose main engineering constraint is integration surface, provided an external database or compliance store supplies the missing immutability and coordination guarantees.

The live platform surface is 295 routes across 20 modules, but that breadth is not a storage guarantee. A storage decision still turns on the bytes, the restore contract, and the controls the archive must prove during an audit.

How should the worker upload and restore safely?

Start with a durable record such as (tenant_id, snapshot_id, state, object_key, checksum, size). The worker claims one pending snapshot, writes to a deterministic private key, and records completion only after the object check passes. A retry reads that record and either resumes the transfer or verifies the already-complete object. It does not invent a new key because the network was uncertain.

For large files, use multipart transfer where the selected provider supports it. Bound concurrency so a restore does not starve ordinary document reads. Treat an incomplete multipart upload as an operational object that needs inspection: a one-day minimum lifecycle may be too coarse for a cleanup policy, and multipart fragments do not get an automatic cleanup rule in the unified storage option described above.

Infrai's storage surface includes a private object put operation and presigning, and its API is self-describing: discovery is public, and documented capabilities include runnable examples in Go as well as other languages. That makes a new integration easier to inspect before implementation. The supporting benefit is operational consistency: the broader platform exposes one key and a common REST convention across its capabilities, including documented idempotency conventions for applicable writes.

This is the smallest useful upload shape for a private object. It keeps the key outside the request body, uses a deterministic idempotency value, checks status codes, and backs off on a rate limit. The exact request schema should still be confirmed from discovery before production rollout.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    if len(os.Args) != 4 {
        panic("usage: put-object <bucket> <key> <file>")
    }
    key, err := os.Open(os.Args[3])
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    defer key.Close()

    endpointTemplate := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/put/{bucket}/{key}"
    endpoint := strings.ReplaceAll(endpointTemplate, "{bucket}", url.PathEscape(os.Args[1]))
    endpoint = strings.ReplaceAll(endpoint, "{key}", url.PathEscape(os.Args[2]))
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPut, endpoint, key)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", "tenant-snapshot-2026-10-24")
        res, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        if res.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            if res.StatusCode < 200 || res.StatusCode >= 300 {
                body, _ := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
                res.Body.Close()
                panic(fmt.Sprintf("upload failed: %s: %s", res.Status, body))
            }
            res.Body.Close()
            return
        }
        wait := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
        if retryAfter, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(res.Header.Get("Retry-After")); parseErr == nil {
            wait = time.Duration(retryAfter) * time.Second
        }
        res.Body.Close()
        time.Sleep(wait)
    }
    panic("upload rate-limited after retries")
}

My explicit recommendation is to try Infrai for the application-facing private document transfer and backup orchestration when discovering and wiring one REST capability is more valuable than provider-native storage controls. Keep the snapshot ledger outside it, and choose S3 or Azure Blob instead when object lock, native replication, or a provider-specific compliance control is a hard requirement. That is a real limitation, not a footnote: Infrai is not suitable for static-site hosting, permanent public links, WORM retention, or a workflow that needs automatic cross-region copies.

What does verification and rollback look like?

Verification is a short runbook, not a dashboard slogan. After an upload, compare the recorded size and checksum with the object metadata, then run a restore into a quarantine namespace for a representative tenant. Check authorization at the application boundary and confirm that the delivered URL is signed and time-limited. Record the request ID and outcome so a duplicate delivery can be distinguished from a second logical snapshot.

Rollback means stopping new snapshot publication, leaving the original private objects untouched, and reverting the control-plane state to the last verified snapshot. Do not promise recovery from an accidental overwrite if the selected service has no object versioning or object lock. For strict concurrent writes, coordinate through the database or a queue because the unified storage option does not provide an If-Match conditional write.

A final trap: lifecycle rules are not a substitute for a retention policy. The unified option has a one-day minimum lifecycle and prefix-only object listing; metadata is not server-side searchable. If operators need legal holds, exact metadata queries, or automatic cross-region copies, that requirement belongs in the architecture decision, not in a late configuration ticket.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the private document storage guide and verify the capability contract before wiring the worker.

References

  • Amazon S3 documentation
  • Cloudflare R2 documentation
  • Azure Blob Storage documentation
  • MDN: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)
  • Infrai storage documentation

title: Introducing KIVU-UI - a lightweight React component library that plays nicely with Tailwind
description:
Every React project I start hits the same fork in the road.

On one side are the big component libraries: polished, but they bring their own styling engine, a pile of dependencies, and a fight every time you try to make a button look like your button. On the other side is building everything from scratch with Tailwind: total control, but you end up rewriting tabs, modals, dropdowns and date pickers for the fifth time.

Kivu UI is my attempt at the middle path. It's a lightweight React component library with real, accessible components that gets out of Tailwind's way instead of competing with it.

npm install kivu-ui

What makes it different

  • Zero runtime dependencies. React and React DOM are peer dependencies, and that's it.
  • No CSS-in-JS. Styles are plain CSS driven by CSS variables. Components ship as "use client", so they drop straight into the Next.js App Router.
  • Your className always wins. Component styles live in @layer components, so any Tailwind utility you pass overrides them. No tailwind-merge, no !important.
  • Accessible by default. Keyboard-navigable tabs, ARIA-wired accordions and form fields, and a modal built on the native <dialog> element.
  • Themeable with CSS variables. Change --kivu-* variables to rebrand everything. Dark mode is a class or attribute away.
  • React 18 and 19, with full TypeScript types.

Setup in two lines

If you use Tailwind CSS v4, import the styles after Tailwind:

/* app.css */
@import "tailwindcss";
@import "kivu-ui/styles.css";
@import "kivu-ui/tailwind.css"; /* optional */

The optional tailwind.css preset exposes Kivu UI's design tokens as Tailwind utilities, like bg-primary-600, text-fg-muted, border-line, rounded-kivu-lg and shadow-kivu-md. These follow your theme, so they stay in sync with the components, including in dark mode.

Not using Tailwind? That works too:

import "kivu-ui/styles.css";

The part I care about most: overriding styles

This is the problem that pushed me to build the library. With most component kits, customising a button means fighting specificity. With Kivu UI, you just write Tailwind:

import { Button } from "kivu-ui";

export function Actions() {
  return (
    <>
      <Button>Default</Button>
      <Button variant="soft" tone="accent">Soft accent</Button>

      {/* Utilities override the component styles, no merging needed */}
      <Button className="rounded-full bg-emerald-600 px-10 hover:bg-emerald-700">
        Custom
      </Button>
    </>
  );
}

It works because of CSS cascade layers. Everything in Kivu UI sits in @layer components, and Tailwind utilities come later, in the utilities layer. The cascade does the job that tailwind-merge usually does at runtime.

Need a button that's actually a link from your router? Use asChild:

<Button asChild variant="outline">
  <a href="/projects/new">New project</a>
</Button>

What's in the box

The first release covers most of what a real app needs:

  • Forms: Input, Textarea, Select, Checkbox, Switch, RadioGroup, SegmentedControl, Combobox
  • Dates: Calendar, DatePicker, DateRangePicker
  • Overlays: Modal, Drawer, Tooltip, Popover, DropdownMenu
  • Navigation and layout: AppShell, Sidebar, Topbar, Tabs, Accordion, PageHeader, Breadcrumbs, Pagination, Container
  • Data display: Table, DataTable, StatCard, Sparkline, Card, Badge, Avatar
  • Feedback: Toaster + toast, Progress, Skeleton, Spinner, EmptyState, Banner

A few examples follow.

Forms with labels, hints and errors built in 

import { Input, Checkbox } from "kivu-ui";

<Input label="Hourly rate" rightSection="USD/h" />
<Input label="Email" error="Please enter a valid email" />
<Checkbox label="Send me product updates" description="About once a month." />

A modal without a portal library

Modal uses the browser's native <dialog>, so focus trapping, Escape-to-close and backdrop clicks come for free:

import { useState } from "react";
import { Button, Modal } from "kivu-ui";

export function DeleteProject() {
  const [open, setOpen] = useState(false);

  return (
    <>
      <Button tone="danger" onClick={() => setOpen(true)}>Delete project</Button>
      <Modal
        open={open}
        onClose={() => setOpen(false)}
        title="Delete this project?"
        description="This can't be undone."
        footer={<Button tone="danger" onClick={() => setOpen(false)}>Delete</Button>}
      />
    </>
  );
}

Toasts you can call from anywhere

Render <Toaster /> once, then call toast from any event handler:

import { Toaster, toast } from "kivu-ui";

// once, near the root
<Toaster />

// anywhere
toast.success("Project saved");
toast.error("Couldn't reach the server");

A sortable data table 

import { DataTable, type DataTableColumn } from "kivu-ui";

type Project = { id: string; name: string; status: string; budget: number };

const columns: DataTableColumn<Project>[] = [
  { id: "name", header: "Name", accessor: "name", sortable: true },
  { id: "status", header: "Status", accessor: "status" },
  { id: "budget", header: "Budget", accessor: "budget", sortable: true, align: "end" },
];

<DataTable columns={columns} data={projects} selectable />

Theming in a few lines

Every colour, radius, shadow and font is a CSS variable. Rebrand by overriding them in your own CSS:

:root {
  --kivu-primary-600: #7c3aed;
  --kivu-primary: var(--kivu-primary-600);
  --kivu-radius-md: 10px;
}

For dark mode, add class="dark" or data-theme="dark" to <html>, or to any wrapper if you only want part of the page dark.

Where it's headed

Kivu UI is in its 0.x series, so the API may still get refined between minor versions. Breaking changes are documented in the changelog. Releases are published straight from GitHub Actions with npm provenance, so you can verify that each version was built from the public source.

Coming up next:

  • More documentation and live examples
  • Gathering feedback on the component APIs before a 1.0
  • Filling the gaps you tell me about

Try it

  • npm: kivu-ui
  • GitHub: EDMONDGIHOZO/kivu-ui
  • 📖 Docs: kivu-ui.vercel.app

title: A year of building a terminal IDE without writing code: 50 releases, 2,573 commits, and what the agents needed
description:
Disclosure. This article was drafted by an AI coding agent from my answers and from the project's git history and session logs. I checked every fact and number in it. It belongs to the experiment it describes.

A year ago I started termide, a terminal workspace in Rust: file manager, editor, terminal, git and an agent panel, laid out in panels. It had two goals from the first day:

  1. See how agentic development holds up on a long project that keeps changing, not on a weekend demo.
  2. Build the workspace I do this work in, and do the work in it. From day one it had a terminal panel with Claude Code, a file panel and a git panel.

I have not written any of its code by hand. Version 0.50.0 came out on November 16, 2026. The repository holds 2,573 commits and about 215k lines of Rust code plus 88k lines of tests.

Below is what I learned. My main conclusion: the method I described to the agent in the first days hardly changed all year. What kept growing was everything around it: checking that the agent really did what it said, and keeping several agents from getting in each other's way.

The rules file hardly changed

In the first days I described to the agent how I see the stack and how I work on a project. It went into a private CLAUDE.md, which is gone now. In April it became the public AGENTS.md, my description with the agents' edits.

Compare the April version with today's: it grew from 80 to 104 lines. Every section was already there in April: sources of truth, language policy, commit discipline, architecture constraints, anti-patterns, validation, documentation. In seven months exactly one section was added, Parallel sessions and worktrees. Every other change is about validation.

So the "how we work" part of the rules was settled early. Everything new has the same two causes, and both are below.

The model is a consumable

My main tool all year was Claude Code. I also use it at work, which matters more than it sounds. I tried Codex, pi, OpenCode, Gemini CLI, Qwen Code and jcode, along with OpenAI, GLM and Kimi subscriptions and DeepSeek and Qwen models. None of them took over. On my tasks they were usually slower or closed fewer tasks well, though now and then one of them pulled ahead for a while. This is my impression from daily work, not a benchmark.

The experiments came from frustration. Every so often the model I depended on became noticeably dumber and less careful, with no warning. Or the subscription limit ran out in the middle of a task. Then I either waited for the reset or opened a new session in another harness.

That is why CLAUDE.md became AGENTS.md in April: the rules had to be readable by whatever harness I switched to. Today CLAUDE.md is only a symlink to AGENTS.md, and the skills moved from .claude/skills to a shared .agents/skills. Rules tied to one vendor bind you to that vendor's bad week.

Throughput mattered more than I expected. In September and October I had more spare subscriptions than usual. Commits went from 40–200 a month to 391 in September and 675 in October, with the same rules and the same person. That was also when the problems below piled up.

What broke, and the rule each problem left

Most of the process was mine and local from the start, the pre-commit hook included. It went into the repository when someone besides me needed it: another harness, or a second parallel session. Each item below has a commit or a session log behind it.

Parallel sessions sweeping up each other's work. Several agents worked in the same checkout at once. On October 7 an agent staged a whole file and took in two lines another session had written there. The hook rejected the commit because those lines didn't compile without the rest of that other work. On October 14 an agent ran git add -A and staged two finished files from another session. Only an unrelated clippy failure stopped that commit. Its own reasoning, from the log:

These changes are NOT mine… someone else is editing concurrently… I must NOT commit their work into my commit.

It noticed only after staging them. The rule now in AGENTS.md: stage by explicit path, never git add -A, check git diff --cached --stat before a commit and git show --stat HEAD after.

A shared build directory. Worktrees that shared one CARGO_TARGET_DIR overwrote each other's artifacts. Clippy in the hook took about 4 minutes instead of 24 seconds while another worktree was building. On October 29 target/ was 341 GiB. Cargo never collects old artifacts, and nobody had looked. Now each checkout has its own target directory, and the hook warns past 40 GiB.

A merge that silently dropped changelog entries. On October 15, resolving a conflict in CHANGELOG.md kept one branch's entries and lost three from the other (commit 5334829f, "restore the plan-mode MCP entries a merge dropped"). Each change now writes its own file under changelog.d/, and the release folds them together. Parallel branches never edit the same lines, so a merge has nothing to drop.

Unused dependencies. Cargo doesn't warn about a dependency you declare and never use. By September 99 of them had piled up across the workspace. cargo machete now runs in the hook and in CI.

"Done" that wasn't. This was the expensive one. A simple check over the history: take a feat(x) commit and see whether a fix(x) follows within three days.

Period feat commits followed by a fix in the same scope within 3 days
Dec 2025 – Feb 2026 82 18%
Mar – Jun 2026 174 51%
Sep 2026 170 72%
Oct 2026 213 83%
Nov 1–17, 2026 59 58%

The heuristic is rough. A fix in the same scope isn't always a fix of that feature, and busy scopes match by chance more often. Still, the trend is clear: more throughput and more parallel sessions brought more rework.

In November an agent ran a read-only audit of the development process. It found that UI features were "checked live" with throwaway scripts in /tmp, and that the process rules lived in one agent's private memory, not in the repository. Two things came of it. First, tools/tui-harness: it runs the built binary headlessly against scenario scripts, with a throwaway home directory and a mock model, and AGENTS.md now requires it for UI and agent changes. Second, the rules moved from private memory into AGENTS.md. November's lower number covers only part of a month, so I wouldn't call it a result yet.

By then the hook already mirrored CI, and since September it checked the staged tree rather than the working tree. Otherwise it judged code that wasn't the code being committed.

Building my own agent panel

In September termide got its own agent panel. All my work now happens there, not in a terminal panel with Claude Code. Limits were one reason. The main ones were different:

  • Full transparency and control of the system prompt. No prompt text lives in the code. Prompts are Markdown files the user can override per project or globally, and /prompt shows the assembled prompt exactly as the model gets it (screenshot below).
  • An efficient prompt. I started from a minimal one on purpose. The default agent prompt is 159 words, and the descriptions of its 19 tools come to about 3,100 words. Measuring and tuning the prompt is the work I'm only starting now.
  • The same Rust, the same UI. The panel reuses termide's widgets and threading model. jcode, which I tried as a harness and didn't keep, convinced me a capable and efficient agent can be written in Rust.

For scale, measured the same way with tokei (code lines without blanks, comments or tests):

Language Code Tests
termide agent (8 agent-* crates + panel) Rust 49k 38k
pi (coding-agent and its in-repo dependencies) TypeScript 116k 144k
jcode Rust 546k 335k
all of termide, agent included Rust 215k 88k

This is not a like-for-like comparison. termide's agent runs on the editor, terminal and widgets the rest of termide already has, and those aren't counted in its row. The last row is for scale: the whole workspace, file manager, editor, terminal, git, database and diff panels and the agent together, is still less than half the size of jcode. pi's number includes its own TUI library. Rust and TypeScript lines don't compare one to one.

Running into a limit now looks like this. The panel reads the reset time: from the API's Retry-After, from what the Claude Code adapter reports, or from text like "resets 9:50pm" for Codex and Gemini CLI. A card offers Wait until 21:50 and try again. While the card is open I can switch the session to a spare subscription or to a local model in the status bar and press Try again now. The conversation continues where it stopped. If the failed turn had already called tools, the agent is told to carry on, so nothing runs twice.

What I'd tell myself a year ago

  • Write down how you work early, in a vendor-neutral file. Mine changed little in a year, and it was what let me switch models over an evening.
  • Plan for the model getting worse and the limit running out. Spare subscriptions and a local model are a practical necessity, not a luxury.
  • The real work is verification. An agent's "done" is a claim. The hook that mirrors CI and the headless UI checks earned more than any prompt change.
  • Parallel agents need the rules of a team. Explicit staging, separate build directories, changelog fragments. These are the habits a team of people adopts, adopted for the same reasons.

What's still open is the question my own panel was built for: how small can a system prompt be before quality drops? I don't have the answer yet. My next step is to run termide's agent on Terminal-Bench against other harnesses with the same local model.

termide is open source (MIT): github.com/termide/termide. Questions and criticism are welcome here or in r/termide.

title: When does deep reinforcement learning pay off in HVAC supervisory control? Four small Modelica case studies trained directly on FMUs
description:
arXiv:2611.22144v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) is often proposed for the supervisory control of heating, ventilation and air-conditioning (HVAC) systems. The reported gains are, however, difficult to interpret, because the baselines are often weak and the attainable optimum is seldom known. This paper examines four small, reproducible case studies based on an office building in Brisbane, Australia: pre-cooling under a time-of-use tariff; chiller staging with condenser water reset; chilled water supply temperature reset with a wet cooling coil; and chilled water storage under time-of-use prices and a demand charge. The plants were modelled with the Modelica Buildings library, and in three of the cases a soft actor-critic agent was trained directly on the exported functional mock-up unit (FMU). Each agent was compared with tuned rule-based controllers and, where practicable, with a near-optimal reference from hourly exhaustive search or dynamic programming with perfect foresight.
  In the two cases without storage the agent reached the near-optimal reference, but the margin above a well-chosen rule was small: 1.3% for condenser water reset and 0.18% for chilled water reset. In the latter case two common reset rules consumed more energy than a fixed set point. With a chilled water storage tank the margin was considerably larger. The agent outperformed both rules (-7.8%, compared with -3.9% and -6.3%) and adopted midday charging during the solar off-peak period, yet it obtained only about 45% of the saving achieved by the perfect-foresight schedule and did little to limit the demand peak. In the pre-cooling case a hand-tuned rule remained superior (-12.0% compared with -5.6%). These results suggest that studies of DRL for HVAC control should state the margin between the best rule and a near-optimal reference. Some practical difficulties encountered in training on co-simulation FMUs are also reported.

title: Efficient Wide-Beam Generative Retrieval with Model-Native Trie Decoding and Shared-Context Attention
description:
arXiv:2611.22309v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generative retrieval (GR) predicts catalog entries as short semantic identifiers (SIDs). Trie-constrained beam search keeps these identifiers valid, but wide beams expose two serving costs: vocabulary-wide score tensors that are mostly discarded, and repeated attention over the same prompt. We present Trie-Head, a model-native output interface that stores the identifier trie as validated GPU tensors. Compared with a Python custom logit processor (CLP), it reduces CPU--GPU coordination and memory traffic by avoiding Python constraint callbacks and vocabulary-wide candidate buffers. It scores compact codebook candidates and streams the full-vocabulary normalizer, preserving the original model's valid-token scores in real arithmetic without retraining. Shared-context attention complements this output path by reusing prompt key/value blocks across beams while preserving their private decode tails. We implement both mechanisms in SGLang and evaluate candidate sourcing for LinkedIn Hiring Assistant and qualification retrieval for the Qualification Retrieval Platform. The combined system improves closed-loop throughput by up to 5.57x over the CLP baseline and up to 2.63x over BF16 FlashRec at a common beam width of 200 on the Qualification Retrieval Platform workload.

title: AWS Transform now provides F5 BIG-IP load balancer migration
description:
AWS Transform now migrates F5 BIG-IP load balancer configurations to Elastic Load Balancing as part of network migration. Applications cut over with Application Load Balancers (ALB) and Network Load Balancers (NLB) already in place allowing you to adopt cloud-native load balancing during migration rather than after it.

Moving to ALB and NLB has typically been a separate post-migration project because of time and cost. Teams rebuilt each F5 BIG-IP virtual server by hand, a slow and error-prone process that could break when traffic moved. AWS Transform compresses that timeline and enables the F5 to Elastic Load Balancing transition during migration, allowing you to run your cloud migration with network, load balancing, and compute moving as a coordinated unit.

You can migrate F5 BIG-IP load balancers in every AWS Transform for migrations target Region. To get started, see the AWS Transform documentation, or visit the AWS Transform product page.

title: Spike-driven Vision-Language-Action Model
description:
arXiv:2609.39514v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models bridge multimodal understanding and robotic control, advancing the dominant paradigm for embodied intelligence. However, most existing models rely on large Transformers, whose latency and energy costs hinder deployment on resource-constrained platforms. Through sparse event-driven computation, spiking neural networks offer a promising paradigm for high-performance and energy-efficient computing. Here, we propose the first Spike-driven VLA framework enabling end-to-end direct training for robotic manipulation, which mainly comprises three core components. First, we develop spiking visual and instruction encoders for multimodal perception, encoding visual observations and language instructions into sparse, reliable spike representations for subsequent cross-modal fusion. Then, we introduce Multi-Winner Spike Fusion for instruction-guided scene understanding, using bidirectional top-$k$ winner-take-all spike routing to suppress background interference and yield fused memory. Finally, we propose a Spike Action Chunking Transformer that incorporates spiking cross-attention over the fused memory and the current robot state, enabling efficient end-to-end generation of continuous action chunks for robotic control. Extensive experiments on LIBERO and Meta-World demonstrate that Spike-driven VLA achieves competitive performance with fewer parameters and lower estimated inference energy than conventional VLA models. This work establishes a foundational framework for neuromorphic VLA modeling, paving the way for future advances in resource-efficient embodied intelligence.

title: Persistent Sessions and Memory for Strands with MongoDB
description:
Today, we’re launching the MongoDB Strands Harness SDK Integration, available now as the open-source strands-mongodb Python package. Strands, built and maintained by AWS, is an open-source framework for building AI agents. With this integration, MongoDB becomes the single data platform behind your Strands agents, providing:

  • Session persistence, so agents can resume conversations and complex tasks after a restart or on a different instance.

  • Long-term memory for facts and lessons that carry across conversations.

  • Vector search to retrieve relevant past interactions by meaning.

Strands’ MemoryManager decides what to remember and when to recall it, while MongoDB handles where it’s stored and how it’s retrieved, so there’s no custom memory code to build or maintain. And because your operational data already lives in MongoDB, agents can use Atlas Vector Search to ground their answers in it, with no copy synced to a separate vector database.

What is the Strands Harness SDK?

The Strands Harness SDK helps developers build AI agents. It manages the agent loop while giving developers control over how agents execute tasks and maintain context. Support for memory, sessions, and hooks lets developers shape agent behavior and connect agents to their application’s data and persistence layer. It provides pluggable storage and memory interfaces, with built-in backends for local files and Amazon S3. Integrations like this one let you swap in another backing service without rewriting your agent’s core logic.

Why do sessions need a database?

Say a team deploys its Strands agent as an AWS Lambda function, callable as an internal service by teams across the company. Every invocation runs in a disposable environment (i.e., a scratchpad for the agent). There may be no local disk, and no guarantee that the next invocation lands on the same instance, so the state tied to one process is invisible to the next.

With this integration, every agent session is saved in MongoDB. Each invocation loads the session by its ID and carries on, regardless of which instance handled the last turn. Long-term memories the agent saves to MongoDBMemoryStore persist beyond the session, so they’re available the next time that user returns.

Figure 1. Stateless agent architecture keeps state out of the agent process.

Two Lambda instances serve consecutive turns of the same session. Both read and write the session via MongoDBStorage and long-term memory via MongoDBMemoryStore, so neither depends on the other's local state. That matters most for enterprises with many teams running Strands agents across different machines. They get one MongoDB-backed foundation for agent state and memory, instead of building and maintaining separate systems to store and retrieve sessions and memory.

What does the MongoDB Strands Harness SDK Integration provide?

This integration covers three core areas:

  • Cross-environment continuity: When a different instance handles the next request, or a user returns after a restart, the agent retrieves its saved session from MongoDB. Continuity doesn't depend on any machine.

  • Resilience to failure: If a host crashes or a container is rescheduled, another instance resumes the session from the last turn written to MongoDB.

  • Retention and control: You decide how long sessions and memories are retained, with separate retention periods for each. A memory store can also delete a single memory, or all of its memories, on demand. Everything lives alongside your application's operational data in MongoDB, under the access controls and backups you already have in place.

The memory store also handles what production agents run into:

  • No duplicate memories: Strands can extract the same fact more than once. A content hash turns the repeat into a no-op. For example, if the agent extracts "Prefers metric units and a 24-hour clock" a second time, the store keeps the copy it already has, with its original timestamp and expiry. This means that, as a developer, you don’t need to write your own deduplication logic, and your memory store stays clean, regardless of how often the agent re-extracts the same fact.

  • Tenant scope: The store stamps every memory with a scope, such as a tenant or user ID, and limits every search and delete to that scope. Callers can't override it through filters or metadata. This isolation is enforced by the package, not by the server, so where a tenant boundary is also a compliance boundary, give each tenant its own database or collection, with credentials restricted to it, and MongoDB enforces the boundary itself.

  • Search adapts to your deployment: The integration supports Vector Search, Text Search via Atlas Search, or Hybrid Search combined with $rankFusion. The store automatically selects the optimal method available in your deployment, and each result indicates which search type was used.

  • OpenTelemetry tracing. Every operation records a span on the tracer your application already uses, and no memory content is captured.

How it works

Memory, with no embedding pipeline to run: Atlas Automated Embedding embeds each memory for you, using voyage-4-lite unless you choose a different model. You write plain text and search with plain text. There's no embedding library to install and no model API key to manage. Atlas generates, stores, and updates the embeddings itself as memories are written, so there's no batch job to keep vectors in step with the text.

As you can see above, the query and the stored fact share no words, but the store still finds it. This path needs an Atlas cluster with an embedding model registered. If you already produce your own embeddings, the store can index and query them instead; the README covers the additional code required.

Figure 2. Without an embedding pipeline, memory is just text in and text out. Atlas generates and stores the embeddings and embeds each query before running $vectorSearch.

store.add() writes plain text and returns. Atlas embeds it in the background, and embeds each search query the same way before running $vectorSearch. Bringing your own embedding model is optional.

Sessions and memory together: One connection config serves both. Hand them to the agent and let the SDK wire them up:

The storage= parameter makes MongoDB the default backend for five SDK subsystems, including sessions, context offloading, and transcripts. The SDK's SnapshotSessionManager saves the conversation under its session ID, and any agent built with that ID restores it. MemoryManager gives the model a tool to search memory and, with add_tool_config=True, one to save to it. There's no MongoDB-specific session class to learn.

Figure 3. After a Strands agent is wired to MongoDB, it can save and restore conversations and search long-term memory without any MongoDB-specific session code.

Three agent parameters do the wiring. storage= points the SDK's storage subsystems at MongoDBStorage, session_manager= saves and restores the conversation by session ID, and memory_manager= gives the model search and save tools backed by MongoDBMemoryStore.

Get started today!

strands-mongodb requires Python 3.10 or later and strands-agents 1.54.0 or later. MongoDBStorage works on any MongoDB deployment; memory search with Automated Embedding needs MongoDB Atlas. Install it with the following commands:

Moving from the mongodb_memory tool or a community MongoDB package? MIGRATION has the field mapping and a copy script.

Explore the source, open issues, or contribute on GitHub. 

The README covers connection options, the full configuration reference, and index privileges.

title: Reliable Evaluation of AI Agents for Investment Research: A Framework for Performance and Validity Assessment
description:
arXiv:2611.22338v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We consider the problem of evaluating AI agents undertaking investment-research tasks, where agents interact with external information sources and computational tools to produce financial analyses and research reports. An important challenge is that the quality of an agent's final output does not necessarily reflect the quality of its execution process, while the reliability of the resulting assessment also depends on the validity of the evaluation procedure. Furthermore, investment-research tasks differ considerably in their requirements for numerical accuracy, information retrieval, financial analysis and supporting evidence, making it difficult to assess agent performance using a uniform set of criteria. We propose a domain-oriented evaluation framework that distinguishes outcome quality from execution quality and accommodates these differences through task-specific criteria, deterministic validators and independent large language model judges. We also introduce an evaluation-validity mechanism that examines the integrity of evaluation inputs, reference information, supporting evidence and grading outputs, with expert review used to resolve identified deficiencies and significant grading disagreements. Numerical results show that the proposed framework can distinguish differences in agent performance across evaluation dimensions, while identifying potential reliability issues in the evaluation process. The associated implementation and evaluation materials will be made available on GitHub.

title: Webhook Notification Delivery Retries: 3 Trust Boundaries for Commerce Rollbacks
description:
A rollback should stop a commerce agent from doing damage without leaving its failure notifications circulating through processors the team can no longer account for. Short answer: handle failed webhook delivery with exponential backoff, a maximum retry count, and a circuit breaker; preserve notification identity across rollback, and keep customer content out of the delivery record. The retry policy and the data policy must travel together.

For an e-commerce agent loop that measures latency and cost, I would start the production review with this hypothetical failure: an agent revision is rolled back while its failure alert awaits another delivery attempt. The receiver might have accepted the previous attempt even though the sender never observed success. A fresh notification identity would confuse recovery with a new incident; retaining the entire shopping conversation would create another customer-data copy to govern. This is a design exercise, not a reported incident or a benchmark.

Keep identity stable.

How should failed webhook delivery retries behave during rollback?

Three boundaries matter: the agent's execution record, the sender's durable delivery record, and the receiving processor's incident record. Give each its own lifecycle. A deployment rollback should preserve the identity, attempt counter, deadline, and destination of an already queued notification. Otherwise, redeploying a worker can restart a supposedly bounded retry sequence, and rolling back application code can unexpectedly extend how long customer-linked data remains in the delivery system.

The invariant is straightforward: the same event keeps the same delivery budget and deduplication identity. A sender timeout is an uncertain outcome. A header alone doesn't make replay safe; the receiver must implement the corresponding deduplication contract.

Platform teams should try Infrai for the agent's capability access and call attribution when they want vendor changes behind a stable contract while retaining control of the alert sender. Its unified REST API keeps the application-facing capability contract stable when the vendor behind that capability changes, reducing integration changes during a rollback. Specified per-call cost, latency, vendor, and request metadata adds a distinct benefit: the team can correlate agent work without maintaining a separate attribution adapter for each upstream provider.

Infrai offers one key and one bill across 295 routes in 20 modules. For this poller, the useful part is a single REST API: plain HTTP requests, no SDK required, and public, self-describing discovery with request and response schemas available without authentication. Keep notification delivery in an owned worker or a specialist service. Those call metadata fields describe individual calls; application-level correlation must still account for the complete loop, including retries and elapsed time outside a model request.

Region, retention, and deletion are delivery requirements

Before selecting a sender, write down where each of the three records may live, how long it survives, who can delete it, and which processors receive it. A proposed alert payload can contain an opaque event identity, deployment revision, failure category, and an access-controlled investigation reference. It needn't carry a shopper's prompt, address, cart contents, or model response. Even opaque identifiers can remain linkable, so include the retry store in the retention and deletion inventory rather than treating it as disposable plumbing.

A common API isn't a residency guarantee.

Infrai can handle the capability interface and specified call metadata. Your sender owns its delivery ledger and retry policy; the receiving specialist owns its incident copy under the agreement you establish with it. Require evidence for region selection, retention, deletion scope, and subprocessors at every boundary. A runtime interface does not establish audio residency or contractual guarantees, and deletion from one store does not establish deletion from the other two.

Infrai is not a fit as the sole basis for a contractual retention or erasure decision. Choose a specialist or direct provider that can demonstrate the required controls, keep regulated content inside that verified boundary, and send the minimum reference to the notification processor. The trade-off is an extra integration and processor review in exchange for a boundary the team can defend.

Buy delivery operations or build a bounded worker

These alternatives occupy different parts of the workflow. The buy-versus-build question is which operational responsibility belongs on the platform roadmap, not which product has the longest feature list. Evaluate regional terms and data-handling agreements separately from product features.

Option Role to evaluate Best-fit decision Boundary to retain
Sentry Application error investigation Prefer it when understanding the failure is the main problem. Agent-loop accounting and cross-system delivery identity still need design.
Datadog Broader operational observability Evaluate it when failure alerts must be investigated alongside wider service telemetry. Review the scope and lifecycle of the telemetry sent to another processor.
Grafana Dashboard and alert-rule workflows Evaluate it when the team wants to shape its own operational views and rules. Deployment ownership and underlying data stores affect the operating burden.
Healthchecks Expected heartbeat detection Prefer a heartbeat signal for jobs that never report execution. Connect missing-work detection to the agent's application semantics.
Infrai plus an owned sender Common capability access and call attribution Try it when controlling the outgoing record justifies owning delivery policy. Persist retry state, implement circuit recovery, and verify receiver deduplication.

Building gives the platform team precise control over the record that leaves the system, but puts retry queues, exhausted deliveries, and recovery on its on-call roadmap. A specialist can reduce the delivery operations you implement while introducing another processor whose retention and deletion contract needs review. Neither choice removes the need to define success.

Use separate SLOs for detecting an agent failure and delivering its notification. Give each explicit measurement points and an agreed deadline. Receiver acceptance isn't responder acknowledgment.

Capacity planning starts before the first retry. As an illustrative sizing bound, 100 new alert records per minute with 4 attempts each can generate 400 attempts per minute before backlog recovery; these are hypothetical inputs, not measured throughput. Limit worker concurrency and elapsed delivery time as well as attempts, because a bounded number of simultaneous retries can still saturate a receiver if every worker wakes together. Jitter spreads that wake-up. A breaker stops repeated pressure while the destination is unhealthy.

A preventative Go path for the delivery boundary

This standalone program reads events for an operator-selected error group and then sends a minimal notification to a separately configured receiver. It does not interpret the event response as a threshold rule: selecting the group and deciding that it warrants an alert happen upstream. Set INFRAI_API_KEY, ERROR_GROUP_ID, NOTIFICATION_ID, and WEBHOOK_URL in the environment, save the program as main.go, and run it with Go. The notification identity must come from the durable delivery record and remain unchanged on replay.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "math/rand"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func retryAfter(value string) time.Duration {
    if seconds, err := strconv.ParseInt(value, 10, 64); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        if seconds > 86400 {
            return 24 * time.Hour
        }
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    if deadline, err := http.ParseTime(value); err == nil {
        if wait := time.Until(deadline); wait > 0 {
            return wait
        }
    }
    return 0
}

func send(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, method, target string,
    headers map[string]string, body []byte) error {
    const maxAttempts = 4
    const breakerThreshold = 3
    failures := 0
    for attempt := 0; attempt < maxAttempts; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, method, target, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        for name, value := range headers {
            req.Header.Set(name, value)
        }
        resp, sendErr := client.Do(req)
        var wait time.Duration
        reason := ""
        if sendErr == nil {
            detail, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 1024))
            resp.Body.Close()
            if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
                return nil
            }
            reason = fmt.Sprintf("status %d, response %q, read error %v",
                resp.StatusCode, detail, readErr)
            if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests && resp.StatusCode < 500 {
                return fmt.Errorf("terminal rejection: %s", reason)
            }
            wait = retryAfter(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"))
        } else {
            reason = sendErr.Error()
        }
        failures++
        if failures >= breakerThreshold {
            return fmt.Errorf("circuit open; retain delivery state: %s", reason)
        }
        if attempt+1 == maxAttempts {
            return fmt.Errorf("attempt budget exhausted: %s", reason)
        }
        backoff := 250 * time.Millisecond * time.Duration(1<<uint(attempt))
        backoff += time.Duration(rand.Int63n(int64(backoff / 2)))
        if wait < backoff {
            wait = backoff
        }
        timer := time.NewTimer(wait)
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            timer.Stop()
            return ctx.Err()
        case <-timer.C:
        }
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("attempt budget exhausted")
}

func run() error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    group := os.Getenv("ERROR_GROUP_ID")
    id := os.Getenv("NOTIFICATION_ID")
    target := os.Getenv("WEBHOOK_URL")
    if key == "" || group == "" || id == "" || target == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set INFRAI_API_KEY, ERROR_GROUP_ID, NOTIFICATION_ID, WEBHOOK_URL")
    }
    destination, err := url.Parse(target)
    if err != nil || destination.Scheme != "https" || destination.Host == "" || destination.User != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("WEBHOOK_URL must be an approved HTTPS receiver without embedded credentials")
    }
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 5 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    eventsURL := strings.Replace("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/errors/events/{error_group_id}",
        "{error_group_id}", url.PathEscape(group), 1)
    if err := send(ctx, client, http.MethodGet, eventsURL,
        map[string]string{"Authorization": "Bearer " + key}, nil); err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("read selected group: %w", err)
    }
    payload, err := json.Marshal(map[string]string{
        "event_id": id,
        "category": "agent_failure",
    })
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    return send(ctx, client, http.MethodPost, target, map[string]string{
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": id,
    }, payload)
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    fmt.Println("notification accepted")
}

The webhook payload is an application-owned example, not an Infrai schema. The receiver must explicitly support the chosen Idempotency-Key contract and atomically deduplicate accepted identities with its side effects; adding the header cannot supply that guarantee. The Infrai credential goes only to the API read. Redirects are disabled so an unexpected destination cannot silently become a new processor boundary. Approve the configured receiver before running the program; this is not a URL-validation service.

The 250-millisecond base, 4-attempt ceiling, 3-failure breaker threshold, and 30-second deadline are demonstration parameters. The breaker can stop attempts before the ceiling. Set production values from the receiver contract and your delivery SLO, and treat a Retry-After beyond the remaining deadline as deferred work or an exhausted deadline. The duration parser bounds extremely large numeric values to a day, still well beyond this program's deadline; it does not send early in that case.

This example has a deliberate limitation: the breaker is terminal within one invocation, and retry state is in memory. A production worker needs persisted attempt counts, a shared destination-scoped open state, and a controlled recovery probe before releasing more traffic. Persist the event identity and deadline across rollback too. Restarting this program is not a production recovery policy, and it must not reset the delivery budget.

Keep error details in an operator-restricted channel with its own retention policy. The code surfaces bounded error bodies to aid diagnosis; those bodies can contain sensitive information and should not become the next notification payload.

When retries need a different signal

Repeatedly sending a rejected payload spends the delivery budget on a deterministic mistake. Correct it through a reviewed recovery path. If duplicate notification effects are unacceptable, require receiver deduplication before enabling automatic retries, and make the deduplication window cover the maximum permitted replay horizon.

Silence is separate.

A job that never starts cannot emit its own failure event, so add a heartbeat-oriented signal such as Healthchecks. Prefer Sentry when deeper error investigation is the immediate need, or evaluate Datadog and Grafana when the decision depends on the surrounding telemetry and operational views. A stable backend contract does not replace those specialist decisions.

For rollback acceptance, check that the old notification retains its identity, remaining attempts, delivery deadline, and data-handling restrictions. If the deployment cannot preserve those properties, pause the sender and repair the state transition before replaying queued records.

Sources

References for the delivery semantics, telemetry concepts, and product roles discussed here:

  • OpenTelemetry logs concepts
  • HTTP semantics and Retry-After
  • Sentry documentation
  • Datadog documentation
  • Grafana documentation
  • Healthchecks documentation

If this capability boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and review the sender and receiver contracts alongside it.

title: Which language is fastest? I ran the same HTML parser in 8 languages: Python caught up with Rust, and Go lost even to Java
description:
This is an English version of my article on Habr (in Russian).

A week ago I wrote about z3l.FastHtmlParser, an HTML parser for .NET that builds a flat list of tags instead of a DOM and parses a page 10–30x faster than HtmlAgilityPack and AngleSharp. Back then it had no CSS selectors, no XPath, and lived only in .NET.

In one week it got CSS selectors and XPath 1.0, and the library itself moved to seven more languages: Go, Rust, Java, TypeScript, Python, PHP and Ruby. These are not "Hello world" ports: each implementation is 6–11 thousand lines — a tokenizer, the HTML5 optional end tag rules, all 2,125 named entities, XPath 1.0 and CSS selectors. The algorithm is the same everywhere, and every port is checked against the original on the same pages.

The result is an experiment you rarely get to run: the same real-world task, eight languages, two operating systems and one CPU. So I can finally answer the question people get flamed for in the comments. Grab your pitchforks.

Setup

  • Same hardware. A physical server with an AMD Ryzen 7 3800X (8 cores, 16 threads).
  • Linux — Ubuntu 26.04 on that server, benchmarks in Docker, official images: dotnet/sdk:10.0, golang:1.27, rust:1.100, maven:3-eclipse-temurin-21, node:26, python:3.14, php:8.4-cli, ruby:4.0.
  • Windows — Windows 10 LTSC in a KVM virtual machine on the same server, 12 vCPUs. Same versions: .NET 10.0.12, Go 1.27.4, Rust 1.100, Java 21.0.13, Node 26.13, Python 3.14.10, PHP 8.4.27, Ruby 4.0.9.
  • PHP runs with opcache and the tracing JIT on both OSes. Ruby runs without JIT, and on Linux also with YJIT and the new ZJIT (the RubyInstaller build for Windows has no YJIT).
  • Strictly one at a time. No benchmark ran alongside another, and Linux and Windows never ran at the same time either. It's a production server running MySQL, RabbitMQ and a dozen services, so background load isn't zero (load average 1–3 out of 16), but it's the same for both OSes.
  • Two tasks. Parsing a page, and scraping — parsing plus extracting 20 books (title, price, rating) or 10 quotes. The pages are saved copies of books.toscrape.com (51 KB), quotes.toscrape.com (11 KB), webscraper.io laptops (38 KB), books ×10 (510 KB), and books with no </li> and </p>. Before measuring, every benchmark checks that all libraries returned the same records.
  • Time is the median per call after warm-up. C# uses BenchmarkDotNet, Go uses testing.B (median of three runs), the rest use the same loop: one second of warm-up, then batches of calls, take the median.
  • Error margin is up to 10%. Repeated runs of the same benchmark differed by up to 10%: C# on books — 55 and 58 μs on Linux, 64 and 59 μs on Windows; Java on Windows — 73 μs yesterday and 66 μs today. So in this article, any difference under 10% is a tie.

Results

Parsing books.toscrape.com, 51 KB (lower is better):

Place Language Linux Windows
1–4 Python (Rust inside) 54 μs 67 μs
1–4 C# 55 μs 64 μs
1–4 Rust 56 μs 61 μs
1–4 Java 59 μs 66 μs
5 Go 84 μs 102 μs
6 Node.js (TypeScript) 183 μs 201 μs
7 PHP + JIT 360 μs 516 μs
8 Ruby + YJIT 818 μs —
9 Ruby 1.60 ms 1.53 ms

The top four are within the error margin.

Parsing, all pages — Linux and Windows

Linux:

quotes, 11 KB 15 μs 16 μs 17 μs 17 μs 24 μs 65 μs 110 μs 466 μs 240 μs
laptops, 38 KB 46 μs 51 μs 47 μs 62 μs 74 μs 173 μs 303 μs 1.40 ms 1.22 ms
books, 51 KB 56 μs 55 μs 54 μs 59 μs 84 μs 183 μs 360 μs 1.60 ms 818 μs
books ×10, 510 KB 563 μs 611 μs 546 μs 617 μs 857 μs 2.27 ms 3.59 ms 15.3 ms 8.02 ms
books without </li> </p> 52 μs 61 μs 55 μs 63 μs 82 μs 234 μs 390 μs 1.83 ms 1.49 ms

Windows:

Page Rust C# Python Java Go Node.js PHP Ruby
quotes, 11 KB 17 μs 20 μs 18 μs 19 μs 29 μs 68 μs 153 μs 455 μs
laptops, 38 KB 50 μs 54 μs 56 μs 66 μs 88 μs 204 μs 448 μs 1.31 ms
books, 51 KB 61 μs 64 μs 67 μs 66 μs 102 μs 201 μs 516 μs 1.53 ms
books ×10, 510 KB 602 μs 637 μs 654 μs 677 μs 944 μs 2.27 ms 5.11 ms 15.4 ms
books without </li> </p> 55 μs 61 μs 63 μs 71 μs 100 μs 224 μs 514 μs 1.91 ms

Scraping 20 books (parse + extract), Linux / Windows. Every port has three ways to search: its own Find methods, CSS selectors and XPath.

Language Find API CSS XPath
Rust 73 / 82 μs 73 / 87 μs 117 / 191 μs
C# 75 / 70 μs 74 / 82 μs 117 / 109 μs
Java 86 / 93 μs 120 / 111 μs 102 / 108 μs
Go 106 / 129 μs 117 / 131 μs 216 / 265 μs
Python 117 / 155 μs 94 / 128 μs 123 / 243 μs
Node.js 230 / 239 μs 285 / 275 μs 269 / 304 μs
