The ports vs. the local champions

Comparing languages is fun, but a user cares about something else: is the port worth taking over what their ecosystem already uses? The ports were written in a week and are clearly less polished than the original. Here's how they stack up against the best each platform had before them.

Parsing books.toscrape.com, 51 KB — how many times faster the port is (Linux / Windows; below 1 means the port is slower):

Language Port, Linux Fastest competitor Port is faster Popular choice Port is faster
Rust 56 μs tl 1.5x / 1.7x scraper (html5ever) 22x / 25x
C# 55 μs HtmlAgilityPack 12x / 12x AngleSharp 21x / 18x
Python 54 μs selectolax (lexbor, C) 8.4x / 6.3x BeautifulSoup 226x / 213x
Java 59 μs Jericho 6.7x / 6.0x jsoup 8.0x / 7.2x
Go 84 μs golang.org/x/net/html 10x / 9.6x goquery 10x / 9.6x
Node.js 183 μs htmlparser2 5.3x / 4.3x cheerio 16x / 9.9x
PHP 360 μs Dom\HTMLDocument (lexbor, C) 1.5x / 1.5x DOMDocument (libxml2, C) 2.6x / 2.8x
Ruby + YJIT 818 μs Nokogiri (libxml2, C) 1.3x / — Nokogiri 1.3x / —
Ruby 1.60 ms Nokogiri (libxml2, C) 0.6x / 0.9x Nokogiri 0.6x / 0.9x

Scraping 20 books — the best of the port's three APIs vs. the best competitor:

Language Port, Linux Fastest competitor Port is faster
Rust 73 μs tl (CSS) 1.7x / 2.1x
C# 74 μs HtmlAgilityPack (XPath) 11x / 12x
Python 94 μs selectolax (CSS) 6.2x / 4.8x
Java 86 μs jsoup (CSS) 8.2x / 7.5x
Go 106 μs goquery (CSS) 9.1x / 8.3x
Node.js 230 μs node-html-parser 6.1x / 4.9x
PHP 514 μs Dom\HTMLDocument (CSS) 1.4x / 1.6x
Ruby + YJIT 1.01 ms Nokogiri (XPath) 1.9x / —
Ruby 2.08 ms Nokogiri (XPath) 0.9x / 1.1x

In seven languages out of eight, the port is faster than anything the ecosystem had — on both OSes and in both tasks. And in Python, PHP and Ruby the main competitors are written in C: selectolax and Dom\HTMLDocument are lexbor; lxml, DOMDocument and Nokogiri are libxml2. Pure PHP beats the C parser built into PHP 8.4 by 1.5x.

The closest competitor is tl in Rust, only 1.5–2x slower. But tl is a zero-copy parser that doesn't decode entities and has no descendant combinator in its selectors, so it does less work.

Ruby is a special case. Without JIT, the port is on par with Nokogiri on Windows (parsing 8% slower, scraping 14% faster) and loses on Linux, where Nokogiri is noticeably faster: 1.6x on parsing. With YJIT the port overtakes Nokogiri: 1.3x on parsing and 1.9x on scraping.

Where does the gap come from? The C libraries do ten times more work: they build a full DOM tree with an object per node, synthesize implicit <html> and <tbody>, and then wrap the found nodes in Python, PHP or Ruby objects. A parser that stores tags as pairs of integer offsets into the source string does exactly what scraping needs, and nothing more.

And now — why every row of these tables will offend somebody.

Claim 1. Python caught up with Rust

On Linux, Python parses the page in 54 μs and Rust in 56. On Windows, 67 and 61.

Of course, this is cheating: the Python version is 790 lines of PyO3 bindings around the Rust version. Inside fh.parse(html) it's not the interpreter running, it's the same machine code as in Rust. And Python being 2 μs faster than Rust itself on Linux is noise and build flags: the Python wrapper is built with fat LTO, the Rust benchmark with thin LTO.

Scraping shows what Python pays for: crossing the boundary. Every found tag and every string becomes a Python object, and the Find API falls 1.6x behind pure Rust (117 μs vs. 73). CSS selectors are only 30% behind (94 μs): the whole search runs inside Rust and the boundary is crossed once. The less often your code jumps between Python and Rust, the closer it gets to Rust.

The provocation is elsewhere, though. In the "Python is slow" debate people tend to forget that in production, Python doesn't run the hot code anyway: numpy, pandas, lxml, selectolax, pydantic-core and orjson are written in C or Rust. Python is the language you call fast code from. And if your task has a native core, a Python service will beat an "honest" Go service that does everything itself.

The moral: a "fast language" is often a language that delegates well.

Claim 2. Go is the slowest of the compiled languages

Go parses the page in 84 μs — 1.5x slower than Rust, C#, Java and even Python. Same on Windows: 102 μs vs. 61–67.

And the Go version is written carefully: 2 allocations per parse, the garbage collector barely shows up in the measurement. It's not the GC, it's the compiler. The Go compiler deliberately optimizes less in exchange for build speed: more modest inlining, fewer bounds checks eliminated, no auto-vectorization. Go does have PGO, but only from a pre-recorded profile (default.pgo), and few people enable it. The JIT in .NET and HotSpot collects the profile itself, at run time, and compiles for the hot paths.

Go is still a great language for services — fast builds, simplicity, predictability. But "Go is fast because it's compiled" is a myth. It's fast compared to Python and Ruby. Not compared to the JVM and .NET.

Claim 3. C# and Java are almost Rust. And "C# beat Rust" is a Windows thing

On Linux, parsing: C# — 55 μs, Rust — 56, Java — 59. Scraping: Rust — 73, C# — 75, Java — 86. A tie, with Java slightly behind.

Windows tells a different story: on scraping, C# is first at 70 μs vs. 82 for Rust, and on XPath the gap is almost 2x: 109 μs vs. 191. The first draft of this article was titled "C# beat Rust". Then I looked at Linux, where Rust and C# are neck and neck, and started digging.

The cause is the allocator. .NET allocates objects on its own heap the same way on every OS: by bumping a pointer. Rust uses the system allocator by default: glibc malloc on Linux, HeapAlloc on Windows. The XPath engine creates lots of small vectors and strings, and the Windows system heap struggles with that. Two lines, and Rust on Windows switches to mimalloc:

#[global_allocator]
static GLOBAL: mimalloc::MiMalloc = mimalloc::MiMalloc;
Rust on Windows HeapAlloc (default) mimalloc For reference: Linux
Parse books, 51 KB 61 μs 55 μs 56 μs
Scrape, Find API 82 μs 69 μs 73 μs
Scrape, XPath 191 μs 125 μs 117 μs

And C# is no longer ahead: 70 μs vs. 69. On Linux mimalloc changes nothing (parsing 55 vs. 56 μs, XPath 117 vs. 117): glibc malloc is already good for this workload.

The moral: a garbage-collected language brings its own allocator, the same everywhere, while Rust gets whatever the OS gives it. On Windows that costs Rust up to 1.5x.

One more note on fairness: the C# version is the original and the most polished: ArrayPool, Span<char>, vectorized IndexOfAny, CollectionsMarshal.SetCount, Dictionary.AlternateLookup to look up by span without allocating strings. But the Java version, which has none of that, is only 5–18% behind Rust. If you want "almost Rust" without the borrow checker, these are your languages.

Claim 4. NativeAOT is slower than JIT, and server GC doesn't help

Since C# is in the top four, let's see how to make it faster. Two popular ideas: compile ahead of time (NativeAOT) and turn on the server garbage collector. BenchmarkDotNet built NativeAOT for the same instruction set the JIT uses on this CPU (x86-64-v3, AVX2), so that's not the issue.

C#, time; in parentheses — relative to regular JIT on the same OS:

Task OS JIT JIT + server GC NativeAOT NativeAOT + server GC
Parse books, 51 KB Linux 58 μs 66 μs (1.14) 75 μs (1.30) 81 μs (1.40)
Windows 59 μs 64 μs (1.08) 83 μs (1.40) 87 μs (1.47)
Parse books ×10, 510 KB Linux 614 μs 625 μs (1.02) 765 μs (1.24) 823 μs (1.34)
Windows 600 μs 626 μs (1.04) 824 μs (1.37) 864 μs (1.44)
Scrape 20 books, Find API Linux 72 μs 80 μs (1.11) 89 μs (1.24) 100 μs (1.40)
Windows 73 μs 75 μs (1.02) 100 μs (1.36) 104 μs (1.41)
Scrape 20 books, XPath Linux 121 μs 150 μs (1.24) 153 μs (1.26) 181 μs (1.50)
Windows 129 μs 132 μs (1.02) 156 μs (1.21) 169 μs (1.31)
Scrape 10 quotes Linux 25 μs 27 μs (1.06) 32 μs (1.27) 35 μs (1.41)
Windows 25 μs 26 μs (1.05) 37 μs (1.45) 38 μs (1.50)

NativeAOT is 20–50% slower than JIT. The main reason is dynamic PGO. The .NET JIT first compiles a method quickly and with instrumentation, watches which branches are hot and which types actually show up at interface calls, and then recompiles for that: devirtualizes calls, inlines the hot code, lays out code so the hot path runs straight through. NativeAOT compiles everything ahead of time, blind. Static PGO for NativeAOT exists, but almost nobody uses it.

Server GC is 2–15% slower, and up to 24% on XPath, where allocations are heaviest. Server GC has a heap per core and a much larger gen0 budget: fewer collections, but new objects land in memory that's no longer in cache. In a single-threaded parser that's a pure loss; server GC pays off when many threads allocate at once.

NativeAOT is about millisecond startup, compact deployment and no JIT at run time. Not about peak speed.

Claim 5. Node.js is 3.3x slower than Rust — and that's a great result

V8 is a marvel of engineering. A dynamically typed language with a JIT stays within 3.3x of Rust on parsing (183 μs vs. 56) and 3.1x on scraping. No other dynamic language in this table comes close: PHP is 2x slower than Node.js, Ruby with YJIT 4.5x.

The main bottleneck isn't even V8, it's JavaScript strings: UTF-16, immutable, no cheap slice views. A parser built on offsets into the source string fits that model well — which is why the gap is so small.

Claim 6. Ruby: YJIT doubles the speed

Ruby 4.0 on Linux — the port vs. Nokogiri:

Task Port, no JIT Port, ZJIT Port, YJIT Nokogiri (libxml2)
Parse books, 51 KB 1.60 ms 1.25 ms 818 μs 1.01 ms
Parse books ×10, 510 KB 15.3 ms 12.1 ms 8.02 ms 9.58 ms
Parse books without </li> </p> 1.83 ms 1.64 ms 1.49 ms 1.01 ms
Scrape 20 books 2.08 ms 1.42 ms 1.01 ms 1.90 ms
Scrape 10 quotes 789 μs 529 μs 375 μs 964 μs

YJIT makes pure Ruby twice as fast on both parsing and scraping. The new ZJIT in Ruby 4.0 gives less for now: +28% on parsing and +46% on scraping. Nokogiri doesn't speed up with JIT at all — its hot code is in C — so with YJIT the pure-Ruby port beats it almost everywhere.

The exception is the page without end tags: the Ruby version spends 14–25% more time on it than on the normal page, and 80% more with YJIT, while Rust, Go and Python don't notice the difference. Something to optimize.

A shame about Windows: RubyInstaller builds have no YJIT, so there Ruby stays an interpreter.

Claim 7. Windows vs. Linux: it's not the VM

Windows runs in a VM on the same server as Linux, so the first suspect is virtualization. Rust with mimalloc clears it: 55 μs in the Windows VM and 55 μs on bare-metal Linux. For this workload virtualization costs almost nothing.

How much slower Windows is than Linux on the same hardware (parsing books, 51 KB):

What Linux Windows Windows slower by
Rust, system allocator 56 μs 61 μs 9%
Rust + mimalloc 55 μs 55 μs 0%
C# (two runs) 55–58 μs 59–64 μs 2–17%
Java 59 μs 66 μs 12%
Node.js 183 μs 201 μs 10%
Go 84 μs 102 μs 22%
Python (Rust inside) 54 μs 67 μs 24%
PHP + JIT 360 μs 516 μs 43%
Ruby 1.60 ms 1.53 ms −4%
lxml (Python, libxml2) 590 μs 1.51 ms 156%
Dom\HTMLDocument (PHP, lexbor) 524 μs 777 μs 48%
Nokogiri (Ruby, libxml2) 1.01 ms 1.41 ms 40%
selectolax (Python, lexbor) 455 μs 421 μs −7%
htmlparser2 (Node.js) 977 μs 870 μs −11%

What follows from this:

  • Runtimes with their own allocator — .NET, the JVM, V8 — perform the same on both OSes, within noise. That holds for third-party libraries on them too: jsoup and AngleSharp differ by 1–3%.
  • Rust and the Python wrapper over Rust slow down on Windows because of the system heap (see claim 3). On XPath in Python the gap is almost 2x: 243 μs vs. 123.
  • Interpreters and C libraries depend on the build. One reason for PHP: the official Windows builds are made with MSVC, which doesn't support computed goto, so the Zend VM runs in the slower CALL mode instead of HYBRID. lxml is 2.6x slower on Windows, Nokogiri 40%. But it goes the other way too: selectolax and htmlparser2 are 7–11% faster on Windows. It all comes down to the specific build of the specific library.
  • Go is 22% slower on Windows, even though it has its own allocator. I have no explanation — hints in the comments are welcome.

A separate provocation: if your PHP service, or your Python service with lxml, runs on Windows, moving to Linux will give you more than rewriting it in another language.

Claim 8. The fastest language isn't the most verbose

Non-blank lines for the same functionality:

Language Lines
TypeScript 5,950
C# 6,950
Java 7,170
Go 8,800
Ruby 8,900
PHP 10,100
Rust 10,750
Python 790 (bindings over Rust)

The Rust version is one of the fastest and the longest. Ruby, famous for being concise, came out longer than C# and Java: when you write a parser in Ruby that has to be fast, idiomatic Ruby ends and manual index juggling in strings begins. TypeScript came out shortest.

Caveats, without which I'd rightly get torn apart

  • One algorithm, one author, one task. HTML parsing is string work and branching; for number crunching, multithreading or I/O the picture may be different.
  • The ports aren't equally optimized. The C# version is the original, the rest are week-old ports. Go and Ruby surely have room to speed up. Pull requests that move your language up the table are welcome.
  • Different benchmark harnesses and up to 10% noise. BenchmarkDotNet, testing.B and a hand-written median loop measure slightly differently, and the server isn't idle. A 10% gap between neighboring rows is a tie; a 2x gap is not.
  • Everything is default. Go without PGO, Rust without target-cpu=native and with the system allocator, as in most projects. Vectorized character search in Rust (memchr) detects AVX2 at run time on its own.
  • Python is Rust. I said it. A pure Python implementation would land around Ruby, or even below.
  • Windows is in a VM. It costs our parsers nothing (Rust + mimalloc), but for libraries that build large DOM trees virtualization may cost more: TLB misses under two-level address translation are more expensive.
  • Single-threaded measurement. In multithreaded scraping, GCs, allocators and threading models come into play — and server GC may look different. That's a topic for a separate article.

Bottom line

If the flame war really needs a one-liner: for parsing, Rust ≈ C# ≈ Java ≈ Python (Rust inside) > Go > Node.js > PHP > Ruby + YJIT > Ruby.

But if you want your scraper to be faster, switching languages isn't the first thing to do:

  • The language, with the same algorithm, gives 1.5x between the top four and Go, 3.3x to Node.js, 6.4x to PHP.
  • The algorithm, within one language, gives 1.5x to 226x over local libraries, and the PHP and Ruby ports beat C libraries.
  • Runtime settings weigh almost as much as the language: NativeAOT instead of JIT is 20–50% slower, the Windows system allocator makes Rust up to 1.5x slower, Windows instead of Linux makes PHP 43% slower.

Data structures matter more than the language, and the runtime and OS matter almost as much as the language.

All eight implementations and the benchmarks are open — run them on your hardware and send me your numbers. For C#, the JIT/NativeAOT and workstation/server GC variants run with one command: dotnet run -c Release --project benchmarks/z3l.FastHtmlParser.Benchmarks -- --runtime-variants --filter '*ParseBenchmarks.FastHtmlParser' '*ScrapeBenchmarks.*_FastHtmlParser*'.

  • C# (original): https://github.com/romanti3172/z3l.FastHtmlParser
  • Go: https://github.com/romanti3172/fasthtmlparser
  • Rust: https://github.com/romanti3172/fasthtmlparser-rs
  • Python: https://github.com/romanti3172/fasthtmlparser-py
  • Java: https://github.com/romanti3172/fasthtmlparser-java
  • TypeScript: https://github.com/romanti3172/fasthtmlparser-js
  • PHP: https://github.com/romanti3172/fasthtmlparser-php
  • Ruby: https://github.com/romanti3172/fasthtmlparser-rb

Disclosure: the ports were written with heavy help from Claude (that's what the meme is about), and this English text is an AI-assisted translation of my original Russian article. The benchmarks and numbers are mine, run on my hardware.

title: Honest Brokers in AI Regulation: How Public Comments Introduce Evidence to Regulators
description:
arXiv:2611.21948v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The regulation of Artificial Intelligence is susceptible to various forms of capture by industry actors that hold undue influence over the policymaking process, due in part to their information advantage in developing these technologies. In the following paper, we investigate the roles of public commenters in providing evidence to potential regulation in the USA. We build a corpus of 40 potential regulations, and 2,664 public comments submitted by a variety of stakeholders. We computationally process these texts to extract evidence meant to inform regulators, in the form of formal citations and informal references. We find significant differences in the type and amount of evidence supplied: Holding comment length constant, business commenters introduce altogether less evidence, and government, university, and civil society commenters provide significantly more research and legal sources. The publication status of cited research is nearly evenly split, with preprints and peer-reviewed articles being introduced by commenters of all types. We further explore patterns of self-citation and find that while it is prevalent amongst all groups, a small cluster of organizations account for over half of all self-citations in our corpus. Our findings complicate a narrative that public comments alone are means to information capture. We interpret these results in terms of the role that commenters attempt to play in the policymaking process-being either an Issue Advocate or an Honest Broker. These findings on the supply of evidence in public comments shed light on an often overlooked form of policymaking that has implications for how and through what sources information is made accessible to regulators of AI.

title: Publisher Signup Migration: Checking Marketing Consent at the Send Boundary
description:
A publisher moving email-and-password signup and sign-in off a managed provider needs a marketing consent check immediately before each recipient's send. Short answer: check that recipient's current category grant, drop recipients without it, and record the dropped count; keep transactional mail outside this marketing filter. An Express middleware check at batch submission is too early when the actual send happens later.

Consider a hypothetical page: a newsletter worker reports an abrupt rise in recipients dropped for missing consent after the account migration. The on-call sees a completed batch and a shrinking audience. A green completion dashboard answers almost nothing. What page fired, which category changed, and did the decision happen before delivery or hours earlier when somebody built the audience?

This is a proposed response trace, not an incident report.

What page should fire before the newsletter batch sends?

Work backward from the drop-count page. An earlier signal should have shown the change in consent decisions during migration validation, while the team could still compare the old account mapping with the candidate mapping and examine the category being checked. A valid account is necessary for sign-in; it isn't evidence that its owner wants a promotional newsletter. Moving those two decisions together makes a quiet migration mistake look like a successful login rollout.

The useful instrumentation belongs at the worker's send boundary. Record the marketing candidates examined, the explicit denials dropped, the checks that couldn't yield a decision, and the messages handed to the sender. Keep these outcomes distinct. An unknown decision should stop that marketing send and remain visible as unresolved work; calling it a denial corrupts the very signal the responder needs.

Count the drops.

The primary signal is the dropped count, because a sudden jump means something upstream changed. Pair it with the number checked so audience growth doesn't automatically become an emergency, and separate the publication's promotional category from transactional categories so account recovery doesn't disappear behind a newsletter policy. This is why a successful batch response is a poor acceptance test: every recipient might have been correctly excluded, yet the batch itself still completed.

For a publisher evaluating Infrai during this migration, the concrete attraction is its public, self-describing discovery surface: request and response schemas plus runnable examples let an engineer inspect the relevant consent capability without adopting another SDK. Publishers moving the marketing worker alongside signup should try Infrai for that consent-check integration when inspecting the contract directly matters.

Infrai uses one key, one wallet, one bill across 295 routes and 20 modules. Its single API key and unified billing reduce credential handling and invoice reconciliation across the backend capabilities the publisher chooses to move. This breadth includes auth, email, storage, scheduling, and observability; consolidating only the capabilities the team actually needs is the relevant operating benefit. Infrai also supplies runnable examples in 10 languages, including Go, so inspecting the consent contract needn't become an SDK translation exercise. None of this establishes migration compatibility; the acceptance traces still have to pass.

Put the decision beside the send

A Node.js and Express application can authenticate the batch-submission request and enqueue its intent. The later worker must still check each recipient. A middleware decision cannot honour a revocation that arrives while the batch waits, and a cached audience export cannot substitute for the current category grant.

Start with a read-only probe of the consent contract. This Go program uses the standard library, reads the API key and recipient details from environment variables, makes an explicit GET request, and prints the actual response without guessing response fields. Set INFRAI_API_KEY, CONSENT_USER_ID, and CONSENT_CATEGORY to your own values; save the program as main.go and run it with go run main.go. The category must be the publication's actual marketing category, not a label invented for this example.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func run() error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    user := os.Getenv("CONSENT_USER_ID")
    category := os.Getenv("CONSENT_CATEGORY")
    if key == "" || user == "" || category == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set INFRAI_API_KEY, CONSENT_USER_ID, CONSENT_CATEGORY")
    }
    endpoint := strings.NewReplacer(
        "{user_id}", url.PathEscape(user),
        "{category}", url.PathEscape(category),
    ).Replace("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/auth/consent/check/{user_id}/{category}")
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 15 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            retryAfter := strings.TrimSpace(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"))
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                candidate := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
                if candidate > delay {
                    delay = candidate
                }
            } else if when, err := http.ParseTime(retryAfter); err == nil {
                if candidate := time.Until(when); candidate > delay {
                    delay = candidate
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("consent check HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("consent check retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

This probe doesn't send email. It lets the engineer inspect the real consent response before writing the worker's decoder against the published schema. A successful HTTP status establishes that the request succeeded; it doesn't establish that consent was granted. Decode the category decision explicitly in the production integration, and keep response bodies out of general-purpose production logs.

The three attempts and 15-second request timeout are example settings, not service limits. A server-specified retry delay can extend the total runtime; a production worker needs a job deadline and durable deferral rather than holding its entire batch indefinitely. When work resumes, repeat the current consent check before sending. Treating an earlier approval as a retry token would recreate the stale-decision problem.

Once the decoder is in place, process each marketing recipient by checking the category, incrementing the dropped count on explicit denial, and invoking the sender only on approval. A check without a usable decision belongs in unresolved work. A retried send needs a stable idempotency key for the same logical message; the read-only probe above performs no write.

There's a subtle limit here: checking immediately before sending narrows the time between the decision and the write, but it doesn't establish an atomic transaction across two services. Don't turn the per-recipient requirement into an unsupported promise about messages a downstream sender has already accepted.

Compare migration work, then model the bill

A useful comparison starts with the boundary each candidate must own. Auth0, Firebase Authentication, and Amazon Cognito are real alternatives worth evaluating for the account migration; the table gives each a distinct evaluation path without pretending that an authentication product name proves marketing consent semantics. Choose the account system and the marketing decision system deliberately.

Candidate Concrete migration evaluation Boundary to prove before committing
Auth0 Evaluate it as the managed identity destination when the publisher wants a dedicated identity-provider decision. Demonstrate the current category decision at the worker, independently of successful sign-in.
Firebase Authentication Evaluate its documented password-authentication integration against the publisher's application changes. Show how the application supplies fresh marketing consent rather than deriving it from a password account.
Amazon Cognito Evaluate its user-pool migration path against the old provider's account mapping. Validate that migrated identity mapping preserves the recipient used for consent checks.
Infrai Evaluate the discoverable consent contract alongside the account-migration work. Validate category mapping and delivery behaviour against the published schemas and the publisher's acceptance cases.

For a team whose difficult requirement is identity migration itself, one of the specialist identity alternatives is the better starting point when its documented migration path matches the existing accounts. A consent-check integration shouldn't decide password migration by accident. Conversely, a team that can already account for identity migration can assess the discoverable consent interface on its own merits. No product in this table gets credit for untested migration compatibility.

Model a workload rather than comparing a nominal request price. For a hypothetical batch with 1,000 marketing candidates, a complete first pass makes 1,000 recipient decisions. If 80 are denied and every other check resolves, 920 messages reach the sender. These are planning inputs, not provider measurements; retries and unresolved decisions add work. A separate transactional batch contributes no checks under this marketing-only policy.

The operating bill therefore includes decision calls, sender submissions, retry work, account-mapping validation, adapter maintenance, and the responder time spent explaining surprising changes. Multiply actual call counts by the applicable billing terms only after the workflow is clear. Infrai specifies per-call cost, latency, vendor, and request metadata, which gives the team inputs for attributing the worker's operating bill. That metadata cannot tell you how many engineering hours a mistaken category mapping will consume. The migration review needs both.

Close the loop without paging on every denial

The acceptance trace should revoke one synthetic reader's marketing grant after audience selection and before processing, then show that reader dropped at the send boundary. A second trace should carry a transactional message through without applying the promotional filter. A third should make the check unresolved and confirm that no marketing send occurs, while the unresolved count remains distinguishable from an explicit denial. These are proposed checks, not reports of a deployment.

Thresholds need the publication's actual batch history. An absolute dropped-count threshold alone will page more often when the audience grows; a ratio alone can make a tiny batch appear catastrophic. Start by reviewing both with batch size and category, then decide which deviations deserve an immediate page and which deserve routine review.

Don't page on every denial.

A denied promotional send is an expected policy outcome. If the threshold wakes someone for ordinary reader revocations, the false-positive cost includes interruption, investigation, and the eventual loss of attention to the next meaningful change; if it tolerates a migration-wide jump, the responder loses the earlier signal this design was meant to provide. That trade-off belongs in the migration acceptance criteria, beside the identity checks, before the newsletter worker takes over.

References

The identity sources below are starting points for evaluating account authentication and migration. They don't establish marketing permission. The OWASP guidance supplies authentication context; each candidate still needs the send-boundary acceptance traces described above.

Further reading

  • OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet
  • Auth0 documentation
  • Firebase password authentication
  • Amazon Cognito user-pool migration

If this boundary fits the publisher's migration, start with the discovery schemas and runnable examples in the Infrai documentation.

title: Uncertainty Quantification for Large Language Diffusion Models
description:
arXiv:2605.14570v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large Language Diffusion Models (LLDMs) are emerging as an alternative to autoregressive models, offering faster inference through higher parallelism. Similar to autoregressive LLMs, they remain prone to hallucinations, making reliable uncertainty quantification (UQ) crucial for safe deployment. However, existing UQ methods are fundamentally misaligned with this new paradigm: they assume autoregressive factorization or use expensive repeated sampling, negating the efficiency of LLDMs. In this work, we present the first systematic study of UQ for LLDMs and propose lightweight, zero-shot uncertainty signals derived from the iterative denoising process, leveraging intermediate generations, token remasking dynamics, and denoising complexity. We further adapt a state-of-the-art UQ method to LLDMs by combining masked diffusion likelihoods with trajectory-based semantic dissimilarity. We prove that expected trajectory dissimilarity lower bounds the masked diffusion training objective, which motivates its usage as an uncertainty score. Comprehensive experiments across three tasks, eight datasets, and four models show that our method achieves a great cost-performance trade-off: it approaches the strongest sampling-based baselines while incurring up to 100x lower computational overhead. Our work demonstrates that LLDMs can deliver both fast inference and reliable hallucination detection simultaneously.

title: Let your coding agent ask a QA agent: connect TestOptim over MCP with one sign-in
description:
Your coding agent says the change is done. A QA agent can check that. TestOptim runs AI tests on your web app and logs each failure as an issue with steps to reproduce. Its remote MCP server lets an MCP client list your projects, start test runs and read those issues.

Until now you had to create an API key and paste it into the client config. Since Nov 10 you can sign in with OAuth instead. Here is the full flow, step by step.

What we tested

We ran this flow with the MCP Inspector (v2.15.0, MCP protocol 2025-11-25). Other clients that support OAuth sign-in for remote servers use the same flow, but we did not test them for this post.

1. Add the server with only its URL

  • Transport: Streamable HTTP
  • URL: https://api.testoptim.com/api/mcp
  • No Authorization header.

The server answers the first request with 401 and a WWW-Authenticate header that points to its OAuth metadata. The client finds the sign-in page from there and registers itself. You do not enter a client ID.

2. Sign in and approve

The client opens TestOptim in your browser. Sign in, then read the consent page. It names the client and lists what it can do:

  • See your projects
  • Start and stop test runs, and read their results
  • Read the issues TestOptim found
  • Start explorations of your app

Select Allow. Only the Owner or an Admin of the organization can approve.

3. The client connects

The browser returns to the client, and the server shows as connected. The client lists 8 tools: list_projects, start_test_run, get_test_run, stop_test_run, list_issues, get_issue, start_exploration and get_exploration.

4. Ask for results

We called three tools:

  1. list_projects returned our 2 projects.
  2. list_issues on one project returned the open issues, with severity and status.
  3. get_issue returned one issue in full: description, 5 steps to reproduce, expected and actual behaviour, the page URL and a screenshot link.

In a coding agent, the same calls look like this: "Run the QA tests on the checkout project and show me the critical issues." The agent calls start_test_run, waits with get_test_run, then reads the results with list_issues and get_issue. A test run uses your plan's test executions, the same as a run started in the app.

5. Remove access when you are done

Each OAuth connection appears in TestOptim under Settings → API keys, named after the client, for example "MCP Inspector (OAuth)". Disconnecting in the client does not remove it. To stop access, revoke it there.

API keys still work

title: Towards Physics-Constrained Rectified Flow for Climate Downscaling: What Projections Can Certify?
description:
arXiv:2611.22283v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Statistical downscaling restores the regional detail behind flooding and crop stress, but diffusion and flow-matching generators can produce sharp fields that break the conservation laws of their coarse input. Physics-Constrained Rectified Flow (PC-RF) is a conditional flow-matching downscaler. Its training penalties target wind divergence, negative precipitation, and mass drift from the coarse total, and a projection after sampling removes the last two exactly. On one corrupted synthetic field with no trained network, the projection drives the Non-negativity Violation Rate (NVR) from 0.236 and the Mass-Conservation Error (MCE) from 0.184 to zero, and the penalties lower the Divergence Error (DE) by about 30%. On ERA5 the projection gives PC-RF and RF-base, the penalty-free rectified-flow baseline, an NVR of exactly zero and an MCE of zero up to float32 rounding. The penalties add no perceptual gain that we can separate from training budget or run-to-run variation. At a matched budget on 2019-2021, PC-RF has no edge over RF-base (SSIM 0.939 vs. 0.942, PSNR 31.81 vs. 31.79, CRPS 0.771 vs. 0.772). Our unprojected CorrDiff reimplementation beats both flow models on PSNR (28.38) and CRPS (1.092) on 2020, yet 45% of its ensemble-mean precipitation cells are negative. On ERA5 a sign error in the divergence operator made that penalty and DE act on a deformation-like term. The fine reference is interpolated from ERA5 and accumulates precipitation over a longer window, so the perceptual scores cannot establish downscaling skill. NVR and MCE need one pass and no fine reference, so we argue they should run first as pass-or-fail checks, with DE as a diagnostic.

title: Aligning Vue 3 Components with OpenAPI Types: Converting CurrentYearTable to TypeScript
description:
In full-stack web applications, frontend models can easily drift out of sync with backend APIs when types are manually redefined or left untyped. By integrating OpenAPI schema generators into the build pipeline, client applications can consume authoritative backend models directly in their Vue components.

In my recent contribution to GitLab's Contributors Platform (MR !3218, closing Issue #868), I converted the CurrentYearTable leaderboard component to TypeScript.

Here is an architectural walkthrough of how we typed props using generated OpenAPI contracts, applied the withDefaults macro, and constructed tests using model factories.

1. The Challenge: Generic Array Props

In the original implementation, CurrentYearTable.vue received leaderboard records using generic JavaScript options:

<!-- Before (JavaScript) -->
<script setup>
import { computed } from 'vue';
import ContributorsTable from '~/common/components/ContributorsTable.vue';

const props = defineProps({
  contributors: {
    type: Array,
    required: true,
  },
  fromDate: {
    type: String,
    default: '',
  },
  toDate: {
    type: String,
    default: '',
  },
});

const filterData = computed(() => ({
  fromDate: props.fromDate,
  toDate: props.toDate,
}));
</script>

While functional, type: Array gave zero insight into what properties a contributor record contained (such as user handles, merged MR counts, or bonus points). If the backend API renamed or removed a property, the frontend would fail silently at runtime.

2. Deriving Prop Types from OpenAPI Specs

Rather than hand-crafting a duplicate Contributor interface that could drift over time, the project generates TypeScript contracts directly from openapi.yaml.

In CurrentYearTable.vue, we imported GetApiV1LeaderboardResponse and indexed its records:

<!-- After (TypeScript) -->
<script setup lang="ts">
import { computed } from 'vue';
import type { GetApiV1LeaderboardResponse } from '~/api/generated';
import ContributorsTable from '~/common/components/ContributorsTable.vue';

const props = withDefaults(defineProps<{
  contributors: GetApiV1LeaderboardResponse['records'];
  fromDate?: string;
  toDate?: string;
}>(), {
  fromDate: '',
  toDate: '',
});

const filterData = computed(() => ({
  fromDate: props.fromDate,
  toDate: props.toDate,
}));
</script>

<template>
  <ContributorsTable
    :contributors="contributors"
    :filter-data="filterData"
  />
</template>

Why this is a best practice:

  1. Single Source of Truth: The TypeScript type GetApiV1LeaderboardResponse['records'] is generated directly from the backend Rails API definition. If an API contract changes, vue-tsc immediately flags any breaking changes across all views.
  2. withDefaults Macro: Provides idiomatic default values for optional string props (fromDate?: string, toDate?: string) without runtime object overhead.

3. Writing Resilient Specs with Model Factories (ADR 005)

Per the project's architectural guidelines (ADR 005: Model Factories in Specs), test fixtures should not be hard-coded object literals with incomplete shapes. Instead, tests use factory functions that populate complete, valid schema defaults.

In CurrentYearTable.spec.ts:

import type { VueWrapper } from '@vue/test-utils';
import { shallowMount } from '@vue/test-utils';
import ContributorsTable from '~/common/components/ContributorsTable.vue';
import { createLeaderboardContributor } from '~/spec/factories/leaderboard';
import CurrentYearTable from './CurrentYearTable.vue';

// Factory generates a valid, complete OpenAPI leaderboard record
const mockContributor = createLeaderboardContributor();

let wrapper: VueWrapper;
const createWrapper = (props = {}) => {
  wrapper = shallowMount(CurrentYearTable, {
    props: {
      contributors: [mockContributor],
      ...props,
    },
  });
};

const findContributorsTable = () => wrapper.findComponent(ContributorsTable);

it('renders ContributorsTable with contributors and default filterData', () => {
  createWrapper();

  expect(findContributorsTable().props('contributors')).toEqual([mockContributor]);
  expect(findContributorsTable().props('filterData')).toEqual({
    fromDate: '',
    toDate: '',
  });
});

it('renders ContributorsTable with custom fromDate and toDate in filterData', () => {
  createWrapper({
    fromDate: '2026-01-01',
    toDate: '2026-12-31',
  });

  expect(findContributorsTable().props('filterData')).toEqual({
    fromDate: '2026-01-01',
    toDate: '2026-12-31',
  });
});

Using createLeaderboardContributor() ensures that our test mocks strictly adhere to the OpenAPI schema without breaking when new fields are introduced.

Key Takeaways

  1. Leverage Generated API Types: Import types directly from OpenAPI or GraphQL code-generators (Response['key']) to eliminate manual duplication and catch breaking API updates.
  2. Use withDefaults(defineProps<{ ... }>(), { ... }): The standard Vue 3 pattern for combining compile-time type definitions with default prop values.
  3. Adopt Model Factories in Tests: Test helpers like createLeaderboardContributor() ensure test mocks always reflect production API contracts.

title: Designing a Reliable Database for an E-Commerce Application
description:
Every successful e-commerce application depends on more than an attractive user interface and smooth shopping experience. Behind the scenes, a well-designed database plays an important role in managing customers, products, orders, payments, and reviews efficiently.

Database design is the process of organizing information into structured tables and defining relationships between them. A good database structure helps maintain data accuracy, minimize duplication, and retrieve information efficiently.

Understanding Relational Database Design

While working on an E-Commerce Management System database using MySQL 5.7, I learned how different types of application data can be organized into separate but connected tables.

The database consisted of seven main tables:

Users: Stores customer account information.

Categories: Organizes products into different categories.

Products: Stores product names, prices, and SKU details.

Orders: Maintains customer order information.

Order Items: Connects products with their respective orders.

Payments: Stores payment-related information.

Reviews: Maintains customer ratings and feedback.

Instead of storing all information in a single table, dividing data into related tables makes the database easier to maintain and manage.

Why Database Relationships Matter

Relationships are essential in relational database management systems.

For example, one customer can place multiple orders, and one product can receive multiple reviews. Similarly, a single order can contain multiple products.

The relationship between orders and products is many-to-many. An intermediate table called order_items handles this relationship by storing the product reference, order reference, quantity, and unit price.

Primary keys uniquely identify records, while foreign keys connect related tables and help maintain referential integrity.

The Importance of Database Normalization

Normalization is another important concept in database design. It helps reduce unnecessary data duplication and maintain consistency.

During this project, I explored three important normal forms:

1NF: Ensures that each column contains atomic values and repeating groups are avoided.

2NF: Ensures that non-key attributes depend on the complete candidate key.

3NF: Removes transitive dependencies so non-key attributes depend on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key.

Applying normalization principles helps create a structured and maintainable database.

Working with SQL JOIN Queries

After creating the tables and inserting sample records, I practised SQL JOIN operations to retrieve information from multiple tables.

I successfully executed queries to combine users with orders, products with categories, order items with orders and products, and reviews with users and products.

These operations demonstrated how related information can be retrieved without storing duplicate data across multiple tables.

Tools and Practical Learning

I used MySQL 5.7 for database implementation, MySQL Workbench for executing SQL queries, and dbdiagram.io for designing the Entity Relationship Diagram.

This project helped me understand how database planning, normalization, constraints, indexes, and relationships contribute to reliable application development.

Conclusion

Database design is a fundamental part of building scalable and maintainable software applications. Through this E-Commerce Management System project, I gained practical experience in relational database design and improved my understanding of MySQL.

title: Semantic Communication via Analog RF Computing: When the Radio Computes the Meaning
description:
arXiv:2611.22100v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Semantic communication (SC) systems transmit continuous latent representations of meaning, but computing the semantic encoder at resource-constrained edge devices incurs substantial energy and memory costs. To address this challenge, we propose an end-to-end SC framework that executes the semantic encoder in the client's RF receiver front end using analog RF computing. A base station (BS) broadcasts encoder weights as RF waveforms, while each edge device reuses its receiver's passive mixer to compute semantic latents at ultra-low energy. These latents are transmitted over the uplink for network-side task inference. We show that analog computing noise across encoder layers and channel noise affecting transmitted latents admit a unified mathematical model. We define a task-posterior semantic distortion metric and derive its second-order decomposition into per-client, per-stage semantic sensitivities. Using this decomposition, we obtain a closed-form semantic-aware water-filling allocation of the total client energy budget across clients, encoder layers, and uplinks, assigning tighter accuracy targets to semantically sensitive stages. This allocation induces a broadcast beamforming problem that accounts for client-specific, per-layer accuracy requirements. We further refine the allocation through stochastic optimization and jointly design it with multi-task noise-aware training of the shared semantic model. MNIST simulations show that, at matched total client energy, the proposed allocation reduces network semantic distortion by 9.2\%-19.2\% compared with uniform precision and 5.1\%-13.1\% compared with client-blind allocation. Noise-aware co-design yields a further 46\% reduction.

title: Python vs R isn’t a debate. It’s a direction.
description:
Here's The Breakdown!

Python:
A general-purpose language used across AI/ML, data science, automation, web development, and production systems.
Strong ecosystem for both building models and deploying them into real applications.
Most widely used in industry because it scales from analysis to full software products.

R:
A statistics-first language built for data analysis, hypothesis testing, and high-quality visualization.
Very efficient for exploratory data analysis and academic/research work, with powerful built-in statistical tools and plotting capabilities.
Less commonly used for large-scale software systems, but still widely used in research and analytics.

Verdict:
Python is the go-to for building real-world AI systems, software, and scalable data products.
R is best when the focus is deep statistical analysis and research-level data work.

Most professionals end up using Python for production and R for specialized analysis.

title: ACH Return Codes Explained: R01, R03, R10 and How to Handle Them
description:
ACH Return Codes Explained: R01, R03, R10 and How to Handle Them

Understanding ACH Return Codes: A Developer's Guide

When you're building a payout system, ACH returns are inevitable. A transaction you thought was settled comes back rejected, and you need to know why and what to do next. The National Automated Clearing House Association (Nacha) publishes a standardized set of return codes—R01 through R85—that tell you exactly what went wrong. This article breaks down the most common ones and how to handle them in code.

The Big Three: R01, R03, and R10

R01: Insufficient Funds

What it means: The recipient's account doesn't have enough money to cover the debit. This is the most common return code.

When it fires: 1–2 business days after the ACH debit is initiated, during the bank's settlement window.

How to handle it:

  • Log the return with timestamp and amount.
  • Mark the payout as "returned" in your database, not "failed"—there's a difference.
  • Notify the recipient (usually via email or in-app).
  • Offer retry options: wait 3–5 business days and retry, or switch to a different payout rail (e.g., Visa Direct for faster settlement). 
async function handleR01Return(payoutId, returnData) {
  const payout = await db.payouts.findById(payoutId);

  payout.status = 'returned';
  payout.returnCode = 'R01';
  payout.returnedAt = new Date();
  payout.retryCount = (payout.retryCount || 0) + 1;

  if (payout.retryCount <= 2) {
    // Schedule retry in 5 business days
    await scheduleRetry(payoutId, addBusinessDays(new Date(), 5));
    await notifyUser(payout.userId, {
      subject: 'Payout returned — will retry',
      message: `Your $${payout.amount} payout was returned due to insufficient funds. We'll retry on ${addBusinessDays(new Date(), 5).toDateString()}.`
    });
  } else {
    // Max retries exceeded; escalate
    payout.status = 'manual_review';
    await notifySupport(payout);
  }

  await db.payouts.save(payout);
}

R03: No Account / Account Closed

What it means: The account number or routing number is invalid, or the account has been closed.

When it fires: 1 business day after initiation (banks catch this quickly).

How to handle it:

  • This is a permanent failure. Do not retry.
  • Flag the recipient's bank details as invalid.
  • Require the user to update their account information before attempting another payout.
  • Consider blocking future payouts to that account until verified. 
async function handleR03Return(payoutId, returnData) {
  const payout = await db.payouts.findById(payoutId);
  const recipient = await db.recipients.findById(payout.recipientId);

  payout.status = 'failed';
  payout.returnCode = 'R03';

  // Mark bank account as invalid
  recipient.bankAccount.status = 'invalid';
  recipient.bankAccount.invalidReason = 'No account or account closed';
  recipient.bankAccount.requiresUpdate = true;

  await notifyUser(payout.userId, {
    subject: 'Bank account information is invalid',
    message: 'The account you provided does not exist or is closed. Please update your bank details.'
  });

  await db.payouts.save(payout);
  await db.recipients.save(recipient);
}

R10: Unauthorized / Unauthorized Debit

What it means: The account holder did not authorize this debit, or the authorization is outside the agreement terms.

When it fires: Up to 60 days after the original debit (this is a consumer dispute).

How to handle it:

  • Investigate immediately. This may indicate fraud or a customer complaint.
  • Halt further payouts to that recipient until resolved.
  • Contact the customer to verify legitimacy.
  • If legitimate, you may need to resubmit with corrected authorization.

title: Plausible Videos Can Lead to Poor Decisions: Diagnosing and CURE-ing World Models for Planning
description:
arXiv:2611.22561v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Action-conditioned world models are increasingly used as world models for planning, yet a world model that makes plausible, realistic-looking videos that are consistent with the training data can produce poor decisions. We address two key questions: (1) when can we trust a world model for planning, and (2) what should we do when we cannot? We introduce CURE (Certify, Upweight, Rollout, Explore), a certificate-guided technique that assesses whether a world model can be trusted for planning and determines what to do next: whether to upweight the training data to debias the model; roll out more samples at test time; or explore by collecting new data where support (how well the training data cover the planner's decisions) is missing. We deploy CURE across multiple domains, spanning simulated physics based on PhyWorld, MuJoCo arm control, and Language-Table pushing in simulation and on real videos. The decisions our certificate trusts have lower regret than those it does not (e.g., 0.06 vs. 0.38 on Language-Table sim and 0.07 vs. 0.38 on MuJoCo contact), whereas video perceptual quality does not identify good decisions. By focusing on decision quality rather than perceptual quality, CURE lowers regret over the best pessimistic decision rule by 10-25% across support levels, and over world-action models, search and policy learning by 41-64%, given the same data.

title: PlaceTally: A Test-Time Memory Model for Constructing Place Graphs
description:
arXiv:2611.22608v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Counting distinct objects in a video is hard when the camera returns to places it has seen. A vision-language model that reads the whole video answers with a few small numbers, and one that reads it in parts counts an object again in every part that shows it. Object trackers need the category before the video is read, or a fixed vocabulary. We observe that a memory for counting does not need to know what it is looking for, only where it has been: objects rarely leave a room between visits, so parts of a video grouped by place share almost no objects, and a place can be recognised before any question is asked. Building on this, we introduce PlaceTally, a question-blind test-time memory model that constructs a place graph for each video. Each video fragment joins the place of its best earlier match or opens a new place, because a strong match is rarely wrong while a true return often matches weakly. A frozen vision-language model counts each place once from at most 128 of its frames, so every read has a bounded input and the memory grows with the number of places; the graph is built 15 times faster than real time. On RevisitCount, our benchmark of real room re-recordings, it scores 62.5% mean relative accuracy on test rooms and 61.2% on held-out rooms, against 51.2% and 44.3% for the same model reading the whole video. It stays level as rooms return more or less often, while a fixed correction of summed visits moves from 38.5% to 61.4%.

title: Say It Another Way: Auditing LLMs with a User-Grounded Automated Paraphrasing Framework
description:
arXiv:2505.03563v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are highly sensitive to subtle changes in prompt phrasing, posing challenges for reliable auditing. Prior methods often apply unconstrained prompt paraphrasing, which risk missing linguistic and demographic factors that shape authentic user interactions. We introduce AUGMENT (Automated User-Grounded Modeling and Evaluation of Natural Language Transformations), a framework for generating controlled paraphrases, grounded in user behaviors. AUGMENT leverages linguistically informed rules and enforces quality through checks on instruction adherence, semantic similarity, and realism, ensuring paraphrases are both reliable and meaningful for auditing. Through case studies on the BBQ and MMLU datasets, we show that controlled paraphrases uncover systematic weaknesses that remain obscured under unconstrained variation. These results highlight the value of the AUGMENT framework for reliable auditing.

title: [백엔드 모의면접] 중복 결제는 어떻게 막을까?
description:
안녕하세요.

인프랩에서 모의면접 서비스를 개발/운영하고 있는 약풍이라고 해요.
최근에 SNS에 오늘의 면접질문 컨텐츠를 연재하고 있었는데, 인프런에도 해당 컨텐츠를 업로드 해달라는 요청들이 있었어요.

오늘부터 주기적으로 이곳에도 5분내로 읽을 수 있는 면접질문을 하나씩 업로드하려고 해요.
재미있게 읽어주시면 감사하겠습니다 🙇

오늘의 백엔드 질문
결제 API에 동일한 요청이 두 번 들어왔을 때, 중복 결제를 어떻게 막으시겠어요?

이력서/포트폴리오에 결제나 주문, 쿠폰 발급이 있으면 나올 수 있는 질문이에요.
실제로 이런 일이 발생할 수 있을까? 싶기도 하지만, 실무에서 종종 발생하는 이슈에요.

이 질문은 결제 요청이 한 번만 온다는 전제로 코드를 짰는지,
혹은 결제 요청이 여러번 전송되어도 한 번만 처리되도록 로직을 작성했는지 검증하는 질문이에요.

답변 키포인트
멱등키(Idempotency-Key)를 누가 만들고 어디에 저장할지
멱등키에 DB 유니크 제약을 걸어 최종 방어선을 설정했는지
처리중과 완료 상태를 구분해 저장하고, 완료면 이전 응답을 그대로 돌려주는 것
재시도와 원요청이 동시에 처리될 때의 경합
외부 PG 응답이 유실됐을 때의 대사(reconciliation)

"버튼 비활성화"처리 만으로는 아쉬운 이유
중복 결제를 이야기할 때 "프론트에서 버튼을 비활성화한다"에서 끝나면 아쉬운 답변이에요.
버튼은 언제든 클라이언트에 의해 조작될 수 있어서, 실제 방어 로직은 서버와 DB에 있어야 하거든요.

같은 키로 들어온 두 번째 요청을 새 결제가 아니라 이미 처리한 요청의 조회로 취급하는 구조인지, 두 요청이 동시에 들어와도 유니크 제약이 하나를 확실히 막아주는지를 같이 설명할 수 있게 준비하는 게 좋아요.

면접에서는
면접에서 이 질문을 받았다면 "재시도 자체를 없앨 수는 없으니, 요청이 여러 번 들어와도 결과는 한 번만 처리한다"라는 식으로 답변을 시작하면 좋아요.

그다음에는 아래 순서로 이어서 설명하면 돼요.

주문마다 멱등키를 만들고, 그 키에 유니크 제약을 건다.
두 번째 요청은 새로 처리하지 않고 저장된 결과를 반환한다.
PG 응답 유실처럼 서버가 통제할 수 없는 경우에는, 주기적인 대사 과정으로 데이터를 보정한다.
이러한 중복 요청 처리 방안은 결제 외에도 다양한 적용할 수 있어요.
쿠폰 발급, 포인트 적립, Kafka의 at-least-once 소비 이슈 모두 연관된 질문으로 나올 수 있어요.

꼬리질문
다음의 꼬리질문도 생각해보세요.

멱등키는 클라이언트와 서버 중 어디에서 생성하는 것이 좋을까요?
DB에서 주문을 조회 후 없으면 insert 하는 방식에는 어떤 문제가 있나요?
같은 멱등키의 요청 두 개가 동시에 들어오면 두 번째 요청에는 어떤 응답을 주시겠어요?
첫 요청이 아직 처리 중일 때 들어온 재시도는 대기시키는 것과 에러를 반환하는 것 중 어느 쪽이 낫나요?
PG에는 결제가 성공했는데 우리 서버가 응답을 받지 못했다면 어떻게 복구하나요?

AI 모의면접으로
나의 면접 스킬을 체크해보세요
프론트엔드,백엔드,FDE 기술면접부터 문화면접까지,
개발자 면접 준비를 실전처럼 연습해 보세요.

title: WM-Quant: Rollout-Aware Post-Training Quantization for JEPA-Style World Models
description:
arXiv:2611.21882v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present WM-Quant, to our knowledge, the first post-training quantization (PTQ) framework designed specifically for JEPA-style world models. Although world models typically feature relatively few parameters, action planning algorithms often require thousands of inferences, which can quickly become computationally expensive. PTQ is a natural way to reduce this cost. However, we show that in world models using autoregressive model predictive control (MPC) rollouts, quantization error can compound with each predictor step, resulting in action rankings from the quantized model becoming near-random. WM-Quant addresses this with three components that build on existing PTQ methods: early-encoder precision, control-path preservation, and rollout-aware scaling. Early-encoder precision protects accurate latent state and goal information to mitigate long-term error propagation. Control-path preservation allows the world model predictor to distinguish between fine-grained actions, significantly improving action rankings and execution. Rollout-aware scaling jointly calibrates encoder and per-step predictor activation ranges with respect to an entire rollout rather than a single prediction, reducing the cumulative rollout error. Across multiple world models, environments, and PTQ methods, WM-Quant substantially improves planning success at low bit-widths, approaching full-precision performance at W4A4.
