title: How the Agnes score works
description:
Agnes gives every frontend repository a health score from 0 to 100, every day there are new commits. A single number is easy to put on a dashboard or a README badge, and just as easy to distrust if you can't see how it was made. So this post explains exactly how the score is calculated, with the real formula and the real numbers. If you think one of them is wrong, I'd like to hear why.

I built Agnes because more and more of our apps and services run entirely on frontend technologies, from the interface down to the API. We needed one system that keeps those codebases healthy and catches security issues, and a score you can follow from day to day tells you more than yet another list of warnings.

What gets analysed

Agnes looks at repositories that are mostly frontend code: at least 60% of the non-blank lines are HTML, CSS (including SCSS, Sass and Less), JavaScript, TypeScript, Vue, Svelte or Astro. Server-side templates (Blade, Twig, Nunjucks, Handlebars) don't count towards that share either way, but the HTML in them is checked too. Generated and vendored folders such as node_modules and dist don't count, and you can leave out more with .gitignore-style rules per project.

The analysis runs the open-source tools frontend teams already use, inside a container with no network access: Oxlint, Biome, ESLint (with the Vue, Svelte, Angular, no-unsanitized and trust-boundary plugins), Stylelint, html-validate, the Svelte compiler, FTA, Knip, jscpd and Secretlint, plus axe-core when the accessibility checks are switched on. Dependencies are read from the lockfile and checked against OSV and the npm registry. Agnes never runs your build, your tests or your scripts, and the code is deleted when the run ends.

Each tool's findings are sorted into categories, and each category gets its own score.

The categories and their weights

Category Weight What it measures
Code smells 35% Lint findings: error-prone patterns, complexity, unused code, CSS and HTML problems
Dependencies 35% Known vulnerabilities, deprecated and outdated packages in the lockfile
Security 15% Committed secrets, HTML injection and similar findings
Duplication 15% The share of the code that is copy-pasted
Accessibility about 10% Optional, off by default: static accessibility checks
Tests 15% Only with a committed coverage report: measured line coverage

The overall score is the weighted average of the categories that could be analysed. A category that can't be analysed (for example dependencies, when there is no lockfile) is left out and the other weights are scaled up to match. Missing data never counts as zero, and it never counts as perfect either.

Tests deserve a note. Without a coverage report, Agnes only knows which source files have a test file next to them. That is shown on the project page, but it doesn't count towards the overall score, because "a test file exists" says very little about whether the code is tested. Once you commit a coverage report (lcov, Istanbul's json-summary, Cobertura or Clover), measured line coverage joins the score at 15%, reaching 100 at 80% coverage.

From findings to a number

Every finding has a severity and a confidence, and each gets a weight:

  • severity: error 3, warning 1, info 0.25;
  • confidence: high 1, medium 0.5, low 0.25.

A finding's penalty is the two multiplied, so a high-confidence error weighs 3 and a low-confidence info weighs 0.0625. A category's penalty is the sum of its findings. Findings a tool reports beyond what the report lists still count, otherwise a repository with more problems would score better.

The penalty then becomes a score with a decay curve:

score = 100 × e^(−penalty / decay)

At zero penalty the score is 100. At a penalty equal to the category's decay value it is about 37. It never goes below 0, and each extra finding costs a little less than the one before. The first problems are the ones that matter most, and a large legacy codebase doesn't end up at a meaningless zero.

How the penalty is measured depends on the category:

  • Code smells are counted per thousand lines (KLOC), because a bigger codebase naturally has more of them. The decay is 40 weighted findings per KLOC. Repositories under 1,000 lines count as 1 KLOC, so a tiny project isn't punished for one warning.
  • Accessibility works the same way, also with 40 per KLOC.
  • Dependencies and security are counted in absolute terms, with decays of 15 and 6. One vulnerable package is one risk whether the project has 2,000 lines or 200,000.
  • Duplication uses the duplicated percentage that jscpd reports, with a decay of 10%.

A worked example

Take a 20,000-line project with:

  • 10 errors and 120 warnings from the linters, all high confidence: a penalty of 10 × 3 + 120 × 1 = 150, or 7.5 per KLOC. Code smells: 100 × e^(−7.5/40) = 83.
  • Dependency findings adding up to a penalty of 5. Dependencies: 100 × e^(−5/15) = 72.
  • One committed secret, an error: a penalty of 3. Security: 100 × e^(−3/6) = 61.
  • 4% duplicated code. Duplication: 100 × e^(−4/10) = 67.

The overall score is the weighted average: 0.35 × 83 + 0.35 × 72 + 0.15 × 61 + 0.15 × 67 = 73.

Scores are shown in four bands: 80 and up is healthy, 60 to 79 fair, 40 to 59 needs work, and under 40 poor. This project is fair, and the single committed secret costs it more than you might expect. That's on purpose.

Which fix is worth the most

A score is only useful if it tells you what to do next. For each rule, Agnes recalculates the score as if all of that rule's findings were fixed, and ranks the rules by the points they would gain. A rule with 40 warnings in a small project can be worth more than one error in a big one, and the ranking shows that directly. AI agents connected to Agnes's MCP server get the same ranking, so they can plan the fixes with the most effect first.

What the score can't tell you

The score is static analysis of the code in your repository. It doesn't run your application, so it can't judge colour contrast, focus handling or anything that only happens in a browser. It doesn't run your tests. Accessibility findings are listed per WCAG success criterion, but they are not an accessibility audit or a compliance statement. A high score means the tools found little to complain about, not that the code is good. A low score means there is work to do, but not that the developers did a bad job: it says nothing about how much was shipped, or under what deadline.

What it is good for is direction: whether a repository is getting healthier or not, and what to fix first.

Free for open source

Agnes is built on open-source tools, so open source gets it for free. On every plan, up to 10 public repositories per team are analysed without counting towards the plan, with up to 100,000 lines each. A public repository can also get a public report page and a README badge that shows its score. Agnes's own html-validate-templates carries one.

The numbers will change

All of these values (the weights, the decays, the severity and confidence weights) sit together in one file in the Agnes codebase, so they can be tuned against real repositories. When they change, the changelog will say so, and scores may move without any change in your code. If a score looks wrong for your repository, I'd like to hear about it: support@agnes.dev.

Curious what your own repository scores? Connecting one takes a minute, and if the number stings a little, at least you'll know which fix to start with: https://agnes.dev. Or see a real report first, no account needed: https://app.agnes.dev/demo

title: Hibernate From Scratch: Understanding JPA, Entities, Repositories & Spring Boot
description:
• A beginner-friendly guide to understanding how Java applications communicate with databases using Hibernate and Spring Data JPA.

Introduction

When building a backend application, one of the most important responsibilities is managing data. Applications need to store information, retrieve records, update existing data, and delete records when necessary.

Traditionally, developers used SQL queries and JDBC (Java Database Connectivity) to communicate directly with relational databases.

Although JDBC provides powerful database access, writing SQL queries and manually mapping database records to Java objects can become repetitive, especially in large applications.

This is where JPA, Hibernate, and Spring Data JPA come into play.

These technologies simplify database operations by allowing developers to work with Java objects instead of writing SQL queries for every database operation.

In this article, we'll explore these concepts from scratch and understand how they work together in a Spring Boot application.

1. Understanding the Fundamentals

Before writing code, let's understand three important concepts.

What is ORM?

ORM stands for Object-Relational Mapping.

It is a technique that maps Java objects to relational database tables.

For example, imagine an application that manages users.

In Java, we might represent a user using a class:

public class User {
    private Long id;
    private String name;
    private String email;
}

In a relational database, the same information might be stored in a table:

users

id name email
1 John john@example.com
2 Sarah sarah@example.com

ORM allows us to connect these two representations.

Instead of manually converting database rows into Java objects, an ORM framework handles much of that work.

What is JPA?

JPA stands for Java Persistence API, now officially known as Jakarta Persistence.

JPA is a specification that defines how Java applications should manage relational data.

It provides standard annotations and interfaces for:

  • Mapping Java classes to database tables.
  • Mapping object properties to database columns.
  • Managing entity relationships.
  • Persisting and retrieving data.
  • Managing entity lifecycle operations.

An important thing to understand is that JPA is not an implementation. It defines the rules and standards that persistence providers must follow.

What is Hibernate?

Hibernate is an ORM framework and one of the most widely used implementations of the JPA specification.

It provides the actual functionality behind many JPA operations.

For example, when we use:

userRepository.save(user);

Hibernate can generate the appropriate SQL statement and execute it against the database.

Hibernate handles tasks such as:

  • Generating SQL queries.
  • Mapping database records to Java objects.
  • Managing entity states.
  • Tracking changes to entities.
  • Handling database relationships.
  • Managing persistence contexts.

In simple terms:

  • JPA defines the standard.
  • Hibernate implements the standard.
  • Spring Data JPA simplifies database access through repository abstractions.

2. How Spring Boot, JPA, Hibernate, and Spring Data JPA Work Together

These technologies are often used together in Spring Boot applications.

Let's understand their relationship.

        Spring Boot Application
                 |
                 v
          Spring Data JPA
                 |
                 v
              JPA API
                 |
                 v
             Hibernate
                 |
                 v
           JDBC Driver
                 |
                 v
          Relational Database
          (PostgreSQL / MySQL)

Each layer has a specific responsibility.

Spring Boot

Provides application configuration and integrates the persistence technologies.

Spring Data JPA

Provides repository interfaces and reduces the amount of database-access code developers need to write.

JPA

Defines the persistence standards and annotations.

Hibernate

Implements JPA and performs the actual ORM operations.

JDBC Driver

Allows Java applications to communicate with the database.

Database

Stores the actual application data.

Understanding this architecture makes it easier to identify which technology is responsible for each operation.

3. Setting Up a Spring Boot Project

Let's create a simple Spring Boot application that uses Hibernate and PostgreSQL.

When creating a project using Spring Initializr, include these dependencies:

  • Spring Web
  • Spring Data JPA
  • PostgreSQL Driver
  • Validation

Spring Boot automatically configures Hibernate as the default JPA provider when the JPA starter is included, unless another provider is configured.

A simplified project structure might look like this:

src/main/java/com/example/demo/
│
├── controller/
│   └── UserController.java
│
├── service/
│   └── UserService.java
│
├── repository/
│   └── UserRepository.java
│
├── entity/
│   └── User.java
│
└── DemoApplication.java

Each package has a specific responsibility:

  • entity: Defines database-mapped Java objects.
  • repository: Handles database access.
  • service: Contains business logic.
  • controller: Handles HTTP requests and responses.

This separation makes applications easier to maintain and extend.

4. Understanding Entities in JPA

An entity is a Java class that represents a database table.

Hibernate uses entity metadata to understand how Java objects should be mapped to database records.

Let's create a User entity.

package com.example.demo.entity;

import jakarta.persistence.*;
import java.time.LocalDateTime;

@Entity
@Table(name = "users")
public class User {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    @Column(nullable = false, length = 100)
    private String name;

    @Column(nullable = false, unique = true)
    private String email;

    @Column(name = "created_at")
    private LocalDateTime createdAt;

    public User() {
    }

    // Getters and setters
}

Let's understand the important annotations.

@entity

Marks a Java class as a JPA entity.

Hibernate recognizes this class as something that should be persisted in the database.

@Table

Specifies the database table associated with the entity.

@Table(name = "users")

Without this annotation, JPA derives the table name from the entity name.

@id

Defines the primary key of the entity.

Every entity must have an identifier.

@GeneratedValue

Specifies how the primary key should be generated.

For example:

@GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)

Common generation strategies include:

  • IDENTITY: Relies on database-generated identity values.
  • SEQUENCE: Uses a database sequence.
  • TABLE: Uses a separate database table to generate identifiers.
  • AUTO: Allows the persistence provider to choose an appropriate strategy.

The best choice depends on the database and application requirements.

@column

Customizes how a Java field maps to a database column.

For example:

@Column(nullable = false, unique = true)
private String email;

This indicates that the column should not accept null values and should contain unique values.

Important: JPA annotations describe mapping and schema-generation metadata. They do not replace proper database constraints and migrations in production applications.

5. Understanding Entity Relationships

Real-world applications rarely contain independent tables.

For example, an e-commerce application might have:

  • Users
  • Orders
  • Products
  • Payments

These tables need relationships to represent how data is connected.

JPA provides four primary relationship annotations.

@OneToOne

Represents a relationship where one record is associated with one other record.

Example: One user has one profile.

@OneToOne
@JoinColumn(name = "profile_id")
private Profile profile;

@OneToMany

Represents a relationship where one record can be associated with multiple records.

Example: One user can have multiple orders.

@OneToMany(mappedBy = "user")
private List<Order> orders;

@ManyToOne

Represents multiple records associated with one record.

Example: Multiple orders can belong to one user.

@ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
@JoinColumn(name = "user_id")
private User user;

@ManyToMany

Represents a relationship where multiple records can be associated with multiple other records.

Example: Students can enroll in multiple courses, and each course can have multiple students.

@ManyToMany
@JoinTable(
    name = "student_courses",
    joinColumns = @JoinColumn(name = "student_id"),
    inverseJoinColumns = @JoinColumn(name = "course_id")
)
private Set<Course> courses;

Understanding relationships is essential when designing a relational database using JPA.

6. What Are Repositories in Spring Data JPA?

After defining entities, we need a way to perform database operations.

This is where Spring Data JPA repositories become useful.

A repository is an abstraction that provides methods for interacting with the database.

Instead of manually writing SQL queries for basic operations, we can extend an existing Spring Data interface.

Let's create a UserRepository.

package com.example.demo.repository;

import com.example.demo.entity.User;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.JpaRepository;

public interface UserRepository
        extends JpaRepository<User, Long> {

}

That's it!

We haven't written any implementation code.

Spring Data JPA automatically provides the implementation at runtime.

By extending JpaRepository, we get access to several useful methods.

Method Purpose
save() Insert or update an entity
findById() Find an entity by its ID
findAll() Retrieve all entities
existsById() Check whether an entity exists
deleteById() Delete an entity by ID
count() Count available records

For example:

userRepository.findAll();

Retrieves all users.

userRepository.findById(1L);

Retrieves a user with ID 1.

userRepository.deleteById(1L);

Deletes the user with ID 1.

Spring Data JPA generates the required database-access implementation behind these methods.

Custom Query Methods

One of the most useful features of Spring Data JPA is query method derivation.

We can define methods based on the properties of an entity.

For example:

public interface UserRepository
        extends JpaRepository<User, Long> {

    Optional<User> findByEmail(String email);

    List<User> findByName(String name);

    boolean existsByEmail(String email);
}

Spring Data JPA analyzes these method names and generates the corresponding queries.

We can also write custom JPQL queries using @Query.

@Query("SELECT u FROM User u WHERE u.email = :email")
Optional<User> findUserByEmail(
    @Param("email") String email
);

JPQL operates on entity classes and their properties rather than directly referencing database table and column names.

7. Understanding the Service Layer

In a properly structured Spring Boot application, controllers should not directly contain database operations.

Instead, we introduce a service layer to manage business logic.

Let's create a UserService.

package com.example.demo.service;

import com.example.demo.entity.User;
import com.example.demo.repository.UserRepository;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

import java.util.List;

@Service
public class UserService {

    private final UserRepository userRepository;

    public UserService(UserRepository userRepository) {
        this.userRepository = userRepository;
    }

    public User createUser(User user) {
        return userRepository.save(user);
    }

    public List<User> getAllUsers() {
        return userRepository.findAll();
    }
}

Why use a service layer?

The service layer provides a place to implement:

  • Business rules.
  • Validation beyond basic input constraints.
  • Transaction management.
  • Coordination between multiple repositories.
  • Application-specific logic.

For example, before creating a user, we might check whether the email address is already registered.

This keeps the controller focused on handling HTTP requests rather than implementing business rules.

8. Connecting the Application to PostgreSQL

Now we need to configure the database connection.

In Spring Boot, database configuration is commonly defined in:

application.yml

spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/demo_db
    username: postgres
    password: your_password
    driver-class-name: org.postgresql.Driver

  jpa:
    hibernate:
      ddl-auto: validate
    show-sql: true
    properties:
      hibernate:
        format_sql: true

Let's understand the configuration.

datasource.url

Specifies the database connection URL.

username and password

Provide database authentication credentials.

ddl-auto

Controls Hibernate's automatic database schema handling.

Common options include:

Value Description
create Creates the schema and may drop existing tables
create-drop Creates the schema and drops it when the session factory closes
update Attempts to update the schema
validate Checks whether the schema matches the entity mappings
none Disables automatic schema management

For production applications, using validate or none alongside a database migration tool such as Flyway or Liquibase is generally a safer approach.

Avoid relying on ddl-auto=update as your production database migration strategy.

9. Understanding the Entity Lifecycle

One of the most important Hibernate concepts is the entity lifecycle.

Hibernate manages entities through different states.

There are four commonly discussed states:

1. Transient

An object is transient when it has been created but is not associated with a persistence context.

User user = new User();
user.setName("John");
user.setEmail("john@example.com");

At this point, the object exists only in application memory.

2. Managed (Persistent)

An entity becomes managed when it is associated with an active persistence context.

For example:

entityManager.persist(user);

Hibernate starts tracking the entity.

Changes made to a managed entity can automatically be synchronized with the database.

3. Detached

An entity becomes detached when it is no longer associated with its persistence context.

For example, after the persistence context is closed, previously managed entities become detached.

Changes to detached objects are not automatically synchronized with the database.

4. Removed

An entity enters the removed state when it is scheduled for deletion.

entityManager.remove(user);

The actual database deletion happens when the persistence context is flushed.

Understanding these states helps explain why Hibernate sometimes executes SQL statements even when we haven't explicitly called a save method.

10. What Is a Persistence Context?

A persistence context is an important part of JPA and Hibernate.

Think of it as an environment that manages entity instances during their lifecycle.

It maintains a collection of managed entities and tracks changes made to them.

For example:

@Transactional
public void updateUser(Long id) {

    User user = userRepository.findById(id)
        .orElseThrow();

    user.setName("Updated Name");
}

Notice something interesting.

We didn't call:

userRepository.save(user);

Yet the updated name can still be persisted.

Why?

Because the entity is managed by the persistence context.

Hibernate detects the changes and synchronizes them with the database during transaction flushing. This mechanism is called dirty checking.

This is one of Hibernate's most powerful features.

11. Understanding Transactions in Spring Boot

A database transaction is a group of operations treated as one logical unit.

Transactions help maintain data consistency.

Spring provides the @Transactional annotation to manage transactions.

Example:

@Transactional
public void transferMoney(
        Long fromAccountId,
        Long toAccountId,
        BigDecimal amount) {

    Account from = accountRepository
        .findById(fromAccountId)
        .orElseThrow();

    Account to = accountRepository
        .findById(toAccountId)
        .orElseThrow();

    from.setBalance(from.getBalance().subtract(amount));

    to.setBalance(to.getBalance().add(amount));
}

Both updates should succeed together.

If an applicable unchecked exception occurs, Spring normally rolls back the transaction.

This prevents a situation where money is deducted from one account but not added to the other.

Transactions are particularly important when multiple database operations depend on each other.

12. Understanding Lazy and Eager Loading

When working with entity relationships, Hibernate needs to determine when related data should be retrieved.

JPA provides two common fetching strategies.

Lazy Loading

Related data is retrieved only when it is accessed.

@OneToMany(
    mappedBy = "user",
    fetch = FetchType.LAZY
)
private List<Order> orders;

Eager Loading

Related data is retrieved eagerly as part of loading the entity, although the exact SQL strategy is provider-dependent.

@ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.EAGER)
private User user;

Lazy loading is generally a good default for collections because it avoids unnecessarily loading large amounts of data.

However, it can introduce the N+1 query problem.

For example, retrieving 100 orders and then accessing each order's user might result in one query to retrieve the orders and additional queries to retrieve users.

Possible solutions include:

  • JPQL JOIN FETCH.
  • Entity graphs.
  • DTO projections.
  • Batch fetching.

Understanding fetching strategies is important for building efficient applications.

13. Putting Everything Together: A Simple REST API

Now let's connect everything.

We'll create a REST controller that exposes user-related endpoints.

package com.example.demo.controller;

import com.example.demo.entity.User;
import com.example.demo.service.UserService;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*;

import java.util.List;

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/users")
public class UserController {

    private final UserService userService;

    public UserController(UserService userService) {
        this.userService = userService;
    }

    @PostMapping
    public User createUser(@RequestBody User user) {
        return userService.createUser(user);
    }

    @GetMapping
    public List<User> getAllUsers() {
        return userService.getAllUsers();
    }
}

We now have two basic endpoints.

HTTP Method Endpoint Description
POST /api/users Create a user
GET /api/users Retrieve all users

The complete request flow looks like this:

       Client Request
             |
             v
       UserController
             |
             v
        UserService
             |
             v
       UserRepository
             |
             v
          Hibernate
             |
             v
         PostgreSQL

When a client sends a request to create a user:

  1. The controller receives the HTTP request.
  2. The service handles the application logic.
  3. The repository executes the persistence operation.
  4. Hibernate translates the operation into SQL.
  5. The JDBC driver communicates with PostgreSQL.
  6. The database stores the record.
  7. The result is returned through the application layers.

This is the basic architecture behind many Spring Boot applications.

Note: This example demonstrates the persistence flow. A production API should use request/response DTOs, validation, exception handling, and appropriate transaction boundaries rather than exposing JPA entities directly.

14. Common Mistakes Beginners Should Avoid

When starting with Hibernate and Spring Data JPA, there are several common mistakes worth understanding.

1. Confusing JPA with Hibernate

JPA is a specification, while Hibernate is an implementation. They are related but not interchangeable concepts.

2. Using entities directly in REST APIs

Returning entities directly can expose internal database structures and create serialization problems, particularly with bidirectional relationships.

Use DTOs instead.

3. Ignoring entity relationships

Incorrect relationship mappings can cause duplicate records, unexpected SQL queries, or data consistency problems.

4. Using EAGER fetching everywhere

Eager loading can retrieve unnecessary data and negatively affect application performance.

5. Ignoring transactions

Operations involving multiple database changes should have appropriate transaction boundaries.

6. Depending on Hibernate to manage production schemas

Use database migration tools such as Flyway or Liquibase to manage schema changes in a controlled and versioned manner.

Conclusion

Understanding Hibernate, JPA, and Spring Data JPA is an important step toward becoming a capable Spring Boot backend developer.

The key concepts to remember are:

  • ORM connects Java objects with relational database tables.
  • JPA defines the persistence specification.
  • Hibernate implements the JPA specification.
  • Spring Data JPA simplifies database access through repositories.
  • Entities represent database records.
  • Repositories provide database operations.
  • Services manage business logic.
  • Persistence contexts track managed entities.
  • Transactions help maintain data consistency.
  • Fetching strategies influence database performance.

Rather than memorizing annotations and methods, focus on understanding what happens behind the scenes when an application communicates with a database.

Once you understand how these components work together, building more complex backend systems becomes much easier.

The best way to learn Hibernate is to build something with it. Start with a simple CRUD application, introduce entity relationships, implement transactions, and gradually explore more advanced persistence concepts.

Happy coding! 🚀

title: Adaptive Memory for Online Reinforcement Learning under Sparse Model Changes
description:
arXiv:2611.21879v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study the discounted reinforcement learning (RL) problem in a setting where the underlying environment changes between deployments. Each deployment provides $H$ observations from a fixed MDP. The reward function and transition kernel are fixed within each deployment. Across deployments, at most an $\epsilon >0$ fraction of the reward and transition kernel entries may change. In this setting, learning each model to deploy from scratch may discard useful observations from past deployments, whereas pooling all past observations can bias the estimates of entries that have already changed. We then propose an algorithm that for each state and action pair, selects how much history to reuse to estimate the reward and probabilities of the next state. We start with observations from the current deployment and add earlier deployment observations one at a time, the most recent first. After each addition, we check whether a single average reward agrees with the estimates from all histories considered until that point. We apply the same check to the distribution of next states. For each estimate, we leverage the last history that passes these aforementioned checks. The optimal control policy is then computed on top of the fitted MDP. We characterize the average gap between the optimal return and the return of the learner's policies over a finite number of deployments. We demonstrate that when $0< |S|\epsilon \leq 2$, with $|S|$ being the cardinality of the state space, our algorithm needs only the observations from the most recent $O(1/\epsilon)$ deployments, and achieves a long-run average gap of at most $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{\epsilon/H})$.

title: A Six-Step Test: Does Your SharePoint AI Assistant Quote Drafts or Old Versions?
description:
An AI assistant answers from the text it indexed. In SharePoint, one procedure rarely exists only once. There is the current major version, the older major versions in version history, a minor draft an editor is still working on, and copies in other places: a PDF export in a project folder, a mail attachment, a file on a Teams channel.

If a superseded passage is in the index, a retrieval step can select it, and the model will write a confident answer from it. The model has no idea which text is authoritative.

What SharePoint keeps by default

Microsoft's support documentation says that for Microsoft 365 customers "versioning is now turned on by default when you create a new library or list, and it will automatically save the last 500 versions of a document."

The version numbers carry meaning: "Major versions are identified by whole numbers, such as 5.0; minor versions are identified by decimal numbers, such as 5.1." A library owner can decide who sees drafts. With draft security applied, "those who have permission only to read the file cannot see the minor version."

At the organisation level, Microsoft Learn states that the default is "Manual version history limits with 500 major version count limit and no expiration." Lowering a library limit does not clean up at once: "up to 20 versions" are removed "for every new version created."

So a rule you replaced two years ago is, by default, still stored in the version history of the same file.

History is one API call away

Microsoft Graph returns the stored versions of a file, newest first, to an app with Files.Read.All or a higher application permission. An indexer can therefore read the stored versions of every file it can reach. Whether it does, and whether it labels what it found, is a design decision of the assistant, not a property of SharePoint.

The test

You can run this alone and free. Allow for the assistant's indexing delay.

  1. Create a test library. In Versioning settings choose major and minor versions, and set draft items to be seen only by users who can edit items.
  2. Upload a short procedure that states: "Procedures are reviewed every 24 months." Publish it as version 1.0.
  3. Edit the sentence to "every 12 months" and publish as version 2.0.
  4. Edit again to "every 6 months" and save without publishing, so it stays as minor draft 2.1.
  5. Give a test account read-only access to the library and wait for the next indexing run.
  6. As that account, ask: "How often are procedures reviewed?"

Reading the result

  • 6 months: this suggests the assistant indexes drafts beyond what SharePoint shows a reader.
  • 24 months: this suggests it reads history without labelling it.
  • 12 months, with the document and version named: the behaviour you want.

Then ask explicitly about previous versions. A good answer marks 1.0 as superseded instead of presenting it as current. Make sure no other copy of the test file exists, and repeat after a second indexing run.

The test applies to any assistant you evaluate, with or without Microsoft Copilot.

What the test does not cover

Copies outside the library, such as PDF exports or mail attachments, are not covered by versioning at all. A version label helps only where the file lives in one place.

The full chapter, with every Microsoft source, is here: Why AI Answers From SharePoint Cite Outdated Documents, and How to Stop It.

Drafted with AI assistance, checked against the cited Microsoft sources and approved by Kaspars Jurjāns.

title: BullMQ Tutorial: Node.js Job Queues That Retry and Recover
description:
Quick answer

BullMQ is a Node.js job queue backed by Redis: your web code adds a job to a queue, and a worker runs it, so slow work never blocks a web request. This post sends three shop orders through a BullMQ queue, charges the two good ones, and watches the third fail and retry because its total is missing.

A customer in Karachi clicks buy on a small online shop. The checkout code charges the card, updates stock, and sends a confirmation email, all inside one web request. Then the email service stalls, the request times out, and the customer clicks buy again. The card is charged twice, and the shop owner hears about it from an angry customer, not a log. A queue breaks that chain. The web request only records the order and hands it to BullMQ, and a worker charges it and sends the email in its own time. If the worker crashes halfway, the order still sits in Redis, waiting for the next worker.

What I would check before using it

My first check: does the work need to outlive the web request? An email, a charge, or a report can take seconds, while a web request should answer fast. When the slow step can fail on its own, a queue earns its place. A quick database write needs only plain code in the handler. For same-time work in one process, plain async code may be simpler; the Node.js REST API post shows where that handler lives.

My second check is who runs Redis. BullMQ stores every job in Redis, so the queue is only as reliable as that server. If nobody owns it, a managed Redis is the honest alternative. Redis is one more service to run, and the Redis Explained: The In-Memory Store That Speeds Things Up post covers what it does.

My third check is what happens when a job fails. Every queue needs a plan for the job that can never succeed: how many retries, how long to wait, and where failures are recorded. Without one, a bad job retries forever while good orders wait. The demo allows three attempts, then fails for good.

My fourth check: are the jobs safe to run twice? A worker can crash after charging a card but before recording it, and BullMQ may run it again. If charging twice is a disaster, the job needs an idempotency key checked before charging.

My verdict, as judgement: adopt BullMQ when background work must not block the user and must survive a crash, and the team runs Node.js and Redis. Skip it for a small script. The recommendation flips the moment nobody owns Redis, or the queue costs more than the job.

Three orders, one worker, and a missing total

Three orders arrive at the same small shop. Ayesha buys a kurta and a dupatta for Rs 12,400, Bilal buys sneakers for Rs 7,800, and Hina buys a handbag and a wallet with no total.

One file defines the queue and the worker, pointing at a local Redis on port 6379. The job checks the total, waits one second to stand in for the charge, and returns a receipt. Every job gets three attempts, one second apart.

/**
 * Order queue for The Practical Developer (BullMQ demo).
 *
 * A small online shop sends each order to a BullMQ queue backed by
 * Redis instead of charging the card inside the web request. A worker
 * picks each job up, charges the order, and returns a receipt string.
 * One order arrives without a total, so the worker throws, BullMQ
 * retries it twice, and then the job fails for good.
 *
 * Run from this folder:
 *   node dispatch_first.js   (sends order 101, no worker running)
 *   node worker.js           (start the worker in another terminal)
 *   node dispatch_rest.js    (sends orders 102 and 103, waits for results)
 */
const { Queue, Worker, QueueEvents } = require("bullmq");

const connection = { host: "127.0.0.1", port: 6379 };

function makeQueue() {
  return new Queue("shop-orders", { connection });
}

async function processOrder(job) {
  const { orderId, customer, items, total } = job.data;
  if (total === undefined || total === null) {
    throw new Error(`order ${orderId} has no total to charge`);
  }
  if (total <= 0) {
    throw new Error(`order ${orderId} has an invalid total: ${total}`);
  }
  await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 1000));
  const joined = items.join(", ");
  return (
    `Order ${orderId} for ${customer}: charged Rs ${total} ` +
    `for ${joined}; confirmation email queued`
  );
}

function makeWorker() {
  const worker = new Worker("shop-orders", processOrder, {
    connection,
    concurrency: 1,
  });
  worker.on("completed", (job, result) => {
    console.log(`Worker: order ${job.data.orderId} completed: ${result}`);
  });
  worker.on("failed", (job, err) => {
    console.log(
      `Worker: order ${job.data.orderId} failed ` +
        `(attempt ${job.attemptsMade}/${job.opts.attempts}): ${err.message}`
    );
  });
  return worker;
}

module.exports = { connection, makeQueue, makeWorker, processOrder };

Two small scripts send the orders: the first sends order 101 with no worker running, the second sends 102 and 103 once the worker starts, then waits for every result.

// dispatch_first.js: send one order BEFORE any worker is running.
const { makeQueue } = require("./queue");

async function main() {
  const queue = makeQueue();
  const job = await queue.add(
    "process-order",
    { orderId: 101, customer: "Ayesha", items: ["kurta", "dupatta"], total: 12400 },
    { attempts: 3, backoff: { type: "fixed", delay: 1000 } }
  );
  console.log("Sent order 101 for Ayesha (Rs 12400, kurta, dupatta)");
  console.log(`Job id: ${job.id}`);
  console.log(`State right after sending: ${await job.getState()}`);
  console.log("No worker is running yet, so the order waits in the queue.");
  require("fs").writeFileSync("first_job_id.txt", String(job.id));
  await queue.close();
}

main().catch((err) => {
  console.error(err);
  process.exit(1);
});

// dispatch_rest.js: send the rest, then collect every result.
const { QueueEvents } = require("bullmq");
const { connection, makeQueue } = require("./queue");

async function main() {
  const queue = makeQueue();
  const events = new QueueEvents("shop-orders", { connection });

  const sent = {};
  sent[102] = await queue.add(
    "process-order",
    { orderId: 102, customer: "Bilal", items: ["sneakers"], total: 7800 },
    { attempts: 3, backoff: { type: "fixed", delay: 1000 } }
  );
  console.log("Sent order 102 for Bilal (Rs 7800, sneakers)");
  sent[103] = await queue.add(
    "process-order",
    { orderId: 103, customer: "Hina", items: ["handbag", "wallet"], total: null },
    { attempts: 3, backoff: { type: "fixed", delay: 1000 } }
  );
  console.log("Sent order 103 for Hina (handbag, wallet, NO total)");
  console.log("Waiting for results...");

  for (const orderId of [101, 102, 103]) {
    const job =
      orderId === 101
        ? await queue.getJob(require("fs").readFileSync("first_job_id.txt", "utf8").trim())
        : sent[orderId];
    try {
      const receipt = await job.waitUntilFinished(events, 30000);
      console.log(`Order ${orderId}: completed - ${receipt}`);
    } catch (err) {
      const state = await job.getState();
      console.log(`Order ${orderId}: ${state} - ${err.message}`);
    }
  }
  await events.close();
  await queue.close();
}

main().catch((err) => {
  console.error(err);
  process.exit(1);
});

Here is the real output. Order 101 was sent with no worker running, so it waited until the worker started and charged it.

$ redis-cli FLUSHALL
OK
$ node dispatch_first.js
Sent order 101 for Ayesha (Rs 12400, kurta, dupatta)
Job id: 1
State right after sending: waiting
No worker is running yet, so the order waits in the queue.

$ node worker.js
Worker started, waiting for orders...

$ node dispatch_rest.js
Sent order 102 for Bilal (Rs 7800, sneakers)
Sent order 103 for Hina (handbag, wallet, NO total)
Waiting for results...
Order 101: completed - Order 101 for Ayesha: charged Rs 12400 for kurta, dupatta; confirmation email queued
Order 102: completed - Order 102 for Bilal: charged Rs 7800 for sneakers; confirmation email queued
Order 103: failed - order 103 has no total to charge

The worker log agrees: order 101 completed even though it was sent first, and order 103 failed three times, one second apart, before BullMQ gave up.

Worker started, waiting for orders...
Worker: order 101 completed: Order 101 for Ayesha: charged Rs 12400 for kurta, dupatta; confirmation email queued
Worker: order 102 completed: Order 102 for Bilal: charged Rs 7800 for sneakers; confirmation email queued
Worker: order 103 failed (attempt 1/3): order 103 has no total to charge
Worker: order 103 failed (attempt 2/3): order 103 has no total to charge
Worker: order 103 failed (attempt 3/3): order 103 has no total to charge

The thing that went wrong is order 103. With no total, the worker threw, BullMQ retried it twice, and then the job failed for good. A missing total never appears on its own, so retrying it is pointless. Retry only failures that time can fix, and fail fast on bad data. Validate the total before the order reaches the queue, and park failed jobs in a dead-letter queue. The Celery Tutorial: Background Jobs in Python That Just Work post shows the same three orders in Python, and the RabbitMQ Tutorial: An Order Queue That Never Loses Work post shows the dead-letter pattern.

Common mistakes and how to fix them

First, starting the worker before Redis is running. The symptom is a connection refused error, or a worker that crashes on its first job. The fix is to start Redis first and check redis-cli ping prints PONG.

Second, retrying bad data forever. The symptom is a worker log full of retries for a job that can never succeed, like order 103, while good orders wait. The fix is to retry only transient errors, and fail fast on bad data by validating first.

Third, forgetting maxRetriesPerRequest: null with newer ioredis versions. The symptom is a warning that BullMQ requires the option, or jobs that behave oddly under load. The fix is to pass maxRetriesPerRequest: null in the connection options, as the BullMQ docs explain.

Fourth, closing the process before the results arrive. The symptom is a script that sends jobs and exits at once, so waitUntilFinished never resolves. The fix is to stay alive until every job reaches a final state, then close the queue and the events, as dispatch_rest.js does.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need Redis to use BullMQ? Yes. BullMQ stores every job in Redis, with no filesystem fallback like the Celery demo used. Local Redis to learn, managed Redis live.

What happens to a job if no worker is running? It waits in Redis. Order 101 stayed waiting until the worker started, then was processed. Nothing was lost.

How is BullMQ different from Celery? They solve the same problem in different languages: Celery is Python with a choice of brokers, BullMQ is Node.js with Redis as its only store. Pick the one your team already runs.

Can I run the worker in the same process as my web server? You can, but you lose the point of the queue: if the server restarts, the worker restarts with it. Run the worker as its own process and keep it alive with PM2 Tutorial: Keep Your Node.js App Running for Good.

What to remember

  • Add slow work with queue.add(), and let the web request answer fast.
  • A job sent with no worker running waits in Redis, it is not lost.
  • Set attempts and backoff per job; retry only failures that time can fix.
  • Make jobs safe to run twice, with an idempotency check.
  • Own Redis: local to learn, managed live.

Where this leaves you

BullMQ earns its place the day a slow step starts breaking web requests that should answer in a blink. The demo proved three things: an order sent before the worker started still got processed, good orders were charged and returned receipts, and the broken order retried twice and then failed loudly instead of vanishing. Start with one queue, one worker, and a local Redis, then move to managed Redis when real users arrive. An empty queue means fast requests, every single time.

Further reading

  • BullMQ guide, queues, https://docs.bullmq.io/guide/queues
  • BullMQ guide, retrying failing jobs, https://docs.bullmq.io/guide/retrying-failing-jobs
  • Celery Tutorial: Background Jobs in Python That Just Work, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/11/celery-python-background-tasks.html
  • RabbitMQ Tutorial: An Order Queue That Never Loses Work, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/11/rabbitmq-python-order-queue.html
  • Redis Explained: The In-Memory Store That Speeds Things Up, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/10/redis-explained-in-memory-store-that.html
  • Build Your First REST API With Node.js and Express, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/10/build-your-first-rest-api-with-nodejs.html
  • PM2 Tutorial: Keep Your Node.js App Running for Good, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/11/pm2-tutorial-nodejs-process-manager.html

title: An AI-Based OSSE Framework to Evaluate Learned Physical Consistency: A Multi-Model Study Using FourCastNet, Aurora, Prithvi WxC, and GraphCast
description:
arXiv:2611.22024v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Observing System Simulation Experiments (OSSEs) are a central methodology for evaluating future atmospheric observing systems. We present the first AI-based OSSE framework to test whether different AI weather models can reproduce comparable physical impact from new observations that traditional physics based models generate. We evaluate four distinct architectural AI models on the Charney conjecture that incomplete historical observations can infer the present state of the atmospheric. We considner- FourCastNet V2, GraphCast, Aurora and Prithvi WxC and integrate each autoregressively over a 60-day forecast horizon. After a 30-day spin-up, we insert ERA5 temperature fields to infer winds and related atmospheric fields. Similar OSSE experiments are conducted for wind insertion. We measure the performance of each model's response to observational information on a 30-day data assimilation cycle forecast with and without data insertion. Distinct architectural AI weather models respond differently to the same OSSE observations. Foundation models (i.e. Prithvi WxC and Aurora), produce the strongest impact. For example, while GraphCast is the weakest, all three of the four models capture the temperature-to-geopotential height response. The two foundational models retain a positive, non-trivial, tropical zonal wind at 500 hPa response to temperature insertion. Various data insertion experiments can vary significantly even within a given architecture. We identify an architecture-specific numerical instability in GraphCast's full 37-level configuration that produces a runaway feedback concentrated at the uppermost levels with ERA5 temperature insertion correctable by excluding levels at or below 100 hPa.

title: Building a Redundant Edge Cluster Out of Three $15/Year Black Friday VPS Nodes
description:
Every Black Friday, developers grab sub-$15/year VPS instances out of impulse, run neofetch, and then let them idle until the renewal invoice hits twelve months later.

Last year, I decided to see how far I could push these throwaway budget boxes. Instead of letting them collect dust, I wired three distinct low-cost nodes across different geographic locations (Los Angeles, Frankfurt, and Singapore) into a self-healing reverse proxy and uptime cluster.

Here is the exact architecture, the configuration workflow, and the hard limits you need to watch out for when running container workloads on budget silicon.

The Architecture: Cheap Edge, Solid Core
The mental model is simple: never put your stateful databases on budget promo nodes.

Instead, treat them as ephemeral edge workers:

       [ Client Requests ]
                │
                ▼
      [ Cloudflare Anycast ]
                │
   ┌────────────┼────────────┐
   ▼            ▼            ▼

[ US Node ] [ EU Node ] [ APAC Node ] <-- $12-$18/yr BF Nodes (Traefik + Wireguard)
└────────────┼────────────┘
│ (Encrypted Wireguard Mesh)
▼
[ Hetzner / Netcup Core ] <-- Production Postgres, Redis & FFmpeg Backend
Anycast Ingress: Cloudflare handles DDoS mitigation and DNS routing to the closest healthy edge node.
Reverse Proxy & SSL: Each node runs Traefik in Docker, automatically negotiating Let’s Encrypt certificates.
Internal Mesh Network: The three edge nodes communicate with my primary production database (hosted on a dedicated Hetzner box) through a private WireGuard overlay network.
Health Checking: If the Los Angeles budget node gets rebooted for unscheduled host maintenance, Cloudflare health checks fail over traffic to Frankfurt in seconds.
Step 1: Minimum Hardware Requirements
You cannot run this stack on just any $10 box. Before you pick up deals from the sales threads, verify these three prerequisites:

Virtualization: Must be KVM. Container-based virtualization (OpenVZ/LXC) often restricts WireGuard kernel modules and causes Docker overlay networking headaches.
RAM: Minimum 1 GB. Docker + Traefik + WireGuard + a lightweight Node.js worker will hover around 350MB–500MB RAM usage. 512MB nodes will trigger the Linux OOM (Out Of Memory) killer the moment you run a package update.
Fair-Share CPU Policy: You don’t need dedicated cores, but avoid hosts that suspend instances if CPU utilization averages above 20% for 15 minutes.
Step 2: Automated Provisioning Script
Once you receive your root credentials, run this minimal hardening and setup script:

!/usr/bin/env bash

set -e

Update & install essential network tools

apt-get update && apt-get upgrade -y
apt-get install -y curl ufw wireguard fail2ban htop

Enable BBR Congestion Control for better throughput on lossy pipes

cat <> /etc/sysctl.conf
net.core.default_qdisc=fq
net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control=bbr
EOF
sysctl -p

Lock down firewall

ufw default deny incoming
ufw default allow outgoing
ufw allow 22/tcp
ufw allow 80/tcp
ufw allow 443/tcp
ufw allow 51820/udp # WireGuard
ufw --force enable

Install official Docker runtime

curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com | sh
Step 3: Zero-Trust Interconnect via WireGuard
Rather than exposing database ports over the public internet, each node connects to the central cluster using a lightweight WireGuard configuration (/etc/wireguard/wg0.conf):

[Interface]
Address = 10.100.0.2/24
PrivateKey = CLIENT_PRIVATE_KEY
DNS = 1.1.1.1

[Peer]
PublicKey = CORE_SERVER_PUBLIC_KEY
Endpoint = core.yourdomain.com:51820
AllowedIPs = 10.100.0.0/24
PersistentKeepalive = 25
Now, any request hitting https://us-proxy.yourdomain.com forwards traffic to 10.100.0.1:3000 through an encrypted tunnel. If the public routing between the US budget node and the European datacenter has bad transit, WireGuard keeps the connection alive without exposing raw database ports to port scanners.

Step 4: The Traefik Edge Deployment
Here is the minimal docker-compose.yml I deploy to each node:

version: '3.8'

services:
traefik:
image: traefik:v3.1
restart: always
command:
- "--providers.docker=true"
- "--providers.docker.exposedbydefault=false"
- "--entrypoints.web.address=:80"
- "--entrypoints.websecure.address=:443"
- "--certificatesresolvers.myresolver.acme.tlschallenge=true"
- "--certificatesresolvers.myresolver.acme.email=admin@yourdomain.com"
- "--certificatesresolvers.myresolver.acme.storage=/letsencrypt/acme.json"
ports:
- "80:80"
- "443:443"
volumes:
- "/var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock:ro"
- "./letsencrypt:/letsencrypt"
networks:
- web

networks:
web:
external: true
What I Learned Running Dirt-Cheap Nodes for a Year
Disk I/O Degrades First: The CPU usually stays fine, but shared disks will inevitably slow down during holidays. Keep your logs written to tmpfs (RAM) instead of hammering the physical disk with verbose access logs.
Reboots Will Happen: Budget providers don’t have redundant hot-swap hardware. Assume your node will reboot without warning once every two months. If your stack is stateless, you won’t care.
Buy Across Different ASNs: Don’t buy three promo instances from three different reseller brands that all sit in the same Racknerd or Colocrossing datacenter. Mix datacenters and network uplinks.

title: TableVista: Benchmarking Multimodal Table Reasoning under Visual and Structural Complexity
description:
arXiv:2605.05955v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We introduce TableVista, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating foundation models in multimodal table reasoning under visual and structural complexity. TableVista consists of 3,000 high-quality table reasoning problems, where each instance is expanded into 10 distinct visual variants through our multi-style rendering and transformation pipeline. This process encompasses diverse scenario styles, robustness perturbations, and vision-only configurations, culminating in 30,000 multimodal samples for a multi-dimensional evaluation. We conduct an extensive evaluation of 29 state-of-the-art open-source and proprietary foundation models on TableVista. Through comprehensive quantitative and qualitative analysis, we find that while evaluated models remain largely stable across diverse rendering styles, they exhibit pronounced performance degradation on complex structural layouts and vision-only settings, revealing that current models struggle to maintain reasoning consistency when structural complexity combines with visually integrated presentations. These findings highlight critical gaps in current multimodal capabilities, providing insights for advancing more robust and reliable table understanding models.

title: What RL on Expert-Built Tasks Teaches Nemotron 3.5 Super
description:
arXiv:2611.22161v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We post-train NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Super (120B total, 12B active parameters) with reinforcement learning (RL) on five expert-built task datasets, one at a time: real-world software engineering, complex constraints, long-horizon tool use, professional chart understanding and enterprise document reasoning. Each run trains a fresh rank-32 LoRA adapter with CISPO on Tinker, with no supervised stage, and each adapter is compared with the base model on the same tasks, harness and settings. On twelve headline benchmarks, eight built by other groups and four by Surge AI, the gains range from +4.5 points on IFBench to +13.8 on GDP_pdf, which rises from 10.4% to 24.2%; SWE-bench Pro V2 rises from 86.9% to 92.1%, Terminal-Bench 2.1 from 63.9% to 70.3%, MultiChallenge from 58.3% to 66.6%, AutomationBench from 14.8% to 27.5% and Chartography from 39.4% to 50.6%. The document adapter, trained without API tools, also gains +8.0 points on AutomationBench. In attempts read side by side with the base model's on tasks each adapter newly solves, the base model's failures recur in a few modes, and each adapter does more often what the base model missed: the tool-use adapter finds the data and the rules before acting, the coding adapter writes its own test or scratch files on SWE-bench Pro V2, the constraints adapter carries earlier turns into its answers, the chart adapter measures the marks in code, and the document adapter reads AutomationBench's spreadsheets.

title: SkillBuffBench: Measuring What Agent Skills Contribute across Harnesses, Models, Skill Access Modes and Memory
description:
arXiv:2611.22017v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agent Skills, file-based packages of procedural knowledge that a coding agent can discover and load on demand, are now shipped by every major agent harness, yet the evidence for how much they help comes almost entirely from settings in which the right Skill is hand-picked for the task and the agent starts from a blank slate. Neither holds in deployment, where an agent chooses from whatever library happens to be installed and frequently carries memory from earlier work. We present SkillBuffBench, a benchmark and paired evaluation protocol that treats Skill access as a three-level factor (no Skill, a curated Skill, and automatic invocation from an installed library), crosses it with memory (off and on), with four agent harnesses and with multiple models (the state-of-the-art proprietary models from Anthropic, Google and OpenAI, and the state-of-the-art open-weight models from Chinese providers), every model being run under every harness, and evaluates the result on research tasks contributed by domain experts together with the Skills they use, currently in materials science and biology, with the suite extended on a rolling basis. Every run is marked by a deterministic verifier; uncertainty is reported with a paired, task-level bootstrap; and cost, agent rounds and wall-clock time are reported alongside the score rather than folded into it. This version of the paper describes the design of the benchmark, its evaluation protocol and its current tasks and Skills. The evaluation is in progress: results will be added once the runs are complete, and the task suite, results and analysis will continue to be updated on a rolling basis.

title: SIDUMN: Self-Supervised Image Denoising Under Symmetric Multiplicative Noise
description:
arXiv:2611.22317v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Self-supervised denoising is challenging when the corruption is multiplicative and signal-dependent. In this letter, we propose SIDUMN, a symmetric noisier framework for self-supervised denoising under mean-one symmetric multiplicative noise. Given noisy observations and the noise law, the method samples an independent synthetic noise factor from the same law and constructs two complementary noisier images by applying the factor and its reflection about one. The denoising network is trained to predict one noisier image from the other, and at inference the reconstructions of $K$ such antithetic pairs are averaged. We show that the population target of the training loss is the clean conditional mean minus a multiplicative cross-term. We further prove that, for any trained network, antithetic averaging never increases the expected squared error of a single noisier-input reconstruction. Numerical results validate the theoretical findings and the proposed method.

title: Amazon RDS now supports fast storage volume initialization
description:
Amazon RDS now initializes storage volumes faster when you perform a point-in-time restore (PITR), create a read replica, or convert a Single-AZ instance to Multi-AZ. Each of these operations creates storage volumes from a snapshot, and the data blocks are downloaded from Amazon S3 before you can access them. With fast storage volume initialization, you get a fully performant DB instance in a predictable amount of time.

Previously, the initialization rate varied with your workload and with which blocks were accessed. As there was no dedicated bandwidth, so you could see increased I/O latency and had no way to tell when an instance would reach full performance. Now, each database instance is initialized at up to 4 TiB per hour, across every gp3 and io2 storage volume attached to the instance. If concurrent initialization across your account exceeds the available bandwidth, the remaining blocks initialize on a best-effort basis, so initialization is never slower than today. Your DB instance stays available and usable while initialization runs.

Fast storage volume initialization is enabled by default and no action is required. To follow progress, use the StorageOperationStatus and StorageOperationPercentProgress fields in the Amazon RDS console, the DescribeDBInstances API, the AWS Command Line Interface (CLI), or AWS SDKs.

This capability is available at no additional cost for RDS for MariaDB, RDS for MySQL, RDS for PostgreSQL, RDS for Db2, RDS for Microsoft SQL Server, and RDS for Oracle, in all commercial AWS Regions and the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. To learn more, see Amazon RDS storage in the Amazon RDS User Guide.

title: Visual Contextual Attack: Jailbreaking MLLMs with Image-Driven Context Injection
description:
arXiv:2507.02844v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: With the emergence of strong vision language capabilities, multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated tremendous potential for real-world applications. However, the security vulnerabilities exhibited by the visual modality pose significant challenges to deploying such models in open-world environments. Recent studies have successfully induced harmful responses from target MLLMs by encoding harmful textual semantics directly into visual inputs. However, in these approaches, the visual modality primarily serves as a trigger for unsafe behavior, often exhibiting semantic ambiguity and lacking grounding in realistic scenarios. In this work, we define a novel setting: vision-centric jailbreak, where visual information serves as a necessary component in constructing a complete and realistic jailbreak context. Building on this setting, we propose the VisCo (Visual Contextual) Attack. VisCo fabricates contextual dialogue using four distinct vision-focused strategies, dynamically generating auxiliary images when necessary to construct a vision-centric jailbreak scenario. To maximize attack effectiveness, it incorporates automatic toxicity obfuscation and semantic refinement to produce a final attack prompt that reliably triggers harmful responses from the target black-box MLLMs. Specifically, VisCo achieves a toxicity score of 4.78 and an Attack Success Rate (ASR) of 85% on MM-SafetyBench against GPT-4o, significantly outperforming the baseline, which achieves a toxicity score of 2.48 and an ASR of 22.2%. Code: https://github.com/Dtc7w3PQ/Visco-Attack.

title: What's inside one AI data answer, and how to build a 'show your work' panel for it
description:
"Revenue is up 18%." Is it? An AI answer about your data that arrives as one sentence gives the reader nothing to check, so they either trust it blindly or come and ask you.

A good answer has parts. This post takes one real response apart and builds the small panel that shows each part in the right place.

The parts

Here is a real answer from FactQL's public sample data, to the question "Who are our top 5 customers by total spend?":

Part Field Where it goes
The answer in words explanation On top, always visible
The rows it came from data.columns, data.rows A table under the answer
The query that ran sql Folded away, one click to open
Where the numbers came from lineage.text A small line, when present

The order is the point: answer first for people in a hurry, rows for people who want to check, the query for the one person who needs it.

The code

Two functions. toView shapes the response and has no DOM in it, so you can unit-test it. renderAnswer draws.

// Turn a raw answer into exactly what the panel shows. No DOM here, so it is easy to test.
export function toView(a, maxRows = 10) {
  const table = a.data ?? {};                       // rows live under "data"
  const columns = table.columns ?? [];
  const rows = (table.rows ?? []).map((row) =>
    row.map((v) => (typeof v === "number" && !Number.isInteger(v) ? Number(v.toFixed(2)) : v)));
  return {
    ok: a.result === "success",
    answer: a.explanation ?? "No answer.",
    columns,
    rows: rows.slice(0, maxRows),
    hiddenRows: Math.max(0, rows.length - maxRows),
    query: a.sql ?? null,                           // folded away by default
    source: a.lineage?.text ?? null,                // "where the numbers came from", when present
  };
}

// The panel itself: answer on top, rows under it, the query behind a click.
export function renderAnswer(a, el) {
  const v = toView(a);
  const add = (tag, text, parent = el) => { const n = document.createElement(tag); n.textContent = text; parent.append(n); return n; };
  el.textContent = "";
  add("p", v.answer);
  if (v.rows.length) {
    const t = add("table", ""), head = add("tr", "", t);
    v.columns.forEach((c) => add("th", c, head));
    v.rows.forEach((row) => { const tr = add("tr", "", t); row.forEach((cell) => add("td", String(cell), tr)); });
    if (v.hiddenRows) add("p", `…and ${v.hiddenRows} more rows`);
  }
  if (v.source) add("p", v.source);
  if (v.query) { const d = add("details", ""); add("summary", "The query that ran", d); add("pre", v.query, d); }
}

Testing the shaping

I ran toView in Node against the real response (18 Nov 2026), with maxRows set to 3:

{
  ok: true,
  answer: 'Your top 5 customers by total spend are Karl Seal, Tim Cary, Russell Brinson, Harry Arce and Daisy Bates. ...',
  columns: [ 'customer_id', 'first_name', 'last_name', 'total_spend' ],
  rows: [ [ 526, 'KARL', 'SEAL', 358.12 ], [ 468, 'TIM', 'CARY', 344.06 ], [ 380, 'RUSSELL', 'BRINSON', 324.04 ] ],
  hiddenRows: 2,
  query: 'SELECT ...',
  source: null
}

Five small decisions, and why

  1. Round floats for display. The raw value was 358.1200000000005. Nobody wants that in a table.
  2. Cap the rows and say how many are hidden. A table of 4,000 rows is not "showing your work".
  3. Use textContent, never innerHTML. Cell values are data. Treat them as text.
  4. Treat optional parts as optional. In my test lineage came back null, so the panel shows that line only when it exists.
  5. Fold the query. Most readers never open it. The ones who do are the ones who would otherwise message you.

When there's no data answer

The second test case is a response with no rows. toView returns the sentence and empty arrays, and the panel shows just the sentence. No empty table, no broken layout.

What do your users ask for first when they doubt a number: the rows, or the query?

title: Your device rebooted at a customer site. What do you know?
description:
Picture a small device you built, a sensor inside a machine at a customer's site a few hundred kilometres away. One morning the customer tells you it restarted during the night. What do you know about why?

On your desk, a debugger would answer that: a cable to the chip and a tool that stops the program and shows where it is. In the field there is no cable, no screen and nobody watching. The device is the only witness, and as we'll see in a moment, by default it forgets everything when it restarts.

ferrite exists for this situation: a device in the field has crashed, and there is no stack trace, no log and nothing that says what happened.

We'll follow one crash twice. First we ask what it leaves behind with nothing in place. Then we let ferrite, an open-source Rust library for this problem, save a small record of the crash, and we turn that record back into the line of code that crashed. Everything runs in QEMU, a program that emulates a computer, here a board with an Arm Cortex-M3 processor, so you can repeat it without hardware. The crash is planted on purpose: this post shows how a crash gets recorded, not how to find a real bug.

What happens when a microcontroller crashes?

A microcontroller is a small computer on one chip, with a processor, memory and peripherals, running one program, the firmware, with no operating system underneath. When the processor meets something it cannot do, such as an instruction it does not know or a memory access that fails, it stops what it was doing and calls a fault handler: a function the program provides for exactly this case. On Cortex-M chips the catch-all one is called HardFault.

Here is the function that will crash for us:

/// The bug we are going to find. `udf` is an instruction the processor
/// refuses to execute, so this function crashes every time.
#[inline(never)]
fn handle_message() {
    unsafe { core::arch::asm!("udf #0") };
}

udf means "undefined": an instruction reserved to be invalid, so running it always faults. #[inline(never)] keeps handle_message a function of its own, so the crash has a name we can find later.

What does the fault handler do if we don't write one? cortex-m-rt, the startup crate this program is built on, provides a default that loops forever (its source). The device freezes. Many products have a watchdog, a hardware timer that resets the chip unless the program checks in regularly, so a frozen device restarts a moment later. I ran this program without ferrite in QEMU, and it printed its first line and then nothing, until I stopped QEMU.

So after the restart, what is left? Before main runs, the startup code gives every global variable its initial value: it zeroes some memory and copies initial values into the rest. Whatever the crashed run knew is overwritten, and the new run starts exactly like the first one. That is why all the customer can tell you is "it restarted".

What would we want the device to tell us?

Suppose the device could leave us a note. What should it say? Three things get us from "it restarted" to a line of code:

  • That it crashed, and the processor's reason. Cortex-M chips keep this in a fault status register, a few bits that tell an undefined instruction apart from, say, a bad memory access.
  • Where it was: the program counter, the address of the instruction that was running.
  • Which build it was running, because an address only means something in the exact program that produced it.

The note also has to travel from the device to someone who can read it. That part comes in later posts. Here the device prints its note.

A note that survives the reset

ferrite brings its own HardFault handler. It copies the registers that matter into a small region of RAM and then resets the chip itself. What makes this work is where it writes. That region is a small block, at most 256 bytes (192 in this build), in a part of RAM the build sets aside under the name .uninit.ferrite. It lies outside the memory the startup code initialises, so the next run's startup leaves it alone. A reset restarts the program, but it does not erase RAM, so the note is still there afterwards. Post 2 looks at this region more closely, including why it does not survive a power cut.

Here is main. Look for two things: init, which tells ferrite about the device, and last_fault, which returns the note if a previous run left one.

#[entry]
fn main() -> ! {
    ferrite_sdk::init(SdkConfig {
        device_id: "qemu-demo-01",
        firmware_version: "0.1.0",
        build_id: 0,
        ticks_fn: || 0,
        ram_regions: &[RamRegion { start: 0x2000_0000, end: 0x2000_FC00 }],
    });

    if let Some(fault) = last_fault() {
        hprintln!("boot: the previous run crashed");
        hprintln!("  pc   = {:#010x}", fault.frame.pc);
        hprintln!("  cfsr = {:#010x}", fault.cfsr);
        debug::exit(debug::EXIT_SUCCESS);
    }

    hprintln!("boot: no crash recorded, handling a message");
    handle_message();
    hprintln!("message handled");
    debug::exit(debug::EXIT_SUCCESS);
    loop {}
}

hprintln! prints to your terminal through a debug channel QEMU provides, and debug::exit ends QEMU. ram_regions tells the fault handler which addresses are safe to read while it collects its note. pc is the program counter, and cfsr is the fault status register.

Before we run it, what should it print? On the first run there is no note, so we should see "no crash recorded", then the crash in handle_message. The handler saves its note and resets, and the program starts again from the top. This time last_fault finds the note, so we should see a second "boot" line from the same QEMU session, and never "message handled".

Running it in QEMU

The project is the program above plus a Cargo.toml and a few build files for this QEMU board, in the ferrite-sdk repository as examples/qemu-fault at commit b51bfed. With QEMU and Rust's thumbv7m-none-eabi target installed, run this in that directory:

cargo build --release
qemu-system-arm -cpu cortex-m3 -machine lm3s6965evb -nographic \
  -semihosting-config enable=on,target=native \
  -kernel target/thumbv7m-none-eabi/release/qemu-fault

I ran it from a fresh checkout of commit b51bfed, with rustc 1.97.0 and QEMU 7.2.22 (Debian 12's package), and it printed:

Timer with period zero, disabling
boot: no crash recorded, handling a message
boot: the previous run crashed
  pc   = 0x00000158
  cfsr = 0x00010000

The first line is QEMU's own message about a timer on the emulated board, not our program's. The rest matches the prediction. When the handler asked for a reset, QEMU restarted the emulated chip and loaded the program again, and like the real chip it left the rest of RAM as it was, so the note survived.

What about cfsr = 0x00010000? Only bit 16 is set, and in Arm's documentation for this register bit 16 is called UNDEFINSTR: the processor tried to run an undefined instruction. That is our udf. So the note already tells us why. Where is the next question.

From an address to a line of code

0x00000158 is only a number. To turn it into a line, we need the file the compiler produced, the ELF file. Besides the program, it can carry debug information: a table from addresses to source lines. Our Cargo.toml asks for it in release builds with debug = 2. The tool addr2line from GNU binutils (in the arm-none-eabi build) looks an address up in that table:

arm-none-eabi-addr2line -f -C -s -e target/thumbv7m-none-eabi/release/qemu-fault 0x00000158

-f asks for the function name, -C turns Rust's encoded symbol names back into readable ones, and -s leaves out the directories. It prints:

qemu_fault::handle_message
main.rs:39

Line 39 of main.rs is the udf line.

There is a condition hiding in that step. We looked the address up in the same file that ran. Change one line above handle_message, rebuild, and the code moves to different addresses: the same 0x00000158 would then point somewhere else, and addr2line would print that other line without complaint. That is why the build belongs in the note. ferrite sends the firmware_version from init with every report, so whoever reads a report knows which release's ELF to look it up in. A version string only identifies a build if it changes with every build, though: our example says "0.1.0" whatever we change, so after that one-line edit its note would still claim 0.1.0. The field meant for the exact build is build_id, which the SDK documents as the first 8 bytes of the ELF's build ID. We left it at 0 here; post 4 is about matching reports to builds.

What a real device does differently

Our program stops after printing so that QEMU exits. A device in the field would carry on with its work after the reset. When it next has a connection, ferrite sends the note, together with the device name and firmware version, to ferrite's server. The server stores the ELF files you upload and runs the addr2line step itself. Making sure each report is looked up in the ELF of the build that produced it is the subject of post 4. After a successful upload, the device clears the note, ready for the next crash.

Let's take stock. With a small block of RAM the startup code does not touch, the program counter and the fault status survived the reset, and the ELF of the same build turned the address into main.rs:39. That rests on one claim we haven't examined: that RAM keeps its contents through a reset. Why does it, how does the program tell a real note from leftover noise, and what happens when the power goes? That's the next post.

Code: github.com/mighty840/ferrite-sdk

title: When Lower Harm Misleads: Auditing Concept Corrections
description:
arXiv:2611.22084v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: An expert who corrects a concept prediction, such as a BI-RADS descriptor in breast ultrasound, expects the diagnosis to improve. Objectives that reduce the harm of such corrections are judged by harm and accuracy, yet harm also falls when a model responds less to every correction or starts from a worse uncorrected prediction, the reference for harm. We propose a correction audit, a reproducible evaluation protocol that separates these explanations: it splits each correction into harm and useful gain on identical events, separates the starting prediction from the correction response, and compares objectives with amplitude baselines matched in source harm. On three breast-ultrasound sources, worst-case correction training, evaluated from the mean-case model's start, lowers harm but gives up more useful gain in all 21 source comparisons pooled over six seeds, raising the corrected negative log-likelihood (NLL); from the same start, selecting between the objectives by harm picks the less helpful model on all three sources. On CUB, a monotonic harm penalty at its reported weight lowers path-level harm in all 80 concept sets while raising the NLL in all 80, almost entirely before any correction. At a fixed start, rescaling both responses to the same source harm reproduces the penalty's mean harm, useful gain and NLL on single-concept corrections within a prespecified margin of 0.0005 nat, although the two responses point in different directions. Lower harm therefore signals better corrections only when it is read together with useful gain, absolute risk and the start it is measured from.
