title: AWS Transform now supports migration to AWS Outposts
description:
AWS Transform now supports AWS Outposts as a migration target. You can migrate workloads onto your Outposts from on-premises environments, another Outpost, or a different Availability Zone or Region. AWS Transform is a collaborative enterprise IT transformation service powered by agentic AI that accelerates cloud migration, application modernization, and continuous tech debt reduction. Run your migration with AI agents in AWS Transform for migrations, or use AWS Transform MGN, the rehost engine within AWS Transform, directly from its console.

If you run workloads on Outposts for low latency, local data processing, or data residency, migrating them has meant manual effort or legacy tooling, often with a detour through the Region and an AMI copy. Now you choose subnets on the Outpost for your migration, and AWS Transform continuously replicates your source servers at the block level, directly from your source environment to the Outpost. You launch test instances before cutover and cut over with minimal downtime.

Migration to Outposts is available in all AWS Transform for migrations target Regions and AWS Transform MGN Regions and requires Amazon EBS on the Outpost. If your Outpost has Amazon S3 on Outposts, you can keep snapshots on the Outpost for data residency or store them in the parent Region. Without it, snapshots are stored in the parent Region.

To get started, see the AWS Transform documentation or visit the AWS Transform product page.

title: Edge-Adaptive Hiera-Seg Model for Building-Integrated Photovoltaic Power Forecasting
description:
arXiv:2611.21680v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Building integrated photovoltaic power forecasting is challenging because facade orientation, rooftop geometry, nearby buildings, vegetation, cloud movement, module temperature, inverter status and edge device reliability jointly affect power generation. This paper proposes an edge-adaptive HieraSeg model for short term BIPV power forecasting with multi-orientation visual-irradiance fusion. RGB facade images, optional thermal cues, irradiance measurements, module temperature, facade orientation, rooftop masks, shading labels, sky condition, historical power and edge device state are aligned into synchronous forecasting windows. HieraSeg extracts hierarchical regions from facade, rooftop, sky, shadow and background images, while the edge-adaptive module changes feature weights under missing frames, latency shifts and local shading changes. The segmentation branch identifies occluded module areas and separates facade, rooftop, sky and background evidence before the forecasting head estimates future BIPV output. Experiments are designed on a simulated multibuilding BIPV dataset with unseen building and unseen orientation tests. The model reports predicted power, confidence interval, dominant evidence, occlusion contribution, orientation contribution and energy-management review priority. This output is intended to show whether the forecast is driven by irradiance change, visible shading, orientation response, stale edge information or recent power history. The framework supports local forecasting at edge controllers with limited communication delay and computing resources, linking visual occlusion, irradiance dynamics and power history to traceable forecasting results for building energy management, microgrid scheduling and BIPV operation planning.

title: Propose with the Gradient, Accept with the Loss: One Hedged Attack for Pixel-Sparse Robustness
description:
arXiv:2611.22596v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A pixel-sparse adversary may change a few pixels of an image to any value. Robustness to such attacks is currently measured with an ensemble, sparse-AutoAttack (sAA), because its members fail in different places: sparse projected gradient descent (sPGD) trusts a first-order model that a full pixel change breaks, and sparse random search (Sparse-RS) ignores the gradient even where it is informative. We show that both attacks are local searches, each a proposal distribution plus an acceptance rule, and ask what such a search can learn from the gradient. A Taylor bound says what to measure, and measurements at the states the search visits give five rules. The sign of the gradient is its most reliable use at a single pixel and sets a new pixel's value. Its ranking of candidate pixels should be followed loosely, and its ranking of the pixels to remove, which is often more reliable, can be followed more closely. A pixel should not be proposed twice before a move is accepted, and acceptance should be decided by the loss alone. These rules define Gradient-guided Random Search (GRS), which runs once and costs one forward and one backward pass per step. On 13 CIFAR-10 configurations and 5 ImageNet models, GRS matches or beats the best single member of sAA and is within one point of sAA itself or stronger on 17 of 18 settings, and it is significantly stronger than sAA on 8. It uses 3 instead of up to 7 forward-pass units, and on CIFAR-10 it runs 3.7 to 5.0 times faster than the members of sAA run in full.

title: Your Rust Code Sets an Environment Variable and the 2024 Edition Calls That Unsafe
description:
The service had one line
at the top of main:

std::env::set_var("TZ", "UTC");

Harmless for years.

Then the team
moved the crate
to the 2024 edition.

It stopped compiling.

The compiler said
set_var is an unsafe function
and needs an unsafe block.

One environment variable.

Unsafe.

Here is the mechanism.

On Linux and most Unix systems,
the environment is a plain C array
owned by the C library.

setenv can move it,
or free old entries,
while it changes it.

getenv reads it
with no lock that Rust controls.

Rust's own std::env functions
take a lock.

C code does not.

And C code
reads the environment
all the time.

Time zone lookups.

DNS resolution.

Locale setup.

Any C library
your crate links.

So one thread sets a variable
while another resolves a hostname,
and the reader can follow a pointer
into memory that was just freed.

A crash.

Or wrong data.

Or nothing,
for months,
and then a crash
nobody can reproduce.

Rust's promise
is that safe code
cannot cause that.

set_var could.

So Rust 1.85,
in February 2025,
shipped the 2024 edition
with set_var and remove_var
marked unsafe.

Older editions still compile them
as safe.

The bug was always there.

The edition only
makes you sign for it.

cargo fix --edition
will wrap the calls
in unsafe blocks for you.

Do not stop there.

An unsafe block
is a promise
that no other thread
can touch the environment.

Check whether you can keep it.

Better moves:

Set the variable
before your program starts,
in the unit file,
the container,
the shell.

Pass configuration
as arguments or structs,
not through the environment.

For child processes,
use Command::env,
which sets it
for the child only.

If it must happen in-process,
do it first thing in main,
before the async runtime,
before any thread,
and write down why.

The 2024 edition
is not adding a danger.

It is pointing at one
your code already had.

– Serguey Asael Shinder

title: Building a Polymarket Trading Bot in Python: Architecture, APIs, and Order Execution
description:
How to design a Polymarket trading bot with Python, market-data integration, order-book analysis, risk controls, and production-ready execution architecture.

A Polymarket bot that can place an order is easy to demonstrate.

Building one that knows whether the order actually filled, survives a disconnected data feed, respects position limits, and recovers correctly after a restart is a different engineering problem.

That's where the complexity begins.

Most introductory tutorials focus on connecting to an API, fetching prices, and submitting a trade. These are useful first steps, but they represent only a small part of a real automated trading system.

If you're building a Polymarket trading bot to operate continuously, the architecture matters as much as the strategy itself.

I'm Casatrick, a developer focused on automated prediction-market trading systems and trading infrastructure.

In this article, I'll walk through the components of a Python-based Polymarket bot, show how to interact with the current API, implement a simple order-book analysis example, and explain the execution and risk-management architecture needed beyond a prototype.

The example is deliberately read-only and paper-only. It does not place real orders or require a private key.

1. Understanding Polymarket's Trading Infrastructure

Polymarket is a prediction-market platform where participants trade contracts tied to the outcomes of real-world events.

Prices generally range from $0 to $1, reflecting market-implied probabilities.

For example, a YES outcome trading at $0.65 represents an implied probability of approximately 65%.

However, the displayed price is not necessarily the price at which a particular trade can execute.

Actual execution depends on the order book, available liquidity, and other market conditions.

For developers, this distinction is important.

A trading bot should not make execution decisions using only a displayed probability.

It needs to understand the market's available buy and sell liquidity.

The APIs and services

The current Polymarket developer ecosystem provides several capabilities:

Component Purpose
Market discovery Find events, markets, and outcome identifiers
CLOB API Retrieve order books and submit eligible orders
Data API Access historical and account-related data
Real-time streams Receive market and order updates
Unified SDK Work with these services through a Python client

The official SDK exposes public and authenticated clients.

A public client is sufficient for discovering markets and reading order books.

Authenticated trading requires an eligible account, supported signing configuration, and the appropriate permissions.

Important: Polymarket's international platform and Polymarket US are separate products. Trading availability depends on jurisdiction. Automated trading must comply with applicable restrictions. Public data access does not imply permission to trade.

Official documentation: https://docs.polymarket.com/

2. The Architecture of a Polymarket Trading Bot

I prefer separating a trading bot into independent components rather than putting everything inside one Python script.

A useful starting architecture looks like this:

           POLYMARKET
         Market Data APIs
                |
                v
       +------------------+
       | Market Data      |
       | Collector        |
       +------------------+
                |
                v
       +------------------+
       | Data Validation  |
       | and Normalization|
       +------------------+
                |
                v
       +------------------+
       | Strategy Engine  |
       +------------------+
                |
                v
       +------------------+
       | Risk Manager     |
       +------------------+
                |
                v
       +------------------+
       | Execution Engine |
       +------------------+
                |
                v
          Polymarket CLOB
                |
                v
       +------------------+
       | Order / Position |
       | Reconciliation   |
       +------------------+
                |
                v
       Monitoring & Logs

Each component has a specific responsibility.

Market Data Collector

Retrieves market information, order books, and relevant trading activity.

Data Validation

Checks timestamps, missing information, invalid values, and whether the system has a sufficiently reliable market view.

Strategy Engine

Evaluates trading rules and generates potential order intentions.

Risk Manager

Checks available risk capacity, position limits, order size, and other restrictions.

Execution Engine

Submits, modifies, or cancels permitted orders and tracks their status.

Reconciliation

Compares internal records against authoritative account and execution information.

Monitoring

Records system health, execution errors, latency, position exposure, and operational events.

Keeping these responsibilities separate makes testing and incident investigation significantly easier.

It also allows a strategy to change without requiring the entire execution system to be rewritten.

3. Setting Up the Python Project

For a new project, use Python 3.11 or later and the current unified Polymarket SDK.

The older py-clob-client has been archived.

For this example, we'll pin the SDK version to avoid unexpected changes during development.

mkdir polymarket-python-bot
cd polymarket-python-bot

python -m venv .venv

Activate the environment.

Windows:

.venv\Scripts\activate

macOS/Linux:

source .venv/bin/activate

Install the SDK:

python -m pip install "polymarket-client==0.20.0"

Create a file:

polymarket-python-bot/
├── bot.py
└── requirements.txt

The dependency file can contain:

polymarket-client==0.20.0

Polymarket's official Python SDK is maintained here:

https://github.com/Polymarket/py-sdk

The unified SDK uses the polymarket Python import package.

4. Connecting to Polymarket Market Data

We can begin without any wallet credentials.

The public client supports reading market information and order books.

import asyncio
import os

from polymarket import AsyncPublicClient


async def main():
    slug = os.environ["POLYMARKET_MARKET_SLUG"]

    async with AsyncPublicClient() as client:
        market = await client.get_market(slug=slug)

        print("Market:", market.question)
        print("Version:", market.version)
        print("Condition ID:", market.condition_id)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

Set POLYMARKET_MARKET_SLUG to the slug of an existing market, then run:

python bot.py

This reads information about one selected market.

There is an important detail developers should understand: Polymarket supports different market protocol versions.

For a binary market, we can select the YES outcome's trading identifier as follows:

yes = market.outcomes.yes

asset_id = (
    yes.position_id
    if market.version == "v2"
    else yes.token_id
)

if asset_id is None:
    raise RuntimeError(
        "No supported YES outcome identifier found"
    )

For older CTF markets, this identifier is a token ID. For Protocol V2 markets, it is a position ID.

The unified SDK abstracts much of the difference, but your code still needs to select the correct identifier.

5. Reading the Order Book

A market's order book shows available buying and selling interest.

For a YES outcome, the book contains bids and asks.

  • Bids: Prices buyers are willing to pay.
  • Asks: Prices sellers are willing to accept.

The spread is the difference between the best ask and the best bid.

book = await client.get_order_book(
    asset_id=asset_id
)

if not book.bids or not book.asks:
    raise RuntimeError(
        "Order book has insufficient liquidity"
    )

best_bid = max(
    level.price for level in book.bids
)

best_ask = min(
    level.price for level in book.asks
)

spread = best_ask - best_bid

print("Best bid:", best_bid)
print("Best ask:", best_ask)
print("Spread:", spread)

Notice that we use max() and min() instead of assuming the order-book levels are already sorted in the required direction.

That avoids a subtle bug found in many introductory examples.

Why the spread matters

Imagine the following hypothetical market:

YES order book

Best bid:   $0.61
Best ask:   $0.64

Spread:     $0.03

Suppose your strategy believes the true probability is approximately 66%.

At first glance, the market may look attractive.

But your estimated probability is not enough to determine whether a trade is worthwhile.

You also need to consider the actual execution price, available shares at that price, applicable fees, and uncertainty in your probability model.

Even a small pricing difference can disappear once execution costs are included.

This is why the strategy engine and execution engine should remain separate.

6. Building a Read-Only Trading Signal Scanner

Now let's combine the previous steps into a single Python example.

This scanner will:

  1. Read a selected Polymarket market.
  2. Fetch its YES order book.
  3. Validate the market snapshot.
  4. Calculate the available spread.
  5. Apply basic order-size and risk checks.
  6. Compare the best ask against an externally supplied probability estimate.
  7. Print a hypothetical trading signal.

It will never place an actual trade.

The probability estimate must come from your own research or model. The example does not generate an edge or claim to predict outcomes.

Complete example: bot.py 

import asyncio
import os

from datetime import datetime, timezone
from decimal import Decimal

from polymarket import AsyncPublicClient


MAX_ORDER_USD = Decimal("25")
MAX_SPREAD = Decimal("0.05")

# Illustrative cost/uncertainty allowance.
# NOT an actual Polymarket fee calculation.
COST_BUFFER = Decimal("0.02")

# Reject market data older than this threshold.
MAX_SNAPSHOT_AGE_SECONDS = 15


async def main():
    slug = os.environ["POLYMARKET_MARKET_SLUG"]

    # Must come from a separate model or research process.
    model_probability = Decimal(
        os.environ["MODEL_YES_PROBABILITY"]
    )

    if not Decimal("0") < model_probability < Decimal("1"):
        raise ValueError(
            "Model probability must be between 0 and 1"
        )

    async with AsyncPublicClient() as client:
        market = await client.get_market(slug=slug)

        yes = market.outcomes.yes

        asset_id = (
            yes.position_id
            if market.version == "v2"
            else yes.token_id
        )

        if asset_id is None:
            raise RuntimeError(
                "Market has no supported YES identifier"
            )

        book = await client.get_order_book(
            asset_id=asset_id
        )

        if not book.bids or not book.asks:
            print("SKIP: Empty order book")
            return

        # Never assume the API arrays are sorted.
        best_bid = max(
            book.bids,
            key=lambda level: level.price
        )

        best_ask = min(
            book.asks,
            key=lambda level: level.price
        )

        spread = best_ask.price - best_bid.price

        if spread <= 0:
            print("SKIP: Invalid or crossed order book")
            return

        # Validate the snapshot's timestamp.
        if book.timestamp is None:
            print("SKIP: Missing snapshot timestamp")
            return

        age = (
            datetime.now(timezone.utc) - book.timestamp
        ).total_seconds()

        if age < -5 or age > MAX_SNAPSHOT_AGE_SECONDS:
            print("SKIP: Unreliable or stale snapshot")
            return

        if spread > MAX_SPREAD:
            print("SKIP: Spread exceeds limit")
            return

        # Meet the market's minimum order size.
        size = max(
            book.min_order_size,
            Decimal("5")
        )

        # This simplified example only considers
        # liquidity at the single best ask.
        if best_ask.size < size:
            print("SKIP: Insufficient top-level liquidity")
            return

        estimated_cost = size * best_ask.price

        if estimated_cost > MAX_ORDER_USD:
            print("SKIP: Order exceeds notional limit")
            return

        # Simple illustrative edge calculation.
        # A production model also needs explicit
        # fee, fill, and uncertainty estimates.
        estimated_edge = (
            model_probability
            - best_ask.price
            - COST_BUFFER
        )

        print("Market:", market.question)
        print("Best bid:", best_bid.price)
        print("Best ask:", best_ask.price)
        print("Spread:", spread)
        print("Hypothetical size:", size)
        print("Estimated cost:", estimated_cost)
        print("Illustrative edge:", estimated_edge)

        if estimated_edge > 0:
            print("PAPER SIGNAL: BUY YES")
        else:
            print("PAPER SIGNAL: NO TRADE")

        print("No order was submitted.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

To run this scanner, configure two environment variables:

export POLYMARKET_MARKET_SLUG="your-market-slug"
export MODEL_YES_PROBABILITY="0.68"

python bot.py

On Windows PowerShell:

$env:POLYMARKET_MARKET_SLUG="your-market-slug"
$env:MODEL_YES_PROBABILITY="0.68"

python bot.py

The probability value 0.68 is only an illustrative input. It is not a prediction or a recommended trade.

What this example demonstrates

Even a basic scanner can enforce several useful rules before generating a hypothetical signal.

It checks for missing liquidity, large spreads, stale data, insufficient top-level depth, and excessive order size.

It also keeps market data and evaluation separate from actual trading.

However, this is still an educational prototype.

It doesn't contain a statistically validated probability model, complete fee calculations, a portfolio-wide risk engine, persistent state, or trade execution.

Those require additional components and testing.

7. How Real Order Execution Works

Once a strategy has been researched and validated, the next step is an authenticated execution workflow.

Polymarket's unified SDK provides a secure client for supported account and trading operations.

Conceptually, an order submission looks like this:

import os

from polymarket import AsyncSecureClient


async def submit_limit_order(
    asset_id: str,
    price: str,
    size: str,
):
    # Explicit opt-in required.
    if os.getenv("ENABLE_LIVE_TRADING") != "YES":
        raise RuntimeError(
            "Live trading is disabled"
        )

    # Eligibility, market state, balance,
    # exposure, and risk checks must occur
    # BEFORE reaching this function.

    client = await AsyncSecureClient.create(
        private_key=os.environ[
            "POLYMARKET_PRIVATE_KEY"
        ],
        wallet=os.environ[
            "POLYMARKET_WALLET_ADDRESS"
        ],
    )

    response = await client.place_limit_order(
        asset_id=asset_id,
        side="BUY",
        price=price,
        size=size,
    )

    if not response.ok:
        raise RuntimeError(response.message)

    return response.order_id

This is an isolated API example—not a complete or approved live-trading implementation. It is deliberately not connected to the earlier paper scanner.

The account must be eligible to trade, the wallet must be correctly configured, and the order must satisfy market-specific constraints.

A robust implementation also needs to check current balances, outstanding exposure, tick size, minimum size, available liquidity, and existing orders immediately before submitting anything.

Never store private keys in source code or commit them to GitHub. Use restricted credentials and secure secret management.

Order submission is not order completion

This distinction is essential.

A successful order-submission response doesn't necessarily mean all requested shares were filled and settled.

An order may remain open, fill partially, be cancelled, or encounter other execution conditions.

Your application needs to distinguish:

Order intent created
        |
        v
Risk validation
        |
        v
Order submitted
        |
        v
Exchange acknowledgement
        |
        v
Open / Partially Filled / Filled / Cancelled
        |
        v
Settlement and position reconciliation

The correct implementation uses authoritative order and trade information rather than assuming the initial HTTP response represents a completed position.

8. The Problem of Partial Fills

Consider a hypothetical strategy that wants to purchase 1,000 YES shares.

It submits an order for the full quantity.

Only 350 shares execute.

The remaining 650 shares are still open.

What should the system do?

A simple bot may immediately submit another 1,000-share order, accidentally increasing its outstanding exposure.

A proper execution engine needs to maintain a more complete state.

Original order:       1,000 shares
Cumulative filled:      350 shares
Remaining quantity:     650 shares

But these numbers should not exist only in memory.

The execution service should persist relevant order IDs and intents, process fills without double-counting, and reconcile against authoritative account records.

If the process restarts, it must not blindly resubmit an order simply because it doesn't remember the earlier acknowledgement.

For the current Polymarket SDK, cumulative fill tracking can use size_matched; individual fills can be matched through account trade records.

That matters because the legacy associate_trades field is deprecated, and an empty value is not reliable evidence that an order has never filled.

9. Risk Management Before Execution

Risk management should be an independent decision layer.

A strategy can identify an opportunity without having permission to execute it.

Before an order reaches the execution engine, I would evaluate several classes of risk.

Risk control Example check
Order size Maximum notional value
Position exposure Maximum exposure per market
Portfolio exposure Combined outstanding risk across markets
Daily loss limit Stop submitting new orders after a defined loss threshold
Data integrity Reject missing or stale market information
Liquidity Check executable size and expected price impact
Execution status Account for outstanding and partially filled orders
Emergency controls Disable order creation and cancel permitted open orders

A production-grade system also needs to distinguish between orders already submitted, executed positions, available balances, and unsettled activity.

For example, imagine a bot that has a $10,000 position limit.

It currently holds $8,000 of exposure and has another $3,000 of outstanding buy orders.

Checking only current holdings would incorrectly suggest that another $2,000 order is acceptable.

The risk engine must also consider the additional exposure that outstanding orders could create.

This is why risk calculations belong in a centralized component rather than scattered across individual strategies.

10. WebSockets, Reconnection, and State Recovery

Polling APIs can be sufficient for initial experiments and less time-sensitive research.

More demanding trading systems may require real-time streams.

But adding WebSockets doesn't automatically make a bot reliable.

The real challenge is maintaining a correct state after interruptions.

Consider this sequence:

  1. The bot receives an order-book update.
  2. It submits a limit order.
  3. The connection drops.
  4. The order partially fills.
  5. The bot reconnects.

If the software assumes the last locally observed state is still correct, it may make decisions using outdated information.

The safer recovery process is:

Connection lost
       |
       v
Pause affected trading
       |
       v
Reconnect
       |
       v
Fetch authoritative state
       |
       v
Reconcile orders and positions
       |
       v
Validate fresh market data
       |
       v
Resume when safe

A production implementation should account for message ordering, duplicate events, missed updates, and synchronization boundaries.

Exactly how state is reconstructed depends on the specific API stream and account workflow.

The goal is not simply keeping a WebSocket connected. It's keeping the bot's understanding of its orders, positions, and market data correct.

11. What I Would Add Before Calling This Production-Ready

At this point, we have demonstrated market discovery, order-book inspection, basic paper signals, and the authenticated order interface.

That's useful, but a production system needs substantially more engineering.

My next priorities would be:

Persistent order state

Record order intentions, exchange order IDs, acknowledgements, fills, and cancellations.

Idempotent execution

Prevent retries or restarts from creating unintended duplicate orders.

Realistic strategy evaluation

Backtest with appropriately timestamped data, fees, market depth, partial fills, and uncertainty around historical execution assumptions.

Portfolio-level risk management

Aggregate exposures across strategies and markets, including open orders.

Monitoring and alerting

Measure feed freshness, execution latency, rejected orders, reconciliation discrepancies, and system availability.

Operational controls

Provide a kill switch, safe restart procedure, controlled deployments, and incident logs.

Security

Protect signing credentials, limit operational permissions, and define a process for rotating or revoking access.

For continuously operating software, these details are not optional decorations.

They determine how the system behaves when things go wrong.

12. Should You Use Python or Rust?

Python is often a strong starting point.

It provides an accessible environment for market-data processing, model development, research, and strategy testing.

It also has an extensive ecosystem for statistical analysis and backend development.

Rust can be useful for specific performance-sensitive or systems-level components where predictable resource usage and tighter runtime control matter.

However, rewriting a trading bot in Rust doesn't automatically improve execution results.

Network latency, exchange processing, market liquidity, and system architecture may dominate the performance characteristics.

Before choosing a language for performance reasons, measure the actual bottleneck.

For many projects, a combination works well:

Python
- Research
- Backtesting
- Strategy development
- Data analysis

Rust or other optimized services
- Selected latency-sensitive components
- Specialized data processing
- Performance-critical infrastructure

Shared operational services
- Risk management
- Order state
- Monitoring
- Reconciliation

Choose technologies based on measured requirements and maintenance costs.

A simpler, reliable architecture is generally preferable to an unnecessarily complex one.

13. The Engineering Questions That Matter

If you're building a custom trading bot or hiring someone to develop one, I would ask these questions before making implementation decisions.

  • What evidence supports the trading strategy?
  • Which markets and protocol versions need to be supported?
  • How quickly does the system need to respond to market changes?
  • How will execution quality be measured?
  • What happens when an order fills partially?
  • How are balances and positions reconciled after an outage?
  • What are the maximum acceptable exposures and losses?
  • Who controls the wallet, keys, and deployment infrastructure?
  • What operational support is required after launch?

A detailed technical specification should answer these questions before a large amount of capital is committed to development.

Final Thoughts

A Polymarket trading bot is not simply an API connection with a BUY button.

It is a trading application composed of market-data processing, strategy evaluation, risk management, execution, reconciliation, and monitoring.

Python makes it possible to build a useful prototype quickly.

The harder problem is turning that prototype into a system that behaves predictably under real market conditions.

I would rather have a bot that rejects a questionable trade for a documented reason than one that executes immediately without understanding its own exposure.

A reliable system makes risks and operational behavior visible. It does not guarantee trading profits.

That's the engineering standard worth aiming for.

Building a Custom Polymarket Trading Bot?

I'm Casatrick, a developer focused on Polymarket trading bots and automated trading infrastructure.

I work on systems involving:

  • Python and Rust trading infrastructure
  • Custom strategy implementation
  • Polymarket API and order-book integration
  • Execution engines and order management
  • Position reconciliation and risk controls
  • Backtesting, monitoring, and deployment

Whether you have an existing strategy, a prototype that needs improvements, or a larger trading infrastructure project, the starting point is understanding the requirements and feasibility.

For a technical project discussion, share your intended architecture, existing code or research, development budget, and expected deliverables.

Explore Custom Polymarket Bot Development — Casatrick

I also publish engineering research and detailed technical guides on my Substack.

References

  • Polymarket Developer Documentation
  • Official Python SDK
  • Discover Markets
  • Prices and Order Books
  • Place Orders
  • SDK Migration Guide
  • Geographic Restrictions

Technical note: Examples reflect the published unified Python SDK interface as reviewed in November 2026. They are illustrative and have not been executed against a live Polymarket account. The read-only scanner requires an existing market slug and a user-supplied probability estimate. Validate code, permissions, market-specific constraints, and API behavior before deployment.

This article is for educational and engineering purposes, not investment advice. Automated trading involves financial risk. Trading must comply with jurisdictional restrictions and platform requirements.

title: On Formal Counterfactual Explanations
description:
arXiv:2611.22010v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Counterfactual explanations are often seen as counterfactual conditionals under closest-world semantics, requiring one to reason over all minimally distant counterexamples. In contrast, formal XAI typically relies on feature-based abductive explanations (AXps) and contrastive explanations (CXps), which admit efficient computation and a minimal hitting-set duality. This paper bridges these perspectives by (i) characterizing closest-world counterfactual explanations explicitly as a disjunctive normal form over all minimally distant counterexample instances, and (ii) introducing conjunctive counterfactual explanations (CFXps), a subclass of counterfactual antecedents restricted to conjunctions of feature literals that guarantee prediction change. The paper establishes structural results connecting CXps, AXps and CFXps: every CXp induces an AXp for its witness instance, and every CXp together with a witness AXp induces a CFXp whose support is precisely determined by that AXp. These theoretical results yield a modular approach for computing CFXps using existing AXp/CXp machinery. Experiments on a representative set of benchmarks using tree ensembles and neural networks show that CFXp extraction is practically efficient. Compared with popular point-based counterfactual explainers, CFXps generally require no more feature changes and can guarantee the counterfactual prediction beyond a single instance.

title: One Year on DEV: The People Made the Platform
description:
I recently got a new badge on my DEV profile. It says One Year on DEV 🎂

I joined on 17 November 2025. I didn't see it coming. The year went by so fast that I only noticed when the badge showed up.


So I wanted to write a post to say thank you. It's not a "lessons learned" article. It's just me talking about the people and the moments that made this year good.

👋 Where it started

When I created my account, I thought DEV was a place to publish articles. I didn't expect much more than that.

Over the year it turned into the place where I read, learn, talk to people, and try new things. Sometimes I open it just to see what people wrote that day.

I joined to share my articles. I stayed because of the people.

Here are a few moments from my year:

Moment Date
Joined DEV 17 November 2025
Started The Startup Café 20 October 2026

title: Refactoring Vue 3 Unit Tests: Moving from Mutable beforeEach State to Functional Factory Helpers in TypeScript
description:
When migrating large Vue codebases to TypeScript, static typing often exposes patterns in our test suites that are brittle or unnecessary. One common pattern in older Vue Test Utils specs is storing a mutable let wrapper variable in the test scope and initializing it inside beforeEach().

In my recent contribution to GitLab's Contributors Platform (MR !3204), I converted the Labelathon page's DetailsSection component to TypeScript and refactored its unit test suite to use functional factory helpers.

Here is a look at why this refactoring improves test clarity, type inference, and test isolation.

The Component: DetailsSection.vue

The DetailsSection component renders instructions and event guidelines using accordion components from bootstrap-vue-next alongside a custom MarkdownRenderer:

<script setup lang="ts">
import { BAccordion, BAccordionItem } from 'bootstrap-vue-next';
import MarkdownRenderer from '~/common/components/MarkdownRenderer.vue';
</script>

<template>
  <BAccordion class="mt-4">
    <BAccordionItem title="Rules & Guidelines">
      <MarkdownRenderer :markdown="guidelines" />
    </BAccordionItem>
    <!-- Additional accordion items -->
  </BAccordion>
</template>

Adding lang="ts" ensures strict compilation of imported third-party components and child component props.

The Spec: Mutable beforeEach vs. Pure createWrapper

The Old Pattern (JavaScript)

Previously, the spec relied on an outer mutable reference:

// Before (DetailsSection.spec.js)
describe('DetailsSection', () => {
  let wrapper;

  beforeEach(() => {
    wrapper = shallowMount(DetailsSection, {
      global: {
        renderStubDefaultSlot: true,
      },
    });
  });

  it('contains the expected content', () => {
    expect(wrapper.html()).toMatchSnapshot();
  });
});

Why avoid this pattern in TypeScript?

  1. Unnecessary State Mutation: A global let wrapper introduces shared state across tests. Tests should be isolated and idempotent.
  2. Type Ambiguity: In TypeScript, declaring let wrapper; defaults to any unless explicitly typed (VueWrapper<InstanceType<typeof DetailsSection>>), which adds boilerplate.
  3. Execution Overhead: If some test cases only test static exports or helpers, beforeEach still mounts the component unnecessarily.

The Modern Pattern (TypeScript)

In DetailsSection.spec.ts, we eliminated beforeEach and the mutable variable in favor of a concise factory helper:

// After (DetailsSection.spec.ts)
import { shallowMount } from '@vue/test-utils';
import DetailsSection from './DetailsSection.vue';

describe('DetailsSection', () => {
  const createWrapper = () =>
    shallowMount(DetailsSection, {
      global: {
        renderStubDefaultSlot: true,
      },
    });

  it('contains the expected content', () => {
    expect(createWrapper().html()).toMatchSnapshot();
  });
});

Why this is better:

  • Automatic Type Inference: createWrapper() naturally returns a typed VueWrapper, avoiding manual type annotations.
  • Pure & Self-Contained: Each test explicitly invokes createWrapper() with optional prop overrides when needed, preventing test leakage.
  • Seamless Snapshot Migration: The Vitest snapshot was smoothly renamed from DetailsSection.spec.js.snap to DetailsSection.spec.ts.snap without breaking snapshot verification.

Key Takeaways

  1. Favor Factory Functions over beforeEach: Pure createWrapper = (props = {}) => ... functions result in cleaner, more readable specs compared to mutating a shared let wrapper variable.
  2. Leverage Type Inference in Tests: By using inline factory functions, Vue Test Utils and Vitest automatically infer wrapper types without verbose casting.
  3. Clean Codebases One Slice at a Time: Converting small presentation components and their specs in focused merge requests keeps review cycles fast and eliminates maintenance debt.

title: Next.js Server Actions: Swallowed Redirects and Body Limits
description:
Server Actions fail in three quiet ways, and none of them throws where the bug actually is.

Symptom. Three failures appear after moving a form to Server Actions. The action validates, redirect("/dashboard") runs, the browser stays on the form. Or every upload over a megabyte dies with 413 Request Entity Too Large / Body exceeded 1mb limit. Or useActionState never updates — the action throws, and all the user sees is a generic An error occurred in the Server Components render with a digest instead of your message.

Cause. redirect() and notFound() do not return; they throw a framework-controlled exception that unwinds the render. A try/catch around the call swallows it, and the action completes normally. Separately, Server Actions deserialise their arguments server-side through a body parser with a fixed size limit, and anything thrown inside an action is serialised across the network boundary — an Error instance, a class instance, or a Date in useActionState state cannot make that trip and is replaced with a digest.

Fix. Call redirect() after the try/catch block or rethrow it with isRedirectError/unstable_rethrow; raise serverActions.bodySizeLimit and validate size before upload; and return plain serialisable objects from actions — { ok: false, fieldErrors } — never caught Error objects.

How an action crosses the boundary

An action is a POST to the current route, RSC-encoded, awaited by the client, whose return value must be serialisable through the same encoding. That single sentence explains all three failures.

// app/actions.ts
"use server";
import { redirect } from "next/navigation";

export async function createPost(prevState: State, formData: FormData): Promise<State> {
  const title = String(formData.get("title") ?? "");

  try {
    if (!title) throw new Error("Title is required");
    await db.post.create({ data: { title } });
  } catch (error) {
    return { ok: false, message: (error as Error).message }; // never rethrow
  }

  redirect("/posts");   // OUTSIDE the try: redirect throws by design
}

Reproduce the swallowed redirect with the snippet above minus the comment: move redirect() inside try and the form posts, the row is created, and nothing navigates, because the catch block returns a state object instead. The same mistake removes the navigation from notFound() and from unauthorized().

Next.js 15 and 16 ship a size limit of 1 MB per action body. It applies to the whole multipart payload, so a 900 KB image plus form fields can exceed it.

// next.config.ts — Next.js 15+ top-level key; Next 14 used experimental
const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  serverActions: { bodySizeLimit: "4mb" },
};

// client: check before the request, so the user gets a real message
const MAX = 4 * 1024 * 1024;
if (file.size > MAX) return { ok: false, message: "File must be under 4 MB" };

A proxy in front of the app has its own limit. Vercel caps request bodies at 4.5 MB for serverless functions, so raising bodySizeLimit past that changes nothing; uploads that large belong in a direct-to-storage signed URL.

Version and boundary reference

Boundary What crosses it Fails when Fix
Client → action arguments FormData, serialisable values File outside FormData, class instances pass FormData, or a base64 string
Action → client return plain object, string, number, array Error, Date, Map, class return { error: string }
Action → framework thrown control-flow errors caught in try/catch isRedirectError / unstable_rethrow
Body parser whole multipart payload over bodySizeLimit raise limit or upload directly
Next.js version Redirect error helper Size limit location
13.4–13.5 isRedirectError in next/dist/client/components/redirect not configurable
14.x isRedirectError (unstable path) experimental.serverActions.bodySizeLimit
15.x unstable_rethrow added serverActions.bodySizeLimit
16.x unstable_rethrow stable behaviour serverActions.bodySizeLimit

Edge cases and the fixes that work

1. Rethrowing the redirect instead of restructuring

When the redirect genuinely belongs inside the guarded block, the framework's own predicate is the correct escape hatch:

import { isRedirectError } from "next/dist/client/components/redirect-error";

try {
  await save(formData);
  redirect("/done");
} catch (error) {
  if (isRedirectError(error)) throw error;   // let the framework unwind
  return { ok: false, message: "Save failed" };
}

That import path is internal and moves between minors. unstable_rethrow(error) from next/navigation is the documented wrapper and covers redirect, not-found, and forbidden in one call.

2. useActionState and non-serialisable state

useActionState keeps the action's return value in React state, which means it is sent through the RSC payload on every update. An Error instance, new Map(), or a Date cannot be encoded and throws Only plain objects, and a few built-ins, can be passed to Client Components from Server Components.

type State = { ok: boolean; message: string; fieldErrors?: Record<string, string> };

export async function updateProfile(_prev: State, formData: FormData): Promise<State> {
  const parsed = schema.safeParse(Object.fromEntries(formData));
  if (!parsed.success) {
    return { ok: false, message: "Check the form", fieldErrors: parsed.error.flatten().fieldErrors };
  }
  await db.profile.update(parsed.data);
  return { ok: true, message: "Saved" };   // plain object, no Date
}

Convert timestamps to ISO strings at the boundary. Error digests exist on purpose: in production an uncaught action error is redacted so an internal stack trace never reaches the browser, which is exactly why a catch that returns error.message must first convert the error into your own string.

3. The 413 that is not the action's limit

Body exceeded 1mb limit comes from the action parser; 413 Request Entity Too Large with no Next.js log line comes from the platform. Check both before changing config:

# platform limit, not framework limit
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" -X POST https://app.example.com/api/upload \
  -F "file=@big.zip"

If the plain route returns 413 while a small action works, the reverse proxy is the limit. For Vercel, request.body above 4.5 MB cannot be raised by configuration at all.

4. revalidatePath order relative to the redirect

Data cache invalidation belongs before the redirect, because the redirect ends the action.

await db.post.update({ where: { id }, data });
revalidatePath("/posts");
revalidateTag("posts");
redirect(`/posts/${id}`);   // last statement, never followed by more work

redirect() returning a typed never means code after it is unreachable and tsc will flag it. That is a feature: use it to prove the action cannot continue after navigation.

5. Actions called outside a form

<form action={}> passes FormData automatically; a startTransition call does not. Passing an object works, but passing a File directly does not — only FormData carries binary through the action encoding.

"use client";
const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition();

<button onClick={() => startTransition(() => publish(post.id))} disabled={isPending}>
  Publish
</button>

6. Error boundaries do not catch action errors in production

An error.tsx boundary catches render errors, and an uncaught action error arrives as a redacted digest that error.tsx never sees unless the client rethrows it. Handle expected failure inside the action and return state; reserve throwing for genuinely broken invariants, where a digest and a server log are the right outcome.

Common mistakes and version gotchas

  • redirect() inside try/catch — swallowed. Move it out or rethrow with unstable_rethrow.
  • redirect() in a setTimeout or after await past the response — the action has returned, so the navigation is lost.
  • Returning Error from an action — not serialisable; return a string or a plain object.
  • useActionState action that does not take (prevState, formData) — React passes the previous state as the first argument and the signature mismatch shows as formData.get is not a function.
  • bodySizeLimit under experimental on Next.js 15+ — ignored, and the 1 MB default stays.
  • revalidatePath after redirect — unreachable; invalidate first.
  • Actions used as event handlers directly — onClick={myAction} posts nothing; wrap in startTransition or use a form.

Related tools. Paste a failed payload and inspect it with the JSON formatter, test a multipart request without the app in the way using cURL to code, and compare the action's serialised state between the versions in a text diff.

title: EcoFlow, Jackery, BLUETTI and Anker SOLIX: Shopify Lessons From Four Portable Power Stores
description:
Cover: EcoFlow official US page, captured 17 November 2026; the article compares four storefronts.

A comparison of storefronts is most useful when the rows describe the same type of decision. These four portable-power pages illustrate different ways to help shoppers navigate information. The following is a US-site observation reviewed on 17 November 2026, not a product-performance ranking, a conversion study, or a claim that every brand uses a particular Shopify plan.

Four observable patterns

  1. EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3: product details, service information and configuration choices appear along the purchase journey. The page also qualifies a central-air-conditioning example with a laboratory condition.
  2. Jackery HomePower: the navigation offers routes by product type and by scenario, including home-backup solution levels.
  3. BLUETTI AC200L: a note on a particular battery connection links to its required cable. The reviewed main option was discontinued; this is historical analysis, not an availability claim.
  4. Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus: a North American power-standard notice is visible near the purchase area and the FAQ distinguishes operating conditions.

Each observation comes from a different page and model. Do not combine their electrical specifications into one fictitious product or compare prices from different regions and dates as if they were simultaneous offers.

Compare purchase journeys without inventing outcomes

Use the same sequence for each site: how a visitor enters the catalog, how the page identifies the specific offer, how conditions are attached to a claim, and how the next relevant step is presented. EcoFlow's scene-based charging explanation, Jackery's category and scenario navigation, BLUETTI's named accessory link and Anker SOLIX's operating-condition FAQ are different kinds of evidence; they should not be scored as if they measured the same thing.

The original article contrasts independent stores with marketplaces and asks whether detailed guidance gives the brand a reason for a customer to stay. That is a useful research question. Page content alone cannot establish that shoppers will not return to a marketplace, that a design reduces returns, or that one brand has the highest conversion rate. A merchant could evaluate those hypotheses with task testing and appropriately collected first-party data.

For a fair editorial comparison, retain source URL, market, date, page type, model and the precise observation for each cell. Pricing, stock and offers should be compared only after aligning market and time; if the required evidence is missing, leave the comparison out. Treat AI-search visibility as a separate experiment, not a guaranteed result of adding markup.

Define the comparison dimension first

For a content team, two reasonable dimensions are the entry path and the way qualifying conditions are presented. A row about “entry path” should contain an observation of the same kind for each site; a row about “conditions” should describe each site's handling of conditions. These are design observations, not proof of customer behavior. If an observation cannot be confirmed for one brand, omit the row until the evidence is complete rather than inventing a value.

The code below displays two editorial comparison rows from a custom.store_comparison page metafield referencing a metaobject. It requires four entries for each row, escaping text rather than mixing live products' attributes. It does not fetch competitor pages or validate that entered observations are true.

{%- comment -%}
  Storefront information architecture comparison; illustrative only.
  Do not infer product performance, electrical safety, or business results.
  Only use verified observations; do not supply invented defaults.
{%- endcomment -%}
{%- assign comparison = page.metafields.custom.store_comparison.value -%}
{%- if comparison != blank -%}
  {%- assign ecoflow_entry = comparison.ecoflow_entry.value -%}
  {%- assign jackery_entry = comparison.jackery_entry.value -%}
  {%- assign bluetti_entry = comparison.bluetti_entry.value -%}
  {%- assign anker_entry = comparison.anker_entry.value -%}
  {%- assign ecoflow_condition = comparison.ecoflow_condition.value -%}
  {%- assign jackery_condition = comparison.jackery_condition.value -%}
  {%- assign bluetti_condition = comparison.bluetti_condition.value -%}
  {%- assign anker_condition = comparison.anker_condition.value -%}
  {%- assign entry_complete = false -%}
  {%- assign condition_complete = false -%}
  {%- if ecoflow_entry != blank and jackery_entry != blank and bluetti_entry != blank and anker_entry != blank -%}{%- assign entry_complete = true -%}{%- endif -%}
  {%- if ecoflow_condition != blank and jackery_condition != blank and bluetti_condition != blank and anker_condition != blank -%}{%- assign condition_complete = true -%}{%- endif -%}
  {%- if entry_complete or condition_complete -%}
<table class="store-comparison">
  <caption>Storefront information architecture comparison</caption>
  <thead><tr><th scope="col">Dimension</th><th scope="col">EcoFlow</th><th scope="col">Jackery</th><th scope="col">BLUETTI</th><th scope="col">Anker SOLIX</th></tr></thead>
  <tbody>
    {%- if entry_complete %}
    <tr><th scope="row">Entry path</th><td>{{ ecoflow_entry | escape | newline_to_br }}</td><td>{{ jackery_entry | escape | newline_to_br }}</td><td>{{ bluetti_entry | escape | newline_to_br }}</td><td>{{ anker_entry | escape | newline_to_br }}</td></tr>
    {%- endif %}
    {%- if condition_complete %}
    <tr><th scope="row">Applicable conditions</th><td>{{ ecoflow_condition | escape | newline_to_br }}</td><td>{{ jackery_condition | escape | newline_to_br }}</td><td>{{ bluetti_condition | escape | newline_to_br }}</td><td>{{ anker_condition | escape | newline_to_br }}</td></tr>
    {%- endif %}
  </tbody>
</table>
  {%- endif -%}
{%- endif -%}

Implementation boundaries and tests

The code is an information-display example, not an install-ready production component. It does not evaluate electrical compatibility, calculate runtime, verify certifications, check inventory, promise shipping or create a working configuration flow. Populate fields only after checking the specific model, market and manufacturer documentation. Shopify's admin or an app must create the definitions first; Liquid does not create metafields.

In a development theme, verify a missing reference, an empty entry, every field by itself and a fully populated entry. Empty values must not create empty headings or false defaults. Test special characters, line breaks, narrow screens, keyboard navigation and the theme's heading hierarchy. Verify actual availability, variant behavior and checkout with the real store integrations. No Shopify production-theme, checkout or physical-product test is claimed here.

The example assumes the reference is rendered in the correct template, that its metaobject has the named multi-line plain-text fields, and that the merchant has made the entry available to the storefront. escape treats content as text; newline_to_br retains its line breaks. See Shopify's metafield and metaobject documentation.

Testing and editorial review

The table hides an incomplete row rather than presenting a four-way comparison with a missing value. Verify all four combinations of missing and present rows, and test long labels on narrow screens. A production implementation should also provide responsive table behavior and preserve the relationship between column and row headers. Re-check each source before use; these pages may change independently. A poster-style comparison, if used, should reflect each site's observed visual identity and be reviewed for factual and typographic accuracy.

title: Our phone CTA bar reads rectangles every frame instead of using IntersectionObserver, and a fast fling is why
description:
CogniPrep's long entry pages are long. A provider hub or an employer guide runs thousands of pixels, and the primary action sits near the top. On a phone, somebody who reads to the end has nothing to tap without scrolling back.

The fix is the oldest pattern on mobile web: a bar pinned to the bottom with the action in it. The interesting part is that almost every decision in the 133 lines is a decision not to do the obvious thing.

It shows between two points, not from a threshold

The bar is not "appears after 400px". It shows after the page's own early call to action has scrolled up under the header, and hides again once the page's closing call to action or the footer comes into view. So it never doubles up with a button already on screen, and it is gone before the footer, which is what stops it covering anything.

Both ends are elements, not offsets. The start is an id passed in as a prop. The end is any element carrying a data attribute, or the footer:

const ends = Array.from(document.querySelectorAll(`[${STICKY_CTA_END_ATTR}], footer`));

Why not IntersectionObserver

This is the part I want to defend, because an observer is the right default and this is the case where it is wrong. The component's own comment states it:

 * Both points are read from element positions on scroll (once per frame), not
 * from IntersectionObserver: a jump straight past the early button, from a fast
 * fling or an in-page link, never intersects it, so an observer would not fire.

An IntersectionObserver reports crossings. If a frame never renders with the element partially in view, there is no crossing to report. Two things on a long page do exactly that: a hard fling on iOS, where the compositor can jump hundreds of pixels between frames, and an in-page anchor link, which teleports past everything in between. In both cases the observer stays silent and the bar never appears, which is the one failure mode a reader notices.

So it reads positions instead, and it reads them as state rather than as events:

const update = () => {
  frame = 0;
  setPastAnchor(anchor.getBoundingClientRect().bottom <= HEADER_HEIGHT_PX);
  setAtEnd(ends.some((end) => end.getBoundingClientRect().top < window.innerHeight));
};
const schedule = () => {
  if (!frame) frame = requestAnimationFrame(update);
};
update();
window.addEventListener('scroll', schedule, { passive: true });
window.addEventListener('resize', schedule);

Three things keep that cheap. The listener is passive, so it cannot block scrolling. The work is coalesced to one requestAnimationFrame per frame no matter how many scroll events arrive. And update() is called once immediately, so a page restored mid-scroll by the browser is correct before the first scroll event rather than after it.

HEADER_HEIGHT_PX is 56, the height of the fixed header, so "scrolled away" means scrolled under the header rather than off the top of the viewport.

The end test is top < window.innerHeight, not a two-sided intersection check. An element above the viewport has a negative top, so "in view or already past it" collapses into one comparison. The bar never comes back once you have reached the end of the page.

The portal, and the one-word reason it is needed

The bar renders through createPortal into document.body. Not for convenience:

 * Rendered into document.body through a portal, so it can be mounted anywhere:
 * `main` carries `contain: paint` (app/globals.css), which would otherwise make
 * it the bar's containing block and pin the bar to the bottom of the page
 * instead of the bottom of the screen.

The stylesheet has this, for unrelated reasons:

@layer base {
  main {
    min-height: calc(100dvh - 3.5rem);
    contain: layout style paint;
  }
}

contain: paint makes the element a containing block for fixed-position descendants. So position: fixed; bottom: 0 inside main is fixed to the bottom of main, which is thousands of pixels down. The bar would work in isolation and fail in place, and the failure would look like "the bar does not show" rather than "the bar is at the wrong offset", because you would have to scroll to the bottom of the document to see it.

A census of this repository in early November counted zero createPortal call sites. There are two now, and this is the one with a written reason.

Four details that cost four lines each

Client-only without a hydration flicker. The bar is invisible until the reader scrolls, so rendering nothing on the server changes nothing on screen:

const isClient = useSyncExternalStore(noSubscribe, () => true, () => false);

A no-op subscribe and a false server snapshot. Static HTML ships without the bar, and the portal arrives after hydration. The practical upshot: the bar is in no page's HTML. You cannot find it by viewing source.

Scroll padding from the bar's real height. While the bar shows, it sets scroll-padding-bottom on the document to its own measured height, so keyboard focus and in-page jumps land above it instead of under it. Measured, not a constant, with the reason given inline: the label can wrap to two lines on a narrow phone.

Hidden properly, not just invisibly. When it is not showing it keeps pointer-events-none translate-y-full opacity-0 and also carries aria-hidden and inert. Opacity zero alone leaves a focusable link in the tab order that nobody can see.

A 48px target and the safe area. The button is min-h-12, and the bar's bottom padding is pb-[max(0.75rem,env(safe-area-inset-bottom))], so the home-bar gesture area on a modern iPhone does not eat the tap. The label is set to wrap rather than truncate, with a comment explaining why: a cut-off label could lose the word "free".

Where it runs, counted from the live site

Five page shells mount it, which puts it on 736 of the 1,093 public URLs:

Surface Pages with the bar
Per-test pages 409
Employer guides 201
Provider hubs 69
Company interview pages 42
Test format pages 15

Each shell names its own anchor id: test-cta, employer-cta, hub-cta, interview-cta, format-cta. Four different names for the same role, which is the kind of thing five parallel edits produce.

The employer number is the one worth noting. There are 214 employer guides, and 201 carry the anchor. The other 13 are guides where no test vendor is evidenced at medium confidence or better, which is a deliberate rule stated in the module that supplies the association: those pages get sibling links but no provider hub link, "because there is no hub that honestly matches the page". Both the early call to action and the bar read the same value, so where there is nothing honest to offer, neither renders. One condition, two surfaces, no special case.

The one loose end

STICKY_CTA_END_ATTR is exported so callers cannot typo the attribute name. All 69 provider hubs write the string by hand instead:

<div data-sticky-cta-end className="...">

A typo there is silent. The bar would simply stay up until the footer, which still looks fine, which is why nothing would catch it. The constant is doing no work until someone imports it.

See it

This one needs a narrow viewport, because the bar is md:hidden and it is not in any page's HTML.

Open the SHL provider hub and set your window to 375px wide, or open it on a phone. View source first and search for pointer-events-none translate-y-full: nothing, because the bar is portalled in after hydration.

Now scroll slowly. The bar arrives the moment the hub's own early button passes under the header, and it leaves again when the closing block at the bottom of the page comes into view. Search the source for data-sticky-cta-end and you are looking at the element that dismisses it.

Then try the hard case. Scroll back to the top, and flick as hard as you can straight to the bottom. The bar never appears, which is correct, because the end block is already in view. Now flick to the middle instead. It is there, having never been given a crossing to observe.

Finally, compare with an employer guide at the same width, where the anchor id is employer-cta instead, and with a per-test page, where it is test-cta. Same 133 lines, three different anchors.

title: CuRSE-Bench: A Benchmark for Probing Cultural Blind Spots in Text-to-Image Safety Evaluation
description:
arXiv:2611.20821v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) safety evaluation typically assigns each prompt or image a single culture-blind harm label, so content that is harmful only within a particular culture can pass as benign. We introduce CultureCraft, an agentic framework that constructs T2I prompts that appear benign under a general-purpose rubric yet carry a latent harmful meaning in a target culture, and use it to build CuRSE-Bench: 10,709 culture-specific prompts and 2,648 culture-general controls over six regions and ten harm axes, each drawn from a predefined knowledge base of documented harm vectors and traceable to at least two independent sources. Scoring every prompt under six region persona judges and a paired culture-blind judge, we find that the culture-blind judge under-rates culture-specific latent harm while matching the persona judges on the controls. Each persona judge, in turn, chiefly decodes its own region's latent harm under our instrument: a selective cultural blind spot that persists in deployed moderators.

title: MedGuardBench: A Patient-Oriented Benchmark for Personalized Guardrail Development
description:
arXiv:2611.22069v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Safety is personal: the same action can be safe for one person but unsafe for another. Yet current guardrails judge content without considering who is affected. Using medication safety, we introduce \textit{patient-conditioned medication guarding}, which predicts a safety verdict and 17 risk categories from a patient profile and prescription. We release \textbf{MedGuardBench}, a drug-disjoint benchmark of 5{,}001 scenarios across 87 medications. We find that standard guardrails rely on surface cues, such as wording and profile presence, rather than patient facts. To address this, we develop \textit{personalized reasoning guardrails} with three components. \textbf{Personalized Reasoning Distillation} links risks to relevant patient fields. \textbf{Context Unrolling (CU)} makes models check each field themselves, reducing false alarms on most backbones; controls show that providing the check does not yield the same benefit. A \textbf{rule-based reward (guided GRPO)} improves unsafe recall and complex-risk detection, including allergies and adverse reactions, on some backbones, but increases false alarms on others. Our models outperform base models and matched no-profile controls in accuracy, while reducing false alarms relative to no-profile controls. Profile removal and swapping confirm that gains come from patient information, not fine-tuning alone.

title: AWS WAF announces simplified onboarding for Bot Control targeted protection
description:
Today, AWS WAF announces a simplified console experience for Bot Control at the targeted inspection level. A single setting, Targeted bot control, turns on targeted protection for your Amazon CloudFront distributions with the configuration AWS recommends. It comes with two additions to the Bot Control managed rule group: bot confidence levels, which summarize the targeted detections on each request as High, Medium, or Low, and a LATEST version that keeps you on the newest detections automatically. Together, they help you protect your applications against sophisticated and AI-powered bots without writing label match rules or changing application code.

The targeted inspection level uses machine learning and client-side signals to detect evasive bots. Previously, acting on those signals meant integrating the AWS WAF JavaScript SDK into every page, learning dozens of labels, and writing label match rules to combine them. Now, the rule group combines the detections into one confidence level per request, with one rule per level, and the Targeted bot control setting adds the rule group, applies the recommended action for each level, sets the version to LATEST, and turns on automatic SDK integration so CloudFront adds the SDK to your pages. You can change any action or start in Count.

The Targeted bot control setting is available today for protection packs (web ACLs) used with Amazon CloudFront. Bot confidence levels and the LATEST version are available in all AWS Regions where AWS WAF Bot Control is available. Standard pricing for the targeted inspection level applies, with no additional charge for the setting or automatic SDK integration. To get started, open the AWS WAF console. To learn more, see Turning on Targeted bot control and Bot confidence levels in the AWS WAF Developer Guide, and read the AWS Security Blog post.

title: How OpenEvidence scales medical search for 650K doctors
description:
OpenEvidence on Vercel

  • Serves 650,000 doctors with medical search

  • Completes production deployments in about five minutes

  • Absorbs traffic spikes without additional capacity provisioning

  • Reduced serverless spend by 90% with Fluid compute

  • Updates doctor- and patient-facing applications independently

OpenEvidence helps physicians find medical evidence during care, whether they’re checking a dosage on intensive care rounds or handling a case outside their specialty without a specialist nearby. Answers draw on peer-reviewed literature and include citations, so doctors can examine the sources behind them.

OpenEvidence’s small team began using Vercel to get early experiments online and kept that workflow as the product grew, relying on the platform to handle web deployments and capacity.

Building software physicians depend on

The stakes are different when software helps inform medical decisions. An incorrect answer can affect how a doctor treats a patient, while an unavailable application can cut off access to evidence when it is needed.

OpenEvidence supported more than 20 million clinical consultations in January 2026. The company also reported that more than 100 million Americans were treated by doctors using OpenEvidence in 2025.

"Honestly, life or death is not inaccurate," says Kush Khosla, Engineering Lead at OpenEvidence. "We operate in situations where it's an ER and they really need to know what's going on. Uptime is very, very important to us."

"A lot of doctors and medical professionals are used to really outdated software," says Andy Yoon, Engineering Lead at OpenEvidence. A more modern experience still needs to meet physicians' expectations of speed, stability, clarity, and information they can trust. The small team needs a way to test updates to the web application before putting them into production and to roll back if something goes wrong.

Keeping releases simple as the audience grows

Andy recalls why Vercel suited the team he joined at OpenEvidence. "I was pretty much the only engineer on our team coming from an actual frontend background," he says. "Most of our team works in Python and machine learning." He adds, "Given the makeup of our engineering team, Vercel really scaled with our needs so well."

The team builds its physician-facing web application with the Next.js framework. When engineers push changes to a development branch, Vercel builds and deploys a preview, giving them a link they can use for live demos and share with colleagues to try new features. Pushing or merging into the production branch then triggers the production build and deployment. If a release needs reverting, the team can roll back to a previous deployment.

That workflow lets the team release multiple times a day, with each change becoming available to a physician audience that Kush thinks about whenever he ships something:

More doctors without more provisioning

Keeping that application available means handling demand the team can’t always anticipate. Andy was scrolling through Slack when he saw the message that OpenEvidence had gone viral on TikTok, reaching around two million views in under a week. He watched traffic climb and checked the logs. Response times stayed fast and error rates remained near zero, and with no additional capacity to provision, he went back to his work.

Beyond sudden spikes, the team has accommodated sustained growth without rebuilding the web application.

"Not once have I had to think, now that we have five times as many doctors, what's happening to page loads or time to first paint," Kush says. "The scaling has happened so naturally that we end up focusing on other things."

A 90% drop in serverless spend

As usage grew, VP of Engineering Micah Smith was watching compute costs. The team enabled Fluid compute for its functions on Vercel, and Micah described the result alongside the wider infrastructure budget:

"We reduced our serverless spend by 90% while maintaining the same performance, and even as we've scaled up to 1000x growth, Vercel is less than 5% of our overall infra spend."

Fluid compute lets multiple requests share a running function instance, so it can handle other work while a request waits for another service, such as a database or an AI backend, to respond. With Active CPU pricing, that waiting time doesn’t incur CPU charges, though memory remains billed while requests are in progress.

A familiar workflow for a new audience

Take Home, OpenEvidence’s first patient-facing application, lets a doctor translate a clinical answer into plain language and share it with a patient, who logs in to review and save the evidence. Clinical-trial matching is also part of the application’s planned direction.

To support this expansion, the team uses a pattern established through dozens of early proofs of concept, each deployed as its own Vercel project with a custom domain. Stakeholders could open those applications and test the workflows for themselves. Getting new projects online in minutes helped the team find product-market fit and made it easier to win early enterprise partnerships.

Take Home has its own project and domain too, so engineers can update the patient experience without deploying the other applications.

With Take Home, evidence that helps a doctor during a consultation can become something a patient returns to afterward.

About OpenEvidence: OpenEvidence helps healthcare professionals find medical evidence at the point of care, with answers sourced, cited, and grounded in peer-reviewed literature. Physicians use it daily across more than 10,000 hospitals and medical centers in the United States. Its mission is to help doctors save lives and improve patient care. Learn more at openevidence.com.

title: Flocking Time and Graph Volume in Nonlinear Cucker-Smale Models with Dynamic Networks
description:
arXiv:2611.22204v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: This study proposes a Cucker-Smale model incorporating dynamic networks and the discrete $p$-Laplacian ($p \in (1,2)$) and analyzes the relationship between flocking time constraints and graph connectivity from both theoretical and experimental perspectives. We establish that this model achieves flocking within finite time and derive a quantitative relationship between the lower bound of flocking time and graph volume. Based on these results, we observe that imposing sufficiently small flocking time induces an increase in network volume, and that larger initial velocity variance requires greater volume under the same time constraint. In our experiments, we trained a transformer-based PPO policy to select network structures at each time step. Under the most stringent time constraint, the maximum average number of connections increased sharply, confirming a threshold effect. The negative correlation between convergence time and average number of connections reflects the theoretical results well. This study provides quantitative evidence for the phenomenon that time constraints induce connection mobilization.

title: Text-Guided Modality Correction for Open-Vocabulary Object Detection
description:
arXiv:2611.22126v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Open-vocabulary object detection (OVD) is essential for detecting objects beyond the categories seen during training. Establishing vision-language associations is crucial for recognizing unseen categories, while integrating complementary visual features across levels supports detection at different scales. However, existing methods often provide insufficient textual guidance for object regions, rely on limited cross-modal alignment strategies, and underuse complementary features across levels, limiting their ability to detect unseen categories and objects of varying scales. To address these limitations, we propose a Text-Guided Modality Correction Network (TMCNet) that incorporates textual guidance into region feature extraction, cross-modal alignment, and multi-scale decoding to strengthen region-category semantic correspondence and promote complementary feature fusion across levels. First, a text-guided modality encoder incorporates textual semantics into queries to guide regional feature aggregation, reducing semantic ambiguity in object representations. Second, a cross-modal alignment module strengthens the correspondence between region representations and category semantics through interactions between visual and textual features. Finally, a progressive text correction decoder combines a top-down pathway with lateral connections to progressively fuse text-guided deep semantic features with shallow visual features at the corresponding scales, preserving both semantic information and spatial detail for objects of different sizes. Experiments on two public datasets, COCO-OVD and LVIS-OVD, demonstrate that TMCNet achieves strong performance in open-vocabulary object detection using simple text queries as guidance. Extending TMCNet to open-vocabulary segmentation also yields performance gains, demonstrating its cross-task applicability and extensibility.
