title: CorrectCast: Selective Multimodal Context for Scale-Aware Residual Correction in Precipitation Nowcasting
description:
arXiv:2611.22178v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Precipitation nowcasting models suffer from errors in intensity, location, and spatial structure. Addressing these errors by retraining nowcaster backbones can be computationally expensive and requires architecture-specific modifications. To overcome these limitations, we propose CorrectCast, a decoupled residual correction framework that refines completed nowcasts while keeping the base nowcaster frozen. By operating on predicted precipitation fields, CorrectCast requires training only a lightweight corrector, reducing computational overhead while providing a unified correction interface across different nowcasting models. Conditioned on the base nowcast and historical quantitative precipitation estimation (QPE) and precipitable water vapor (PWV) observations, the corrector selects multimodal context and employs scale-aware modulation to estimate residual corrections. On the Mississippi River Basin (MRB) and contiguous United States (CONUS) datasets, CorrectCast improves six base nowcasters spanning extrapolation-based, deterministic, and generative approaches, with absolute gains in mean CSI averaging 0.0233 and 0.0290 across the six models, respectively.

title: Self-hosting an LLM server on a GPU SageMaker Code Editor space with Kronk
description:
Some teams do not want prompts or models to leave hardware they control. This post walks through running Kronk, an open-source Go model server built on llama.cpp, on a GPU instance behind Amazon SageMaker Studio's Code Editor, with an install that survives restarts and no public endpoint.

What we built

  • A SageMaker Studio domain in VPC-only mode, with subnets that reach the internet through a NAT gateway.
  • A Code Editor space on ml.g5.2xlarge (one NVIDIA A10G, 24 GB) with a 100 GB EBS volume.
  • A lifecycle configuration (LCC) that installs Kronk once, repairs CUDA library paths, and starts the server on every app start.
  • Access to the API and the admin UI through an SSM tunnel. Nothing is exposed on the network.

Kronk serves OpenAI-compatible chat, embeddings and reranking endpoints, plus an Anthropic-compatible Messages API and a browser admin UI. By default it listens on 127.0.0.1:11435.

Why Code Editor

Code Editor is a VS Code-based IDE, so writing and running non-Python code in it (here a Go server and a Go client) feels like working on a local machine, with a terminal and an EBS-backed home directory. We did not try a JupyterLab space, which also has a terminal and exposes ports through /jupyterlab/default/proxy/<port>/. The trade-off for Code Editor is in the networking section below.

The lifecycle configuration

An LCC for a Studio app must finish within five minutes, and a download plus library install can take longer. The pattern that works is an LCC that does almost nothing: it writes a launcher script to EBS and runs it with nohup in the background. The launcher is idempotent, so it installs only on the first start.

The version below is the one that ended up working:

#!/bin/bash
# CodeEditor LCC: persist the Kronk model server. Returns fast; heavy work runs under nohup.
set -u
KDIR=/home/sagemaker-user/kronk-bin
mkdir -p "$KDIR"

cat > "$KDIR/start-kronk.sh" <<'EOS'
#!/bin/bash
# Idempotent and instance-agnostic: installs Kronk once (on EBS), makes sure the CUDA backend's
# shared libraries resolve, then (re)starts the server detached on loopback.
set -u
KDIR=/home/sagemaker-user/kronk-bin
KVER=1.33.2
LOG="$KDIR/start.log"
EXTRA="$KDIR/cuda-libs"          # pip-installed CUDA libs live on EBS (installed once)
exec >> "$LOG" 2>&1
echo "=== $(date -u) start-kronk begin ==="

unset HTTP_PROXY HTTPS_PROXY http_proxy https_proxy
export NO_PROXY=localhost,127.0.0.1 no_proxy=localhost,127.0.0.1
export KRONK_BASE_PATH=/home/sagemaker-user/.kronk
export KRONK_WEB_API_HOST=127.0.0.1:11435   # loopback only; reach it via the CE proxy
export PATH="$KDIR:$PATH"

HAS_GPU=0
if nvidia-smi -L; then HAS_GPU=1; else echo "no NVIDIA GPU detected -> cpu"; fi

curl -sS -m 15 -o /dev/null -w "github reachability http=%{http_code}\n" https://github.com || echo "WARN: github unreachable"

if [ ! -x "$KDIR/kronk" ]; then
  echo "Installing kronk v$KVER"
  curl -fsSL --retry 3 --connect-timeout 20 -o "$KDIR/kronk.tgz" \
    "https://github.com/ardanlabs/kronk/releases/download/v${KVER}/kronk_${KVER}_linux_amd64.tar.gz" || { echo "download failed"; exit 1; }
  tar -xzf "$KDIR/kronk.tgz" -C "$KDIR"
  f=$(find "$KDIR" -type f -name kronk -perm -u+x | head -1)
  [ -n "$f" ] && [ "$f" != "$KDIR/kronk" ] && mv "$f" "$KDIR/kronk"
  chmod +x "$KDIR/kronk"; rm -f "$KDIR/kronk.tgz"
fi
"$KDIR/kronk" --version || true

if [ "$HAS_GPU" = 1 ]; then export KRONK_PROCESSOR=cuda; else export KRONK_PROCESSOR=cpu; fi
"$KDIR/kronk" libs --local || echo "WARN: libs install failed"

# --- Make the CUDA backend's dependencies resolve (generic across images/instances) ---
if [ "$HAS_GPU" = 1 ]; then
  CUDA_SO=$(find "$KRONK_BASE_PATH/libraries" -name 'libggml-cuda.so' 2>/dev/null | head -1)
  if [ -n "$CUDA_SO" ]; then
    missing() { LD_LIBRARY_PATH="${LD_LIBRARY_PATH:-}" ldd "$CUDA_SO" 2>/dev/null | awk '/not found/{print $1}'; }
    add_libdirs() {  # add every dir that holds libcublas* to LD_LIBRARY_PATH
      for d in $(find /usr/local/cuda* /opt/conda "$EXTRA" -name 'libcublas*.so*' 2>/dev/null | xargs -r -n1 dirname | sort -u); do
        case ":${LD_LIBRARY_PATH:-}:" in *":$d:"*) ;; *) export LD_LIBRARY_PATH="$d:${LD_LIBRARY_PATH:-}";; esac
      done
    }
    add_libdirs
    M=$(missing)
    if [ -n "$M" ]; then
      echo "CUDA backend still missing: $M -> installing via pip into $EXTRA"
      MAJOR=$(echo "$M" | grep -o 'so\.[0-9]*' | head -1 | cut -d. -f2)
      case "$MAJOR" in 12) PKGS="nvidia-cublas-cu12";; *) PKGS="nvidia-cublas nvidia-cublas-cu${MAJOR:-13}";; esac
      mkdir -p "$EXTRA"
      for p in $PKGS; do
        python3 -m pip install --quiet --target "$EXTRA" "$p" && { echo "pip installed $p"; add_libdirs; [ -z "$(missing)" ] && break; } || echo "pip $p failed"
      done
      M=$(missing)
    fi
    if [ -z "$M" ]; then echo "CUDA deps OK; LD_LIBRARY_PATH=${LD_LIBRARY_PATH:-}"; else echo "WARN: unresolved CUDA deps: $M (Kronk will fall back to CPU)"; fi
  else
    echo "WARN: libggml-cuda.so not found under $KRONK_BASE_PATH/libraries"
  fi
fi

# Env file so interactive shells (kronk CLI, tests) match the server
cat > "$KDIR/env.sh" <<EOF
export PATH="$KDIR:\$PATH"
export KRONK_BASE_PATH=$KRONK_BASE_PATH
export KRONK_PROCESSOR=$KRONK_PROCESSOR
export LD_LIBRARY_PATH="${LD_LIBRARY_PATH:-}"
EOF

"$KDIR/kronk" server stop || true
"$KDIR/kronk" server start --detach
sleep 8
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "health http=%{http_code}\n" http://127.0.0.1:11435/v1/models || true
grep -o '"gpu-count":[0-9]*' "$KRONK_BASE_PATH/kronk.log" | tail -1
echo "=== $(date -u) start-kronk done ==="
EOS
chmod +x "$KDIR/start-kronk.sh"

# Fire and forget so the LCC finishes well under the 5-minute limit
nohup "$KDIR/start-kronk.sh" > "$KDIR/nohup.out" 2>&1 &
disown
echo "kronk launcher started in background"
exit 0

Things to note:

  • Kronk and its models live under /home/sagemaker-user, on EBS, so the 640 MB model and the 217 MB CUDA library bundle are downloaded once.
  • The version is pinned (1.33.2). The project releases often.
  • The server binds to loopback. The UI and API are reached through the tunnel described below.

Problems we hit

1. A dead proxy. An older LCC in the domain set HTTP_PROXY to a proxy host that no longer existed, so the first install failed after a 137-second timeout. Checking the route tables showed the subnets already had 0.0.0.0/0 through a NAT gateway, so the proxy was not needed. Lesson: do not copy proxy settings from old LCCs without checking that the proxy exists.

2. The default Code Editor image was not allowed. The domain's default Code Editor image was a custom one that the user profile could not launch (not present in list of custom images). Setting the first-party sagemaker-distribution-gpu image on the space and the app fixed it.

3. The LCC must be allowed on the user profile. CreateApp rejects an LCC that is not in the user profile's (or domain's) LifecycleConfigArns. Updating a profile replaces the whole list, so read the existing settings first.

4. It ran on the CPU. The first chat worked, but nvidia-smi showed 0 MiB used and the reply came back at 18.9 tokens per second. The Kronk log said "gpu-count":0 and memory-topology: cpu-only. ldd on libggml-cuda.so showed libcublas.so.13 => not found: the driver was fine, but the linker could not find the cuBLAS library the CUDA backend needs. The libraries were present under /opt/conda, just not on the search path. The launcher now reads ldd, adds the directories that contain libcublas*, falls back to pip install --target if they are missing, and logs what it decided. After that the log showed "gpu-count":1 and the same request ran at about 352 tokens per second (346 in the admin chat).

To confirm the fix, open System > Running in the admin UI after a request. With the model on the GPU, the resource budget shows CUDA0 with the model's 4.44 GiB reserved there and only about 158 MiB in system RAM. In the CPU run, the same plan was cpu-only, with the memory charged to system RAM.

One caveat: the admin Info page still prints a warning that "ggml enumerated no GPU device". We believe that is the page's own probe running without the library path that the launcher sets for the server, but we did not confirm it. The speed (about 350 tok/s against 19), the Running page and the server log all agree on the GPU.

5. Code Editor has no /proxy/<port>/ path. In JupyterLab you can open a local server at /jupyterlab/default/proxy/<port>/. Code Editor in the new Studio does not offer that, and we got Unsupported URL path. The answer was remote access.

Reaching the UI without exposing anything

Enable RemoteAccess on the space (this requires recreating the app), make sure the execution role can start SSM sessions, and add an SSH entry on your laptop that uses the AWS-provided sagemaker_connect helper. Then forward the port:

ssh -L 11435:127.0.0.1:11435 <your-space-host-alias>

and open http://localhost:11435.

If you prefer a GUI, desktop VS Code with the AWS Toolkit can connect to the same space over SSM. In the AWS Explorer, open SageMaker AI, then Studio, find the running space, and click the remote-access icon next to it.

The Ports panel then forwards 11435 for you, and you can browse the Kronk files on EBS (kronk-bin, .kronk) next to a terminal on the GPU instance.

You also need the Session Manager plugin and credentials that allow sagemaker:StartSession. One caution: if your connect helper script runs with set -x, it prints the SSM stream URL and session token to the terminal. Remove the -x.

Calling it from Go

The server speaks the OpenAI chat-completions format, so a client needs only the standard library. This one does the same thing as the curl command and prints the speed numbers that Kronk returns in usage:

// Minimal client for a Kronk model server (OpenAI-compatible chat completions).
// Does the same thing as:
//
//  curl http://127.0.0.1:11435/v1/chat/completions \
//    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
//    -d '{"model":"unsloth/Qwen3-0.6B-Q8_0","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Say hi"}]}'
//
// Run on the instance (VS Code remote window) or on your laptop through the
// SSM tunnel (ssh -L 11435:127.0.0.1:11435 <host>); both reach http://127.0.0.1:11435.
package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "flag"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

type message struct {
    Role    string `json:"role"`
    Content string `json:"content"`
}

type request struct {
    Model     string    `json:"model"`
    Messages  []message `json:"messages"`
    MaxTokens int       `json:"max_tokens,omitempty"`
}

type response struct {
    Choices []struct {
        Message struct {
            Content          string `json:"content"`
            ReasoningContent string `json:"reasoning_content"`
        } `json:"message"`
        FinishReason string `json:"finish_reason"`
    } `json:"choices"`
    Usage struct {
        PromptTokens     int     `json:"prompt_tokens"`
        CompletionTokens int     `json:"completion_tokens"`
        TotalTokens      int     `json:"total_tokens"`
        TokensPerSecond  float64 `json:"tokens_per_second"`
        TTFTMillis       float64 `json:"time_to_first_token_ms"`
    } `json:"usage"`
    Error any `json:"error"`
}

func main() {
    baseURL := flag.String("url", envOr("KRONK_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:11435"), "Kronk base URL")
    model := flag.String("model", "unsloth/Qwen3-0.6B-Q8_0", "model ID exactly as listed by /v1/models")
    prompt := flag.String("prompt", "Say hi", "user prompt")
    maxTokens := flag.Int("max-tokens", 0, "max completion tokens (0 = server default)")
    showReasoning := flag.Bool("reasoning", false, "also print reasoning_content")
    flag.Parse()

    body, err := json.Marshal(request{
        Model:     *model,
        Messages:  []message{{Role: "user", Content: *prompt}},
        MaxTokens: *maxTokens,
    })
    if err != nil {
        fatal(err)
    }

    req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, strings.TrimRight(*baseURL, "/")+"/v1/chat/completions", bytes.NewReader(body))
    if err != nil {
        fatal(err)
    }
    req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    // Only needed if you later enable authorization on the server.
    if key := os.Getenv("KRONK_API_KEY"); key != "" {
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
    }

    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 5 * time.Minute}
    start := time.Now()
    resp, err := client.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        fatal(err)
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()

    raw, err := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
    if err != nil {
        fatal(err)
    }
    if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusOK {
        fatal(fmt.Errorf("HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, strings.TrimSpace(string(raw))))
    }

    var out response
    if err := json.Unmarshal(raw, &out); err != nil {
        fatal(fmt.Errorf("decode response: %w\n%s", err, raw))
    }
    if len(out.Choices) == 0 {
        fatal(fmt.Errorf("no choices in response: %s", raw))
    }

    c := out.Choices[0]
    if *showReasoning && c.Message.ReasoningContent != "" {
        fmt.Printf("[reasoning]\n%s\n\n", strings.TrimSpace(c.Message.ReasoningContent))
    }
    fmt.Println(strings.TrimSpace(c.Message.Content))
    fmt.Printf("\n-- finish=%s prompt=%d completion=%d tok/s=%.1f ttft=%.0fms wall=%s\n",
        c.FinishReason, out.Usage.PromptTokens, out.Usage.CompletionTokens,
        out.Usage.TokensPerSecond, out.Usage.TTFTMillis, time.Since(start).Round(time.Millisecond))
}

func envOr(k, def string) string {
    if v := os.Getenv(k); v != "" {
        return v
    }
    return def
}

func fatal(err error) {
    fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "error:", err)
    os.Exit(1)
}

Run it from your laptop through the tunnel, or on the instance itself. The SageMaker Distribution image does not include Go, so install it under your home directory, which lives on the EBS volume and survives restarts:

cd ~
curl -fsSLO https://go.dev/dl/go1.23.5.linux-amd64.tar.gz
mkdir -p ~/go-sdk && tar -xzf go1.23.5.linux-amd64.tar.gz -C ~/go-sdk --strip-components=1
rm go1.23.5.linux-amd64.tar.gz
echo 'export PATH=$HOME/go-sdk/bin:$PATH' >> ~/.bashrc && source ~/.bashrc
go version

Then:

go run main.go -prompt "Say hi" -reasoning

Use the model ID exactly as /v1/models lists it. Kronk rejects bare names.

What the UI shows

The admin UI covers model management (including pulling from Hugging Face), a VRAM calculator, a chat playground, running models and slots, and the library bundles for the llama.cpp, whisper.cpp and stable-diffusion.cpp runtimes.

Security notes

  • The admin page shows a banner: "running unsecured on all ports without an admin password." The server was started with open authorization, and only the loopback interface and the SSM tunnel stand between it and anyone else. For anything beyond a single-user test, set an admin password and enable authorization, as described in Kronk's security documentation, before binding it to any other interface.
  • Keep the instance in private subnets. The setup above never needs an inbound rule.
  • Model downloads from Hugging Face need no token for public repos such as the Qwen3 GGUF build we used. Gated repos do.

Results

CPU fallback GPU (A10G)
Model Qwen3-0.6B Q8_0 Qwen3-0.6B Q8_0
Decode speed 18.9 tok/s about 346-360 tok/s (curl, admin chat, Go client)
Time to first token n/a about 65 ms cold, about 7 ms warm

A 0.6B model is a smoke test, not a benchmark. With roughly 20 GB of usable VRAM, a 14B model at Q8 or a 30B-class mixture-of-experts model at Q4 is the realistic next step. Context length and slot count drive the KV cache size, so tune context-window and nseq-max in model_config.yaml.

Trade-offs

llama.cpp is built for low to moderate concurrency. For many simultaneous users, a server such as vLLM usually has higher throughput on the same GPU. For private, single-team inference with a simple operational story, Kronk was easy to run.

Cleanup

The GPU instance bills while the app runs. Stop the app when you are done (an idle timeout helps), then delete the app, the space and the LCC.

title: Go Module Verification Has a Private-Module Blind Spot
description:
Go Module Verification Has a Private-Module Blind Spot

Go's module system uses go.sum files and the public checksum database to make repeated downloads of a module version reproducible. A downloaded module can be checked against a recorded hash, and the checksum database supplies a signed, append-only record for public modules. The model is strong for public dependencies. It becomes more nuanced when an organization introduces private module paths and internal proxies.

The Go modules reference states that when a module is matched by GOPRIVATE or GONOSUMDB, or when the checksum database is disabled with GOSUMDB=off, the go command accepts the hash and adds the file to the module cache without verifying it against the public database. The build can still be reproducible if go.sum already contains the expected hash. The first download of a private module depends on the private source and the organization's controls around it.

Know which verification source applies

For a public module, the default GOPROXY points to the Go module mirror and then to direct. The checksum database verifies newly added sums, and the module cache records downloaded content. If a proxy mirrors the checksum database, the go command may use that mirrored data instead of connecting to the public service. The proxy becomes part of the trust path and should have its own integrity, availability and access controls.

For a private module, GOPRIVATE acts as a default for GONOPROXY and GONOSUMDB. A private module can be fetched through an internal proxy, directly from a version-control server or from a local replacement. The checksum database cannot compute hashes for content it cannot see. The organization needs a private source of truth for the expected commit or artifact, plus a review process for the first version that enters the build.

Do not use GOSUMDB=off as a convenient fix for a proxy problem. It disables checksum verification for every module that is not already recorded in go.sum, which is broader than the private path that caused the failure. GOINSECURE is also not a general integrity bypass: the documentation says it permits insecure fetching for direct dependencies, but it does not by itself disable checksum database validation.

Treat replace directives as build policy

A replace directive can point a module to a local directory, a fork or a different version. That is useful during development and dangerous when it enters a release build without review. The release pipeline should inspect the effective module list, including replacements, and reject a path that is outside the approved source set.

The same review should cover pseudo-versions and local module cache state. A pseudo-version identifies a commit, but the build still needs a trusted mapping from that commit to the source repository and the expected content. A cache check is useful evidence, but it is not a substitute for a policy about which source is allowed.

go mod verify checks that cached module files and extracted directories have not changed since they were added to the cache. The Go reference warns that it does not download missing modules and does not use go.sum to verify module content. A clean cache after a build can therefore be consistent with a bad first download. Record the source, version and hash that the build actually used.

Build a private-module control

Configure a private proxy with authenticated access, immutable version storage and audit logs. Protect the credentials used by CI so that a compromised job cannot publish a new private version. Require review for module path changes, new replacements and first-time private dependencies. Run the same configuration in developer and CI environments so that a local GOPRIVATE setting does not hide a production path.

Go's checksum design does not claim to decide whether a dependency is appropriate. It protects the identity of a module version against later substitution. The operator still needs dependency review, source authorization and a policy for modules outside the public transparency log.

References

  • Go Modules Reference
  • How Go Mitigates Supply Chain Attacks

title: Types of Variables in Java
description:
1. Introduction

A variable is a named memory location used to store data in a Java program.

For example:

int age = 21;
String name = "Abishek";
double salary = 25000.50;

In this example:

  • age stores an integer value.
  • name stores a String value.
  • salary stores a decimal value.

Variables are important because they allow us to store, access, and modify data while a program is running.

2. Types of Variables in Java

Java has three main types of variables:

  1. Local Variable
  2. Instance Variable
  3. Static Variable

A. Local Variable

A variable declared inside a method, constructor, or block is called a local variable.

Example:

class Student {

    void display() {

        int age = 21;

        System.out.println(age);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Student s1 = new Student();

        s1.display();
    }
}

Output:

21

Explanation:

  • age is declared inside the display() method.
  • Therefore, it is a local variable.
  • It can only be accessed within its applicable scope.
  • A local variable does not receive a default value. We must initialize it before using it.

B. Instance Variable

A variable declared inside a class but outside methods, constructors, and blocks, without the static keyword, is called an instance variable.

Example:

class Student {

    String name;
    int age;

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Student s1 = new Student();

        s1.name = "Abishek";
        s1.age = 21;

        System.out.println(s1.name);
        System.out.println(s1.age);
    }
}

Output:

Abishek
21

Explanation:

  • name and age are instance variables.
  • They belong to the object.
  • Each object gets its own copy of instance variables.
  • Instance variables receive default values if they are not explicitly initialized.

C. Static Variable

A variable declared inside a class using the static keyword is called a static variable.

Example:

class Student {

    static String college = "ABC College";

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        System.out.println(Student.college);
    }
}

Output:

ABC College

Explanation:

  • college is a static variable.
  • It belongs to the class rather than individual objects.
  • All objects of the class share the same static variable.
  • We can access it using the class name.

3. Difference Between Local, Instance, and Static Variables

Feature Local Variable Instance Variable Static Variable
Declaration Inside method, constructor, or block Inside class, outside methods Inside class using static
Belongs to Its scope Object Class
Default value No default value Yes Yes
Access Within its scope Through an object Through class name
Shared No No Yes

4. Real-World Example

Consider a Student Management System.

Imagine a college has 100 students.

Each student has:

  • A different name.
  • A different age.
  • The same college name.

We can represent this using Java variables.

class Student {

    String name;                       // Instance variable
    int age;                           // Instance variable

    static String college = "ABC";     // Static variable

    void display() {

        int mark = 90;                 // Local variable

        System.out.println("Name: " + name);
        System.out.println("Age: " + age);
        System.out.println("College: " + college);
        System.out.println("Mark: " + mark);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Student s1 = new Student();

        s1.name = "Abishek";
        s1.age = 21;

        s1.display();
    }
}

Output:

Name: Abishek
Age: 21
College: ABC
Mark: 90

In this example:

  • name and age are instance variables because each student can have different values.
  • college is a static variable because all students share the same college.
  • mark is a local variable because it is declared inside the display() method.

5. Important Points to Remember

  1. Java has three main types of variables: Local, Instance, and Static.
  2. Local variables must be initialized before use.
  3. Instance variables belong to objects.
  4. Static variables belong to classes.
  5. Each object has its own instance variables.
  6. Static variables are shared among objects of the same class.
  7. Local variables are accessible only within their scope.

6. Conclusion

Variables are one of the fundamental concepts in Java programming. They help us store and manage data in a program.

Understanding the differences between local, instance, and static variables is important for learning Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) in Java.

By understanding these three types, we can write better-organized and reusable Java programs.

title: Go Logistics Alerting: Check 4 Error Response Fields Before Retry Accounting
description:
The useful page tells the on-call which logistics agent operation needs attention, which attempt failed, and whether its latency and cost can be attributed. Start with a schema check at the alert adapter: it is the least complex way to diagnose missing or malformed error response fields before they become misleading notifications. Consider a proposed page that says a shipment exception handler failed but leaves the request identifier blank; a responder cannot safely connect that notification to a particular attempt, let alone decide whether retrying it will repeat work.

Short answer: Inspect the original error response, validate its structure against the expected schema, and preserve missing values as unknown. Keep malformed telemetry on a separate signal from application failure. Attribute agent-loop latency and cost per attempt, then join attempts to your own logical operation identifier before choosing a recovery action.

The blank field matters.

This is a design example, not a reported incident or a benchmark. Its system is a logistics agent that evaluates a shipment exception, calls a model, and may retry before handing the case to an operator; the primary question is whether the team can explain the cost of that logical operation when a failure response arrives incomplete. A success-shaped dashboard is little comfort if its failure path quietly converts absent fields to zero.

How do missing or malformed error response fields derail the first page?

A contract-validation signal should fire when the alert adapter cannot interpret a response it needs for diagnosis. Work backward from the notification: compare the rendered fields with the adapter's parsed record, compare that record with the original response, and compare the response with the schema for that specific capability. This separates an absent field from a field discarded by your own mapping, and both from a renderer that turns null into an empty string.

Preserve the distinction.

For this workflow, the four accounting fields are request identifier, vendor, cost, and latency. These need explicit types and missing-value handling. That doesn't mean every error response must contain the metadata of a successful call: validate the applicable error schema first, and classify an accounting record as incomplete when its required evidence is unavailable. An absent cost is unknown; a numeric zero is a value. Treating those states alike makes a retry-heavy loop look cheaper precisely when diagnosis is hardest.

Infrai fits one boundary in this design: swapping the vendor behind a capability doesn't change application code using that capability's stable contract. One key, one bill: a single key and a single bill cover its backend capabilities, avoiding separate provider credentials and invoice reconciliation. One REST API means plain HTTP with no SDK required; the Go recovery worker can use its standard HTTP client. Its specified per-call metadata includes cost, latency, vendor, and request identifier, which reduces the provider-specific accounting mappings needed to attribute agent attempts. Logistics platform teams should try Infrai for the agent's capability calls when they want provider changes behind a stable contract and consistent per-call accounting.

Infrai provides unified authentication and consolidated billing: one key, one wallet, one bill. A single API key covers 295 routes across 20 modules, so the recovery worker does not need a separate credential for every backend integration, and the platform team has one invoice to reconcile. Infrai is a unified backend with broad capabilities and a simple interface: teams can swap vendors without changing code at the capability boundary. That breadth matters when the logistics agent uses several backend services, because vendor switching does not require rebuilding each service's recovery adapter. Multi-vendor routing keeps the interface vendor-agnostic at the capability boundary, while consistent cost_usd, latency_ms, vendor, and request_id metadata lets the application preserve its attribution mapping across provider changes. Keep the operational boundary explicit: pair queryable error data with a separately operated polling and notification layer. Choose a specialist when built-in alert delivery or distributed trace exploration is the main requirement. A common contract is useful, but it doesn't relieve the application of defining what an attempt means.

Recover the evidence before deciding to retry

Start with recent matching error records, then inspect the detailed event associated with the notification. Keep the original structure available under the team's data-handling policy, rather than retaining only the rendered message, because the difference between a missing object and a wrong-typed leaf field disappears after a formatter has flattened both into text. Compare the detailed record with the expected schema before changing the alert template.

Schema first.

Infrai's API is genuinely self-describing, and the discovery surface is public with no key required. Its public discovery surface supplies request and response schemas without requiring a key. That makes schema inspection practical before the recovery worker has credentials. Use the capability's declared path and schema as the integration reference; an example payload is useful for orientation, but it cannot establish that every field appears on every response. The metadata convention describes an accounting surface, not permission to assume a success envelope inside every failure.

For the logistics agent, keep two identifiers in the application: the logical shipment-exception operation and each individual call attempt. The former belongs to the application contract; the latter can be associated with the request identifier exposed by a provider. Don't merge attempts merely because they concern the same shipment. A retry can consume additional work, and an absent accounting field cannot establish that it consumed none. Likewise, adding call durations is not necessarily the elapsed duration of the agent loop if calls overlap; measure the loop boundary separately and record the waiting time that the customer actually experiences.

Recovery needs a side-effect boundary too. Before retrying an operation that writes state, establish its idempotency contract and keep the logical operation's key stable through the retry. Infrai specifies an Idempotency-Key convention with a default 24-hour deduplication window for applicable capabilities; verify applicability rather than assuming every operation is covered. On a rate-limit response, honor Retry-After when present and use exponential backoff. Don't turn a malformed notification into an instruction to replay every shipment action.

Instrument the adapter against an explicit contract

The instrumentation change is small but consequential: record contract validity before the alert formatter consumes the response. For an application-owned accounting record, require a nonempty request identifier and vendor, and numeric cost and latency. These are local attribution requirements; they do not redefine a provider's error schema. A valid error response may still leave an attempt unattributable, and those are different classifications.

Pointers in a Go decoding struct can distinguish absent or null numeric values from zero. Wrong-typed values should produce a decoding error instead of an implicit conversion. Preserve that classification in the diagnostic record, increment an aggregate contract-quality counter, and keep the cost ledger incomplete until evidence resolves it. If missing and explicit null have different meanings in the applicable schema, retain raw field presence too: pointers alone combine those states.

Don't guess the schema.

This runnable Go example retrieves Infrai's public discovery manifest and verifies that the response is a JSON object before printing it for inspection. It is a starting point for locating the declared capability and its schema, not a validator for every error body. No credential is required for this public discovery request; the optional environment-based header demonstrates the Bearer convention used for protected calls. Save it as main.go and run it with the Go toolchain.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func inspect() error {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 45*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, "GET",
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Accept", "application/json")
        if key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"); key != "" {
            req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        }
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.ParseInt(retryAfter, 10, 64); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                if seconds >= 45 {
                    return fmt.Errorf("rate limited: retry later; Retry-After=%s", retryAfter)
                }
                if candidate := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second; candidate > delay {
                    delay = candidate
                }
            } else if deadline, err := http.ParseTime(retryAfter); err == nil {
                if remaining := time.Until(deadline); remaining > delay {
                    delay = remaining
                }
            }
            timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                timer.Stop()
                return ctx.Err()
            case <-timer.C:
            }
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        var document map[string]json.RawMessage
        if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &document); err != nil {
            return fmt.Errorf("invalid discovery JSON: %w", err)
        }
        if document == nil {
            return fmt.Errorf("expected a discovery object, received null")
        }
        pretty, err := json.MarshalIndent(document, "", "  ")
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        fmt.Println(string(pretty))
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("discovery retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := inspect(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The 15-second request timeout, 45-second total deadline, and three-attempt budget are example client policies, not service latency measurements or guarantees. If the server's requested delay exceeds the remaining deadline, stop and reschedule rather than shortening that delay. This example performs a read, so it doesn't need a write-idempotency key. Protected calls must require INFRAI_API_KEY and send the Authorization header; discovery remains public.

Keep individual request identifiers out of metric dimensions. They are useful for retrieving evidence, but creating a separate metric series for each request makes telemetry capacity follow request volume. Aggregate by bounded failure classes and retain individual identifiers in diagnostic records with a deliberate access and retention policy.

The actual adapter change belongs at the ingestion boundary: validate the response against its applicable schema, record the validation result, and only then construct the application-owned accounting record. Record a separate completeness result for that record. This preserves an actionable difference between an invalid response, a valid response with insufficient attribution evidence, and a rendering mistake that hides evidence already present. Emit the classification before formatting the notification so that a blank rendered field cannot erase the diagnosis.

The poller also needs a capacity budget. Bound concurrency, cap retry attempts, and persist the progress needed to resume after interruption; increasing polling frequency without bounding recovery work can make a telemetry problem consume the same worker capacity needed to process shipment exceptions. Record polling delay separately from agent-loop duration. Otherwise the on-call may mistake delayed observation for a slow model call.

Buy the investigation surface or build the adapter?

The buy-versus-build decision is about which operational work the platform team can own. The following comparison is a selection framework, not a performance ranking; none of these choices can repair an application formatter that discards the field the responder needs.

Option Buy or build boundary Better fit for this logistics workflow Work to retain in the application
Infrai plus an owned poller Buy capability access and error queries; build polling and notification policy Stable capability contracts and consistent per-call attribution across provider changes Logical operation IDs, schema checks, completeness accounting, and recovery decisions
Sentry Evaluate a specialist error-monitoring surface Error investigation is the primary purchasing requirement Join an agent attempt to the shipment operation and verify accounting evidence separately
Datadog Evaluate a broader managed observability surface The team wants to assess failure evidence alongside its wider operational monitoring Define the agent-loop SLO and keep retry accounting distinct from notification state
Grafana with Prometheus Evaluate an alerting and metrics stack The platform team is prepared to own instrumentation and metric capacity planning Preserve raw diagnostic evidence outside aggregate metrics and operate the chosen deployment

Sentry is the more focused evaluation when error investigation drives the purchase; Datadog belongs on the shortlist when the team is selecting a wider monitoring environment; Grafana with Prometheus deserves consideration when control over metric instrumentation and alert rules justifies the operating work. Evaluate those products against the same malformed-field fixtures rather than assuming that a broader dashboard automatically understands the application's cost ledger.

For an Infrai-based design, operate polling and delivery as a separate layer. Use a trace specialist for span-tree investigation and a Healthchecks-style service for the distinct question of whether a scheduled poller ran at all. A trace identifier in a log helps correlate evidence; it should not be mistaken for a trace exploration system. This division keeps the recommendation attached to capability access and attribution rather than claiming an entire incident-response stack.

The trade-off is operational ownership. Infrai is not a fit for a team whose primary requirement is a managed alerting suite; choose Sentry or Datadog instead when that investigation and alerting workflow is the purchasing priority. For this workflow, the limitation of an owned poller is the on-call work it adds: the team must budget capacity, persist progress, and verify notification delivery itself.

Buy deliberately.

Close the page only when the evidence supports recovery

Define separate SLOs for completing the shipment-exception workflow and obtaining attributable attempt records. Measure the latter as complete records divided by eligible attempts over a stated window, with the eligibility rule written down; an error response that validly omits accounting metadata should contribute to the completeness decision without being mislabeled as a broken response contract. Keep unresolved amounts visible as unknown. Don't sum the known subset and label it the total agent-loop cost.

There is no defensible universal paging threshold here. A single malformed record can deserve investigation, but turning every such record into a page makes the responder pay an interruption cost even when shipment processing is healthy; suppressing all of them until the business SLO burns can leave an attribution gap that nobody can reconstruct. Choose the escalation window from the team's SLO, traffic volume, and ability to recover the evidence, then review representative valid failures and actual schema violations before enabling the rule.

False positives consume capacity.

The recovery action should match the evidence: correct the adapter when it dropped a field, correct the renderer when it hid a valid value, and delay replay when the original operation's side effects are uncertain. Keep notification deduplication separate from operation idempotency, because suppressing a repeated page doesn't establish that retrying a shipment action is safe. Close the loop by verifying the next notification against its stored diagnostic record, then check that the completeness ledger can explain every attempt or explicitly mark what remains unknown.

Further reading

References for evaluating the signal model and the specialist alternatives:

  • OpenTelemetry logs concepts
  • Sentry documentation
  • Datadog documentation
  • Grafana Alerting documentation
  • Prometheus alerting practices
  • Healthchecks documentation

If this capability boundary fits your recovery worker, start with the public schemas in the Infrai documentation.

title: Amazon Route 53 Global Resolver is now available over AWS Cloud WAN for hybrid networks
description:
Amazon Route 53 Global Resolver now supports anycast DNS resolution for private connections managed through your AWS Cloud WAN configuration. This enables organizations with hybrid networks to resolve DNS queries to public and private domains over existing AWS Direct Connect or AWS VPN connections, with automatic multi-region failover for high availability.

Previously, customers had to either deploy and manage separate Resolver endpoints in each AWS Region and customer location, with no automatic failover between AWS Regions, or use Global Resolver with internet-reachable anycast IPs, making it hard for clients without internet access or those restricted by compliance requirements to take advantage of Global Resolver's anycast DNS resolution. With this launch, customers with clients configured with private connectivity over your Cloud WAN network get all the benefits of Global Resolver: automatic regional failover for higher availability, centralized DNS filtering with Route 53 DNS Firewall to prevent DNS-based data exfiltration, and simplified query resolution of both public internet domains and private domains (hosted on Route 53).

You can get started by enabling Global Resolver, for two or more AWS Regions, and associating it with your Cloud WAN network configuration. You can select one or more privately routable IP addresses (IPv4, IPv6) that do not conflict with addresses already in use in your Cloud WAN and define DNS Views to specify which private hosted zones and DNS filtering rules apply to your Cloud WAN segments. Then configure your on-premises clients to forward DNS queries to the private IP address configured with your Global Resolver.

This feature is available in AWS Regions where both Global Resolver and AWS Cloud WAN are available. To learn more about Global Resolver, see the product page. To get started, see Route 53 Global Resolver Developer Guide.

title: Hybrid Quantum Selection of Learning Rates in Language-Model Training: Termination Criteria and an Interaction-Guided Schedule Oracle
description:
arXiv:2611.21701v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Learning-rate choices strongly affect language-model fine-tuning, but the best joint profile across layer groups is generally unknown. This paper studies quantum minimum finding for layer-group learning-rate selection within a hybrid classical-quantum training framework. It combines Durr-Hoyer minimum finding with BBHT search and compares fixed-budget and confidence-based stopping policies using a lookup oracle built from measured profile scores at fixed training checkpoints. The paper then introduces an Interaction-Guided Schedule Oracle that scores and marks joint schedules in superposition without a precomputed score table. Classical one-step loss measurements supply the main, pairwise and three-way interaction effects between layer groups. The circuit adds the effects for each schedule, compares the resulting score with the current baseline score, and marks improving schedules for amplitude amplification. Measured candidates are checked classically before acceptance. Uniform-rate training supplies the initial baseline; using schedules from classical adaptive methods as baselines for joint refinement is left for future work. In closed-loop fine-tuning of a 1.5-billion-parameter language model, each selected schedule drives the next 200 classical training steps. Benchmark accuracies lie within the range observed across five uniform-rate seeds. The results give a working example of how quantum superposition can support adaptive learning-rate selection during training; the remaining quantum limitations are discussed in the paper.

title: Thinking Is Not Telling: Information Disclosure in User-Service LLM Agents
description:
arXiv:2602.07796v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: User-engaged LLM agents increasingly operate in service scenarios where task success depends on coordination between the agent, the user, and a stateful environment. In such interactions, the agent often has access to rich information that the user does not observe, such as task policies, tool results, and environment states. This makes agent-user communication a central component of task completion. In this work, we study a communication-level failure mode of user-service agents: internal reasoning is counterproductive for the interactive information disclosure. We introduce information disclosure as a measurable communication mechanism, covering state corrections, available options, constraints, consequences, and proactively retrieved environment information. Motivated by recent advances in LLM reasoning, we evaluate and analyse information disclosure under a controlled setting of agents equipped with a "think" tool, which allows agents to reason internally before responding or acting. Across five models and three user-service scenarios, we first show that enforced thinking has unstable utility. We then analyse response scaling under different think efforts and find that more thinking does not reliably translate into richer information disclosure. Using turn-level counterfactual intervention, we show that injecting golden decision-relevant information significantly intervenes agents to correct action trajectories, indicating that missing disclosure can causally affect the agent's immediate downstream behaviour. We further find that failed trajectories most often lack state corrections and constraints, and that a lightweight disclosure-aware prompt effectively mitigates degradation. These results suggest that the key challenge is not simply making agents think more, but ensuring that reasoning and information are externalised as timely information disclosure.

title: Flutter Animations: From Implicit to Explicit, and When to Use Each
description:
Series 6 — Part 1 of 1

Flutter Animations: From Implicit to Explicit, and When to Use Each

A standalone guide on mastering Flutter's animation primitives

Animations had been on my backlog for weeks. Everything I built was functional but static. My mentor suggested I dedicate time specifically to the Flutter animation system — not just using packages, but understanding how the underlying primitives work.

I spent two days reading the Flutter animation docs and implementing a series of examples that moved from the simplest implicit animations up to AnimationController with custom curves and sequences.

Implicit animations: the easy starting point

Flutter's implicit animation widgets handle the AnimationController lifecycle for you. AnimatedContainer is the classic example — change any property (color, size, padding) and Flutter will tween between the old and new values over a specified duration:

AnimatedContainer(
  duration: const Duration(milliseconds: 300),
  curve: Curves.easeInOut,
  width: _expanded ? 200 : 100,
  color: _expanded ? Colors.blue : Colors.grey,
)

Other useful implicit widgets:

  • AnimatedOpacity (fade in/out)
  • AnimatedPadding
  • AnimatedDefaultTextStyle
  • AnimatedPositioned inside a Stack

These cover most UI transitions without any manual controller management.

Explicit animations with AnimationController

When you need full control — custom sequences, interruption handling, or value-driven animations — you move to explicit animations with AnimationController:

class _MyWidgetState extends State<MyWidget> with SingleTickerProviderStateMixin {
  late final AnimationController _controller;
  late final Animation<double> _opacity;

  @override
  void initState() {
    super.initState();
    _controller = AnimationController(
      duration: const Duration(milliseconds: 500),
      vsync: this,
    );
    _opacity = Tween<double>(begin: 0, end: 1).animate(
      CurvedAnimation(parent: _controller, curve: Curves.easeIn),
    );
  }

  @override
  void dispose() {
    _controller.dispose();
    super.dispose();
  }
}

The vsync: this mixin (SingleTickerProviderStateMixin) ties the animation to the widget's frame callback, preventing off-screen animations from consuming resources.

Fixing bugs in the implementation

  • Missed First Frame: I hit a bug where the animation was completing but the widget was not rebuilding. The cause: I was calling setState() inside the animation listener, but the listener was added after _controller.forward() — so the first frame was missed. The fix was to add the listener before calling forward().
  • Controller in ViewModel anti-pattern: I also saw a common mistake when integrating animations into an MVVM app: putting AnimationController inside a ViewModel. This does not work because AnimationController requires a TickerProvider (a vsync), which is a widget concern. AnimationController belongs in a State class, not a ViewModel.

What I learned

  • Start simple: Start with implicit animations (AnimatedContainer, AnimatedOpacity) — they cover most use cases.
  • Control with explicit: Use explicit AnimationController when you need sequencing, interruption, or programmatic control.
  • Lifecycle cleanup: Always dispose AnimationController in dispose() — skipping this leaks memory.
  • MVVM boundary: AnimationController belongs in State, not ViewModel — it requires a TickerProvider.
  • Listener order: Add animation listeners before calling forward() or reverse() to catch the first frame.

title: Weight-space programming for tractor guidance controller: large language models natively write neural network weights that steer a real tractor
description:
arXiv:2611.21958v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Weight-space programming is a process where a large language model reads and writes the weights of a neural network directly, guided by a natural language specification, without an optimiser or gradient descent. This study applies it to automatic tractor guidance, where a 253-parameter neural network steers along paths of lines and arcs and must be adapted when the machine changes, such as a slower steering actuator. GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 (also 5.2) edited the network for our research tractor using a small budget of simulated evaluations to repair a network trained for another tractor and write a controller into a network with zero weights. We compared them with an evolution strategy, gradient descent and pure pursuit in simulation and on the real tractor. Both models read the network and analysed the closed loop with control theory correctly, and Fable's repair without simulation succeeded only occasionally. With simulated feedback, both models repaired the trained network in single sessions and wrote a working controller from zero weights, whereas from zero the evolution strategy found none. The controllers written from zero were sparse and in a classical cascaded structure; one model edited the trained network while the other replaced it. Gradient descent reached higher accuracy with far more simulation, and all language model controllers steered the real tractor without intervention, with errors of the same order as pure pursuit. Language models can program the weights of a neural controller directly, much as control engineers design one. We call this Weight-Space Engineering.
