title: Shifting Five Percent Should Not Be a Leap of Faith: Canary Traffic Between Clouds
description:
A canary release inside one cloud is a familiar exercise. Shift a small share of traffic, watch error rates and latency, promote or roll back. A canary that moves traffic between clouds is a different exercise, and treating it as the same one is how teams end up either too frightened to move anything, or moving everything at once because the small step never worked reliably.

The difference is not the percentage. Five percent between clouds crosses boundaries that five percent inside one provider never touches: a different load balancer, a different health model, often a different data path for the requests that follow the first one, and a rollback that has to work across the same boundaries in reverse. Designing for that, in advance, turns a leap of faith into a routine operation.

Start with where the decision is made

Traffic can be shifted in more places than most diagrams show, and each place has a different blast radius.

DNS weighting is the simplest lever and the bluntest. Records are cached by resolvers and clients for longer than the time to live suggests, some clients ignore it altogether, and a rollback through DNS is a waiting game rather than a switch. It works for coarse, slow moves between largely independent endpoints. It is a poor choice for a canary that needs to be reversed in minutes.

A global load balancer or traffic manager in front of both clouds gives a real switch: weights change in one place, new connections follow the new split quickly, and health based removal is automatic. The cost is that this layer becomes a critical dependency for both clouds, so its own health, limits, and failure behaviour need the same attention as the services behind it.

Routing the canary through an existing private interconnect or hub adds a third option: keep the public entry point fixed, and change where traffic goes after it arrives. That keeps client behaviour unchanged and makes the shift observable in one place, but it can add a detour. Measure the added latency before the canary, not during it, because a slow canary looks like a failing new version even when the code is fine.

Pick one decision point for a given move, write it down, and make sure everyone on the call knows which lever will be pulled and which levers will not be touched. Most failed canaries involve two levers changing at once and no way to tell which one caused the result.

A request is rarely the whole journey

Shifting the first request is easy to test. Shifting the session that follows is where cross cloud canaries break.

If a user lands on the new cloud for the first request and is sent back to the old cloud for the next one, because a session cookie points at a local store, a websocket reconnects to a different endpoint, or a file upload resumes against a different backend, the failure looks intermittent and user specific. It is neither. It is a locality problem.

Before any traffic moves, list what has to stay together: session state, uploaded files in progress, long lived connections, queued jobs started by the request, and callbacks from third parties that still point at the old address. For each item, decide whether it is shared between clouds, replicated with a known lag, or pinned so that a started journey finishes where it began. Pinning is underrated. For many services the safest canary rule is simple: new sessions may start on the new cloud, existing sessions finish on the old one, and nothing migrates mid flight.

The same question applies to data writes. If the canary writes to a local database that replicates back slowly, a rollback does not just move traffic, it strands the writes made during the canary window. Test that path deliberately: write during a trial shift, roll back, and confirm those records are visible and correct from the old side before calling the design ready.

Health has to mean the same thing in both places

Each cloud defines health in its own way, with its own probe interval, threshold, and view of what a healthy target is. During a canary those differences stop being trivia.

A target that flaps twice in the new cloud may be removed and returned automatically, swinging the effective traffic share well away from the planned five percent. A probe that checks a shallow status endpoint will report healthy while the deeper dependency, a database connection, an identity endpoint, a queue, is failing for real users. And if the two clouds report latency in different ways, the comparison that decides promotion is not a comparison at all.

Align three things before shifting anything. First, probe the same meaningful path in both clouds, ideally a lightweight request that exercises the real dependencies without creating real work. Second, set matching intervals and thresholds for the duration of the move, so removal behaviour is predictable. Third, agree in advance on the numbers that will decide the outcome: error rate, tail latency, and one business signal such as completed checkouts, finished jobs, or successful logins, each compared against the old cloud over the same window, not against a memory of last week.

Watch the split you actually have, not the split you set

A weight is an intention. The delivered split is what resolvers, connection reuse, retry behaviour, and a small number of very heavy clients actually produce. During a cross cloud canary, log the cloud that served each request at the entry point and report the real percentage alongside the configured one. A canary that was meant to be five percent but delivered thirty percent explains a lot of confusing results, including a capacity problem on a new cloud that was sized for five.

Retries deserve special attention here. A client that retries a failed request against the other cloud can turn a small error rate on the new side into duplicated work and a misleading success rate. Decide whether cross cloud retries are allowed during the move, and if they are, make them visible as retries in the logs rather than letting them blend into normal traffic.

Capacity follows the same logic. Size the new cloud for the share after next, not the first share. If the plan is five, then twenty five, then fifty percent, the canary should prove the path can carry the next step, or the promotion decision is being made on evidence that does not cover it.

Rollback is a traffic shift too

Rollback gets planned as a single sentence, move traffic back, and then discovered to be a project of its own. Write it as a procedure with the same care as the forward move: which lever changes, in what order, what happens to sessions started on the new cloud, what happens to data written there, and how long until the old cloud is carrying everything again, measured rather than assumed.

Then rehearse it at the smallest share. A rollback practised at five percent, in daylight, with notes taken, is worth far more than a confident rollback plan that has never run. Many teams find the rehearsal is where the real defects are: a missing route back, a health probe that prevents the old targets rejoining, a dashboard that only shows the new cloud. Finding those at five percent is the entire point of starting small.

A short checklist before the first shift

  1. One named decision point for the shift, and one named lever for rollback.
  2. A locality list covering sessions, uploads, long lived connections, jobs, and callbacks, each shared, replicated, or pinned.
  3. A write and read back test across the rollback boundary.
  4. Matching health probes, intervals, and promotion criteria in both clouds.
  5. Logging that reports the delivered traffic split, not only the configured weight.
  6. Capacity on the new cloud sized for the next step, not only the first.
  7. A rehearsed rollback at the smallest share, timed end to end.

None of this requires a new platform. It requires treating the space between clouds as part of the release, not as plumbing that will look after itself. Teams that design that space deliberately, with private connectivity, consistent routing, and one place to see both sides of a move, find that five percent really can be five percent, and that promoting it is a decision based on evidence rather than nerve. That is the kind of cross cloud connectivity work described at cloudverg.com, where VergMesh and VergRail are used to keep multi cloud paths consistent enough for moves like this to be routine.

A canary between clouds will never be as simple as a canary inside one cloud. It can, however, be just as calm, provided the traffic decision, the locality rules, and the way back are designed before the first percent moves.

title: FLARE: A Full-Lifecycle Dense Supervision Paradigm for Long-Horizon Coding Agents via Generative Reward Model
description:
arXiv:2609.23808v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: While test-time scaling enhances Large Language Model (LLM) agents in long-horizon software engineering (SWE), sparse binary rewards (Pass/Fail) create a severe credit assignment crisis and waste failed exploratory trajectories. Current trajectory optimization and scaling methods are costly and structurally limited, relying on heuristic state reuse without causal diagnosis or delayed scalar scoring without actionable online guidance. We propose FLARE (Full-Lifecycle Alignment and Reward Engine), a novel dense supervision paradigm driven by a lightweight Generative Reward Model (GRM). First, RADAR, an offline causal-aware diagnostic framework, extracts high-fidelity, hindsight-free supervision through causal-chain backtracking to distill a GRM providing real-time, step-level risk feedback. Second, FLARE uses this GRM to continuously optimize the agent across its entire lifecycle. During inference, FLARE acts as an Active Scaffold, autonomously intercepting high-risk generation steps for localized breakpoint re-execution, drastically reducing compute overhead. During post-training, the GRM's structured signals serve as process-supervised reranking scores for Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and step-level dense rewards for Reinforcement Learning (RL), mitigating policy collapse in sparse environments. Extensive evaluations show that FLARE establishes a new Pareto frontier across the agent lifecycle: FLARE (N=1) outperforms Global Rollout (N=5) with a 5x reduction in token consumption. Extending FLARE to training overcomes the sparse reward problem in long-horizon interactive tasks, delivering relative performance gains of 19.13% in SFT through process-aware data curation and a consistent 9.19% improvement in RL.

title: GP--RL--MPC: Uncertainty-Aware Reinforcement Learning-Augmented Model Predictive Control with Gaussian Process Postdecision State-Value Functions
description:
arXiv:2611.22038v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We propose Gaussian Process Reinforcement Learning-Augmented Model Predictive Control (GP--RL--MPC), which uses a learned critic as the MPC terminal penalty to account for costs beyond the prediction horizon. Gaussian process regression (GPR) enables data-efficient critic learning from limited, noisy rollouts within optimistic approximate policy iteration (OAPI), with soft updates mitigating policy chattering. A tunable risk coefficient weights GP epistemic uncertainty in the terminal cost, regulating sensitivity to uncertain critic predictions. The postdecision state formulation shifts disturbance averaging offline to account for aleatoric uncertainty from the terminal transition onward. Under matching objectives and admissible actions, a one-step horizon recovers greedy value-space RL. After fitting GP hyperparameters by exact marginal likelihood, we construct a sparse deterministic training conditional (DTC) posterior using inducing points selected by pivoted Cholesky (PC), reducing online evaluation costs as the training dataset grows. In a continuous stirred-tank reactor (CSTR) subject to exogenous disturbances, GP--RL--MPC with an appropriately selected risk coefficient and policy screening reduces the sum of squared errors (SSE) by an average of 80.52% relative to an otherwise matched baseline MPC across five random seeds (sample standard deviation: 3.48%).

title: Joint-ID: Transformer-based Joint Image Enhancement and Depth Estimation for Underwater Environments
description:
arXiv:2611.22212v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Underwater imaging is a challenging task due to factors such as scattering, absorption, and turbulence, which degrade image quality and limit visibility. In this paper, we propose a novel approach for enhancing underwater images that leverages the benefits of joint learning for simultaneous image enhancement and depth estimation. We introduce Joint-ID, a transformer-based neural network that can obtain high-perceptual image quality and depth information from raw underwater images. Our approach formulates a multi-modal objective function that addresses invalid depth, lack of sharpness, and image degradation based on color and local texture. We design an end-to-end training pipeline that enables joint restoration and depth estimation in a shared hierarchical feature space. Additionally, we propose a synthetic dataset with various distortions and scene depths for multi-task learning. We evaluate Joint-ID on synthetic and standard datasets, as well as real underwater images with diverse spectra and harsh turbidity, demonstrating its effectiveness for underwater image enhancement and depth estimation. Furthermore, we demonstrate the ability of Joint-ID to perform feature matching and saliency detection for visually guided underwater robots. Our proposed method has the potential to improve the visual perception of underwater environments and benefit applications such as oceanography and underwater robotics. Supplements are available at: https://sites.google.com/view/joint-id/home

title: Stop Endorsing Java Developers. Start Publishing Their Failure Receipts.
description:
What if the best endorsement of a Java developer was not a compliment, but a bug they successfully defeated?

Let me ask you something.

If I write on LinkedIn:

"I am an excellent Java developer with strong Spring Boot and Microservices experience."

Would you believe me?

What if 10 colleagues endorse that statement?

Would that prove I can handle a production issue at 2 AM when a critical API suddenly starts timing out?

Probably not.

I believe the software engineering industry needs a different way to recognise developers.

Not another certificate.

Not another skill badge.

Not another collection of LinkedIn endorsements.

I propose something different: The Failure Receipt.

  1. What is a Failure Receipt?

A Failure Receipt is a technical record of a real engineering problem solved by a developer and independently reviewed by another engineer.

Think of it as a technical endorsement backed by evidence.

Every receipt contains five things:

The failure: What was broken?
The investigation: How did the developer identify the root cause?
The solution: What did they change and why?
The verification: Which tests prove the fix works?
The reviewer: Who independently reviewed the solution?

For example:

A Spring Boot application starts responding slowly when 500 concurrent requests arrive.

Instead of simply claiming:

"I am good at performance optimisation."

The developer produces a Failure Receipt.

Problem: API response latency increased under load.
Investigation: Identified inefficient database access.
Solution: Improved query execution and introduced appropriate indexing.
Verification: Compared benchmark results before and after the change.
Review: Another Java engineer independently reviews the implementation.

Now the endorsement has a story, evidence and technical reasoning.

  1. Why should Java developers care?

Java developers work on systems where reliability matters.

Consider these real engineering situations:

A memory leak in a long-running application.
A deadlock caused by concurrent execution.
An inefficient Hibernate query.
A failing Kafka consumer.
A slow Spring Boot REST endpoint.
An unexpected transaction rollback.

A list of technologies on a CV cannot demonstrate how someone handles these situations.

A documented engineering investigation can provide much stronger evidence.

  1. The Failure Receipt format

I propose the following open format:

yaml
failure_receipt:
developer: "Developer Name"
technology: "Java / Spring Boot"

incident:
problem: "API latency increased"

investigation:
root_cause: "Inefficient database access"

solution:
change: "Query optimisation"

verification:
test: "Automated regression test"
benchmark: "Before-and-after measurements"

independent_review:
reviewer: "Reviewer Name"
status: "Reviewed"

This is a conceptual example, not a real production incident.

The important principle is that every claim should be traceable to evidence.

Confidential company information should never be published without permission.

  1. My proposed five-level recognition model

I would introduce five recognition levels:

Level 1 – Bug Hunter

Identifies and reproduces a technical problem.

Level 2 – Root Cause Investigator

Demonstrates an understanding of why the problem occurred.

Level 3 – Solution Engineer

Implements and tests an appropriate solution.

Level 4 – Reliability Contributor

Demonstrates measurable improvements in reliability or performance.

Level 5 – Engineering Mentor

Helps other developers understand and solve similar problems.

These are proposed community recognition levels, not formal professional certifications.

  1. Imagine a developer's public profile

Instead of displaying:

Java: 99 endorsements
Spring Boot: 85 endorsements
Microservices: 72 endorsements

Imagine displaying:

4 independently reviewed debugging cases.
3 verified performance improvements.
2 architecture decisions reviewed by senior engineers.
5 open-source problem-solving contributions.

That tells a much more meaningful professional story.

  1. An invitation to the Java community

I want to explore this concept with other Java developers.

My first challenge is simple:

Can we replace one generic skill endorsement with one real engineering problem that someone has successfully solved?

If you are a Java developer, share:

The most interesting production-style bug you have solved.
How you identified the root cause.
What you changed.
How you proved your solution worked.

If you are a senior engineer, would you independently review and validate another developer's Failure Receipt?

Let's see whether we can create a more meaningful culture of technical recognition.

My belief:

A developer should not be recognised only for the technologies they know.

They should also be recognised for the problems they can solve, the engineering decisions they make and the knowledge they share.

Perhaps the future of developer endorsement is not another badge.

Perhaps it is a documented failure that became a successful engineering solution.

What do you think? Would you trust a developer's Failure Receipt more than a traditional skill endorsement?

title: Seeing What Still Holds: How Waiting Control Changes Cooperative Recovery
description:
arXiv:2611.22368v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Changing the holding reference during a fixed-duration wait can reverse the ranking of visual recovery methods. We introduce AuditEmbodied, a paired execution and trajectory evaluation framework that independently varies holding references and waiting duration while keeping recovery executors frozen. A 960-execution factorial on 20 initialization seeds compares CAD-feedback and landmark-based recovery from identical post-wait physical states within each holding and waiting condition. Protected completion requires successful recovery under the declared execution constraints. At a 1 s wait with registered wrist references, their protected completion counts change from 6/40 versus 19/40 under registered holding to 34/40 versus 22/40 under position-only holding. Trajectory analysis localizes the main separation to grasp formation: small observation-time target residuals precede large tracking errors. Joint diagnostics and controlled interventions characterize persistent tracking constraints. On fresh seeds, gradual position reanchoring improves CAD recovery's long-wait completion by 42.5 percentage points and reduces mean complete recovery time by 6.06 s relative to registered holding. Additional evaluations with pretrained policies, handover, and a mass-matched geometry characterize holding-reference sensitivity across executors and physical regimes. These findings establish holding reference as an explicit evaluation condition for comparing visual recovery performance.

title: From Perception to Simulation: Unveiling and Empowering Mental Spatial Dynamics in MLLMs
description:
arXiv:2611.22541v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Spatial reasoning is a fundamental component of world understanding for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). While existing research has advanced the perception of spatial relations in static scenes, the domain of dynamic spatial simulation remains relatively unexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce MentalGrid, a benchmark focused on spatial reasoning tasks that require models to simulate evolving spatial states without intermediate visual feedback. Extensive evaluation on our benchmark reveals a significant deficiency in the spatial simulation capabilities of existing models. Specifically, we find that performance is constrained by perceptual limitations in simple simulation scenarios and hindered by inadequate multi-step reasoning as complexity increases. To address these challenges, we propose a three-stage curriculum learning framework utilizing 16k specialized spatial reasoning samples. This approach yields SpatialWalker, which achieves a 33.8% average improvement over its base model, surpassing proprietary models like Gemini-3-Flash in spatial simulation. Furthermore, SpatialWalker demonstrates robust generalization, maintaining a 4.9% average gain on out-of-domain benchmarks, demonstrating the pivotal role of spatial simulation as a fundamental building block for broader spatial intelligence.

title: I Benchmarked Vexlo Cloud India Singapore and USA Nodes Against Railway ($5 vs $45 a month)
description:
Let us be real for a second. Usage-based cloud pricing sounds cute until your side project gets a tiny traffic spike and Railway or Render hits you with a $60 bill for vCPU seconds and outbound bandwidth.

I wanted to see if a flat-rate PaaS could actually hold up across global regions without throttling containers, so I benchmarked Vexlo Cloud over the weekend.

What I Tested

I deployed a Dockerized Node.js backend, a Next.js frontend, and a managed Redis plus Postgres stack. Here are the raw numbers from the run.

  • Cold GitHub Push to Live HTTPS took 42 seconds using their automated build pipeline.
  • Global Edge Regions include India (Mumbai) at 14ms regional ping, plus dedicated Singapore and USA nodes for international traffic.
  • Monthly Cost stayed locked at ₹149 a month via instant UPI in India, or $5 a month in USD and 16 other global currencies with zero egress overage fees.

The Bill Shock Math

If you want to see the exact price gap for your own stack, play around with the Railway Pricing Calculator and the Render Pricing Calculator they built. Seeing per-seat fees and RAM multipliers side by side makes it pretty obvious why indie devs are moving back to predictable flat-rate containers.

One Click Self Hosted Stacks

Instead of manually writing Traefik labels and SSL configs on a raw Ubuntu VPS, their 1-Click Open Source Templates let you deploy self-hosted tools in under a minute across India, Singapore, or USA servers. I tested Deploy n8n on Vexlo and Deploy Uptime Kuma and both spun up with persistent volumes and valid TLS automatically.

Backups are automated out of the box, the infra team already manages hosting for 1,500+ developers, and you can export your data anytime with zero lock-in. Check out their Developer Docs and Runbooks if you are debugging Docker OOM errors or Indian payment gateway webhooks.

title: Wrong Input, Wrong Threshold: Re-evaluating Adversarial Facial Privacy
description:
arXiv:2611.21923v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Published face-privacy methods report protection above 90% against black-box recognition models. That number comes from an evaluation protocol with two independent defects, reported in a measure that cannot size either one. The input is wrong: methods published since 2022 feed the network the whole photograph, or a detector's box, where deployed systems detect, align to a landmark template and crop. Re-scoring the same files through a realistic front end costs a standard transfer attack 56% of its dodging protection and a budget-allocating attack 7%, with no image regenerated. The measure is wrong: that loss is a difference of success rates, so it saturates, moving by 8.2x over a budget sweep while the effect beneath it moves by 1.34x. We therefore report the paired cosine shift, in which both thresholds cancel algebraically, so the input defect holds without committing to a calibration. Measured that way it is 2.2x and 10.7x larger on three unseen recognizers, and at matched budget it reverses the L-infinity transfer ranking: the one surveyed method that aligns at evaluation gains 0.18 where MI-FGSM loses 0.05. The cause is a resampling mismatch, not perturbation lost outside the crop; optimising through a differentiable alignment operator largely removes it, adding +24 to +58 points on unseen recognizers and a commercial system, with a residual on one of them. The thresholds are wrong: the four constants inherited since 2021 hold the false-accept rate near its nominal 1% on aligned crops but admit 2.3-5.4% on whole images, with an opposite-signed bias across dodging and impersonation, the two tasks reported side by side. Differentiable alignment and gallery scoring are not new: the first generation of this literature used both, and we show what dropping them cost.

title: Redict Is Deprecated: How to Migrate to Valkey When It Rejects Your dump.rdb
description:
Redict is deprecated. The announcement went up on November 17, 2026, and it says Redict 7.3.6 is the final release. That release from October 2025 patched CVE-2025-49844 and three other CVEs. Nobody will patch the next one.

If you run Redict, or you package it for a distro, you have to move. The announcement makes migrating to Valkey sound like a config rename. For at least one person in the Lobsters thread it wasn't: Valkey refused the existing dump.rdb, and the reason is a single integer in a header file. I'll go through why that happens and the one config line that should get you past it. Then come three migration paths (RDB copy, replication, Docker Compose) and what I'd do if you'd rather go back to Redis 8.

Why the Redict project gave up

Redict forked Redis OSS 7.2.4 in March 2024 under LGPL-3.0. The bet was that a copyleft fork would protect the community from the next licence rug-pull. The announcement admits the bet lost on two fronts. Valkey got the momentum, and Redis went back to an OSI licence when Redis 8 added AGPLv3 next to RSALv2 and SSPLv1 in May 2025.

The author, Drew DeVault, recommends Valkey and specifically advises against going back to Redis. The argument is that Redis still requires a contributor licence agreement, and a CLA is what makes a relicence possible in the first place. One commenter in the Lobsters thread credited antirez for the return to open source and hoped Redis had learned from its mistakes, but admitted to being pessimistic. The company already relicensed once, in March 2024, and it still holds a CLA that lets it do it again. For me that's reason enough to stay off Redis.

Valkey vs Redis 8 vs staying on Redict

Redict 7.3.6 Valkey 9.1 Redis 8.x
Licence LGPL-3.0 BSD-3-Clause AGPLv3 / RSALv2 / SSPLv1 (your pick)
Governance Independent fork, now deprecated Linux Foundation Redis Ltd., CLA required
Security fixes None after 7.3.6 3 years per minor (policy) Ongoing (8.4.2 was a security release)
Managed hosting Effectively none ElastiCache, Memorystore, Aiven, DigitalOcean Redis Cloud
Loads a Redict RDB Yes With rdb-version-check relaxed (see below) Not a supported path

The managed-hosting row decides it for a lot of teams. When AWS launched ElastiCache for Valkey it priced it 33% below the other engines on serverless and 20% below on node-based clusters, and existing reserved-node discounts carry over. Valkey 9.1 shipped in May 2026 with automatic TLS certificate reloading and database-level ACLs.

There's one case where I'd pick Redis 8: if you want the bundled query engine, JSON and time series modules, and AGPL is fine for your use.

Why a plain container swap to Valkey fails: RDB version 12

The announcement's container advice is to "pull the valkey container instead". In the Lobsters thread, legoktm reports that this failed for them because "the RDB formats were incompatible". Because they only used Redict as a cache, they deleted the dump and moved on.

The cause is in the headers. Redict's src/rdb.h has carried #define RDB_VERSION 12 since the 7.3.0 tag. Valkey's src/rdb.h says:

RDB 11 is the last open-source Redis RDB version, used by Valkey 7.x and 8.x.
RDB 12-79 are reserved for Redis non-compatible RDB formats

Valkey 9 numbers its own format 80 and up. When a stock Valkey sees version 12, it treats the file as foreign and refuses it. Valkey's own migration guide only promises compatibility with Redis OSS 7.2 and earlier, and a Redict dump isn't one of those.

The escape hatch is a config flag. Valkey 8.1 added rdb-version-check (#1604), and #2543, merged for 9.0, extended relaxed mode to foreign formats. In relaxed mode Valkey loads only the types and opcodes it understands and errors out on anything else. Redict 7.3.0's rdb.h defines the same object types (0 through 21) and opcodes that Valkey 9.0 reads, including the cluster-only SLOT_INFO opcode, so a Redict dump shouldn't contain anything relaxed mode has to reject. Per the shipped valkey.conf, the setting "also applies to replication and the RESTORE command", so it covers all three migration paths below. The default is strict.

I haven't seen anyone publicly confirm a full Redict-to-Valkey load in relaxed mode yet, so do it on a copy first.

Step 0: find out what you actually have 

redict-cli INFO server | grep -E 'redict_version|redis_version'
redict-cli INFO keyspace
redict-cli CONFIG GET dir
redict-cli CONFIG GET dbfilename
redict-cli CONFIG GET appendonly

Write down the key counts from INFO keyspace, because you'll compare them at the end. If the instance is a pure cache and you can survive a cold start, skip all of this: stop Redict, start Valkey on an empty data dir, and you're done. That's what legoktm did.

Path 1: RDB copy (short downtime, simplest)

Stop the writers first, then take a fresh snapshot:

redict-cli SAVE
cp /var/lib/redict/dump.rdb /var/backups/redict-dump.rdb

Move the config over, as the announcement suggests (/etc/redict.conf to /etc/valkey.conf), and add the line from the section above. Stop Redict, then copy the dump into Valkey's data dir (paths vary by distro, so check what CONFIG GET dir told you):

cp /var/lib/redict/dump.rdb /var/lib/valkey/dump.rdb
chown valkey:valkey /var/lib/valkey/dump.rdb

The config:

# valkey.conf
dir /var/lib/valkey
dbfilename dump.rdb
rdb-version-check relaxed
appendonly no

Leave appendonly no for the first start. The Valkey migration doc warns that with AOF enabled, the copied RDB won't be imported. Start Valkey and check:

valkey-cli INFO keyspace
valkey-cli INFO server | grep -E 'server_name|valkey_version'

Valkey still reports redis_version:7.2.4 for client compatibility, so check valkey_version to see what's really running. When the key counts match, run valkey-cli BGSAVE so the data is rewritten in Valkey's own format. If you use AOF, turn it on at runtime with valkey-cli CONFIG SET appendonly yes, which builds the AOF from the data already in memory. Flipping it to yes in the file and restarting can bring Valkey up from an empty AOF instead of your RDB. Run valkey-cli CONFIG REWRITE so appendonly yes is saved to valkey.conf, then edit the file to set rdb-version-check back to strict. That takes effect on the next restart.

Path 2: replication cutover (near-zero downtime)

Run Valkey next to Redict, with rdb-version-check relaxed in its config (plus masterauth if Redict has a password), and point it at Redict:

valkey-cli REPLICAOF redict-host 6379
valkey-cli INFO replication   # wait for master_link_status:up

Once the replica has caught up, pause writes in the app, check that master_repl_offset matches on both sides, and promote:

valkey-cli REPLICAOF NO ONE

Point the clients at Valkey and resume. The write pause only has to cover the offset check and the client switch. The Valkey docs warn that writes which reach the old primary during the switch can be lost, so don't skip the pause.

Path 3: the Docker Compose swap 

services:
  cache:
    # was: registry.redict.io/redict:7.3.6
    image: valkey/valkey:9.1
    command: ["valkey-server", "/usr/local/etc/valkey/valkey.conf"]
    volumes:
      - ./valkey.conf:/usr/local/etc/valkey/valkey.conf:ro
      - cache-data:/data
volumes:
  cache-data:

Keep the same named volume and the dump comes along. Make sure dir in the config matches the mount path and that valkey.conf has rdb-version-check relaxed for the first boot. Run docker compose exec cache valkey-cli INFO keyspace before you let traffic back in. If you don't add the flag, you get exactly what legoktm hit.

Going back to Redis 8 instead

Redis 8.2's rdb.h also says RDB_VERSION 12. That looks convenient, but the two version 12s were defined independently, and Redict's own compatibility page says switching back from Redict to Redis is not supported. I wouldn't trust a raw file copy here. Use a client-level copy (RIOT or RedisShake, both listed in Valkey's migration doc) against a staging Redis 8 first, then compare key counts. You'll also need to rename redict-cli to redis-cli in your scripts and swap the systemd units back.

The checklist

  • INFO keyspace counts recorded before you start
  • Backup copy of dump.rdb kept outside the data dir
  • rdb-version-check relaxed for the first load only, then back to strict
  • AOF off on first boot, then enabled with CONFIG SET appendonly yes once the data is loaded
  • Scripts updated for valkey-cli (although redis-cli still works against Valkey)
  • Distro packagers: ship a redict to valkey transition package so people get the upgrade instead of quietly running an unpatched server

I'm moving everything to Valkey, and the CLA is the reason I'm not considering Redis. If you think that's the wrong call, I'd like to hear the argument. What are you running in production now: Valkey, Redis 8, or something else like DragonflyDB or KeyDB? And did your Redict data survive the move?

Sources

  • Redict is deprecated and the Lobsters discussion
  • Redict 7.3.6 release notes
  • Redict compatibility with Redis
  • Redict rdb.h at 7.3.0, Valkey rdb.h, Redis 8.2 rdb.h
  • Valkey migration guide and valkey.conf (9.0)
  • Valkey PR #2543: relaxed RDB check for foreign formats
  • Valkey release and support policy
  • Valkey 9.1 release post
  • Redis: now available under AGPLv3 and antirez: Redis is open source again
  • Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey announcement

title: Layerwise Learning-Rate Scaling in Vision Networks: Effective-Rate Identification, Power-Mean Aggregation, and Budget Dependence
description:
arXiv:2611.21696v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Layerwise learning-rate scaling assigns different learning rates to different parts of a network. Although established in fine-tuning pretrained models, its effects in vision networks trained from scratch are commonly assessed by training each candidate recipe. We show that, in this setting, the rate-related component of a layerwise strategy is well summarized by an effective learning rate computable directly from its multiplier profile. Across matched-control comparisons, changes in test accuracy closely track changes in training loss (r = -0.996), which supports an optimization-progress explanation of the short-budget rate effect. Increasing the untuned base learning rate tenfold shifts the rate-matched contrast upward in all six tested architectures (p = 0.016) and increases the number of architectures in which a published discriminative schedule, excluded from model fitting, outperforms the uniform control from two to five of six (p = 0.031). Within the evaluated strategy space, a parameter-weighted power mean with exponent 0.35 (95% confidence interval [0.20, 0.50]) accounts for 42.6% of within-architecture variance, compared with 36.4% for the arithmetic mean. Ranking candidates by this scalar without training improves the selected candidate's mean percentile rank from the 26th to the 10th and reduces its mean accuracy shortfall relative to the best candidate from 3.70 to 1.12 points. The rate-related effect decays as the training budget increases; relative to tuned baselines, the overall strategy effect falls within the prespecified practical-equivalence margin in two of three architectures. A separate grouping-related contrast can persist at long budgets, although its direction and magnitude depend on the architecture.

title: FieldGuide: A Corpus Map for Token-Efficient Agentic Document Exploration
description:
arXiv:2611.21647v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generative AI agents can help journalists explore large document collections. But exploratory workflows can require substantial token use and time, especially when the task is broad and the relevant subquestions are not yet known. This paper introduces FieldGuide, an agent-facing corpus map that organizes a document collection into a topic hierarchy and exposes tools for corpus orientation, scoped search, and bounded reading. I evaluate FieldGuide on five journalistic document-exploration tasks using 38 Chicago Police Department public-records documents, comparing it with raw-file access and retrieval-augmented generation. Across the five tasks, FieldGuide used 27% fewer tokens and 41% less elapsed time than raw-file access; relative to RAG, it used 38% fewer tokens and 21% less elapsed time. An accuracy audit identified four minor issues in FieldGuide's responses, comparable to the other conditions. In blind ratings of generated reporting leads, FieldGuide's mean ratings were higher than RAG's and lower than the raw-file condition's. These descriptive results suggest that corpus orientation may reduce runtime token use and elapsed time without severe accuracy failures. They also motivate further study of whether selective access limits broad, cross-document discovery.

title: Kengele: an alarm for when an activist goes missing, that nobody can switch off
description:
When an activist disappears, the first hours matter.

In Kenya, the national human rights commission counted more than 80 abductions and enforced disappearances after the 2024 protests. In January 2025, several abducted young men were released within hours of public outcry. Kenyan activist Boniface Mwangi and Ugandan activist Agather Atuhaire were freed after their detention in Tanzania became public.

Speed of public pressure is what gets people out. Today the alarm depends on someone noticing and phoning around, over networks that can be watched or switched off. Uganda and Tanzania both shut down the internet around their elections.

So I'm building Kengele (Swahili for "bell"), an open-source alarm for when an activist goes missing.

Not for real use yet. Kengele is in the design and early build stage. Nobody should rely on it until an independent security review is done.

How it works

  1. Watch windows. Before a protest, a court visit or a risky trip, the activist sets check-ins, for example every 90 minutes from 2pm to 8pm.
  2. The alarm lives on the guardians' phones. Each check-in is a signed, encrypted message to 3 to 5 guardians (family, a lawyer, an organisation). If one doesn't arrive, every guardian's app raises the alarm on its own. Seizing the activist's phone stops nothing.
  3. Duress PIN. If someone forces the activist to check in, the duress PIN shows a normal screen and quietly raises the top-level alarm.
  4. Guardians confirm first. Nothing goes public until 2 of 3 guardians confirm. The alert text is locked under a key split among the guardians (Shamir secret sharing), so one guardian, even a coerced one, cannot publish early.
  5. Public alert and legal packet. Once confirmed, the activist's pre-written alert is published on Nostr, and the lawyer gets a ready habeas corpus packet.
  6. A captor can't call it off. After an alarm starts, the activist's own all-clear ends nothing. Only guardians, after a voice or video check, can stand it down.

Built for shutdowns

  • The clock only runs while the network is up. In a blackout, deadlines pause instead of firing hundreds of false alarms, then the alarm fires the moment the network returns.
  • Encrypted SMS fallback. Every message is exactly 228 bytes and fits in two SMS. A panic looks identical to a normal check-in on the wire.
  • Carry and deliver later. Messages are signed and encrypted, so any phone can carry them and deliver them when it finds a network, with the original signed time intact.
  • Per-route clocks. An SMS only proves SMS works. Each activist's clock pauses only when every route they use is down.

What it deliberately doesn't do

No servers to switch off. No custody of anyone's money. No GPS trail. No accounts or phone numbers. And it doesn't prevent an abduction. It shortens the time between a disappearance and public pressure.

Where it is

Written in Go, on Nostr (NIP-44 encryption, NIP-59 gift wrap) and BIP-340 signatures. So far:

  • a published threat model, written before the code
  • the signed, encrypted message format
  • the guardian watcher with the shutdown-aware clock
  • Nostr transport that hides sender and timing from relays
  • the SMS spec
  • 2-of-3 guardian confirmation and the coerced all-clear rule

Ten pull requests merged, every one race-tested.

Next: the Android app, OpenTimestamps proof, a legal fund guardians can unlock, Bluetooth mesh through bitchat, and an independent security review.

Prior art

The closest tool, Círculo by Guardian Project and ARTICLE 19, says on its site that its service shut down on 15 November 2026. It needed the internet and its own servers. Amnesty's Panic Button was retired after false alarms. Kengele is designed around both lessons.

Get involved

Security reviewers, Go and Android developers, Nostr folks and Swahili translators are all welcome. Start with the Start here issue.

Code: github.com/altradits/kengele (MIT)

Ukinyamaza, kengele inalia. If you go quiet, the bell rings.

title: ARG-Avatar: Animation-Rendering Guidance for Efficient Feedforward Avatar Reconstruction
description:
arXiv:2611.22207v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reconstructing animatable 3D human avatars from images is important for applications such as gaming and augmented reality. Feedforward methods make avatar reconstruction accessible by reducing inference time to a few seconds, but recent approaches rely heavily on scaling model capacity, training data, and computation. We ask whether such scaling is necessary. To this end, we introduce ARG-Avatar, an efficient feedforward framework with only 68M trainable parameters that achieves SOTA reconstruction quality. Our key insight is that 3D animation and rendering already provide strong geometric correspondences that existing methods largely attempt to learn from data. In light of this, we design the Foreground Avatar Coordinate RoPE attention (FACRoPE) and Intermediate Token Rendering (ITR) pipeline to guide avatar tokens to attend to their corresponding patches. Experiments across multiple datasets show that ARG-Avatar consistently outperforms prior methods when using two or more input images. Compared with LHM++, ARG-Avatar uses approximately 9$\times$ fewer trainable parameters, 4.8$\times$ fewer training sequences, and 14$\times$ less training compute, while running 6$\times$ faster and achieving a 2.7 dB PSNR improvement on the out-of-distribution NeuMan benchmark.

title: Similar Is Not Useful: Selecting In-Context Demonstrations by Closed-Loop Utility
description:
arXiv:2611.22295v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Retrieval-augmented vision-language-action (VLA) policies fill their context with the demonstrations whose frames look most like the current observation under frozen DINOv2 embeddings. We ask whether visual similarity selects the demonstrations that make the policy succeed. For a frozen retrieval-augmented VLA (RICL on $\pi_0$-FAST, LIBERO), we make the demonstration pool swappable at run time and score each demonstration's utility by regressing the closed-loop success of 60 fixed-size pools on their membership. On initial states disjoint from those used for scoring, pools of the five highest-utility demonstrations succeed on 66.4% of 760 paired episodes across 19 tasks, pools of the five most similar on 55.7%, and random pools on 55.5%. Utility beats similarity by 10.8 points ($p=3.2\times10^{-6}$; positive on 15 of 18 untied tasks), including on 12 tasks the policy was never primed on, and similarity-selected pools do no better than random ($+0.1$ points). Within a task, a pool's visual similarity to the test scenes tracks its success at Spearman 0.10; across tasks, similarity separates tasks whose scenes differ and falls to chance when two tasks share a scene. The gain comes from on-task closed-loop evidence: best-of-ten direct search over pools recovers two-thirds of it with 100 rollouts. Against the shipped 20-demonstration pool, utility-curated pools of five lead by 7.0 points over 560 paired episodes from two evaluation runs ($p=0.006$), and utility-ordered retrieval inside the full pool leads by 4.5 points ($p=0.055$).

title: Claude Fable 5.2 now available on AI Gateway
description:
Claude Fable 5.2 from Anthropic is now available on AI Gateway.

Fable 5.2 is built for open-ended technical work and improves on earlier Fable models in coding, reasoning, and vision. It can run long, ambiguous tasks unattended, and works as an orchestrator that hands simpler tasks to smaller models, or as an advisor that other Claude models consult on harder problems. It also communicates more clearly and generates output faster than earlier Fable models. Effort runs from low to max, with high as the API default.

Fable 5.2 has cybersecurity and biology safety classifiers enabled. Access to Claude Fable 5.2 requires data retention. Anthropic does not support Zero Data Retention for the model. Prompts and completions are retained for 30 days and are not used to train Claude. If your team has ZDR turned on, AI Gateway returns an error instead of sending the request to Fable 5.2.

To keep requests served when a classifier is triggered, use model fallbacks. Add a models array to providerOptions.gateway, and AI Gateway tries each model in order when the cybersecurity classifier declines a request.

Call it through the AI SDK, the Chat Completions, Responses, and Anthropic Messages APIs, or a coding agent connected to AI Gateway. Use anthropic/claude-fable-5.2 as the model name:

This request falls back to Opus 5.5, then Sonnet 5.5, if the cybersecurity classifier declines it. The models option works the same way on every AI Gateway API format.

To use it in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and more, install the latest Vercel CLI and run setup:

Try Claude Fable 5.2 in the model playground.

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting, Zero Data Retention support, budgets for API keys, routing rules, and more.

AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and does not charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests.

title: Does the Voice Matter? Evaluating Frustration Detection on Deployed Clinical Voice-Agent Calls
description:
arXiv:2611.21001v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Autonomous voice agents now conduct routine clinical follow-up calls, so some automated triage is unavoidable. A patient becoming frustrated is one thing that triage should catch. These systems typically read only the transcript the speech-to-text stage produces, not the voice, and whether that is enough is largely untested on real clinical speech. We study per-turn frustration detection on real patient calls from a deployed clinical voice agent: 150 turns from six calls labelled by three annotators, with a length-matched acted corpus as a control, and 714 turns from 30 calls. Patient turns are overwhelmingly short: across the deployed calls, roughly 59% are one or two words, against 13% in the full acted corpus, and a corpus accuracy gap remains even after the acted set is length-matched. On one-word turns, transcript-only detection does not exclude chance. Across five audio-capable language models, the transcript flags 3 or 4 of the 39 frustrated one-word turns in the 30 calls, and a classifier given only the word count reaches 57.3%. Whether audio helps depends on the model and on the instruction. Asked to attend to delivery, two Gemini 2.5 models gain 3.0 pp over the transcript across 30 calls (-1.0 to 7.5 pp). Of the turns they confidently clear, 6.9% were in fact frustrated for audio against 13.0% for the transcript, a difference of 6.1 pp (2.2 to 10.4 pp). Across the 30 calls, given one prompt identical for both inputs, no model's audio-text interval excludes zero. Under the input-specific prompts, a newer Gemini model and two smaller open models do worse with audio than with the transcript (-3.5, -8.6 and -10.6 pp). A WavLM probe trained on the clinical calls matches the best prompted model overall (71.6%) but misses every frustrated one-word turn in the 24 added calls. When a patient's turn is short, the transcript alone is not enough to rule out frustration.

title: When Your Agent Leaves the Process: What Strands A2A Reveals About Cross-Process Token Accounting and Failure Reporting
description:
When you move an agent from a local function call to a remote HTTP endpoint, you lose three things: shared memory, a unified token ledger, and a single failure surface. Strands A2A, an open protocol for agent-to-agent communication, exposes these gaps with production telemetry from nine real runs.

The evidence is specific. A caller reports zero tokens for a run that consumed 2369 on the remote side. A remote tool raises an exception, yet the orchestrator marks the task completed. A reply times out, but the receipt already exists on disk. These are not edge cases. They are the default behavior when orchestration crosses process boundaries without new accounting primitives.

The Setup: Two Processes, One Port, No Shared Ledger

The test task is minimal. A fixture holds three invented per-node token counts. An agent must call sum_tokens to add them, then call save_draft to write a brief. Earlier experiments ran this inside one process using swarms, graphs, and workflow tools. This version splits the writer into a second OS process and calls it over HTTP.

Strands Agents SDK wraps the writer as an A2AServer and the caller as an A2AAgent. Both processes share one port and one file on disk. They share nothing else. No memory, no token counter, no exception stack.

The protocol is A2A (Agent-to-Agent), which defines discovery, invocation, and result serialization. The SDK marks its A2A integration as experimental in a log line. That warning is accurate.

Token Accounting Across Process Boundaries

Inside one process, you inspect an agent's token counters directly. Across a process boundary, you get a string and a status code.

Nine runs show the caller's AgentResult reporting zero tokens for work that consumed 2369 tokens on the remote side. The remote agent increments its own counter. The caller never sees it. The HTTP response does not include token metadata. The A2A protocol does not define a token ledger field.

You can add a custom header or embed token counts in the response body, but neither is standard. Without a shared ledger, each process maintains its own view. The caller sees zero. The remote agent sees 2369. Both are correct within their own scope.

This is not a bug. It is a missing primitive. Cross-process orchestration needs a token accounting layer that survives HTTP serialization.

Failure Propagation: When Completed Means Crashed

A remote tool raises an exception. The orchestrator marks the task completed anyway.

The failure happens inside the remote process. The exception propagates to the A2A server, which logs it and returns a 200 status code with a generic error message. The caller receives the response, parses the status, and marks the task completed.

The orchestrator has no visibility into the remote stack trace. It sees a successful HTTP transaction. The task state is completed, not failed. The error message is a string in the response body, not a structured failure signal.

To propagate failures correctly, you need:

  • A status field in the A2A response that distinguishes success, partial success, and failure.
  • A structured error object with exception type, message, and trace.
  • A retry policy that interprets remote failures as retriable or terminal.

Without these, a remote crash looks like a successful no-op.

Receipt Timing: When the Reply Times Out but the Write Succeeded

A reply times out. The receipt already exists on disk.

The remote agent calls save_draft, which writes a file. The write succeeds. The agent prepares a response. Before the response reaches the caller, the HTTP timeout fires. The caller logs a timeout error. The file remains on disk.

The caller has no proof that the write succeeded. The timeout could mean:

  • The remote agent crashed before writing.
  • The remote agent wrote, then crashed before replying.
  • The remote agent wrote and replied, but the network dropped the response.
  • The remote agent is still running, and the reply will arrive late.

The only way to know is to check the file. But the caller does not know the file path unless the remote agent advertised it in the task definition. Even then, the caller must poll the filesystem or wait for an out-of-band signal.

This is a coordination problem. The receipt (the file) and the reply (the HTTP response) are decoupled. The receipt is durable. The reply is ephemeral. The caller needs a way to correlate them.

Architecture: How Strands A2A Wires Two Processes

The SDK provides two classes: A2AServer and A2AAgent.

A2AServer wraps an agent and exposes it over HTTP. It handles discovery, invocation, and result serialization. The server runs in a separate process, typically started with uvicorn or another ASGI server.

A2AAgent wraps an HTTP client and presents a remote agent as a local tool. The caller treats it like any other agent, but under the hood, every method call becomes an HTTP request.

The protocol defines three endpoints:

  • GET /discovery: Returns agent metadata, including available tools and input schema.
  • POST /invoke: Accepts a task definition and returns a result.
  • GET /status/{task_id}: Returns the current state of a running task.

The SDK uses FastAPI for the server and httpx for the client. The protocol is JSON over HTTP. No gRPC, no message queue, no shared memory.

Here is the server setup:

from strands_agents import Agent, A2AServer
from fastapi import FastAPI

writer_agent = Agent(
    name="writer",
    tools=[sum_tokens, save_draft],
    model="amazon.nova-pro-v1:0"
)

app = FastAPI()
a2a_server = A2AServer(agent=writer_agent)
a2a_server.mount(app, path="/writer")

The caller setup:

from strands_agents import A2AAgent

remote_writer = A2AAgent(
    base_url="http://localhost:8000/writer",
    timeout=30.0
)

result = remote_writer.run(task="Add tokens and save brief")

The caller sees result.status, result.output, and result.tokens. The tokens field is always zero unless the remote agent explicitly includes it in the response.

Failure Modes and Observability Gaps

Failure Mode Caller Sees Remote Reality Missing Primitive
Remote tool raises exception status=completed, generic error string Exception logged, task aborted Structured failure signal in response
HTTP timeout before reply Timeout error, no result Write succeeded, reply prepared Durable receipt correlation
Remote agent crashes mid-task Timeout or connection error Partial state, no cleanup Idempotency token, state snapshot
Token counter incremented remotely tokens=0 in caller result tokens=2369 in remote logs Shared token ledger or response metadata
Network partition during invoke Retry or timeout Task may run twice Idempotency key, deduplication

The table shows five failure modes. None are handled by default. Each requires a custom solution.

What You Need to Build

If you run agents across process boundaries, you need:

  1. Token ledger: A shared counter or a response field that propagates token usage back to the caller.
  2. Failure signal: A structured error object in the A2A response, not a string in the body.
  3. Receipt correlation: A way to prove a write succeeded even when the reply times out. Options include polling a known file path, using a message queue for receipts, or embedding a receipt hash in the response.
  4. Idempotency: A task ID or invocation token that prevents duplicate execution when the caller retries after a timeout.
  5. State snapshots: A way to resume or roll back a remote task that crashes mid-execution.

None of these are in the A2A protocol today. You build them yourself or accept the gaps.

When to Use Cross-Process Orchestration

Use it when:

  • You need to isolate agents for security, resource limits, or language boundaries.
  • You want to scale agents independently (different instance types, regions, or clusters).
  • You are composing agents from multiple teams or vendors.

Avoid it when:

  • Token accounting matters and you cannot instrument the remote agent.
  • Failure propagation must be precise and you cannot add structured error handling.
  • Latency is critical and the HTTP round-trip is too expensive.
  • You need transactional guarantees across tool calls.

Technical Verdict

Cross-process agent orchestration is not a protocol problem. It is a missing primitives problem. A2A defines how to serialize a task and parse a result, but it does not define how to account for tokens, propagate failures, or correlate receipts with replies.

If you control both sides of the boundary, you can extend the protocol with custom headers, response fields, or out-of-band signals. If you do not, you accept zero token visibility, opaque failures, and receipt timing gaps.

The Strands SDK marks A2A as experimental. That is the right label. The protocol works for discovery and invocation. It does not work for production observability or failure recovery without additional infrastructure.

Build the ledger, the failure signal, and the receipt correlation yourself, or keep your agents in one process.

Source Links

  • Orchestrating Agents: Your Agent Leaves the Process
  • Strands in Action GitHub Repository

title: RiDEx: Reward-Informed Directional Exploration for Diffusion Reinforcement Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.22052v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reward-based diffusion post-training updates model parameters from task rewards. While existing approaches improve sampling and policy optimization, they still rely largely on isotropic random perturbations in a high-dimensional latent space for exploration. Such variation often spends the perturbation budget on changes with little influence on the target reward, making exploration inefficient. We study where diffusion models should explore and how to learn from that exploration. We introduce Reward-Informed Directional Exploration (RiDEx), which concentrates local exploration in reward-relevant subspaces of the denoising velocity field. Conditional residuals or differentiable reward gradients propose the subspace, and equal-and-opposite perturbations at the same generation state measure its terminal reward response. The reward difference supplies signed local supervision in the explored coordinates, while all generated images contribute to global DiffusionNFT learning. RiDEx thereby couples exploration-space selection with feedback about the changes it produces. On Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium, RiDEx attains the highest peak rewards among the evaluated methods on four alignment and preference tasks. Its gradient-direction instantiation achieves 15x and 29x target-attainment speedups over DiffusionNFT on HPSv2 and PickScore, measured in H200 GPU hours. Controlled experiments confirm that reward-aligned directions elicit stronger responses at equal perturbation magnitude, and that applying their measured credit improves curve-average reward across all four tasks.
