title: Amazon OpenSearch Serverless now supports ingest pipelines
description:
Amazon OpenSearch Serverless now supports ingest pipelines, so you can clean, enrich, and vectorize documents inside your collection as they are indexed, without running separate preprocessing infrastructure. Teams building search, log analytics, and generative AI applications can replace data-prep code in Lambda functions or ETL jobs with transformations that apply consistently to every document, regardless of how it is ingested.

You can use ingest pipelines to normalize and clean data with processors such as copy, date, dot_expander, join, lowercase, uppercase, remove, rename, set, and trim. For semantic and AI search, you can chunk long text with text_chunking and generate embeddings at ingest time with text_embedding, text_image_embedding, and sparse_encoding. The ml_inference processor calls any model you have connected and lets you map its input and output fields yourself. You create and manage pipelines with the familiar OpenSearch _ingest/pipeline APIs. You can test a pipeline against sample documents with the _simulate API before sending it live traffic, then apply it as an index's default pipeline or on individual indexing and bulk requests.

Pipeline processing uses your collection's indexing OpenSearch Compute Units (OCUs) and is billed the same way as other indexing activity. If you use a remote model with an ML processor, the model provider bills inference separately. Ingest pipelines are available in all AWS Regions where Amazon OpenSearch Serverless is available.

To get started, see Ingest pipelines in Amazon OpenSearch Serverless in the Amazon OpenSearch Service Developer Guide. To learn more about OpenSearch Serverless, visit the Amazon OpenSearch Serverless product page.

title: Lock-Screen Controls for a Web Soundboard: the Media Session API, Honest Metadata and Handlers Only for What You Support
description:
Most of the clips on a soundboard are over before anyone could reach for a lock screen. A one-second "bruh" does not need a media card on the phone's notification shade. But a soundboard is rarely only one-second clips. People loop a background track, play a long reaction audio, or leave a board open in a tab while they switch apps. That is when the operating system's media controls start to matter, and when a soundboard that ignores them feels unfinished.

This post walks through the Media Session API from the point of view of a grid of soundboard buttons: when the page should claim the session at all, what the card should say, which hardware and lock-screen buttons it should answer, and how to leave nothing stale behind when the clip ends.

The helpers are plain ES modules. They take the browser objects as arguments, so I could test the logic in Node 20+ with node:test and small fakes. The tests check the decisions, not the audio. What actually appears on a lock screen, a smartwatch or a headset button still depends on the browser and the operating system, and you should check it on the devices you care about.

What the Media Session API does

navigator.mediaSession is the page's way of telling the browser, and through it the operating system, three things:

  1. What is playing. You set navigator.mediaSession.metadata to a new MediaMetadata({ title, artist, album, artwork }). That is the text and image on the media card.
  2. Which controls work. You call navigator.mediaSession.setActionHandler(action, handler) for actions such as play, pause, seekto or nexttrack. Passing null removes a handler.
  3. Where playback is. playbackState can be "playing", "paused" or "none", and setPositionState({ duration, playbackRate, position }) describes the progress bar.

The browser decides when to show a media card. Your page does not get to force one onto the screen, and very short sounds may never get one. What you control is whether the card, when it does appear, tells the truth.

Decide when the board should claim the session

A board full of short clips is a strange fit for a media card. If every tap replaced the metadata, the card would flicker between titles faster than anyone could read it. If you register a nexttrack handler, the headset's skip button now does something on a page that has no idea what "next" means.

So the first decision is not about metadata at all. It is about which plays deserve a session:

  • Long clips. A full reaction audio, a song snippet, an ambient loop.
  • Loop mode. Anything the person set to repeat, because they will want to stop it from outside the tab.
  • Not one-shots. A short hit that ends on its own does not need a pause button on the lock screen.

In the helper below that becomes shouldClaimSession({ duration, loop }). The default threshold is eight seconds. That number is a design choice for this sketch, not a browser rule, so set your own after watching how people use your board.

Honest metadata

The card shows a title, a secondary line and an image. For a sound button the mapping I use is:

  • title: the sound's own name, trimmed, with a readable fallback such as "Untitled sound" instead of an empty string.
  • artist: the site or board name. It answers "where is this coming from?" when the tab is hidden.
  • album: the category the sound sits in, so "Memes" or "Games" rather than a made-up album.
  • artwork: only images with an absolute https URL and a sizes value such as 512x512. A path that depends on the current page, or an image without sizes, is skipped rather than guessed.

Resist the urge to put marketing on the card. "Vine boom" is more useful than "Vine boom - the best free sounds online". The card is a control surface, and it is read at a glance on a locked phone.

Register only the actions you can honour

This is the part that is easiest to get wrong. The API lets you register many actions, and it is tempting to register all of them "just in case". Each one you register is a promise: the button on the headset or the lock screen will now do something.

For a soundboard clip that is playing in loop mode, the honest set is usually small:

  • play and pause, because a looping clip should be stoppable from outside the tab.
  • stop, where the browser supports it, so the card can go away.
  • seekbackward, seekforward and seekto if your player can actually seek. For a short loop, a two-second step is enough.
  • previoustrack and nexttrack only if the board has a real queue, such as a playlist mode. A grid of unrelated buttons usually does not.

There is one more detail: browsers do not all support the same actions, and some of them throw when you register one they do not know. Wrapping each setActionHandler call in its own try means one unsupported action does not stop the others from being registered.

The helpers

Here is the module. It does not touch the DOM or create audio. It decides what to tell the session and wires actions to a small player object that you provide.

// Media Session helpers for a browser soundboard. Plain ES modules, no dependencies.
// The browser objects (navigator.mediaSession, MediaMetadata, HTMLAudioElement) are passed in,
// so the logic can be tested in Node with small fakes.

export const ACTIONS = ["play", "pause", "stop", "seekbackward", "seekforward", "seekto", "previoustrack", "nexttrack"];

/** Build the plain object you pass to `new MediaMetadata(...)` for one sound. */
export function metadataFor(sound, { board = "Soundboard", site = "", artwork = [] } = {}) {
  const title = String(sound.title || "").trim() || "Untitled sound";
  const art = artwork
    .filter((a) => a && /^https:\/\//.test(a.src) && /^\d+x\d+$/.test(a.sizes || ""))
    .map((a) => ({ src: a.src, sizes: a.sizes, type: a.type || "image/png" }));
  return { title, artist: site, album: sound.board || board, artwork: art };
}

/** Clamp numbers so setPositionState() never throws (position must stay within 0..duration, rate must not be 0). */
export function positionStateFor(duration, position, playbackRate = 1) {
  if (!Number.isFinite(duration) || duration <= 0) return null;
  const rate = Number.isFinite(playbackRate) && playbackRate !== 0 ? playbackRate : 1;
  const pos = Math.min(Math.max(Number.isFinite(position) ? position : 0, 0), duration);
  return { duration, playbackRate: rate, position: pos };
}

/** Map an <audio> event name to navigator.mediaSession.playbackState. */
export function playbackStateFor(eventName) {
  if (eventName === "playing" || eventName === "play") return "playing";
  if (eventName === "pause") return "paused";
  return "none"; // ended, emptied, error
}

/**
 * Register only the handlers the board can honour. Unsupported actions throw in some browsers,
 * so each call is wrapped. Returns the actions that were actually registered.
 */
export function installHandlers(session, player, { allowSkip = false, seekStep = 2 } = {}) {
  const wanted = {
    play: () => player.play(),
    pause: () => player.pause(),
    stop: () => player.stop(),
    seekbackward: (d) => player.seekBy(-(d && d.seekOffset ? d.seekOffset : seekStep)),
    seekforward: (d) => player.seekBy(d && d.seekOffset ? d.seekOffset : seekStep),
    seekto: (d) => player.seekTo(d.seekTime),
  };
  if (allowSkip) {
    wanted.previoustrack = () => player.previous();
    wanted.nexttrack = () => player.next();
  }
  const registered = [];
  for (const action of ACTIONS) {
    const fn = wanted[action] || null;
    try {
      session.setActionHandler(action, fn);
      if (fn) registered.push(action);
    } catch {
      // the browser does not know this action; leave it alone
    }
  }
  return registered;
}

/** Remove everything when the board is closed or the clip ends, so the lock screen does not show a stale card. */
export function clearSession(session) {
  session.metadata = null;
  session.playbackState = "none";
  for (const action of ACTIONS) {
    try { session.setActionHandler(action, null); } catch { /* unsupported */ }
  }
}

/** Short clips rarely need a lock-screen card. Claim the session only for long clips or loop mode. */
export function shouldClaimSession({ duration, loop = false }, minSeconds = 8) {
  return Boolean(loop) || (Number.isFinite(duration) && duration >= minSeconds);
}

A few choices in there are worth calling out:

  • positionStateFor() clamps the position into 0..duration and replaces a zero playback rate with 1. setPositionState() throws when the position is past the duration or the rate is zero, which is easy to hit with a looping clip that reports its time a little late. Returning null for a duration that is not a finite positive number lets the caller simply skip the call.
  • installHandlers() registers null for actions the board does not want. That clears handlers left over from an earlier clip, which matters when the same tab plays a long track and then a short one.
  • clearSession() resets the metadata, the playback state and every handler. Call it when the clip ends, when loop mode is turned off and the clip finishes, or when the board is closed.

Wiring it to an audio element

In the browser the glue is short. This sketch uses an HTMLAudioElement; the same idea works with an AudioBufferSourceNode if your player exposes play, pause, stop and seeking.

import { metadataFor, positionStateFor, playbackStateFor, installHandlers, clearSession, shouldClaimSession } from "./media-session.mjs";

const session = "mediaSession" in navigator ? navigator.mediaSession : null;
const audioEl = document.querySelector("#board-audio");

function startSound(audio, sound, { loop = false } = {}) {
  audio.loop = loop;
  audio.src = sound.src;
  const playing = audio.play(); // call play() inside the tap handler, before any await

  if (!session) return playing;
  if (!shouldClaimSession({ duration: sound.duration, loop })) {
    clearSession(session);
    return playing;
  }

  session.metadata = new MediaMetadata(metadataFor(sound, {
    site: "My Soundboard",
    artwork: [{ src: "https://example.com/icons/board-512.png", sizes: "512x512" }],
  }));

  installHandlers(session, {
    play: () => audio.play(),
    pause: () => audio.pause(),
    stop: () => { audio.pause(); audio.currentTime = 0; clearSession(session); },
    seekBy: (s) => { audio.currentTime = Math.max(0, audio.currentTime + s); },
    seekTo: (t) => { audio.currentTime = t; },
  });
  return playing;
}

// call startSound(audioEl, sound, { loop }) from each button's pointerdown or click handler
for (const name of ["playing", "pause", "ended"]) {
  audioEl.addEventListener(name, () => {
    if (!session) return;
    session.playbackState = playbackStateFor(name);
    if (name === "ended" && !audioEl.loop) clearSession(session);
  });
}

audioEl.addEventListener("timeupdate", () => {
  if (!session || !session.setPositionState) return;
  const state = positionStateFor(audioEl.duration, audioEl.currentTime, audioEl.playbackRate);
  if (state) session.setPositionState(state);
});

Two things in that glue are easy to miss.

First, audio.play() is called inside the tap handler before anything else. The session setup can happen after it. If you await something first, some browsers will no longer treat the call as part of the user's gesture.

Second, setPositionState is feature-checked. It is newer than the rest of the API, and calling a missing method throws.

The tests

The fakes are deliberately dull: a session object that records handlers and throws for actions named as unsupported, and a player that records calls.

import test from "node:test";
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import { metadataFor, positionStateFor, playbackStateFor, installHandlers, clearSession, shouldClaimSession } from "./media-session.mjs";

function fakeSession(unsupported = []) {
  const handlers = {};
  return {
    handlers, metadata: undefined, playbackState: "none",
    setActionHandler(action, fn) {
      if (unsupported.includes(action)) throw new TypeError(`unsupported ${action}`);
      handlers[action] = fn;
    },
  };
}
function fakePlayer() {
  const calls = [];
  const rec = (name) => (...a) => calls.push([name, ...a]);
  return { calls, play: rec("play"), pause: rec("pause"), stop: rec("stop"), seekBy: rec("seekBy"),
           seekTo: rec("seekTo"), previous: rec("previous"), next: rec("next") };
}

test("metadata keeps only absolute https artwork with sizes", () => {
  const m = metadataFor({ title: "  Vine boom ", board: "Memes" }, { site: "Example Board", artwork: [
    { src: "https://example.com/a-512.png", sizes: "512x512" },
    { src: "/icons/board-96.png", sizes: "96x96" },
    { src: "https://example.com/b.png" },
  ] });
  assert.equal(m.title, "Vine boom");
  assert.equal(m.album, "Memes");
  assert.deepEqual(m.artwork, [{ src: "https://example.com/a-512.png", sizes: "512x512", type: "image/png" }]);
});

test("metadata falls back to a readable title", () => {
  assert.equal(metadataFor({ title: "" }).title, "Untitled sound");
});

test("position state is clamped and never uses a zero rate", () => {
  assert.deepEqual(positionStateFor(2.5, 3.1, 0), { duration: 2.5, playbackRate: 1, position: 2.5 });
  assert.deepEqual(positionStateFor(2.5, -1), { duration: 2.5, playbackRate: 1, position: 0 });
  assert.equal(positionStateFor(NaN, 0), null);
  assert.equal(positionStateFor(0, 0), null);
});

test("audio events map to playbackState", () => {
  assert.equal(playbackStateFor("playing"), "playing");
  assert.equal(playbackStateFor("pause"), "paused");
  assert.equal(playbackStateFor("ended"), "none");
});

test("unsupported actions are skipped, not fatal", () => {
  const s = fakeSession(["stop", "seekto"]);
  const p = fakePlayer();
  const reg = installHandlers(s, p);
  assert.deepEqual(reg, ["play", "pause", "seekbackward", "seekforward"]);
  s.handlers.seekbackward({});
  s.handlers.seekforward({ seekOffset: 5 });
  assert.deepEqual(p.calls, [["seekBy", -2], ["seekBy", 5]]);
});

test("track buttons are only offered when the board can skip", () => {
  const s = fakeSession();
  assert.ok(!installHandlers(s, fakePlayer()).includes("nexttrack"));
  assert.equal(s.handlers.nexttrack, null);
  assert.ok(installHandlers(s, fakePlayer(), { allowSkip: true }).includes("nexttrack"));
});

test("clearSession removes metadata and handlers", () => {
  const s = fakeSession(["stop"]);
  installHandlers(s, fakePlayer());
  s.metadata = { title: "x" }; s.playbackState = "playing";
  clearSession(s);
  assert.equal(s.metadata, null);
  assert.equal(s.playbackState, "none");
  assert.equal(s.handlers.play, null);
});

test("short one-shot clips do not claim the session", () => {
  assert.equal(shouldClaimSession({ duration: 1.4 }), false);
  assert.equal(shouldClaimSession({ duration: 1.4, loop: true }), true);
  assert.equal(shouldClaimSession({ duration: 30 }), true);
});

Output from Node:

✔ metadata keeps only absolute https artwork with sizes (1.402085ms)
✔ metadata falls back to a readable title (0.125806ms)
✔ position state is clamped and never uses a zero rate (0.259309ms)
✔ audio events map to playbackState (0.11789ms)
✔ unsupported actions are skipped, not fatal (0.38821ms)
✔ track buttons are only offered when the board can skip (0.189353ms)
✔ clearSession removes metadata and handlers (0.147715ms)
✔ short one-shot clips do not claim the session (0.098102ms)
ℹ tests 8
ℹ suites 0
ℹ pass 8
ℹ fail 0
ℹ cancelled 0
ℹ skipped 0
ℹ todo 0
ℹ duration_ms 57.243399

These tests prove the decisions: which actions get registered, what gets cleared, how numbers are clamped. They do not prove that a particular phone shows the card the way you expect. For that, open the board on the devices you support, play a long clip, lock the screen and press every control the card shows. If a button appears that your board cannot honour, remove its handler.

Checks before you ship

A short list I run when a board gains lock-screen controls:

  1. Tap a one-second clip. No media card should appear, or if the browser shows one anyway, it should disappear when the clip ends.
  2. Start a loop, lock the phone, press pause. The loop stops. Press play. It resumes from the same place.
  3. Press the skip buttons on a headset. If the board has no queue, nothing should happen.
  4. Switch from a long clip to a short one. The old title should not stay on the card.
  5. Close the tab. The card goes away.
  6. Look at the artwork. It loads from an absolute https URL and is not a stretched favicon.

Where this fits

Lock-screen controls do not make short sound buttons faster or funnier. They make the longer, looping and background uses of a board behave like the rest of the person's media. The work is mostly restraint: claim the session only when the play deserves it, describe it in plain words, answer only the buttons you can honour, and clean up when you are done.

If you keep those four rules, the API is small. The helpers above are under a hundred lines, and most of that is the code that says no.

title: RICoT: Recurrent Interleaved Chain-of-Thought for Page Stream Segmentation
description:
arXiv:2611.22382v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have renewed interest in Page Stream Segmentation (PSS), splitting a multi-page file into its constituent documents. Yet published LLM methods still frame the task as boundary classification over one or a few neighboring pages, and commercial document-splitting APIs do not disclose their methods. We reimagine PSS for LLMs as a sequential process over the whole stream and propose RICoT (Recurrent Interleaved Chain-of-Thought), a prompting framework that works through the pages as a reader would: within a sliding window it reasons about each page and commits its boundary decision before moving on, and across windows it carries forward a compact record of what it has read, keeping per-call cost bounded. We also introduce FinancePSS-205, a benchmark of 205 real-world, de-identified financial page streams, to be released publicly. On FinancePSS-205, RICoT matches or outperforms pairwise and windowed prompting with the same backbone for each of three open-weight LLMs; on a TABME test subset, RICoT with GLM-5 reaches document F1 0.847 and boundary F1 0.915, above published zero-shot results. A 2B-parameter student, trained on a larger teacher's decisions with and without the page-level reasoning, performs comparably in both modes and comes within 0.05 document F1 of the strongest prompted model on FinancePSS-205.

title: Can Language Models Learn to Forecast Stock Prices?
description:
arXiv:2609.36914v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We study whether language models can learn to forecast stock returns through training. We build BETA, a chronological sandbox over S&P 500 stocks in which a model calls tools to retrieve prices, indicators, and news available up to a decision date, and then forecasts the stock's future return. Evaluating frontier models in this sandbox reveals three weaknesses: their scores decline as the test period approaches the present while a simple momentum baseline stays stable, they predict gains far more often than gains occur, and they predict moves much smaller than those that are realized. We first fine-tune on filtered, hindsight-generated tool-use trajectories for historical tasks judged predictable from the evidence available at the time. We then apply reinforcement learning with rewards based on realized returns. During RL, long investigations frequently exceed the context window. We therefore introduce a selective compaction tool that allows the model to compress chosen portions of its interaction history. Selective compaction changes the context available to subsequent decisions, so policy updates must preserve the context in which each action was generated. Meanwhile, rollouts vary substantially in the number and length of their trainable turns, making a shared group-level baseline less effective. We address these challenges with Context-Aligned Turn-Level PPO, which uses a turn-level critic and computes policy updates using each turn's actual context. The resulting models, which we call AURA, substantially reduce all three weaknesses. Training improves the 8B model's score from 24.0 to 47.0 and the 30B model's from 27.4 to 54.7, with the latter surpassing all evaluated frontier models on our benchmark and achieving its largest margin on the most recent test period. These results suggest that agentic RL can improve performance on tasks with noisy, delayed real-world outcomes.

title: Reciprocal Rank Fusion k=60: My #1 BM25 Match Fell to Position 31
description:
I typed ERR_CONN_4012 into my hybrid search and got 30 pages about connection errors in general. The one runbook that actually contained the string ERR_CONN_4012 sat at position 31.

BM25 had ranked it #1. Of course it did: exact token, rare token, short doc. The vector index didn't have it in its top 50 at all. Then Reciprocal Rank Fusion merged the two lists and quietly buried the only correct answer below every vaguely related page.

Nothing was broken. Reciprocal Rank Fusion with k=60 did exactly what the formula says. This post is about that formula, why the textbook default punishes "one retriever is very sure" results, and what I changed.

TL;DR

  • Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) scores each doc as sum(1 / (k + rank)) across retrievers. With the common default k=60, rank #1 is worth 1/61 = 0.0164 and rank #50 is worth 1/110 = 0.0091. The curve is almost flat.
  • Any doc ranked 61st or better in both lists beats a doc ranked #1 in only one list. In general, the cutoff is rank k + 1.
  • Exact-match queries (error codes, SKUs, function names) are exactly the case where BM25 is right and embeddings miss, so RRF demotes them by design.
  • If a reranker only sees the fused top 20, the buried doc never even gets a second chance.
  • Fixes: detect identifier queries and pin exact matches, retrieve deeper on the vector side, lower k or weight BM25, and widen the rerank window.

How does Reciprocal Rank Fusion actually score documents?

Reciprocal Rank Fusion ignores raw scores and uses only rank positions. Each retriever contributes 1 / (k + rank) for every doc it returned, and a doc missing from a list contributes zero.

def rrf(rankings: list[list[str]], k: int = 60) -> dict[str, float]:
    scores: dict[str, float] = {}
    for ranking in rankings:
        for rank, doc_id in enumerate(ranking, start=1):
            scores[doc_id] = scores.get(doc_id, 0.0) + 1.0 / (k + rank)
    return dict(sorted(scores.items(), key=lambda x: -x[1]))

That's the whole algorithm. It's popular for good reasons: BM25 scores and cosine similarities live on completely different scales, and RRF sidesteps calibration entirely. No normalization, no tuning, works out of the box. Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Weaviate, Qdrant and most RAG tutorials reach for it, and k=60 is the number almost everyone copies from the original 2009 paper.

The trouble is what k=60 does to the shape of the curve.

Why does RRF with k=60 bury exact keyword matches?

RRF with k=60 makes appearing in two lists worth far more than ranking first in one. Here are the actual numbers:

Situation RRF score
#1 in BM25, absent from vector list 1/61 = 0.01639
#50 in both lists 2/110 = 0.01818
#61 in both lists 2/121 = 0.01653
#62 in both lists 2/122 = 0.01639 (tie)

Read the second row again. A document that both retrievers considered mediocre, 50th place each, outscores the document BM25 was most confident about.

The break-even is easy to derive. A doc at rank r in both lists beats an exclusive #1 when:

2 / (k + r) > 1 / (k + 1)
       k + r < 2k + 2
           r < k + 2

So with k=60, every doc ranked 61st or better in both lists outranks your exclusive #1. If each retriever returns 50 results, that means every single overlapping doc wins.

That's where position 31 came from. My query hit 30 generic "connection error / timeout / retry" pages that both BM25 and the embedding model liked. All 30 appeared in both top-50 lists. The runbook appeared in one. Final position: overlap count plus one. It's not bad luck, it's arithmetic.

Why do embeddings miss error codes in the first place?

Embedding models compress meaning, and an identifier like ERR_CONN_4012 has very little meaning to compress. The tokenizer chops it into pieces like ERR, _, CONN, _, 401, 2, and the model maps the whole thing to roughly "some connection error." Every page about connection errors lands nearby.

BM25 sees the opposite picture. The full token is rare across the corpus, so its IDF is huge, and the one doc containing it shoots to the top.

This split is the entire reason hybrid search exists. The queries where one retriever is decisively right and the other is lost are the queries hybrid search was supposed to save. Flat RRF treats that disagreement as noise and votes it down.

Does a reranker fix bad RRF fusion?

A cross-encoder reranker only fixes RRF if the correct doc is inside the window it reranks. A lot of pipelines fuse, take the top 20, and rerank those. My runbook was at 31, so the reranker never saw it. The most accurate component in the pipeline was handed a list that didn't contain the answer.

If you rerank, the window has to be at least as large as the plausible overlap between your retrievers. With two top-50 lists, the worst case for an exclusive #1 is position 51. I rerank the fused top 60 now. It costs more cross-encoder calls, but a reranker that sees the answer is cheaper than one that confidently orders 20 wrong ones.

How do you fix Reciprocal Rank Fusion for exact-match queries?

Four changes, roughly in order of impact.

1. Detect identifier queries and pin exact matches

If the query contains something that looks like a code, the user wants that string. Don't make them win a popularity contest for it.

import re

IDENT = re.compile(r"\b(?:[A-Z]{2,}[_-][A-Z0-9_-]+|[A-Z]+-\d+|0x[0-9a-fA-F]+|\w+\(\))")

def hybrid_search(query, bm25, vec, k=60, n=50):
    bm = bm25.search(query, n)
    vc = vec.search(query, n)
    fused = list(rrf([bm, vc], k=k))

    idents = IDENT.findall(query)
    if idents:
        exact = [d for d in bm[:5] if any(i in doc_text(d) for i in idents)]
        fused = exact + [d for d in fused if d not in exact]
    return fused

The check against doc_text matters. BM25's top 5 can still contain partial matches on ERR or CONN, and you only want to pin docs that contain the literal string.

2. Retrieve deeper on the vector side

An exclusive #1 loses because the other list gives it zero. Give the other list a chance to give it something. If the vector search returns 500 instead of 50 and the runbook shows up at rank 400, it earns 1/460 = 0.00217 extra:

1/61 + 1/460 = 0.01857   (runbook)
2/110        = 0.01818   (doc at #50 in both)

Now it beats every doc ranked 50th in both. It still loses to shared docs near the top, but it climbs out of the basement. Deeper ANN retrieval is cheap compared to the LLM call that follows.

3. Lower k, or weight the retrievers

Lower k makes top ranks matter more. From the break-even above, an exclusive #1 is beaten by docs in both lists down to rank k + 1:

k Exclusive #1 loses to shared docs ranked...
60 1 through 61
20 1 through 21
10 1 through 11
1 1 through 2

Weighted RRF multiplies each retriever's contribution. Be careful: the weight also boosts shared docs' BM25 half, so it's weaker than it looks. With BM25 weight 2 and k=60, a shared doc at rank r scores 3/(60+r) against the exclusive doc's 2/61. Shared docs still win down to rank 31. Weight 3 still lets shared docs win down to rank 21. Weights help, but they don't solve the identifier case alone.

I ended up with k=20 as the default and kept the identifier pin as the real fix.

4. Look at disagreement, don't average it

The most useful debugging change was logging, per query, how many docs appeared in only one list and where they landed after fusion. A doc that's #1 in one retriever and missing from the other is a signal, not an outlier. If that pattern shows up on a large share of your queries, your two retrievers are answering different questions and flat fusion is hiding it.

When is RRF k=60 still the right choice?

RRF with k=60 is a fine default when your queries are natural-language questions and both retrievers mostly agree. In that regime, the flat curve smooths out noise from either retriever, and consensus really is a good proxy for relevance. It's also hard to beat for zero-tuning setups.

It's the wrong default for corpora full of identifiers: runbooks, API references, ticket histories, log search, product catalogs, legal citations. There, the query often has exactly one correct answer, and only the lexical retriever knows it.

So why did my #1 BM25 match fall to position 31?

Reciprocal Rank Fusion with k=60 gives rank #1 a score of 1/61 and rank #50 a score of 1/110, so the rank curve is nearly flat and showing up in two lists dominates ranking high in one. Mathematically, any document ranked k + 1 or better in both lists beats a document ranked #1 in only one. My runbook was BM25's #1 and absent from the vector top 50, so it landed behind all 30 documents that appeared in both lists. To fix it, detect identifier-style queries and pin literal matches, retrieve deeper on the vector side so exclusive hits earn partial credit, lower k (I use 20), and rerank a window wide enough to include the worst-case position of an exclusive #1.

Written by the developer behind Preterview, an interview prep platform.

title: OpenWhistle: A Large-Scale Longitudinal Dataset and Benchmark of Bottlenose Dolphin Vocalizations
description:
arXiv:2609.34839v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Recent advances in bioacoustics have been driven by large-scale corpora and standardized benchmarks, yet existing resources are overwhelmingly bird-centric and shallow per species, limiting their use for studying the structure of a single species' communication system. This gap is particularly acute for cetaceans: despite bottlenose dolphins (Tursiops truncatus) being a compelling case of complex vocal communication among non-human mammals, existing dolphin datasets are small, fragmented, and largely closed. We introduce OpenWhistle, the largest publicly available dataset of dolphin vocalizations. It comprises approximately 180,000 whistles (114 hours) recorded over five years from a stable pod of five individuals in a semi-natural environment, paired with a curated subset of 8,354 expert-annotated whistles and reproducible evaluation protocols for whistle-type detection and classification. We further release the full processing pipeline for whistle detection, segmentation, and categorization. To demonstrate its utility, we pretrain a Wav2Vec2.0 model adapted to dolphin acoustics on the OpenWhistle corpus and show that it learns effective representations, outperforming general-purpose bioacoustic models such as AVES and BioLingual on both tasks while leaving meaningful headroom for future work. By releasing the dataset, pipeline, and evaluation protocol, we provide the first open dolphin whistle dataset tailored for training self-supervised models, laying the groundwork for advancing dolphin communication research and developing models that capture fine-grained acoustic structure within species.

title: CEVA: Complementary Evidence Verification via Frame-Level Reorganization for Short-Video Fake News Detection
description:
arXiv:2611.22141v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Short-video platforms are now a common way for the public to follow unfolding events. Their rapid, visually persuasive format also makes fake news easier to spread. Unlike text-image posts, short-video news interleaves multiple modalities and changing scenes, making it difficult to identify which frames verify a claim. Existing detectors either pool sampled frames homogeneously or select them by text-frame similarity. Both overlook that aligned frames may repeat a misleading claim, whereas less dominant context may challenge it. We present CEVA (Complementary Evidence Verification Approach), to our knowledge the first short-video fake news detection framework to explicitly organize frames by their evidential roles before multimodal fusion. Its Dual-Branch Complementary Reorganization (DBCR) module separates explicit-alignment frames from candidate complementary-context frames, and cross-modal fusion with bidirectional contrastive regularization operates on the reorganized evidence. On FakeSV and FakeTT, CEVA achieves the best overall results among the compared methods. Under fixed frame budgets and backbones, DBCR outperforms uniform, random, and similarity-based selection and improves two structurally different detectors. Together, these results establish pre-fusion evidence organization as an effective and transferable component of short-video fake news detection.

title: How to find out what 1,000 websites are built with (and what you can't see from outside)
description:
Disclosure: SiteGauge, which publishes this article, built the tool used in the second half. The article was drafted by an AI model (Claude). The detection script was tested, and the output and figures shown come from real runs of the tool.

A browser extension will tell you what one website is built with. That stops being useful at about the twentieth tab. If you have a list of 1,000 prospects, competitors or customers and want to know which run Shopify, which use HubSpot, and which still have no cookie banner, you need to do the detection yourself, in bulk.

This article shows how the detection works, gives you a small script you can run today, and then shows the bulk version with real output.

What a website gives away in one request

You do not need a browser, and you do not need to run any JavaScript. A single request for the home page already carries most of the evidence:

Where to look Example What it tells you
Response headers x-shopid, server: cloudflare, x-powered-by: Craft CMS Platform, CDN, server software
Cookie names _shopify_y, CraftSessionId Platform and tools that set a cookie on the first visit
Meta tags <meta name="generator" content="WordPress 6.8"> CMS, often with its version
Script and stylesheet addresses /wp-content/…, /_next/static/…, static.klaviyo.com CMS, framework, every third-party tool that loads a script
Inline scripts the Google Tag Manager snippet Tag managers and what they are set up to load
DNS records MX, SPF and TXT records of the domain Email provider, sending services, tools the domain was verified with

Two of these are easy to get wrong.

Folder names only count in the page's own scripts and stylesheets. A page that links to a PDF in somebody else's /wp-content/ folder is not a WordPress site. Match the folder in <script> and <link> tags, not anywhere in the HTML.

DNS describes the organisation, not the page. A company whose domain is verified with Shopify does not necessarily run this website on Shopify. Keep what you learn from DNS in separate columns.

A script for one website

Here is the idea in 30 lines of Python, standard library only:

import re
import urllib.request


def detect(url):
    """Return the technologies a page gives away in its first response."""
    req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers={"User-Agent": "tech-check-example/1.0"})
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=20) as resp:
        headers = {k.lower(): v for k, v in resp.getheaders()}
        html = resp.read(2_000_000).decode("utf-8", "replace")

    found = []
    generator = re.search(r'<meta[^>]+name=["\']generator["\'][^>]+content=["\']([^"\']+)', html, re.I)
    if generator:
        found.append(f"generator says: {generator.group(1)}")
    if re.search(r'<(?:script|link)[^>]+/wp-(?:content|includes)/', html):
        found.append("WordPress")
    if "x-shopid" in headers or "cdn.shopify.com" in html:
        found.append("Shopify")
    if "/_next/static/" in html:
        found.append("Next.js")
    if "googletagmanager.com/gtm.js" in html:
        found.append("Google Tag Manager")
    if "cloudflare" in headers.get("server", "").lower():
        found.append("Cloudflare")
    return found


print(detect("https://wordpress.org/"))

This works, and for five technologies on ten websites it is all you need.

It gets harder as the list grows. You will need a few hundred rules instead of five. You will need time-outs, retries on www., and a polite rate per host. Sites that block automated requests have to be told apart from sites that are down. Tools loaded through a tag manager never appear in the HTML, so you have to read the tag manager's container file as well. None of it is difficult. All of it takes time.

The bulk version

We packaged that work as an Apify Actor: Website Technology & Tech Stack Detector. It knows about 500 technologies in more than 60 categories, reads the tag manager container and the domain's DNS, and returns one row per website with the evidence for every match.

The input is a list of domains:

{
  "websites": ["apify.com", "crawlee.dev", "wordpress.org"]
}

With curl

For a short list, one call runs the Actor and returns the rows:

curl -s -X POST \
  "https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/sitegauge~website-technology-detector/run-sync-get-dataset-items" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $APIFY_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"websites": ["apify.com", "crawlee.dev", "wordpress.org"]}'

This synchronous endpoint waits at most five minutes. Use it for up to a few hundred websites, and the client below for longer lists.

With Python 

import os
from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_TOKEN"])

domains = [line.strip() for line in open("domains.txt") if line.strip()]
run = client.actor("sitegauge/website-technology-detector").call(run_input={"websites": domains})

rows = list(client.dataset(run.default_dataset_id).iterate_items())

One thing to watch: this is the syntax of version 3 of apify-client, where call() returns an object. Many examples online still use the older run["defaultDatasetId"], which fails on a current install.

What comes back

This is the row for wordpress.org from a run on 18 November 2026, shortened:

{
  "input": "wordpress.org",
  "finalUrl": "https://wordpress.org/",
  "status": "analyzed",
  "technologyCount": 12,
  "cms": "WordPress",
  "analytics": "Google Analytics",
  "tagManagers": "Google Tag Manager",
  "emailSenders": "Help Scout",
  "connectedServices": "Google Search Console",
  "technologies": [
    { "name": "WordPress", "category": "CMS", "version": "7.2",
      "evidence": ["header link: api.w.org", "meta generator: WordPress 7.2", "loads: /wp-content/"] },
    { "name": "PHP", "category": "Programming language", "version": null,
      "evidence": ["implied by WordPress"] },
    { "name": "nginx", "category": "Web server", "version": null,
      "evidence": ["header server: nginx"] }
  ]
}

In the same run, apify.com came back with Next.js and React, Google Analytics and Mixpanel, HubSpot, Intercom, OneTrust, Amazon CloudFront, Google Workspace for email and Amazon Route 53 for DNS.

The evidence list is the part that matters most in practice. When a result looks wrong, you can see in one line why the tool said so.

Filtering the list

The category columns (cms, ecommerce, marketing, liveChat, cookieConsent and so on) are plain text, so filtering is one line:

def uses(row, column, name):
    return name in (row.get(column) or "")

shopify_with_klaviyo = [
    r["input"] for r in rows
    if uses(r, "ecommerce", "Shopify") and uses(r, "marketing", "Klaviyo")
]

no_cookie_banner = [
    r["input"] for r in rows
    if r["status"] == "analyzed" and not r.get("cookieConsent")
]

If you would rather not write code, the Actor's Output tab exports the same table as CSV or Excel.

What it costs and how long it takes

  • Price: $2 per 1,000 analyzed websites, plus Apify's small start fee per run. Websites that are blocked, unreachable or disallowed by robots.txt are in the results and are not charged. A free Apify account is enough to try it.
  • Speed: about 550 websites per minute at the default memory setting, measured on a mixed list of 736 well-known sites. Slow and dead domains lower that figure, because each one is given up to 20 seconds to answer.

What you cannot see from outside

No tool of this kind can see everything, and it helps to know the limits before you trust a list:

  • Only the first request counts. Tools that load after a click, after cookie consent, or only on inner pages such as the checkout are not seen.
  • Server-side software that leaves no public trace is invisible. A site can run on almost anything behind a CDN and tell you nothing.
  • Some sites refuse automated requests. They show up with the status blocked, not as a site without technologies. Read the status column before you count.
  • A missing result is not proof of absence. "No analytics found" means none was visible in the first response.

Being a good visitor

For each website the Actor reads robots.txt, requests the home page once and, where the page uses Google Tag Manager, reads the public container file. It identifies itself in its user agent, respects robots.txt and does not try to get around blocks. It reads public pages and public DNS records. It does not collect names, email addresses or other personal data.

If you try it on your own list and a technology is missing or wrongly matched, open an issue on the Actor's Issues tab. Wrong matches are fixed first.

More tools and the running ledger: https://sitegaugehq.github.io

title: Analyzing Learned Convnet Features with Dirichlet Process Gaussian Mixture Models
description:
arXiv:1702.07189v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Convolutional Neural Networks (Convnets) have achieved good results in a range of computer vision tasks the recent years. Though given a lot of attention, visualizing the learned representations to interpret Convnets, still remains a challenging task. The high dimensionality of internal representations and the high abstractions of deep layers are the main challenges when visualizing Convnet functionality. We present in this paper a technique based on clustering internal Convnet representations with a Dirichlet Process Gaussian Mixture Model, for visualization of learned representations in Convnets. Our method copes with the high dimensionality of a Convnet by clustering representations across all nodes of each layer. We will discuss how this application is useful when considering transfer learning, i.e.\ transferring a model trained on one dataset to solve a task on a different one.

title: A 200 OK After Redirects Is Not a Direct 200: Testing Internal Links in Node.js
description:
A link check can report success and still miss the thing you wanted to test.

Suppose your acceptance rule is: “This internal link must reach its destination without an HTTP redirect.” Checking only (await fetch(url)).status === 200 does not express that rule. With default redirect handling, the response can describe the final destination rather than the first response.

This example isolates that distinction with a disposable local server. It is a synthetic regression test, not a crawl of a client website or evidence of an SEO improvement.

AI disclosure: This article and its code were generated by an AI assistant. The executable example was run locally on Node.js v24.22.3. The test output below comes from that run; the routes and page content are invented fixtures.

Two assertions, two different questions

“Does the destination eventually return 200?” and “Does this exact URL return 200 directly?” are different checks.

Fixture First response Result with normal following
/direct 200 200
/old 301 to /direct?source=example 200
/chain 302 to /old 200 after two hops
/loop 307 to itself Cannot finish successfully
/missing 404 404

The table describes the server defined below. The script deliberately follows only /old; its other assertions inspect the first hop. It does not run a redirect loop to exhaustion.

A successful eventual response is useful evidence, but it is not evidence of a redirect-free link. In this test, redirect: 'manual' makes the first response observable. The expected status is exactly 200, not just response.ok, which also includes other 2xx statuses.

A copy-and-run regression test

Save the following as redirect-check.mjs and run node redirect-check.mjs. It uses Node's built-in HTTP server, assertions and fetch. No package installation, account, credentials or public target is needed. The server binds only to loopback and chooses a temporary port.

import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { createServer } from 'node:http';

// Local, synthetic fixtures only. Nothing is fetched from the public internet.
const server = createServer((req, res) => {
  const url = new URL(req.url, 'http://fixture.invalid');
  if (url.pathname === '/direct') {
    res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'text/plain' });
    res.end('Example page');
  } else if (url.pathname === '/old') {
    res.writeHead(301, { Location: '/direct?source=example' });
    res.end();
  } else if (url.pathname === '/chain') {
    res.writeHead(302, { Location: '/old' });
    res.end();
  } else if (url.pathname === '/loop') {
    res.writeHead(307, { Location: '/loop' });
    res.end();
  } else {
    res.writeHead(404);
    res.end('Not found');
  }
});
await new Promise(resolve => server.listen(0, '127.0.0.1', resolve));
const origin = `http://127.0.0.1:${server.address().port}`;

async function firstHop(href) {
  const requested = new URL(href, origin);
  // This demo accepts only its own fixture origin, not arbitrary URLs.
  if (requested.origin !== origin || requested.username || requested.password) {
    throw new Error('Outside the local fixture origin');
  }
  const response = await fetch(requested, {
    method: 'GET', redirect: 'manual', signal: AbortSignal.timeout(2000)
  });
  const result = {
    status: response.status,
    location: response.headers.get('location'),
    direct200: response.status === 200
  };
  // Release resources; this check does not need the page body.
  await response.body?.cancel();
  return result;
}

try {
  const followed = await fetch(`${origin}/old`, {
    signal: AbortSignal.timeout(2000)
  });
  assert.equal(followed.status, 200);
  assert.equal(followed.redirected, true);
  assert.equal(new URL(followed.url).pathname, '/direct');
  await followed.body?.cancel();
  console.log('Default fetch: /old -> status 200, redirected true');

  const cases = [
    ['/direct?source=example#details', 200, null, true],
    ['/old', 301, '/direct?source=example', false],
    ['/chain', 302, '/old', false],
    ['/loop', 307, '/loop', false],
    ['/missing', 404, null, false]
  ];
  for (const [href, status, location, direct200] of cases) {
    const actual = await firstHop(href);
    assert.deepEqual(actual, { status, location, direct200 });
    console.log(`${href}: ${actual.status}; direct200=${actual.direct200}`);
  }
  await assert.rejects(firstHop('https://example.com/'), /Outside/);
  console.log('PASS: default-follow check, five first-hop cases, origin guard');
} finally {
  server.closeAllConnections();
  await new Promise(resolve => server.close(resolve));
}

What the run actually established

The recorded output was:

Default fetch: /old -> status 200, redirected true
/direct?source=example#details: 200; direct200=true
/old: 301; direct200=false
/chain: 302; direct200=false
/loop: 307; direct200=false
/missing: 404; direct200=false
PASS: default-follow check, five first-hop cases, origin guard

The first assertion demonstrates the false shortcut: /old produces a final 200, but redirected is true. The five manual checks distinguish direct success, a permanent redirect, the start of a chain, a self-redirect and a missing URL. The final assertion rejects an input outside the fixture origin before any request is made.

The checker does not follow a Location header. In particular, the /loop test is one request, not an unbounded traversal. It cancels response bodies it does not need and uses a timeout. Assertions stop the run on a mismatch, while the finally block closes the server.

Apply the rule to a link, not just a destination

For an authorised check of a site you maintain, record the source page, the original href and the first response separately. If a replacement is appropriate, verify the intended destination and update that specific link. Do not delete a redirect simply because one internal link no longer needs it; old bookmarks and external references may still depend on it.

Keep query parameters and fragments intentional. In the fixture, the redirect supplies ?source=example; a replacement that drops it would not preserve the same URL. The #details fragment in the direct fixture is not sent in an HTTP request. A 200 therefore says nothing about whether a matching HTML anchor exists. Validate the actual anchor separately.

Use GET when you need to test GET behaviour. A HEAD-only check is a different request and can produce different results on some servers. Conversely, do not casually fetch arbitrary user-supplied URLs: the small origin guard here is tailored to a fixed local fixture, not a complete security design for a public URL-checking service.

Boundaries of this test

This is a Node.js example, not code for a browser console. Browser Fetch can expose manual redirects as opaque responses; do not assume you will be able to read the same status and headers there. Node's built-in fetch uses Undici, whose documentation explains its manual-redirect behaviour.

A direct 200 also does not establish that the content is correct, in the right language, indexable or canonical. It will not detect a JavaScript redirect, a meta-refresh, a soft-404 page or a broken fragment. Those require additional checks. Keep this assertion narrow: for this GET request, the first HTTP response is 200.

References

  • Node.js: built-in fetch
  • Undici: specification compliance and manual redirects

title: SpecSearch: Towards Hardware-Aware Efficient Speculative Decoding
description:
arXiv:2611.22296v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates large language model (LLM) inference, but its optimal configuration depends jointly on workload characteristics, GPU hardware, and available memory. For example, on the RTX~5090, the state-of-the-art speculative drafter DFlash achieves $3.50\times$ the throughput of autoregressive (AR) decoding at low concurrency, but only $0.76\times$ at high concurrency with short outputs. We present SpecSearch, a hardware-aware search engine that jointly optimizes decoding strategy, draft length, and precision across workload--GPU pairs. Its analytical cost model captures memory and compute constraints to identify feasible configurations and narrow the search space for throughput optimization. Guided by this model, calibration measurements are collected from multiple GPUs. Using the measurements, a Jev-based predictor learns to select high-throughput decoding configurations on held-out GPUs without requiring deployment-GPU calibration. The predictor is parameter-efficiently trained on calibration data, while adapting a frozen Qwen3-4B using LoRA adapters and a linear correction layer. Across NVIDIA RTX~5090, H100, L40 and AMD MI300X GPUs, SpecSearch with full calibration achieves an average of $2.01\times$ the throughput of AR and $1.36\times$ the throughput of SD, both served by vLLM. The proposed Jev-based predictor closely matches this search performance with $1.30\times$ throughput improvement over SD with vLLM, while eliminating the need for held-out GPU calibration. Additionally, it retains $97.36\%$ of the throughput achieved by SpecSearch that utilizes full calibration.

title: A Hybrid Exact-Heuristic Solver for the Integrated Passenger and Parcel Transportation Problem
description:
arXiv:2611.22043v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We describe the solver we submitted to the second round of the SOICT 2026 contest on the Integrated Passenger and Parcel Transportation problem, a selective pickup-and-delivery routing problem with time windows, open routes and heterogeneous taxis. The solver is a single-file, standard-library Python program that combines (i) a constant-time insertion test based on latest-arrival slack, (ii) greedy insertion, local search and an Adaptive Large Neighborhood Search (ALNS) with simulated-annealing acceptance, and (iii) an exact route-selection engine that enumerates, for every taxi, the best feasible route for each request set and then solves the resulting set-packing problem by branch-and-bound strengthened with route-based large neighborhood search, Lagrangian bounds and reduced-cost fixing. The engine is chosen automatically from the instance size, and an independent verifier and a watchdog guarantee that a valid answer is always printed. On the official evaluation (38 scored instances, 5-minute limit) the solver obtained a total benefit of 487,237, finished every run within 277 s and used at most 279 MB; 28 of the 38 instances terminated well before the limit.

title: What is GhostMap that Aqua Security detected in IronWorm and Atomic Arch?
description:
Aqua Security details GhostMap, a concealment component identified in IronWorm malware samples distributed via compromised software packages.

Learn how the stealth tool hides selected processes and network connections.

GhostMap does the hiding; it's not the entire malware. Aqua examined IronWorm, which was distributed via compromised software packages. Previous research had reported that IronWorm targeted developer secrets, such as login credentials and digital access keys.

How GhostMap was installed

The researchers examined the file included in the package [email protected]When they ran it with administrator privileges, the file copied itself elsewhere on the system and created a service that remained installed. The service launched GhostMap.

The test did not show that the program could obtain administrator privileges on its own or start without them.

What could he be hiding?

In tests, some programs didn't appear in a regular list of what was running. However, researchers were able to find them from other parts of the system. They reappeared in the lists when GhostMap was stopped.

The connection used by IronWorm did not appear in any of the connection lists in all three tests. However, another check still showed it, without revealing which program had opened it.

Aqua also found program names and internal structures in the Atomic Arch sample that matched GhostMap. This does not prove that the two campaigns were run by the same operator. The detailed testing of what it could hide and how it could be detected was on the IronWorm sample that Aqua tested.

What did Aqua's tool detect?

Aqua's Tracee tool detected three programs that could change data in the memory of other applications. In the test, it recorded all 48 calls involving reading directories. This suggests that it was able to detect the activity, not prevent it.

Aqua confirmed that IronWorm stored test data on the system itself. It did not observe any successful sending of data outside the system, nor did it confirm successful execution of remotely authenticated commands.

For systems that may have been exposed, Aqua suggests comparing the lists of programs seen with preserved executables and known paths. /proc/PIDIt also suggests checking for unrecognized services and programs associated with eBPF. Before removing a suspicious file, administrators should keep its information and any additional information stored with it.

title: MemT-1.0: Towards Memory-Native Evolution
description:
arXiv:2610.26825v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Memory-native evolution requires making memory an intrinsic capability of foundation models, enabling them to continuously accumulate and utilize information. To this end, we introduce MemT-1.0, a new architecture of memory foundation models that internalize memory as part of model computation. Building on Metis, MemT-1.0 employs Gated DeltaNet-2 with a stable token-level memory update mechanism within each turn. We further introduce Mixture-of-Storage to scale native memory capacity. Following a deliberate backbone preparation, we develop a two-stage training pipeline consisting of continued pre-training and post-training, supported by 34B tokens of training data and efficient training and inference infrastructure. We release a model family comprising MemT-1.0-Nano, MemT-1.0-Flash, and MemT-1.0-Pro, and conduct a comprehensive evaluation of memory and general capabilities. The results show that they outperform the parametric memory baselines on average and remain competitive with retrieval-augmented methods, while largely preserving general capabilities. At a history length of 128K tokens, MemT-1.0-Nano achieves approximately $1.86\times$ end-to-end inference speedup and a $66\times$ reduction in persistent storage relative to full context KV cache. By internalizing retrieved procedural experience, MemT-1.0 improves task success on agentic tasks, providing a practical step toward memory-native evolution.

title: RLDE: A Reinforcement Learning Framework for Interpretable Iterative Document Editing
description:
arXiv:2611.22039v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Improving the quality, clarity, and flow of long documents remains a challenging problem in NLP, as human editing typically occurs through iterative refinement rather than a single-pass rewrite. Most existing automated systems act as black-box generators or rely on supervised learning, limiting interpretability and failing to capture the sequential nature of revisions. In this paper, we propose RLDE, an automated end-to-end metric-driven RL framework that formulates document revision as a reference-free MDP problem (unsupervised with respect to paired document-revision targets). Working with a limited action space (NOOP, INSERT, DELETE, REPLACE), RLDE leverages Pointer Networks for dynamic span selection at the token level and sends generative actions to the frozen BART-base model to obtain context-aware suggestions. PPO agents learn to optimize a multi-objective reward function based on readability, perplexity, and grammar metrics with the help of a novel SBERT-based Semantic Preservation Penalty constraint to avoid deletion degeneracy. Evaluations on the BEA-2019 dataset showed statistically significant results (p < 0.01) across all metrics, where Flesch Reading Ease increased from 49.8 to 59.4, perplexity decreased from 63.7 to 39.8, while preserving 93% of semantic information. When compared to Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompt-engineered models like GPT-4 and LLaMA-2, RLDE shows high performance at a very low computational inference cost. Moreover, the quality of edits generated by RLDE has been verified via human evaluations, scoring 4.9/5 for meaning preservation and 4.4/5 for edit quality.

title: Building a Production-Ready Localization and Internationalization System in Angular
description:
A Complete Architecture Using Angular 22, ngx-translate, RxJS, and Tailwind CSS

1. Introduction

Localization is often treated as a simple feature: add a language dropdown, create two JSON files, and replace hardcoded strings with translation keys.

However, this approach is not sufficient for a real-world application.

Imagine building an enterprise dashboard used by employees in different countries. Some users prefer English, while others prefer Arabic. When a user changes the language, the entire application must respond immediately.

This includes:

  • Navigation menus and page titles.
  • Dashboard statistics and product information.
  • Form labels, placeholders, and validation messages.
  • Dates, currencies, and numbers.
  • Text direction and layout.
  • Notifications and dynamically generated messages.
  • Content loaded from APIs.

A production-ready localization system must also consider performance, maintainability, lazy loading, caching, fallback languages, and testing.

In this article, we'll build a realistic Angular application with English and Arabic support and design its localization architecture as if we were implementing it for a real company.

By the end, we'll have a system that supports runtime language switching, RTL/LTR layouts, feature-based translation files, and a reusable translation service.

2. Understanding Internationalization and Localization

Before writing code, it's important to understand two concepts.

Internationalization (i18n)

Internationalization is the process of designing an application so it can support multiple languages and regional conventions without requiring major code changes.

For example, an application should not assume that:

  • Every language reads from left to right.
  • Every country uses the same date format.
  • Every currency uses the same symbol.
  • Every language has the same pluralization rules.

Internationalization focuses on preparing the application for different cultures and languages.

Localization (l10n)

Localization is the process of adapting an internationalized application to a specific language or region.

For example:

English Arabic
Dashboard لوحة التحكم
Products المنتجات
Settings الإعدادات
Welcome back مرحباً بعودتك
Save changes حفظ التغييرات

Localization also includes date formatting, number formatting, currency conventions, and text direction.

The distinction is important:

Internationalization is an architectural decision. Localization is the implementation of that decision for specific languages and regions.

3. Project Architecture

We'll build a small enterprise dashboard called Global Commerce Dashboard.

It will contain three main pages:

  1. Dashboard: displays statistics and recent activity.
  2. Products: displays a list of products.
  3. Product Details: displays information about a selected product.

We'll also implement shared components such as:

  • Navbar.
  • Language Switcher.
  • Reusable Button.
  • Reusable Input.

Why Feature-Based Architecture?

A common mistake is organizing an entire application by technical type:

components/
services/
models/
pages/
pipes/

This structure may work for small applications, but it becomes difficult to maintain when features grow.

Instead, we'll organize the application around business features.

Each feature owns its components, routes, models, and feature-specific translations.

Project Structure 

src/
│
├── app/
│   │
│   ├── core/
│   │   ├── localization/
│   │   │   ├── translation.service.ts
│   │   │   ├── translation.types.ts
│   │   │   ├── missing-translation.handler.ts
│   │   │   └── locale.config.ts
│   │   │
│   │   ├── interceptors/
│   │   └── guards/
│   │
│   ├── shared/
│   │   ├── components/
│   │   │   ├── navbar/
│   │   │   ├── language-switcher/
│   │   │   ├── button/
│   │   │   └── input/
│   │   │
│   │   └── pipes/
│   │
│   ├── features/
│   │   ├── dashboard/
│   │   │   ├── dashboard.component.ts
│   │   │   └── dashboard.routes.ts
│   │   │
│   │   └── products/
│   │       ├── components/
│   │       ├── pages/
│   │       │   ├── products-list/
│   │       │   └── product-details/
│   │       ├── models/
│   │       └── products.routes.ts
│   │
│   ├── app.component.ts
│   ├── app.config.ts
│   └── app.routes.ts
│
├── assets/
│   └── i18n/
│       ├── en.json
│       ├── ar.json
│       │
│       └── features/
│           └── products/
│               ├── en.json
│               └── ar.json
│
└── styles.css

Notice that we're separating global translations from feature translations.

This is important because a large application may have dozens of features, and loading every translation file during application startup would waste bandwidth and increase initial loading time.

4. Choosing the Translation Library

Angular provides two main approaches to internationalization.

Angular Built-in i18n

Angular's built-in i18n system is useful when translations are managed during the build process.

It works particularly well for applications that:

  • Have predefined language versions.
  • Don't need frequent runtime language changes.
  • Prefer separate localized application builds.

However, runtime switching between languages requires a different deployment and application architecture.

ngx-translate

For this application, we'll use ngx-translate.

It provides:

  • Runtime language switching.
  • JSON-based translation files.
  • Lazy loading.
  • Interpolation.
  • Translation fallback.
  • Reactive translation updates.
  • Standalone provider APIs.
  • Hierarchical translation services for lazy-loaded features.

Another important detail is that ngx-translate v18 uses Angular Signals internally while still supporting RxJS-based APIs.

We'll use RxJS in our application-level abstraction to expose a consistent reactive interface.

Architecture decision: ngx-translate handles the translation engine, while our TranslationService handles application-specific localization behavior.

This separation prevents components from depending directly on the translation library.

5. Project Setup

Create the Angular application:

ng new global-commerce-dashboard \
  --standalone \
  --routing \
  --style css \
  --strict

cd global-commerce-dashboard

Install the translation dependencies:

npm install @ngx-translate/core @ngx-translate/http-loader

Install Tailwind CSS:

ng add tailwindcss

Angular CLI provides an official Tailwind integration that configures the required dependencies and styles.

We can also verify the Angular version:

ng version

For this implementation, use the compatible ngx-translate v18 release.

Why Strict Mode?

Strict mode helps detect problems before runtime.

For example:

  • Incorrect types in translation parameters.
  • Nullable values.
  • Invalid component inputs.
  • Inconsistent service contracts.

Localization code frequently handles dynamic values, so strict typing is particularly valuable.

6. Designing the Translation Files

We'll start with the global translation files.

src/assets/i18n/en.json

{
  "app": {
    "name": "Global Commerce",
    "welcome": "Welcome back, {{name}}",
    "loading": "Loading...",
    "save": "Save",
    "cancel": "Cancel",
    "search": "Search"
  },
  "navigation": {
    "dashboard": "Dashboard",
    "products": "Products",
    "settings": "Settings"
  },
  "dashboard": {
    "title": "Dashboard",
    "subtitle": "Here's what's happening with your business.",
    "statistics": {
      "revenue": "Total Revenue",
      "orders": "Total Orders",
      "customers": "Customers",
      "products": "Products"
    },
    "activity": {
      "title": "Recent Activity"
    }
  },
  "common": {
    "actions": "Actions",
    "viewDetails": "View Details",
    "noData": "No data available",
    "error": "Something went wrong"
  }
}

src/assets/i18n/ar.json

{
  "app": {
    "name": "التجارة العالمية",
    "welcome": "مرحباً بعودتك، {{name}}",
    "loading": "جاري التحميل...",
    "save": "حفظ",
    "cancel": "إلغاء",
    "search": "بحث"
  },
  "navigation": {
    "dashboard": "لوحة التحكم",
    "products": "المنتجات",
    "settings": "الإعدادات"
  },
  "dashboard": {
    "title": "لوحة التحكم",
    "subtitle": "إليك آخر المستجدات المتعلقة بنشاطك التجاري.",
    "statistics": {
      "revenue": "إجمالي الإيرادات",
      "orders": "إجمالي الطلبات",
      "customers": "العملاء",
      "products": "المنتجات"
    },
    "activity": {
      "title": "النشاط الأخير"
    }
  },
  "common": {
    "actions": "الإجراءات",
    "viewDetails": "عرض التفاصيل",
    "noData": "لا توجد بيانات",
    "error": "حدث خطأ غير متوقع"
  }
}

Why Nested Translation Keys?

Instead of creating hundreds of unrelated keys:

{
  "dashboardTitle": "Dashboard",
  "dashboardRevenue": "Total Revenue",
  "dashboardOrders": "Total Orders"
}

We organize translations by domain:

{
  "dashboard": {
    "title": "Dashboard",
    "statistics": {
      "revenue": "Total Revenue",
      "orders": "Total Orders"
    }
  }
}

This improves readability and makes the translation structure easier to maintain.

It also makes it easier to compare the English and Arabic dictionaries.

7. Configuring ngx-translate

Now we'll configure the translation engine.

app.config.ts

import {
  ApplicationConfig,
  inject,
  provideAppInitializer
} from '@angular/core';

import {
  provideHttpClient
} from '@angular/common/http';

import {
  provideRouter
} from '@angular/router';

import {
  provideTranslateService,
  TranslateService
} from '@ngx-translate/core';

import {
  provideTranslateHttpLoader
} from '@ngx-translate/http-loader';

import {
  firstValueFrom
} from 'rxjs';

import { routes } from './app.routes';
import { TranslationService } from './core/localization/translation.service';

export const appConfig: ApplicationConfig = {
  providers: [
    provideRouter(routes),

    provideHttpClient(),

    provideTranslateService({
      loader: provideTranslateHttpLoader({
        prefix: '/assets/i18n/',
        suffix: '.json'
      }),

      lang: 'en',
      fallbackLang: 'en'
    }),

    provideAppInitializer(() => {
      const translationService = inject(TranslationService);

      return firstValueFrom(
        translationService.initialize()
      );
    })
  ]
};

Understanding the Configuration

provideTranslateService() registers the root translation service.

The HTTP loader retrieves translation files using the selected language.

For example:

/assets/i18n/en.json
/assets/i18n/ar.json

The fallbackLang option defines the language used when a translation is missing from the active language.

The application initializer ensures that the preferred language is loaded before the application starts rendering its main content.

This helps prevent untranslated content from briefly appearing during startup.

8. Creating a TranslationService Abstraction

This is one of the most important architectural decisions.

We don't want every component to inject TranslateService and independently manage:

  • localStorage.
  • Language validation.
  • RTL/LTR configuration.
  • Browser language detection.
  • Language switching.
  • Error handling.

Instead, we'll create a centralized abstraction.

8.1 Translation Types

translation.types.ts

export const SUPPORTED_LANGUAGES = [
  'en',
  'ar'
] as const;

export type SupportedLanguage =
  typeof SUPPORTED_LANGUAGES[number];

export type TextDirection = 'ltr' | 'rtl';

export interface LanguageConfig {
  code: SupportedLanguage;
  label: string;
  direction: TextDirection;
  locale: string;
}

export const LANGUAGE_CONFIG: Record<
  SupportedLanguage,
  LanguageConfig
> = {
  en: {
    code: 'en',
    label: 'English',
    direction: 'ltr',
    locale: 'en-US'
  },

  ar: {
    code: 'ar',
    label: 'العربية',
    direction: 'rtl',
    locale: 'ar-EG'
  }
};

Why define a language configuration instead of using simple strings?

Because language is more than a translation file.

Each language may have its own:

  • Text direction.
  • Date conventions.
  • Number formatting.
  • Currency conventions.
  • Regional settings.

Centralizing these properties makes it easier to add new languages later.

8.2 Implementing the Service

translation.service.ts

import {
  Injectable,
  inject,
  signal
} from '@angular/core';

import {
  TranslateService
} from '@ngx-translate/core';

import {
  BehaviorSubject,
  Observable,
  catchError,
  from,
  map,
  of,
  switchMap,
  tap
} from 'rxjs';

import {
  LANGUAGE_CONFIG,
  LanguageConfig,
  SupportedLanguage
} from './translation.types';

@Injectable({
  providedIn: 'root'
})
export class TranslationService {

  private readonly translate = inject(TranslateService);

  private readonly storageKey = 'app-language';

  private readonly currentLanguageSubject =
    new BehaviorSubject<SupportedLanguage>('en');

  readonly currentLanguage$ =
    this.currentLanguageSubject.asObservable();

  readonly currentLanguage = signal<SupportedLanguage>('en');

  readonly direction = signal<'ltr' | 'rtl'>('ltr');

  readonly locale = signal('en-US');

  readonly languages = Object.values(LANGUAGE_CONFIG);

  initialize(): Observable<SupportedLanguage> {

    const language = this.getInitialLanguage();

    return this.translate
      .setFallbackLang('en')
      .pipe(
        switchMap(() => this.translate.use(language)),
        map(() => language),
        tap(() => this.applyLanguage(language))
      );
  }

  switchLanguage(
    language: SupportedLanguage
  ): Observable<SupportedLanguage> {

    if (!LANGUAGE_CONFIG[language]) {
      return of(this.currentLanguage());
    }

    return this.translate.use(language).pipe(
      map(() => language),
      tap(() => this.applyLanguage(language)),
      catchError(error => {
        console.error('Language switching failed', error);

        return of(this.currentLanguage());
      })
    );
  }

  private applyLanguage(
    language: SupportedLanguage
  ): void {

    const config: LanguageConfig =
      LANGUAGE_CONFIG[language];

    this.currentLanguage.set(language);

    this.direction.set(config.direction);

    this.locale.set(config.locale);

    this.currentLanguageSubject.next(language);

    localStorage.setItem(
      this.storageKey,
      language
    );

    document.documentElement.lang = language;

    document.documentElement.dir =
      config.direction;
  }

  private getInitialLanguage(): SupportedLanguage {

    const savedLanguage =
      localStorage.getItem(this.storageKey);

    if (this.isSupportedLanguage(savedLanguage)) {
      return savedLanguage;
    }

    const browserLanguage =
      navigator.language.split('-')[0];

    if (this.isSupportedLanguage(browserLanguage)) {
      return browserLanguage;
    }

    return 'en';
  }

  private isSupportedLanguage(
    language: string | null
  ): language is SupportedLanguage {

    return (
      language !== null &&
      Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(
        LANGUAGE_CONFIG,
        language
      )
    );
  }
}

Why Use BehaviorSubject?

We need a reactive stream that notifies components when the active language changes.

For example:

this.translationService.currentLanguage$
  .subscribe(language => {
    console.log('Current language:', language);
  });

A BehaviorSubject immediately emits the latest language to new subscribers.

This is useful for components that are created after the user has already changed the language.

We also expose Signals for convenient integration with Angular templates.

Why Apply the Language After Loading?

Notice the order:

return this.translate.use(language).pipe(
  map(() => language),
  tap(() => this.applyLanguage(language))
);

We first load the translation dictionary, then update the application's language state.

This avoids updating the UI direction while the requested translation is still loading.

Production Consideration: SSR

The example above targets a browser-rendered application.

If we introduce Angular SSR, direct access to localStorage, navigator, and document must be protected using Angular's platform abstractions.

Also, user-specific language state must not be shared between server requests.

Now we can build a reusable component.

language-switcher.component.ts

import {
  Component,
  inject
} from '@angular/core';

import {
  TranslatePipe
} from '@ngx-translate/core';

import {
  TranslationService
} from '../../../core/localization/translation.service';

import {
  SupportedLanguage
} from '../../../core/localization/translation.types';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-language-switcher',
  standalone: true,
  imports: [TranslatePipe],
  template: `
    <div class="flex items-center gap-2">

      <button
        type="button"
        (click)="changeLanguage('en')"
        [class.font-bold]="
          translation.currentLanguage() === 'en'
        "
        aria-label="Switch to English"
      >
        English
      </button>

      <span aria-hidden="true">|</span>

      <button
        type="button"
        (click)="changeLanguage('ar')"
        [class.font-bold]="
          translation.currentLanguage() === 'ar'
        "
        aria-label="التغيير إلى العربية"
      >
        العربية
      </button>

    </div>
  `
})
export class LanguageSwitcherComponent {

  readonly translation = inject(TranslationService);

  changeLanguage(language: SupportedLanguage): void {
    this.translation.switchLanguage(language)
      .subscribe();
  }
}

Why Is This Component Reusable?

It doesn't know anything about:

  • Dashboard.
  • Products.
  • Routing.
  • Translation file locations.
  • localStorage implementation.

Its only responsibility is allowing users to select a language.

This is an example of the Single Responsibility Principle.
