13. Feature-Based Lazy Loading

A large enterprise application should not load every page during the initial application startup.

Angular Router supports lazy loading through loadComponent and loadChildren.

app.routes.ts

import {
  Routes
} from '@angular/router';

export const routes: Routes = [

  {
    path: 'dashboard',
    loadComponent: () =>
      import('./features/dashboard/dashboard.component')
        .then(m => m.DashboardComponent)
  },

  {
    path: 'products',
    loadChildren: () =>
      import('./features/products/products.routes')
        .then(m => m.PRODUCT_ROUTES)
  },

  {
    path: '',
    pathMatch: 'full',
    redirectTo: 'dashboard'
  },

  {
    path: '**',
    redirectTo: 'dashboard'
  }

];

This gives us lazy-loaded feature bundles.

But there's another performance issue.

What happens when the application has 20 features and each feature contains hundreds of translation keys?

Loading all translation dictionaries at startup is still unnecessary.

We need to lazy-load translations independently.

14. Lazy Loading Feature Translation Files

This is where ngx-translate's hierarchical services become useful.

We'll keep global translations in the root service and give the Products feature its own child translation service.

Our structure will be:

assets/i18n/
│
├── en.json
├── ar.json
│
└── features/
    └── products/
        ├── en.json
        └── ar.json

Products English Translation

assets/i18n/features/products/en.json

{
  "products": {
    "title": "Products",
    "subtitle": "Manage your product inventory",
    "name": "Product Name",
    "price": "Price",
    "status": "Status",
    "details": "Product Details",
    "inStock": "In Stock",
    "outOfStock": "Out of Stock",
    "add": "Add Product",
    "items": "{count, plural, =0 {No products} one {One product} other {# products}}"
  }
}

Products Arabic Translation

assets/i18n/features/products/ar.json

{
  "products": {
    "title": "المنتجات",
    "subtitle": "إدارة مخزون المنتجات",
    "name": "اسم المنتج",
    "price": "السعر",
    "status": "الحالة",
    "details": "تفاصيل المنتج",
    "inStock": "متوفر",
    "outOfStock": "غير متوفر",
    "add": "إضافة منتج",
    "items": "{count, plural, =0 {لا توجد منتجات} one {منتج واحد} two {منتجان} few {# منتجات} many {# منتجاً} other {# منتج}}"
  }
}

The pluralization strings above use ICU MessageFormat syntax. To interpret them, we need a MessageFormat compiler rather than the default ngx-translate parser.

We'll discuss pluralization implementation separately.

Products Routes

products.routes.ts

import {
  Routes
} from '@angular/router';

import {
  provideChildTranslateService
} from '@ngx-translate/core';

import {
  provideTranslateHttpLoader
} from '@ngx-translate/http-loader';

export const PRODUCT_ROUTES: Routes = [

  {
    path: '',
    providers: [
      provideChildTranslateService({
        loader: provideTranslateHttpLoader({
          prefix: '/assets/i18n/features/products/',
          suffix: '.json'
        })
      })
    ],

    children: [

      {
        path: '',
        loadComponent: () =>
          import('./pages/products-list/products-list.component')
            .then(m => m.ProductsListComponent)
      },

      {
        path: ':id',
        loadComponent: () =>
          import('./pages/product-details/product-details.component')
            .then(m => m.ProductDetailsComponent)
      }

    ]
  }

];

Why Use a Child Translation Service?

The child translation service is connected to the root service.

It inherits the active language and can resolve translations from its parent when a key is not available locally.

For example:

<h1>{{ 'products.title' | translate }}</h1>

The Products feature loads its own translation dictionary.

However:

<button>{{ 'common.save' | translate }}</button>

Can still resolve a global translation from the root service.

This gives us two levels:

  • Root translations for application-wide content.
  • Child translations for feature-specific content.

This is much cleaner than creating one enormous JSON file.

Important: Child translation providers are scoped to their route. Don't register a new independent root translation service inside every feature, because that can break shared language state.

17. Interpolation

Translation messages often contain dynamic values.

For example:

Welcome back, Abanoub

We shouldn't construct translated messages manually.

Instead, define a placeholder in the translation file:

{
  "welcome": "Welcome back, {{name}}"
}

Arabic:

{
  "welcome": "مرحباً بعودتك، {{name}}"
}

Then use:

<h1>
  {{ 'app.welcome' | translate: { name: 'Abanoub' } }}
</h1>

The translation engine replaces the placeholder with the supplied value.

The important advantage is that the translator controls the complete sentence.

This matters because word order can differ significantly between languages.

Avoid building translated sentences by concatenating multiple translated fragments.

For example, this is fragile:

const message =
  translatedWelcome + userName + translatedSuffix;

A language may require a completely different sentence structure.

18. Pluralization

Pluralization is more complicated than adding an s to a word.

English commonly uses:

  • One product.
  • Two products.
  • Five products.

Arabic has more complex plural categories:

  • Zero.
  • One.
  • Two.
  • Few.
  • Many.
  • Other.

We should never implement pluralization by manually checking whether a number equals one.

Option 1: Angular I18nPluralPipe

For simple cases, Angular already provides I18nPluralPipe.

Example:

import {
  Component
} from '@angular/core';

import {
  I18nPluralPipe
} from '@angular/common';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-product-count',
  standalone: true,
  imports: [I18nPluralPipe],
  template: `
    <p>
      {{
        productCount
          | i18nPlural: pluralMessages : locale
      }}
    </p>
  `
})
export class ProductCountComponent {

  productCount = 5;

  locale = 'en-US';

  pluralMessages = {
    '=0': 'No products',
    '=1': 'One product',
    other: '# products'
  };

}

For Arabic, we can define additional categories after registering Arabic locale data.

Option 2: ICU MessageFormat

For larger applications, a MessageFormat compiler is a better choice when translators need to manage complex plural and gender rules directly inside translation messages.

ngx-translate provides an integration point through its TranslateCompiler API.

A compatible MessageFormat compiler can be configured through provideTranslateCompiler().

The message might look like:

{count, plural,
  =0 {No products}
  one {One product}
  other {# products}
}

Arabic can use its own categories:

{count, plural,
  =0 {لا توجد منتجات}
  one {منتج واحد}
  two {منتجان}
  few {# منتجات}
  many {# منتجاً}
  other {# منتج}
}

The compiler interprets these rules using the selected language's pluralization behavior.

For an enterprise application with complex messages, I'd choose ICU MessageFormat because it keeps linguistic rules inside the translation dictionaries instead of spreading them across Angular components.

19. Date and Number Localization

Changing text is only one part of localization.

Consider these values:

2026-11-12
125000

They may need different representations depending on the user's locale.

Date Formatting

Angular's DatePipe supports locale-aware formatting.

Example:

import {
  DatePipe
} from '@angular/common';

@Component({
  standalone: true,
  imports: [DatePipe],
  template: `
    {{ today | date:'longDate':undefined:locale() }}
  `
})
export class ExampleComponent {

  readonly today = new Date();

  readonly locale = inject(
    TranslationService
  ).locale;

}

The date format changes when the locale changes.

Registering Locale Data

Angular requires locale data to be registered for locales that aren't included by default.

In the application bootstrap configuration:

import {
  registerLocaleData
} from '@angular/common';

import localeAr from '@angular/common/locales/ar';

registerLocaleData(localeAr);

For applications supporting several locales, register the necessary locale data for each supported language.

Number Formatting

Angular's DecimalPipe also accepts a locale argument.

{{ amount | number:'1.2-2':locale() }}

Example:

amount = 125000.50;

The output will follow the selected locale's number conventions.

Currency Formatting 

{{ amount | currency:'EGP':'symbol':'1.2-2':locale() }}

Don't assume that changing the language automatically changes the currency.

Language, locale, and currency are related but separate concepts.

An Egyptian Arabic user may prefer Arabic text while still viewing prices in USD.

Currency should usually be controlled by business or user preferences, not inferred exclusively from the selected language.

20. RTL and LTR Support with Tailwind CSS

One of the biggest mistakes in multilingual interfaces is assuming that translating text automatically produces a correct RTL layout.

It doesn't.

Arabic requires proper direction-aware styling.

For example:

<div class="text-start">
  Content
</div>

This is preferable to:

<div class="text-left">
  Content
</div>

Similarly:

<div class="ms-4">
  Content
</div>

Uses logical margin spacing rather than physical left/right spacing.

Logical CSS Properties

Prefer:

.card {
  margin-inline-start: 1rem;
  padding-inline: 1.5rem;
  text-align: start;
}

Instead of:

.card {
  margin-left: 1rem;
  padding-left: 1.5rem;
  text-align: left;
}

Logical properties adapt automatically to the document direction.

Direction-Aware Layout

Use:

<div
  class="flex items-center justify-between"
  [attr.dir]="translation.direction()"
>

For elements containing English product codes, emails, or phone numbers inside an Arabic page, use:

<span dir="ltr">
  support@example.com
</span>

This prevents mixed-direction content from displaying incorrectly.

Important RTL Testing Areas

Always test:

  • Navigation menus.
  • Icons and directional arrows.
  • Breadcrumbs.
  • Forms and validation messages.
  • Tables.
  • Dropdown menus.
  • Modals.
  • Pagination.
  • Charts.
  • Dates and numbers.

RTL is a layout concern, not simply a text-alignment concern.

21. Fallback Language and Missing Translation Handling

Imagine the Arabic dictionary doesn't contain:

products.discount

But the English dictionary does.

We want the application to display the English fallback instead of showing an empty value or crashing.

We already configured:

provideTranslateService({
  fallbackLang: 'en'
})

This gives ngx-translate a fallback dictionary.

However, there may be cases where the key is missing from both dictionaries.

For development, we should make missing keys easy to identify.

A custom missing translation handler can help.

missing-translation.handler.ts

import {
  Injectable
} from '@angular/core';

import {
  MissingTranslationHandler,
  MissingTranslationHandlerParams
} from '@ngx-translate/core';

@Injectable()
export class AppMissingTranslationHandler
  implements MissingTranslationHandler {

  handle(
    params: MissingTranslationHandlerParams
  ): string {

    console.warn(
      `[Missing Translation] ${params.key}`
    );

    return `⟦${params.key}⟧`;
  }
}

Then register it inside the translation service configuration using ngx-translate's provider helper:

import {
  provideMissingTranslationHandler
} from '@ngx-translate/core';

provideTranslateService({

  fallbackLang: 'en',

  loader: provideTranslateHttpLoader({
    prefix: '/assets/i18n/',
    suffix: '.json'
  }),

  missingTranslationHandler:
    provideMissingTranslationHandler(
      AppMissingTranslationHandler
    )

});

The important idea is that missing translations should be visible during development.

For production, the behavior can be adjusted according to the product requirements, but silently hiding translation problems is not a good practice.

22. Translation Caching Strategy

Translation files are mostly static resources.

We don't want to download the same translation dictionary every time the user navigates between pages.

There are several caching layers:

1. ngx-translate In-Memory Store

Once a language is loaded, ngx-translate keeps its translation data in memory.

This helps prevent unnecessary requests when switching between components that use the same translation service.

2. Browser HTTP Cache

Configure your server or CDN to return suitable cache headers for versioned translation assets.

For example:

Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable

This is appropriate when translation file URLs include content hashes or version identifiers.

For non-versioned URLs, use shorter caching policies or revalidation.

3. CDN Caching

In enterprise environments, translation files can be served through a CDN.

This reduces latency for users in different geographic regions.

4. Cache Invalidation

Translation changes must become visible after deployment.

A common approach is to use content-hashed asset filenames or include an application release version in translation asset paths.

Don't assume that localStorage is a suitable translation cache.

Persisting the selected language is useful, but caching the complete translation dictionary in localStorage introduces invalidation and stale-data problems.

23. Browser Language Detection

We already implemented browser language detection in:

navigator.language

The initialization order is:

  1. Read the saved language.
  2. If it is supported, use it.
  3. Otherwise, inspect the browser language.
  4. If supported, use it.
  5. Otherwise, use English.

For example:

Saved language: ar
Browser language: en-US
Selected language: ar

The saved user preference takes priority over browser preferences.

This is important because users should not have their selected language unexpectedly changed every time they open the application.

24. Integrating Localization with Angular Router

A language switch should not navigate the user away from the current page.

For example:

/products/15

If the user changes from English to Arabic, the application should remain on:

/products/15

The route itself doesn't need to change because language is managed globally.

Our TranslationService already updates the active language without reloading the application.

For larger applications, there are two possible routing strategies.

Strategy A: Global Language State 

/dashboard
/products
/products/15

The language is stored separately.

This is the approach we're using in this project.

It's suitable for internal dashboards and authenticated business applications.

Strategy B: Language-Based URLs 

/en/dashboard
/ar/dashboard
/en/products/15
/ar/products/15

This approach is more suitable for public websites where SEO and sharing localized URLs are important.

A route guard can validate the language segment and update the translation service before rendering the page.

For our dashboard, global language state is simpler and avoids unnecessary routing complexity.

25. Reusable Buttons and Inputs

Reusable components should not own application translations.

Instead, they should receive translation keys from their parent components.

For example:

button.component.ts

import {
  Component,
  input
} from '@angular/core';

import {
  TranslatePipe
} from '@ngx-translate/core';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-button',
  standalone: true,
  imports: [TranslatePipe],
  template: `
    <button
      type="button"
      class="rounded-lg bg-blue-600 px-4 py-2 text-white"
      [disabled]="disabled()"
    >
      {{ label() | translate }}
    </button>
  `
})
export class ButtonComponent {

  label = input.required<string>();

  disabled = input(false);

}

Usage:

<app-button label="app.save" />

The component doesn't need to know what the Save button means.

It only knows that it receives a translation key.

The same principle applies to reusable input components.

For example:

<label>
  {{ labelKey | translate }}
</label>

<input
  [placeholder]="placeholderKey | translate"
/>

This approach improves reusability across different features.

26. Testing the TranslationService

Localization should be tested like any other important application service.

We need to verify:

  • The default language.
  • Language switching.
  • Language persistence.
  • Direction changes.
  • Unsupported language handling.

Example:

translation.service.spec.ts

import {
  TestBed
} from '@angular/core/testing';

import {
  TranslateService
} from '@ngx-translate/core';

import {
  of
} from 'rxjs';

import {
  TranslationService
} from './translation.service';

describe('TranslationService', () => {

  let service: TranslationService;

  const translateMock = {
    use: jasmine.createSpy().and.returnValue(of({})),

    setFallbackLang: jasmine.createSpy()
      .and.returnValue(of({}))
  };

  beforeEach(() => {

    localStorage.clear();

    TestBed.configureTestingModule({
      providers: [
        TranslationService,
        {
          provide: TranslateService,
          useValue: translateMock
        }
      ]
    });

    service = TestBed.inject(TranslationService);

    translateMock.use.calls.reset();

  });

  it('should be created', () => {

    expect(service).toBeTruthy();

  });

  it('should initialize with English by default', (done) => {

    service.initialize().subscribe(language => {

      expect(language).toBe('en');

      expect(service.currentLanguage()).toBe('en');

      done();

    });

  });

  it('should switch to Arabic', (done) => {

    service.switchLanguage('ar').subscribe(language => {

      expect(language).toBe('ar');

      expect(service.direction()).toBe('rtl');

      expect(
        localStorage.getItem('app-language')
      ).toBe('ar');

      done();

    });

  });

});

The mock isolates our application abstraction from the actual HTTP translation loader.

For integration tests, we should also test the real translation provider and verify that the correct JSON files are loaded.

27. Testing the Language Switcher Component

We should test the user interaction itself.

language-switcher.component.spec.ts

import {
  TestBed
} from '@angular/core/testing';

import {
  of
} from 'rxjs';

import {
  LanguageSwitcherComponent
} from './language-switcher.component';

import {
  TranslationService
} from '../../../core/localization/translation.service';

describe('LanguageSwitcherComponent', () => {

  const translationMock = {

    currentLanguage: () => 'en',

    switchLanguage: jasmine.createSpy()
      .and.returnValue(of('ar'))

  };

  beforeEach(async () => {

    await TestBed.configureTestingModule({

      imports: [
        LanguageSwitcherComponent
      ],

      providers: [
        {
          provide: TranslationService,
          useValue: translationMock
        }
      ]

    }).compileComponents();

  });

  it('should switch to Arabic when Arabic is clicked', () => {

    const fixture =
      TestBed.createComponent(LanguageSwitcherComponent);

    fixture.detectChanges();

    const buttons =
      fixture.nativeElement.querySelectorAll('button');

    buttons[1].click();

    expect(
      translationMock.switchLanguage
    ).toHaveBeenCalledWith('ar');

  });

});

This test verifies that selecting Arabic calls the correct service method.

In a larger application, we should add tests for:

  • Browser language detection.
  • Invalid stored language values.
  • Failed translation requests.
  • Missing translation fallback.
  • Direction switching.
  • Feature translation loading.
  • Date and number formatting.

28. Common Mistakes in Production

Here are some mistakes worth avoiding.

1. Hardcoding User-Facing Text

Bad:

<h1>Products</h1>

Better:

<h1>{{ 'products.title' | translate }}</h1>

2. Concatenating Translated Sentences

Bad:

'Welcome ' + username + ' back'

Better:

{
  "welcome": "Welcome back, {{name}}"
}

3. Assuming RTL Means Text Alignment Only

Changing text-align doesn't solve all RTL problems.

Use logical spacing, direction-aware layouts, and proper testing.

4. Loading Every Translation at Startup

This creates unnecessary network traffic.

Use global dictionaries for shared content and feature-specific translation chunks for lazy-loaded features.

5. Mixing Language and Currency

Arabic doesn't automatically mean Egyptian Pound.

Language, locale, timezone, and currency should be modeled separately.

6. Directly Injecting TranslateService Everywhere

This creates unnecessary coupling.

Use a TranslationService abstraction to centralize application behavior.

7. Ignoring Missing Keys

Missing translation keys should be detectable during development and covered by automated checks.

8. Using Index-Based Translation Keys

Avoid:

{
  "text1": "Dashboard",
  "text2": "Products"
}

Prefer meaningful names:

{
  "navigation": {
    "dashboard": "Dashboard",
    "products": "Products"
  }
}

9. Translating Backend Business Values Blindly

The backend should return stable identifiers or structured business data.

For example:

{
  "status": "PENDING"
}

The frontend can map that identifier to:

{
  "status": {
    "PENDING": "Pending"
  }
}

This prevents the backend from becoming dependent on a specific frontend language.

29. Enterprise-Level Architecture

For a larger company, I would extend this architecture in several directions.

29.1 Centralized Translation Management

Instead of manually editing JSON files across multiple teams, use a translation management platform.

A typical workflow:

Developer
    |
    v
Translation Keys
    |
    v
Translation Management Platform
    |
    v
Professional Translators
    |
    v
Review and Approval
    |
    v
Translation API / JSON Export
    |
    v
Angular Application

This makes translation updates easier to coordinate across development, product, and localization teams.

29.2 Backend Translation API

In some systems, translations are managed dynamically by the backend.

For example:

GET /api/translations/en
GET /api/translations/ar

The response might be:

{
  "orders": {
    "title": "Orders",
    "status": "Order Status"
  }
}

A custom TranslateLoader can retrieve dictionaries from an API rather than static assets.

Example:

import {
  Injectable,
  inject
} from '@angular/core';

import {
  HttpClient
} from '@angular/common/http';

import {
  TranslateLoader
} from '@ngx-translate/core';

import {
  Observable
} from 'rxjs';

@Injectable()
export class ApiTranslateLoader
  implements TranslateLoader {

  private readonly http = inject(HttpClient);

  getTranslation(
    language: string
  ): Observable<Record<string, unknown>> {

    return this.http.get<Record<string, unknown>>(
      `/api/translations/${language}`
    );

  }
}

This can be useful when non-developers need to update translations without rebuilding the frontend.

However, it introduces additional concerns:

  • API availability.
  • Authentication.
  • Cache invalidation.
  • Version compatibility.
  • Translation deployment consistency.

For smaller applications, static JSON files are usually simpler.

29.3 Translation Versioning

In production, translation dictionaries should have versions.

For example:

{
  "version": "2026.11.1",
  "translations": {
    "dashboard": {
      "title": "Dashboard"
    }
  }
}

This helps identify stale translation data and coordinate frontend and backend deployments.

29.4 Translation Validation in CI/CD

A CI pipeline should verify that:

  • All required translation files exist.
  • JSON files are valid.
  • Required keys exist in every supported language.
  • Nested structures are consistent.
  • No unused keys remain.
  • Interpolation parameters are consistent.
  • Feature translation files follow naming conventions.

For example, a validation script could compare English and Arabic dictionaries and fail the build when required keys are missing.

This prevents translation problems from reaching production.

29.5 Observability

Translation failures should be observable.

We can record:

  • Failed translation requests.
  • Missing translation keys.
  • Unsupported language selections.
  • Translation loading duration.
  • API errors.

These events can be sent to an observability platform such as Sentry or an internal monitoring service.

Don't log sensitive interpolation values or user-specific content.

30. SEO Considerations for Multilingual Applications

SEO requirements depend on the type of application.

For an authenticated dashboard, SEO may not be important because most pages aren't publicly indexed.

For a public multilingual website, however, it becomes a major architectural concern.

Consider these URLs:

/en/products
/ar/products

Search engines can discover separate localized versions.

We should also configure:

HTML Language Attribute 

<html lang="ar" dir="rtl">

Alternate Language Links 

<link
  rel="alternate"
  hreflang="en"
  href="https://example.com/en/products"
/>

<link
  rel="alternate"
  hreflang="ar"
  href="https://example.com/ar/products"
/>

<link
  rel="alternate"
  hreflang="x-default"
  href="https://example.com/products"
/>

Server-Side Rendering

For public content, Angular SSR can improve how localized pages are delivered to search engines and users.

However, SSR must be designed carefully so one user's language preference doesn't leak into another server-rendered request.

The language should be resolved per request through the URL, request headers, or an appropriate user preference.

31. Final Architecture Review

Let's review the responsibilities of each layer.

Layer Responsibility
TranslationService Application localization state
ngx-translate Translation engine
TranslationLoader Loading JSON dictionaries
LanguageSwitcher User language selection
Navbar Navigation and shared UI
Feature Routes Lazy loading and feature translation scope
Angular Pipes Date and number formatting
Tailwind CSS Responsive and direction-aware styling
Backend API Business data and optional dynamic translations

The most important architectural principle is separation of concerns.

The translation library should not control business logic.

Components should not manage persistence.

Feature modules should not duplicate global localization behavior.

And the backend should not depend on a specific frontend language.

32. Conclusion

Building a multilingual Angular application requires more than translating labels.

A production-ready localization architecture must account for language state, runtime updates, text direction, regional formatting, translation loading, caching, routing, testing, and deployment.

In this implementation, we used:

  • Angular standalone architecture.
  • Feature-based project organization.
  • ngx-translate v18.
  • RxJS and Angular Signals.
  • Lazy-loaded translation dictionaries.
  • Hierarchical translation services.
  • English and Arabic support.
  • RTL/LTR switching.
  • localStorage persistence.
  • Browser language detection.
  • Interpolation and pluralization.
  • Locale-aware date and number formatting.
  • Tailwind CSS logical utilities.
  • Unit and component tests.

These decisions give us a foundation that can grow from a small dashboard into a larger enterprise application without turning localization into a collection of unrelated components and utility functions.

The goal isn't simply to make the application speak multiple languages.

The goal is to make localization a first-class part of the application's architecture.

title: A Link You Can Just Open
description:
This essay was first published on the Zyaku blog.

Here is a small scene I keep imagining.

It's late in the evening and the power has been out for an hour. In a family group on someone's phone, a cousin forwards a link: a local reporter's post about which roads are under water and which bridge is closed. The phone has one bar. The person holding it taps the link.

A page loads, slowly. It doesn't show the post. It shows a form. Email. Password. Confirm password. A code is on its way to your inbox. The bar flickers, and the code never comes. They close the tab, go back to the group and ask, "What does it say?" Then they wait for someone with better signal to type it out.

Nothing in that scene is broken. Every part works the way somebody designed it. That's what bothers me about it.

This week we changed it on Zyaku. When someone shares a public post with you, you can now read it without signing up. Zyaku asks you to join only when you want to do more than read: like, comment, follow or save. And anyone, with an account or without one, can report a post.


A forwarded link should open to the words, not to a form.

The wall in front of the words


Most links lead to a gate before they lead to anything else.

Most apps put the sign-up wall right in front of the content, and I understand why. Every visitor who turns into an account is something a team can point to at the next meeting. A link someone opens, reads and closes counts for nothing. So the wall goes up early, and its cost lands on the person who only wanted to read one thing.

I've stood on the wrong side of that wall more times than I can remember. Usually it costs me a minute. On a bad connection, in a bad hour, it can cost the whole point of the link. A shared post is often a message from someone you trust: I think you should see this. Turning that into a registration form is a strange way to treat a recommendation.

So now the post comes first. You see who wrote it, their words and pictures, and the labels Zyaku puts on posts: whether something was made with AI, whether media was altered, whether a claim is disputed, and how sure Zyaku is about the post itself. If you want to join the conversation, Zyaku asks you then, and after you sign up it brings you straight back to the post you were reading.

For people who do join, there's a small new welcome too. New accounts now get a Start here card on Home for their first couple of weeks, with one first step that fits what they said they do. Creators can practise posting with no signal: write something, switch the connection off and on, and watch what Zyaku would show while a real post waits. The practice post is never sent. I like that a first lesson can be a rehearsal with nothing at stake.

Ask at the counter


Anyone can read the rates on the wall. The paperwork waits for the counter.

Before I built software, I spent years in finance. One habit from that world took me a long time to see clearly. You ask for someone's papers when money is about to move, not when they walk through the door.

Anyone can stand in a bank and read the rates on the board. The identity checks, the forms and the signatures come at the counter, when there's something real to protect. Ask too early and you don't make anything safer. You make people leave, and you end up holding information you had no reason to collect.

That's how a shared post works now. Reading asks for nothing. Doing something that touches other people, like a comment or a follow, asks you to be someone.

We took the idea one step further than I first expected to. When you open a shared post without an account, Zyaku sets no cookie, keeps nothing in your browser and doesn't count your visit. We also ask search engines not to list these previews, so a post shared with a few people doesn't quietly become a page for the whole web.

That last part has a cost, and I'd rather name it. We won't know how many people opened a link and left. Somebody building a growth chart would love that number. I decided I'd rather not have it than take it from people who never agreed to anything.

Some doors stay shut


Opening one door made us decide which ones stay closed.

Opening the door for reading made us think hard about what should never sit behind it.

Not every post opens without an account. Emergency and crisis messages don't, and neither do posts tied to a place during a crisis. A message someone wrote in a frightening moment, saying where they are, wasn't written for strangers, and a forwarded link can travel much further than its author ever meant it to. Posts by anyone under eighteen don't open this way either. Nor do followers-only posts, mature posts or paid work. A comic chapter is still something readers pay for, and creators still get paid for the chapter they unlock.

Anything outside those rules gets the same short answer as a post that doesn't exist: this post can't be shown here. It doesn't explain why, on purpose. Sometimes the reason itself gives something away.

And while I'm on safety, the line I repeat in every one of these essays: Zyaku is not an emergency service. If you're in danger, call your local emergency number first.

In the language you read in


An open door helps more when you can read what's behind it.

An open door doesn't help much if what's behind it is in a language you can't read. So the other half of this week was about language.

Any journalism article on Zyaku can now be read in any of the languages Zyaku offers, and your choice is remembered for next time. Posts on your screen are now translated together, so they show up in your language much sooner. The shared-post preview, the Start here card and the Zyaku AI screen now appear in every language we support, not only in English.

When Zyaku translates a post, it says so. You can see that the translation was made by AI and what language it came from, and the original is one tap away. I care about that label as much as the translation. A reader deserves to know when the words in front of them aren't the words the writer chose.

This one is personal. I think in a mix of Hindi and English, like a lot of people I grew up with, and most software has treated that as a mistake to correct. A report written in one language by a reporter in one town should be able to reach a reader somewhere else without either of them doing anything special. That's the whole job.

What isn't finished


Some of this is done. Some of it is still on the bench.

Plenty.

Only ordinary posts, pictures, videos and clips open without an account for now. Comics and paid pieces still ask you to sign in, and some of that is deliberate rather than unfinished.

Reports from people without an account can be misused. We limit how often they can come from one place, and they go into the same queue as every other report. I don't think that's the final answer, and I'll keep watching it.

The phone apps aren't public yet, so everything here is about a link opened in a browser. And signing up on one bar of signal is still heavier than it should be. Letting people read first fixes the first minute. It doesn't fix every minute after that.

Underneath all of this, the offline core keeps moving too. HoldSend, our open-source library for writing offline and publishing exactly once, is public under the Apache license, and an early version is now on npm for anyone to try. Its interface may still change, and its own README says plainly that it isn't ready for production.

The first thing we ask


Read first. Decide later.

The first thing a product asks of a stranger says a lot about it. For a long time the answer across most of the internet has been: tell us who you are. I'd like Zyaku's answer to be: nothing yet.

Back in that dark room, the link opens. The post is there. The person reads which bridge is closed, types it into the family group, and goes back to waiting for the lights. Nobody had to make an account to be useful to each other.

So here's my question for you. What's the last link you gave up on because it wanted an account before it would show you anything? I'm curious what you were trying to read, and whether you ever found it another way.

Rohit Kashyap

Founder & CEO, Zyaku · Founder, TAMVEL

What's new on Zyaku · About the founder

title: Celigo Platform MCP and the Celigo CLI: What They Do and How to Set Them Up Safely
description:
Originally published on integrationstars.com. Facts checked against Celigo's developer documentation on November 3, 2026.

Celigo now gives you two first-party ways to work with an integrator.io account outside the UI:

  • Platform MCP: a hosted MCP server, run by Celigo, that lets an AI client (Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, VS Code and others) read, build, run and troubleshoot your account in plain language. Generally available since June 18, 2026. Endpoint https://api.integrator.io/celigo-mcp (plus EU, AU and CA). Nothing to install.
  • Celigo CLI (@celigo/celigo-cli): every REST resource as a celigo <resource> <verb> command, with profiles, JSON/YAML/table/CSV output and --jq filtering. Generally available since April 5, 2026; needs Node.js 22+; MIT licensed.

Both call the same REST API with the same permissions. Neither can do more than the signed-in user or the token could do through the API.

Which one to use

You want to Use
Ask questions and make one-off fixes in plain language Platform MCP
Script repeatable changes or run checks in CI Celigo CLI
Let a coding assistant build and troubleshoot from your machine Celigo CLI (with Celigo skills loaded)
Call integrator.io from your own code or a runtime without Node.js REST API

A common pattern: diagnose in a chat client, then turn the fix into a reviewed CLI change.

Not to be confused with the Celigo MCP Server (the mcpServers resource you build to expose your own tools) or MCP Management (Celigo's gateway for governing MCP access). A tool you defined in an MCP Server can only do what you built it to do; Platform MCP can do anything your user or token can.

What an agent can change

list_* tools read, upsert_* tools create or update, and delete_resource deletes. Four details from Celigo's tool reference:

  • Delete never blocks. Dependents come back as warnings, "but the delete always proceeds".
  • An update is a full replace. upsert_* with an _id is a PUT of the whole document; patch_flow exists for single-field flow edits.
  • Stored secrets are guarded. Since the October 28 update, upsert_connection keeps a stored secret when the ****** mask is sent back.
  • Failed writes are not retried. A write that fails with a 5xx or network error may have run, so check before retrying.

Five guardrails before production

  1. Bind the session to a sandbox. OAuth sign-in picks one account and one environment; a bearer token is already bound to its account and environment.
  2. Use a scoped token. Celigo warns a full-access token "can read, change, and delete everything in your account". Custom-scoped tokens are limited to the resources you select.
  3. Use CLI permission modes, and know their limit. Profiles run in read, operate or full (default full). A mode "never adds to what the credential itself may do": it is a seatbelt, the token scope is the lock. Platform MCP's docs describe no equivalent modes.
  4. Ask for the plan before every write. In the CLI: celigo push --dry-run.
  5. Read the audit log by source. list_audit_log_entries filters by source, including mcp and cli. A separate token per agent makes each change attributable.

Integrations in git: pull, review, push 

npm install -g @celigo/celigo-cli
celigo login

# Pull one integration into a folder and put it in git
celigo pull --integration <integration-id> --dir ./acme --no-symlinks
cd acme
git init && git add . && git commit -m "baseline"

# After editing: check, plan, then write back
celigo status
celigo diff
celigo lint
celigo push --dry-run
celigo push

# Write the same tree into another environment
celigo promote --to sandbox

Safety rules worth knowing: lint runs offline against Celigo's published API schemas; push refuses any resource changed since your pull; push refuses connection documents that still hold the ****** mask; a tree is bound to the API host and token owner it was pulled with; promote needs full mode on the target.

Where we would start (our recommendation, not Celigo's)

  1. Read-only triage in chat, against a sandbox or with a read-scoped token.
  2. Operational actions (retries, error resolution) with confirmation. They change destination systems, so treat them as writes.
  3. Structural changes (new flows, mappings, deletes) only through pull, pull request and push.

Full guide, with the release timeline and FAQ: integrationstars.com. Sources: Celigo Developer Platform, Platform MCP, Platform MCP tools, Celigo CLI, profiles and permission modes, local tree, 2026 changelog, @celigo/celigo-cli on npm.

title: Multi-Region DR on AWS/Azure/GCP: What RTO/RPO Tiers Actually Cost in India (2026)
description:
If you've only ever tested failover in a staging environment, here's the gap between the demo and production reality: picking an RTO number is really picking an architecture, and the architecture is really picking a cost.

There are four patterns worth knowing cold. Backup-and-restore is cross-region snapshots plus a runbook — cheap (+10–20% over single-region spend), slow (4–24hr RTO). Pilot-light keeps a synced database and pre-wired networking in region two with compute scaled to near-zero — a solid middle ground (+20–40%, 1–4hr RTO). Warm-standby runs a genuinely live, scaled-down stack in region two continuously — this is where most production systems should land (+40–70%, 15–60min RTO). Active-active runs full capacity in both regions simultaneously behind a load balancer, with real-time bidirectional replication — expensive (+80–150%+) but near-zero RTO. Treat those percentages as planning ranges, not quotes: your real premium depends on how much of the stack you replicate, how you size the standby, and how chatty your data layer is.

Three things that bite engineers who haven't built this before: cross-region egress isn't free (₹1.5–2.5/GB between India regions adds up fast on a chatty database), reserved-capacity discounts (25–70% off on-demand) materially change which tier is affordable, and nobody budgets for the quarterly failover drill that actually proves the DR plan works instead of just existing on a diagram.

If you're building on India infrastructure specifically: AWS's Mumbai (ap-south-1) + Hyderabad (ap-south-2) pair, Azure's Central India + South India pair, and GCP's asia-south1 + asia-south2 pair are the natural defaults — not just for latency, but because RBI's payment-data localisation rule means DR copies of payment data can't legally live offshore anyway.

We wrote up the full RTO/RPO cost breakdown, including an INR pricing table by business size, here: Multi-Region Cloud Architecture & Disaster Recovery Cost for Indian Businesses in 2026.

title: Cost Optimization Hub now supports stopping idle Amazon EC2 instances
description:
AWS Cost Optimization Hub now lets you stop idle Amazon EC2 instances directly from your recommendations. Cost Optimization Hub consolidates and prioritizes cost optimization recommendations across your AWS accounts and Regions, including idle resources. Previously, stopping an idle instance required you to leave Cost Optimization Hub and identify the specific instance in the Amazon EC2 console. Now you can stop it from the Savings opportunities page in Cost Optimization Hub.

When you choose Stop next to an idle instance recommendation, a confirmation shows the instance, its account and Region, what the instance loses when it stops, such as instance store data and data in memory, and what continues to bill, such as EBS volumes and Elastic IP addresses. Stopping does not terminate the instance or delete its EBS volumes, and you can start it again from the EC2 console. Stop needs no separate setup and uses your existing permissions. To receive idle resource recommendations, turn on Cost Optimization Hub and AWS Compute Optimizer.

This feature is available at no additional charge in all AWS Regions except the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions and the China Regions.

To get started, open Cost Optimization Hub in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console and go to Savings opportunities. To learn more, see the Cost Optimization Hub product page and user guide.

title: How to check your Rust port against the Python original (with five real bugs it caught)
description:
You rewrote a Python library in Rust. The benchmarks look great and the test suite is green. One question is left, and it is the one your users care about: does it still do exactly what the old code did?

Your tests can't fully answer that. They check the inputs you thought of. The differences hide in the inputs nobody thought of.

The good news is that a port comes with something most code never has: a complete specification. It's the old code. You don't need to read the Rust or reason about it. Run both versions on the same input and compare what comes back. Repeat until they disagree.

Here is how to do that in practice, and five places it found real bugs.

The idea in one function 

def same(input):
    return python_version(input) == rust_version(input)

Everything else is detail. Where do the inputs come from? How do you compare outputs fairly? What if one side raises and the other doesn't?

Doing it with equiv

I use equiv, an open-source checker written in Rust. It generates inputs and runs each side in its own Python process. It stops at the first input where they disagree. Every run writes a receipt you can re-run byte for byte, which matters when you hand a bug to a maintainer.

Point it at both versions of a function:

equiv review port.py original.py parse str --errors-agree

--errors-agree counts it as agreement when both sides raise, because a port rarely raises the exact same exception class. One side raising while the other returns is still a difference.

If the port is a new release of the same package, give each side its own environment:

equiv review new.py old.py fn str \
  --reference-python old-env/bin/python \
  --candidate-python new-env/bin/python \
  --versions-of yourpackage

Each side reports which version it actually loaded, so you never compare the wrong build by accident.

A note on limits: this is testing, not proof. A clean run means the two versions agreed on every input it tried, and the output says how many. It works on functions that take and return plain Python values.

Five real examples

1. django-rusty-templates: a panic and a wrong count

django-rusty-templates is a Rust implementation of Django's template engine. Compared with Django's own engine across 27 checks:

  • wordwrap panicked on text starting with a non-breaking space.
  • This one is my favourite: 
'a<b'|capfirst|length

(that is, capitalise the string, then count its characters)

Django says 3. The Rust version said 6, because it escaped < to < too early and then counted the extra characters.

Seven differences in all (#587, #593), all fixed in five merged pull requests.

2. LiteLLM: a regression in a release candidate

LiteLLM moved parts of its core to Rust in 1.110. Running the last Python release (1.109.1) against the release candidate, each in its own environment:

  • temperature=1 was suddenly refused for 72 of 405 Claude model names that the previous release accepted (#51394, fixed in #52341).
  • The Rust-backed tokenizer differed from tiktoken on lone surrogates and very large token IDs (#51601, fixed in #51720).

3. sqlfluff: feed it SQL its tests never run

sqlfluff ships a Rust parser next to its Python one, and its CI already compares them on its own fixtures. They agree on all 16,442 statements. The trick was to give each dialect's parser SQL written for other dialects, which CI never does. Three parsers split. In one T-SQL statement, Python read the word day as a date part and Rust read it as a column name (#9095, fixed the next day).

4. ua-parser: three engines, one user agent

uap-python has three interchangeable engines, one of them in Rust. For Applebot's desktop crawler, the Python engine said "Mac" and the Rust engine said "Spider" (#334). The maintainer traced it to one rule and wrote a fix (uap-core#675). Running all three engines over the 17,820 user agents in the project's own tests: 9 disagreements before the fix, none after.

5. dulwich: a panic that except Exception can't catch

dulwich is Git in pure Python with a Rust speed-up for sorting tree entries. With names containing a slash, the Rust comparison stopped being a consistent ordering. Below 21 entries it sorted differently. From 21 entries it panicked, and a PyO3 panic is a BaseException, so ordinary except Exception handling doesn't catch it. The maintainer reproduced it and merged a fix the same day (#2582).

What I'd do if I were porting a library today

  1. Keep the old version runnable until the new one has been compared with it. Once you delete it, you lose your specification.
  2. Test the inputs nobody chose:
    • text that isn't English, including non-breaking spaces;
    • empty values and huge values;
    • inputs from a neighbouring format (another SQL dialect, another user agent family);
    • every input form the API accepts, not just the documented one.
  3. Treat a panic in the port as a bug, even if Python raised too. Python callers can't catch it the normal way.
  4. Decide which side is right before you ship. In the ua-parser case, the Rust engine was the correct one. Either way, your users shouldn't be the ones who find out.

The full write-up, with every issue and pull request linked, is on my site: Running Rust ports against the Python they replace.

If you're porting a library and want a second pair of eyes on it, I'm happy to run it against the original. Say hello in the comments.

title: Auditors Struggle to Catch Sabotage In End-to-End Transcripts of AI Safety Research
description:
arXiv:2611.21832v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As AI systems are increasingly used to automate AI R&D, misaligned systems could sabotage research intended to improve model safety and alignment. To stress-test defenses against such sabotage, we use a human expert as a proxy saboteur on AI safety research. We conduct a red-team/blue-team game where a human researcher runs AI safety experiments from scratch and auditors try to tell which were sabotaged and how. Given access to the full research transcript and the ability to run experiments, human auditors mostly fail to distinguish sabotaged from benign research: they achieve an AUROC of 0.59, not significantly better than chance, and fully identify the specific sabotage in only 17% of cases. Despite not being allowed to run experiments, the best frontier models outperform human auditors (Fable 5.1: AUROC 0.73, 32% full identification) within noise and weaker models perform comparably. When the saboteur chooses which experiments are attacked, rather than being required to sabotage every question given, sabotage identification drops further. Our results suggest that research sabotage by expert-level agents is difficult to detect with current auditing methods and provide a new setting for studying research sabotage.

title: Discovery of new antiviral agents through artificial intelligence: in vitro and in vivo results
description:
arXiv:2611.22230v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: In this research, we employed a deep reinforcement learning (RL)-based molecule design platform to generate a diverse set of compounds targeting the neuraminidase (NA) of influenza A and B viruses. A total of 60291 compounds were generated, of which 86.5% displayed superior physicochemical properties compared to oseltamivir. After narrowing down the selection through computational filters, nine compounds with non-sialic acid-like structures were selected for in vitro experiments. We identified two compounds, DS-22-inf-009 and DS-22-inf-021 that effectively inhibited the NAs of both influenza A and B viruses (IAV and IBV), including H275Y mutant strains at low micromolar concentrations. Molecular dynamics simulations revealed a similar pattern of interaction with amino acid residues as oseltamivir. In cell-based assays, DS-22-inf-009 and DS-22-inf-021 inhibited IAV and IBV in a dose-dependent manner with EC50 values ranging from 0.29 uM to 2.31 uM. Furthermore, animal experiments showed that both DS-22-inf-009 and DS-22-inf-021 exerted antiviral activity in mice, conferring 65% and 85% protection from IAV (H1N1 pdm09), and 65% and 100% protection from IBV (Yamagata lineage), respectively. Thus, these findings demonstrate the potential of RL to generate compounds with promising antiviral properties.

title: Illusory Truth or Salient Anomaly? Model-Dependent Responses to Repeated Poisoned Passages in RAG-Style Contexts
description:
arXiv:2610.41012v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Repeated passages in retrieved evidence may influence how language models identify misinformation, even when those passages restate a single underlying claim rather than provide independent support. We compare four instruction-tuned models on 200 claims from the BEIR SciFact test split using paired, fixed seven-document contexts. The minority condition contains one poisoned document and six non-target documents, whereas the majority condition contains the original poisoned document, five paraphrases, and one non-target document. Poison detection rates increase from 45.5% to 66.0% for Apertus-8B and from 4.0% to 15.5% for Aya-Expanse-8B, but decrease from 80.0% to 47.5% for Mistral-Nemo and from 25.0% to 9.5% for Gemma-3-12B-IT. All four paired comparisons are statistically significant. These contrasting results suggest that repeated poisoned evidence does not affect all models in the same way. One possible interpretation is that repetition makes the poisoned claim more conspicuous to some models, potentially facilitating its detection, while other models may treat repeated formulations as reinforcing evidence, potentially reducing their ability to identify the poisoned claim. Although these interpretations require further investigation, the findings highlight the importance of model-dependent responses to repeated evidence in retrieval-augmented settings.

title: EGS: A Complementary Safety Framework for Educational LLMs
description:
arXiv:2611.22203v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) offer strong potential for personalized education, but adolescent-facing deployment raises risks of toxic, biased, misleading, or developmentally inappropriate content. We argue that educational safety should move beyond binary refusal: student queries are often ambiguous or curiosity-driven, requiring contextual guidance rather than simple blocking. We introduce the Educational Guardrail System (EGS), a lightweight, model-agnostic runtime framework that complements intrinsic alignment through query moderation, scenario-aware pedagogical guidance, and response moderation. EGS triages inputs by risk level, redirects gray-zone queries with category-specific educational interventions, and audits outputs before delivery. Experiments across general and education-specific benchmarks show that EGS improves moderation performance, refusal quality, and jailbreak robustness across diverse LLMs. These findings suggest that defense-in-depth guardrails can strengthen safety while preserving the pedagogical utility required in educational LLMs. Our code and model weights will be publicly available to support community adoption.

title: One button sent people to the wrong page. We checked all 41, and 14 didn't go where they said.
description:
On Tuesday morning I opened the page a small clothing shop was about to get from us: a short video of one of their products, and under it a single button that said "Make one with your own character."

It was a product, not a character. And the button didn't open anything that makes a video. It opened the page where you build a new character from scratch.

This post is about that one button, the 40 others we checked because of it, and the rule we wrote so it stops happening.

TL;DR
We audited all 41 calls to action on our site and in our emails. 14 didn't go where their words said. We fixed 7 the same day, 7 sit on pages we froze on purpose, and a test now fails the build if a button drifts.

The words said one thing and the link did another

I build RefVid, a small tool where you upload a few photos of a product or a character once, then make short videos that keep it looking the same in every shot. Every finished video gets a public share page, and that page has one job: let whoever watches it make their own.

The share page picked its words from a fallback. When a video wasn't made from a template, the page assumed it was about a character, wrote "Keep your own character the same in every shot", and pointed the button at the character builder (we call saved characters and products "elements").

So a shop owner watching a video of their own product would read "character" and land on a form asking them to create one. Nothing on that page says "video".

My first fix sent it to a second wrong page

The obvious patch: read the subject's type. If the clip shows a product, say "Make one with your own product". That went in at 11:15 UTC.

Then I looked at where it actually led. With no template recorded, the new button opened our marketing page for product videos. The words were right now. The destination was a page that explains the thing instead of starting it.

That fix lasted 22 minutes. The second one, at 11:37, is what this post is really about, because by then the question had changed from "why is this button wrong?" to "how many buttons are wrong?"

So we listed every button on the site: 41 of them

We went through every page type and every email we send, and wrote down each call to action as a row: the file, the words, where it goes for a signed-in visitor, and where it should go.

41 rows. 27 were fine. 14 were not. These are the 7 we fixed that day:

Words on the button Where it lives Went to Now goes to
Make one with your own character Share page, clip with no template Character builder New video
Make one with your own product Share page, product clip, no template Marketing page New video
Make one with your own subject Gallery, clip with no template Character builder New video
Make your own series Series index, episodes, making-of pages Photo picker, then builder New video
Try it in the studio Prompt blocks on making-of pages Photo picker, then builder New video
(sign in) Invite welcome sheet, no template Character builder New video
Make another "Your video is ready" email That subject's page New video, same subject

The part that surprised me: the same action, "start a new video", was written four different ways in the code. One helper went to the builder, one component opened a photo picker first, one link went to the marketing page, and the email linked to the subject's own page. Every one of them made sense on the day it was written. Together they meant a visitor couldn't predict where "make one" would take them.

Not one label changed in the fix. The words were already right in all 7 languages we ship. Only the destinations moved.

The rule: one label, one destination, defined once

We wrote it down as four rows, and every button on the site now has to be one of them:

The button means Example words Goes to
Make one like this (template known) "Use this template" New video with that template filled in
Start a new video (no template) "Make one with your own…", "Try it", "Make another" New video, nothing preset
Create a character or product Only words that say so: "New element" The builder
Go to the studio "Studio", "Open the studio" The studio home

And each row is built by exactly one function. "Start a new video" is one helper call; nothing else in the codebase is allowed to assemble that link by hand. If you want to see the "make one like this" row working, any card in our template gallery goes straight into a new video with that template filled.

The same bug, in an email, cost a user 124 credits

The same morning a support email arrived. A user had signed up on their phone, added their own photo, and somehow never started a video. Our follow-up email said, more or less: the photo you added is already saved; open the link and press Generate.

The link carried their saved photo in the URL:

/studio/t/product-black-friday?subject=<their photo>

They opened it in their mail app, signed out. Our middleware redirected them to sign in and rebuilt the destination from the path only:

/login?intent=template:product-black-friday

The subject was gone. After sign-in, the template page did what it does when you have no photo: it loaded the template's sample product, a perfume bottle. They pressed Generate, exactly as the email told them, and 124 of their 129 signup credits went into a sample perfume ad they never asked for.

We refunded the credits and added extra, and fixed the redirect so the intent keeps everything it was given:

template:<slug>[:fresh][:subject-<id>]

In the 30 days before, 72 people got that exact "your photo is already saved" email. One of them hit this. That's a small number, and it is also every credit that person had.

It's the same mistake as the button, one layer down: the words promised a destination, and something between the click and the page threw part of it away.

Tests now fail the build if a button drifts

A rule I have to remember will fail again. So the rule is a test. cta-one-destination.test.ts reads the source and fails when:

  • any file outside a short allow-list sends someone to the builder (each allowed file has a one-line reason next to it),
  • a start link is assembled by hand instead of through the one helper,
  • the share page points at a marketing page,
  • a share button says "product" and opens the builder, or says "character" and opens a product page, checked in all 7 languages.

A second test follows the email link as a signed-out visitor through the sign-in redirect and checks that the saved photo is still in the URL where sign-in lands.

What we haven't fixed yet

7 of the 14 wrong buttons are still wrong, on purpose, for now.

They sit on pages we froze on 8 November: our home page, our pricing page and our cartoon series hub. Those are the pages an AI assistant had started sending visitors to, and we decided not to touch them at all while we watched whether that traffic held. We are now unfreezing pages one at a time, each change measured against its own before-numbers. These three haven't had their turn.

Words on the button Page Goes to today Should go to
Make one with your own subject Home, gallery Character builder New video
Make your own series Series hub, header Photo picker, then builder New video
Make your own series Series hub, closing block Photo picker, then builder New video
Generate (own photos, no template) Home, composer Builder with the photos New video with the photos
Make this (an ad format) Home, ad strip The sample subject's page New video with that prompt
Start free Pricing Studio home New video
One clip Pricing Studio home New video

The guard test knows about the three that open the builder: their files sit on its allow-list, each marked "frozen page". When a page thaws, its line comes off the list and the test forces the fix; the other four are on the audit list waiting for the same day. Until then, if you land on our home page and press one of those, you'll see the old behaviour.

A question for you

If you searched your own app today for every button that says "start", "try" or "make one", how many different places would they lead, and would you be able to say which one is right?

title: Literary Language Mashup: Curating Fictions with Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.21649v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In this paper, we propose an alternative approach to human evaluation of literary fictions by employing LLMs themselves as evaluators within the GrAImes framework. We apply this methodology to assess human-written and AI-generated microfictions in Spanish, to five PhD professors in literature and sixteen literary enthusiasts, and to short stories in both Spanish and English. By comparing the evaluations performed by LLMs with those of human judges, we examine the degree of alignment and divergence between both perspectives, thereby assessing the feasibility of LLMs as auxiliary literary evaluators. Our analysis focuses on the alignment of responses from LLMs with those of human evaluators, providing insights into the potential of LLMs in literary assessment. The conducted experiments reveal that while LLMs cannot be regarded as substitutes for human judges in the evaluation of literary microfictions and short stories, with a Krippendorff's alpha reliability coefficient less than 0.66, they can serve as a valuable tool that offers an initial perspective on the editorial quality of the texts in question. Overall, this study contributes to the ongoing discourse on the role of artificial intelligence in literature, underlining both its methodological constraints and its potential as a complementary resource for literary evaluation.

title: A reconnect schedule is a thundering-herd problem
description:
Our device agent has two reconnect schedules stacked on top of each other, and one guard behind
them. They look like tuning, but they set how the whole fleet meets the relay after an outage.

We have not published a measurement of a real relay restart, and this post does not claim one.
What follows is the design, read from the agent's code and checked with a simulation of the
library's backoff.

Schedule one: the socket library, with jitter

When the relay drops the connection, the socket library reconnects on its own first. The agent
asks for a 5 second first delay and a 60 second cap (session_manager.go:498-499). The delay
doubles on each attempt up to the cap. Each delay is randomised by up to half either way (the
library's default factor of 0.5, third_party/socket.io-client/constants.go:15-16), and then
clamped back into 5 to 60 seconds (Duration() in the library's backo2.go, v3.0.6).

That clamp is the part we got wrong. Every delay that jitter pulls below 5 seconds becomes exactly
5 seconds. We ran the library's own backo2.go 10,000 times with our settings. The first retry
landed between 5.0 and 7.5 seconds, and 5,005 of the 10,000 landed on exactly 5,000 ms. A relay
restart drops every socket at about the same moment, so about half the fleet's first attempts are
scheduled for the same 5 second delay, within whatever spread there was in noticing the drop.

The same thing happens from the other side at the cap. From the fifth retry on, the doubled delay
is already 60 seconds, jitter spreads it over 30 to 60, and the clamp puts about half on exactly
60 seconds: 5,011, 4,954 and 4,995 of 10,000 for the fifth, sixth and ninth retry. The second to
fourth retries are not clamped and are spread out.

There is one more random delay, and this one has no clamp. If the relay is shedding /init load
it answers temporarily_unavailable to an exchange, registration or token refresh
(init.socket.server.ts:243). The agent then waits a random 5 to 60 seconds and tries again, up
to three times (initBackoff, throttledRetries and retryWhileThrottled in
session_manager.go:47, :59-60, :811). That wait only matters for a device that runs an
/init exchange, and after a relay restart not every device does.

Which devices go back through /init

A device holds a session token for ten days (deviceJwtExpirationSeconds is 864000 in
src/config.json:52). The agent gets one in each Start() and hands it to the socket library
once. The library re-sends that same token on every reconnect, and the agent has no way to give
it a newer one (session_manager.go:501-506).

A connected device does also go back to /init every 24 hours
(refreshTokenTickerInterval, :84, scheduledRefresh, :630). But that rotates the stored
refresh credential only. The session token on the wire stays the one from the last Start(). The
relay checks its signature and expiry on every handshake (session.socket.server.ts:224), and a
rotation does not invalidate it, because the row the token names keeps its identity
(init.socket.server.ts:592-596). So after a relay restart the fleet splits in two:

  • Session token under ten days old. The library reconnects /session with the token it has. No /init exchange runs, so the clamped library delay is its only spread.
  • Session token older than that. The relay refuses it. The device shows as not connected, and the next 60-second tick runs Start() (main.go:272). That refreshes over /init inside retryWhileThrottled (session_manager.go:461-463), which is where the relay sheds load and the random 5 to 60 second wait spreads those devices out.

The age that counts is the time since the process last ran Start(), not since the device first
connected.

Schedule two: the agent's own loop, without jitter

Behind the library sits a plain loop in main.go (:21, :231-232):

  • 60 seconds. The agent checks its connection once a minute.
  • 5 quick retries. If the connection is still gone, it tears it down and rebuilds it from scratch on each of the next ticks, up to five times.
  • 30 minutes. After five rebuilds it waits until thirty minutes have passed since the last one, then starts over.

No jitter here, no exponential curve. Each agent's ticker starts when the agent starts, so ticks
land at different seconds for different devices. That is the only spread this loop has.

What each schedule protects

Now say the relay comes back slow, or falls over again under load.

The library schedule is the one the relay meets first. Its first wave is half a wall: about half
the fleet scheduled for exactly 5 seconds, the rest spread over the next 2.5. After that the doubling thins
it out, until the cap gives half of the stragglers the same 60 second delay again.

The outer loop guards against something else: a device rebuilding its whole connection every
minute, forever. Each rebuild closes the previous connection first, so the library's own retries
on it end there. After the fifth, the loop leaves the last rebuild standing and stays quiet for
thirty minutes. What happens next depends on how far that rebuild got. If it had already created
its /session socket, that socket keeps retrying at the capped, jittered pace and brings the
device back by itself. If the relay was unreachable at /init, setup never finished. The /init
socket may reconnect, but it does nothing more, because the connect handler returns until setup
is done (handleInitConnect, session_manager.go:717-719). That device waits for the
thirty-minute mark.

In short: after a few quick tries in the first minute, a device starts at most one
rebuild a minute, and five of them. The library path does move partly in step, because of the
clamp, and the outer loop has no jitter at all. Those are the two things we would change first if
the fleet grew: a lower floor or our own jitter for the library, and jitter for the loop.

A failure that never retries

One case skips the loop. If the relay says the device's credential is no good, the agent exits
with code 2 instead of retrying (ExitCodeAuthFailure, main.go:16, :223-225, :275-278).
Only a refusal that is not also marked transient counts (requiresCredentialReset,
session_manager.go:120). A device with a dead credential hammering the relay every minute would
be a herd of its own.

Why you cannot just tune it

Change a sixty-second cap to ten and you have not tuned one device. You have changed the load on
your relay from every device, at once, on the next release. You cannot roll it back from the relay,
because the devices you would need to reach are the ones running the change.

That is why we treat these numbers as a fleet contract, not a setting. Changing them is a
load test you plan.
