title: Google Trends gives scrapers decoy data. Here's how to check yours
description:
I'm a data scientist and a professional data engineer, and an MSc student in Computer Science and Engineering, where the courses I chose are about data and AI. I started working with Google Trends when pytrends, the popular Python library for it, was archived in April 2025.

Something didn't match

Then I noticed something was wrong with my tool: what I saw in my normal browser and what my tool got didn't match. The rising related queries for "python" in my tool were things like "walmart near me". I was surprised, and curious.

So on 7 November 2026 I compared one search, "python", United States, past 12 months, panel by panel: what the Google Trends website showed in my browser, and what Google sent to my automated request.

What I found

Panel Website, in my browser Automated request
Interest over time 53 weeks identical, 53 of 53
Interest by state 51 states identical, 51 of 51
Interest by city 34 cities 3 cities
Rising related queries "python docs", "python 3.15"… "walmart near me", "lidl near me", "cheap flights 2024", "how to cook pasta"…
Related topics 38 topics none

Interest over time and interest by state were identical for both. But the website showed 34 cities in the browser, while the request got only 3. I mean, are you kidding me?

What surprised me more was the rising related queries. They were totally different. The website showed "python docs", while the request got "walmart near me", "lidl near me", "cheap flights 2024" and "how to cook pasta". Only 2 of 25 were the same.

And related topics? 38 on the website. Guess how many the request got. Yes: zero. :D

Why?

I think Google does this by labelling our requests: it treats a real browser as a normal user, and our automated request as a scraper. The requests labelled as scrapers got the decoys.

Why Google does this instead of sending an error is what confuses me. Why, Google? Why send decoy data?

Who should worry

People who use rising queries for content ideas, SEO, keyword research or research papers should worry about this. The decoys look normal, and nothing tells the user that they are fake.

For example, someone finds "baby diapers" as a rising keyword and starts making baby-diaper videos, while the trend he's chasing doesn't even exist.

Check your own tool in one minute

You can really check this in just one minute:

  1. In your tool, get the rising related queries for "python", United States, past 12 months.
  2. Open the same search on trends.google.com in your normal browser.
  3. Compare them.

If the keywords don't match, then boom: you've been fooled by Google, and so has the tool you were using.

What to do instead

I think what people should do is use only the panels that actually match. For something like related queries, use the download button on the Google Trends website itself. And once a month, compare that download with your tool.

Full disclosure

After discovering the issue, I fixed my Google Trends scraper. It now returns only the panels that actually match the website, and leaves out related queries, related topics and cities. I check it myself against the website every month, so I don't get the fake data.

Let me know: is your tool sending decoys too?

title: How One Base64 Bug Can Leak Your Java Heap (Java4Shell, CVE-2026-114938)
description:
How One Base64 Bug Can Leak Your Java Heap (Java4Shell, CVE-2026-114938)

Most Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) coverage on day one was either "your servers are on fire" or "it only crashes the JVM." Both skip the mechanism, and the mechanism tells you who is at risk. This post walks through why the bug exists, what the sources actually established, and what a defender can watch for.

I have not reproduced the bug. Everything below comes from public write-ups by Upwind, Endor Labs, Equixly, Qualys and Calif, and I flag where they disagree.

TL;DR

Claim Status
Heap write past the output array on x86-64 with AVX-512 VBMI Reproduced by Endor Labs (under an emulator) and Upwind (on real hardware)
JVM crash from a remote request Consistent across sources
Pre-auth RCE in named products Claimed by Calif, no public proof-of-concept
Attacker-controlled write contents Not supported, the written bytes are constant
Exploited in the wild None reported, not in CISA KEV as of November 17

Why an intrinsic exists at all

HotSpot ships a pure-Java Base64 decoder. When the JIT sees that decoder running hot, it can replace the Java loop with an intrinsic, a hand-written assembly stub for the target CPU. On x86-64 with AVX-512 VBMI, the stub decodes wide blocks at once.

Equixly makes two points that matter for exposure. The intrinsic replaces the Java code only after the JIT compiles the decoder, which on a busy server happens within seconds. And the vector path only engages above a length threshold. Endor Labs gives the threshold as 31 bytes on Java 21, 25 and 27, and 128 bytes on Java 17.

That is why the shortest triggers differ by version. 65 characters is enough on 21, 25 and 27. 17 needs 129.

The tail bug

The block loop handles most of the input. The last characters, including padding, go through a tail routine. Per Upwind, a malformed string ending in a stray = makes the tail calculate a negative output length. A small write becomes a full 64-byte write, 62 bytes beyond the end of the output array. Endor Labs measured 62 bytes for a single = tail and 63 for ==.

Two properties follow from the measurements.

First, the overflow content is fixed. Endor Labs says the bytes stay the same regardless of the input data. An attacker controls the length of the input and the heap layout around the destination array, not the bytes that get written.

Second, Java still rejects the input afterwards with an IllegalArgumentException. The exception is a useful tell, as the detection section below shows, but it fires after the damage.

Upwind also ran 300,000 well-formed inputs and saw no overflow, so ordinary traffic is not at risk. The trigger is a malformed string.

What the fix looks like

Endor Labs reports the fix as JDK-8393212, "Base64 optimization improvements," a four-line change that adds a guard before the size computation and routes short padded tails to the scalar path. Engineers committed it under embargo on October 14, 2026. Endor Labs also notes that on November 17 the public jdk17u, jdk21u and jdk25u repositories did not yet carry the fix, while Oracle's builds had shipped.

The vulnerable code arrived in 17.0.6 in January 2023 through a backport from JDK 18, and Equixly flags the 17.0.6 starting point as its own inference from backport history.

From crash to code execution

The crash path is simple. If the 62 stray bytes land on a live object, they overwrite its header, and the usual result is a SIGSEGV inside garbage collection, per Endor Labs. Equixly warns the crash log will not mention Base64, because the garbage collector reads the damaged object later.

Calif claims much more, in five stages.

Stage Claimed step
1 Corrupt an array length
2 Corrupt a second array to leak heap contents, which Calif calls JavaBleed
3 Repair object headers so the JVM keeps running
4 Groom the heap remotely so the overflow lands on a chosen object
5 Write into the JVM code cache

Endor Labs marks every one of these as Calif's claim. Calif says there is no universal exploit, and that each target needs its own decoder route, writable buffer, readable feedback channel and heap layout. The sources I read do not discuss address space randomization at all, so I will not call it a barrier or a bypass.

This is why your exposure depends on the application and not just the JVM. A service that decodes attacker data with Base64.getDecoder() on a hot path, and reflects some of the result, has the shape Calif describes. A service that never decodes attacker input is a crash risk at worst. Whether HTTP Basic or JWT parsing in a given product qualifies is an open question in the sources, so I treat it as unknown.

What does not reach the bug

Per the write-ups, these cases never reach the bug.

  • The MIME decoder takes the scalar path.
  • Third-party Base64 libraries that do not call java.util.Base64 do not reach the intrinsic.
  • ARM64 hosts, including Graviton, Ampere and Apple silicon, have no such stub. Equixly ran 794 crafted inputs on Temurin 17.0.21 for arm64 and saw no stray writes.
  • x86-64 without AVX-512 VBMI, such as Skylake-SP, Cascade Lake and AMD before Zen 4.

One discrepancy to know about: Equixly requires AVX-512 BW as well as VBMI, while Cyber Security News names only VBMI. Qualys lists four CPU flags (avx512f, avx512bw, avx512vbmi, bmi2) and says all four must appear.

Detection engineering

You cannot detect this with a dependency scan, since the flaw is in the runtime. You detect it at the edge, in the logs and on the host.

Edge rules

The malformed shape is checkable without decoding. Padded Base64 has a length divisible by 4, so a token ending in = or == with a length that is not a multiple of 4 fails on sight. Upwind's heuristic adds a size floor of 32 characters. Endor Labs suggests 65 as the lower bound when you run mixed Java versions. Equixly offers this rule for the Authorization header.

^Basic\s+(?:\S{4})*\S{0,2}=$

I have not tested it. Run it in log-only mode against production traffic first, because a wrong rule that blocks real logins is its own outage.

Application logs

Every trigger throws after the write. A burst of IllegalArgumentException from java.util.Base64 in a request handler, clustered by source address, is the signal Endor Labs recommends. Paced or fragmented Base64 traffic at a high rate from one source fits the same pattern, since heap grooming needs repeated attempts.

Host signals

  • New hs_err_pid*.log files with a SIGSEGV in a GC copy routine and a compiled Base64$Decoder.decode0 frame
  • Repeated JVM restarts of one service
  • Java processes that spawn a shell or open new outbound connections
  • Oversized or binary-looking responses from endpoints that echo decoded input, which would match the leak stage Calif describes 
# Recent JVM crash logs and their crash lines
find / -name 'hs_err_pid*.log' -mtime -2 2>/dev/null | while read -r f; do
  echo "$f"; grep -m1 -E '^# (SIGSEGV|Problematic frame)' "$f"
done

A crash log alone is not evidence of an attack. JVMs crash for plenty of other reasons. A cluster of crashes that line up with decode-heavy requests from one source is.

Where the sources disagree

I kept a list while reading, and you should keep your own.

  • Oracle's status. Equixly wrote that the fix was still pending. Qualys, Upwind and Cyber Security News say Oracle shipped fixed builds on November 17.
  • Severity. Qualys attributes the 9.2 (CVSS 4.0) to the researchers, Equixly to South Korea's NCSC, and nobody has published a vector string. Cyber Security News calls the 8.1 (CVSS 3.1) the OpenJDK advisory score, and Equixly says Oracle has not said which of its November flaws carries that score.
  • Java 8. Qualys and Cyber Security News list Oracle's 8u511b33-perf Performance Pack as affected. The same sources call standard Java 8 not affected.
  • The CVE mapping. Endor Labs marks the mapping from this bug to CVE-2026-114938 as not confirmed, because it could not retrieve the OpenJDK advisory. Check the CVE record yourself before you cite it in a ticket.

The bottom line

The mechanism is narrow: one assembly tail, one hardware feature, one malformed input shape. The reach is wide, because it sits in the runtime that bundled products carry. The honest status on November 17 is a proven crash, a claimed code execution chain and a patch that exists.

If you only do one thing, put a malformed-padding check in front of your Base64 decoding paths and an alert on the exception, then patch on your normal fast track. If a public exploit lands next week, you will already be watching the right signal.

What would you want your WAF to tell you about a bug class it cannot see inside the runtime?

GDS K S · thegdsks.com · building Glincker · follow on X @thegdsks

A bug in the runtime is a bug in everything that runs on it.

Sources: Upwind, Endor Labs, Equixly, Qualys, Cyber Security News, Calif.

title: Bandit Online Submodular Minimisation Using Zeroth-Order Oracles
description:
arXiv:2611.22130v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: We consider online submodular minimisation under bandit feedback, where at each round a decision maker plays a subset and observes only its cost, while the cost functions, and hence their minimiser, change over time. Existing bandit methods only guarantee static regret, which compares against a single fixed subset and is a weak benchmark when the minimiser moves. This paper provides, to the best of our knowledge, the first method with guarantees for tracking a moving minimiser in this setting. We propose a zeroth-order method built on a two-point oracle for the Lov\'asz extension whose two evaluations are both subsets that can be played. The perturbed and base points are rounded by a common random threshold, and drawing the smoothing direction from the unit sphere makes the base evaluation a zero-mean control variate, so the oracle is an unbiased estimator of the smoothed gradient. We establish dynamic regret bounds of order $O\big((1+\sqrt{P^\ast_N})N^{3/4}\big)$ in general and $O\big((1+\sqrt{P^\ast_N})N^{2/3}\big)$ under a sufficiently small drift, where $P^\ast_N$ is the path length of the minimiser sequence, together with the corresponding $O(N^{3/4})$ and $O(N^{2/3})$ static regret bounds. Numerically, the method attains lower regret than the algorithm of (Hazan and Kale (2012)), with the advantage growing with the path length.

title: Ramu Kaka's Notebook: How Bitcask Stores Data Without Ever Erasing Anything
description:
Remember Ramu Kaka?

If you read Danni, Johny and the Java Feature Flag Problem, you know Ramu Kaka. He runs the tea stall in front of the hospital. He was our feature flag.

Turns out Ramu Kaka is also a database engineer. He just doesn't know it.

Half the hospital drinks chai on credit. Ward boys, nurses, Johny (obviously), and sometimes even Big-B on night shift. Ramu Kaka tracks all of it in a notebook.

His rules are simple:

  1. He never erases anything. Pen only. Crossing out looks dishonest.
  2. Every new chai, every payment, he writes a new line at the bottom.
  3. When the notebook is full, it goes into the drawer and he starts a new one. Old notebooks are never written to again.
  4. He doesn't remember anyone's balance. He remembers which notebook and which line has their latest entry.

Johny asks "Kaka, how much do I owe?" Kaka doesn't flip through 40 pages. He goes straight to notebook 3, line 112, reads one line, done.

Congratulations👏. That is Bitcask.

Bitcask: A Log-Structured Hash Table for Fast Key/Value Data by Justin Sheehy and David Smith (Basho Technologies, 2010). Six pages. Readable in one chai break. It came out of Riak.

No LSM levels. No bloom filters. No B-tree page splits. An append-only log plus a hash map. That's the whole trick.

On disk: the notebook drawer

A Bitcask instance is just a directory. Only one OS process may open it for writing at a time.

Inside, exactly one file is active. When it crosses a size threshold, it's closed and a new active file is created. Once closed, on purpose or because the server died, a file is immutable. Never opened for writing again.

  bitcask-dir/
  ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │  active data file   <── appends only, one writer
  │  older data file    (immutable)
  │  older data file    (immutable)
  │  older data file    (immutable)
  └──────────────────────────┘

Ramu Kaka's drawer. One open notebook on the counter, the full ones in the drawer. Writes are sequential. No seeking around to patch an old line.

One line in the notebook

Every put appends one entry:

 ┌───────┬────────┬────────┬──────────┬───────────┬─────────────┐
 │  crc  │ tstamp │ key_sz │ value_sz │    key    │    value    │
 └───────┴────────┴────────┴──────────┴───────────┴─────────────┘
          └─────────────────── covered by crc ─────────────────┘
  • crc: checksum over everything after it in the entry
  • tstamp: a 32-bit local timestamp (the paper marks it internal-only, not exposed)
  • key_sz, value_sz: sizes, so you know where key ends and value ends
  • key, value: the actual bytes

A data file is these entries glued one after another. No header pages, no free lists, no slots.

Johny buys another chai? Kaka doesn't edit the old line. He writes a new one. The old line stays. It's just not the latest anymore. Same in Bitcask: an update is a new append. The old value is still on disk.

Johny clears his tab? Kaka writes JOHNY - CLEARED. That's a tombstone. In Bitcask, delete is a write of a special tombstone value, removed on the next merge.

In memory: Ramu Kaka's brain (the keydir)

After the append, Bitcask updates an in-memory hash table called the keydir. For every key, a fixed-size record points at the most recent entry:

 keydir (in RAM)
 ┌─────────┐    ┌─────────┬──────────┬───────────┬────────┐
 │ "johny" │ -> │ file_id │ value_sz │ value_pos │ tstamp │
 ├─────────┤    ├─────────┼──────────┼───────────┼────────┤
 │ "big-b" │ -> │ file_id │ value_sz │ value_pos │ tstamp │
 ├─────────┤    ├─────────┼──────────┼───────────┼────────┤
 │ "nurse" │ -> │ file_id │ value_sz │ value_pos │ tstamp │
 └─────────┘    └─────────┴──────────┴───────────┴────────┘

Values are not in RAM. Every key is. Ramu Kaka remembers every customer's name and where their line is. He does not remember amounts.

On a write, the keydir is atomically updated to the newest location. Any later read sees it.

The basic flow

put(key, value)

  1. Build the entry: tstamp | key_sz | value_sz | key | value, and compute a CRC over it.
  2. Append crc | entry to the end of the active file. Sequential write.
  3. Optionally fsync (sync_on_put). Safer, slower.
  4. Only after the append succeeds, point the keydir at it: key -> (file_id, value_sz, value_pos, tstamp).
  5. If the active file crossed the size limit, close it. It's immutable now. Open a fresh active file.

get(key)

  1. Look up the key in the keydir. Not there? Not found.
  2. Seek to value_pos in file_id, read value_sz bytes. Done.

That's at most one disk seek. Often not even that. Bitcask leans on the OS page cache on purpose and has no internal read cache of its own.

delete(key)

  1. It's just a put, with a special tombstone value.
  2. Remove the key from the keydir.

Ramu Kaka's rule: write the line first, then remember where you wrote it. Flip that order, and a reader can follow a pointer to bytes that don't exist yet.

Merge: Sunday cleanup

Kaka never erases, so the drawer keeps growing. Johny has 300 lines of chai history and exactly one of them matters.

Bitcask merges the non-active (immutable) files into a fresh set with only the live, latest version of each key. Overwritten values and deleted keys are gone.

On Sunday, the nephew copies only each customer's current balance into a fresh notebook. The old notebooks go to the raddi-wala.

The active file isn't touched, so writes keep flowing while the merge runs.

Hint files: when Ramu Kaka gets a fever

One day Ramu Kaka gets dengue and comes back after a week. His memory is blank.

Slow option: read every notebook from the first page. That's what Bitcask does on open if it has nothing better: scan all data files to rebuild the keydir.

Faster option: while merging, the nephew writes a small index card next to each fresh notebook. Name, which line, how long the entry is. No amounts.

That's a hint file. Instead of values, it holds tstamp, key_sz, value_sz, value_pos, and the key. On open, Bitcask scans the hint file instead. Much smaller, much quicker startup.

The data files are the commit log. No separate replay. No WAL sitting next to the data. The log is the data.

The bill (trade-offs nobody puts on the poster)

Bitcask is simple. Simple is not free.

  • Every key must fit in RAM. The keydir grows with the number of keys and must fit entirely in RAM. Values can be much larger than RAM, but keys can't. Huge keyspace with tiny values? Bad fit. Ramu Kaka can handle the hospital. Not the whole of Bangalore.
  • No range scans. The keydir is a hash table. list_keys and fold walk the whole store. Need ordered iteration? Use an LSM-tree or a B-tree.
  • Space amplification until merge. Every overwrite leaves garbage on disk until a merge runs. Write-heavy workloads on the same keys burn disk fast.
  • Startup time without hints. No hint files means a full scan of every data file. Fine at small size. Painful when the drawer is big.
  • Single writer. One process opens a Bitcask for writing. A deliberate simplification, not a bug. Still a constraint.

Torn writes and the CRC

Say the power dies mid-append. Half an entry on disk. Chai spilled on the last line.

That's what the crc is for. On recovery you recompute it. Mismatch = this entry is garbage. A torn entry can only be at the tail of the active file, the only one ever appended to. The sane move (my design choice, not something the paper spells out) is to treat the first bad entry at the tail as the end of the log and truncate there.

CRC does not bring the lost write back. It only stops you from serving corrupted bytes as if they were real.

fsync deserves its own post, coming next. For now: write() returning success only means the bytes are in the OS page cache, not on disk.

Still relevant in 2026?

Yes. The hardware got faster. The ideas didn't expire.

  • Append-only is everywhere. Postgres writes a WAL before touching data. Kafka is basically one giant append-only log. Same Ramu Kaka rule: never erase, just add a line.
  • Sequential writes still win. SSDs made random reads cheap, but appending to the end of a file is still the simplest, most predictable write you can do.
  • RAM is bigger now. "All keys must fit in memory" scared people in 2010. In 2026, plenty of workloads fit comfortably.
  • Crash recovery is still the hard part. CRC per entry, replay the log, ignore the torn tail. Every storage engine has to answer this question.
  • It's small enough to understand. You can hold the whole design in your head in one evening. Try that with an LSM tree.

So why does Ramu Kaka matter to me?

Cause I am mad or its fancy. I wanted to implement in rust.

Want to see me to pick fight with borrow checker? Follow along on X: @nimxch.

Read the paper: Bitcask: A Log-Structured Hash Table for Fast Key/Value Data, Justin Sheehy & David Smith, Basho Technologies, 2010.

title: RegimeCouncil: Paired-Evidence Routing For Memory Conflict Governance In LLM Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.22113v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Language agents rely on long-term memory to personalize responses across extended interactions, yet stored facts quietly go stale as the world changes, and an agent often learns that using memory hurt only through delayed feedback after acting on an outdated record. Before the memory store is updated, how far should that negative feedback propagate: should it suppress memory use only on future queries for that same fact (a local policy), or also across other stored facts (a global policy)? Existing memory systems implicitly fix one of these two sharing scopes at design time. We formulate this online scope choice under hidden validity and delayed feedback as memory conflict governance, and prove that neither fixed policy is sufficient on its own. We then propose RegimeCouncil, a lightweight paired-evidence router that retains both scopes as advisors and arbitrates between them online without retraining the LLM. Using revealed comparisons between answering with memory and answering without memory (the no-memory anchor), a Local Advisor tracks the latest outcome on the queried fact alone, while a Global Advisor pools recent outcomes across all stored facts. A Meta Governor follows the Local Advisor by default to avoid cross-fact interference and switches to the Global Advisor only when global pooling accumulates a strictly positive recent utility margin, guaranteeing finite-time switching under delayed feedback. Across LongMemEval update streams and real-world historical drift on TempLAMA and TAQA with Qwen3-30B-A3B and GPT-4o, RegimeCouncil outperforms the better fixed-scope policy by 5.2-7.3 points on primary disagreement episodes and across all 30 held-out settings, while ablations show that removing any of its three modules reduces accuracy by 2-7 points.

title: NEBench R1: a Reasoning Benchmark for Evaluating Nuclear Domain Competence in Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.21682v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being explored for knowledge-intensive and safety-critical applications in nuclear engineering. However, existing nuclear-domain benchmarks provide limited content coverage or focus primarily on answer accuracy without systematically evaluating the quality of the underlying reasoning. This study introduces NEBench R1, a reasoning-oriented benchmark comprising 7,546 unique multiple-choice questions extracted from U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) reactor operator licensing examinations covering 18 nuclear facilities. Each question is classified according to the NRC Knowledge and Abilities catalogs and accompanied by an official explanation serving as a reference for reasoning evaluation. Six LLMs were evaluated, with overall accuracy ranging from 34.0% to 73.9% across three distinct performance tiers. To assess reasoning quality, an LLM-based judge evaluated correctly answered responses using a multidimensional rubric. Although responses generally demonstrated strong problem comprehension, they scored lower in factual and procedural accuracy and distractor analysis, indicating that correct answers were not necessarily supported by technically sound justifications. Response clarity was also weakly indicative of technical quality. Furthermore, longer reasoning traces were associated with lower accuracy in both frontier reasoning models, suggesting that reasoning length may reflect question difficulty rather than improved problem-solving performance. Reasoning-token consumption may therefore provide an additional signal for identifying potentially unreliable responses. NEBench R1 establishes a benchmark for evaluating both answer accuracy and reasoning quality, providing a foundation for assessing the domain competence and reliability of LLMs in nuclear engineering.

title: Asking What Matters: Disagreement-Guided Ambiguity Detection for Interactive Text-to-SQL
description:
arXiv:2611.21645v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Interactive text-to-SQL requires an LLM agent not only to generate executable SQL, but also to decide which uncertainty to clarify within a limited interaction budget. However, current clarification policies have three limitations: (i) they target surface ambiguity without testing its SQL impact; (ii) they miss ambiguities implicit in schema routes or domain knowledge; and (iii) they spend limited turns on unfocused or redundant questions. These limitations expose a critical challenge: identifying SQL-impacting ambiguity before the intended SQL is known. In this paper, we propose DisGuAD, a Disagreement-Guided Ambiguity Detection framework that specializes clarification selection. DisGuAD treats disagreement among plausible SQL interpretations as direct evidence of which uncertainty matters to the final query. Specifically, it constructs a query-term inventory, elicits contrastive SQL interpretations through complementary probe families, compares their canonical SQL components, and attributes recurring differences to user-facing clarification targets. A lightweight prioritization and dialogue-state mechanism then selects one high-impact unresolved target for clarification. Experiments on BIRD-Interact Lite and Full with two LLM backbones demonstrate consistent improvements in task success and clarification quality. Compared with the original interaction policy, DisGuAD improves normalized Reward by 4.40--8.97 points and raises overall critical-ambiguity coverage from 48.62% to 82.75% and from 45.76% to 85.14%. Its clarification signals further improve two independently designed static text-to-SQL frameworks by up to 13.97 Reward points while keeping their SQL generators fixed. These results demonstrate that disagreement among plausible SQL queries provides actionable evidence for selecting clarification targets that matter to downstream generation.

title: Token Commitment as a Control Surface for Steering Masked Diffusion Generation
description:
arXiv:2611.21669v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Masked diffusion models repeatedly predict provisional tokens before a sampler decides which predictions become permanent. Existing inference-time steering methods primarily modify activations, logits, or denoising trajectories, while treating this commitment policy as a fixed decoding detail. We instead study token commitment as a diffusion-specific control surface and separate it into two decisions: which tokens to commit and how many tokens to commit at each step. For the first, we introduce counterfactual target-aware commitment, which ranks unresolved positions by a mixture of model confidence and leave-one-token-out target contribution. For the second, we introduce calibrated adaptive budgets driven by target progress and confidence. Across language and vision-language settings in the LLaDA family, multiple targets, two activation-steering methods, and an unsteered control, both mechanisms yield empirically monotonic target-quality trade-offs in every configuration we evaluate. Adaptive schedules also recover competitive operating points relative to scorer-free stochastic schedules matched in average denoising cost. Because both mechanisms require only a scalar score evaluated on a provisional completion, they apply unchanged when the target is an automatic proxy for task success rather than an output attribute: NLI entailment for dialogue summarization and CLIPScore for captioning, neither of which corresponds to a single reusable steering direction. We reproduce the behavior of both mechanisms on a second masked-diffusion family, Dream-7B, for one control target and one task-success target. These results characterize commitment--which provisional predictions become irreversible, and how rapidly--as an interpretable control surface for steering masked diffusion generation under the conditions we test.

title: Java4Shell CVE-2026-114938: Is Your Server Next? Find Every Vulnerable JVM
description:
Java4Shell CVE-2026-114938: Is Your Server Next? Find Every Vulnerable JVM

CVE-2026-114938 (Java4Shell) is a heap out-of-bounds write in OpenJDK's AVX-512 Base64 decoder. I covered the background in a separate post. This one is the runbook: how to find the JVMs that matter, what to run, what to change and how to prove it worked.

I have not run this against a vulnerable machine. The commands come from the Qualys, Upwind, Endor Labs and Equixly write-ups, and I only checked that the shell and Java snippets parse. Test in staging first.

TL;DR

Step Goal Time
1. Inventory Find the real runtime behind every Java process minutes per host
2. Hardware check Split hosts by AVX-512 VBMI seconds
3. Patch Move to a vendor build that carries the fix your restart window
4. Mitigate Apply a JVM flag where you cannot patch one restart
5. Verify Prove the flag or build is live in the running process seconds
6. Watch Alert on crash and decode patterns ongoing

1. Inventory the JVM that actually runs

Your shell's java tells you very little. Jenkins, Jira, Confluence, Keycloak and Elasticsearch ship or select their own runtime. Equixly and Endor Labs both call this out. Ask the process.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# jvm-inventory.sh: one line per running JVM with its real binary and version
set -u
for pid in $(pgrep -f '[j]ava'); do
  exe=$(readlink -f "/proc/$pid/exe" 2>/dev/null || echo unknown)
  ver=$(jcmd "$pid" VM.version 2>/dev/null | grep -m1 -E 'JDK|OpenJDK' || echo "jcmd unavailable")
  printf '%s\t%s\t%s\n' "$pid" "$exe" "$ver"
done

jcmd must run as the same user as the target JVM. If it prints "jcmd unavailable", the process may be a minimal runtime without the JDK tools. Fall back to "$exe" -version.

Version triage, using the ranges Qualys and Upwind list.

Line Affected Fixed Oracle build
17 17.0.6 and later, before the fix 17.0.21.1
21 up to 21.0.13 21.0.13.1
25 up to 25.0.5 25.0.5.1
27 up to 27.0.1 27.0.1.1
8 Oracle Enterprise Performance Pack 8u511b33-perf 8u513-perf
11, 17.0.0 to 17.0.5, standard 8 not affected none needed

A version number is not proof. Endor Labs warns that an LTS build with a matching number may still lack the commit, because the fix is tracked as JDK-8393212. Treat the vendor advisory as the source of truth, and note that Qualys lists Corretto 17.0.21.1.2 as released.

2. Check the hardware

Only x86-64 hosts with AVX-512 VBMI reach the vulnerable routine. Run this on each host or container node.

grep -m1 '^flags' /proc/cpuinfo | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -E '^(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)$' | sort

Per Qualys, you are on the hardware side of the risk only when all four flags appear. Intel Ice Lake and later server parts and AMD Zen 4 and later qualify. ARM64, including Graviton and Apple silicon, does not.

In Kubernetes, pods inherit the node's CPU, so check the node and not the image.

# Which nodes would run the vulnerable path
for node in $(kubectl get nodes -o name); do
  pod="cpucheck-${node#node/}"
  kubectl debug "$node" -q --image=busybox --profile=general -- \
    sh -c "grep -m1 '^flags' /proc/cpuinfo | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -c avx512vbmi" 2>/dev/null \
    | sed "s|^|$node  avx512vbmi=|"
done

Remember Qualys's caution: a resize or an instance family change can move a workload onto an affected CPU later. A host that passes today is not a permanent pass.

3. Patch

Patching is the only complete fix, and the vendors say so. The steps that bite people are all about the running process.

  • Rebuild container images from a base that carries the fixed JDK, then redeploy. Replacing files on disk does not change a JVM that is already running.
  • Restart every Java process. Without a restart you have patched a file, not a process.
  • For bundled runtimes, take the application vendor's update, not a hand-swapped JDK, unless the vendor documents it.
  • For Temurin, Zulu, Microsoft, Red Hat and distro packages, confirm the fixed build in the vendor advisory. Equixly could not confirm those on November 17.

4. Mitigate where you cannot patch yet

Both Qualys and Upwind recommend one flag first.

-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics

It turns off the fast decoder on any architecture. Qualys warns that large Base64 workloads may slow down, and Upwind reports it stopped the overflow on every affected version they tested. In a container, set it through the environment.

ENV JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics"

Two alternatives appear in the write-ups, and each has a trap.

Flag Trap
-XX:UseAVX=2 Disables all AVX-512, so it can slow unrelated work. On ARM the JVM refuses to start.
-XX:DisableIntrinsic=_base64_decodeBlock Without -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions the JVM will not start. Pushed through JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS, Upwind calls it a fleet-wide outage.

A reverse proxy is not a control. Qualys says so plainly, and CISA's size-limit advice does not stop this bug on its own.

5. Verify in the running process

Setting a flag in a manifest proves nothing until you ask the process.

# Flag state inside a live JVM
jcmd <pid> VM.flags | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -E 'UseBASE64Intrinsics|UseAVX'

# Or ask a fresh JVM what it would do with your options
java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep -E 'UseAVX|UseBASE64Intrinsics'

You want UseBASE64Intrinsics = false in the process. Remove the flag after the patch lands, because it costs speed.

6. A guard in your own code

If you decode untrusted Base64 with java.util.Base64, you can reject the malformed shape before the decoder sees it. Upwind's detection heuristic is a Base64-alphabet token of 32 or more characters that ends in = and whose length is not a multiple of 4. Well-formed padded Base64 always has a length divisible by 4.

import java.util.Base64;

public final class SafeBase64 {
    private SafeBase64() {}

    /** Rejects padded input whose length cannot be valid Base64 before decoding. */
    public static byte[] decode(String input) {
        if (input.endsWith("=") && input.length() % 4 != 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("malformed base64 padding");
        }
        return Base64.getDecoder().decode(input);
    }
}

This is defense in depth. It narrows the input, and it does not replace the patch. I have not tested it against Calif's chains, which are unpublished.

7. Detection

Endor Labs and Equixly suggest the same few signals.

  • Authorization headers or request fields where Base64 ends in = or == and the length is not a multiple of 4. Equixly offers a WAF rule for the header: ^Basic\s+(?:\S{4})*\S{0,2}=$. I have not validated it.
  • Bursts of IllegalArgumentException from java.util.Base64 in request handlers, because every trigger throws after the write.
  • New hs_err_pid*.log files. Equixly warns the log will not name Base64, because the crash comes later when the garbage collector reads the damaged object. Endor Labs describes a SIGSEGV in a GC copy routine with a compiled Base64$Decoder.decode0 frame, clustered by source IP.
  • Java processes that start a shell or open new outbound connections, which Qualys lists as a monitoring signal. 
# Quick sweep for recent JVM crash logs and their crash frame
find / -name 'hs_err_pid*.log' -mtime -2 2>/dev/null | while read -r f; do
  echo "$f"; grep -m1 -E '^# (SIGSEGV|Problematic frame)' "$f"
done

8. Priorities

Qualys orders the work like this: internet-facing identity providers first, then Jira, Confluence, Jenkins and Artifactory, then other internet-facing Java services, then internal Kafka, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker. The first group is first because Calif's pre-auth claims name them.

The bottom line

The slow part of this incident will not be the patch. It will be learning which of your processes are Java and which JDK they use. Run the inventory script once, keep its output, and you will have the answer ready for the next runtime bug too.

How many of your JVMs would the script find that nobody on your team knew about?

GDS K S · thegdsks.com · building Glincker · follow on X @thegdsks

You cannot patch a runtime you have not inventoried.

Sources: Qualys, Upwind, Endor Labs, Equixly, CISA alert.

title: Three Booleans Is Not a State Machine: Modelling UI Logic That Can't Be in Two States at Once
description:
I review a lot of component code. The most common bug pattern I see is not a typo. It is this:

const [isLoading, setIsLoading] = useState(false);
const [isError, setIsError] = useState(false);
const [isSuccess, setIsSuccess] = useState(false);

Three booleans, eight combinations, three of which are legal. The other five are bugs waiting for a slow network.

Why the bug is structural, not careless

Everyone knows not to set isLoading and isSuccess at the same time. Nobody sets them deliberately. They happen because the flags are set in different places, on different async paths, sometimes in an await that resolves after the component re-rendered.

Add a quantity and a retryCount and the handshake gets worse. Add a "pending but optimistic" case and you have invented a fourth flag, and now four booleans give you sixteen states where five are legal.

This is the classic argument for a discriminator:

type Status =
  | { kind: "idle" }
  | { kind: "validating" }
  | { kind: "submitting"; optimistic: boolean }
  | { kind: "error"; message: string; retryable: boolean }
  | { kind: "success"; orderId: string };

One variable, five states, no illegal combinations by construction. TypeScript will force you to handle each case. This is a finite state machine, and you do not need a tool to get the benefit.

When you do need a tool

A plain discriminated union is enough for a lot of components. The tool starts earning its place when transitions have conditions that non-engineers need to see and tune.

Consider a product card with these rules:

  • hover reveals quick-add, unless the item is out of stock
  • quick-add is disabled while submitting
  • a failed request retries twice, then shows an error
  • success shows a toast and resets after 2.4s
  • changing quantity while submitting cancels the previous request
  • reduced-motion users skip the success animation but still see the toast

That is not a union. That is a graph, and the people who care most about the exact timing and states are designers, not the person writing the reducer.

How Exode models it

The editor's logic surface is a hierarchical state machine with typed inputs, transitions and listeners.

  • Inputs: boolean, number, string, colour. These are the machine's interface to the app.
  • States: idle, hover, submitting, error, success, with sub-states where needed.
  • Transitions: guarded by input values and events.
  • Listeners: fire an animation, set another input, navigate, or call a webhook.

The compiled component exposes the same interface, so the app drives it with props:

<ExodeUICanvas
  artboard="product-card"
  inputs={{ quantity, status, outOfStock }}
  onTrigger={(name) => {
    if (name === "addToCart") handleAdd();
  }}
/>

And the motion for each state is part of the same file — the success spring, the error shake, the toast timing. There is no separate "animation spec" document to drift.

The refusal case

A state machine is not automatically better. I have seen statecharts with four states that should have been two CSS classes, and diagrams nobody updates because the code moved on.

Three signs you should not use one:

1. The logic is a pure function of props. isOpen && <Panel /> does not need a machine.

2. Nobody will maintain the diagram. A state machine that drifts from the code is worse than a boolean, because it lies with confidence.

3. The states are mostly visual variants. Hover, focus, pressed and disabled are CSS pseudo-classes. Do not put them in a graph.

The interesting middle is the awkward case: three to eight states, real async, shared with a designer. That is where a visual machine pays for itself.

The five-state rule of thumb

If you can describe a component's behaviour as a sentence — "it is idle, then submitting, then success or error" — write the union and move on.

If describing it takes a paragraph with the word "unless" in it twice, draw the graph.

A migration that worked

I moved a checkout button from booleans to a machine last quarter. The old code had four flags and a useEffect that reset them, and one bug where a fast double-click could set isSuccess and isError in the same tick.

The new version had five states and one status prop. The failure path was a transition, not a flag being set in a catch. The double-click bug became structurally impossible because submitting has one exit and the click handler is ignored inside it.

The diff was smaller than the original component. That is the part people do not expect: a correct state model is usually less code, because you stop writing the guard clauses that patch an incorrect one.

The general principle

State is not a bag of facts. It is a position in a graph. Every time you add a boolean, ask what combinations it makes legal — and whether all of them should be.

Most of the time, one discriminated union is the whole answer. Sometimes you need a visual machine because a designer has to see it. Both are better than isLoading && !isError && isSuccess === false.

UX Baba writes about interaction design and front-end architecture. The state machine surface described here is part of the Exode editor — exodeui.com if you want to draw one.

title: From Imperfective Paradox to Moorean Absurdity: Single-Chain Reasoning Lock-In and Multi-Candidate Verbalization Across Aspectual and Pragmatic Ambiguity
description:
arXiv:2611.22188v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Natural language entailment and coherence judgments often depend on whether an event merely occurred, reached a telic culmination, satisfied a plan, or was evaluated under multiple pragmatic standards. We test observable consequences of the single-chain premature lock-in hypothesis across four preregistered, sealed formal experiments on Qwen3-8B-Q8_0 (16,640 formal units, temperature=0.0): 15 of 16 hypothesis slots retain confirmatory status (12 rejecting H0 under within-experiment Holm control at alpha_fam=0.05; E3_H3 demoted to descriptive status). In Experiment 1, Direct-CoT vs. MCU differs by 25.00 pp on telic high-confidence completion (Holm p=1.31239e-05), while NLI-CoT collapses by -91.25 pp on uninterrupted atelic items (Holm p=1.81805e-21). Multi-Candidate Verbalization (MCV) elicits K=5 weighted estimates in one call, separating the prompt from unweighted (MCU) and self-weighted (MCW) readouts. Mandarin (E2) and English (E3) expose an Interruption-Anchored Realis Paradox under NLI-CoT. In Experiment 4, MCU-CF raises perceived coherence on implicit Moorean sentences by 26.64 pp over Direct-CoT (Holm p=0.0006), alongside Direct-CF - Direct-CoT = 29.15 pp and MCU-CoT - Direct-CoT = 17.31 pp. A 1,800-call OpenAI ablation and a stage="dev" P16.7 cross-model extension (4,240 planned/collected units across five external models: 4,222 valid, 18 format-missing, 0 transport-missing; <2% missing per slice; OpenAI gpt-4o-mini at top_logprobs=20 achieves 1,000/1,000 valid units) show that discrete NLI-CoT and scalar Direct-CoT judgments dissociate across models. Confirmatory effects concern observable prompt-and-readout protocols; internal premature lock-in remains a hypothesis. All code, stimuli, preregistered analysis plans, and verification tools are available at https://github.com/asj252/llm-judgment-studies.

title: BATMoS: Budget-Aware Guidance Allocation for Efficient Video Diffusion
description:
arXiv:2611.22028v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The effectiveness of a video diffusion model's inference budget depends on where computation is spent along the denoising trajectory. Across eight equal-budget inference configurations, VBench total scores span 4.80 points, highlighting the importance of explicit allocation design. Our key insight is that guidance evaluations are not equally valuable across diffusion time: retaining the sampling updates while selectively reusing guidance can preserve generation quality with fewer denoiser evaluations. We introduce BATMoS (Budget Aware Temporal Mixture of Strategies), which routes between fresh classifier-free guidance and cached guidance using a single pretrained denoiser. A magnitude-based temporal rule assigns guidance reuse to low-magnitude blocks and reserves fresh guidance for the remaining blocks, with a single integer controlling the computation budget. The resulting schedule requires no additional router training or per-budget threshold search. Evaluated on CogVideoX-2B with 4,720 videos per configuration across all sixteen official VBench dimensions, BATMoS achieves the highest total score among the eight allocation policies and comes within 0.10 points of full classifier-free guidance using 20\% fewer branch evaluations. BATMoS also composes with feature reuse, reducing computation from 80 to 62 effective branch evaluations with a 0.11-point decrease in total score. These findings make temporal guidance allocation a practical mechanism for extracting more generation quality from a fixed inference budget.

title: 1,719 A/B runs, 31 verdicts, and a graph still gated
description:
"Is there a real knowledge graph in my second brain?" There is - and in June I decided against the one I picture

Anton is making himself a podcast about how his second brain actually works: knowledge graph, vector search, RAG. He pictures the graph as Obsidian with everything linked and no orphans, or a detective board with red threads between facts. The questions: is there a real graph like that; how does RAG differ from a vector database and from retrieval; can the graph be linked properly to the vector base and RAG; an audit - how many orphan notes, is that bad, do new notes link to old ones automatically, what to improve; and separately, is it better to link distilled knowledge or raw.

Every one of those has an answer on his own shelf, and two of them he wrote himself.

The detective board is the exact architecture he ruled out on 15 June. His own memo decision-unified-search-layer (origin: anton, status: active, the output of a full Alpha Protocol pass) states it plainly in its "what not to take" section: global GraphRAG - no. Expensive in GPU and tokens, poor at incremental updates. And the next line is the whole answer to today's question: "the graph is only a thin domain graph (entity tables + same_as), not an LLM graph over all notes." Red threads between every pair of facts is the shape he rejected five months ago, on the grounds of corpus size.

The terms are defined in the same memo as a pipeline rather than a glossary. Query → intent → exact entity lane → native SQL lane → BM25 lane → vector lane → RRF fusion → reranker → snippets → optional LLM synthesis. Read off that line: retrieval is the whole pipeline, the vector base is one lane of four, RAG is retrieval with the LLM synthesis step attached. Plus a hard rule from the same page: the LLM is final synthesis only - never inside retrieval, never for resolving identities.

The graph is not theoretical. It has been measured, and it came out break-even. A/B verdict of 25 July: 262 promotions, but 18 distinct queries (the nightly run cycles one gold set of 12 questions), 8 live runs in the month, and 31 verdicts from Anton: 16 signal, 15 noise. The recommendation was to keep the wiki-graph gated - no harm found, but not fit for default. The entity lane had zero data points, because its nightly task had been off since 11 July (a BT-diff that ran 7.5 hours; fixed down to 9 minutes).

The audit he is commissioning has already been run - by his own instrument, 47 days ago. Vault-Orphans.html, scan of 2 October: 226,869 live markdown files, 71,460 orphans with zero inbound links, 31.5%.

And here is the part that matters. Those 31.5% are not a verdict, because the threshold already exists and it is tiered. The vault-hygiene memo of 7 July, point D4, verbatim: "orphans - tiered policy, NOT zero orphans." Curated layer: insights with no inbound links under 15%, reachability from a MOC above 90% for concepts and decisions and above 80% for insights, broken links under 0.5%. Archive layer (~100k imports): orphans are normal by design, requiring only metadata and retrievability.

The table against those thresholds:

  • 02-Decisions/_Inbox - 16,288 of 16,302 (99.9%): an inbox, not a curated layer
  • 01-Conversations/* and _session-md/* - roughly 20,000 at 100%: carved out by the contract itself
  • 07-People - 481 of 19,040 (2.5%): curated, healthy
  • distilled meeting notes - 63 of 615 (10.2%): inside the 15%
  • 10-Tasks - 1,001 of 1,942 (51.5%), 02-Decisions/Portugal 79.2%, Construction 60.1%: these are over

So three quarters of all orphans sit in precisely the folders his own contract declares legitimate orphans. Where the threshold applies, the vault passes. The genuine violations are three, and they are small: the task journal and two project folders.

But the number that matters most is a different one. Brain-Health.html, 2 October: search server alive, index 248 MB, 84,799 chunks over 25,813 files (11% of the corpus - exactly what the three-layer rule prescribes), TurnState ledger 44,855 turns. And the line next to it: A/B - 1,719 runs, verdicts 16 / 15. In July there were 31 judgments at the same 16:15. Two and a half months and 1,719 runs later, the judgment count has not moved. The machine keeps running the comparison; nobody grades it. That is why the graph has been gated since July.

The local dashboard on this node (AB-Recall-Graph-vs-Vector.html, 7 August) says the same and is candid about its own blindness: 0 clean measurements out of the 20 required; 288 rows but 12 distinct queries (24 repeats of one set); the graph contributes a median of 2.0 new notes per query and in 33.3% of queries contributes nothing; and, printed on the dashboard: only novelty is counted, because ab_eval.py never writes scores or gold references - "this does not answer the argument as a whole."

"Distilled or raw" was settled on 6 June and runs as a standing rule. The three-layer architecture: bulk goes to SQLite at zero LLM tokens; meaning goes to RAG over the curated markdown (about 5k high-signal documents, explicitly not the 1.5M raw messages); reading and judgment stay in markdown with the graph over it. One line: bulk → DB, meaning → RAG, judgment → markdown. The distilled layer is what gets linked and embedded; the raw layer is kept findable in the database instead. The post frames it as an open trade-off between noise and detail; the architecture resolved it by sending each to a different layer.

And linking the graph into the vector base has a measured cost. DR26-08-06 tested whether retrieval composes when shards are merged. Stable additivity survives on fixed dense embeddings plus a pointwise reranker. What breaks it: corpus-level normalisation, global thresholds, dedup and near-dup, listwise cross-encoders - and graph expansion. Jaccard runs about 0.85-0.95 for pure dense; "with BM25, MMR or a graph, noticeably lower", no number given. So "link the graph to the vector base and RAG" is not free: the graph is the lane his own research named as the one that degrades composition.

"Do new notes link automatically" - the contract exists, the lint is alive. The link-at-birth rule: any automated writer putting a note into a curated layer gives it, in the same pass, at least one typed outbound link and one road in from a MOC. Deliberate orphans are carved out - raw imports, session transcripts, bus artefacts, drafts: "that is an archive, not a graph." Live run of the lint on this node: window 26 hours, notes born 0, violations 0. The watchdog answers; zero here means nothing was born on this node in the window, because the automated writers live on the hub.

⚠️ What I did not do. The quality half of the audit - recall@k, how often the graph brings back the note that mattered - cannot be taken from this node: brain_ask.py, the embeddings and turnstate.db live where the GPU is, and the sync whitelist deliberately leaves .npy and .pkl behind. The freshest quality figure in existence is that same 16:15 over 18 distinct queries.

⚠️ Caveats. The orphan scan is dated 2 October and is 47 days old: it is the last measurement, not today's state; a fresh full re-count over all 332,643 files was started on this node and had not finished when the chain closed. The graph and index figures come from dashboards of 2 October and 7 August and were not re-taken. The passport of orphan_scan.py itself admits tested: no.

The full story, in two versions:
📖 For humans, the longread: https://github.com/tonydzi/clawrush/blob/main/longreads/20261116.md
🤖 For machines, the devlog: https://github.com/tonydzi/clawrush/blob/main/devlog/20261116.md. Just hand this link to your coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor) and it will figure everything out: it is written for machines.

🔗 All our channels and contacts in one place: https://linktr.ee/PaloAltoAI

Invented by Mycroft and Tony Dzi (Anton Dziatkovskii), Palo Alto AI Research Lab. Proudly made in Silicon Valley.

title: How I made a phone animation go from ~35 fps to ~140 fps: draw once, then only move it
description:
I build InviteMeOut, an app for invitations and small-business pages that open with an animation: a wax seal that breaks, curtains that part, a towel that wipes dust off a car. The opening is the first thing a guest sees, so it has to be smooth on a three-year-old phone, not just on my laptop.

One of them wasn't. Here's what was wrong and the rules I follow now.

The slow version

The opening for a car-detailing business page wipes a layer of dust off the screen with a towel. The first version did it the "obvious" way:

  • a full-screen SVG mask that grew as the towel moved,
  • feGaussianBlur and feTurbulence filters for soft, dusty edges,
  • the towel itself as a filtered SVG, animated with SMIL,
  • a scale on the whole layer, and a backdrop-filter: blur() pill floating on top.

In Chrome's phone emulation it ran at about 35 fps. On a real phone it was worse. Every frame the browser had to re-run the filters over the whole screen, re-rasterize the mask, and re-blur whatever sat under the pill.

The fast version

Same look, different work per frame:

  1. The dust is a <canvas> drawn once. Each frame only erases the new strip the towel just covered, using globalCompositeOperation = "destination-out". Nothing is redrawn from scratch.
  2. The towel is rendered once and only moved, with transform: translate3d(...). The GPU moves a texture it already has.
  3. Sheen, glints and dust puffs are transform + opacity only. These two properties can be animated without layout or repaint.
  4. The backdrop-filter element is removed before the animation starts. A blur over something that changes every frame is one of the most expensive things you can ask a phone to do.
  5. Sizes are in px, not SVG viewBox units, so the same towel looks the same on a narrow phone and a wide one.

Result in the same emulation: about 140 fps, and smooth on real phones.

The rules I use for every opening now

  • Draw heavy textures once (a canvas or a static image), then never redraw them.
  • Animate only transform and opacity.
  • No animated masks, filters or background-position.
  • No backdrop-filter over anything that moves.
  • Measure before calling it done. I use a tiny requestAnimationFrame logger that records frame times in phone view: 
const times = [];
let last = performance.now();
function tick(now) {
  times.push(now - last);
  last = now;
  if (times.length < 300) requestAnimationFrame(tick);
  else {
    const avg = times.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) / times.length;
    console.log("avg fps:", Math.round(1000 / avg), "worst frame ms:", Math.max(...times).toFixed(1));
  }
}
requestAnimationFrame(tick);

One more thing: sound needs a tap

Phones won't play audio until the user touches the page. Instead of fighting that, the tap that breaks the seal (or starts the wipe) is the same gesture that starts the music. It feels intentional, and it's the only reliable way.

If you want to see the openings in action, they're at invitemeout.app. Free on the web and on the iPhone. I'm building it solo, so feedback on what stutters on your phone is very welcome.

title: Multi-Label Agreement: A Flexible Framework for Inter-Annotator Reliability
description:
arXiv:2610.37292v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Reliable evaluation of inter-annotator agreement (IAA) is important for assessing the consistency of annotation processes. While established IAA metrics such as Cohen's kappa, Fleiss' kappa, and Krippendorff's alpha are commonly applied in single-label settings, multi-label tasks require additional decisions about how full label sets, joint selections, and joint omissions should be compared.
  In this work, we present Multi-Label Agreement (MLA), a flexible framework for evaluating agreement in multi-label annotation tasks. MLA preserves the full binary label vectors assigned to each item and uses average pairwise Hamming agreement, thereby accounting for both joint selections and joint omissions. Its pooled-marginal form is not a mathematically independent coefficient: it is a chance-disagreement-weighted average of label-wise Fleiss/Scott-type coefficients and is closely related to Krippendorff's alpha with normalized Hamming distance. The framework supports pooled-marginal, Gwet AC1, and fixed-baseline normalizations, yields item-level, label-level, and corpus-level results, and includes a conditional minimum-agreement diagnostic. Through a worked example and Monte Carlo simulations, we show how the resulting values depend on label prevalence, the declared label inventory, and the selected model of expected agreement. We also provide a Python implementation. MLA thus offers a transparent and interpretable framework for multi-label agreement analysis without claiming that one normalization is universally preferable.

title: "Introducing KaDeep Studio: know what's ready to ship, on every platform and in every market"
description:
It's launch week. Your team is shipping a new payments feature to India, the UAE, Japan and Mexico, on web, iPhone, Android and desktop, in five languages.

The test dashboard says 27 of 31 passing. The translation tracker says 79% reviewed. The accessibility audit is from last quarter. Three tools, and still no clear answer. So the person who owns the release makes the call on gut feel.

Today we're launching KaDeep Studio, so that call is never made on gut feel again.

KaDeep Studio is one AI agent that tests your release on every platform, in every language you sell, checks accessibility on the way, and gives your team one clear go or no-go, with the evidence behind it.

👉 Start free · 📅 Book a walkthrough · ⭐ Open-source CLI

1. Ask in plain English

"Test Kasu Money 1.1 on web, Android, iPhone and desktop, in all five languages."

No selectors and no scripts. The agent reads your specs, explores the live product and writes a test plan you approve. From one spec, it wrote 40 test cases in 3.4 minutes.

2. It tests every platform

One agent drives web (Chrome, Safari, Firefox, Edge), Android and iOS (cloud phones, emulators or real devices), and desktop apps on Windows and macOS.

Every step is recorded with the screen, console and network log. When your app changes, the agent updates the affected steps and asks for approval before saving them. Apps on localhost or behind a VPN run on a paired computer.

It also finds what scripts miss: in one session, it tapped Send three times quickly and caught the wallet charging the customer three times. Bugs go to Jira with evidence, and the agent re-checks each fix on the same platform and language.

3. Then it takes you global

Translating files isn't enough. The product has to work in every language. In KaDeep, localization lives in the same Studio:

  • 100+ file formats, from app strings to PDFs and courses, returned in the format they arrived in
  • Guardrails: an estimate before any spend, free translation-memory matches, enforced glossaries, a second model reviewing, and human review for legal and finance text
  • Checked on screen: it catches what files can't show, like Hindi tab labels clipped or an Arabic layout that doesn't mirror

4. Accessible under any law

Every run checks accessibility on web and mobile. When procurement asks for proof, KaDeep produces an expert-signed VPAT® against WCAG 2.2 AA, Section 508, ADA and EN 301 549. No row is ever decided by AI alone.

5. One clear decision

Release Ready brings journeys, platforms, languages, accessibility and bugs into one view that answers one question: ready to ship? If not, it shows exactly why. If your team ships anyway, the decision is recorded with every sign-off. A person always makes the call, with the full picture.

What it changes for your business

  • Leaders get "can we ship?" answered with reasons, not opinions.
  • Engineering covers every platform and language without growing headcount at the same rate.
  • Growth teams launch new markets with every journey tested in that language.
  • Sales has a current VPAT® ready when procurement asks.

Faster releases, lower cost of quality, less risk in every market.

Proven on a full release

Before launch, we ran a complete 4-market release for Kasu Money, a demo wallet we built: web and Android, four languages, a 26-person demo team. KaDeep wrote 40 test cases from the spec, ran ~400 web runs, filed and re-checked 52 bugs, translated 606 strings, found both seeded accessibility issues, and flagged a slowdown from 418 ms to 10.2 s. On release day, it held the release until six stakeholders signed off on the record. → Read the case study

For developers

Two open-source (Apache-2.0) npm packages:

npx kadeep                                   # talk to the agent from your terminal
npx kadeep init                              # add a go / no-go release gate to CI
claude mcp add kadeep -- npx -y kadeep mcp   # let Claude Code or Cursor run your tests

Every pull request gets a verdict:

✓ Smoke: 12/12 passed (2m 41s)
✗ Checkout: 3/4 passed (1m 05s)
    ✗ Pay by card [DEFECT] · Expected "Order placed" to be visible

NO-GO · 1/2 required checks passed · 3m 47s

The gate starts in shadow mode, so it reports without blocking until your team trusts it. It works with every major CI, and runs on your own model keys or through Claude Code, Codex and Cursor.

kadeep-ai / kadeep-cli

KaDeep Studios CLI and releasegate: AI end-to-end testing from your terminal, CI/CD and coding agents (MCP). Run tests on web, mobile and desktop and get a go / no-go for every release.

title: Measuring Facebook Group Health for Filipino Communities in 30 Lines of JavaScript
description:
By MD Fozla Rabbi, SEO Specialist

Admins of Filipino Facebook groups love the member count. But a group with 8,000 members and three comments a week is basically a ghost town.

Here's a tiny Node.js script that turns a weekly activity log into a few honest health numbers.

The data

Facebook's Group Insights shows posts, comments, reactions and active members. Copy a few weeks into a JSON file:

[
  { "week": "2026-W43", "members": 7810, "active": 640, "posts": 41, "comments": 210 },
  { "week": "2026-W44", "members": 7955, "active": 702, "posts": 48, "comments": 265 },
  { "week": "2026-W45", "members": 8120, "active": 655, "posts": 37, "comments": 190 }
]

The script 

const weeks = require("./group-weeks.json");

function health(w) {
  const activeRate = (w.active / w.members) * 100;
  const commentsPerPost = w.comments / Math.max(w.posts, 1);
  return { week: w.week, activeRate, commentsPerPost };
}

const rows = weeks.map(health);

for (const r of rows) {
  console.log(
    r.week.padEnd(9),
    "active " + r.activeRate.toFixed(1) + "%",
    "| comments/post " + r.commentsPerPost.toFixed(1)
  );
}

const first = rows[0];
const last = rows[rows.length - 1];
const trend = last.activeRate - first.activeRate;
console.log("Active-rate trend:", (trend >= 0 ? "+" : "") + trend.toFixed(1), "points");

What the numbers mean

  • Active rate above ~8% is healthy for a buy-and-sell or local community group.
  • Comments per post above 4 means people actually talk, not just post ads.
  • Growing members with a falling active rate usually means low-quality joins or too many sell posts.

In the sample above, members went up but the active rate dipped. Classic sign the group needs more conversation posts and fewer link drops.

Practical fixes admins use

Weekly question threads in Taglish. Pinned rules about selling days. Welcome posts that tag new members. Boring stuff. Works.

For a fuller strategy, this guide on how to grow a Facebook group in the Philippines covers rules, content calendars and promotion. BoostingPH also has an API if you want to wire growth services into your own tools.

title: Long-Context Generation Is a Sampling Problem (When You Turn Up the Heat)
description:
arXiv:2611.22148v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Open-weight language models are widely observed to get worse the longer they generate. Often, attempts to fix this involve more training. At high temperature, The sampler, i.e. the rule that picks the next token out of the model's probabilities, decides whether long and agentic generation survives and/or thrives. We test 29 open-weight models from 1B to 122B parameters on ten established benchmarks plus needle retrieval out to one million tokens, covering SWE-bench Verified coding agents, long chain-of-thought reasoning, long-form writing, long structured output and long-context reading. Samplers that keep their pool of candidate tokens small and steady as temperature rises don't lose accuracy. Samplers that let in low-probability tokens fall apart. At temperature 2, coding agents running top-p, top-k or Top-H resolve 0 of 100 GitHub issues, while the same agents running top-nsigma resolve 46 to 62 and win every issue the two samplers disagree on, on three Qwen3.5 models. Over all benchmarks top-nsigma keeps a median 100% of its temperature-1 score where top-p keeps 26%. Counting how many tokens each sampler lets through explains why. In one Llama-3.1-8B story, going from temperature 1 to 2 grows top-p's pool from 4 tokens to 51,845 while top-nsigma stays at 3. Across 133 combinations of sampler setting and temperature, the typical pool size predicts judged quality (Spearman correlation of -0.77), and when we pick the pool at temperature 1 and only apply temperature afterwards, Top-H, min-p and p-less stop collapsing. At the default temperature of 1 most samplers perform about the same, We release all code and data to the public.
