title: Streaming On-Policy Distillation: Decoupling Three Clocks for Stage-Wise Supervision Consumption
description:
arXiv:2611.22298v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In on-policy distillation (OPD), response completion, supervision delivery, and parameter updates need not share the same granularity. We develop streaming OPD by decoupling these three clocks: a response repeatedly delivers newly generated segments while generation continues, retaining the full causal prefix at each delivery and computing loss only on new positions. A consumption protocol then organizes supervision budgets, position selection, staleness handling, and update scheduling, allowing control over quantity, coverage, and version lag across training stages. In GSM8K experiments distilling Qwen3-4B into Qwen3-0.6B with VERL, supervised-budget matching reduces the early gap between best test accuracies over seven common candidates from 4.55 to 2.42 points. Synchronous continuation from the same checkpoint reaches 73.39% best test accuracy over seven common candidates at u=384,...,576, versus 74.30% synchronous and 71.95% budget-matched (differences -0.91 and -2.35 points); an unpaired extended record reaches 76.12%. Freshness filtering and disagreement-overlap selection improve local peaks but do not establish sustained advantages. A system prototype shows lower data-supply waiting times without establishing an equal-update speedup. Quality recovery and supply-side benefits are assessed separately; end-to-end gains must account for continuation cost.

title: When AUC Meets Generative Reconstruction: A Unified Principle for Balanced Visual Representation Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.22094v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) require visual encoders that extract fine-grained visual features while constructing semantically disentangled and discriminative representations. Conventional methodologies encounter a fundamental trade-off: contrastive learning enhances inter-class discrimination by suppressing intra-class variability, whereas generative reconstruction emphasizes perceptual fidelity but lacks explicit comparative supervision. The naive aggregation of these objectives via composite loss functions often induces optimization conflicts and instability due to gradient interference within the shared latent space. To resolve this, we introduce a unified representation-learning paradigm that reformulates generative reconstruction as a discriminative ranking problem within the generative output manifold. Our approach maintains perceptual reconstruction as a supervisory signal and integrates a ranking-based discriminative constraint by systematically ordering matched and mismatched reconstruction outputs. This formulation embeds discriminative information seamlessly into the generative process, alleviating the risk of loss competition. Specifically, we propose AUC Generative Reconstruction (AUCGR), which optimizes the area under the ROC curve (AUC) by ensuring higher scores for matched pairs than for mismatched pairs, and Partial AUC Generative Reconstruction (pAUCGR), which addresses supervision bias by focusing on mismatched comparisons within reliable feature subspaces. The proposed objectives are designed to be plug-and-play, requiring no architectural modifications to existing generative reconstruction frameworks. Theoretical analysis establishes rigorous connections to AUC/pAUC optimization and provides generalization guarantees. Extensive experiments validate that our method advances both discriminative accuracy and fine-grained perceptual representation.

title: Sample-Aligned Decoders for Latent Generative Models
description:
arXiv:2611.22458v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Latent generative models synthesize images by decoding generated latents, yet their decoder is trained only to reconstruct encoder latents and never sees the latents it decodes at test time, so the residual errors of the generator are rendered directly into the final image. Existing remedies retrain the generator, add cost at every sampling step, or make the decoder robust to perturbed real latents, assuming that generator errors resemble such perturbations. We find that they do not. Generated latents lie on the encoder latent manifold as closely as real ones, yet follow a different distribution. The decoder should therefore be adapted to the distribution of generated latents, which raises two challenges: (1) unpaired supervision, since a generated latent has no ground-truth image, and (2) latent-space drift, since a decoder freed from paired targets forgets the latent space it must decode. We propose Sample-Aligned Decoders (SAD), a post-training framework that fine-tunes only the decoder of a frozen generator at no inference cost. Generated-Sample Distribution Alignment matches decoded generated latents to unpaired real images in a frozen foundation-model feature space, and Encoder Anchor Preservation keeps the decoder close to the original one on encoder latents. Our analysis shows that the alignment is effective only on generated latents, where it corrects each sample in proportion to how much more often the generator produces such latents than the encoder; on encoder latents it can only work against the anchor. SAD improves four state-of-the-art ImageNet generators across three tokenizers, e.g., FID-50K from 1.15 to 0.98 for REPA-E, complements discriminator guidance, and extends to text-to-image generation. Our code and models are available at https://torpedo2003.github.io/SAD/.

title: Does the Model Use What It Cites? Counterfactual Tests of Grounded Reasoning Chains in Small Video-Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.21940v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A grounded reasoning chain cites a frame span and a box for every step, so a reader can check where the model looked. Whether the answer depends on the cited region is a different question. We test it by intervention: the regions a model cited in its own chain are blacked out, and the share of correct answers that flip is compared with blacking out boxes of the same size elsewhere on the same frames. The paired difference, the cite gap, needs no annotation. We apply it to 2-3B video-language models trained on exact CLEVRER chains and on pseudo-labelled NExT-QA chains. With the same weights, the cite gap is 0.089 on CLEVRER and 0.003 on NExT-QA. Pooled over models, masking the cited boxes flips 2.2 times as many correct answers as the control on CLEVRER and 1.1 times as many on NExT-QA, also among the answers that depend on the video at all, while the boxes pass a grounding check on both. Masking the cited entity on every frame, instead of the cited box, flips 1.9 times as many answers as its control. The NExT-QA chains were supervised to cite two frames of entities that stay visible on most frames, so this outcome is what the supervision predicts; the point is that the usual check on grounded chains cannot see it. A citation can be verifiable and relevant without the answer depending on it, and a test of grounded reasoning should remove what a chain names, not only where it points.

title: DAP-MR: Degradation-Aware Prompt-Magnitude Routing for Real-World Ultrasound Super-Resolution
description:
arXiv:2611.22331v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When super-resolution models designed for natural images are used on ultrasound scans, relying on semantic text prompts can lead to unreliable results. The tags these models generate often do not match the actual restoration needs, and specialized medical terms may be misunderstood by general-purpose text encoders. Instead, prompts focused on common image degradations are more directly useful for guiding restoration. However, using a single prompt to describe both the type and severity of image degradation can entangle these factors, making it hard for the model to know how strong the degradation is. To address this limitation, we introduce Degradation-Aware Prompt--Magnitude Routing (DAP-MR). Each degradation type is represented by a dedicated token initialized from the contextualized EOS embedding of a degradation-oriented prompt and subsequently adapted during ultrasound SR training. A separate magnitude router predicts a continuous, input-dependent magnitude that modulates the corresponding token. Thus, language provides a degradation-aware initialization for what should be restored, while magnitude routing supplies an explicit signal for how strongly it should influence restoration. DAP-MR can be added to both one-step and multi-step diffusion super-resolution frameworks without changing their core structures. Our experiments--on synthetic datasets with both in-domain and under anatomical-domain shift, as well as unpaired real-world ultrasound data--show that DAP-MR delivers better restoration quality and generalizes more consistently across different domains.

title: Large Language Models as Nonlinear Dynamical Systems: The Three Clocks of Depth, Training, and Generation
description:
arXiv:2611.21983v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Language models are dynamical systems. A transformer is iterated over its layers, over the steps of its training and over the tokens it generates, and on each of these three clocks it shows behavior that nonlinear dynamics has studied for a century: fixed points, bifurcations, synchronization, chaos and noise-driven escape from potential wells. The two communities rarely meet, so this behavior is often rediscovered under new names. We build a bridge between them. To describe, we condense about 200 papers into the Three-Clock Dictionary, which maps fifteen concepts of nonlinear dynamics onto each clock and marks every correspondence as proved, measured or conjectured, and we show each concept in a mechanical system and in a language model side by side. To explain, we derive reduced-order models: the softmax is a Boltzmann distribution, gradient descent an Euler step on a nonlinear spring, a loss spike a ball thrown out of a stiff valley, attention on the circle a Kuramoto model, and a repetition loop a well that deepens while it is occupied. We then test these explanations on open language models, on a laptop CPU. Escape from repetition loops in GPT-2 and Pythia follows the Arrhenius law with the logit gap as the barrier, and the barrier deepens and then saturates, so the temperature needed to leave a loop falls like $1/\ln N$ with the generation length $N$ and rises with model size. Coherent text lives in a narrow window of temperatures, which a small reasoning model shares at its recommended temperature. Training makes each Pythia layer more expansive, and a small transformer trains at a multi-mode edge of stability. The third step, solving problems of language models, is still ahead: controllers derived from the escape analysis remove loops but do not yet beat the best fixed temperature. We state twelve open problems where nonlinear dynamics could get there.

title: AWS Control Tower now supports existing Amazon S3 bucket for log delivery
description:
AWS Control Tower now lets you use an existing Amazon S3 bucket in your landing zone to store AWS Config and AWS CloudTrail logs. Previously, AWS Control Tower required you to use the Amazon S3 bucket it creates and manages for log storage. Now, customers who want full control of bucket policies, lifecycle rules, and logging infrastructure can consolidate centralized logs in an Amazon S3 bucket they already manage.

You can use your own Amazon S3 bucket for both AWS Config and AWS CloudTrail, giving you full control of bucket policies, lifecycle rules, and logging infrastructure. You can switch between self-managed and AWS Control Tower managed buckets at any time, and your Amazon S3 buckets are preserved during landing zone updates, resets, and decommissioning. The bucket must be owned by an AWS account in your organization, be located in your AWS Control Tower home Region, and be preconfigured with the bucket policy that AWS Control Tower requires.

This feature is supported in landing zone version 4.0 and later and is available in all commercial AWS Regions, the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, and the AWS European Sovereign Cloud where AWS Control Tower is available.

To learn more about configuring self-managed Amazon S3 bucket for your AWS Control Tower landing zone, visit the AWS Control Tower documentation.

title: ThermLeT: Transformer-based Temperature Prediction for 2.5D Chiplet Architecture
description:
arXiv:2611.21954v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: The drive toward heterogeneous 2.5D chiplet packages promises unmatched performance and customization, yet the resulting density amplifies thermal challenges. To facilitate rapid design space exploration, we present ThermLeT, a multimodal transformer-based, scale invariant surrogate that integrates power density maps, spatial coordinate embeddings, material properties and heat transfer rate to predict steady state temperature in 13 ms, about four orders of magnitude faster than conventional finite element solvers such as ANSYS. To train the transformer model, we also create a dataset of 6,221 chiplet layouts perturbed from three representative architectures. On a 150 sample test set, ThermLeT achieves an RMSE of 3.16{\deg}C and an MAE of 2.24{\deg}C, improving accuracy by 35% over ThermEDGe and by 71% over HotSpot, while running approximately 6x and 11x lower inference latencies respectively. Ablation studies confirm robust generalization to unseen floorplans. Code and dataset available at https://github.com/MicroSystemsDesignLab/ThermLeT

title: Java String.format() Cheat Sheet: %s, %d, %.2f, Flags and Locale
description:
On a laptop with German regional settings, String.format("%.2f", 0.5) returns "0,50" instead of "0.50" — and the very next Double.parseDouble(...) fails with NumberFormatException: For input string: "0,50". Surprises like this disappear once you understand how string formatting in Java actually works.

String formatting in Java means building a string from a template in which format specifiers (%d, %s, %.2f and others) are replaced with argument values. Formatted output is produced by String.format(), String.formatted() (Java 15+), System.out.printf() and the java.util.Formatter class, which powers all of them. You can format numbers, strings, characters, dates and times.

String.format(), printf() and formatted(): which one to use

If you need the result as a string, use String.format() or "template".formatted(); if you want to print it right away, use System.out.printf(); if the text is assembled in several steps or written to a file, use the Formatter class. All of them understand exactly the same template syntax.

Method What it returns Since When to use it
String.format(template, args...) A new string Java 5 You need the formatted string itself (Java's sprintf)
"template".formatted(args...) A new string Java 15 Same as above, but shorter; great with text blocks
System.out.printf(...), System.out.format(...) The same PrintStream; prints to the console Java 5 Formatted console output
PrintWriter.printf(...) The same PrintWriter; writes to a stream Java 5 Writing to a file or a network stream
new Formatter(...).format(...) The same Formatter; accumulates the result Java 5 Building text from several calls, writing to an Appendable or a file

System.out is a static field of type PrintStream, which is why it has the printf() and format() methods. They are two names for the same method: printf() exists to make C programmers feel at home. Unlike print() and println(), which print a single value as is, printf() takes a template plus any number of arguments. Under the hood, every method in the table uses Formatter.

Throughout this lesson, the output in comments is shown for Locale.US. With a locale such as German or French, you will see a comma instead of the decimal point (details in the Locale section).

public class PrintfExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.printf("Formatted string: %.2f%n", 1000.0 / 3.0);
        System.out.format("%s, next year you will be %d%n", "John", 23);

        String str = String.format("Price: $%.2f", 99.5);
        System.out.println(str);

        String greeting = "Hello, %s! You have %d new messages.".formatted("Anna", 5);
        System.out.println(greeting);
    }
}
// Output:
// Formatted string: 333.33
// John, next year you will be 23
// Price: $99.50
// Hello, Anna! You have 5 new messages.

The formatted() method shines with text blocks (Java 15+): you write the template as is, without concatenation or \n.

String json = """
        {"name": "%s", "age": %d}
        """.formatted("Anna", 30);
System.out.print(json);
// Output: {"name": "Anna", "age": 30}

Format specifier syntax

A format specifier is a part of the template that starts with % and describes how to print the next argument. Its general form is %[argument_index$][flags][width][.precision]conversion; only the % sign and the conversion character are required, everything else is optional.

%[argument_index$][flags][width][.precision]conversion
Part What it sets Example
argument_index$ Argument number (starting at 1), followed by $ %2$s — the second argument
flags Alignment, sign, leading zeros, grouping separators %-10s, %,d, %+d
width Minimum field width in characters %8d
.precision Digits after the decimal point for numbers; maximum length for strings %.2f, %.3s
conversion Conversion type (required) d, s, f, x

The argument index lets you reuse one value several times or change the order of arguments. The %<s form means "the same argument as the previous specifier":

public class ArgumentIndexExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.printf("Hello %1$s!%n%1$s, how are you?%n"
                        + "Welcome to the site %2$s%n",
                "John", "www.site.com");
        System.out.printf("%d in hexadecimal: %<x%n", 255);
    }
}
// Output:
// Hello John!
// John, how are you?
// Welcome to the site www.site.com
// 255 in hexadecimal: ff

Java format specifiers: table

The conversion character defines how the argument is interpreted: %d is an integer, %f a floating-point number, %s a string, %c a character, %b a boolean. The argument type must match the specifier, otherwise you get an IllegalFormatConversionException at runtime.

Specifier What it prints Example Result
%d Decimal integer (int, long, BigInteger…) format("%d", 42) 42
%s / %S String representation (toString()) format("%S", "java") JAVA
%f Floating-point number in decimal notation, 6 digits after the point by default format("%f", 3.14159) 3.141590
%e / %E Floating-point number in scientific notation format("%e", 12345.678) 1.234568e+04
%g / %G Floating-point number: scientific notation if, after rounding, the value is less than 10^-4 or at least 10^precision, otherwise decimal. Precision = total number of significant digits (6 by default) format("%g", 12345.678) format("%g", 0.00001234) 12345.7 1.23400e-05
%a / %A Floating-point number in hexadecimal notation format("%a", 1.0) 0x1.0p0
%x / %X Integer in hexadecimal format("%X", 255) FF
%o Integer in octal format("%o", 8) 10
%c / %C Character (char or an int code point) format("%c", 65) A
%b / %B Boolean: false for null, the value itself for a Boolean, true for any other object format("%b", null) false
%h / %H The argument's hash code in hexadecimal format("%h", "hi") d01
%t / %T Date and time (with a suffix: %tY, %tF…) format("%tY", LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 16)) 2026
%n The platform-specific line separator format("a%nb") a and b on separate lines
%% A literal % sign format("%d%%", 50) 50%

Uppercase variants (%S, %X, %E, %G, %A, %B, %H, %C, %T) work like their lowercase counterparts but convert the result to upper case: %x gives ff, %X gives FF; %b gives true, %B gives TRUE. There are no uppercase forms of %d, %f and %o.

What does this code print?

System.out.printf("%b %b %b%n", "false", null, 0);

Answer: true false true. The string "false" is not a Boolean but an ordinary non-null object, so %b turns it into true. The number 0 also gives true: in Java, unlike C, zero does not mean "false". Only null becomes false.

Width and precision

Width (%10s) sets the minimum number of characters in a field: a shorter value is padded with spaces on the left, or on the right with the - flag. Precision (%.2f) sets the number of digits after the decimal point for floating-point numbers, rounding with HALF_UP; for strings (%.3s) it sets the maximum length, and the rest is cut off.

public class WidthPrecisionExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        double x = 1000.0 / 3.0;
        System.out.println("Unformatted: " + x);
        System.out.printf("[%.2f]%n", x);
        System.out.printf("[%8.2f]%n", x);
        System.out.printf("[%-8.2f]%n", x);
        System.out.printf("[%10s][%-10s]%n", "Java", "Java");
        System.out.printf("[%.3s]%n", "Formatter");
        System.out.printf("[%3s]%n", "Formatter");
    }
}
// Output:
// Unformatted: 333.3333333333333
// [333.33]
// [  333.33]
// [333.33  ]
// [      Java][Java      ]
// [For]
// [Formatter]

The last line shows a non-obvious detail: width is a minimum, not a maximum. A longer value is printed in full, and your columns drift apart. To truncate a string you need precision: %-10.10s always prints exactly 10 characters.

Width and alignment are what you need to print a table in the console:

public class TableExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.printf("%-10s%8s%n", "Item", "Price");
        System.out.printf("%-10s%8.2f%n", "Bread", 45.5);
        System.out.printf("%-10s%8.2f%n", "Coffee", 89.9);
    }
}
// Output:
// Item         Price
// Bread        45.50
// Coffee       89.90

Formatting float and double with %f

The %f, %e and %g specifiers accept float, double, their wrappers and BigDecimal; there is no separate specifier for float and no %lf for double. Integer specifiers never convert floating-point values: %d with a float argument throws IllegalFormatConversionException: d != java.lang.Float.

float price = 19.99f;
double discount = 12.5;
System.out.println(String.format("%.2f", price));
System.out.println(String.format("%.1f%%", discount));
System.out.println(String.format("%08.3f", -3.14159));
// Output:
// 19.99
// 12.5%
// -003.142

Format flags

Flags go right after % (or after the argument index) and control alignment, the sign of a number, leading zeros and grouping separators. Several flags can be combined: %,(.2f prints a negative number in parentheses and with grouping separators.

Flag What it does Example Result
- Left-justify (requires a width) format("[%-5d]", 42) [42 ]
0 Pad with zeros instead of spaces (numbers only, requires a width) format("%05d", 42) 00042
+ Always print the sign format("%+d", 42) +42
space Put a space before positive numbers (to line them up with negative ones) format("[% d]", 42) [ 42]
, Locale-specific grouping separators format("%,d", 1234567) 1,234,567
( Enclose negative numbers in parentheses format("%(d", -42) (42)
# Alternate form: 0x prefix for %x, 0 for %o format("%#x", 255) 0xff 
public class FlagsExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.printf("%,.2f%n", 10000.0 / 3.0);
        System.out.printf("%,(.2f%n", -10000.0 / 3.0);
        System.out.printf("%09.2f%n", 10000.0 / 3.0);
    }
}
// Output:
// 3,333.33
// (3,333.33)
// 003333.33

Incompatible flags throw an exception: + together with a space, or - together with 0, gives IllegalFormatFlagsException, and - or 0 without a width gives MissingFormatWidthException.

The Formatter class

The java.util.Formatter class is the engine behind formatted output in Java: String.format() and printf() create one internally. You use Formatter directly when the text is built from several format() calls or when the result should go straight into a StringBuilder, a file or a stream.

The format() method of Formatter converts its arguments according to the template and appends the result to the accumulated text, which you get back with toString(). A minimal Java Formatter example:

import java.util.Formatter;

public class FormatterExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Formatter formatter = new Formatter();
        formatter.format("This %s is about %n%S %c", "book", "java", '8');
        System.out.println(formatter);
    }
}
// Output:
// This book is about
// JAVA 8

The Formatter(Appendable, Locale) constructor writes directly into a StringBuilder and sets the locale at the same time. Formatter implements Closeable, so when it writes to a file, close it with try-with-resources. All constructors and conversions are listed in the official Formatter Javadoc.

import java.util.Formatter;
import java.util.Locale;

public class FormatterBuilderExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        Formatter formatter = new Formatter(sb, Locale.US);
        formatter.format("%-8s%6.2f%n", "Tea", 3.5);
        formatter.format("%-8s%6.2f%n", "Coffee", 12.0);
        System.out.print(sb);
    }
}
// Output:
// Tea       3.50
// Coffee   12.00

Locale: dot or comma

Number and date formatting depends on the locale: without an explicit Locale, String.format() and printf() use the system default (Locale.getDefault(Locale.Category.FORMAT)). In German and French the decimal separator is a comma, and the grouping separator is a dot or a space, so the same program prints different strings on different machines.

import java.util.Locale;

public class LocaleExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        double price = 1234.567;

        System.out.println(String.format(Locale.US, "%,.2f", price));
        System.out.println(String.format(Locale.GERMANY, "%,.2f", price));
        System.out.println(String.format(Locale.FRANCE, "%,.2f", price));
        System.out.println(String.format(Locale.ROOT, "%.2f", price));
        System.out.println(String.format(Locale.GERMANY, "%.2f", 0.5));
    }
}
// Output:
// 1,234.57
// 1.234,57
// 1 234,57
// 1234.57
// 0,50

The French line looks like it contains an ordinary space, but it does not: since Java 13 (CLDR locale data) the French grouping separator is the narrow no-break space U+202F, and older JDKs used the no-break space U+00A0. A test such as assertEquals("1 234,57", result) typed with a regular space fails, and so does parsing that string back with code that expects plain spaces.

format() and printf() have an overload that takes a Locale as the first parameter. formatted() has no such overload — it always uses the default locale. The new Locale("de", "DE") constructor is deprecated since Java 19; use the constants (Locale.GERMANY), Locale.forLanguageTag("de-DE") or Locale.of("de", "DE") (Java 19+) instead.

Rule of thumb. For data that another program will read (CSV, JSON, SQL, logs that get parsed), pass Locale.ROOT or Locale.US explicitly. Rely on the default locale only for text that a human reads.

Formatting dates and times

The %t specifier (or %T for upper case) with a suffix prints part of a date or time: %tY is the year, %tm the month, %td the day, %tB the month name, %tH:%tM hours and minutes, %tF the ISO date. The argument can be a LocalDate, LocalDateTime, Date, Calendar or long.

import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.util.Locale;

public class DateFormatExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        LocalDate date = LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 16);
        System.out.println(String.format("%tF", date));
        System.out.println(String.format("%1$tm/%1$td/%1$tY", date));
        System.out.println(String.format(Locale.US, "%1$tB %1$te, %1$tY", date));
    }
}
// Output:
// 2026-10-16
// 10/16/2026
// October 16, 2026

Note the %1$: without the index, every %t specifier expects its own argument, and the template "%tm/%td/%tY" with a single date throws MissingFormatArgumentException. For complex date patterns, modern code usually reaches for java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter.

Common mistakes and the exceptions they throw

The compiler does not check format strings: mistakes surface only at runtime as unchecked exceptions, subclasses of IllegalFormatException (which extends IllegalArgumentException). Here are the most frequent cases and how to fix them:

Code What happens How to fix it
format("%d", 3.5) IllegalFormatConversionException: d != java.lang.Double Use %f for floating-point values or cast with (int)
format("%s and %s", "A") MissingFormatArgumentException: Format specifier '%s' Pass all arguments or reuse one with %1$s
format("%-05d", 7) IllegalFormatFlagsException: Flags = '-0' Pick one flag: %-5d or %05d
format("%i", 7) (a habit from C) UnknownFormatConversionException: Conversion = 'i' Java prints integers only with %d
format("Save 50%") UnknownFormatConversionException: Conversion = '%' Escape the percent sign: 50%%
format("%s", "a", "b") No exception, output a — the extra argument is silently ignored Match the number of specifiers and arguments (IDEs highlight this)
format("%d", (Integer) null) No exception, output null Check the value for null beforehand

%n or \n? Use %n in templates: it inserts the line separator of the current OS (\r\n on Windows, \n on Linux and macOS). \n always produces a single LF character — correct only when a file format or protocol requires exactly that.

DecimalFormat and MessageFormat

Besides String.format(), the java.text package offers two formatting classes: DecimalFormat formats a number by a pattern such as #,##0.00, and MessageFormat inserts arguments by number in curly braces {0}, {1} — the approach used in UI localization bundles.

import java.text.DecimalFormat;
import java.text.DecimalFormatSymbols;
import java.text.MessageFormat;
import java.util.Locale;

public class TextFormatExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        DecimalFormat df = new DecimalFormat("#,##0.00",
                DecimalFormatSymbols.getInstance(Locale.US));
        System.out.println(df.format(1234567.891));

        System.out.println(MessageFormat.format("File {0} contains {1} lines", "data.txt", 1500));
        System.out.println(MessageFormat.format("File {0} contains {1,number,#} lines", "data.txt", 1500));
    }
}
// Output:
// 1,234,567.89
// File data.txt contains 1,500 lines
// File data.txt contains 1500 lines

A MessageFormat quirk: numbers in {1} are formatted with the locale's grouping separators, so 1500 becomes 1,500. The {1,number,#} format prints the number without separators. Another one: a single quote in a MessageFormat pattern is an escape character, so an apostrophe has to be doubled — "Don''t" prints Don't.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is there a sprintf equivalent in Java?

Yes: String.format() (or "template".formatted() in Java 15+) returns the formatted string, and System.out.printf() corresponds to C's printf. The syntax is similar but not identical: there is no %i or %u, %n is the line separator, and %b accepts any object. More in the section Common mistakes and the exceptions they throw.

Does Java have f-strings or string interpolation?

No. Java has no equivalent of Python's f-strings: you cannot write variable names inside a string literal. String Templates (STR."Hello \{name}") appeared as a preview feature in JDK 21 (JEP 430) and JDK 22 (JEP 459), but they were removed in JDK 23 and are not part of the language. The closest options are "Hello, %s!".formatted(name), String.format() or plain concatenation "Hello, " + name + "!".

What is the difference between printf() and println()?

println() prints a single value and always adds a line break. printf() takes a template and any number of arguments, but adds no line break on its own — you have to put %n into the template.

Which is faster: String.format() or concatenation with +?

Concatenation is noticeably faster: every String.format() call parses the template and creates a Formatter. In loops and hot code, build strings with + or a StringBuilder, and keep String.format() for places where readability and alignment matter. All concatenation options are compared in Java String Concatenation.

How do I keep two decimal places without rounding?

%.2f always rounds with HALF_UP: String.format("%.2f", 1.999) gives 2.00. To drop the extra digits instead, use BigDecimal: new BigDecimal("1.999").setScale(2, RoundingMode.DOWN) returns 1.99.

title: Preventing Duplicate Contact Names From Silently Corrupting Your Lending Ledger
description:
When building an expense or lending tracker, contact management seems trivial at first glance:

"Just let the user type a name in a text field: 'Rahul'. Save it to SQLite. Done."

In practice, free-form text input without identity modeling quickly degenerates into chaos.

Consider what happens over a year of real-world usage:

  • You lend Rs. 500 to Rahul (your coworker).
  • Three months later, you lend Rs. 2,000 to Rahul (your cousin).
  • Next week, you record a dinner split with Rahul P (the same coworker).

If your app relies on naive string matching or creates unindexed rows for every entry, you face two destructive failure modes:

  1. The Silent Merge: The app assumes every "Rahul" is the same person. Your cousin's loan is merged into your coworker's balance sheet!
  2. The Duplicate Explosion: The app creates three separate cards for "Rahul", "rahul", and "Rahul P.", scattering loan installments across different entries and making it impossible to see total debt in one place.

Here is how FinLedger architected a contact disambiguation engine (PersonDao.kt, LendingDialogs.kt) to eliminate name collisions and duplicate entities.

The Pitfalls of Naive Contact Management 

flowchart TD
    subgraph Failures["The Twin Traps of Free-Form Contact Entry"]
        UserTypes["User Enters Name: 'Rahul'"]

        UserTypes --> Trap1["Failure Mode 1: The Silent Merge
        App matches existing 'Rahul' by string equality.
        Cousin's loan merged into Coworker's record!
        Privacy breach and accounting confusion."]

        UserTypes --> Trap2["Failure Mode 2: Duplicate Explosion
        App creates new entity for every string variance:
        'Rahul', 'rahul ', 'Rahul Patil'.
        Dozens of fragmented cards clutter the UI."]
    end

To build a reliable ledger, an application must decouple identity (who the person actually is) from display labels (what their name looks like on screen).

The FinLedger Architecture: Relational Person Entities

In FinLedger, contacts are first-class domain entities managed by PersonDao.kt, decoupled from individual loan or split records:

flowchart TD
    subgraph PersonArchitecture["Centralized Person Relational Model"]
        Input["User Types Contact Name: 'Rahul'"] --> Normalizer["String Normalizer:
        Trim whitespace, lowercase comparison"]

        Normalizer --> MatchQuery{"Query PersonDao:
        Does an existing contact match
        normalized string 'rahul'?"}

        MatchQuery -->|No Match Found| CreateNew["Create New Person:
        Generate immutable UUID.
        Store name, optional phone & note."]

        MatchQuery -->|Match Found| Disambiguate["Surface Disambiguation Dialog:
        Display matching contacts with metadata:
        - Rahul Patil (Coworker, +91 98XXX)
        - Rahul Verma (Cousin)"]

        Disambiguate --> UserDecision{"User Selects Action"}

        UserDecision -->|Select Existing| BindExisting["Bind to Existing Person ID:
        Aggregates under existing debt history"]

        UserDecision -->|Create Distinct| CreateDistinct["Create New Distinct Person:
        Assign unique UUID. Prompt for nickname/note."]
    end

Let's examine how each safeguard functions in detail:

1. Case-Insensitive String Normalization

Before querying the database, candidate names pass through a strict string sanitizer:

  • Trims leading and trailing whitespace.
  • Collapses multiple internal spaces into a single space.
  • Compares using Unicode-aware case insensitivity (COLLATE NOCASE).

This ensures that typing "Rahul Patil", "rahul patil", or "Rahul Patil " immediately identifies the candidate as the same person rather than spawning three fragmented records.

2. The Interactive Disambiguation Prompt

When you create a loan or split expense and enter a name that matches one or more existing records, FinLedger refuses to make an assumption.

In LendingDialogs.kt, an interactive disambiguation sheet appears:

  • "A contact named 'Rahul' already exists. Is this the same person?"
  • The sheet surfaces the contact's contextual metadata: their phone number suffix, personal note (e.g., "Design Team"), and current outstanding balance.
  • If it is the same person, tapping their card binds the new loan to their existing personId.
  • If it is a different person, tapping "Create as New Person" prompts you to enter a distinguishing note or last name (e.g., "Rahul (Cousin)") and assigns an independent, unique UUID.

3. Immutable Relational Keys (personId)

Every debt record (LendingEntity) and repayment (LendingRepaymentEntity) references the person via an immutable foreign key: personId: String (a UUIDv4).

Because the database relations are bound to the immutable UUID rather than the human-readable string:

  • If you later edit Rahul's display name to "Rahul Patil (Tech Lead)", that edit updates a single row in the persons table.
  • All historical loans, partial repayments, and split expenses across the last three years stay perfectly connected with zero broken references.

Key Takeaway

Contact names in human language are inherently ambiguous; software identifiers must never be.

By establishing a centralized, UUID-driven Person repository with case-insensitive normalization and proactive disambiguation prompts, FinLedger guarantees that doing business with people of the same name never corrupts your financial records.

FinLedger is a privacy-first, offline-first personal finance application for Android that models bank accounts, credit cards, and cash without double-counting.

title: pgSherpa: a free PostgreSQL monitoring companion for macOS
description:
CortexRidge has released pgSherpa, a free desktop companion for PostgreSQL on macOS, now available on the Mac App Store.

pgSherpa sits in a corner of the screen and polls one or more PostgreSQL servers (PostgreSQL 12 to 18). When something needs attention it says so in a sentence, with the rows behind it:

  • Health: lock-wait chains, long-running and idle-in-transaction sessions, replication lag and replication slots, vacuum and transaction ID wraparound, connection limits.
  • Security: the server's version compared with the latest PostgreSQL minor release and the CVEs fixed since, plus configuration such as SSL, MD5 passwords and superuser count.
  • Cloud: backups, failovers, maintenance windows and replicas for DigitalOcean Managed Databases, Supabase and Amazon RDS / Aurora PostgreSQL, read from the provider's API.
  • SQL: a query box with PostgreSQL completion and \h syntax help for the server's own version. Every statement runs in a read-only transaction unless the user switches it to write.
  • Reports: ready-made views of pg_stat_activity, pg_locks, pg_stat_statements, vacuum progress, indexes and replication.

pgSherpa needs only a role with pg_monitor. It installs no extension and no agent on the server, and it has no account and no telemetry; passwords and keys stay in the macOS Keychain.

It runs on macOS 12 or later, on Apple silicon and Intel Macs.

  • Mac App Store: https://apps.apple.com/app/id6833955115
  • More information: https://cortexridge.com/

title: HubEgo-100K: In-the-Wild Egocentric Video of Skilled Work for Robot Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.21938v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Robot policies trained by imitation generalize poorly outside the environments and objects seen in training. Published data-scaling studies find that generalization grows with the diversity of training environments and objects rather than with more demonstrations per environment. Robot data is costly to collect across many environments, whereas egocentric human video can be recorded in the wild at scale; existing egocentric video, however, mostly shows daily-life activity and contains little skilled work in real workplaces. We present HubEgo-100K, a dataset built for diversity. This version of the paper covers the first release, v1.0: 10,124 hours of 1080p egocentric video with synchronized 100 Hz inertial (IMU) data from one head-mounted phone camera. In v1.0, 12,227 contributors record their own unscripted work in 15,548 environments (each one contributor's own setting of one type, such as their kitchen or workshop) across 11 setting types, 30 work categories, 56 task types and 35 action families, with 83% of hours in workplace settings. The release comprises 72,754 episodes with machine-generated action and language annotations, in LeRobot and MCAP formats under CC BY 4.0. We measure diversity along each axis, show that inside v1.0, with episodes in random order, new contributors and words keep appearing, and relate the measurements to published evidence on six data properties tied to policy performance, including hand visibility and inertial sensing. We also document collection, curation, privacy measures and data format, and provide a datasheet. Later versions of this paper will add benchmarks and cover further releases toward 100,000 hours.

title: Is 4-Bit Quantization More Than Noise to a Chat Model's Safety Behaviour? Attributing Behavioural Shifts with Matched Perturbations
description:
arXiv:2611.22186v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Chat models on phones and laptops are usually 4-bit copies of the model that was evaluated, and audits of such copies disagree about what quantization does to refusal. A 4-bit build is one of many weight perturbations of the same size, so a change in its behaviour could come from its specific rounding error or from any perturbation that large. In a pre-registered study of three 3-4B chat models, with paired tests, blind human labels and an 8-bit null, we find two 4-bit shifts of opposite sign: with a compliant reply prefilled, Qwen2.5-3B continues into harmful content more often, and on held-out jailbreaks Llama-3.2-3B complies 10.3 points less often. Matched perturbations separate the two. Shuffled and Gaussian versions of the error average close to zero, while scaling the real error, from its mirror image to twice its size, changes behaviour near-linearly. At half the real error, Llama's likelihood is almost unchanged, yet it already complies 5.8 points less often, and llama.cpp's Q4_K_M, at the same bits per weight, moves neither model. Refusal under 4-bit quantization depends on the specific rounding error, not on bits per weight or likelihood, so each build has to be compared with its original.

title: Your List Endpoint Runs 101 Queries to Show 100 Orders
description:
Your list endpoint runs 101 queries to show 100 orders.

A list I reviewed loaded 100 orders, then asked the database for each order's customer, one at a time.

1 query for the list.
100 more for the customers.

That is the N+1 problem. The page was slow, the database was busy, and the team's first idea was a bigger database.

What the code usually looks like

The endpoint fetches the orders, then loops over them to fetch each customer:

const orders = await db.query(
  `SELECT id, total, customer_id FROM orders
   ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 100`
);

for (const order of orders) {
  const [customer] = await db.query(
    `SELECT name FROM customers WHERE id = ?`,
    [order.customer_id]
  );
  order.customerName = customer?.name;
}

One query for the list, then one query per row inside the loop. With 100 orders that is 101 queries. With 1,000 orders it would be 1,001. The query count grows with the list, and that is the real problem.

Why it stays hidden for so long

The data is correct. Every order shows the right customer name, so no test fails and no user reports a bug. In development the list has ten rows, so eleven queries feel fast. The problem only shows up when real data arrives, and by then the slow page looks like a database problem, not a code problem.

The wrong fixes

A bigger database pays more for the same 101 queries. The queries are the problem, not the machine running them.

A cache hides the extra queries until the data changes, then the first request after the change pays the full cost again. It also adds a whole new thing to keep correct.

An index makes each of the 101 queries faster, without removing 100 of them. Faster queries that should not exist are still queries that should not exist.

The fix: ask for the data together

One query can return the orders with the customer name already in each row:

SELECT o.id, o.total, c.name
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
ORDER BY o.created_at DESC
LIMIT 100;

One query, 100 rows, the customer name already in each row.

Two details in that query matter.

First, it is a LEFT JOIN, not a plain JOIN. If an order can exist without a customer, a plain JOIN would silently drop those orders from the list. LEFT JOIN keeps every order and leaves the customer name empty where there is no customer.

Second, it has an ORDER BY. Without it, LIMIT 100 returns whichever 100 rows the database happens to find first, and that set can change between requests, which breaks paging. With ORDER BY, the database sorts first and then takes the newest 100 orders.

When a join is the wrong fix

The join above works cleanly because each order has exactly one customer. Joining a many-to-one relation keeps one row per order.

A one-to-many relation behaves differently. Join orders to order_items, and an order with five items becomes five rows. LIMIT 100 now counts rows, not orders, so you might get 30 orders, and the last one can be cut off halfway through its items.

For that case, use two queries instead. Page the orders first, then fetch all their items in one go:

SELECT id, total FROM orders
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 100;

SELECT order_id, sku, qty FROM order_items
WHERE order_id IN (/* the 100 order ids */);

Then group the items by order_id in your code. That is still two queries for any list size, which is the whole point.

If you use an ORM

Use its eager loading, like include in Prisma or Sequelize. It may run 2 queries instead of 1, and that is fine. What matters is that the query count stays the same as the list grows:

const orders = await prisma.order.findMany({
  take: 100,
  orderBy: { createdAt: 'desc' },
  include: { customer: true },
});

The ORM fetches the orders, then fetches the customers for those orders in one more query. Two queries for any list size beats one query per row. This two-query approach is also why ORMs handle one-to-many relations like order items without the row multiplication problem.

How to spot it in your own code

Count the queries per request, not the time per query. Turn on query logging in development, open a list page, and look at the count. Then change the page size from 10 rows to 100 rows. If the query count jumps with the row count, you have an N+1 hiding in that endpoint.

Fix the shape of the query first. Speed comes after, and only where it is still needed.

How many queries does your list endpoint run today? Drop the number in the comments.

title: Amazon WorkSpaces Applications adds support for smart card redirection
description:
Amazon WorkSpaces Applications now supports smart card redirection on single-session and multi-session fleets, so users can access the smart card connected to their local device from applications inside their streaming session. It also extends smart card sign-in, previously limited to single-session fleets, to multi-session fleets. This launch helps public sector, healthcare, and other regulated organizations that use Common Access Card (CAC) or Personal Identity Verification (PIV) cards run those workflows on multi-session fleets.

Administrators can turn smart card sign-in for Active Directory and smart card redirection on or off independently for each stack. Smart card sign-in lets users sign in to domain-joined streaming instances with their smart card instead of a password, while redirected smart cards support in-session authentication, digital signing, and email encryption. For example, a government agency can move CAC users from single-session to multi-session fleets and keep CAC sign-in.

These capabilities are available today in all AWS commercial and AWS GovCloud (US) regions that offer WorkSpaces Applications.

To get started, turn on either setting under User settings for your stack, use a Windows image with the latest WorkSpaces Applications agent, and connect with the WorkSpaces Applications client for Windows. New stacks have both settings turned off by default, and existing stacks that use smart card redirection keep it turned on. To learn more, see Create a stack in the Amazon WorkSpaces Applications Administration Guide, or visit the Amazon WorkSpaces Applications product page.

title: Depth-Aware Activation Steering via Attention Residuals
description:
arXiv:2611.21655v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Activation steering is a simple, training-free way to modulate LLM behavior, yet existing methods typically inject vectors at a single layer and lack mechanisms for depth-aware propagation or internal verification. We combine two recent ideas - Attention Residuals (AttnRes) providing learnable cross-layer pathways, and Jacobian-lens (J-space) concept readout - into a lightweight depth-aware steering pipeline. On two small open models (Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3.5-0.8B), distributing a persona vector according to AttnRes-style depth weights yields stronger internal alignment (deeper-layer concept cosine and rank, p<0.0001) and stronger behavioral shifts than single-layer injection. The effect is sign-specific: reverse vectors invert all six metrics, random directions degrade alignment (p<0.0001), and a short LoRA fine-tune erases the imprint. Injection rewires attention strictly downstream of the injection point (upstream JS = 0.00000). Three practical findings follow. First, a layer-wise geometric decomposition of cosine readouts: at the injection layer 123% of the increase is arithmetic, while 5-11 layers downstream 100% is dynamical. Second, an intensity window: effects are monotone over 0.3-0.7, then generation collapses (617 to 306 to 25 chars). Third, metric discipline: keyword-rule metrics fail LLM-judge validation (kappa <= 0.09), and two rule-based conclusions were retracted. Training the depth weights on a steering objective (200 steps, frozen backbone) raises final alignment 10x on held-out prompts. Cross-persona vectors retain 96-99% of the effect: specificity holds against random, not semantic, directions. We contribute a practical, low-overhead depth-aware steering method with a careful evaluation protocol. Code and data are released.

title: DNeo: Your Parallel Draft Model Needs Better Target Feature Encoding
description:
arXiv:2611.21925v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Speculative-diffusion decoding uses a small parallel drafter model to generate b draft tokens in one forward pass, which then undergo parallel verification via a larger target model. Faster inference can be achieved when multiple draft tokens pass verification simultaneously. Recent parallel draft architectures (DFlash, DSpark) improve draft quality by conditioning on rich features computed by the target, through a mechanism known as feature encoding. However, standard feature encoding mechanisms have three limitations: (1) they are lossy, applying encoding projections that are destructive to the underlying target feature-space via a discovered effect known as residual mixing, (2) they are memory-less, with no record of previously processed proposals, and (3) they utilize features sampled uniformly from across the target layers, omitting important hidden states. To address these issues, we propose Mixture-of-Features Attention (MoFA), a lightweight feature-encoding approach equipped with a working memory that encodes previously rejected proposals. Leveraging MoFA, rejection memory, and a set of further enhancements, including 2-tap causal convolutions, prefix-only cross-attention, and non-uniform target layer selection, the final architecture, DNeo, achieves 1.3x faster generation speed than SoTA (DFlash-2) without impacting drafter footprint or generation quality. DNeo marks a new state of the art in high quality, fast LLM inference.

title: RDS Extended Support Charges on the AWS Bill? A MySQL 8.0 or PostgreSQL 13 Database Passed Its End of Standard Support
description:
As of November 18, 2026, this post sums up the official pages linked here.

The problem

Your Amazon RDS line on the AWS bill went up this month. Nobody changed an instance size, added storage or bought anything new. The database runs the same version as last month. The new cost is RDS Extended Support.

This can catch many teams this year. RDS for MySQL 8.0 reached its RDS end of standard support on July 31, 2026. RDS for PostgreSQL 13 reached it on February 28, 2026. In this post we show what the charge is and why it started without anyone clicking anything. We also show how to find the databases behind it and stop it safely.

Root cause: an old major version keeps running, for a fee

Here is how AWS describes it. Extended Support "allows you to continue running a database on a major engine version" past its RDS end of standard support date. AWS charges extra for this. (RDS Extended Support)

Charges start "the day after the RDS end of standard support date." (RDS Extended Support charges)

For the two versions most teams ask about, AWS's own calendars show:

Version RDS end of standard support Extended Support year 1 pricing starts Year 3 pricing starts RDS end of Extended Support
RDS for MySQL 8.0 31 July 2026 1 August 2026 1 August 2028 31 July 2029
RDS for PostgreSQL 13 28 February 2026 1 March 2026 1 March 2028 28 February 2029

(Sources: MySQL on Amazon RDS versions and Release calendar for Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. MySQL 5.7, PostgreSQL 11 and PostgreSQL 12 are already past their end of standard support too; see the same pages.)

The MySQL page also notes that "MySQL 5.7 and 8.0 are now only available under RDS Extended Support."

Why nobody "turned it on"

Enrollment is the default in many setups:

  • With the AWS CLI or RDS API, if you "don't specify the RDS Extended Support setting, Amazon RDS defaults to enabling RDS Extended Support." AWS adds that the same default applies when you automate with CloudFormation or other services. It keeps the database available past the end of standard support. In the console, the setting "isn't selected by default." (Creating a DB instance with RDS Extended Support)
  • When an enrolled database reaches the date, RDS enrolls it automatically. AWS says this "doesn't change the database engine and doesn't impact the uptime or performance of your DB instance." (RDS Extended Support)

So the database keeps working exactly as before. The only thing that changes is the bill.

How the charge is priced

For provisioned RDS for MySQL instances, AWS says "RDS Extended Support is priced per vCPU per hour." The price also depends "on the AWS Region and calendar date." (Amazon RDS for MySQL pricing)

The pricing pages give these examples:

  • RDS for MySQL 5.7 in US East (Ohio): "$0.100 per vCPU-hr between March 1, 2024 to February 28, 2026. Starting March 1, 2026, you will be charged $0.200 per vCPU-hr." (Amazon RDS for MySQL pricing)
  • RDS for MySQL 5.7 on a db.r5.large in US East (N. Virginia) in the first year: "$0.200 per hour, or 2 vCPUs x $0.100 per vCPU-hr." (same page)
  • RDS for PostgreSQL 12 in US East (Ohio): "$0.100 per vCPU-hr between March 1, 2025 to February 28, 2027. Starting March 1, 2027, you will be charged $0.200 per vCPU-hr." (Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL pricing)

These are AWS's worked examples, not the rate for every version and Region. Read the pricing page for your engine, version and Region before you estimate a bill. The formula AWS gives is simple: number of vCPUs x the hourly rate for your Region and pricing year, for every hour the instance runs.

Five details make the bill bigger than people expect. All five come from the FAQ on the MySQL and PostgreSQL pricing pages and the charges page:

  1. Multi-AZ standbys pay too. With one standby, you are charged "on both your primary and standby instances." With two readable standbys, on the primary and both standbys.
  2. Read replicas pay too, if they run a major version past its end of standard support.
  3. Reserved Instances do not help. "RDS Extended Support charges are independent of instance charges. Therefore, Reserved Instance discounts are not applicable to RDS Extended Support charges."
  4. A restore can start a new charge. Snapshots themselves are not charged. But restoring a DB snapshot "to a new DB instance after end of standard support" is charged "RDS Extended Support pricing for that instance." The same applies if you create a new instance on that version.
  5. The price goes up in year 3. The first two years use the year 1 and 2 rate. Year 3 pricing starts "on the first day of the third year."

Step 1: find the databases behind the charge

List every DB instance with its engine, version and enrollment:

aws rds describe-db-instances \
  --query 'DBInstances[].[DBInstanceIdentifier,Engine,EngineVersion,DBInstanceClass,MultiAZ,EngineLifecycleSupport]' \
  --output table

AWS says that if Extended Support is available for a database, the response includes EngineLifecycleSupport. The value open-source-rds-extended-support means the database is enrolled. The value open-source-rds-extended-support-disabled means enrollment was turned off. (Viewing enrollment in RDS Extended Support)

Enrollment alone is not a charge. AWS notes that "Charges for RDS Extended Support only start when your DB engine version has reached the RDS end of standard support." So the list you care about is: enrolled and on a major version whose end of standard support has passed. For Aurora clusters and Multi-AZ DB clusters, run describe-db-clusters as well, because the setting lives at the cluster level.

In the console, the Databases page has an RDS Extended Support column. If you do not see it, AWS says to turn it on under the Preferences icon. (same page)

The command lists one Region at a time, so run it in every Region you use (add --region).

Step 2: check the dates for each version

You can read the support dates from the CLI instead of a web page:

aws rds describe-db-major-engine-versions \
  --engine mysql \
  --major-engine-version 8.0

AWS says the response includes SupportedEngineLifecycles, with a start and end date for standard support (open-source-rds-standard-support) and for Extended Support (open-source-rds-extended-support). This works for the open source engines (MariaDB, MySQL and PostgreSQL), not the commercial ones. (Viewing support dates, describe-db-major-engine-versions)

Use --engine postgres for PostgreSQL.

Step 3: stop the charge the right way

AWS lists two things that stop the charge. One is upgrading "to an engine version that's covered under standard support." The other is deleting "the database that's running a major version past the RDS end of standard support date." (RDS Extended Support charges)

Option A: plan and test a major version upgrade (the usual fix)

Upgrade to a major version with a long standard support window, not just the next one. AWS warns that "The charges will restart if your target engine version enters RDS Extended Support in the future." (same page) Two examples from the calendars:

  • MySQL: 8.4 has RDS end of standard support on 31 July 2029.
  • PostgreSQL: 14 reaches its RDS end of standard support on 28 February 2027, only a few months away. PostgreSQL 16 runs to 28 February 2029, and 17 to 28 February 2030.

For RDS for MySQL, MariaDB and Aurora MySQL, AWS says you can use Blue/Green Deployments to move off an Extended Support version. This works as long as Blue/Green supports your engine, Region and version. (Amazon RDS for MySQL pricing FAQ)

If you upgrade in place, know what the command does. The CLI reference covers --engine-version. It says: "Changing this parameter results in an outage and the change is applied during the next maintenance window unless the ApplyImmediately parameter is enabled." A major upgrade with a non-default parameter group needs a parameter group from the new version's family. You must also set --allow-major-version-upgrade. (modify-db-instance) Test on a restored copy first. That copy is charged Extended Support while it runs on the old version.

Option B: delete what nobody uses

Old read replicas, a forgotten test database, a copy restored "just to check something." Each one is charged on its own. If it is not needed, take a final snapshot and delete it. Snapshots are not charged Extended Support. (Amazon RDS for MySQL pricing FAQ)

Be careful with "just turn it off"

You can change enrollment at any time with the EngineLifecycleSupport setting. In the CLI, that's --engine-lifecycle-support open-source-rds-extended-support-disabled. But AWS warns about disabling it on a database "that is already past its standard support end date." In that case, "the instance or cluster automatically upgrades to the next supported major version." (RDS Extended Support)

That is a major version upgrade you did not test, and if the database is in production, it happens to production. Use this only after the application has been tested on the new version.

Step 4: stop new charges from appearing

  • Set the option on purpose in code. Because the CLI and API default to enrollment, add --engine-lifecycle-support (or EngineLifecycleSupport) to your create and restore scripts so the choice is visible. AWS notes that if you set open-source-rds-extended-support-disabled and the end of standard support has passed, creating the instance "will always fail." That is a useful guard against new databases on old versions. (Creating a DB instance with RDS Extended Support)
  • Put the next dates on the calendar. PostgreSQL 14 (28 February 2027) is the next big one for many teams. Run the Step 1 command a few months ahead of each date.

When it still goes wrong

  • The charge came back after an upgrade. You upgraded to a version that later reached its own end of standard support. AWS's example: a PostgreSQL 11 database upgraded to 12 on April 30, 2024 was charged again from March 1, 2025. (RDS Extended Support charges)
  • The bill is bigger than one instance should cost. Count the standbys and read replicas. Each is charged.
  • You bought Reserved Instances and the line is still there. RI discounts do not apply to this charge.
  • Extended Support has an end too. AWS says it is available "for up to 3 years past the RDS end of standard support date." After that, RDS "will automatically upgrade your major engine version." (RDS Extended Support)

What to check first

  1. Which DB instances and clusters are on MySQL 5.7, MySQL 8.0, PostgreSQL 11, 12 or 13, and are they enrolled?
  2. How many vCPUs does each have, counting standbys and read replicas?
  3. Which ones can be deleted, and which need an upgrade plan?
  4. Is the target version far enough from its own end of standard support?
  5. Do your create and restore scripts set --engine-lifecycle-support on purpose?

Docs checked (November 18, 2026)

  • Amazon RDS User Guide, Amazon RDS Extended Support with Amazon RDS (what it is, automatic enrollment, changing enrollment, forced upgrade when disabled past the date, up to 3 years)
  • Amazon RDS User Guide, Amazon RDS Extended Support charges (start date, standbys, what stops the charge, charges restarting, the PostgreSQL 11 example)
  • Amazon RDS User Guide, Creating a DB instance or a Multi-AZ DB cluster with RDS Extended Support (CLI and API default to enrollment, console does not, disabled option makes creation fail past the date)
  • Amazon RDS User Guide, Viewing enrollment in RDS Extended Support (EngineLifecycleSupport values, console column, enrollment vs charges)
  • Amazon RDS User Guide, Viewing support dates for engine versions and AWS CLI describe-db-major-engine-versions (SupportedEngineLifecycles)
  • Amazon RDS User Guide, MySQL on Amazon RDS versions (MySQL 5.7, 8.0 and 8.4 dates)
  • Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL Release Notes, Release calendar for Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL (PostgreSQL 13, 14, 16 and 17 dates)
  • AWS CLI, modify-db-instance (--engine-lifecycle-support values, --engine-version outage note, --allow-major-version-upgrade)
  • Amazon RDS for MySQL pricing and Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL pricing (per vCPU-hour pricing, the Ohio and N. Virginia examples, Multi-AZ, read replicas, Reserved Instances, snapshots and restores, Blue/Green)

title: AWS Lambda now supports customer-managed runtimes, giving platform teams centralized control over runtime contents and updates
description:
AWS Lambda now supports customer-managed runtimes for Lambda Event Functions (formerly Lambda functions). Customer-managed runtimes are a standalone resource type that fully decouples runtime management from function deployment. Platform teams gain centralized control over the runtime contents, updates, access, and lifecycle, including the ability to push updates to shared components without per-function redeployments. Application teams consume the runtime from their functions in the same way as a Lambda-managed runtime, preserving their familiar developer experience.

Many organizations require every function to include approved components, such as SDKs, certificates, and security or monitoring tools. Previously, sharing these through Lambda Layers or container images meant redeploying every function to pick up a change. With customer-managed runtimes, platform teams manage these components in a central runtime, packaged as OCI container images in Amazon ECR and compatible with existing Docker and CI/CD tooling. Functions pick up updates automatically as Lambda recycles execution environments, so there's no need to redeploy each function or coordinate rollouts. Updates can be scheduled and staged to match change control policies, with centralized health metrics and rapid rollback. With this launch, the existing custom runtimes feature is renamed "bring your own language."

AWS Lambda customer-managed runtimes is now generally available in all commercial AWS Regions. There is no additional charge for customer-managed runtimes; functions are billed at standard Lambda rates and standard Amazon ECR pricing applies to runtime images.

To get started, build your runtime as a container image in Amazon ECR, starting from a Lambda base image or from scratch, then create a runtime, a version, and an alias. Application teams reference the runtime alias in their function configuration and keep deploying their code as .zip files. Share runtimes with other accounts or an AWS Organization by using a resource-based policy. You can create and manage customer-managed runtimes using the AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, CloudFormation, or AWS CDK. To learn more, see the customer-managed runtimes documentation and launch blog post.

title: Sleep2Word: Peripheral-to-EEG Translation via Duration-Aware Wordization
description:
arXiv:2611.21643v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Estimating full-night electroencephalography (EEG) spectrograms from peripheral measurements could extend EEG-informed sleep analysis to recordings acquired without EEG. This task requires compact representations of signals with different temporal structures. We introduce Sleep2Word, a framework for translating respiration, electrocardiography (ECG), or photoplethysmography (PPG) into EEG spectrograms through duration-aware physiological words. Building on context-dependent chunking, Sleep2Word groups physiological embeddings into variable-duration chunks and jointly quantizes their content and duration into modality-specific wordbooks. A block-autoregressive translator then predicts target EEG word identities and occurrence-specific duration refinements within fixed-duration blocks. This design accommodates independent source and target wordbooks, limits temporal drift, and shortens the autoregressive decoding path. Trained on over 20K PSG cases across 9 datasets, Sleep2Word consistently outperforms existing spectrogram generation baselines in EEG spectrogram reconstruction, sleep staging, arousal detection, and survival prediction. Compressing full night sequences by up to 69.7%, the learned words yield a favorable accuracy-compute trade-off. Sleep event analysis further shows that the learned words capture physiologically plausible associations across modalities, suggesting their potential for interpretable cross-modal analysis.

title: Fragmented Markers, Mixed Results: A Systematic Review of AI Coding Assistants and Developer Productivity
description:
arXiv:2611.21632v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: AI coding assistants are increasingly embedded in software engineering practice, yet the literature still offers no cumulative, easily interpretable picture of their effects on software developer productivity. The central problem is not a lack of studies, but a lack of comparability: prior work operationalizes productivity through heterogeneous markers, settings, and reporting styles, making cross-study conclusions difficult. To address this, we conduct a staged systematic literature review. In the first stage, we synthesize studies that explicitly examine developer productivity. In the second, we extend the scope to productivity-related developer outcomes using SPACE as a theory-informed lens, capturing human-centered evidence that explicit productivity studies often omit. Across both stages, we analyze how productivity is operationalized, which confounding factors are discussed, and how reported effects are distributed.
  We identify 187 unique productivity and productivity-related markers, while individual studies typically only use five, revealing a broad but highly fragmented evidence base. Explicit productivity research is dominated by time-, output-, and artifact-oriented proxies, whereas the broader SPACE-aligned corpus makes satisfaction, psychological aspects, and well-being substantially more visible. Reported effects are often positive, but this pattern is stronger in perceived and tendency-based findings than in objective or statistically evaluated ones. Overall, the literature suggests that AI coding assistants can support productivity, but current evidence does not yet support simple, context-independent conclusions. The key contribution of this review is therefore a structured basis for making productivity evidence more interpretable, multidimensional, and comparable across studies.

We've released version 6.22 of Google Cloud CCaaS.

The timing of the update to your instance depends on the deployment schedule that you have chosen. For more information, see Deployment schedules.

Feature

Transcript separation for chat

You can now configure Google Cloud CCaaS to deliver a separate transcript file for each participant segment in a chat, instead of one combined transcript per session. Under Settings > Chat > Chat Transcript, select Per Segment in Transcript Separation to generate individual transcript files for each agent, virtual agent, or supervisor who joins the chat—helpful for identifying which participant handled each part of a transferred or escalated conversation. Your consumers still receive a single, full-chat transcript regardless of this setting.

For more information, see Chat transcripts and chat history.

By default, this capability is inactive. Contact Google Cloud Support to turn it on for your instance.

Feature

Campaign-based scheduled callbacks

Agents can now schedule a callback during an outbound campaign call. The callback belongs to the campaign, not to an individual agent, and the dialer calls the consumer back in the time slot they chose. Administrators set slot length, capacity, booking window, and expiry for each campaign, and supervisors can track upcoming, completed, and expired callbacks from the campaign list.

For more information, see Campaign management.
