title: Testing World Models on Actions They Have Never Seen: Held-Out Plans, Forecast Accuracy and Price Rules in Retail
description:
arXiv:2611.22537v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A world model is trusted to answer "what if": how its world responds to an action it has never seen. We give a test of that trust for any action-conditioned world model: actions held out of training by design and scored against a known answer; whether forecast accuracy predicts accuracy on those actions; and the same structure given to simpler models. We run it in retail, where the action is a price and promotion plan, across 2,853 fitted models. First, forecast accuracy is a fair guide between kinds of model (rank correlation with error on new plans 0.32 to 0.66) and a poor guide between versions of one world model: where merchants plan into high-demand weeks the link reverses, down to -0.69. Second, training the world model to learn the effect of actions (JEPA pretraining, a latent consistency check, adaptation at the plan date) leaves its error on new plans unchanged. Third, in generated worlds the recorded regular price and three price rules improve it. Given the same rules, a log-linear model is best when its curve can match the truth; in a world whose curve lies outside the rules, the world model with the rules is ahead of the log-linear model with the rules in 36 of 40 worlds, and does as well without its recurrent cell. On real data (Breakfast at the Frat, The Complete Journey and M5) the rules lower the world model's error on pure price cuts deeper than any it saw (0.63 to 0.56 on the Frat; 0.45 to 0.44, within chance, on The Complete Journey), but not on lasting price moves. Fourth, a small share of random test plans helps every model a little. In a generated dosing world, a stress test in a second domain, the first finding repeats, and the built-up drug level lowers the world model's error (2.86 to 1.91) though it still predicts only 0.12 to 0.32 of the true gain. The test carries to any domain where a world model is asked about actions outside its history.

title: ConfGuard: a physics-grounded reference monitor for predictive-maintenance large-language-model agents
description:
arXiv:2611.22288v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large-language-model agents now close the industrial predictive-maintenance loop, reading sensor windows, retrieving procedures and dispatching work orders. Two attack channels meet there: injected text in a retrieved document can hijack the decision, and a bounded sensor perturbation can corrupt the remaining-useful-life estimate behind it. Recent agent defenses police data provenance and tool privilege but cannot tell whether a prognostic quantity is physically plausible. ConfGuard is a reference monitor with a physics-grounded policy. Its conformal monitor tests each prediction, anchored to the asset's admitted history, against degradation physics: capped remaining life never rises and falls at most one cycle per cycle. Calibrating its threshold over whole asset trajectories lets the operator set the expected share of a clean asset's windows the running monitor escalates. A physics-policy validator checks the agent's maintenance-urgency decision against the decision a deterministic policy derives from the same interval. On all 10,196 C-MAPSS test windows the monitor cuts a covert attacker's reach on healthy assets from 0.529 to 0.046 and closes suppression of failing assets (0.151 to 0), escalating 0.027 of clean windows against a 0.05 target, while the fixed physical range it replaces leaves both attacks open. Behind a Qwen3-14B planner the composed monitors hold urgency-class injection to 0.00 and the universal sensor attack to 0.12, against 0.29 and 0.54 for a defended prompt. An adaptive attacker defeats a Mahalanobis detector on 0.504 of windows and adversarial training on 0.485. We report an attack class the projection misses.

title: Building a Gherkin editor and two-way Git sync on Atlassian Forge: eight things I learned
description:
I spent October and November 2026 building Gherkin Studio, a BDD app for Jira Cloud, on Atlassian Forge. It lets a team write Gherkin scenarios inside a Jira story, syncs the .feature files both ways with GitHub, GitLab.com or Bitbucket Cloud, and shows CI results on each story. Atlassian approved it on the Marketplace on 18 November.

Forge runs your code on Atlassian's infrastructure, so there is no server to keep alive. It also has limits you only meet once real data arrives. These are the eight that cost me the most time, with the numbers I measured.

1. One storage value holds at most 240 KiB

Forge's key-value storage refuses any single value over 240 KiB. That sounds generous until you store a whole story's scenarios in one value, or an index of every step your team has written (for autocomplete), or a CI result for a story with hundreds of scenarios.

What I did: every place that writes a value now checks its size in bytes first, and my local test double of Forge storage refuses anything over 240 KiB, so the limit fails in tests instead of in production. The step index is capped by bytes, not by count.

2. A web trigger that takes too long gets a 424

CI pipelines post a Cucumber JSON report to a Forge web trigger. My first version checked each story in the report one after another. With 500 stories that took 56 seconds, and Forge stopped the trigger with HTTP 424.

Checking ten stories at a time (a small mapLimit helper, no library) brought the same 500 stories down to 6.7 seconds. Forge also refuses request bodies around 6 MB with a 413; 4.5 MB went through.

3. Slow work belongs in a queue, not in a resolver

The optional AI drafts call the Anthropic API. A short story took 16–20 seconds; a detailed one took more than 22, which is too long for a UI resolver. The call now runs in a Forge async event consumer with timeoutSeconds: 300, and the panel polls for the result. A long story takes about 40 seconds and nothing times out.

One trap: Forge retries an async event after an error or a timeout. Since the API call costs money, the job is marked as running before the paid call, so a retry does not pay twice.

4. Each Git host says "conflict" differently

Two-way sync means detecting when the file in Git changed since the last sync. The three hosts report a stale write in three ways:

  • GitHub: 409 when the file's SHA is stale; 422 when the SHA is missing.
  • GitLab: 400, with a message such as "changed since you started editing it".
  • Bitbucket Cloud: 400, "The parent commit specified (…) is not the head of branch". Not 409.

All three answer 404 for a missing file, but also for a missing branch or repository. So before telling a user "the file was deleted in Git", the app tests the connection.

When both sides changed, nothing is overwritten. The app shows a line-by-line diff and the user picks Jira's version, Git's version or the text in the editor.

5. Jira can stop showing a module without an error

My status panel used jira:issueGlance. During review it simply stopped appearing on my test site, even with the old manifest. The docs now say the glance is replaced by the issue context module. Moving to jira:issueContext, with the same dynamic properties, brought it back under "Apps" on the story. I kept the glance for older views.

6. Deleting a story sends more events than the docs suggest

When an issue is deleted, the app removes that story's data in a trigger on avi:jira:deleted:issue. The docs say cascading events are not emitted, but a subtask deleted together with its parent did get its own event on my site. Deleting a whole project is a single avi:jira:deleted:project event, with no list of its issues.

7. Licensing exists only in production

context.license is only present in the production environment of a paid app. In development and staging it is undefined, so the code treats "undefined" as licensed and only "inactive" as read-only. You can test the inactive path by installing on a separate developer site with an inactive license.

8. The free compute is large

Forge includes 200,000 GB-seconds a month per app. A month of heavy testing on my site used 282. For a small app, compute cost is not the problem; storage limits and timeouts are.

What I would do again

  • Fake Forge storage locally with the real limits, so tests fail where production would.
  • Measure with real data before choosing a design. Every limit above showed up only with realistic sizes.
  • Read what each Git host actually returns instead of what the docs imply.

If you build on Forge and hit something I missed, I'd like to hear it in the comments.

I'm the developer of Gherkin Studio, the app described here. It's on the Atlassian Marketplace, free for up to 10 users. This post first appeared on gherkinstudio.com.

title: Selective Column Loading in GORM for Leaner Catalog Queries
description:
Our ads table contains JSONB fields, long text, contact data, timestamps, and other detail-page fields. A catalog card needs only a small subset. Loading that subset keeps the list query and its data contract lean.

The Problem

The default GORM pattern loads all columns:

var ads []model.Ad
db.Where("marketplace_category_id = ?", categoryID).Find(&ads)
// SELECT * FROM ads WHERE marketplace_category_id = ...

That transfers and scans fields the card never reads. Large text and JSONB values can make the waste more visible, but the effect depends on row width, PostgreSQL TOAST behavior, the query plan, and network latency.

The Fix: Explicit Selection

A simplified version of our list query explicitly selects the fields needed by catalog cards:

var ads []*model.Ad
db.Model(&model.Ad{}).
    Select(
        "ads.catalog_id",
        "ads.title",
        "ads.currency",
        "ads.price",
        "ads.image",
    ).
    Where("ads.is_published = ? AND ads.marketplace_category_id = ?", true, categoryID).
    Order("created_at DESC").
    Limit(24).
    Find(&ads)

Fields that were not selected keep their Go zero values, so the returned model must not escape into code that assumes it is fully populated. A dedicated projection struct makes that contract more explicit:

type CatalogCard struct {
    CatalogID uint   `gorm:"column:catalog_id"`
    Title     string `gorm:"column:title"`
    Currency  string `gorm:"column:currency"`
    Price     string `gorm:"column:price"`
    Image     string `gorm:"column:image"`
}

var cards []CatalogCard
db.Model(&model.Ad{}).
    Select("catalog_id", "title", "currency", "price", "image").
    Where("is_published = ? AND marketplace_category_id = ?", true, categoryID).
    Find(&cards)

GORM can infer a smaller projection when querying a model into a smaller struct, but an explicit Select is easier to audit and remains clear if the destination changes.

Measure the Impact

Selective loading reduces bytes sent to Go and avoids scanning or unmarshalling omitted fields. It does not guarantee a particular latency improvement: PostgreSQL may still need to visit the same heap pages, and another part of the query may dominate.

Use EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) for the database plan and a Go benchmark or production trace for allocations and end-to-end latency. Compare representative data, not estimates based only on Go struct sizes.

Index Strategy

Selective columns only help if the query itself is fast. Our catalog's common predicates and sort order have a matching composite index:

CREATE INDEX idx_ads_marketplace_list
    ON ads (
        country_id,
        is_published,
        is_owner_active,
        marketplace_category_id,
        offer_type,
        created_at DESC
    );

Column order and optional filters must follow real query patterns. Adding every filter to one index creates a large index that may not help. Confirm usage with the query plan, and remember that an index can speed reads while making writes and maintenance more expensive. On a busy existing table, assess lock impact and consider CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY; it cannot run inside a transaction block and can leave an invalid index after failure.

The Rule

Our convention is:

  • list methods explicitly select card fields;
  • detail and edit methods may load the full model;
  • a partially loaded model should stay inside the read path that created it.

Find vs. Scan

Scan() is not required for a non-model projection. With Model(&model.Ad{}), GORM can use Find(&cards) and still retain the model context, including its table and applicable scopes. Scan(&cards) is also useful for custom projections and aggregate queries.

The important part is to inspect the generated SQL and understand which GORM scopes you intend to apply. The GORM query documentation shows the smart-select behavior.

This article is based on lessons from building Towami, a multi-country marketplace and white-label storefront platform. Follow for more practical notes on Go, HTMX, infrastructure, and SaaS.

title: Rigging UI Elements: Bones and IK Outside of Character Animation
description:
Bones are associated with characters, and that association keeps designers from using them where they would save the most time: interface elements that need to bend.

This is a practical guide to the cases, the workflow, and the limits.

What a bone rig actually buys you

A keyframe rig says: at 200ms, this vertex is here. At 400ms, it is there.

A bone rig says: this vertex is 60% influenced by the upper arm and 40% by the forearm. Move the arm and the vertex follows, everywhere, forever.

That indirection is the value. You animate the skeleton — a handful of rotations — and the geometry follows. Change the artwork, and the rig still works. Change the pose, and the skin deforms consistently.

For UI, that means:

  • a mascot that leans, blinks and gestures without re-keyframing every path
  • an illustration that squashes on press without distorting its neighbours
  • a decorative arrow that bends along a curve instead of being redrawn
  • a loading skeleton that breathes with a single parameter
  • a hero object whose parts stay attached when the layout changes

The workflow, in the order it matters

1. Decide what the skeleton is, not what the drawing is.

Look at the artwork and ask: what are the levers? A tail has three. A ribbon has four. An arm has two plus a hand. Bones should be fewer than you think; a rig with twelve bones for a shape that needs three is harder to animate, not easier.

2. Parent the hierarchy properly.

Master bone at the root, children for the limbs or segments, each rotated around a sensible pivot. In Exode this is the master/child bone distinction in the hierarchy panel, and the pivot is what makes a rotation look like a joint rather than a spin.

3. Bind, then weight.

Auto-binding on selection is convenient and destructive if you are not careful — the audit notes on the Exode repo list exactly that problem and the fix that shipped. The safe sequence is: bind the mesh, then paint weights, then test extreme poses before you animate.

Weights are the craft. A vertex at 100% on one bone will crease. A vertex split 50/50 will bend smoothly. The batch weighting and the live weights table exist because doing this one vertex at a time is how rigs get abandoned.

4. Add IK only where you need it.

Inverse kinematics solves the pose from a target: drag the hand, the elbow follows. It is magic for a character reaching for something. It is overkill for a two-bone ribbon you will animate directly.

Exode supports IK chains; the rule is to use them at the end of a chain, not the root, or the whole rig becomes a puppet you cannot pose precisely.

5. Animate the skeleton, never the mesh.

Once the rig is bound, all animation should be bone rotations and root position. If you catch yourself keyframing individual vertices, the rig is wrong.

The UI-specific details nobody tells you

Layout and rigs interact badly if you let them. A bone rig lives in the coordinate space of its container. If the container reflows on a breakpoint, the rig must be positioned by layout, not by absolute coordinates, or it will detach on mobile. This is the single most common bug in "responsive mascot" work.

Rigs need a rest pose that matches the design. If the rig's neutral pose is not the design's default, every state has a permanent offset. Bind at the pose you will ship.

Reduced motion needs a rig-free fallback. A static image at the rest pose is the honest fallback. Do not run a cut-down rig animation for users who asked for less motion; show the still.

Export the rig, not a video. A baked sprite sequence loses the interactivity you built the rig for. If the rig is in the design artefact, the compiled component carries it.

Where the tooling is still catching up

The honest part.

Mesh deformation in Rive and Spine is deeper than in Exode today. If the brief is "a cape that ripples with wind", those tools have more mature free-form deformation and more artist-facing controls.

Exode's rigging audit lists eight gaps it closed — destructive auto-bind, single-vertex selection, read-only weights, edit-mode exit, static weight visuals, destructive re-binding, no independent Bézier handle weighting, and rigid normalisation. That is a real list, and the fact that it is public is a good sign. It is not the same as a decade of character rigs.

So the split I use:

  • Character as art object, shipped inside a canvas or game: Rive or Spine.
  • Character or shape inside a responsive interface, driven by app state: rig it where the layout and state live.

A small example

A brand mark that reacts to a form field:

  • idle: rest pose
  • focus: slight lean toward the field, one bone rotation
  • invalid: a single shake on the root bone, damped
  • success: a squash-and-stretch envelope plus a small bounce

Four states, one rig, two bone rotations and an envelope. No keyframed paths, no per-state redraw, and the whole thing scales with the container because it is inside the layout.

That is the case for bones outside character animation: it turns "redraw it four times" into "rotate a lever".

The rule I would give a team

If an element needs to bend in more than one state, rig it. If it only ever translates or fades, keyframe it and move on. Bones are a multiplier on reuse, and reuse is the only reason they are worth the setup.

UX Baba writes about interaction design and the unglamorous parts of craft. Exode's bone system is part of the editor at exodeui.com.

title: Temporal Pseudo-RGB Encoding for Label-Free Detection of VEEV Infection in Human Brain Endothelial Cells
description:
arXiv:2611.21892v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Label-free detection of viral infection is central to antiviral screening and pathogen surveillance. Most deep-learning methods analyze individual frames and do not model temporal progression. We evaluate temporal pseudo-RGB encoding, which stacks three time-offset brightfield frames ($t{-}6$ h, $t{-}3$ h, $t$) as the red, green, and blue channels of a single image so that morphological change becomes color and an ImageNet-pretrained convolutional neural network (CNN) can be trained on infection trajectories without architectural modification. In human brain microvascular endothelial cells (HBMVEC) infected with Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus (VEEV) TC-83, a multi-task network predicts infected-versus-mock status and time post-infection in one forward pass. Across three experimental runs under leave-one-row-out cross-validation, with all 36 wells scored out of fold, the encoding reaches 91.6% accuracy against 87.4% for the single-frame model (paired difference $+4.2$ percentage points, 95% CI $[+2.5, +6.1]$; sign-flip $p = 3\times10^{-5}$; well-level inference, conditional on three runs). At the late-phase endpoint (40-48 h), where floating cells and debris can make conventional brightfield images difficult to interpret, the advantage widens to $+23.9$ points (95% CI $[+19.2, +28.9]$). Time post-infection is recovered on the fixed row split with MAE = 1.31 h ($R^2 = 0.975$). Among the temporal models tested the encoding has the highest mean accuracy, at a fraction of the cost of the recurrent and 3D convolutional alternatives, though only its margin over the single-frame model is resolved; the tested ViT-B/16 backbone showed no corresponding gain, so the finding is limited to convolutional backbones and this virus-cell system.

title: I used to read TV audiences live. Now I read app reviews the same way.
description:
In 2013 I worked as an applied anthropologist at a market research firm in Mexico City. One of my jobs: when a TV network premiered a telenovela, I watched the audience, not the show.

While each episode aired, I followed what people wrote on social media in real time. How they felt about the characters and the story, and how that changed from scene to scene. The network learned how people felt while it was still happening, not weeks later in a survey.

That method has a name: netnography, ethnography of online communities. Thirteen years later, now as a frontend engineer, I used it again for a UX case study on a Mexican mobile carrier. No TV this time: 55 public comments from app stores and a Facebook community.

It turned out to be the most useful research I did in the whole project. And any developer can do it this Friday afternoon.

Why it works

Surveys ask people questions. Reviews and community posts are people talking without anyone asking. Nobody writes a one-star review to be polite. They write it at the exact moment something failed, in their own words, often with details you'd never think to ask about.

That's what I learned in focus groups too: what people say when you ask them is not always what they do. Unprompted conversation gets closer to what they actually do.

How to do it, step by step

1. Pick where people already talk. App Store and Google Play reviews, public Facebook groups, Reddit, your own support tickets. Start with public reviews: they're the easiest and raise the fewest ethical questions.

2. Collect 50 to 100 recent comments. Six months back is enough. Copy them into a spreadsheet, one per row.

3. Paraphrase, don't copy. Write what each person says in your own words, without names. That protects them, and it forces you to understand the comment before you classify it.

4. Code each comment by theme. Start with no categories; let them appear as you read. After 15 or 20 comments, patterns show up. In my case: "the app hides the basics", "I paid but it doesn't work", "support never answers", "I don't trust this".

5. Count. Counting turns impressions into evidence. "Users struggle with login" is an opinion. "In 6 of 55 comments, the registration banner hid the login button" is a finding a product manager can act on.

6. Stop at saturation. When new comments stop producing new themes, you have enough. For me that happened around comment 45.

7. Go see it yourself. Every theme is a hypothesis. Open the app and try to reproduce it. When I did, the registration banner was there, asking me to register a line I had already registered.

What I found

Here's what 55 comments looked like once coded:

Theme Comments
The app hides the basics (balance, usage, login) 12
Paid or completed, but not working 8
Support: slow, bots, no human 7
Trust and security 5
Unclear plan conditions 5

The biggest theme wasn't a bug. It was information hierarchy: promotions came first, and what people opened the app to do came second. No crash report would ever show you that.

The limits (say them out loud)

  • Reviews skew negative. Happy people rarely write. Netnography shows you where it hurts, not how many people hurt.
  • It's not a replacement for talking to users. It tells you what to ask them.
  • Private groups need permission. If a community is closed, ask the admins or stay with public sources.
  • Never publish anything that identifies someone: no names, no screenshots with faces, no exact quotes that can be searched back to a person.

The real lesson

In 2013 I read audiences so a TV network could adjust a story. In 2026 I read reviews to figure out why people couldn't find their balance. The method didn't change. What changed is that now I can also fix what I find.

That's the case I'd make to any developer: you don't need a research team to start listening. You need a spreadsheet, an afternoon, and the discipline to count before you conclude.

You can read the full case study, with the redesign and prototypes, on my site: Activated doesn't mean working.

title: Can Vision-Language Models Truly Understand Images? A Benchmark Beyond Commonsense Bias
description:
arXiv:2611.22360v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved impressive performance on a wide range of vision-language tasks. However, it remains unclear whether their predictions are grounded in the visual content itself or are largely driven by statistical co-occurrence patterns and commonsense correlations learned from large-scale image-text corpora. Existing vision-language benchmarks predominantly consist of samples that conform to human commonsense, allowing models to achieve strong performance by exploiting dataset priors rather than genuinely understanding image content. To address this limitation, we present ContraSense, a systematically constructed benchmark for evaluating faithful vision-language understanding. ContraSense consists of carefully curated counter-intuitive image-text pairs that deliberately violate common expectations, substantially reducing the effectiveness of statistical biases and requiring models to rely on visual evidence for reasoning. We conduct comprehensive evaluations on a diverse set of representative open- and closed-source MLLMs. The results reveal a substantial performance gap between current MLLMs and humans: even the strongest closed-source model achieves only about 60\% accuracy, compared with 96.04\% for human participants. These findings demonstrate that current MLLMs still struggle with faithful visual understanding and highlight the need for more robust multimodal reasoning grounded in image content. The ContraSense benchmark is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/LingLin00/ContraSense.

title: Heave-Ho: Decentralized Long-Horizon Multi-Humanoid Collaboration
description:
arXiv:2611.22275v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Collaboration promises to extend humanoid capabilities beyond what individual robots can achieve. However, realizing this potential requires coordinated whole-body interactions, coherent long-horizon planning, and precise synchronization across robots. We introduce Heave-Ho, a decentralized framework for long-horizon collaborative multi-humanoid loco-manipulation. At the low level, we develop a multi-agent post-training framework that adapts a humanoid foundation tracking model to physically coupled interactions between humanoids, enabling coordinated decentralized control from local observations alone. At the high level, we train a vision-language planner and design a speech-based leader-follower coordination mechanism to synchronize decentralized execution without network communication. Trained with two identical humanoids, our system scales to teams of up to ten robots and generalizes to heterogeneous teams without retraining. To benchmark these capabilities, we introduce HH-Bench, comprising 12 tasks involving teams of 2 to 10 humanoids, including heterogeneous teams. Systematic evaluations show that Heave-Ho consistently outperforms baseline methods, while real-world experiments demonstrate robust decentralized collaboration across challenging tasks.

title: October 27, 2026
description:
AlloyDB for PostgreSQL

Announcement

The following AlloyDB AI functions and improvements are available in Preview:

  • The ai.extract function lets you extract structured data from unstructured text directly within your database queries without needing external extraction pipelines. For more information, see Extract structured data.

  • The ai.classify function lets you categorize unstructured text into predefined labels directly within your database queries. For more information, see Classify text.

  • Parameter names and signatures for AI query engine functions (ai.analyze_sentiment, ai.summarize, and ai.agg_summarize) are updated. For more information, see Model endpoint reference.

    • The prompt and prompts parameters are renamed to input and inputs in scalar and batch functions respectively.

    • An optional additional_instructions parameter is added to ai.summarize and ai.agg_summarize to provide custom instructions to guide summary formatting, length, and tone.

    • ai.agg_summarize supports multiple positional signatures, including passing optional additional instructions and specifying model IDs.

Apigee X

Feature

The Apigee API Health & Availability dashboard is now generally available in Cloud Monitoring to help you monitor the health, performance, and availability of your Apigee API proxies in real time:

  • Golden signal scorecards: track aggregate Traffic (requests per second), Error Rate (5xx), and Latency (p95) scorecards.
  • Status code and error trends: visualize the Request Rate by Status Code chart over time and identify problematic APIs using the dedicated 5xx Error Rate by Proxy and 4xx Error Rate by Proxy charts.
  • Granular filtering: filter telemetry by project_id, location, and proxy_name to troubleshoot specific regions or proxies.

For more information, see API Monitoring.

Bigtable

Feature

You can use Apache Avro schema bundles to query individual fields within Avro records stored as serialized bytes in Bigtable. You can query your Avro data using GoogleSQL for Bigtable, continuous materialized views, and logical views. This feature is in Preview.

Cloud DNS

Announcement

Starting January 5, 2027, CNAME chasing behavior will change so that Cloud DNS follows CNAME chains between public and private zones. If your private zones or response policies have overlapping domain names with public CNAME targets, queries might resolve to unintended internal IP addresses or return resolution errors.

The following table outlines the current and updated behaviors.

Source of CNAME answer Current behavior (until January 5, 2027) New behavior (starting January 5, 2027)
Cloud DNS public zone Subsequent queries search only public DNS zones and internal DNS. Private zones, forwarding zones, and response policies are ignored. Subsequent queries follow the complete VPC name resolution order: response policies, private zones, forwarding or peering zones, internal DNS, and public zones.
Cloud DNS private zone Subsequent queries search only authorized private zones. Public DNS zones are ignored. Subsequent queries follow the complete VPC name resolution order. If the target isn't found in authorized private zones, Cloud DNS queries public DNS zones.
Cloud DNS response policy zone Cloud DNS systems don't perform queries for CNAME answers received from response policy local data rules. Subsequent queries follow the complete VPC name resolution order. If the target isn't found in response policies or private zones, Cloud DNS queries public DNS zones.

Review your CNAME chasing needs before January 5, 2027. Test your DNS query paths using dig or nslookup to identify CNAME chasing scenarios.

  • Look for private-to-public CNAME chasing scenarios: Look for CNAME answers from response policies or private zones that don't match any response policy or record in a private zone. Previously, these queries resulted in a NXDOMAIN answer but after January 5, 2027, these scenarios might match a record in a public zone or continue to be NXDOMAIN responses.
  • Look for public-to-private CNAME chasing scenarios: Look for CNAME answers from public zones that don't match any record in a public zone. Previously, these CNAME chasing scenarios would have resulted in a NXDOMAIN response. After January 5, 2027, these scenarios might match a response policy or record in a private zone or continue to be NXDOMAIN responses if the private zone doesn't have the record.
  • For CNAME chasing scenarios under your control: As best practice, configure matching time-to-live (TTL) values for all records in the CNAME chain.

Announcement

Starting January 5, 2027, Cloud DNS will disable full responses to DNS queries of type ANY (QTYPE=ANY) in public authoritative zones. Instead, a single resource record will return for ANY queries, chosen from the existing resource record sets that match the query.

Standard traffic from web browsers, applications, and API traffic query specific record types directly and are therefore unaffected with no action required.

However, certain legacy scripts, automated health checkers, debugging commands (for example, dig example.com ANY), or custom third-party monitoring systems that explicitly query ANY records will receive the first available record instead of a full zone inventory. You must complete the following configuration updates before January 5, 2027:

  • Identify legacy queries: Review internal tools, deployment scripts, or third-party DNS monitoring configurations for commands or API calls that request the ANY record type. Cloud DNS logs in Cloud Logging can be helpful with this.
  • Transition to specific queries: Update the tools to query the specific, individual record types they require (for example, querying for A, AAAA, MX, or TXT records separately).
  • Retrieve full zone records: If you use ANY queries to retrieve all records in a zone, use the Cloud DNS REST API (resourceRecordSets.list), the gcloud CLI (gcloud dns record-sets list), or the Google Cloud Console instead.

Risks associated with not making these changes include the following:

  • False monitoring alarms: Automated uptime or DNS monitoring tools checking ANY responses may misinterpret the new response as a system failure and trigger false alerts.
  • Broken automation pipelines: Internal deployment or CI/CD scripts that rely on parsing a full zone dump with an ANY query will fail to retrieve the expected data payload and may crash.
  • Disrupted IT diagnostics: Network administrators running manual legacy troubleshooting commands will no longer see a quick summary of all domain records, which could delay active network incident diagnostics.

  • Connect ESXi nodes and VLAN-tagged Dynamic NICs directly to your VPC subnets without requiring private services access peering.

For more information, see VMware solution on Google Cloud overview and Compare VMware Engine models.

title: Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938): The Bug That Leaked Before Its Patch
description:
Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938): The Bug That Leaked Before Its Patch

On November 17, 2026, a security firm called Calif published a write-up titled "Write once, RCE everywhere." The bug it describes, tracked as CVE-2026-114938 and nicknamed Java4Shell, lives in java.util.Base64, a class most of us have called without a second thought. Endor Labs calls the fix four lines. The names on the affected list are Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate.

I spent the day reading the advisories and vendor write-ups so you don't have to. Some of what you will see on social media has a reproduction behind it. Some is Calif's claim with no public proof yet. I'll keep the two apart, because the difference decides how fast you need to move.

TL;DR

Question Short answer
What is it CVE-2026-114938, nicknamed Java4Shell, a heap out-of-bounds write in OpenJDK's hardware-accelerated Base64 decoder
How big is the write 62 bytes past the end of the output array, per Upwind and Endor Labs
Who is at risk HotSpot 17.0.6 and later, plus 21, 25 and 27, on x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 VBMI
Who is not ARM64, older Xeons, AMD before Zen 4, Java 8 and 11 (standard builds), and the MIME decoder
Exploitation No exploitation in the wild reported, not in CISA KEV as of November 17
Is there a fix Oracle shipped fixed builds on November 17, other vendors on their own schedules

How a Base64 string becomes a crash

Base64 decoding is boring work, so HotSpot does not do it in plain Java. Once the JIT decides the decoder is hot, it swaps the Java loop for a hand-written assembly routine that uses AVX-512 to chew through the input in wide chunks. That gives the speedup, and it also hosts the bug.

The routine has a special path for the last characters of the string. Per Upwind, a malformed string that ends in a stray = makes that tail code calculate a negative output length. A small write turns into a full 64-byte write, 62 bytes past the end of the array. Java then notices the input is invalid and throws an exception. By that point the bytes are already in memory.

Those bytes are a constant. Endor Labs says the content of the overflow is the same whatever you send. The attacker does not choose what gets written. They choose where it lands by shaping the heap.

If the bytes land in free memory, nothing happens. If they land on a live object, they destroy its header. Endor Labs puts the usual result as a SIGSEGV inside garbage collection. That is the part everyone agrees on: a remotely triggerable JVM crash.

The part people argue about

Calif says the overflow escalates much further. In their write-up, a chain of five stages corrupts an array length, uses a second array to leak heap contents, repairs object headers, grooms the heap remotely and finally writes into the JVM's code cache. Their claimed results are pre-auth RCE on default installs of Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate, and post-auth RCE on Kafka, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker.

Here is what I could and could not confirm.

  • Calif reports that they found the bug with AI help in about an hour and had a first working exploit about two hours later. That is their timeline, not an independently checked one.
  • No public proof-of-concept shell exists. Calif is withholding the product-specific exploits and published a safe reproducer only.
  • Calif itself says there is no universal exploit. Each target needs its own decoder route, writable buffer, feedback channel and heap layout.
  • Equixly, writing the same day, calls RCE unproven and calls a JVM crash the realistic outcome.

Both readings can be true at once. A crash needs no skill. Code execution needs a skilled attacker per product, but the defenders' clock is Calif's own statement that product exploits will follow.

The numbers that matter

Number What it is Source
62 Bytes written past the array for a single = tail (63 for ==) Upwind, Endor Labs
65 Shortest trigger length on Java 21, 25 and 27 Endor Labs, Equixly
129 Shortest trigger length on Java 17 Endor Labs, Equixly
9.2 CVSS 4.0 score, attributed to the researchers Qualys, Endor Labs
8.1 Oracle's CVSS 3.1 score for the November update Qualys, Endor Labs
11 Java SE fixes in Oracle's November update, all remotely exploitable without auth Endor Labs
Jan 2023 Backport of the vulnerable decoder into 17.0.6 Endor Labs
Oct 14, 2026 Fix committed under embargo Endor Labs

The sources disagree on several details. Equixly attributes the 9.2 score to South Korea's NCSC while the others attribute it to Calif, and nobody has published a CVSS vector string. Treat the score as a signal, not a measurement.

Why this one has legs

Three things make this more than a routine patch Tuesday item.

The first is the reach. This is not a library you can grep for in a lockfile. The flaw sits in the runtime itself, so dependency scanning of pom.xml or build.gradle will not surface it. Endor Labs says so directly, and that is the main reason I expect this to linger in fleets for months.

The second is that you can be vulnerable by accident of hardware. Qualys warns that a workload on an unaffected CPU can land on an affected one after a resize or an instance type change. The same container image, the same JVM flags, a different answer.

The third is the leak. Per Upwind and Endor Labs, the bug reportedly leaked before its patch was ready. The NCSC in South Korea told public institutions to inspect their Java runtimes on November 16, a day before the fix shipped.

What I would do before lunch

Start by finding out which JVM each service really runs. The java on your shell path is often not the one your service uses, especially for Jenkins, Jira, Confluence, Keycloak and Elasticsearch, which bundle their own runtime.

# The real runtime behind a running service, not the first java on PATH
for pid in $(pgrep -f '[j]ava'); do
  echo "pid $pid  $(readlink -f /proc/$pid/exe)"
  jcmd "$pid" VM.version 2>/dev/null | sed -n '2,3p'
done

# Does this host have the CPU feature at all
grep -m1 '^flags' /proc/cpuinfo | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -E '^(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)$'

Qualys says a host meets the hardware condition only when all four flags appear. If the second command prints nothing, the host is not exposed to this particular code path, though I would still patch it.

Then patch. The Oracle fixed builds named by Qualys are 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1 and 27.0.1.1, and Corretto 17.0.21.1.2. For Temurin, Zulu, Microsoft, Red Hat and your distro packages, check the vendor advisory, because I could not confirm their fixed builds today. Remember that a running JVM does not change when you replace files on disk. Rebuild images and restart processes.

If you cannot patch today, the workaround both Qualys and Upwind recommend is a JVM flag.

java -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics -jar app.jar

It switches off the fast decoder, so heavy Base64 workloads may slow down. Test before rolling it out. One warning from Upwind that I want to repeat: a variant circulating online, -XX:DisableIntrinsic=_base64_decodeBlock, stops the JVM from starting on its own and becomes a fleet-wide outage when pushed through JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS. Endor Labs lists it only together with -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions. Skip it and use the flag above.

The bottom line

I have not reproduced this myself, and I would not trust any article that claims to have run Calif's chains without Calif's code. What the public record supports today is a real, remotely triggerable memory-safety bug in the runtime that carries a vendor fix and a one-line mitigation. Whether it becomes the next Log4Shell depends on whether Calif's promised product exploits arrive before your restart window closes.

Here is the question I would put to your team today: if someone asked you to list every JVM your company runs, including the ones inside vendor appliances, how long would that take?

GDS K S · thegdsks.com · building Glincker · follow on X @thegdsks

The scariest runtime bugs are the ones your dependency scanner cannot see.

Sources: Upwind, Endor Labs, Qualys, Equixly, Calif.

title: Leveraging Segmentation Representations for Efficient Classification: A Self-Configuring Framework Based on nnU-Net
description:
arXiv:2611.22380v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We propose a self-configuring framework that extends the nnU-Net workflow to both segmentation and classification in 3D medical imaging. Building on nnU-Net's self-configuring method, the framework reuses representations learned by a segmentation model for image-level classification. Its encoder features and predicted segmentation probabilities are used by a lightweight classifier. Two information-sharing strategies are investigated. In the frozen-backbone branch, features are augmented with region-of-interest information, predicted foreground volume, and segmentation confidence. In the adaptation branch, the final encoder stage is partially fine-tuned for classification, with an auxiliary segmentation loss to preserve segmentation-related information. Additional five-fold experiments showed that more complex configurations did not consistently improve classification performance. On the public validation leaderboard, our selected framework achieved an Overall score of 0.8056. In the official FLARE 2026 Task 2 final evaluation, our framework ranked first overall, achieving the highest DSC, NSD, and AUROC across all four testing tasks, including two hidden testing tasks. Local inference measurements also remained below the challenge limits of $60 \mathrm{s}$ per case and $4 \mathrm{GB}$ GPU memory. These results demonstrate the practical value of reusing segmentation representations for classification while maintaining a simple and efficient framework.

title: Make the agent leave existing CSS Module class names alone unless the PR is a rename
description:
The bug is a misaligned icon. The diff also renames .wrap to .container, .btn to .button, and .iconLeft to .iconStart “for clarity.” Every snapshot, every test id that happened to use a class, and every overlapping PR now conflicts. The layout fix is two lines.

I’ve started telling agents to leave existing CSS Module (and BEM, and CSS-in-JS hashed) class names alone unless the ticket is a rename. A bugfix is not a vocabulary exercise.

Why the rename sneaks in

The model likes tidier names. It will “improve consistency” in any file it already opened. CSS Modules make that look safe: the name is local, TypeScript will catch broken imports. What TypeScript will not catch is a snapshot, a visual test, a documented class in a README, or a sibling branch that edited the same module.

The churn also hides the real change. Reviewers scan a 40-line class rename and miss the gap that actually fixes the icon.

This is the same discipline as “don’t clean up unrelated imports in a UI bugfix,” applied to class identifiers.

A simple naming policy

  • Bugfixes and features reuse the current class names
  • Renames are their own PR, with no behavior change
  • New classes are fine — add .iconSlot, do not rename .wrap to make room
  • Do not “align” names with a different component in passing

If the team is mid-migration from .btn to .button, point the agent at that migration branch or do the rename there, not in a visual bug ticket.

What to put in the prompt 

Do not rename existing CSS Module class names (or the imported identifiers) in this PR.
You may add a new class.
If a name is genuinely wrong, leave a comment and we will do a rename-only follow-up.
Keep the diff limited to the layout bug.

In review, if the class map moved and the computed styles barely did, send it back.

Selectors in tests are the other casualty. If a Playwright or Testing Library query used a class because no test id existed, a “clarity” rename breaks the test without changing the product. The right follow-up is a test id, in a small PR, not a rename mixed into the layout fix.

The same restraint applies to styled-component display names and CSS-in-JS keys that appear in snapshots. If the agent rewrites those while fixing gap, you will review typography instead of the icon.

Global class names in CSS Modules (:global(.legacy)) are even more dangerous to rename in passing, because they may be referenced from another package or a server-rendered shell. If the agent touches a :global selector in a layout bugfix, treat that as a crossing of the rename boundary and send the PR back.

Reject / send back

Reject

  • A drive-by rename of three or more classes in a bugfix
  • “Consistency with another file” as the reason inside a layout PR
  • A rename that forces snapshot and translation updates with no behavior change, mixed into a functional fix

Accept

  • A new class for a new slot
  • A rename-only PR, isolated and mechanical
  • The two-line layout fix that leaves the identifiers alone

title: A small Node.js fixture for incomplete streaming tool arguments
description:
AI-assisted draft prepared for the AI Relay Check account. The examples below use local fixtures.

Valid JSON can still miss a required tool argument. If a stream ends early, the same tool may never receive a complete invocation. A local fixture separates argument parsing from the backend, and it can be run before testing a paid route.

Start with a tool whose required arguments are a string named label and an integer named count. Use known values and check the results before executing any tool.

import assert from "node:assert/strict";

function readFixtureArguments(chunks, complete) {
  if (!complete) throw new Error("Incomplete tool invocation");
  const args = JSON.parse(chunks.join(""));
  if (args.label !== "sample" || args.count !== 2) {
    throw new Error("Unexpected tool arguments");
  }
  return args;
}

assert.deepEqual(readFixtureArguments(['{"label":"sample",', '"count":2}'], true),
  { label: "sample", count: 2 });
assert.throws(() => readFixtureArguments(['{"label":"sample"}'], true), /Unexpected/);
assert.throws(() => readFixtureArguments(['{"label":"sample",'], false), /Incomplete/);

In a live client, set the completion flag from the actual protocol event and associate fragments with the correct invocation ID. Then return a mock result and confirm the model continues using that result. A transport-level HTTP 200 alone cannot validate the tool workflow.

title: ARC-2: Continuous Compliance Through Delta Management
description:
arXiv:2611.21811v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: ARC 1 introduced a three-layer governance architecture for autonomous systems comprising model safety validation, cognitive certification (CRAB), and operational authorization (LEA). However, it did not address how compliance should be maintained after deployment.
  This paper introduces Delta Management, a continuous governance framework that measures deviations between a system's current operational state and its certified baseline, defined as a region rather than a fixed point. Compliance is assessed through continuous monitoring instead of static certification.
  Four extensions are proposed. First, CRAB evaluation incorporates the worst verified behavioral deviations, with isolated outliers quarantined pending confirmation to prevent unjustified restrictions. Second, a layered trigger taxonomy distinguishes hard safety violations, critical single-dimension failures, correlated multi-system degradation, and risk-weighted composite indicators, each triggering proportionate responses. Third, a graduated safe transition protocol separates withdrawal of operational authorization from physical shutdown, consistent with established safety standards and EU AI Act requirements. Fourth, environmental delta is introduced as a distinct baseline validity condition: environmental drift beyond the certified Operational Design Domain (ODD) triggers recertification or ODD revision rather than automatic authority contraction.
  Together, these extensions transform ARC from a deployment-time certification architecture into a continuous framework for monitoring, evaluating, and enforcing compliance throughout the operational lifecycle of autonomous systems. The framework addresses the continuous compliance obligations established by EU AI Act Article 72(2).

title: From Sorry to QED: Refining LLM Math Proofs via Angelic Execution
description:
arXiv:2611.22103v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can now generate Lean proof scripts that capture the high-level structure of many mathematical arguments. However, these scripts frequently fail on complex theorems: a single missing side condition or misapplied lemma can cause the prover to abort early and discard an otherwise viable proof outline. This paper presents MathEye, a framework that converts imperfect LLM-generated proof scripts into fully verified Lean proofs by combining symbolic reasoning with minimal human interaction. At the core of MathEye is angelic proof checking, an optimistic execution model that replaces failing proof fragments with placeholders while preserving the overall structure of the argument. This optimistic check produces an angelic proof that isolates the exact proof obligations that the LLM fails to discharge. Because these unresolved obligations are often logically interdependent, asking a mathematician to address every placeholder directly is inefficient. To minimize human effort, MathEye performs residual analysis over a proof dependence graph that captures symbol-level data flow in the angelic proof. By formulating obligation selection as a MaxSAT optimization problem, MathEye selects a minimal-cost set of essential obligations whose resolution suffices to complete the entire proof. MathEye presents these essential obligations to the mathematician in ordinary mathematical language and uses the mathematician's answers to automatically reconstruct the complete Lean proof. Experiments on 30 real-world benchmarks across analysis and algebra show that MathEye solves 93.3% of the problems while reducing the number of required user interactions by 55%.

title: TempQuant: Learning Adaptive Temperatures for Quantized Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.22128v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed at low precision, yet quantization can degrade their performance. We study how quantization interacts with decoding settings such as the sampling temperature and top-p by examining how it distorts the model's next-token probabilities. Measuring entropy during generation across deployed temperatures, we find that quantization warms the model on average, and that temperature matters much more for the performance of a quantized model than for its full-precision counterpart. Because quantization and temperature both shape the next-token distribution, we investigate how much the sampling settings can undo what quantization changes, through our method TempQuant, which learns the quantized model's temperature and top-p to bring its next-token probabilities closer to the full-precision model's. We learn these settings at two granularities. The first is a single global setting per requested temperature, which finds nearly the same temperatures that tuning on labeled answers would, without any labels. Model cards typically recommend sampling a quantized model with the same settings as its full-precision counterpart, while we find that different settings can substantially improve its accuracy. On 3-bit Qwen3-4B, for example, global TempQuant raises MATH accuracy from 34% under the configuration recommended for Qwen's quantized releases to 51%. The second sets the temperature and top-p for every token, motivated by our finding that tokens whose rankings flip under quantization tend to need warming, while tokens whose rankings are preserved tend to need cooling. When quantization degrades accuracy substantially, TempQuant recovers much of it, and when degradation is lighter, it still brings the quantized model's behavior closer to the full-precision model's.

title: Apache Data Lakehouse Weekly: November 11 to 18, 2026
description:
New this week: a condensed newsletter for data lakehouse and AI. Starting now, there is a shorter companion email that sums up the week in both the data lakehouse and AI worlds in one quick read. It is built for readers who want the headlines from both topics without two long issues. This longer newsletter is not going anywhere. It will keep coming every week with the same depth. To get the new condensed newsletter, subscribe at developer.dremio.com, where you can also download free books on Apache Iceberg, Apache Polaris, and the open lakehouse.

Three words sum up this week across the six projects: ship, settle, and specify. Polaris shipped 1.9.0 after a license problem forced a second release candidate. Arrow pushed out a wave of Rust, Go, and Java releases. DataFusion voted on three releases and on taking in a distributed execution library as a subproject. Then the spec work. Iceberg opened a formal vote to add materialized views to the view spec, a feature the community has debated for years. Parquet argued over page sizes, encryption, and what a statistic like distinct_count really promises. Ossie kept working on the hard questions of how a semantic model should behave when real engines read it.

A second thread ran under all of it. Several projects talked openly about how AI tools fit into open source work. Polaris moved toward an Assisted-by: line in commit messages. Iceberg C++ and Arrow debated whether automatic Copilot reviews help or just add noise. Ossie looked at an opt-in AI review bot. These are small process threads, but they show communities writing down their norms before the tools decide for them.

Apache Iceberg

Materialized views go to a vote

The biggest moment on the Iceberg list this week came on November 16. Jan Kaul called a vote to add materialized views to the Iceberg view spec, based on PR #11041. The vote followed a request for broader review that Jan sent on November 10 on behalf of the materialized view working group.

The design is simple to explain. A materialized view is an Iceberg view whose version carries a pointer to a storage table. The storage table is a normal Iceberg table that holds the precomputed results. Readers that do not understand materialized views ignore the pointer and run the view query directly. That choice matters. It means existing view consumers keep working with no changes, and engines can adopt the feature on their own schedule.

Refresh state lives in the snapshot summary of the storage table. It records which view version was materialized, when the refresh started, and the state of every source at refresh time. Tables are tracked by snapshot ID and views by version ID. With that record, any engine can decide whether the stored results are still fresh without asking the engine that wrote them.

Support on the vote thread was wide. Nevin Zheng, Marius Grama, Walaa Eldin Moustafa, Andrei Tserakhau, Benny Chow, Talat Uyarer, John Zhuge, Alex Stephen, Aastha Agrrawal, Pachu Shrinivas, and Huang-Hsiang Cheng all posted +1 votes. Alex Cruise voted +1 and raised two late questions. Walaa asked to keep the vote thread for votes and move the discussion to a new thread or the biweekly sync. Why does this matter for lakehouse teams? Materialized views have lived inside individual engines for a long time, each with its own format and refresh logic. A shared spec means one engine can build a materialized view and another can read it and check its freshness. That turns a vendor feature into a property of the table format.

V4 takes shape, one argument at a time

A cluster of threads this week all point at the next format version. The most pointed one asked whether V4 should stop writing ORC and Avro data files. Maximilian Michels called it a tough one and then said he was +1 on dropping write support for both. His reasoning was blunt. Avro and ORC are not first-class citizens today, and the community has clearly chosen Parquet. He was firm that readers must keep reading both formats for backward compatibility.

Péter Váry pushed back on a single-format future. He argued that Iceberg needs at least two live, active columnar formats to keep innovation and composability alive. His picks were Parquet for stability and Vortex for newer work, while noting the community should decide. Zheng Hu proposed a different angle: give the file format API feature flags, so a table rejects features its file format does not support. That approach decouples table format evolution from what each file format can do. Renjie Liu and Ankit Kumar also joined in.

Huaxin Gao started a deep thread on cross-engine determinism for functions in stored expressions. The problem is real. Some V4 features compute a value at write time and compute it again later, possibly in a different engine. Check constraints, stats-only fields in the index spec, and derived columns all fall into that bucket. If two engines disagree on the result of a function, the table breaks in quiet ways.

Péter proposed replacing the current boolean deterministic flag with a volatility enum based on PostgreSQL's categories: VOLATILE, STABLE, and IMMUTABLE. He proposed deprecating the old flag with a defined mapping during a transition. Andrei Tserakhau backed the enum and added a key rule: what matters is whether a value gets computed again later, not the function on its own. Check validation, virtual columns, and stats-only expressions need IMMUTABLE. A value computed once and stored as the source of truth can be VOLATILE. Alex Cruise, Matt Butrovich, and Szehon Ho also weighed in.

On the vector type, Russell Spitzer laid out the options for float16 and int8 elements. The V4 vector(E, D) type stores fixed-length numeric arrays like embeddings, with a guarantee that every non-null value has exactly D finite, non-null elements. The proposed element types are the existing int, long, float, and double. Requests for float16 and int8 keep coming. Andrei voted to leave them out of V4 and add them as separate element types in V5 if needed. He pushed back on treating float16 as a storage choice for vector(float, D), since that forces every reader to support every encoding for a small size gain. Péter added a data point: with Parquet byte-stream split encoding, his benchmark showed float16 about 10% smaller. He asked the group to judge the options from the view of AI and ML workloads, since those drive the vector type in the first place.

Daniel Weeks created a rest-v4-changes branch to collect REST catalog spec changes for V4 tables, with the first changes in PR 17642. The branch holds only OpenAPI spec edits, which keeps rebases small. Jean-Baptiste Onofré promised a review.

Neelesh Salian also opened a thread on making format version 3 the default, following the same process the community used for the V2 switch. Java and Go already support most of V3. PyIceberg cannot write V3 yet, and iceberg-rust is still working through it. Gang Wu added that iceberg-cpp supports most V3 features except the variant type. Neelesh pointed to work in iceberg-verification to add V3 reference tables so implementations can confirm they read V3 the same way.

Derived columns, such as storing Hilbert values, will move forward as a separate effort. Ruobing Wang, Aastha Agrrawal, and Ajantha Bhat signed up to help with reviews.

The Kafka Connect CDC thread got sharper. Andrei summarized the proposal: the sink's coordinator converts each commit's equality deletes into deletion vectors before committing, so the sink never commits an equality delete. CDC is opt-in, and append-only stays the default. koodin9 posted benchmarks on PR 18003. With increasing IDs, a conversion stays under 0.4 seconds. With random UUID keys on a 10,000-file table, every file gets read, and conversion takes 2 to 42 seconds depending on storage latency. Maximilian confirmed the goal is to stop writing equality deletes entirely, but doubted that ad-hoc scanning scales. Grant Nicholas raised commit contention: writing deletion vectors instead of equality deletes creates contention with other writers like compaction, which hurts low-latency CDC workloads.

This is one of the most practical debates on the list. Equality deletes are cheap to write and expensive to read. Deletion vectors flip that trade. CDC pipelines sit right on the fault line, and the community is now measuring where the costs land.

Apache Parquet

A new committer and a spirited week

The Parquet PMC welcomed Russell Spitzer as a committer, announced by Julien Le Dem. The thread collected 26 messages of congratulations, the busiest thread on the list. Russell already works across Iceberg and Parquet, and this week showed why that matters. He started one of the most important Parquet threads of the year.

Breaking DataPageV2 encryption, on purpose

Russell's thread opened with a hook: "I want to Break DataPageV2 Encryption in Parquet-Java". The problem is real. When modular encryption arrived, it treated DataPageV1 as one blob. Levels and values lived together, and encryption covered the whole thing, the same way compression did. DataPageV2 is different. Levels are not compressed with values. A V2 page holds uncompressed levels followed by compressed values. The parquet-java writer reused existing patterns and ended up writing unencrypted levels next to encrypted values. That breaks compatibility with every other Apache implementation.

Russell's position: fix it, even if it breaks older parquet-java readers. Julien Le Dem recalled that applying compression only to values in V2 was intended, since levels encoded with the RLE hybrid do not compress well and per-page compression stays optional. He agreed that encryption should cover the whole page and that this looks like an artifact of how encryption was implemented. Gidon Gershinsky, Antoine Pitrou, Prateek Gaur, and Xinli Shang all joined the 10-message thread. For anyone relying on Parquet modular encryption with V2 pages in Java, this thread is required reading.

A separate proposal from Akil Raza looked at extending Parquet Modular Encryption beyond AES to value-level protection and externally supplied cryptography. Adam Reeve asked whether finer-grained keys already cover the use case, and noted that envelope encryption with a custom KMS client already lets organizations plug in their own service.

Page sizes, statistics, and encodings

Alkis Evlogimenos proposed removing the 8KB page size recommendation from the configuration guide. His case was clear. Pages compress independently, so small pages limit compression. They also inflate page indexes: for the same data, 8KB pages mean roughly 128 times as many entries as 1MB pages. parquet-java, Arrow C++, and Arrow Rust all target 1MB pages by default. Andrew Pilloud agreed and added that most blob stores are tuned for reads of 1MB or more. At 8KB, reading and decoding page headers likely costs more than reading the data. Jigao Luo, Prateek Gaur, Russell Spitzer, and Andrew Lamb also weighed in. This is a docs change, but docs drive defaults in new writers, so it matters.

The distinct_count thread turned into a debate on intent. Adrian Garcia Badaracco proposed classifying the field as inexact. Daniel Weeks was fine with a clarification but objected to redefining it as an estimate. He felt the argument leaned on the field never being clearly specified, rather than on what it was introduced to do. Adrian asked for evidence that anyone ever understood the field as exact. Query engines use this statistic for planning, so the answer has teeth.

Encoding work moved forward too. Gunnar Morling reported that Hardwood now supports ALP encoding for floating-point data and interoperates bit-exactly with parquet-java's implementation in both directions. He described one difference: Hardwood builds each column chunk's preset from eight sample vectors spread across the whole chunk. Gang Wu, Antoine Pitrou, and Prateek Gaur also took part. Andrew Lamb responded to Prateek's FastLanes benchmark breakdown and recommended naming the proposal FASTLANES, since the term already has mindshare. Prateek worried the term is overloaded but said he was fine with it.

Neelesh Salian split the logical type out of the earlier WIRE proposal into a standalone SERIALIZED_VALUE logical type for serialized messages, following Micah's suggestion. Projection will come later as a separate proposal once one or more engines agree to use it. Matt Topol pushed back. He still does not see the use case, since these messages are usually intermediate data passed between systems, not something written raw to Parquet for storage. He suggested a struct column for the readers and writers that care. Julien Le Dem and Scott Haines also joined.

The FILE logical type kept moving. Gunnar asked what is left to merge fixtures for the FILE type, and Andrew Lamb promised to review it. In a related thread on ambiguity when inline and uri are both set, Daniel Weeks said inline values are meant to match the referenced part of the external file, and a mismatch is an error state the spec should not try to define. Stefan Grafberger summarized the agreement: writing both is useful, inline is a copy of the referenced data, and readers are not required to recheck the external data, though they can with a checksum.

Thomas Kissinger posted objections on the extensible decimal floating-point type, focused on the BID encoding. He called it overloaded and non-trivial, with almost no ecosystem support across languages. Divjot Arora shared a page-first data layout proposal that builds on the earlier non-contiguous pages idea and uses the modular footer. His core point: the row group and column chunk structure works when columns are uniform in size but breaks down when sizes or densities vary. Jiayi Wang posted updates to the modular footer Thrift definitions and asked for help auditing which existing metadata fields to keep, remove, or redesign.

Gabriel was clear about how it fits next to Ballista. Apache Ossie (Incubating)

Relationships, joins, and what consumers guess

Ossie's list ran 81 messages, and the theme was precision. The semantic model spec is now meeting real engines and BI tools, and every gap shows up as two consumers guessing differently.

The busiest thread was a GitHub discussion on how semantic engines should interpret Ossie relationship definitions, with 10 messages. Julian Hyde added a caveat to an earlier point: his answer assumed the database has referential integrity. Christian Eubank replied that referential integrity helps if the model is anchored at Orders, but BI users often expect a query grouped by state name to include states with no orders at all. Referential integrity resolves the rows that exist. It does not say what to do with the dimension rows that have no facts.

Damian Waldron raised a related gap in a thread titled "Join type is not carried by a relationship, and consumers are guessing differently". He asked whether that is settled, since consumers fill the gap in different ways, and at least one of them was losing rows. He positioned it next to Matthew Mullins's explicit relationship cardinality proposal, which covers multiplicity but not join type. Matthew agreed to drop OneToMany and keep the existing from/to semantics after JB's points on backward compatibility and the risk of silent fan-out. He also accepted PascalCase for enum values to match other enumerations. Damian also posted a thread on model expressions versus query semantics, noting that for ThoughtSpot some expressions are not model-only at all, because the query completes their meaning. He said he measured this, and it changed what their converter emits.

Core spec details

Several core spec threads tightened definitions. Julian Hyde, Harel Shein, Chris Eubank, Jakub Moravec, and Matthew Mullins discussed what Dataset.source should guarantee. Harel, from the OpenLineage technical steering committee, introduced himself and noted that OpenLineage settled on almost the same structure: dataset identity as a namespace plus a name. Julian listed the lineage questions a business user asks, like when a dataset was last updated, how often it refreshes, and which Parquet files fed a query result. The overlap with OpenLineage is a strong signal. Semantic layers and lineage systems are converging on the same identity model.

Aleksandr Kosachev opened a thread on time zones. The spec defines CURRENT_DATE without a zone, so CAST(created_at AS DATE) on a zoned timestamp returns different dates depending on each engine's session or server zone. He proposed landing the Layer 1 primitives first, starting with AT TIME ZONE, and then a model-level default zone. JB agreed with the two-step plan and argued for a fixed rule on skipped and repeated times rather than an error. His reasoning: a model passes its tests, then a query fails one night a year because of one row.

David Schwarzenbacher reported that lazy consensus passed on ROUND tie-breaking and true division for OSSIE_SQL_2026. ROUND(x, d) now rounds half away from zero, so ROUND(2.5, 0) is 3 and ROUND(-2.5, 0) is -3. Johannes Zemlin flagged a grammar issue on the precedence of ||: the merged ANTLR grammar and the sqlglot-based validator read a || b + c differently. Chris Eubank proposed allowing AGG(source.measure) in dataset-scoped metrics in PR 726. JB started lazy consensus on PR 705 to reject keys and ontology lists that name the same thing twice. He also flagged that converters disagree on which expression wins when a field has both top-level SQL and a tagged ANSI_SQL entry.

Testing, converters, and new implementers

Chris Eubank asked for PPMC approval of the DuckDB dependency for the OST test harness in Julian's PR 667, which introduces the OST file type for query conformance testing. Yufei Gu confirmed the Python DuckDB package is MIT licensed, which the ASF lists as Category A. Ayush Saxena, Joshua Klahr, and JB also voted. Related discussions proposed moving expected results to .ost tables for compliance query cases, following PR 741's change for the wide table suite.

Converter work kept growing. William Kelley proposed case-insensitive vendor and dialect names with uppercase as the canonical form, so Hex, hex, and HEX all match. Chris supported it as a light PR. Mahmoud Hassanen opened PR 202 for ClickHouse dialect support across converters for Holistics, Lightdash, OrionBelt, and more. Tony, working toward his first open source contribution, introduced Athena support for the Tableau converter. Kyoung Min Kim followed up on vendor-specific validation with PR 759.

New implementers showed up too. Emran Said, CEO of NNumbers in Brazil, introduced the company as an Ossie implementer. They wrote an Ossie model over their demo lakehouse tables against spec 0.3.0.dev0 and consume it on their governed data platform. That is the kind of independent implementation an incubating spec needs.

The ontology track and the road to a first release

The ontology working group stayed active. Ankit Tandon posted notes from the November 10 sync. Purvaja Narayanaswamy supported forming an Actions working group. Her framing is sharp: metrics and the ontology let an agent read the business, but they say nothing about the operations that change it. She asked the working group to keep a boundary already drawn in the thread. Ossie describes an operation. It does not execute or authorize it. Johnson Zhao offered an interoperability example from earlier experiments. Birendra Sahu opened PR 748 for optional knowledge references on ontology concepts and metrics, linking definitions to business rules and source evidence. A GitHub discussion asked whether Ossie should consider competency questions for ontology requirements.

On project mechanics, JB welcomed Justin Talbot as a committer. He announced release prep for 0.3.0-incubating, with final PRs for the release guide and legal checks, and a new milestone on GitHub. Yufei proposed separating release and spec versions, so validator and parser fixes ship without bumping the spec. JB preferred a complete bundle for the first release, spec plus validator plus docs, then decoupling after that. JB also proposed the first Ossie workshop and meetup, with sponsors secured and a January target in Seattle or the Bay Area. Yufei proposed opt-in AI code reviews using Orca, a bot he built that uses project context from an LLM wiki built from dev list history. He noted Polaris is already trying it.

Cross-Project Themes

Specs are where the real work happens now

Look at what took the most energy this week. Iceberg voted on materialized views and argued about determinism, vectors, and file formats for V4. Parquet debated page sizes, encryption scope, and whether a statistic is exact. Ossie worked through join types, time zones, and operator precedence. None of these are features you see in a demo. All of them decide whether two engines get the same answer from the same data.

That is the core promise of the open lakehouse. You keep one copy of your data in open formats and point any engine at it. The promise only holds if the specs are precise. Huaxin's determinism thread and Damian's join-type thread are the same problem in two projects: a value or a result that depends on which engine computed it. The communities are closing those gaps one definition at a time.

Engines shape specs more than specs shape engines

Several threads showed real engine behavior forcing spec decisions. Spark's DROP TABLE ... PURGE never asks the catalog to purge, which changes how Polaris designs soft-delete. Parquet-java's DataPageV2 writer left levels unencrypted, and now the spec's intent has to be restored by breaking old readers. iceberg-go found that a V2 to V3 upgrade brought deleted rows back. DataFusion's 56.0.0 needed a second candidate partly to unblock datafusion-python.

The takeaway for practitioners: test the paths between versions and between engines, not just the happy path inside one engine. Upgrades, mixed readers, and cross-engine reads are where the bugs live.

Release discipline is spreading

Polaris is moving toward ATR and reproducible SBOMs. Arrow Java is moving to a quarterly cadence. Arrow Rust is maintaining three older majors in parallel. Iceberg cut a 1.12.x branch to prepare a patch. DataFusion pushed three releases in a week. Ossie is preparing its first complete incubating release and debating how to split spec and release versions. Mature open source projects treat releases as a product. That is good news for anyone building on top of them.

AI tools need norms, and communities are writing them

The AI process threads deserve attention. Polaris is putting an Assisted-by: requirement in AGENTS.md. Iceberg C++ wants Copilot auto-reviews off because of false positives and noise. Arrow found that repo-level Copilot settings bill individual contributors. Ossie is weighing an opt-in review bot built on project context. Each community is deciding where AI helps and where it gets in the way. AGENTS.md showing up as the place to encode a contribution rule is worth noting too. The file is turning into a real part of project governance.

Looking Ahead

Watch the Iceberg materialized view vote close and see whether Alex Cruise's late questions lead to follow-up spec PRs. Expect more V4 movement on the volatility enum, vector element types, and the ORC and Avro question. A 1.12.1 patch release looks likely. In Polaris, watch the 1.10.0 plan for mid-December and whether ATR becomes part of it. Arrow Java 20.0.0 and Arrow Rust 60.2.0 votes should close soon. DataFusion 56.0.0 RC2 and the datafusion-distributed IP clearance are next. In Parquet, follow the DataPageV2 encryption fix and the page size recommendation change. Ossie's 0.3.0-incubating release prep and January workshop are the milestones to track there. And if you have an Iceberg or open lakehouse story to tell, the Iceberg Summit 2027 CFP closes January 10.

Keep Learning

If this newsletter helps you keep up with the open lakehouse, my books go deeper. They cover Apache Iceberg, Apache Polaris, Apache Arrow, Apache Parquet, agentic AI, and how to architect a lakehouse that works across engines. You can find the full catalog of more than 50 titles, from hands-on guides to deep architecture references, in one place.
