title: A job retry should not hide the next job in GitLab CI
description:
A pipeline view should help answer one question quickly: what is still running, waiting, or blocked? In glab ci view, a retry could make that answer incomplete. The retry showed up correctly, but an unrelated item later in the list could disappear. A downstream pipeline trigger could still exist in GitLab while the terminal view gave no sign of it.

This was a rendering bug. The fix does not change which CI jobs run or when a downstream pipeline starts. It changes which entries the CLI keeps when it builds the view.

Three entries are enough to reproduce it

The CLI collects pipeline jobs, then appends downstream pipeline triggers before building the display list. Here is the input order from the regression test, with the downstream entry representing a trigger:

ID  stage   name
 1  test    unit        original attempt
 2  test    unit        retry
 3  deploy  downstream distinct entry

Expected display: unit attempt 2, then downstream (ID 3). The old code returned only unit attempt 2. That is what made the bug easy to miss: the deduplication looked correct if you only checked which retry won.

Where the row went

The old helper did two things. It recorded the last entry for each job key, then used the first repeated key to decide how many output slots to allocate. It assumed duplicates marked the beginning of a retry-only suffix. Here, the second entry repeats test/unit, so the output gets only one slot. The helper fills that slot with attempt 2. It has already seen the downstream entry, but never gives it a slot.

That assumption might hold for one neatly ordered input. It does not hold after the caller appends another stream of entries. The first duplicate tells you that one job was seen before. It tells you nothing about the next entry.

Keep the position and replace the attempt

The proposed fix gives each distinct (stage, name) pair an output index on its first appearance. Every subsequent appearance updates the job at that index. The loop continues through the entire slice, so a new key still receives a new slot after any number of repeats.

input entry       decision                   rows after the step
test/unit #1      append at index 0          [unit #1]
test/unit #2      replace index 0            [unit #2]
deploy/downstream append at index 1          [unit #2, downstream #3]

Using a Go struct as the map key also keeps the two fields separate. The old concatenation made ("ab", "c") and ("a", "bc") both become abc. A struct key distinguishes them without a separator or escaping rule. The scan takes one pass and uses a map entry per distinct key. It preserves the first appearance order and shows the last supplied attempt for each job. This is separate from deciding the configured order of pipeline stages.

The same test failed before and passed after

To isolate the change, the focused test ran against the old helper with only the new test added, then again with the patch:

go test -count=1 -run '^Test_latestJobsKeepsJobsAfterRetry$' ./internal/commands/ci/view
Code under test Observed result
Old helper plus new test Failed. Expected two entries, got one. The missing entry was downstream (ID 3).
Patched helper plus the same test Passed. The test checks that the retry and the downstream entry both survive, in order.

The GitLab merge request includes the patch and the regression test. The full CI-view package tests and the MR pipeline passed. The MR is still open, so this is a proposed fix.

If your own display code collapses repeated events, put an unrelated item immediately after the first duplicate in the test. Then assert the exact output order as well as the winning attempt. That variation catches truncation bugs that a list ending in retries can hide.

AI-assisted writing.

title: Beyond Reconstruction: A Unified Framework for Trustworthy and Explainable EEG Artifact Removal Evaluation
description:
arXiv:2611.21781v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Deep-learning methods have achieved strong performance in EEG artifact removal, but evaluation remains dominated by reconstruction metrics such as error, correlation, and signal-to-noise ratio. Although these metrics assess similarity to clean EEG, they do not establish whether models effectively suppress artifacts, preserve neural activity, or provide reliable explanations. To address these limitations, we propose TriX-EEG, a three-level framework for trustworthy and explainable EEG artifact removal. Level 1, Signal Validity (SV), evaluates reconstruction quality and neural band-power preservation. Level 2, Removal Faithfulness (RF), assesses the removed component through artifact error and residual artifact/neural leakage. Level 3, Explanation Reliability (ER), examines model behavior through temporal alignment, causal relevance, and stability. We evaluate TriX-EEG using nine published neural denoisers across three public benchmarks derived from EEGDenoiseNet and the PhysioNet Motion Artifact Contaminated EEG Dataset, covering EOG, EMG, and motion artifacts. Results show that reconstruction metrics alone are insufficient for trustworthy denoiser assessment: RF complements it by revealing whether errors stem from residual artifact or suppressed neural activity, while ER captures distinct aspects of explanation behavior, supporting joint evaluation of three aspects within a unified framework rather than reliance on any single factor. External validation on an independent EEG/EOG dataset and the BCI Competition IV-2a motor-imagery dataset further demonstrates broadly consistent rankings under dataset shift. Higher-ranked denoisers generally preserve more task-relevant information or cause less downstream performance degradation. Overall, TriX-EEG provides a comprehensive basis for EEG denoiser assessment, encouraging models that are not only accurate but also faithful and explainable.

title: Marketplace SMS OTP API: Template Evidence for Login, Resend, Cancel and Renewal Notices
description:
A marketplace choosing an SMS OTP API for 2FA login needs resend and cancel controls, plus an auditable record for subscription renewal notices. The least complex starting point is an application-owned, versioned template registry feeding a messaging provider, with a separate record for each delivery attempt.

TL;DR: Use an SMS OTP API with verification, resend, and cancel controls for login. Keep the compliance notice and its approved template version in a separate evidence trail. Choose template ownership first; then choose the transport. A successful OTP check does not establish delivery of a renewal notice.

For a Python AI application team already integrating several backend services, Infrai is worth trying for the SMS authentication transport and notice delivery integration: a single API key and unified billing reduce credential sprawl and invoice reconciliation across services. Its public, self-describing discovery schemas offer a second useful advantage: developers can inspect request and response contracts before connecting an agent tool to a sending operation. That makes the notebook-to-prod handoff more concrete without asking a language model to invent parameters.

Infrai's consolidation model is one key, one bill: one API key covers backend services through a single REST API. For this workflow, the useful reduction is the number of credentials and billing relationships the team operates.

Infrai provides one REST API for 295 routes across 20 modules. Infrai's HTTP API needs no SDK: the template inspector below uses Python's standard library rather than adding a vendor dependency to the notebook environment. The practical benefit is a consistent interface for the template contract and the messaging adapter. Infrai's public discovery supplies request and response schemas with no key required, so the team can inspect the contract before implementing the sending adapter.

Keep evidence explicit.

The data flow is straightforward: select an approved template revision, render it with renewal data, store the rendered content alongside its inputs, submit the message, and associate the provider's message identifier with the local record. A polling worker retrieves delivery state and appends observations. Authentication follows its own challenge lifecycle; resend and cancellation controls belong there, even when both flows share a transport provider.

What should the template owner preserve before sending?

Start with an executable contract. The following Python example uses only the standard library. It retrieves Infrai's template-creation schema, then creates an in-memory SQLite ledger, records a fictional marketplace renewal notice, and rejects reuse of the same notice identifier with different content. Discovery is public; this example reads the API key from the INFRAI_API_KEY environment variable to use the same credential pattern as the eventual authenticated integration. It inspects the contract without creating a template or sending a message.

The example dates and identifiers are test fixtures. They aren't suggested notice periods or legal requirements. The sample wording is a rendering fixture, not approved compliance copy.

import hashlib
import json
import os
import sqlite3
import time
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from email.utils import parsedate_to_datetime
from urllib.error import HTTPError
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen


def template_contract():
    url = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/email.template.create"
    headers = {"Authorization": "Bearer " + os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]}
    for attempt in range(4):
        request = Request(url, headers=headers, method="GET")
        try:
            with urlopen(request, timeout=20) as response:
                if response.status != 200:
                    raise RuntimeError(f"Unexpected HTTP {response.status}")
                return json.load(response)
        except HTTPError as error:
            reason = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
            if error.code != 429 or attempt == 3:
                raise RuntimeError(f"HTTP {error.code}: {reason}") from error
            delay = 2 ** attempt
            retry_after = error.headers.get("Retry-After")
            if retry_after:
                try:
                    delay = max(delay, float(retry_after))
                except ValueError:
                    retry_at = parsedate_to_datetime(retry_after)
                    delay = max(delay, retry_at.timestamp() - time.time())
            time.sleep(delay)
    raise RuntimeError("Discovery retry budget exhausted")


contract = template_contract()
print("Template request schema:", json.dumps(contract["params"], indent=2))


db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("""
    CREATE TABLE notices (
        notice_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
        template_revision TEXT NOT NULL,
        inputs_json TEXT NOT NULL,
        rendered_body TEXT NOT NULL,
        body_sha256 TEXT NOT NULL,
        recorded_at TEXT NOT NULL
    )
""")


def record_notice(notice_id, revision, template, values):
    inputs_json = json.dumps(values, sort_keys=True)
    body = template.format_map(values)
    digest = hashlib.sha256(body.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()
    evidence = (revision, inputs_json, body, digest)
    existing = db.execute(
        """SELECT template_revision, inputs_json, rendered_body,
                  body_sha256 FROM notices WHERE notice_id = ?""",
        (notice_id,),
    ).fetchone()
    if existing is not None:
        if existing != evidence:
            raise ValueError("Notice identifier already has different evidence")
        return existing[3]
    with db:
        db.execute(
            "INSERT INTO notices VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)",
            (notice_id, *evidence, datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()),
        )
    return digest


template = (
    "{marketplace}: Your {plan} subscription renews on {renewal_date}. "
    "Review renewal settings in your seller account."
)
values = {
    "marketplace": "Example Market",
    "plan": "Seller Plus",
    "renewal_date": "2026-12-15",
}
notice_id = "seller-482-renewal-2026-12"
first = record_notice(notice_id, "renewal-en-v3", template, values)
assert record_notice(notice_id, "renewal-en-v3", template, values) == first

changed = dict(values, plan="Seller Pro")
try:
    record_notice(notice_id, "renewal-en-v3", template, changed)
except ValueError:
    print("Changed content rejected for the existing notice identifier")
else:
    raise AssertionError("Expected conflicting evidence to be rejected")

print("Recorded notices:", db.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM notices").fetchone()[0])
db.close()

This catches a small but consequential trap: rendering a retry from the latest template can change the content associated with an earlier notice. Preserving the revision and rendered body lets the worker reuse the original artifact. The digest helps detect content differences; it doesn't prove that the recipient received anything, and this mutable local database is not a tamper-evident archive.

Content identity comes first.

Production needs a persistent store, access controls, concurrency handling, and a retention policy approved for the marketplace's obligations. Resolve concurrent duplicate inserts transactionally. Keep recipients and provider identifiers in the protected delivery record, and treat provider submission as a separate operation with its own idempotency control. A local uniqueness check alone cannot prevent duplicate remote sends after a worker crashes.

That's the useful notebook boundary: a tiny executable example establishes the invariant, while production work supplies durability and delivery reconciliation.

Two template arrangements, two evidence invariants

The first viable arrangement keeps templates in the application release process. A reviewed revision and its rendering inputs produce a stored artifact, which the delivery adapter submits. Its invariant is that every notice identifier resolves to one approved rendering, even if the application deploys a newer template before a retry.

Choose this arrangement when renewal copy changes alongside product behavior, when several transports must share wording, or when an AI feature helps draft text but must not control the final send. The cost is real: your team owns the review interface, revision history, localization checks, and release discipline. For a small Python team, a versioned registry may be enough initially; building a full editing console immediately would consume time better spent evaluating delivery behavior.

The second arrangement keeps editable templates in the messaging provider's template system. The application's evidence ledger records the approved revision and preserves the rendered artifact used for the send. Its invariant is that an auditor can reconstruct the actual notice without depending on whatever the template editor displays today.

Editing ownership changes the handoff.

This can suit an operations team that owns copy outside application releases. Before choosing it, test how the candidate exposes template revisions and rendered content, and how edits interact with retries. Don't assume those semantics from the existence of a template feature. If the selected system cannot supply the evidence your process requires, preserve the approved rendering in the application or choose a different system.

For this marketplace, application-owned templates are the better default when engineers also own the renewal rules. Provider-owned editing becomes attractive when the people approving notices need an independent publishing workflow. Either arrangement still needs a delivery ledger.

Compare providers at the ownership boundary

There are several credible candidates. Twilio Verify and Vonage Verify are authentication-focused alternatives to evaluate for the login portion; Amazon SNS belongs in the messaging transport evaluation. Those are different purchasing decisions. None should inherit ownership of compliance copy merely because it can participate in message delivery.

The table defines the decision and the acceptance test for each candidate. It does not treat an untested behavior as a verified feature.

Candidate Where it belongs in this design What to establish before selecting it
Twilio Verify A specialist candidate for the OTP lifecycle Test challenge expiry, resend behavior, cancellation semantics, and required US/EU destinations against the current contract. Keep notice evidence separately.
Vonage Verify Another specialist candidate for authentication Compare its challenge workflow with the application's cooldown and recovery rules. Verify the specific channels and regional conditions the product needs.
Amazon SNS A candidate for a transport-centered implementation Establish delivery evidence, sender requirements, and where the application must own authentication and template state. Include that application work in the comparison.
Infrai A shared backend interface for SMS OTP and messaging integration Inspect discovery schemas, use its OTP verification and resend/cancel controls, and design delivery observation around polling. Preserve approved content in the chosen template registry.

The trade-off is polling latency. Infrai is not a fit for a requirement that mandates push-driven delivery processing; evaluate Twilio Verify or Vonage Verify against that requirement before selecting a specialist. Confirm the exact event semantics rather than assuming them. Infrai's events use a pull model, so polling interval and reconciliation behavior must fit the notice's operational deadline.

Test that deadline explicitly.

Regional fit also needs evidence. “US/EU” in a project ticket is not proof of sender approval, recipient reachability, or compliance with the marketplace's particular obligations. Check the intended destinations and registration requirements before connecting the production send action.

How should an SMS OTP API separate login resend and cancel from renewal notices?

The exciting part of eval-driven development here is how little model inference the critical path needs. A model can suggest draft wording during preparation; approved renewal notices can use deterministic rendering. That keeps prompt cost out of routine retries and makes content comparisons repeatable. Never ask an agent to rewrite a notice while retrying the same logical send.

Build a small evaluation matrix around concrete transitions: the first login challenge, a resend during cooldown, a resend after cooldown, a cancellation, a verification attempt after cancellation, and a renewal notice retried after its template changes. Define the application's expected result for each case, then check that the chosen provider's documented behavior supports it. These are acceptance cases, not claims that every vendor implements identical state transitions.

Cancellation deserves particular care. A cancel request is not evidence that a previously delivered message disappeared. Record the provider's actual response and observed state, and distinguish stopping a challenge from proving delivery of a notice. Likewise, an accepted send request should not be relabeled “delivered” by the application.

Acceptance isn't delivery.

For SMS OTP, put cooldowns, IP and device throttles, and per-country rules in the application. Resend is a user experience control, not an abuse policy. Keep authentication codes out of model prompts and routine logs; they add no value to evaluating renewal wording.

Email can carry the notice while SMS handles login. If email also serves as an authentication recovery channel, give the application explicit responsibility for that challenge lifecycle. Avoid coupling a compliance deadline to the assumption that both channels have identical scheduling and cancellation semantics.

Make the operational handoff reviewable

Before launch, assign a named owner to template approval and a separate owner to delivery reconciliation, even if one person fills both roles. Confirm that each notice resolves to an approved revision, preserved rendering, protected recipient record, and provider message identifier. Store state observations with their observation times. Polling provides observations at intervals; it should not be described as an instantaneous event stream.

Then rehearse the awkward cases: a worker stops after submission, an old revision is retried, a challenge is canceled while a resend is being processed, and delivery remains unresolved at the review deadline. Decide who investigates an unresolved record. Preserve uncertainty rather than manufacturing a success state.

For email, DKIM is useful context for message authentication, but it is not a substitute for delivery evidence or proof that the recipient read a notice. Keep those claims separate in the audit interface. The result should let a reviewer answer a concrete question: which approved notice did this marketplace attempt to deliver, and what evidence exists about that attempt?

Further reading

References for evaluating the separate authentication, messaging, and email-authentication boundaries:

  • Twilio Verify documentation
  • Vonage Verify documentation
  • Amazon SNS documentation
  • RFC 6376, DomainKeys Identified Mail

If the shared backend boundary fits your team, start with the first-party SMS OTP resend and cancel guide and evaluate it against your template and evidence invariants.

title: A test run that can hang forever is broken
description:
This one covers November 10 to 17. It was a week about tests that finish: my workflow kit moved onto Node's own test runner and learned to end a run that has stopped doing anything. The rest went into a new engine for my awesome lists, a deploy fix in my framework, and how my machines upgrade Node.

A hung npm test is not a slow one

workkit is my workflow kit for Claude Code: GitHub issues as the work list, labels as the pipeline, hooks that enforce the rules. Agents run most of my test suites now, usually in the background. A suite that waits on a socket that never closes does not fail. It just sits there, and so does the agent waiting on it.

Version 0.94 puts every root npm test and every workkit prove under a supervisor. It checks the run every five minutes (tests.check changes that), and each check asks two questions. Was the run's log written since the last check? Did any of its processes use the processor? Processor time counts as work once it reaches 1 percent of one core over the check.

The verdicts are simple:

  • Output or work: alive. Nothing happens.
  • Neither, two checks in a row: frozen. The evidence goes in the log, one line per process, then the run is ended with exit code 124.
  • No output for six checks, but working: a look. The run keeps going, and the call attached to it prints the evidence and exits 125.

A busy run is never ended, however long it takes. A frozen one ends with a line that says why:

detach: no output and no processor use for <N> minutes, so the run was ended (exit 124)

Inside a run there is a second bound. The runner ends a suite file's whole process group after 600 seconds (TEST_DEADLINE=<seconds> sets another) and reports one timed-out failure, so one stuck file costs a line in the report instead of the whole run.

Why it matters: "it's still running" used to be a guess. Now it is a measurement, and the two exit codes tell an agent whether to wait or to go look.

The runner is Node's now

The other half of the week was the runner itself. Since version 0.95, a workkit suite is plain node:test: describe, test, the usual hooks, and an expect with Jest's matchers, exported from workkit-core/test. Any suite runs alone with node <file>. The kit's own case engine, with its group, assertEq and selfRun, is gone.

Removing an API means migrating everyone on it, so the release shipped workkit convert. It rewrites an old-shape suite in place and maps each statement one for one: group('x') becomes describe('x', ...), assertEq(actual, wanted) becomes expect(actual).toBe(wanted). It only rewrites a file it fully understands. Cases made in a loop, a whole-file skip or a setup line between cases leave the file byte for byte, with one line saying where and why:

converted <path> (<n> cases)
left <path>:<line> <why>

A file already on Node's functions is left alone, so a second run changes nothing. My own machine-setup repo moved over the same week.

The next release built on that base: --filter=<text> runs only the cases whose full name, describe path included, holds the text, and a bare run at a monorepo root also runs each workspace member's own npm test.

Why it matters: Node's runner is the one every JavaScript developer can already read. The kit stops maintaining a test framework and keeps only the parts that are its job: finding suites, bounding them, and recording proof.

24 copies of the same bots, now one engine

I maintain 24 public awesome lists. Each one had its own copy of the same three jobs: a pull request check that judges a new entry, a weekly sweep for dead links and archived repos, and a daily sync of the shared text. Each copy had its own scripts and tests. A fix meant 24 commits.

awesome-kit is new this week, and it holds that code once. A list now carries three short workflow files, each calling the kit's composite action with one command:

jobs:
  sweep:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: ianwieds/awesome-kit@v2
        with:
          command: sweep

GitHub fetches the kit at the tag the list names, so a kit release reaches every list without a commit to any of them. Moving a list onto it deleted 1,628 lines from each one, about 39,000 lines across all 24.

The 2.0 release added awesome-kit setup. Run in a fresh repo, it scaffolds every missing file a list needs, writes the three workflows, runs sync, and sets the repo's description and topics through gh. It never overwrites a file the list owns, and since 2.0.1 it fails before any write when the config names a different repo than origin.

Two details I like. The pull request check runs on pull_request_target, so it can comment on a fork's PR, but it checks out only the base branch and reads the head README as data, never code. And the daily job keeps one empty commit on a maintenance branch, so GitHub never pauses the Monday sweep after 60 quiet days.

Why it matters: a new list starts with one command, and a fix reaches every list at its next run.

Deploys that stop growing the repo

omega is my framework for shipping a website, backend, desktop app and browser extension from one project. Each deploy pushes a snapshot to a deploy ref, and every snapshot chained on the one before, so the mirror grew by a full copy per deploy.

A change now on main (not in a release yet) re-roots that chain on GitHub's side before each deploy. Through the git data API, the deploy ref's tip becomes a parentless copy of its own tree, the push waits until the ref reads that root, and the new snapshot chains on it. The ref then holds one root, the latest snapshot, and any admin publish since. Nothing older.

Why it matters: a deploy mirror should cost the same on deploy 500 as on deploy 5.

Node upgrades that cannot strand a terminal

One private story, from the scripts that set up my machines. They used to move the default Node to the newest release as soon as it installed. If a global package then failed to install, every new terminal opened on a Node with missing tools.

Now a new release becomes the default only once its global packages are in. A failed install leaves new terminals on the release that worked. Globals install only when missing or behind, so the package firewall I route npm through keeps its 133 MB binary between runs.

Why it matters: an upgrade is stage first, then flip the pointer. Flip it first and a half-finished upgrade is the default.

Next week I want the supervisor's two exit codes wired into how my agents react to a stuck run. What does your test runner do when a test never returns? Comments are open.

title: Scaling Laws for Vision-Language Fusion
description:
arXiv:2611.22351v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have emerged as central foundation models combining multimodal perception with text comprehension. While VLMs are traditionally built via late fusion by continued pre-training an off-the-shelf language model on multimodal (image-text) data, mixing modalities from the start of pre-training (early fusion) has recently gained traction. However, the fundamental trade-offs between these paradigms remain poorly understood, resulting in expensive and heuristic-driven training recipes. In this paper, we systematically analyze the learning dynamics of these multimodal pre-training processes, showing that validation losses during vision-language fusion can be modeled by separating the base learning trajectory, where different data types contribute at distinct rates, from a distribution shift driven by the competition between modalities. We derive a scaling law that unifiedly describes these dynamics, enabling accurate loss predictions across mixture ratios, training steps, and model sizes. Crucially, our law characterizes the trade-off between early and late fusion: under a fixed data budget, early fusion preserves text performance while late fusion favors vision performance, yielding a trade-off that increasingly tilts toward early fusion as model size scales. Extensive experiments confirm that our scaling law reliably captures multimodal learning dynamics and governs fusion decisions.

title: Localizing Agri-tech: Building a Multilingual Next.js App for Rural India
description:
Localizing Agri-tech: Building a Multilingual Next.js App for Rural India

If you build an app for a farmer in Nashik or a trader in Haveri using standard English UI patterns, you’ve already lost. In the Indian agri-tech landscape, English isn't just a barrier; it’s a trust-killer. When we started building KhetiSetu, we knew that supporting Hindi, Marathi, and Kannada wasn't a "nice-to-have" feature—it was the core product requirement.

The challenge with multilingual apps in the Indian context isn't just swapping strings. It’s about handling varying script densities, managing "Hinglish" terminology that farmers actually use, and ensuring that a low-end Android device on a 3G connection doesn't choke on massive translation bundles.

Here is how we architected our Next.js App Router to handle high-performance localization across three major Indian languages.

The Architecture: Middleware-based Routing

We opted for a sub-path routing strategy (e.g., /hi/mandi, /kn/mandi). This is superior to cookie-only localization because it allows farmers to share links via WhatsApp that preserve the language context. If a farmer in Karnataka shares a crop listing with a peer, the recipient should see it in Kannada immediately.

In Next.js, we leverage the middleware.ts to intercept requests and redirect users based on their preferred language or geographic IP if no locale is present.

// middleware.ts
import { NextResponse } from 'next/server';
import type { NextRequest } from 'next/server';
import { match as matchLocale } from '@formatjs/intl-localematcher';
import Negotiator from 'negotiator';

const locales = ['en', 'hi', 'mr', 'kn'];
const defaultLocale = 'hi';

function getLocale(request: NextRequest): string {
  const negotiatorHeaders: Record<string, string> = {};
  request.headers.forEach((value, key) => (negotiatorHeaders[key] = value));

  const languages = new Negotiator({ headers: negotiatorHeaders }).languages();
  return matchLocale(languages, locales, defaultLocale);
}

export function middleware(request: NextRequest) {
  const pathname = request.nextUrl.pathname;
  const pathnameIsMissingLocale = locales.every(
    (locale) => !pathname.startsWith(`/${locale}/`) && pathname !== `/${locale}`
  );

  if (pathnameIsMissingLocale) {
    const locale = getLocale(request);
    return NextResponse.redirect(
      new URL(`/${locale}${pathname.startsWith('/') ? '' : '/'}${pathname}`, request.url)
    );
  }
}

export const config = {
  matcher: ['/((?!api|_next/static|_next/image|favicon.ico).*)'],
};

Solving the "Dictionary Debt"

In a marketplace like KhetiSetu, content is dynamic. We have static UI elements (buttons, labels) and dynamic data (crop names, variety names).

For static UI, we use a dictionary pattern. Instead of a heavy library that loads everything on the client, we fetch only the necessary JSON on the server side using the [locale] layout segment.

The Directory Structure 

app/
  [locale]/
    layout.tsx
    page.tsx
    mandi/
      page.tsx
dictionaries/
  en.json
  hi.json
  mr.json
  kn.json

We load these dictionaries using a simple asynchronous getter. This ensures that the Hindi translations aren't being sent to a user viewing the app in Kannada, keeping the payload small for users on spotty rural networks.

Language Script Avg. Word Length (Relative) Line Height Adjustment
English Latin 1.0x Standard
Hindi Devanagari 1.2x +15% for Matras
Marathi Devanagari 1.2x +15% for Matras
Kannada Kannada 1.1x +20% for Ottu-aksharas

The "Vernacular-First" UI Challenge

One of the biggest mistakes engineers make is assuming that a 16px font size works across all scripts. Devanagari (Hindi/Marathi) and Kannada scripts have complex "matras" (diacritics) and "ottu-aksharas" (stacked consonants).

If you use a standard line-height: 1.2, the top and bottom of the Kannada characters will often get clipped on mobile browsers. We had to implement script-specific CSS variables to handle this.

/* globals.css */
:lang(hi), :lang(mr) {
  --base-font-size: 17px;
  --base-line-height: 1.6;
}

:lang(kn) {
  --base-font-size: 16px;
  --base-line-height: 1.8;
}

.body-text {
  font-size: var(--base-font-size);
  line-height: var(--base-line-height);
}

Furthermore, "Translation" is often the wrong word. We focus on "Transcreation." For example, the word "Submit" doesn't have a direct, natural-sounding equivalent in a rural context. In Hindi, we use "आगे बढ़ें" (Move forward) or "जमा करें" (Deposit/Submit), depending on the action. Using overly formal Sanskritized Hindi makes the app feel like a government form rather than a tool for the community.

Handling Dynamic Data and SEO

For an agri-tech marketplace, SEO is vital. If a farmer searches for "सोयाबीन भाव" (Soybean price) in Marathi, we need our Marathi-specific pages to rank.

Next.js makes this easier with generateMetadata. We ensure that each page includes hreflang tags, telling Google that the /hi/, /mr/, and /kn/ versions of a page are equivalents.

export async function generateMetadata({ params: { locale } }) {
  const baseUrl = 'https://khetisetu.com';
  return {
    alternates: {
      canonical: `${baseUrl}/${locale}`,
      languages: {
        'hi-IN': `${baseUrl}/hi`,
        'mr-IN': `${baseUrl}/mr`,
        'kn-IN': `${baseUrl}/kn`,
      },
    },
  };
}

Performance: The 2-Second Rule

Farmers are often using $100-150 Android phones. These devices have limited CPU power to parse large JavaScript bundles. By using Next.js Server Components, we move the localization logic—the heavy lifting of mapping keys to strings—to the server.

The client receives the final HTML with the correct Hindi or Kannada strings already rendered. There is no "flash of un-localized text" (FOUT) where the user sees "SUBMIT_BUTTON" for half a second before it turns into "जमा करें".

Conclusion: Engineering for Trust

Building for the Indian agricultural sector requires a shift in mindset. You aren't just writing code; you're building a bridge across a digital divide. By utilizing Next.js's middleware and server-side rendering, we've managed to provide a seamless experience for Hindi, Marathi, and Kannada speakers on KhetiSetu without sacrificing performance.

Localization in agri-tech isn't about translating words; it's about respecting the user's language enough to make the technology invisible. When a farmer sees their local Mandi prices in their own script, the barrier to entry vanishes. And in the world of Indian agriculture, that is the ultimate engineering goal.

title: Every Camera Grows Up: Camera-Height Regression in Interactive Video World Models
description:
arXiv:2611.21782v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Interactive video world models serve as simulators for embodied agents: from a starting image and an action trajectory, they generate the views the agent would see. The starting image fixes how high the camera is, for example 0.15 m for a floor robot or 2.2 m for an overhead camera, and a faithful simulator must keep this height as the camera moves. We show that six recent open-weight models fail to do so: as motion replaces the starting view with generated content, they move the camera toward human eye level, a failure we call camera-height regression. Our benchmark, EyeHeight, pairs six rendered elevations (0.15 m to 2.2 m) and four calibrated real-world rig heights with scale-free multi-view height estimation. All six models lose their initial height during a $180^\circ$ turn-and-walk rollout: initialized at 0.15 m, only 0-20% of clips end within $1.3\times$ of the starting height as inferred viewpoints converge to human heights of 1.1 m to 1.5 m, whereas ground-truth renders remain within a few percent. In Matrix-Game models, homography-tracked floor motion stays consistent with constant elevation during rotation even as newly outpainted room geometry yields a higher reconstructed viewpoint. Regression grows with rotation angle, begins while the start frame remains in context, and largely reverses in SANA-WM when a $360^\circ$ turn restores the initial view. We trace this pull to human-centric video priors in which floor-level views are nearly absent: in SANA-WM, textual height cues and dense floor-disparity maps do not prevent it, whereas classifier-free text guidance during the first half of denoising strengthens it. Combining unguided sampling with height-balanced fine-tuning recovers more retention but costs 5 MUSIQ points, a loss fixed during those same early steps. Viewpoint drift alone shifts the paths predicted by visual navigation policies.

title: Knowing Which, Not How Much: Language Models Order Party Positions They Cannot Place
description:
arXiv:2611.21878v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Language models are increasingly asked where real actors stand: what a party's platform prioritises, what an institution has committed to. Such judgments are gradable, carrying both an order and a magnitude. Nearly every benchmark that tests them asks about one entity at a time, then reads that score as the model's knowledge of the domain. Order and magnitude, however, need not be acquired together. Text about social entities carries far more comparison than measurement, so a model may hold a dependable ordering with no anchored scale beneath it. We ask whether a model can place a documented social position on a scale or only order the actors it compares, and what that means for how such knowledge is measured. We test this on party positions in Japan and South Korea, where the Comparative Manifesto Project's coded data supplies a rare external answer key. Asked to order four parties, models beat the strongest fixed-answer baseline by more than a factor of two; asked to place one party on the same scale, they fall below it. The ordering survives inside those failed placements, and supplying the coded values lifts placement to near ceiling. Comparative and absolute questions about the same fact therefore measure different things here, and for party issue salience a benchmark built from one cannot speak for the other.

title: Why I Chose Node.js Caching for SaaS Export Signed URLs: Rate-Limit Control
description:
Short answer: For a Node.js SaaS export pipeline, cache still-valid signed URLs, persist the export job and object key, and use exponential backoff with idempotent retries around presign calls; object storage should deliver the bytes directly.

File exports are a storage problem and a request-shaping problem. A presign endpoint should not run on every export-page refresh. My default is to persist the export job and object key, cache one still-valid signed URL for a short window, then retry with exponential backoff when the presign call is rate-limited.

That is the whole fix in one sentence. Keep the app in charge of access decisions; let storage deliver the finished object.

Infrai is one option for that presign boundary, using one key and one bill across backend capabilities while its public discovery surface describes request and response schemas with runnable examples, so wiring the capability does not require learning a new SDK first.

What changes between a refresh storm and a controlled download?

Picture the request path as a small diagram in words: browser asks for an export, API checks the export record, API reuses a cached URL or signs once, and the browser downloads directly from the bucket. In the failure mode, every refresh repeats the signing step, several workers retry immediately, and the rate limiter sees a burst for the same object.

I once debugged a similar shape with a counter rather than a dashboard: 12 refreshes in a minute became 12 signing calls for one key. The useful number was not download bandwidth. It was duplicate presign work. A short cache window and a stable export record removed that multiplication.

The record needs an application-owned idempotency key, such as accountId:exportId. Store the object key, job state, and the signed URL expiration timestamp. If a user requests the same export again, return the existing job while it is valid. If the URL is near expiry, sign a replacement once and update the record under a database lock or queue. In a busy SaaS tenant, that coordination also has to cover a worker finishing at the same moment that a browser refresh arrives: the winner writes the URL and expiry, while the loser rereads the record instead of issuing a second presign call. This is where a tiny mutex or transactional compare-and-set earns its keep, because retrying a duplicate signing request can make a rate-limit incident look like a storage outage even when downloads themselves are healthy.

The catch is that access control and delivery simplicity pull in different directions. A long-lived public URL is easy to share, but this storage setup does not provide a public-read ACL or a permanent public URL. Keep the link private and short-lived when the export contains account data.

How should Node.js handle presign rate limits, caching, and retries?

Here is a minimal TypeScript sketch. It uses one storage route, an explicit method, bearer authentication, a client idempotency key, and Retry-After when the service supplies it. The response body is checked instead of assuming a 200.

type PresignResult = { url: string; expires_at?: string };

const baseUrl = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";
const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

async function presign(bucket: string, key: string, idempotencyKey: string): Promise<PresignResult> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 5; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(
      `${baseUrl}/storage/object/presign/${encodeURIComponent(bucket)}/${encodeURIComponent(key)}`,
      {
        method: "POST",
        headers: {
          Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
          "Content-Type": "application/json",
          "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKey,
        },
        body: JSON.stringify({}),
      },
    );

    if (response.ok) return (await response.json()) as PresignResult;

    const body = await response.text();
    if (response.status !== 429 || attempt === 4) {
      throw new Error(`presign failed (${response.status}): ${body}`);
    }

    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
    const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter) && retryAfter > 0
      ? retryAfter * 1000
      : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
  }
  throw new Error("unreachable");
}

In production, put the result in Redis or your database with an expiry comfortably before the signed URL expires. Add a per-export mutex so two concurrent requests do not both discover a cache miss and sign twice. The retry loop is for transient pressure, not a substitute for that coordination.

Do not use the trial balance for persistent writes; the storage facts mark that balance as restricted. Also watch the bucket rather than guessing. Export files accumulate quietly, and lifecycle cleanup has a one-day minimum expiration, so hourly cleanup is not an option here.

Which storage choice fits a private export pipeline?

The table is intentionally about boundaries, not a winner badge. Verify current regional, retention, and deletion terms with the provider before committing regulated data.

Option Strength in this workflow Boundary to check
Amazon S3 Mature object storage and presigned-download pattern You own policy, region selection, lifecycle rules, and the number of SDKs and credentials in the app
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible object storage option for teams already using Cloudflare Confirm the regions, retention controls, and egress assumptions that fit your users
Azure Blob Storage Natural fit when the rest of the SaaS runs on Azure identity and regions Confirm equivalent signed-link, deletion, and processor-contract details
Infrai storage One REST API with a public discovery surface and runnable examples, so a Node.js service can inspect a capability before wiring it No public URLs, object versioning, object lock, cross-region replication, or self-service CORS route; lifecycle expiry is at least one day

I recommend trying Infrai for the presign step when your team values a self-describing API and wants one authenticated surface across backend capabilities. Discovery exposes request and response schemas plus runnable examples, and the same key and conventions can reduce integration bookkeeping around the export service. That does not move your processor boundary: the object still lives with the selected storage vendor, and your legal and regional requirements remain yours to verify.

Stick with direct S3, R2, or Blob APIs when you need provider-specific replication, WORM-style retention, public hosting, or browser upload CORS that you must configure yourself. This gateway is not suitable when an accidental overwrite must be recoverable through versioning or when an hourly lifecycle policy is mandatory. Your mileage may vary by jurisdiction; I am not sure a generic API layer can satisfy a contract that names a particular processor or region, so get that answer in writing.

What should you measure after the fix?

Start with four counters: presign requests, 429 responses, cache-hit rate, and exports requested per job id. Add object count and bucket usage so cleanup is visible. A healthy trace should show many page views leading to one presign call, followed by direct downloads.

When a job is complete, retain its object key and status long enough for the product policy, then delete the object and record together. The storage lifecycle route can help with the retention floor, but application deletion is still the clear path for an account-erasure request. Keep logs free of signed URLs; log the export id, key hash, status, latency, and request id instead.

The practical rule is simple: cache the permissioned link, not the permission decision. Re-check ownership in your API, reuse the signed URL only inside its validity window, and make retries boring.

Further reading

  • Capability index
  • Storage discovery example
  • OWASP File Upload Cheat Sheet
  • AWS EFS managed file system
  • Amazon S3 presigned URLs
  • Cloudflare R2 presigned URLs
  • Azure Blob shared access signatures
  • Node.js fetch API

For the storage presign schema and a runnable starting point, see the storage capability index.

title: From Ideal to Real: Integrating Language Models into Smart Home for Human-Centric IoT Safety and Security Fuzzing
description:
arXiv:2611.22457v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Integrating IoT devices into household systems offers enhanced control over living environments. However, as these devices become pervasive in critical sectors such as healthcare, transportation, and home automation, they expose inter-rule vulnerabilities that may lead to privacy breaches, data theft, and physical harm. Traditional fuzz testing methods, which often operate in simulated environments assuming ideal human decisions, fail to account for the complexities of human interactions that can influence device operations in smart homes, potentially leading to unforeseen consequences. To reveal the impact of real human decisions and discover unexpected inter-rule vulnerabilities, we introduce an enhanced version of IoT Fuzz for smart homes by integrating large language models to emulate human decision-making processes. Our novel approach adds a layer of realism and unpredictability to the testing environment, more accurately capturing the diverse and dynamic nature of human interactions in smart home settings.

title: RTLReviewBench: LLM Hardware Reviewers Rarely Miss Bugs but Routinely Reject Correct RTL
description:
arXiv:2611.21678v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Hardware teams increasingly ask large language models (LLMs) to review register-transfer level (RTL) code, yet it is unclear whether a model can tell a correct module from a buggy one without simulating it. We introduce RTLReviewBench, a benchmark of 114 matched pairs of buggy and correct Verilog modules. Each pair shares one specification, most buggy modules are real failures of LLM code generators, and every label is confirmed by simulation. Evaluating 12 commercial and open-weight models, we find a consistent asymmetry: reviewers rarely accept buggy code but often reject correct code, producing more than five false rejections for every missed bug. Synthetic mutants hide part of the problem: on the same designs, models miss far fewer injected bugs than real ones. Asking a model to reason before it commits to a verdict sharply reduces false rejections for weaker reviewers, and a controlled ablation shows that where the reasoning appears in the output matters more than the instruction to reason, whereas sampling and majority voting do not help. A blinded audit further shows that some correct "buggy" verdicts rest on false technical claims. We release the benchmark, a harder split for future models, all model responses, and the evaluation code at https://github.com/yasirmahmud/RTLReviewBench

title: BQ-LoRA: Binary-Quantized Low-Rank Adapters as Implicit Regularizers for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
description:
arXiv:2611.22334v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning of quantized large language models is dominated by QLoRA, which combines 4-bit weight quantization with FP16 low-rank adapters. We ask whether the FP16 adapter precision is necessary. Replacing it with a single binary bit per adapter parameter, combined with a learned per-layer scale $s$ and a Scaled Straight-Through Estimator, reduces adapter storage by 13-16x. We introduce two variants -- NormScale, which binarizes under a norm-preserving scale with a clipped STE, and LearnThresh, which makes the binarization threshold learnable -- unified under a framework we call BQ-LoRA. Our main theoretical contribution is a tight characterization of the BQ-LoRA hypothesis class: it has bounded entrywise norm, a typical-set spectral norm bound that is $\Theta(r)$ times sharper than the worst case, a full-rank, near-isotropic update, and consequently a Rademacher complexity that yields an explicit $\tilde{O}(s_{\max}\alpha\sqrt{d_{out}/(rn)})$ generalization bound. FP16 LoRA has no comparable a priori norm or isotropy control. On Qwen2.5 (1.5B-72B), BQ-LoRA exceeds QLoRA's benchmark averages at every scale by 0.8-3.5 points; on LLaMA-2 (7B/70B) it remains competitive at the same storage reduction but does not uniformly lead the strongest FP16-adapter baselines (LoftQ at 7B, QLoRA at 70B). On Qwen2.5-7B the binary adapter preserves the 4-bit base WikiText-2 PPL within 0.06 (9.86 vs. 9.80) while QLoRA worsens it by 0.59. The reduction applies to inference-time adapter storage and serving; training memory matches QLoRA and step time rises by under 4%. We translate the storage saving into a deployment study, BQ-SGMV, by extending Punica's SGMV kernel with a binary inner-product primitive: the same A100-80GB holds 15.6x more adapters in HBM, and our research prototype eliminates cache misses under a skewed synthetic workload.

title: ReMoE: An Interpretable Mixture-of-Experts Framework for Human Mobility Recovery Forecasting Across Disasters
description:
arXiv:2611.22133v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Human mobility often declines sharply following disasters and subsequently exhibits complex recovery dynamics. Effective forecasting of this recovery is critical for timely assessment and resource allocation. However, existing approaches are often developed for individual events and operate as black boxes, limiting their transferability and interpretability beyond the events they were trained on. Recent studies have identified recurring post-disaster mobility recovery types across disasters, suggesting that recovery knowledge may be transferable. Motivated by this, we propose ReMoE, an interpretable mixture-of-experts framework for cross-disaster mobility recovery forecasting. ReMoE uses a feature-guided router to adaptively combine specialized experts that learn these heterogeneous yet reusable recovery types, producing a region-specific recovery pattern. It further refines this pattern through residual correction informed by forecasts of future hazard conditions. We evaluate ReMoE on a large-scale mobility dataset covering 18 disaster events spanning hurricanes, floods, winter storms, and wildfires. ReMoE is competitive in-distribution and achieves the strongest performance on unseen events and hazard types, with larger gains under greater distribution shifts. Further analyses show that ReMoE yields interpretable learning outcomes and maintains robust performance under uncertainty. Broadly, ReMoE offers a transferable and traceable forecaster that can support anticipatory post-disaster assessment.

title: Juice 1.0 Is Here — Building UI Without Fighting Your Markup
description:
After years of development, experimentation, architectural decisions, and more CSS than I care to admit, Juice has officially reached v1.0.0.

And I couldn't be more excited to finally say that.

For those who haven't followed my previous articles, Juice is an open-source, attribute-first CSS and UI library I've been developing as part of CitrusWorx's WebEngine ecosystem.

It started with a relatively simple question:

What if building interfaces felt more like describing what you wanted, rather than constantly wrestling with how to style it?

That question eventually became Juice.

Today, I'm excited to share its first major release.

The Problem I Wanted to Solve

Modern frontend development is incredibly powerful.

We have mature frameworks, sophisticated design systems, utility-first CSS libraries, component ecosystems, and tooling that would have seemed unimaginable a decade ago.

But somewhere along the way, building a relatively simple interface started requiring an increasingly complicated collection of abstractions.

Sometimes you need a component library.

Sometimes you need a CSS framework.

Sometimes you need a JavaScript framework just to make everything work together.

And sometimes, all you really want is a card with a heading, some content, and a button.

I kept asking myself whether we could make the everyday parts of UI development simpler without sacrificing the flexibility needed for more sophisticated applications.

I didn't want to reinvent CSS.

I wanted to rethink how we interact with it.

Enter Juice: Attribute-First UI Development

Juice takes a different approach to expressing layout and presentation.

Instead of relying entirely on lengthy class lists or custom component abstractions, Juice allows developers to describe their interfaces directly through HTML attributes.

For example, here's a conceptual illustration of the attribute-first approach:

<div stack gap="4">
  <div card padding="4">
    <h2>Welcome to Juice</h2>
    <p>
      Build interfaces with expressive markup.
    </p>
  </div>
</div>

The idea is straightforward:

Your markup describes the structure. Your theme defines the visual identity. Juice connects the two.

Attributes such as stack, row, grid, gap, padding, card, and surface make layout intentions visible where the interface is actually being constructed.

This isn't about replacing every CSS rule with an attribute.

It's about providing a more expressive foundation for the things developers do repeatedly.

More Than Another CSS Framework

One of the most important architectural decisions behind Juice was making it useful independently of WebEngine.

Although Juice is being developed as part of the larger CitrusWorx ecosystem, it isn't intended to require developers to adopt that entire ecosystem.

You should be able to use Juice in a standalone project, integrate it into an existing application, or combine it with the frontend technologies you already enjoy.

That independence matters to me.

I don't believe developers should have to replace their entire toolchain just to benefit from one useful library.

Juice is designed around a CSS-first foundation, with JavaScript capabilities available where they make sense.

Its broader architecture also brings together design tokens, themes, components, and optional runtime behavior.

The goal is to provide a consistent UI foundation without forcing every application into the same architecture.

Why Themes Matter

One of the principles driving Juice is the separation of structure and identity.

A layout shouldn't have to be completely rewritten just because an application needs a different visual personality.

The same structural building blocks should be reusable across projects while themes control how those building blocks look and feel.

For CitrusWorx, this is especially important.

WebEngine is intended to support a growing ecosystem of applications and developer tools.

Having a shared visual foundation means we can establish consistency without requiring every application to look identical.

That's the balance I'm working toward with Juice.

What v1.0.0 Actually Means

Reaching version 1.0 isn't the same as declaring a project finished.

If anything, it means accepting a new level of responsibility for the foundation you've created.

During the 0.x development cycle, I spent a considerable amount of time exploring the boundaries of what Juice should become.

There were questions about how attributes should behave, how themes should work, how much JavaScript belongs in a CSS-first library, and how to organize the different pieces into something developers can reasonably understand.

There was also the temptation to keep adding features.

Another component.

Another runtime.

Another abstraction.

Another improvement before calling it ready.

Eventually, though, a library needs to stop being an endless experiment and start becoming something people can actually build with.

Juice v1.0.0 represents that transition.

It's a commitment to a public foundation that developers can begin adopting, testing, and helping improve.

It doesn't mean every idea on the roadmap has been implemented.

It means the project has reached its first major milestone, and future improvements can build on that foundation.

Juice and the Bigger WebEngine Picture

If you've followed my Road to WebEngine series, you know Juice isn't being developed in isolation.

It's one part of a much larger effort at CitrusWorx to build an ecosystem of modular, interoperable developer technologies.

Another major part of that ecosystem is Sig.js, our JavaScript library for building reactive interfaces.

With Sig.js and Juice both reaching their first major releases, two important pieces of the WebEngine vision are beginning to come together.

Sig.js addresses how interfaces are constructed and updated.

Juice addresses how those interfaces are structured and presented.

They have different responsibilities, and that's intentional.

I want developers to be able to adopt individual pieces of WebEngine without being forced into an all-or-nothing framework decision.

The broader vision is ambitious, but it's being built one library, one package, and one release at a time.

Getting Started

Juice v1.0.0 is available on npm.

npm install @citrusworx/juiceui@1.0.0

You can explore the package and source code here:

npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/@citrusworx/juiceui/v/1.0.0

GitHub: https://github.com/citrusworx/webengine/tree/master/libraries/juice

Whether you're interested in attribute-driven styling, design systems, frontend architecture, or simply exploring a different approach to building interfaces, I'd love for you to take a look.

What's Next?

Reaching v1.0.0 doesn't mean development slows down.

It means the focus changes.

Moving forward, I want to spend more time improving the developer experience, refining documentation, expanding practical examples, addressing issues that emerge from real-world usage, and continuing to evolve the library without losing sight of its original purpose.

I also want to explore how Juice can make UI development more accessible to people who aren't necessarily frontend specialists.

Because I believe good developer tools should make creativity easier, not introduce unnecessary barriers.

A Personal Milestone

Building something like Juice takes a surprising amount of persistence.

There are days when everything comes together beautifully.

And there are days when you find yourself questioning an architectural decision you made three months earlier.

But that's part of engineering.

You experiment.

You discover limitations.

You rethink assumptions.

You improve the design.

And eventually, you ship.

For me, Juice reaching v1.0.0 is another step toward turning CitrusWorx from a collection of ideas and experiments into a real ecosystem of software that other developers can use.

There's still an enormous amount of work ahead.

But today, I'm celebrating this milestone.

Juice 1.0 is here.

If you try it, I'd genuinely appreciate your feedback. Tell me what works, what doesn't, and what you think an attribute-first UI library should do differently.

Thanks for following along on the Road to WebEngine.

We're just getting started.

Built with curiosity, persistence, and a whole lot of CSS.

title: From Repositories to Training Environments: Scaling Long-Horizon Coding Agents with Environment Evolution Loop
description:
arXiv:2611.21152v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Training coding agents for long-horizon tasks requires environments with verifiable feedback. Existing pipelines often follow a linear process that ends with validation, establishing usability but providing little guidance on improving training value. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) often requires model rollouts or model training followed by downstream evaluation, with costs and feedback delays amplified on long-horizon tasks. How can we use timely, reliable proxy signals to improve training value and synthesize environments at scale? We present RepoFactory, an automated pipeline that converts real repositories into verifiable environments where agents build complete projects from scratch given a language specification. Its Environment Evolution Loop optimizes a multiplicative objective combining validity, structural coupling, and implementation scope through proxy feedback. RepoFactory produces 10,159 environments across 17 software domains. Training Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on these environments yields RepoHorizen-35B-A3B, which achieves gains of 22.6 percentage points on NL2Repo-Bench and 8.5 points on average across five benchmarks covering long-horizon coding and agentic tasks in real-world production settings, compared with 17.5 and 6.4 points without environment evolution. These results highlight the training value of RepoFactory environments and the additional gains from the Environment Evolution Loop.

title: Amazon Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall now supports automated allow-list generation
description:
Amazon Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall now automatically generates domain allow-lists from your VPCs' observed DNS query traffic, helping you enforce least-privilege DNS access and reduce the risk of DNS-based data exfiltration.

Previously, implementing a least-privilege model required security teams to manually analyze DNS query logs to identify the domains their VPCs depend on before deploying allow-list rules. This created operational overhead and delayed enforcement of a deny-by-default (walled-garden) posture.

With automated allow-list generation, DNS Firewall analyzes DNS query traffic using a lookback window configurable from 1 hour to 7 days to create an allow-list of observed domains. It then continuously monitors DNS queries and flags newly observed domains, so you can review them before adding them to the allow-list. You can deploy the rule across multiple VPCs and accounts using AWS Firewall Manager or Route 53 Profiles.

This capability is available at no additional cost to DNS Firewall Advanced customers, in all AWS Regions where Route 53 DNS Firewall is supported, except in AWS GovCloud (US) and Amazon Web Services China Regions. To get started, use the Route 53 DNS Firewall console, AWS CLI, or API.

title: Latent Fact Composition under Next-Token Training
description:
arXiv:2611.21921v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Controlled studies of latent two-hop reasoning train transformers to predict only the answer, whereas language models are trained to predict every token. We ask whether a model trained on every token learns to answer two-hop questions whose intermediate entity appears in no two-hop training example. We build a synthetic corpus with such questions. On this corpus every term of the loss can be computed exactly. A looped transformer, a standard transformer and DiscoLoop answer almost none of these questions. We therefore introduce the Baton family of looped transformers. They pass the intermediate entity to the second loop as a token embedding. When trained to predict only the answer, two of its three variants answer these questions almost perfectly. We then relate the success and failure of each model to three design conditions. Experiments that change one condition at a time agree with this hypothesis. When Baton is trained on every token, however, its accuracy on these questions rises and then declines. We further split the gradient of the next-token loss into three terms. Removing the two terms that depend on the particular training set raises the peak accuracy but does not remove the decline. The decline arises in the second hop while the model still recalls both facts.

title: DEFTS: Data-Efficient, Training-Free Few-Shot Learning for CLIP in the Text Subspace
description:
arXiv:2611.21993v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) achieves impressive zero-shot image classification performance by comparing image embeddings against class-specific text embeddings. While recent few-shot methods leverage labeled training samples to improve upon this zero-shot baseline, they often predominantly rely on image embeddings and underutilize the semantic structure of the text embeddings. In this paper, we introduce DEFTS, a data-efficient, training-free few-shot classification method strictly in the text subspace. We first demonstrate empirically that while raw text embeddings can be suboptimal as direct classifiers, the linear subspace they span remains highly discriminative. DEFTS therefore proposes to reduce the image-text modality gap by projecting estimated image prototypes directly into this subspace. Importantly, by expressing these prototypes as linear combinations of text embeddings, DEFTS reduces a high-dimensional estimation problem to the derivation of just a few coefficients. These coefficients are then computed via a Bayesian posterior mean, using a prior naturally centered on the original text embedding coordinates. Extensive experiments across 12 image classification benchmarks demonstrate that DEFTS significantly improves upon existing training-free methods.

title: 9 PostgreSQL fixes that took real queries from ~100 ms to under 1 ms (with EXPLAIN output)
description:
Most "slow database" problems I see are not exotic. They are the same handful of patterns: a missing index on a foreign key, a function wrapped around a column, an OFFSET that reads 200,000 rows to show 20.

I ran each pattern below on a 1,000,000-row orders table in PostgreSQL 16.6, captured EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) before and after the fix, and kept the numbers as they came out. Your timings will differ — the shape of the plan is what matters.

Fix Before After
Index the foreign key 67.7 ms 0.10 ms
Composite index (equality first, then sort column) 80.0 ms 0.20 ms
Expression index for lower(email) 14.2 ms 0.07 ms
Rewrite date(created_at) = … as a range 100.2 ms 0.31 ms
Partial index for the hot slice 82.3 ms 0.15 ms
Covering index (INCLUDE) 41.2 ms 3.9 ms
Keyset pagination instead of OFFSET 28.2 ms 0.11 ms
pg_trgm for ILIKE '%text%' 168.5 ms 1.1 ms
Planner estimate instead of exact count(*) 84.1 ms 0.07 ms

1. Index your foreign keys

PostgreSQL creates an index for a primary key, not for a foreign key. So this innocent query:

SELECT id, status, total, created_at FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 4242;

reads the whole table:

Gather  (actual time=2.554..67.674 rows=10 loops=1)
  ->  Parallel Seq Scan on orders  (actual time=16.595..43.016 rows=3 loops=3)
        Filter: (customer_id = 4242)
        Rows Removed by Filter: 333330
        Buffers: shared hit=96 read=15055
Execution Time: 67.727 ms

The giveaway is Rows Removed by Filter: 333330 per worker — a million rows checked to return ten. One index later:

CREATE INDEX orders_customer_id_idx ON orders (customer_id);

Bitmap Heap Scan on orders  (actual time=0.032..0.058 rows=10 loops=1)
  ->  Bitmap Index Scan on orders_customer_id_idx
        Index Cond: (customer_id = 4242)
        Buffers: shared hit=6
Execution Time: 0.104 ms

From 15,151 buffers to 16. Rule: every foreign key you filter or join on deserves an index.

2. Composite index: equality columns first, then the range/sort column 

SELECT id, customer_id, total, created_at FROM orders
WHERE status = 'pending' AND created_at >= '2026-06-01'
ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50;

An index on (status, created_at) lets PostgreSQL jump straight to pending, read rows already in date order and stop after 50. Column order matters: equality first, then the range or sort column. 80 ms → 0.2 ms.

3. Expression index for lower() and friends

WHERE lower(email) = '…' cannot use a plain index on email. Index the expression itself:

CREATE INDEX customers_lower_email_idx ON customers (lower(email));

14.2 ms → 0.07 ms.

4. Keep the column bare (sargable queries) 

-- slow: function on the column hides it from the index
WHERE date(created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC') = '2026-03-15'
-- fast: same rows, as a range
WHERE created_at >= '2026-03-15 00:00+00' AND created_at < '2026-03-16 00:00+00'

100.2 ms → 0.31 ms. No new index needed — just let the existing one work.

5. Partial index for the small slice you query all the time

If 5% of orders are pending and your dashboard only ever asks for those, index only them:

CREATE INDEX orders_pending_created_idx ON orders (created_at) WHERE status = 'pending';

Smaller, faster to maintain, 82 ms → 0.15 ms.

6. Covering index for index-only scans

When the index already contains every column a query needs, PostgreSQL can skip the table (Index Only Scan, Heap Fetches: 0) once the visibility map is current — i.e. after VACUUM:

CREATE INDEX orders_customer_total_idx ON orders (customer_id) INCLUDE (total);
VACUUM orders;  -- updates the visibility map so the heap can be skipped

41 ms → 3.9 ms for a GROUP BY customer_id over 2,000 customers.

7. Keyset pagination instead of OFFSET

OFFSET 200000 still reads and throws away 200,000 rows. Remember the last id you showed:

SELECT id, customer_id, total FROM orders WHERE id > 200000 ORDER BY id LIMIT 20;

Same cost on page 1 and page 10,000. 28 ms → 0.11 ms.

8. ILIKE '%text%' with pg_trgm

A B-tree cannot help a leading wildcard. A trigram GIN index can:

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_trgm;
CREATE INDEX orders_note_trgm_idx ON orders USING gin (note gin_trgm_ops);

168 ms → 1.1 ms.

9. Do you really need an exact count(*)?

For a "≈ 1.2M orders" badge, the planner's statistics are instant and usually within a few percent after ANALYZE:

SELECT reltuples::bigint AS estimated_rows FROM pg_class WHERE oid = 'orders'::regclass;

84 ms → 0.07 ms.

Bonus: a correctness trap, not a speed one

x NOT IN (SELECT y …) returns no rows at all if the subquery contains a single NULL. Use NOT EXISTS instead. It is not faster here — it is right.

How to find these in your own database

  1. Turn on pg_stat_statements and sort by total_exec_time — fix the queries that cost the most in total, not the slowest single run.
  2. Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on the top offenders. Look for Seq Scan with a large Rows Removed by Filter, and for big read= buffer counts.
  3. Change one thing, re-run, compare. Keep what helps; drop indexes nobody uses (pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan = 0).

I packaged this workflow — the 10 lessons with full before/after plans, a reproducible 1M-row demo dataset and 12 read-only diagnostic scripts (top queries, unused and duplicate indexes, vacuum health, blocking locks and more) — as the PostgreSQL Performance Playbook ($29, 30-day money-back guarantee).

Just want the one-page version? The free PostgreSQL Performance Checklist (PDF, $0) puts these checks on a single printable page.

If you want more SQL practice first, two well-reviewed resources from other creators on Gumroad:

  • SQL Practice Problems – Professional Package — 97 challenge problems (written for SQL Server/MySQL).
  • Decode PostgreSQL — how PostgreSQL works, explained without heavy code.
