title: When Does Discrete Ricci Curvature Help? An Edge-Level Analysis of Curvature-Enhanced GCNs for PPI Prediction
description:
arXiv:2611.21849v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Curvature-enhanced graph convolutional networks (CGCN) incorporate Ollivier-Ricci curvature (ORC), grounded in optimal transport theory, into message passing, motivated by the claim that curvature-weighted edges alleviate "over-squashing" at structural bottlenecks. But does CGCN's improvement actually come from mitigating over-squashing? We investigate this on four real-world protein-protein interaction (PPI) datasets, comparing CGCN against a standard GCN at the level of individual edges rather than aggregate metrics alone. While CGCN improves aggregate AUC, AUPR, and F1 across all four datasets, this gain is concentrated almost entirely on low-degree edges, while performance on low-curvature (bottleneck) edges systematically degrades in three of four datasets, the opposite of what the over-squashing motivation predicts. Examining the learned edge-weight function directly, together with clustering-validity metrics, edge-distance ratios, and a layer-depth ablation across four depths, we find evidence for an alternative account: curvature-weighting sharpens the separation between clusters, which improves intra-cluster predictions at the cost of inter-cluster (bottleneck) ones. We test this account against topologically defined communities rather than the classification labels used elsewhere. Additionally, we offer practical guidance on when to prefer CGCN over standard GCN, depending on whether intra- or inter-cluster predictions matter most.

title: Introducing the Apache Spark Optimization Agent for Amazon EMR Serverless
description:
Amazon EMR Serverless now offers the Apache Spark optimization agent, which analyzes completed Spark job runs and delivers cost and performance optimization recommendations in seconds. You can select a cost or performance goal, and the agent returns specific configuration changes with the telemetry evidence and plain-language reasoning behind each suggestion. The agent can analyze a single run or compare it against a known-good baseline to pinpoint what changed. You access it from the EMR Serverless console or through the SageMaker Unified Studio MCP Server.

The agent takes the job's configuration, logs, and Spark telemetry together with your chosen intent and returns recommendations computed by a deterministic recommendation engine. The engine reads all job artifacts together to identify what is driving runtime and cost: too little parallelism, a skewed join key, memory pressure forcing spill, idle executors, or capacity provisioned beyond what the job uses. The configurations the engine targets are the settings most commonly tuned across millions of Spark jobs running on AWS. When cost and performance trade off, the recommendation improves the metric you asked for while keeping degradation of the other within defined limits. The engine also evaluates a best practices checklist covering platform-level improvements such as upgrading to a newer Spark version or using Graviton processors. Each recommendation is labeled by the surface it modifies: infrastructure, Spark configuration, code, or data layout. Data engineers can also use the agent during development to tune configurations before promoting to production. All access is authenticated with AWS IAM and logged in AWS CloudTrail.

The Apache Spark Optimization Agent is available at no additional charge in all Regions where EMR Serverless is available, except GovCloud (US) and China Regions, for EMR release versions 7.6 and later. To get started, see Apache Spark Optimization Agent for Amazon EMR Serverless.

title: VisHead-Spec: Head-Routed Visual Attention for Multimodal Speculative Decoding
description:
arXiv:2611.21839v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates vision-language models(VLMs) while preserving the target model's outputs, but its speedup diminishes under high concurrency serving as the system becomes more compute bounded as the batch size increases. This problem is pronounced for multimodal speculative decoding as the long range of the image tokens in the prompt can significantly increase the computational cost during draft token prediction. The block-diffusion drafters (e.g. DFlash, DSpark) can effectively speed up the draft model efficiency by predicting multiple draft tokens in one forward pass, but their speedup for VLMs under high concurrency is still modest (<9%). In order to understand this gap, we examine the information flow between different modalities from target model to draft model and identify the sparsity pattern of visual attention between the target and draft models: only small set of key-value heads in the draft model need direct visual feature attention in the context and only visual features from top level layers in the target model need to be attended in the context. We therefore propose VisHead-Spec, which selects a small, fixed set of key-value (KV) heads to attend to all image features from top level layers in the target model and restricts the remaining heads to text features. On Qwen3-VL-8B and MMSpec, VisHead-Spec-8 lets 8 of the drafter's 40 KV heads read the image while keeping accepted length within 0.3% of the block-diffusion draft model baseline (i.e. DSpark). At batch size 64, its throughput gain over autoregressive decoding increases to 16.0%, compared with 9.5% for DSpark; at batch size 1, its speedup remains comparable to DSpark.

title: Vercel Tracing is now generally available
description:
Vercel Tracing is now generally available on all plans. You can now search and inspect traces from the dashboard or the Vercel CLI, and new Next.js projects get tracing by default. Pricing is unchanged from the beta.

Browse and search traces in the dashboard

In beta, you could only open a trace per request from the Logs page. The new Traces page shows every trace and span in one place, for a project or your whole team. Switch between a Spans list and a Traces list, filter each, and search with Kibana Query Language (KQL). A Live mode streams new traces as they arrive. A query like span.name:db* AND span.duration > 500 narrows to slow database spans by name and duration.

Search traces from the CLI

The Traces page uses the same KQL as vercel traces search --query, so a query built in the dashboard runs in the CLI unchanged. Search covers every project in your team, or one project with the --project flag. Inspect a single trace with vercel traces inspect <request-id>, and manage a project's sampling rules with vercel traces config.

Automatic tracing for new Next.js projects

In beta, nothing was collected until you added a sampling rule. Starting with Next.js 16.5, new projects created on Vercel that include at least one Node.js function get tracing turned on after their first successful build. Vercel adds one sampling rule tracing 100% of requests in all environments and injects instrumentation at build time, so traces include Next.js framework spans with no setup. To opt out, remove all sampling rules in Settings → Tracing.

Longer retention

In beta, traces followed your runtime log retention. Hobby now keeps traces for 3 days instead of 1 hour, Pro for 14 days instead of 1 day, and Enterprise for 14 days instead of 3 days.

Read the Tracing documentation to learn more.

title: CoSphere-SLAM: Multi-Agent Panoramic Gaussian Splatting SLAM with Spherical Loop Closure
description:
arXiv:2611.22235v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Dense collaborative mapping is essential for search and rescue, building inspection, and warehouse automation, where panoramic cameras capture the entire surroundings in a single frame. Unlike pinhole agents that share views only at similar headings, panoramic agents observe overlapping scenes at any 3D orientation, yet searching full rotations also produces mutually consistent false loop closures across distinct symmetric rooms. Moreover, continuous monocular scale drift splits rigidly merged maps at revisited surfaces, while depth noise at short baselines distorts loop translation directions. To address these challenges, we propose CoSphere-SLAM, the first multi-agent Gaussian splatting SLAM framework for panoramic cameras, whose spherical loop closure aligns spherical features over $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ via fast Fourier correlation across arbitrary orientations and rejects symmetric false closures through global $\mathrm{Sim}(3)$ consensus. Building on these closures, directional global optimization solves a per-keyframe $\mathrm{Sim}(3)$ pose graph with log-scale regularization to correct scale drift while separating optical-flow translation directions from depth-based magnitudes. Finally, omnidirectional Gaussian fusion transforms each Gaussian with its keyframe similarity and renders Gaussians at their maximum ray response to jointly refine poses and maps. Experiments on indoor and cross-session multi-agent panoramic benchmarks demonstrate that CoSphere-SLAM achieves state-of-the-art trajectory accuracy and rendering quality among single-agent and multi-agent methods. Project website: https://cosphere-slam.github.io.

title: Quantum-Classical Separation in Probability Distribution Transport via Nonlocal Games
description:
arXiv:2611.21840v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: In many-body physics and generative artificial intelligence, locality provides a natural notion of phase equivalence: two quantum states or classical probability distributions are regarded as in the same phase when local dynamics can reversibly transform one into the other. This raises a fundamental question: can local quantum dynamics transport classical probability distributions in ways that local classical dynamics cannot? We establish a quantum-classical separation in distribution transport: two classical distributions can be connected exactly and reversibly by a constant-depth local quantum circuit, whereas classical stochastic transport requires a substantially larger spatial range. We demonstrate this separation explicitly on a one-dimensional chain and develop a general construction principle on graphs, based on nonlocal games. Moreover, the source distribution can itself be generated by a simple local classical process, establishing a quantum advantage in distribution generation as well. Our results reveal a fundamental distinction between classical and quantum local reversibility, even when both the initial and final states are entirely classical.

title: ClearTalk: Data-Driven Mandarin Articulation Analysis and Personalized Communication Support for Children with Dysarthria
description:
arXiv:2611.21639v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Children with dysarthria may experience reduced intelligibility and difficulty expressing everyday needs. ClearTalk is a smartwatch-based system that converts Mandarin speech-recognition differences into interpretable articulatory profiles for personalized practice and staged communication. Target and recognized utterances are aligned at the syllable level, summarized across seven articulatory positions, and ranked by a count-sensitive asymmetric heuristic. For 13 dysarthric speakers from the Mandarin Dysarthria Speech Corpus, system syllable-level accuracy showed a Pearson correlation of 0.908 with expert intelligibility, with an R-squared value of 0.824 and a p-value below 0.001. The system-selected priority targets achieved an 86.7 percent overlap with the consensus of three blinded speech-language pathologists; across 210 target consonants, automated labels achieved 86.7 percent agreement, a Cohen's kappa of 0.76, and a macro-F1 score of 0.81. In a balanced single-session pilot with 15 children, mean pre/post gains were 14.4, 29.4, and 27.7 percentage points for mild, moderate, and severe groups, while communication-round completion rates were 81.3, 66.7, and 48.0 percent. These findings support the feasibility of using interpretable patterns of speech errors to guide wearable articulation practice and communication assistance.

title: Verifica el estatus de un CFDI y si tu proveedor está en la lista 69-B del SAT con Python
description:
Si trabajas en cuentas por pagar, un ERP o una fintech en México, recibes facturas todo el día. Casi todas están bien. Las que no, suelen caer en dos casos que el XML no te avisa:

  1. El CFDI ya no está vigente. El emisor lo canceló (a veces después de que lo recibiste) o el SAT no lo tiene registrado.
  2. El emisor aparece en una lista del SAT, sobre todo la del artículo 69-B del Código Fiscal de la Federación: los contribuyentes que el SAT presume que emiten facturas por operaciones inexistentes (los famosos EFOS).

En este artículo armamos en Python un flujo pequeño que puedes meter en tu proceso de recepción de facturas: leer el XML, validar formatos sin red, consultar al SAT y tomar una decisión (pagar, revisar o bloquear).

Por qué importa revisar

Un CFDI cancelado deja de tener efectos fiscales. Si lo pagaste y lo deduces, el problema aparece meses después, en una revisión. Y la cancelación puede ocurrir después de que el XML entró a tu sistema, así que el XML que guardaste no basta: hay que preguntarle al SAT.

Las listas del SAT son otro riesgo:

  • Artículo 69-B. Cuando el SAT concluye que un contribuyente no tenía capacidad para realizar las operaciones que facturó, lo publica primero como presunto y, si no desvirtúa, como definitivo. Las facturas de un definitivo se consideran sin efectos fiscales, y quien las usó para deducir o acreditar tiene que demostrar que la operación sí existió o corregir su situación fiscal. Hay también quienes lograron salir: desvirtuados y con sentencia favorable.
  • Artículo 69. Contribuyentes con créditos fiscales firmes, no localizados, cancelados, con sentencia condenatoria por delito fiscal, entre otros. No invalida las facturas por sí solo, pero es una señal que tu equipo de cumplimiento querrá ver.
  • Artículo 69-B Bis. Transmisión indebida de pérdidas fiscales.

No soy abogado; para la interpretación de cada caso, habla con tu contador. Lo que sí podemos automatizar es el cuándo revisar:

  • Al recibir la factura, para rechazar de inmediato lo que no existe o ya está cancelado.
  • Antes de programar el pago, porque entre la recepción y el pago pueden pasar 30, 60 o 90 días, y en ese tiempo el emisor puede cancelar o aparecer en una lista.
  • Periódicamente sobre las facturas ya pagadas, si tu operación lo justifica.

Parte 1: sin red, leer el XML

Empezamos con lo que no cuesta nada. Para hacer la consulta al SAT necesitas tres datos del CFDI: el UUID (folio fiscal, dentro del TimbreFiscalDigital), el RFC del emisor y el RFC del receptor. El total lo guardamos para conciliar.

Este es un XML de ejemplo sintético. Los RFC EKU9003173C9 y URE180429TM6 son los que el SAT usa en sus ambientes de prueba, el UUID es inventado y los sellos están vacíos. No es una factura real:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!-- EJEMPLO SINTÉTICO: RFC de pruebas del SAT, UUID inventado, sin sellos reales -->
<cfdi:Comprobante xmlns:cfdi="http://www.sat.gob.mx/cfd/4"
    xmlns:tfd="http://www.sat.gob.mx/TimbreFiscalDigital"
    Version="4.0" Serie="A" Folio="1024" Fecha="2026-11-10T12:30:00"
    SubTotal="10000.00" Moneda="MXN" Total="11600.00"
    TipoDeComprobante="I" Exportacion="01" MetodoPago="PPD"
    LugarExpedicion="64000">
  <cfdi:Emisor Rfc="EKU9003173C9" Nombre="ESCUELA KEMPER URGATE" RegimenFiscal="601"/>
  <cfdi:Receptor Rfc="URE180429TM6" Nombre="UNIVERSIDAD ROBOTICA ESPAÑOLA"
      DomicilioFiscalReceptor="65000" RegimenFiscalReceptor="601" UsoCFDI="G03"/>
  <cfdi:Conceptos>
    <cfdi:Concepto ClaveProdServ="81111500" Cantidad="1" ClaveUnidad="E48"
        Descripcion="Servicio de desarrollo de software" ValorUnitario="10000.00"
        Importe="10000.00" ObjetoImp="02"/>
  </cfdi:Conceptos>
  <cfdi:Complemento>
    <tfd:TimbreFiscalDigital Version="1.1"
        UUID="6F3C2A1B-0D4E-4B7A-9C21-5E8F7A6B3D10"
        FechaTimbrado="2026-11-10T12:31:05" RfcProvCertif="SPR190613I52"
        SelloCFD="..." NoCertificadoSAT="00000000000000000000" SelloSAT="..."/>
  </cfdi:Complemento>
</cfdi:Comprobante>

Con la librería estándar alcanza. Lo único delicado son los namespaces: en CFDI 4.0 el comprobante usa http://www.sat.gob.mx/cfd/4 y el timbre http://www.sat.gob.mx/TimbreFiscalDigital.

import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET
from decimal import Decimal

NS = {
    "cfdi": "http://www.sat.gob.mx/cfd/4",
    "tfd": "http://www.sat.gob.mx/TimbreFiscalDigital",
}

def leer_cfdi(ruta):
    raiz = ET.parse(ruta).getroot()
    if raiz.get("Version") != "4.0":
        raise ValueError(f"Se esperaba CFDI 4.0, llegó {raiz.get('Version')}")
    emisor = raiz.find("cfdi:Emisor", NS)
    receptor = raiz.find("cfdi:Receptor", NS)
    timbre = raiz.find("cfdi:Complemento/tfd:TimbreFiscalDigital", NS)
    if timbre is None:
        raise ValueError("El XML no trae TimbreFiscalDigital (¿no está timbrado?)")
    return {
        "uuid": timbre.get("UUID").upper(),
        "rfc_emisor": emisor.get("Rfc"),
        "rfc_receptor": receptor.get("Rfc"),
        "total": Decimal(raiz.get("Total")),
        "tipo": raiz.get("TipoDeComprobante"),
    }

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(leer_cfdi("factura_ejemplo.xml"))

$ python3 leer_cfdi.py
{'uuid': '6F3C2A1B-0D4E-4B7A-9C21-5E8F7A6B3D10', 'rfc_emisor': 'EKU9003173C9', 'rfc_receptor': 'URE180429TM6', 'total': Decimal('11600.00'), 'tipo': 'I'}

Usa Decimal para el total, nunca float; vas a compararlo contra montos de pago.

Validar el formato del RFC

Antes de gastar una consulta, descarta lo que ni siquiera tiene forma de RFC: 3 letras para personas morales o 4 para físicas, una fecha AAMMDD y 3 caracteres de homoclave, el último un dígito o A.

import re
from datetime import date

# 3 letras (moral) o 4 (física) + AAMMDD + homoclave de 3
RFC_RE = re.compile(r"^([A-ZÑ&]{3,4})(\d{2})(\d{2})(\d{2})([A-Z\d]{2}[A\d])$")

def rfc_con_formato_valido(rfc: str) -> bool:
    m = RFC_RE.match(rfc.strip().upper())
    if not m:
        return False
    aa, mm, dd = (int(g) for g in m.group(2, 3, 4))
    try:
        # el año de 2 dígitos es ambiguo; 2000 es bisiesto y sirve para validar 29-feb
        date(2000 + aa, mm, dd)
    except ValueError:
        return False
    return True

if __name__ == "__main__":
    for rfc in ["EKU9003173C9", "URE180429TM6", "XAXX010101000",
                "EKU9013173C9", "ABC12345", "eku9003173c9"]:
        print(f"{rfc:14} {rfc_con_formato_valido(rfc)}")

$ python3 rfc_formato.py
EKU9003173C9   True
URE180429TM6   True
XAXX010101000  True
EKU9013173C9   False
ABC12345       False
eku9003173c9   True

EKU9013173C9 falla porque el mes 13 no existe. Ojo: el formato correcto no significa que el RFC exista ni que esté activo. Para eso necesitas al SAT.

Parte 2: consultar al SAT con el API de MexCheck

Para no tener que automatizar el portal Verifica CFDI ni descargar y sincronizar los CSV de las listas, uso dos endpoints de MexCheck:

  • POST /v1/cfdi/verify: pregunta al portal Verifica CFDI del SAT si el comprobante existe y si está vigente o cancelado. Recibe uuid, rfc_emisor y rfc_receptor (o el XML completo en el campo xml, nunca ambos). Tarda unos 3 segundos.
  • POST /v1/rfc/sat-lists: regresa en qué listas (69, 69-B, 69-B Bis) aparece un RFC. Es una consulta a una base local sincronizada con las publicaciones del SAT, así que responde en milisegundos.

La autenticación es con el header x-api-key. La llave va en una variable de entorno, MEXCHECK_API_KEY, nunca en el código.

Qué significa cada respuesta

/cfdi/verify regresa found, status, uuid, message y cfdi (el registro tal como lo imprime el SAT: estado, es_cancelable, estatus_cancelacion, fecha_cancelacion, motivo, folio_sustitucion, total con formato de moneda, etc.):

found status Qué hacer
true vigente Sigue el flujo.
true cancelado Bloquea. Revisa motivo y folio_sustitucion (motivo 01 trae la factura que lo sustituye).
false no_encontrado El SAT no lo tiene. Si se timbró hace menos de 72 horas puede no estar registrado todavía: reintenta más tarde.
false rechazado El portal rechazó la solicitud (por ejemplo, un XML ilegible). message trae la razón.
null null No se pudo contactar al SAT. Reintenta; no se cobra.

Si llega un status que no está en la tabla, la documentación pide tratarlo como ni vigente ni cancelado; por eso el código de abajo lo manda a revisión.

/rfc/sat-lists regresa {"rfc": ..., "sat_lists": [...]}. Cada elemento trae article (69, 69b o 69b_bis), sub_list, situation, name y, cuando la lista lo publica, person_type, state y first_publication_date. Lista vacía = el RFC no aparece en ninguna.

Cliente con reintentos

Los reintentos importan porque el SAT a veces no responde. found: null, 429, 500 y 504 se reintentan con backoff; 401 (llave), 402 (sin saldo) y 422 (datos inválidos) no, porque repetir no cambia nada. El timeout va a 95 segundos: una consulta puede tardar hasta 90, y si cortas antes, la consulta se cancela y no recibes respuesta.

import os
import time
import requests

BASE_URL = "https://mexcheck.com/v1"
HEADERS = {"x-api-key": os.environ["MEXCHECK_API_KEY"]}
REINTENTABLES = {429, 500, 504}

def _post(ruta, cuerpo, intentos=4):
    """POST con reintentos para found:null, 429, 500 y 504 (no se cobran)."""
    for intento in range(intentos):
        r = requests.post(f"{BASE_URL}{ruta}", json=cuerpo,
                          headers=HEADERS, timeout=95)  # el API puede tardar hasta 90 s
        if r.status_code in REINTENTABLES:
            time.sleep(2 ** intento)
            continue
        r.raise_for_status()  # 401, 402 o 422: no tiene caso reintentar
        datos = r.json()
        if "found" in datos and datos["found"] is None:  # SAT no respondió
            time.sleep(2 ** intento)
            continue
        return datos
    return None  # sin respuesta definitiva: deja la factura en cola

def verificar_cfdi(uuid, rfc_emisor, rfc_receptor):
    return _post("/cfdi/verify", {"uuid": uuid, "rfc_emisor": rfc_emisor,
                                  "rfc_receptor": rfc_receptor})

def listas_sat(rfc):
    return _post("/rfc/sat-lists", {"rfc": rfc})

Si prefieres mandar el XML completo, el SAT además revisa los sellos y llena sello_cfdi y sello_timbre_fiscal: curl -F xml=@factura.xml -H "x-api-key: $MEXCHECK_API_KEY" https://mexcheck.com/v1/cfdi/verify.

La decisión

Aquí va la regla de negocio. La mía es conservadora: bloquear si el CFDI está cancelado o el emisor es 69-B definitivo; mandar a revisión todo lo demás que no esté limpio (presuntos, artículo 69, no encontrados, estatus raros). Ajústala con tu área fiscal.

def decidir_pago(cfdi_resp, listas_resp):
    """Regresa (acción, motivos). Acciones: pagar, revisar, reintentar, bloquear."""
    if cfdi_resp is None or listas_resp is None:
        return "reintentar", ["SAT o el API no dieron respuesta definitiva"]

    bloqueos, revisiones = [], []

    status = cfdi_resp.get("status")
    if status == "cancelado":
        c = cfdi_resp["cfdi"]
        bloqueos.append(f"CFDI cancelado el {c.get('fecha_cancelacion')} (motivo {c.get('motivo')})")
    elif status == "no_encontrado":
        revisiones.append("SAT no encuentra el CFDI (si se timbró hace menos de 72 h, reintenta después)")
    elif status != "vigente":
        revisiones.append(f"Estatus inesperado: {status!r} - {cfdi_resp.get('message')}")

    for l in listas_resp.get("sat_lists", []):
        situacion = (l.get("situation") or "").upper()
        if l["article"] == "69b" and "DEFINITIVO" in situacion:
            bloqueos.append(f"Emisor en 69-B como {l['situation']}")
        elif l["article"] == "69b" and ("DESVIRTUADO" in situacion or "FAVORABLE" in situacion):
            revisiones.append(f"Emisor estuvo en 69-B ({l['situation']}); guarda la evidencia")
        else:
            revisiones.append(f"Emisor en art. {l['article']} / {l.get('sub_list')}: {l['situation']}")

    if bloqueos:
        return "bloquear", bloqueos + revisiones
    if revisiones:
        return "revisar", revisiones
    return "pagar", []

Probarlo sin gastar créditos

Para no tocar el API real mientras desarrollas, simulo requests.post con respuestas que tienen exactamente la forma del esquema OpenAPI (los valores son inventados). Escenarios: todo limpio, SAT caído una vez, un 429 seguido de un emisor en 69-B definitivo, un CFDI cancelado y el SAT caído en todos los intentos:

$ python3 test_mock.py
vigente + limpio                 -> ('pagar', [])
SAT caído 1 vez, luego vigente   -> ('pagar', [])
429 y luego vigente + EFOS       -> ('bloquear', ['Emisor en 69-B como Definitivo'])
cancelado + limpio               -> ('bloquear', ['CFDI cancelado el 2026-11-12T09:15:00 (motivo 02)'])
SAT caído siempre                -> ('reintentar', ['SAT o el API no dieron respuesta definitiva'])

Valido además esos mocks contra el openapi.json con jsonschema, prohibiendo campos extra, para no depender de campos inventados. En tu CI puedes hacer lo mismo: el esquema está en la documentación.

Parte 3: que tu agente de IA lo haga por ti (MCP)

Si construyes la integración con Claude Code, Cursor u otro cliente MCP, puedes conectar el servidor MCP de MexCheck para que el asistente lea la documentación y ejecute consultas reales mientras escribe el código. Las herramientas relevantes son cfdi_verify y rfc_sat_lists, que reciben los mismos campos que el endpoint REST y regresan el mismo JSON.

Claude Code:

claude mcp add --transport http mexcheck https://mexcheck.com/mcp

Cursor (.cursor/mcp.json):

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "mexcheck": { "url": "https://mexcheck.com/mcp" }
  }
}

No hay llave que pegar: la primera vez que el asistente usa una herramienta de tu cuenta, abre el navegador para que inicies sesión. Un detalle: el MCP es para desarrollar. En producción tu servidor llama al API REST con su llave, como en el código de arriba. Y las consultas por MCP cuestan lo mismo que por REST.

Costos

Pago por uso a $0.015 USD por crédito:

  • /v1/cfdi/verify: 5 créditos ($0.075 USD). Las respuestas found: null y los errores 422 no se cobran; un no_encontrado sí, porque el SAT contestó.
  • /v1/rfc/sat-lists: gratis con cualquier plan activo; 1 crédito ($0.015 USD) en pago por uso.

Las cuentas nuevas reciben $5 USD de crédito al registrarse. Los planes mensuales están en la página de precios.

Resumen

  • Del XML sacas UUID, RFC emisor, RFC receptor y total sin red y sin dependencias.
  • Valida el formato del RFC antes de consultar, pero no lo confundas con validar que existe.
  • Consulta el estatus del CFDI al recibirlo y otra vez antes de pagar.
  • Revisa al emisor contra 69-B (y 69) en los mismos dos momentos.
  • found: null significa "reintenta", no "no existe".
  • Deja que la regla de bloqueo la defina tu área fiscal; el código solo la aplica.

La documentación completa está en mexcheck.com/docs y puedes crear una cuenta en mexcheck.com.

Soy Adrian Rangel, fundador de MexCheck. Los RFC, UUID y respuestas de este artículo son de ejemplo; el código lo probé contra respuestas simuladas, no contra facturas reales.

title: Adrianzhi Kuan Ong（王志寬）︱比特幣ETF、日經歷史新高與日本結束負利率：資本正在重新尋找方向
description:
2024年剛過去不到三個月，全球市場已經出現了三個值得長期記錄的變化。
1月，美國現貨比特幣ETF獲批。
2月，日經225指數突破1989年的歷史高點。
3月，日本央行結束持續多年的負利率政策。
一個發生在數位資產，一個發生在股票市場，一個發生在貨幣政策。


看似沒有關係，但從全球資產配置角度，它們共同指向一個變化：
全球資本正在重新尋找方向，而過去相對獨立的市場正在被重新連接。
日本正在經歷的，不只是一次股市上漲
2015年至2019年，我長期參與日本及亞洲市場的量化投資組合管理。
因此，日經指數重新突破1989年的高點，對我而言並不僅僅是一個數字。
日本從來不缺優秀企業。
汽車、機器人、工業自動化、半導體設備、精密製造等領域，一直存在大量具有全球競爭力的公司。
過去真正制約估值的，是經濟增長預期、資本效率和股東回報。
現在這些因素正在發生變化。
企業治理改革、資本效率提升、股票回購以及國際資金重新配置，共同推動市場重新評估日本資產。
所以我更願意把這一輪行情理解為：
資本正在重新發現一個被低估多年的市場。
日本結束負利率，重要的是「方向變了」
日本央行結束負利率政策。
利率水平仍然很低，但金融市場真正重要的變化，有時並不在於幅度，而在於：
方向發生了改變。
日本長期低利率，使日元成為全球重要的融資貨幣之一。
過去幾年，美國快速加息，而日本保持寬鬆，美日利差擴大，進一步強化了日元融資套利交易。
如果未來日本逐漸正常化貨幣政策，而美國進入降息週期，利差方向可能發生變化。
這並不意味著套利交易馬上逆轉。
但市場需要開始思考：
如果大量建立在舊利率環境上的資金開始重新配置，會發生什麼？
趨勢建立的時候往往很平靜。
真正需要警惕的，是擁擠交易開始退出的時候。
比特幣正在進入傳統金融體系
另一邊，比特幣也經歷著完全不同的結構變化。
美國現貨比特幣ETF獲批的重要意義，並不只是比特幣價格上漲。
它意味著傳統投資者可以通過更加熟悉的金融工具獲得數位資產敞口。
2022年FTX倒閉時，我曾經寫過：
數位資產真正缺少的不只是技術，還有信任。
ETF不能消除數位資產的波動、槓桿和監管風險，但它正在改變市場基礎設施和機構參與方式。
數位資產與傳統金融之間的邊界，正在進一步縮小。
這也意味著未來比特幣可能越來越受到美元、利率、全球流動性和機構風險偏好的影響。
進入主流，並不意味著風險消失，而意味著它開始進入更大的全球資本網絡。
投資正在變成一個更複雜的資訊問題
日本股票、日元、美國利率、全球股票、黃金、原油、比特幣……
這些資產看起來彼此不同，但背後可能通過利率、匯率、流動性和資金流形成一張複雜的網絡。
這也是過去一年我越來越認真思考人工智能與量化投資結合的原因。
傳統量化模型擅長處理價格、成交量、估值和宏觀數據。
但今天的投資系統還需要面對新聞、央行聲明、企業公告、政策文件以及大量即時資訊。
市場真正缺少的已經不是資料。
而是：
如何更快理解資料之間正在發生的關係。
未來的系統化投資，可能逐漸形成一條更加完整的鏈條：
資訊採集 → AI理解 → 資料重構 → 信號識別 → 量化分析 → 策略決策 → 風險控制 → 交易執行。
但這裡必須記住一個原則：
資訊不等於信號，信號不等於策略，策略也不等於收益。
資料需要驗證，模型需要測試，交易成本需要計算，風險更需要控制。
AI真正值得研究的價值，不是替投資者猜測明天哪個市場上漲。
而是幫助我們在越來越複雜的全球資本網絡中，更快發現變化、更早理解關聯，並用系統化的方法做出決策。
從1999年進入資產管理行業，到今天二十五年，我越來越相信：
長期有效的投資能力，不是永遠擁有同一個答案。
而是在市場改變之後，
仍然能夠發現變化，並提出新的問題。
—— Adrianzhi Kuan Ong（王志寬）

title: November 09, 2026
description:
AI Hypercomputer

Feature

Generally available: Pathways on Cloud is now generally available on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). Major features include the following:

  • Single-controller execution model: Coordinate multi-slice and multi-host Cloud TPU workloads from a single Python client process. Pathways uses asynchronous dispatch and centralized scheduling to support both Single Program, Multiple Data (SPMD) and Multiple Program, Multiple Data (MPMD) workloads. For example, training and reinforcement learning (RL) loops.
  • Resilient and elastic training: Keep training jobs running across hardware interruptions with resilient training, including the following capabilities:
    • Elastic training: Dynamically scale down to healthy Cloud TPU slices during unplanned hardware failures and scale back up when replacement slices rejoin without restarting the entire job.
    • Suspend-resume: Automatically save and restore high-bandwidth memory (HBM) state to Cloud Storage during planned GKE preemption events.
    • Hot-swapping: Remap interrupted workloads onto standby or lower-priority Cloud TPU slices.
  • Colocated Python sidecar containers: Run custom Python code directly on Cloud TPU host VMs alongside Pathways workers. For example, multi-host data loading with Grain or RemoteIterator, and distributed asynchronous checkpointing with Orbax.
  • Interactive mode and Shared Pathways Service: Run, inspect, and debug JAX workloads interactively from a notebook or terminal using interactive mode, or share a long-running pool of Cloud TPU slices on demand across multiple users and jobs with the Shared Pathways Service.
  • Cluster Director, Cluster Toolkit, and GKE integration: Launch JAX workloads on the Pathways runtime using Cluster Director or Cluster Toolkit (gcluster with --pathways and --pathways-headless), or by deploying Kubernetes JobSet manifests on GKE.
  • pathwaysutils utility package: Use the pathwaysutils Python package for advanced features such as the Shared Pathways Service, elasticity, and experimental.reshard for device-side data transfers across hosts over Inter-Chip Interconnect (ICI) or Data Center Network (DCN).
  • Standard libtpu.so layering and custom libtpu.so support: Pathways is layered over the standard libtpu.so shared library and provides a way to dynamically link in a user-provided libtpu.so at runtime using PathwaysJobSet.with_custom_libtpu in pathwaysutils.
  • Single-process profiling, observability, and compilation cache: Capture end-to-end JAX profiler traces across the client, proxy, resource manager, and Cloud TPU hosts from a single process. Reuse compiled XLA modules with a persistent compilation cache on Cloud Storage, and view Pathways control and data plane metrics in Cloud Monitoring.
  • Agentic workload debugging: Troubleshoot failed, crashing, or stalled Pathways workloads on GKE using the pathways-workload agent skill. With this skill, AI agents can inspect Cloud Logging container logs, node kernel logs, and GKE events to help identify root causes and fixes.
  • Supported Cloud TPU versions, JAX versions, and container images: Supports TPU7x (Ironwood), TPU v6e (Trillium), TPU v5p, and TPU v5e for JAX versions 0.12.0.1, 0.12.0, 0.11.2, 0.11.1, 0.11.0, 0.10.2, and 0.10.1, with container images published in Artifact Registry:
    • Image locations:
      • Pathways resource manager and worker: us-docker.pkg.dev/cloud-tpu-v2-images/cloud-pathways/server:TAG
      • IFRT proxy server: us-docker.pkg.dev/cloud-tpu-v2-images/cloud-pathways/proxy_server:TAG
      • Colocated Python sidecar: us-docker.pkg.dev/cloud-tpu-v2-images/cloud-pathways/colocated_python_sidecar:TAG
    • Image tags: Replace TAG with one of the following tags, which are created automatically when a Pathways build passes qualification tests and is promoted to production:
      • YYYYMMDD-jax_JAX_VERSION: Pinned tag created by combining the UTC promotion date (YYYYMMDD) with -jax_ and the verified JAX version (JAX_VERSION) after per-version qualification tests pass. For example, 20261108-jax_0.12.0.1.
      • jax-JAX_VERSION: Rolling tag updated after per-version qualification tests pass to point to the most recent verified image for that JAX release. For example, jax-0.12.0.1 or jax-0.12.0.
      • latest: Rolling tag updated when a build passes qualification tests against the most recent supported JAX release.

For more information, see Introduction to Pathways on Cloud.

AlloyDB for PostgreSQL

Feature

The following AlloyDB AI features and improvements are generally available (GA):

  • Smart batching for AI functions: AI function acceleration is generally available for ai.if, ai.rank, ai.analyze_sentiment, ai.summarize, ai.extract, ai.classify, and ai.generate on AlloyDB clusters running PostgreSQL 17 and later. Smart batching automatically batches and offloads eligible AI operations for asynchronous evaluation. It improves query execution speed without requiring you to rewrite queries into complex array structures. In PostgreSQL 18 and later, this feature is enabled by default. For more information, see Accelerate performance for queries with AI functions.

  • Sentiment analysis: the ai.analyze_sentiment function is generally available on AlloyDB clusters running PostgreSQL 17 and later. This built-in function classifies the sentiment of text as positive, negative, or neutral directly within SQL queries in real time. For more information, see Analyze text sentiment.

Anthos Config Management

Change

Upgraded the Open Telemetry image from 0.152.0 to 0.159.0 to pick up vulnerability fixes. To understand the changes in each release, review the full changelog for opentelemetry-collector-contrib.

Anti Money Laundering AI

BigQuery

Feature

To support your FinOps practices, you can now opt in to compute cost attribution in BigQuery editions. This feature attributes billed compute charges directly to the query projects that use your administration project's reservation capacity. Allocating costs based on actual commitment and autoscaling slot usage lets you accurately track project-level costs and manage internal chargebacks. This feature is available in Preview.

Feature

Query performance troubleshooting and job and system performance comparison in the BigQuery jobs explorer are generally available (GA). For more information, see Troubleshoot job performance and Diagnose performance regressions by comparing jobs and systems.

When you create or schedule a pipeline, you can specify the maximum number of concurrently executed pipeline tasks. This feature is generally available (GA).

You can use compression functions in GoogleSQL to compress or decompress bytes or string values by using the Zstandard (Zstd) lossless data compression algorithm. The following functions are supported:

  • ZSTD_COMPRESS
  • ZSTD_DECOMPRESS_TO_BYTES
  • ZSTD_DECOMPRESS_TO_STRING

These functions are in Preview.

Bigtable

Feature

You can use the Google Cloud console to create and manage Apache Avro schema bundles for your Bigtable tables. You can also view Avro schema bundle definitions in Bigtable Studio. This feature is in Preview. For more information, see Create and manage Avro schemas.

title: As Student Rollouts Continue, Visual Backdoors Keep Growing
description:
arXiv:2611.22446v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Conventional knowledge distillation can facilitate the propagation of backdoors from teacher models to student models. However, how this risk manifests in On-Policy Distillation (OPD) remains insufficiently studied. OPD has recently emerged as an important post-training paradigm for Vision-Language Models (VLMs). Unlike traditional offline distillation, OPD does not require teacher-generated responses. Instead, it uses the teacher's probability distributions to supervise response trajectories generated online by the student. Since the initial student model typically generates benign responses and receives no explicit supervision from malicious target responses, OPD appears to offer some inherent resistance to backdoor propagation.
  In this paper, we challenge this intuition and reveal a more subtle risk of visual backdoor propagation in OPD. Through experiments across multiple model families and datasets, together with theoretical analysis, we identify three main findings. First, unlike the relatively gradual propagation observed in traditional offline distillation, backdoors rarely emerge in OPD at low poisoning ratios. However, the attack success rate rapidly approaches 100% once a critical threshold is exceeded. Second, backdoor propagation does not depend on explicit malicious responses. Instead, it is driven by the continuous accumulation of anomalous probability mass assigned by the teacher. Finally, based on these findings, we propose a novel trigger design that enables visual backdoor propagation with zero explicit trigger injection. These findings further reveal an overlooked mechanism of backdoor propagation in OPD and highlight its potential security risks.

title: How to Find and Fix Slow Interactions (INP) in a React App
description:
A filter that takes a moment to respond can make an otherwise polished React app feel broken. The button registers the click, but the selected state appears late, the list freezes, or the interface ignores the next input while it catches up.

To improve Interaction to Next Paint (INP) in React, start with real-user data, identify the slow interaction, and trace its work in the browser. Then fix the cause: unnecessary component rendering, expensive synchronous JavaScript, layout and paint work, or a combination. Do not begin by adding memo to every component.

This guide uses React 19.3.1 and browser APIs available in modern Chromium-based browsers. The examples are illustrative implementation patterns, not benchmark results or a claim that a particular application was tested. The React Compiler is optional; manual profiling still matters.

TL;DR: diagnose before optimizing

  1. Find the affected page and interaction in field INP data, segmented by mobile and desktop.
  2. Reproduce the gesture in Chrome DevTools with a realistic CPU profile.
  3. Separate input delay, event-handler processing and presentation delay.
  4. Use React DevTools Profiler to see which components rendered and how much React rendering contributed.
  5. Apply the smallest relevant fix, then compare the same interaction and confirm the field metric improves.

INP is not a React-only metric. It measures the time from a user interaction until the browser presents the next frame. React rendering can contribute, but so can unrelated JavaScript, style recalculation, layout, paint, third-party scripts and work that was already occupying the main thread.

What INP measures

Interaction to Next Paint is a Core Web Vital that assesses responsiveness across a page visit. It observes qualifying click, tap and keyboard interactions and reports a representative high-latency interaction. The metric is evaluated at the 75th percentile of page visits, separately for mobile and desktop.

The current web.dev guidance defines these thresholds:

INP at the 75th percentile Assessment
200 ms or less Good
Above 200 ms and up to 500 ms Needs improvement
Above 500 ms Poor

These are assessment thresholds, not a promise that every interaction below 200 ms feels identical on every device. Use the field distribution to understand the experience of real visitors. A lab trace helps explain a specific interaction; it does not replace field measurement.

An interaction's latency has three useful parts:

  • Input delay: time between the user's gesture and the start of the event callbacks. A busy main thread can delay the callbacks before your click handler runs.
  • Processing duration: time spent running the event handlers associated with the gesture.
  • Presentation delay: time after the handlers finish until the browser can render and present the next frame.

This breakdown changes how you debug. If input delay dominates, inspect tasks that ran before the event. If processing dominates, inspect handlers and synchronous work they trigger. If presentation dominates, inspect React rendering, style, layout and paint after the handlers.

Source: web.dev: Interaction to Next Paint.

Find the slow interaction in field data first

Start with the users who experience the problem, not a development machine that may be substantially faster than theirs.

Use a Real User Monitoring (RUM) setup or the Chrome UX Report data available through your performance tooling. Look beyond the page-level INP value. You need to know which URL or route is affected, whether the issue is concentrated on mobile, and which interaction is responsible. Useful context includes the interaction target, event type, timing breakdown and whether the slow visit happened during or after page load.

If you instrument your own RUM pipeline, the web-vitals library provides an INP measurement and attribution build. Send measurements with enough context to group them by route, device class and interaction target. Avoid collecting raw user-entered content or other sensitive values just to label an interaction. A stable selector or component-level identifier is usually more useful than the text inside a field.

A field report such as “the orders page has poor INP on mobile” is a starting point, not a diagnosis. Narrow it to “changing the status filter on the orders page” or “opening the account menu after initial load.” Then reproduce that exact gesture.

Field data can also reveal issues that local testing misses: a third-party script, a slow device, a long-running task after navigation, or a page state that your test account does not contain. If field data is unavailable, use a reproducible user report as a temporary lead and mark the diagnosis as provisional.

Reproduce and profile the interaction

1. Record the browser trace

Open the affected route in Chrome, open DevTools, and select Performance. Use the live metrics view to observe local INP while interacting. Start a runtime recording, perform the exact gesture once, and stop the recording. Repeat with the relevant page state and CPU throttling that approximates the field environment.

Find the Interactions track. Select the slow interaction and inspect its input delay, processing time and presentation delay. Then inspect the Main track around the same time. Look for long JavaScript tasks, repeated event handlers, style recalculation, layout and paint. The flame chart and Bottom-up view help identify which functions account for the work.

Do not assume a long task that happens near the click is necessarily caused by the click. Check the call stack and timing boundaries. A task that starts before the user gesture can increase input delay even if it has nothing to do with the target component.

Chrome DevTools documents the Interactions track, the timing breakdown and the runtime recording workflow in its Performance panel reference.

2. Inspect React rendering separately

The React Developer Tools Profiler answers a narrower question: which React components rendered for this update, and how much render time did the profiled tree consume?

Open the Profiler tab, start recording, perform the interaction, and inspect the resulting commit. Look for a small state change causing a large part of the page to render. Check whether expensive children rendered even though their relevant inputs did not change. Also inspect Effects that update state after a render; chains of Effects can create additional commits.

For a focused measurement in code, wrap the relevant subtree in React's <Profiler>:

import { Profiler, type ProfilerOnRenderCallback } from 'react';

const onRender: ProfilerOnRenderCallback = (
  id,
  phase,
  actualDuration,
  baseDuration,
  startTime,
  commitTime
) => {
  // Send sampled, non-sensitive diagnostics to your dev logger.
  console.debug('React commit', {
    id, phase, actualDuration, baseDuration, startTime, commitTime,
  });
};

export function OrdersPage() {
  return (
    <Profiler id="orders-results" onRender={onRender}>
      <OrdersResults />
    </Profiler>
  );
}

actualDuration describes the time spent rendering the profiled tree for that update. baseDuration estimates the cost of rendering the entire subtree without optimizations. The Profiler adds overhead and is disabled in ordinary production builds by default; use the React DevTools Profiler for interactive investigation, or a profiling-enabled build when you need production measurements. Do not treat the callback's render duration as the full INP value: it does not include all browser work or time before React starts rendering.

See the React Profiler reference.

Fix the cause, not the symptom

The following table maps common trace patterns to the first fix worth testing. It is a diagnostic guide, not a claim that every symptom has only one cause.

Symptom in the trace or UI Likely area to inspect First fix to test
Typing or toggling rerenders an entire page State is too high in the tree Move transient state closer to the component that owns it
A click updates a large results panel synchronously Urgent and non-urgent updates are coupled Mark the expensive result update as a Transition
Search input feels blocked by filtering Input and result rendering share one update priority Defer the value used by the expensive results subtree
Scrolling a large table is sluggish Too many DOM nodes and row renders Virtualize the visible rows
A click triggers parsing, sorting or transformation work CPU-heavy synchronous JavaScript Move pure computation to a Web Worker
React render time is high for unchanged props Repeated expensive component work Memoize the measured subtree, or evaluate React Compiler
Browser trace shows layout or paint after React work DOM size, layout or visual effects Reduce DOM/layout work and avoid forced synchronous layout

1. Render less: localize state and split components

A common source of unnecessary work is placing short-lived state too high in the component tree. If typing in a search box updates state owned by the page shell, every descendant may be asked to render again.

Move the state to the smallest component that needs it. Keep the expensive results panel separate from unrelated controls. This improves the component boundary before introducing memoization.

Before:

import { useState } from 'react';

function OrdersPage({ orders }: { orders: Order[] }) {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState('');
  return (
    <main>
      <Header />
      <SearchBox value={query} onChange={setQuery} />
      <OrdersTable orders={orders} query={query} />
      <BillingSidebar />
    </main>
  );
}

After:

import { useState } from 'react';

function OrdersPage({ orders }: { orders: Order[] }) {
  return (
    <main>
      <Header />
      <OrdersWorkspace orders={orders} />
      <BillingSidebar />
    </main>
  );
}

function OrdersWorkspace({ orders }: { orders: Order[] }) {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState('');
  return (
    <section>
      <SearchBox value={query} onChange={setQuery} />
      <OrdersTable orders={orders} query={query} />
    </section>
  );
}

The state now belongs to the workspace that needs it. This does not guarantee that the table is cheap, but unrelated page regions no longer need to be part of the same update path. Keep component boundaries aligned with state ownership and actual UI responsibilities.

2. Keep urgent input responsive with Transitions

A filter selection often has two consequences: the control must reflect the user's choice immediately, while a large result panel can update at a lower priority. React Transitions let you mark the latter update as non-urgent so React can interrupt background rendering to handle more urgent work.

import { useState, useTransition } from 'react';

function StatusFilter() {
  const [status, setStatus] = useState('all');
  const [visibleStatus, setVisibleStatus] = useState('all');
  const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition();

  function handleChange(nextStatus: string) {
    setStatus(nextStatus); // Update the control urgently.
    startTransition(() => {
      setVisibleStatus(nextStatus); // Update expensive results non-urgently.
    });
  }

  return (
    <>
      <select value={status} onChange={e => handleChange(e.target.value)}>
        <option value="all">All</option>
        <option value="open">Open</option>
        <option value="closed">Closed</option>
      </select>
      {isPending && <span aria-live="polite">Updating results…</span>}
      <OrdersTable status={visibleStatus} />
    </>
  );
}

Transitions change scheduling priority; they do not make the underlying calculation faster. Keep controlled text-input updates urgent—React does not allow a Transition to control a text input. For asynchronous actions, state updates after an await may need another startTransition wrapper. See useTransition.

3. Defer expensive results while keeping input immediate

When a component receives a value from a parent and you cannot directly wrap the parent's setter, useDeferredValue can let an expensive subtree lag behind the immediate value. The input remains controlled by the current query; the results use the deferred query.

import { useDeferredValue, useState } from 'react';

function ProductSearch({ products }: { products: Product[] }) {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState('');
  const deferredQuery = useDeferredValue(query);

  return (
    <>
      <input
        value={query}
        onChange={event => setQuery(event.target.value)}
        aria-label="Search products"
      />
      <ProductResults products={products} query={deferredQuery} />
    </>
  );
}

useDeferredValue does not impose a fixed delay and does not prevent network requests. It allows React to prioritize the current update and attempt the deferred render in the background. If the results subtree is not expensive, deferring it adds complexity without a meaningful benefit. Read the useDeferredValue reference.

4. Virtualize long lists

Rendering thousands of rows creates work for React and the browser. It also creates a large DOM that can increase style, layout and paint costs. Virtualization renders only the rows around the visible viewport and reuses a small window as the user scrolls.

Use a maintained virtualizer when the list has variable row heights, accessibility requirements, sticky headers or complex grid behavior. The simplified example below demonstrates the fixed-height principle; it intentionally omits keyboard navigation, dynamic measurements and scroll restoration, so do not treat it as a complete table implementation.

import { useState } from 'react';

function VirtualList({ items }: { items: Item[] }) {
  const rowHeight = 40;
  const viewportHeight = 400;
  const [scrollTop, setScrollTop] = useState(0);
  const start = Math.max(0, Math.floor(scrollTop / rowHeight) - 3);
  const count = Math.ceil(viewportHeight / rowHeight) + 6;
  const visible = items.slice(start, start + count);

  return (
    <div
      style={{ height: viewportHeight, overflowY: 'auto' }}
      onScroll={event => setScrollTop(event.currentTarget.scrollTop)}
    >
      <div style={{ height: items.length * rowHeight, position: 'relative' }}>
        {visible.map((item, index) => {
          const itemIndex = start + index;
          return (
            <div
              key={item.id}
              style={{
                position: 'absolute',
                top: itemIndex * rowHeight,
                height: rowHeight,
                width: '100%',
              }}
            >
              {item.label}
            </div>
          );
        })}
      </div>
    </div>
  );
}

For production, validate focus behavior, screen-reader semantics, row measurement and overscan. A virtualized list can also make browser find-in-page and selecting content behave differently; decide whether those trade-offs fit the interface.

5. Move CPU-heavy work off the main thread

Transitions and deferred values help React schedule rendering. They do not move arbitrary JavaScript computation to another thread. If a click handler parses a large file, transforms a dataset or performs expensive search over a large collection, move pure computation to a Web Worker where practical.

src/workers/search.worker.ts:

self.addEventListener('message', (event: MessageEvent<{ items: Item[]; query: string }>) => {
  const { items, query } = event.data;
  const normalized = query.toLowerCase();
  const matches = items.filter(item =>
    item.label.toLowerCase().includes(normalized)
  );
  self.postMessage(matches);
});

src/search.ts:

const searchWorker = new Worker(
  new URL('./workers/search.worker.ts', import.meta.url),
  { type: 'module' }
);

export function searchInWorker(items: Item[], query: string) {
  return new Promise<Item[]>(resolve => {
    const onMessage = (event: MessageEvent<Item[]>) => {
      searchWorker.removeEventListener('message', onMessage);
      resolve(event.data);
    };
    searchWorker.addEventListener('message', onMessage);
    searchWorker.postMessage({ items, query });
  });
}

This is a minimal communication example, not a complete worker lifecycle abstraction. A real implementation should handle worker errors, cancellation or stale responses, termination, and large payload costs. Workers cannot access the DOM. They are useful for CPU-bound work that can operate on data and return a result. Structured cloning or transferring data has a cost, so measure the whole path rather than assuming a worker always wins. See web.dev's off-main-thread guide.

6. Memoize only when profiling justifies it

memo, useMemo and useCallback can reduce repeated work, but they also add comparison, dependency and maintenance costs. Start by removing unnecessary state updates, localizing state, simplifying rendering and eliminating expensive work. Then use the Profiler to identify components that repeatedly render with unchanged inputs and have meaningful render cost.

React 19.3 supports the stable React Compiler, which can automatically memoize components, values and functions when it can safely analyze them. It is an optional build-time tool, not an automatic feature of every React 19 app. Check your build-tool integration, compiler diagnostics and rollout strategy before enabling it. With the compiler enabled, manual memoization is usually less necessary, but existing useMemo and useCallback calls should be evaluated carefully rather than removed wholesale.

References: React Compiler introduction, React memo.

Prevent regressions with monitoring and budgets

A local trace tells you whether a change improved the reproduced interaction. Field monitoring tells you whether real users experienced the improvement across devices, routes and page states. Keep both in the workflow.

For each high-value interaction, define an owner and a reviewable budget. A useful budget is not simply “React render under X milliseconds”; INP includes browser work outside React. Instead, set a field INP objective aligned with the Core Web Vitals assessment threshold, and track the interaction-level causes that your team can act on. Segment by mobile and desktop and watch the 75th percentile over a stable reporting window.

Add performance checks to release review:

  • Monitor INP by route and device segment, and alert on sustained regressions rather than one noisy visit.
  • Keep a small set of repeatable interaction scenarios for filters, menus, search, forms and large tables.
  • Record a browser trace before and after a substantial interaction change.
  • Re-check third-party scripts and analytics handlers; instrumentation itself can create main-thread work.
  • Use production-like builds and realistic data. Development mode and synthetic data can distort the result.
  • Treat a good page-level score as a signal, not proof that every important interaction is responsive.

Do not invent a target for a component's render duration without measuring the application and its devices. Establish a baseline first, then set an engineering budget that reflects your actual user experience.

What to do next

Slow React interactions are rarely fixed by one universal hook. Field data identifies the experience to investigate; the browser trace shows where time is spent; the React Profiler tells you how much of that work belongs to rendering. Apply the narrowest fix, then verify it in both the lab and the field.

Use the React Production-Readiness Checklist to review performance alongside the other concerns that affect a production React application. For the wider engineering context behind apparently small UI features, read Frontend Is Easy… Until You Actually Build Something.

References

  • Interaction to Next Paint (INP) — web.dev
  • Optimize INP — web.dev
  • Performance features reference — Chrome DevTools
  • React Profiler
  • useTransition
  • useDeferredValue
  • React Compiler
  • React memo
  • Use web workers to run JavaScript off the browser's main thread — web.dev

title: VTT: Reading Vehicle Size and Powertrain Type from Motion Trajectory Across Unseen Car Models
description:
arXiv:2611.22109v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vehicle size and powertrain information can enrich trajectory data for traffic analysis and simulation. We present VTT, a dataset and benchmark for identifying these attributes from motion and controller area network (CAN) signals across unseen car models. The dataset contains 9,062 drives, about 3,950 h, from 1,431 vehicles and 174 car models. It provides three footprint-based size classes, powertrain labels, and evaluation on unseen car models and unseen drivers. Using 60-s windows, we compare four sequence architectures, statistical features and physical features proposed by large language models. Training with auxiliary physical targets, data augmentation and task-specific weighting raises drive-level macro-F1 to 92.6-93.0% for battery-electric versus combustion vehicles and from 62.9% to 67.1% for size classification. On public logs from 4,061 additional drivers, the full-input model identifies powertrain correctly for 86 of 88 car models; size accuracy is 63.2%, close to the internal vehicle-level result of 63.5%. Physical-feature analysis links powertrain recognition to deceleration behaviour and size recognition to steering response. Errors near size-class boundaries and limited gains from longer observations highlight the importance of label resolution and training-fleet coverage for cross-model generalisation.

title: Limite 1B - Violetto: Technical Report
description:
arXiv:2611.21646v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present Limite 1B - Violetto, a one-billion-parameter model designed for high-throughput mathematical reasoning. Limite is trained from scratch on 237 billion tokens from a carefully curated, mathematics-centric corpus and supports context lengths of up to 131k tokens. Its architecture and training recipe were developed together to maximize reasoning capability while keeping training and inference costs low. Post-training combines knowledge distillation, targeted supervised fine-tuning, and RLVR on a curated curriculum. Limite achieves 94.01% on AIME 2026 and 74.25% on BeyondAIME, placing it among models many times its size on our evaluation suite. The model is deliberately only lightly instruction-tuned: it is intended primarily as a single-turn mathematical solver and as a fast, parallel component of larger systems, rather than as a general-purpose assistant. We release the model, its base and value checkpoints, and an optimized serving implementation under the Apache 2.0 license.

title: Swagger UI is from 2011. It’s Time to Upgrade to Scalar.
description:
You've built a modern backend with TypeScript, NestJS, or Fastify. Clean architecture, type-safe APIs, and everything working perfectly.

Then someone opens your /docs endpoint.

And there it is. The same old Swagger UI.

Don't get me wrong. Swagger UI is great and has served developers for years. But API documentation can look and feel much better.

That's where Scalar comes in.

What Is Scalar?

Scalar is an open-source API documentation tool that gives your OpenAPI documentation a cleaner, more modern interface.

Think of it as Swagger UI, but with a better developer experience.

Here's what makes it interesting:

  • Modern UI: Clean layout, dark mode, and customizable themes.
  • Built-in API client: Test endpoints directly without switching to Postman.
  • Code snippets: Generate request examples in JavaScript, Python, Go, and more.
  • Authentication: Support for Bearer tokens, API keys, and other OpenAPI security schemes.
  • OpenAPI support: Works with your existing OpenAPI specifications.

And the best part?

You don't need to change your backend or rewrite your API schemas.

Swagger UI vs. Scalar

Here's a quick comparison:

Feature Swagger UI Scalar
UI Design Traditional accordion layout Modern, clean interface
Dark Mode Requires customization Built-in
API Testing Basic Try it out Integrated API client
Code Snippets Configurable request snippets Multiple languages and clients
Authentication Bearer, API keys, OAuth2 Bearer, API keys, OAuth2
Search Endpoint filtering Integrated reference search
Customization CSS and configuration Built-in themes and configuration
OpenAPI 3.1 Supported Supported
Open Source Yes Yes

Both tools do the job, but Scalar focuses more on the overall developer experience, especially when exploring and testing APIs.

How Easy Is It to Integrate?

If you're using Fastify with @fastify/swagger already configured, it's just a few lines.

Install Scalar:

npm install @scalar/fastify-api-reference

Register it in your Fastify application:

await fastify.register(
  import('@scalar/fastify-api-reference'),
  {
    routePrefix: '/docs',
    configuration: {
      theme: 'purple',
    },
  }
);

Now open:

http://localhost:3000/docs

That's it. Your existing OpenAPI specification now has a modern documentation interface.

Scalar also supports NestJS, Express, Next.js, and other frameworks.

Should You Replace Swagger UI?

Not necessarily.

Swagger UI is still actively maintained and supports OpenAPI 3.1, authentication, and interactive requests.

Scalar simply offers a different, more polished experience for exploring and testing APIs.

If you're happy with Swagger UI, there's no reason to rush.

But if you want better-looking, developer-friendly API documentation without much effort, Scalar is definitely worth trying.

Final Thoughts

We spend hours improving our backend architecture, performance, and code quality.

Why not give the same attention to our API documentation?

A great API deserves a great developer experience.

Give Scalar a try on your next project.

What do you use for API documentation — Swagger UI, Scalar, or something else?

title: ElevenLabs on AI Gateway
description:
Vercel and ElevenLabs are partnering to bring 14 ElevenLabs models to AI Gateway. To celebrate the launch, all ElevenLabs models are 50% off on AI Gateway for the first 14 days, through November 9th.

AI Gateway supports six different types of ElevenLabs audio models:

  • Speech to text: Transcribe recordings or caption live audio as people speak.

  • Streaming text to speech: Start playing audio while a language model is still writing its reply, so users don't have to wait for the full answer.

  • Realtime voice agents: Let users talk to your app and listen to it respond out loud in a single live session. Useful for support lines, tutors, and in-app assistants.

  • Music: Describe a track in plain text and get back a finished song or instrumental at the length you need.

  • Sound effects: Generate game and interface sounds, or ambience that loops cleanly, from a short description.

  • Multi-voice dialogue: Voice a whole conversation in one call, with a different voice for each speaker.

All of these audio models are accessible through a single gateway API key. Your app or agent can transcribe what a user says, reason over it with your choice of hundreds of models, then answer in an ElevenLabs voice. You can also create soundtracks with generated music and sound effects.

Every request lands in the same usage, cost, and trace views as your other AI Gateway traffic.

Model types

AI Gateway gives you access to 14 ElevenLabs models, spanning speech to text, realtime voice, and music.

Speech and transcription

Scribe v2 Realtime turns a user's speech into text while they are still talking. A language model of your choice then writes the answer. Eleven Flash v2.5, a low-latency ElevenLabs voice model, reads that answer aloud as it streams in, so the user hears the reply begin before the model finishes writing it.

Because each step is its own model, you can swap the transcription, language, or speech model without touching the rest of the pipeline.

In the example below, a user asks whether they’ll make a connecting flight. The text model combines flight status and gate distance to answer, then the speech model delivers the response.

Realtime voice agents

Eleven Realtime v1 Max and Eleven Realtime v1 Mini run the whole spoken conversation in one model, which suits conversations where users expect natural back-and-forth, like a support call or an in-app assistant. Both models take the user's audio in and speak a reply back over a single WebSocket session, so there's no separate transcription or speech step to wire up.

Eleven Realtime hears “Can I change the delivery address for my order?” and responds “I can help with that. What’s your order number?” over one WebSocket session.

In the browser, connect with the useRealtime hook from @ai-sdk/react, which handles the WebSocket connection, microphone capture, and audio playback. In the hook's sessionConfig, set an ElevenLabs voice ID and turnDetection: { type: 'semantic-vad' }. These models support semantic voice activity detection (VAD) to decide when the user has finished speaking, but they don't support server-vad. The realtime guide walks through the full browser setup.

Music and sound effects

Music v2.5 and Music v2 compose original music from a text description. Name a genre, a mood, or the instruments you want, and the model returns a finished track at the length you ask for, with or without vocals. For more control, you can lay out a song section by section and give each section its own style and length.

Sound Effects v2 works the same way for shorter sounds, such as footsteps, a door slamming, or rain that loops under a game level.

All three models use generateSpeech, with text describing the sound you want instead of words to read aloud. This example requests a 30-second track:

Multi-voice dialogue

Eleven v4, Eleven v4 Turbo, and Eleven v3 perform a script with several speakers in a single request. You assign a voice to each line, and each change of voice starts a new turn. A two-host podcast or a scene with a full cast comes back as one continuous recording, so there are no separate clips to stitch together.

About AI Gateway

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting, Zero Data Retention support, budgets for API keys, routing rules, and more.

AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and doesn't charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests.

The AI Gateway audio docs have examples across the ElevenLabs models. Browse all audio models on AI Gateway, and try ElevenLabs at 50% off until November 9th.

title: When Detection Does Not Guarantee Resistance: Reasoning and Poisoned Context in RAG
description:
arXiv:2608.17153v5 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) exposes large language models to knowledge-poisoning attacks, where misinformation injected into retrieved documents can influence model outputs. Prior work has shown that models may detect contradictory evidence yet still allow it to influence their responses, revealing a gap between monitoring and control. We investigate whether deliberative reasoning changes this relationship. Because attack success and poison detection alone do not reveal whether detected poison continues to influence the final answer, we use two complementary measures: Cordon Rate, the probability that a model detects poison and nevertheless produces a poison-aligned answer, conditioned on a non-poison-aligned no-RAG response; and Leakage Rate, the probability that poisoned context influences the answer despite an explicit instruction to ignore retrieved documents. Across 200 SciFact questions, we compare reasoning-disabled and reasoning-enabled configurations of DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Qwen3.6-Plus. For DeepSeek-V4-Flash, reasoning reduces Cordon Rate from 0.205 to 0.075 and Leakage Rate from 0.235 to 0.140, despite increasing Attack Success Rate from 0.233 to 0.298 and decreasing Poison Detection Rate from 0.965 to 0.665. Qwen3.6-Plus shows the same qualitative pattern. These results demonstrate that poison detection and downstream influence capture distinct aspects of poisoning behavior.

title: AdaRSI: On-Demand Recursive Self-Improvement for Embodied Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.20474v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Failures in long-horizon embodied tasks can arise from how a vision-language-action model (VLA) is called or from its execution capabilities. We introduce AdaRSI, an on-demand recursive self-improvement framework in which a coding agent first refines its tools and procedures, then adapts sub-steps that remain unreliable after testing alternative instructions and approaches. The agent collects demonstrations, tests their utility through temporary fine-tuning probes, and pools accepted data across tasks to train a specialist VLA that works alongside the original executor. At the end of each development round, its records are summarized into shared experience that guides subsequent diagnosis and data collection. On unseen composite tasks in RoboCasa365, AdaRSI raises success from 4.6% to 13.3%. On perturbed LIBERO-Pro 2.0 tasks, success rises from 32.9% to 49.1%. On RoboCasa365's Composite-Unseen suite, it achieves higher success than adapting every manipulation sub-step, using 34% of the GPU time and 36% of the demonstrations. On a real robot, the agent autonomously collects demonstrations and adapts the executor to recover fallen bottles, improving task completion.

title: Margin Dynamics for Large Language Model Alignment
description:
arXiv:2611.21766v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Practitioners choose among LLM alignment methods largely by trial and error. We provide a theoretical foundation: each pairwise method defines a vector field on the probability simplex that governs how the model redistributes mass between preferred and dispreferred completions. Projecting onto a single preferred/dispreferred pair reduces this to a one-dimensional margin ODE with a closed-form solution. These solutions reveal that DPO margins grow without bound (logarithmically as $O(\log t)$ in the gradient-flow limit) while IPO margins converge to a finite $1/(2\tau)$; that label noise induces a qualitative phase transition in DPO (unbounded $\to$ bounded) but affects IPO only quantitatively; and that gradient concentration under asymmetric weighting governs trainability at scale. We confirm all three predictions across five model families spanning four benchmarks. The closed-form solutions also enable principled method design: we prove that adding any label smoothing $\varepsilon > 0$ to SimPO creates a finite margin attractor at $\Delta^* = \beta^{-1}\log((1-\varepsilon)/\varepsilon)$, while $\varepsilon = 0$ (standard SimPO) has no attractor. We test this across three models (8B-9B) and confirm the prediction: the theory-derived configuration (TPO-S, $\varepsilon = 0.05$) is competitive with the strongest baselines, attaining the highest mean IFEval score among the compared methods on all three, validating that the predicted finite attractor is a usable operating point rather than proposing a new state-of-the-art loss.

title: A single inference process underlies the behavior and neural circuits of working memory
description:
arXiv:2611.22054v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Working memory holds past inputs online for future behavior. Despite decades of research, accounts of working memory remain divided across levels of analysis, with long-standing debates on whether its capacity reflects discrete slots or continuous resources, how attention improves recall, and whether its representations rely on persistent neural firing or activity-silent states. Here we show that MemGP, a theory that is specified at the computational, algorithmic, and circuit levels of analysis simultaneously, can explain diverse behavioral and neural phenomena in working memory. At the computational level, MemGP casts working memory as probabilistic inference over a continuous function on feature space, with a variational objective that balances memory strength against a Gaussian-process prior. At the algorithmic level, writing, storing, and reading of memories correspond to approximating this posterior with a finite set of inducing points, the resource that all items share. In simulations, MemGP reproduces load-dependent precision loss, attentional benefits during maintenance, and inter-item attraction and repulsion, in each case revealing multiple complex computational dependencies. At the circuit level, the algorithm analytically (without training) maps onto a recurrent circuit, including its architecture and dynamics. Beyond reproducing neural phenomena such as delay-dependent drift, this analytical map deduces center--surround connectivity, a property long assumed in attractor models, and a structured combination of persistent activity and synaptic weights to hold memories. Thus, a single inference objective not only jointly predicts the behavioral and neural signatures of working memory, but also addresses, across several instances and different levels of analysis, existing competing explanations.
