title: What developers think of HTML right now
description:
🚀 Frontend Focus

#​767 — November 18, 2026 | Read on the web

🗳️ The State of HTML 2026 Results

The State of HTML 2026 results are now out covering what developers are using, loving and struggling with, plus how much they use AI. Declarative, element-based features are winners, while form controls remain difficult. Some highlights:

  • <details>/<summary> (72.5%) and <dialog> (67.8%) are the most used interactivity features, and use of the Popover API has reached 40% now that it works in every major browser.

  • <select> and date inputs are the hardest elements to style, and customizable select is the feature most held back by browser support (Firefox is yet to ship it).

  • <datalist> usage jumped from 30% to 44%, yet positive sentiment fell from 44% to 34%, with respondents citing styling, accessibility and browser bugs.

  • Native data tables with built-in sorting and filtering topped the wishlist, ahead of tabs, comboboxes and switches. HTML includes came up again.

In his overall conclusion, Polypane creator Kilian Valkhof sees the frustration shifting from browsers doing things differently to browsers simply not having caught up yet, with mobile OSes a particular sore spot. He ends: "Our industry might be in turmoil, but I think our foundation is in good shape."

Devographics

A Form Platform That Fits Your App — Design complex forms visually and render them in React, Angular, or Vue. Keep full control over your backend and data. Create custom themes or use style adapters, extract form responses from PDFs and images with AI, and generate or fill existing PDF forms.

SurveyJS sponsor

🤖 Top 10 Things AI Gets Wrong in Web Development — The Chrome team tested frontier coding agents and found they pass only about 50% of web best-practice checks unguided, but ~90% with Modern Web Guidance installed. The areas they get wrong include accessibility, performance and security.

Philip Walton (Google)

Introducing the Cross-Origin Storage API — A new API proposal from the Chrome team to enable sites to share large assets (like AI models, fonts, common libraries, etc.) meaning end users would save bandwidth by only having to download them once.

Thomas Steiner

⚡️ IN BRIEF

  • 🔦 jQuery 4.1 and 3.8 are out. 3.8 is the last planned feature release of the 3.x line, which now gets critical fixes only.

  • 📑 Or perhaps you don't need jQuery at all? The long-standing 'You Don't Need jQuery' guide has had a major update, swapping IE fallbacks for modern one-liners.

  • 🌐 Chrome 158 is now stable, with the install element, media state pseudo-classes like :playing and :paused, and the start of XSLT's staged removal. Plus there's a look at what's new in the DevTools.

  • ⛓️‍💥 A cautionary tale about using link shorteners: some old Bitly links were recently hijacked, repurposing where they sent people.

  • 🌅 As we mentioned last month, Arc is going away on December 22, so Chris Coyier rounds up the browsers worth trying instead.

📙 Articles, Opinions & Tutorials

Charts in HTML and CSS — A neat gallery of column and bar charts, heatmaps, donuts, line charts and more, built from just HTML and CSS (no JavaScript or SVGs). It's all built upon semantic markup, so if you strip away the stylesheet, they remain readable tables or lists. There's also an agent skill.

Keith Cirkel

Charts That Do Analytics? Yes, With One Script — Give your users forecasts and anomaly detection in the chart itself. Orbit for Highcharts, free for 60 days.

Highcharts sponsor

The CSS caret-* Properties and Custom Caret Accessibility — A thorough look at the newer caret-shape and caret-animation properties alongside caret-color for styling the text cursor. Covers caret browsing, WCAG rules, and how author styles can trump users' caret preferences.

Sara Soueidan

What Safari on Apple HomeView Means for Your Site — Safari now runs on Apple's square, 7-inch, voice-driven display. Most sites 'just work' but Jen flags some assumptions that break, like a shorter viewport than usual, an iOS user agent on a non-iPhone, and voice users who need labeled controls.

Jen Simmons (WebKit)

PropFLIP: Because It Flips with Props — Adam takes four @property custom properties and uses them, along with a transition, to create a neat flip effect. A sprinkling of JS helps bring it all together.

Adam Argyle

Giving AI Agents a Better Way to Debug CSS
Amit Merchant

Building an atproto Link Aggregator
Johanna Larsson

🧰 Tools, Code & Resources

Allo: Your Friendly Neighborhood Font — A really nice, free, open source typeface with variable weights and roundness options, automatic optical sizing, plenty of alternates, and much more. The site does an excellent job of showing it all off. Repo here.

Josh Puckett

📊 Who Shipped First? Chromium vs Gecko vs WebKit — A look at 'which browser engine got there first' for a huge range of Web platform features. Patrick used the web-features data for this and Chromium/Chrome, perhaps unsurprisingly, has a clear lead in introducing new features.

Patrick Brosset

Your Chart Renders Fast. The Query Behind It Doesn’t — Tiger Cloud keeps dashboard queries fast as data grows, and it’s still Postgres underneath. $1000 credit to start.

Tiger Data (creators of TimescaleDB) sponsor

🐞 BugShot: Chromium Extension for Streamlined Bug Reporting — Adds a side panel for turning browser bugs into a report that includes captures, annotations, recordings, and logs. It can then submit reports directly to Jira, GitHub, Linear, Notion, and more.

SinhyeokKang

Astrobook: A Minimal Storybook Alternative — An alternative to the popular Storybook UI component playground that supports React, Vue, Preact, Svelte, Solid, Lit, and Astro. The demo site includes multiple framework examples.

Ocavue

Aura: Ambient Gradients Built from Layered CSS Blend Modes — 200+ customizable gradients that offer a soft, atmospheric look that feels 'like light'. Click any gradient to preview it live, browse sub-categories (mesh, nebula, lattice, glass, etc.), and export as PNG, SVG, CSS, Tailwind, etc. GitHub repo.

Cristian Olivera

📰 Classifieds

⚡️ Add lightning-fast 1D/2D barcode scanning to your web app with STRICH. On-device processing, free trial and demo!

📱 No Mac needed. Expo Simulators gives your coding agent a cloud iOS Simulator to test its own work, on Linux or Windows.

🧾 Generating invoices or reports from JSON? Foxit compares 10 PDF generator APIs on templates, HTML rendering and how each one bills.

title: Context Has a Price: Adding and Removing Context for LLM Coding Agents under Prefix Caching
description:
arXiv:2611.22238v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Coding agents repeatedly send their conversation history to a language model. Adding useful code may reduce search, while removing old tool outputs may shorten later prompts. But do these changes reduce the cost of solving a task? We study this as a measurement problem in more than 20,000 runs of open models on SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench and Loc-Bench. We account separately for uncached input, cached input and output tokens. Three findings emerge. First, in our main evidence-package experiments, retrieved code reduces read and search commands by 18--34%, but increases cost by 33--42% when cached input costs one tenth of uncached input, without a measurable improvement in resolution. Second, removing old observations can either save money or increase cost: the same approach saves 19--36% without a cache discount but increases cost by 38--116% with a tenth-price cache. Third, shorter prompts do not guarantee cheaper runs because agents may respond by taking more steps. We also find that concurrent experiments can share cached prefixes and distort cost comparisons. These results show why context-management methods should be evaluated using both token prices and the agent's subsequent behavior.

title: MedImgAnnotator: batch wise medical image annotation and preprocessing tool
description:
arXiv:2611.22450v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The curation of large cohort datasets for developing deep learning models demands annotating or editing over the AI-predicted labels. However, openly available annotation tools are time-consuming, as they involve complex navigational steps and do not support batch processing. This study aimed to develop a simple, fast, semiautomated batch-annotation tool named MedImgAnnotator. The tool was created by integrating editing tools, image mask pair matching logic, preprocessing functions, object detection tool, and a plugin management system. Its performance was evaluated in terms of active annotation time and ease of use by the developer and 12 users using open-source MR and CT scans. Additionally, the tool had been used by the MICCAI 2026 CARE Challenge liver segmentation best performance winner to annotate liver masks from 6412 MRI volumes. The evaluation results showed that MedImgAnnotator reduced active annotation time from 206.5+/-32.87 (average active annotation time of openly available tools) seconds to 59 seconds. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test of 12 users evaluation results recorded P values of 0.032 and 0.008 for the active annotation time and higher ease of use rating metrics, respectively, indicating that the current tool significantly reduces annotation time and enhances ease of use. Moreover, the tool utilization for annotating different regions of interest from different modality scans and body regions shows its usability across modalities and areas of interest. MedImgAnnotator, which significantly reduces active annotation time for large imaging cohorts, is available as an executable file and as a Python script. Access link: https://ewunateassaye.github.io/developed-tools/medimgannotator.html

title: How I Used Aggregation Pipelines to Fix No-Op Updates and Keep Error Clarity in Axion
description:
Hey friends! 👋🏻

I wanted to share a cool backend fix I implemented while adding the comments editing feature to my microforum, Axion. It's about handling no-op updates cleanly without breaking error handling.

In the past, some of my editing routes would update the content unconditionally. Even if the old and new content were exactly the same, the database would still run the update, hit the disk, and change the timestamps. It was inefficient honestly.

And letting MongoDB update the timestamps on identical content breaks data integrity. It lies to you—saying the last update happened at X time when nothing actually changed. Plus, it would return modifiedCount === 1 just because a timestamp field got changed, which ruins the tracking of actual content changes.

When adding comment updates, I wanted to avoid this behavior entirely.

The Naive Approach. I could have simply used { content: { $ne: content } }. But this creates a blindspot in my logic. If the database returns 0 matched documents, you can't differentiate between two completely different scenarios:

  1. Does the document actually exist and belong to the logged-in user?
  2. Did the query just fail because the new content matches the old content?

To give a proper response to the client, I needed to know the difference.

My Solution: Aggregation Pipeline Updates. Instead of a basic update, I relied on an aggregation pipeline inside the update operation. And that's my logic:

  1. It first finds a document created by the current logged-in user where the _id matches the given comment ID.
  2. If found, it updates the content and timestamps only if the old content differs from the new content.
  3. Finally, it checks matchedCount === 0. If it's 0, we know that the document wasn't found (or the user doesn't own it) and can throw a proper 404 error here.

Oh, yeah, and to end this cleanly, I included a changed field in the HTTP response, setting its value to modifiedCount !== 0. This tells the frontend exactly whether an actual database write occurred or if it was a harmless no-op.

Handling the "(Edited)" Badge Properly. While doing this, I also needed a way for the frontend to show an "(Edited)" badge on updated comment cards.

I didn't want to rely on a single boolean like isEdited: true because it doesn't provide the metadata of when the update happened if I ever need it. I also rejected the idea of just comparing createdAt against updatedAt. Like, what if a background script or admin tool ever modifies a document for maintenance? updatedAt changes, and the system would falsely tell users the comment was edited when it wasn't.

So, I came up with a cleaner approach: adding a third field called editedAt. For non-edited comments, it stays null. The moment a real edit happens, it stores the exact timestamp of that edit. Maybe I don't show the edit timestamp to users right now, but if I ever want to in the future, the data will be there. It's a matter of handling "what if" scenarios cleanly from day one.

At the end of the day, losing precise error handling isn't worth saving a few lines of code.

Thanks for hanging out and reading through! How do you handle these annoying no-op updates and edit tracking in your backend? Let's talk in the comments below. See you next time! 🌟

title: Three States for Async Product Image Jobs: Accepted, Downloaded, Approved
description:
AI-generated tutorial from CartVisual, based on the cited vendor documentation. The job states below are an illustrative integration design.

An image-edit job can be accepted before the edited file exists. In a catalog pipeline, confusing those events can cause two problems: a duplicate paid request when polling is slow, or a broken SKU image when a status URL ends up in the asset table.

Keep the job receipt separate from the asset

Store the provider job ID and the immutable source revision together as soon as the API acknowledges the request. Keep the lookup URL in the task record. Claid’s async image-editing documentation, for example, distinguishes the task lookup from the completed result’s output object. If the response does not include a lookup URL, the documented route also accepts the task ID.

Make the merchant approval a distinct transition

Transition Required evidence
Submitted to accepted A provider job ID that can be looked up
Accepted to downloaded A completed response and a file your worker actually read
Downloaded to approved A check against the SKU, dimensions and source reference

If polling times out after acceptance, keep the receipt and reconcile that job. A local timeout does not tell you that the provider stopped. If the download fails after completion, retry the download according to the provider’s documented access and expiry rules. Both paths avoid submitting another generation merely to recover a file.

A useful test for your worker

Create a fake status response pointing to a fake task lookup. Assert that the worker never writes that URL into the product’s live image field. Then feed it a completed response with a fixture file and confirm that the file reaches a review state. You can test both branches with local fixtures and without making a paid provider request.

For a worked Claid example and the documented field names, see CartVisual’s async image handoff guide and the official Claid async API reference.

title: The File Watcher That Looked Like a Permissions Problem
description:
Running a small file-watching tool on a managed Mac produces three failures in quick succession, and all three look like the same thing.

First npm install -g stops and asks for a password. Then, once it's installed, macOS throws up a dialog about accessing files in a folder you own. Then, pointed at a real project tree, it dies with EMFILE: too many open files. Every one of those reads as "this machine won't let me do it, I need admin rights."

None of them needs admin rights. They're three unrelated mechanisms that happen to fail in the same register, and the way out is different for each.

TL;DR: The sudo prompt is about where npm writes, not what the tool does — install as a devDependency, via npx, or with npm config set prefix ~/.npm-global. The privacy dialog is TCC, a per-user consent for ~/Desktop/~/Documents/~/Downloads granted to your terminal app, not to root. The EMFILE is macOS's default ulimit -n 256 meeting chokidar 4, which dropped fsevents and now opens one watch per directory — raise the soft limit to the hard limit (no root needed) or switch to --poll. Details below, from copy-watch.

What Actually Needs Admin Rights Here?

Only the write target. npm install -g defaults to a prefix under /usr/local, which is root-owned, so npm asks for a password — for its own bookkeeping, not for anything the installed program will later do. A watcher reading ./dist and writing ~/Sites/preview never touches a privileged path at runtime.

Three ways around it, in descending order of how often they're the right call:

# 1. As a project dependency — resolved via node_modules/.bin, nothing global
npm install --save-dev copy-watch

# 2. No install at all
npx copy-watch ./dist ~/Sites/preview --initial

# 3. Global, but inside $HOME
npm config set prefix ~/.npm-global
echo 'export PATH="$HOME/.npm-global/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.zshrc

If Node itself came from nvm, fnm, or Homebrew in user context, the prefix is already writable and none of this applies — which is why the problem is so easy to misfile as machine policy. It's a property of your Node install, not of the tool.

The runtime rule is the boring one: everything under $HOME is yours to write, everything outside it (/Library, /usr/local, /Applications) is root's. Choose ~/Sites or ~/Projects as a mirror target and the question never comes up.

Why Does macOS Ask for Permission on a Folder I Own?

Because ownership isn't the only gate. ~/Desktop, ~/Documents, and ~/Downloads sit behind TCC — Apple's privacy layer — and the POSIX bits say yes while TCC says ask-first.

Two details make this confusing in exactly the wrong way:

  • The grant is per application, not per script. macOS asks once, on first access, and records the answer against Terminal or iTerm — the process that spawned you. Every script you ever run from that terminal inherits the decision. Which is why the dialog appears once, for one tool, and then never again for anything.
  • Declining is sticky and silent. Say no once and every later attempt fails as EACCES or EPERM, with no second prompt. That is the error most likely to get misread as "I need sudo," because it's the same errno you'd get from a genuinely privileged path.

The repair is in System Settings → Privacy & Security → Files and Folders → your terminal app. A user decision, not an admin one. It's worth making the tool say so directly rather than letting the raw errno mislead:

onError: (err) => {
  if (err?.code === 'EPERM' || err?.code === 'EACCES') {
    console.error(
      `Fehler: kein Zugriff auf ${err.path ?? 'den Pfad'}.\n` +
        '  Auf macOS koennen ~/Desktop, ~/Documents und ~/Downloads geschuetzt sein.\n' +
        '  Beim ersten Zugriff fragt das System einmalig nach — die Freigabe erfolgt\n' +
        '  fuer das Terminal-Programm unter Systemeinstellungen > Datenschutz & Sicherheit\n' +
        '  > Dateien und Ordner.',
    );
    return;
  }
  console.error(`Fehler: ${err.message}`);
}

The principle generalizes to every entry on this list: when an errno has a known non-obvious cause on this platform, attach the remedy to the error. The user is going to search the message anyway — save them the trip. The descriptor case below gets the same treatment.

Why Do I Get EMFILE on a Deep Tree?

This one is a real resource limit, and it got noticeably easier to hit in the last major version of chokidar.

Chokidar 4 dropped the optional fsevents native dependency. That's a genuine win at install time — no node-gyp, no Xcode Command Line Tools, no compile step, so the "without admin rights" story holds all the way through installation. The cost shows up at runtime: instead of one FSEvents stream covering an entire subtree, you get one fs.watch per directory.

Meanwhile macOS starts shells at ulimit -n 256. A node_modules tree — assuming you didn't ignore it, which is why it's in the default ignore list — will exhaust that before it finishes the initial scan.

The soft limit can be raised to the hard limit by any user:

ulimit -n 4096      # current shell only; put it in ~/.zshrc to persist
ulimit -Hn          # the ceiling — high enough on modern macOS

Only going above the hard limit needs root, and you almost certainly don't. So: check at startup and warn below 1024, rather than letting it surface as a crash halfway through a scan.

The zero-configuration alternative is --poll, which trades CPU for descriptors — it stats on an interval instead of holding watches. On a build output directory that's a bad deal. On a mount, as below, it isn't a choice at all.

Transient shortages deserve a retry rather than a hard failure, and only for the two errnos that actually mean "come back later":

const FD_ERRORS = new Set(['EMFILE', 'ENFILE']);

async function withRetry(fn, retries = 5) {
  let lastError;
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt <= retries; attempt++) {
    try {
      return await fn();
    } catch (err) {
      if (!FD_ERRORS.has(err?.code)) throw err;
      lastError = err;
      await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 50 * (attempt + 1)));
    }
  }
  throw lastError;
}

The if (!FD_ERRORS.has(...)) throw err line is the important one. A retry loop that swallows every error turns a permissions bug into a hang, which is a strictly worse thing to debug than the original crash.

Why Doesn't It Work on a Network Share?

Because kernel change notifications frequently don't cross the mount. SMB, NFS, /Volumes/…, VM shared folders, Docker bind mounts — writes land, and no event ever arrives. The watcher sits there looking healthy and does nothing, which is the worst failure mode on this list because there's no error to search for.

There is no clever fix. Polling is the only mechanism that works, because it asks instead of waiting to be told:

copy-watch ./src /Volumes/team-share/inbox --poll --interval 1000

The useful diagnostic heuristic: if the source path starts with /Volumes/ or came out of mount, assume events don't work until proven otherwise, and start with --poll.

Why Doesn't My LaunchAgent Inherit ulimit?

Because launchd is not your shell and never read your ~/.zshrc. Two things break the first time you try to run a watcher at login, and both are worth knowing before you spend an evening on them:

<key>ProgramArguments</key>
<array>
  <string>/Users/you/.nvm/versions/node/v22.4.0/bin/node</string>
  <string>/Users/you/tools/copy-watch/bin/cli.js</string>
</array>
<key>SoftResourceLimits</key>
<dict><key>NumberOfFiles</key><integer>4096</integer></dict>

ProgramArguments needs absolute paths — launchd has no login-shell PATH, so a bare node isn't found, and with nvm the correct path points at a specific version directory (which node gives it to you). And the descriptor limit you set in your shell is invisible here; it has to be declared as SoftResourceLimits.

The part that's genuinely good news: a LaunchAgent in ~/Library/LaunchAgents runs in your user context and needs no sudo at all. It's /Library/LaunchDaemons — system-wide, running before login — that requires root, and it's the wrong tool for a per-user file mirror anyway.

launchctl bootstrap gui/$(id -u) ~/Library/LaunchAgents/local.copy-watch.plist
launchctl print   gui/$(id -u)/local.copy-watch      # status
launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u)/local.copy-watch      # stop

What's the Generalizable Lesson Here?

  • "Asks for a password" is a claim about a path, not about a capability. Trace which file the failing operation wants to write before concluding the machine is locked down — most of the time the answer is to move the write into $HOME.
  • On macOS, POSIX permissions are no longer the whole story. TCC can deny access to a directory you own, the denial is recorded against your terminal app rather than your script, and it surfaces as an ordinary EACCES with no hint about which layer said no.
  • When you drop a native dependency, you move a cost rather than remove it. Losing fsevents bought a compile-free install and paid for it in file descriptors — a good trade, but only if the new failure mode is documented where people will hit it.
  • Attach the remedy to the error message for platform-specific errnos. EMFILE plus "run ulimit -n 4096, no admin needed" is the difference between a fixed problem and an abandoned tool.
  • The silent failure — a watcher on a network mount that never fires — is worth more defensive attention than any of the loud ones. Loud failures get searched; silent ones get blamed on the tool being flaky.
  • Cross-check platform assumptions in CI. Running the smoke tests across macOS, Linux, and Windows on three Node versions is how you find out that a path-normalization shortcut works on exactly one of them.

The companion piece to this one — why a file watcher deletes the file you just saved — covers the other half of the problem: the timing heuristics that make mirroring survive an editor's atomic save.

title: Best Web Design and Development Blogs to Follow: 33 Checked
description:
TL;DR: We checked which of the best web design and development blogs still publish. These 33 blogs and newsletters each published an editorial post in the 90 days to 18 Nov 2026. The React blog has the longest gap: 70 days since its 9 Sep 2026 post. Start with Smashing Magazine for design, Josh W. Comeau and web.dev for front-end, the release blog for each framework you ship, and Frontend Focus for email. Of the 21 blogs on our 2018 list, 7 still pass.

Last checked 18 Nov 2026. Next check: January 2027.

This list is for front-end developers and web designers, especially at small agencies, who built an RSS reader years ago and now find half of it silent or full of Black Friday deals. It names the best web design and development blogs that still publish real articles, with a date you can check for each, and the good ones that missed out.

At Netling, an AI assistant is now our team's first stop for an answer. That works when you know what to ask. A short feed tells you about the change you did not know to look for, such as WebKit's spatial CSS developer preview on 16 Nov 2026 or the Node.js security releases on 11 Nov 2026. It is also where we check what the assistant told us.

In April 2018 I published a list of 21 blogs on our old site (archive copy). What happened to each of them is near the end.

How we chose these blogs, and what "still active" means

Every blog and newsletter here passed the same five rules, checked on 18 Nov 2026:

  1. Recent: an editorial post in the 90 days to 18 Nov 2026.
  2. Regular: at least four editorial posts in the 12 months to 18 Nov 2026. Newsletters instead need at least three issues in the 90 days.
  3. On topic: web design or development is the main topic, meaning at least five of the newest ten editorial posts, by our reading of the titles.
  4. Free: you can read it without paying.
  5. Vendors labelled: vendor blogs are allowed, and we label them.

An editorial post is a written article, or a roundup of other people's articles. Sponsored posts, deals, event and course promotions, single-product reviews and podcast episodes do not count. Neither do roundups of templates, fonts, plugins, tools or hosting.

A script read the dates in each blog's own feed and set those items aside by their titles. Feeds show only their newest items, so when every editorial item in the feed falls inside 90 days, the count is a floor and we write "at least". Codrops and Design Shack block scripts, so we checked their home pages in a browser.

Rule 3 is our judgement from titles, and we say where a blog passed narrowly. The longest gap among the picks is the React blog's 70 days. Four well-known blogs sit just beyond the 90-day line: Hongkiat (103 days), Post Status (117), A List Apart (141) and MDN Blog (156).

The best web design and development blogs at a glance

This is the skim version, with each blog's newest editorial post as of 18 Nov 2026. The full entries below add the 90-day count and the feed URL.

Design and UX

  • Smashing Magazine (17 Nov): practical articles on UX, accessibility, CSS and AI in design work.
  • Nielsen Norman Group (13 Nov): UX research findings and definitions (sells training).
  • UX Collective (16 Nov): product-design essays from many authors (Medium-hosted).
  • Pixels of the Week (8 Nov): Stephanie Walter's weekly pick of UX and design links.
  • Codrops (17 Nov): creative front-end, WebGPU and motion tutorials and case studies.

CSS and front-end

  • CSS-Tricks (16 Nov): CSS techniques (owned by DigitalOcean).
  • Josh W. Comeau (20 Oct): long interactive tutorials on CSS and React.
  • Ahmad Shadeed (5 Nov): CSS layout experiments.
  • Rachel Andrew (2 Nov): CSS layout from a CSS Working Group member.
  • Piccalilli (13 Nov): front-end craft and The Index links (sells courses).
  • CodePen Blog (16 Nov): Chris Coyier's Chris' Corner column (vendor).
  • Frontend Masters Blog (16 Nov): frequent front-end tutorials (vendor).

Browsers, standards, performance and accessibility

  • web.dev (2 Oct): monthly Baseline and "new to the web platform" digests (Google).
  • Chrome for Developers (7 Oct): Chrome release and API posts (vendor).
  • WebKit (16 Nov): Safari features and release notes (Apple).
  • Bram.us (22 Oct): new CSS and DevTools features.
  • CSS Wizardry (11 Nov): weekly web-performance notes.
  • Adrian Roselli (10 Nov): accessibility and WCAG in detail.
  • Zach Leatherman (14 Oct): web components and Eleventy.

JavaScript, frameworks and back-end

  • React blog (9 Sep): releases and security advisories.
  • Next.js blog (17 Nov): releases and monthly security notices (Vercel).
  • Nuxt blog (28 Oct): Nuxt and Vue-ecosystem releases.
  • Node.js blog (17 Nov): every release and security release.
  • Laravel News (16 Nov): daily Laravel and PHP news.
  • SitePoint (17 Nov): tutorials, in a mixed feed.

WordPress, industry and agency life

  • Make WordPress Core (17 Nov): developer notes before each release.
  • The Repository (17 Nov): daily WordPress news.
  • Speckyboy (16 Nov): web design and the agency business.
  • Web Designer Depot (17 Nov): opinion and design trends.
  • Boagworld (5 Nov): a fortnightly column on UX and agency practice.

Newsletters

  • Frontend Focus (11 Nov): weekly front-end news.
  • JavaScript Weekly (17 Nov): weekly JavaScript news.
  • CSS Layout News (4 Nov): monthly CSS layout links.

Best web design and UX blogs

Smashing Magazine

Smashing Magazine publishes practical articles on UX, accessibility, CSS and AI in design work. Its newest article asks how accessibility testing can keep up when AI speeds up the build. Its conference promotions sit in the same feed, and we left them out of the count.

Newest editorial post: 17 Nov 2026 · Editorial posts in the last 90 days: 18 · Feed: https://www.smashingmagazine.com/feed/

Nielsen Norman Group

Nielsen Norman Group turns its UX research into one or two short articles a week. Read it for evidence-based guidance and for the definitions your clients' UX teams already use. NN/g is a training and consulting firm, so expect links to its courses.

Newest editorial post: 13 Nov 2026 · Editorial posts in the last 90 days: at least 18 · Feed: https://www.nngroup.com/feed/rss/

UX Collective

UX Collective publishes product-design essays from many independent authors every day. It is hosted on Medium, and some stories are member-only: signed out, we could read two of the three newest. Skim the titles and open what fits your work.

Newest editorial post: 16 Nov 2026 · Editorial posts in the last 90 days: at least 10 · Feed: https://uxdesign.cc/feed

Stephanie Walter's Pixels of the Week

Stephanie Walter publishes Pixels of the Week, a weekly pick of UX and design links with short notes (8 Nov, 1 Nov and 25 Oct 2026). It is the quickest way in this group to see what UX practitioners are reading.

Newest editorial post: 8 Nov 2026 · Editorial posts in the last 90 days: 9 · Feed: https://www.stephaniewalter.design/feed/

Codrops

Codrops covers creative front-end work: WebGL and WebGPU effects, GSAP motion tutorials and case studies of experimental sites. Its 17 Nov post builds an infinite carousel of cloth posters with WebGPU. The feed blocks scripts, so we counted posts on its home page in a browser.

Newest editorial post: 17 Nov 2026 · Editorial posts in the last 90 days: at least 7 (the home page shows 9 to 17 Nov only) · Feed: https://tympanus.net/codrops/feed/

Best CSS and front-end blogs

CSS-Tricks

CSS-Tricks still publishes CSS techniques, such as staggering scroll-driven animations with animation-range-start. DigitalOcean has owned it since March 2022 and runs it as a standalone site. We left its 13 Nov Black Friday deals post out of the count.

Newest editorial post: 16 Nov 2026 · Editorial posts in the last 90 days: at least 13 · Feed: https://css-tricks.com/feed/

Josh W. Comeau

Josh W. Comeau writes long, interactive tutorials on CSS and React. He posted 8 times in the 12 months to 18 Nov 2026, most recently on 26 May, 6 Jul and 20 Oct, so this is a low-volume feed where each post is worth the time. The newest, The Future of CSS, looks ahead to Interop 2027.

Newest editorial post: 20 Oct 2026 · Editorial posts in the last 90 days: 1 (8 in 12 months) · Feed: https://www.joshwcomeau.com/rss.xml

Ahmad Shadeed

Ahmad Shadeed writes CSS layout articles built around visual experiments, such as his 15 Sep post on aligning icons with their labels. Read it when you want to understand why a layout breaks, as well as how to fix it.

Newest editorial post: 5 Nov 2026 · Editorial posts in the last 90 days: 5 · Feed: https://ishadeed.com/feed.xml

Rachel Andrew

Rachel Andrew is a member of the CSS Working Group and writes about CSS layout and newer features such as margin-trim. Her 2 Nov post is on making CSS features generic. Read it for the reasoning behind the spec.

Newest editorial post: 2 Nov 2026 · Editorial posts in the last 90 days: 5 · Feed: https://rachelandrew.co.uk/feed

Piccalilli

Piccalilli publishes front-end craft articles several times a week, plus The Index, a weekly issue of links (#205 on 6 Nov, #206 on 13 Nov 2026). It is creator-run and sells courses, and we excluded its course promotion. Its feed shows only five items.

Newest editorial post: 13 Nov 2026 · Editorial posts in the last 90 days: at least 4 · Feed: https://piccalil.li/feed.xml

CodePen Blog

The CodePen Blog is a vendor blog, but it carries Chris' Corner, a CSS and front-end column by Chris Coyier, who founded CSS-Tricks. The rest of the feed is podcast episodes, often about CodePen features, so we counted only the column.

Newest editorial post: 16 Nov 2026 · Editorial posts in the last 90 days: 8 · Feed: https://blog.codepen.io/feed/

Frontend Masters Blog

The Frontend Masters Blog belongs to a company that sells video courses, but the articles are free and arrive several times a week. A recent one builds diagrams and graphs with modern CSS alone.

Newest editorial post: 16 Nov 2026 · Editorial posts in the last 90 days: at least 10 · Feed: https://blog.master.dev/feed/

Browser, standards, performance and accessibility blogs

web.dev

web.dev is Google's site for web developers. Its blog publishes a monthly digest of what reached Baseline and what is new to the web platform. That makes it a quick way to see which features are newly safe to use across browsers.

Newest editorial post: 2 Oct 2026 · Editorial posts in the last 90 days: 5 · Feed: https://web.dev/static/blog/feed.xml

The Chrome for Developers blog covers Chrome releases and new APIs, such as what is new in WebGPU in Chrome 155 and 156. It is a vendor blog, and its feed holds only ten items, so the real cadence is higher than our count.

The WebKit blog is where Apple's engine team explains new Safari features and release notes. On 16 Nov 2026 it introduced a developer preview of spatial CSS. If your clients' visitors use iPhones, this feed tells you what Safari will support next.

Bram.us

Web development newsletters worth the inbox space

A newsletter needed at least three issues in the 90 days to make the list. Three did:

  • JavaScript Weekly: weekly JavaScript news. Issue 811 went out on 17 Nov 2026. Feed: https://cprss.s3.amazonaws.com/javascriptweekly.com.xml
  • CSS Layout News: monthly CSS layout links. Issues 345, 346 and 347 went out on 17 Sep, 8 Oct and 4 Nov 2026. Feed: https://csslayout.news/feed/

Piccalilli's The Index and Stephanie Walter's Pixels of the Week also read like weekly newsletters. CSS Weekly is missing on purpose, and the next section says why.

Good blogs that didn't make the list, and why

These fail one of the rules on 18 Nov 2026. Several are still worth reading if you know what you are getting. Awwwards, Dribbble and Siteinspire appear on other lists, but they are galleries for inspiration, not blogs, so we did not test them.

Slow but deep

Sara Soueidan posted two editorial pieces in the 12 months to 18 Nov 2026, the newest on 16 Nov about styling the text caret accessibly. A List Apart published two articles in that time, the newest on 30 Jun 2026, so it misses the 90-day line too. Both fail rule 2, and both deserve a feed slot if you accept long gaps.

Good, but mostly about other things

About four of Brad Frost's newest ten posts are on web design; the rest are music, personal posts and app links. Read him for design-systems work. Chris Coyier's personal blog is mostly personal, and his CSS writing now goes into Chris' Corner on the CodePen Blog. The freeCodeCamp News site is free and good for juniors, but only 4 of its newest 10 tutorials are web development.

Quiet for now

The MDN Blog last posted on 15 Jun 2026; use MDN as a reference, not a feed. The official Vue blog has not posted since "Announcing Vue 3.5" on 1 Sep 2024, so follow the Nuxt blog and Vue's GitHub releases instead. Post Status's newest item in its public feed is from 24 Jul 2026, 117 days before the check, so it misses the 90-day line for now.

Changed format

WP Tavern's feed shows no written post since 9 Jan 2025, and its home page now lists only weekly podcast episodes. CSS Weekly sent one issue in the 90 days: #640 on 12 Nov 2026 came 203 days after #639.

What happened to our 2018 list of the best web design blogs

On 12 April 2018 I published "20 Best Web Design and Development Blogs To Follow" on our old site. By then we had been building websites for ten years (Netling started in 2008). The intro promised "10 must-read blogs", "in no particular order", and then listed 20 plus a bonus, so 21 in all. It gave no rule for what made the cut, and no entry said when the blog had last posted.

Eight years on, I put all 21 through the same rules as the 2026 list, so you can see how a list like this ages. Seven of my 21 picks still pass.

The bigger change is in the kind of blog that made the cut. My 2018 list had no blogs run by the projects or browser makers themselves, and no newsletters. This year's list has eight of the first (React, Next.js, Nuxt, Node.js, Make WordPress Core, WebKit, Chrome for Developers and web.dev) and three newsletters. It also has eight personal blogs, each written by one person, from Josh W. Comeau to Adrian Roselli.

The split is 2 closed or absorbed, 9 with no editorial post in the 90 days, 3 active but off-topic, and 7 still passing: 21 in total. The off-topic group is our reading of their newest posts.

Closed or absorbed (2)

InVision announced on 5 Jan 2024 that its design and collaboration services would shut down, and accounts stayed open until 31 Dec 2024 (Silicon Republic). Its domain, invisionapp.com, now redirects to Miro.

Scotch.io joined DigitalOcean on 16 Dec 2019, which removed the paywall on its tutorials. The domain now redirects to DigitalOcean's community site.

No editorial post in the 90 days before 18 Nov 2026 (9)

These sites missed the 90-day line on 18 Nov 2026. Most are still online, and some still post roundups.

  • Hacking UI: no new post since 11 May 2018, a podcast episode a month after our list went up.
  • Envato Tuts+ Web Design: no new post found since 27 Jun 2025, 509 days before the check.
  • Hongkiat: about monthly (13 editorial items in 12 months) until 7 Aug 2026, then nothing for 103 days.
  • A List Apart: two articles in 12 months, the newest on 30 Jun 2026.
  • Onextrapixel: no editorial post since 5 Feb 2026, and only font roundups since; the newest item is from 24 Apr 2026.
  • David Walsh Blog: newest editorial post 20 Nov 2025. The only item since is a sponsored post on 9 Nov 2026.
  • Design Bombs: newest editorial post 27 Jul 2026, with font, template and plugin roundups since.
  • WPKube: all ten items in its feed, from 20 Feb to 14 Sep 2026, are product reviews or plugin roundups.
  • Design Shack: on 18 Nov 2026 its home page listed only template, font, mockup and preset roundups.

Active, but no longer mainly about web design (3)

  • Designmodo now sells email and website design tools, and its newest posts are a Black Friday sale, a deliverability webinar and email how-tos.
  • Toptal Blog, a talent marketplace's blog, has 2 web development posts among its newest 10. The rest cover NLP, robotics, Spring Batch, data structures and marketing.
  • Backlinko is an SEO site, owned by Semrush since January 2022.

Still pass the rule (7)

Smashing Magazine, Codrops, CSS-Tricks, SitePoint, Web Designer Depot, Speckyboy and Boagworld all made the 2026 list, and their entries above carry the dates.

Our reading, and not a law: the blogs that held up kept one clear topic, or have a named person writing them. Four of the nine that went quiet, Onextrapixel, Design Bombs, WPKube and Design Shack, drifted into asset roundups. The other five slowed down or stopped. When you prune your own reader, a feed that has turned into font and template lists is the first to go.

How to follow these blogs without drowning in them

Make one folder per group in your RSS reader. Most readers accept a pasted feed URL, so the ones above are all you need. Twice a year, check the date of each feed's newest editorial item, not its "last built" date. MDN's feed was rebuilt on 17 Nov 2026, but its newest post is from 15 Jun 2026. Drop anything quiet for 90 days.

When a blog is the wrong place to learn

For exact API behaviour, use MDN's reference pages and the specs. For a framework upgrade, use the official migration guide: a release post tells you a deadline exists, and the guide tells you what to change. For a bug on a deadline, start with the project's GitHub issues.

Frequently asked questions

What are the best web development blogs to follow?

For most front-end work, start with Smashing Magazine, CSS-Tricks, Josh W. Comeau, web.dev and the WebKit blog, plus Frontend Focus as your one newsletter. Add the release blog for each framework you ship. Designers, WordPress developers and agency owners get their own short sets at the end of this post.

Is CSS-Tricks still active?

Yes. Its newest editorial post was on 16 Nov 2026, with at least 13 in the 90 days before 18 Nov 2026, and DigitalOcean has owned it since March 2022. Founder Chris Coyier now writes Chris' Corner on the CodePen Blog.

What is the best newsletter for front-end developers?

Frontend Focus (weekly, issue 766 on 11 Nov 2026) for broad front-end news, JavaScript Weekly (issue 811 on 17 Nov 2026) for JavaScript, and CSS Layout News (monthly) for layout. CSS Weekly sent one issue in the 90 days, so check it before relying on it.

Are web design blogs still worth reading?

Yes, if you keep the list short. Search and AI tools answer the question you bring. A feed shows you what changed while you were not looking, such as the React Server Components security advisories in December 2025 or the WordPress 7.2 developer notes on 17 Nov 2026.

How can I tell whether a blog is still active?

Open its RSS feed and read the newest item's date, not the feed's "last built" date: MDN's feed was rebuilt on 17 Nov 2026, but its newest post is from 15 Jun 2026. Then check that the newest items are editorial: David Walsh's newest item is sponsored, and his last editorial post was on 20 Nov 2025.

Where to start: a short set for your role

Start with the set that fits your job, and add more only when you keep up with these:

  • Designer: Smashing Magazine, Nielsen Norman Group and Pixels of the Week.
  • Front-end developer: Josh W. Comeau, web.dev and the WebKit blog.
  • WordPress developer: Make WordPress Core and The Repository.
  • Agency owner: Boagworld and Speckyboy.

Everyone should add Frontend Focus as the one newsletter, plus the release blog for each framework you ship (React, Next.js, Nuxt or Node.js). Re-run the 90-day check every six months, and drop what has gone quiet. We will re-check this list in January 2027 and update every date.

If you run a small agency and these blogs are how your team stays sharp, but you are short on build capacity, our white label web development team builds sites under your brand. Tell us about the project when one comes up.

Originally published at netling.digital.

title: Per-customer API limits in six stacks: where the check has to run
description:
Every per-customer limit I've wired up comes down to the same five steps: work out which customer is calling, check their rate limit, reserve part of their quota, run the handler, then count what the request actually used. Those steps don't change between frameworks. What changes is where the framework lets you run code before and after a handler, what it tells you about the route that matched, and whether anything still runs once the response has gone out.

This post skips the rate limiting algorithm itself and looks at where the check ends up in each framework and what caught us out. The examples use the UsageRail SDKs, which I work on. Most of the constraints below come from the frameworks and would hit your own middleware too; a few, such as the synchronous consumer in Next.js, come from our SDK.

Three questions decide the placement:

  1. Does the check run before or after your own authentication?
  2. Which route can you record: /v1/items/:id, or /v1/items/42?
  3. Where does the work after the response run: a timer, a shutdown hook, or something like waitUntil?

Express: order is coverage

Express middleware applies to routes registered after it, and that is most of the placement rule:

import express from "express";
import { usageRail } from "@usagerail/node/express"; // import before your routers

const app = express();
app.get("/health", (req, res) => res.send("ok")); // registered first, never checked

app.use("/v1", usageRail({
  appKey: process.env.USAGERAIL_APP_KEY,
  auth: "api-key", // Authorization: Bearer <key>, or x-api-key
}));

Import order matters for a different reason. Express doesn't keep a router's mount path as you wrote it, so the SDK records mount paths as routers are mounted, which only works for routers mounted after the import. A router mounted before the import is still checked as long as its requests pass through the UsageRail middleware, but its usage is grouped by the concrete path, so /tenants/42/reports becomes its own row for every tenant. If you identify callers yourself, put your auth middleware first, set auth: "custom" and pass a consumer function that reads req.user.

On the client side, both refusals are a 429. On a rate-limit 429, Retry-After is the seconds until the customer's bucket has a token again. On a quota 429, it's the seconds left in the billing period, which can be days. A retry helper that sleeps on that header can park a job for 12 days, so clients should retry short waits and surface long ones.

Hono: reserve before the handler runs

Middleware registered with app.use("/v1/*", ...) runs before it knows which handler will answer. That matters when the quota is counted in units, because the reservation has to happen before the handler runs. The SDK matches the raw path against the route templates you've configured and takes the largest reservation among the templates that match. After the handler returns, it reads the route that actually ran with routePath(c) and records the usage there.

The other Hono-specific thing: the middleware doesn't touch the process, because Hono also runs where there isn't one. On Node.js you add two things yourself: flushOnExit(rail.engine), which sends pending counts at shutdown (without it they're lost), and fileSnapshotStore, which saves the key list so a restarted process can check keys before its first sync.

Streaming takes more care. In this Hono example that meters streamed tokens per customer, an SSE response counts once when the stream opens, and the units from track() are added when it ends or the client disconnects. Pass track() the running total after each chunk: it replaces the previous value, so calling track(1) per chunk records the whole stream as 1.

Next.js route handlers: wrap each one

App Router route handlers have no app.use, and middleware.ts runs before the handler without ever seeing the status it returns. So the check wraps the handler itself, and you pass the route template, because a route handler isn't told which file it came from:

// app/v1/items/[id]/route.js
import { rail } from "@/lib/usagerail"; // usageRail({ ..., waitUntil: after })

export const GET = rail.route("/v1/items/[id]", async (request, { params, usage }) => {
  const { id } = await params;
  const item = await loadItem(id);
  usage.track(item.size); // optional: count units instead of requests
  return Response.json(item);
});

middleware.ts still has a job if you use your own auth. The consumer function has to return synchronously, so a database lookup goes in middleware, which passes the account ID on in a request header. Make the middleware overwrite that header on every request, or a caller can send their own. The work after the response moves into after() from next/server, since a frozen instance may never fire a timer. If the platform stops an instance before that work finishes, the unsent counts are gone. In our October 2026 tests of after() on Vercel, every successful response was counted, including a burst of 70 requests at once that started 70 new instances.

Cloudflare Workers: set up on the first request

On Workers the code looks like the Hono version with serverless: true, plus nodejs_compat in the Wrangler config, because the SDK uses node:crypto. Two platform rules forced real changes. Workers refuse to generate random values while the module is loading, and the SDK creates an instance ID when it starts, so with serverless: true it sets itself up on the first request instead. Leave serverless: true out and the Worker fails to start. And there's no process to hook, so reporting, key-list refreshes and quota lease renewals go into c.executionCtx.waitUntil after each response, at most one batch every 0.5 seconds per isolate.

When we moved per-customer keys and quotas from Node.js into a Worker, revocation changed too. With no background sync, a request that finds the key list more than 20 seconds old tries to refresh it first, waiting up to 1 second, so a revoked key normally stops working within about 20 seconds, even on an isolate that sat idle. If UsageRail can't be reached, the isolate keeps using the list it already has, and a list more than 24 hours old isn't trusted.

Django REST framework: in front of DRF, not inside it

DRF's throttles handle "N requests per minute per user" well. We needed limits that come from each customer's plan plus a quota per billing period, and putting those quota checks in a plain Django middleware in front of DRF means they run before DRF does. With SessionAuthentication that's fine, because Django's AuthenticationMiddleware has already set request.user. With TokenAuthentication, a consumer that reads request.user still finds an anonymous user when the middleware runs, so those requests are recorded as anonymous: not rate limited, not counted against a quota and never billed. The fix is to call the auth class from the consumer:

# myapp/usage.py, set as USAGERAIL["consumer"] in settings.py
from rest_framework.authentication import TokenAuthentication
from rest_framework.exceptions import AuthenticationFailed


def consumer(request):
    try:
        result = TokenAuthentication().authenticate(request)
    except AuthenticationFailed:
        return None
    if result is None:
        return None
    user, _token = result
    return str(user.pk)

That costs a second token lookup per request. Running first has two other effects. Refused requests never reach DRF's exception handler or renderers, so a custom error format has to be set in on_reject. And router URLs are recorded as the regular expressions DRF builds, which route weights have to match exactly.

LiteLLM: count where you know the customer

LiteLLM isn't a web framework, but many LLM APIs get their token counts from it. If you sell an API and call models through the LiteLLM Python SDK, LiteLLM knows the tokens and has no idea which of your customers the call was for. To count LiteLLM token usage per customer, keep the check in your API layer. Here a FastAPI middleware checks the limits and the endpoint passes in the token count:

# Inside the FastAPI endpoint, after the model call
response = await litellm.acompletion(model=model, messages=messages)
# Prompt plus completion tokens, as reported by the provider
request.state.usagerail.track(response.usage.total_tokens)

The middleware decides whether to let the request in before the model runs, so each route needs a reservation sized for the most tokens one API request can use. For a single model call that's your max_tokens plus the largest prompt you accept. If one request makes several model calls, reserve for all of them, and add the actual tokens up before calling track(), because it replaces the value instead of adding to it. If you also run the LiteLLM proxy, its virtual keys can carry their own budgets and rate limits, and the two can run side by side.

What doesn't move

A few things were the same in all six:

  • Rate limit buckets live in memory, per process, per instance or per isolate. On Vercel or Workers that means a customer can get the full limit on every instance unless you split it across them. Our page on per-customer API rate limiting covers the token bucket and the response headers.
  • Refused requests and 4xx or 5xx responses aren't billed. They're still recorded, and they don't use up quota.
  • What happens at the limit is a pricing decision. A plan that stops at the quota answers 429 quota_exceeded with Retry-After set to the seconds left in the period. Prepaid credits answer 402 insufficient_credits once the balance is gone. A plan that bills overage keeps serving past the included units and puts the extra on the customer's invoice; rate limits still apply.

If your stack puts this check somewhere else, I'd like to hear where it ended up and what broke first.

I work on UsageRail. The examples use its Node.js (@usagerail/node) and Python (usagerail) SDKs.

I used AI to help draft this post.

title: Our import worker was killed for memory and the last log line we had was thirty thousand rows old
description:
Our supplier catalogue import is a Python worker running in Kubernetes. It reads each supplier's product file, validates every row and reports progress with print, one line per thousand rows, naming the supplier and the row. Run it on a laptop and you can watch it count through the file.

In October it was OOMKilled every night on one supplier's file. kubectl logs --previous ended at row 41,000, so we spent a morning reading rows 41,000 to 42,000 for anything that could blow up memory. They were ordinary. Running the same file locally showed memory climbing only after row 63,000, where the supplier had started pasting whole HTML pages into the description column, and the kill came about eight thousand rows after that.

The logs were not wrong. They were late. When Python's standard output is a terminal it is line buffered, and each print appears at once. In a container, standard output is a pipe to the runtime, and Python buffers it in blocks of a few kilobytes, writing only when the block fills or the program exits normally. Our progress lines were short, so one block held thirty of them. A process killed for memory receives SIGKILL, which nothing can catch, and whatever sat in the buffer is never written. We had been reading the last line that happened to be flushed, not the last line the worker printed.

Nothing had ever made us suspicious, because our tracebacks always arrived. Since Python 3.9, standard error is line buffered even when it is not a terminal, so errors came through promptly and progress did not.

Every Python base image we build now sets PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1. The worker reports progress through the logging module, whose stream handler flushes after every record, and it writes one JSON object per line with the supplier, the row and its own memory use. The import also streams the description column and rejects any field over a size limit, which was the actual bug.

In a terminal, print means now. In a container it means eventually, and a process killed for memory never gets to eventually.

– Sergey Shinder

title: How Many Training Labels Are Wrong? Auditing a Fitted Model through Gradient Allocation
description:
arXiv:2611.22449v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: How many labels in a training set are wrong, and which ones? The usual answers read a held-out set or the model's outputs. A held-out reading depends on how the held-out set was drawn, and an output-based reading fails once the model has fitted its wrong labels, because the loss of a fitted wrong label is small and the prediction agrees with it. We read the answer from the per-example gradients of a single trained model. Each example, together with its label, asks the network to change in a particular way. We normalise the magnitudes of its gradient into a gradient allocation and compare it with the mean allocation of every class. An example is flagged when relabelling it as its nearest other class makes its allocation fit better than under its own label, and the share of flagged examples is the reading of the noise rate. The rule has no threshold and needs no clean data, no held-out set and no further training. After the model has fitted 99-100% of its wrong labels, the allocation still separates wrong from right labels with an AUC of 0.94-0.96 on the noisiest human labels of CIFAR-10N, where a feature-space margin falls to 0.79-0.84 and the loss, the gradient norm and the self-influence of an example to 0.73-0.76. On such a fitted model, readings of the noise rate from predictions or feature margins fall to 0-6% at true rates of 8-58% on CIFAR-10 with ViT-S, while the audit reads 54-96% of the true rate, and at least 93% of the examples it counts carry wrong labels. On a briefly trained model, before the wrong labels are fitted, the reading lies within 1.7 percentage points of the true noise rate on CIFAR-10 from 0% to 58% noise. Confident learning, which trains four further models, separates wrong labels about as well (AUC 0.925-0.998 against 0.900-0.995) and mostly reads the noise rate more closely, at a lower precision. An audit of 5,000 examples takes 14 to 27 seconds on one GPU.

title: Gemini price increases: Carbon and Argon double on 1 December 2026, Flash on 1 January 2027
description:
Google's pricing page lists scheduled price increases for several Gemini models. If you have workloads on them, your costs change on fixed dates, with no change in usage.

Written with AI assistance. Figures were read from Google's pricing page on 18 November 2026; check it again before you budget.

What the page says

All prices are USD per 1 million tokens, standard paid tier.

Model Now Scheduled change
Gemini 4 Carbon $2 in / $10 out $4 in / $20 out from 1 December 2026
Gemini 4 Argon $2 in / $10 out $4 in / $20 out from 1 December 2026
Gemini 3.8 Flash $0.75 input $1.50 input from 1 January 2027
Gemini 3.6 Flash $0.75 input $1.50 input from 1 January 2027
Gemini 4 Hydrogen $1.50 input no change listed on the page

The pattern on the page is that these standard prices double. Batch prices on the same page double too, for example Carbon batch input goes from $1 to $2.

A worked example

A workload of 10 million input and 2 million output tokens a month on Carbon or Argon:

  • Until 30 November: 10 x $2 + 2 x $10 = $40
  • From 1 December: 10 x $4 + 2 x $20 = $80

Same usage, double the bill.

What you can do

  • Re-run your estimate with the new rates before the date, not after the invoice.
  • Test a cheaper tier for tasks that do not need the biggest model. Quality differs, so measure it on your own prompts.
  • Use batch and caching where the provider offers them. They help, but batch prices rise as well.
  • Compare providers on their own pages: Anthropic (https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing) and OpenAI (https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/pricing).

Source: Google's pricing page, https://aistudio.google.com/docs/pricing

I keep a dated page that switches to the new rate automatically on the effective date: Gemini 4 pricing. It runs in your browser and is not a substitute for checking Google's page.

title: The Hidden Cost of MoE Diffusion Decoding: Profiling and Fixing the Sampler
description:
arXiv:2611.21852v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Masked diffusion language models (dLLMs) decode by iteratively denoising a full canvas of tokens, so every forward pass runs a per-token sampling and stopping pipeline over the entire canvas-by-vocabulary logits tensor. We profile single-user decoding of a 26B-parameter diffusion Mixture-of-Experts model on a bandwidth-bound edge accelerator (NVIDIA GB10) and report a result that is easy to miss: after weight quantisation, this logits pipeline, not the expert GEMMs, is the single largest consumer of decode time. Unlike autoregressive decoding, where sampling touches one position's logits per committed token, diffusion decoding processes S times as many logit entries per output token, where S is the number of denoising steps. We show this pipeline is largely redundant or fusable and remove it in two lossless tiers: a bit-exact tier whose output is byte-identical to the reference decoder, and an accuracy-parity tier using a fused single-pass entropy kernel and Gumbel-max sampling. Combined with a W4A16 expert kernel, the full stack reaches 2.4-2.7 times end-to-end speedup over bf16 at unchanged benchmark accuracy on GSM8K, HumanEval, and MATH, on a single 273 GB/s device. We confirm the finding on a second, independently built diffusion MoE (LLaDA2.0-mini: pipeline 28.8% of decode, fused W4A16 3.3 times at accuracy parity) and show it disappears on a dense diffusion model (3.6%). The cost is specific to MoE diffusion, where quantisation makes the backbone cheap. Code and quantised weights are released.

title: Bringing the Semantic Web to GitLab Pages: Implementing RFC 9110 Content Negotiation in Go
description:
The Semantic Web and Linked Open Data (LOD) initiatives rely on a foundational principle: a single persistent URI (e.g., https://example.com/alice or https://example.com/ontology) should be accessible to both humans in their web browsers and machines consuming semantic data models.

Through HTTP Content Negotiation, a browser requesting Accept: text/html receives a styled HTML page, while an RDF crawler or knowledge-graph ingestion pipeline requesting Accept: text/turtle or Accept: application/ld+json receives machine-readable triples from the exact same URI.

In my recent contribution to GitLab Pages (MR !1384, closing Issue #1135), I designed and implemented RFC 9110-compliant content negotiation for static sites hosted on GitLab Pages.

Here is an engineering deep-dive into how we implemented media-type negotiation, specificity weighting, and cache safety in Go.

1. The Problem: Extensionless URLs in Static Hosting

Historically, GitLab Pages mapped extensionless HTTP requests (GET /research-paper or GET /) exclusively to .html (or index.html).

For scientific organizations, academic publishers, and open-data projects hosting ontologies on GitLab Pages:

  • A browser requesting /schema received schema.html.
  • A machine or graph database sending Accept: application/rdf+xml or Accept: text/turtle still received HTML or a 404 error.

Because static sites couldn't resolve semantic file variants without forcing users to type explicit extensions like schema.ttl, GitLab Pages could not serve Linked Data in compliance with W3C best practices.

2. Designing an RFC 9110 Compliant Accept Parser in Go

HTTP content negotiation is defined in RFC 9110 (Section 12.5.1). A robust content negotiation parser must handle:

  1. Quality Values (q): Entries with higher weights (q=1.0 vs q=0.5) take priority. Zero quality (q=0) rejects the type.
  2. Specificity Weighting:
    • Exact type/subtype: application/ld+json (highest precedence)
    • Subtype wildcards: text/* (medium precedence)
    • Global wildcards: */* (lowest precedence)

We built a parser that parses candidate media types and orders them by quality and specificity:

type MediaRange struct {
    Type       string
    Subtype    string
    Quality    float64
    Specificity int
}

When a client sends:

Accept: text/html;q=0.8, text/turtle;q=0.9, */*;q=0.1

The parser evaluates text/turtle ($q=0.9$) first, followed by text/html ($q=0.8$), and finally the wildcard fallback.

3. Mapping Media Types to Semantic File Extensions

GitLab Pages now recognizes common Linked Data and Semantic Web formats:

MIME Media Type File Extension Format Description
text/turtle .ttl Terse RDF Triple Language
application/ld+json .jsonld JSON for Linked Data
application/rdf+xml .rdf Resource Description Framework XML
application/n-triples .nt N-Triples
text/n3 .n3 Notation3
application/owl+xml .owl Web Ontology Language
text/html, application/xhtml+xml .html HyperText Markup Language

Resolution Algorithm:

  1. When receiving a request for /dataset:
  2. Inspect the client's Accept header.
  3. For each candidate media type in descending preference order, test if the corresponding file exists on disk (e.g., dataset.ttl, dataset.jsonld, dataset.rdf).
  4. If a match is found, serve that file with the matching Content-Type header.
  5. If no semantic file matches or no Accept header is provided, safely fall back to the default dataset.html.

4. Cache Correctness: Why Vary: Accept is Crucial

In static web hosting and CDNs, caching responses correctly is just as important as serving them.

If a CDN caches dataset.html for GET /dataset, a subsequent request from an RDF crawler with Accept: text/turtle would mistakenly receive the cached HTML from the CDN edge server!

To prevent cache poisoning:

  • Whenever content negotiation takes place, GitLab Pages appends: 
  Vary: Accept
  • This instructs CDNs, reverse proxies, and browsers that the cached representation depends strictly on the incoming Accept header.
  • Direct extension requests (e.g., GET /dataset.ttl) bypass negotiation and do not emit unnecessary Vary headers.

5. Testing & Verification

The feature is covered by unit tests and end-to-end integration tests in TestReader_ContentNegotiation:

  • Directory Indexes: GET / with Accept: application/rdf+xml serves index.rdf.
  • Quality Fallbacks: Verifying that q=0.9 wins over q=0.7.
  • Graceful HTML Fallback: If an unsupported media type is requested, standard HTML is delivered without breaking normal user navigation. 
go test -v ./internal/vfs/zip -run '^TestReader_ContentNegotiation$'

Conclusion

With this contribution, thousands of static websites hosted on GitLab Pages can now serve both human-friendly documentation and Linked Open Data from identical canonical URLs.

Special thanks to the GitLab Pages maintainers for their thorough reviews and guidance throughout this implementation!

Check out the merged implementation on GitLab:

👉 GitLab Pages MR !1384

title: You Embedded Questions and Documents the Same Way and Your Model Expected Them Labelled
description:
The search over the help centre
was built in a week.

An open embedding model.

Every article,
split and embedded.

Every customer question,
embedded the same way.

Nearest neighbours.

Done.

It worked.

Mostly.

Short questions did badly.

"refund card"
returned other short things.

Titles.

Headings.

Fragments that looked
like the question,
not the answer to it.

The team tried bigger chunks,
smaller chunks,
a reranker.

Nobody had read
the model card to the end.

The model was from the E5 family.

Its card says
every input should start with
"query: "
or
"passage: ".

And then, in the FAQ,
plainly:
yes, you need the prefix,
or you will see
a performance drop.

Here is the mechanism.

Some embedding models
are trained asymmetric.

During training,
questions carried one label
and documents carried another.

The model learned
two slightly different jobs.

For a query:
what is this person looking for.

For a passage:
what does this text contain.

Leave the labels off
and both sides
get embedded as the same kind of thing.

Then a short question
sits nearest
to other short text,
because that is what
it most resembles.

Similar wording wins.

The answer loses.

And nothing errors.

The scores still come back
between zero and one,
the top result still looks plausible,
and the dashboard stays green.

The fix was two strings:

query: refund card
passage: To refund a card payment...

Then re-embed every document,
because the stored vectors
were made without the label.

E5 is not alone.

Nomic's text model
wants "search_query: "
and "search_document: ".

BGE suggests
an instruction
in front of short queries.

Others want none at all.

So the prefix
is part of the model's interface,
like an argument
a function cannot work without.

Your code will not fail
when you forget it.

It will just return
something close
to the right answer,
every day,
forever.

Read the model card
to the last line.

Then write a test
with ten real questions
and the article each one should find.

– Serguey Asael Shinder

title: Unsupervised Multi-modal Medical Image Registration via Invertible Translation
description:
arXiv:2611.22152v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In medical imaging, the alignment of multi-modal images plays a critical role in providing comprehensive information for image-guided therapies. Despite its importance, multi-modal image registration poses significant challenges due to the complex and often unknown spatial relationships between different image modalities. To address this, we introduce a novel unsupervised translation-based multi-modal registration method, termed Invertible Neural Network-based Registration (INNReg). INNReg consists of an image-to-image translation network that converts multi-modal images into mono-modal counterparts and a registration network that uses the translated mono-modal images to align the multi-modal images. Specifically, to ensure the preservation of geometric consistency after image translation, we introduce an Invertible Neural Network (INN) that leverages a dynamic depthwise convolution-based local attention mechanism. Additionally, we design a novel barrier loss function based on Normalized Mutual Information to impose constraints on the registration network, which enhances the registration accuracy. The superior performance of INNReg is demonstrated through experiments on two public multi-modal medical image datasets, including MRI T1/T2 and MRI/CT pairs. The code is available at https://github.com/MeggieGuo/INNReg

title: We measured 9 video models' real per-second cost (bills included)
description:
Video generation is the one part of the API market where nobody publishes an honest unit price. Every provider quotes "per second", but what one second actually costs depends on resolution, duration rounding, whether frames are billed as input, and how the task is settled. So we did the boring thing: we called nine video models with an identical 4-second prompt, then read the billing delta from the upstream account before and after each call.

All numbers below are paid, measured, USD per second of generated video. Prompt: a calm sea at sunrise, duration 4s, single call each, CNY→USD at 6.8 (we settled in CNY).

Measured upstream cost

Model Upstream cost (USD/sec) 4s call (USD) Wall time
grok-imagine-video 0.0132 0.053 67s
veo-3.1-fast 0.0199 0.080 55s
grok-imagine-video-1.5 0.0212 0.085 90s
gemini-omni-flash-1.1 0.0265 0.106 61s
gemini-omni-flash-1.2 0.0265 0.106 61s
veo-3.1 0.0331 0.132 48s
doubao-seedance-2.0-fast 0.0802 0.321 139s
doubao-seedance-2.0 / 2.5-flash 0.0997 0.399 134–158s
wan3.0-video-prime 0.2118 0.847 140s

Three findings that surprised us:

1. The spread is 16×. grok-imagine-video and wan3.0-video-prime are the same task at the same length, and one costs 16 times the other. If you are picking a video model by "which one looks newer", you are picking your bill at random.

2. Wall time does not track price. The cheapest model finished in 67s; the second cheapest took 55s; the most expensive took 140s. Cheap and slow is a real trade-off, but "expensive" bought us nothing in latency either.

3. Some models are simply not there. kling-3.0, kling-3.0-omni and kling-3.0-motion-control returned 502/400 on submit; seedance-2.0* and gemini-omni-flash (non-1.1/1.2) returned model_not_found with no available channel. Five of sixteen candidates did not produce a single frame. We removed them from our catalogue rather than letting them fail after your credit is held.

What it means if you are buying

A 4-second clip at 0.0132/sec costs 5 cents. The same clip at 0.2118/sec costs 85 cents. Run 100 clips a month and the choice is $5 versus $85 — for outputs most people cannot tell apart without a side-by-side.

Two practical rules we now apply internally:

  • Price per second × duration is the only comparable number. Per-call pricing hides the duration multiplier; per-resolution pricing hides the frame billing.
  • Test the settle, not the submit. A task that returns queued proves nothing. We only treat a model as available after the file URL comes back and the billing delta lands.

How we call them

Our gateway exposes the same nine models behind one endpoint, so switching is a one-line change:

curl https://tapixai.com/v1/videos \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TAPIX_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model":"veo-3.1-fast","prompt":"a calm sea at sunrise","duration":4}'

Then poll the returned id:

curl https://tapixai.com/v1/videos/$TASK_ID -H "Authorization: Bearer $TAPIX_KEY"

You get status: queued → completed and a file URL. Billing is per second of generated video, charged only when the task completes; a failed task releases the hold.

We publish these numbers because we would rather you trust a bill you can reproduce than a comparison table you cannot. If a cheaper model appears upstream, it shows up in our catalogue the next morning.

New accounts start with $1 of credit — enough for roughly 5–50 of the clips above depending on which model you try. No card required.

title: What Claude actually gets from a screen recording, token counts for 4 ways to send it
description:
Claude can't open your screen recording. Anthropic's vision docs list JPEG, PNG, GIF and WebP as input formats, and for a GIF only the first frame is used. Codex and ChatGPT take images too, not MP4.

So when a bug needs a 43 second repro, something has to turn the video into what the model can read. I tried four ways on the same recording: 43 seconds, 3 screens, a few clicks on X.com.

1. Still frames

Each frame is an image, and Claude 4.7 counts image tokens in 28px patches: ceil(width/28) x ceil(height/28). A 1440x900 frame is 52 x 33 = 1,716 tokens.

One frame per screen is 3 frames, about 5,150 tokens. One frame per second is 43 frames, about 73,800 tokens, and once a request carries more than 20 images the per-image size limit gets stricter.

Either way the clicks are gone. You see the screen before and after, not which button was pressed.

2. One tall stitched page

Stitching the whole flow into one long image looks clever and costs almost nothing. That's the problem.

Claude 4.7 shrinks any image to 2576px on the long edge (older models 1568px). A 2540x18410 page arrives as 355x2576, about 1,196 tokens, and 16px body text ends up around 2.2px tall. On older models it's 216x1568 and 1.4px.

The same thing happens with Playwright fullPage: true captures. Odilon Hugonnot's CLAUDE.md for mobile redesign uses full-page screenshot scripts at 375 to 768px, and on a long mobile page those get squeezed the same way before Claude checks them. Crop to the viewport, or slice the page into tiles with a small overlap so a line cut at the seam still shows whole in one tile.

3. Gemini, which does take video

Gemini is the one model here that accepts video. It samples 1 frame per second at about 100 tokens per second at default resolution, so the 43 second clip is about 4,300 tokens.

Cheapest of the four. It still only sees one frame a second, so a quick click between two samples can disappear, and you're outside Claude or Codex for that question.

4. The recording as JSON

This one skips pixels. SlimSnap records the screen with voice and writes JSON next to the MP4: one frame per screen with its text and positions, every click with the control it hit and the screen it led to, and each spoken sentence tied to the element under the pointer.

The same 43 seconds came to 6.3k tokens of JSON.

It costs more than Gemini and far less than a frame per second. What you get for it is that "I clicked Save and nothing happened" reaches the model as the actual control plus the screen that came after.

Which one to send

You want to show Send
One screen One cropped screenshot
A long page Viewport-sized tiles, not one tall image
A flow, and you use Gemini The MP4
A flow, and you use Claude or Codex One frame per screen, or JSON with the clicks

Reproduce the numbers

Tokens for one image on Claude 4.7:

python3 -c "import math;w,h=1440,900;print(math.ceil(w/28)*math.ceil(h/28))"

The size Claude actually sees for a tall page:

python3 -c "w,h=2540,18410;s=2576/max(w,h);print(round(w*s),round(h*s))"

A still at each screen change, to send as frames:

ffmpeg -ss 4.5 -i repro.mp4 -frames:v 1 screen2.png
