title: Fidelity Regret: Measuring Simulator Misspecification in Verifiable Design
description:
arXiv:2611.22263v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: RLVF assumes the verifier evaluates the quantity of interest. In genetic-circuit design, a topological verifier can establish that a program is a valid circuit computing the target function, whereas ranking its physical performance requires a simulator. We measure fidelity regret, the reference simple regret incurred when a cheap simulator selects the design, over a 21,362-design combination subspace spanning 5 measured gate libraries and 3 organisms. Exact ordered-assignment checks retain positive regret in every tested cell while shifting magnitudes in both directions. Mean normalized regret is 0.369 over 72 cells and only 6 have zero regret. The discrepancy depends strongly on the reference axis: the yeast library SC1C1G1T1 has mean regret 0.113 for cytometry quality and 0.801 for growth burden, and every evaluated library--circuit-size pair has positive burden regret. Topological verification ties all valid gate assignments, while an oracle whitelist subject to retaining at least 25% of the design space leaves positive regret in 30 of 52 cells. Design-space optimization and feedback-guided search with frozen language models reach the high-regret regions; on a matched zero-regret control, additional optimization instead reduces regret. At a matched modeled-cost budget, mitigation is budget- and library-dependent. An in-sample fixed rule spending $\alpha{=}0.34$ of the budget re-scoring top cheap-simulator designs achieves mean excess regret 0.016, compared with 0.305 for cheap-only and 0.034 for reference-only selection, improving on cheap-only in 330 of 360 cells. More broadly, any workflow optimized through a simulator or digital twin can satisfy its verifier yet perform poorly on the intended physical objective. Fidelity regret provides a transferable template for detecting this gap before optimization and comparing budget-aware remedies across scientific domains.

title: October 28, 2026
description:
AlloyDB for PostgreSQL

Announcement

The following AlloyDB AI and vector search features and improvements are generally available (GA):

  • The alloydb_scann extension supports four-level tree (4LT) ScaNN vector indexes on PostgreSQL 17 and later, providing support for tables with up to 10 billion vector rows. For more information, see Four-level ScaNN tree indexes.

  • 4LT ScaNN vector indexes support automatic index maintenance. For more information, see Create a ScaNN index and Maintain vector indexes automatically.

  • You can enable streaming functionality for ScaNN vector indexes by setting the scann.satisfy_limit parameter to relaxed_order. When enabled, the vector scan continues searching through additional leaf partitions until it finds enough results to satisfy the LIMIT clause of your query, improving recall on filtered searches. Additionally, you can enable this feature for parallel process scans by setting the scann.enable_parallel_satisfy_limit database flag to on. For more information, see ScaNN index reference and Best practices for tuning ScaNN indexes.

  • Vector assist simplifies the deployment and management of your AlloyDB vector workloads by helping you set up production-ready vector search capabilities, including embedding generation, query optimization, and index creation for vector types such as Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW). For more information, see Vector assist overview.

  • For AlloyDB for PostgreSQL instances running PostgreSQL 17 and later, the maximum supported value for num_leaves when building ScaNN vector indexes is increased from 30,000,000 to 104,857,600. For more information, see Create a ScaNN index and ScaNN index reference.

  • You can use the external_search_fdw extension to connect to external search clusters and query their data directly from your database using the following search sources:

    • Elasticsearch

    • Solr

    • OpenSearch

  • AlloyDB supports the rum extension for high-performance full-text search operations on PostgreSQL 17 and earlier. The rum extension extends standard GIN indexes by storing positional information directly in the index, letting you perform faster phrase searches and relevance ranking without accessing the table data. For more information, see Create and manage a RUM index.

Fixed

AlloyDB provides more accurate memory usage estimation and prevents out-of-memory (OOM) errors when you build a ScaNN four-level tree index. This feature is in Preview. This update improves the stability of index builds by enforcing memory limits and improving memory estimation under constrained conditions.

Feature

Identity and Access Management (IAM) group authentication is generally available (GA) for new and existing AlloyDB clusters running PostgreSQL 15 and later. With IAM group authentication, you can manage database roles and privileges at the group level across primary instances and read pool instances, including first-time sign-ins directly to read pool instances. You can also preserve individual and IAM group user configurations when you migrate from a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL backup.

For more information, see IAM database authentication overview and Manage IAM authentication.

Security

In response to GCP-2026-071, Google is updating AlloyDB managed components. The fix to the certificate store is shipped in a new maintenance version that AlloyDB applies during scheduled maintenance, so you don't need to manually update AlloyDB managed instances. You can also apply the fix by performing self-service maintenance.

Depending on how you connect to AlloyDB, take the following actions:

  • If you use the AlloyDB Auth Proxy, then upgrade it to v1.17.2 or later. If you run the standalone proxy binary, then also update the host's certificate authority (CA) certificates.

  • If you use the AlloyDB Language Connectors, then update the language runtime and operating system CA certificates (for example, Go 1.26.10 or 1.27.3 or later).

Application Integration

Security

A Deserialization of Untrusted Data vulnerability was discovered in the SubWorkflow task in Application Integration versions prior to September 11, 2026. For more information, see the GCP-2026-074 security bulletin.

Feature

Application Integration agent skills

Application Integration agent skills are available in the public google/skills repository: application-integration-basics, application-integration-authoring, and application-integration-troubleshooting. AI coding agents that use these skills can help you set up Application Integration; build, publish, and run integrations through the REST API; and troubleshoot failed runs. For more information, see Application Integration agent skills and Build an integration with an AI agent.

Bigtable

Feature

You can configure Bigtable tables with microsecond timestamp granularity to capture and store high-frequency data. By supporting microsecond precision for cell timestamps, Bigtable helps you prevent data loss from write collisions in workloads with high event rates. This feature is generally available (GA) for instances in the Enterprise Plus edition. For more information, see Data type enforcement in Bigtable.

Cloud Asset Inventory

Feature

The following resource types are publicly available through the ExportAssets, ListAssets, BatchGetAssetsHistory, QueryAssets, Feed, and Search (SearchAllResources, SearchAllIamPolicies) APIs.

  • Google Cloud Migration Center
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/DiscoveryClient
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/Group
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/ImportJob
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/PreferenceSet
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/ReportConfig
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/Settings
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/Source

Cloud Database Migration Service

Feature

Database Migration Service for homogeneous SQL Server migrations now supports Distributed Availability Group (DAG) migrations in general availability (GA).

With DAG migrations, you can use gcloud CLI and Database Migration Service API to migrate databases from self-managed SQL Server Enterprise Edition instances directly to Cloud SQL for SQL Server over a private network connection. DAG migrations don't require exporting backup or transaction log files to Cloud Storage, and support post-promotion reverse replication for zero-data-loss failback.

For more information, see About Distributed Availability Group (DAG) migrations and Migrate from self-managed SQL Server using Distributed Availability Groups.

Cloud SQL for MySQL

Feature

Managed replica indexes for Cloud SQL for MySQL are generally available (GA). This feature lets you automatically retain and restore secondary indexes on read replica instances when Cloud SQL re-creates a replica.

Previously, re-creating a read replica deleted custom secondary indexes because primary backups don't have replica-only index definitions. With managed replica indexes, Cloud SQL tracks secondary index metadata on the primary instance, replicates this metadata to read replicas, and automatically rebuilds secondary indexes after replica re-creation.

Managed replica indexes are supported on instances that are running Cloud SQL for MySQL 8.0 or later, Cloud SQL Enterprise edition or Cloud SQL Enterprise Plus edition, and maintenance version R20260726.00_05 or later.

For more information, see Read replica indexes overview and Create and manage read replica indexes.

Confidential Space

Announcement

A new Confidential Space image (261001) is available. This image removes compromised CA certificates from the OS trust store. See the security bulletin for more details.

This image also adds support for running workload containers as a non-root user. Workload authors can require non-root execution with the tee.launch_policy.nonroot_container launch policy, and workload operators can enable it with the tee-nonroot-container metadata variable. For more information, see Non-root container execution.

Gemini Enterprise

This location is available in GA with allowlist. To get access to this location for use with Gemini Enterprise, contact your Google account team.

For more information, see Data residency for Gemini Enterprise.

For Gemini Enterprise apps, we recommend associating each Agent Gateway with a single regional Agent Registry instance in the same project and region as the gateway. Use the us-central1 registry for global and us apps, and the europe-west1 registry for eu apps.

This note updates the September 9, 2026 entry. For more information, see Register your agents and destination resources.

Fixed

CodeMender updates (v0.17.0)

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Support bundle diagnostics: Introduce cm support-bundle to collect environment metadata, configuration policies, health reports, and session logs into a compressed archive for streamlined troubleshooting.
  • Plain output mode: Add the persistent --plain flag (configurable via the CM_PLAIN environment variable or output.plain in config.yaml) to suppress decorative emojis, ANSI escape sequences, and Unicode borders for compatibility with screen readers and CI/CD log pipelines.
  • Dedicated exit codes for setup failures: Assign distinct exit codes (such as code 10 for credential issues) to configuration and authentication failures, preventing CI/CD pipelines from confusing environment setup issues with security findings.
  • Tailored CI/CD credential guidance: Provide environment-specific authentication guidance when running inside automated CI/CD systems such as GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Buildkite, and Jenkins instead of interactive login prompts.
  • Single-line JSONL statistics: Add the --jsonl flag to cm stats to output single-line JSON records with model and team attribution for seamless integration with Cloud Logging and log aggregation pipelines.
  • Granular sandbox and policy flags: Replace the overloaded --unrestricted flag with orthogonal flags (--sandbox=false) and configurable command policies to decouple container sandboxing from execution safety controls.
  • Sandbox configuration protections: Mount .git/hooks, .git/config, and .codemender read-only within writable execution sandboxes during cm fix and cm verify to prevent modifications to repository security policies.
  • Bug fixes:
    • Added a security warning when commands are executed with both sandbox isolation disabled and interactive approval skipped.
    • Enforced allowedRoots path boundaries across host discovery and remediation file operations to prevent traversal via dangling symlinks.
    • Supplied exact finding line ranges to remediation agents during cm fix to eliminate manual file scanning overhead.
    • Updated cm report import to properly treat findings without location data as file-level findings rather than defaulting to the first line.
    • Ensured cm session cancel routes requests to the session's original region regardless of local environment overrides.
    • Fixed finding status tracking in cm verify so unexploitable verdicts update the local state database rather than leaving findings open.

For more information, see the CodeMender documentation.

Google SecOps

Fixed

Tools power-up: Environment filtering in Get Integration Instances

There was an issue where the Get Integration Instances action in the Tools power-up didn't correctly filter environments with names that contain an ampersand (&). This issue has been fixed in version 85.0 of the Tools power-up.

For more information, see Get Integration Instances.

title: TeleChat to Xing4: Advancing Frontier Agentic Models on Domestic Chips and Frameworks
description:
arXiv:2611.22115v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present Xing 4, a series of large language models that extends the TeleChat lineage through coordinated advances in model architecture and training infrastructure on Ascend. This report describes the design principles and systems engineering behind the series, spanning architecture selection, large-scale pretraining, and reasoning and agentic post-training. We study how sparse activation, attention design, model depth and width, and speculative decoding balance model capacity with computation, memory access, and execution overhead. Our pretraining infrastructure builds on MindSpore HyperParallel, combining topology-aware hybrid sharding, efficient distributed optimizer execution, and coordinated management of long-sequence workloads and activation memory. CPU affinity and core isolation further reduce host scheduling interference. Together, these mechanisms support the pretraining of a 285B-parameter model on 8,192 Ascend 910C cards, providing a concrete setting for the architectural and systems studies. For post-training, we introduce TeleGym, a unified agent execution platform that connects execution, evaluation, and trajectory construction to policy optimization. Disaggregated asynchronous execution, bounded oversampling, and partial rollout accommodate heterogeneous task durations while preserving trajectory continuity across policy updates. Together, these advances establish an Ascend-oriented training foundation for the continued development of Xing 4 across model scales and increasingly demanding reasoning and agent workloads.

title: Vercel MCP now supports Client ID Metadata Documents
description:
Any MCP client can now ask to connect to Vercel MCP. You still log in and approve each connection, but the client no longer has to be reviewed by Vercel first. Previously, Vercel reviewed and allowlisted each client and its redirect URIs by hand, and anything not on the list was rejected.

To connect, a client publishes a Client ID Metadata Document (CIMD), a JSON file on its own domain that describes it, and uses that file's HTTPS URL as its OAuth client_id. This follows the MCP authorization spec, which now recommends CIMD over Dynamic Client Registration.

Because Vercel hasn't reviewed these clients, the consent screen shows where each one comes from: its name, its logo, and the hostname that serves its metadata document, for example "Claude Code by claude.ai". CIMD clients don't get the Vercel verified badge, so the hostname is what you're trusting when you approve.

Apps already registered with Vercel are unchanged.

Read the Vercel MCP documentation to connect your client.

title: DiscoveryAgent: A Framework for Scientist-centric Agentic AI
description:
arXiv:2611.21950v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI agents can assist scientific research, but balancing autonomous investigation with scientists' ability to inspect and redirect ongoing work remains a central design challenge. We present DiscoveryAgent, a domain-agnostic, scientist-centric system that combines autonomous investigation with scientist-directed hypothesis steering. Scientists select, refine, or replace hypotheses between research rounds, while audit agents interrogate checkpointed records to trace claims, reproduce analyses, and inform subsequent decisions. Across two predictive modeling tasks, DiscoveryAgent produced the best variable-star classifier among evaluated baselines and, with scientist steering, a protein variant-effect predictor surpassed by only one of 106 ProteinGym baselines. We develop a rigorous checkpointing system that enables highly capable audit agents, a scalable form of oversight for agentic research. Audit agents autonomously identify errors at higher rates than previous AI scientist agents, and scientists collaborating with audit agents identify 14x more valid errors versus scientists performing manual review. In three case studies led by domain experts across physical science, social science, and life science, we developed a multimodal photometric-redshift estimator that resolves complementary failures of images and photometry, achieving 0.971 AUROC for low-redshift classification; documented an 83% rise in Florida homeowners-insurance premiums from 2013 to 2023, with a growing, regressive burden; and identified CD4+ T-cell relay genes, which both receive and exert broad transcriptional regulation, enriched for autoimmune disease associations. Together, these results show how autonomous research can expand scientists' empirical reach while centering their authority over research direction and their ability to understand and challenge the evidence.

title: Your Go Function Returned a Nil Error and the Caller Saw an Error Anyway
description:
The order service
had a validation step.

It returned an error
if the quantity was wrong,
and nothing if it was fine.

type QtyError struct{ Qty int }

func (e *QtyError) Error() string {
return fmt.Sprintf("bad quantity %d", e.Qty)
}

func validate(o Order) error {
var err *QtyError
if o.Qty <= 0 {
err = &QtyError{o.Qty}
}
return err
}

The caller did the usual thing:

if err := validate(o); err != nil {
reject(o, err)
}

Every order was rejected.

Including the good ones.

Then the log line
that printed the reason
crashed with a nil pointer dereference.

Here is the mechanism.

In Go,
an interface value has two parts.

A type.

And a value.

It equals nil
only when both are empty.

validate returns error,
which is an interface.

Inside, err was a *QtyError
that happened to be nil.

Returning it
put the type *QtyError
into the interface,
with a nil pointer as the value.

Type filled in.

Value empty.

So err != nil
was true.

An interface holding a nil pointer
is not a nil interface.

The Go FAQ has a whole entry on it,
titled
"Why is my nil error value not equal to nil?"

And Error() ran
on a nil *QtyError,
reached for e.Qty,
and panicked.

The fix is small.

Return the interface,
not the concrete pointer:

func validate(o Order) error {
if o.Qty <= 0 {
return &QtyError{o.Qty}
}
return nil
}

That nil
is the untyped kind,
and it reaches the caller
as a true nil.

The rule underneath:

never declare a variable
of your own error type
and return it as error.

Declare it as error,
or return nil by name.

The same trap waits
anywhere a nil pointer
is handed to an interface.

A nil *bytes.Buffer
passed as an io.Writer.

A nil *Config
stored in an any.

Each one
looks like nothing
and compares as something.

When a check says
something is there
and you can see nothing,
ask what type
it was wrapped in.

– Serguey Asael Shinder

title: How Much of SAR Vehicle Recognition Is the Vehicle? Background Shortcuts, Angle Gaps and Partial Libraries on MSTAR and ATRNet-STAR
description:
arXiv:2611.21827v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Deep networks score near 99% on the MSTAR vehicle benchmark, and the newer ATRNet-STAR benchmark was built to be harder. We ask how much of these scores comes from the vehicle itself. With a modern network (ConvNeXt-Small, 3 seeds) we first reproduce the known MSTAR result: with the central 96x96 pixels zeroed out, accuracy is still 73.3% (chance 10%). The same shortcut is present in ATRNet-STAR, which was collected across several scenes: with the vehicle removed, accuracy is 63.3% on the 40-class SOC split (chance 2.5%). Under the official scene-change split, the background stops helping and starts hurting. Accuracy is 22.8% on full chips and 30.8% when only the vehicle is shown. A SAR foundation model, SARATR-X, leans on the background more than ConvNeXt does (+4 to +6 points with the vehicle removed, in every seed) and does not solve the scene change. We then hold the amount of training data fixed and vary the depression angles used for training. Accuracy is set mainly by the gap to the nearest training angle: 57% at 15 degrees, 39% at 30 degrees and 26% at 45 degrees. Adding more training angles does not help. Finally, when most classes have training images at the test angle and a few do not, the missing classes do worse than when no class has them: 9.0% instead of 22.4% at a 45-degree gap. Most of their images are assigned to known classes. We recommend reporting background-only and target-only controls, and the angle gap, next to any accuracy figure. Code is public.

title: Encoding, Decodability, and Use: A Five-Layer Framework for Benchmark Measurement Audits with Evidence from UAV Intent Recognition
description:
arXiv:2611.22434v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Benchmark accuracy is routinely read as evidence that a model understands the construct the benchmark measures. We propose and instantiate on AeroIntent a five-layer framework that decomposes that reading into observation, representation, decoding, use, and behaviour. The framework separates encoding, decodability, and use as distinct levels. In the instantiation, the observation layer is unreliable on 7 of the 20 Drone programs and floors the direct visual correlate of radial velocity at a 0.26\% scale change. The representation layer exposes two task-designed RGB features with nominal signals. RAFT flow radial bias reaches $r=+0.257$ ($p=0.030$), and bounding-box optical-flow divergence reaches $r=+0.203$ ($p=0.029$). No multi-feature readout gives a fold-mean test correlation above the cluster minimum detectable effect (MDE), and the largest positive global out-of-sample correlation is $r=+0.080$. The decoding layer sets the MDE at $|r|=0.599$ at the multi-feature Bonferroni threshold ($\alpha=0.00714$, power 0.80), and the observed $r=+0.080$ has power 0.00. Two injection experiments establish the MDE's condition from both sides: aligned injections are detected at or above the simulated power, and orthogonal injections are not detected. The use layer finds accuracy consistent with program memory (program-identity 0.937/0.597/0.210) and multi-region static cues. The behaviour layer is consistent with accuracy not requiring a radial-velocity readout (appearance 0.6552 vs bounding-box trajectory 0.4080, cluster-level paired $\Delta=+0.2471$, $p=0.0132$).

title: A Log-Timescale Perturbation Bound for Selective State Space Models at Every Sequence Length
description:
arXiv:2611.21952v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Mamba models deployed on streaming data, such as limit order book updates, run far past the sequence lengths they were trained on. A guarantee on how much a small change of input can move the hidden state therefore has to hold at every length. The closest existing bound we know of measures the change of the timescale additively, and it grows linearly with the sequence length unless the timescale is bounded away from zero. In this paper, we measure the change on a log scale instead. The key observation is that the decay factor of each step then moves by at most a fixed fraction of that step's input weight, so the per-step errors cannot pile up. Using this, we prove that two runs of a selective-scan cell from a common start stay within a bound that holds at every length, shrinks to zero with the size of the change and needs no lower bound on the timescale. We give a construction showing that, for small changes, this bound is within a factor of about 2 of the best possible, and we extend it to the update used in Mamba's released code when the timescale is bounded above. We then evaluate block-level bounds built from the theorem on two small models trained on one day of order book data. With a bounded timescale, a bound built on the existing analysis is tighter than ours for at most the first 8 steps. With Mamba's softplus timescale, whose certified lower bound is as small as $10^{-21}$, it is looser at every length. Our bounds hold for every input to a block, but they remain more than five orders of magnitude above the changes that gradient attacks find.

title: ALOHA Lightning: Learning Fast and Precise Manipulation
description:
arXiv:2611.21919v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Learning from human demonstrations has enabled robots to acquire a wide range of manipulation skills, but learned policies typically execute far slower than ordinary humans. This speed gap is mainly due to lack of an interface for collecting demonstration data at high speed, and the difficulty in training policies that can robustly execute high-speed motions. In this paper, we present ALOHA Lightning (Flash ALOHA), a system for learning fast and precise robotic manipulation. Our system uses kinesthetic teaching to intuitively collect near-human-speed demonstrations on a backdrivable bimanual platform, yielding natural and fast trajectories. We also present a learning pipeline that enables smooth high-speed execution through test-time action smoothing and aligns the visual data distribution between data collection and deployment with masking. Given 50 demonstrations for each task, ALOHA Lightning autonomously completes bimanual tasks such as ball tossing and catching, folding shorts, battery insertion, and bussing tables for over 80% success rates while close to human speed. Project website: https://flash-aloha.github.io/

title: Autoscaling Adds Waiters, Not Ovens. Here's What Actually Breaks at 10x Load
description:
A signed enterprise deal or a viral campaign puts the same pressure on a platform: 10x the normal traffic, arriving faster than anyone budgeted for. The instinct is to trust autoscaling to absorb it, and autoscaling does its job exactly as designed. The problem is what it was designed to scale. It adds more stateless application instances, which were already the most elastic part of the system, and does nothing for the database connection pool, the cache origin, or the shared job queue underneath them. Manoj Yerrasani, VP of Global Platform Engineering at NBCUniversal, put it plainly after operating at Super Bowl scale: "auto-scaling is a lie." More app servers just means more processes competing for the same fixed set of database connections, and that competition is where the outage actually starts.

Four questions that predict where a platform breaks first

The Load Shape Audit is four diagnostic questions, not a tool you install:

  • Request shape: how many backend calls does a single user action trigger? A page load that fans out to six API endpoints multiplies your real request volume by six before traffic even grows.
  • Data shape: how many different access patterns are competing on one database? Write-heavy configuration writes and read-heavy analytics queries fighting over the same connection pool degrade both.
  • Tenant shape: does one large tenant's workload saturate a shared resource, connection pool, job queue, cache, search index, and degrade service for every smaller tenant on the same infrastructure?
  • Failure shape: when something has to give, is there a predetermined priority order, or does the system degrade randomly?

Signal 3 is the one most platforms discover the hard way. Neon's production analysis and the AWS whitepaper on SaaS tenant isolation both document the same pattern: one noisy tenant degrading everyone sharing its infrastructure.

The pattern that fixes the most common request-shape failure

When a cache misses under load, the naive implementation lets every concurrent request for that same uncached key hit the database independently, ten simultaneous cache misses become ten identical queries. The fix is request collapse, also called singleflight: the first request triggers the real query, and every other request for the same key waits on that one result instead of firing its own.

const inFlight = new Map();

async function getWithSingleflight(key, fetchFn) {
  if (inFlight.has(key)) {
    return inFlight.get(key); // piggyback on the request already running
  }
  const promise = fetchFn()
    .finally(() => inFlight.delete(key));
  inFlight.set(key, promise);
  return promise;
}

That's a handful of lines, and it turns a thundering herd of duplicate queries into one query with N waiters. It's also exactly the kind of fix that autoscaling can't provide, because the problem was never a shortage of application instances.

Isolating the noisy neighbor, in order of cost

Tenant-shape problems get fixed in escalating stages, and jumping straight to the most expensive one wastes engineering time you don't have during an incident:

  • Row-level isolation at the database layer. PostgreSQL row-level security enforces tenant boundaries in the database itself, not in application code that a future developer might bypass.
  • Per-tenant connection pools and job queue lanes. A large tenant gets its own lane instead of competing with everyone else for the same shared pool.
  • Full tenant silo. Dedicated infrastructure per tenant, the most expensive option, reserved for the tenants whose load actually justifies it.

What this looked like on a real platform

Brocoders rebuilt Adact's platform on Node.js and Nest.js with a split database layer, PostgreSQL for write-heavy campaign configuration, MongoDB for read-heavy analytics, so the two access patterns stopped fighting over the same connection pool. Server-side rendering behind CloudFront collapsed what had been multiple API calls per page load into a single request. That architecture held through a campaign that generated 18,000 leads in 10 days and sustained over 2 million requests at peak across more than 3 million visitors in six months, without the app-server layer being the thing that mattered most. We run full-stack delivery with our own DevOps, no outsourced infra, so the team building the feature is the same team that has to answer when a connection pool saturates at 2am.

Pre-launch checklist before you trust autoscaling with a 10x event

  • Run expected load in staging at least twice before launch, not once, and not in production.
  • Freeze configuration changes the week of launch. Ben Maurer's 2015 analysis of Facebook outages found human error during change windows was a leading cause, not raw traffic.
  • Map every shared resource: connection pools, caches, job queues, search indexes, and who else is competing for each one.
  • Write explicit traffic-tier priorities before you need them: what's protected (checkout, auth), what degrades gracefully (recommendations), what gets dropped with a message.
  • Set numeric thresholds for architectural work, not vibes: "at X concurrent users the read path splits, at Y tenants we move to per-tenant pools."
  • Don't build the full silo model preemptively. Every extra service boundary adds deployment surface and on-call pages before the load that justifies it arrives.

If you're staring down a 10x traffic event and want a second technical opinion on which layer actually breaks first, brocoders.com is a reasonable place to start that conversation.

title: AWS Lambda adds support for GPU instances on Lambda Managed Instances
description:
AWS Lambda now supports GPU-accelerated Event Functions on Lambda Managed Instances using EC2 G-series instances. You can now run GPU-accelerated workloads including AI inference, media processing, 3D rendering, scientific computing, and financial simulations on Lambda without managing GPU drivers, frameworks, or scaling. Lambda runs multiple invocations concurrently in each execution environment and scales responsively based on GPU utilization, CPU utilization, and concurrency to keep your GPUs busy and reduce costs. GPU-accelerated functions integrate with the same 200+ AWS event sources as other Event Functions, so you can add GPU compute as another step in your serverless application.

Running GPU workloads today requires customers to provision hardware, manage driver and framework dependencies, and build custom scaling and capacity management. With this launch, you can go from code to a running GPU workload in minutes. Lambda provides GPU base images preconfigured with frameworks such as vLLM, SGLang, and PyTorch. You can run workloads with large artifacts using container images and NVMe ephemeral storage of up to 32 GB each. To reduce startup time, Lambda supports Seekable OCI (SOCI) lazy loading and streaming artifacts directly from Amazon S3. For resilience, you can select G-series instance types from multiple generations in the allowed instance types for your capacity provider. Lambda provisions instances from the newest generation that meets your function requirements and falls back to older generations when capacity is unavailable.

GPU-accelerated Event Functions on Lambda Managed Instances is available in all AWS Commercial Regions where Lambda Managed Instances and EC2 G-series instances are available. You can configure GPU-accelerated functions using the AWS Console, AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, AWS CloudFormation, AWS CDK, or AWS SAM. You can also use this feature through coding assistants such as Kiro, Claude Code, or Codex by installing the Lambda Managed Instances skill from the Agent Toolkit for AWS. You pay the EC2 On-Demand price (Savings Plans and Reserved Instances apply) for your instance, plus a 9.75% Lambda management fee and $0.20 per million requests. To learn more, visit the AWS Lambda Developer Guide and AWS Lambda Pricing.

title: RICE-PO: Turning Retrieval Interactions into Credit Signals for Reasoning Agents
description:
arXiv:2605.26352v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Retrieval is increasingly moving from one-shot matching toward interactive reasoning, where language agents iteratively inspect evidence, reformulate queries, and search again. Training such agents raises a credit-assignment challenge: executable actions such as queries or summaries can be directly evaluated by the retriever, while latent reasoning steps are not directly observable and only affect future executable actions. This asymmetry makes outcome-level reward assignment unreliable, as the same final reward may credit reasoning steps that did not actually shape retrieval success. We propose RICE-PO, a critic-free policy optimization framework that converts retrieval interactions into localized learning signals. RICE-PO selects high-uncertainty executable actions as anchors, evaluates local counterfactual branches using retrieval metrics, and propagates credit to latent reasoning steps only when reasoning-to-action influence is strong and future residual effects are stable. On BRIGHT and BEIR, RICE-PO consistently outperforms prompt-based agents and group-based RL baselines under the same retriever setting. These results show that the structure of agent-environment interaction itself can provide useful supervision for training reasoning-based retrieval agents.

title: Giga Energy Secures $1 Billion AI Cloud Deal for 60 MW Data Center in Hunting County, Texas
description:
U.S.-based AI data center developer Giga Energy has signed a 10-year, USD 1 billion lease with an unnamed AI cloud provider for Project Clay, a 60 MW GigaBase AI data center campus in Hunt County, Texas.

Giga broke ground on the project in July and will develop, own, and operate the campus, which the customer will use for AI computing capacity. The site is slated to be ready for service in spring 2027.

*GigaBase Targets Faster Data Center Deployment
*
Alongside the lease announcement, Giga officially unveiled GigaBase, its data center system engineered to tackle lengthy construction timelines, heavy water consumption, and strain on local utilities.

As part of its expansion into Data Center Projects in the US, the company says Project Clay will be completed in under eight months, less than half the time of traditional builds.

Power Strategy Taps Underutilized Capacity
A cornerstone of the project is an investment in new electrical infrastructure that draws on underutilized capacity from dedicated power infrastructure in the county.

The design ensures the campus does not pull from distribution capacity serving existing homes and businesses.

Giga positioned the project against the priorities laid out by Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, who has called for data centers to pay for their own power, deploy water-efficient cooling technologies, prevent infrastructure costs from shifting onto residents, and ensure communities benefit from growth.

This is exactly the kind of AI infrastructure Texas needs," said Brent Whitehead, president and co-founder at Giga Energy.

"Communities shouldn't have to choose between economic growth and protecting local resources. We've engineered our GigaBase system and development approach so they don't have to."

Cooling System Runs Independently of Local Water
Project Clay replaces open-loop evaporative cooling with a fully closed-loop system that operates independently of local water supplies, whether municipal or groundwater, to cool its IT equipment.

According to the company, the facility consumes no water for compute operations.
The only local water use will come from sinks and employee bathrooms, comparable to a small business office and on par with the annual usage of two homes. Giga frames this approach as aligning with Texas' growing emphasis on water-efficient data center development in drought-prone regions.

Jobs and Tax Revenue Head to Hunt County

The roughly 30-acre campus will serve hyperscale and AI cloud customers while, according to Giga, generating lasting economic value for the county.

The build phase is expected to create approximately 300 construction jobs, with 24 permanent full-time positions carrying estimated annual salaries of USD 116,000 to USD 180,000.

The project is also projected to generate millions in new recurring annual tax revenue that the company says can help fund local schools, infrastructure, emergency services, and other essential public needs.
"We believe AI infrastructure should leave a community stronger than it found it. That means creating high-paying jobs, expanding the local tax base, and making long-term investments that benefit residents for decades," said Whitehead.

"Hunt County is gaining an economic engine that will support schools, public services, and future growth for generations."

*Off-Site Manufacturing Drives the Schedule
*
At the heart of the GigaBase system is a factory-first construction model in which much of the facility is manufactured off-site before final assembly in the community.

Giga says this approach significantly shortens construction schedules, reduces truck traffic, minimizes disruption to local roads and housing, and allows communities to realize economic benefits sooner.
The company describes the resulting campus as faster to build, lighter on local infrastructure, and purpose-built to be a long-term community partner.

Giga has previously promoted the concept under the banner "shovel-ready to rack-ready in 9 months" when introducing the GigaBase system.

Company Background and the Deal's Significance

Giga Energy is a U.S.-based manufacturer, developer, and operator of modular AI data centers, actively contributing to the growth of data center projects and infrastructure development in the US.

The company operates factories in Long Beach and Houston, has delivered more than 7 GW of electrical infrastructure, and has more than 258.5 MW of critical IT capacity completed and under development.

The 10-year, USD 1 billion lease represents a significant commercial milestone for the young company as it scales its modular approach. The customer, an AI cloud provider, has not been publicly named.

With demand for AI infrastructure accelerating across the United States, Giga leaders say the next generation of data centers must do more than power technology and must also earn the trust of the communities where they are built.

The company frames Project Clay as that philosophy in practice, pairing large-scale computing capacity with measures intended to avoid burdening existing residents and utilities.

title: Every Heist Needs a Mastermind. So Does Your Backend.
description:
Every app you use runs a small heist behind the scenes.

Say you order a pair of shoes. One part of the system checks that the shoes are in stock. Another takes your payment. A third ships the box. Each one is a service, a small program with one job. Think of them as a crew: the inside guy, the safecracker and the driver.

Now picture that crew with no plan. They just message each other and hope it works out. The stock check says yes, the payment is still pending, and the driver leaves anyway. Nobody notices anything went wrong until the customer calls asking about an order they were never charged for, or one that never showed up.

Every heist needs a mastermind. In software, that’s called an orchestrator.

The orchestrator holds the plan and tells each service when to move. The driver doesn’t leave until the payment clears. If the payment fails, it tries again. If it still fails, the shoes go back on the shelf so you don’t end up shipping something nobody paid for. And every move is written down, so when something goes wrong, you can see exactly what happened and when.

That’s orchestration. It isn’t about making each service smarter. It’s about having one place that knows the whole plan.

title: EviDARL: Evidence-Centric Dual-Agent Reasoning via Alternating Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Table Question Answering
description:
arXiv:2611.22310v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Despite advances in LLM-based table reasoning, most studies focus on single-table settings. Multi-table QA requires multi-hop reasoning over complex table relationships and evidence dispersed across long contexts, often without verifiable intermediate traces. To address these challenges, we introduce EviDA, an evidence-centric dual-agent framework comprising an Evidence Construction Agent and a Reasoning and Answering Agent. The Evidence Construction Agent generates and executes table-manipulation programs over complete tables to produce question-specific evidence and verifiable intermediate traces, simplifying subsequent reasoning. The Reasoning and Answering Agent then performs multi-hop reasoning over this evidence to derive final answers. We further introduce EviDARL, which combines agent-specific fine-grained rewards with parameter-efficient alternating reinforcement learning to improve collaboration between the agents. By optimizing each agent in turn while holding the other fixed, EviDARL enables bidirectional adaptation between evidence construction and answer reasoning. Experiments on MMQA and TQA-Bench demonstrate that EviDARL substantially outperforms competitive open-model and multi-table reasoning baselines under constrained model and training budgets.

title: EmbedGym: Letting Coding Agents Develop and Debug Embedded Firmware Without Physical Hardware
description:
arXiv:2611.21845v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Modern coding agents perform well on general software benchmarks because they can run code and unit tests in a closed loop. Embedded firmware development, however, breaks this loop: a program that compiles can still fail on real hardware due to pin polarity, bus protocol, timing, or networking bugs that an agent at a text terminal cannot observe. Existing embedded coding agents either skip hardware execution, drive GPIO-only simulators with multi-second delays, or test on physical boards in a static environment. In this paper, we present EmbedGym, an interactive virtual hardware environment that lets coding agents develop and debug embedded firmware without physical hardware. EmbedGym uses instruction-level microcontroller unit (MCU) emulators to execute the same binary that would be flashed onto a physical board, connects them to 41 peripheral models, an analog circuit simulator, and virtual WiFi/Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) endpoints, and exposes an interface for agents to change sensor inputs, press buttons, and inspect hardware states. On top of it, we build EmbedGym-Bench, which consists of 598 tasks across 6 MCU-framework pairs graded by hidden timed test vectors, using a five-stage multi-agent workflow that synthesizes peripheral models and tasks from datasheets and driver libraries. We expose EmbedGym to a coding agent at three levels and evaluate eight models over more than 14K trajectories. Even when compilation succeeds 99.7% of the time, 19.9% of compiled firmwares fail at runtime (up to 73% on individual targets). In contrast, interactive hardware testing in EmbedGym increases pass rates across models by +4.9% to +14.7% (up to +31% on individual targets). Our results also show that an agent with EmbedGym outperforms prior embedded agent frameworks, and lightweight models with EmbedGym match frontier models without it at 30-70x lower cost.

title: Treat Java Objects Like JSON
description:
Treat Java Objects Like JSON

Java is powerful, but working with nested objects can be tedious. Getters, setters, null checks, conversions — a lot of code for simple operations.

What if you could use JSONPath, JSON Schema, and JSON Patch directly on Java objects?

That's what SJF4J (Simple JSON Facade for Java) does. No intermediate JSON trees, no serialization required.

Start with an Ordinary Java Object

Consider two simple classes:

public class User {
    public String name;
    public int age;
    public Address address;
}

public class Address {
    public String city;
}

Nothing special here. No annotations, interfaces, or base classes.

Now suppose we have a User instance:

User user = ...;

Navigate with JSONPath

With SJF4J, we can use JSONPath directly on this object:

JsonPath path = JsonPath.parse("$.address.city");

// Read
String city = path.getString(user);

// Update
path.put(user, "Shanghai");

That's it.

No serialization, no intermediate JSON tree, and no conversion back to a Java object.

We're simply treating the Java object as a JSON-like structure.

The same approach works with Map, List, arrays, and other supported object models.

Validate with JSON Schema

JSONPath is just the beginning.

Suppose we want to validate a User against a JSON Schema:

JsonSchema schema = JsonSchema.fromJson("""
{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "name": { "type": "string", "minLength": 1 },
    "age": { "type": "integer", "minimum": 0 }
  },
  "required": ["name"]
}
""");

ValidationResult result =
    schema.createPlan().validate(user);

Yes, user is still an ordinary Java object.

SJF4J supports JSON Schema Draft 2020-12, 2019-09, and 7, allowing the same validation rules to work across different data representations.

Modify with JSON Patch

We can also apply standard JSON Patch operations directly:

JsonPatch patch = JsonPatch.fromJson("""
[
  {
    "op": "replace",
    "path": "/name",
    "value": "Alice Zhang"
  }
]
""");

patch.apply(user);

The original User object is updated in place.

This can be useful for applying structured updates without writing property-specific mutation logic.

How Does It Work?

The key is OBNT (Object-Based Node Tree), SJF4J's unified structural model.

Instead of converting everything into a dedicated JSON tree, SJF4J recognizes three basic structural concepts:

Node Java representations
Object POJO, Map, JsonObject
Array List, Java array, JsonArray
Value String, Number, Boolean, custom values

This allows JSON-oriented operations to work consistently across different Java object representations.

Think of it as a common structural vocabulary for data that already exists in memory.

Runtime Flexibility, Compiled Speed

Dynamic structural operations are convenient, but Java also has a powerful advantage: the compiler.

SJF4J takes advantage of this through Compiled APIs, using annotation processing to generate optimized Java implementations at compile time.

For example:

@CompiledNavigator
interface UserNavigator {
    @GetByPath("$.address.city")
    String getCity(User user);
}

Instead of interpreting the JSONPath expression at runtime, the generated implementation can access Java fields directly:

// Simplified generated code
public String getCity(User user) {
    if (user == null) return null;
    Address address = user.address;
    return address == null ? null : address.city;
}

The result is ordinary Java code: readable, debuggable, and easy for the JVM to optimize.

And the performance difference can be substantial.

In SJF4J's benchmarks, Compiled APIs achieve up to 50× faster execution than their Runtime counterparts in selected workloads. Actual gains depend on the operation and data structure.

This gives developers the flexibility of dynamic JSON-oriented APIs, alongside the performance benefits of statically generated Java code.

Beyond JSONPath

SJF4J brings several related capabilities together:

  • Binding: JSON/YAML serialization and deserialization.
  • Navigation: JSONPath and JSON Pointer.
  • Validation: JSON Schema.
  • Mapping: Object-to-object mapping.
  • Patching: JSON Patch and Merge Patch.

It also supports multiple backends, including Jackson 2/3, Gson, Fastjson2, JSON-P, and SnakeYAML.

The goal isn't to replace all these libraries. It's to provide a consistent way to work with structured data, regardless of its underlying Java representation.

Final Thoughts

Java gives us a robust type system and a powerful compiler. JSON gives us a flexible structural model and a rich set of standards.

SJF4J brings these strengths together.

We can work with native Java objects using JSON semantics, and when performance matters, compile those operations into optimized Java code.

That's the idea behind SJF4J: JSON semantics, native Java objects, and compile-time performance.

If you're interested:

  • GitHub — SJF4J
  • Documentation
  • Benchmarks

Feedback and ideas are welcome!

title: KVUse: Reusable-KV User Memory for Efficient LLM Recommenders
description:
arXiv:2611.21920v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Memory-augmented recommenders built on large language models (LLMs) maintain a natural-language profile of each user. These profiles are updated by a user profile update path that revises the profile as new interactions arrive and are consumed by downstream task paths like ranking. Because these user profiles are stored as text in the user memory, every ranking LLM call that consumes them must splice them in the prompt and calculate the KV cache of them during the prefill phase. Given these ranking LLM calls are prefill heavy (long prompt but short decoded output) and repeatedly called, these repeated prefill of user profile text dominates the serving. Prefix caching cannot remove it, because these user profiles are preceded by different text in different calls. We present KVUse, which stores the user profiles as reusable key-value (KV) caches instead of text. KVUse trains lightweight LoRA writers by self-distillation, so that the user profile update call produces the reusable KV of the user profile while decoding it, and the LLM can read these reusable KV at new positions and behind new context without recomputation. KVUse also has a customized KV scheduler that uploads the stored reusable KV of the next batch while the current batch is computed, hiding the KV transfer from host memory behind GPU computation. On four InstructRec datasets with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, KVUse shows no statistically significant difference in ranking quality from full prefill over continuous memory update rounds. Under saturated load, KVUse raises the throughput of the downstream scoring path by 4.0x-4.5x and of the profile update path by 1.4x-1.9x.

title: Cross-Modal StateKV Injection for Communication in Multi-LLM Systems across Temporal Segments
description:
arXiv:2611.22304v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Video understanding with multiple multimodal language models requires a communication interface that can transfer complementary visual observations. Text-based communication is interpretable, but introduces an intermediate generation stage and can omit information relevant to subsequent reasoning. We study Cross-Modal StateKV Injection, a provider--carrier framework that communicates through key--value (KV) states at visual-token positions. Provider models observe complementary video frames; their visual KV states are aligned and projected into the carrier representation space and integrated through gated residual updates. Injection preserves the carrier KV-cache sequence length, while retaining the additional computation required by the providers and the communication module. The reported experiments on MLVU and Video-MME compare carrier-only inference, text-based communication, and StateKV with two provider architectures. Results show modest, task-dependent accuracy gains and lower reported latency than the evaluated text-communication baseline, with some categories remaining unchanged or decreasing. Increasing provider-side frame coverage offers additional gains on selected tasks without extending the carrier cache. These findings motivate further study of visual KV communication under explicitly controlled observation and computation budgets.

title: SandBAR: A Band-Asymmetric Architecture for Underwater Image Restoration with Removable Frequency Scaffolding
description:
arXiv:2611.22355v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Light scattering, absorption and turbidity degrade underwater imagery through complementary frequency tendencies: large-scale, channel-dependent appearance distortions and local high-frequency detail loss. This band asymmetry motivates different forms of restoration for global colour and local structure. Our primary contribution is SandBAR, a novel unified band-asymmetric architecture for underwater image restoration. Rather than treating frequency processing as an isolated module, SandBAR organises the restoration pipeline around band asymmetry at the block, encoder and objective levels. Within this architecture, we introduce a novel band-asymmetric sandwich block with a reserved post-attention repair slot and the Split-band Parallel Asymmetric Repair Kernel (SPARK), a novel module that applies channel-aware large-support correction to the low band, which predominantly carries large-scale appearance distortions, and lightweight local refinement to the detail-bearing high band, thereby restoring global colour while preserving fine structure. To deliver the global cast to the depth at which the network represents global structure, a learnable low-frequency guidance path injects a low-pass view of the input into the deep encoder, and a three-scale spatial-frequency objective supervises the same axis throughout the decoder. Building on the reserved post-attention slot, we further introduce Post-attention Scaffold Training (PaST), a novel removable nonlinear scaffolding scheme that trains the permanent SandBAR graph under band-specific capacity and runs it at inference without that capacity. SandBAR reaches 29.89 / 28.92 / 22.77 dB on EUVP / LSUI / UIEB and establishes a new three-domain mean state of the art on the benchmark family, exceeding the strongest published result by approximately 1.0 dB. PaST adds no parameters or FLOPs at inference and preserves matched latency.

title: Stop Paying Twice for the Same LLM Answer
description:
A semantic cache for LLM calls with MongoDB Vector Search and Automated Embedding, in about 60 lines of Python.

Users ask the same questions in different words. "What is your refund policy?" and "How do refunds work?" are the same request, but an exact-match cache sees two different strings and pays for two LLM calls. A semantic cache fixes this by matching on meaning instead of text.

In this post I build one on MongoDB. The new part is Automated Embedding: MongoDB creates the embeddings for you, so there is no separate embedding pipeline to run. I will also show the guard that decides what should never be cached, because that part matters more than the cache itself.

Why an exact-match cache is not enough

A normal cache keys on the exact prompt string. That works for repeated system calls, but not for people. Small changes in wording, spacing or word order all count as a miss.

A semantic cache stores each prompt with its answer. For a new prompt it runs a vector search over the stored prompts. If the closest one is similar enough, it returns the stored answer and skips the LLM call. If not, it calls the LLM and stores the new pair.

Most of the work is in two decisions: which prompts are safe to cache, and how similar "similar enough" is.

Let MongoDB do the embedding

On May 7, 2026, MongoDB announced Automated Voyage AI Embeddings in Vector Search as a public preview. You declare an autoEmbed field in the index, and MongoDB embeds the text when documents are written and when you query. Here is the index for the cache collection, using PyMongo 4.20:

from pymongo.operations import SearchIndexModel

INDEX = "prompt_cache_idx"

def create_indexes(coll):
    model = SearchIndexModel(
        name=INDEX,
        type="vectorSearch",
        definition={"fields": [
            {"type": "autoEmbed", "modality": "text",
             "path": "prompt", "model": "voyage-4"},
            {"type": "filter", "path": "tenant"},
            {"type": "filter", "path": "llm_model"},
        ]},
    )
    coll.create_search_index(model=model)
    # plain TTL index: cached answers expire after 1 day
    coll.create_index("created_at", expireAfterSeconds=86_400)

Two details matter here. The tenant and llm_model filter fields keep one customer's answers away from another's, and stop an answer from an old model being served after you switch models. The TTL index is a normal MongoDB feature: documents are deleted automatically a day after created_at, so stale answers do not live forever.

The lookup

With autoEmbed, the query takes plain text instead of a vector. I ask for the single nearest prompt and read its score:

THRESHOLD = 0.95  # illustrative, tune on your own traffic

def cache_lookup(coll, prompt, tenant, llm_model):
    pipeline = [
        {"$vectorSearch": {
            "index": INDEX,
            "path": "prompt",
            "query": {"text": prompt},
            "filter": {"tenant": tenant,
                       "llm_model": llm_model},
            "numCandidates": 50,
            "limit": 1,
        }},
        {"$project": {"answer": 1, "prompt": 1,
                      "score": {"$meta": "vectorSearchScore"}}},
    ]
    hit = next(coll.aggregate(pipeline), None)
    if hit and hit["score"] >= THRESHOLD:
        return hit
    return None

vectorSearchScore is between 0 and 1, where 1 means most similar. The value 0.95 is only a starting point. The right number depends on your model and your users, so log the score of every lookup and look at real near-misses before you trust any threshold.

Not every prompt should be cached

This is where a semantic cache can hurt you. "Cancel order 48213" and "Cancel order 48214" are almost identical as text, but returning the first answer for the second request is a real bug. The same goes for anything personal or time-sensitive.

So I put a simple guard in front of the cache:

import re

UNSAFE = re.compile(
    r"\d{3,}|@|\b(today|now|latest|current)\b", re.I)

def is_cacheable(prompt: str) -> bool:
    """Skip prompts with IDs, emails or time words."""
    return not UNSAFE.search(prompt)

I ran this guard locally on six sample prompts. My first version also blocked the words "my" and "me", and it rejected "How do I reset my password?", which is one of the most cacheable questions there is. After removing those words, the run gave: password reset, refund policy and file formats are cacheable; the order number, the email address and "latest prices" are skipped. A regex is a blunt tool, and in a real system you would also check the route or intent, but the point stands: decide what to exclude before you decide the threshold.

The full flow then checks the guard on both read and write:

from datetime import datetime, timezone

def answer(coll, prompt, tenant, llm_model, call_llm):
    if is_cacheable(prompt):
        hit = cache_lookup(coll, prompt, tenant, llm_model)
        if hit:
            return hit["answer"], "cache"
    text = call_llm(prompt)
    if is_cacheable(prompt):
        coll.insert_one({
            "prompt": prompt, "answer": text,
            "tenant": tenant, "llm_model": llm_model,
            "created_at": datetime.now(timezone.utc),
        })
    return text, "llm"

Before you ship it

  • Automated Embedding is a preview feature, and MongoDB's docs say not to use it in production yet. Check the current prerequisites for your cluster tier before you build on it.
  • Embedding calls are billed, both when you write and when you query. A cache saves LLM tokens but adds embedding cost, so measure both.
  • When your source documents change, cached answers can go stale before the TTL ends. Add a version field to the filter, or clear the collection on deploy.
  • Return the cache source ("cache" or "llm") in your logs. Without it you cannot measure the hit rate or debug a wrong answer.

I only ran the pure Python parts here (the guard and the index model). The vector search calls need an Atlas cluster with Automated Embedding enabled.

Takeaway

A semantic cache is a small amount of code: one index, one $vectorSearch stage and one threshold. The hard part is deciding what must never be cached. Scope by tenant and model, block IDs and time-sensitive prompts, give everything a TTL, and tune the threshold on real logs, not on a guess.

Sources

  • How to index fields for vector search (autoEmbed) – MongoDB Docs
  • $vectorSearch aggregation stage – MongoDB Docs
  • The Bottleneck in Enterprise AI Isn't the Model. It's the Data – MongoDB Blog
  • TTL indexes – MongoDB Manual
  • PyMongo on PyPI

  • X (@aiwithsatyam)
  • GitHub

title: How Zapier turns ideas into working software in hours with Vercel
description:
Zapier on Vercel

  • Interactive partner demos in under two hours with v0, replacing a process that could take weeks

  • First versions of three internal applications, each built in one day

  • A shared daily briefing for more than 60 marketers, replacing individual efforts to assemble the same information

  • 3.3 million sandboxes created in one month, isolating the code execution behind Zapier’s AI workloads

Before the industry had a word for agents, Zapier was building them. Today Zapier is the AI orchestration platform connecting AI to the workflows, data, and systems businesses use every day.

Zapier has been a Vercel customer since they began using Vercel for web experiences several years ago. They stayed, and expanded, because every team that needed to ship quickly found the same answer: speed, with the security guardrails already in place. As they grew, so did their adoption of Vercel as more teams found new uses for the platform. Today, Vercel supports work across engineering, partnerships, and marketing, from customer-facing AI to interactive partner demos and internal applications.

The needs vary by team, but the priority is getting useful work into people’s hands quickly. A backend engineer can create an interactive demo of an integration inside a partner’s product. In marketing, a former product marketer with no prior deployment experience can share tools containing sensitive information through a company-approved environment and keep improving them as colleagues use them.

Zapier’s teams are moving faster and doing more than they could before. When the next launch comes around, building on Vercel is a given.

From weeks of prototype work to a demo in under two hours

Every partnership Zapier signs extends what its customers can automate. The Powered by Zapier team is how those partnerships become product, helping SaaS and AI companies embed Zapier’s automation capabilities directly into their own tools, so users can automate without ever leaving the partner’s app. The stakes are high, because Zapier relies on this team to make its platform the entry point to all the software in the world. The problem was speed: collaborating outside the organization took forever, with every prototype requiring screenshots, design time, and frontend resources, and weeks could pass before a partner saw anything clickable.

With v0, the team can create a fully interactive, multi-view prototype in under two hours, showing an embedded Zapier experience inside the partner’s own product.

Chu’s background is in backend development, not frontend engineering or design, but v0 lets her build these experiences without coordinating a separate design and frontend effort for every partner conversation. Partners can click through the flow and share it with colleagues, using the prototype as a blueprint for implementation alongside the API documentation.

Sharing sensitive internal data securely

In marketing, Joe Stych set out to make the team’s scattered knowledge easier to use. He had spent years in product marketing before becoming a agentic go-to-market engineer, but had never worked out of a Git repository or deployed an application.

At an internal hackathon, he built Marketing Hive, a shared source for positioning, messaging, personas, and competitive intelligence. Sharing his local prototype meant making sensitive information accessible to colleagues without exposing it to everyone else.

“The Hive holds our positioning, personas, and competitive intel, so I couldn't just send people a link. On Vercel it was behind our SSO from the first deploy, so I could share it without exposing it” says Joe Stych, Senior Lead, Agentic GTM at Zapier.

Zapier’s data and security teams had already endorsed Vercel. Stych deployed through the company’s approved internal tooling environment, with access gated behind Zapier’s single sign-on.

He develops in Cursor and keeps code and source material in GitLab, where changes trigger Vercel builds and deployments. If an update needs to be undone, he can roll back the deployment.

The first versions of three of his internal applications took about a day each. In roughly two months, a hackathon project had grown into production software used across marketing. It was built by someone who had never deployed anything before.

Internal apps for marketing and sales

Marketing Hive holds the knowledge. Marketing OS puts it to work. It gives more than 60 marketers a daily briefing in Slack and a dashboard with what changed across marketing, one update from each team, a win worth celebrating, and progress against goals. Each marketer can start from the briefing instead of assembling the same information from separate channels.

“The first five minutes of your day, you need to look at the Marketing OS update,” says Dan Slagen, Zapier’s CMO.

Readers mark what they found useful, helping Stych prioritize improvements. The briefings also spark discussions in a marketing channel open to everyone at the company.

Stych is building a sales coaching application that brings together account context and industry messaging before a call. Afterward, it reviews the Gong recording to highlight what worked and suggest changes to the talk track.

For the internal applications, he checks reported numbers and the evidence behind claimed insights. Decisions about positioning remain with people, and he says additional safeguards will come before agents publish without human review.

Model access and isolated code execution

Beyond Marketing OS, a separate team at Zapier uses AI Gateway to send requests to AI models on behalf of customers using Zapier products.

A common endpoint lets an application change or add models without maintaining a separate integration for each provider. Failover gives requests another route when a provider cannot serve them, while unified reporting lets a team see their usage across providers in once place.

What's next

Zapier’s relationship with Vercel began with web experiences and expanded as the company grew, with more teams finding uses for the platform as their needs changed. Today its role spans the software Zapier runs for customers and the tools its people build for one another, and every thread is still widening.

The clearest picture of where it leads is in marketing, where other teams are starting to borrow the pattern. The goal is more versions across the company, and perhaps a Revenue OS for Zapier’s customer-facing teams next, each built the way the first one was, by someone close to the problem. First comes trust. Stych still checks reported numbers and the evidence behind claimed insights, and additional safeguards will come before agents publish without human review.

Across all of it, Vercel helps Zapier put useful work into people’s hands and keep adapting it to the needs of the business.

title: PCGRL for Complex Platformers: Synthesizing Playable and Diverse Levels via Inflated Envelopes and Forward Curricula
description:
arXiv:2611.22250v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Procedural Content Generation via Reinforcement Learning (PCGRL) has emerged as a promising paradigm for automated game development. However, existing PCGRL frameworks still suffer from severe exploration bottlenecks and scaling limitations when faced with long-sequence generation tasks governed by strict rigid-body rules and non-linear kinematic boundaries (e.g., platformer constraints). Consequently, traditional approaches frequently fail to maintain reliable level solvability on large-scale canvases. To address these challenges, we present a physics-aware, curriculum-guided PCGRL framework. First, we construct an "Inflated Volume Envelope" mechanism, which provides a physics-constrained representation that incorporates continuous kinematic feasibility into the discrete state space of the MDP. Second, to alleviate the sparse reward challenge induced by extremely long decision sequences, we introduce intermediate state-transition feedback and a multi-stage forward extension curriculum learning framework, enabling informative value estimation and stable credit assignment over long-horizon trajectories. Finally, to resolve the issue where deterministic policies after convergence generate highly monotonous map paths with a lack of diversity, we activate high-entropy stochastic inference during the synthesis phase, regularized by a post-hoc parallel rejection filtering mechanism. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework significantly enhances structural diversity while maintaining high physical playability across multi-scale environments. Comparative evaluations across multi-scale canvases demonstrate that our framework maintains superior convergence stability and dimensional scalability, reliably synthesizing solvable levels where traditional PCGRL baselines degrade.

title: From Temperature-Limited to Battery-Limited Legged Locomotion
description:
arXiv:2611.22231v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: On legged robots, sustained locomotion often ends in thermal shutdown rather than battery depletion: the heat of walking concentrates in a few joint motors, which overheat long before the battery is empty. We train thermally aware locomotion policies by reinforcement learning without ever observing temperature, and demonstrate this on a Unitree Go2 quadruped. We first identify a coupled 13-node lumped RC thermal network, fitted on two runs of a single robot and calibrated against the measured electrical power, that predicts all twelve motor temperatures with a mean RMSE below 1 $^\circ$C across different robot instances, gaits, payloads, and speeds. Under a sustained gait, the temperatures the motors will settle at follow directly from the gait-averaged squared torques and joint speeds. Our core contribution is a reward that drives down the hottest predicted asymptotes: thermal time constants exceed the credit-assignment horizon of reinforcement learning by orders of magnitude, but predicted asymptotes respond to torque and joint speed within a single gait cycle, so the policy learns to lower and spread heat with no temperature input. On the robot, the policy turns sustained locomotion from temperature-limited to battery-limited: with a 5 kg payload at 1 m/s, a learned baseline reaches thermal shutdown after 19 minutes (1.1 km), whereas our policy runs the battery down after 174 minutes (10.0 km) with its hottest motor 14 $^\circ$C below the shutdown threshold in a 26 $^\circ$C room; on an unloaded factory circuit with stairs and ramps, the baseline overheats after 25 laps (6.2 km), while our policy completes 47 (11.2 km) on one battery with 22 $^\circ$C of margin.

title: Bridging Instant Payment Switches (ISO 20022 / Real-Time Rails) and Core Banking Mainframes (COBOL COMP-3)
description:
High-throughput domestic instant payment switches — from UPI and IMPS in India to Pix in Brazil, SEPA Instant in Europe, and FedNow in the United States — settle front-end ISO 20022 messages in milliseconds. Yet behind the API gateway, the authoritative system of record in Tier-1 banks frequently remains an IBM Z mainframe executing CICS, Db2, and COBOL COMP-3 packed-decimal batch and online ledgers.

When Global Capability Centers (GCCs) and core-banking modernization squads attempt to strangle or bridge these estates using naive LLM code translation, two silent failure modes appear immediately:

  1. IEEE-754 Binary Float Drift on COMP-3 Nibbles: A COBOL PIC S9(13)V99 COMP-3 field packs two decimal digits per byte with a trailing sign nibble (0xC positive, 0xD negative, 0xF unsigned). Mapping packed decimals into binary floats introduces sub-paisa / sub-cent rounding drift across millions of daily clearing legs.
  2. Dual-Write Timeout Ambiguity Between Instant Switches and CICS: When an ISO 20022 pacs.008 credit transfer times out at 1,500 ms while a CICS LUW (SYNCPOINT) commits downstream, naive retry loops double-post the ledger unless bounded by deterministic idempotency keys and outbox reconciliation.

Reference Blueprint: Deterministic ISO 20022 to COMP-3 Airlock 

from decimal import Decimal, ROUND_HALF_EVEN

def unpack_comp3(buf: bytes, scale: int) -> Decimal:
    digits = "".join(f"{b >> 4}{b & 0x0F}" for b in buf[:-1])
    high, sign = buf[-1] >> 4, buf[-1] & 0x0F  # <1>
    raw = Decimal(f"{digits}{high}").scaleb(-scale)  # <2>
    if sign not in (0x0C, 0x0D, 0x0F):
        raise ValueError(f"Invalid COMP-3 sign: {hex(sign)}")
    signed = -raw if sign == 0x0D else raw
    quantum = Decimal(10) ** -scale
    return signed.quantize(quantum, rounding=ROUND_HALF_EVEN)  # <3>
Annotation Architectural Description
<1> Sign-Nibble Isolation: Extracts the high-order final digit and EBCDIC sign nibble (0x0C/0x0D/0x0F) without intermediate float casting.
<2> Exact Base-10 Scaling: Applies Decimal.scaleb(-scale) to honour implied V99 copybook decimal alignment deterministically.
<3> Banker Rounding Invariant: Enforces ROUND_HALF_EVEN quantization prior to ledger comparison or Z3 equivalence verification.

Six Exit Gates for Core-Banking & GCC Modernization Teams

  • SMF-Weighted GraphRAG Lineage: Rank live CICS transaction hot-paths from production SMF Type 110 telemetry before slicing a single COBOL paragraph.
  • OIDC-to-RACF Identity Airlocks: Map cloud OIDC JWTs to RACF IDIDMAP / PassTickets so zero-trust audit trails remain unbroken.
  • Z3 Concolic Equivalence Proofs: Prove mathematically that refactored Java/Go/Rust services produce identical outputs across every boundary condition.
  • 30-Day Shadow Dual-Run Parity: Reconcile full billing-cycle clearing files bit-for-bit before retiring LPAR MSU capacity.

Open-Access Workbench & Worldwide Editions

  • Interactive Browser Lab (COMP-3 Hex Decoder & 4HRA MSU-to-Cloud TCO Estimator): digbijoylabs.github.io/iron-silicon-bridge
  • Open-Access Working Paper (CERN Zenodo DOI): doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24243905

    • Canonical Architecture Overview
    • Amazon India Edition (INR) · Worldwide 13-Country Storefronts & 10-Language Hub
