title: Best Static Website Hosting Services in 2026
description:
TL;DR

  • Use Render Static Sites when your frontend runs alongside a backend API, background workers, or a database on the same platform.
  • Pick Netlify when your team relies on shareable preview links for every pull request before merging.
  • Choose Vercel when your team already builds with Next.js and exports a static site.
  • Before committing, check three deal-breakers that vary by host: commercial plan rules, whether hitting a cap pauses your live site, and SPA deep-link rewrites.

Shipping a static site like a React, Vue, or docs build sounds routine on paper. You run a build, get a folder of HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files, and upload them. In practice, picking the wrong host creates real headaches.

Once your site leaves localhost, you still have to connect your Git repo for auto-deploys, configure HTTPS on a custom domain, and add rewrite rules so refreshing /account/settings does not return a 404. You also need to watch the bill: does every pull-request preview eat into your monthly quota, and will one busy project pause every other site on the team?

A small frontend team should not face server-style surprises just to publish static files. Below, I compare nine static hosts, explain which workflow each fits best, break down pricing traps, and share a pre-launch checklist before you switch DNS.

Static site hosting comparison at a glance

Static hosting serves prebuilt HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and assets for docs sites and single-page apps (SPAs). If a request needs server-side rendering or backend code execution, you need an application service alongside static hosting. Inspect your build output directory to be sure.

Managed hosts serve files over a content delivery network (CDN) and handle TLS certificates automatically. This table compares managed Git and CLI workflows from provider docs.

Product and plan Git deploys, previews, and build limits Custom domains, HTTPS, and routing Pricing and usage limits
Render Static Sites Git deploys, PR previews Managed SSL, root/www redirect, rewrites Render pricing, plan bandwidth and build allowances
Netlify (Credit plans) Git deploys, PR previews Custom domains, HTTPS Shared team credits, exhaustion can pause all team sites
Vercel (Hobby) Git deploys, previews (100/day) Domains, HTTPS Personal use only, commercial sites need paid plans
Cloudflare Pages (Free) Git deploys, previews (500/mo, 1 concurrent, 20-min max) 100 domains/project, 2,000 static / 100 dynamic _redirects Free build limits, 25 MiB max per file
DigitalOcean App Platform Repo deploys, 1-hour build max Domains, HTTPS, routing varies by setup 3 free static apps, bandwidth billing applies
AWS Amplify Hosting Managed Git deploys, previews Custom domains, SSL Separate build, storage, bandwidth billing, account-dependent free tier
Azure Static Web Apps Repo deploys, staging Managed SSL, config routing No bandwidth overage on Free, per-preview and total storage caps
Firebase Hosting CLI deploys, preview links Domains, SSL, config rules Project storage and bandwidth, Spark limits can stop serving
GitHub Pages Repo publishing, workflow build rates Custom domains, HTTPS No free hosting for commercial SaaS or e-commerce

Watch the difference between build concurrency (how many builds run at once), build duration (how long one build can run), and deploy frequency (daily or monthly caps). A high monthly cap still leaves your team waiting if concurrency is capped at one.

Which static website host fits your site?

Render Static Sites for a frontend alongside application services

I pick Render when a static frontend belongs to an app that also needs an API, background workers, or a database. Its dedicated static site service serves files over a CDN without an application server, while Render web services and Render Postgres share the same dashboard. One platform means one set of permissions, deploys, and bills.

When moving a domain over, Render automatically pairs your root domain and www subdomain with a main-domain redirect (custom domains), and supports redirect and rewrite rules for SPAs. Check Render pricing for current plan allowances before locking in your team setup.

Netlify for pull-request preview workflows

I look at Netlify when reviewing live preview links on every pull request is central to how a team works. The key billing rule to watch on Netlify is the difference between preview builds and production deploys.

Under Netlify's credit-based pricing plans, creating a Deploy Preview uses 0 credits (though visitors loading that preview still count toward web requests and bandwidth), while successful production deploys consume credits. Read the credit rules carefully. Because running out of shared team credits can pause all projects, including live production sites, a shared team budget is an uptime risk as well as a billing concern.

Vercel for Next.js frontend workflows

I shortlist Vercel when a team is already built around Next.js and wants tight frontend preview links. Remember that static hosting only covers prebuilt HTML, CSS, and JS files. If your Next.js app needs server-side rendering, middleware, or API routes, check Vercel's compute pricing and limits separately.

Vercel Hobby limits you to 100 deployments per day and is strictly for personal, non-commercial use. Company or client sites need a paid plan, so check Vercel pricing for per-seat fees and included usage before building a team budget around the starter tier.

Cloudflare Pages for Git-based publishing within file limits

Cloudflare Pages works well when your repo uses standard Git deploys and your output fits its limits. Keep Cloudflare Pages separate from Workers Static Assets: Cloudflare publishes a Pages-to-Workers migration guide, so check current guidance before starting a new project.

On the Free plan, Cloudflare allows 500 builds per month, one concurrent build, a 20-minute build timeout, and a 25 MiB max size per file. That per-file cap matters most if your site serves large downloads or videos. Also check _redirects limits (2,000 static and 100 dynamic rules) and test what happens to your live site if a build fails or hits a quota.

DigitalOcean App Platform for small static-only apps

I consider DigitalOcean App Platform when a team already runs servers on DigitalOcean and wants to group a few small static sites in one place. DigitalOcean advertises three free static-only apps on its App Platform pricing page. Because one app can hold multiple components, check the billing docs to see how components are counted and when adding a backend service moves you off the free static tier.

Routing also takes a bit of checking. DigitalOcean's limits and URL-routing guide behave differently depending on the rule type, so verify your exact domain redirects, path redirects, and SPA fallback rules before moving DNS.

AWS Amplify Hosting for managed publishing with pay-as-you-go billing

AWS Amplify Hosting fits teams already on AWS who want Git-connected deploys without wiring up an S3 bucket and CloudFront distribution by hand. AWS's static website guide keeps those two paths separate.

Amplify's pricing page charges separately for build minutes, stored files, and bandwidth served. A busy docs repo and an asset-heavy download site therefore hit completely different parts of the bill. Before relying on a free tier, check whether your AWS account is still eligible for its introductory free offer.

Azure Static Web Apps for Azure-centered teams

Azure Static Web Apps makes sense for teams already anchored in Azure who want built-in staging environments for pull-request reviews. Watch the storage limits: Azure's quotas docs cap storage both per environment and across all environments combined, which limits how many open PR previews you can keep around.

Free plans do not allow paid bandwidth overages, and the plans and quotas pages list slightly different custom-domain counts for Standard, so confirm the exact limit in your subscription. Use the configuration guide to set SPA fallback routes and excluded paths.

Firebase Hosting for Firebase-centered teams

Firebase Hosting works cleanly for static sites and SPAs whose teams already use the Firebase CLI and preview links. Its hosting configuration keeps redirects, rewrites, and headers in firebase.json alongside your code, so teammates can review routing changes right in Git.

Keep Firebase Hosting separate from Firebase App Hosting. Firebase's product comparison reserves App Hosting for server-rendered apps. Before choosing Spark or Blaze, review storage, bandwidth, and limit rules, because hitting Spark limits can take the site offline and Blaze usage is shared across your Firebase project.

GitHub Pages for eligible project and documentation sites

GitHub Pages is a natural fit for open-source project sites and repository docs. Read GitHub's intended-use policy before assuming it covers company sites: it forbids free hosting for online businesses, e-commerce sites, and commercial SaaS, even though organization docs may qualify.

Check deep-link routing early too. Generated docs sites with an HTML file per page work out of the box, while React or Vue SPAs break when someone refreshes a sub-page unless a rewrite rule serves index.html.

What your team actually pays

Static hosting bills vary by deploy frequency and asset size. A docs site that deploys twenty times a day burns build minutes and deploy credits while barely touching bandwidth. A marketing site with large videos or downloads barely touches build limits while burning through bandwidth and request caps.

Check pricing for Render, Netlify, Vercel, DigitalOcean, or AWS Amplify, and add up six cost items:

  1. Plan base fee and per-seat charges
  2. Build minutes and extra concurrent builds
  3. Production-deploy credits
  4. Outbound bandwidth and request volume
  5. Storage for production and open preview builds
  6. Hosting-related DNS or domain fees (separate from domain registration)

Also check how a provider handles hitting a cap, through alerts, spending limits, automatic top-ups, overage fees, or hard pauses. Confirm whether a limit stops only new deploys or takes your live site offline too, especially when projects share one team budget.

Choose the host and verify it before switching DNS

Pick the provider whose deploy flow, plan rules, and limit behavior match your team, then test four things on a staging URL before updating production DNS:

  1. Confirm your build finishes inside the timeout and PR previews update on new commits.
  2. Refresh a nested SPA route like /account/settings directly, and check that a missing file like /assets/missing.js returns a real 404 instead of index.html.
  3. Verify SSL certificates issue cleanly and www redirects to your root domain (or vice versa) in one hop.
  4. Push a broken build on a test branch to confirm your last working deploy stays live and can roll back fast.

If your static site is the frontend for an app that also needs an API, background workers, or a PostgreSQL database, start with Render Static Sites so you can deploy frontend and backend services from the same workspace without splitting bills and permissions across providers.

Frequently asked questions

What is the best hosting service for static websites?

The best choice depends on your stack and workflow. Pick Netlify for shareable PR preview links, Vercel for Next.js static exports, and Render Static Sites when your frontend runs alongside backend APIs and databases. Verify commercial rules, routing support, and cap behavior.

Can I host a commercial static website for free?

Yes, if the provider's terms allow business use and your traffic stays within free limits. Check Vercel's fair-use rules and GitHub Pages' restrictions on commercial SaaS and online businesses before deploying company sites there.

Does a React or Next.js app count as a static website?

Yes, if your build outputs plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files without server-side rendering or middleware. Client-side routing works on static hosts, though refreshing nested URLs usually requires an SPA rewrite rule.

Can a static website use a database?

Yes. Static hosting only covers frontend file delivery. Your browser app can read and write dynamic data through a secured backend API, such as pairing Render Static Sites with a Render web service and Render Postgres in one workspace.

Can I move hosts without changing my domain?

Yes. Keep your domain at your registrar and point DNS records to the new host. The files are portable, so focus on translating redirect rules, SPA fallbacks, and cache headers, then test the preview URL and SSL certificate before updating DNS.

title: Comparing Implicit and Explicit Language Attitudes toward the Dutch multiethnolect Straattaal in Humans and Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.22335v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: While language attitudes have been extensively studied in humans, the extent to which large language models (LLMs) encode similar associations between language varieties and social attributes remains unclear. Contemporary sociolinguistic research distinguishes between explicit attitudes, which stem from deliberative processing, and implicit attitudes, which arise from automatic processing. This study investigates whether LLMs exhibit human-like implicit and explicit language attitudes toward the Dutch multiethnolect Straattaal, particularly its association with migrant communities. We use closely matched designs to assess attitudes in humans and LLMs. For humans, we use an Implicit Association Test (IAT) and an explicit rating task. For LLMs, we use the LLM Word Association Test (LLM WAT) and the same explicit rating task. Human participants strongly associate Straattaal with individuals with a migration background at both implicit and explicit levels. In the LLM WAT, Straattaal is consistently associated with individuals with a migration background, with stronger associations observed in larger and newer models. When presented with the same explicit rating task as human participants, LLMs produce comparable response patterns. Overall, the findings suggest that many LLMs encode language attitudes resembling those observed in humans, however we also highlight important questions about how concepts and measures developed to study human attitudes should be interpreted in LLMs. This highlights the relevance of incorporating sociolinguistic perspectives and language variation into NLP research to better identify and mitigate socially and linguistically embedded biases.

title: Turning dead scroll padding into a little animated fire
description:
Every chat list ends somewhere, and ours used to end in nothing. The last conversation row sat above a blank strip of screen, and that strip existed for a practical reason: three floating action buttons live in the bottom-right corner, and the last row had to scroll clear of them. The padding was correct. It was also dead space that every user paid for on every short list.

Now an animated footer emoji sits in that space — a little fire by default. This is the decision record for turning reserved padding into a feature without changing the scroll geometry, and for keeping an animated footer emoji in Flutter cheap enough to leave on.

The blank strip we were already paying for

The chats list reserves room for the tallest stack of floating buttons: search, the extra button some accounts get, and contacts. A mini floating button occupies 48 dp vertically, gaps sit between them, and the scaffold adds its own margin above the safe area. The result is roughly 184 px of reserved height at the end of the list.

That number is not decoration. It is the reason the last row can be tapped instead of sitting under a button. It is also why the empty state and the populated list share the same bottom padding: the geometry should not change just because the content did.

So the constraint was fixed before the feature existed. We were not looking for space to add; we were looking at space we had already bought and never used.

Do not add a footer below the list

The tempting implementation is a column: the list, then a footer underneath it. It looks harmless, and it quietly changes two things.

First, it adds scroll length. The list now ends later than it used to, so the last row travels further before it settles. Second, it makes the geometry depend on whether the footer is enabled. Turn the decoration off and the list gets shorter; turn it on and it grows. A preference should not resize the conversation list.

The version we shipped puts the footer inside the scroll view instead, as the last sliver. The list's total extent stays the same whether the emoji is on, off, or replaced by an empty box of the same size.

SliverFillRemaining is margin-top: auto

The footer is a SliverFillRemaining with hasScrollBody: false. On a list shorter than the viewport, it receives all the leftover height, which pushes its child to the real bottom. In CSS terms it is margin-top: auto; in a chat list it means a two-row list has one enormous gap between the second row and the emoji, rather than a small decoration floating in the middle of the screen.

On a long list there is no leftover height, so the sliver falls back to a minimum. That minimum is the height of the button stack, which preserves the original reason the space existed: the last row still clears the buttons.

return SliverFillRemaining(
  hasScrollBody: false,
  child: ConstrainedBox(
    constraints: BoxConstraints(minHeight: AppFab.stackHeight(3)),
    child: Align(
      alignment: Alignment.bottomCenter,
      child: FriendsFooterEmoji(scrollController: controller),
    ),
  ),
);

The Align matters as much as the sliver. Without it, the emoji would stretch or sit at the top of the expanded area. With it, the unused height lives above the emoji and the decoration stays pinned to the bottom edge.

Same geometry with the switch off

When the footer is disabled, the widget still renders a square of its normal size with nothing inside. It does not return SizedBox.shrink(), because collapsing the box would remove height from the sliver and shorten the list. The switch would then change scroll behaviour as well as appearance.

That is the rule in one sentence: the setting decides what is painted, never how far the list scrolls.

It also makes the toggle feel instant. There is no relayout of the rows, no jump in the scroll position, and no re-measure of the viewport: one box goes from containing an animation to containing nothing.

An animated footer emoji in Flutter, centred clear of the buttons

The floating buttons are right-aligned, so the footer is centred horizontally. That keeps it visually clear of the stack without needing to know the width of a button or the exact device inset.

An 8 px gap plus the device's bottom inset separates the emoji from the screen edge. The list's own bottom padding already accounts for the dock and the button stack, so the footer is not compensating for them again; it is only adding breathing room.

The result is a decoration that looks placed rather than dropped. On a wide desktop window it stays centred while the buttons remain at the far right.

Reuse the registry, do not build a second one

The emoji comes from the same 85-emoji bundled animation registry used by emoji-only messages. That gives the picker one set of choices, the renderer one lookup, and the fallback one rule: if the emoji has no bundled animation, draw the glyph.

The picker only offers emoji that do have an animation, so the chosen footer always moves unless the app-wide motion level is off. A stored value that is not in the registry is ignored rather than rendered as a mystery glyph, which protects against an old or hand-edited setting.

Reusing the registry also means the footer inherits variation-selector normalisation and the same asset-loading behaviour as the rest of the app. There is no footer-specific asset pipeline to keep alive, and no second list of emoji to drift out of date. The same set also powers animated reaction chips.

Glyphs in the grid, motion in the preview

The picker shows the full bundled set. Playing all of those Lottie compositions at once would be absurd: the sheet would ask the device to decode and loop dozens of animations for a choice the user has not made yet.

So the grid renders plain text glyphs. One animated preview at the top shows the current selection. Tapping an emoji updates the preview only; the sheet stays open, and nothing is saved until the user presses Apply.

That extra step is deliberate. An animation is a poor thing to judge from a still frame, and a footer is something the user will see every day. Previewing first and committing second means the choice is made after seeing the motion.

Two settings that follow the account

The feature stores two values: which emoji, and whether the footer is enabled. Both travel through the same settings map as the other appearance options. There is no new endpoint and no new persistence format.

Because the whole settings map is pushed together, the footer choice follows the account across devices exactly like the theme, the chat background or the animation switches. Sign in on a new device and the same emoji is waiting at the bottom of the list.

An unknown emoji in the stored settings is ignored. That keeps the renderer's promise simple: the footer either shows something from the registry or shows the default, never a missing asset.

The first frame after a restart

Like the other appearance settings, the footer values are cached locally as well as synced. The cache is read at startup, before the profile request returns, so the first frame already has the right emoji and the right switch state.

Without that, a list could render with the default fire, then swap to the chosen emoji a moment later. On a slow connection the flash could last long enough to notice, and a decoration that flickers on every launch is worse than no decoration at all.

The cache is a bridge, not a second source of truth. The server value still wins once it arrives.

Motion off means a still glyph

The master motion level is respected. When it is off, the footer renders the emoji as text at a proportional size instead of playing the animation. No loop, no ticker, no exception for decoration.

That mirrors the emoji-message fallback, so the whole app has one answer to "what happens when someone turns motion off": the content stays, the movement does not.

Decoration should be silent

The footer is wrapped in ExcludeSemantics. It carries no information: it is not a button, it does not show a count, and it does not indicate state. A screen reader announcing "fire" at the end of a list of conversations would be noise dressed as content.

Excluding it also keeps the semantics tree honest. The list ends where the conversations end, and the decoration is invisible to assistive technology in the same way a background pattern is.

The ticker budget at the bottom of a long list

A looping animation at the end of a long list is a small but permanent cost. If the user is reading the top of a hundred conversations, the footer is nowhere near the viewport, and its ticker has no reason to run.

The footer mutes its animation while the list is more than 400 px from the end. Scrolling back towards the bottom re-enables it before it comes into view, so the motion is already running by the time the user sees it. The check also tolerates the brief moment when one controller is attached to two scroll views during a tab or search swap; in that case it animates rather than asserting.

This is the same principle as the lazy message list: do not pay for what nobody can see.

What it costs, and what it buys

The cost is one looping composition, muted when far from the bottom, plus a sliver that already had to reserve space. The scroll length is unchanged, and empty tabs show no footer at all.

What it buys is harder to measure: a list that feels finished at the bottom instead of stopping in a blank strip. The space was already reserved; the only new decision was to treat it as part of the design.

The short version

  • The chats list already reserved about 184 px so the floating buttons would not cover the last row.
  • Put the footer inside the scroll view as a sliver; do not add a footer below the list.
  • Use SliverFillRemaining with hasScrollBody: false so a short list gives all unused height to the footer.
  • Keep a minimum height equal to the button stack so a long list still clears the buttons.
  • Render an empty box of the same size when the switch is off, so the geometry never changes.
  • Reuse the bundled emoji registry and keep the glyph fallback for anything unregistered.
  • Show glyphs in the picker grid and animate only the preview; require Apply before saving.
  • Sync the emoji and the switch through the existing settings map, with a local first-frame cache.
  • Mute the ticker when the footer is far from the viewport, and exclude it from semantics.

FAQ

Why not put the emoji in the floating button stack? Because the stack is interactive and right-aligned. The footer is decoration and belongs in the list's own space, where it can be centred and scrolls with the content.

Does the footer appear on empty tabs? No. Empty tabs keep their existing centred message and show no footer.

What happens if the chosen emoji loses its animation? The stored value is validated against the registry when applied and when read from the cache. An unknown value is ignored, and the default remains.

Does the footer change the scroll position when it is toggled? No. The box keeps its size and the sliver keeps its extent, so only the painted content changes.

Is this safe in encrypted chats? The footer is on the chats list, not inside a conversation. It is presentation only and does not touch message content.

title: No Webfonts, No Frameworks: The Performance Budget I Keep on My Tool Pages
description:
When I rebuilt my video downloader as plain PHP pages on shared hosting, I made one decision before writing a line of code: no webfonts, no frameworks, no build step. Every tool page on ramrom.io is hand-written HTML, one shared CSS file, and a small vanilla JavaScript file. That is the whole front end. It sounds old-fashioned, and honestly it is. But it is a deliberate choice, and it has held up through every page I have added since.

Why I started from zero

A tool page has one job. A visitor pastes a link, taps a button, and gets a file. Everything on the page that does not serve that job is weight the visitor has to download on a phone, quite possibly on a slow mobile connection. A framework would have been comfortable for me, the developer. It would not have been comfortable for the visitor. The download starts with a network request either way, but a 40KB page that renders in a blink beats a 400KB page that looks fancier.

So I set a budget, in plain words rather than a spreadsheet: the homepage should stay under 100KB, and no tool page should need more than one CSS file and one JavaScript file. If something did not fit inside that budget, it did not ship.

What "no webfonts" actually costs me

The first thing people notice is the type. I use the system font stack: -apple-system, Segoe UI, Roboto, sans-serif. The text looks like the rest of the visitor's phone, which is fine, because nobody visits a downloader to admire the typography. Dropping webfonts saved a render-blocking request and a flash of unstyled text on every single visit.

The same thinking applies to CSS. There is one shared stylesheet for all eight tool pages. A fix to a button style lands everywhere at once, and the browser caches the file after the first page, so the second tool page a visitor opens is even lighter. I did not need a design system. I needed one file I could read top to bottom in a minute.

JavaScript, kept small on purpose

The JavaScript is one shared engine file. It handles the paste, the resolve call, the quality dropdown, and the download. Nothing else. I write it by hand, no bundler, and I minify it before uploading, then I test the download flow still works after minifying.

Because there is no framework, there is no framework update to chase and no dependency that can go stale. When I add a feature, I add a few lines to a file I already understand. When something breaks, the file I need to read is the file I wrote.

The trade-offs I accept

This approach is not free. Hand-written pages mean I repeat markup across pages, and a layout change means editing several files. I have accepted that cost because the pages are small and the layout rarely changes. I also accept that the site will never win a design award. It is blue and white, with plain buttons and plain text. That is fine. A tool page is not a portfolio piece.

The one place I almost broke the rule was dark mode. I thought about it, then did not ship it. The blue-and-white theme works, the pages are readable in daylight, and a dark theme would have doubled the CSS I maintain for a feature nobody asked for.

The lesson

A performance budget is not a number in a report. It is a question I ask before adding anything: does this help the visitor download their video faster? A webfont does not. A framework does not. A third analytics script does not. So they stay out, and the page stays fast on the worst connection I can test on, which is a real phone on a real Pakistani mobile network, not a fast office connection.

If you are building a single-purpose tool, try writing the page with nothing in it first, then add only what the job needs. You will be surprised how little that turns out to be.

title: PURE: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Multi-Granularity Multimodal Identity Matching
description:
arXiv:2611.22343v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Identity matching asks whether two records denote the same identity, yet the answer depends on the target granularity. Two records may match at the base level but not at the variant level: they share an underlying design while differing in attributes such as color or size. Final matching accuracy does not separately characterize the capabilities involved. To study this problem, we use e-commerce as a challenging real-world domain. We introduce PURE, a diagnostic benchmark for multi-granularity multimodal identity matching covering four capability dimensions: Perception, Understanding, Reasoning, and Evidence-grounded Judgment. The benchmark comprises 1,457 multiple-choice questions across 14 tasks, derived from real-world matching pairs and verified by two domain experts. Across ten recent MLLMs, overall scores range from 47.1% to 86.0%. Understanding receives the highest mean score and Judgment the lowest, with weaknesses in visual difference localization and variant-level rule judgment. Modality ablations show that models benefit from multimodal evidence but can incorrectly identify conflicts between matching records. In direct matching, most models recognize matching pairs more reliably than non-matching pairs at the base level, whereas the reverse holds at the variant level. PURE therefore reveals what aggregate matching accuracy hides: not only whether models judge a pair correctly, but where they struggle to interpret evidence and apply matching criteria.

title: Spatially local mini-batching for implicit neural representations
description:
arXiv:2611.22236v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Neural surrogates based on implicit neural representations (INRs) are typically trained on mini-batches spread over the whole domain, since a generic INR loses accuracy when every point of a batch lies in one small region. We show that low-rank neural representations (LRNRs), INRs whose weight matrices are products of shared bases with coefficients emitted by a small hypernetwork, can be trained with spatially local mini-batches. Each step uses the points of one time snapshot of an adaptive-mesh numerical solution inside one small cell, with snapshots and cells drawn according to the refinement of the mesh. We posit that such training is enabled by the structural property of LRNRs, as a local step reaches the shared bases only through the $r$ coefficients of each layer, and keeps one cell from rewriting the network. By a Kolmogorov-width argument, we show that when restricted to a small cell, the hidden states of LRNRs lie close to a low-dimensional subspace, which suggests the local steps only affect low-rank subspaces of the shared bases. On six hyperbolic-conservation-law problems with solutions computed using adaptive mesh refinement, one local training recipe reaches 1.1-2.3% relative $L^2$ error with a tenth of the parameters of a dense network of the same width. Finally, we provide a comparison by training a hypernetwork-SIREN, a DeepONet, and a Fourier neural operator (FNO) of the same size with the same local batches and training budget. We observe that these baselines reach 16-78% where the LRNR reaches 4.9%. Interestingly, we also observe that local training has a significant effect on the per-cell low-dimensional structure even in a wide generic hypernetwork-SIREN.

title: Stop Early, Stay Simple: Evidence Acquisition for Power System Fault and Attack Diagnosis
description:
arXiv:2611.21695v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Diagnostic models for cyber-physical power systems usually inspect every telemetry source for every event, although some events are clear from one source and others need several. We ask when a learned policy for choosing that evidence is worth its added complexity. To answer this, we present ActiGrid, a benchmark framework for active evidence acquisition that pairs a classifier trained to tolerate missing modalities with a Double Deep Q-Network (DQN), which either requests another source or stops and diagnoses but never operates grid actuators. On the public TU Delft digital substation and MSU/ORNL power system attack benchmarks, we compare the DQN with fixed subsets and orders, calibrated entropy stopping, a greedy value of information rule, and tree ensembles trained per subset. The learned policy does adapt to what it observes, yet it is statistically indistinguishable from entropy stopping on TU Delft and Pareto dominated by simple controls on MSU/ORNL, while compact subset classifiers outperform it while reading fewer sources on both benchmarks. Entropy stopping run over those subset classifiers reaches the highest mean Macro-F1 on TU Delft (0.928 while reading 57% of the sources) but brings no saving over a static three source subset on MSU/ORNL, where no method exceeds 0.45 Macro-F1. Selective acquisition can pay off, but on these benchmarks it does not need a learned policy.

title: Arabic Safety Alignment as Selective Refusal: An Empirical Study of SFT, DPO, and Guard Calibration
description:
arXiv:2608.29378v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Arabic large language models must refuse harmful prompts without over-refusing benign or sensitive prompts, yet a single refusal rate hides this trade-off. We evaluate it using benign refusal B and harmful-prompt refusal H, where H measures refusal rather than harmful compliance. Across five Arabic-capable models and 130 runs on the full human-written AraSafe set, refusal-only supervised fine-tuning (SFT) collapses toward blanket refusal, whereas selected mixed-SFT configurations reach H = 90% to 93% at B = 14% to 23%; four selected configurations exceed the H = 90% target in all three runs, while Fanar does so in two of three. Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and inference guards change B and H differently across models rather than acting as uniform upgrades. In a blinded 300-response audit, annotator binary-refusal agreement is 89.0% (kappa = 0.78); Qwen3Guard and Aya Expanse 32B reach 88.7% and 91.0% accuracy, respectively, with no conclusive paired difference. Selected SFT raises H on Arabizi for all five models, but none reaches 90%, showing only partial transfer from Modern Standard Arabic. Overall, the results support model-specific operating-point selection: set a deployment target and retain only interventions that improve it.

title: How Mercor ships internal apps and billions of production tokens on one platform
description:
Mercor on Vercel

  • Batch jobs cut from 12 hours to 2 hours

  • 18M requests and 63B tokens routed through AI Gateway in 10 days

  • Expert access provisioned in seconds via Vercel Passport

  • Over 2,000 projects created by hundreds of internal builders

Mercor connects hundreds of thousands of domain experts with frontier AI labs, helping those labs generate the human data they need to train and evaluate leading models. It also runs large batches of automated grading jobs to evaluate models for labs and enterprises.

Demand arrives in bursts that can push model traffic to peak capacity for days, even as individual evaluation or labeling jobs carry 24-hour deadlines. With so little time to deliver, requests waiting on a provider’s rate limits can put a client’s deadline at risk.

Mercor’s business teams also need applications tailored to each engagement, giving experts a way to see their tasks and progress without waiting for changes to the core platform.

For Aaron Brown, Mercor’s Head of Security, enabling more people to build means making it easier to give them the access they need and keep track of how they use it. Mercor uses Vercel AI Gateway to manage model access and Vercel Passport to handle secure access to their applications.

When model capacity becomes a customer deadline

Mercor’s mix of direct integrations and third-party gateways could not provide enough token-per-minute capacity for its open-model workloads when demand surged. As requests hit provider limits and entered retry queues, time-sensitive batch jobs stretched beyond 12 hours, consuming more than half of a client’s 24-hour deadline.

AI Gateway provided more inference capacity and failover routing between providers when requests hit rate limits, helping batch work continue instead of waiting in retry queues. Mercor reports that those jobs now finish in 2 to 3 hours, leaving more time to complete the rest of the client’s work. In its first 10 days on Gateway, the team routed 18 million requests and 63 billion tokens, without hitting rate limits.

Mercor continues to use multiple gateways and vendors, valuing Vercel for its combination of model access, controls, and hands-on support when the team needs more capacity. Engineers also get one API for leading foundation model providers and a growing catalog of open models, so they can try a new model without building another provider integration.

Giving engineers room to experiment within limits

As model use grew, Mercor needed to understand where token spend was going, but its previous setup offered little visibility into usage by team and project. A single loop error in a script could exhaust the available budget.

Hundreds of Mercor engineers now use open models through AI Gateway with per-user keys that carry expiration dates, token limits, and spend limits. Security can give experimentation a budget and an end date, then use the usage records to see which user, project, and workload is driving consumption. Engineers can try different models through the same gateway under those controls, without managing another set of provider credentials each time.

Managing access as business teams build

A few hundred people across Mercor’s business teams now build applications on Vercel, where the company’s project count has grown from fewer than a dozen to roughly 2,000. Many of those projects are temporary environments for a specific client engagement.

One production use case gives experts detailed views of their project tasks and progress. Rather than ask engineering to add every engagement’s interface to the core platform, business teams build the interfaces themselves and share them with the experts doing the work.

To share those applications, teams need to control who can sign in without taking on a separate authentication setup for every project. Passport provides that common authentication layer, handling sign-in to Vercel deployments through an existing identity provider.

Mercor’s identity team built a product called Audiences, integrating Vercel Passport as a first class primitive, to automate access provisioning. Once a team selects the experts who need access, Audiences creates the IdP group, Vercel connection, and Passport configuration. With that workflow, Mercor reports provisioning access in seconds for audiences ranging from dozens of experts to tens of thousands. Offboarding works the same way in reverse. Because access is derived from the IdP group, removing the group at the end of an engagement removes access to the project, so no stale access is left behind.

Limiting what each agent can do

Alongside those applications, Mercor uses agents to answer questions from experts in its marketplace, automate HR workflows, and help employees navigate internal systems. Mercor’s approach is to give each agent narrow permissions suited to its job, rather than everything available to the person who invoked it.

For agents that use open models through AI Gateway, Mercor can also scope model access, set expiration dates, and cap spending. That governs their model use while Mercor separately determines which systems and actions each agent can access.

What’s next

Mercor expects more open models to power its internal agents and systems, and more teams outside engineering to build tools for experts. As that work grows, the company wants teams to spend less time setting up model integrations and application authentication so they can respond to client workloads with tight deadlines.

The aim is to make the secure path the fastest path, with shared model access and repeatable authentication workflows helping experts get the tools they need and labs get their work back on time. Mercor wants to support that growth without security work increasing at the same rate.

About Mercor: Mercor is an AI data company that organizes human intelligence for AI training and evaluation. Its network of more than 5M experts, from doctors to lawyers to engineers, powers benchmarks, enterprise evals, RL environments, post-training and agent deployments.
