title: The night the queue ran dry at 1:40
description:
Here's the rule everything else hangs on: the one who builds a thing never gets to say it's done.

Every piece of work in our house goes through three hands. One writes the spec: what "done" means, in clauses you can check. One builds against it. Then the spec's author returns as the acceptor and measures the result herself, with her own commands, not the builder's word. A builder can be brilliant and quietly wrong; acceptance catches that.

A good acceptance doesn't stop at "the tests pass". It breaks the code on purpose to see whether the tests notice. On one recent feature the acceptor planted ten small bugs in a copy of the code — a dropped check, a flipped reply — and the suite caught all ten. One survivor would have sent the feature back.

Acceptance started on the night machinery itself, before it ran, and found three defects in its own spec — one the "now ≥ 08:00" clause, which read literally would end every night begun the evening before, because a time of day is not a deadline. The suite grew from 43 to 68 as they were fixed.

The ask

In early October I wrote down something simple: stop choosing the night's work by hand every evening. Keep one standing backlog for all projects, give the night a signal that I'm asleep, and let it work until morning. One hard condition: at 08:00, the usage window still open must be at least half free.

The rest of the design followed. One backlog file; every item carries a project, a status, a stops-at line naming the last step we may take without a human, and who added it. The status vocabulary is closed: proposed, ready, in-flight, parked, done, dropped. One rule matters most: only the acceptor may move an item to ready. The runner picks nothing else — that is why a night is safe, and shallow.

There were two triggers: a command on the command line, and a physical tag by the bed. The tag path worked — 112 scans — but the last was in September and none in the 23 days after, so it had quietly left my routine. A tag daemon also kills a bound command after 30 seconds, so the command had to stand on its own. The supervisor runs detached, locked by a file lock in Python.

Each tick is one item, end to end: a spec check, one build, acceptance, a status update, a line in the morning report. Two failed ticks in a row end the night, and a tick that stops to ask for approval counts as failed, not as something to retry quietly.

The budget gate

The runner refuses to start work without knowing what it costs, and a budget gate is only as honest as its gauge. On the evening of the first run there was no gauge at all: the usage script returned "status: unknown", the proxy console an empty five-hour window, and a direct endpoint call failed with a 401.

The cause turned out to be duller than a bug. The script preferred any credentials file on disk, and that one was stale — last written in early September, its token long expired — while the live token sat in the keychain. The 401 came from the dead token, and so did the later rate limit with its long Retry-After. A keychain call answered 200 at once. Two answers, "unknown" and "empty", were one problem in different clothes.

What shipped is a single poller: one job writes one gauge file, and it alone may call the usage endpoint on a schedule. One call per cycle; after a rate limit it waits for the server's Retry-After, otherwise it doubles the wait. Its first run answered 200 with small numbers; the parser read "GO".

The handover between gauge and runner is where the night stumbled. The runner started just after midnight with the variable pointing at a missing gauge file, and its first gate said HOLD: gauge unknown. Restarted with the variable set, it read GO. The report that survives opens at 01:04 — my start, not a fault. One gauge detail stayed unresolved: all three gates read the same numbers, and the reading aged — 30 minutes, then 44, then 58 — though the poller should have refreshed every few minutes.

What happened

Three items were ready. All three ran, exit 0, all ending ready→done, all accepted on the first pass, in 13, 14 and 8 minutes. One fixed a reminder banner that forgot it had been dismissed after a reload. Another packaged a mobile release path and only ran it as a dry run: it reported success and produced an unsigned archive — exactly what a dry run is for.

The report's "waiting on a human" section held two more lines, both fences working: a deployment waiting for a date, and a real upload needing the paid developer team signed in. The night's last line said: 01:40 — queue empty. The deadline was 08:00, and the budget nowhere near a stop row.

The night ended because there was nothing left to do — the design working as written. "Only the acceptor makes things ready" exists so nothing unvetted runs while nobody is watching. The cost: a night goes only as deep as the vetting done in daylight. A gate built to stop a night running too hot never acted at all.

What changed afterwards

The next morning I wrote down: the backlog needs to be thought about much further ahead — research, gathering and writing tasks too, maybe even a book — so that when one task blocks there is something to switch to. Then I narrowed it: an idea to think through together, not an order. Nothing new was opened; by ten I looked at the result and said keep it as it was.

The backlog side came first. Before that pass, ready stood at zero; after it, thirty-five items: three proposed, twenty-two ready, four parked, six done. The ready ones sat in four lanes — five builds, eight research, four gathering, five writing — interleaved so no two neighbours share a project, which a script checked: zero adjacent pairs. A floor of fifteen ready items became the warning line. The non-code items carry their own acceptance floor: sources, recorded statuses, an explicit Unknown list, no decisions taken for me.

The runner side got the fields that make that possible: optional lane, predecessor and builder per item; a lint that errors on a bad lane or on a predecessor naming a missing item; one function shared by the supervisor, the lint and the dry-run, so the three cannot disagree about what is ready. Then the switch rule: a project-wide block — red CI, a dirty tree, an unreachable host, expired auth — parks every ready item of that project in one tick with one waiting line, so the night moves on instead of failing twice and stopping. The suite went from 68 to 90 tests, and the gate stayed byte-for-byte unchanged, checked by comparing syntax trees.

The prediction that didn't hold

At twelve minutes a tick, twenty-two items is roughly four and a half hours; research and writing run longer. After the refill I expected budget, not the queue, to end most nights. The nights that followed all ended like the first: 22 ready and 23 ticks, empty at 05:36; 25 ready and 25 ticks, empty at 04:19; 19 ready and 19 ticks; 31 ready and 31 ticks. Not one stopped on the budget.

A prediction isn't a measurement, and the measurement said the queue was still the wall — the refill bought depth, not immunity. A deeper queue ends the same way, only later.

title: A flat T-shirt photo has no back or sides. So we draw them before the video starts.
description:
This afternoon, recording a tutorial for a feature we'd just shipped, I pressed Remove old photos, watched two flat T-shirt photos leave the row, opened a video template, and there they were again.

The button had done exactly what the code told it to. It changed what was on screen and never touched the saved product.

That button is the last step of a feature we built today: turning flat product photos into four studio views before a video is made. Here's why the feature exists, how it works, and the two state bugs it shipped with.

TL;DR
A video model given one flat photo of a shirt has to invent the back and sides when the clip turns it. So RefVid now draws four studio views (front, back, left, right) from your flat-lay photos first. On day one, removed photos came back on reload, and a closing dialog briefly announced "Your 0 new views are ready."

A flat photo shows one side, and a turning video needs four

A lot of clothing gets photographed the cheap way: laid flat, shot from above. That's a fine photo for a product page.

It's a poor photo for a video. Ask a model for a slow turn or a floating spin, and halfway through it has to show a side it has never seen. It doesn't know what the back print looks like, how the sleeve falls, or whether there's a print at all. So it makes something up, and the made-up back is what the viewer sees for half the clip.

A prompt can say "white tee, logo on the back," but it can't say what the logo looks like. The model needs pictures of every side. Drawn views can't recover details your photos don't show; what they do is give the video model one consistent shirt from four angles instead of one flat one.

So the studio draws the views first

I build RefVid, a small tool where you upload a few photos of a product or a character once, then make short videos that keep it looking the same in every shot. Today we shipped a step that sits in front of the video.

When a product's main photo is in the composer, a small wand sits on its corner:

Clicking it opens a card. You tick up to three source photos (the first ticked one is treated as the front) and the views you want. The button spells out the total before you press it:

The whole flow, start to finish:

Step You do What happens
1 Add the flat photos to a product, front first They become the product's photos
2 Click the wand on the main photo The Draw product views card opens
3 Tick source photos and views The button shows the total, e.g. Draw 4 views · 120 credits (30 a view)
4 Press Draw About a minute later the views take the product's first places
5 Press Remove old photos The flat photos are deleted from the product
6 Pick a template (floating product, 360 turntable) The video starts from the four views

The views are ghost-mannequin shots: the shirt filled out as if someone were wearing it, nobody inside, floating over light grey. Underneath is an image model; RefVid writes its instructions. A view is charged once it's stored, and a view that fails gives its credits back.

The sides are drawn from the new front, not the flat photo

Four views drawn independently would be four independent guesses. The front might get a slightly boxier cut, the left side a slightly different white, and a turning video would stitch those into a shirt that changes shape mid-spin.

So the drawing runs in two rounds. First the front and back, straight from your flat photos. Then the left and right, with the front that was just drawn as their first picture. The sides never see a wrinkled shirt on a floor; they copy a studio shot that already has the light, the grey and the cut decided. The back doesn't need the front (your back photo already says what's there), so two rounds are enough, not three.

Here is the result on our test shirt: flat photos on the left, the four views on the right, and a close-up of the back print.

The delete button changed the screen and left the saved photos alone

Once the views exist, the flat photos get in the way. If they stay in the row, the video model gets both a crisp studio front and a wrinkled shirt on a wooden floor: two versions of one shirt to reconcile. So when the views land, RefVid asks: Happy with them? Remove the old photos from this product…

The first version of that button removed the flat photos from the clip being composed. The row looked right.

But the composer doesn't own a product's photos. Open a template link or reload, and it rebuilds the row from the photos stored on the product, which nobody had touched. The flats came straight back, and the next video would have started from all six pictures: the exact mix the button was meant to prevent.

The same-day fix makes the button mean what it says: it deletes the old photos from the product itself, the same as pressing × on the product's page. One guard went in with it: nothing is deleted unless every new view is already stored, so a half-finished drawing can't leave a product with no photos.

When a button's label is a verb, check which copy of the data the verb reaches. "Remove" in a composer and "remove" on a product look identical on screen.

The dialog counted views that were already gone

The second bug: for a fraction of a second, as that dialog faded out, its title read "Your 0 new views are ready."

The count came from the same state that told the dialog to be open. Closing cleared that state at once, but the fade-out was still running, so the dialog rendered its last frames with nothing in them. It now keeps the views it was showing until it has fully gone.

What it can't do

  • Very small text and busy all-over patterns come out softer. A big logo holds up; a care label or a dense print doesn't always. Check each view against your photos and redraw the one that's off (30 credits for one view).
  • Products that aren't worn float. A bottle, a shoe or a box is drawn upright and floating in the same grey studio. Fine for a turntable; not a lifestyle shot.
  • No back photo, no back print. Upload only the front and the back is drawn plain in the shirt's colour. It doesn't invent a print you didn't show it.
  • The example is synthetic. The tee in every screenshot is a RefVid logo tee, and its "flat-lay photos" were themselves made with an image model, so this walkthrough doesn't show how it does on a photographed garment.
  • Look at the left view above. It has thin dark marks along its edges that the source photos don't support; a shirt seen exactly side-on wouldn't show them.

Try it

The walkthrough, with a screenshot for every step, is on the tutorial page, and there's a 2:43 narrated video if you'd rather watch.

Which button in your app changes what's on screen but leaves the saved data untouched, and how did you find out?

Written with AI assistance from our own build notes and tickets.

title: Data-Efficient Algal Bloom Segmentation in Freshwater Bodies Using a Three-Stage Transfer Learning Pipeline with Attention-Enhanced Decoding
description:
arXiv:2611.22064v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Harmful algal blooms threaten water quality and public health, yet automated segmentation of bloom regions in freshwater imagery is limited by scarce pixel-level annotations. We present a transfer-learning pipeline that adapts a Swin Transformer U-Net with SCSE decoder attention from ImageNet-1K to water-body segmentation (RIWA, LaRS) and then to algal blooms, together with a model-assisted annotation protocol that expands the labelled algae corpus from 145 to 655 images. In a single-seed ablation on a 41-image validation split (checkpoint S2-A4 and its variants), corpus expansion is the dominant factor (+11 mIoU points); water-body pretraining helps only on the expanded corpus (+1.1 points over ImageNet initialization); SCSE attention adds 0.3 points; and a learnable positional encoding lowers mIoU by 0.6 points and is omitted. Adding 476 images, 188 of them algae-free, reduces false-positive area on non-water scenes from 22.6% to 4.9%. Against nine baselines on a 256-image test split, a separately trained checkpoint of the same architecture (S2-A13) reaches mIoU 0.919 and the highest algae IoU (0.902); a near-duplicate audit indicates train/test overlap in this split, so these scores are likely optimistic.

title: React Intersection Observer: Detect Elements Entering the Viewport
description:
Key Takeaways

  • Intersection Observer detects when an element enters or leaves the viewport.
  • It is a native browser API that works easily with React.
  • React developers commonly combine it with useRef, useEffect, and useState.
  • Common applications include lazy loading, scroll animations, infinite scrolling, analytics, and video control.
  • threshold controls how much of an element must be visible.
  • rootMargin allows detection before an element reaches the viewport.
  • One observer can monitor multiple elements.
  • Always disconnect the observer when it is no longer required.

Index

  1. Introduction
  2. What Is Intersection Observer?
  3. How It Works
  4. Basic React Example
  5. Important Options
  6. Practical Use Cases
  7. Lazy Loading
  8. Scroll Animations
  9. Infinite Scrolling
  10. Visibility Analytics
  11. Video Control
  12. Reusable Custom Hook
  13. Common Mistakes
  14. Performance Tips
  15. Stats
  16. Interesting Facts
  17. FAQs
  18. Conclusion

1. Introduction

Modern web applications frequently need to know whether an element is visible to the user.

For example:

  • Load an image only when the user approaches it.
  • Start an animation when a section appears.
  • Load more products when the user reaches the bottom.
  • Track whether an advertisement was viewed.
  • Play a video only while it is visible.

One traditional solution is to listen for the scroll event and continuously calculate element positions.

React applications can instead use the browser's Intersection Observer API.

It provides a simple way to react when an element enters or leaves a particular area, usually the browser viewport.

2. What Is Intersection Observer?

Intersection Observer is a browser Web API that allows JavaScript to detect when one element intersects with another element or the viewport.

In simple terms:

Intersection Observer answers the question: "Is this element currently entering, inside, or leaving the visible area?"

For example:

User scrolls
     ↓
Element approaches viewport
     ↓
Intersection detected
     ↓
Callback executes
     ↓
React performs an action

It is useful because developers do not need to repeatedly calculate an element's position during scrolling.

3. How It Works

The basic Intersection Observer flow is:

Create observer
      ↓
Select target element
      ↓
Observe target
      ↓
Element intersects viewport
      ↓
Callback executes
      ↓
Perform required action

Basic JavaScript:

const observer = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {
    console.log(entries[0].isIntersecting);
});

observer.observe(element);

isIntersecting tells us whether the target is currently intersecting the observer's root.
In React, the same API can be connected to a DOM element using useRef().

4. Basic React Example

A simple React implementation looks like this:

const ref = useRef(null);
const [visible, setVisible] = useState(false);

useEffect(() => {
    const observer = new IntersectionObserver(([entry]) => {
        setVisible(entry.isIntersecting);
    });

    if (ref.current) {
        observer.observe(ref.current);
    }

    return () => observer.disconnect();
}, []);

The reference is attached to the element:

<div ref={ref}>
    {visible ? "Visible" : "Not Visible"}
</div>

What happens?

When the element enters the viewport:
isIntersecting = true

When it leaves:
isIntersecting = false

React can then change the UI, start an animation, request data, or perform another action.

5. Important Intersection Observer Options

Two options are particularly important.

threshold

threshold determines how much of the target should intersect before the observer reports the threshold crossing.

For example:

{ threshold: 0 }
Useful when detecting an element as it begins entering the viewport.

{ threshold: 0.5 }
Useful when approximately half of the element should be visible before taking action.

{ threshold: 1 }
Useful when the target needs to be completely visible for the threshold condition.

Multiple thresholds are also possible:
{ threshold: [0, 0.5, 1] }

rootMargin

rootMargin changes the effective observation area.
Example:
{ rootMargin: "200px" }

This can detect an element before it actually reaches the visible viewport.

This is particularly useful for preloading.

For example:

Image is 200px away
       ↓
Observer detects image
       ↓
Start loading
       ↓
User reaches image
       ↓
Image is ready

6. Practical Use Cases

Intersection Observer is most useful when the requirement is related to visibility.

Common applications

Lazy Loading
Load images or content only when they approach the viewport.

Scroll Animations
Start an animation when a section becomes visible.

Infinite Scrolling
Load the next set of records when the user reaches the bottom.

Analytics
Track when users actually see a particular section or advertisement.

Video Control
Play or pause a video based on its visibility.

On-Demand Content
Fetch expensive data only when the user reaches the relevant section.

7. Practical Example: Lazy Loading

Imagine an e-commerce application containing hundreds of product images.

Loading every image immediately is unnecessary because the user may never scroll far enough to see many of them.

Intersection Observer can detect when an image approaches the viewport.

const observer = new IntersectionObserver(([entry]) => {
    if (entry.isIntersecting) {
        setLoadImage(true);
        observer.disconnect();
    }
}, {
    rootMargin: "200px"
});

The process becomes:

Page loads
   ↓
Image is far away
   ↓
Do nothing
   ↓
User scrolls
   ↓
Image approaches viewport
   ↓
Observer triggers
   ↓
Load image

Where can you use this?

  • E-commerce product lists
  • Image galleries
  • News websites
  • Social feeds
  • Portfolio websites

For basic image lazy loading, native HTML also provides:

Intersection Observer is more useful when custom loading behavior is required.

8. Practical Example: Scroll Animations

Modern websites often animate sections as users scroll.
For example:

Section outside viewport
        ↓
Opacity: 0

User scrolls
        ↓
Section becomes visible
        ↓
Opacity: 1

React can use Intersection Observer to add a CSS class.

const observer = new IntersectionObserver(([entry]) => {
    if (entry.isIntersecting) {
        setVisible(true);
        observer.disconnect();
    }
});

CSS can then handle the animation:

.section {
    opacity: 0;
    transform: translateY(30px);
}

.section.visible {
    opacity: 1;
    transform: translateY(0);
}

*Suitable for : *

  • Landing pages
  • Portfolio websites
  • Corporate websites
  • Product pages
  • Marketing websites

The important idea is to let Intersection Observer detect visibility and CSS handle the animation.

9. Practical Example: Infinite Scrolling

Infinite scrolling is another common use case.

Imagine a product listing:

Product 1
Product 2
Product 3
...
Product 20

       Sentinel

A small element called a sentinel is placed at the bottom.

When the sentinel enters the viewport:

Sentinel visible
      ↓
Request next page
      ↓
Receive products
      ↓
Add products
      ↓
Sentinel moves downward

Example:

const observer = new IntersectionObserver(([entry]) => {
    if (entry.isIntersecting) {
        loadMoreProducts();
    }
}, {
    rootMargin: "300px"
});

Where can you use it?

  • Social media feeds
  • E-commerce listings
  • Search results
  • News feeds
  • Video feeds

In production, also manage loading states so multiple API requests are not triggered simultaneously.

10. Practical Example: Visibility Analytics

Suppose a page contains an advertisement.
Simply rendering the advertisement does not necessarily mean the user saw it.

Intersection Observer can detect when it becomes visible.

const observer = new IntersectionObserver(([entry]) => {
    if (entry.isIntersecting) {
        trackAdView();
        observer.disconnect();
    }
}, {
    threshold: 0.5
});

Here, the application can use a visibility threshold appropriate to its analytics requirements.

The same approach can be used for:

  • Advertisement impressions
  • Product visibility
  • Article sections
  • Marketing content
  • Feature usage

11. Practical Example: Video Control

Intersection Observer can also control media based on visibility.

For example:

Video enters viewport
       ↓
Play

Video leaves viewport
       ↓
Pause

Example:

const observer = new IntersectionObserver(([entry]) => {
    if (entry.isIntersecting) {
        video.play();
    } else {
        video.pause();
    }
}, {
    threshold: 0.5
});

This can be useful for:

  • Short-video feeds
  • Product videos
  • Educational websites
  • Social media interfaces

Browser autoplay policies still need to be considered when automatically playing videos.

12. Reusable Custom Hook

If Intersection Observer is used throughout a React project, creating a custom hook can avoid repeated code.

A simplified hook can look like:

function useIntersectionObserver(options) {
    const ref = useRef(null);
    const [visible, setVisible] = useState(false);

    useEffect(() => {
        if (!ref.current) return;

        const observer = new IntersectionObserver(
            ([entry]) => setVisible(entry.isIntersecting),
            options
        );

        observer.observe(ref.current);

        return () => observer.disconnect();
    }, [options]);

    return [ref, visible];
}

A component can then use:

const [ref, visible] = useIntersectionObserver({
    threshold: 0.2
});

This is useful when many components need the same visibility behavior.

Benefits

  • Less duplicated code
  • Easier maintenance
  • Reusable logic
  • Cleaner React components

13. Common Mistakes

Forgetting Cleanup
Always disconnect the observer when the component is removed.
return () => observer.disconnect();

Creating Unnecessary Observers
If multiple elements need to be monitored, one observer can often observe multiple targets.
observer.observe(element1);
observer.observe(element2);
observer.observe(element3);

Triggering API Calls Repeatedly
For infinite scrolling or data loading, protect against duplicate requests.

For example:

Already loading?
↓
Yes → Don't request again
No → Start request

Using Intersection Observer for Everything
It is designed for intersection and visibility.
It is not a replacement for:

  • click
  • mousemove
  • keydown
  • Drag and drop
  • General event handling

14. Performance Tips

Use rootMargin intelligently

For example:
rootMargin: "200px"
can provide extra time for content to load before it becomes visible.

Disconnect one-time observers
If an action only needs to happen once:
observer.disconnect();
or:
observer.unobserve(element);

Avoid unnecessary React state updates
Only update state when the visibility change affects the application.

Combine it with other optimizations
Intersection Observer works well alongside:

  • Image optimization
  • Pagination
  • Code splitting
  • Native lazy loading
  • API caching
  • Virtualized lists

15. Stats

  • **Browser Support: **Intersection Observer is supported by approximately 97% of global web users. Source: https://caniuse.com/intersectionobserver
  • Multiple Targets: One IntersectionObserver instance can observe multiple target elements, reducing the need to create separate observers for each element. Source: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/IntersectionObserver/observe
  • Threshold Configuration: Developers can configure a single threshold or an array of thresholds to detect different intersection ratios. Source: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/IntersectionObserver/IntersectionObserver
  • **Asynchronous Observation: **The API reports intersection changes asynchronously, helping developers avoid repeatedly calculating element positions during scrolling. Source: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Intersection_Observer_API
  • **Native Browser API: **Intersection Observer is a browser feature and does not require a React-specific library. Source: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Intersection_Observer_API

16. Interesting Facts

  • Framework Independent: Intersection Observer is a native JavaScript API that works with React, Vue, Angular, and plain JavaScript.
  • Multiple Elements: A single observer instance can monitor multiple elements, making it useful for lists, cards, and page sections.
  • Early Detection: The rootMargin option can detect elements before they enter the viewport, enabling content preloading.
  • Multiple Use Cases: Beyond animations, Intersection Observer supports lazy loading, analytics, infinite scrolling, and media playback control.
  • Native Lazy Loading: For simple image lazy loading, the browser's built-in loading="lazy" attribute may be sufficient. Intersection Observer is more useful when custom application logic is needed.

17. FAQs

What is Intersection Observer?
It is a browser API that detects when an element enters or leaves an observation area such as the viewport.

Is Intersection Observer part of React?
No. It is a browser API that can be integrated into React using hooks.

What is isIntersecting?
It indicates whether the observed element is currently intersecting the observer's root.

What is threshold?
It controls the intersection ratio at which the observer reports a threshold crossing.

What is rootMargin?
It changes the effective observation area and can allow detection before an element actually enters the viewport.

Can Intersection Observer be used for infinite scrolling?
Yes. A sentinel at the bottom of a list can trigger the next API request.

Can it be used for animations?
Yes. It can add a CSS class when an element becomes visible.

Can it lazy-load images?
Yes. However, native loading="lazy" may be sufficient for basic image loading.

Can one observer monitor multiple elements?
Yes. A single observer can monitor multiple targets.

Should I create a custom hook?
If your project uses Intersection Observer in several components, a custom hook can make the code cleaner and reusable.

18. Conclusion

Intersection Observer provides a simple solution for a common frontend requirement:

"Do something when this element becomes visible."

Instead of continuously calculating element positions during scrolling, developers can let the browser report intersection changes.

The basic React pattern is:

useRef()
   ↓
DOM element
   ↓
IntersectionObserver
   ↓
Intersection detected
   ↓
React state/action

Its most common applications include:

  • Lazy loading
  • Scroll animations
  • Infinite scrolling
  • Analytics
  • Video control
  • On-demand API requests

The two options developers should understand first are:
threshold
rootMargin

For reusable applications, a custom React hook can further simplify the implementation.

Intersection Observer is therefore an important API for React developers who want to build interfaces that load, animate, or react to content based on what the user is actually seeing.

Quotes

“The best optimization is often the work you don't perform until it is actually needed.”

“Great web experiences deliver the right content at the right moment.”

“Performance is not only about doing things faster; it is also about avoiding unnecessary work.”

title: What is a researcher’s worth?
description:
Why the debate over research isn’t a technology story – and why effortless AI makes human friction our scarcest asset.

We’re no stranger to this question.

For many years, research practitioners have talked with one another about how to “mature” teams so that they understand the value of our work in bringing success to their ventures. Or when we share the results of our research, we are peppered with questions about whether the findings are real, whether the methods are too weak or lack representativeness, or whether our subjects are even telling the truth when they express to us what they need.

But it’s not just research practitioners. Researchers in academia have been stripped of the funding they need to advance science. Academic departments have shuttered, and scholars’ voices have been dismissed as part of major civic scientific efforts, like the Census, the Environmental Protection Agency, or the Department of Education.

Put in this context, contemporary discourse around artificial intelligence replacing our jobs feels less like “the reason” than one reason among many when people question whether researchers (and research, in general) matter.

Over the last ten years, I’ve worked as an industry researcher while keeping a foot in academia, and have had some of the best work experiences of my life. There is a joy and a magic I find in what happens when you bring experts of different disciplines together – research, business, engineering, design, and more – to solve complex puzzles.

So if that cross-disciplinary magic is so real — and so productive — why do researchers in both companies and public life spend so much of their careers on the defensive? Most hot takes right now answer that question with new kinds of work: prompt faster, automate your synthesis, prove your return on investment.

As a social scientist, I think those takes miss what is actually happening. The debate over a researcher’s worth isn’t really a technology story. It’s a story about how institutions handle inconvenient truths.

Why institutions put research on trial.

Back in 2020, I wrote about one of my favorite scenes from the all-too-accurate show, Silicon Valley. In the episode, technologists watch through a one-way mirror as focus group participants give honest feedback about their app. One participant explained that the app made them feel “totally freaked out,” and another explained that it “made me feel stupid.”

Behind the mirror, the exec got angry. “Clearly none of these people get it, maybe this is a bad group…everyone that I showed the beta to loved it.” His colleague explained that this was the fifth focus group and they all shared the same feedback. She then realized he only gave the beta to his engineer friends. “I wanted to give it to people who would understand what I’m trying to do so I could get useful feedback,” he said. “And with all due respect, I gave it to you — the one person without a computing background – and you said it felt engineered.”

Those of us who love the craft of research love talking about research methods. But I find that in many cases, debates about methods in settings like these are not about finding what’s valuable. Methodological nitpicking is a way to avoid disruptions to a preferred plan. In this way, it is a shield against uncertainty – ironically, the very thing that research tries to disambiguate.

Social scientists argue that when under pressure, organizations gravitate toward commensuration – a process by which people working together flatten a messy, pluralistic set of realities into a single spreadsheet metric. The truth is, we do live in a world with a lot of unknowns, and the “winners” of today’s marketplace may not be the same in a few months or years. Under that uncertainty, it is tempting to flatten complex human behavior into click metrics – and flatten researchers into headcount cost compared against a chatbot – mistaking a tidy spreadsheet for certainty.

What AI actually changed: a mirror that rarely talks back.

In 2020, the lead technologist in Silicon Valley had to walk through the door and argue with human beings using their products. In 2026, they don’t have to do that anymore. They can swap the humans behind the glass for a synthetic AI persona trained to give feedback in specific ways.

I’m not here to say that AI is bad for science. I actually love a lot of the applications of artificial intelligence I get to use. I’m more troubled by the discourse around artificial intelligence and research in industry – how people talk about it – and the way it is compared to the human worth of social scientists.

For one, when organizations treat research as theater to rubber-stamp decisions they have already made, synthetic users and LLM summaries offer “good enough” reassurance at a fraction of the cost. Replacing hard-to-reach or marginalized communities with LLM agents doesn’t actually include them, either. It builds statistical caricatures out of dominant internet texts while erasing human consent and real-world inequities – the kind of blind spot that lets an automated camera “touch-up” feature quietly lighten darker skin tones if real people aren’t in the room.

And think about how culture actually moves. A few years ago, if you asked a model trained on historical averages what romance audiences wanted, it would tell you to center a man and a woman falling in love – it never would have bet on a breakout love story about two men playing hockey. Models fed past averages and synthetic data lose the tails of the distribution, the emerging subcultures and edge cases where the future actually starts. Meanwhile, algorithmic platforms mistake digital traces for human intent: a frustrated user clicking three times to fix a broken output looks like “high engagement” in behavioral logs.

Artificial intelligence is an interesting tool, not a good social scientist. But today, AI is giving anxious institutions the frictionless validation they secretly always wanted.

Looking in our own mirror.

Listen, I don’t think researchers are perfect by any means. We’re human after all! I actually think that researchers both in industry and academia accidentally made our worth easy to caricature.

Often professions survive or shrink based on what they claim jurisdiction over – what we diagnose problems to be, to what we attribute their causes, and how we offer treatment. In 2020, I warned that industry research was used too tactically (“go run a focus group”) as a way to drive impact. But over the last decade, much of industry research leaned into method gatekeeping – measuring our worth by how many people we interviewed or surveyed, or how many “insights” we delivered, or how many slide decks were shared.

At the same time, in academia, career incentives rewarded the world’s smartest experts for speaking mainly to peers behind journal paywalls rather than embedding social science into civic and institutional design. For example, a senior professor in my field asked me how I’d like the discipline to advance. I said that we should consider hiring clinical professors to more genuinely bring our findings to the field. He actually laughed at me. “Save it for social work,” he said.

I’m of the opinion that neither of these approaches has really helped anyone. In the former, we have traded using appropriate and defensible methods, asking big questions, and discussing complicated answers for a “study complete” checkbox. In the latter, we have siloed the magic of expert discovery almost entirely to the few people who read a published paper.

Where the magic of research lives.

Why does bringing research, engineering, design, and business together feel like magic? David Stark showed that breakthrough innovation happens in what he calls “heterarchies” – teams that hold competing accounts of worth in creative tension rather than collapsing everything into shipping speed. When AI coding tools let teams spin up twenty working prototypes in a week, velocity is no longer the scarce resource. Knowing which human dream is worth building becomes the scarcest asset in the room. For example, when do you pause a team buried in fifty usability bug fixes to instead ask whether we’re focused on the right value?

Some unfortunate news for my colleagues: humans don’t follow linear product models. They improvise inside their own social groups and cultural ecosystems. They react and adapt to major changes in their lives.

Engineers see systems; product managers see markets and funnels; and social scientists see social structure.

Social scientists can find and explain why youth culture over the last twenty years has shifted from public broadcasting to more intimate pockets of the internet. Or why a certain design aesthetic feels exciting in one region and troubling in another, shaped by the cultural meanings people there share. Or how chaotic-looking livestreams with tens of thousands of people are actually held together by the patterned, organized activities of moderators who keep conversation focused and fun.

In The Tacit Dimension, Hungarian-British polymath Michael Polanyi wrote that “we can know more than we can tell.” A vast amount of human knowledge is nonverbal. It includes how we think about cultural norms that we can’t summarize in a survey, or sometimes even in the context of an interview. My bet is that unguided LLMs can’t uncover that tacit knowledge on their own. But social scientists can. We triangulate methods and hold magnifying glasses up to a social problem in a variety of ways, including by testing our assumptions against an accumulated body of scholarly work in purposefully specific subfields.

Worth is built together.

Whether in a product sprint, a university lab, or a public agency, a researcher’s worth was never the focus group they run, how big or small their sample size is, or the paper they publish. Our worth is how we apply our training and our lens to the messy, plural, inconvenient realities of human life, even when institutions are tempted by easy mirrors that boil experience down to a lone metric.

To my research peers: bring your expertise and critical thinking to the work that you do. Show value to your teams by how you and your work “make the strange familiar, and the familiar strange” in the pursuit of a shared understanding grounded in human experience.

To my academic colleagues: get out of the ivory tower. Meet people who do research and engage in practice for purposes that have nothing to do with publishing. Learn new ways to talk about your work that shed both academic-ese and didactic habits in favor of two-way learning.

To my partners in research: resist the seduction of a mirror that always agrees with you. When AI makes spinning up twenty new ideas effortless, speed stops being your competitive edge – knowing what is actually true about people outside your building is. Invite the friction of someone trained to tell you when your favorite plan doesn’t match how humans really live.

We’ve spent years talking about how to “mature” organizations into valuing research, as if worth were a favor. It isn’t. Worth is built together.

Dr. Matt Rafalow is a senior staff researcher at YouTube, and a visiting scholar at University of Southern California. The views expressed in this article reflects the individual opinions of the author.

What is a researcher’s worth? was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Sample-efficient Personalization of Large Language Model Alignment with Multidimensional User Preference Data
description:
arXiv:2611.22210v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Preference alignment has become a central tool to align large language models (LLMs) with human values and desired behavior, and its online variant can further advance their capabilities beyond what static data alone offer by repeatedly generating and labeling new responses with human feedback. But costly, time-consuming annotations limit its scalability, making sample efficiency essential, and existing methods typically seek to improve it by expanding coverage of the response space or selecting pairs with the highest uncertainty for comparison. Although they are effective, these methods quantify uncertainty from the perspective of the LLM, which may differ from the uncertainty perceived by the user: a pair can appear highly uncertain to the LLM even when past comparisons from the user already imply a clear ordering. In this paper, we propose multidimensional preference-guided online direct preference optimization (MPG-DPO), which leverages low-cost multidimensional evaluations from automated verifiers on the user historical comparisons to construct a personalized preference cone guiding response selection for online preference alignment. Specifically, it first discards responses that are confidently dominated under the estimated user preference, then selects two responses that are competitive under the retained preference cone yet exhibit the strongest unresolved disagreement. Theoretical analysis shows that, with high probability, the fraction of queries spent on cone-dominated responses vanishes as learning progresses. Experiments across multiple LLM families show that MPG-DPO outperforms strong contenders under matched query budgets.

title: asyncpg DuplicatePreparedStatement on PgBouncer: Why Supabase Breaks Your Pool
description:
A FastAPI service works locally, then fails in production with asyncpg.exceptions.DuplicatePreparedStatementError: prepared statement "__asyncpg_stmt_1__" already exists, or with ConnectionFailureError: connection is closed mid-request. The database is Supabase or PgBouncer, the connection string came from the dashboard, and no application code changed.

Neither error is about your SQL. Both come from using a client-side statement cache against a pooler that does not keep a session.

Why the statement collides

asyncpg prepares statements and caches them per connection, keyed by SQL text, up to statement_cache_size (100 by default). Each prepared statement gets a server-side name like __asyncpg_stmt_1__.

Under a direct connection that name is unique per session, so the cache is a pure win. Under transaction pooling, PgBouncer hands every transaction a possibly different server connection: the cache no longer describes anything real, and two clients that both prepared __asyncpg_stmt_1__ can land on the same server session, where the second prepare fails with SQLSTATE 42P05.

import asyncpg

# correct for the Supabase transaction pooler (port 6543) and PgBouncer transaction mode
pool = await asyncpg.create_pool(
    dsn,
    min_size=1,
    max_size=5,              # small: the pooler multiplies, not the app
    statement_cache_size=0,  # no server-side prepared statements
    max_cached_statement_lifetime=0,
    command_timeout=30,
    server_settings={"application_name": "api"},
)

With SQLAlchemy, set it at the dialect level too, because SQLAlchemy builds the asyncpg pool itself:

create_async_engine(
    "postgresql+asyncpg://user:pass@host:6543/postgres",
    poolclass=NullPool,                     # let the pooler pool
    connect_args={
        "statement_cache_size": 0,
        "prepared_statement_cache_size": 0, # SQLAlchemy's own layer
        "server_settings": {"application_name": "api"},
    },
)

Both knobs exist because there are two caches: asyncpg's, and SQLAlchemy's prepared-statement cache on top of the same driver. Setting only one is the most common half-fix.

Which endpoint you are actually on

Endpoint Port Prepared statements App pool size Use for
Direct connection 5432 supported, cache them your real budget migrations, LISTEN/NOTIFY
Session pooler 5432 supported per session small long sessions, ORMs without pooling
Transaction pooler 6543 not supported across transactions 1–5 per worker most web traffic
Transaction pooler + cache 6543 collisions any never

When you see DuplicatePreparedStatementError the cache met a transaction pooler; TooManyConnectionsError means the app pool is larger than the pooler budget; InvalidPasswordError usually means the username is postgres instead of postgres.<project-ref>.

Reproduce it instead of guessing

A single-worker test never reproduces the collision. Run the same query from many coroutines against the pooler — if it passes with statement_cache_size=0 and fails without it, the diagnosis is confirmed. Do not "fix" it by catching DuplicatePreparedStatementError and retrying: the retry prepares the same name on another server connection and the error moves instead of disappearing.

ConnectionFailureError is not a bug in your query

The pooler recycles server connections aggressively — Supabase's transaction pooler closes idle ones long before a typical web worker notices. asyncpg keeps the client object and only learns the socket is gone when it writes. Retry only on ConnectionFailureError and InterfaceError, never on a query error: replaying an INSERT that failed before commit is fine, replaying one that timed out after commit is not.

async def fetch_one(pool, sql, *args):
    for attempt in range(2):
        try:
            async with pool.acquire() as conn:
                return await conn.fetchrow(sql, *args)
        except asyncpg.ConnectionFailureError:
            if attempt:
                raise

pool_pre_ping narrows the window after an idle close but does not remove the need to retry. Keeping min_size=1 and running an occasional SELECT 1 from a background task keeps a warm client, so the first request after a quiet period does not fail.

Transaction pooling also gives one server connection per transaction — exactly what async with conn.transaction() needs, and exactly what a bare SET does not survive. Use SET LOCAL for statement_timeout or search_path, and keep advisory locks, LISTEN, temporary tables, cursors and Alembic migrations on port 5432, where a session exists.

Two traps specific to Supabase

The direct host is IPv6-only. db.<project-ref>.supabase.co resolves to IPv6 unless the IPv4 add-on is enabled, so a container or CI runner without IPv6 gets socket.gaierror: [Errno -9] Address family for the host is not supported. It looks like DNS and is not; use a pooler host, and note the pooler username is postgres.<project-ref>.

Your pool size is multiplied by the pooler. Four uvicorn workers with max_size=20 demand 80 server connections from a pooler that may allow far fewer, and the failure only appears under load. Keep a handful per worker (max_size = 5) and let the pooler queue; NullPool is the simplest correct choice for serverless.

Checklist before you file a bug

  • Both cache switches set to 0.
  • Port 6543 only for traffic that does not need a session.
  • max_size small, per worker.
  • Retry on ConnectionFailureError / InterfaceError only.

Format the failing statement with the SQL formatter before hunting a syntax difference, diff two connection strings character by character with the text diff tool, and split a copied postgres:// URL into its parts with the URL parser.

The longer version, with the pool sizing table and the keepalive snippet, is on my site: asyncpg DuplicatePreparedStatement on PgBouncer and Supabase.

title: Data Cache is moving to Runtime Cache
description:
Data Cache is exiting beta and moving to Runtime Cache. Next.js fetch caching and unstable_cache will switch over on every version without code changes. On Pro, each project and environment gets its own Runtime Cache storage allocation, with 8x the space of Data Cache’s previous team-wide pool. Enterprise projects get 10x their previous Data Cache storage.

Once your team migrates, Data Cache reads and writes that were previously unbilled are charged at Runtime Cache pricing. Rates start at $0.40 per million read units and $4.00 per million write units, and vary by region.

Hobby teams get 1 million read units and 200,000 write units free each month across all projects. On Pro, usage draws from your $20 infrastructure credit each month, and anything beyond it is billed at regional rates. For Enterprise pricing, contact your account team.

Migration

Teams created on or after October 30, 2026 use Runtime Cache by default.

If your team already uses Data Cache:

  • Hobby: We’ll migrate your team on November 29, 2026.

  • Pro: We’ll notify you of your migration date and when billing changes take effect.

  • Enterprise: Your account team will contact you with migration details.

Before you migrate, review your project's Data Cache usage in Observability. To cut unnecessary reads and writes, follow the optimization guide or copy the agent prompt into your coding agent. In the Runtime Cache dashboard, you can also select Optimize with Vercel Agent.

Starting October 30, existing Hobby and Pro teams can opt in early from your team's CDN settings. Runtime Cache pricing applies as soon as you opt in.

You can also disable fetch and unstable_cache caching in CDN settings, which sends more requests to your data sources but doesn’t stop your migration.

Read about the architecture and recent improvements in the blog post.

Yelp has moved its Cassandra fleet from legacy self-managed Kubernetes clusters to Amazon EKS by re-pointing existing EBS volumes at new pods, rather than streaming data between nodes.

By Claudio Masolo

title: RoboTeam: Benchmarking Vision-Based Multi-Agent Control of Many Robot Arms in Real Time
description:
arXiv:2611.22138v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Multimodal agents can now control robot arms by calling tools and writing code. Existing benchmarks fall short in three ways: most test one or two arms on short tasks, many pause the world while the agent thinks, and many give it ground-truth object positions. We present RoboTeam, a simulated benchmark where agents control 4 to 16 robot arms in real time from camera images alone. Its 36 tasks are long jobs that the arms must do together, such as passing timbers or building a picture from hundreds of cubes. We start from the most flexible agent system, the adaptive system, where one agent decides when to fork delegates. With it, gpt-6.1-sol and opus-5.5 complete 28 and 27 tasks, and four other models at most 3. But at a high price: a typical task takes gpt-6.1-sol 3.5 hours and 218 million input tokens, and a third of its steps fail at least once and must be retried. We then compare it with three fixed systems: single-agent, hierarchical, and decentralized. All four complete a similar number of tasks but differ in time and tokens. The hierarchical and decentralized systems are faster but use up to 1.9 times the tokens, and the single agent uses fewer tokens but takes 1.6 times as long, so the adaptive system lies between them. Even so, no model or system is yet fast, cheap, and reliable at once. RoboTeam measures these limits where earlier benchmarks cannot: long multi-arm jobs, camera images only, and a world that never pauses.

title: How to build a bounded after-hours clinic FAQ reply (open-source demo)
description:
A clinic website can answer "When do you open?" after reception closes. It should not improvise an answer to "Should I take antibiotics?" Those questions need different handling, even when someone puts both in the same message.

This walkthrough uses an MIT-licensed fictional dental-clinic demo. It illustrates approved operational answers, a booking link and explicit fallbacks. It is not client work, a medical device or a clinically validated system. There are no claimed booking increases or customer results.

Disclosure: This article was drafted and checked by an AI assistant on Ahmed Fouad's behalf. The demo was also built with AI assistance. Commands and implementation details below were checked against the public repository; its tests are developer-written regression checks, not an independent safety evaluation.

1. Draw the boundary before choosing a model

Keep the first version narrow: opening hours, accessibility, location, published fees and the clinic's existing booking route. Get the wording approved by the person responsible for clinic information. Give unknown questions a useful contact route rather than a plausible answer.

For a UK-facing deployment, keep general signposting visible: call 999 for emergencies; contact NHS 111 for urgent concerns when appropriate. Check the wording against NHS emergency guidance and NHS 111, then have the clinic approve it. NHS 111 online is England-only; confirm the appropriate route for the clinic's nation. Outside the UK, obtain local wording instead of copying those numbers.

Never present keyword detection as triage. A missed keyword does not mean someone is safe. Do not collect symptoms, patient records, dates of birth or contact details in this demonstration. A request for a person should lead to a clear human route, without pretending someone has been notified.

2. Run the kit without accounts or API keys

Download the ZIP from GitHub, or clone it:

git clone https://github.com/AHMEDFOUAAD/clinic-after-hours-faq-assistant.git
cd clinic-after-hours-faq-assistant

Open index.html in your browser. There is no build step. Try "What are your opening hours?", "How do I book an appointment?" and "I want to speak to a real person". The booking button opens a labelled placeholder, not an appointment calendar. The handover message does not contact reception.

Despite the chatbot interface, no language model runs at runtime. faq-data.js contains invented operational FAQs; engine.js selects canned replies with deterministic keyword matching. AI-assisted development is different from sending every visitor message to an AI provider. This version makes the boundaries easier to inspect and avoids runtime model fees.

3. Understand the reply order

The engine checks routes before attempting an FAQ match:

emergency signposting
→ personal-data warning
→ clinical-question refusal
→ human-contact request
→ approved FAQ match
→ unknown-question fallback

These are internal software labels, not clinical classifications. The emergency and clinical patterns are incomplete regular expressions. They can miss unfamiliar phrasing, misspellings or a different language.

FAQ matching normalizes text, removes common words and scores overlapping keywords. It returns an approved answer only when the match clears its threshold and uncertainty check. Otherwise it refuses to guess. It can still return irrelevant answers for nonsense such as "teeth whitening for cats". A passing test suite does not fix that limitation.

4. Replace the fictional content carefully

Work through SETUP.md rather than replacing the clinic name alone:

  • Replace every invented answer in faq-data.js with approved public wording. Keep who approved it and when outside the public repository.
  • Set bookingUrl to the clinic's existing approved HTTPS booking page. Do not add a patient-data form to the demo.
  • Replace the canned reception contact wording with a real, approved route. Do not publish private staff details.
  • Check fees, holiday hours and availability statements. Name the person responsible for future changes.

The source fields are fictional page labels, not documents fetched by a retrieval system. Changing a label does not verify an answer. Read the underlying clinic material yourself.

For a static preview, the setup guide lists the files to copy to an approved host. _headers is host-specific; other hosts need equivalent configuration. Keep fictional previews labelled DEMO and excluded from search indexing. Hosting these files does not connect email, WhatsApp, SMS or a booking calendar.

5. Test failures, not just friendly questions

With Node.js 22 or newer, run:

node tests/run-tests.js
node tests/unseen-probe.js
node --test tests/public-kit.test.js tests/interface.test.js

The checked revision passed its 36 scripted checks, 18 probe questions and three Node subtests. The historical unseen-probe name is misleading: those questions are now public and are not an independent evaluation.

Ask the clinic to supply fresh questions and paraphrases. Include mixed administrative and medical questions, requests for a person, unsupported services, personal details and incorrect assumptions. Check booking destinations, keyboard access and narrow screens. Confirm that input renders as plain text.

This kit does not transmit questions or persist chat history; questions remain in page memory until reload. Hosting visit logs and external booking pages have separate privacy implications. Review them too.

6. Treat a live auto-reply as a separate integration

AFTER-HOURS-REPLY.md provides sample wording, not a connected responder. A real email or form workflow needs channel permissions, opening-hour and holiday rules, duplicate-reply prevention, retention decisions and a named person who handles replies. Agree those before adding automation. If reporting is needed, prefer counts over copying message content.

Deliver editable source, approval notes and update instructions, then remove temporary access. Never put patient data or credentials in GitHub issues.

You can adapt and self-host the free demo kit without hiring anyone. For done-for-you setup, contact Ahmed through his Fiverr profile to agree a fixed scope; enquiries, orders and payments stay on Fiverr.

title: Towards Optimism-Pessimism Trade-off in Model-based Offline-to-Online Reinforcement Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.22172v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Model-based offline-to-online reinforcement learning (RL) enables sample-efficient adaptation by leveraging offline pre-training for online fine-tuning. However, the distribution shifts between offline and online stages often hinder fine-tuning performance. Many existing methods encode the optimism-pessimism trade-off through a single-objective formulation. Selecting its trade-off coefficient through online fine-tuning can require costly bi-level optimization. We identify the balance established during offline training as a key challenge: in our motivating experiments, optimistic policies adapt better to novel tasks, whereas pessimistic policies perform better on the same online tasks. To address this challenge, we propose a bi-objective formulation that captures this trade-off, yielding a Pareto policy pool during offline training. This policy pool enables adaptive selection during online fine-tuning across diverse online tasks. To generate the pool, we introduce Multi-Objective Soft Actor-critIC (MOSAIC), which solves bi-objective problems and constructs diverse Pareto policies. After offline training, a contextual bandit algorithm hierarchically selects the most suitable policy for fine-tuning at each online interaction step. Empirically, our pipeline, Hierarchical Pareto Policy Pool (HiP3), achieves the strongest aggregate performance across both same and novel online tasks and maintains its advantage under stronger distribution shifts. Comprehensive ablations further clarify the roles of the policy pool, MOSAIC-based pool construction, and the online selection mechanism.

title: Reconfiguring Procedural Knowledge for Compositional Robot Skill Adaptation
description:
arXiv:2611.22174v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: General-purpose behavior models increasingly internalize broad procedural knowledge during training, making their adaptation to new goals and skill interfaces less a problem of learning entirely new behaviors than of reconfiguring existing competence. We study this capability as reconfigurability, the ability to realize new behaviors by cost-efficiently restructuring existing components and relations under sparse governing information, where task specifications provide high-level goals and procedure specifications expose a limited set of reusable factors, leaving the concrete bindings and compositions required for execution underdetermined. We propose RecPo, a framework that represents skills task-agnostically through multiple procedure views and materializes executable skill sequences by composing stored transitions to realize task-specific changes. RecPo maintains a procedure knowledge base of skill-induced transitions, with each view exposing a reusable factor and preserving local skill connectivity. At deployment, it interprets task specifications through the same views and resolves the resulting compositional queries over the stored relations to bind skills for execution. On long-horizon tasks in an extended Franka Kitchen benchmark, RecPo achieves 91.9% ordered completion with 1.0 ms of task inference per episode across varying procedure support and task-record sparsity. Real-robot studies further demonstrate adaptation through local memory edits without task-specific retraining.
