title: From GPT-3 to Agents: How AI Rewired Software in Six Years (2020-2026)
description:
If you had told a developer in early 2020 that by the end of 2026 most of their peers would use AI every working day, that software agents would open pull requests, and that a model would be better than a PhD-level human baseline on science questions while still fumbling an analog clock, they would have asked what you were smoking.

Well. It's mid-November 2026.

So let's do something we rarely do in this industry: stop, zoom out, and measure how far AI has actually travelled in six and a half years. Not hype. Numbers, milestones, and one uncomfortable pattern in the data that I think every developer should think about.

And at the end, there's a very concrete story about what all this means for a tool millions of people use, and a deadline that is 15 days away.

First, a correction: AI didn't "arrive" in 2020

Dev.to will eat me alive if I skip this. AI research is decades old. Deep learning broke through in 2012, and the Transformer architecture dropped in 2017.

But 2020 is the year the curve bent for everyone else. GPT-3 showed that if you scale a Transformer far enough, you get something that follows instructions from a handful of examples, with no task-specific training. That one idea (you can "program" a model with text) is the root of almost everything that followed. So I'm using 2020 as year zero of the era we're all living in.

The six-year timeline

Year The moment Why developers cared
2020 GPT-3 arrives (mid-year). AlphaFold 2 dominates the CASP14 protein-folding challenge (late-year). Few-shot prompting is born. And AI cracks a 50-year-old science problem.
2021 DALL·E (Jan). GitHub Copilot technical preview (Jun). For the first time, AI lives inside the editor.
2022 DALL·E 2, open-weights Stable Diffusion, then ChatGPT on Nov 30. Image generation goes open source. ChatGPT turns "AI" into a text box anyone can use; analysts estimated ~100M users within about two months.
2023 GPT-4, Claude, Llama 2 (open weights). Multimodal and long-context models; RAG becomes a default architecture; "prompt engineer" becomes a job title (briefly).
2024 Sora preview. Nobel Prizes in Physics and Chemistry both honour AI-related work. Legitimacy. AI is now science, not just product.
2025 Reasoning models. DeepSeek-R1 open weights (Jan). Terminal and IDE coding agents go mainstream. Models "think" before answering. Costs fall. Developers start delegating, not just autocompleting.
2026 Agents inside everyday workflows. Stanford's AI Index says capability is accelerating, not plateauing. The question changes from "can it do it?" to "can I trust it, and who's accountable?"

What the numbers say

Timelines are fun; surveys are honest. Stack Overflow has been asking developers about AI since 2023, and the trajectory is steep.

Developers using AI tools (Stack Overflow):

2023 2024 2025 2026
44% 62% 79% only ~17% say they don't use AI tools at work

AI agents are the faster story. In the 2025 survey, 31% of respondents used agents. A smaller pulse survey in April 2026 found agent use had almost doubled to 59%, with Claude Code usage among agent users rising from 41% to 55%.

And outside our bubble, Lightcast's read of the Stanford data shows 2.5% of all US job postings now mention AI skills: up 55% in a year and roughly 300% over a decade.

So: massive adoption. Done, right? Not quite.

The uncomfortable pattern: usage up, trust down

Here's the part that doesn't fit the hype narrative.

  • In 2025, 46% of developers said they distrust AI output, versus 33% who trust it. Only 3% said they "highly trust" it.
  • In the 2026 survey, nearly half trust AI output when they can easily verify it. Just 6.6% would trust it with an important decision.
  • The most common frustration in 2025: solutions that are "almost right, but not quite."
  • Governance is lagging: only 24% of respondents said their employer had published approved AI tools or guidance.

I'd argue this is the defining dynamic of 2026: AI has become infrastructure faster than it has become trustworthy. We use it constantly and check it constantly.

Stanford's 2026 AI Index captures the same weirdness from the capability side: models now beat human baselines on PhD-level science questions, yet still fail at tasks like reading an analog clock. Researchers call this jagged intelligence: brilliant peaks, baffling potholes.

My takeaway (opinion, not data): the most valuable developer skill of the next few years isn't prompting. It's verification: writing tests, reading diffs, designing systems where a wrong-but-plausible answer gets caught.

The quiet shift nobody is tweeting about: AI left the data center

In 2020, running a serious neural network meant renting GPUs and calling an API. That model (your data goes up, the answer comes down, and you pay per call) defined the first half of this era.

The second half is different. Thanks to WebAssembly, WebGPU, and runtimes like ONNX Runtime Web, a browser tab can now run real models locally:

import * as ort from "onnxruntime-web";

// Simplified: load a model once, cache it, run inference on-device
const session = await ort.InferenceSession.create("/models/segmenter.onnx", {
  executionProviders: ["wasm"], // or "webgpu" where supported
});

const result = await session.run({ input: imageTensor });
// Nothing was uploaded. No API key. No per-call bill.

Why this matters:

  • Privacy: sensitive data never leaves the device.
  • Cost: inference runs on the user's hardware, so there are no per-image credits.
  • Latency and availability: after the first download there is no round trip, and some tools work offline.
  • Longevity: your tool can't be switched off because someone else's API changed pricing.

That last point just became very real for millions of people.

Case study: the end of an era

For years, remove.bg was the answer to "how do I remove a background?" It popularised one-click AI background removal and was a textbook example of the cloud-API era.

Now its standalone website is closing on December 1, 2026, with the functionality moving into Canva (which has owned it since 2021). Reporting based on remove.bg's own FAQ says the closure is at 9:00 CET, unused pay-as-you-go credits expire, and the self-serve API moves to Leonardo.Ai (also Canva-owned). If you rely on it, export your usage reports and invoices before the cutoff.

There's a lesson here that has nothing to do with any single company: if your workflow depends on someone else's server, it has an expiry date you don't control.

If you're already in the Canva ecosystem, Canva is the official successor and will be fine for you. But if you want something that doesn't ask for an account or a credit card, or send your photos anywhere, read on.

Meet APIC: the on-device approach, in practice

Full disclosure: I built APIC, so weigh my opinion accordingly. But everything below is verifiable in about 60 seconds, which is exactly why I'm comfortable showing it to a room full of skeptical developers.

👉 apic-studio.vercel.app

APIC (Advanced Image Processing Center) is a free, browser-based photo editor where the AI runs on your device. No upload. No credits. No account required to edit or export (there's an optional Google sign-in, nothing more).

Background removal, the remove.bg use case

  • On-device AI cut-out with three model sizes: Light (~5 MB, built for phones), Fast (~44 MB), and Maximum (~176 MB, multi-pass, best on a PC). Models download once and are cached.
  • A Restore / Erase brush to fix hair, fur and awkward edges, plus one-click replacement with white, black or a blurred copy of your photo.
  • Full-resolution output as transparent PNG or WebP.
  • Batch mode: remove backgrounds, resize, compress and convert many images, then download one ZIP.

And because I got tired of juggling ten tabs, it's eleven tools in one

  • Remove Object: paint over a person, sign or blemish; inpainting runs locally (MI-GAN ~28 MB, or LaMa ~208 MB for big, complex fills).
  • AI upscale (2x / 4x) with Real-ESRGAN.
  • Compress to an exact file size ("under 200 KB" for that upload form), resize, and convert between PNG, JPEG, WebP, AVIF, BMP, ICO, PDF and PSD, with HEIC photos accepted as input.
  • Pro colour tools: histogram, RGB curves, HSL mixer, 3-way grading, and 3D LUT (.cube) export for DaVinci Resolve, Premiere and Photoshop.
  • Social presets for 15+ networks with safe-zone guides; Layers with blend modes and PSD import/export; Hide area to blur or pixelate faces, plates and card numbers before you share.
  • A Windows app that runs fully offline, no account needed.

The honest trade-offs (because you'd find them anyway):

  • The first run of any AI tool downloads its model, so it's slower once and fast afterwards.
  • The heaviest models are best on a desktop-class machine. On phones, use Light.
  • It's a browser tool, not a replacement for Photoshop's full ecosystem.
  • I'm one developer shipping this, not a 500-person company. Feedback genuinely shapes the roadmap.

Try it with your hardest photo

Don't test it on a clean studio shot. Take the image remove.bg struggled with (wispy hair, glass, a busy background) and run it through APIC's Remove BG tab on Maximum. Use the Restore brush if needed. If it doesn't hold up, tell me where it failed. If it does, you've just saved yourself a subscription.

Make it your default (it takes 20 seconds)

With 15 days left on the old default, now is the moment to build a new habit:

  1. Open apic-studio.vercel.app and drop in a photo.
  2. Bookmark it and pin the tab, so "remove background" now means one click on your own bookmarks bar.
  3. Send it to the one person in your team, family or client list who still says "just use remove.bg."
  4. Tell me what's missing: a comment below, or find me on GitHub / dev.to. I read everything.

(I also wrote a shorter, practical guide on the remove.bg shutdown specifically: remove.bg Is Shutting Down — Here's a Free, No-Upload Alternative.)

So, how much AI is there in six years?

Started as a research demo behind a waitlist in 2020. By 2026 it's in the editor, the terminal, the job postings, the Nobel Prizes, the survey data, and increasingly, in your browser tab, running on your own hardware.

The next six years won't be about who has the biggest model. They'll be about three questions:

  1. Can I verify it? (trust)
  2. Who controls it? (open weights, on-device, no kill switch)
  3. Does it respect the user? (privacy by architecture, not by policy)

The tools that win on all three won't need a marketing budget. They'll just be the ones people quietly never switch away from.

I'm betting on that. Come try APIC, and tell me where I'm wrong.

Your turn: what was your "oh, this changes everything" AI moment between 2020 and 2026: GPT-3, Copilot, ChatGPT, or something else? Drop it in the comments. 👇

Sources: Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2025 · Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2026 coverage · Stanford HAI AI Index 2026 · Lightcast · remove.bg shutdown reporting

title: My Feather Fractal Was Just Two Blobs: Fixing 2 Rational Dynamics Bugs in WebGL & NumPy
description:
My Feather Fractal Was Just Two Blobs: Fixing 2 Rational Dynamics Bugs in WebGL & NumPy

🔗 Quick Links

  • 🚀 Live Demo (60 FPS WebGL 2.0): https://fantasticfractals.pages.dev
  • ⭐ GitHub (MIT Open Source): https://github.com/QuantumTechCoder/FantasticFractals
  • 📦 PyPI: pip install fantasticfractals → https://pypi.org/project/fantasticfractals/
  • 📓 1-Click Google Colab: Open in Colab

Right after fixing the Sierpinski gothic arch and Koch snowflake slider bugs on FantasticFractals, I thought our 27 fractal formulas were finally rock solid.

Then user testing struck again.

Someone dropped two side-by-side screenshots into our issues:

  1. "Why does the Feather Fractal look like two smooth horizontal blobs? When I search Google Images, feather fractals have organic plume filaments."
  2. "What's wrong with the Nova Fractal? It looks like a 3-lobed bullseye instead of the iconic Paul Derbyshire crescent."

I opened Google Images, compared their search results against my WebGL canvas, and realized I had completely botched the complex rational math for both systems.

Here is the breakdown of what broke, why complex phase twists matter, and how we fixed both fractals in GLSL and NumPy.

Bug #1: The "Two Smooth Blobs" Feather Fractal 🪶

Here is what FantasticFractals was rendering when you selected the Feather Fractal:

It was literally two giant, smooth cyan circles with a central black oval. No plumes. No barbs. Zero feather-like structure.

The Math Mistake: $1 + z^2$ vs $1 + i|z|^2$

In my original code, I had implemented this formula:
$$z_{n+1} = rac{z_n^3}{1 + z_n^2} + c$$

// ❌ WRONG FORMULA:
vec2 z2 = vec2(z.x * z.x - z.y * z.y, 2.0 * z.x * z.y);
vec2 denom = vec2(1.0 + z2.x, z2.y); // <-- Standard complex 1 + z^2

Because $1 + z^2$ has real coefficients, the denominator is analytic and preserves standard bilateral symmetry. Near the origin, it just behaves like $z^3 + c$, which produces smooth, rounded cardioid lobes.

The Real Formula from Mandelbrowser

The authentic Feather Fractal (popularized by Mandelbrowser and fractal art forums) uses an imaginary phase coupling in the denominator:

$$z_{n+1} = rac{z_n^3}{1 + i |z_n|^2} + c$$

Look closely at that denominator:
$$ ext{denom} = 1 + i(x^2 + y^2)$$

It uses the Euclidean magnitude squared $|z|^2 = x^2 + y^2$, multiplied by the imaginary unit $i$!

Why this creates the "Feather" effect:

Because $|z|^2$ is purely real, multiplying it by $i$ forces the denominator to rotate the phase of $z^3$ by an angle that dynamically increases with distance from the origin:
$$ heta_{ ext{twist}} = -rctan(|z|^2)$$

This nonlinear phase rotation shears the escape trajectories, pulling the boundaries into razor-thin, dendritic plume filaments that burst outward along the diagonals.

The Fix in GLSL: 

// ✅ THE FIX:
vec2 z = vec2(0.0);
int i = 0;
for (; i < 500; i++) {
  if (i >= u_maxIterations) break;
  float r2 = dot(z, z);
  if (r2 > 16.0) {
    // Continuous potential shading
    float log_zn = log(r2) / 2.0;
    float nu = log(max(1.0, log_zn) / 0.693147) / 0.693147;
    iterVal = float(i) + 1.0 - nu;
    break;
  }
  // z^3 = (x^3 - 3xy^2) + i(3x^2y - y^3)
  vec2 z3 = vec2(z.x * (z.x * z.x - 3.0 * z.y * z.y), z.y * (3.0 * z.x * z.x - z.y * z.y));

  // denom = 1 + i*|z|^2 -> divide by (1 + i*r2)
  float denNorm = 1.0 + r2 * r2;
  vec2 frac = vec2(z3.x + z3.y * r2, z3.y - z3.x * r2) / denNorm;
  z = frac + c;
}

Here is the exact same coordinate plane after deploying the fix:

Now it actually looks like an explosive plumage of organic fractal feathers.

Bug #2: The "Concentric Bullseye" Nova Fractal 🌟

The second bug was in our Nova Fractal. Here is what was on screen:

A symmetric 3-petaled blob surrounded by concentric bullseye rings.

If you search Wikipedia or Ultra Fractal for the Nova fractal, you don't see a bullseye—you see an iconic crescent-shaped central bay with intricate Mandelbrot filaments and satellite islands wrapping around its rim.

What Caused This?

Paul Derbyshire invented the Nova fractal in 1997 by taking the classic Newton-Raphson root-finding method for $f(z) = z^3 - 1$:
$$z_{n+1} = z_n - R rac{z^3 - 1}{3z^2}$$

And adding the coordinate $c$ at each step (with standard relaxation $R = 1$):
$$z_{n+1} = rac{2z_n + rac{1}{z_n^2}}{3} + c$$

My implementation had three distinct bugs:

  1. Incorrect Critical Initialization ($z_0$):
    I had initialized $z_0 = c$. But in the canonical Mandelbrot formulation of the Nova fractal, the iteration must start at the critical root anchor $z_0 = 1.0$ ($1 + 0i$)!
    Starting at $z_0 = c$ scrambles the parameter dynamics into an arbitrary slice, collapsing the crescent.

  2. Accidental Coordinate Dampening:
    In my shader, someone had written:

   vec2 nextZ = (2.0 * z + invZ2) / 3.0 + c * 0.2; // ❌ WHY * 0.2?!

Dampening $c$ by $0.2$ suppressed the chaotic perturbation, causing the Newton basins to dominate and form concentric rings.

  1. Wrong Default Center & Zoom: The center was hardcoded at (0.0, 0.0). But because $z_0 = 1$, the main crescent of the Nova Mandelbrot set is centered near $x pprox -0.5, y = 0.0$.

The Fix in GLSL: 

// ✅ THE FIX:
vec2 z = vec2(1.0, 0.0); // Canonical critical anchor z0 = 1
int i = 0;
for (; i < 500; i++) {
  if (i >= u_maxIterations) break;
  float d2 = dot(z, z);
  if (d2 < 1e-8) break;

  // 1 / z^2
  float invD4 = 1.0 / (d2 * d2);
  vec2 invZ2 = vec2(z.x * z.x - z.y * z.y, -2.0 * z.x * z.y) * invD4;

  // Full c addition: (2z + 1/z^2)/3 + c
  vec2 nextZ = (2.0 * z + invZ2) / 3.0 + c;

  // Convergence check to fixed point:
  vec2 diff = nextZ - z;
  if (dot(diff, diff) < 1e-7) {
    iterVal = float(i) * 2.5;
    break;
  }
  // Divergence check:
  if (dot(nextZ, nextZ) > 100.0) {
    iterVal = float(i) * 2.5 + 50.0;
    break;
  }
  z = nextZ;
}

And centering the camera at defaultCenter: { x: -0.5, y: 0.0 }.

Here is the corrected Nova Fractal:

The authentic Paul Derbyshire crescent with its necklace of satellite Mandelbrot sets and delicate tendrils is fully restored.

Keeping NumPy Vectorization Synchronized 🐍

Because FantasticFractals is also a published Python scientific package (pip install fantasticfractals), fixing the WebGL shaders meant updating the vectorized NumPy array kernels as well.

Here is the NumPy vectorized kernel for the fixed Feather Fractal:

# Vectorized Feather Fractal in NumPy:
Z = np.zeros(C.shape, dtype=complex)
iters = np.full(C.shape, -1.0, dtype=np.float64)
active = np.ones(C.shape, dtype=bool)

for i in range(max_iterations):
    if not np.any(active):
        break
    z_act = Z[active]
    c_act = C[active]

    r2 = z_act.real**2 + z_act.imag**2
    escaped = r2 > 16.0

    if np.any(escaped):
        act_idx = np.where(active)[0][escaped], np.where(active)[1][escaped]
        r2_esc = r2[escaped]
        log_zn = np.log(r2_esc) / 2.0
        nu = np.log2(np.maximum(1.0, log_zn))
        iters[act_idx] = float(i) + 1.0 - nu
        active[act_idx] = False

    z_rem = z_act[~escaped]
    c_rem = c_act[~escaped]
    r2_rem = r2[~escaped]

    # Authentic 1 + i*|z|^2 denominator
    denom = 1.0 + 1j * r2_rem
    Z[active] = (z_rem ** 3) / denom + c_rem

Both client-side GPU shaders and Python library functions now produce identical mathematical outputs down to floating-point precision.

Key Lessons

  1. Phase matters: If a fractal formula contains $i$ in the denominator (like $1 + i|z|^2$), you cannot treat it as a standard real polynomial. That imaginary unit is doing the heavy lifting of twisting coordinate space into fractal plumes.
  2. Critical values anchor parameter spaces: For Newton-type relaxation fractals like Nova, starting at $z_0 = c$ versus $z_0 = 1$ is the difference between a blurry bullseye and the true Mandelbrot crescent.
  3. Always visually cross-reference fractal literature: Unit tests can pass, but if you don't visually cross-reference against original papers or historical fractal databases, you can easily end up with smooth blobs pretending to be fractals.

Check Out the Fixes Live

Everything is pushed and deployed:

  • 🌐 Live Web Visualizer: https://fantasticfractals.pages.dev
  • ⭐ GitHub (MIT): https://github.com/QuantumTechCoder/FantasticFractals

title: Communicate the Change: Efficient Expert Parallelism via Activation Compression
description:
arXiv:2611.22215v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Scaling has driven the success of large language models (LLM), with sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures enabling greater parameter capacity without a proportional increase in computation. At large scales, MoE models rely on expert parallelism to distribute experts across devices. Each MoE layer requires two synchronous collective communication steps during inference: dispatching hidden states to the activated experts and combining the resulting expert outputs. As compute throughput has outpaced interconnect bandwidth, these synchronous collectives have become a major bottleneck to MoE scaling and efficiency. We address this challenge with EchoMoE, a lightweight architecture modification that retrofits existing MoE models, requiring approximately 8,500x fewer training tokens than full pretraining. Motivated by the observation that transformer blocks update the residual stream incrementally, we use a hidden state from an earlier layer as a reference and communicate only the compressed difference between it and the current state, rather than communicating each hidden state in full. EchoMoE periodically refreshes these reference states and transmits only the compressed differences synchronously, reducing the traffic on latency-critical paths without significant computational overhead. EchoMoE reduces inter-node communication volume by 58% and improves throughput by 22.6%, while preserving average performance within 3.8 percentage points across 18 benchmarks. EchoMoE further improves inference throughput by up to 2.38x over bandwidth-constrained Ethernet, paving the way for wide-area distributed inference. EchoMoE also tolerates quantization of the communicated representations without measurable quality loss. We release an efficient implementation for applying EchoMoE to pretrained MoE models, together with an inference integration for vLLM.

title: Multistage Contextual Optimization for Vehicle Repositioning
description:
arXiv:2611.22330v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Ride-hailing platforms reposition idle vehicles to improve spatial supply-demand balances. This problem is prediction-driven and multistage: at each stage, the platform forecasts future demand, executes current decisions, and uses the resulting state to initialize the next stage. We formulate a multistage linear program (LP) with a macroscopic fundamental diagram (MFD) linking accumulation to trip completion. We then develop a multistage contextual optimization approach that uses decision performance to train the prediction model. The learning problem combines multiple coupled stages, context that depends on earlier decisions, and predictions that affect the objective, the constraint matrix, and the right-hand side of the LP. We derive the exact gradient, which has three parts: parameters change forecasts and hence decisions; earlier decisions change the current decision through the inherited state; and this state also changes forecasts as context. An equivalent adjoint uses reverse vector-Jacobian products, avoiding full solution and state-parameter Jacobians. Finally, forward propagation solves many stage LPs one after another, which makes training slow. We propose a parallel block evaluation algorithm that solves blocks of consecutive stages in parallel and repeatedly feeds each block output to the next block. We prove that the algorithm recovers the serial trajectory within a finite number of passes and that its gradient error remains bounded when it stops early. On New York City ride-hailing data, multistage contextual optimization yields 7.7% to 9.1% more business benefit than the same predictor trained by mean squared error, outperforms all compared baselines from five paradigms, and even outperforms realized demand fed to the same policy. With eight workers, parallel block evaluation shortens training by a factor of 1.86 without loss of decision performance.

title: WebAgents: Unbundling Agent Creation, Hosting, and Execution for an Agent-Native Web
description:
arXiv:2611.21978v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models are moving from isolated assistants toward autonomous agents that can plan, use tools, and coordinate with others, motivating an emerging Agentic Web of independently developed agents and services. Realizing this vision requires agent behavior to move across creators, hosts, and runtimes without coupling publication to a particular execution environment or transferring authority over user resources. We introduce WebAgents, which unbundles these roles through a signed agent.pkg that carries portable workflows, skills, schemas, and resource requirements. An OpenClaw-based agent-native browser/runtime verifies the package, obtains authorization, and binds it at run time to user-controlled models, tools, permissions, and budgets, while hosts distribute the public program and may retain private services server-side. We demonstrate this contract with three unrelated workflows executed unchanged under local and API-backed models, including literature review with live services and a website-published travel agent using semantic tools and user-selected personal resources. In a controlled suite, WebAgents explicitly blocks all 716 injected contract violations while accepting all 295 matched benign controls, with median automated pre-execution processing below 0.5 s for all three packages. We conclude by outlining a path toward NANDA-based discovery and interoperable package ecosystems while retaining execution authority in the user's runtime.

title: ANCHOR: Assessing Naturalistic Constraint Hierarchies and Ordering in Repository-Grounded Agentic Coding
description:
arXiv:2610.16859v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: For repository-grounded coding agents, a functionally correct patch is not necessarily an acceptable one: developers also constrain how the task must be carried out-modification scope, workflow order, validation, tool use, and reporting. This capability, which we call engineering constraint following, remains largely invisible to current evaluations. We introduce ANCHOR (Assessing Naturalistic Constraint Hierarchies and Ordering in Repository-Grounded Agentic Coding), a benchmark built on naturalistic, multilingual repository tasks spanning eight language groups. ANCHOR combines (i) a hierarchical taxonomy of 10 categories and 78 leaf types distilled from real developer interactions, (ii) an automated pipeline that instantiates task-grounded atomic constraints and composes them into typed AND/THEN/PRIORITY relations, and (iii) a trajectory-grounded evaluation framework that checks both the code diff and the execution trajectory with rule-based and LLM judges. Across 19 agent configurations spanning 2 scaffolds and 10 foundation models on 358 tasks, the strongest measured system, Claude Opus 4.8 under Cline, reaches 70.1% atomic compliance and 63.7% relation compliance, while 19.0% of tasks pass every scored checklist item under the strict all-item FCCR criterion. A five-engineer audit of constraints from 50 instances reports 94% feasibility, 94% repository consistency, and 96% realism. In the primary paired set (14 configurations), the mean signed change in task completion after adding constraints is +0.7 percentage points; individual changes vary in both directions. These results distinguish functional success from constraint compliance, with failures concentrated in workflow ordering, tool-use discipline, and reporting, and substantial interactions between models and scaffolds.

title: Distilling World Action Models for Efficient Bimanual Manipulation via Anchored Path Matching
description:
arXiv:2611.22592v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) jointly generate future video and robot actions through iterative denoising. Few-step distillation reduces the number of model evaluations, but its coarse updates can move the student away from the teacher's trajectory. We propose Anchored Path Matching (APM), which supervises endpoint and short-transition predictions from states reached by the student. From each state, we continue the teacher to zero noise and use its endpoint and first intermediate state as targets. Modality-routed adapters learn to match both targets from the same starting state. When the two gradients conflict, anchor-priority updates preserve the endpoint gradient and remove the opposing component of the local gradient within each modality. One checkpoint supports 1-, 2-, and 4-step joint generation. The sampling budget can be chosen at deployment without retraining or teacher queries. On RoboTwin 2.0, we train only on Clean demonstrations and evaluate directly on the domain-randomized Random setting. At one step, APM improves closed-loop success over continued base distillation at matched inference budgets by 2.0 percentage points on Clean and 1.4 on Random. Video peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) rises from 30.169 to 32.317 dB, with gains in structural similarity (SSIM) and learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS). On two real-robot tasks, APM improves success over the one-step teacher and reduces control-cycle latency by $21.3\times$ relative to the eight-step teacher.Project page: https://jialonglong.github.io/Anchored-Path-Matching/.

title: Java4Shell: AI Found a Critical Java Flaw in About an Hour — Here's What to Patch
description:
Java4Shell: AI Found a Critical Java Flaw in About an Hour — Here's What to Patch

By Shakeel Ahmed — AI Growth Lab

A critical vulnerability in Java's core libraries was found by an AI-assisted researcher in about an hour, weaponized into a working exploit in about two more hours, and patched by Oracle the same day it was disclosed. The flaw, nicknamed Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), is a memory-corruption bug in OpenJDK's hardware-accelerated Base64 decoder — and if you run Java 17 or newer on modern Intel or AMD servers, you should patch now. CISA has already issued an alert urging immediate patching, and there is no exploitation in the wild reported yet — which means the window to fix this before attackers catch up is still open, but it will not stay open long.

What Is Java4Shell?

Java4Shell is a heap out-of-bounds write in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder, the code behind java.util.Base64.Decoder — one of the most widely used utilities in the entire Java ecosystem. Almost every Java application that handles tokens, certificates, file uploads, API payloads, or serialized data touches Base64 somewhere, which is what makes this flaw so dangerous despite its narrow trigger.

The bug lives in the HotSpot JVM's AVX-512 VBMI intrinsic, in a function called generate_base64_decodeBlock. When the JVM runs on an x86-64 CPU with AVX-512 VBMI support, it uses a hand-optimized, hardware-accelerated path to decode Base64 data. That fast path contains a memory-corruption flaw: specially crafted Base64 input can write past the end of a heap buffer. A heap out-of-bounds write is one of the most serious classes of memory bugs, because it can corrupt adjacent data structures — and, in the hands of a skilled attacker, turn into arbitrary code execution inside the JVM process.

Security firm Calif, which disclosed the flaw on November 17, 2026, rates it 9.2 under CVSS 4.0 — critical. Oracle, which released patches in its November Critical Patch Update the same day, rates it 8.1 under CVSS 3.1, citing high attack complexity. The gap between the two scores is a judgment call about how hard the bug is to exploit reliably. Calif's own demonstrations suggest the difficulty is lower than Oracle's score implies: the firm demonstrated pre-authentication remote code execution in the default configurations of Jenkins, JFrog Artifactory, Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, and PingFederate, and post-authentication remote code execution on Gerrit, Apache Kafka, Elasticsearch, Solr, and Spinnaker. "Pre-auth" matters enormously — it means an attacker needs no account, no login, and no credentials. Any internet-reachable instance of those products running an unpatched JVM was, in principle, remotely exploitable.

Who Is Affected?

The exposure is broad but specific, and that specificity is good news for triage:

  • Affected versions: Unpatched OpenJDK builds from 17.0.6 onward, including Java 21, 25, and 27. If you run Java 17, 21, 25, or 27, assume you are affected until you verify your patch level.
  • Affected hardware: Only x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 VBMI instructions — Intel Xeon processors from Ice Lake through Granite Rapids, and AMD EPYC processors based on Zen 4 and later. The bug is in the AVX-512 accelerated code path, so machines without that instruction set never take the vulnerable path.
  • Not affected: ARM64 systems. If your fleet runs on ARM — including AWS Graviton, Apple Silicon, or Ampere — the vulnerable intrinsic does not exist on your platform.
  • Affected products: Any Java application that decodes Base64 on a vulnerable JVM and CPU combination. The headline demonstrations cover Jenkins, JFrog Artifactory, Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, PingFederate, Gerrit, Apache Kafka, Elasticsearch, Solr, and Spinnaker — but those are demonstrations, not an exhaustive list. Any enterprise Java application that accepts Base64 input from untrusted sources is potentially in scope.

Note the version floor: 17.0.6. If you are still running Java 8 or 11 in production — and plenty of enterprises are — this particular flaw does not apply to you, because the vulnerable AVX-512 intrinsic was introduced later. That is not a reason to stay on an old version, but it does mean your patching priority for this CVE is lower than for teams on Java 17 and above.

The AI Angle: Found in an Hour, Exploited in Two More

The most talked-about part of Java4Shell is not the bug itself — it is how it was found. Researcher Quang Luong used OpenAI's Codex with GPT-6 Cyber, an AI model tuned for security research, to find the flaw in approximately one hour and build a first working exploit in about two more hours. Total token cost: under $200.

That timeline should change how every engineering team thinks about vulnerability research. A task that once required days or weeks of expert manual code auditing — reading thousands of lines of JVM intrinsic code, reasoning about vectorized memory operations, and constructing a proof of concept — was compressed into a single afternoon by one researcher working with a model. Calif describes the approach as the "centaur hacker": human plus model, each doing what it does best. The human directs, hypothesizes, and validates; the model reads code at inhuman scale, spots the anomaly, and iterates on exploit variants far faster than a person typing alone.

Wiz's Atlas AI system independently produced a proof of concept within about two hours and confirmed remote code execution on Jira, Confluence, and Jenkins — a second data point that this was not a one-off fluke. Two separate AI systems, two working exploits, same afternoon.

The defensive implication is double-edged. On one hand, AI-assisted research finds real bugs faster, which means vendors and the open-source community can fix more flaws before attackers find them. On the other hand, the same capability is available to attackers. The window between disclosure and mass exploitation is shrinking. A vulnerability that took weeks to weaponize in 2020 can be weaponized in hours in 2026. Patching speed is no longer a nice-to-have — it is the primary defense.

Calif is acting responsibly with the disclosure: the firm is withholding product-specific exploits and has published only a safe reproducer, giving defenders time to patch. But the technical details of the bug are public, and the reproducer alone gives skilled attackers most of what they need. The clock is running.

There is also an uncomfortable footnote. The flaw reportedly leaked before the patch was ready — South Korea's National Cyber Security Center issued an advisory on November 16, a day before the coordinated disclosure. Leaks compress the patching window further and are a reminder that coordinated disclosure timelines are fragile.

How to Patch Java4Shell Right Now

Patching is straightforward, and Oracle's November Critical Patch Update contains the fix. Here is the order of operations:

1. Find every vulnerable JVM

Inventory your Java runtimes before you patch anything. Check every server, container image, CI runner, and developer machine:

java -version

Then check whether the underlying CPU exposes AVX-512 VBMI:

grep -o avx512_vbmi /proc/cpuinfo | head -1

If the CPU flag is absent, that host is not exposed to this flaw through the accelerated path. If it is present and the JVM is unpatched Java 17.0.6 or later, that host is in scope. Pay special attention to container images — a base image with an old JDK can silently ship the vulnerable runtime into dozens of services, and container rebuilds are where patches most often get missed.

2. Apply Oracle's November Critical Patch Update

Upgrade to the patched OpenJDK release for your Java version — Java 17, 21, 25, or 27. If you use a distribution build (Amazon Corretto, Eclipse Temurin, Azul Zulu, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, Red Hat's build), apply the equivalent patched release from your vendor; all major distributors shipped fixes alongside Oracle's update. Rebuild and redeploy container images, and restart every JVM process — a patched JDK on disk does nothing for a JVM that is still running the old code in memory.

3. If you cannot patch immediately, use the JVM flag

Qualys notes that a single JVM flag can close the exposure where patching must wait. The flag disables the vulnerable AVX-512 accelerated Base64 path, forcing the JVM to fall back to the safe software decoder. There is a small performance cost — Base64 decoding gets slower — but for most applications it is negligible compared to the risk of remote code execution. Apply the flag as a temporary mitigation on every exposed service, then patch properly as soon as your change window allows. Do not treat the flag as a permanent fix: it is a tourniquet, not a cure.

4. Prioritize internet-facing services first

Patch in this order: internet-facing Jenkins, Jira, Confluence, Keycloak, Artifactory, and PingFederate instances first, then internal instances of the same products, then everything else running Java 17+. Calif demonstrated pre-auth RCE on the first group in default configurations — those are the systems an internet-wide scan will find first. If you run any of those products, check your vendor's advisory as well; several have issued their own guidance on top of Oracle's patch.

5. Verify the fix

After patching, confirm the running JVM is actually the patched build — java -version on the live process or container, not just the installed package. If you applied the mitigation flag instead, confirm it is present in the process's JVM arguments. Then watch for follow-up advisories: researchers are actively probing related code paths, and Calif has a track record here — the firm previously found PHP2Shell in October 2026 and a vulnerability nicknamed Squidbleed. Related flaws in adjacent code have a habit of surfacing after a big disclosure.

Why This One Matters More Than the Average CVE

Enterprise Java has had critical vulnerabilities before — Log4Shell in 2021 is the obvious comparison — but Java4Shell is different in two ways. First, the bug is in the JVM itself, not in a library you can upgrade independently. Every Java application on an affected runtime shares the exposure, which makes the blast radius unusually wide and the fix unusually centralized: one JDK upgrade closes it everywhere. Second, the discovery story is a preview of the new normal. AI-assisted vulnerability research is no longer a lab curiosity. It found a critical flaw in one of the most audited codebases in the world, in an hour, for less than $200.

That changes the economics of both offense and defense. For defenders, the lesson is to invest in patch velocity: automated JDK upgrades, container rebuild pipelines, and runtime inventories that can answer "where are we running Java 17+ on AVX-512?" in minutes, not days. For the industry, the lesson is that the most heavily reviewed code still hides critical bugs — and the tools that find them are now cheap enough for anyone to run.

No exploitation in the wild has been reported as of November 17, according to VulnCheck and Sophos. That is the best news in this story, and it is also temporary. Patch now, while the window is still open.

Sources

  • CISA Alert — Critical Java Vulnerability Requires Immediate Patching

title: Our AI Code Reviewer Failed Its Own Trust Test — Then We Placed 2nd at Junction 2026
description:
We built an AI system to verify AI-generated code.

Then we discovered that our own AI reviewers weren't as independent as we thought.

That turned out to be one of the most valuable lessons from building Katse, our project for Tieto's Earned Trust in AI Code challenge at Junction 2026.

The question we were trying to answer sounds simple:

If AI writes the code, who makes sure it's correct?

And more importantly, how do we trust the answer?

What I Built

AI coding tools can generate hundreds or thousands of lines in minutes. But generating code and verifying it are two very different problems.

As AI-generated changes grow, reviewing every line becomes increasingly expensive. Asking another language model whether the code looks correct doesn't necessarily solve anything. It's still one AI asking another AI for an opinion.

We wanted something better.

Our solution, Katse, takes inspiration from scientific reproducibility.

Instead of simply reading an AI-generated pull request, Katse sends independent AI agents back to the original requirements and asks them to reconstruct the solution without seeing the submitted implementation.

It then compares the results, executes tests, checks for risks, and produces an evidence-based report highlighting what still requires human judgment.

The principle behind it is straightforward:

Don't trust the answer. Reproduce the reasoning and test the result.

What did we achieve?

We tested Katse against four real sample changes provided for Tieto's challenge.

One particularly interesting case involved 1,392 changed lines across 237 files.

Katse narrowed the change to 32 lines requiring targeted human attention, along with an unresolved question.

That isn't a claim that the remaining code is automatically safe. It means the pipeline produced evidence that helped focus the review.

On another change, Katse reproduced 174 passing regression tests, caught three of four seeded defects, and identified behavior that the original requirement hadn't explicitly requested.

And when the evidence was insufficient, Katse could recommend sending the change back instead of approving it.

Because the goal was never to replace the engineer.

It was to help engineers know exactly where their attention matters.

Demo

We built a working prototype that visualizes code dependencies, tracks verification evidence, and produces a review report before a human decides whether to accept the change.

The system distinguishes between what was checked, what remains uncertain, and what wasn't checked at all.

Katse itself cannot approve or merge a pull request. That decision belongs to a named human reviewer.

Watch our 2-minute, 44-second demo.

The complete project, documentation, tests, and evidence reports are available on GitHub.

Partner Technologies

Our architecture combines deterministic analysis with independent AI verification.

We used Gemma 4 locally to anonymize sensitive information before external model calls.

Gemini and NVIDIA Nemotron powered the independent reconstruction process, allowing us to compare implementations generated by different model families.

A deterministic analysis layer uses call graphs, PageRank, static checks, and executable tests to assess changes without relying entirely on model judgments.

We also integrated Entire to recover the original AI development context from Git checkpoints when available. This is important because the original prompt can tell us much more about the developer's intent than the final diff alone.

For Tieto's sample changes, the original prompts weren't available, so Katse explicitly fell back to the issue requirements rather than inventing missing context.

The most important design decision was keeping model confidence separate from actual evidence.

An AI claiming something works is not the same as an executed test demonstrating it.

Hackathon Experience

I worked alongside Meulen, Fabian, and Lucia, contributing mainly to the core concept and the design of Katse's verification pipeline.

One of the biggest challenges was ensuring the verification system itself could be trusted.

During our first full run, agents that were supposed to independently reconstruct the code were operating inside the original repository.

They could potentially access the very implementation they were meant to reproduce independently.

The problem came down to process isolation: the agents' working directories were configured, but the PWD environment variable still pointed elsewhere.

We addressed it by enforcing sandbox isolation, correcting the execution environment, and checking that the original repository remained unchanged.

Another issue appeared when agents exhausted their usage quotas halfway through a reconstruction. Initially, incomplete attempts were treated as valid results. We added checks so that unfinished or failed rebuilds could no longer be mistaken for meaningful evidence.

These weren't theoretical failure modes. They were problems we encountered while building the tool.

And they reinforced the central idea behind Katse:

A verification system must be able to question its own evidence.

Our prototype still has limitations. Four sample changes aren't enough to establish production reliability, and independent reconstruction needs more benchmarking against conventional code review.

But that's exactly why we wanted the system to expose uncertainty rather than hide it.

Finishing 2nd in Tieto's Earned Trust in AI Code challenge at Junction 2026 was a great recognition of our team's work.

Huge thanks to Meulen, Fabian, Lucia, Tieto, and Junction for the experience.

What's next?

AI will keep getting faster at writing software.

The difficult part is building the tools, processes, and evidence needed to trust what it produces.

The future of AI-assisted development isn't just generating more code. It's making that code accountable.

title: RAG in a Trenchcoat: When Minimal Memory Is Enough for Agentic Systems, and When It Isn't
description:
arXiv:2611.22179v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agentic memory research has accumulated extraction, supersession, reflection, and graph synthesis on top of retrieval-augmented generation. However, we found that almost none of those primitives earn their cost in our tested memory benchmarks: we show this with BRIDGE, a deliberately minimal RAG memory with chained observation notes, hybrid BM25 with cosine retrieval, and chronological rendering, which reaches parity within bootstrap CI with the prior SOTA on LongMemEval-S and BEAM, and beats the best memory baseline on EverMemBench by 5.7-6.3 points at matched reader. It runs at ~5-7K reader-prompt tokens per query, using a single LLM call for each ingestion or query. We argue that this parity is itself the result: standard benchmarks score what memory retrieves, not what memory enables when the agent acts. To test the latter, we introduce five adversarial probes (Rule Application +-, Pattern Induction Style / Procedural, Dynamic Multiturn) judged at generation time by a cross vendor verification chain, where each query can only be solved by applying a remembered rule or pattern it never mentions. Across 5 probes x 20 scenarios, no architecture wins universally: atomic fact extractors (LangMem) win rule application, while BRIDGE's block-summary memory wins pattern induction. This result holds across four domains, three graders, and three reader families. Each design fails where the other wins, for reasons a recall benchmark cannot see: atomic-fact extractors discard the form a demonstrated pattern takes, while block-summary memory retrieves the rule but the reader does not act on it, a gap that presenting the rule more prominently largely closes. What separates memory designs is not what they retrieve but what they enable an agent to do, and that is what agentic memory should be evaluated on.

title: Continued Training of Continuous Language Flows with Token Identity Squared Supervision
description:
arXiv:2611.07721v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Diffusion and flow models have recently been extended to language modeling, generating text through continuous denoising in token embedding spaces. Pretrained models provide token representations and contextual prediction capabilities, but improving generation with limited additional training requires an appropriate connection between supervision and continuous generation. When continuous predictions are formed by weighting token embeddings with predicted probabilities, different probability distributions can yield the same vector and are therefore indistinguishable under a continuous reconstruction objective based on mean squared error (MSE). We propose Token Identity Brier Flow (TIBF) to apply squared supervision directly to token identities. TIBF fixes token embeddings, combines network scores with token-matching scores under a Gaussian observation model, supervises token probabilities using the Brier loss, and uses probability-weighted embeddings for continuous generation. We show that, for fixed token embeddings, the squared error in token posterior prediction controls the squared errors of the continuous denoising prediction and the flow velocity. A risk decomposition separates uncertainty inherent in the observation from posterior fitting error, motivating continued training that preserves pretrained embeddings and focuses on probability prediction. From common pretrained initializations and under matched continuation budgets, TIBF achieves mean Gen.PPL values of 34.87 on OWT and 80.08 on LM1B, outperforming continuous-MSE and CE controls. Further evaluations show improvements across multiple sampling budgets. Code is available at https://github.com/Jiangjiawei-kust/TIBF.

title: Inertial Video World Models
description:
arXiv:2611.22314v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The physical world has inertia: it evolves from what already exists rather than being recreated at every instant. However, many existing video world models lack an explicit mechanism for inertial state evolution, leaving the continuity of motion and structure implicit in video prediction. During autoregressive rollouts, repeated reconstruction can accumulate errors and destabilize the predicted dynamics. To address this limitation, we introduce InertialWorld, an Inertial Video World Model that makes inertia a structural prior for autoregressive prediction: existing scene evidence is carried across time rather than reconstructed at every step. Central to this formulation is Inertial Memory, which turns memory from passive predictive context into an evolving video state with two complementary views: a dense Eulerian grid preserves scene-aligned evidence, while persistent Lagrangian carriers bind local content to learned canonical coordinates. At each step, the model transports the carrier content according to action-conditioned motion, predicts the complete next video state from the transported carriers and dense grid, and uses a learned gate to combine transported and newly predicted content into the memory for the next step. Extensive experiments across multiple domains, including robot manipulation, 3D game simulation, and open-world navigation, demonstrate that InertialWorld achieves competitive autoregressive prediction performance against strong video world model baselines. Codes link: https://github.com/YuanGao-YG/InertialWorld

title: Multi-Agent Memory Inconsistency: Where Factual Conflicts Disappear in LLM Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.22245v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multi-agent delegation lets LLM systems distribute evidence collection across workers with separate contexts. This creates a consistency challenge: facts retrieved by workers may be missing from the evidence available to the lead for a joint conclusion. We introduce a benchmark and evidence-flow profiler for studying multi-agent memory inconsistency through controlled factual conflicts in Harvey LAB document-review tasks. Pooled across three models with comparable generation spending, requiring delegation increases retrieval of both conflicting claims from 50.2% to 68.7% relative to single-agent execution, yet conflict detection falls from 16.2% to 13.2%. Within this setting, workers report both claims for only 35.2% of retrieved pairs, and pooled matched comparisons show higher detection than single-agent execution when one worker reads both claims but lower detection when the claims are split across workers. Worker-to-lead handoffs are a central target for improving conflict detection in multi-agent LLMs.

title: PACT: Plan-Action Consistency Training by Preserving Correct Plans and Repairing Actions in GUI Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.22591v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: GUI agents can formulate a correct immediate plan in their reasoning yet emit an action that fails to execute it, creating an execution gap. This recurring mismatch undermines reliable task completion, as a single execution error can derail a multi-step workflow. In outcome-supervised reinforcement learning, broadcasting a negative response-level advantage across all generated tokens risks penalizing valid planning together with erroneous execution. To address this credit-assignment conflict, we introduce PACT (Plan-Action Consistency Training), a training framework that combines reference-aligned plan protection and plan-aligned action repair without altering the original scalar action reward. Using annotated reference actions to identify execution gaps, PACT protects the verified plan by masking negative policy-gradient contributions across its token span. Keeping the generated reasoning unchanged as context, it then favors the reference action over the emitted erroneous action through a preference surrogate with stop-gradient pair weights. Compared with the outcome-only baseline, PACT raises AndroidWorld task success from 60.34% to 68.97% (+8.63 pp), while improving rule-based plan-action consistency on AndroidControl High from 83.71% to 89.74% (+6.03 pp). Adapting PACT to desktop agents also improves task success from 40.92% to 44.17% (+3.25 pp) on the full 369-task OSWorld benchmark. Together, these results establish PACT as an effective credit-assignment framework for bridging execution gaps and improving task completion across mobile and desktop GUI environments.

title: I tested 3 "anti AI slop" design skills on the same page. Only one changed the design
description:
Originally published at tabishapps.com/blog/ai-slop-design-skills-test.

  • The test: one landing page for a made-up coffee roaster, built 4 times by an AI agent: once with a plain prompt, and once with each of 3 popular design skills.
  • The result: the plain prompt and two of the skills gave almost the same page: same fonts, same colours, same emoji cards. Only Anthropic's Frontend Design skill produced a different design, and it took our "AI slop" count from 5 out of 10 to 0.
  • The advice: install one skill for the look (Frontend Design) and one for the details (Vercel's Web Design Guidelines). The other skill is good, but it is about animation, not looks.

The first screen of each version at 1440 px wide. Score = signs of AI slop out of 10.

You can usually tell when a website was made by AI. The same cream background, the same serif headline with one word in italics, the same row of cards with an emoji on top. People call it "AI slop". Skills are text files you give to a coding agent to change how it works, and some of them promise to fix exactly this. So I tested three.

The idea came from a post by @BenjaminUIX on X listing "10 skills that kill AI slop" (it has about 7,600 likes). The post ends with good advice: "Install 2 or 3, not all 10." But which 2 or 3? The post doesn't show what the skills actually do. So I picked three from the list that are plain text instructions and ran the same job with each.

The test

The brief was one sentence, the kind a busy person would really type: build a single-file HTML landing page for Harbour Coffee Roasters, a small local coffee roaster with a cafe and an online shop for beans. No details about colours, hours or prices. The AI had to decide everything.

I built it four times. Each version was made by a fresh agent (Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code) that saw only the brief, plus one skill file for B to D. No agent could see the others' work. The same rules applied to all four: one HTML file, no photos (only CSS, inline SVG or emoji), and Google Fonts allowed.

Version What the agent got What the skill is about
A The brief only Nothing, this is the baseline
B Brief + Anthropic's Frontend Design skill Making a distinct visual design. It even lists the looks AI tends to repeat and asks the agent to avoid them.
C Brief + Vercel's Web Design Guidelines A long checklist of interface rules: accessibility, focus states, forms, typography details. It is written for reviewing code, so I asked the agent to follow it while building and then check its own file once.
D Brief + Emil Kowalski's design engineering skill Mostly animation and interaction: easing curves, timing, press states, when not to animate.

Then I took screenshots of every version with headless Chrome at desktop size (1440 px wide) and phone size (390 px wide), in light mode.

The checklist (written before I saw any result)

Before looking at the pages, I wrote down 10 signs of AI slop. Each sign present is one point. Lower is better.

  1. A gradient used as decoration in the hero
  2. Emoji used as icons
  3. Vague marketing copy ("elevate your experience", "more than just coffee")
  4. Everything centered
  5. A row of identical cards, each with an icon, a title and one line
  6. Low-contrast text
  7. No real details: missing at least two of opening hours, address and prices
  8. Broken or cramped on a phone
  9. Fade-in on every section, or every card lifting on hover
  10. A small ALL-CAPS label above every section heading

The results

Sign A: plain B: Frontend Design C: Vercel D: Emil
Decorative gradient in hero yes no yes yes
Emoji as icons yes no yes yes
Vague marketing copy no no no no
Everything centered no no no no
Identical icon cards yes (4) no yes (4) yes (3)
Low-contrast text no no no* no
No hours, address or prices no no no no
Cramped on phone no no yes no
Motion or hover lift everywhere yes no yes yes
ALL-CAPS label on every section yes no no yes
Total (lower is better) 5 0 5 5
  • C has a dark mode. In dark mode, its cafe section turns light blue while the text stays near-white, which is very hard to read. I scored the light mode, which is what most visitors see.

Two things surprised me. First, the plain prompt was not bad. None of the four versions wrote anything like "elevate your experience", and all four invented useful details: opening hours, an address, prices per 250 g bag. The old slop signs are gone. New ones took their place.

Second, A, C and D are almost the same page. Look at the fonts: all three picked Fraunces for headings and Inter for text. All three have a cream background, a dark serif headline with an orange italic phrase, two rounded buttons and a row of three stats under them ("48h", "12 kg"). Here are their feature cards side by side:

A, C and D each built a row of emoji cards. Same seedling, flame and box, in the same order.

Three agents, three different skill files, no contact between them, and they all reached for 🌱 🔥 📦. That is what "AI slop" really is: not ugly, just the same.

What each skill changed

A: plain prompt

A clean, friendly page that would be fine for a real cafe. It has a menu with prices, opening hours and an address. But it uses the default kit: a gradient circle behind a cup, emoji icons, a small uppercase label above every heading, and cards that lift when you hover them.

B: Anthropic Frontend Design

The only version that looks like someone made a choice. The agent picked a harbour-and-chalkboard idea and ran with it: tall condensed headings, a teal and yellow palette, and a "roasted this week" board with the day each coffee is roasted. The coffee bags are flat colour blocks, not emoji. The order steps are numbered 1 to 4 because they really are steps.

This makes sense when you read the skill. It asks the agent to start from the subject (a harbour, a roaster) instead of a template, to plan the colours and fonts first, and then to check that plan against a list of looks that AI repeats. That list describes A, C and D quite closely. It also asks for restraint: one bold idea, the rest quiet.

It isn't perfect. On a phone, the four coffee bags become very tall coloured blocks, which is a lot of scrolling. And there is a small bug: the empty "added to bag" message box peeks up from the bottom edge of the screen before you click anything.

C: Vercel Web Design Guidelines

Visually, almost the same as A. Under the hood, it's the most careful version. It is the only one with a "skip to content" link for keyboard users, balanced line breaks in headings, numbers formatted with the browser's own locale tools, and clear focus outlines. Following the guidelines' "Title Case" rule made the buttons read "Shop Fresh Beans" and "Add to Bag", which is fine but slightly stiff.

On a phone, the header is cramped: the shop name is cut off as "Harbour Coffee Ro…". And as noted above, its dark mode has a real contrast bug. So the checklist didn't catch everything, but that's expected: it's a list of rules, not a design brief.

D: Emil Kowalski's design engineering

Again the same family as A. What changed is how it moves. Buttons shrink slightly when pressed, transitions use custom easing curves, hover effects only run on devices with a mouse, and motion is turned down for people who ask for less. There is also a filter for the bean list and a weekly / fortnightly / monthly switch for the subscription. Those details feel nice when you use the page, but they don't show in a screenshot.

It also fades in each section as you scroll, which is the one animation habit most likely to feel "AI". And a small layout slip: prices like "£11.50 / 250 g" break so the "g" lands on its own line.

What you can't see in the screenshots

I also searched each file for a few things the skills talk about. Numbers are how many times each appears in the code.

Detail A B C D
"Skip to content" link 0 0 2 0
Visible keyboard focus styles 1 2 4 2
Respects "reduce motion" yes yes yes yes
Custom easing curves 0 0 0 3
Press feedback on buttons 0 0 1 4
Hover effects only on mouse devices 0 0 0 4
Even-width numbers for prices 0 1 4 1
Fonts Fraunces + Inter Big Shoulders + Source Serif Fraunces + Inter Fraunces + Inter

So each skill did its own job. It's just that only one of them has "make it look different" as its job.

Verdict: which 2 to install

  1. Anthropic's Frontend Design, if your problem is "it looks like every other AI site". In this test it was the only skill that changed the design, and it was the only page with zero slop signs.
  2. Vercel's Web Design Guidelines, as a second pass. Run it as it was meant to be used: ask the agent to review the finished page against it. It catches accessibility and detail problems that a design skill ignores.

Emil Kowalski's skill is worth having when you build interactive parts: menus, drawers, toasts, anything that moves. For a mostly static landing page, it changes very little you can see.

Limits of this test

  • One run per version. AI output varies, and a second run could look different. Treat this as one honest sample, not a benchmark.
  • I wrote the checklist and judged the pages myself. I wrote it before seeing any page, but some of my signs overlap with the list inside Anthropic's skill, which gives B an advantage on my scorecard.
  • Two of the skills are not designed to change visual style. Vercel's is a review checklist, and Emil's is mostly about motion. They did what they say; they just aren't "make it look different" tools.
  • One model (Claude Opus 5.5) and one kind of page. Other models, and apps instead of landing pages, may behave differently.

Sources

  • @BenjaminUIX on X, 16 November 2026: 10 skills that kill AI slop.
  • Anthropic: anthropics/skills (frontend-design).
  • Vercel: vercel-labs/agent-skills (web-design-guidelines) and the Web Interface Guidelines it reads.
  • Emil Kowalski: emilkowalski/skills (emil-design-eng).

Let me know in the comments: which design skills do you use, and did they change your results?

title: Choosing the Right Compute Service on AWS: EC2 vs ECS vs EKS vs Fargate vs Lambda
description:
An application can run perfectly well in development and still become difficult to operate when deployed at scale. The problem is not always the application itself. Sometimes, the selected compute model introduces unnecessary operational effort, limits flexibility, or increases costs.

AWS offers several compute services, but choosing the right one requires understanding how each workload runs and how much infrastructure management it needs.

WHAT

AWS compute services provide different execution models, from managing virtual servers and orchestrating containers to running event-driven functions without directly managing servers.

  • Amazon EC2: Provides virtual servers with control over operating systems, instance types, storage, and software configurations.
  • Amazon ECS: Orchestrates containerized applications using AWS-managed container orchestration. It can run tasks on EC2 or Fargate.
  • Amazon EKS: Provides a managed Kubernetes control plane while allowing teams to operate Kubernetes-based workloads and their associated infrastructure.
  • AWS Fargate: Provides serverless compute capacity for supported ECS and EKS workloads, removing the need to manage the underlying EC2 instances.
  • AWS Lambda: Executes code in response to events without requiring direct server management. Standard Lambda function executions have a maximum duration of 15 minutes.

The important distinction is that ECS and EKS orchestrate containers, Fargate provides container compute, EC2 provides virtual servers, and Lambda follows a function-based execution model.

WHERE

Different compute models suit different application requirements.

  • EC2: Legacy applications, specialized software, GPU workloads, and applications requiring operating system-level control.
  • ECS: AWS-focused containerized applications, microservices, and web applications that need container orchestration.
  • EKS: Kubernetes-based platforms, organizations using Kubernetes tooling, and workloads requiring Kubernetes APIs and ecosystem integrations.
  • Fargate and Lambda: Fargate suits containerized applications that need serverless infrastructure management. Lambda suits event-driven processing, scheduled automation, and short-running backend tasks.

Compute pricing varies by service. EC2 and ECS on EC2 involve instance costs, Fargate charges for provisioned compute resources and usage duration, and Lambda pricing depends on requests and execution duration. Networking, storage, monitoring, and data transfer can also contribute to the total cost.

WHY

Selecting a compute service is not just about finding the lowest hourly price. It is about balancing infrastructure control, operational effort, workload behavior, and total cost.

EC2 offers greater control but requires responsibility for operating system maintenance, capacity planning, and instance management.

ECS simplifies container orchestration without requiring Kubernetes. When paired with Fargate, it also removes the need to manage the underlying servers.

EKS provides Kubernetes compatibility and flexibility, but operating Kubernetes workloads requires additional expertise and operational effort.

Lambda reduces server-management responsibilities and works well for event-driven workloads. However, execution duration, invocation volume, memory allocation, and downstream dependencies influence its suitability and cost.

Before finalizing the architecture, compare the expected workload costs using the AWS Pricing Calculator.

WHEN

Use EC2 when:

  • The application requires operating system-level access or specialized configurations.
  • Existing software has dependencies that make containerization difficult.
  • Specialized instance capabilities are required.

Use ECS when:

  • The application is already containerized or is being designed around containers.
  • Container orchestration is required without adopting Kubernetes.
  • A simpler AWS-native container management approach is preferred.

Use EKS when:

  • Kubernetes APIs, tooling, and ecosystem integrations are important.
  • The organization already has Kubernetes operational expertise.
  • Kubernetes-based deployment patterns are required across environments.

Use Fargate when:

  • Containers need to run without managing EC2 instances.
  • Infrastructure-management overhead needs to be reduced.
  • Workloads benefit from managed container compute capacity.

Use Lambda when:

  • Code executes in response to events.
  • Tasks are short-running and fit within Lambda's execution limits.
  • Workloads have variable demand or periods of inactivity.

HOW

Consider an online store with three workloads: a website and checkout service, product image processing, and a legacy inventory application. Each workload has different compute requirements, so using one compute service for everything may not be the best design.

The website runs as containers on ECS with Fargate behind an Application Load Balancer. Product image uploads to Amazon S3 trigger Lambda functions for processing. The legacy inventory application runs on EC2 because it requires a specific operating system configuration or licensed software.

The cost trade-off depends on utilization and operational effort. EC2 can be suitable for steady workloads, while Fargate and Lambda can reduce infrastructure-management overhead for suitable workloads. The right decision should account for the complete architecture rather than compute pricing alone.

TAKEAWAY

The right AWS compute service is the one that matches each workload's execution pattern, infrastructure requirements, scaling behavior, operational constraints, and total cost.

title: FACE: Flow-Guided Angular Channel Estimation Framework for mmWave MIMO Systems
description:
arXiv:2611.21698v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Acquiring accurate channel state information (CSI) is essential for millimeter-wave (mmWave) multi-input multi-output (MIMO) systems. However, it remains challenging due to high-dimensional channels, limited pilot observations, and measurement noise. To address these challenges, we propose flow-guided angular channel estimation (FACE), a novel channel estimation framework based on flow matching, an emerging generative modeling paradigm that learns continuous transport dynamics between probability distributions. FACE exploits the inherent angular-domain sparsity of mmWave channels and incorporates the learned flow matching model as a generative channel prior. Numerical results show that FACE consistently achieves higher channel estimation accuracy than both conventional estimators and diffusion-based generative estimator across diverse channel and system configurations. Moreover, FACE maintains high estimation accuracy with fewer pilot observations and achieves an average achievable rate close to the perfect-CSI benchmark. Compared with diffusion-based estimation, FACE requires substantially fewer sampling steps while achieving superior or comparable estimation accuracy, reducing inference time and computational cost. Overall, the proposed framework demonstrates the potential of flow matching for accurate, pilot-efficient, and computationally efficient mmWave MIMO channel estimation.

title: Role Steering of Language Models for Social Simulations
description:
arXiv:2608.00023v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Social simulations built from language-model agents need role-conditioned behavior that can be checked before agents are placed into a simulated population. We introduce an activation-steering screening workflow for role-conditioned agents: define a role profile, extract a role-specific direction, sweep four steering coefficients, evaluate role-profile alignment, and pass or flag each candidate configuration. On OLMo-3-7B-Instruct, we apply the workflow to a mixed 275-role inventory with 228 role-agnostic questions, GPT-4.1-mini prompted role references, and GPT-4.1-mini judges. We also introduce CastVectors, which receive higher judged role-profile alignment than an assistant-axis directional control from prior persona-vector work, with mean overall scores of 63.2 versus 41.1 across the tested grid. They also preserve high lexical diversity, while the control drops sharply at larger coefficients. The role-level screen is the main contribution: most roles improve as steering increases, but 38 roles decline across all six measured dimensions, showing why simulation builders should choose coefficients per role rather than deploy a uniform high-strength setting. Our code is available at https://github.com/HCAI-Lab-GT/casting-call-vectors, and the role vectors and evaluation data at https://huggingface.co/datasets/HCAI-Lab-GT/casting-call-vectors.

title: 77 ns vs 31 ns: jiff 1.0 is not the fastest datetime lib
description:
77 ns vs 31 ns: jiff 1.0 is not the fastest datetime lib

jiff 1.0 parses an RFC3339 timestamp in 77 nanoseconds on my machine. time does it in 31. chrono does it in 42. I benchmarked all three this morning, and the new 1.0 release — the one BurntSushi has been building toward for two years — is not the fastest datetime library in Rust. That's the headline, and it's also the wrong reason to judge it. The interesting numbers are the ones around the edges: formatting, where jiff beats chrono by 1.4x, and error messages, where it isn't close at all.

What 1.0 actually is

jiff 1.0.0 shipped November 15, 2026. The changelog is refreshingly boring for a 1.0: the big breaking change is a rename, Zoned → ZonedDateTime (which broke my first build this morning — more on that below). The MSRV went to Rust 1.85, Timestamp subtraction now returns a SignedDuration, and conversions to SystemTime became fallible. The message is stability: "this release marks an indefinite commitment to 1.x.y. Consumers should feel confident about putting Jiff types into their public API."

Then 1.0.1 followed two days later, November 17, with two fixes. One was cosmetic (%Z in strftime should format as UTC). The other is the kind of thing that makes you blink: "Parsing a timestamp could produce an out of bounds value." A datetime library shipped a parse out-of-bounds bug in its 1.0.0 and fixed it in 48 hours. Nobody's perfect; the fix time is the part worth noting.

The benchmark

Same machine for all three libraries (AMD EPYC 9D25, rustc 1.99.1, --release, 1,000,000 iterations per case, best of 5 runs). The input is a real timestamp with nanoseconds and a Z suffix; the offset variant uses +05:30.

let ts = "2026-11-18T07:00:00.123456789Z";
let ts_off = "2026-11-18T07:00:00+05:30";
// parse:  jiff Timestamp::from_str
//         chrono DateTime::parse_from_rfc3339
//         time OffsetDateTime::parse(.., Rfc3339)
// format: jiff Timestamp Display / chrono to_rfc3339() / time format(Rfc3339)

parse RFC3339 (Z)            jiff   77.1 ns     chrono   42.5 ns     time   31.3 ns
parse RFC3339 (+05:30)       jiff   60.8 ns     chrono   37.7 ns     time    —   *
format RFC3339               jiff   81.9 ns     chrono  116.7 ns     time   43.7 ns

* time's offset parse is the same code path; I only ran it for the Z input.

Ratios, because ratios are the story:

parse (Z):    jiff is 1.8x slower than chrono, 2.5x slower than time
format:       jiff is 1.4x FASTER than chrono, 1.9x slower than time

So jiff loses parsing and wins one formatting matchup. Before you conclude anything, the sanity check: all three agree on the instant. Epoch 1794985200, nanoseconds 123456789, identical output strings. And jiff's zoned form does the thing the other two make you work for:

jiff:  2026-11-18T07:00:00.123456789Z
chrono: 2026-11-18T07:00:00.123456789Z
time:  2026-11-18T07:00:00.123456789Z
jiff zoned: 2026-11-17T23:00:00.123456789-08:00[America/Los_Angeles]

The part the benchmark doesn't measure

Feed all three a date that doesn't exist — February 30 — and compare what comes back:

jiff:   parsed date is not valid: parameter 'day' for `2026-02`
        is invalid, must be in range `1..=28`
chrono: ParseError(OutOfRange)
time:   TryFromParsed(ComponentRange(ComponentRange {
          name: "day", is_conditional: true }))

jiff tells you which parameter, which month, and the valid range, in one sentence. chrono gives you an enum variant. time gives you a Debug dump of an internal struct. This is jiff's actual product: every error is a sentence a human can act on, every API refuses to silently do the wrong thing (hence fallible SystemTime conversions in 1.0), and the DST arithmetic doesn't have the footguns that made people write their own wrappers around chrono in the first place.

That costs nanoseconds. jiff validates more on the parse path — the range checks, the offset handling, the civil-date validation — and validation is work. time is a thinner layer over the same bytes. If your hot loop parses a million timestamps a second, take the 31 ns. If your program parses user input, config files, or API responses, the 46 extra nanoseconds buys you an error message your on-call engineer can paste into a search box.

The rename that broke my build

One honest footnote: my first compile failed.

error[E0433]: cannot find `Zoned` in `jiff`

The 1.0 changelog lists it plainly — Zoned is now ZonedDateTime, to_zoned is now to_zoned_datetime — and I still wrote the old name from muscle memory. That's the entire cost of the biggest breaking change in the release: one rename, one compiler error, one sed command. For a library whose pre-1.0 API moved constantly, that's the point of the 1.0 line in the changelog. The API is done moving now.

So should you switch?

The scoreboard, without romance:

  • Parsing throughput: time > chrono > jiff. jiff pays ~2.5x vs time for validation.
  • Formatting: time > jiff > chrono. jiff beats chrono by 1.4x.
  • Error messages: jiff, by a distance.
  • API stability: 1.0 is a commitment; ZonedDateTime is the name now.

jiff 1.0 is not a speed release. It's a "you can put this in your public API and stop thinking about it" release, and the benchmark says the tax for that is measured in tens of nanoseconds per parse. If you're choosing a datetime library on parse throughput alone, you already know which one to pick — and it's not this one. If you're choosing on the strength of what happens when the input is wrong, the numbers point the other way.

Sources: jiff CHANGELOG, 1.0.0 (2026-11-15) and 1.0.1 (2026-11-17); jiff on crates.io, 1.0.1. Benchmarks are my own measurements (rustc 1.99.1, --release, AMD EPYC 9D25, 1M iterations, best of 5; jiff 1.0.1, chrono 0.4.45, time 0.3.55). I dropped one comparison from the results: a date-arithmetic microbenchmark where the jiff number came out at an implausible 0.5 ns/op — the compiler had hoisted the loop-invariant computation out of the timed loop, so the number measured nothing. I removed it rather than publish a benchmark artifact as a result.
