title: Sparse Integer Fourier Transform and Its Application In Machine Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.21976v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: The Discrete Fourier transform, mainly implemented by Fast Fourier Transform (FFT), has been essential for numerous domains, such as digital signal processing and feature extraction in materials design. However, current FFT methods suffer from extensive non-trivial multiplications and twiddle-factor operations in the big data era. To improve the computational efficiency of FFT, this study proposes Sparse Integer Fourier Transform (SIFT), a method that leverages the fast computing of sparsity and small integers, and applies the Radix-n method to derive an FFT. The 2N-point DFT matrix in Radix-n FFT is decomposed into four sparse integer matrices. A diagonal matrix containing complex twiddle factors is efficiently approximated using an optimization strategy while the remaining matrices retain sparsity and integer entries. For radix-32 FFT, SIFT reduces the estimated arithmetic cost by 75%, with RMSE below $2.3765\times10^{-8}$ and MAPE below 0.01089%. We evaluate frequency extraction in a numerical test and an engineering case. In the numerical test, MAPE and RMSE are below 2.016% and $2.536\times10^{-6}$, respectively. For wind turbine fault diagnosis, SIFT extracts compact spectral features that retain fault information while reducing the classifier's input dimensionality relative to the full time series.

title: PromptPack: Training-Free Augmentation of Diffusion Editors for Intent-Aligned Spatial and Semantic Control
description:
arXiv:2611.21865v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Many image-editing tasks require confining changes to intended spatial regions while exactly preserving user-designated source content. Instruction-driven editing pipelines often leave such user-intent underspecified, while inpainting editors condition generation on explicitly defined edit support but not on the spatial assignment of individual edit concepts. PromptPack addresses both limitations by equipping diffusion editors with two explicit 'Edit Guides': an edit-role partition that labels each pixel as 'Keep,' 'Permit,' or 'Modify' to specify where edits may occur, and a regional-prompt assignment that maps spatial regions to text prompts to specify which concepts apply where. These guides may be manually specified or, for source-object edits, automatically derived from a text-grounded SAM 3 mask. Without retraining, PromptPack injects independently embedded regional prompts into the editor's fixed-length text sequence and uses the Edit Guides to spatially mask attention, gate flow updates, and restore protected source pixels. We integrate PromptPack into FlowEdit FLUX, FlowEdit SD3, and FLUX Kontext and demonstrate improved requested-concept placement and protected-content preservation across all three integrations on PIE-Bench++. In a pairwise user study, PromptPack achieves an 87% preference rate over FlowEdit FLUX, establishing PromptPack as a practical, training-free interface for intent-aligned diffusion editing.

title: Building a 7 deadly sins test without judging the user
description:
Someone finishes a personality quiz and gets “Pride: 75.” What should they do with that? Does it mean they are unusually proud, that three-quarters of their personality is pride, or simply that they agreed with a few statements?

Working on a 7 deadly sins test made that ambiguity hard to ignore. Calculating a number is straightforward. Giving someone enough context to read it fairly takes more care.

The project uses the 7 deadly sins as themes for an entertainment quiz. The interesting development problem is what happens between an answer, a score, and the sentence a person remembers afterward.

Start with the question behind the search

“Which deadly sin am I?” invites a single, memorable answer. That makes a character reveal a reasonable part of the experience. But I want that reveal to leave room for a second question: “Which of my answers led here?”

For this project, I treat the reader's task as three connected steps: answer recognizable situations, understand the resulting pattern, and decide whether any of it is worth discussing or sharing.

That framing affects the interface. The character needs supporting context. The scores need an explanation. Sharing needs to be a choice.

There is also a scope decision to make early: these are original characters inspired by everyday habits, not matches from The Seven Deadly Sins anime. A familiar phrase should not leave someone guessing which experience they opened.

Make a 7 deadly sins test score explainable

The homepage Quick Quiz has 21 questions, with three assigned to each theme. It asks people to think about the past four weeks, which gives the answer a time frame rather than asking them to summarize their whole life.

Each usable answer has a value from 0 to 4. Some statements point in the opposite direction, so their values are reversed before averaging. Each theme is then scaled independently to 0–100.

Here is a simplified JavaScript illustration of that calculation:

// Illustrative answers for one theme, not a real user's result.
const answers = [
  { value: 3, reverse: false },
  { value: 2, reverse: false },
  { value: 0, reverse: true },
];

const values = answers.map(({ value, reverse }) =>
  reverse ? 4 - value : value
);

const score =
  (values.reduce((sum, value) => sum + value, 0) / values.length) * 25;

console.log(score); // 75: average of 3, 2, and 4, scaled to 100

The arithmetic is easy to inspect. It does not establish that the questions are a validated measure of personality.

Here, 75 describes responses within one question group. It is not a percentile, a probability, or a measure of moral worth. The seven scores do not need to add up to 100.

The other detail worth handling explicitly is missing information. “This situation doesn't apply to me” should not quietly become zero. In the Quick Quiz, those answers are excluded, and each theme needs at least two usable answers before the user can finish.

If you are building something similar, define that rule before designing the result screen. Otherwise, an unanswered question can accidentally become a confident conclusion.

A concrete example: “Which deadly sin am I?”

Imagine someone who often defends their work immediately when corrected. They also keep thinking about achievements that went unnoticed. In this quiz, those situations contribute to the pride theme.

That is enough to make a reading about recognition and defensiveness relevant. It is not enough to explain their relationships, work history, or reasons for reacting that way.

A useful next step is small: the next time feedback arrives, ask one curious question before explaining your side. The person can try it, disagree with it, or decide the situation needs more context.

There is no need to force a winner, either. If several scores are close, the result should make that visible. The project includes mixed, balanced, and quieter outcomes so the headline can acknowledge the pattern instead of flattening it.

You can inspect that answer-to-result flow in the 7 deadly sins quiz I'm building. The Quick Quiz is free, with no account or result paywall. It pairs an original character with seven scores and the responses behind them, so there is something to examine after the reveal.

Sharing deserves its own design decision

A result that feels fine in a private browser tab may feel different in a group chat.

The project lets people make an illustrated card, choose playful or gentle wording, and decide whether to include scores. A result link excludes individual answers, but anyone holding the link can read the selected information. Shared links cannot be revoked.

Those details belong near the sharing action. A person should understand what will leave the page before copying it.

Friend comparison has a similarly narrow purpose: compare two profiles from the same quiz version and start a conversation. It does not calculate compatibility or establish who has the “better” personality.

For me, the useful design constraint is keeping the character, score, and explanation consistent about what they know. This is entertainment and a prompt for reflection. It cannot diagnose someone, provide a religious judgment, or establish a permanent identity.

A 7 deadly sins test can still be playful within those limits. If you want a concrete example to explore, the Quick Quiz puts the questions, explanation, and optional sharing in one flow. The part I would carry into another project is simple: make the result easy to question, as well as easy to share.

title: CutAgent: Creative-Gene-Driven Planning and Experience-Guided Self-Refinement for High-CTR E-commerce Advertising Video Creation
description:
arXiv:2611.22418v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: E-commerce advertising video creation requires both high-level creative planning and reliable multi-modal production. However, existing methods often map product attributes directly to scripts or editing decisions without explicitly modeling advertising strategies, narrative structures, and production styles. They also have limited ability to reuse past production failures. To address these limitations, we propose $\textbf{CutAgent}$, a dual-agent framework that formulates advertising video creation as a Plan--Execute--Self-Evolve process. CutAgent comprises two collaborative agents, $\textbf{GeneAgent}$ and $\textbf{VideoAgent}$, connected by a structured creative gene that bridges product understanding and video production. GeneAgent maps multi-modal product inputs---textual attributes together with product images---to creative genes that specify narrative units and production rules. To train GeneAgent, we construct $\textbf{CutAgent-70K}$ with approximately 70K samples of product attributes/images, reverse-extracted creative genes, cleaned clip pools, and real-world CTR, and apply high-CTR supervised fine-tuning followed by CTR-guided GRPO. Guided by the generated gene, VideoAgent retrieves category-then-gene failure--correction experiences from a long-term memory as constraints for shot-script planning, then coordinates material retrieval, narration, subtitles, music, and timeline rendering. Independently, a reflection loop diagnoses quality defects, revises deficient production decisions, and writes verified corrections back to memory for later retrieval. Experiments on $\textbf{CutAgent-Eval}$ show that CutAgent outperforms representative baselines in e-commerce advertising video creation, achieving the highest online CTR of $\textbf{2.21\%}$.

title: We Moved Our Branch Shared Drives Into Azure and Nine Branches Could Not Reach Them Because Their Broadband Blocked One Port
description:
Each of our branches has a shared drive for the documents that do not belong in any system: cutting lists for the timber saw, photographs of damaged deliveries, the yard rota, the price lists suppliers send as spreadsheets. For years these lived on a small server in each branch. Last spring we retired the servers and moved the drives to Azure Files, which presents cloud storage as an ordinary Windows network drive.

We piloted it at head office and at our two largest branches, and it was excellent. Drives mapped at sign in and files opened quickly. We scheduled the remaining branches over three weekends.

On the Monday after the second weekend, nine branches rang to say their drive had gone. Windows reported that the network path could not be found. The branches that worked and the branches that did not had the same PCs, the same build and the same settings.

They did not have the same internet. Our larger sites connect over a private network that reaches Azure through our own link. The smaller branches use business broadband with direct internet access, and the nine that failed were all with one provider. Azure Files speaks SMB, the Windows file sharing protocol, over TCP port 445, and that provider blocks port 445, as many do. The port was abused by worms for years, and SMB was never designed to cross the open internet. Microsoft's documentation warns about exactly this, in a section we had not read because our pilot sites never needed it.

For two days those branches emailed files to one another while we arranged a fix. Each branch router now builds a VPN tunnel to our Azure network, and the drives are reached through a private address inside it, so the broadband provider sees only encrypted VPN traffic. That is how it should have been designed from the start.

Our migration checklist now records how every site connects to the internet, and every pilot includes at least one site of each kind. We had tested the product well. We had tested it only from the places where it was always going to work.

– Serguey Shinder

title: Turning handwritten notes (60-120 page PDFs) into Anki flashcards: a workflow that doesn't lose content
description:
Scanning a 100-page notebook, feeding the whole PDF to a model, and asking for flashcards produces a deck that looks complete and isn't. The failure is quiet: cards come out fine, but whole sections of the notebook never made it in, and you find out during revision. Here is the pipeline that fixes it, in the order that matters.

The short version: pilot the OCR on 5 pages, split the PDF into chunks, transcribe before you generate, check coverage against a fact list, verify each card against the source, and import into a staging deck before it touches your real one. Total setup is about an hour for a 120-page notebook, mostly scripting the split.

Why the naive approach fails

Three separate failure modes get blamed on "the model":

  1. OCR errors. Handwriting, formulas, subscripts, and anything where layout carries meaning degrade transcription quality. A card built on a misread term teaches the wrong fact permanently — I've seen a generator turn "photic" into "aphotic", the exact opposite.
  2. Coverage loss. A model given 100 pages summarizes toward what it thinks is important. Your exam syllabus and its idea of importance are not the same list.
  3. Card design errors. Multi-fact cards, cloze deletions with two deletions, and derivations crammed onto cards all fail silently during review.

Fixing #1 and #2 at the source is cheaper than fixing bad cards later.

Step 0: pilot the OCR on 5 pages

Before any pipeline work, put five representative pages through your best vision model and count the errors yourself. Dense handwriting, mixed notation, and diagram-heavy pages are where it breaks. If you're seeing more than a couple of real errors per page, stop — you'll spend more time fixing cards than typing them. This ten-minute check decides whether the whole project is worth it.

Step 1: split the PDF into chunks

Never generate from the whole document. Split by semantic unit: one section, or 3-5 pages at a time. You don't need a GUI for this:

# qpdf: pages 1-5 into one file, and so on
qpdf input.pdf --pages . 1-5 -- chunk_01.pdf

or with pypdf in a few lines of Python if the page ranges vary.

Step 2: transcribe before you generate

Run OCR per chunk, but keep the transcript as its own file instead of letting the model go straight from image to cards. Two reasons:

  • You can skim a transcript in 30 seconds and catch misreads; you can't catch them inside finished cards.
  • If the transcript is wrong, you re-run one chunk. If cards are built on a wrong transcript, you re-run everything downstream.

Step 3: the coverage check

This is the step almost everyone skips, and it's the one that actually prevents silent loss. For each chunk:

  1. Ask the model for a numbered list of the facts worth testing from the transcript — before asking for any cards.
  2. Generate cards from the same chunk.
  3. Map every card back to a number on that list.
  4. Generate again for any fact with no card.

On a 120-page notebook this is the difference between "some cards" and "the syllabus". It takes maybe 20 minutes for the whole document and it's the only step that catches sections the model quietly dropped.

Step 4: the verification pass

For each generated card, re-ask its question against the original transcript with the card's answer hidden. Anything that disagrees gets deleted, not patched — a patched card that's still wrong is worse than a missing card, because you'll trust it later. Then read 20 random cards from the batch by hand. If more than a couple are wrong, don't trust the batch; the transcript or the prompt is the problem, not the cards.

Formulas and diagrams

Stop trying to make plain text cards out of them. Definitions, conditions, and "given X, which relation applies and why" work fine as cards. Worked derivations belong in your notes; labelled anatomical or schematic diagrams belong in image occlusion, not in a text card. Forcing them into text produces cards that are wrong in subtle ways.

Import and triage

Import everything into a staging deck, not your real one. Review the batch, move keepers over, delete the rest. Anki's own search makes triage fast, and a bad batch never pollutes your scheduling history.

Tools

Nothing in this pipeline requires a subscription:

  • Splitting: qpdf or pypdf.
  • OCR: any vision-capable model you already have access to.
  • Generation: same model, per chunk, with the coverage checklist.
  • Import: AnkiConnect (writes decks straight into a running Anki), or a CSV / .apkg export if you prefer files.

Disclosure

I build AnkiMate, a Chrome extension that covers the middle of this pipeline: it turns a web page, a selected text, a PDF, or a YouTube transcript into basic and cloze cards and writes them into Anki through AnkiConnect, using on-device AI by default or your own API key. Free tier is 3 generations a day; Pro is a $19.9 one-time license (regular $29.9), no subscription. Closed source, and largely built with AI assistance.

Two honest limits: it does not do handwriting OCR (that's your Step 0 and Step 2), and it does not do the coverage check or the verification pass — those stay manual, because they need your judgment about what matters. The workflow above matters more than the tool.

title: idl-codegen: عميلان بأنواع محددة لـ TypeScript و Dart من Anchor IDL
description:
برنامج Anchor يصف نفسه في ملف IDL: تعليماته (instructions)، وحساباته، وأنواعه، وأحداثه، وأخطاؤه، وبذور (seeds) عناوين الـ PDA. جهة البرنامج تولّدها لك macros الخاصة بـ Anchor. أما جهة العميل (client) فمنها يبدأ العمل اليدوي. على أحدهم أن يكتب الدالة التي تحوّل الوسائط بترميز Borsh، وتضع أمامها الـ discriminator المكوّن من 8 بايتات، وترتّب الحسابات بالترتيب الصحيح مع أعلام signer وwritable الصحيحة، وتشتق عناوين الـ PDA من نفس البذور التي يستعملها البرنامج.

كتابة ذلك مرة واحدة أمر مقبول. لكن كتابته مرتين، بـ TypeScript لتطبيق الويب وبـ Dart لتطبيق Flutter، تعني نسختين يجب أن تبقيا متطابقتين مع البرنامج ومع بعضهما. وبايت واحد خاطئ في إحداهما يعطي معاملة تفشل على السلسلة برسالة خطأ لا تشرح الكثير.

idl-codegen يقرأ ملف Anchor IDL (مواصفة 0.30 وما بعدها) ويكتب العميلين معًا. والـ README يبدأ بتحذير يجب ذكره هنا أيضًا: المشروع لم يخضع لتدقيق أمني. العملاء المولَّدون يبنون التعليمات ويفكّون ترميز الحسابات، ولا يوقّعون ولا يرسلون شيئًا. راجع الكود المولَّد مقابل برنامجك قبل استعماله مع أموال حقيقية، وجرّب على devnet أولًا.

ماذا يقدّم

أمر واحد ينتج مجموعتين من الملفات:

  • TypeScript: الملفان <name>.ts وborsh.ts، ويعتمدان على @solana/web3.js v1.
  • Dart: الملفان <name>.dart وborsh.dart، ويعتمدان على package:crypto، وهما موجّهان لتطبيقات Flutter.

كل عميل يحتوي نفس المكوّنات.

معرّف البرنامج. الثابت PROGRAM_ID في TypeScript و<name>ProgramId في Dart.

الأنواع. في TypeScript تحصل على interfaces، وعلى الـ enums في شكل اتحادات { kind: ... }، وعلى دوال encodeX / decodeX. وفي Dart تحصل على أصناف (classes) فيها encode وstatic decode. الـ enums التي بلا بيانات تصبح enum عادية في Dart، والتي تحمل بيانات تصبح أصنافًا من نوع sealed.

بناء التعليمات. الدالة createXInstruction(accounts, args) تُرجع TransactionInstruction في TypeScript. ونسخة Dart تأخذ وسائط مسمّاة وتُرجع Instruction. الحسابات التي لها address ثابت في الـ IDL، مثل System Program، تأخذه كقيمة افتراضية. والحسابات الاختيارية تأخذ معرّف البرنامج كقيمة افتراضية، وهذا عُرف Anchor للتعبير عن "None".

فك ترميز الحسابات. الدالة decodeXAccount(data) تتحقق من الـ discriminator قبل الفك، وفي TypeScript توجد أيضًا isXAccount.

الأحداث (events). الدالة decodeXEvent(data) في اللغتين.

دوال PDA. الدالة findXPda(...seeds) تُولَّد من pda.seeds في الـ IDL: البذور الثابتة، وبذور الحسابات، وبذور الوسائط، وحالات seeds::program مثل حسابات التوكن المرتبطة (ATA). وعميل Dart يأتي بدالة findProgramAddress خاصة به.

الأخطاء والثوابت. في TypeScript: ERRORS و<Name>Error.fromCode(). وفي Dart: <name>Errors و<Name>Exception.fromCode(). ومعها قيم #[constant] المعرّفة في البرنامج.

تحويل الأنواع يتبع نفس الفكرة في الجهتين: u64 وi64 وu128 وi128 تصبح bigint / BigInt؛ والأعداد الصحيحة الأصغر تصبح number / int؛ وpubkey يصبح PublicKey / Pubkey؛ وbytes يصبح Uint8Array / Uint8List؛ وOption<T> يصبح T | null / T?. أما tuple structs وtuple variants فتصبح values: [...] في TypeScript وfield0, field1 في Dart.

طريقة الاستعمال

تحتاج Node.js 20 أو أحدث. انسخ المستودع وشغّل المولّد من مجلد المشروع:

git clone https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/idl-codegen
cd idl-codegen
pnpm install
pnpm gen target/idl/my_program.json --ts app/src/generated --dart mobile/lib/generated
# or after `pnpm build`:  node dist/cli.js <idl.json> --ts <dir> --dart <dir>

الوسيط الأول هو ملف الـ IDL الذي كتبه anchor build. والخياران --ts و--dart هما مجلدا الإخراج. كود TypeScript المولَّد يحتاج @solana/web3.js v1 في تطبيقك، وكود Dart المولَّد يحتاج package:crypto.

ثم في تطبيق الويب:

import { createIncrementInstruction, findCounterPda } from "./generated/counter_todo.js";
const [counter] = findCounterPda(wallet.publicKey);
const ix = createIncrementInstruction({ authority: wallet.publicKey, counter }, { by: 1n });

ونفس النداء في تطبيق Flutter:

import 'generated/counter_todo.dart';
final (counter, _) = findCounterPda(authority: me);
final ix = createIncrementInstruction(authority: me, counter: counter, by: BigInt.one);

المقطعان يشتقان نفس الـ PDA ويبنيان نفس بايتات التعليمة. التوقيع والإرسال يبقيان في كودك أنت، بالمحفظة وطبقة الـ RPC التي يستعملها تطبيقك أصلًا.

كيف اختُبر

الكود المولَّد لا ينفع إلا إذا وثقت في البايتات، ولهذا يدور أغلب قسم الاختبارات في الـ README حول هذه النقطة.

  • اختبارات golden. كل IDL في test/fixtures/ يُولَّد ثم يُقارن بايتًا ببايت مع test/golden/. الملفات هي counter_todo وescrow، وهما IDL حقيقيان من مشاريع Anchor مجاورة، وkitchen_sink المكتوب يدويًا ليغطي كل الأنواع: مجموعات حسابات متداخلة، وحسابات اختيارية، وenums تحمل بيانات، وtuple structs، وu128/i128، وf64، ومصفوفات ثابتة الطول، وseeds::program.
  • مترجمات صارمة. كود TypeScript المولَّد يمرّ من tsc --strict، وكود Dart المولَّد يمرّ من dart analyze --fatal-infos. ويُتجاوز فحص Dart إن لم يكن dart موجودًا في الـ PATH.
  • السلوك. دوال PDA تطابق PublicKey.findProgramAddressSync، بما فيها عناوين ATA. بيانات التعليمة هي الـ discriminator متبوعًا بوسائط Borsh. والحسابات تمرّ بدورة encode ثم decode وتعود كما كانت، مع التحقق من الـ discriminator.
  • بين اللغتين. برنامج Dart في test/golden/dart/bin/check.dart يبني نفس التعليمات وعناوين PDA وبايتات الحسابات، والاختبار يتحقق من أن ناتجه يطابق عميل TypeScript بايتًا ببايت.

هذا الفحص الأخير كشف خطأً حقيقيًا. على Dart 3.9 VM كانت الدالة BigInt.modPow تُرجع نتائج خاطئة لبعض المدخلات ذات 255 بت، فتعطّل فحص وقوع النقطة على منحنى ed25519 الذي تعتمد عليه findProgramAddress. لذلك يستعمل كود Dart المولَّد الآن خوارزمية square-and-multiply خاصة به.

ما يجب معرفته

  • غير مدقَّق. العملاء يبنون التعليمات ويفكّون البيانات فقط، لكن تعليمة خاطئة قد تحرّك أموالًا بعد أن توقّعها. قارن الناتج مع برنامجك وجرّبه على devnet أولًا.
  • الأنواع العامة (generics) مرفوضة. الـ IDL الذي يستعمل generics لا يُولَّد منه شيء.
  • بعض بذور PDA تصبح بايتات خام. البذور التي تقرأ بيانات حساب (path: "list.next_id") أو حقلًا من وسيط من نوع struct تتحول إلى وسيط bytes خام. وإن كانت تعليمة أخرى تشتق نفس الحساب من وسيط بسيط، يستعمل المولّد ذلك الشكل الأبسط.
  • coption لم يُختبر مع برنامج حقيقي. هو مدعوم في الترميز وفك الترميز، لا أكثر.
  • ملفات IDL القديمة تحتاج تحويلًا. ملفات IDL السابقة لـ Anchor 0.30 يجب تحويلها أولًا بالأمر anchor idl convert.
  • web3.js v1. ناتج TypeScript موجّه إلى @solana/web3.js v1.

لماذا بنيته

المشكلة هي التكرار. ملف الـ IDL يحتوي أصلًا كل ما يحتاجه العميل: أنواع الوسائط، وترتيب الحسابات، والـ discriminators، والبذور، ورموز الأخطاء. كتابة العميل يدويًا تعني نسخ هذه المعلومات إلى كود، ثم نسخها مرة ثانية عندما يوجد تطبيق موبايل بـ Dart بجانب تطبيق ويب بـ TypeScript. بعدها يجب تكرار كل تغيير في البرنامج في مكانين، ولا شيء ينبّهك عندما يتأخر أحدهما عن الآخر.

توليد العميلين من نفس الـ IDL يلغي خطوة النسخ، ويجعل اختبار أحد الناتجين مقابل الآخر ممكنًا. إذا أنتج عميل TypeScript وعميل Dart نفس البايتات لنفس المدخلات، ووافق عميل TypeScript مكتبة @solana/web3.js في عناوين PDA، يضيق المجال كثيرًا أمام اختلاف صامت. وخطأ BigInt.modPow مثال جيد على قيمة هذه المقارنة: لا شيء في كود Dart كان يبدو خاطئًا، ولم تكشفه إلا مقارنة البايتات.

الكود

المولّد، وملفات الاختبار، وملفات golden، والاختبارات موجودة على GitHub: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/idl-codegen. الرخصة MIT، والـ issues والـ pull requests مرحّب بها.

نُشر في الأصل على abdeldjalilchougui.biz.

title: 96 rows out of 47,114: when 92% of your joins return nothing and 97% of the rest return the wrong match
description:
A join returns rows. That is all it promises. It does not promise the rows mean anything.

We learned this the expensive way. A league dashboard was reading 46 competitions. The database holds 751 for the same predictions. Nobody had changed a query; nobody had deleted a row. The join had been succeeding for months — returning thousands of rows, every one attached to the wrong match.

This is the audit, run against production: ai_predictions (47,209 rows, 47,114 graded), matches (85,580) and nami_matches (89,601). The lesson is narrower than "test your joins": row counts cannot validate a join, and the only thing that can is a semantic assertion on the payload.

The join everyone writes

ai_predictions has a column named match_id. matches has a primary key named id. The query writes itself:

SELECT m.competition_id, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM ai_predictions p
JOIN matches m ON m.id = p.match_id
WHERE p.settled
GROUP BY 1;

It runs in under a second. It returns 46 rows. It is wrong.

The first warning sign is parent coverage, which nobody computes because the query already returned data:

SELECT
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ai_predictions WHERE settled)                            AS settled,
  COUNT(*)                                                                       AS joined_by_id,
  ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) / (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ai_predictions WHERE settled), 2) AS pct
FROM ai_predictions p JOIN matches m ON m.id = p.match_id
WHERE p.settled;

settled  joined_by_id  pct
  47114          3736  7.93

92.07% of graded predictions have no parent in matches. On a foreign key that is a catastrophe. Here it produced silence, because a join returning some rows looks like one that works.

The resolved rows are worse than the missing ones

The 7.93% that resolved are not correct. They are collisions — two unrelated integer sequences that happen to overlap. Three independent checks prove it, and any one alone would have caught it.

Check 1 — the scores disagree. A prediction stores the final score it was graded against; so does the match row. If the join is real they must match.

SELECT COUNT(*) AS comparable,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE p.match_home_score = m.home_score
                          AND p.match_away_score = m.away_score) AS agree,
       ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE p.match_home_score = m.home_score
                          AND p.match_away_score = m.away_score) / COUNT(*), 2) AS pct
FROM ai_predictions p
JOIN matches m ON m.id = p.match_id
WHERE p.settled AND p.match_home_score IS NOT NULL AND m.home_score IS NOT NULL;

comparable  agree  pct
      3581     96  2.68

97.32% of resolved rows hang off a match with a different final score. The same check against the correct key returns 99.77% — coming up.

Check 2 — the calendar disagrees. Compare the day the prediction was written with the day the joined match kicked off:

|created_at - kickoff|    rows
0 days                       0
1-3 days                     6
4-30 days                2,479
31-180 days              1,251

Zero same-day. Six within three days. 3,730 rows point at a match that had already been played — sometimes weeks before the prediction existed.

Check 3 — the labels disagree. Join both tables to the same 3,736 predictions and compare competition IDs: 3,736 of 3,736 disagree, 100%. And the true competitions behind those rows number just 4 — four real competitions scattered across 46 invented ones.

That is the failure mode: a broken join does not produce empty output. It produces plausible, confidently wrong output, and the error is concentrated rather than random.

Why nothing stopped it: three ID spaces, zero foreign keys

The schema holds more than one identity per match, and every one is a bare integer:

matches.id                 811  ..  92,780         (dense, curated)
matches.nami_id        4,336,437 .. 4,670,168      (vendor natural key)
nami_matches.nami_id   4,336,437 .. 4,670,170
nami_matches.id              3 .. 25,340,015       (sparse surrogate)
ai_predictions.match_id  3,974 .. 24,360,892

The ranges overlap, which is why the collision rate is 7.9% instead of 0%. The column type cannot tell the spaces apart, and neither can the planner. The constraint that would have failed loudly is missing:

SELECT conname, conrelid::regclass AS tbl, confrelid::regclass AS ref
FROM pg_constraint
WHERE contype = 'f' AND conrelid::regclass::text IN ('ai_predictions','matches');

matches_competition_id_fkey  matches  competitions
matches_home_team_id_fkey    matches  teams
matches_away_team_id_fkey    matches  teams

matches has three outbound foreign keys. ai_predictions has none — its match_id, model_id and user_id are unconstrained integers, each a join waiting to mis-resolve.

The key that is actually correct

ai_predictions.match_id references nami_matches.id, the sparse surrogate of the raw feed. Not matches.id, not matches.nami_id. Same query, different target:

WITH joined AS (
  SELECT p.id, p.created_at, n.match_time,
         p.match_home_score AS p_home, p.match_away_score AS p_away,
         n.home_score_regular AS n_home, n.away_score_regular AS n_away
  FROM ai_predictions p
  LEFT JOIN nami_matches n ON n.id = p.match_id
  WHERE p.settled
)
SELECT COUNT(*)                                                        AS settled,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE match_time IS NULL)                      AS no_parent,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE created_at > match_time)                 AS written_after_kickoff,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE n_home IS NOT NULL AND p_home IS NOT NULL
                          AND (p_home <> n_home OR p_away <> n_away))  AS score_mismatch,
       ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE n_home IS NOT NULL AND p_home IS NOT NULL
                          AND p_home = n_home AND p_away = n_away)
             / COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE n_home IS NOT NULL AND p_home IS NOT NULL), 2) AS score_agreement_pct
FROM joined;

settled  no_parent  written_after_kickoff  score_mismatch  score_agreement_pct
  47114          0                     81             106                99.77

100% parent coverage, zero orphans, scores agreeing on 46,680 of 46,786 comparable rows. The league dimension goes from 46 competitions to 751 and from 3,736 rows to 47,114 — a 12.6× larger evidence base, obtained by changing one identifier in an ON clause.

The residual deserves naming rather than rounding: 81 rows written after kickoff and 106 score disagreements (0.23%). Those are real defects, not join errors. A working key does not mean a clean table; it means the defects are visible at the right grain instead of laundered into wrong-parent rows.

The missing bridge

matches remains worth keeping — curated competition and team foreign keys, lottery classification, scheduling metadata. It is just reachable by four hops, not one, since matches.nami_id resolves against nami_matches.nami_id for 85,314 of 85,580 rows (99.69%):

ai_predictions.match_id -> nami_matches.id -> nami_matches.nami_id
                        -> matches.nami_id -> matches.id

The fix: make the join assert on its own payload

A foreign key on nami_matches.id prevents future orphans, and we added one. But it would not have caught this bug: match_id values inside matches.id's range are valid children of matches.id, because they happen to be. Referential integrity was never violated. Semantics were.

So the durable fix is a validated view that carries the assertion inside it:

CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW v_predictions_graded AS
SELECT p.id AS prediction_id, p.model_id, p.created_at,
       p.prediction_direction, p.hit, p.hit_1x2,
       n.id AS nami_match_id, n.competition_id, n.match_time,
       n.home_score_regular, n.away_score_regular,
       (p.match_home_score = n.home_score_regular
        AND p.match_away_score = n.away_score_regular) AS score_consistent,
       (p.created_at <= n.match_time)                  AS written_before_kickoff
FROM ai_predictions p
JOIN nami_matches n ON n.id = p.match_id
WHERE p.settled
  AND p.match_home_score IS NOT NULL
  AND n.home_score_regular IS NOT NULL;

Consumers read the view, not the table. The two booleans then become a contract test that fails the build instead of the dashboard:

import psycopg2

DSN = "postgresql://user:pass@127.0.0.1:5433/soccerdream"
SQL = """
WITH t AS (
  SELECT p.created_at, p.match_home_score AS p_home, p.match_away_score AS p_away,
         n.match_time, n.home_score_regular AS n_home, n.away_score_regular AS n_away
  FROM ai_predictions p LEFT JOIN nami_matches n ON n.id = p.match_id
  WHERE p.settled)
SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE n_home IS NULL),
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE created_at > match_time),
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE p_home = n_home AND p_away = n_away),
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE n_home IS NOT NULL AND p_home IS NOT NULL)
FROM t
"""

def test_join_integrity():
    with psycopg2.connect(DSN) as conn, conn.cursor() as cur:
        cur.execute("SET statement_timeout = '120s'")
        cur.execute(SQL)
        n, orphans, late, agree, comparable = cur.fetchone()
    assert round(100.0 * (n - orphans) / n, 2) >= 100.0, f"orphans={orphans}/{n}"
    assert round(100.0 * agree / comparable, 2) >= 99.5, "score disagreement too high"
    assert late <= 200, f"late-written rows={late} exceed known defect class"

Against the old join target the first assertion fails by 92 points. Against the correct one it passes with 0 orphans, 99.77% agreement and 81 late rows — three numbers a reviewer can argue with.

What the wrong join cost

naive matches.id correct nami_matches.id
rows reached 3,736 47,114
competitions 46 751
score agreement 2.68% 99.77%
orphans unmeasurable 0
rows both joinable and semantically true 96 46,680

96 of 47,114. 0.20%. That is the end-to-end correctness of the join as written; every per-league rate built on it was a statistic about collisions.

The generalisable part is that join success rate is a vanity metric: it measures whether two integer domains intersect, which in any schema with more than one surrogate key they always will. The only metric that means something is semantic agreement on a field both sides independently observed — here the final score, plus the calendar. Two checks, a few lines of SQL, available the whole time.

For every join in your reporting layer, name the field that would have to agree if the join were real. If you cannot name one, you do not have a join. You have a Cartesian product with good manners.

Analytics and research content. Not betting advice. 18+

本内容仅供数据分析与研究参考，不构成任何决策建议。

title: pgjumbo: a new free desktop client for PostgreSQL
description:
pgjumbo is a new desktop client for PostgreSQL 12+, free to use, for Windows, macOS and Linux, with query, data and administration tools.

pgjumbo connects to PostgreSQL 12+, including Amazon Aurora and RDS with IAM authentication, directly, over SSL or through an SSH tunnel. Installers are available for Windows (x64 and ARM64), macOS (Apple silicon and Intel) and Linux (AppImage, .deb and .rpm).

Version 1.0.2 includes:

  • An object explorer and inspector with each object's CREATE script, statistics and dependencies.
  • A Query Tool with completion, syntax errors from PostgreSQL's own parser as you type, parameters, EXPLAIN as a table or a diagram, and results that can be sorted, filtered, compared and exported.
  • A data editor that shows the statements before it saves them.
  • Backup and restore built on pg_dump, pg_dumpall and pg_restore: choosing objects and rows, server backups as a folder of archives, reading an archive's contents before restoring, and restoring into a new database.
  • Maintenance: what each table needs and what holds VACUUM back, VACUUM, ANALYZE and REINDEX as reviewed steps with progress, and autovacuum settings per table.
  • Server activity, configuration, roles and privileges, logs, replication, pg_cron jobs and LISTEN/NOTIFY.

Changes to objects are shown as SQL and reviewed before they run, and on servers marked Production, destructive statements ask for confirmation first.

Download pgjumbo · Release notes for 1.0.2

title: Weight-Space Programming Doesn't Need Transformers
description:
arXiv:2611.22055v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Standard neural architectures such as the Transformer were chosen because they train well with gradient descent and run fast on GPUs. In weight-space programming, a large language model (LLM) writes target weights by hand without gradient-based training, so those reasons no longer apply. Should we keep the Transformer? Given minimal guidance, ten labeled examples, and a sandbox, mainly on multiple-choice questions, we task three frontier LLMs with either generating the weights of a fixed architecture or designing the architecture themselves. When free to design, all three compile plain-text facts into a sparse table queried by a fixed procedure, reaching up to 54.4% test accuracy. An LLM-designed model achieves higher test accuracy than the most accurate released Transformer that the same LLM wrote while using about 1,800x fewer parameters. Without gradients, they choose a table, in which the LLM can state what each weight means and can find and rewrite a wrong one. Each wrong answer points to one row, and removing a row changes about one other answer. From this, we propose an associative-memory-based model up to 17x faster on GPUs than a same-sized Transformer. We also test pretrained weights, other benchmarks, and tasks where models generate answers. Pretrained LLMs remain more accurate; the claim concerns which structure to build when writing weights.

title: LoCaR: Localized Canvas Retrieval With Frozen Vision-Language Model
description:
arXiv:2611.22131v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Whole image embeddings can under represent small objects and local attributes that distinguish relevant images for localized queries. We present LoCaR, a training free framework for localized text to image retrieval with frozen vision language models. LoCaR constructs and utilizes independent proposals (SAM2) focusing on the object so as to get a more localized representation that independently encodes each region using the frozen visual encoder. We further study paired-support adaptation as an optional residual that uses matched text region exemplars without updating the underlying encoders. We also introduce LOCFG, a Visual Genome derived benchmark designed to evaluate localized retrieval for smaller and more challenging referents. Across several vision language backbones, our results show that improving the region representation itself is the main source of gain.

title: Understanding React Hooks: useState, useEffect, and useContext
description:
Introduction

React is a popular JavaScript library used to build interactive user interfaces. One of its most powerful features is Hooks.

Hooks allow functional components to use React features such as state management, side effects, and shared data without writing class components.

Among the most commonly used React Hooks are:

  • useState()
  • useEffect()
  • useContext()

Let's understand each hook, how it works, and when to use it.

1. useState() – Managing Component State

What is useState?

useState() is a React Hook that allows us to create and manage state inside a functional component.

State is data that can change over time. Whenever the state changes, React re-renders the component to display the updated information.

Syntax 

const [state, setState] = useState(initialValue);
  • state: Stores the current value.
  • setState: Updates the state.
  • initialValue: Defines the initial state.

Example: Counter Application 

import React, { useState } from 'react';

function Counter() {
    const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

    return (
        <div>
            <h2>Count: {count}</h2>

            <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>
                Increment
            </button>

            <button onClick={() => setCount(count - 1)}>
                Decrement
            </button>
        </div>
    );
}

export default Counter;

How does it work?

  1. Initially, the count value is 0.
  2. When the user clicks Increment, setCount() updates the state.
  3. React detects the state update.
  4. React re-renders the component with the new value.

Real-world use cases:

  • Counter applications
  • Form input handling
  • Toggle buttons
  • Shopping cart quantities
  • Showing and hiding components

2. useEffect() – Handling Side Effects

What is useEffect?

useEffect() is a React Hook used to perform side effects in functional components.

A side effect is an operation that interacts with something outside the component's rendering process.

Examples include:

  • Fetching data from an API.
  • Setting up timers.
  • Updating document titles.
  • Subscribing to external events.

Syntax 

useEffect(() => {
    // Side-effect logic

    return () => {
        // Cleanup logic (optional)
    };
}, [dependencies]);

Understanding the dependency array

The dependency array controls when the effect runs.

1. Without a dependency array

useEffect(() => {
    console.log("Component rendered");
});

Runs after every render.

2. Empty dependency array

useEffect(() => {
    console.log("Component mounted");
}, []);

Runs after the initial render.

3. With dependencies

useEffect(() => {
    console.log("Count changed");
}, [count]);

Runs after the initial render and whenever count changes.

Example: Fetching API Data 

import React, { useState, useEffect } from 'react';
import axios from 'axios';

function Products() {
    const [products, setProducts] = useState([]);

    useEffect(() => {
        axios.get('https://dummyjson.com/products')
            .then(response => {
                setProducts(response.data.products);
            });
    }, []);

    return (
        <div>
            {products.map(product => (
                <h3 key={product.id}>
                    {product.title}
                </h3>
            ))}
        </div>
    );
}

export default Products;

How does it work?

  1. The component renders.
  2. useEffect() executes after the initial render.
  3. Axios sends a request to the API.
  4. The API returns product data.
  5. setProducts() updates the state.
  6. React re-renders the component with the products.

Real-world use cases:

  • Fetching API data
  • Authentication checks
  • Event listeners
  • Timers and intervals
  • Synchronizing with external systems

3. useContext() – Sharing Data Between Components

What is useContext?

useContext() is a React Hook that allows components to access shared data without passing props manually through multiple component levels.

This problem is commonly known as Prop Drilling.

Understanding Prop Drilling

Imagine we have three components:

  • App (Parent)
  • Home (Child)
  • Profile (Grandchild)

If App contains user information and Profile needs that information, we might have to pass props through Home even when Home doesn't need the data.

Context API helps solve this problem.

Step 1: Create a Context 

import { createContext } from 'react';

export const MyContext = createContext();

Step 2: Create a Provider 

import React, { useState } from 'react';
import { MyContext } from './MyContext';
import Home from './Home';

function App() {
    const [user, setUser] = useState({
        name: "Raja",
        age: 22
    });

    return (
        <MyContext.Provider value={{ user, setUser }}>
            <Home />
        </MyContext.Provider>
    );
}

export default App;

Step 3: Access Context in Another Component 

import React, { useContext } from 'react';
import { MyContext } from './MyContext';

function Profile() {
    const { user, setUser } = useContext(MyContext);

    return (
        <div>
            <h2>{user.name}</h2>
            <h3>{user.age}</h3>

            <button onClick={() =>
                setUser({ ...user, age: 23 })
            }>
                Update Age
            </button>
        </div>
    );
}

export default Profile;

How does it work?

  1. createContext() creates a context.
  2. The Provider makes data available to its descendant components.
  3. The value prop contains the shared data.
  4. useContext() accesses that data.
  5. Components can use the shared state and update it through its setter.

Real-world use cases:

  • User authentication information
  • Shopping cart data
  • Theme switching (dark/light mode)
  • Language preferences
  • Global application settings

4. Difference Between These Three Hooks

Hook Main Purpose Example
useState Manage component state Counter
useEffect Handle side effects API fetching
useContext Share data between components Shopping cart

5. Can We Use These Hooks Together?

Absolutely! These hooks are often used together in real-world React applications.

For example, in an e-commerce application:

  • useState() manages the cart items.
  • useEffect() fetches products from an API.
  • useContext() shares cart information between Product and Cart components.

Each hook has a different responsibility, but together they help build scalable and interactive applications.

Conclusion

React Hooks make functional components more powerful and easier to manage.

Understanding useState, useEffect, and useContext is an important step toward becoming a React developer.

title: Your Terraform IaC Module Should Say No Before Your Cloud Bill Does: Cloud High Availability for $0 (Part 2 - IaC Implementation)
description:
What if your terraform plan failed the moment a change left the Always Free tier, and told you which limit you hit?

You get exactly that with this open-source Terraform module on Oracle Cloud: two Ampere A1 VMs with no public IP behind a load balancer, SSH only through OCI Bastion, and plan-time guardrails that reject any configuration leaving Always Free unless you switch to paid mode. Part 1 - Architecture Decisions helps you decide whether this architecture fits your project and which trade-offs you accept. Here you see the code, how it is tested, and how you deploy it.

  • Terraform Registry: devsahamerlin/alwaysfree-and-flexible-ha-compute-service/oci
  • Ready-to-run example: examples/example-1
  • GitHub: devsahamerlin/terraform-oci-alwaysfree-and-flexible-ha-compute-service

The constraint, and the Terraform IaC design goals

The Always Free limits your tenancy has to respect: Ampere A1 at 1,500 OCPU hours and 9,000 GB hours per month, which means 2 OCPUs and 12 GB in total (halved from 4 and 24); 1 flexible load balancer at 10 Mbps; 200 GB of boot and block volumes; 5 volume backups; everything in your home region. Cross one of them and your tenancy starts billing.

Goal Success criterion
$0 by default Your terraform plan refuses any configuration that leaves Always Free
Private by default No public IP on your VMs, SSH only through OCI Bastion, only 80/443 exposed
High availability At least 2 VMs behind a health-checked load balancer
Scale without a rewrite free_tier_mode = false switches to paid shapes, same architecture
Opt-in features Database, storage, DNS and container registry behind enable_* flags
Verifiable fmt, validate, TFLint, Checkov and a mocked terraform test on every pull request; Terratest on a real tenancy

Non-goals: multi-region, Kubernetes, and deploying your application. The module provisions your infrastructure; your app arrives through cloud-init or your own pipeline.

Your VMs live in a private subnet with assign_public_ip = false, and are spread round robin across your region's availability domains (count.index % length(ads)); in single-AD regions, OCI picks the fault domains for you. They reach the internet for updates through a NAT gateway, and OCI services (Object Storage, Autonomous Database, Container Registry) through a service gateway. The public subnet only holds your load balancer and the Bastion endpoint, and its security list only opens 80 and 443.

Your load balancer is pinned to the free shape, distributes traffic round robin and health-checks each VM over HTTP, so a dead VM leaves the pool:

shape = "flexible"
shape_details {
  minimum_bandwidth_in_mbps = 10
  maximum_bandwidth_in_mbps = 10
}

Your SSH access goes through the OCI Bastion service, with managed SSH sessions. The module creates one session per VM and prints a ready-to-use command for you:

ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_rsa \
  -o ProxyCommand="ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_rsa -W 10.0.2.15:22 -p 22 <session_ocid>@host.bastion.<region>.oci.oraclecloud.com" \
  -p 22 ubuntu@10.0.2.15

You set the Bastion's client allow list with allowed_ssh_cidrs. If you leave it at 0.0.0.0/0, Terraform warns you through a check block.

Guardrails as plan-time preconditions

Each Always Free limit is a precondition with its own error message, so you know what to change:

resource "null_resource" "free_tier_guard" {
  lifecycle {
    precondition {
      condition     = !var.free_tier_mode || local.total_requested_ocpus <= local.max_free_ocpus
      error_message = "Always Free validation failed: ${local.total_requested_ocpus} OCPUs requested (vm_count x vm_ocpus), the Always Free limit is ${local.max_free_ocpus} OCPUs. Set free_tier_mode = false to scale beyond it."
    }

    precondition {
      condition     = !var.free_tier_mode || local.total_requested_load_balancers <= local.max_free_load_balancers
      error_message = "Always Free validation failed: ${local.total_requested_load_balancers} load balancers requested, Always Free includes ${local.max_free_load_balancers}. ..."
    }
    # + shape, memory, 200 GB of block storage, no scheduled backups
  }
}

Your plan fails before any resource is created, which is when you want to hear about cost. The rules sit on a null_resource rather than in variable validations because they combine several variables (vm_count × vm_ocpus, both load balancer flags, total storage), and validations can only reference other variables from Terraform 1.9, while the module supports 1.5 and later. The limits themselves are four values in locals.tf, so when Oracle changes the allowance, you update one line per limit.

Going paid is one flag for you, with the same subnets, Bastion and load balancer logic. In paid mode your Autonomous Database can also use a private endpoint in a dedicated subnet:

free_tier_mode    = false
vm_count          = 3
vm_shape          = "VM.Standard.E4.Flex"
vm_ocpus          = 2
vm_memory_gb      = 16
enable_backend_lb = true
enable_backups    = true

Testing: a mocked provider first, then a real cloud

The module you deploy goes through three layers of tests:

  • terraform fmt -check, terraform validate, TFLint and Checkov on every pull request.
  • terraform test with a mocked OCI provider on every pull request: 17 runs that need no cloud account and no credentials. They check that each Always Free guardrail rejects its case, what every enable_* flag creates, and the outputs, including one apply of the full paid stack against the mocks.
  • Terratest on a real tenancy: a smoke test (network and one VM), destroyed right after. The full-stack test sends an HTTP request through the load balancer and expects a 200 from the app.

You can test your own module without a cloud in a few lines: a mock_provider block, fake values for the attributes your code indexes (here, availability domains, the service gateway's services and the load balancer IP), and expect_failures on the guard resource:

mock_provider "oci" {
  source = "./tests/mocks"
}

run "rejects_more_than_2_ocpus" {
  command = plan

  variables {
    vm_ocpus = 2 # 2 VMs x 2 OCPUs = 4
  }

  expect_failures = [null_resource.free_tier_guard]
}

Technical trade-offs you accept

Each one is written down in the README and in .checkov.yaml, with when you should revisit it:

  • Stateful security lists (Checkov CKV_OCI_17). Return traffic is handled for you, so your rules stay simple and hard to get wrong. Stateless rules only pay off at very high throughput, and you have a flag for that.
  • Oracle-managed encryption keys (Checkov CKV_OCI_9 / CKV_OCI_3). AES-256 at rest with nothing for you to operate. Switch to customer-managed keys in OCI Vault if you store PCI, PHI or PII data.
  • Always Free ATP on a public endpoint. Always Free Autonomous Databases can't use private endpoints, so your access relies on the mTLS wallet and the admin password. Paid mode gives you a private endpoint; an access list is on the roadmap.
  • Terraform-managed Bastion sessions. You get a working SSH command right after apply, but sessions expire after 3 hours, so your next plan recreates them. Making them optional is on the roadmap.
  • 10 Mbps load balancer. The free shape. Raise it in paid mode, or put a CDN in front of your static assets.

Results: what you get from the Terraform module

  • $0/month with the defaults: 2 Ampere A1 VMs (1 OCPU / 6 GB each), a 10 Mbps load balancer, Bastion with one session per VM, a private versioned bucket and one 50 GB block volume per VM. That's 30 resources in your plan, all inside Always Free.
  • Guardrails that work: 6 scenarios checked with terraform plan against a real tenancy. The free defaults (30 resources) and a paid E4.Flex setup (33 resources) pass; 4 OCPUs / 24 GB, two load balancers, and storage with backups are rejected with a message that tells you which limit you crossed.
  • Tests without a cloud account: 17 terraform test runs against a mocked OCI provider, which you can run yourself without credentials.
  • Security posture: no public IP on your VMs, only 80/443 exposed, IMDSv1 disabled, in-transit encryption for boot volumes. Checkov: 10 checks passed, 0 failed, with each exception documented. TFLint: 0 issues.
  • Terraform first, OpenTofu-compatible: built and tested with Terraform (validated with 1.10), and it also validates with OpenTofu 1.11 if your team needs it.
Item Cost
2 × A1 VMs, 200 GB of volumes, 1 load balancer, Bastion, bucket (≤ 20 GB) $0 (Always Free)
Autonomous Database (Always Free, optional) $0
Second load balancer, scheduled backups, non-A1 shapes Paid (blocked while free_tier_mode = true)
DNS zones, Container Registry (optional, off by default) Not listed in Always Free, check OCI pricing

What's next: explicit fault-domain placement for single-AD regions, an access list for the free ATP, optional Bastion sessions, identity-domain support for the registry IAM resources, frontend HTTPS with your own certificate, and a clearer error when atp_admin_password is missing: today, if you enable the database without it, you see the provider's Missing required argument before the module's own message.

Try the Terraform module

Add it to your project from the Terraform Registry:

provider "oci" {
  region = "eu-marseille-1" # your tenancy home region
  # Authentication: ~/.oci/config, environment variables, or user_ocid/fingerprint/private_key_path
}

module "ha_stack" {
  source  = "devsahamerlin/alwaysfree-and-flexible-ha-compute-service/oci"
  version = "~> 1.0"

  tenancy_ocid      = var.tenancy_ocid
  region            = "eu-marseille-1" # your home region
  ssh_public_key    = file("~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub")
  allowed_ssh_cidrs = ["203.0.113.10/32"] # curl ifconfig.me
  cloud_init_config = file("${path.module}/cloud-init.yaml") # your app must listen on :8080 for the LB health check
}

Or clone the repository and run the bundled example, which ships a small Nginx page showing which VM answered:

git clone https://github.com/devsahamerlin/terraform-oci-alwaysfree-and-flexible-ha-compute-service.git
cd terraform-oci-alwaysfree-and-flexible-ha-compute-service/examples/example-1
cp terraform.tfvars.example terraform.tfvars   # OCIDs, key paths, home region
terraform init && terraform apply

Your first apply takes about 15 minutes, most of it waiting for the Bastion plugin to start on your VMs. Then check the load balancing:

LB=$(terraform output -raw frontend_load_balancer_public_ip)
for i in 1 2 3 4; do curl -s "http://$LB/" | grep -o 'vm-[0-9]*'; done

Hosting your side project shouldn't need a budget line, and "free" shouldn't mean "insecure". If this module saves you an afternoon of VCN plumbing, star the repo, open an issue with what you'd like next, or send a pull request, and share what you build with it.

  • 👉 Terraform Registry: https://registry.terraform.io/modules/devsahamerlin/alwaysfree-and-flexible-ha-compute-service/oci
  • 👉 GitHub: https://github.com/devsahamerlin/terraform-oci-alwaysfree-and-flexible-ha-compute-service

In Part 1 - Trade Offs , you will see the trade offs of this system

title: Save Points for Law Firm Intake Forms: A Game Design Lesson
description:
Anyone who played games before autosave remembers losing an hour of progress to a power cut or a missed save point. Modern game design treats that kind of loss as the game's fault. Progress is saved quietly at sensible moments, and a crash costs a few seconds at most.

Law firm intake forms rarely get the same care. A person filling out a criminal defense contact form is often stressed, on a phone, and interrupted. A call comes in, the browser reloads, the screen locks, and everything they typed about the arrest is gone. Some will start again. Many will not. If you build sites for defense firms, a save point in the intake form is a small piece of work with a real payoff, as long as you handle the privacy side carefully.

What games get right about saving

Good save systems share a few habits. They save without asking, so the player never has to think about it. They save at natural checkpoints, such as entering a new area, rather than every frame. They tell the player when a save happened with a small, unobtrusive icon. And they make it easy to start fresh when the player wants to.

Each of those maps onto a form. Save quietly as the user types, at the moment a field loses focus. Show a short "Saved on this device" note. Offer a clear way to wipe the saved data. Restore it automatically if the page reloads.

The privacy problem games do not have

A saved game holds a character's inventory. A saved intake form can hold a description of an arrest, a charge, a court date and a phone number. That changes the design.

The device may be shared. A person might fill out the form on a family computer, a work laptop or a friend's phone. Anything stored in the browser can be seen by the next person who opens it. For that reason, persistent storage that survives closing the browser is a poor fit for defense intake. Session-scoped storage is a better default: in current browsers, sessionStorage data survives a reload but is cleared when the tab is closed, and it is not shared with other tabs.

It also helps to be selective about what gets saved at all. Contact details and simple choices, such as the type of charge from a dropdown, are the fields people most hate retyping. The long free-text description of what happened is the most sensitive. A reasonable compromise is to save the structured fields and leave the free-text box out, or to save it only if the firm decides the trade-off is worth it after discussing it with the lawyers.

A minimal implementation

Here is a small sketch using sessionStorage. It saves listed fields when they lose focus, restores them on load, and clears everything on submit or when the user asks.

const KEY = "intake-draft";
const form = document.querySelector("#intake");
const SAVED = ["name", "phone", "email", "charge_type", "county"];

function save() {
  const data = {};
  SAVED.forEach(n => { data[n] = form.elements[n]?.value || ""; });
  try { sessionStorage.setItem(KEY, JSON.stringify(data)); } catch (e) {}
}

function restore() {
  try {
    const data = JSON.parse(sessionStorage.getItem(KEY) || "{}");
    SAVED.forEach(n => { if (data[n] && form.elements[n]) form.elements[n].value = data[n]; });
  } catch (e) {}
}

function clearDraft() {
  try { sessionStorage.removeItem(KEY); } catch (e) {}
}

form.addEventListener("focusout", save);
form.addEventListener("submit", clearDraft);
document.querySelector("#clear-draft").addEventListener("click", () => { clearDraft(); form.reset(); });
restore();

The try blocks matter. Storage can throw in private browsing modes or when the browser blocks site data, and the form has to keep working either way. Clearing on submit should happen after you confirm the submission succeeded if the form posts by script, so a network error does not wipe the draft.

Telling the user what happened

Games show a spinning icon in the corner. A form can show a line of small text under the submit button that changes to "Saved on this device until you close this tab" after the first save. That one sentence tells the person their work is safe and tells them how long it stays. Next to it, a "Clear this form" link gives them control on a shared device.

Keep the message honest. Do not say "saved" in a way that suggests the firm has received anything. Only the submit button sends the information.

Making the form shorter matters more

A save point helps people who get interrupted. It does nothing for people who give up because the form asks too much. Before building any of this, look at which fields the firm actually uses at the first call. Some intake forms ask for date of birth, case number and a long narrative that the lawyer will cover by phone anyway. A guide to designing an intake form a frightened caller will finish goes through trimming the form itself.

Track the effect with your existing form analytics. Compare form starts with completed submissions for a few weeks before and after adding the save feature. Small sites will need longer to see a pattern.

Questions about saving intake form progress

Should the form use localStorage so drafts survive closing the browser?

For criminal defense intake, that is risky on shared devices. Session-scoped storage is the safer default unless the firm has a clear reason and tells users plainly.

Does saving in the browser send anything to the firm?

No. Data in sessionStorage stays on the device until the user submits the form.

Does the firm need to mention this in its privacy policy?

Ask the firm to review its privacy policy with whoever maintains it. Describing local draft saving in plain words is good practice.

SBD Marketing works only with criminal defense firms, one firm per city, and helps them with website design, SEO for the charges they defend, visibility in AI search tools and SEO audits. Its notes on UX lessons from video game design cover more ideas from games that apply to law firm sites.

title: SarcasTraps: Effect of Sarcasm on Turkish Hate Speech Detection
description:
arXiv:2610.16957v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Standard hate speech detection datasets often emphasize explicit harmful language, but directed harm can also be expressed indirectly, without clearly hateful wording. Sarcasm is one such form of indirect expression, as it can convey harmful intent through mock praise, exaggeration, humor, or apparent politeness. In this paper, we introduce SarcasTraps, a targeted external test set for analyzing the effect of sarcasm on Turkish hate speech detection. SarcasTraps contains 479 entries annotated along two dimensions: hate speech and sarcasm. We train classifiers using BERTurk and XLM-RoBERTa on two existing Turkish hate speech datasets and evaluate them on SarcasTraps, using it strictly as an external test set. We also evaluate GPT-4.1 and Llama-3.3-70B in a zero-shot setting on SarcasTraps. Results show that sarcasm substantially affects hate speech detection. Fine-tuned encoder models lose recall on sarcastic hate, while zero-shot LLMs maintain higher recall but suffer substantial precision drops on sarcastic examples. These findings show that both fine-tuned hate speech detectors and zero-shot LLMs struggle when sarcasm is involved, and SarcasTraps provides quantitative evidence of this challenge through a targeted Turkish test set. Due to the presence of sensitive and hateful language, SarcasTraps will be shared upon request for academic research purposes. Warning: This paper has examples from the dataset which contains offensive and hateful content towards groups of people.

title: EgoHandWAM: Probing the Role of Hand Motion in Egocentric World Action Modeling
description:
arXiv:2611.22151v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: How much does hand motion tell us about what a first-person camera will see next? EgoHandWAM forecasts three-dimensional wrist and fingertip trajectories and a future visual feature from the current image and recent hand states. We train on 751,065 EgoDex windows using a frozen DINOv2 encoder. On held-out development sessions, the action-only model reduces two-second wrist endpoint error from 60.26 to 56.48~mm relative to a stationary forecast. It still underestimates long reaches. Adding future-feature supervision gives nearly identical trajectory accuracy. With the recorded hand history, the visual head reduces smooth L1 error by 1.32\% relative to copying the current feature. Shuffling histories across sessions erases this gain. In a separate four-task probe, adding recorded future displacements to observed context and future tracking-validity masks reduces visual-feature error by 3.93\%. Masks alone give little improvement. A trajectory predicted from the same observations adds little. On two simulated RoboTwin tasks, substituting aligned human examples for an auxiliary batch of robot examples gives no consistent increase in task success across three training seeds.

title: What Is a Cloud-Native CMS? Required vs. Optional Features
description:
A cloud-native CMS assumes that any server can disappear at any moment. When that happens, editors stay logged in, uploads are still there and visitors notice nothing. Everything else follows from this: the application runs as identical, replaceable instances and keeps its state in services outside of them.

Many products are called cloud-native because they run on AWS or offer an API. Neither says much. WordPress on an EC2 instance is still WordPress on a single server, only rented from Amazon.

The CNCF definition talks about scalable, resilient, observable and loosely coupled systems. Below, I translate that into eight concrete requirements for a CMS, list the features that are often mixed up with them, and compare hosted and self-hosted setups.

The eight requirements

If a CMS misses one of these, it's a traditional CMS that happens to run in the cloud.

  1. Stateless instances. It doesn't matter which instance answers a request. Sessions, shared caches and locks are stored in Redis or the database. Purely local speed-ups like OPcache or compiled templates are fine, as long as no other instance depends on them.
  2. Object storage for files. Uploads go to S3, Azure Blob, Google Cloud Storage or a compatible service instead of a local uploads/ folder. The same applies to generated files such as thumbnails, resized images and exports, which are easy to forget. A fresh instance with an empty disk must be able to serve every file.
  3. Horizontal scaling. You handle more traffic by adding instances behind a load balancer rather than buying a bigger server. That only works if the first two points hold. Adding instances automatically is a separate step and not required.
  4. Cluster-safe background work. A scheduled task runs once per schedule, regardless of how many instances are up, either through a single scheduler or a distributed lock. Slow jobs go into a queue processed by separate workers.
  5. Configuration from the environment. Credentials, endpoints and feature flags are read from environment variables or a secrets manager, as described in the 12-factor app. The same build runs in development, staging and production.
  6. Automated deployments. CI/CD ships container images or immutable bundles. Nobody logs into a server to change files or install plugins, and rolling back means deploying the previous image. Database migrations run once per release, as their own deploy step or under a lock (in Laravel: php artisan migrate --isolated), and never from every instance at startup.
  7. Health checks. Each instance has an endpoint the orchestrator can probe, so a broken instance is removed and replaced without waking anyone up.
  8. Logs as streams. Logs go to stdout or a log service. Log files inside a container disappear with it.

I'll use PagibleAI, an MIT-licensed CMS package for Laravel, as the example here. It relies on Laravel's filesystem, cache, queue and logging abstractions, so most of this is configuration rather than code. Requirements 1, 2, 4, 5 and 8 look like this in the .env file:

# credentials via IAM role, or AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID / AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY
FILESYSTEM_DISK=s3
AWS_BUCKET=cms-media
AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=eu-central-1

REDIS_HOST=redis.internal
SESSION_DRIVER=redis
CACHE_STORE=redis
QUEUE_CONNECTION=redis

LOG_CHANNEL=stderr

Scheduled tasks that must not overlap get ->onOneServer(), which takes a lock in the shared cache.

Laravel also ships an /up route for health checks, which PagibleAI inherits. By default it only confirms that the app boots. To include the database or Redis, listen for the DiagnosingHealth event and throw an exception if a dependency is unreachable. Use such a check for readiness only: if the database goes down, Kubernetes should stop sending traffic, not restart every pod.

The examples assume the container serves HTTP itself on port 8080, for example with FrankenPHP, Octane or nginx in front of PHP-FPM. PHP-FPM alone doesn't speak HTTP. In Kubernetes you point the probes at the route:

readinessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /up
    port: 8080
  periodSeconds: 10
livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /up
    port: 8080
  initialDelaySeconds: 20

Without Kubernetes, a Docker health check does the same for Compose, Swarm and most container platforms (the image needs curl installed):

HEALTHCHECK --interval=10s --timeout=3s CMD curl -fsS http://localhost:8080/up || exit 1

Other stacks have the same building blocks. Strapi and Payload use upload providers or storage adapters for S3 and can keep sessions and cache in Redis, and most Go and Python systems read these settings from the environment. Check that your CMS supports them out of the box and doesn't silently write to local disk somewhere.

Optional features

The following features show up in many cloud-native systems and often get treated as part of the definition. They are useful in the right situation, but a CMS can meet all eight requirements without any of them.

Feature Useful when
Headless API (REST, GraphQL) Websites, apps or kiosks share the same content
Server-rendered pages You want a website without building a separate frontend
CDN and edge caching Visitors are spread around the world or traffic comes in spikes
Autoscaling Load varies a lot during the day or the year
Serverless Traffic is low or very bursty and you want to pay per request
Kubernetes You already run a cluster (for a single site it's usually overkill)
Multiple regions You have strict uptime targets or data-residency rules
Multi-tenancy One installation serves many sites or customers
Realtime collaboration Several editors work on the same pages at once
Audit logs and metrics Compliance requires it or the editorial team is large
AI and agent access (e.g. MCP) You produce or translate a lot of content

Headless is the one most often confused with cloud-native. Headless describes how content gets to the frontend. Cloud-native describes how the system is run. A headless CMS may still depend on a single server, and a cloud-native CMS can render plain HTML. PagibleAI does both from the same content model: server-rendered Blade themes for websites, a read-only JSON:API for apps and static-site builds, and a GraphQL API for the editor and custom tools.

Cloud-native vs. traditional CMS

The main difference is where state is kept. A classic WordPress, Joomla or Drupal installation stores code, uploads, cache and sessions on the disk of one server. A cloud-native CMS keeps none of that on the instance.

If the server on the left fails, everything on it is gone until it's restored. On the right, an instance can be replaced at any time because nothing on it has to survive.

Aspect Traditional Cloud-native
Deployment unit One long-lived server Identical instances built from one image
Scaling Bigger server More instances
Server failure Site down until repaired Traffic goes to other instances, the broken one is replaced
Updates In place, via admin UI or FTP New image, rollback by redeploying the old one
Extensions Installed on the live server Added at build time
Configuration Files on the server Environment variables, secrets manager
Cost Low and fixed for small sites Grows with usage, more services to run

The traditional setup still has its place. For a single site with modest traffic, one well-maintained server is simpler and cheaper than a set of managed services. The cloud-native approach starts to pay off with traffic spikes, uptime targets, many sites, or teams that want every change to go through review and CI.

Moving a traditional CMS into the cloud rarely makes it cloud-native. Plugins that write to the local disk, cron jobs that expect a single server and updates through the admin panel all cause trouble once a second instance exists. Teams usually work around this with offload plugins, a shared file system like NFS or EFS and a rule against installing plugins in production. That works, but every workaround needs maintenance.

Hosted or self-hosted

Whether a CMS is cloud-native and who runs it are two separate questions. The same architecture is available as a service or as software you deploy yourself, and that choice affects cost and risk more than most features do.

With a hosted CMS, the vendor runs a multi-tenant service and you get an editor and an API. Contentful, Sanity, Storyblok and Contentstack work this way. With a self-hosted CMS, you deploy the software to infrastructure you control, such as AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, a European provider or your own Kubernetes cluster. Strapi, Payload, Directus and PagibleAI are in this group. PagibleAI is built for the integration case: it installs with composer require aimeos/pagible into an existing Laravel application and shares its database, login and deployment pipeline instead of running as a separate service.

Aspect Hosted Self-hosted
Operations Done by the vendor Done by your team or an agency
Time to first content Minutes Hours to days
Pricing Usually by seats, locales, API calls or records Infrastructure plus staff time
Data location The vendor's regions Any region or provider
Customization Vendor's extension points and webhooks Full access to the source
Integration with your app Through the API Can share code, database and login
Limits Plan quotas and rate limits Your infrastructure
Lock-in Proprietary content model and API Usually open source, data in your own database
Security Shared with the vendor Yours, on top of the provider's infrastructure

Quotas and the tiers that include regional data hosting differ a lot between vendors and change often, so check the current pricing pages.

Hosted is the better fit if you have nobody to run infrastructure, need to launch quickly and the plan limits will cover your growth for the next few years. Self-hosting makes more sense if compliance rules decide where your data lives, if the CMS has to be tightly integrated with an existing application, if usage-based pricing would outgrow your budget, or if you need to change how the system behaves in code.

There is also a mix of both: self-hostable software that the vendor or a hosting partner runs for you. You start with the convenience of a hosted service and can take over operations later without migrating your content.

Checking a "cloud-native" claim

These questions help with any vendor or project. If the answer to one of the first seven is no, the system runs in the cloud but isn't cloud-native.

  1. Can I stop any running instance under load without users losing their session or uploads?
  2. Do files go directly to object storage, without a shared network file system?
  3. Can I run three instances behind a load balancer without sticky sessions?
  4. Does each scheduled task run once, no matter how many instances are up?
  5. Are all settings and secrets passed in through the environment?
  6. Are extensions and the content model part of the build, and do migrations run once per release?
  7. Is there a health check endpoint, and do logs go to stdout or a log service?
  8. For hosted products: can I export all content and files in an open format?

You can try the first question in a few minutes with Docker Compose, as long as a reverse proxy sits in front of the app service:

docker compose up -d --scale app=3

# log in to the admin, upload an image, then stop one replica
docker stop $(docker compose ps -q app | head -n 1)

# reload the admin: still logged in, image still there?

If you were logged out or the image is missing, state is stored on the instance.

This only tells you something if uploads go to object storage. A shared Docker volume makes a single-server setup pass as well, and that doesn't help you once instances run on different hosts.

Conclusion

A cloud-native CMS costs a bit more effort upfront and gives you resilience, scaling and repeatable releases in return. Whether you buy it as a service or run it yourself depends on your operations capacity, how costs grow with usage, where your data has to live and how much control you need over the code.

How many of the checks does your current CMS pass? If you want to see how a CMS supports these requirements in code, the PagibleAI source is a good starting point.
