title: FM-Mamba: An Efficient Native 2D Selective State Space Model with Stability-Aware Discretization
description:
arXiv:2611.22061v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: When applied to two-dimensional features such as images, Mamba-based methods either flatten the feature map into 1D sequences and fuse multiple scans, which breaks spatial adjacency and multiplies computation, or recurse directly on the 2D grid but rescale the recurrence with a fixed input-independent factor and aggregate only the predecessors on a single anti-diagonal, leaving the discrete step unconstrained by 2D stability theory. We propose \textbf{FM-Mamba}, a native 2D selective state space model built on the general Fornasini--Marchesini (FM) model. Its coupled recurrence evolves along both spatial axes; cross-axis coupling induces a discrete diagonal-predecessor term $\tilde A_0$, and two independent input-dependent step sizes $\Delta_1(i,j)$, $\Delta_2(i,j)$ govern propagation along the two axes, so that the coefficients adapt per position and per direction. A normalized ratio $r_k=a_{0,k}/(a_{1,k}a_{2,k})$ yields a closed-form piecewise bound on the two step sizes; when a configuration falls outside the stable interval the steps are projected onto this bound, and the criterion is re-verified per position after training, which suppresses systematic local amplification without global damping. The recurrence is executed by a dual-diagonal wavefront scan: each update gathers information from two anti-diagonals, and the input enters the current state through a single projection, so that neither training nor inference flattens the feature map. Code is available at https://github.com/BitSsm/FM-Mamba-Runtime

title: AWS Lambda durable functions now supports pausing and deleting executions
description:
AWS Lambda durable functions now lets you pause a running durable execution and resume it later without losing its progress. When you resume an execution, it continues from its last checkpoint on the same function version. By default, time spent paused doesn't count toward the execution timeout. You can also now delete a completed execution's data before its retention period ends.

With Lambda durable functions, you can build resilient multi-step applications and AI workflows that run for up to one year, with built-in checkpointing and automatic retries. With this launch, when a downstream service is degraded or a model provider's rate limit is reached, you can pause affected executions while you resolve the issue instead of letting the retries run out. You can also delete an execution's history, checkpoint data, and input and output payloads after it succeeds, fails, stops, or times out. For example, you can delete an execution whose input contains personal data, or clean up failed executions that a bug left behind.

You can pause, resume, and delete executions using the Lambda console, the AWS CLI, or the AWS SDKs in all AWS Regions where AWS Lambda durable functions is available.

To learn more, see Managing durable executions in the AWS Lambda Developer Guide, or visit the AWS Lambda durable functions product page. If you build with an AI coding assistant such as Kiro, the Agent Toolkit for AWS gives it skills and guidance for building on AWS.

title: Socket.IO Tutorial: Real-Time Order Updates in Node.js
description:
Quick answer

Socket.IO is a library that lets a Node.js server push events to connected browsers the moment something happens, instead of waiting for the browser to ask. This post builds a live order-status feed: order 1042 moves from received to packed to delivered, and each change reaches the customer instantly. It fits order tracking, chat, and live dashboards.

A customer buys a kurta and a dupatta, pays Rs 12,400, and then waits. The shop page says "processing" and the customer refreshes, waits, refreshes again. The usual fix is polling: the browser asks the server every few seconds whether anything changed. Most of those requests return the same answer, and the one that matters can still arrive seconds late. A push model flips the pattern: the server speaks first, the moment the order changes. Socket.IO is the most used way to do that in Node.js, and this post puts it to work on a real order, with one event that goes missing.

What I would check before using it

My first check is whether the update is worth pushing at all. A live feed earns its place when the reader waits on something that changes at an unknown time: an order status, a chat reply, a delivery location. If the data only changes when the user acts, a normal request is simpler and cheaper.

My second check is how many clients need the same event. Socket.IO shines when one event fans out to many browsers: each order gets a room, and only the customer in that room hears about it. If every event goes to exactly one client, a plain WebSocket may be less machinery. The WebSockets Explained: Real-Time Data Without Polling post covers the raw transport underneath.

My third check is what happens when a connection drops. Networks drop and phones switch from Wi-Fi to mobile data, and Socket.IO reconnects on its own. But reconnection does not replay the events missed in between. If a missed update matters, the client must ask for the current state after reconnecting. The demo replays nothing, which suits a status feed and not a payment.

My fourth check is the team cost. Socket.IO adds a persistent connection per client, which changes how the server is deployed: sticky sessions behind a load balancer, or the Redis adapter for several servers. For one small server that cost is trivial; for a fleet it is a design decision.

My verdict, as judgement: adopt Socket.IO when users wait on events they cannot predict and the server should speak first. Skip it when a request on demand already answers the question. The recommendation flips the moment events must never be missed, or the deployment cannot hold persistent connections.

One order, three updates, and a silent listener

Order 1042 belongs to Ayesha: a kurta and a dupatta for Rs 12,400. The shop wants her browser to learn about each change the moment it happens, without polling. The server below puts each client in a room named after the order id and emits an order-update event at each step: received, packed, delivered.

// server.js: live order-status feed.
// Run: node server.js (listens on port 3000).
const http = require("http");
const { Server } = require("socket.io");

const server = http.createServer();
const io = new Server(server, { cors: { origin: "*" } });

const STEPS = [
  { status: "received", note: "Payment confirmed, order received" },
  { status: "packed", note: "Kurta and dupatta packed at the warehouse" },
  { status: "delivered", note: "Order handed to Ayesha in Karachi" },
];

io.on("connection", (socket) => {
  console.log(`client connected: ${socket.id}`);
  socket.on("join-order", (orderId) => {
    const room = `order-${orderId}`;
    socket.join(room);
    console.log(`client ${socket.id} joined ${room}`);
    STEPS.forEach((step, index) => {
      setTimeout(() => {
        const update = { orderId, ...step };
        io.to(room).emit("order-update", update);
        console.log(`sent order-update: ${orderId} -> ${step.status}`);
      }, 400 * (index + 1));
    });
  });
  socket.on("disconnect", () => {
    console.log(`client disconnected: ${socket.id}`);
  });
});

server.listen(3000, () => {
  console.log("Socket.IO server listening on http://localhost:3000");
});

The first client has a small bug: it listens for order_status, with underscores, while the server emits order-update, with a hyphen. Socket.IO never warns about a listener that matches nothing.

// client-buggy.js: the wrong event name, on purpose.
// Run: node client-buggy.js
const { io } = require("socket.io-client");

const socket = io("http://localhost:3000");
const received = [];

socket.on("connect", () => {
  console.log(`connected as ${socket.id}`);
  socket.emit("join-order", 1042);
});

// BUG: the server emits "order-update", not "order_status".
socket.on("order_status", (update) => {
  received.push(update);
  console.log(`update: order ${update.orderId} is ${update.status}`);
});

setTimeout(() => {
  console.log(`after 2.5s: received ${received.length} updates`);
  console.log("nothing arrived: the event name does not match the server");
  socket.disconnect();
  process.exit(0);
}, 2500);

Here is the real output. The buggy client connects fine, joins the room, and hears nothing, while the server log shows all three updates going out.

=== buggy client (wrong event name) ===
connected as gI1iughH...
after 2.5s: received 0 updates
nothing arrived: the event name does not match the server

The fix is one word: listen for order-update, exactly what the server emits.

// client-fixed.js: only the listener name changes.
// FIXED: listens for "order-update", exactly what the server emits.
socket.on("order-update", (update) => {
  received.push(update);
  console.log(`update: order ${update.orderId} is ${update.status} (${update.note})`);
});

Now the same run delivers every update, in order.

=== fixed client (correct event name) ===
connected as b2w_1A6K...
update: order 1042 is received (Payment confirmed, order received)
update: order 1042 is packed (Kurta and dupatta packed at the warehouse)
update: order 1042 is delivered (Order handed to Ayesha in Karachi)
after 2.5s: received 3 updates

=== server log ===
Socket.IO server listening on http://localhost:3000
client connected: gI1iughH...
client gI1iughH... joined order-1042
sent order-update: 1042 -> received
sent order-update: 1042 -> packed
sent order-update: 1042 -> delivered
client disconnected: gI1iughH...
client connected: b2w_1A6K...
client b2w_1A6K... joined order-1042
sent order-update: 1042 -> received
sent order-update: 1042 -> packed
sent order-update: 1042 -> delivered
client disconnected: b2w_1A6K...

The bug failed in the quietest possible way: no error, no crash, just a listener waiting for an event that would never arrive. The server did its job perfectly, which is what makes this mistake hard to spot. When a Socket.IO client hears nothing, check the event name first, character by character, before doubting the connection. The Build Your First REST API With Node.js and Express post shows the request side of the same stack, where a wrong route at least returns a 404.

Common mistakes and how to fix them

First, the event name mismatch from the demo. The symptom is a client that connects cleanly and receives nothing, with no error anywhere. The fix is to match the event name exactly on both sides, and to keep event names in one shared list or constants file instead of typing them twice from memory.

Second, broadcasting every update to every client. The symptom is a customer watching another customer's order change, because the server used io.emit. The fix is rooms: socket.join("order-1042") on the server, then io.to("order-1042").emit(...) so only that order's room hears it.

Third, a client that never connects because of CORS. The symptom is the browser console showing a cross-origin error while the server looks healthy. The fix is to pass the cors option when creating the server, as the demo does, and to list the real front-end origin instead of "*" in production.

Fourth, assuming an emitted event always arrives. The symptom is a customer stuck on "packed" after a network drop, because the update fired while they were offline. The fix is to treat emits as fire-and-forget: on reconnect, have the client ask for the current order state.

Frequently Asked Questions

How is Socket.IO different from plain WebSockets? Socket.IO is built on the WebSocket transport and adds rooms, automatic reconnection, event names, and a fallback to HTTP long polling. Plain WebSockets give you a raw pipe and leave the rest to you.

Do I need a separate server for Socket.IO? No. It attaches to the HTTP server your app already uses, so it can share a port with an Express app. The demo uses a plain Node.js HTTP server.

What happens when a client disconnects? Socket.IO reconnects automatically, and the client can rejoin its rooms on the connect event. Events sent while the client is away are lost unless the server stores them.

Can Socket.IO scale to many users? Yes, with the Redis adapter, which lets several Socket.IO servers share events. A single server handles a small shop easily; the adapter becomes the answer when one process is no longer enough.

What to remember

  • Socket.IO pushes events from server to browser, so the browser stops polling.
  • Event names must match exactly on both sides; a mismatch fails silently with no error.
  • Rooms keep each customer's updates private.
  • Reconnection is automatic, but missed events are not replayed unless you store them.
  • Attach Socket.IO to your existing HTTP server, and set CORS to your real front-end origin.

Where this leaves you

Socket.IO earns its place the moment a user is waiting on something the server knows first: an order moving through the warehouse, or a reply landing in a chat. The demo proved the two things that matter: the server pushed three real updates to the right room, and the one failure was a silent name mismatch fixed by a single word. That quiet failure is the lesson. Start with one event and one room, then add reconnection handling before real customers depend on it. A feed that speaks first feels instant, and that is what keeps a customer from refreshing.

Further reading

  • Socket.IO docs, getting started, https://socket.io/docs/v4/
  • Socket.IO docs, tutorial, https://socket.io/docs/v4/tutorial/introduction
  • Socket.IO docs, rooms, https://socket.io/docs/v4/rooms/
  • WebSockets Explained: Real-Time Data Without Polling, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/11/websockets-explained-real-time-data.html
  • Build Your First REST API With Node.js and Express, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/10/build-your-first-rest-api-with-nodejs.html
  • Express Explained: Node's Minimal Web Framework Guide, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/10/express-explained-nodes-minimal-web.html
  • React useEffect Explained: When to Use It and Skip It, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/10/react-useeffect-explained-when-to-use.html
  • FastAPI Explained: Python APIs at Full Speed, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/10/fastapi-explained-python-apis-at-full.html

Waqas Shahid is a software engineer from Karachi with more than 12 years of experience, including 6+ years in engineering leadership. He writes The Practical Developer.

title: Why does hosting a simple app still require 4 different tabs?
description:
Every time I spin up a new project on a fresh VPS, I tell myself it’ll take ten minutes. Two hours later, I have four browser tabs open, three terminal sessions running, and I’m still wiring things together.

If you look at the average small-to-medium setup right now, nothing actually lives in one place anymore. Your code is sitting on GitHub. Your compute is on a cloud VPS provider. DNS is buried inside Cloudflare or whichever domain registrar had a promo that year. And then you’re manually configuring databases, SSL certificates, reverse proxies, and transactional email somewhere else.

None of these tools are bad. In fact, most of them are great at what they do. The annoying part isn't the individual tools, it's the constant context-switching and glue work just to keep a straightforward application online.

How a "simple" deployment turns into tab sprawl

When you’re deploying your first side project, juggling a few logins feels normal. You set up Nginx or Caddy, point an A record, spin up a Postgres container, and forget about it.

The real headache starts six months later, or when you’re managing ten client sites, a couple of WordPress installs, and a few staging environments. Suddenly, routine maintenance turns into a detective game.

Take a typical Tuesday afternoon bug: a client messages saying their contact form stopped sending emails and the site feels sluggish.

To figure out what’s happening, you have to jump across four different interfaces:

  1. Check the domain registrar or DNS provider to make sure an SPF, DKIM, or MX record didn't get overwritten during a recent migration.
  2. SSH into the box to run htop and df -h because maybe a rogue log file ate up the remaining disk space, or PHP/Node workers are spiking RAM.
  3. Inspect the database container or service to see if slow queries are locking up connections during traffic bursts.
  4. Check your reverse proxy or SSL renewal cron to verify a certificate didn't quietly fail to renew overnight.

None of these problems are hard to fix on their own. What eats your time is hunting across disconnected dashboards and terminal windows just to get a clear picture of what your server is actually doing.

The problem with traditional control panels

Naturally, people reach for server control panels to avoid doing everything over SSH. And for a long time, that was the standard answer.

The catch is that most legacy control panels were built for massive shared-hosting resellers, not modern developers or small teams running lean VPS instances. If you spin up a $6 or $12 VPS with 2GB of RAM, installing a heavy traditional panel can easily eat up 40% to 50% of your memory before your actual application even serves its first request.

​On top of the resource bloat, the licensing models have gotten pretty wild. Paying more for the control panel license than you pay for the underlying cloud server itself doesn't make much sense when you just want to host a few apps, databases, and mailboxes cleanly.

On the flip side, going completely bare-metal without any UI works great, until you need to hand a project over to a teammate, onboard a junior developer, or quickly check server health from your phone while you're away from your desk.

What actually makes a setup sustainable

After dealing with enough fragmented setups, you start realizing that most projects don't need enterprise orchestration or a dozen external SaaS add-ons. They just need fewer moving parts and visibility in one place.

​When your core infrastructure lives under one roof, the day-to-day workflow changes completely:

  • Deployment stays predictable: Spinning up a static site, a WordPress instance, or a custom app follows the same clean flow instead of custom bash scripts every single time.
  • Server health isn't a mystery: You shouldn't have to SSH in and run four CLI commands just to see if CPU, RAM, or disk space is creeping toward a bottleneck. Having live metrics right next to your active services saves hours of guesswork.
  • Backups and security aren't afterthoughts: Scheduled backups, firewall rules, and audit logs are much easier to maintain when they live inside the same dashboard where you manage your domains and databases.
  • Low overhead: A control plane should stay out of the way. If your server has 2GB of RAM, your apps deserve that memory—not the management interface.

Why we started building Vexlyx

That exact frustration with multi-tool clutter and bloated panels is what led us to build Vexlyx.

We wanted a single, lightweight dashboard where you can manage your projects, domains, databases, mailboxes, backups, and firewall rules on one server, without sacrificing performance or dealing with five different logins.


A look inside the Vexlyx dashboard—monitoring server health, active deployments, and scheduled backups in one place.

​Instead of stitching together separate tools just to see what's running, everything from live CPU/RAM usage to recent deployment activity and scheduled backups sits in one clean view.

​How are you running your stack right now?

I’m genuinely curious how other developers and small agencies here approach this:

  • Do you prefer keeping DNS, mail, databases, and app hosting completely separated across different providers, or do you try to consolidate everything onto one panel?
  • If you’re self-hosting client sites on a VPS, what part of server maintenance ends up eating the most unexpected time?

Drop your setup in the comments, always interested to see what’s holding up well in production for other folks.

title: TUSI: A Citation-Grounded Graph-Based Benchmark
description:
arXiv:2611.21823v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Evaluating retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems in Persian law remains challenging because benchmarks lack realism, grounding, and coverage of legal reasoning. Existing resources are either synthetically generated from statutory texts, lacking natural information needs, or derived from informal legal question--answer sources without explicit linkage to authoritative legal documents, making them unsuitable for rigorous evaluation of grounded legal reasoning. To address this gap, we introduce TUSI-Bench, a structured Persian legal benchmark designed for the evaluation of RAG-based systems. TUSI-Bench is built upon a multi-layered legal knowledge framework containing 7,261 legal articles and integrating codified statutes, legal commentaries, doctrinal writings, and Supreme Court unification rulings. We also construct a legal knowledge graph linking articles and concepts for structure-aware retrieval. Based on this foundation, TUSI-Bench provides two complementary evaluation tasks: (i) TUSI-QA, an open-ended question answering benchmark containing 1,999 questions that requires grounded responses with explicit legal citations, and (ii) TUSI-Bar, a multiple-choice benchmark containing approximately 500 four-option questions derived from Iranian Bar examination questions. Furthermore, we propose a graph-based retrieval baseline that leverages relational structure within the legal knowledge graph. Experimental results demonstrate that incorporating graph-based relations improves retrieval recall by up to 8 percentage points compared to standard baselines, highlighting the importance of structured legal representations for RAG systems. The proposed benchmark provides a standardized resource for evaluating grounded legal reasoning in Persian and enables future research on structured legal intelligence.

title: Decoding Without a Decoder: Direct Pixel Prediction from Diffusion Transformers
description:
arXiv:2611.22287v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Latent diffusion models rely on a decoder to map denoised latents to pixels, adding complexity and inference cost. We introduce Decoding Without a Decoder (DWD), which lets a finetuned diffusion transformer produce final pixels directly through a linear head. Unlike previous methods, where the denoising output leads to final pixels, DWD separates the two roles: the original denoising head continues to drive sampling, then the new DWD head predicts the pixels at the final step. We extend pretrained latent models with DWD efficiently by finetuning only the last few transformer blocks, training the DWD head with pixel quality losses while anchoring the denoising head to the pretrained model to preserve the sample trajectory. Across latent image and video generators, DWD removes the decoder and reduces inference cost while maintaining or even improving pixel quality. On Wan video generation, it visibly reduces detail distortion and flickering, lowering warping error by 23%. Remarkably, the same separation also improves pixel diffusion models that do not even use a decoder: a final-step DWD head produces substantially better texture detail in text-to-image generation, and improves ImageNet FID from 1.55 to 1.43, a new state of the art among pixel flow models.

title: Decision models take 26% of requests; Anthropic now wins new teams 2:1
description:
AI Gateway Production Index — November 2026

Every month, AI Gateway routes more than 100 trillion tokens between production applications and AI labs. That traffic gives us a view of what AI usage looks like in today’s enterprise and startup landscape across language, decision, voice, image, and video models. We publish it here monthly. See the Production Index reports from August, September, and October.

November 2026 Summary

  • In six weeks, decision models grew to one in four gateway requests, while accounting for half a cent of every dollar spent. Close to a third of all paid teams used one in October. Among teams processing over 10 billion tokens a month, seven in ten used a decision model.

  • About 11% of paid teams used a voice model in October, up from 4% in July.

  • OpenAI and Anthropic now reach about the same share of paid teams, and new teams in October picked Anthropic nearly two to one. OpenAI’s share of gateway spend, meanwhile, is up by two-thirds since December.

  • More than half of language-model requests went to models less than two months old, up from less than three in ten. Within one month of a typical model’s peak usage, three in four of the teams using it have moved on.

Decision models account for 26% of all requests

Production AI is splitting into two jobs: generation and judgment. Until recently, when software needed to make a quick call, a team could use either a fixed rule that was cheap but rigid, or a language model that was smart but slow and expensive.

Decision models are now a third option. They classify, score, or pick between choices instead of generating text, and cost about a seventieth as much per request as a language model.

They arrived on AI Gateway in mid-September, and there are now 15 decision models available from eight different vendors. In October, nearly a third of paid teams on AI Gateway used a decision model. About 11% of paid teams used a decision model without sending a single request to a text-generating model.

Decision models cost far less per token and give very short answers, so even though they received about one in four gateway requests in October, they accounted for just 0.53% of total spend.

Almost all of that request volume went to Jev from TypeSafe AI, which alone received nearly four times Anthropic’s total requests. For every $1 teams spent on Jev, they spent $64 on Anthropic models.

Decision models are most common among the teams that run the most AI. Just over one in five teams running fewer than 10 million tokens used a decision model in October. At 100 million to 1 billion tokens, nearly half used one. Above 10 billion, seven in ten did.

This is partly because big teams use more of everything. The top 1% of teams by spend use a median of 29 different models, and the bottom tenth use only one. It’s also volume. The more requests a team sends, the more it has to gain from a model that makes simple decisions faster and far more cost-effectively.

Voice adoption is up 2.6x since July

About one in nine paid teams used a voice model in October, up from one in 24 in July, an increase of 161%.

New teams are using voice, and existing teams are adding it. Among teams that paid in both July and October, the share using voice went from 5% to 14%.

Teams that use voice are also using more of it. The share of teams sending at least 100 voice requests a month grew fivefold, and six in ten of September’s voice teams returned in October, up from fewer than half in July.

A spoken conversation with an AI app takes three steps:

  • A voice model turns the user’s speech into text

  • A language model writes the reply

  • Another voice model reads the reply back to the user

Most voice teams use just one or two of these pieces. Use of speech-to-text models has nearly tripled since July, and text-to-speech has more than tripled.

Some models do all three steps on their own. In July, about a quarter of voice teams used one of these all-in-one models, and one in six assembled the pieces themselves. By October, those numbers had swapped.

For most teams, voice is a new way for users to talk to an app or agent they already have. Teams’ preferred language models stay in the middle, and they can add voice at one end or both.

Anthropic wins new teams two to one, and OpenAI’s share of spend is up two-thirds

Last December, 70 of every 100 paid teams on AI Gateway used an OpenAI model and 48 used an Anthropic model. By October, the two labs were nearly level, with OpenAI at 55 and Anthropic at 54.

Both labs now reach more of the teams that have been on the gateway since December, but Anthropic’s reach grew more. The share of these teams using Anthropic rose from about half to two-thirds, while OpenAI’s rose from about three in four to four in five.

Most of Anthropic’s gain came from new teams. In October, it was the first-choice lab for nearly twice as many of them as OpenAI.

But among the biggest teams, both labs already have nearly everyone. More than nine in ten of the top 1% by spend use both Anthropic and OpenAI. With these teams, the labs now compete for how much of the work each one gets.

On that measure, Anthropic still leads, but OpenAI has gained ground. OpenAI now takes nearly 15 cents of every dollar spent on the gateway, up from about 9 in December, while Anthropic’s halved to about 32 cents over the same period.

Most AI traffic now runs on models less than two months old

Teams are moving to new models almost as fast as labs release them. More than half of October’s language-model requests went to models less than 60 days old. Before September, that share had never passed three in ten.

Within each model family, a new version arrives every 61 days at the median, and a typical model peaks within a month of launch. Four weeks later, three in four of the teams using it at its peak aren’t using it anymore, whether or not a successor has shipped in the family. Most of those teams are still on AI Gateway, using other models.

Teams switch models frequently, usually to something newer, and often to another lab. In October, about half of teams running at least 10 million tokens a month changed their most-used model. Four in five of those moved to a more recent release, and six in ten moved to a different lab.

Older models stay in use, often alongside a newer primary model. Seven in ten teams running at least 10 million tokens a month still used a model at least ten months old in October, but for the typical team it ran less than 3% of its tokens.

AI models now have a half-life of about six weeks. That means that, to the teams using them, labs are only as good as their latest model and have to re-earn their business with every new one.

Also in October’s data

  • Opus 5.5 was the top model by spend in its first full month. It took about one in seven dollars across all teams. Four of the six most widely used models on AI Gateway are Anthropic’s: Sonnet 5.5 (reaching 26% of paid teams), Haiku 5.5 (22%), Haiku 4.5 (20%), and Opus 5.5 (18%). Jev (28%) and GPT-6 Luna (19%) are the other two.

  • Image and video both had their biggest month yet on AI Gateway. More teams than ever are putting spend on them, and the largest teams are adopting them the fastest. About a third of the top 1% of teams by spend now use an image model, up from a quarter in July. One in six use a video model, up from one in ten.

  • OpenAI’s newest image model, GPT-Image-2.5 Sunburst, took the lead in image spend in its first full month, followed by its Flare and GPT-Image-2 models. ByteDance’s Seedance 2.5 led video spend for a third month running, ahead of Google’s Veo 3.1 and Kuaishou’s Kling 3.0.

About this data

This report uses anonymized, aggregate traffic routed through Vercel AI Gateway through October 2026.

A few notes on measurement:

  • Spend is estimated at published list prices; actual bills may differ.

  • Paid teams are teams with at least one paid request in the month. Team size is measured by a team’s total tokens that month.

  • Decision models are the models classified as decision models in the AI Gateway model list.

  • Each model version is counted separately. A model’s age is measured from that version’s first day on AI Gateway, and gateway history begins October 20, 2025.

  • Switching rates compare paid teams with at least 10 million tokens in both September and October. A team’s most-used model is measured by tokens.

  • Voice figures begin June 22, 2026. Teams that “assembled the pieces” used speech-to-text, a language model, and text-to-speech on the same day.

  • A new team’s first-choice lab is the lab it sent the most language-model requests to in its first month.

  • All figures use the most recent data and protocol available; prior months may be revised as methodology is updated.

title: GridDriver: On-Board BEV-Based Language Planning and Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2611.21924v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Bird's-Eye-View (BEV)-conditioned large language models (LLMs) enable language-interactive driving, but onboard deployment requires efficient perception and continuous planning alongside autoregressive language generation. We present GridDriver, an efficient BEV-conditioned LLM framework combining trajectory prediction, structured driving indicators, natural-language navigation, driving explanations, and scene question answering. Lightweight spatio-temporal BEV perception and spatially structured tokens provide scene context to a shared LLM, while frame-wise scheduling interleaves trajectory prediction with asynchronous language generation. GridDriver achieves competitive performance on public benchmarks, reaching 87.9% PDMS on NAVSIM and 57.6% accuracy on nuScenes-QA with a shared planning and QA checkpoint. Spatial representation analyses demonstrate improved geometric information retention and trajectory prediction compared with Q-Former compression. The system achieves 32.7 ms standalone planning latency and 9.4 plans/s in an onboard ROS 2 pipeline. We further evaluate planning on our own data recordings and demonstrate open-loop onboard operation on a research vehicle. Across public benchmarks and real-world evaluations, we identify strengths and limitations of the BEV-based approach.

title: Learning to Edit IFC Building Models: Verifiable Checkers as the Training Signal for Dependency-Aware Editing Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.22307v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Editing a building information model in the Industry Foundation Classes (IFC) schema requires propagating changes to dependent elements while preserving unrelated entities. Existing language-model agents for IFC editing use prompted models without learning from edit outcomes. Target-file comparisons do not specify which alternative edits are allowed or which unrelated entities must remain unchanged. We present IfcGym, a CodeAct environment in which a language model edits IFC through executable code and four checkers verify validity relative to the input model, intent, dependency and preservation against a task specification. Their conjunction is strict success. IfcEdit distils verified teacher episodes into a Qwen3.5-9B student through supervised fine-tuning (SFT), then applies Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with strict success as the reward. On IfcEditBench, 1,990 editing tasks on 13 held-out real projects, the final student reaches 86.78% strict success, from 79.15% after SFT. The paired confidence interval for the difference from its teacher includes zero; the same recipe on a 27B model reaches 91.76% and exceeds the teacher. On the public benchmarks BIM-Edit and BIBIMBAP the final student scores 55.19 and 54.50. On IfcEditBench, the students outperform all prompted models except the teacher under matched tool access; both evaluated frameworks also score lower. Rewarding all four checkers yields 4.83 points more strict success than rewarding intent and validity alone.

Second, the service adds three new routing capabilities:

- PID remapping on MediaConnect router reassigns transport stream PIDs inline, without transcoding.
- Clean switch aligns input transitions on video boundaries for a more seamless switching experience.
- SRT merge input mode bonds redundant SRT streams of the same content, reconstructing a clean feed when one path degrades to add resilience for lossy or long-haul contribution.

These capabilities are available in all AWS Regions where MediaConnect Router is available.

To learn more, see the AWS Elemental MediaConnect documentation.

title: Java4Shell pode abrir acesso remoto por falha no decodificador Base64 do Java
description:
Falha no decodificador Base64

A Calif, startup de cibersegurança, anunciou a Java4Shell, vulnerabilidade no decodificador Base64 do Java que pode permitir acesso remoto não autorizado a sistemas internos. Segundo a empresa, o pesquisador Quang Luong identificou a falha com apoio do GPT-6 Cyber, modelo da OpenAI voltado à pesquisa de segurança digital.

A Calif afirma que o Java está presente em sistemas de cerca de 90% das empresas da lista Fortune 500 e é usado em bancos, hospitais, companhias aéreas, empresas de tecnologia e órgãos governamentais.

Como a falha pode ser explorada

O problema ocorre quando o decodificador processa uma sequência malformada: 64 letras A seguidas de um sinal de igual. O comportamento inesperado pode provocar operações indevidas na memória e, em condições normais, encerrar o processo. Os pesquisadores dizem ter usado heap grooming — a organização de dados na memória para influenciar o comportamento do programa — para avançar até um possível acesso não autorizado.

A Calif demonstrou a exploração no Keycloak, sistema de autenticação e gerenciamento de acesso usado por milhares de organizações, entre elas CERN, Hewlett Packard, UnitedHealthcare e NASA. O The New York Times informou ter verificado a descoberta de forma independente e relatou que o teste de demonstração levou menos de uma hora.

Correção e resposta das empresas

A Oracle publicou uma atualização de segurança na terça-feira, 17 de novembro. A Agência de Segurança Cibernética e de Infraestrutura dos Estados Unidos (CISA) recomendou que as organizações instalem a correção imediatamente. Google e Microsoft estavam entre as empresas notificadas durante a divulgação coordenada, que envolveu os países da aliança Five Eyes: Estados Unidos, Canadá, Austrália, Nova Zelândia e Reino Unido.

O Google afirmou que implementou proteções e atualizações em seus serviços após ser informado sobre a falha. Também desenvolveu mecanismos para verificar se ela havia sido explorada e publicou orientações para clientes.

IA e pesquisa de segurança

A Java4Shell é a segunda grande vulnerabilidade que a Calif diz ter identificado com auxílio de modelos da OpenAI nas últimas semanas. No mês anterior, a startup encontrou falhas no PHP. O caso mostra como a IA pode acelerar a busca por vulnerabilidades e a criação de demonstrações de exploração, ajudando equipes de defesa e também podendo reduzir o esforço necessário para ataques.

Thai Duong, diretor-executivo da Calif, afirmou que a exploração não é simples, o que dá tempo para empresas e desenvolvedores instalarem as correções. Ele alertou que sistemas sem atualização nos próximos cinco a dez anos ainda poderão ficar expostos. Na mesma semana, o FBI emitiu um alerta sobre hackers que estariam usando ferramentas autônomas de IA contra órgãos públicos e empresas em diferentes países.

Confira mais em: https://guiadeti.com.br/noticias/falha-java4shell-no-java-pode-permitir-acesso-remoto-a-sistemas-internos/

title: Bad Apples in the Kitchen: How LLM Teams Detect, Correct, and Calibrate Against Their Misaligned Members
description:
arXiv:2611.22342v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: What protects an LLM team when one teammate quietly goes wrong? Most multi-agent LLM work assumes cooperative partners and inspects chat between turns before acting. Real-time embodied cooperation does not allow this pause: chat runs alongside action, so a teammate whose words stay cooperative while behavior diverges can cause damage faster than the team can name what is happening. We study this case by injecting three theory-grounded misaligned agents into a custom four-player Overcooked environment, each stressing a different joint-action layer (speech-action mismatch, role invasion, and aggregate-progress disruption), and decompose robustness into three sequential gates of detection, correction, and calibration through a 3x4x2 design (n=720 episodes). Nearly all trolls are eventually named, but recovery follows only when attribution and situational diagnosis appear in the same utterance; direct source-attribution prompting improves the hardest case only by degrading the troll-free baseline by 37.5%. Robustness, then, depends less on detection alone than on whether team chat combines attribution with diagnosis in a single utterance, suggesting that sensitivity to misalignment should be targeted rather than uniformly raised.

title: V2V Communications Using Blockchain-Enabled 6G Technology and Federated Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.21932v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: This study proposes an interesting approach for vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V) communication, which integrates blockchain technology, federated learning (FL), and allocation optimization of latency and resources. The research evaluates the proposed system using various performance metrics such as packet delivery ratio (PDR), model accuracy, and latency and demonstrates its superiority over existing techniques. Furthermore, the system provides enhanced security through consensus optimization and k-anonymity for data privacy. Overall, the proposed system is a promising solution for efficient and secure V2V communication in the era of connected and autonomous vehicles. Moreover, the proposed approach achieves higher reliability, lower latency, and better resource utilization compared to traditional 5G.

title: Public HTTPS Queue Subscription or Polling Consumer for Webhook Recovery
description:
Short answer: for a weekly digest sent to active developer-tool customers, choose the delivery shape that makes operational recovery explicit. Use a public HTTPS push subscription when an existing webhook processor can authenticate, persist an attempt, and return quickly; use a polling consumer when the processor is private or when the application must own leasing and retry timing. In both cases, the durable boundary is an idempotent customer-send record plus an audit trail, not the transport.

This is an architecture decision record about recovery, not a contest between queue interfaces. A digest may be generated once and delivered twice, because a worker can lose its connection after the provider accepts the request but before the acknowledgement arrives. The business result still must be one digest per customer and period. That means the system needs a uniqueness rule such as (customer_id, digest_week), an attempt record for every delivery, and a reconciliation path that can distinguish “not tried,” “accepted,” “timed out,” and “already applied.” Exactly-once effects are an application property built on at-least-once delivery.

What should a webhook processor record when polling consumers retry failed jobs?

The first review question is not latency. It is: who can restart work after a partial failure?

With push, an external delivery service reaches a public HTTPS handler. The handler verifies the request, records the delivery identifier, performs bounded work, and acknowledges only after the digest state is committed. A handler that returns success before its database transaction is durable creates a recovery hole: the delivery system may stop retrying while the customer still has no recorded send.

With polling, a worker reaches the queue from an outbound network connection, leases a message, commits the idempotent send record, and acknowledges last. The worker is easier to keep private, but its liveness, lease duration, shutdown behavior, and retry schedule become your responsibility. That is a reasonable trade when security policy forbids public ingress or when the retry decision depends on application state that changes between attempts.

The weekly schedule belongs outside this decision. A scheduler should enqueue a digest job with a stable period identifier; it should not perform the customer send itself. If the scheduler runs again after a deploy, the uniqueness constraint turns the repeated enqueue into an observable duplicate rather than a second customer-facing effect.

Compare push versus polling recovery boundaries

Compare the options by failure ownership. The table is intentionally narrower than a feature checklist.

Option Network shape Recovery owner Suitable when Main limitation
Public HTTPS push subscription Delivery service calls your endpoint Handler and delivery policy The webhook processor is already public and independently monitored Public ingress, authentication, and burst capacity are part of the queue design
Polling consumer Worker calls the queue Worker, lease policy, and acknowledgement logic The processor must stay private or needs application-controlled timing A healthy process and queue metrics must be maintained
Broker dead-letter route Broker moves rejected messages Broker topology plus an operator A team already operates a broker and needs a clear redrive boundary Dead letters do not replace business reconciliation or idempotency

Neither option prevents duplicates. A timeout after the email provider accepted a request is indistinguishable from a timeout before acceptance unless the provider offers a durable idempotency key. Generate that key from the customer and digest period, store it with the attempt, and use the same key on every retry. Record the response classification separately from the business result; a transport success is evidence about delivery, not proof that the customer read the message.

This is where compliance concerns become practical. An audit trail should answer who or what scheduled the digest, which customer-period key was processed, which attempt number ran, what external request identifier was used, and why the next retry was or was not scheduled. Logs alone are a poor substitute because retention, redaction, and sampling policies can remove the very evidence needed during reconciliation.

Code path for a repeatable customer send

The critical path should be deliberately uneventful: receive, validate, claim, apply, record, acknowledge. The claim and application must be safe to repeat. Here is a generic polling shape; the queue adapter is intentionally separate from the customer-send transaction.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "database/sql"
    "fmt"
)

type Job struct {
    ID         string
    CustomerID string
    Period     string
}

type Queue interface {
    Receive(context.Context) (Job, error)
    Ack(context.Context, string) error
    Retry(context.Context, string, string) error
}

func handle(ctx context.Context, db *sql.DB, q Queue, send func(context.Context, Job, string) error) error {
    job, err := q.Receive(ctx)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }

    key := fmt.Sprintf("%s:%s", job.CustomerID, job.Period)
    tx, err := db.BeginTx(ctx, nil)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer tx.Rollback()

    // The unique customer-period key makes a redelivery harmless.
    result, err := tx.ExecContext(ctx,
        `INSERT INTO digest_sends (customer_id, period, status)
         VALUES (?, ?, 'claimed') ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`,
        job.CustomerID, job.Period)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if n, _ := result.RowsAffected(); n == 0 {
        return q.Ack(ctx, job.ID)
    }
    if err := tx.Commit(); err != nil {
        return err
    }

    if err := send(ctx, job, key); err != nil {
        _ = q.Retry(ctx, job.ID, err.Error())
        return err
    }
    if _, err := db.ExecContext(ctx,
        `UPDATE digest_sends SET status = 'sent' WHERE customer_id = ? AND period = ?`,
        job.CustomerID, job.Period); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    return q.Ack(ctx, job.ID)
}

The example leaves one important policy visible: claiming before the external send can create a stuck claimed row if the process dies. That is not a reason to remove the claim. Add a lease expiry and a reconciliation job that can safely re-open stale claims, while retaining the original attempt history. The alternative is to send first and write afterward, which makes duplicate sends more likely when the write fails. There is no transaction spanning your database and an arbitrary mail or webhook provider, so the design must expose this boundary instead of pretending it is atomic.

Three words: ack last.

Privacy constraints on private ingress

The rejected option in this ADR is public push. Select polling when the webhook processor has no permitted public ingress, when a private network is a hard requirement, or when an operator needs to pause leasing during reconciliation. A polling worker is also the clearer choice when the retry schedule depends on a customer’s current subscription state and the application must inspect that state before re-enqueueing.

Push is the better operational shape when the processor already has public HTTPS ingress, can reject unauthenticated requests before changing state, and has independent alarms for delivery silence and handler saturation. It reduces the need to run a continuously pulling process, but it does not remove capacity planning, deduplication, or audit requirements.

The catch is recovery ownership. Push is not suitable when nobody owns the public endpoint or when the delivery policy cannot be inspected during an incident; stick with a private polling worker until those controls exist. A broker with dead-letter exchanges can also be a sound choice for a team that already operates that topology, although dead-lettering still needs an application-level redrive rule and a ledger of outcomes.

Test reconciliation as the schedule's second clock

Test the failure boundaries, not only the happy path. A useful test kills the worker after the external provider accepts the idempotency key, then checks that a redelivery creates one customer-period effect and two auditable attempts. Another pauses the consumer beyond its lease, starts a second consumer, and verifies that the claim rule prevents concurrent business effects. A third replays an old scheduler message after the period has closed and confirms that the system records the decision without sending a second digest.

Metrics should make recovery visible: age of the oldest pending job, attempts by outcome, stale claims, acknowledgement latency, and the count of customer-period conflicts. Alerting on queue depth alone misses a silent public endpoint and a worker that is acknowledging messages while its final status update fails.

I'm not sure a queue dashboard, by itself, can answer every audit question; retention and export behavior vary, and the question should be verified before approval. Keep the durable evidence in an application-owned attempt table, then use the queue's metrics as operational signals. Your mileage may vary on retry intervals, but the decision rule should remain stable: select the ingress that gives the team a clear, testable recovery owner.

title: Privacy Boundaries for Email Test Fixtures
description:
Email testing is often described as a delivery problem: did the message arrive, did the link work, and did the UI show the right state? In a real application, it is also a privacy problem.

A test fixture can contain a name, an account identifier, a password-reset URL, a team invitation, or a billing detail. Even when the data is synthetic, a shared mailbox and a long retention period can turn a small QA convenience into a surprisingly durable data store.

This is where a temp mail workflow can be useful, but only if the fixture is designed as a controlled security boundary. The mailbox is not the whole solution. The useful design includes ownership, access, expiry, logging, and a plan for what happens when a test fails.

Why email fixtures are a privacy boundary

An email fixture sits between at least three systems:

  1. The application under test, which creates the message.
  2. The delivery layer, which may retry or queue it.
  3. The test runner or reviewer, which reads the message and acts on it.

Each system can copy data. A CI log may capture a message identifier. A browser test may save a screenshot. A retry queue may retain the payload longer than expected. The inbox itself may keep messages after the test has finished.

That makes fixture design closer to threat modeling than to choosing a convenient test address. Ask who can read the mailbox, which credentials are stored in CI, whether links can be replayed, and how quickly the data disappears. The answers should be part of the test contract, not tribal knowledge.

Map the data before choosing a mailbox

Start with a small data-flow map for each email scenario. It does not need to be a polished architecture diagram. A table in the test repository is often enough:

Data Created by Needed by Retention goal
Recipient address Fixture factory Application and test Test duration
Message ID Mail adapter Logs and assertions Short CI retention
Verification token Application Browser test Until consumed or expired
Message body Mailbox One assertion Avoid saving

This exercise finds accidental persistence early. For example, the message body may be needed for one assertion, while the message ID is enough to diagnose a timeout. Keeping both forever is rarely justified.

The same map also helps teams choose the right boundary. A local fake transport may be best for unit tests. An isolated mailbox is more appropriate for an end-to-end check of rendering, delivery, and link behavior. A shared personal inbox is usually the least auditable option.

Design a fixture with a short, explicit lifecycle

A reliable fixture has a lifecycle that can be explained in one paragraph:

  1. Allocate a unique address or namespace for the test run.
  2. Associate it with a run ID, not with a developer's personal identity.
  3. Wait for a message with a bounded timeout.
  4. Extract only the fields needed for the assertion.
  5. Consume or invalidate the token.
  6. Delete the mailbox or let its documented expiry policy finish.

The run ID matters because it prevents parallel jobs from reading one another's messages. It also makes cleanup and investigation easier. A test can use a small adapter rather than scattering provider-specific calls throughout the suite:

type MailFixture = {
  address: string;
  runId: string;
  waitForMessage: (subject: string, timeoutMs: number) => Promise<string>;
  dispose: () => Promise<void>;
};

const fixture = await mailFixtures.create({ runId });

try {
  await app.requestVerification(fixture.address);
  const body = await fixture.waitForMessage("Verify your account", 30_000);
  expect(extractLink(body)).toMatchObject({ path: "/verify" });
} finally {
  await fixture.dispose();
}

In practise, cleanup still needs to be idempotent. The test runner can be interrupted, the provider can return a transient error, or the assertion can fail before the message is read. A cleanup job with a short maximum age is a useful second line of defense.

Make failures useful without keeping message bodies

Teams often retain too much data because debugging an intermittent email failure is hard. A better compromise is to record structured evidence:

  • run ID and test name;
  • provider request and message IDs;
  • timestamps for creation, delivery, and assertion;
  • normalized subject and selected header values;
  • failure category, such as timeout, wrong recipient, or invalid link.

Avoid copying full message bodies into CI logs. If a failure needs deeper inspection, allow a restricted, time-limited diagnostic path and document who can use it. That approach preserves observabilty without making every build artifact a searchable archive of emails.

It is also worth testing the negative path. Verify that an expired token is rejected, that a token cannot be used twice, and that a message sent to the wrong fixture is not accepted. Replay-safe email verification jobs offer a useful perspective on making these states explicit. For flows that change an existing address, replay windows for email change tokens are another related design consideration.

A practical review checklist

Before adding an email fixture to CI, ask:

  • Is this test exercising the real delivery boundary, or would a fake transport be more precise?
  • Does every parallel run have an isolated address or namespace?
  • Are credentials scoped to the smallest mailbox operation needed?
  • Is the token short-lived and single-use?
  • Does cleanup run when the test fails and when the job is cancelled?
  • Are logs storing IDs and classifications instead of message bodies?
  • Is the expiry policy written down and monitored?
  • Can a reviewer reproduce the scenario without using a personal inbox?

The last question catches a cultural problem as much as a technical one. When a team searches for “tamp mail com” or another rough phrase while looking for a quick test mailbox, the real requirement is usually isolation and repeatability. Those properties should be provided by the test design, not left to search luck.

Closing thought

Email fixtures are small, but they cross application, infrastructure, and human boundaries. Treating them as privacy boundaries leads to simpler choices: use synthetic data, assign a run ID, limit access, retain evidence selectively, and make expiry observable.

The result is not just safer testing. It is a test suite that explains its failures, behaves predictably under parallel CI, and does not quietly accumulate a second inbox full of data nobody meant to keep. The fixture are disposable; the design around them should be durable.

title: Browser Back Button Testing: Can a Peer Return to the Same SaaS Task?
description:
Browser Back button testing should check whether someone can return to the same useful task, not merely whether the address changes. For a SaaS review queue, that means checking the filter, sort order, selected item and place in the list. Write down which state should survive before asking a founder peer to try the demo.

A public demo often follows the cleanest route: open the queue, select a record, finish. A peer may take a different route. They open the wrong record, go back, inspect another, then use Forward. The question is whether the product helps them continue without rebuilding the context they already supplied.

The queue below is a fictional example and a proposed manual test plan. It is not a report of testing Buildside or another product. Use the same reasoning when building in public and inviting someone to review a navigable prototype.

Define the task that Back should restore

Imagine an app for reviewing incoming requests. A person selects “Needs review,” sorts the oldest requests first and scrolls to a sample request called Cedar. They open Cedar to inspect its details. Before taking any action, they press the browser's Back button.

The useful destination is the filtered queue they just left. Returning to a general dashboard would make the person navigate again. Returning to an unfiltered queue could make Cedar harder to find. Returning to the same route with the wrong filter is still a loss of task context.

Write the expectation in plain words: “Back returns to Needs review, oldest first, with Cedar or its former location easy to find.” This is more useful than “Back works.” It also leaves room for a legitimate change, such as another reviewer processing Cedar while the detail page was open.

Separate requirements from nice touches. Restoring a filter may be essential. Restoring the exact pixel position may be less important than keeping the same nearby records visible. Decide which distinction matters for your workflow before classifying every visual difference as a bug.

Separate URL state from temporary state

A route can identify a record without describing the full task. A queue address might include a status filter and sorting choice. A selected tab, an expanded explanation or a temporary note may live elsewhere. Listing those pieces helps you ask what a return visit is supposed to recover.

MDN's guide to working with the History API explains how a single-page app can add and update session-history entries and respond to navigation. Its example also addresses the initial history entry. Those browser mechanisms support navigation; they do not choose the correct product behavior for your queue.

For this fictional app, make the filter and sorting choice shareable through the URL. Treat an unsent note as a separate concern with an explicit expectation. This is a proposed design choice for this scenario, not a rule that every interface must store every preference in its address.

Ask one practical question for each piece of state: would losing this force someone to repeat meaningful work? If yes, describe the recovery or preservation rule. If no, avoid adding persistence simply because it is technically possible. Restoring an obsolete detail panel can be confusing too.

Run one clean Back and Forward journey

Start with sample data that contains enough requests to make the filter and ordering visible. Write down the browser, starting URL, filter, sort and sample record. Use fictional names and safe content so your public evidence does not expose customer information.

Open Cedar, press Back once and observe the queue before clicking anything else. Is Needs review still selected? Is the ordering still oldest first? Can you identify where you left off? Record the result separately for each expectation rather than giving the entire journey a single pass label.

Next, press Forward once. The expected destination is Cedar's detail view in this scenario. Check whether the record identity and visible information match the current task. A detail page that opens but displays a different request is a more serious problem than a lost scroll position.

Do not compensate for a failure while recording it. If you reset the filter out of habit, the next observer cannot tell whether navigation restored it. Capture the state first, then recover. The short interruption is part of the experience a peer is trying to describe.

Test changed data without demanding a frozen screen

Now give the return journey a reason to differ. In the fictional scenario, another reviewer marks Cedar complete while its details are open. When you go Back, Cedar may no longer belong in Needs review. That absence can be correct.

The requirement should preserve orientation while respecting the authoritative data. The queue might keep its filter and order, show the surrounding requests and explain that Cedar was completed. It should not silently recreate an old list just to reproduce a screenshot.

Write a second expectation: “Back preserves the queue context, but completed requests leave this filter.” This prevents two reviewers from reporting contradictory results because one expects exact visual restoration and the other expects fresh data. Both care about continuing the task; they differ about what that requires.

Keep this check separate from simultaneous-edit conflict handling. You are examining navigation after a known data change, not claiming that a quick peer review covers every multi-user race. A useful public test has clear boundaries.

Compare refresh and direct entry

Browser Back, refresh and opening a link in a new tab are different journeys. Test them separately. After restoring the queue, refresh it. Then copy the visible queue URL into a new tab. Which parts of the task remain, and which deliberately reset?

In this example, the shareable filter and sort should remain because they describe the queue being requested. A transient expanded row may reset. If the direct link instead opens the default queue, a peer cannot reproduce the view simply by using the link you shared.

Try a direct link to Cedar as well. It may be reasonable for the app's internal “Back to queue” link to choose a defined default when no prior queue exists in that tab. That is a different control from the browser's Back button. Name the control in your notes.

Also describe the starting condition. “Back left the demo” is ambiguous if Cedar was the first page in a fresh tab. A report should say whether the reviewer entered through a queue or opened the detail URL directly. The route history changes the interpretation.

Share a bounded review request in public

A build-in-public update can show the route through the task and the uncertainty you want checked. For example: “In this sample queue, open Cedar from Needs review and use browser Back. Please tell me whether the filter and your place survive. Sample data only.”

That invitation gives a peer a concrete job. It does not require them to become a routing specialist or inspect your code. A founder community such as Buildside provides a relevant context for sharing the work and asking for feedback, but the quality of the request still depends on the task you describe.

Include the intended behavior alongside a short recording or safe screenshot. A visually smooth return is not enough if the wrong requests appear. Ask the reviewer to report the visible filter, record identity and action they used, not merely whether the transition felt fast.

Turn the observation into a decision

Keep a small record containing the starting condition, action, expected state, observed state and consequence. “Back cleared Needs review, so I had to find Cedar again” is actionable. “Navigation is weird” needs another conversation before it can guide a change.

After a repair, repeat the journey that failed using the same safe fixture. Then check the adjacent Forward and refresh journeys, since the change may affect their behavior. Ask a peer to retry only when you can explain what changed and which observation would resolve the remaining question.

Do not turn a few successful reviews into a reliability claim for every browser, route or device. They are evidence about the journeys actually attempted. The useful result is narrower: a person could leave a record, return to the relevant queue and continue the task without reconstructing its context.

title: Saga в микросервисах: оркестрация или хореография?
description:
Большинство из вас, вероятно, уже слышали про паттерн Saga в микросервисной архитектуре. Он помогает координировать бизнес-процесс, который проходит через несколько сервисов и не может быть выполнен одной общей транзакцией.

Каждый участник Saga фиксирует локальное изменение. Если один из последующих шагов не удаётся, система запускает компенсирующие действия, чтобы привести процесс в допустимое состояние. Но кто должен управлять последовательностью этих шагов — сами сервисы или отдельный координатор?

Что выбрать: оркестрацию или хореографию?

При хореографии сервисы реагируют на события друг друга, и отдельного управляющего компонента нет. При оркестрации отдельный координатор задаёт порядок действий, отслеживает состояние процесса и определяет, что делать при сбоях.

Выбор зависит от сложности бизнес-процесса и необходимого уровня контроля. Сравним оба подхода на одном примере.

Пример: оформление заказа

Хореография: сервисы реагируют на события

Рассмотри процесс создания заказа. Сервис заказов, который публикует событие OrderPlaced. Сервис складских остатков проверяет наличие товара и пытается его зарезервировать. Затем он публикует событие StockReserved или StockUnavailable.

После StockReserved платёжный сервис обрабатывает оплату и публикует PaymentCompleted или PaymentFailed. Когда оплата прошла, сервис доставки создаёт отгрузку.

Весь процесс не принадлежит одному сервису: каждый участник реагирует на нужные ему события. Сервисы остаются независимыми, но состояние заказа распределено между обработчиками. Чтобы понять, что произошло при сбое, может потребоваться проследить цепочку событий в нескольких сервисах.

Например, если оплата не прошла, сервис складских остатков должен получить событие об ошибке и снять резерв. Если после успешной оплаты не удалось создать отправление, нужен следующий шаг восстановления: повторить попытку, отменить платёж или передать заказ на ручную обработку.

Пока процесс короткий, а реакции простые, за хореографией легко следить. По мере появления ветвлений и сценариев восстановления она становится сложнее.

Оркестрация: один компонент управляет шагами

Вместо этого ход процесса может управлять Saga заказа:

  1. Запросить у сервиса складских остатков резервирование товаров.
  2. После подтверждения запустить оплату.
  3. После успешной оплаты запросить создание отправления.
  4. Если оплата не прошла — попросить снять резерв.
  5. Если создание отправления завершилось ошибкой — повторить попытку или запустить согласованный сценарий восстановления.

Оркестратор хранит состояние заказа и решает, что делать при сбое или таймауте. Процесс проще наблюдать, но сам координатор тоже нужно сопровождать и эксплуатировать. Его задача — управлять последовательностью шагов, а не забирать у сервисов бизнес-логику и владение данными.

Как выбрать

Хореография Оркестрация
Процесс Короткий, преимущественно линейный Длительный или с ветвлениями
Состояние процесса Восстанавливается по событиям Хранится координатором
Обработка ошибок Распределена между участниками Задана в логике процесса
Основная цена С ростом процесса сложнее проследить его целиком Нужно эксплуатировать дополнительный компонент

Если шаги просты и сервисы могут независимо реагировать на события, хореографии может быть достаточно. Если команде важно отслеживать состояние каждого заказа, обрабатывать таймауты и управлять несколькими сценариями отказа, оркестрация даёт процессу явного владельца.

Одно остаётся неизменным: компенсация — не откат транзакции. Снять резерв товара или отменить платёж — новое действие, которое тоже может завершиться ошибкой. Обработчики должны быть идемпотентными; повторы, таймауты, зависшие заказы и ручное восстановление нужно предусмотреть заранее.

title: AI Coding Agents, Rust Migrations, and OpenJDK Security: A Practical Field Guide
description:
The interesting part of a new developer tool is not the launch announcement. It is whether you can put it through a small, measurable experiment.

Here are five current projects and topics worth testing, with a bounded first step for each. The goal is not to declare a winner; it is to find where the tool fits your workflow.

1. Claude Code: Require evidence before accepting a fix

What it is: Claude Code is Anthropic’s terminal-based coding agent. It can inspect a repository, modify files, run development commands, and respond to failures.

Why now: The Claude Code team’s recent verification write-up reached 256 points and 165 comments on Hacker News at the time of this report. The discussion reflects a practical concern: an agent saying “fixed” is not the same as reproducing the bug, running the correct tests, and checking for regressions.

Tutorial angle: Start with a small, reproducible bug in a sample repository. Write or seed a regression test that fails before the fix. Then ask Claude Code to:

  1. Reproduce the failure and show the command output.
  2. Add or update a regression test.
  3. Implement the smallest possible fix.
  4. Run both the targeted test and the full test suite.
  5. Review its own diff for unrelated changes.

A useful prompt is:

Fix this bug. First add a regression test and demonstrate that it
fails for the reported reason. Then make the smallest change that
passes it. Run the targeted test and the full suite, show both
results, and review the final diff. Do not claim the issue is
fixed unless the required commands exit successfully.

Keep the initial repository disposable. You are evaluating the verification loop, not trying to complete a large migration on day one.

Difficulty: Intermediate

Start today:

  • Install Claude Code with curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash

2. rust-anything: Port behavior before you port code

What it is: rust-anything is an assistant for incrementally rewriting an existing application in Rust. Its approach focuses on comparing the rewritten implementation with the behavior of the original.

Why now: The rust-anything repository reportedly collected 1,292 GitHub stars between its November 16 creation and this report. The interest is understandable: big-bang rewrites often hide behavioral differences until much later.

Tutorial angle: Port one small surface area, such as a single CLI command or HTTP endpoint:

  • Record golden outputs from the existing implementation.
  • Generate the Rust equivalent.
  • Run both versions against the same inputs.
  • Compare stdout, stderr, exit codes, and response bodies.
  • Investigate every mismatch before accepting the port.
  • Commit each port separately so it can be reverted.

Choose behavior with clear edges. Date formatting, Unicode handling, and partial failures are more useful first tests than a complicated business workflow.

Also decide what “equivalent” means before generating code. Matching a response byte-for-byte may be too strict for one endpoint and too loose for another.

Difficulty: Intermediate

Start today:

  • Clone the project with git clone https://github.com/erkamyaman/rust-anything.git

3. FrontierHarness: Evaluate the harness, not only the model

What it is: FrontierHarness is an evaluation harness for comparing models inside different agent harnesses. A harness includes the system prompts, tool loops, context management, and scaffolding surrounding a model.

Why now: FrontierHarness Eval v1.1 reached 329 points and 161 comments on Hacker News at the time of this report. That points to a gap familiar to anyone running coding agents: a model can perform well on a generic benchmark but behave differently when it has your tools, prompts, and repository.

Tutorial angle: Build a small benchmark from three representative repository tasks, such as:

  • Fix a bug and add a regression test.
  • Add an endpoint to an existing service.
  • Refactor a module without changing its public API.

Run the same task snapshots through several model-and-harness pairings. Record:

  • Task completion rate
  • Test pass rate
  • Number of tool calls and turns
  • Time and token usage
  • Unrelated changes in the final diff
  • Whether the agent recovered after a failed command

Use those results to create a routing rule—for example, “use model A for test-driven fixes and model B for bounded refactors”—rather than selecting one model for everything.

Difficulty: Intermediate

Start today:

  • Open the FrontierHarness Eval v1.1 quickstart and locate its first example task

4. Java4Shell: Triage OpenJDK Base64 exposure

What it is: Java4Shell is a newly disclosed OpenJDK vulnerability involving attacker-controlled Base64 data that can lead to remote code execution.

Why now: The Java4Shell disclosure reached 450 points on Hacker News, making runtime verification an immediate priority for teams operating Java services.

Tutorial angle: Treat this as an inventory and patching exercise, not an exploit exercise:

  1. Record the Java runtime version used by each service.
  2. Find the boundaries where untrusted data enters Base64 decoders.
  3. Compare those runtimes with the fixed versions in the vendor advisory.
  4. Upgrade affected services and redeploy every instance.
  5. Add a harmless regression test that confirms malformed or unexpected encoded input is rejected safely.
  6. Verify the updated runtime in the deployed environment, not only on a build server.

Inventorying decoding boundaries is more useful than searching for one suspicious function. The dangerous path may cross a controller, queue consumer, plugin loader, or configuration service.

Test only in an isolated environment. Do not run third-party proof-of-concept payloads against production systems.

Difficulty: Intermediate

Start today:

  • Run java -version 2>&1 and compare the runtime version with the advisory

5. open-orange: Test Cloudflare Worker portability

What it is: open-orange is an open-source compatibility layer designed to run Cloudflare Workers and Durable Objects on AWS, GCP, Azure, or self-hosted infrastructure.

Why now: The open-orange repository reportedly reached 659 GitHub stars within days of its November 12 creation. Portable serverless runtimes are appealing because they can reduce infrastructure coupling without forcing an immediate application rewrite.

Tutorial angle: Build a deliberately small Worker that uses a Durable Object, then:

  1. Run it locally through open-orange.
  2. Exercise the Worker’s routing behavior.
  3. Write and read Durable Object state.
  4. Switch the target backend without changing application code.
  5. Compare responses, persistence, concurrency behavior, and error handling.
  6. Record any Cloudflare-specific APIs that do not translate cleanly.

Include failure cases in the comparison. Portability is more convincing when requests, timeouts, storage failures, and concurrent updates behave consistently.

Difficulty: Intermediate

Start today:

  • Clone the runtime with git clone https://github.com/rivet-dev/open-orange.git

Building in public: my lead-gen engine

My lead-gen engine discovers and enriches Hong Kong SME leads before preparing them for outreach. In the latest run, it discovered 1,776 leads, enriched 201, and contacted 231. The gap between discovery and enrichment is the clearest constraint, so the next iteration should measure successful enrichment and reply quality rather than focusing only on discovery volume.

  • Discovered leads: 1,776
  • Enriched leads: 201
  • Contacted leads: 231

Start with this today

Pick Java4Shell because runtime exposure is quick to check.

Run:

java -version 2>&1

Compare the output with the Java4Shell disclosure and vendor guidance. If the version or deployment configuration is uncertain, check the runtime inside the actual container or deployment image rather than relying only on your local machine.

Picks of the week

  • Claude Code for teams that need agents to show verification evidence.
  • rust-anything for incremental, behavior-preserving Rust migrations.
  • FrontierHarness for choosing models based on real harness performance.
  • Java4Shell for immediate OpenJDK runtime triage.
  • open-orange for testing whether a Worker can move between clouds.

Which of these would you put through a five-minute test first, and what result would convince you to adopt it?
