title: Higher-Order Interaction Reconstruction via Integral Physics-Informed Neural Networks
description:
arXiv:2611.21935v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reconstructing higher-order interactions is a fundamental challenge in complex networked systems, with applications in ecological, social, and biological networks. This inverse problem is inherently difficult due to the combinatorial complexity of higher-order structures, the strong nonlinearity of the underlying dynamics, and the prevalence of noisy and sparse observations. In this article, we propose a novel integral physics-informed neural network (IntegralPINN) framework for higher-order interaction reconstruction. Instead of { penalizing derivative-based physics residuals,} we adopt an integral formulation over temporal intervals, which naturally suppresses high-frequency noise and mitigates derivative-induced instability. We further introduce a continuous parameterization of interaction tensors, enabling tractable identification of higher-order structures via gradient-based optimization. We provide theoretical analysis establishing a noise-robust error bound that is independent of derivative amplification when the integration window satisfies an excitation condition. Extensive experiments on ecological dynamics, social contagion, and neuronal synchronization systems demonstrate that IntegralPINN achieves accurate and robust reconstruction under noisy and sparse observations, outperforming state-of-the-art approaches.

title: Designing an RF switch matrix for automated test
description:
A switch matrix looks like a simple box: N inputs, M outputs, and a controller. In practice most of the engineering effort goes into three decisions that are hard to change later — port topology, isolation budget, and control architecture. This note walks through the trade-offs that show up when specifying matrices for semiconductor ATE, satellite payload test benches and EMC labs.

Start from the measurement, not the port count

The first question is not "how many ports" but "what gets measured through the path". A matrix that routes a vector network analyzer to 24 devices under test has different requirements from one that switches a spectrum analyzer between eight antenna feeds.

Two numbers drive everything:

  • Insertion loss budget. Every switch in the path adds loss, and that loss changes the calibration reference. A 4x24 matrix built from cascaded SP6T switches can easily put 1.5 dB between instrument and DUT if the topology is careless.
  • Isolation requirement. Cascaded switches multiply isolation, but only if unused ports are terminated. An open port reflects energy back into the matrix and it shows up as crosstalk on the measured port.

The second point is the one that bites most often. A matrix built from 80 dB switches can measure 60 dB of isolation if a single unused port is left open. Terminating every unused port in 50 ohms is not a refinement, it is part of the specification, which is why the load's return loss and power rating matter as much as the switch.

Reflective or absorptive switching

Mechanical coaxial switches are usually reflective: when a port is deselected the signal bounces back. In a well-terminated matrix that is acceptable, and it keeps cost and insertion loss low.

PIN diode switches come in both flavours. The absorptive version terminates the off port internally so the source always sees a matched load. For receive chains with low noise amplifiers, or any path where a reflection can stress a sensitive front end, absorptive is the safer default. The price is a little more insertion loss and a little more bias current.

Waveguide paths above 26 GHz change the calculus again. Waveguide switches are reflective by construction, and the flange interface matters more than the switch itself: a WR28 switch mounted on a mismatched flange will show worse return loss than the datasheet suggests.

Control architecture, the part everyone underestimates

A matrix is only as good as its driver. Three decisions determine whether the system is pleasant to work with:

  1. Switching element choice. Mechanical switches give low loss and high isolation but switch in milliseconds. When the sequence needs microsecond transitions, the matrix wants PIN diodes on the fast paths and mechanical switches elsewhere, in a hybrid arrangement.
  2. Logic level and latching. TTL inputs can be driven straight from a tester's digital IO. 28 V control is common in industrial and military racks. Latching elements hold state with power removed, failsafe elements return to a defined port. Choosing the wrong one shows up as intermittent path errors months later.
  3. State readback. Without readback the controller cannot tell "commanded" from "actually switched". A matrix that reports its true position saves hours of debugging when a sequence fails at 3 a.m.

Termination, cooling and the boring details

High port count matrices concentrate power. Absorptive switches and terminations dissipate what the DUT reflects, and a rack of 24 ports can turn a few watts of reflected power into a thermal problem. Finned coaxial loads and terminations exist for exactly this reason.

The mechanical details matter as well: connector grade (2.92 mm versus 2.4 mm versus 1.85 mm), torque consistency across operators, and whether the matrix is serviceable when one switch fails. A matrix designed as one sealed unit becomes scrap when a single port dies.

A short specification checklist

  • Port count and topology, with the full path loss budget written down
  • Isolation target, and the termination plan for unused ports
  • Switching speed per path, and whether hybrid mechanical/PIN is needed
  • Control logic, latching behaviour and state readback
  • Connector types and grades, matched across the whole path
  • Worst case power dissipation and the cooling path

Most of these are cheap to get right at design time and expensive to fix once the rack is built. If you are specifying a matrix for a new test bench, the numbers worth arguing about are loss, isolation and termination. The rest follows.

title: The Receiver Should Refuse the Second Copy — Your Retry Loop Never Will.
description:
Yesterday's fix was on the sending side. A slow receiver took 2.5 seconds to answer, the sweeper checked every second, heard silence, and sent the same order three times. The fix was a claim row: one row per delivery key, claimed once, so the second and third ticks had nothing to send. Three deliveries became one.

Then itsvicmoreno asked the question that undoes that fix, politely, in the comments. What if the acknowledgement is lost AFTER the write? The receiver has already taken the order, already charged the card, already sent the email. The sender never hears back, decides the delivery failed, and sends it again. The claim row cannot help you there. The sender did its job, the row says done or it says nothing useful, and a second copy is already on its way. Does the fix live only in the sweeper, or does the receiving end have a say?

I ran that exact case on my own machine. One event, evt-1042, a $29.00 payment confirmation for order ORD-1042. The same event delivered twice, the second send waiting for the first reply, so the second copy arrives after the first write has fully landed. Two receivers, side by side, with the same side effects: a charge line, a confirmation email line, and one stock decrement each time a delivery is accepted. The only difference is that one of them keeps a table of keys it has already processed, and checks it before doing anything else.

My claim is simple, and I expect some of you to disagree with it. A smarter retry loop will never be enough. The receiver has to be able to say no to the second copy, because the receiver is the last place where a duplicate can still be stopped before it becomes a second charge.

Problem 1: the plain inbox charged twice for one order

The plain receiver has no duplicate check at all. Every delivery it accepts is a real delivery, as far as it knows. Here is what two copies of evt-1042 did to it:

Plain inbox Receiver with a processed-keys table
Deliveries received 2 2 (1 accepted, 1 refused)
Charges 2, $29.00 twice, $58.00 in total 1, $29.00
Confirmation emails 2 1
Stock decrements 2, stock 10 down to 8 1, stock 10 down to 9
Second copy's reply 200, processed 200, duplicate, refused

Both runs gave the same numbers, twice each, at 00:07:04 and 00:07:08 for the plain receiver, 00:07:06 and 00:07:11 for the one with the table. The plain receiver logged two deliveries for one order, charged $58.00 for a $29.00 order, sent the customer the same confirmation twice, and took two items out of stock for one sale. Nothing about the second copy looked wrong when it arrived. It had the same key, the same order, the same amount, and it arrived after a perfectly normal gap. A receiver that cannot recognise a key it has already seen has no way to know it has been paid twice.

That is the shape of the bug itsvicmoreno pointed at. The sender-side claim is a good fix for the slow case, and I am not taking that back. But the lost-acknowledgement case walks straight past it. The sender believes the first delivery failed. From the sender's side, resending is the correct, careful thing to do. The duplicate is not a mistake in the retry logic. It is the retry logic working as designed, on wrong information.

Problem 2: the table works, and the order of the two steps is the whole trick

The second receiver keeps a small table, one row per delivery key. When a delivery arrives, it checks the table first. If the key is already there, it refuses the copy before any side effect runs, and still answers 200, so the sender stops retrying. If the key is new, it writes the key into the table first, and only then charges, emails, and decrements stock.

The reply matters as much as the refusal. The second copy got {"status":"duplicate","refused":true} with a 200 behind it. A refused copy that answers with an error would look like another failed delivery, and the sender would send it a third time, then a fourth. A refusal has to sound like success to the sender, because from the sender's point of view the order did go through. It went through the first time.

And the order of the two steps inside the receiver is the whole trick. Key first, then side effects. If you charge first and write the key second, there is a gap between the two, and a crash in that gap leaves a charge with no record of it. The next copy arrives, the table says it is new, and the customer is charged again. Writing the key first closes that gap in one direction: a crash after the write leaves a recorded key with no charge, which is a missing charge you can reconcile, not a double charge you have to refund. One of those is a bookkeeping problem. The other is a customer with two charges on their statement.

The check itself is small. In the receiver, before anything else happens:

if (keys.includes(evt.delivery_key)) {
  // refuse: already processed, no side effects
  res.end(JSON.stringify({ status: 'duplicate', refused: true }));
  return;
}
// record the key FIRST, then charge, email, decrement stock
writeKeys([...keys, evt.delivery_key]);

That is the entire defence. A lookup, a refusal, and a write that happens before the money moves.

Problem 3: the table does not remove the duplicate, only its cost

Be honest about what the table buys you. The second copy still arrives. It still costs a delivery, a lookup, and a reply. On a bad day, when every acknowledgement is being lost, the table does not reduce the traffic at all. It reduces the damage the traffic can do. Two copies still cross the wire. Only one of them touches money, email, or stock.

That is a narrower win than the headline version, and it is worth saying plainly, because it decides where this fix belongs. The table is not a replacement for the sender-side claim. It is the second layer, the one that catches the copy the claim could not stop. The claim stops the sweeper resending a delivery that is still in flight. The table stops the receiver acting on a delivery that already landed. You need both, because they guard different moments, and the lost-acknowledgement case is the one that slips between them.

Problem 4: the honest limits of this test

Three limits, because the test was small. First, my two copies arrived one after the other, in order, never at the same instant. Two copies landing at the exact same moment, both checking the table before either has written, were not tested, and a race like that is exactly where a simple lookup breaks. A real table wants the check and the write to happen as one step, not two, and I did not test that step.

Second, the crash window I described above, between writing the key and running the side effects, was not tested either. I know the order matters. I did not prove what happens when the receiver dies inside it. A real table wants the key write and the side effects in one transaction, or a reconciliation pass that finds recorded keys with no charge. My test had neither.

Third, I reset the table before each run. Whether the keys survive a receiver restart, and for how long they should be kept before they are cleared, are both open questions my test does not answer. A table that forgets is a table that charges twice, just later.

So the claim stands, narrowed to what the numbers support. The sender-side claim fixed the slow receiver. It does not fix the lost acknowledgement, because in that case the sender is right to resend. The receiver-side table does fix it: the second evt-1042 was refused, one charge instead of two, one email instead of two, stock 9 instead of 8. The fix belongs at the receiving end, in a table checked before the money moves, with the key written before the side effects run.

If you run webhooks, you have met this one. What did your duplicate cost you, a double charge, a double email, a customer asking why they got two copies of the same thing? And what caught it in the end, a table like this one, a claim on the sending side, or something else entirely?

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

title: Better Calibrated, Better Planned: Uncertainty-Aware Multi-ASV Informative Path Planning for Oil Spill Monitoring
description:
arXiv:2611.21783v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Monitoring oil spills with fleets of Autonomous Surface Vehicles (ASVs) requires mapping a heterogeneous pollutant field from sparse, noisy measurements under tight time and energy budgets. Informative Path Planning (IPP) addresses this problem by coupling a reconstruction model, which infers the field and its uncertainty, with a planner that decides where to sample next. Prior work has focused on planning strategies and has largely relied on Gaussian Processes (GPs), leaving the calibration of the model's uncertainty underexplored. We study how uncertainty calibration conditions multi-vehicle IPP with a fleet of ASVs that coordinates online through a shared uncertainty map. We introduce Evidential Deep Learning (EDL) as an uncertainty-calibrated information model. We benchmark EDL, Monte Carlo Dropout and Deep Ensembles against a GP in closed loop with five planners on physics-based oil spill simulations. Across 60 maps, the choice of model dominates the outcome, explaining 80\% of the variance of the final reconstruction error, against 1\% for the planner among the deep models. EDL achieves the lowest error and the highest IoU under every planner, is the best calibrated model and runs at 3.9 ms per step. With 50 cells per vehicle it reconstructs the spill better than MC Dropout and Deep Ensembles with 150. Deep Ensembles become more confident as their error grows, whereas EDL is unaffected. Robustness of the information model to the data its own planner collects is therefore a requirement of uncertainty-aware IPP.

title: OfficePrism: Benchmarking Agents on Single-Domain Operations Across Enterprise Business Functions
description:
arXiv:2611.22262v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Broad workplace scores can mix competence within one business function with the extra cost of coordinating across functions and systems, making failures hard to localize. OfficePrism evaluates this prerequisite through 420 single-domain enterprise tasks spanning seven business functions under shared, benchmark-defined L1--L3 task-structure levels. Each task runs in a fresh environment combining a shared synthetic organization with one function-specific domain and yped state access. Our pipeline uses grounded records, business rules, and tool schemas to jointly construct a Chinese-language ticket, a hidden executable reference witness, and an expected response, followed by automated filtering and human curation. The same task set is evaluated through full-schema and search-and-dispatch packages. Across 124 model--harness--package configurations, the per-case joint natural-language-and-database pass rate ranges from 22.6% to 76.4%, with a median of 67.9%. L1 is highest in all 124 configurations, and L2 exceeds L3 in 122. Among 50 configurations sharing the same harness and model labels across both packages, search scores higher in 30, ties in one, and scores lower in 19.

title: MCTS Is Counting the Wrong Thing: Learning Exploration Counts for LLM Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2611.22301v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) has powered landmark successes in reinforcement learning, yet its gains in LLM reasoning can remain modest despite substantial search effort. We identify an overlooked bottleneck: what MCTS counts. Standard UCT assigns independent visit counts to textual branches, allowing different formulations of the same reasoning strategy to repeatedly receive exploration bonuses. Our theoretical analysis shows that this count fragmentation can impair exploration efficiency, as quantified by increased cumulative regret. To address this problem, we introduce Learned Pseudo-Count MCTS (LPC-MCTS), which changes only the exploration statistic in UCT. A lightweight Coin-Flipping Network head on the policy's hidden representations estimates representation coverage, enabling related branches to share exploration evidence. Across 5 mathematical-reasoning and 7 search benchmarks, LPC-MCTS consistently outperforms strong MCTS baselines. Holding each LPC-MCTS-trained policy fixed, replacing standard MCTS counts at inference improves average mean@16 accuracy across 5 mathematical benchmarks by 3.79 percentage points on Qwen2.5-7B and 2.71 points on Qwen3-4B. Applying LPC-MCTS during both training and inference yields gains of 4.96 and 4.37 points over standard MCTS, respectively. Together, our theory and experiments show that changing what MCTS counts can substantially improve its exploration efficiency and reasoning performance.

title: HyCoInfer: Cloud-Edge Collaborative Inference for Large Language Models on Heterogeneous GPU-FPGA Architectures
description:
arXiv:2611.22086v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) serving relies predominantly on cloud GPUs, yet autoregressive decoding is memory-bound and often leaves their arithmetic units underutilized. Edge FPGAs offer attractive decoding efficiency, but are ill suited to sustaining a high-concurrency serving workload alone. This paper presents HyCoInfer, a heterogeneous cloud-edge serving system that assigns prefill to cloud GPUs and distributes decoding across cloud GPUs and edge FPGAs. The design addresses three barriers to practical offloading: capacity balancing across heterogeneous accelerators, the large KV cache crossing a constrained wide-area link, and the latency added by heterogeneous execution. HyCoInfer incorporates FPGA decode capacity into GPU prefill/decode role partitioning and places requests according to queue load, prompt length, and network state. It further combines layer-wise pipelined transfer, decoder-side precomputation, and bandwidth-adaptive KV cache compression based on residual vector quantization. We implement HyCoInfer using two NVIDIA V100 GPUs and an AMD Xilinx Alveo U280 and evaluate it over 100-1000 Mbps links. At 500 Mbps, HyCoInfer delivers up to 4.11 times the request goodput of cloud-only vLLM and reduces mean end-to-end latency by up to 61.1%. Across different network conditions and workloads, the system improves overall serving capacity, with the largest gains on communication-intensive tasks, and reduces per-request energy.

title: Ein Binary für alle Geräte: Ich habe das Cloud-Abo durch einen eigenen Dateiserver ersetzt
description:
Kleine Designagentur: drei Workstations, zwei Notebooks, ein PC in der Werkstatt, dazu überall Handys. Das Problem war nie der Speicherplatz, sondern auf welcher Maschine die Datei liegt.

Cloud-Laufwerke: Sync-Konflikte, sobald zwei Leute dieselbe Datei öffnen, plus Jahresgebühr. Messenger: Größenlimits und Neukomprimierung. Remote-Desktop: gut für einen Klick, aussichtslos für eine 300-MB-Rohdatei.

Also habe ich die Dateiauslieferung zurück auf eine eigene Maschine geholt — mit Banyan (榕树), einem plattformübergreifenden Dateibrowser als einzelnes Binary.

Was er macht, in den Begriffen der Oberfläche:

  • Mehrgeräte-Verbund – ein Konto auf Handy, Desktop und Tablet gleichzeitig. Dateien lassen sich direkt in einen Ordner auf einem anderen Gerät schieben, ohne Herunterladen und erneutes Hochladen.
  • Über 100 Formate ansehen – Bilder, Video, Audio, PDF, Office, CAD, Archive, Quellcode, Schriften. Alte .doc/.xls werden nicht gerendert, dort erscheint die eingebettete Vorschau statt einer Fehlermeldung.
  • Markierungen und Wasserzeichen – Text- oder Bild-Wasserzeichen, Unterschrift, Stempel, Freihandnotizen, genau dort platziert, exportiert als markiertes PDF.
  • Teilen mit einem Klick – Link ohne Anmeldung, mit Zählern für Aufrufe und Downloads.
  • Remote speichern – direkt in einen Ordner eines anderen Geräts speichern.
  • Alle Plattformen – Windows, macOS, Linux, FreeBSD, Android; anderswo per Browser.

Die Installation ist altmodisch einfach: entpacken, starten, Browser öffnen. Keine Laufzeitumgebung, keine Container. Der erste Start legt Datenbank und config.json an; beim Update werden Daten migriert, Originaldateien bleiben als Sicherung erhalten.

Zwei Details, die ich nicht erwartet hatte: DWG wird über LibreDWG vektorisiert, ich sehe also die Revision eines Plans, ohne CAD zu starten. Und Ordner lassen sich verschlüsseln (AES-256-GCM, auf der Platte immer Chiffrat, Entschlüsselung nur im Speicher) — praktisch für Verträge auf einer geteilten Maschine.

Ehrliche Lücken: v1.0.0, für iOS und HarmonyOS gibt es noch keine Pakete (Android hat eine APK); das Hilfezentrum ist praktisch leer; mehrere Freigabeordner erfordern Handarbeit in config.json; kein Hosting-Angebot, eine eigene Maschine ist nötig.

Demo ohne Konto, nur Lesen: http://visio.ikootoo.com:8688/

Transparenz: Ich nutze es täglich und habe dem Autor ein paar Fehlerberichte geschickt. Kein bezahlter Beitrag.

title: Why Punitive Streaks Make Users Quit—And What I Built Instead for a Step Tracker
description:
Traditional habit and fitness apps love strict daily streaks. On paper, the psychology makes sense: once someone hits a 25-day streak, loss aversion keeps them coming back every single day so they don't break the chain.

Until life happens.

Someone gets sick, travels across time zones, or misses a single day of walking—and watches a 40-day streak reset to zero. In behavioral psychology, that triggers the "what-the-hell effect": once the streak is broken, the user feels like they've already failed, closes the app, and never opens it again.

Designing a Non-Punitive Care Loop
While building Fitness Quest, I wanted walking to feel rewarding without turning a missed day into a guilt trip. Instead of a binary streak counter that resets to zero, daily steps translate into cumulative care progress for virtual pet companions (Lumi and Luna).

Here is how the loop differs from standard streak trackers:

Progress pauses instead of resetting: If you skip a walk or take a rest day, your pet doesn't get sick, lose health, or die. Your progress simply waits until your next walk.

Micro-wins over rigid thresholds: Even a short 10-minute walk contributes visible care progress rather than failing an arbitrary 10,000-step daily quota.

Emotional attachment without anxiety: Users open the app to check on their companion rather than to avoid a red warning notification.

What This Taught Me About Consumer Utility UX
Most developer-built productivity and health tools over-index on strict metrics—red charts, broken chains, and aggressive push notifications. Designing around forgiveness instead of punishment lowers daily pressure, which paradoxically makes people stick with the habit longer.

Have you ever abandoned an app specifically because you broke a long streak? What retention mechanics actually keep you coming back without feeling forced?

title: Why I Built 100% Client-Side File Converters (WebP to PNG, MP3 to OGG & ZIP to PDF) With Zero Server Uploads
description:
Have you ever tried to convert a single .webp image to .png or transcode an .mp3 clip to .ogg online, only to run into:

  1. A "Please wait while uploading to our server..." progress bar
  2. A hidden 2-file daily limit or paywall
  3. Uncertainty about who is storing your personal screenshots, PDFs, or audio recordings?

Modern browsers are surprisingly powerful. Between the HTML5 Canvas API, Web Audio API, JSZip, and WebAssembly, you almost never need a remote backend server to convert everyday media files.

Over the past few months, I built ExactSolver — a free browser-based toolkit of 180+ client-side utilities and 400+ technical calculators where 100% of file processing happens locally in the user's browser.

How Client-Side Conversion Works Under the Hood

1. Lossless Image Conversion (WebP to PNG)

When a user drops a .webp image into our WebP to PNG Converter:

  • The file is read locally via FileReader / URL.createObjectURL().
  • It is decoded onto an offscreen HTML5 <canvas> preserving full 24-bit RGBA alpha transparency.
  • canvas.toBlob(callback, 'image/png') exports a clean, lossless PNG directly into browser memory for instant download.
  • Bytes uploaded to a server: 0.

2. Browser Audio Transcoding (MP3 to OGG)

Audio files are often large and slow to upload on standard residential connections. On our MP3 to OGG Converter, browser decoding and encoding allow users to convert audio clips into open-source OGG Vorbis format directly from RAM without waiting on server queues.

3. Fonts & Archive-to-PDF Workflows

We applied the exact same privacy-first architecture to:

  • Online Font Converter for web typography and icon vector assets
  • ZIP to PDF Converter for unpacking images/documents from a .zip archive in-memory and merging them into a single clean PDF
  • Download & Upload Time Calculator for estimating real-world Mbps vs. MB/s transfer times (including TCP/IP overhead)

Why Client-Side Architecture Matters

  • Zero Privacy Risk: Invoices, legal PDFs, client assets, and personal photos never touch a third-party server.
  • Instant Batch Speed: No upload bottleneck—conversion runs at your local CPU speed.
  • 100% Free Forever: Because computation runs in the user's browser, the tools stay free with no arbitrary file limits.

If you're a developer or creator who regularly converts files or needs quick engineering/unit math, check out the full toolkit at ExactSolver.com. Feedback on what formats or tools to add next is always welcome!

title: Your Paris Christmas week has three closure days in it
description:
Christmas falls on Fri Dec 25 this year, and a lot of Indian tech workers are turning the week after it into a first trip to Paris. The usual order is flights, then hotel, then "we'll fit the Louvre and Versailles into whichever days are free."

The question nobody asks

"Which of my days is each place actually closed?"

Say you land Fri Dec 25 and fly out Wed Dec 30:

  • Fri Dec 25: the Louvre and the Palace of Versailles are both closed.
  • Mon Dec 28: Versailles (Palace and Trianon) is closed every Monday.
  • Tue Dec 29: the Louvre is closed every Tuesday.

Put Versailles on Monday and the Louvre on Tuesday, which looks tidy on paper, and you get neither.

What to check before you book

  • Swap them: Louvre on Monday, Versailles on Tuesday. Or use Sat Dec 26 and Sun Dec 27, when both are open.
  • From Sat Dec 19 to Mon Jan 4, the Louvre requires a timed reservation for every visitor, so book the slot when you book the flights. Non-EEA visitors pay €32.
  • The Louvre stays open till 9 PM on Wednesdays and Fridays, so your departure day can still work if your flight is late.
  • Treat Christmas Day as an arrival and walking day, not a sightseeing day.

Where SearchSpot fits

SearchSpot is a human-backed AI travel concierge that asks these questions before you pay. It puts you before commissions, so it has no reason to push the flight that lands you on the wrong days just because it looks cheap. It hunts for the best value wherever and whenever it shows up.

If you want it to line up your Paris dates against the closures: searchspot.ai/get-app?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=community&utm_campaign=searchspot-community

title: Five Tailwind breakpoints ship in our CSS, two of them do all the work, and one changes nothing at all
description:
Responsive design is usually discussed as a design decision and shipped as a pile of sm: and lg: prefixes nobody audits afterwards. I wanted the audit: how many media queries does our stylesheet contain, how many of them ever fire on a real page, and how much changes when they do.

The subject is Nakodo, 76 public pages served by Next 16, styled with Tailwind v4, 154,378 bytes of CSS in two files.

Every media query in the stylesheet

Pulling the CSS and brace-matching each @media gives 41 top-level blocks (one more is nested inside another) holding 22,155 bytes, which is 14.4% of the stylesheet:

Condition Blocks Rules Bytes
(min-width:40rem) = sm, 640px 3 138 7,755
(min-width:64rem) = lg, 1024px 2 55 3,128
(min-width:48rem) = md, 768px 2 27 1,352
(min-width:80rem) = xl, 1280px 2 5 174
(min-width:96rem) = 2xl, 1536px 1 1 27
(min-width:420px) 1 1 74
(min-width:360px) 1 1 48
not all and (min-width:40rem) = max-sm 1 4 137
not all and (min-width:64rem) = max-lg 1 1 29
(hover:hover) 8 49 4,492
(prefers-reduced-motion:no-preference) 10 45 4,130
(prefers-reduced-motion:reduce) 3 4 310
(forced-colors:active) 6 6 499

Two things stand out before any page is loaded. The sm blocks are 45 times the size of the xl blocks, and the entire 2xl breakpoint is this:

@media (min-width:96rem){.container{max-width:96rem}}

.container has zero uses in 69,066 lines of application code. A media query ships for a screen size we never designed for, carrying a rule for a class we never use.

Every responsive prefix in the source 

sm:        367 uses in 72 files
lg:        135 uses in 25 files
md:         50 uses in 23 files
xl:          5 uses in  3 files
2xl:         0 uses in  0 files
max-sm:      4 uses in  1 file
max-lg:      1 use  in  1 file
min-[420px]: 2 uses in  2 files
min-[360px]: 1 use  in  1 file

Five of those 5 xl: uses: two xl:table-cell and one xl:block plus xl:ml-0 in the results table behind the login, and one xl:grid-cols-5 in the marketing footer. That last one is the only xl: utility that reaches a public page, and it is there once per page, 76 times in total:

<nav aria-label="Footer" className="grid grid-cols-2 gap-x-8 gap-y-8 sm:grid-cols-3 xl:grid-cols-5">

Counting prefixes in the delivered HTML of all 76 pages:

Prefix Uses Pages carrying it Distinct utilities
hover: 5,143 76 10
sm: 1,795 76 48
lg: 802 76 25
md: 347 76 9
motion-reduce: 339 66 2
group-hover: 319 70 1
min-[360px]: 76 76 1
xl: 76 76 1
2xl: 0 0 0

The nine distinct md: utilities across the whole public site are md:block, md:flex, md:gap-8, md:grid-cols-2, md:grid-cols-3, md:hidden, md:order-none, md:table and md:text-sm. That is the complete vocabulary of our 768px breakpoint.

Which widths actually change a page

Class counts are not behaviour. The test that matters is: render the same page at one pixel either side of each boundary and count the elements whose layout-relevant computed styles differ. I drove Chrome through the DevTools protocol, setting the viewport with Emulation.setDeviceMetricsOverride before each load, and compared display, flex-direction, text-align, order, position, visibility, font-size and the number of grid columns for every element in the body.

page                                    elements  359/360  419/420  639/640  767/768  1023/1024  1279/1280  1535/1536
/pricing                                     978        0        0        3       12          5          1          0
/glossary                                    721        0        0        2        8          3          1          0
/guides/how-to-find-youtube-influencers      856        0        0        7        8          3          1          0
/for/agencies                                739        0        0        3        8          3          1          0

Including padding and gap changes adds about four more elements at 640 per page. Nothing else moves.

So on a typical public page of this site, out of 700 to 1,000 elements:

  • 640px restyles two to seven elements. One of them is always the footer nav going from two columns to three.
  • 768px restyles eight to twelve, almost all of them display: a mobile block becoming a table cell, a hidden element appearing.
  • 1024px restyles three to five.
  • 1280px restyles exactly one element on every page, and it is the footer nav again, going from three columns to five. Measured in the browser: 232px 232px 232px becomes 126.398px 126.398px 126.398px 126.398px 126.406px.
  • 1536px restyles nothing. The media query fires (matchMedia("(min-width:96rem)").matches flips to true at exactly 1536), and because the only rule inside it targets an unused class, the page height is identical: 5,208px either side on the home page, 7,068px on the glossary.

That last line is the measurement I wanted. A week ago I checked that our pages render identically at 1280px and at 4K and concluded the design simply stops caring above a certain width. Now I know the mechanism: it stops caring at 1,280px, where one footer gains two columns, and the breakpoint above that is a no-op shipped by the framework's default theme.

The two custom boundaries never fire on a public page at all. min-[420px]:grid-cols-4 is on a stats row behind the login, and min-[360px]:inline-flex is one header button:

<Button asChild className="hidden min-[360px]:inline-flex">

That button is hidden below 360px because it was the one thing that would not fit when I checked the site at 320px. A one-pixel audit found it; a one-rule media query fixed it.

What I take from this

The honest summary is that this site has two breakpoints, not five. 640px handles phone-to-tablet, 768px handles the few places where a table replaces a stack, 1024px handles the sidebar layouts, and the top two exist because they came with the toolkit.

Three changes, in order of how much they are worth:

  1. Delete nothing. The 27 bytes of the 2xl block and the 174 of xl are not a performance problem, and container may be used later. Saying "we audited this and it is fine" is a legitimate outcome, and the audit took an hour.
  2. The nine md: utilities are a vocabulary small enough to write down, so write it down. A responsive scale nobody can recite is a scale nobody can use consistently, and ours fits in one line of a design note.
  3. The footer is the only element on the public site that responds to the top two breakpoints. If I ever want to prove that a layout change is design rather than habit, that is the element to start from.

You can reproduce the whole thing from outside: load the pricing page, the glossary or any guide at 1279px and 1280px, and watch the footer columns. Everything above the footer will be byte-for-byte the same.

title: The IBS effect in ETFs: section 4.4 of 151 Trading Strategies, replicated in Python and R
description:
This is a standalone version of an article first published on quantstr.at. The Python and R code, the data files and the line-by-line walk-through are in the original.

TL;DR

  • Strategy: Section 4.4 of 151 Trading Strategies sorts ETFs by Internal Bar Strength (IBS), where the close sits within the day's range, and bets on mean reversion the next day.
  • What we did: an attempt to replicate Pagonidis (2014), The IBS Effect: Mean Reversion in Equity ETFs, on Yahoo Finance data for 31 of its 33 ETFs (two are no longer available), first over the original window to 5 December 2013 and then on the 13 years since.
  • Result in the original window: the average next-day return after the lowest IBS bucket was 0.353% and after the highest −0.134% (original: 0.350% and −0.126%). A long-short rule earned 30.8% a year per ETF before costs.
  • Since 2013: the gap between the lowest and highest bucket fell from 0.49 to 0.19 percentage points a day. The same rule earned 9.2% before costs and −0.1% after 5 basis points per trade.
  • The book's decile rule: 38.6% a year before costs since 2013, 16.4% at 2 basis points and −10.4% at 5. It turns over its portfolio about 3.5 times a day, so the cost assumption decides the result.

The idea

IBS = (Close − Low) / (High − Low). It is 0 when the close is the low of the day and 1 when it is the high. Pagonidis finds that ETFs that closed near their low tend to rise the next day and those that closed near their high tend to fall.

IBSi​(t)=racPiC​(t)−PiL​(t)PiH​(t)−PiL​(t)

The single-ETF rule goes long when IBS is 0.2 or below and short when it is 0.8 or above, for one day. The book's version ranks the ETFs each day, buys the lowest tenth and sells the highest tenth with equal weights.

Replication: average next-day return by IBS bucket (%)

0 to 0.2 0.2 to 0.4 0.4 to 0.6 0.6 to 0.8 0.8 to 1
Pagonidis (2014), to 5 Dec 2013 0.350 0.096 0.025 −0.032 −0.126
Ours, to 5 Dec 2013 0.353 0.099 0.032 −0.048 −0.134
Ours, after 5 Dec 2013 0.142 0.072 0.025 −0.005 −0.044

Gap between lowest and highest bucket: 0.49 points in the original window (original: 0.476). Probability of a positive next day: 57.2% after the lowest bucket and 46.4% after the highest (original: 56.8% and 46.2%).

The rule, before and after 2013

Average annual return per ETF of the long-short rule (compounded):

After 2013 the effect is positive in 29 of 31 ETFs but weaker, and trading costs matter: at 5 basis points per trade the rule is about break-even.

IBS as a filter for RSI

Pagonidis combines IBS with Cutler's RSI(3): buy below 10, hold while RSI(3) is 40 or below, and in the filtered version hold only while IBS is 0.5 or below. The sum of daily returns without the filter is 121.9% in the original window (original: 119.0%); with the filter 119.4% (original: 128.6%), in about half the days. We reproduce the halving of time invested but not the improvement in return in that window. After 2013 the filter helps: 30.4% against 20.3%.

The book's decile rule

Annual growth rate of the dollar-neutral decile rule, before and after costs:

Cost per unit traded To 5 Dec 2013 After 5 Dec 2013
None 337.9% 38.6%
2 bps 268.3% 16.4%
5 bps 184.1% -10.4%
10 bps 84.1% -42.1%

Break-even cost is roughly 3.9 basis points. Fills at the close are assumed, which is idealised because the final IBS is only known once the close is set.

Limitations

  • Yahoo adjusted prices differ from the vendor in the original, and two ETFs (GXG, RSX) are missing. The ETFs that remain survived to today.
  • This is an attempt to replicate; where choices were not stated (range and volume medians, tie-breaking, the cost model) they are ours and are listed in the original article.
  • No bid-ask spread, market impact or borrow costs in the replication tables. Not investment advice.

Conclusion

The IBS effect reproduces closely in the original window: next-day returns after low-IBS days were 0.49 percentage points higher than after high-IBS days. Since 2013 the gap has narrowed to 0.19, and whether anything is left after trading costs depends on assumptions a backtest cannot settle.

Reference: Pagonidis, A. S. (2014). The IBS Effect: Mean Reversion in Equity ETFs. Working paper, NAAIM. Book: Kakushadze, Z. and Serur, J. A. (2018), 151 Trading Strategies, Section 4.4.

The full article, with the Python and R code: https://quantstr.at/quant-strategies/mean-reversion/?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=syndication

title: A Temporal Algebraic Framework for Data Stream Evaluation Under Delayed Labels and Distribution Shifts
description:
arXiv:2611.21914v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In data streams, labels often arrive late or only for some instances, class prevalence drifts, and rare classes vanish from short windows. Standard evaluation then confuses a degraded decision boundary with a change in prevalence, and is biased when labels are delayed or selected by the model. We extend an algebraic framework that obtains pooled (micro) and per-class (macro) measures from one confusion matrix to streams, weighting the counts in time by exponential fading or a sliding window; the update costs O(m^2) per step, whatever the stream length, and each pooled measure stays a weighted combination of the per-class ones. Delayed and selective feedback enter as an observation mask: until its label arrives, an instance is counted with the model's calibrated class probabilities, and the bias of this interim estimate is driven by their calibration error. Audited conventions report no value for a class without verified instances. We separate prior shift from concept drift by monitoring prior-free coordinates (recall and specificity) and attribute a change in a measure to the two sources with a first-order Jacobian decomposition. On synthetic streams and four real datasets, a detector on these coordinates with a memory per class raises no excess false alarms under label shift, unlike the Jacobian alarm and error-rate detectors. The correction for delayed labels recovers recall in some real settings and is only partial for precision, specificity and F1. Twenty-five statements are checked in Lean 4, and the code is in the aggmetrics package.

title: M$^3$-Test: Coverage Gaps in Joint-Perturbation Testing of Visual Question Answering
description:
arXiv:2611.22329v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A visual question answering (VQA) model can pass every image-only and question-only test yet fail when the same changes occur together. Standard robustness reports average over conditions and therefore cannot say which accepted requests remain vulnerable. We introduce M3-Test, a coverage audit that aligns each clean input with its single-modality variants and a complete 5x5 family, 4x4 strength joint library, so that any reduced test suite can be replayed on the same requests. Across 2.6 million responses from four vision-language models, joint failures affect 26-29% of the Qwen questions that pass all 40 single-modality tests, although fewer than 0.6% of their joint records fail. Passing the 25 maximum-strength corners does not close this gap: 11-14% of the accepted questions still fail elsewhere in the library. Re-executing the archived failures reproduces about 90% of them, against a 0.3-0.6% flip rate among matched passing controls, and re-checking the most fragile failure records supports 80-89% of them. On the evidence examined, neither execution noise nor grading error can fully account for the gap. The same aligned grids make previous evaluations reusable. On held-out images, a risk order learned from other models discovers about 80% of affected Qwen questions within 25 additional queries, compared with 65-68% for maximum-first and 53-57% for pairwise covering arrays. M3-Test thus turns a passing robustness suite into a request-level account of what remains untested, supporting acceptance, regression review and test allocation.

title: SpatialMind: Adaptive Multi-Level Geometric Fusion for Spatial Reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.22415v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) demonstrate promising capabilities in 2D visual understanding, yet remain limited in 3D spatial reasoning. Recent studies explore integrating 3D reconstruction models into MLLMs. However, these approaches either use a single geometric granularity across all tasks or adopt a fixed multi-level fusion scheme, regardless of task-specific reasoning requirements. Through systematic experiments on multi-level geometric fusion, we find that spatial tasks at different cognitive levels (e.g., distance estimation vs. route planning) require geometric representations of different granularities, revealing that fixed fusion cannot accommodate diverse spatial reasoning requirements. To bridge this gap, we propose SpatialMind, a task-adaptive framework for dynamically integrating multi-level geometric representations. SpatialMind employs GeoFus, a multi-layer geometric fusion module built around a gating network jointly conditioned on textual instructions, visual semantics, and geometric representations. This network adaptively modulates the contributions of shallow, intermediate, and deep geometric features across the layers of the LLM decoder. Furthermore, we introduce a negative-entropy regularization loss to mitigate gate collapse. Gate visualizations indicate that GeoFus adapts geometric granularity to task requirements. Experiments demonstrate that SpatialMind achieves competitive performance across spatial benchmarks, attaining a state-of-the-art score of 72.3 on VSI-Bench. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/zhaosb-star/SpatialMind.

title: Eight in Ten LLMs Leak System-Prompt Secrets: Nevan, an Agentic Capture-the-Flag Study
description:
arXiv:2611.21956v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: We audit instruction-hierarchy enforcement across 363 text-in/text-out models from the OpenRouter catalog. The research question we answer with this experiment is which models disclose a protected secret embedded in the system prompt, and through which techniques. Each model guards a secret 16-character flag set in its system prompt, while an artificial intelligence (AI) agent (OpenCode, powered by DeepSeek V4.1 Flash), steered by a human researcher, tries to persuade it to emit the flag. The flag was exfiltrated from 296 of the 363 models, plus four models released after the initial catalog freeze, for 300 captures in total. Of these, 170 involved a non-English language pivot, most often French. Each capture shows that a model ranked a user request above its system instruction at least once. It does not show that the model provably resists untested attacks, nor that it would consistently leak semantically sensitive data, nor that it is vulnerable to harmful-content jailbreaks. For practitioners, we draw three lessons: do not store secrets in system prompts, enforce critical behavior outside the model with output validation and deterministic checks, and do not let a large language model (LLM) judge be the sole decider of consequential outcomes.

title: I Built an AI Loop That Finds "Lost My Work" Bugs and Fixes Them Until the Test Passes
description:
We've all done it. You fill in a long sign-up form, a job application, or a checkout, press Back or Refresh, and everything you typed is gone. These "lost my work" bugs are everywhere, and unit tests rarely catch them because they only show up in a real browser.

For the KaneCLI Online Hackathon by TestMu AI, I built StillHere: a loop that catches these bugs in a real browser and keeps fixing them until the test passes.

What it does

StillHere runs a closed loop:

  1. Find it. Kane CLI drives a real Chrome session through a journey described in plain English: fill in a checkout, open another page, press Back, press Refresh, and check the cart, details, and current step are still there.
  2. Fix it. If anything is wiped, Kane's failure report becomes a repair prompt for the Codex coding agent, which fixes the app without weakening the test.
  3. Prove it. The exact same Kane objective re-runs, unchanged, until it passes.

It works for any form or multi-step flow via --objective, not just checkout.

How I built it

Node.js with no dependencies. StillHere calls Kane CLI with --agent, parses its NDJSON result, writes a failure report with evidence and screenshots, and pipes a repair prompt to codex exec. A sample shop with a real Back/Refresh bug is included, and npm run demo:loop resets the bug so you always see fail, fix, pass. Built solo with Codex.

What Kane caught

In the recorded run, pressing "Back to checkout" wiped the order: the cart, the customer's details, and the review step were all gone. Codex fixed it by saving state in sessionStorage plus browser history and restoring it on load and Back. Kane then passed through both Back and Refresh. The test was never changed to make it pass.

Challenges

Chrome crashed when launched from a sandbox, so Kane runs from a normal terminal. Long Kane runs timed out, so the default timeout became 300 seconds. I also made sure a run with no final Kane result counts as incomplete, not as a failure for the agent to "fix."

What I learned

Verifying in a real browser catches bugs a mock never would, and keeping the test fixed is what makes an AI fix trustworthy.

What's next

A GitHub Action that runs the loop on every pull request, plus ready-made objectives for sign-up, login, and multi-step forms.

Try it

  • Code and setup: https://github.com/Mzee04/stillhere
  • Demo: https://youtu.be/4R3yvR5oKvg

What "lost my work" bugs have you run into?

title: Argon gc and restore now emit JSON
description:
Four argon commands printed only text, so a script could not read their result: argon gc and the three argon restore subcommands, preview, reset, and branch. A human could read the output, but nothing else could. The fix in argon-lab/argon#99 registers all four in the shared -o/--output list, so they take -o json like the rest of the CLI, and documents the shape of what they emit.

What changed

cli/cmd/output.go gains gcCmd, restorePreviewCmd, restoreResetCmd, and restoreBranchCmd in the shared output list. That single registration is what makes -o json available on all four.

The JSON bodies are built by small functions, gcReportJSON, restorePreviewJSON, restoreResetJSON, and restoreBranchJSON, so their shape is testable without a live project or WAL. That matters here because gc and restore need a real project to exercise end to end.

The shapes:

  • gc emits dry_run, branches (each branch name plus its cutoffs map), and entries_removed. Branches with no cutoffs are omitted, and branches is an empty list rather than null when nothing is reclaimable.
  • restore preview emits branch, current_lsn, target_lsn, operations_to_discard, and affected_collections, which is an object, empty rather than null.
  • restore reset emits branch, target_lsn, and backup_branch only when a backup branch was created.
  • restore branch emits the new branch name and the LSN it was forked at.

Why the registration test exists

A shape test alone would not catch the real defect. The PR includes TestGCAndRestoreAcceptJSONOutput, which fails before the change with gc has no --output flag and the same for the three restore subcommands. The shape tests, TestGCReportJSONShape and TestRestoreJSONShapes, pass on their own because they call the builder functions directly. Only the registration test proves the flag is wired to the command. The PR runs both, plus the whole ./cmd/ package.

Verification from the PR 

$ cd cli && go build ./...          # ok
$ go test ./cmd/ -run 'TestGCReportJSONShape|TestRestoreJSONShapes|TestGCAndRestoreAcceptJSONOutput' -v
=== RUN   TestGCAndRestoreAcceptJSONOutput
--- PASS: TestGCAndRestoreAcceptJSONOutput (0.00s)
=== RUN   TestGCReportJSONShape
--- PASS: TestGCReportJSONShape (0.00s)
=== RUN   TestRestoreJSONShapes
--- PASS: TestRestoreJSONShapes (0.00s)
PASS
ok      argon-cli/cmd   0.012s
$ go test ./cmd/                    # whole package, existing tests included
ok      argon-cli/cmd   5.562s

gofmt -l cmd/ prints nothing and go vet on the package is clean. The repository build was run inside the nested cli module, which is where these commands live. The change is 6 files, 195 lines added and 1 removed, and it closes issue #75.

Why this matters this week

The week's trending projects are dominated by coding agents and the tooling around them: GitHub Trending lists agent skill bundles, MCP servers, and workflow orchestrators, and dev.to's trending clusters include AI coding agents and the risks of agents reading untrusted input. The honest link is narrow. An agent that drives a CLI cannot parse prose, so a command that only prints text is opaque to it. This PR makes gc and restore readable by a script or agent, with named fields instead of scraped sentences. That is the whole change, and it is enough.

Sources checked on 18 November 2026: trendshift.io/weekly, github.com/trending, and dev.to/trending.

The rule to carry

When a command already has a shared output mechanism, add new subcommands to it instead of inventing a second flag. Then split the work into two tests: one that calls the builder and checks the shape, and one that checks the flag is registered on the command. The first proves the data is right, the second proves a user can actually ask for it. Fixing only one leaves either a correct shape nobody can request, or a flag that emits nothing.

The diagram for this piece is short. Four commands on the left, the fields they now emit on the right:

Four commands, one shared output flag, documented fields instead of prose.

title: RPMem: Learning Long-Term Recurrent Parametric Memory Across Sessions for LLM Agents
description:
arXiv:2609.23466v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Long-running LLM agents require memory that persists and evolves across sessions. Text-based memory retrieves and reconstructs past interactions at every query, making long-horizon performance increasingly dependent on retrieval quality and contextual reasoning as histories grow. Parametric memory encodes experience directly into model computation, but existing approaches provide limited support for cross-session memory evolution. Their coupling to a specific backbone further restricts memory reuse after model replacement. We introduce RPMem, a two-stage architecture that compiles each session into a model-independent latent memory through forward computation and selectively integrates it with retained memory via a task-trained recurrent gate. The consolidated memory is then mapped to backbone-specific low-rank adaptation (LoRA) parameters, allowing the encoding capability to transfer when the backbone is replaced. Evaluation across three long-term memory benchmarks and five diverse backbones demonstrates broad generalization with near-constant update cost and memory footprint. With Qwen3-8B on PERMA, RPMem reaches 85.52%, outperforming the strongest parametric and text-based baselines by 5.32 and 12.98 percentage points, respectively. Ablations validate the complementary roles of session compilation and cross-session consolidation, while dynamics analyses reveal that the gate acquires task-specific memory integration strategies. These results establish RPMem as a lifecycle-independent parametric memory framework that maintains evolving cross-session memory that remains reusable across backbone replacements. Our code is available at https://github.com/Quark-Medical/rpmem/tree/main.

title: From syllable representation via gesture generation to articulation: A spiking neural model
description:
arXiv:2611.22499v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Speech production requires a transformation from phonological representations into coordinated vocal-tract movements. This paper presents a spiking neural sensorimotor model within the Neural Engineering Framework and Semantic Pointer Architecture. Each syllable occurrence has a neural oscillator whose evolving phase coordinates its gestures and initiates the next syllable. Phase-dependent commands recruit separate neural populations for vocalic, oral-constriction, velopharyngeal, and glottal actions (gestures). Neural ramp integrators shape the rise and fall of gesture activation. Together with articulatory targets, these trajectories determine the extent and time course of articulatory movements. Opponent neural populations provide control signals to a geometric articulatory model.
  Thirty reference recordings cover an input corpus of eight lexical words, an alternative realization of one word, a syllable sequence, and isolated syllables. Two additional paired simulation subcorpora of sixty runs each, covering two words and one syllable sequence, assess activation reliability across neural realizations. Adjusting gesture command amplitudes increased successful realizations from 57/60 to 60/60 under the specified criteria, with ramp rate factors held constant.
  The model demonstrates how neural oscillator and ramp dynamics generate articulatory timing under specified phasing rules. It complements a preceding mental-lexicon model through an ordered syllable interface. Continuous online execution across all components and connection to the acoustic extension remain further integration steps. Accessible code and synchronized visualization support inspection of the neural activation trajectories and resulting vocal-tract movements.

title: Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938): is your Java server affected?
description:
Java4Shell is the nickname for CVE-2026-114938, a memory-corruption bug in the Base64 decoder that OpenJDK uses on x86-64 machines with AVX-512 VBMI. The security group Calif says a 65-character string, 64 letter A's followed by an equals sign, makes the decoder write 62 bytes past the end of a 50-byte array. OpenJDK and Oracle published fixes on November 17. If you run Java 17 or newer, the question is whether any of your servers can reach the broken code path, and that takes about four checks.

TL;DR

  • Calif reports that OpenJDK's AVX-512 Base64 decoder writes 64 bytes into a 50-byte array for a 65-character padded input, so 62 bytes land past the end. Java rejects the input afterwards, which is too late.
  • Scope: OpenJDK 17.0.6 and newer on x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 VBMI (Intel Ice Lake or later, AMD Zen 4 or later). ARM64 is not affected. Standard Java 8 and 11 are not on this CVE.
  • OpenJDK and Oracle list it at CVSS 3.1 8.1; Calif scores it 9.2 on CVSS 4.0. Fixed builds exist from Oracle and Amazon Corretto, and Temurin is releasing as testing finishes.
  • Calif says it reached code execution in eleven products. Those are Calif's own tests, the recipes are withheld, and Calif says there is no universal exploit.
  • The mitigation that works everywhere is -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics. When I checked on November 18, the CVE was not on CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list.

What is Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938)?

Base64 packs three bytes into four text characters. It shows up in login headers, file uploads and network messages, so almost every Java server decodes it somewhere. To decode it faster, HotSpot, the JVM inside OpenJDK, can swap in a hand-written assembly routine once a decode call site has been compiled by C2, the optimizing JIT compiler. The routine uses AVX-512 VBMI instructions to process 64 bytes at a time.

Calif, a security research group, found the bug in that routine. Its write-up credits Quang Luong, who says he told the Codex coding agent to audit the JIT compiler, intrinsics, widely used APIs and cryptography. Most of what came back was junk, he says, and then it flagged the Base64 decoder. Calif says it took one hour to find the bug and two more hours to build the first working exploit, for under $200 in tokens. I have not verified any of that; it is Calif's account. Calif is also the team behind PHP2Shell, which I covered on October 22.

How does the Base64 overflow work?

Take the published trigger: 64 letter A's followed by one equals sign.

AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA=

(On older OpenJDK 17 builds Calif says the trigger is 128 A's plus the equals sign.) Sixty-four A's decode to 48 bytes. With the padding character, Java reserves a 50-byte result array for the 65-character input. The assembly handles the final tail with one 64-byte store and a mask that says which bytes to write. Calif's pseudocode shows where it goes wrong:

output_len := (input_length / 4) * 3
if input[input_length - 1] == '=':
    output_len -= 1
output_mask := bzhiq(-1, output_len)

For a one-character tail the first line gives zero, the padding branch subtracts one, and the length becomes minus one. The mask instruction bzhiq does not clip an index of 64 or more, so the mask comes out as all ones and the store writes all 64 bytes. The store starts at offset 48 of a 50-byte array, so 62 bytes land past the end, on whatever object the allocator placed next door. Only then does Java notice the input is malformed and throw IllegalArgumentException. The error is correct and it is late.

The fix in public OpenJDK is small. The November security branch (pull request 33936, CSPU26_11) contains a four line change in stubGenerator_x86_64.cpp, committed under the title "Base64 optimization improvements". It adds a check that sends padded tails shorter than four characters to the Java code instead:

+    // A padded Base64 tail shorter than one complete block is handled by Java.
+    __ cmpl(length, 4);
+    __ jcc(Assembler::less, L_bruteForce);

OpenJDK's advisory does not name this commit; I tie it to the CVE by its place in the security branch and by how well it matches Calif's description.

From a fixed spill to code execution: what Calif claims

The spill is mostly a constant pattern, and only its landing position is controllable. Calif says it aims the spill at the length field of a neighboring array, which turns the fixed write into a bounded, chosen-value write. A second array whose length is corrupted and whose data is copied into the response becomes a heap read, which Calif compares to Heartbleed. From there Calif describes warming up the decoder until the JIT selects the fast path, an optional rehearsal round, the trigger, disclosure, repair of damaged objects and an application-specific final step.

Calif says its initial testing reached code execution in default configurations of Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate without a login, and in Kafka brokers, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker after one. It also lists sample Struts and Spring Boot applications, and a client-side route in which a Java program opens a TLS connection to a malicious server. These are Calif's own results. The product recipes stay private until people have had time to patch, and I found no product advisory in the vendor pages I checked that confirms them.

Calif is open about the limits. There is no universal exploit; every target needs its own profile: a route to the decoder, a live writer, a way to read the result back, a heap layout and an application action. The attack is sensitive to network jitter, and Calif says it rented a server in the same cloud region as its target to reduce it. Some chains need request streaming, so a proxy that buffers the whole request body, such as nginx by default, removes their timing. Calif adds that this is not a general mitigation: Elasticsearch runs from a single complete request, so buffering does not stop that chain.

What is confirmed, and by whom?

  • Vendors. OpenJDK's advisory dated November 17 lists CVE-2026-114938 under hotspot/compiler at CVSS 3.1 8.1, affecting 17, 21, 25 and 27. Oracle's November Critical Security Patch Update lists the same score and credits Quang Luong of Calif.io. Oracle JDK 17.0.21.1 has a release date of November 17.
  • Distributions. Amazon's Linux Security Center shows Corretto 17, 21 and 25 packages as fixed on November 17. Adoptium says Temurin builds with the fix are being published as testing completes. Red Hat's bulletin says it is expediting fixes and that JVMs on ARM64, or on x86-64 CPUs without AVX-512 VBMI, are not known to be affected.
  • Government. CISA's alert of November 17 urges immediate patching and suggests validating Base64 input at the application boundary and limiting unauthenticated access as temporary controls.
  • Exploitation. The CVE was not in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog (version 2026.11.17) when I checked on November 18. That says nothing about the future. The security firm Hadrian says it crashed Spring Security and Tomcat login checks on a Temurin 17 build in a lab, and reached code execution in a lab service that decodes request bodies; that is Hadrian's claim, and it says reliable code execution is very hard to reproduce.

Which of your servers can run the broken code?

Four conditions have to line up for a JVM to be in scope.

  1. An x86-64 chip with AVX-512 VBMI. Calif names Intel Ice Lake, Sapphire Rapids, Emerald Rapids and Granite Rapids, and AMD Zen 4 or newer. On Linux, Calif's check prints the relevant CPU flags: 
grep -m1 '^flags' /proc/cpuinfo | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -E '^(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)$'

All four flags must appear. A virtual machine sees the CPU features its hypervisor exposes, so run the check inside the guest that runs the JVM.

  1. A Java build in range. OpenJDK 17.0.6 and newer, which means Corretto, Temurin, Microsoft, Zulu, Liberica, SapMachine, Red Hat OpenJDK and Oracle builds that have not yet taken the fix. Standard Java 8 and 11 are not on this CVE; Oracle also lists its Java 8 performance build.
  2. A warmed-up decoder. The C2 compiler selects the routine only after the Base64 call site has been compiled, so a freshly started JVM is still on the Java implementation. Semgrep's detection README says AWS Lambda's Java bootstrap limits the JIT in a way that keeps the intrinsic unused by default; I have not verified that myself, so read it before relying on it.
  3. Input an attacker can reach. The vulnerable decoder has to receive attacker-controlled data, through an authentication header, an upload, a token or a message.

If any of the four is missing, the JVM is out of scope for this bug. You should still update, because the checks above depend on hardware that cloud providers and migrations change.

How do I fix or mitigate Java4Shell?

Option Works on Notes
Update to the fixed build for your Java line everything Oracle JDK 17.0.21.1 shipped on November 17; check your vendor for the matching Corretto, Temurin or distribution build
-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics every architecture disables the hardware Base64 routine; Aikido notes that programs decoding a lot of Base64 may run slower
-XX:UseAVX=2 x86-64 only disables AVX-512; OpenJDK on ARM does not recognize the flag and will fail to start
Rebuild container images containers patching the host leaves the JDK inside an old image as it was

Calif and Adoptium both recommend -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics as the interim control.

What Calif says we should delete

Calif's closing argument is that the fast decoder helps programs that decode enormous amounts of Base64, while everyone else carried the assembly too. It calls the cleanup vibe-uncoding, and the phrase is theirs; Calif notes that an apparently unused feature can have hidden dependencies.

Verdict: SHIP IT

I stamped the patch SHIP IT. It is small, public and already built by the main vendors, and the one flag works everywhere. Calif's code execution claims stay Calif's until someone else shows them, so update without panic and check which machines are actually in scope.

FAQ

Is Java4Shell exploited in the wild?

I found no source saying so. CISA urged patching, and the CVE was not on its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list when I checked on November 18.

Does Java4Shell affect ARM and Graviton servers?

Calif, Red Hat and Amazon say ARM64 is not affected, because the vulnerable routine is x86-64 AVX-512 code. Do not set -XX:UseAVX=2 on ARM; the JVM will refuse to start.

Does it affect Java 8 and Java 11?

OpenJDK's advisory marks Java 17, 21, 25 and 27. Red Hat and Adoptium say Java 8 and 11 are not affected. Oracle separately lists its Java 8 performance build.

Is the 65-character string enough to take over a server?

Calif says the string only causes the overwrite. Turning it into code execution needed a separate, bespoke recipe for each product, which Calif has not published.
