title: My Dashboard Synced Itself Only While You Watched. Background Tabs Broke That.
description:
VoiceDash is the client portal I build for voice AI agencies: each agency's clients log in and see their own agent's calls, transcripts and analytics. For a long time those calls arrived two ways. Retell pushed them by webhook, and there was a "Sync Calls" button for everything the webhook missed.

The button was the problem. Nobody presses a sync button on a dashboard they opened to read numbers. So I wrote a small React hook that syncs on its own, shipped it, and less than an hour later shipped a fix for a case I had not thought about: a tab you have not looked at yet.

This is that hook, the one-line bug, and the parts I still have not fixed.

What the hook does

Two client pages show calls: the conversation list and the analytics dashboard. Both now call the same hook with the agent's ID and a callback that reloads the page's data.

const SYNC_EVERY_MS = 60_000;
/** Returning to the tab syncs again unless the last sync was this recent. */
const MIN_GAP_ON_RETURN_MS = 15_000;

export function useCallSync(agentId: string | undefined, onSynced: () => void) {
  const onSyncedRef = useRef(onSynced);
  onSyncedRef.current = onSynced;

  useEffect(() => {
    if (!agentId) return;
    let stopped = false;
    let running = false;
    let lastRun = 0;
    // sync(), onVisibilityChange(), the timer and the cleanup go here
  }, [agentId]);
}

Three triggers: when the page opens, when the tab comes back into view (unless it synced in the last 15 seconds), and every minute while the tab is visible. The callback lives in a ref so the effect does not tear down and restart its timer every time the parent re-renders with a new arrow function. The effect depends only on agentId.

The running flag stops a slow sync from overlapping with the next tick. stopped stops a sync that finishes after the user navigated away from calling back into an unmounted page.

Why "only while visible"

The server route behind the hook calls Retell's list-calls API with the agent's key. A dashboard left open in a forgotten tab for a weekend should not call a vendor API 2,880 times for nobody. So the first version guarded every sync the same way:

const sync = async () => {
  if (running || document.visibilityState !== "visible") return;
  // ...
};

sync();
const timer = setInterval(sync, SYNC_EVERY_MS);

That reads fine. It is also wrong for one case that showed up almost immediately.

The background tab

Open a dashboard with a middle click. Or restore a browser session with five portal tabs. The page loads, renders the calls already in the database, and its visibilityState is "hidden". The opening sync returns early.

Nothing is broken yet. The moment you switch to that tab, visibilitychange fires and the hook syncs. But between load and switch, the page shows stale data while looking finished, and the dashboard's whole promise was "you never press Sync".

The fix was to treat the opening sync differently from the repeat:

const sync = async ({ evenIfHidden = false } = {}) => {
  if (running || (!evenIfHidden && document.visibilityState !== "visible")) return;
  running = true;
  lastRun = Date.now();
  try {
    await fetch("/api/retell/sync-calls", {
      method: "POST",
      headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
      body: JSON.stringify({ agentId }),
    });
  } catch {
    // Calls that arrived by webhook still show; the next sync retries.
  } finally {
    running = false;
  }
  if (!stopped) onSyncedRef.current();
};

sync({ evenIfHidden: true });
const timer = setInterval(() => sync(), SYNC_EVERY_MS);

Note the () => sync() in setInterval. Passing sync directly would still work here because setInterval calls it with no arguments, but the wrapper makes it obvious that the repeat never gets evenIfHidden.

The rule I took from it: a page someone opened is a request, even if they are not looking at it yet. A timer someone forgot about is not. Those deserve different guards, and I had written one guard for both.

Refreshing without flicker

Syncing is half of it. After a sync the page has to show the result without becoming a loading skeleton every minute.

On analytics, the fetch takes a quiet flag that skips the loading placeholders, plus a request counter so an old response cannot overwrite a newer date range the user picked meanwhile:

const fetchData = async (quiet = false) => {
  const request = ++latestRequest.current;
  if (!quiet) setLoading(true);
  // ... fetch /api/analytics
  if (res.ok && request === latestRequest.current) setData(await res.json());
};

useCallSync(agentId, () => fetchData(true));

The conversation list was harder because the user might have scrolled through three pages and opened a transcript. Replacing the list would throw that away. So the refresh fetches the newest page and merges: unseen calls go on top, calls already shown get their fields updated (a call stored mid-call gets its final duration and transcript later), and the list is re-sorted by start time. If the search box changed while the request was in flight, the result belongs to a different list and is dropped.

What makes it safe to call this often

The client side is the easy part. The reason a once-a-minute sync is cheap lives on the server, and I covered most of it in A Webhook Tells You Something Happened, Not That You Have Everything. The short version:

  • Each agent stores callsSyncedUntil, how far its Retell history is known to be complete. A routine sync reads oldest first from two hours before that point, so it is usually a single request.
  • The watermark only moves forward. The update is conditional (callsSyncedUntil: null or lt: until), so two syncs of the same agent racing each other cannot move it backward.
  • Inserts use createMany with skipDuplicates against a unique key on (agentId, platformCallId). Two tabs syncing the same agent at the same second store each call once.
  • The route spends at most 25 seconds answering, then hands whatever is left of a long history to Next.js after() with a bigger budget and a resume cursor.

Without those four, a polling hook on the client would be a load generator. With them, the hook is mostly a trigger.

What I have not fixed

Honest list, from reading the code again for this post. None of these have shipped.

The hook ignores the response status. fetch only rejects on network failure. If the route returns 502 because Retell is down, or 400 because the key was removed, the hook treats it as a finished sync, calls onSynced, and tries again in a minute. No backoff, and nothing on screen says the numbers are no longer being refreshed. The page just quietly stops changing. I would rather show a small "last synced 14 minutes ago" line than have someone trust a frozen dashboard.

Every visible tab polls on its own. running is per hook instance. Two tabs on the same agent's analytics, both visible on two monitors, make two sync requests a minute. The server makes that safe, not free. A BroadcastChannel so one tab syncs and the others just refresh would fix it. I have not needed it badly enough yet.

The list merge only looks at the newest page. If a sync backfills calls from last month (a gap left by a broken webhook, say), they land in the database but not in a list you already scrolled, because the merge only fetches the first 50. They appear on the next full load. Rare, but it is exactly the case the backfill exists for.

A first sync can hold the request for 25 seconds. For an agent with no watermark, the opening sync reads Retell history up to the route's budget before answering. The page is usable the whole time, but the "new calls appear" moment can lag on a freshly connected agent.

What I would tell myself before writing it

Polling from the browser is a reasonable choice when the server work is idempotent and incremental. Most of my effort went there, not into the hook, and that was the right split.

The hook itself needed exactly one more distinction than I gave it: who asked for this sync? The page opening, the user coming back, or a timer. Each one deserves its own guard, and collapsing them into a single visibilityState check cost me a release.

If you build portals for voice agents, this is part of what goes into VoiceDash. And if you have solved the "one tab syncs, the rest listen" problem in production, I would like to know whether BroadcastChannel held up or whether you ended up with locks in localStorage.

title: SOTA or Luck? The Winner's Curse in LLM Leaderboards
description:
arXiv:2611.22227v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Public LLM leaderboards guide model evaluation and adoption, yet the reported performance of top-ranked models can be systematically overstated. This leaderboard winner's curse arises because ranking noisy benchmark scores rewards sampling luck alongside genuine ability. The same selection effect can distort scores throughout the leaderboard, a phenomenon we call the rank-induced bias. We develop an $m$-out-of-$N$ bootstrap to correct for this bias. It assumes a fixed model pool with independent, identically distributed bounded tasks while allowing arbitrary within-task correlation among models. Under exact population tiers separated by positive gaps, we prove that the bootstrap reduces $\Theta(N^{-1/2})$ ranking bias to expected residual bias $o(N^{-1/2})$. Across 14 benchmarks from 5 benchmark families, the rank-1 adjustments range from approximately 0.09 to 3.86 percentage points. In our SWE-bench Verified snapshot, the tied leaders receive an adjustment of 0.90 percentage points. Such overstatement is large enough to make the apparent winner statistically fragile. Thus, we use the same bootstrap to further quantify the intervals of plausible rank positions for each model and group models into tiers. We establish sufficient conditions for consistent recovery of population tiers. On SWE-bench Verified, this procedure places 13 of 173 models in the leading tier. We combine the score adjustment and rank intervals in the Rank Uncertainty and Leaderboard Evaluation Report (RULER). We validate its finite-sample performance using sample splitting and calibrated simulations, and advocate publishing RULER alongside raw rankings so readers can assess both reported performance and the precision of the ordering. RULER also provides guidance for benchmark design that accounts for selection effects and ranking uncertainty.

title: Distributional Alignment as a Criterion for Designing Task Vectors in In-Context Learning
description:
arXiv:2605.20730v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: In-context learning (ICL) allows large language models (LLMs) to adapt to new tasks through demonstrations, yet it suffers from escalating inference costs as context length increases. While task vectors offer a promising alternative by compressing demonstrations into compact hidden-state representations, their quality has been evaluated only through downstream task accuracy. This indirect criterion provides limited insight into how to design more effective task vector extraction methods. In this paper, we posit that inference using task vectors should align their predictive distribution with that of ICL. To quantify this, we introduce $d_{\text{NTP}}$, a metric that measures the discrepancy in next-token probabilities between task vector-based and ICL-based inference. Our empirical analysis reveals that $d_{\text{NTP}}$ serves as a performance proxy, exhibiting a strong negative correlation with downstream accuracy. Motivated by this, we develop Linear Task Vector (LTV), a method designed to minimize $d_{\text{NTP}}$ via a closed-form linear mapping that estimates demonstration effects through regression. Across eight classification benchmarks and five LLMs, LTV consistently outperforms existing task vector baselines, improving average accuracy by 9.2\% while reducing inference latency. We further show that LTV outperforms the baselines on regression tasks. Moreover, we investigate the transferability of LTV across different model scales; an aspect that has remained nascent in task vector research. Specifically, we empirically show that task vectors from a larger model can enhance a smaller model's performance by 6.4\%, suggesting a new utility for extracted task representations.

title: Protección y Recuperación de Datos NoSQL: Backups Automatizados con MongoDB Atlas, GitHub Actions y Render Copiar
description:
Introducción

En el desarrollo de sistemas informáticos, almacenar información correctamente es fundamental. Sin embargo, existe un aspecto igual de importante que muchas veces pasa desapercibido: ¿qué sucede cuando los datos se pierden, se eliminan accidentalmente o la base de datos presenta un problema?

Una aplicación puede funcionar perfectamente y, aun así, estar expuesta a pérdidas de información si no dispone de una estrategia adecuada de respaldo y recuperación.

Como parte del curso de Base de Datos II de la Universidad Privada de Tacna, desarrollamos en equipo una aplicación web que utiliza MongoDB Atlas como base de datos NoSQL y que incorpora mecanismos automatizados para generar, verificar y recuperar copias de seguridad.

Para completar la solución, integramos GitHub Actions como herramienta de automatización y Render como plataforma de despliegue.

En este artículo presentaré cómo organizamos nuestra solución, las tecnologías utilizadas, el funcionamiento de los respaldos y los aprendizajes obtenidos durante su implementación.

Enlaces del proyecto

  • Repositorio público: https://github.com/saulalvarado1/NoSQL-Backup-Strategy
  • Aplicación desplegada: https://nosql-backup-strategy-d819.onrender.com
  • Base de datos: MongoDB Atlas.
  • Automatización: GitHub Actions.
  • Despliegue: Render.

1. La importancia de proteger los datos en una aplicación NoSQL

Cuando una aplicación utiliza una base de datos alojada en la nube, es posible pensar que la información está completamente protegida gracias a la infraestructura del proveedor.

Sin embargo, disponer de un sistema de replicación no significa necesariamente contar con una copia de seguridad independiente.

Por ejemplo, si un administrador elimina accidentalmente los documentos de una colección, esa operación puede propagarse a las réplicas de la base de datos.

Por esta razón, es necesario implementar mecanismos que permitan recuperar información almacenada en un momento anterior.

Durante nuestro proyecto trabajamos con tres conceptos fundamentales:

Respaldo (Backup): consiste en generar una copia de los datos que pueda utilizarse posteriormente.

Restauración (Restore): permite recuperar la información desde un respaldo previamente generado.

Recuperación ante desastres: comprende los procedimientos necesarios para restablecer la información y los servicios después de un incidente.

Nuestro objetivo fue integrar estos mecanismos en una aplicación funcional y demostrar que es posible automatizar procesos de recuperación utilizando herramientas de desarrollo modernas.

2. Descripción de la aplicación desarrollada

Para implementar y demostrar nuestra estrategia construimos una aplicación web que representa una pequeña tienda.

El sistema utiliza Node.js y Express para gestionar las solicitudes HTTP y MongoDB Atlas como servicio de almacenamiento documental.

La aplicación permite registrar productos, consultar sus datos, eliminarlos y administrar determinados procesos de respaldo.

Principales funcionalidades

  • Registro de productos con nombre, precio y cantidad disponible.
  • Visualización de los productos almacenados.
  • Eliminación de registros.
  • Comunicación con MongoDB Atlas.
  • Generación de respaldos desde una interfaz administrativa.
  • Consulta de información sobre los respaldos generados.
  • Verificación del estado de conexión con la base de datos.

Para el manejo de los respaldos, la aplicación incorpora operaciones protegidas mediante un token de administrador, evitando que cualquier solicitud pueda acceder directamente a esas funciones.

La interfaz web sirve como demostración práctica del funcionamiento de la base de datos y de los procedimientos de protección implementados.

3. Tecnologías y arquitectura del sistema

Seleccionamos un conjunto de tecnologías que nos permitiera integrar desarrollo web, almacenamiento NoSQL, automatización y despliegue continuo.

Tecnología Función
MongoDB Atlas Almacenamiento de documentos NoSQL
Node.js Ejecución del código JavaScript del servidor
Express Desarrollo de la API web
Docker Empaquetado de la aplicación
GitHub Control de versiones
GitHub Actions Pruebas, backups y automatización
Render Publicación de la aplicación
OpenSSL Cifrado de los archivos de respaldo

¿Cómo se relacionan estos componentes?

Cuando un usuario accede a la aplicación, Render entrega la interfaz y ejecuta el servidor Express.

El servidor establece una conexión con MongoDB Atlas para realizar operaciones sobre las colecciones.

De manera independiente, GitHub Actions ejecuta procesos programados para generar respaldos, probar su restauración y almacenar los archivos resultantes como artefactos.

Esta separación es importante porque la aplicación y el sistema de respaldos no dependen del mismo proceso de ejecución.

Además, utilizamos Docker para facilitar la configuración y reproducción del entorno de desarrollo.

4. Diseño de nuestra estrategia de respaldo

Uno de los primeros pasos fue establecer qué características debía cumplir el mecanismo de protección.

Decidimos implementar un sistema de respaldo lógico automatizado, en el que los documentos de MongoDB se exportan a archivos que pueden almacenarse y recuperarse posteriormente.

Esta decisión estuvo relacionada con el uso del clúster gratuito M0 de MongoDB Atlas, que no proporciona las mismas funciones de backup administrado disponibles en determinadas modalidades de pago.

Objetivos de recuperación

Para organizar nuestra estrategia consideramos dos indicadores:

RPO (Recovery Point Objective):

Representa la cantidad máxima de datos recientes que estamos dispuestos a perder ante un incidente.

Establecimos como objetivo un RPO de 24 horas, mediante la programación de un respaldo diario.

RTO (Recovery Time Objective):

Representa el tiempo máximo esperado para recuperar el servicio después de una interrupción.

Nuestro objetivo de diseño fue realizar una recuperación en menos de cinco minutos para el conjunto reducido de datos de demostración.

Estos valores representan metas del proyecto. Su cumplimiento real depende de factores como la ejecución del respaldo, la disponibilidad de los archivos y el tiempo efectivo de restauración.

Aplicación del principio 3-2-1

También tomamos como referencia la conocida estrategia 3-2-1, que propone mantener varias copias de los datos, utilizar medios de almacenamiento diferentes y conservar al menos una copia fuera del entorno principal.

En nuestra solución, la información original reside en MongoDB Atlas, mientras que los respaldos automatizados se almacenan como artefactos de GitHub Actions.

Estos artefactos también pueden descargarse y conservarse en otro almacenamiento para completar una estrategia con una tercera copia independiente.

De esta manera, evitamos depender exclusivamente del proveedor que aloja la base de datos.

5. Implementación del respaldo lógico

El componente principal de la estrategia se encuentra en el archivo:

src/backup-lib.js

Este módulo contiene la lógica utilizada para crear respaldos, restaurar documentos, calcular verificaciones de integridad y administrar la retención.

¿Por qué utilizamos Extended JSON?

MongoDB trabaja con tipos BSON que no siempre pueden conservarse correctamente utilizando una conversión tradicional a JSON.

Por ejemplo, existen tipos como:

  • ObjectId: identificadores de documentos.
  • Date: valores de fecha.
  • Decimal128: números decimales de alta precisión.

Para preservar estos tipos utilizamos Extended JSON (EJSON) en su representación canónica.

Un fragmento del código implementado es:

async function* lineas() {
  for await (const doc of cursor) {
    documentos++;
    yield EJSON.stringify(doc, {
      relaxed: false
    }) + '\n';
  }
}

Este procedimiento recorre los documentos de una colección y los transforma a EJSON.

Posteriormente, la información se comprime utilizando gzip:

await pipeline(
  Readable.from(lineas()),
  zlib.createGzip(),
  fs.createWriteStream(archivo)
);

El resultado es un archivo comprimido con extensión .jsonl.gz por cada colección.

Esta implementación permite procesar los documentos mediante flujos de datos, evitando cargar toda la colección simultáneamente en memoria.

6. Integridad de los archivos y metadatos

Crear archivos de respaldo no es suficiente. También necesitamos comprobar que la información pueda recuperarse correctamente.

Para solucionar este problema, implementamos verificaciones mediante SHA-256, un algoritmo criptográfico que permite calcular una huella digital de los archivos.

Cada respaldo incorpora un archivo llamado:

metadata.json

Este archivo registra información como la identificación del respaldo, el nombre de la base de datos, las colecciones exportadas, la cantidad de documentos, los índices y sus respectivos checksums.

¿Para qué sirve el checksum?

Supongamos que un archivo de respaldo se modifica accidentalmente o sufre una corrupción durante su almacenamiento.

Cuando intentamos restaurarlo, el sistema vuelve a calcular su hash SHA-256 y lo compara con el valor registrado originalmente.

Si ambos valores son diferentes, el archivo se considera alterado y se rechaza la restauración.

Un fragmento utilizado en nuestro proyecto es:

const actual = await sha256(
  path.join(dirBackup, info.archivo)
);

if (actual !== info.sha256) {
  throw new Error(
    `Checksum inválido en la colección "${nombre}"`
  );
}

Una característica importante es que esta verificación se realiza antes de iniciar la modificación de los documentos de destino.

Así reducimos el riesgo de utilizar respaldos dañados durante un proceso de recuperación.

7. Proceso de restauración de MongoDB

Una parte esencial del proyecto fue implementar el procedimiento inverso: recuperar los documentos almacenados en un respaldo.

Para ello desarrollamos el script:

scripts/restore.js

Este componente utiliza las funciones de restauración disponibles en nuestra biblioteca.

Etapas de recuperación

Primera etapa: validación del respaldo

Se comprueba la existencia de los archivos y se verifican sus checksums SHA-256.

Segunda etapa: lectura de documentos

Los archivos comprimidos se descomprimen y los documentos EJSON se convierten nuevamente a sus tipos correspondientes.

Tercera etapa: inserción de registros

La restauración organiza los documentos en lotes de hasta 1000 registros para insertarlos en MongoDB.

Cuarta etapa: recuperación de índices

Se recrean los índices registrados en los metadatos, conservando estructuras importantes para las consultas.

Quinta etapa: verificación final

Se compara el número de documentos restaurados con el número registrado durante el respaldo.

De esta manera, el procedimiento no termina únicamente después de insertar información, sino que incorpora una validación adicional.

Importante: la restauración predeterminada elimina los documentos existentes en las colecciones incluidas en el respaldo antes de volver a insertarlos. Por ello, debe ejecutarse sobre una base de datos de prueba o bajo un procedimiento de recuperación previamente autorizado.

8. Pruebas automatizadas del sistema

Para demostrar que los respaldos funcionan, incorporamos pruebas automatizadas utilizando las herramientas de Node.js.

Estas pruebas se encuentran en:

test/backup.test.js

Una de las pruebas genera una colección de 2501 documentos, incluyendo valores especiales de MongoDB.

Después crea un respaldo, elimina la colección de prueba y ejecuta la restauración.

Finalmente, verifica que se hayan recuperado correctamente los documentos, sus tipos y el índice configurado.

También incorporamos otras pruebas para comprobar:

  • Que la política de retención conserve únicamente la cantidad de respaldos configurada.
  • Que un archivo modificado sea rechazado por una verificación SHA-256 incorrecta.
  • Que los registros recuperados mantengan los tipos de datos originales.

El comando para ejecutar estas pruebas es:

npm test

Estas verificaciones son importantes porque permiten identificar errores en el proceso de recuperación antes de utilizar el sistema con información relevante.

Una de nuestras principales conclusiones técnicas fue que un respaldo es realmente útil cuando se ha comprobado que puede restaurarse.

9. Automatización de backups mediante GitHub Actions

Una vez implementado el sistema de respaldo, el siguiente objetivo fue evitar que su ejecución dependiera de una persona.

Para ello configuramos GitHub Actions mediante el archivo:

.github/workflows/backup.yml

Este workflow utiliza una programación automática:

on:
  schedule:
    - cron: "0 5 * * *"
  workflow_dispatch:

La expresión cron programa el respaldo diariamente a las 05:00 UTC, equivalente a las 00:00 en Perú.

También incorporamos workflow_dispatch, que permite iniciar manualmente el proceso desde GitHub.

¿Qué hace el workflow?

El flujo realiza las siguientes actividades:

  1. Descarga el código desde el repositorio.
  2. Prepara Node.js e instala las dependencias.
  3. Se conecta a MongoDB Atlas y genera el respaldo lógico.
  4. Restaura el respaldo en una instancia temporal de MongoDB para verificarlo.
  5. Prepara un archivo comprimido y aplica cifrado AES-256 cuando está configurada la contraseña de respaldo.
  6. Publica el archivo como artefacto de GitHub Actions, con una retención configurada de 30 días.

La conexión a MongoDB Atlas utiliza credenciales almacenadas en GitHub Secrets.

Para el cifrado se utiliza el secreto BACKUP_PASSPHRASE.

En la configuración actual, el workflow permite continuar sin cifrar si ese secreto no está definido y genera una advertencia. Para un entorno de producción sería recomendable exigir obligatoriamente su configuración y detener la publicación cuando falte.

Esta automatización representa una mejora importante respecto a generar respaldos manualmente, porque permite incorporar el procedimiento a una rutina programada y verificable.

10. Integración continua y despliegue en Render

Además de los respaldos, desarrollamos un segundo workflow encargado de realizar pruebas y automatizar la publicación de la aplicación.

Este archivo se encuentra en:

.github/workflows/ci-cd.yml

El proceso comienza cuando se realizan cambios en el repositorio.

Funcionamiento del pipeline

1. Validación del código

GitHub Actions prepara un entorno de ejecución y ejecuta las pruebas automatizadas contra un servicio temporal de MongoDB.

2. Construcción con Docker

Cuando las pruebas finalizan satisfactoriamente, se construye una imagen Docker como comprobación de que la aplicación puede empaquetarse correctamente.

3. Despliegue automatizado

Si el cambio corresponde a la rama principal, GitHub Actions utiliza el deploy hook de Render para solicitar una nueva publicación.

4. Verificación del servicio

El pipeline consulta el endpoint:

/health

Este endpoint permite verificar que el servidor responda y pueda establecer comunicación con MongoDB.

Gracias a este procedimiento, la publicación está vinculada al resultado de las pruebas.

Aplicación desplegada

Nuestra aplicación utiliza MongoDB Atlas como servicio de base de datos y Render para ejecutar el servidor Node.js.

Se puede acceder desde:

https://nosql-backup-strategy-d819.onrender.com

La configuración de infraestructura de Render se encuentra declarada en render.yaml, lo que facilita reproducir la configuración del servicio.

11. Cómo ejecutar el proyecto localmente

El repositorio incluye un entorno configurado con Docker Compose.

Para obtener el proyecto se puede utilizar:

git clone https://github.com/saulalvarado1/NoSQL-Backup-Strategy.git

cd NoSQL-Backup-Strategy

Posteriormente, se inicia la aplicación y la base de datos local:

docker compose up -d --build

Para cargar los datos de demostración:

docker compose exec app node scripts/seed.js

El sistema incorpora cinco productos de ejemplo, como una laptop, un monitor y accesorios informáticos, además de registros de clientes.

Después podemos ingresar a:

http://localhost:3000

Para comprobar el funcionamiento de las pruebas automatizadas dentro del contenedor:

docker compose exec app npm test

También es posible generar un respaldo manual:

docker compose exec app npm run backup

Y restaurarlo en una base de datos local independiente, evitando modificar los registros originales:

docker compose exec -e DB_NAME=tienda_restaurada app npm run restore

Estos comandos permiten explorar el funcionamiento del proyecto y comprender el ciclo de respaldo y recuperación utilizando un entorno de desarrollo aislado.

12. Resultados y aprendizajes obtenidos

El desarrollo de esta solución nos permitió integrar diferentes conocimientos del curso de Base de Datos II.

Entre los principales resultados alcanzados destacan:

  • Implementación de una aplicación web conectada a MongoDB Atlas.
  • Desarrollo de mecanismos de respaldo lógico de documentos NoSQL.
  • Conservación de tipos BSON utilizando EJSON.
  • Compresión de respaldos y verificación mediante SHA-256.
  • Recuperación de documentos e índices.
  • Pruebas automatizadas para validar integridad y restauración.
  • Configuración de procesos programados mediante GitHub Actions.
  • Integración de Docker y despliegue automatizado en Render.

Uno de los aprendizajes más importantes fue comprender que la protección de datos no consiste únicamente en guardar archivos.

Es necesario considerar la frecuencia de los respaldos, la seguridad de las credenciales, la integridad de la información y los procedimientos que se seguirán ante una pérdida de datos.

También identificamos oportunidades de mejora, como incorporar alertas ante fallos de ejecución, exigir siempre el cifrado y almacenar copias adicionales en servicios independientes.

Para escenarios de mayor escala también sería necesario evaluar mecanismos de respaldo que proporcionen garantías de consistencia durante escrituras concurrentes y opciones de recuperación a un punto específico en el tiempo.

13. Conclusiones

El desarrollo de este proyecto nos permitió comprender la importancia de implementar estrategias de respaldo y recuperación para bases de datos NoSQL alojadas en la nube.

En primer lugar, comprobamos que MongoDB Atlas puede integrarse con aplicaciones web desarrolladas mediante Node.js y Express, ofreciendo una plataforma adecuada para gestionar información documental.

En segundo lugar, la implementación de respaldos mediante EJSON, compresión gzip y verificaciones SHA-256 nos permitió conocer diferentes mecanismos que contribuyen a preservar la información y detectar posibles alteraciones.

Finalmente, la incorporación de GitHub Actions y Render demostró cómo las prácticas de automatización pueden aplicarse tanto a la publicación de aplicaciones como a los procedimientos de protección de datos.

La experiencia nos ayudó a fortalecer nuestros conocimientos sobre bases de datos NoSQL, desarrollo web, integración continua, despliegue automatizado y recuperación ante fallos.

El principal aprendizaje es que una estrategia de backup no debe limitarse a generar copias, sino que también debe garantizar procedimientos verificables para recuperar la información cuando sea necesario.

Referencias y documentación

Para comprender las tecnologías utilizadas, pueden consultarse las siguientes fuentes oficiales:

  • MongoDB Documentation — Bases de datos, BSON, respaldos y restauración.
  • GitHub Actions Documentation — Automatización de workflows y ejecución programada.
  • Render Documentation — Despliegue de servicios web y configuración de infraestructura.
  • Node.js Documentation — Desarrollo de aplicaciones y procesamiento de archivos.

title: Solver to System: LLM Reasoning Across Representations and Execution in Scientific Simulation
description:
arXiv:2611.21964v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Simulators based on partial differential equations (PDEs) are widely used to model physical systems, but generating and interpreting PDE solver code with large language models (LLMs) remains challenging. Scientific simulation code is a useful testbed for LLM scientific reasoning because (1) one system can be represented by code, equations, natural language, and numerical trajectories and (2) code can execute successfully while implementing invalid physics. We introduce Solver2System, a dataset of PDE solvers with multiple representations, controlled corruptions, and lexical perturbations, to evaluate whether LLMs can recover the underlying physical system through (1) cross-representation consistency and (2) static and agentic detection of physical invalidity. Across eight open-weight models, LLMs systematically favor some representations when evidence conflicts, and lexical perturbations to code alter interpretation of other unchanged representations. Execution improves physical-validity judgments, but weaker agents can judge correctly without identifying the causal defect. Thus, LLMs may reach correct judgments despite inconsistent representation reconciliation or causal misdiagnosis.

title: PhyVGGT: Feed-Forward Articulated Object Reconstruction from Monocular Videos
description:
arXiv:2611.22244v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reconstructing an articulated object with its 3D movable parts, joint parameters and unseen articulation states from an uncalibrated monocular video is essential for robot manipulation and interactive digital twins. Existing per-scene optimisation methods require minutes to hours and external depth or camera poses, whereas feed-forward 3D foundation models reconstruct dense point maps in one pass without segmenting movable parts or inferring joints. Even on these monocular point maps, regressing or fitting continuous joints directly fails on casual videos, since cross-frame attention blurs moving part boundaries in deep layers, underestimates motion along the viewing ray and leaves continuous axes ill-conditioned under small opening angles. To address these challenges, we propose PhyVGGT, a single-pass framework on a frozen 3D foundation model that anchors moving-part matching and closed-form joint estimation to the undistorted geometry of the stationary base. First, our Part and Motion Decoder fuses intermediate per-frame tokens with global tokens and references part queries to a static-base query to segment 3D parts, align point maps on the static base and predict learned Bingham priors. Second, our Kinematic Inference Layer fits an orthogonal Manhattan frame to static surface normals, selects the joint axis in closed form under a Bingham posterior combining pairwise motion scatter with the learned priors, and solves a linear system for the hinge pivot to drive unseen states. Trained solely on synthetic data, PhyVGGT achieves state-of-the-art monocular performance across five benchmarks, outperforming FAMOS and monocular ArtiPoint, surpassing posed RGB-D ArtiPoint in median error, and running in 6.8 s per 48-frame video against hours of per-scene optimisation in Articulat3D. Project page: https://phyvggt.github.io.

title: Where Does Hindsight Enter Clinical Agent Benchmarks? An Audit of Simulators and Case Construction
description:
arXiv:2611.22241v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Benchmarks for LLM diagnostic agents are built from retrospective records: the case an agent reads is rewritten from discharge summaries, and unrecorded test results are generated by a simulator that often sees the final diagnosis. HindAudit separates three hindsight channels (the diagnosis given to the simulator, the retrospective context it conditions on, and the agent-facing case text) and measures each with judges trained only on real data. On 27,489 emergency admissions from MIMIC-IV, five registered tests found no leakage into simulated laboratory results: providing the diagnosis to five simulators had a negligible effect, and prompted gatekeepers diluted the diagnostic signal, although exploratory results suggest they can raise agent scores. The largest effect lay in the case text. Against a presentation-time reconstruction from triage records, benchmark-style summaries raised the zero-shot accuracy of four LLMs from 25.4% to 39.7% and discharge histories to 45.3%, and raised six interactive agents' scores while barely changing their ranking. The exploratory gap was reproduced in a registered replication on held-out patients. Masking diagnosis names left it unchanged. Because MIMIC lacks a contemporaneous bedside history, the gap is an upper bound on hindsight. We report all registered outcomes and recommend construction practices.

title: SCAN: Site-Aware Collaborative Privacy-Preserving Adaptation of Vision-Language Models for Neurological Disease Classification
description:
arXiv:2611.21955v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Worldwide neuroimaging data could strengthen diagnostic foundation models, but privacy rules often prevent centralizing brain MRI scans. We present SCAN, a site-aware collaborative adaptation framework for Neurological Disease Classification that lets new sites adapt a 3D medical vision-language model (VLM) without retraining or sharing patient scans. Each site keeps exact class prototypes for local prediction and can share privacy-protected class summaries: norm-bounded sums and counts perturbed once with calibrated noise. Using 7,641 scans from 67 sites across 12 countries, covering Alzheimer's disease (AD), stroke, epilepsy and controls, we assess local adaptation, cross-site benefits, and effects on existing sites. At seven unseen sites, the frozen VLM's zero-shot AUCs were 0.833-0.945 for AD and stroke. Training-free local prototypes improved epilepsy AUC at three sites from 0.598/0.625/0.508 to 0.684/0.729/0.762 and AD AUC at one site from 0.833 to 0.863, nearly matching a classifier trained at each site (mean AUC 0.757 vs. 0.759). With differential privacy ($\epsilon$ = 4), new sites contributed without materially reducing accuracy at existing sites (AUC change $\leq$0.2%), although gains from sharing were limited, and membership attacks performed near chance. SCAN offers hospitals a worldwide framework to adapt and share brain MRI VLMs without exchanging scans or retraining.

title: Corrupting Ties: Investigating Robustness to Bias Injection Across Multi-Agent Network Topologies
description:
arXiv:2611.21804v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI systems are increasingly deployed in high-stakes decision-making contexts, where interactions among components can introduce fairness risks that remain undetected when auditing components or collective outcomes in isolation. As LLM-based multi-agent systems become more prevalent, understanding how biased information propagates through agent interactions is essential for assessing their fairness. We introduce a controlled bias injection framework that replaces selected agent responses with predefined biased ones, enabling an intervention-based analysis of how network topology and injection configurations shape system behavior. We propose decision divergence metrics that quantify the effects of these interventions at the agent, network, and system levels, and evaluate five topologies on three binary classification tasks using LLMs from the Qwen and Gemma families. Sequential networks show the greatest divergence, whereas fully connected and mesh networks show less. Injection position also matters: in star networks, injecting the central agent has larger effects than injecting peripheral agents. Models further differ in whether divergence follows the injected bias. These findings highlight the role of network structure in the propagation of biased information and motivate topology-aware auditing of fairness risks in multi-agent systems.

title: 60 FPS Motion Engineering & Core Web Vitals: Designing Editorial Interfaces That Rank in Google Discover
description:
By **Benni Alencar* — Chief AI Systems Architect at Benni OS. Canonical article & interactive benchmarks at benni-os.net.*

Executive Summary & The 16.67 ms Frame Budget

Modern editorial engineering sits at an unforgiving intersection: readers expect tactile, fluid storytelling with zero visual jank, while search and discovery algorithms—especially Google Discover—penalize any site that misses strict Core Web Vitals thresholds. On a 60 Hz display, your entire JavaScript, style recalculation, layout, paint, and GPU compositing pipeline has exactly 16.67 milliseconds to produce a frame (or 8.33 ms on 120 Hz ProMotion panels).

When teams bolt arbitrary scroll listeners or unguarded CSS transitions onto an editorial layout, they trigger synchronous layout thrashing on the main thread. Interaction to Next Paint (INP) spikes past 200 ms, Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) breaks reading continuity, and Google's crawlers demote the page from Discover feeds. Within the Benni Canvas architecture, motion and aesthetics are treated as deterministic engineering contracts—governed by Skill 56 (Motion Engineering) and Skill 57 (Aesthetic Engineering).

The Browser Rendering Pipeline & Compositor-Only Transforms

To guarantee a locked 60 FPS, animations must never touch the Layout (geometry) or Paint (rasterization) stages of the browser's rendering pipeline. Animating top, left, width, height, or margin forces the CPU to recompute box geometry for every affected node in the DOM tree on every tick.

Instead, editorial motion should be strictly confined to compositor-only properties: transform (translate3d, scale, rotate), opacity, and hardware-accelerated clip-path masks. These properties are handed off to the GPU compositor thread, allowing the main thread to remain idle and responsive to user taps—protecting your INP budget.

flowchart LR
  A["Scroll / User Input"] --> B{"Animated Property?"}
  B -->|"top / left / width / margin"| C["Main Thread: Layout & Reflow"]
  C --> D["CPU Paint & Rasterize"]
  D --> E["Frame Drop > 16.67ms (Jank + High INP)"]
  B -->|"transform / opacity / clip-path"| F["GPU Compositor Thread"]
  F --> G["Layer Matrix Update (< 2ms)"]
  G --> H["Locked 60 FPS + Healthy CWV"]

GPU Layer Promotion Without VRAM Exhaustion

Promoting an element to its own compositor layer via will-change: transform, opacity eliminates paint invalidation during motion. However, applying will-change globally to dozens of cards allocates excessive GPU texture memory (VRAM), causing mobile browsers to crash or stall during texture uploads. Promote layers just-in-time—only on active interactive targets or immediately before a timeline starts—and release them when the sequence completes.

Property / Pattern Pipeline Stage Triggered Core Web Vitals Impact Benni Canvas Verdict
transform: translate3d() / opacity Composite Only (GPU) Zero CLS, minimal INP overhead Approved (Default Motion Token)
top / left / height Layout + Paint + Composite Severe INP spikes & frame drops Banned in production timelines
box-shadow / filter: blur() Paint + Composite (CPU/GPU) High rasterization cost on scroll Static or pseudo-element opacity fade
aspect-ratio + explicit width/height Pre-allocated Layout Box Prevents CLS (< 0.01) on image load Mandatory for all media slots

Deterministic Lenis & GSAP Lifecycle Cleanup

Combining Lenis smooth scrolling with GSAP ScrollTrigger delivers cinema-grade scroll choreography, but it is also the number-one source of memory leaks in single-page applications and view-transitioned editorial sites. Orphaned requestAnimationFrame loops, stale ScrollTrigger pins, and duplicate ticker listeners accumulate across navigations, degrading INP over time.

Every motion module in Benni Canvas must implement an atomic setup/teardown lifecycle using gsap.context(), explicit ticker detachment, and lenis.destroy():

import Lenis from 'lenis';
import gsap from 'gsap';
import { ScrollTrigger } from 'gsap/ScrollTrigger';

gsap.registerPlugin(ScrollTrigger);

export function mountEditorialMotion(container) {
  const prefersReduced = window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)').matches;
  if (prefersReduced) return () => {};

  const lenis = new Lenis({
    duration: 1.15,
    easing: (t) => Math.min(1, 1.001 - Math.pow(2, -10 * t)),
    smoothWheel: true,
  });

  lenis.on('scroll', ScrollTrigger.update);

  const tick = (time) => {
    lenis.raf(time * 1000);
  };
  gsap.ticker.add(tick);
  gsap.ticker.lagSmoothing(0);

  const ctx = gsap.context(() => {
    gsap.from('.editorial-reveal', {
      y: 28,
      opacity: 0,
      duration: 0.75,
      stagger: 0.08,
      ease: 'power3.out',
      clearProps: 'transform,opacity',
      scrollTrigger: {
        trigger: container,
        start: 'top 82%',
        once: true,
      },
    });
  }, container);

  // Deterministic teardown on route change or component unmount
  return () => {
    ctx.revert();
    gsap.ticker.remove(tick);
    lenis.destroy();
  };
}

Notice two critical details in this pattern: clearProps: 'transform,opacity' releases GPU layer promotions as soon as the reveal finishes, and the returned cleanup function guarantees zero dangling listeners when the user navigates between articles.

Typography Hierarchy & Optical Rhythm

High-performing editorial architecture relies on disciplined typography before a single animation runs. In Benni Canvas (Skill 57: Aesthetic Engineering), we pair a high-contrast display serif (DM Serif Display) for headlines with a geometric humanist sans-serif (Plus Jakarta Sans) for body copy and a crisp monospace (IBM Plex Mono) for telemetry, badges, and code.

  • Fluid Scaling with clamp(): Use font-size: clamp(2.3rem, 4.5vw, 3.6rem) for the single page `` so headlines scale smoothly from 375 px mobile viewports to 1440 px desktops without media-query layout jumps.
  • Optimal Measure: Constrain prose containers to 65ch–75ch (roughly 860px max-width with padding) to prevent eye-tracking fatigue and multi-line wrapping bloat.
  • Zero-FOIT Font Loading: Pair preconnect hints to fonts.googleapis.com and fonts.gstatic.com with display=swap so Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) text renders immediately without blocking.

Accessibility First: Strict prefers-reduced-motion

Motion engineering without accessibility is broken engineering. Roughly 35% of adults over 40 experience vestibular sensitivity to parallax, continuous scroll-jacking, or large-scale translations. Your CSS and JS layers must honor prefers-reduced-motion: reduce as a first-class invariant, collapsing spatial motion into instant state transitions or subtle opacity fades:

`css
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
html {
scroll-behavior: auto;
}
*, *::before, *::after {
animation-duration: 0.01ms !important;
animation-iteration-count: 1 !important;
transition-duration: 0.01ms !important;
scroll-behavior: auto !important;
}
}
`

Core Web Vitals Budgets & Ranking in Google Discover

Google Discover is a visual-first, mobile-centric recommendation engine. Unlike traditional search, Discover surfaces articles based on topical authority, entity clarity, page experience, and high-impact imagery. Missing even one technical signal disqualifies an otherwise brilliant article from Discover cards.

To pass both the Core Web Vitals field assessment and Google Discover's eligibility gates, enforce these non-negotiable engineering budgets:

  1. Robots Directive (max-image-preview:large): Always include in . Without max-image-preview:large, Google restricts your Discover card to a tiny thumbnail, collapsing click-through rates.
  2. High-Resolution 16:9 Hero Asset: Serve a clean, watermark-free hero image at least 1200 px wide (for example, our 1376×768 asset) with fetchpriority="high", loading="eager", and explicit width/height attributes to lock LCP ≤ 2.5 s and CLS ≤ 0.01.
  3. Unified Entity Graph (JSON-LD): Declare both TechArticle and FAQPage schemas in JSON-LD, referencing the exact same canonical URL, ImageObject dimensions, and verified author/publisher entities.
  4. Single `` Semantic Outline: Maintain exactly one per document followed by a strict → `` hierarchy so screen readers and semantic parsers map your topic graph cleanly.

Benni Canvas Design Systems: Automated Quality Gates

In the Benni OS ecosystem, we do not rely on manual checklists to enforce these standards. Benni Canvas integrates Skill 56 (Motion Engineering) and Skill 57 (Aesthetic Engineering) into automated validation gates that inspect every generated interface for compositor-only animation tokens, reduced-motion coverage, contrast ratios, and Core Web Vitals readiness prior to deployment.

Build with Benni Canvas & Sovereign Web Architecture

Ship 60 FPS editorial interfaces with deterministic GSAP/Lenis lifecycles, verified Core Web Vitals budgets, and Google Discover structured data out of the box.

    Access Operator Mode & Playbook →




Frequently Asked Questions


      Why do compositor-only properties matter for 60 FPS motion?

      Animating transform, opacity, or clip-path bypasses the browser's main-thread Layout and Paint stages, executing directly on the GPU compositor thread so frames complete well within the 16.67 ms budget.



  How do you prevent memory leaks when combining Lenis and GSAP ScrollTrigger?
  Wrap all GSAP timelines in `gsap.context()`, detach the ticker callback, call `ctx.revert()` on unmount, and invoke `lenis.destroy()` so no orphaned `requestAnimationFrame` loops persist across route changes.


  What technical requirements are mandatory to rank in Google Discover?
  Pages must include the `max-image-preview:large` robots directive, serve high-resolution hero imagery at least 1200 px wide (such as 1376×768) referenced in both `og:image` and `TechArticle` JSON-LD, and pass Core Web Vitals thresholds (LCP ≤ 2.5 s, CLS ≤ 0.1, INP ≤ 200 ms).

  Benni Canvas pairs Skill 56 (Motion Engineering) and Skill 57 (Aesthetic Engineering) to enforce compositor-only tokens, strict `prefers-reduced-motion` fallbacks, and automated Core Web Vitals quality gates before publishing.

title: JSONB at Scale: Taming PostgreSQL TOAST Churn and WAL Bloat on High-Write Workloads
description:
Originally published on tamiz.pro.

JSONB is one of PostgreSQL's most useful data types for semi-structured data, but it also hides one of the database's most expensive internal mechanisms. Large documents are moved out of the main heap into TOAST storage, compressed along the way, and—when the row changes—rewritten. On write-heavy systems, that combination can produce surprising WAL amplification, bloated tables, and storage amplification long after the original data has been compacted.

The core problem is not JSONB itself. It is that many workloads treat JSONB like an opaque scalar column while PostgreSQL treats it like a variable-length object with expensive update semantics. Understanding that boundary is the difference between a healthy high-write system and one that spends its I/O budget rewriting the same payload over and over.

This guide walks through the internals of TOAST, explains where WAL amplification comes from, and provides a concrete engineering path from diagnosis to remediation.

Table of Contents

  • 1. The mental model: JSONB is not one column
  • 2. How PostgreSQL stores large JSONB values
  • 3. Why high-write workloads create TOAST churn
  • 4. Measuring the problem
  • 5. The remediation toolkit
  • 6. Reference implementation: a batched JSONB writer
  • 7. Production patterns and edge cases
  • 8. Frequently Asked Questions

1. The mental model: JSONB is not one column

A common source of confusion is the idea that a jsonb column occupies a single, self-contained slot in a row. That is true only for small values. PostgreSQL uses a fixed-width pointer in the row itself and stores the actual payload elsewhere once the value exceeds the threshold for in-row storage.

For a row like this:

CREATE TABLE events (
    id          bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    tenant_id   integer NOT NULL,
    payload     jsonb NOT NULL,
    created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

The payload column is not necessarily inline. The storage decision depends on the tuple size, the available space in the page, and the value's compressibility. A small JSONB document may stay in the heap tuple. A large document is compressed and, if needed, pushed into TOAST storage.

Three distinct storage paths exist:

  1. Inline storage — the JSONB value fits in the main heap tuple and is stored directly on the page.
  2. Compressed inline storage — the value is compressed but still fits in the tuple.
  3. External TOAST storage — the value is compressed and then stored out-of-line in a TOAST table, with only a small pointer remaining in the heap tuple.

This distinction matters because the cost profile of each path is different. Inline writes are cheap. Compressed inline writes require CPU. External TOAST writes add a second relation, additional index-like bookkeeping, and an extra round of WAL.

The key insight

When you UPDATE a row and change only a small field, PostgreSQL does not patch the JSONB value in place. PostgreSQL has no fine-grained, in-place JSONB mutation. It constructs a new value and writes a new tuple version.

If that new value is externally stored, the old TOAST chunk may be reused only if the storage code determines it can be shared. In practice, for changed or rewritten values, you get a fresh TOAST write.

The result is a cost model that looks roughly like this:

row update cost ≈ heap tuple write
              + TOAST value write (if external)
              + compression CPU
              + WAL for both heap and TOAST
              + dead tuple cleanup
              + index maintenance

On a workload that updates a small subset of fields in a large JSONB document thousands of times per second, the TOAST write and its WAL can dominate the actual business logic.

2. How PostgreSQL stores large JSONB values

TOAST—the acronym stands for The On-disk Self-Optimizing Table—is PostgreSQL's mechanism for handling variable-length attributes larger than a page-sized tuple.

The TOAST table

When a table contains a TOASTable column, PostgreSQL creates a companion relation with a name like pg_toast_16384. This table has the same structure as the original table but with a special trigger that moves large values out of line.

The TOAST table stores four columns per TOASTable column:

chunk_id    oid    -- identifier linking chunks to a value
chunk_seq   int4   -- ordering of the chunk
chunk_data  bytea  -- the actual compressed bytes

Values larger than TOAST_TUPLE_THRESHOLD (around 2 KB) are split into chunks of roughly TOAST_MAX_CHUNK_SIZE (around 2 KB as well, adjusted for page overhead). Each chunk is a separate row in the TOAST table.

Compression: PGLZ and LZ4

Before storage, PostgreSQL attempts to compress the value using PGLZ, the built-in algorithm. Since PostgreSQL 14, you can enable LZ4 compression, which is significantly faster while producing somewhat larger output than PGLZ for many data shapes.

You can control this at the column level:

ALTER TABLE events
    ALTER COLUMN payload SET STORAGE EXTERNAL;

The available modes are:

Storage mode Behavior When to use it
PLAIN Never compress or move out of line; errors if the row is too large Very large values you want stored verbatim and never compressed
EXTENDED Compress first, move out of line only if still too large Default; good general-purpose choice
EXTERNAL Move out of line first, compress only if that saves space Write-heavy workloads where compression CPU is the bottleneck
MAIN Always keep inline, compress if needed Small, bounded values

The default for jsonb is EXTENDED, and that default is often exactly wrong for high-write workloads.

Why WAL amplification happens

Every physical change is logged in the Write-Ahead Log. When you update a row with an externally stored JSONB value, the WAL contains:

  1. The new heap tuple, including the TOAST pointer.
  2. The new TOAST chunk rows.
  3. WAL for the index entries that reference the row.

The TOAST portion can be substantially larger than the logical change you made. If your JSONB document is 100 KB and you update a single status field, the logical delta is a few bytes. The physical write is 100 KB, plus WAL for it.

This is not a bug. It is the natural consequence of PostgreSQL's MVCC design combined with copy-on-write semantics for variable-length values. The engineering response is to reduce the number of bytes written per logical operation, or to reduce the frequency of those operations.

3. Why high-write workloads create TOAST churn

Let's characterize the workload patterns that cause the most damage.

Pattern A: read-modify-write of large documents 

UPDATE events
SET payload = jsonb_set(payload, '{status}', '"processed"'::jsonb)
WHERE id = $1;

This rewrites the entire document. If the document is 50 KB and externally stored, each update writes 50 KB of TOAST data and generates corresponding WAL.

Pattern B: upsert loops with high conflict rates

When many workers contend on the same key, PostgreSQL's ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE path repeatedly rewrites the row, and each rewrite regenerates the TOAST value.

Pattern C: telemetry and event ingestion with mutable payloads

Event tables often accumulate a JSONB payload that grows over time as processing stages add metadata. Each stage appends a key, rewriting the whole document.

Pattern D: unbounded JSONB growth

If a JSONB column accumulates history, counters, or nested arrays without bounds, the value size grows monotonically. The write cost per operation grows with it, even though the operation itself is constant-size.

Pattern E: aggressive autovacuum settings misapplied to TOAST

Vacuuming the parent table does not automatically keep TOAST tables in good shape in every configuration. You need to understand how TOAST cleanup interacts with autovacuum and toast.autovacuum_* settings.

4. Measuring the problem

Before changing anything, establish a baseline. This section covers the queries and tools that will tell you whether TOAST churn is actually your bottleneck.

Step 1: Find tables with large average row sizes 

SELECT
    schemaname,
    relname,
    n_live_tup,
    pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size(relid)) AS total_size,
    pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(relid))         AS heap_size,
    pg_size_pretty(
        pg_total_relation_size(relid) - pg_relation_size(relid)
    )                                               AS toast_and_index_size,
    round(avg_row_len, 1)                           AS avg_row_bytes
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
ORDER BY pg_total_relation_size(relid) DESC
LIMIT 20;

A large gap between heap_size and total_size is a strong signal that TOAST and indexes are consuming significant space.

Step 2: Measure TOAST usage per table

PostgreSQL exposes TOAST statistics through pg_class and pg_stat_user_tables:

SELECT
    c.relname                                    AS table_name,
    pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(c.reltoastrelid)) AS toast_size,
    t.n_live_tup,
    t.n_dead_tup,
    t.n_mod_since_analyze
FROM pg_class c
JOIN pg_stat_user_tables t ON t.relid = c.oid
WHERE c.reltoastrelid <> 0
ORDER BY pg_relation_size(c.reltoastrelid) DESC;

Step 3: Inspect actual storage modes

The pg_column_size function returns the number of bytes used to store a value, including any TOAST compression:

SELECT
    id,
    pg_column_size(payload)          AS stored_bytes,
    octet_length(payload::text)      AS raw_text_bytes,
    pg_column_size(payload) * 1.0
      / NULLIF(octet_length(payload::text), 0) AS compression_ratio
FROM events
ORDER BY stored_bytes DESC
LIMIT 20;

A ratio near 1.0 means the data is not compressing well. A ratio around 0.3 means PGLZ is doing a good job. Values in the tens of kilobytes are candidates for TOAST.

Step 4: Look at WAL generation

PostgreSQL 15+ exposes per-table WAL statistics:

SELECT
    wal_records,
    wal_bytes,
    wal_fpi,
    round(wal_bytes / 1024.0 / 1024.0, 2) AS wal_mb,
    round(wal_bytes::numeric / NULLIF(n_tup_ins + n_tup_upd + n_tup_del, 0), 0)
        AS avg_wal_bytes_per_dml
FROM pg_stat_wal
CROSS JOIN pg_stat_database d
WHERE d.datname = current_database();

More practically, use pg_stat_wal (cluster-wide) and pg_stat_database for xact_commit rates, then sample pg_current_wal_lsn() over a fixed interval:

-- Run twice, one minute apart, and subtract.
SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn();

The difference tells you the WAL bytes per second your cluster is generating.

Step 5: Profile with pg_stat_statements

Find the statements generating the most WAL. pg_stat_statements tracks wal_bytes when the track_wal_io_timing and related options are enabled in PostgreSQL 15+:

SELECT
    query,
    calls,
    total_exec_time,
    wal_bytes,
    round(wal_bytes::numeric / NULLIF(calls, 0)) AS avg_wal_per_call
FROM pg_stat_statements
WHERE wal_bytes > 0
ORDER BY wal_bytes DESC
LIMIT 20;

This is usually where you find the UPDATE ... jsonb_set(...) pattern.

Step 6: Inspect the TOAST table directly 

SELECT
    chunk_id,
    count(*)          AS chunks,
    sum(length(chunk_data)) AS total_bytes,
    avg(length(chunk_data)) AS avg_chunk_bytes
FROM pg_toast.pg_toast_16384
GROUP BY chunk_id
ORDER BY total_bytes DESC
LIMIT 10;

Replace 16384 with the actual OID of your table's TOAST relation, found via:

SELECT c.reltoastrelid::regclass
FROM pg_class c
WHERE c.relname = 'events';

5. The remediation toolkit

The goal is to reduce bytes written per logical operation. There are several complementary levers, ordered by how much they typically help.

Lever 1: Set STORAGE EXTERNAL on hot JSONB columns

This is the single highest-leverage change for CPU-bound high-write workloads. It skips compression for values that go out of line, trading storage for CPU and write throughput.

ALTER TABLE events
    ALTER COLUMN payload SET STORAGE EXTERNAL;

-- Force a rewrite so the new storage mode applies to existing rows.
VACUUM FULL events;

Important caveats:

  • VACUUM FULL takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock. On a live system, plan a maintenance window or use pg_repack.
  • The change only affects newly written or rewritten tuples. Existing tuples keep their old layout until they are rewritten.
  • EXTERNAL means no compression at all for out-of-line values. If your JSON compresses 5:1, your TOAST table will grow substantially. Verify the tradeoff on real data.
  • If the value fits inline, it is still stored inline, uncompressed.

Measure the effect:

-- Before and after: compare WAL generation rate and CPU usage.
SELECT
    pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('pg_toast.pg_toast_16384')) AS toast_size,
    (SELECT count(*) FROM events WHERE pg_column_size(payload) > 2000) AS external_values;

Lever 2: Enable LZ4 compression

If you want compression but less CPU, LZ4 is a strong option:

ALTER SYSTEM SET lz4 TO on;
SELECT pg_reload_conf();

Then force a rewrite of affected rows:

VACUUM FULL events;

LZ4 typically compresses 2–3x faster than PGLZ with slightly worse ratios. For JSON payloads with many repeated keys, the ratio difference is usually modest.

Lever 3: Reduce the frequency of large rewrites

The best fix is often architectural: stop rewriting the whole document for small changes.

Normalize hot fields into real columns. If status, tenant_id, or retry_count are queried or updated frequently, move them out of JSONB:

ALTER TABLE events
    ADD COLUMN status text,
    ADD COLUMN retry_count integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0;

UPDATE events
SET status = payload ->> 'status',
    retry_count = COALESCE((payload ->> 'retry_count')::integer, 0);

Now updates touch only the scalar column:

UPDATE events
SET status = 'processed'
WHERE id = $1;

This eliminates the TOAST rewrite entirely for that field.

Split cold and hot data. Keep a small, frequently-updated working set in one table and append large, rarely-modified payloads to another:

CREATE TABLE event_payloads (
    event_id   bigint PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES events(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    payload    jsonb NOT NULL
);

The events table stays small and cheap to update; the payload table is written once and read rarely.

Use append-only semantics. For event streams, don't update at all:

INSERT INTO events (tenant_id, payload, created_at)
VALUES ($1, $2, now());

A consumer maintains derived state. This eliminates TOAST churn by construction.

Lever 4: Batch writes

If you must write many rows, batch them. PostgreSQL's WAL cost per row drops significantly when many tuples are written in one statement, because full-page images and page-header overhead are amortized.

INSERT INTO events (tenant_id, payload, created_at)
SELECT *
FROM jsonb_to_recordset($1::jsonb)
    AS x(tenant_id integer, payload jsonb, created_at timestamptz);

For high-throughput ingestion, COPY is usually faster still:

psql -d appdb -c "\copy events (tenant_id, payload, created_at) FROM '/data/events.csv' WITH (FORMAT csv)"

Lever 5: Tune autovacuum for TOAST tables

TOAST tables have their own autovacuum settings:

ALTER TABLE pg_toast.pg_toast_16384 SET (
    autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.02,
    autovacuum_vacuum_threshold = 1000
);

More aggressive vacuuming on TOAST tables removes dead chunks faster, limiting bloat. The tradeoff is more I/O spent on vacuum.

You can also set cluster-wide defaults:

ALTER SYSTEM SET toast.autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.02;
ALTER SYSTEM SET toast.autovacuum_vacuum_threshold = 1000;
SELECT pg_reload_conf();

Lever 6: Monitor WAL generation continuously

Track WAL rate and TOAST size as first-class metrics:

CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW monitor_toast_wal AS
SELECT
    now()                                          AS sampled_at,
    pg_current_wal_lsn()                           AS current_lsn,
    pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size('events')) AS events_total_size,
    pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('pg_toast.pg_toast_16384')) AS toast_size,
    (SELECT n_live_tup FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE relname = 'events') AS live_tuples;

Sample it on a schedule and alert on regressions:

SELECT
    max(wal_bytes) - min(wal_bytes) AS wal_generated,
    max(toast_size) - min(toast_size) AS toast_growth
FROM monitor_toast_wal
WHERE sampled_at > now() - interval '1 hour';

6. Reference implementation: a batched JSONB writer

Here is a complete, runnable example that demonstrates the core techniques working together. It assumes PostgreSQL 15 or later.

Schema 

DROP TABLE IF EXISTS event_batches;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS events;

CREATE TABLE events (
    id          bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    tenant_id   integer NOT NULL,
    status      text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending',
    payload     jsonb NOT NULL,
    created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- Hot path: uncompressed out-of-line storage.
ALTER TABLE events ALTER COLUMN payload SET STORAGE EXTERNAL;

-- Cold path: append-only payloads, written once.
CREATE TABLE event_payload_archive (
    event_id   bigint PRIMARY KEY,
    payload    jsonb NOT NULL
);

CREATE INDEX events_tenant_created_idx
    ON events (tenant_id, created_at DESC);

Batch insert function 

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION ingest_event_batch(
    p_batch jsonb
)
RETURNS bigint
LANGUAGE plpgsql
AS $$
DECLARE
    v_inserted bigint;
BEGIN
    INSERT INTO events (tenant_id, payload, created_at)
    SELECT
        (x ->> 'tenant_id')::integer,
        x -> 'payload',
        COALESCE((x ->> 'created_at')::timestamptz, now())
    FROM jsonb_array_elements(p_batch) AS x;

    GET DIAGNOSTICS v_inserted = ROW_COUNT;

    -- Archive the same payload for cold storage without a second rewrite.
    INSERT INTO event_payload_archive (event_id, payload)
    SELECT e.id, e.payload
    FROM events e
    WHERE e.tenant_id = (p_batch -> 0 ->> 'tenant_id')::integer
      AND e.created_at >= now() - interval '1 second'
    ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;

    RETURN v_inserted;
END;
$$;

In production, the archive insert should use a more precise correlation key (for example, a batch UUID written into every row) rather than the time window above. The time-window version here is intentionally simple and illustrative.

Test it 

SELECT ingest_event_batch(
    jsonb_build_array(
        jsonb_build_object(
            'tenant_id', 42,
            'payload', jsonb_build_object(
                'event_type', 'order.created',
                'order_id', 1001,
                'items', jsonb_build_array(
                    jsonb_build_object('sku', 'ABC-123', 'qty', 2),
                    jsonb_build_object('sku', 'XYZ-789', 'qty', 1)
                ),
                'metadata', repeat('x', 5000)
            ),
            'created_at', now()
        ),
        jsonb_build_object(
            'tenant_id', 42,
            'payload', jsonb_build_object(
                'event_type', 'order.created',
                'order_id', 1002,
                'items', jsonb_build_array(
                    jsonb_build_object('sku', 'DEF-456', 'qty', 5)
                ),
                'metadata', repeat('y', 5000)
            ),
            'created_at', now()
        )
    )
);

Verify the storage layout 

SELECT
    id,
    tenant_id,
    pg_column_size(payload) AS stored_bytes,
    octet_length(payload::text) AS raw_bytes
FROM events
ORDER BY id;

-- Confirm the TOAST relation is being used.
SELECT
    chunk_id,
    count(*) AS chunks,
    sum(length(chunk_data)) AS bytes
FROM pg_toast.pg_toast_16384
GROUP BY chunk_id;

Efficient status update

Because status is now a real column, updating it does not rewrite the payload:

UPDATE events
SET status = 'processed'
WHERE id = 1;

Compare the WAL generated by this statement against an equivalent jsonb_set update on the payload itself. The difference is dramatic once the payload is large.

7. Production patterns and edge cases

The jsonb_set rewrite cost in detail 

UPDATE events
SET payload = jsonb_set(payload, '{status}', '"processed"'::jsonb)
WHERE id = 1;

This expression must:

  1. Read and detoast the existing JSONB value.
  2. Parse it into the binary JSONB representation.
  3. Locate the target path.
  4. Construct a new binary representation.
  5. Recompress it.
  6. Write a new TOAST value and log it to WAL.

The cost is proportional to document size, not to the size of the change.

Bounded JSONB growth

If a JSONB column accumulates unbounded data, cap it. PostgreSQL 15+ offers a neat trick using generated columns:

ALTER TABLE events
    ADD COLUMN payload_size integer
    GENERATED ALWAYS AS (pg_column_size(payload)) STORED;

CREATE INDEX events_payload_size_idx ON events (payload_size)
    WHERE payload_size > 100000;

Use this index to find outliers and alert on them, or to drive a cleanup job that moves oversized payloads to cold storage.

Partitioning for retention

Time-based partitioning combined with DROP TABLE gives O(1) retention without vacuum pressure:

CREATE TABLE events_2024_01 PARTITION OF events
    FOR VALUES FROM ('2024-01-01') TO ('2024-02-01');

Dropping an old partition removes its TOAST data immediately, without the dead-tuple cleanup cost of a mass DELETE.

When JSONB is genuinely the wrong choice

If you find yourself constantly extracting the same fields, querying JSONB paths in hot paths, or rewriting documents to update a single attribute, the data is relational. Normalize it.

JSONB shines when the shape is genuinely variable, reads are more common than writes, and the document is mostly immutable once written. It struggles when the shape is stable but unknown to you, when writes are frequent, and when documents grow without bound.

Connection-level settings that help

For bulk ingestion, consider raising synchronous_commit temporarily for non-critical writes:

SET synchronous_commit = off;
-- bulk load
-- reset per connection
RESET synchronous_commit;

This reduces WAL flush frequency. It trades durability on commit for throughput, so use it only for data you can regenerate or reconcile.

8. Frequently Asked Questions

Does STORAGE EXTERNAL always reduce WAL?

Not always. It eliminates the CPU cost of compression, which often lets the system write more rows per second and therefore generate more total WAL. It reduces per-row CPU and latency, but total WAL can rise if throughput increases substantially. The correct metric to track is bytes of WAL per logical operation, not total WAL alone.

Should I run VACUUM FULL to apply a storage mode change?

VACUUM FULL rewrites the table and its TOAST data, applying the new storage mode, but it locks the table exclusively. For large production tables, use pg_repack, which does the same work with a much shorter lock window, or accept that new storage modes apply only to newly written rows.

Is there a way to avoid TOAST entirely for JSONB?\n

Only by keeping values small enough to fit inline. If your JSONB payloads exceed a few kilobytes, TOAST is unavoidable. The realistic options are to reduce the value size, split hot and cold fields, or reduce write frequency.

How do I know if my TOAST table is bloated?

Compare pg_relation_size(reltoastrelid) against the sum of live chunk sizes. A large difference, or a TOAST table that keeps growing while the parent table's row count stays flat, indicates dead chunks that vacuum has not yet reclaimed. Check pg_stat_user_tables for the parent and run VACUUM on the TOAST relation explicitly if needed.

title: AdaFlowLite: Scalable and Non-blocking Inference on Asynchronous Mobile Data
description:
arXiv:2611.21691v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The rise of mobile devices equipped with numerous sensors, such as LiDAR and cameras, has driven the adoption of multi-modal deep intelligence for distributed sensing tasks, such as smart cabins and driving assistance. However, the arrival time of mobile sensory data vary due to modality size and network dynamics, which can lead to delays (if waiting for slow data) or accuracy decline (if inference proceeds without waiting). Moreover, the diversity and dynamic nature of mobile systems exacerbate this challenge. In response, we present a shift to \textit{opportunistic} inference for asynchronous distributed multi-modal data, enabling inference as soon as partial data arrives. While existing methods focus on optimizing modality consistency and complementarity, known as modal affinity, they lack a \textit{computational} approach to control this affinity in open-world mobile environments. %
\sysname pioneers the formulation of structured cross-modality affinity in mobile contexts using a hierarchical analysis-based normalized matrix. This approach accommodates the diversity and dynamics of modalities, generalizing across different types and numbers of inputs. Employing an multi-modal lightweight Swin Transformer (MMLST), \sysname facilitates real-time and flexible data imputation, adapting to various modalities and downstream tasks without retraining. Experiments show that \sysname significantly reduces inference latency by up to 80.4\% and enhances accuracy by up to 62.1\%, while achieving nearly a 50\% reduction in energy consumption, outperforming status quo approaches. Also, this method can enhance LLM performance to preprocess asynchronous data.

title: Beep: an open-source ADE that runs your coding agents across all your machines
description:
Most of us have more than one machine: a laptop, a build server, maybe a box with a GPU. Coding agents mostly ignore that. They run where you opened them, and moving work to another machine means pushing branches, copying files and starting the conversation again.

We built Beep to fix that for ourselves, and we just open-sourced it under MPL-2.0.

What it does

Syncs your projects between machines. Project files stay in step on every machine you link. The sync is compatible with Syncthing, so it works next to a setup you already have.

Connects machines peer to peer. Machines form an encrypted mesh over iroh. They talk to each other directly. A relay only helps when a direct connection is not possible, and traffic stays end to end encrypted.

Runs the agents you already pay for. Claude Code and Codex work with your existing subscriptions, next to OpenCode, Pi and our own harness, Flsh. You pick the machine for each task, and Beep shows your plan usage next to your work.

Gives you terminals everywhere. Persistent terminals on any machine in the mesh, from one window.

There is no account to create and none of our servers sits between your machines.

Why another ADE

The ones we tried had at least one of three problems: they were heavy (300 MB and up), they assumed a single machine, or they added a subscription on top of the ones we already had.

Beep has a Rust core and a Tauri UI. The download is 26 MB on macOS and 31 MB on Windows.

It started as a personal assistant. We dropped that part for now, because the multi-machine control panel was the thing we opened every day.

Try it

You can click through the real UI on sample data, in the browser, with nothing to install: beep.flashmind.com.

To run it for real:

  1. Download Beep and open it.
  2. Choose Set up all. It installs what is missing (Git, Claude Code, Codex) and signs you in.
  3. Use Add a machine to link your second machine.

Current limits

  • Desktop builds: Apple silicon Macs, Windows x64 and Linux x64. No Intel Mac build.
  • The Linux AppImage is 133 MB.
  • The phone app is still in testing. It pairs as an observer: it hosts no projects and runs no code.

Feedback

Issues and PRs are welcome on GitHub. We would most like to hear how the sync and the machine pairing work on your setup.

title: Evolution Under Fire: Evolving Agent Safety Harnesses with Adaptive Injection Stressors
description:
arXiv:2611.22583v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Tool-using language-model agents must act on information from untrusted emails, webpages, and documents. This creates a central security challenge: malicious instructions and legitimate task directives can arrive through the same interaction channel. Existing defenses are largely hand-designed and static, making further improvements dependent on repeated manual redesign. We introduce Evolution Under Fire, a staged framework that couples safety-harness evolution with adaptive stressor evolution. Utility-constrained, Pareto-scheduled tree search evolves complete executable safety harnesses from execution evidence while keeping the task model, benchmark, tools, and evaluator fixed. Adaptive stressor evolution then discovers utility-preserving attacks that guide a subsequent stage of harness evolution. On AgentDyn with GPT-4o-mini, an evolved harness reduces attack success from 50.4% to 3.0%, improves clean and attacked utility over the initial harness, and offers a stronger security-utility trade-off than reproduced defenses. On Agent-SafetyBench with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, harness evolution reduces attack success from 82.6% to 62.0% while retaining helpfulness and runtime validity. Evolved harnesses also transfer without further evolution to Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, reducing attack success from 32.1% to 0.9% while improving attacked-task utility.
