title: Cloud Rightsizing: How to Choose a Smaller Instance Without Breaking Production
description:
Or how to stop paying for CPU cores that spend most of their lives doing absolutely nothing.

Cloud infrastructure has a funny habit: making it bigger is easy, making it smaller is scary.

A developer needs a powerful EC2 instance for a temporary workload. You provision 8 vCPUs and 32 GB of RAM. The job finishes, the workload changes, and the instance stays.

Three months later, it's still running, consuming your cloud budget while wondering why nobody gives it anything interesting to do.

I've seen this more times than I'd like to admit.

That's why cloud rightsizing matters. It's not about buying the cheapest possible infrastructure. It's about giving workloads the resources they actually need without turning production into an experiment.

CPU Is Not the Whole Story

Let's say you have an instance with:

  • 8 vCPUs
  • 32 GB RAM
  • Average CPU utilization: 12%
  • Average memory utilization: 38%

The obvious reaction: "Let's move to two vCPUs!"

Not so fast.

Looking at average CPU utilization and immediately resizing an instance is like deciding someone doesn't need a car because you saw them walking yesterday.

Before making a decision, I'd check five things:

  • CPU: Average usage, peaks, and sustained load. A server averaging 12% might hit 85% during batch processing.
  • Memory: Low CPU doesn't mean low RAM requirements. Your application might be keeping a large cache in memory.
  • Network: Some workloads are CPU-light but network-heavy.
  • Historical behavior: A quiet Tuesday isn't a capacity planning strategy.
  • Expected growth: Today's oversized instance might be tomorrow's perfectly reasonable configuration.

One attractive percentage in a dashboard is not an infrastructure strategy.

Why 90 Days of Data Matter

When investigating an oversized resource, I want historical context.

In our Rightsizing implementation, we use 90-day historical usage data in recommendation reporting, including CPU and memory utilization charts. We also consider network activity and associated costs.

Why 90 days?

Because infrastructure workloads have habits. Scheduled jobs, weekly reports, monthly processing, traffic spikes — all those things that nobody remembers until something breaks.

Of course, 90 days isn't a magic number. Seasonal workloads or recently changed applications may require a different observation period.

The goal is simple: make decisions based on actual behavior, not guesses.

A Practical Rightsizing Workflow

Here's how I'd approach an optimization candidate.

1. Find the right resource

Start with a specific cloud account and workload. Collect usage and cost data over a meaningful period.

In Binadox Rightsizing, you can configure the analysis period and apply filters such as cloud region and operating system.

Don't try to resize half your infrastructure on Monday morning. That's a great way to make your incident management team very popular.

2. Understand future requirements

Historical data tells you what happened, not necessarily what happens next.

Define whether the workload is expected to remain stable, grow, or decrease.

An instance that looks oversized today might be perfectly reasonable if traffic is expected to double next month.

3. Compare configurations

Don't choose an instance based on price alone.

Compare:

  • vCPU count and memory.
  • Instance family and capabilities.
  • Historical utilization.
  • Expected monthly cost.
  • Workload requirements.

The cheapest instance isn't necessarily the best one.

Reducing RAM from 32 GB to 8 GB might look great on a spreadsheet. Until your application needs 10 GB and starts swapping.

Congratulations, you've optimized your cloud bill and introduced a memory problem.

4. Validate before changing production

Recommendations should be treated as hypotheses, not commandments.

Check for resource spikes, scheduled jobs, application dependencies, and upcoming traffic changes.

Test the proposed configuration outside production where possible. Then monitor latency, error rates, CPU, memory, and network activity.

I'd much rather discover a problem in staging than in an incident report.

From Recommendations to Actual Savings

There's one problem with cloud cost optimization that often gets overlooked.

Finding an oversized instance doesn't mean anyone will resize it.

Someone still needs to review the recommendation, compare configurations, estimate savings, create a ticket, get approval, apply the change, and verify the result.

Meanwhile, engineers have 47 other things to finish this week.

Manually rightsizing cloud infrastructure is tedious. You collect metrics, compare instance types, calculate costs, check historical usage, prepare tickets, and repeat everything for the next resource.

So We Automated the Boring Part

At some point, manually checking every instance starts feeling like a second job.

Open CloudWatch, check CPU, investigate memory, compare instance types, calculate potential savings, repeat for the next resource. And then do it all again next month.

We decided this part could be automated.

That's how we built Rightsizing in Binadox. It analyzes CPU, memory, network activity, and costs, then suggests alternative instance configurations based on historical usage.

You can see what you're running now, what could replace it, how the estimated monthly cost would change, and how the resource behaved over time. Recommendations can also be turned into tickets, with Slack and email notifications to keep everyone in the loop.

The important thing is that it doesn't blindly resize production. Engineers review the suggestions and decide what to apply.

I wouldn't claim that automation eliminates the need for engineering analysis. It doesn't. But it does eliminate a lot of repetitive data collection and manual comparison.

And honestly, I'd rather have our engineers spend that time debugging something interesting than comparing EC2 instance prices in spreadsheets.

That's a much better use of their skills.

title: Can AI Help Explain AI? Effects of Multimodal LLM-Generated Explanations on Perceived Understanding and Perceived Trust in XAI Visualizations
description:
arXiv:2611.21638v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) aims to make machine learning models understandable, yet many XAI visualizations remain difficult for end-users to interpret. Here, we evaluate whether augmenting XAI outputs with textual explanations from multimodal LLMs improves perceived understanding and perceived trust. We conducted a pre-registered within-subject experiment ($N = 128$) across seven decision scenarios and five XAI methods, with and without LLM generated explanations. The explanations improved perceived understanding and perceived trust by 0.35 and 0.26 points on five-point scales (both $p < .001$). The gain appeared in all seven scenarios, did not differ between local and global explanations, and was largest for participants with the least prior XAI exposure. A mediation analysis indicates an indirect effect on perceived trust through perceived understanding. These results suggest that multimodal LLMs can provide a useful interpretive layer for XAI beyond expert audiences.

title: How Much Distribution Shift Can a Clustering Withstand? Exact Split and Merge Certificates for Structured Transports
description:
arXiv:2611.22000v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In clustering, the distribution of the population being clustered is often uncertain or changes over time, so the true distribution may shift away from the nominal distribution used to form the clustering. Once the clustering is committed and each member is assigned to a cluster, such shifts may change the distribution of each cluster. They can make a cluster too spread out for one representative at a given resolution, motivating a split, or bring distinct clusters close enough to share a representative at that resolution, motivating a merge. We make these split and merge events precise using a local stability criterion built on the phase-transition analysis in deterministic annealing. This notion of stability enables us to quantify how robust a clustering is against such events. Furthermore, motivated by applications in which uncertainty and population change are structured, we study shifts whose displacements are restricted to a prescribed subspace. The smallest structured shifts that reach the respective thresholds define the split and merge radii, for which we obtain exact semidefinite programming (SDP) reformulations. The split SDP has only two scalar decision variables. These convex reformulations enable us to combine the radii into a robustness certificate for the full clustering that gives the size of the smallest structured shift that reaches any monitored split or merge threshold.

title: Amazon ECR now supports global authentication tokens for private registries
description:
Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) now supports global authentication tokens for private registries. Previously, you needed to request a separate authentication token in each AWS Region where you push or pull container images. Now, you can request a single token from the AWS Sign-In CreateBearerToken API and use it across all ECR private registries in the same AWS partition.

Teams that run proxy services to route container pulls across Regions, a common pattern for optimizing latency or availability, previously had to request, refresh, and coordinate a separate token for every Region behind the proxy. With global tokens, the proxy manages one token for all Regions in the AWS partition. Global tokens are valid for 12 hours by default, but can be configured to be as low as 5 minutes. These tokens work with the Docker CLI, and the Amazon ECR Docker Credential Helper. Existing regional authentication tokens continue to work as before.

Global authentication tokens are available in all commercial AWS Regions where Amazon ECR is supported. To learn more, see Private registry authentication in the Amazon ECR User Guide.

title: crdt-sync: محرك مزامنة local-first صغير بـ Rust، مع CRDT و sqlite و websocket
description:
شخصان يعدّلان الملاحظة نفسها. أحدهما في قطار بلا تغطية، والآخر على مكتبه. وكلاهما يواصل الكتابة. حين يخرج القطار من النفق، كيف يجب أن تكون الملاحظة؟

الجواب الكلاسيكي أن يكون الخادم هو الحَكَم: كل تعديل يذهب إليه، وهو يقرر الترتيب، والعميل الذي بلا اتصال ينتظر. تطبيقات local-first (المحلي أولًا) تقلب هذا. كل جهاز يحمل نسخة كاملة، والتعديلات تُطبَّق فورًا ودون اتصال، والأجهزة تتبادل التغييرات كلما استطاعت الوصول إلى بعضها. والشرط الصعب: بعد تبادل كل شيء، يجب أن تتطابق كل النسخ، مهما كان الترتيب الذي وصلت به التغييرات.

هياكل البيانات التي تضمن ذلك تسمّى CRDT، أي conflict-free replicated data types. و Automerge و Yjs هما المكتبتان المعروفتان المبنيتان عليها. وهما مكتبتان ناضجتان وفيهما تحسينات كثيرة، فقراءتهما طويلة إن كان هدفك أن تفهم كيف تعمل الفكرة.

crdt-sync محرك مزامنة local-first صغير بـ Rust. المستندات أشجار من CRDT، وراءها سجل عمليات (operation log) و vector clocks. النسخ (replicas) تعدّل دون اتصال، وتخزّن العمليات في sqlite، وتتزامن عبر خادم websocket مبني بـ axum ببروتوكول من رسالتين. ويسمّي الـ README جمهورَيه: المطورون الذين يريدون فهم كيف تعمل تطبيقات local-first من الداخل، ومن يحتاج نقطة انطلاق مدمجة ومقروءة لمزامنة مستندات صغيرة بين أجهزة وخادم يتحكم فيه.

ماذا يقدّم

أربعة أنواع CRDT. المستند شجرة مبنية من هذه:

  • LwwRegister، سجل من نوع last-writer-wins: الختم الأعلى (Lamport، ثم replica) هو الذي يفوز.
  • LwwMap، خريطة فيها سجل LWW لكل مفتاح. الحذف كتابة لـ "لا شيء"، والقيمة قد تكون قيمة بسيطة أو كائنًا متداخلًا.
  • OrSet، مجموعة observed-remove تفوز فيها الإضافة (add-wins): كل إضافة تنشئ وسمًا (tag) فريدًا، والحذف يزيل فقط الوسوم التي رآها.
  • Rga، للنص. كل محرف يُدرج بعد محرف مرجعي، والإدراجات المتزامنة في الموضع نفسه تُرتَّب حسب الختم، والحذف يترك شواهد (tombstones).

سجل العمليات. كل تعديل هو Op له معرّف (replica, seq)، حيث seq يعدّ 1 و2 و3 وهكذا لكل نسخة، ومعه ختم Lamport، والكائن المستهدف، والفعل. ولأن الأرقام التسلسلية بلا ثغرات، فإن vector clock من الشكل replica → highest seq يقول بالضبط أي العمليات تملكها نسخة ما. والسؤال "هل رأيت العملية X" مقارنة واحدة.

التسليم بأي ترتيب. الدالة Doc::apply_remote تقبل العمليات بأي ترتيب وأي عدد من المرات. المعروفة تُهمل. والباقية تنتظر في قائمة حتى تُدمج تبعياتها: العملية السابقة من النسخة نفسها، والكائن المستهدف، والمحرف الذي يأتي الإدراج بعده، والوسوم التي رآها حذف من المجموعة.

بروتوكول مزامنة من رسالتين. الرسالة StateVector(clock) يُجاب عنها بـ Ops(missing)، والرسالة Ops(ops) تُدمج. الطرفان يرسلان الـ state vector عند الاتصال، فجولة واحدة في كل اتجاه تكفي ليصير الاثنان محدَّثين. ثم ينقل الخادم العمليات المدمجة حديثًا إلى كل عميل آخر على المستند نفسه.

ترميز مدمج. أعداد LEB128 varint، وجدول نسخ لكل دفعة حتى يأخذ معرّف العملية بايتًا أو اثنين، وأرقام تسلسلية وأختام Lamport مرمَّزة بالفرق (delta)، واختصارات من بايت واحد لحالتي "الكائن نفسه كالعملية السابقة" و"إدراج بعد العملية السابقة". ويذكر الـ README أن كتابة 1000 محرف تُرمَّز في أقل من 8 KB. والـ decoder يرفض المدخل المبتور أو العدائي دون panic ودون حجز ذاكرة مفرط.

خادم وتخزين. خادم axum يقدّم GET /sync/{doc} كـ websocket بإطارات ثنائية (binary frames)، وGET /docs وGET /docs/{doc} بصيغة JSON. يحتفظ بـ Doc واحد في الذاكرة لكل مستند مفتوح، يُحمَّل من sqlite عند أول استعمال، ويضيف العمليات المدمجة إلى sqlite قبل نقلها. والتخزين جدول واحد، ops(doc, replica, seq, body)، يُكتب بـ INSERT OR IGNORE فيكون الحفظ idempotent.

طريقة الاستعمال

ثبّت الملفين التنفيذيين crdt-server وcrdt-cli من GitHub بواسطة Cargo، أو أضِف المكتبة إلى مشروعك:

cargo install --git https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/crdt-sync --locked
cargo add --git https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/crdt-sync

البداية السريعة في الـ README تشغّل خادمًا وعميلين، لكل عميل قاعدة بياناته المحلية، من نسخة محلية للمستودع:

cargo run --release --bin crdt-server -- --listen 127.0.0.1:3030 --db server.db

# two clients, each with its own local database (works offline)
alias c='cargo run -q --release --bin crdt-cli -- --server ws://127.0.0.1:3030 --doc notes'
c --db alice.db insert title 0 "Meeting notes"
c --db alice.db add tags work
c --db alice.db sync
c --db bob.db sync
c --db alice.db set status draft        # concurrent edits while "offline"
c --db bob.db set status final
c --db bob.db add tags urgent
c --db alice.db sync && c --db bob.db sync && c --db alice.db sync
c --db alice.db show
c --db bob.db watch                     # stay connected, print every remote change
curl 127.0.0.1:3030/docs/notes          # the server's copy as JSON

Alice و Bob كلاهما يكتب status وهو "غير متصل"، و Bob يضيف وسمًا. وبعد المزامنة، يحمل الاثنان المستند نفسه:

{
  "status": "final",
  "tags": ["urgent", "work"],
  "title": "Meeting notes"
}

السجل احتفظ بواحدة من الكتابتين المتزامنتين، وهي نفسها على كل نسخة. والمجموعة احتفظت بالوسمين معًا.

أوامر الـ CLI هي: show، info، set KEY VALUE، del KEY، insert KEY INDEX TEXT، erase KEY INDEX COUNT، add KEY VALUE، remove KEY VALUE، sync، watch.

وكمكتبة:

use crdt_sync::{Doc, ObjId, ObjKind, sync::sync_pair};

let mut a = Doc::new(1);
let (text, _) = a.map_new(ObjId::Root, "body", ObjKind::Text)?;
a.text_insert(text, 0, "hello")?;
let mut b = Doc::new(2);
sync_pair(&mut a, &mut b);            // state vectors, then missing ops
b.text_insert(text, 5, " world")?;
a.map_set(ObjId::Root, "title", "greeting")?;
sync_pair(&mut a, &mut b);
assert_eq!(a.to_json(), b.to_json()); // {"body":"hello world","title":"greeting"}

ما يجب معرفته

قسم الحدود في الـ README طويل وصريح. اقرأه قبل أن تبني على المشروع:

  • لا مصادقة ولا صلاحيات في الخادم. كل من يستطيع الوصول إليه يستطيع قراءة كل مستند والكتابة فيه. شغّله على localhost أو خلف proxy يقوم بالمصادقة.
  • السجلات تكبر بلا نهاية. لا ضغط (compaction)، ولا snapshots، ولا تنظيف للشواهد. والمستند يُعاد بناؤه بإعادة تشغيل سجله كاملًا.
  • النص للملاحظات لا للكتب. البحث في RGA مسح خطي، وهناك عملية لكل محرف.
  • مجموعة صغيرة من الأنواع. لا نص منسَّق، ولا قوائم كائنات، ولا عدّادات، ولا نقل. والإنشاء المتزامن لكائن متداخل تحت المفتاح نفسه يُبقي كائنًا واحدًا (LWW)، والتعديلات على الآخر تُخفى.
  • تحقق محدود من الأطراف. العمليات القادمة من طرف معطوب، والتي تستهدف كائنًا غير موجود أو من نوع خاطئ، تُسجَّل وتُتجاهل. ولا يوجد تحقق ممن يحق له الكتابة بأي replica id.
  • الأمر watch يطبع التغييرات البعيدة فقط. والتعديلات تتم بتشغيلات منفصلة للـ CLI.

ما تم اختباره. الأمر cargo test يشغّل 17 اختبار وحدة، و6 خصائص proptest، و4 اختبارات من البداية إلى النهاية (end-to-end). الخاصية الأساسية هي التقارب (convergence): ثلاث نسخ تقوم بإدراجات وحذوف عشوائية في النص، وإضافات وحذوف في المجموعة، وكتابات في السجل، وتعديلات وحذوف في الخريطة، بينما تُسلَّم مجموعات جزئية عشوائية من سجلات بعضها مخلوطة ومكررة. وفي النهاية يستلم الجميع كل شيء بترتيب مبعثر، مرتين. ويجب ألا تبقى عند أي نسخة عمليات معلّقة، وأن تتساوى الساعات والـ JSON، على 300 حالة. وخصائص أخرى تتحقق من تقارب البروتوكول بمزامنات ثنائية في حلقة، ومن أن النص في نسخة واحدة يطابق نموذج Vec<char>، ومن أن البايتات العشوائية والرسائل المقلوبة بعض بتاتها لا تسبب panic في الـ decoder.

والاختبارات من البداية إلى النهاية تغطي دمج تعديلات عميلين دون اتصال، وخادمًا أُعيد تشغيله يقدّم المستند نفسه من sqlite، وعميلًا متصلًا يستلم التعديلات المنقولة، وعمليتَي crdt-cli تعدّلان دون اتصال ثم تتقاربان. وكفحص إضافي، يذكر الـ README أن كسر قاعدة الترجيح في LWW أو ترتيب الإخوة في RGA يجعل خصائص التقارب تفشل بعد حالات قليلة.

لماذا بنيته

فكرة local-first سهلة القول وصعبة التصديق إلى أن ترى كل قطعة: كيف تُعرَّف العملية، ولماذا يكفي vector clock لمعرفة ما ينقص الطرف الآخر، وماذا يعني "انتظر التبعيات" في الكود، وكيف يُدمج نص يكتب فيه شخصان في الموضع نفسه. المكتبات الناضجة تجيب عن كل هذا، لكن وسط كثير من التحسينات.

أردت المسار كله في كود صغير يُقرأ من أوله إلى آخره: الـ CRDT، والسجل، والترميز الثنائي، والتخزين، والبروتوكول، والخادم. وأردت أن يُتحقق من ادّعاء التقارب باختبارات خصائص لا ببضعة أمثلة مختارة باليد، لأن الأخطاء في هذا النوع من الكود تسكن في التداخلات التي لا تخطر على بال أحد.

الكود

الكود والاختبارات موجودة على GitHub: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/crdt-sync. الرخصة MIT. اعتبره نقطة انطلاق مقروءة للمستندات الصغيرة، مع الحدود المذكورة أعلاه.

title: Continual-ARC: Measuring Skill Acquisition over a Working Lifetime
description:
arXiv:2611.14505v3 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Agent harnesses have emerged as a promising mechanism for continual learning, alongside test-time parametric learning. However, the current benchmarks have several limitations: they generally focus on a single applied domain, serve each instance only once, and assume a single family of learner, so memory-based and weight-based systems are rarely compared on the same scale. We propose Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream built from the three ARC-AGI editions, whose tasks need no domain knowledge. The same tasks return after dormant gaps with fresh instances, while new tasks keep arriving. On each instance, the learner may pay for demonstrations, submit answers, or act inside the harness, with retries permitted on incorrect submissions, which are paid for. Each instance is scored based on the share of this feedback budget consumed. Since a learner may keep anything between instances, memory-based and weight-based systems are scored on the same scale. After the stream, the learner is frozen and tested on fresh instances of the tasks it met, which measures memorization, and on unseen tasks, which measures generalization. We run an agent harness with frozen weights, with and without persistence, on Qwen3.5-9B and GLM-5.3 Flash, comparing them with two prompting floors, a program-induction method and Qwen3.5-9B's weights trained to imitate GLM-5.3 Flash. Persistence in the harness generally does not improve memorization unless provided with explicit expert guidance. Most harness-based methods still learn less than a floor that simply caches each task's demonstrations, across all models we tested. Harness-based methods gain little or nothing on unseen tasks, whereas weight-based learning shows substantial gains. This opens the door to future weight-based continual learning that could teach models to drive harnesses in new domains.

title: What are the best Shadeform alternatives for buying GPU time?
description:
Shadeform is good at one job: finding a GPU virtual machine across 30+ clouds and launching it from one account, so the right alternative depends on whether you also want someone to finish the run for you. Nodus takes the job itself, runs it on the cheapest capacity that will finish it, and restores its checkpoint if a machine is lost, at $2.60 per NVIDIA H100 SXM hour on the Nodus pricing page.

SkyPilot is the open-source choice for your own cloud accounts, Vast.ai has some of the lowest H100 sticker prices, and Runpod suits per-second container pods. We build Nodus, so read with that in mind. Every fact about another company links to its own docs or pricing page, and every sum is written out.

What does Shadeform actually do for you?

Shadeform is a broker for VMs, not a job runner. Its docs describe a cloud GPU marketplace where you compare availability, price and specs across 30+ providers, then launch through one console, REST API, shade CLI or MCP server. Each instance is a plain VM you SSH into, with an optional startup script, container and persistent volume.

The pricing model is simple. Shadeform's FAQ says it charges the same rate as going direct to the provider, with no extra fee, and passes your payment through. By default it launches into its own account with each provider (Shade Cloud), so you never sign up with them. You can also link your own provider account to spend existing credits or a negotiated rate.

The same FAQ is clear about the limits. Shadeform inherits each provider's SLA, and its Docker launch option starts a container on your VM rather than running a serverless one. On spot instances, a reclaimed machine is terminated, and the guide asks you to checkpoint to a volume, make jobs resumable, and poll and relaunch yourself.

Which Shadeform alternative fits which buyer?

Pick by who handles the run after launch. Shadeform and Vast.ai hand you a machine. SkyPilot and Nodus take a job and keep it going.

Option What you buy Who restarts a lost run H100 price signal Good fit
Shadeform VMs from 30+ clouds, one bill You, from your own checkpoints Single H100 listings $1.66 to $5.99, average $3.47 Finding the cheapest live VM across clouds
Nodus Jobs, Workspaces, Sandboxes, Functions Nodus, from the last committed checkpoint H100 SXM $2.60 Runs that should finish without babysitting
SkyPilot Open-source scheduler over your accounts SkyPilot managed jobs Whatever your clouds charge Teams with several cloud accounts and credits
Vast.ai Marketplace GPU instances You H100 SXM from $1.70, median $1.73 Lowest sticker price, flexible hosts
Runpod Per-second container pods You H100 SXM $4.39 Secure, from $2.69 Community Containers on one provider

Sources: Shadeform H100 directory and FAQ, Nodus pricing and attempts and recovery, SkyPilot managed jobs, Vast.ai pricing, Runpod pricing. Prices checked November 18, 2026.

One caveat on the Shadeform row. Its cheapest single-H100 listing is a PCIe VM, while the Nodus rate is for the H100 SXM, so the cards are close but not identical. Shadeform's directory also changes as providers come and go, and its own cheapest-GPU guide shows that the lowest listed price is not always available.


Shadeform's spread is the story: its listings run from below Nodus to more than twice the Nodus rate.

Is Nodus cheaper than Shadeform for an 80-hour H100 run?

Nodus is cheaper than the average Shadeform H100 listing and dearer than the cheapest one. Take a fine-tune that needs one H100 for 80 hours, priced at each listed rate.

Option Rate per GPU-hour 80 GPU-hours
Shadeform, lowest listing $1.66 $132.80
Vast.ai H100 SXM median $1.73 $138.40
Nodus H100 SXM $2.60 $208.00
Runpod Community, from $2.69 $215.20
Shadeform, average listing $3.47 $277.60
Runpod Secure $4.39 $351.20
Shadeform, highest listing $5.99 $479.20

Each row is the rate times 80: for example $2.60 x 80 = $208.00 and $3.47 x 80 = $277.60. Against the average Shadeform listing, Nodus saves $69.60 on this run. Against the cheapest listing, Nodus costs $75.20 more, if that listing is live when you need it and the run never loses its machine.


At list prices the cheapest VM wins a clean run; the average Shadeform listing costs 33% more than Nodus.

How much rework can a cheaper listing absorb before Nodus wins?

The cheapest rate only stays cheapest while the run goes cleanly. When a VM is lost and your scripts restart from scratch, you pay again for the hours you redo. That gives a simple break-even rule we use when pricing runs:

A listing at price p beats Nodus only if p x (1 + r) is below $2.60, where r is the share of the run you expect to redo.

Solving for r gives the rework each Shadeform price tier can absorb. These assume the Nodus run redoes nothing, which is close to true for a checkpointed Job that loses only the minutes since its last checkpoint.

  • $1.66 listing: 2.60 / 1.66 = 1.566, so it stays cheaper until you redo 56.6% of the run.
  • $1.99 listing: 2.60 / 1.99 = 1.307, so the limit is 30.7%.
  • $2.48 listing: 2.60 / 2.48 = 1.048, so the limit is 4.8%.
  • $2.50 listing: 2.60 / 2.50 = 1.040, so the limit is 4.0%.

On the 80-hour run, 4.0% is 3.2 hours. Losing one machine late in the run without a good resume path wipes out the saving from a $2.50 listing. The $1.66 listing has far more room, which is why it is a fair pick for short, restartable work.


Below about $2 a GPU-hour, a listing can survive real rework; near $2.50, one bad restart erases the gap.

What happens on Nodus when a machine is lost mid-run?

Nodus starts a new attempt somewhere else and restores your files. Its attempts and recovery page describes the sequence. On a reclaim notice, Nodus asks your program for an urgent checkpoint while it prepares a replacement, which starts only once the old machine is provably gone. A machine that stops sending heartbeats gets a replacement prepared after 20 seconds and is declared lost after 60 seconds on shared capacity.

The contract is files, not memory. Your program writes weights, optimizer state and its step counter to /nodus/state, and the checkpoint guide shows the Job spec defaults:

recovery:
  continuity: Checkpointed      # restore the latest checkpoint into each new attempt
  checkpoint:
    paths: [/nodus/state]       # up to 64 absolute paths, all saved in one checkpoint

That is the work Shadeform's spot guide leaves to you: the polling, the relaunch and the restore. For a wider view of the same pattern across providers, see how GPU capacity failover works.

Where is Shadeform the better choice?

Shadeform is the better choice when you want a VM, not a managed run. If your team lives in SSH, tmux and its own scripts, a plain machine with no new job format is the shortest path. Shadeform gets you one from many providers without opening many accounts.

It also wins on price discovery. One API call sorted by price across 30+ clouds is hard to beat for finding the cheapest live H100, and its lowest listing in this check, $1.66, is below the Nodus rate. Short jobs that restart cleanly can bank that difference.

Three more cases favour it. You can link your own provider accounts and launch into them to spend existing credits. Shadeform offers reserved contracts, with a 12-month minimum term on its pricing page. And if you already use SkyPilot, Shadeform has a SkyPilot guide that adds its catalog as one more cloud.

Are SkyPilot, Vast.ai and Runpod better fits for some teams?

Yes, each one fits a narrower buyer than Shadeform or Nodus.

SkyPilot is the closest to Nodus in spirit. It is open source under Apache 2.0 and runs jobs on Kubernetes, Slurm, reserved GPUs or 20+ clouds that you hold accounts with. Its managed jobs recover from preemptions, node crashes and GPU errors, and your job can reload its latest checkpoint. You run the software and keep the provider bills.

Vast.ai is the sticker-price option. Its pricing page lists the H100 SXM from $1.70 per hour, with a 30-day median of $1.73. Like a Shadeform VM, you handle restarts yourself. Our Vast.ai alternatives post goes deeper.

Runpod fits teams that want per-second container pods on one provider. Its pricing page lists the H100 SXM at $4.39 per hour on Secure Cloud and from $2.69 on Community Cloud. See our Runpod alternatives guide for the trade-offs.

Can you connect a Shadeform account to Nodus?

No. Nodus's cloud accounts docs list AWS, GCP, Azure and a set of API-key clouds such as Lambda, Nebius and Runpod, and Shadeform is not among them. If you hold credits with one of the listed clouds, you can connect that account directly and have Nodus spend those credits before Nodus capacity (Beta).

How do you move a Shadeform workflow to Nodus?

Keep your training script and point its saves at /nodus/state. Then submit it as a Job from the project directory, with a dry run first. The commands come from the install and quickstart pages:

pip install nodus-compute
nodus login
nodus run --name finetune --gpu H100 --image nodus/pytorch \
  --max-cost 25 --timeout 8h --dry-run -- python train.py

The dry run uploads the directory and shows the estimate without starting anything. Remove --dry-run to submit. --max-cost sets a hard dollar limit for the Job, and nodus describe job/finetune shows its attempts, placement and cost. Your SSH key, startup script and polling loop go away; the state directory replaces them.

If you want to compare GPU types before committing, a Sweep runs the same Job across several GPUs and reports the cheapest and fastest cell. Our post on running one training job across several GPU clouds covers the wider design.

FAQ

Does Shadeform have more GPUs than going to a provider directly?

No. Its FAQ says it taps each provider's on-demand pool, so what you see on Shadeform is what you would see at the provider. What it adds is one search, one account and one bill across them.

Does Nodus work the same way as Shadeform?

No. Shadeform lists VMs for you to launch and manage, while Nodus runs the work itself. You submit a Job, Function or TrainingJob, Nodus picks the capacity, and recovery and billing are per run.

Do Shadeform spot instances resume automatically?

No. Its spot guide says a reclaimed instance is terminated and marked preempted, and billing stops. Restarting it, on spot or on-demand, is up to your own polling and relaunch code.

Can an AI agent buy GPU time through Shadeform or Nodus?

Both have a hosted MCP server. Shadeform's lets Claude Code, Cursor or Codex find and manage instances. The Nodus server creates resources only after an accepted dry run and runs under the person's own projects and spending limits.

Which data centers do Shadeform GPUs run in?

Shadeform's FAQ says it guarantees all GPUs are in Tier 3 or Tier 4 data centers. Machine SLAs are the underlying provider's, which Shadeform shares on request.

Originally published on the Nodus blog.

title: REEL: Brain-Guided Video Generation and Selection by Reranking Encoder Embeddings with Linear Decoding from fMRI data
description:
arXiv:2611.21907v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Visual brain decoding from functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data has made remarkable progress in recent years, driven by increasingly powerful artificial intelligence (AI) models and the growing availability of large-scale public datasets. However, despite the impressive advances achieved in static image decoding, the reconstruction of videos from fMRI signals remains challenging due to the temporal mismatch between rapidly changing video stimuli and the slow dynamics of the blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) response. We evaluate a Bayesian-inspired proposal-and-rerank strategy on CC2017 and the BOLD Moments Dataset (BMD), using a linear semantic decoder, a pretrained video generator, and three neural encoding streams with ridge readouts and learned pooling in two streams. We refer to this framework as REEL (Reranking Encoder Embeddings with Linear decoding). Compared with a single generated candidate, reranking increases mean Video 50-way accuracy from 0.2359 to 0.2434 across three CC2017 participants and from 0.3653 to 0.3920 across ten BMD participants. These findings suggest an alternative and conceptually simpler strategy for improving video brain decoding, highlighting the potential of our approach as a complementary direction to increasingly complex pipelines.

title: Cost culture is not a finance initiative
description:
It's not a quarterly review. It's not an optimization project. It's not something you do when the bill gets uncomfortable

It's the way a team thinks about resources by default

When an engineer spins up a new service and the first question they ask is "what will this cost to run and is that justified by what it delivers" - that's cost culture

When a developer sets a log retention policy without being asked because they know unretained logs are waste - that's cost culture

When a team lead reviews the impact on the cloud bill as part of the definition of done for a new feature - that's cost culture

The difference between teams with cost culture and teams without it is not that the first group cares about money more

It's that the first group has made cost visibility a default condition of how they work

You can't have cost culture without visibility. If engineers can't see what their services cost, they can't factor cost into their decisions. The information isn't there

You can't have cost culture without ownership. If cloud costs belong to "the company" or "DevOps" or "whoever handles billing", they belong to nobody. Cost culture requires cost ownership at the service level, the feature level, the team level

You can't have cost culture without psychological safety. If the only time cost gets discussed is when the bill is already too high, engineers learn that cost conversations are bad news conversations. They stop raising the issues they see early because raising an issue means being associated with a problem

Cost culture is built when people feel safe flagging inefficiencies before they become expensive

When the finding is celebrated, not interrogated

When "I found $800 a month we're wasting on this forgotten service" is received as a win, not a question about how it got there

The environment shapes the behavior

Build the right environment and the behavior follows

title: TIBECG: Temporal Information Bottleneck for Lead-Specific Demographic Privacy in ECG Waveform Release
description:
arXiv:2611.21694v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Transmitting an electrocardiogram (ECG) waveform can expose demographic information beyond an intended diagnostic task. We evaluate TIBECG, an architectural temporal information bottleneck, on individual leads extracted from hospital twelve-lead recordings. A 2,302,337-parameter processor varies its latent length while retaining the same nine-score consistency objective, without age or sex labels in protector fitting. Across 6,386 recordings, ten folds, 12 leads and 21 lengths, retrospective selections retained at least 95% of each lead's clean macro-F1. Their weaker age/sex interval gain exceeded the best eligible conventional transformation on all leads, by a median 22.08 percentage points. The implemented sampling-rate comparison shows that direct downsampling usually suppresses demographic inference more strongly but at a larger loss of diagnostic utility, whereas TIBECG favors utility preservation. Selection stability also varies by lead. Lower latent Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence does not reliably rank residual sex leakage at a fixed length. These findings support lead-specific evaluation of waveform processing, not validated consumer deployment or expert-readable reconstruction. When the waveform-input diagnostic classifier is hosted as part of a proprietary cloud service rather than deployed on the device, waveform transmission is required to obtain its scores.

title: A Visual Information Extraction System Using Multimodal Large Language Models for Scanned Cognitive and Behavioral Assessments
description:
arXiv:2611.22252v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Objective. Paper-based assessments are common in patient care, but handwriting and scanning artifacts make these forms difficult to process at scale. This study proposes a modular, multimodal LLM-based system with human oversight for extracting fields and scores. We conducted a qualitative analysis of the use of LLMs for hand-drawing analysis.
  Materials and Methods. The system processes cognitive assessments (i.e., MMSE, MoCA, Mini-Cog) and the NICHQ Vanderbilt Assessment using two modules: 1) a form classifier that assigns a scanned page to a form type, followed by a corresponding 2) score extractor that extracts fields and scores into a schema. A human-in-the-loop design utilizing dual-model validation engages human annotators when two LLMs disagree, limiting manual review to challenging pages only.
  Results. End-to-end accuracy for cognitive assessments was 88%, with most form types exceeding 90%. For the NICHQ Vanderbilt, overall accuracy reached 97.5%, with all form types above 96%. The human-in-the-loop design further improved cognitive assessment accuracy to 97.5% while reducing manual work by 63.8%. In the Mini-Cog Clock Drawing task, qualitative analysis showed that 62.3% of all extraction errors stemmed from ambiguous drawing, in which cases the LLM provided reasonable readings.
  Discussion. Compared to current manual data extraction, our LLM-based system reduces processing time by 10 to 20 times and costs by over 12 times. The modular design allows seamless expansion to additional form types.
  Conclusion. Our system provides an accurate, scalable, and cost-efficient solution for structuring data trapped in handwritten paper forms for clinical decision support.

title: A Lightweight TypeScript Router for Building Modern Backend Applications
description:
Introducing Xanout: A Lightweight TypeScript Router for Building Modern Backend Applications

I've been working on Xanout, a lightweight, TypeScript-first server router designed to make backend development simpler and more flexible.

The idea behind Xanout is straightforward: provide developers with a clean routing system built around web standards without introducing unnecessary complexity.

What is Xanout?

Xanout is a server-side routing library for building HTTP applications and backend services.

It provides a simple foundation for handling HTTP requests, defining routes, and organizing server-side application logic.

What can you build with Xanout?

Xanout can be used as a foundation for building:

  • REST APIs — Create structured APIs for web and mobile applications.
  • Authentication systems — Implement login, registration, authorization, and session-based authentication.
  • Backend services — Build application backends and business logic.
  • API gateways — Organize and manage HTTP endpoints.
  • Microservices — Develop lightweight HTTP-based services.
  • Middleware-driven applications — Handle authentication, logging, validation, error handling, and request processing.

Why Xanout?

Some of the ideas behind the project:

  • TypeScript-first development.
  • Lightweight routing architecture.
  • Web-standard APIs and interfaces.
  • Flexible middleware handling.
  • Simple and developer-friendly API design.

I want developers to focus on building their applications rather than dealing with unnecessary framework complexity.

Project Links

  • Website & Documentation: https://xanout.devnax.com/
  • GitHub Repository: https://github.com/devnax/xanout

What's Next?

Xanout is still evolving. I'm working on improving its architecture, developer experience, and overall capabilities.

If you're interested in TypeScript, backend development, or open-source projects, I'd appreciate your feedback.

Feel free to explore the project, share your thoughts, or contribute.

Thanks for reading!

title: What Does an Agent Need? Bundle-Aware Agent Resource Composition
description:
arXiv:2611.22030v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: An agent resource's value depends on its backbone and companion resources and is known only after execution. Token-based generators remain tied to their training catalog, while independent resource scoring misses complementarities and reused bundles target other tasks. We formulate Task-Conditioned Agent Resource Composition (AgentComposition): jointly selecting a backbone model and a tool-skill bundle to maximize end-to-end execution utility. Our Retrieval-Grounded Bundle-Aware Agent Generation retrieves candidate resources and past configurations of similar tasks. A fine-tuned generator reads resource descriptions and recombines candidates through constrained beam search, allowing new resources without retraining. A bundle-aware critic ranks complete configurations using a large language model (LLM) teacher and historically successful configurations as execution proxies, and adapts to execution feedback when available. We evaluate reference recovery, offline execution with judged and native rewards, and online recommendation with real execution, building AgentSelect-Exec with 5,060 executed configurations. Our method recovers the complete reference configuration within ten candidates for 67.73% of AgentSelect queries, nearly twice the strongest baseline, and leads all baselines on SkillsBench. The proxy-trained critic raises the top-ranked agent's execution score from 7.58 to 8.37 out of 10; execution feedback increases it to 8.78, above the strongest baselines. Four target-domain queries suffice to adapt the generator to SkillsBench. Agents recommended online outperform the strongest baselines under both an LLM judge and native verifiers. These results support learning and transferring joint resource composition from task experience.

title: ReMaRL: Learning to Unmask and Remask in Frozen Diffusion Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.22576v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Masked diffusion language models generate tokens in parallel, and the order in which tokens are unmasked affects final-answer accuracy. Several methods learn unmasking policies from task rewards, but these policies cannot remask earlier predictions. Remasking lets the model correct those predictions using newly generated context. Heuristic rules guide both unmasking and remasking, while supervised remaskers learn to detect token errors. Neither approach directly optimizes these decisions for final-answer correctness. To address this gap, we introduce ReMaRL (Remasking with Reinforcement Learning), a lightweight policy that learns which tokens to unmask, retain, or remask. We train this roughly 0.3M-parameter policy with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) from final-answer rewards while keeping the diffusion model frozen. With LLaDA-8B-Instruct, ReMaRL achieves the highest scores among the compared unmasking and remasking policies within the tested inference budgets of 4-32 model calls on math and 8-16 calls on code.

title: SLED: Sensor SLicing from Edge to Datacenter
description:
arXiv:2611.21937v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Modern sensing systems generate large volumes of heterogeneous data streams from multiple sensor modalities, increasing reliance on datacenters for computation, artificial intelligence/superintelligence (AI/SI) inference, and AI/SI training. Each sensor stream may have different network and compute requirements depending on its type and data volume. However, current wireless systems typically allocate resources at the device level, leading to contention among co-located sensor streams, where bulk data transfers may starve latency-critical telemetry. To this end, this paper introduces Sensor Slicing (SL). SL provides deterministic, medium access control (MAC)-level isolation for individual sensors within a single user equipment (UE) in open radio access networks (O-RAN). Using agentic coding techniques, SL is implemented in two O-RAN-compliant packages, reducing development time by 400 times (2 h 40 min [OCUDU] vs. 6.5 weeks [OAI]), 228-fold fewer human prompts (4 vs. 913), and less than half the tokens (0.64B vs. 1.43B). An associated end-to-end framework, SLED, is implemented to establish per-sensor radio and network isolation across edge, campus, and remote high-performance computing (HPC) tiers. Over-the-air wireless experiments demonstrate that while conventional network slicing causes critical delays to increase more than 2,300-fold under high traffic load, SLED maintains stable latency. Scaling evaluations on the two RAN stacks show that throughput remains within 0.9% and 1.4% of expected allocations even as the number of sensor slices increases. The results demonstrate that SLED preserves latency-critical telemetry while effectively utilizing resources across the sensor-to-HPC pipeline. The SLED software and evaluation datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/UNL-CPN-Lab/SLED-Sensor-SLicing-from-Edge-to-Datacenter.

title: pytrends 429 TooManyRequestsError: why it happens and 3 ways to fix it (2026)
description:
Disclosure: I built the Apify Actor mentioned in fix 3, so I'm biased. Apify links here are referral links. Fixes 1 and 2 don't need it at all.

Your Google Trends script worked yesterday. Today it stops with:

pytrends.exceptions.TooManyRequestsError: The request failed: Google returned a response with code 429

Here is what that error means, what state pytrends is in today, and three ways to get past it, starting with the free ones.

Why it happens

pytrends doesn't use an official API. It sends the same requests the trends.google.com website sends, and Google rate-limits them. When Google answers with HTTP status 429 ("Too Many Requests"), pytrends raises TooManyRequestsError. Google doesn't publish the limit, so there is no safe number of requests per minute to aim for. The same script can work from your laptop and fail from a cloud server or a shared IP.

Two details from the pytrends 4.9.2 source that help:

  • TooManyRequestsError is a subclass of pytrends.exceptions.ResponseError. Catch TooManyRequestsError for 429s only, or ResponseError for any other failed response.
  • Every call is a request. Creating a TrendReq() makes one request (it fetches a Google cookie). build_payload() makes one, interest_over_time() makes one, and related_queries() makes one per keyword. A loop that creates a new TrendReq and a new payload for every keyword makes requests faster than it looks.

Is pytrends still maintained?

No. As of 18 November 2026:

  • The GeneralMills/pytrends repository is archived (read-only). Its last commit is from 22 April 2023.
  • The latest release on PyPI is 4.9.2, uploaded in April 2023.

So nobody is going to ship a fix for the 429s upstream. Google's own Trends API is still an alpha. Its page still says Google is "accepting applications for alpha testers", so you can't count on getting access.

Fix 1: send fewer requests, back off on 429, cache everything (free)

Most 429s go away if you stop sending requests the moment Google pushes back, and stop asking for data you already have:

  • Reuse one TrendReq object instead of creating one per keyword.
  • Batch up to five keywords per payload. pytrends' README allows up to five terms per build_payload. Note that batched keywords share one 0–100 scale (they are compared against each other), which is either exactly what you want or not, depending on the analysis.
  • Back off exponentially on TooManyRequestsError, with some random jitter, instead of retrying immediately.
  • Cache results on disk. Last year's weekly interest doesn't change, so fetch it once. 
import json, random, time
from pathlib import Path
from pytrends.request import TrendReq
from pytrends.exceptions import TooManyRequestsError

CACHE = Path("trends_cache")
CACHE.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
pytrends = TrendReq(hl="en-US", tz=0)   # create once, reuse for every call

def interest(keywords, timeframe="today 12-m", geo="", max_tries=5):
    """Interest over time for up to 5 keywords, cached on disk, with backoff on 429."""
    name = f"{'+'.join(keywords)}_{timeframe}_{geo}".replace(" ", "_").replace("/", "-")
    path = CACHE / f"{name}.json"
    if path.exists():
        return json.loads(path.read_text())

    for attempt in range(max_tries):
        try:
            pytrends.build_payload(keywords, timeframe=timeframe, geo=geo)
            df = pytrends.interest_over_time()
            break
        except TooManyRequestsError:
            wait = 60 * 2 ** attempt + random.uniform(0, 15)   # ~1, 2, 4, 8, 16 minutes
            print(f"429, sleeping {wait:.0f}s")
            time.sleep(wait)
    else:
        raise RuntimeError(f"Still rate-limited after {max_tries} tries: {keywords}")

    data = {kw: {d.strftime("%Y-%m-%d"): int(v) for d, v in df[kw].items()}
            for kw in keywords if kw in df}
    path.write_text(json.dumps(data))
    return data

for batch in (["python", "rust"], ["golang"]):
    result = interest(batch)
    print({kw: list(series.items())[-1] for kw, series in result.items()})
    time.sleep(random.uniform(5, 10))   # pause between batches

I ran this on 18 November 2026. The first run fetched both batches, and the second run read them from trends_cache/ without contacting Google. The wait times are a starting point, not a number Google publishes. If you still see 429s, make them longer.

This is the right fix for notebooks, weekly reports and anything that can run slowly.

Fix 2: pytrends' built-in retries and proxies (free, with a catch)

TrendReq takes retries, backoff_factor and proxies arguments. Its full signature in 4.9.2 is:

TrendReq(hl='en-US', tz=360, geo='', timeout=(2, 5), proxies='',
         retries=0, backoff_factor=0, requests_args=None)

The catch: retries and backoff_factor crash on current urllib3. pytrends builds its retry policy with urllib3's old method_whitelist argument, which urllib3 2.x no longer accepts. On a fresh install (pytrends 4.9.2, requests 2.34.2, urllib3 2.8.0) the first request fails with:

TypeError: Retry.__init__() got an unexpected keyword argument 'method_whitelist'

If you want them anyway, pin urllib3 below 2 in that environment:

pip install pytrends "urllib3<2"

from pytrends.request import TrendReq

pytrends = TrendReq(
    hl="en-US", tz=0,
    timeout=(10, 25),
    retries=2, backoff_factor=0.5,
    proxies=["https://my-proxy.example:8080"],   # a list; HTTPS proxies with a port
)

Things I confirmed in a venv with urllib3 1.26.20:

  • It works: the retry policy is accepted and normal requests go through.
  • Retries cover 429, 500, 502 and 504. When they run out, you get requests.exceptions.RetryError ("too many 429 error responses"), not TooManyRequestsError. If you turn retries on, catch both. (I checked this against a local test server that always answers 429. With retries=2 it was hit three times before the error.)
  • proxies must be a list. The README says only HTTPS proxies work and you need the port number. pytrends moves to the next proxy after each successful response, and drops a proxy from the list if it raises a proxy error while fetching the cookie.

Pinning an old urllib3 can clash with other packages, so keep it in its own virtualenv. Proxies help only if they are IPs Google isn't already throttling.

Fix 3: send only the blocked keywords to a hosted scraper

If you need the data now and don't want to manage proxies, keep pytrends for the requests that work and send only the 429s to a hosted service. I use my own Google Trends Scraper on Apify for this. It costs $0.003 per keyword result ($0.001 per "trending now" item, if you use that mode). Searches with no data and failed searches aren't charged, and users on Apify's Silver and Gold Store discount tiers get 10% and 20% off.

pip install -U pytrends apify-client
export APIFY_TOKEN="your-token-here"   # Apify Console → Settings → API & Integrations

import os
from pytrends.request import TrendReq
from pytrends.exceptions import TooManyRequestsError
from apify_client import ApifyClient

def via_apify(keywords, timeframe="today 12-m", geo=""):
    client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_TOKEN"])
    run_input = {"keywords": list(keywords), "timeframe": timeframe}
    if geo:
        run_input["geos"] = [geo]
    run = client.actor("logicbase_systems/google-trends").call(run_input=run_input)
    out = {}
    for row in client.dataset(run.default_dataset_id).iterate_items():
        if row.get("status") == "ok":
            out[row["keyword"]] = {p["date"][:10]: p["value"] for p in row["interestOverTime"]}
    return out

def get_interest(keywords, timeframe="today 12-m", geo=""):
    pytrends = TrendReq(hl="en-US", tz=0)
    out, blocked = {}, []
    for kw in keywords:              # one keyword per request = each on its own 0-100 scale
        try:
            pytrends.build_payload([kw], timeframe=timeframe, geo=geo)
            df = pytrends.interest_over_time()
            out[kw] = {d.strftime("%Y-%m-%d"): int(v) for d, v in df[kw].items()}
        except TooManyRequestsError:
            blocked.append(kw)
    if blocked:
        out.update(via_apify(blocked, timeframe, geo))
    return out

series = get_interest(["python", "rust"])
print({kw: list(s.items())[-1] for kw, s in series.items()})

Both paths return the same shape, {keyword: {"YYYY-MM-DD": value}}. I ran the snippet on 18 November 2026 both ways: once normally, with pytrends answering, and once with pytrends forced to raise TooManyRequestsError so both keywords went to Apify. The fallback run took about 3 seconds inside Apify and returned two 0–100 weekly series. The latest points were within one of the values pytrends had returned a minute earlier (Google Trends samples its data, so small differences between requests are normal). Two keywords cost $0.006 plus a tiny start fee. On a machine Google isn't throttling, the function never calls Apify at all.

Each row from the Actor also has a summary (average, peak, peak date, latest), related queries and interest by region. The full Google Trends in Python walkthrough covers comparisons, CSV export and trending-now by country, so I won't repeat it here.

Which one should you pick?

Situation Pick
Notebook, weekly report, anything that can run slowly Fix 1: reuse, batch, back off, cache
You already have good HTTPS proxies and can pin urllib3<2 Fix 2: pytrends' retries / proxies
Production job, low or bursty volume, no proxy setup Fix 3: fall back to a hosted scraper for the 429s only

One last thing: a ResponseError with a code other than 429, or an empty DataFrame, is not a rate limit, so slowing down won't fix it. Check your geo code, timeframe string and keyword first.

title: KV-LTM: Persistent Per-Session KV Caches as Long-Term Memory for Personal Assistants
description:
arXiv:2611.21998v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Personal assistants accumulate months of conversations, but today's long-term memory stacks put derivation or selection between a question and its evidence. In a system-level comparison on LongMemEval, two commercial assistants scored well below the same model reading the history offline [1], consistent with, but not isolating, content loss between write and read. We propose KV-LTM: a memory tier storing each session's raw text plus its KV cache under a fixed reader model, answering by restoring cached sessions and appending the question. KV-LTM is complementary to, not a replacement for, retrieval and indexing. Text is the memory of record; the cache is a recompute-free prefill accelerator, degrading gracefully to text. We specify the design: storage record, budget-derived retention, append-only read path, and bounded aggregation. We size it analytically: across pinned BF16 full-attention (GQA) and latent-cached MLA configurations, per-token state spans approximately 31K-328K bytes (the pinned KDA+MLA hybrid differs: approximately 8.1K bytes/token plus a fixed per-session recurrent term), giving approximately 0.34-3.6 TB per user-year at a declared 30K-token/day scenario, against approximately 49 MB of raw text; per-query cost is modelled as regime-conditional transfer, attention, decode, aggregation, and compute. We define an evaluation protocol needing no persistent-cache implementation for logical QA evaluation: per-session prefill emulates valid cache reuse under the same model/input-state contract and ideal arithmetic, with named arms, controlled baselines, and a preregistered reader-model gate; a separate minimal real-cache replay tests numerical equivalence and measures the cost axis, with outcomes not assumed. KV-LTM trades storage for avoided re-prefill compute and write-time fidelity, within a declared retention budget.

title: Thinking Harder Doesn't Lead to Better Choices: Reasoning Effort Increases the Confidence but Not the Correctness of LLM Shopping Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.22033v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous shopping agents that process multimodal product listings (consisting of visual and text data) and recommend purchases on behalf of consumers. Naturally, one might assume that models with more thinking power would make higher-quality purchasing decisions. To test this belief, we ask two questions about such agents: does asking a model to think harder make it choose better products, and does the confidence it reports tell us the likelihood it may be wrong? We benchmark ten frontier models on three product-choice benchmarks built from WebShop, Amazon's SQID and Wayfair's WANDS platforms to see if LLMs with more thinking power actually make better-quality product purchase decisions. Across all three benchmarks, we found that increasing the thinking effort does not increase decision quality in a statistically meaningful way. The same change in thinking effort raises stated confidence at a statistically significant level, so extra thinking buys confidence rather than correctness. We also measure the calibration of these models (how well their reported confidence percentage matches their true correctness percentage) in these tasks and show that most models are not well-calibrated at every effort level. We also find that errors are strongly shared: when one model errs in a task, several others tend to err on that same task. Furthermore, on tasks where several models all err, a large number of them pick the same wrong product.

title: Troubleshooting AI Coding Assistants 2026: Stats & Solutions
description:
Originally published at nlocoding.com

43% of engineers spend more time debugging AI-generated code than writing it.

43%engineers spend more time debugging AI-generated code

AI coding assistants are supposed to save time—yet the reality is often more complicated. With tools like GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, and OpenClaw now everywhere, developers see a 40% reduction in coding time but face recurring headaches: misconfigurations, security risks, and code that needs constant correction. In 2026, troubleshooting AI coding assistants is no longer an edge case; it’s a daily survival skill (learn.ryzlabs.com).

Most troubleshooting in 2026 targets recurring code issues

70% of developers encounter recurring issues with AI-generated code, leading to wasted hours and increased frustration (learn.ryzlabs.com). This is not a minor annoyance: it’s the defining reality for anyone using these tools. Code suggestions that look helpful on the surface can mask subtle errors, bad patterns, or outright breakages. The solution isn’t to stop using AI coding assistants, but to build a habit of systematic review and small-batch testing. You’ll notice the code seems fine—until it isn’t. That’s where discipline beats automation.

⚠️Common Mistake: Trusting AI-generated code without reviewing logic or security. Most problems are repeat offenders.

Misconfigurations are the leading cause of AI assistant errors

67% of developers cite misconfigurations as the top source of errors in AI-assisted coding (learn.ryzlabs.com). This isn’t about some obscure edge case; it’s the default pitfall. Whether environment variables are missing, permissions are set wrong, or integrations are half-done, the assistant’s output becomes unreliable. The fastest fix: double-check configuration before blaming the AI. Configuration drift is the new silent killer of productivity. A single misspelled path or outdated API key, and suddenly the assistant’s magic is gone.

💡Pro Tip: Maintain a checklist for environment and tool configuration. Automate sanity checks in CI wherever possible.

Security flaws in 2026 AI coding agents expose real risks

Recent incidents show security isn’t theoretical. Grok Build exposed thousands of apps, with 94.7% accessible without login (techradar.com). OpenClaw’s privileged access across platforms makes it a potential single point of catastrophic failure (techradar.com). A developer’s worst day isn’t a build error—it’s discovering the AI assistant leaked sensitive data or gave attackers a backdoor. Every integration adds risk. The actionable move: review data flows, restrict permissions aggressively, and never treat AI-generated code as inherently safe. Security theater is out, real auditing is in.

AI coding assistants accelerate work—until structured-output tasks break

AI coding assistants reduce coding time by 40%, making them essential for any modern workflow (learn.ryzlabs.com). But speed isn’t everything. Even the most advanced models, like those recently released by Microsoft and Google, still fail on structured outputs (axios.com; tomsguide.com). Complex APIs, nested data, or intricate conditional logic remain weak spots. The fix is to use assistants for scaffolding or boilerplate, but own the structure yourself. Chasing full autonomy is a mirage. Here’s the thing nobody tells you: sometimes it’s faster to write the tricky parts by hand.

"Even the most advanced AI models fail more often than you think on structured outputs—raising doubts about the effectiveness of coding assistants." — techradar.com

Debugging AI-generated code now takes more time than writing from scratch for many engineers

43% of engineers report spending more time debugging AI-generated code than writing it (learn.ryzlabs.com). This is the paradox: AI tools promise speed, but the debugging process often eats up that gain. The main culprits are silent logic errors, style mismatches, and non-obvious dependency issues. The solution is not to abandon AI, but to treat debugging as a first-class workflow: write tests early, use static analysis, and make every AI commit go through a review—even if it’s just you reading it twice. Blind trust is expensive. Skepticism pays dividends.

AI assistant updates in 2026 drive productivity—but only when maintained

Microsoft’s upgrade to Copilot Chat in Visual Studio improved task completion rates from 103 to 124 out of 157 coding tasks (windowscentral.com). Yet, many assume once the assistant is set up, no further attention is needed. Updates matter: they patch vulnerabilities, boost accuracy, and widen the range of supported workflows. Skipping them is like running old antivirus software—it might look fine until it fails catastrophically. Always check for updates, and schedule reviews to catch deprecations before they bite.

The AI coding assistant tool landscape: comparison table

Tool Specialty Notable Feature
GitHub Copilot Code Suggestions Integrated with Visual Studio Code
Claude Code Code & PC Troubleshooting System diagnostics on Windows/macOS
OpenClaw Multiplatform Assistant Privileged access across apps
Grok Build App Coding Agent Rapid multi-app generation
Kimi AI K2.6 MoE Coding Open-weight expert model

FAQ: Troubleshooting AI Coding Assistants 2026

What is the most common cause of errors in AI coding assistants?Misconfigurations are the leading cause, with 67% of developers citing them as the most frequent source of AI-assisted coding errors.

Are AI-generated code snippets secure by default?No, AI-generated code is not inherently secure. Security flaws can be introduced if the code is not reviewed and tested carefully.

Do AI coding assistants need regular updates?Yes. Regular updates are crucial for fixing bugs, patching vulnerabilities, and improving performance. Neglecting updates leads to security and reliability risks.

Can AI coding assistants fully automate the development process?No. AI coding assistants require human oversight and intervention to ensure code quality, maintain security, and handle complex logic.

Where troubleshooting AI coding assistants goes next

The promise of AI coding assistants is real—40% less coding time is not a fantasy. But the frustrations are just as real: 70% of developers still see recurring issues, and nearly half spend more time debugging than writing from scratch. The lesson is not to reject these tools, but to treat them as powerful, fallible colleagues. Trust, verify, and automate your checks. In 2026, troubleshooting isn’t a chore; it’s the core skill that separates productive teams from those drowning in silent errors. If you’re still chasing the dream of a fully autonomous coding AI, you’re missing the real battle: making the assistant work for you, not the other way around.

title: 5 Database Performance Checks for Mining IT Teams
description:
Our Mining database performance checklist
Enterprise applications, asset management platforms and reporting tools depend on databases that remain available and responsive. A slow application may be caused by inefficient queries, storage contention, missing maintenance or infrastructure capacity rather than an issue in the application itself.
For mining businesses operating across sites and offices, the following checks help IT teams prioritise database reliability.
1. Check query and workload performance
Review slow-running queries, execution plans, locking, wait events and changes in peak usage. Establish a performance baseline for each critical workload and identify whether recent changes have increased response times.
Ask: Can we identify the queries responsible for the largest performance impact?
2. Review capacity and resource contention
Assess CPU, memory, storage latency, disk utilisation and database growth. Check that capacity forecasts reflect seasonal processing, reporting and planned application changes. Cloud database sizing should be reviewed alongside cost.
Ask: Do we know when our critical environments will reach capacity thresholds?
3. Verify backup and restore capability
Successful backup jobs do not prove that recovery will meet business requirements. Test restores, confirm recovery point and recovery time objectives, and verify dependencies such as encryption keys, configuration and connectivity.
Ask: When was the last successful recovery test, and what did it prove?
4. Review patching, versions and privileged access
Identify unsupported database versions, delayed security patches, unnecessary privileges and configuration drift. Plan upgrades around application compatibility, maintenance windows and rollback procedures.
Ask: Which databases present the greatest security or support risk today?
5. Confirm proactive monitoring and ownership
Ensure alert thresholds reflect business-critical services, not just server availability. Document who receives alerts, who investigates them and how incidents escalate outside business hours.
Ask: Would our team detect degradation before users report it?
What to do next
Record each check as Pass, Needs attention or Not assessed. Prioritise systems by business criticality and assign an owner and target date to each finding. title: DSADiff: Data Structure-Aware Diffusion for Crystal Structure Prediction via Mitigating Complexity- and Imbalance-Induced Biases
description:
arXiv:2611.22050v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Crystal Structure Prediction (CSP) is an important step in accelerating the generation and discovery of new materials. In recent years, diffusion-based CSP methods have made significant progress. However, existing models still suffer from generation bias when facing diverse materials spaces, while systematic approaches for tracing the sources of such performance variations remain limited. To address this issue, we propose LAS (Layered Analysis Strategy), a mechanism analysis framework that identifies crystal complexity and elemental composition imbalance as two key factors affecting generation difficulty and further reveals their relationships with model generation performance. Building on these findings, we further propose DSADiff (Data Structure-Aware Diffusion), a data structure-aware diffusion model that transforms the key factors identified by LAS into a unified generation difficulty representation and uses it to jointly drive feature modeling and training strategy optimization. This enables the model to adapt its representation and generation capability to samples with different data structures and difficulty levels, thereby mitigating learning bias across samples. Experiments on three CSP benchmark datasets, including Carbon-24, demonstrate that DSADiff consistently improves both Match Rate and RMSE, with a maximum Match Rate improvement of 9%, surpassing existing state-of-the-art methods and achieving new state-of-the-art performance. This work deepens the understanding of diffusion-based CSP models from the perspective of generation bias and provides a new direction for designing less biased generative models for complex materials spaces.

title: It's My Turn! Interpretable Methods Reveal Developmental Differences from Mother-Child Conversational Dynamics
description:
arXiv:2611.21969v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Understanding conversational interactions between mothers and children is an important challenge for computational behavioral modeling. Existing methods use traditional statistical approaches and subjective measures of conversational dynamics, without incorporating temporal or probabilistic modeling. We developed an interpretable computational framework that combines sequence analysis, information-theoretic measures, and Bayesian hierarchical modeling to characterize temporal conversational dynamics in parent-child play. We applied this framework to interactions from 94 mother-child dyads with two-year-old children. Sequence analysis revealed that dyads with lower language development (as defined by scores on the Bayley developmental test) exhibited more heterogeneous conversational organization and fewer serve-and-return exchanges than higher-development dyads, a reciprocal turn-taking pattern in which one partner initiates communication and the other responds. Mutual information analyses suggested differences in conversational predictability between lower- and higher-development dyads, although the bootstrap confidence intervals overlapped. Bayesian hierarchical models estimated temporal trajectories for maternal consecutive turns, child responses following maternal speech, and overlapping responses; HDIs showed that trajectories differed in whether they excluded 0, but there were no statistically credible differences between the Bayley groups. Overall, these results indicate that children with higher developmental scores have more organized and predictable communication styles, with more ``serve-and-return" patterns with their mothers. These results demonstrate that interpretable computational representations of conversational dynamics capture developmental differences beyond simple measures of speech quantity.

title: AVIF vs WebP vs JPEG in 2026: one photo, same width, real bytes
description:
This is a web performance benchmark of image formats. AVIF came out 51% smaller than JPEG on our test photo at the same 1920 px width. WebP came out 39% smaller. Support is no longer the excuse: 95.35% of users can see AVIF.

We took one 9.8 MB camera photo (4964 × 2782), resized it to 1920 × 1076, and encoded it with the same engine at Auto quality:

Format Bytes vs JPEG
JPEG q85 183.7 KB +31%
JPEG Auto 140.3 KB base
WebP Auto 85.5 KB −39%
AVIF Auto 69.3 KB −51%

Yet almost nobody ships it

The 2025 Web Almanac found only 0.7% of LCP images in AVIF. WebP support sits at 96.74%, AVIF at 95.35% (caniuse, August 2026 data). The gap between "supported" and "shipped" is mostly build tooling.

Three things that trip people up

  1. Quality numbers don't transfer. AVIF q80 is not JPEG q80. On one test image AVIF q80 weighed 159.5 KB, while JPEG q80 weighed 82.1 KB. Tune each format on its own scale.
  2. <picture> order matters. The browser takes the first type it supports, not the smallest file. Put AVIF first.
  3. Measure decode on a cheap phone. We measured bytes, not decode time. AVIF decode costs more CPU, and that lands in LCP's render delay.

The setup we ship 

<picture>
  <source type="image/avif" srcset="hero-800.avif 800w, hero-1920.avif 1920w" sizes="100vw">
  <source type="image/webp" srcset="hero-800.webp 800w, hero-1920.webp 1920w" sizes="100vw">
  <img src="hero-1920.jpg" width="1920" height="1076" alt="..." fetchpriority="high">
</picture>

Are you serving AVIF in production yet? If not, what's blocking you: encode time, CDN, or the CMS?

Method and the full comparison: https://blinkimg.com/blog/avif-vs-webp-vs-jpeg?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=avif-webp-jpeg

title: Beyond Bitwidth: Deployment-Constrained Mixed-Precision Quantization for Multilingual LLM Inference on NVIDIA Blackwell
description:
arXiv:2611.21974v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Low-bit LLM quantization is useful only if a model preserves service-relevant accuracy, executes through supported GPU kernels, and meets measured memory and latency limits. We study Qwen3-8B on NVIDIA B200 with vLLM, including INT2/INT3, GPTQ, NVFP4, and mixed-precision configurations. We verify native packed execution and precision on all 144 fused linear modules and evaluate Korean, English, numerical, and reasoning quality under preregistered gates. Packed INT2 and INT3 execute, but all seven tested INT2 grids degenerate on generation. Isolated module-restoration effects are strongly non-additive; Korean and reasoning sensitivity rankings disagree, and a promising INT4/INT8 development candidate fails independent final evaluation. A configuration with 16-bit activations, 98 NVFP4 weight-only modules, 46 INT8 modules, and an INT8 output head passes all gates on the untouched FINAL-81 set (5,168 items): 5.917 GiB of weight-loading memory (limit 5.98), Korean teacher-correct retention 0.904 (gate 0.90), and TPOT ratio 0.939 relative to BF16. It improves paired accuracy over NVFP4 W4A4 by +1.4 percentage points (Bonferroni-adjusted interval [+0.2, +2.6]), compared with +3.4 points on the selection set. This comparison changes both activation precision and INT8 protection; exploratory analyses suggest that the activation change contributes substantially, but the isolated allocation effect is not established. Final checkpoints were not retained, and bitwise rebuild reproducibility remains unverified.

title: Pathology Randomization for Synthetic Priors and Zero-Shot Detection
description:
arXiv:2611.21975v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Hospital brain imaging archives hold a diverse array of pathology at sample sizes beyond prospective studies, particularly for underrepresented populations and diseases. To unlock uncurated clinical data and scale analysis, methods are needed to detect abnormalities across contrasts and resolutions. Synthetic data has provided robust, contrast-agnostic models for a variety of human neuroimaging tasks in healthy anatomy, but pathology detection and other tasks in clinical settings still require real patient data, contrast-specific models, or disease-specific generators. We propose PathoDraw, a generative model of brain MRI with pathology. A conditional distribution of lesions given the healthy anatomy is drawn into the label map before contrast-agnostic rendering, and a single network estimates healthy anatomy with exact signed intensity deviation of any input scan. The contrast-agnostic 3D UNet learns the healthy labels under the lesion and the signed deviation directly and identifies pathology via robust tissue statistics and learned features, despite no training on real pathology. We show zero-shot detection on public stroke, tumor, and white matter hyperintensity datasets as well as archived clinical data, spanning $T_1$w, FLAIR and $T_2$w at various resolutions under a recent unsupervised anomaly detection benchmark protocol. Our single model exceeds or performs comparably to contrast-specific anomaly detectors trained on real scans and keeps healthy anatomy intact. The same generator trains networks for super-resolution and for registration in the presence of pathology. Our model, robust across acquisition and disease, enables the use of uncurated, archived data for clinical analysis. Our code is available at https://github.com/agr78/Pathology-Randomizer.
