title: crdt-sync: a small local-first sync engine in Rust, with CRDTs, sqlite and websockets
description:
Two people edit the same note. One is on a train with no signal, the other at a desk. Both keep typing. When the train leaves the tunnel, what should the note look like?

The classic answer is to make the server the judge: every edit goes to it, it decides the order, and a client without a connection waits. Local-first apps turn this around. Each device holds a full copy, edits apply immediately and offline, and devices exchange changes whenever they can reach each other. The hard requirement is that after exchanging everything, all copies are identical, no matter in which order the changes arrived.

Data structures with that guarantee are called CRDTs, conflict-free replicated data types. Automerge and Yjs are the well-known libraries built on them. They are mature, optimized libraries, which makes them a long read if your goal is to learn how the idea works.

crdt-sync is a small local-first sync engine in Rust. Documents are trees of CRDTs, backed by an operation log and vector clocks. Replicas edit offline, store operations in sqlite, and sync through an axum websocket server with a two-message protocol. The README names its two audiences: developers who want to understand how local-first apps work underneath, and those who need a compact, readable starting point for syncing small documents between devices and a server they control.

What it does

Four CRDT types. A document is a tree built from these:

  • LwwRegister, a last-writer-wins register: the highest (Lamport, replica) stamp wins.
  • LwwMap, a map with an LWW register per key. A delete is a write of "nothing", and a value can be a scalar or a nested object.
  • OrSet, an observed-remove set with add-wins behaviour: each add makes a unique tag, and a remove deletes only the tags it observed.
  • Rga, text. Each character is inserted after a reference character, concurrent inserts at the same spot are ordered by stamp, and deletes leave tombstones.

An operation log. Every edit is an Op with an id (replica, seq), where seq counts 1, 2, 3 and so on per replica, plus a Lamport timestamp, a target object and an action. Because sequence numbers have no gaps, a vector clock replica → highest seq says exactly which operations a replica has. "Have I seen op X" is one comparison.

Delivery in any order. Doc::apply_remote accepts operations in any order, any number of times. Known ones are dropped. The rest wait in a pending list until their dependencies are integrated: the previous op of the same replica, the object they target, the character an insert goes after, and the tags a set-remove observed.

A two-message sync protocol. StateVector(clock) is answered with Ops(missing), and Ops(ops) is integrated. Both ends send their state vector on connect, so one round trip each way brings both up to date. The server then relays newly integrated operations to every other client on the same document.

A compact encoding. LEB128 varints, a per-batch replica table so op ids take one or two bytes, delta-coded sequence numbers and Lamport times, and one-byte shortcuts for "same object as the previous op" and "insert after the previous op". The README states that typing 1000 characters encodes to under 8 KB. The decoder rejects truncated or hostile input without panicking or over-allocating.

A server and storage. The axum server exposes GET /sync/{doc} as a websocket with binary frames, plus GET /docs and GET /docs/{doc} as JSON. It keeps one in-memory Doc per open document, loaded from sqlite on first use, and appends integrated ops to sqlite before relaying them. Storage is one table, ops(doc, replica, seq, body), written with INSERT OR IGNORE so saving is idempotent.

How to use it

Install the two binaries, crdt-server and crdt-cli, from GitHub with Cargo, or add the library to a project:

cargo install --git https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/crdt-sync --locked
cargo add --git https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/crdt-sync

The README's quick start runs a server and two clients, each with its own local database, from a clone of the repository:

cargo run --release --bin crdt-server -- --listen 127.0.0.1:3030 --db server.db

# two clients, each with its own local database (works offline)
alias c='cargo run -q --release --bin crdt-cli -- --server ws://127.0.0.1:3030 --doc notes'
c --db alice.db insert title 0 "Meeting notes"
c --db alice.db add tags work
c --db alice.db sync
c --db bob.db sync
c --db alice.db set status draft        # concurrent edits while "offline"
c --db bob.db set status final
c --db bob.db add tags urgent
c --db alice.db sync && c --db bob.db sync && c --db alice.db sync
c --db alice.db show
c --db bob.db watch                     # stay connected, print every remote change
curl 127.0.0.1:3030/docs/notes          # the server's copy as JSON

Alice and Bob both set status while "offline", and Bob adds a tag. After syncing, both hold the same document:

{
  "status": "final",
  "tags": ["urgent", "work"],
  "title": "Meeting notes"
}

The register kept one of the two concurrent writes, the same one on every replica. The set kept both tags.

The CLI commands are show, info, set KEY VALUE, del KEY, insert KEY INDEX TEXT, erase KEY INDEX COUNT, add KEY VALUE, remove KEY VALUE, sync and watch.

As a library:

use crdt_sync::{Doc, ObjId, ObjKind, sync::sync_pair};

let mut a = Doc::new(1);
let (text, _) = a.map_new(ObjId::Root, "body", ObjKind::Text)?;
a.text_insert(text, 0, "hello")?;
let mut b = Doc::new(2);
sync_pair(&mut a, &mut b);            // state vectors, then missing ops
b.text_insert(text, 5, " world")?;
a.map_set(ObjId::Root, "title", "greeting")?;
sync_pair(&mut a, &mut b);
assert_eq!(a.to_json(), b.to_json()); // {"body":"hello world","title":"greeting"}

Things to know

The README's limitations section is long and plain. Read it before you build on this:

  • No authentication or authorization on the server. Anyone who can reach it can read and write every document. Run it on localhost or behind an authenticating proxy.
  • Logs grow forever. There is no compaction, no snapshots and no tombstone garbage collection. A document is rebuilt by replaying its whole log.
  • Text is for notes, not books. RGA lookups are linear scans, and there is one op per character.
  • A small set of types. No rich text, lists of objects, counters or moves. Concurrent creation of a nested object under the same key keeps one object (LWW), and edits made to the other are hidden.
  • Limited peer validation. Ops from a buggy peer that target a missing object or the wrong kind are logged and ignored. There is no check of who may write which replica id.
  • watch only prints remote changes. Edits are made with separate CLI invocations.

What is tested. cargo test runs 17 unit tests, 6 proptest properties and 4 end-to-end tests. The main property is convergence: three replicas perform random text inserts and deletes, set adds and removes, register writes and map sets and deletes, while random subsets of each other's logs are delivered shuffled and duplicated. In the end everyone receives everything in a scrambled order, twice. All replicas must have no pending ops, equal clocks and equal JSON, over 300 cases. Other properties check protocol convergence over pairwise syncs in a ring, that single-replica text matches a Vec<char> model, and that random bytes and bit-flipped messages never panic the decoder.

The end-to-end tests cover offline edits from two clients merging, a restarted server serving the same document from sqlite, a live client receiving relayed edits, and two crdt-cli processes that edit offline and converge. As a sanity check, the README notes that breaking the LWW tie-break or the RGA sibling ordering makes the convergence properties fail within a few cases.

Why I built it

The idea behind local-first is easy to state and hard to trust until you have seen every piece: how an operation is identified, why a vector clock is enough to know what a peer is missing, what "wait for dependencies" means in code, and how text can merge when two people type at the same position. The mature libraries answer all of this, but inside a lot of optimization.

I wanted the whole path in one small codebase that can be read end to end: the CRDTs, the log, the binary encoding, the storage, the protocol and a server. And I wanted the convergence claim to be checked by property tests and not by a few hand-picked examples, because the bugs in this kind of code live in the interleavings nobody thinks of.

Get the code

The source and the tests are on GitHub: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/crdt-sync. It is MIT licensed. Treat it as a readable starting point for small documents, with the limits listed above.

Originally published at abdeldjalilchougui.biz.

title: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights
description:
arXiv:2611.21885v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Language models are trained once, frozen and deployed: improving one again takes another training run, and a prompt, a scaffold or extra computation at inference is gone once the task ends. A frontier model has been shown to edit the weights of a much smaller one. We ask whether a model can rewrite its own weights to make itself better, and find that it can, by its own reasoning, with no gradients and no training; we call this self-rewriting. Given its weights, graded answers and the ability to run itself, a 27B model diagnoses its failure and edits the weights behind it. It surpasses itself: its own edit makes it 6.6 points more accurate on 490 problems it never saw, in a test fixed in advance, and another session's edit also makes it significantly better. It keeps getting better: it submits an edit only when its own tests support it, each edit replacing the last, and over its first eight such sessions its accuracy only rises. Unlike test-time scaling, the gain persists in its weights and adds no cost per answer; unlike training, it needs no pre- or post-training infrastructure, only an open model and hours on one GPU. It repairs a damaged copy of itself: it locates the corrupted matrix and rewrites it with values of its own, never reading the undamaged weights; found on text math problems alone, the repair lifts the copy on six image benchmarks it never saw from 7% to 70% accuracy, 83% of the undamaged model's. And the ability emerges with scale: across four sizes of one family, the 2B model makes no edit and the 4B and 9B models break themselves; only the 27B model works on itself as a human would, comparing its hidden states on answers that finish and on answers that run out of tokens, weakening the direction that separates them. Like a human, a model need not separate training from inference; improving a language model may come to take a conversation rather than a training run.

title: My dual-axis chart was lying about zero
description:
A commenter on Reddit looked at one of my charts for about ten seconds and found a bug I had shipped to everyone.

The chart was a combo chart: revenue as bars on the left axis, profit margin as a line on the right axis. Pretty standard dashboard stuff. Their question was simple: "where is zero on the right axis?"

It wasn't where the bars started.

What went wrong

Two axes on one chart means two sets of tick labels sharing one set of grid lines. My first version got half of that right. The right axis picked the same number of ticks as the left, each one a round number, so every label sat neatly on a grid line.

What it never did was force the two zeros onto the same line.

Take revenue from $0 to $62K and a margin between −10% and 35%:

  • Left axis: 0, 20K, 40K, 60K, 80K (five lines)
  • Right axis: five lines, round step, must cover −10% to 35%, so: −20%, 0%, 20%, 40%, 60%

Look at the second line. The right axis says 0%, the left says $20K. The bars stand on the bottom line, but the margin's zero floats one line above it.

Now give one month a −5% margin. The dot lands above the bars' baseline. Anyone skimming the chart reads it as "slightly positive". It's a loss.

Every label was a round number, every tick sat on a grid line, and the chart was still wrong.

The fix

When the chart starts at zero, both axes now get the same number of steps below zero and the same number above it, the most either axis needs. Zero becomes one shared grid line, by construction.

The left axis keeps its own round step. The right axis tries a few candidates (1, 2 or 5 times a power of ten) and keeps the one with the best score:

// fewer lines is calmer, but an axis its values barely use squashes the line
const filled = (hi - lo) / (step * (below + above))
const score = below + above + 4 * (1 - filled)

The first term prefers fewer grid lines. The second punishes a step so large that the data only fills a sliver of the axis, which would flatten the line into a near-straight squiggle.

Same data, after the fix:

  • Left: −20K, 0, 20K, 40K, 60K, 80K
  • Right: −10%, 0%, 10%, 20%, 30%, 40%

Both zeros sit on one line, and the −5% month now dips below it, where a loss belongs.

Two smaller changes came with it:

  • The solid grid line moved from the bottom of the chart to zero, where the bars actually stand.
  • alignZero={false} turns it off, for the rare chart where two independent domains really are what you want.

What I took from it

Tests wouldn't have caught this. Every output was a valid, round, evenly spaced set of ticks. The bug only exists when you read the chart the way a person does, comparing one axis against the other.

So: show your charts to someone with negative numbers in their data. Mine all had happy, positive margins.

The component is free and MIT if you want to poke at it: https://dashral.com/components/combo-chart?utm_source=devto&utm_campaign=zero-baseline

title: MAI Code 2 y MAI Code 2 Flash: los modelos de programación con IA de Microsoft llegan a GitHub Copilot con precios promocionales
description:
Microsoft lanzó MAI Code 2 y MAI Code 2 Flash, sus modelos de programación con IA, en GitHub Copilot el 17 de noviembre de 2026: en los benchmarks de la propia Microsoft, MAI Code 2 rinde el 98% de GPT-6.1 Sol al 40% del costo, con precios promocionales en Copilot desde $0.05 por millón de tokens de entrada.

Qué cambió

Microsoft anunció MAI Code 2 y MAI Code 2 Flash el 17 de noviembre de 2026, en Ignite, como sus modelos de programación con IA para el trabajo empresarial diario, y ambos ya están en GitHub Copilot. MAI Code 2 está pensado para llevar código a producción: depuración profunda, implementación en varios archivos, razonamiento sobre todo el repositorio e interfaces de usuario. MAI Code 2 Flash es el hermano de alto volumen para explicaciones de código, ediciones puntuales, correcciones rutinarias e iteración rápida. El registro de cambios de GitHub sitúa MAI Code 2 en los planes Copilot Pro, Pro+, Max, Business y Enterprise, y MAI Code 2 Flash en todos los planes, incluidos Free y Student, para suscriptores elegibles con planes anuales. MAI Code 2 Flash también está en vista previa de acceso limitado en Microsoft Foundry.

En sus evaluaciones, promediadas sobre DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal Bench 2.1, SWE-Atlas y FrontierCode v1.1, MAI Code 2 rinde el 98% de GPT-6.1 Sol al 40% del costo, y el 96% de Claude Opus 5.5 al 5% del costo; en evaluaciones ciegas de frontend, los revisores lo prefirieron frente a GPT-6 Sol el 67% de las veces. MAI Code 2 Flash iguala a GPT-6 Luna al 65% del precio y a Claude Haiku 5.5 al 20%, en DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal Bench 2.1 y SWE-Atlas (cifras de Microsoft). GitHub lista en su documentación de precios de Copilot las tarifas promocionales hasta el 17 de mayo de 2027: MAI Code 2 a $0.50 de entrada / $2.50 de salida por millón de tokens, y Flash a $0.05 / $0.25, el doble después. Microsoft dice que aún no están afinados para investigación científica fundamental ni trabajo agéntico de muy largo horizonte, y al 17 de noviembre de 2026 Artificial Analysis aún no publicaba páginas de ninguno.

Cifras

Métrica MAI Code 2 MAI Code 2 Flash
Precio de entrada por 1M de tokens (promocional) $0.50 $0.05
Precio de salida por 1M de tokens (promocional) $2.50 $0.25
Rendimiento 98% de GPT-6.1 Sol al 40% del costo (4 benchmarks) Iguala a GPT-6 Luna al 65% del precio (3 benchmarks)
Tarifas promocionales hasta 17 de mayo de 2027 17 de mayo de 2027

Por qué importa

Si tu equipo ya paga GitHub Copilot, MAI Code 2 te da una opción predeterminada más barata para el trabajo diario que llena la mayoría de los sprints —depuración, refactors y cambios en varios archivos— con tarifas promocionales muy por debajo de los precios insignia, sin proveedor nuevo ni migración. Envía las correcciones rutinarias y las explicaciones a MAI Code 2 Flash, reserva MAI Code 2 para el trabajo de producción, y tus créditos de Copilot rinden más durante el mes; solo ten en cuenta que los modelos apuntan a la programación empresarial diaria, no a problemas de investigación ni ejecuciones autónomas muy largas.

title: Measuring Human-AI Alignment as an Early Indicator for Effective Collaboration in Hybrid SE Teams
description:
arXiv:2611.21633v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: As AI agents increasingly integrate into software engineering (SE) processes, ensuring effective collaboration in these hybrid teams becomes a critical challenge. While existing metrics focus on observing dynamic run-time performance, there is a lack of systematic, static measurements for early human-AI alignment -- the degree to which an AI's actions and granularity map to human expectations. This position paper proposes a research agenda to develop an SE-specific alignment metric suite drawing principles from software architecture, organizational psychology, and human-computer interaction. Furthermore, it outlines a validation methodology using concepts and techniques from business process monitoring (BPM) and introduces static assessment tools leveraging declarative BPM languages to ensure agents adhere to specific project constraints.

title: WHBench: Evaluating Frontier LLMs with Expert-in-the-Loop Validation on Women's Health Topics
description:
arXiv:2604.00024v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used for medical guidance, but women's health remains under-evaluated in benchmark design. We present the Women's Health Benchmark (WHBench), a targeted evaluation suite of 47 expert-crafted scenarios across 10 women's health topics, designed to expose clinically meaningful failure modes including outdated guidelines, unsafe omissions, dosing errors, and equity-related blind spots. We evaluate 22 models using a 23-criterion rubric spanning clinical accuracy, completeness, safety, communication quality, instruction following, equity, uncertainty handling, and guideline adherence, with safety-weighted penalties and server-side score recalculation. Across 3,102 attempted responses (3,100 scored), no model mean performance exceeds 75 percent; the best model reaches 72.1 percent. Even top models show low fully correct rates and substantial variation in harm rates. Inter-rater reliability is moderate at the response label level but high for model ranking, supporting WHBench utility for comparative system evaluation while highlighting the need for expert oversight in clinical deployment. WHBench provides a public, failure-mode-aware benchmark to track safer and more equitable progress in womens health AI.

title: InfuseLoop: Cross-Trajectory Latent Injection for Scalable Parallel Looped Transformers
description:
arXiv:2611.22426v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Parallel Looped Transformers (PLTs) use otherwise idle decoding compute by overlapping recurrent iterations. However, vanilla PLTs scale poorly with depth: they exhibit training-loss spikes, and their quality gains shrink as more loops are added. The benefit of additional loops depends on the information available to each iteration, so we examine whether the existing computational dependencies limit effective depth scaling. We find that only the preceding in-trajectory state is passed across loop boundaries, even though completed cross-trajectory representations are already available. Based on this finding, we propose InfuseLoop, a cross-trajectory latent injection mechanism. It aggregates causally available hidden states from later prediction trajectories through lightweight attention residuals. This design preserves token-parallel training and concurrent loop execution, and requires only $O(Rd)$ additional hidden-state storage. Experiments show that InfuseLoop eliminates training-loss spikes and improves validation-loss scaling up to eight loops. At eight loops, InfuseLoop reduces perplexity by 3.4--17.1% relative to vanilla PLTs and by 10.5--37.3% relative to the non-looped baseline. It also improves average downstream accuracy by 0.84 and 1.99 percentage points over these two baselines. InfuseLoop incurs only 0.3% decoding time over vanilla PLTs and 23.3% over the non-looped baseline, while keeping the same logical KV-cache footprint as vanilla PLTs.

title: Cancellation-Free Constrained SquareCB for Safe Controller Selection
description:
arXiv:2611.21880v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study constrained contextual bandits, in which a learner chooses one of $K$ actions in each round to minimize loss while keeping the expected cost of its play below a budget. Existing reductions to online regression weight the cost by a Lagrange multiplier learned from past constraint residuals, so slack in some rounds can offset violations in others. We instead run SquareCB proposed in \citep{foster2020beyond} with a rectified weight on the cost: it is zero when the estimated cost is within the budget, and otherwise just large enough to bring it back to the budget. Under realizability and Slater's condition with margin $\delta$, the algorithm attains regret $O(\sqrt{KT\,\mathrm{Reg}_{\mathsf{Sq}}(T)}/\delta)$ and cancellation-free violation $\sum_t(V_c^{p_t}-b)^+=O(\sqrt{KT\,\mathrm{Reg}_{\mathsf{Sq}}(T)})$, where $\mathrm{Reg}_{\mathsf{Sq}}$ is the error of the regression oracle. The same bounds hold when the budget must be met in every context, potentially adversarially chosen contexts. In controller selection for a safe-control-gym quadrotor and a BOPTEST building, the violation is 6 to 9 times lower than that of primal-dual and virtual-queue baselines, with a lower or comparable regret.

title: Computed Permutation Trellis Coding: Near-Optimal Quantization from Two Multiplications and a 64-Byte Table
description:
arXiv:2611.22019v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: We propose Computed Permutation Trellis Coding (CPTC), a low-bit quantization format for tensors written once and read many times. Formats that round each value on its own, such as INT4 and FP4, waste a large part of their bits against the information-theoretic ideal. Trellis codes recover this loss by encoding values jointly, but prior decoders either need a large lookup table for their best quality or compute values with a hash that restricts what they can decode. CPTC's decoder multiplies its state by two coefficients and adds the top bits of the products to index a 64-byte table. Because that sum is not uniformly distributed, the rarely used ends of a small table can hold values far out in the tails. One decoder serves every bit width from 1 to 6, reproduces the standard integer and floating-point formats exactly, and comes within 0.07 bits of the ideal at 4 bits. It matches a random-permutation trellis code whose table is thousands of times larger, and exceeds every QTIP codebook. In LLM weight quantization without fine-tuning, CPTC has the lowest KL divergence to the unquantized model at every tested bit width on Llama 3.1 8B and 70B Instruct against QTIP's codebooks (by up to 27%). The decoder has been built into the AWS Trainium 4 AI accelerator, where it runs at the throughput of the native FP4 and FP8 formats for a negligible fraction of the systolic array's area. Fused encoding kernels quantize an 8B model's linear layers in under two minutes on one GPU and, in cycle-level simulation, on one Trainium 4 chip.

title: Perception into Imagination: Executable Memory for World Models
description:
arXiv:2611.22294v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Physical agents must use what they previously saw or touched after visibility or contact is lost. Their actions change the implications of these remembered facts. We introduce executable perceptual memory (EPM), a world-model framework that advances explicit perceptual state alongside neural latent dynamics during imagination. Its evolving read-out informs reward prediction, value estimation and policy learning. We align reward inputs with the transitions that produced them and supervise the reward head on open-loop rollouts of recorded actions. On Memory Maze $13\times13$, EPM reaches 30.37 return at 1M interactions, compared with 23.37 when the same evolving read-out informs only policy and value on a common perceptual front end: a gain of 7.00 [3.80, 10.21]. The complete method also improves control on $9\times9$ and in MiniWorld. Probes of remembered, out-of-view arrivals show stronger reward anticipation in both visual implementations. Concentration, tactile recovery and real tactile frames demonstrate complementary roles of remembered facts in imagined-policy training, motion-dependent decisions and sensory-content retention. EPM connects persistent perception to the predicted consequences and learning signals of a world model for Physical AI.

title: Captors can force the PIN. They still can't switch the alarm off.
description:
The short version, for everyone: Kengele is a free safety alarm for activists. If captors force an activist to unlock their phone and say "I'm safe", the alarm now keeps ringing. Only 2 of the activist's 3 trusted contacts can switch it off, and only after seeing or hearing them on a call. The rest of this post shows exactly how, with code you can run yourself.

Kengele is an open-source alarm for activists in East Africa. Ukinyamaza, kengele inalia: "if you go quiet, the bell rings."

Why it exists

  • Amnesty International counts over 83 enforced disappearances around Kenya's 2024 and 2025 Gen Z protests.
  • When someone disappears, how fast the public finds out often decides how fast they are released. Today that depends on someone noticing and phoning around.
  • The closest tool for human rights defenders, Círculo, says on its own site that its service shut down on 15 November 2026. It depended on one organisation's servers.

How it works, in plain words

  1. Before a risky event, the activist sets a time window, for example "2pm to 8pm, check in every 90 minutes".
  2. They check in from their phone. Each check-in goes to 3 to 5 guardians: family, a lawyer, a trusted organisation.
  3. If a check-in doesn't arrive, each guardian's phone raises the alarm on its own. There is no central server, so there is nothing to shut down or seize.

For developers: check-ins are signed, encrypted Nostr events (NIP-17/44/59) sent over public relays. The watcher logic runs on each guardian's device.

The problem this update fixes

Kengele already had a duress PIN: a second PIN that unlocks to a normal-looking screen but quietly raises the alarm. But a captor can force someone to give their real PIN and send "I'm safe". Before this change, that was enough to end the alarm.

The new rule (PR #31)

Once an alarm has gone off (a missed check-in, a panic button or a duress PIN):

Who says "safe" What happens
The activist alone Guardians see "the activist says they are safe". The alarm keeps ringing.
The activist + 1 guardian Not enough. The activist's word never counts towards the vote.
2 of 3 guardians The alarm stands down.

Each guardian also has to speak to the activist by voice or video before their "safe" can be sent. The app enforces this. It isn't just a guideline.

And the activist's "I'm safe" never delays a public alert. If guardians are already confirming the alarm, their confirmations keep counting.

Proof

Without reading code: every change is public. Open pull request #31 to see what changed, when, and the written reasoning. The cover image shows the project's automatic checks (tests) running. Each PASS means the rule held.

For developers: the guardian's all-clear is built by GuardianAllClearEvent, which returns ErrNotVerified unless it receives a record of a voice or video call (body.go#L128-L140). The record stays on the guardian's device and is never sent.

The core test (confirm_test.go#L328):

func TestActivistAllClearAloneEndsNothing(t *testing.T) {
    // After a panic, captors force the activist to unlock with the real
    // PIN and send an all-clear. The alarm must stay, and the release must
    // still happen when a second guardian confirms.
    ...
    o = expect(t, None)(f.clearFrom(t, tl, f.activist.priv, 1, t0, t0))
    if !o.ActivistSaysSafe || o.By != NotCleared || tl.Epoch() != 1 {
        t.Fatalf("activist all-clear ended the alarm: %+v epoch=%d", o, tl.Epoch())
    }
    ...
    // The pending confirmation survived, and the second one releases.
    expect(t, Release)(f.confirm(t, tl, 2, 1, t0.Add(time.Minute), t0.Add(time.Minute)))
}

Run it yourself (needs Go 1.24 or newer):

git clone https://github.com/altradits/kengele
cd kengele
go test -race -v -run 'AllClear|PlusOne|Coerced' ./internal/confirm

Our run (Go 1.26.5, commit 00783f7):

--- PASS: TestSingleCoercedGuardianCannotPublish (0.16s)
--- PASS: TestActivistAllClearAloneEndsNothing (0.09s)
--- PASS: TestActivistPlusOneGuardianIsNotEnough (0.07s)
--- PASS: TestGuardianAllClearNeedsVerification (0.00s)
--- PASS: TestAllClearByTwoGuardians (0.07s)
--- PASS: TestAllClearRaces (0.27s)
--- PASS: TestConcurrentActivistAllClearAndConfirms (0.14s)
ok      github.com/altradits/kengele/internal/confirm   2.142s

What it still can't stop

Being honest about the limits matters more than the feature (threat model §4.5):

  • Captors can pressure the activist during the video call too. Pick guardians who know the activist well, and agree a spoken code word in advance.
  • If 2 of 3 guardians are compromised, they can switch the alarm off. That's the trade-off by design, so pick guardians who don't live, work or get arrested together.

Status and how to help

Kengele is still being designed and is not for real use until an independent security review is published.

  • No coding needed: digital-security reviewers, Swahili translators, and anyone who works with activists and can tell us what we're missing.
  • Developers: Go, Android/Kotlin, Nostr, Bitcoin (miniscript, OpenTimestamps).

Start with CONTRIBUTING.md.

title: Learning Calibrated and Samplable Predictive Distributions of Surface-Ocean $\Delta p$CO$_2$ Using Tabular Diffusion Models
description:
arXiv:2611.21769v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The ocean absorbs almost 30% of anthropogenic CO$_2$ emissions, but quantifying this sink requires estimating surface-ocean CO$_2$ from observations that are sparse in space and time. Most existing machine-learning estimates of this field are deterministic, giving a single value per grid point, with uncertainty approximated post hoc via residuals, ensembles, or prescribed distributions. We instead learn a conditional predictive distribution for each observation: using Treeffuser, a conditional diffusion model with gradient-boosted-tree score functions, we estimate the full predictive distribution of $\Delta p$CO$_2$ (the sea-air $p$CO$_2$ difference) from 13 environmental, spatial, and temporal predictors. On a held-out SOCAT test set, Treeffuser attains the lowest continuous ranked probability score among the uncertainty-quantification methods evaluated (8.229 $\mu$atm) and the coverage closest to the nominal 68% / 95% levels (0.686 / 0.930), while retaining point-prediction skill comparable to a deterministic XGBoost baseline (RMSE 18.4 vs. 17.7 $\mu$atm; $R^2$ 0.77 vs. 0.79). These results show that conditional diffusion can provide well-calibrated, observation-level uncertainties while largely preserving point-prediction skill. Because Treeffuser is generative, its samples can support probabilistic analyses of $\Delta p$CO$_2$; extending this to spatially coherent field reconstruction will require modeling dependence across grid cells and evaluation on spatially held-out data.

title: Speed Insights now measures soft navigations
description:
Speed Insights now measures soft navigations: client-side route changes that update page content without a full reload. This means you can now track performance as users move through your app, not just on full-page loads.

Speed Insights captures LCP, FCP, INP, and CLS for soft navigations and includes these measurements in your Real Experience Score. TTFB is not captured because there is no new document request.

Soft-navigation tracking is enabled by default for all projects using Speed Insights, with no action required. It works with modern web frameworks such as Next.js, SvelteKit, and Nuxt, in Chromium-based browsers.

In your project's Speed Insights dashboard, use the new Navigation Type filter to view All, Hard, or Soft navigation data.

Soft-navigation events count toward Speed Insights Plus usage. Existing Plus customers will receive an email with details about when billing for these events begins. For projects that newly enable Plus, these events are billed from the start.

To disable soft-navigation tracking, set softNavs to false in your application code and redeploy. This option requires @vercel/speed-insights version 2.1.0 or later:

Learn more in the Speed Insights documentation.

Read more

title: How to catch an expiring or broken SSL certificate before your visitors do
description:
Many TLS certificates now live 90 days, and the maximum lifetime for all public certificates is dropping in steps (200 days since March 2026, 47 days by 2029). Auto-renewal handles most of it, until a DNS change, a moved server or a forgotten subdomain breaks the renewal and nobody notices until visitors see a browser warning.

Here is what to check, how to do it for free with tools you already have, and how to run the same checks on a long list of domains.

The four problems to look for

1. Expiry. The certificate is past its end date, or will be soon. You want a warning weeks ahead, not on the day.

2. Wrong name. The certificate is valid but does not cover the name the visitor typed. Typical after a migration: example.com is covered, www.example.com or shop.example.com is not.

3. Broken chain. The server does not send its intermediate certificate. Desktop browsers often repair this on their own, so the site "works for me", while API clients, payment callbacks and bots fail.

4. Self-signed or private CA. Fine on an internal tool, a problem on anything public.

Option A: openssl for one host

openssl is installed on most Linux and macOS machines and ships with Git for Windows:

openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -enddate -ext subjectAltName

This prints who the certificate is for, who issued it, its end date and every name it covers. -servername matters: without it, a server hosting several sites may hand you the wrong certificate. To check the chain, look for Verify return code: 0 (ok) in the output of the first command alone.

Option B: a short Python script for a list

Python's standard library can do a strict check, the same way an API client would, with no extra package:

import socket, ssl
from datetime import datetime, timezone

def check(host, port=443, warn_days=30):
    ctx = ssl.create_default_context()  # verifies the chain and the hostname
    try:
        with socket.create_connection((host, port), timeout=10) as sock:
            with ctx.wrap_socket(sock, server_hostname=host) as tls:
                cert = tls.getpeercert()
    except ssl.SSLCertVerificationError as e:
        return f"BAD {host}: {e.verify_message}"
    except OSError as e:
        return f"ERR {host}: {e}"
    end = datetime.fromtimestamp(ssl.cert_time_to_seconds(cert["notAfter"]), timezone.utc)
    days = (end - datetime.now(timezone.utc)).days
    return f"{'OK ' if days > warn_days else 'BAD'} {host}: {days} days left"

for line in open("domains.txt", encoding="utf-8"):
    if line.strip():
        print(check(line.strip()))

Expired certificates, wrong names, self-signed certificates and missing intermediates all end up in the BAD branch with the reason. One limit: when verification fails, Python does not give you the certificate, so you see why it failed but not its dates or names. For that, fall back to the openssl command above. Run the script daily from cron or a scheduled task and you have a basic monitor.

Option C: a hosted checker for bulk jobs

Disclosure: this one is ours. We publish SSL Certificate Checker on Apify. You paste a list of domains, host:port pairs or full URLs, and it does one TLS handshake per host, up to 100 in parallel. Unlike the script above, it still reads and reports the certificate when it is not trusted.

from apify_client import ApifyClient  # pip install apify-client

client = ApifyClient("YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN")
run = client.actor("extas_corp/ssl-certificate-checker").call(
    run_input={"domains": ["example.com", "smtp.example.com:465"], "warnDays": 21})
for item in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items():
    if not item["ok"]:
        print(item["host"], item.get("daysLeft"), item["warnings"], item["error"])

A certificate served for the wrong host comes back like this (shortened):

{
  "host": "wrong.host.badssl.com",
  "ok": false,
  "trusted": false,
  "trustError": "Hostname mismatch, certificate is not valid for 'wrong.host.badssl.com'.",
  "subject": "*.badssl.com",
  "daysLeft": 45
}

Each row also has the issuer, validFrom / validTo, all alternative names, a wildcard flag, the TLS version and cipher. ok is true only when the certificate is trusted, not expired and not expiring within warnDays. DNS, connection and timeout errors are reported on their row and do not stop the run.

It is free during launch: you only pay Apify's own platform usage, which the free monthly credit covers for normal use. Limits: it is not a full TLS security scan (no cipher enumeration, no vulnerability tests), revocation is not checked, STARTTLS ports such as SMTP 587 are not supported, and a CDN may serve a different certificate in another region than the one the check runs from.

What to put on the list

  • Every hostname, not only the main domain: www, apex, api, mail, old marketing subdomains.
  • Mail and other TLS services on their own ports (465, 993).
  • The vendors you depend on: an expired certificate on a payment or webhook endpoint breaks your site too.

Run it daily, alert only on BAD, and the next expiry becomes a ticket instead of an outage.

title: PACD: Provenance-Aware Consensus Decoding for Mitigating Cross-Modal Hallucinations in Omnimodal Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.22456v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Omnimodal large language models (Omni-LLMs) integrate audio, video, and text for multimodal reasoning, yet remain vulnerable to cross-modal hallucinations, where one modality improperly influences predictions about another. Existing training-free decoding methods mitigate these errors through modality perturbation or relevance-based weighting. However, due to interference from irrelevant modality cues during fusion and difficulty detecting shared errors, these methods may suppress correct unimodal predictions and allow erroneous consensus to persist. To address these limitations, we propose Provenance-Aware Consensus Decoding (PACD), a training-free framework for mitigating cross-modal hallucinations. PACD comprises two complementary paths based on whether the branches reach consensus. For non-consensus cases, Relevance-Guided Candidate Arbitration identifies task-relevant unimodal evidence and selectively arbitrates between predictions using alternative candidates. For consensus cases, Provenance-Based Consensus Recovery leverages the outranking principle to evaluate the consistency and strength of layer-wise modality evidence for alternative answers, selectively resolving erroneous consensus under confidence constraints. Extensive experiments on four Omni-LLMs and five benchmarks across two tasks demonstrate the superiority of PACD. Compared to existing methods, PACD achieves up to 27.6% relative improvement over standard decoding across CMM, AVHBench, and SVHalluc for cross-modal hallucination mitigation, and an average relative improvement of 7.7% over best baseline across OmniVideoBench and FutureOmni for general audio-visual reasoning.

title: RetiDual-Select: Reliability-Aware Specialist-Generalist Routing for Retinal OCT under Image-Quality Shift
description:
arXiv:2611.22117v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Adaptive fusion can repair a static ensemble's errors, but can also overturn correct decisions. RetiDual-Select combines retinal specialist RETFound with the image encoder of the medical vision-language model MedSigLIP, separating candidate fusion, routing safety and predictive review. Calibrated product-of-experts (PoE) fusion is the static reference, a small gate proposes an alternative for each image, a validation-frozen harm guard decides whether that candidate may replace the reference, and a separate score prioritizes review. Static PoE reached the highest or joint-highest clean accuracy on all three datasets. At a clean 2% accepted-error target the review policy accepted 94.3% of Kermany-4 images at 99.89% selective accuracy, and 92.4% of OCT-C8 at 98.65%. Both branches were correct on 95.0% and 91.8% of clean images; only 4.4% and 6.2% had exactly one correct branch. Across 15 prespecified synthetic conditions, adaptive gains were concentrated in severe contrast reduction, where this routing opportunity widened roughly ninefold; percentile rescaling largely removed the effect, linking it to compressed dynamic range. In post-hoc validation-only analyses, gain was higher when the gate followed the more reliable branch, and a frozen guard cut the worst-condition OCT-C8 loss from 1.39 to 0.36 percentage points. Adaptive routing was useful when image quality created a reliability opportunity and the gate followed it; otherwise the system retained Static PoE or deferred for review. The findings are bounded by the synthetic perturbations evaluated and do not establish robustness to natural acquisition or scanner shift.

title: tmol: a GPU-accelerated implementation of the Rosetta energy function for machine learning
description:
arXiv:2611.21857v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Physics-inspired forcefields complement generative machine learning models, showing better generalization beyond the training distribution. However, these forcefields are typically slow to evaluate, and their derivatives are difficult to integrate into ML frameworks. We introduce tmol, a GPU-native PyTorch library implementing the state-of-the-art RosettaGenFF forcefield. tmol supports efficient batched differentiable scoring and whole-structure refinement with up to 362-fold throughput increase (batched). Used as a reward in generative protein design, tmol increases hydrogen bonds and water bridges at designed interfaces.

title: A plain checklist to see if ChatGPT and Google AI can read your website
description:
Many business sites look fine to people but are hard for search engines and AI tools to read. Here is a short checklist you can run in about 15 minutes.

  1. Can crawlers get in? Open yourdomain.com/robots.txt. Make sure it does not block Googlebot or the AI crawlers you want (GPTBot, PerplexityBot, ClaudeBot).
  2. Is there a sitemap? Open yourdomain.com/sitemap.xml. It should list your real pages and nothing broken.
  3. Does each page have one clear title and one H1 that say what the page is about?
  4. Do your answers appear as plain text near the top of the page? AI tools quote short direct answers, so put the answer first and the detail after.
  5. Do you have basic structured data (Organization, and FAQ where it fits)? Test it with Google's Rich Results Test.
  6. Is the page fast and readable on a phone? Run PageSpeed Insights.
  7. Is your business name, site and contact the same everywhere you are listed?

Fix these in order. None of them needs a big budget. They just need someone to check.

We are Liftup Technologies, a team of 10 in Pune that has worked on websites, SEO and automation since 2015. We built a free tool that checks the AI side of this: https://liftup.tech/tools/ai-visibility-checker/

title: Growing Clusters Lower the Bar: Profile Accretion in LLM-Based Incremental Entity Resolution
description:
arXiv:2611.22485v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Incremental entity resolution pipelines ask a large language model (LLM) whether a new record belongs to an existing cluster and show it the records already linked. Analyses of matching oracles assume that the answer depends only on the records compared. For the LLM matchers we test, it depends on cluster size, and the model lowers its bar for joining a cluster as the cluster grows. On French procurement suppliers from FOPPA, with SIREN identifiers as ground truth, we hold the new record fixed and vary only the number of verified members shown. Sixteen members instead of one raise the false match rate on similarly named companies by \dfmrMin--\dfmrMax{} percentage points in six open-weight models, while their area under the ROC curve rises by only \aucGainMin--\aucGainMax. In Claude Sonnet~5 and Haiku~5.5 the rise is \clSonD{} and \clHaiD{} points. The shift persists with street addresses, prompt variants and the BatchER and ComEM formats, and one false merge raises acceptance of the intruder's other records in every open model. It does not arise on Czech and Bulgarian TED notices, where one record with its full address already identifies the company. In online linking on confusable blocks, a single threshold set on labelled data raises recall by a factor of \fxRRmin--\fxRRmax{} for five models with no detectable loss of precision and no extra LLM calls.

title: Improved Convergence Rates for Stochastic Multi-Gradient Descent which Close the Gap: A Proof by AI
description:
arXiv:2607.18174v2 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: For smooth nonconvex stochastic multi-objective optimization, stochastic multi-gradient descent (SMG) computes an approximate steepest common descent direction of the objectives from stochastic gradients. Under standard assumptions, this note establishes a new convergence rate for SMG in terms of the squared Pareto-stationarity (PS) measure. With a constant stepsize and linearly growing mini-batches, the expected squared empirical PS measure at the algorithm's output is $\tilde{O}(T^{-1})$ after $T$ iterations. This improves on the $\tilde{O}(T^{-1/4})$ bound obtained by Chen et al. (JMLR, 2024) for linearly growing batches, without requiring bounded gradients. Here, $\tilde{O}(\cdot)$ suppresses logarithmic factors. The key to the rate improvement is to exploit the Lipschitz continuity of the PS measure, defined by the norm of the multi-gradient descent algorithm (MGDA) direction, rather than the $(1/2)$-H\"older continuity of the MGDA direction used by Chen et al. (2024). For variants of MoCo and MoCo+ with exact MGDA updates and constant batch sizes, the analysis gives expected squared empirical PS rates of $O(T^{-1/2})$ and $\tilde{O}(T^{-2/3})$, respectively. These bounds match the corresponding single-objective momentum rates up to logarithmic factors. The proof was accidentally discovered while the author was preparing homework for a graduate course: ChatGPT 5.4 Thinking Extended generated the initial proof strategy for the main SMG result in response to an author-written homework-solution prompt; the author then verified and reorganized the resulting argument. The appendices document the prompt, summarize the student submissions with LLM disclosures, and present additional proofs and results on momentum-based stochastic MGDA.

title: Eyes in the Update? Learning Where Rewards Land in Multimodal Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2611.22438v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal post-training has moved from broad instruction tuning toward reinforcement learning for image and video reasoning, where outcome rewards can improve final-answer accuracy. Yet these rewards are assigned to complete generated trajectories, while visual evidence is used only at sparse and uneven positions inside the response. Recent work has begun to make multimodal RL more token-sensitive through grounding signals or external token-level weighting. We ask a more specific question: can the allocation of the same trajectory-level reward be inferred from the model's own multimodal computation, rather than from an auxiliary annotator, perception module, or process label? We propose Gaze-RL, a representation-driven policy optimization method that redistributes completion-level advantage through a latent reward landing field. The field is computed from internal cross-modal geometry and local predictive uncertainty, assigning larger update weight to positions that are both visually anchored and decision-bearing while remaining mean-one, so the total credit of each rollout is preserved and only its positionwise allocation changes. Gaze-RL requires no process supervision, auxiliary perception module, or architectural modification, and improves both Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL3.5 across a broad range of image and video benchmarks.

title: Bring Live MongoDB Atlas Data Into Microsoft 365 Copilot
description:
The federated Copilot connector for MongoDB Atlas gives organizations a governed way to bring live operational data into the flow of work across Copilot experiences.

To operate efficiently, businesses require timely information about the systems that underpin their organizations. For example, they need to be able to answer questions like: Which incidents are open? Which orders are delayed? What fields and data types are present in the customer collection? The answers they need often live in operational applications built on MongoDB Atlas, while the questions are asked in the productivity tools people use every day.

To help close that gap, MongoDB is excited to introduce a federated Copilot connector for MongoDB Atlas. Now generally available, the connector enables users to ask Microsoft 365 Copilot questions about live data in MongoDB Atlas, bringing operational context into the same experience where people collaborate, analyze information, and make decisions.

The connector surfaces MongoDB Atlas data across Microsoft Copilot experiences, including Copilot Chat, Researcher in Copilot, Copilot Cowork, Microsoft Word, Excel, and Teams, with additional experiences planned to follow.

Bring operational data into the flow of work

The connector brings MongoDB Atlas to Microsoft Copilot through MongoDB’s managed remote Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. When a user asks a relevant question, Copilot can query Atlas in real time—instead of relying on a static copy of the data.

This creates a more direct path from a business question to the information needed to answer it, and helps users—who may not have MongoDB expertise—access and analyze live operational data through an AI assistant.

Now, business users can use conversational prompts to:

  • Retrieve live business data without writing database queries.

  • Find and filter customers, transactions, products, orders, content, or operational events.

  • Get quick counts and key performance indicators, such as the number of delayed orders or high-value customers.

  • Summarize and rank data to identify top categories, products, regions, trends, averages, and other business insights.

For example, a user might ask Copilot to summarize the open incidents in an Atlas cluster supporting a payments application, identify delayed orders, or describe the fields and data types in the customer collection for a loyalty service. By industry, a supply chain team can investigate inventory, shipment, and warehouse exceptions. A financial services team can explore customer records, fraud alerts, and transaction investigations. And a retailer can ask questions about orders, loyalty, customer service, and personalization.

The connector can also help power business copilots and agents. Organizations can ground Copilot and other AI assistants in current MongoDB Atlas data for customer service, sales, operations, and decision support, bringing live operational context into the workflows where teams already work.

Connect to live data without migrating or indexing it

Organizations using MongoDB Atlas do not need to migrate their operational data, re-platform their applications, or rebuild their integrations to use the connector.

To do so, an administrator simply approves and enables the connector in the Microsoft 365 admin center. Users then sign in, and their existing Atlas permissions carry through to each query.

MongoDB Atlas remains the system of record. The connector queries Atlas directly rather than indexing a copy of Atlas data into Microsoft 365, so the information returned to users reflects the current state of the underlying application data.

This federated approach helps organizations connect their productivity layer to operational data while keeping that data in the environment where it is managed.

Put governance into every interaction

Making operational data more accessible requires controls that organizations can understand and manage. The connector is designed to support that approach through:

  • Permission-aware access: Each query runs as the signed-in user and honors the permissions already defined in MongoDB Atlas.

  • Administrator control: Admins approve the connector and can manage deployment through the Microsoft 365 admin center.

  • Read-only access: The connector is designed for read-only interaction with Atlas data.

  • Auditability: Administrators can audit connector activity in Microsoft Purview.

  • No separate search index: The connector queries Atlas on demand instead of indexing a copy of Atlas data in Microsoft 365.

Together, these controls give organizations a practical way to make operational information available through Copilot without giving up the governance model around the source data.

A foundation for more productive work

AI-powered productivity depends on access to relevant business context. By connecting Microsoft Copilot and other AI assistants to live MongoDB Atlas data through a federated connection, MongoDB and Microsoft are helping organizations make operational information easier to use without adding a data-movement project or another application to maintain. Users can get answers, summaries, and insights from live data through natural language, while technical teams retain control over the underlying systems and permissions.

For organizations already running MongoDB Atlas on Azure and Microsoft 365 Copilot, the connector provides a way to build on existing investments. Teams can explore high-value operational questions, validate measurable business outcomes, and develop repeatable patterns for bringing current data into everyday decisions.

The result is a simpler path from question to context to action—grounded in the systems organizations already use and governed by the permissions they already have.

title: Vork Research Preview Targets Agent-Written 3D and VFX
description:
Vork is available as a source-available, free research preview of a headless 3D and VFX engine built for AI agents. An agent can define an entire scene in code—including shaders, materials, cameras and physics—render it on the GPU, inspect the output and revise the code without operating an editor. Developers can write ordinary scene JSON directly or generate it through Python and TypeScript SDKs, giving agent workflows a documented rendering interface rather than a graphical control path. The project describes these capabilities in its repository.

Code is the control surface

The project says its core API fits in about 2,500 tokens. Vork is written in Rust and Slang, renders through Vulkan and Metal on Linux, Windows and macOS, and exposes public hooks that can change camera rays, material response, light propagation and film response without modifying the renderer itself. Those hooks and implementation details are documented in the README.

A local workflow starts with vork init, which creates a project containing a renderable JSON scene; initialization flags can also provide editable TypeScript or Python scene files. Render quality is configured separately from scene content: std/previs is intended for iteration, std/draft uses scene-ray lighting, std/final is the default delivery profile, and std/path enables path transport. The repository documents the commands and the distinct purposes of these profiles.

Scene authoring and command-line help do not require a GPU. Rendering requires Apple Silicon or an NVIDIA or AMD GPU with Vulkan ray-query support, while the project also offers remote rendering through vork cloud. By default, the renderer combines raster visibility with hardware ray-traced lighting; a path tracer is available separately. Vork’s hardware requirements and rendering modes are listed by the project.

Benchmark caveats limit the comparison

Vork reports that its million-bird demonstration rendered 192 frames at 1080p in 97 seconds on one NVIDIA L4. It projects that Blender EEVEE would take 13–18 minutes at the same sample count, and separately reports timings 1.1–2.3 times faster than EEVEE for default stills and movies and about 8–11 times faster for the bird flock. These are Vork’s published measurements and projections.

The project explicitly calls these results timings rather than equal-quality speedups. Its draft and final measurements used four and eight samples respectively with OIDN on an NVIDIA L4, while the Blender 5.2.1 results were retained baselines rather than fresh runs and used different settings. Driver caches and clocks were not controlled; Vork’s movie times include startup and scene loading, while Blender’s exclude those stages after a still-image prime. The benchmark notes disclose these methodological differences.

Visual review also found softer edges, grainier defocus, wall mottling and changes to sparse or spectral highlights at the tested budgets. Nineteen earlier comparisons failed the experiment’s declared no-worse FLIP condition, and that quality experiment was not repeated for the reported build. The project includes both findings among its benchmark qualifications.

Analysis: Programmability shifts the verification burden

Analysis: Vork’s more consequential proposition is its interface design, not the headline speed range. A compact scene API and programmable GPU hooks give an agent direct control over rendering behavior instead of asking it to manipulate an editor. That could make custom effects and simulations easier to express as code, but it also expands the scene-specific programs that a team must inspect, test and reproduce. The project’s small API, editor-free workflow and public program hooks support this interpretation.

The unresolved trade-off is control versus verification. Vork’s documentation warns that increasing samples cannot restore transport omitted by a render profile and recommends inspecting path-rendered output when necessary. It also says its furnace tests, analytic oracles and render tests can catch errors but do not guarantee that every scene is physically exact. Teams evaluating the preview therefore still need shot-specific visual checks; the published timing comparison cannot settle whether its faster profiles preserve the properties a particular production requires. Those rendering and validation limits are stated in the project documentation.

title: Why I Rewrote type-tune from TypeScript to Rust 🦀
description:
Hoi hoi! 👋

I'm @nyaomaru, a frontend engineer who loves TypeScript and gambas, not crabs! 🦐

And yet, somehow, I ended up building a tool in Rust. 🙀🦀

Recently, I released a new open-source CLI tool called type-tune.

necoz-oss / type-tune

A Rust-powered CLI to find shared TypeScript types and move them safely. 🦀

type-tune

Give shared TypeScript types a better home. 😸

Scan. Review. Move. Validate.

type-tune is a Rust-powered CLI that finds shared TypeScript type aliases and interface declarations and helps move them without manually chasing imports.

It creates a reviewable plan, updates supported type imports and re-exports, and validates the rewrite with TypeScript. You decide what moves and where.

Guides for installation, the first scan, and the review workflow live in the official documentation. Releases are listed on GitHub Releases, and the package is type-tune on npm.

Why type-tune?

Types often start next to a component or utility, then end up shared across a project. Moving them later means tracking imports, local dependencies, and barrels by hand.

  • Discover shared types with deterministic candidate IDs.
  • Review plan.md and choose the destination before making changes.
  • Rewrite supported type-only imports, aliases, and simple barrels while keeping compatibility re-exports at the original…
View on GitHub

type-tune finds shared TypeScript types and helps move them to a better place without manually updating imports, dependencies, and barrel exports.

But why is a TypeScript tool created by a TypeScript lover written in Rust? 🤔

🐈 It All Started with TypeScript

Naturally, the original implementation of type-tune was written in TypeScript.

It was already complete by September, with nearly 20,000 lines of TypeScript, including tests, comments, and blank lines.

Around that time, I happened to watch this video by DHH.

I didn't agree with everything, but I particularly liked the idea of taking advantage of this era to pursue things that genuinely excite us.

Of course, outside of personal projects, I don't think we can simply hand everything over to AI. Someone still needs to understand and maintain the software.

But while watching the video, a simple thought crossed my mind.

If it's possible to go from Rails to Rust, why not TypeScript to Rust? 🦀

🦀 From TypeScript to Rust

I already had a working implementation, design documents, tests, and well-defined TypeScript types.

For example, translating a data model like this:

type CandidateKind = "typeAlias" | "interface";

type Candidate = {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  kind: CandidateKind;
  referrers: string[];
};

Into something like this:

enum CandidateKind {
    TypeAlias,
    Interface,
}

struct Candidate {
    id: String,
    name: String,
    kind: CandidateKind,
    referrers: Vec<String>,
}

Of course, migrating the entire application involved much more than translating type definitions.

But having an existing design and implementation made it much easier.

With the help of AI, I completed the migration in less than a month while working on it as a side project.

The results were satisfying 😻

  • Better execution performance.
  • Native binary distribution.
  • No Rust development environment required for npm users.

You can still install type-tune like any other familiar TypeScript development tool.

pnpm add -D type-tune

The npm launcher requires Node.js 22+, but the core implementation runs as a native binary.

So far, so good!

Except for one little problem. 😿

🙀 type-tune Got Faster. Its Developer Got Slower.

I barely knew Rust. 😹

I'm comfortable reviewing AI-generated TypeScript code, but with Rust, I'm still learning the fundamentals.

For example, consider ownership and borrowing.

In TypeScript, this is perfectly fine:

function printName(name: string) {
  console.log(name);
}

const name = "OrderSummary";

printName(name);
console.log(name); // OK

However, a similar implementation in Rust doesn't compile.

fn print_name(name: String) {
    println!("{}", name);
}

fn main() {
    let name = String::from("OrderSummary");

    print_name(name);
    println!("{}", name); // Error: value borrowed after move
}

The ownership of name is transferred to print_name.

One way to fix this is to borrow the value instead.

fn print_name(name: &str) {
    println!("{}", name);
}

fn main() {
    let name = String::from("OrderSummary");

    print_name(&name);
    println!("{}", name); // OK
}

Another option is to clone the value.

print_name(name.clone());
println!("{}", name); // OK

Both solutions compile, but cloning unnecessarily can introduce additional allocations.

So when AI generates a .clone(), I need to understand whether it's actually necessary or whether borrowing would be more appropriate.

The same applies to visibility boundaries.

For example, making an internal helper public might solve an accessibility issue:

pub fn resolve_destination() {
    // ...
}

But if the function is only used within the same crate, exposing it publicly may be unnecessary.

pub(crate) fn resolve_destination() {
    // ...
}

And if it's only used within its own module, it can remain private.

fn resolve_destination() {
    // ...
}

The compiler accepts all three declarations, but each represents a different architectural decision.

I'm also still learning when macros are appropriate and when ordinary functions are sufficient.

AI can generate code that compiles, but I still need to understand whether its design choices are appropriate.

In TypeScript, I can make these decisions relatively quickly. In Rust, I often need to stop and learn something before continuing my review.

AI can generate Rust code much faster than I can understand it.

I wanted to accelerate the development of my side project, but I introduced a new bottleneck.

Myself.

What a wonderful optimization! 😹

🎨 Creating Without Learning

Of course, I could just vibe code.

I could keep pressing Enter whenever AI asks for approval and probably release features faster.

But for me, creating something without learning anything is just another task.

And I believe that if I keep doing nothing but those tasks, I'll gradually lose my ability to create.

I enjoy using AI to learn unfamiliar concepts and explore new approaches.

But I don't want to spend my time simply producing things without understanding them.

I don't want to become a very expensive Enter key. 😹

Do I regret choosing Rust?

Not at all!

It was a valuable experience, and I'm grateful that we live in a time when we can challenge ourselves like this so easily.

Now, let's talk about what I actually built!

🛠️ The Design Behind type-tune

One architectural decision remained unchanged throughout the migration.

Scan / Plan / Apply

Consider a typical TypeScript project.

src/
├── features/
│   ├── orders/
│   │   └── order-page.ts
│   ├── dashboard/
│   │   └── dashboard.ts
│   └── reports/
│       └── reports.ts

Initially, a type belongs to the orders feature.

// features/orders/order-page.ts

export type OrderSummary = {
  id: string;
  total: number;
};

But as the application grows, other features start importing it.

// features/dashboard/dashboard.ts

import type { OrderSummary } from "../orders/order-page";

export function calculateRevenue(orders: OrderSummary[]) {
  return orders.reduce((sum, order) => sum + order.total, 0);
}

// features/reports/reports.ts

import type { OrderSummary } from "../orders/order-page";

export function createReport(order: OrderSummary) {
  return `${order.id}: ${order.total}`;
}

The type is still useful, but its original location may no longer be appropriate.

Tools like Knip help us remove unused code.

type-tune tackles a different problem: reorganizing types that are still in use.

🔍 1. Scan 

pnpm exec type-tune scan --project tsconfig.json

type-tune analyzes exported type aliases, interfaces, references, and relevant dependencies to identify potential extraction candidates.

No source code is modified.

📋 2. Plan

Finding a type that can be moved doesn't necessarily mean it should be moved.

That's why type-tune generates a reviewable plan.

pnpm exec type-tune plan \
  --project tsconfig.json \
  --out .type-tune/plan.json \
  --markdown .type-tune/plan.md

It generates two files:

  • plan.json — Candidate metadata and validation information.
  • plan.md — A human-readable, editable plan.

Every candidate is ignored by default.

Here's a simplified example of plan.md:

- [ignore] <candidate-id> `OrderSummary`
  - kind: `typeAlias`
  - from: `src/features/orders/order-page.ts`
  - to: `src/features/orders/types/order.ts`

You can approve the candidate and customize its destination.

- [ignore] <candidate-id> OrderSummary
+ [apply] <candidate-id> OrderSummary
    - kind: typeAlias
    - from: src/features/orders/order-page.ts
-   - to: src/features/orders/types/order.ts
+   - to: src/domains/orders/types/order-summary.ts

Perhaps it belongs in a shared directory, a domain-specific module, or exactly where it is now.

That's an architectural decision.

You decide what moves and where.

🚚 3. Apply

Preview the selected changes:

pnpm exec type-tune apply \
  --plan .type-tune/plan.json \
  --markdown .type-tune/plan.md \
  --dry-run

Then apply them:

pnpm exec type-tune apply \
  --plan .type-tune/plan.json \
  --markdown .type-tune/plan.md

The resulting project structure:

src/
├── domains/
│   └── orders/
│       └── types/
│           └── order-summary.ts  ← Moved!
└── features/
    ├── orders/
    │   └── order-page.ts
    ├── dashboard/
    │   └── dashboard.ts
    └── reports/
        └── reports.ts

The type now lives in its new home.

// domains/orders/types/order-summary.ts

export type OrderSummary = {
  id: string;
  total: number;
};

Supported imports are updated automatically.

- import type { OrderSummary } from "../orders/order-page";
+ import type { OrderSummary } from "../../domains/orders/types/order-summary";

And the original module retains a compatibility re-export.

// features/orders/order-page.ts

export type { OrderSummary } from "../../domains/orders/types/order-summary";

type-tune also validates the rewrite using the TypeScript compiler and rolls back changes if normal validation fails.

You should still review the resulting diff and run your project-specific tests and builds.

🧩 Automate the Work, Not the Decisions

Why separate Scan, Plan, and Apply?

Because discovering opportunities, making architectural decisions, and executing changes are different responsibilities.

type-tune even supports optional AI-assisted review:

pnpm exec type-tune plan \
  --project tsconfig.json \
  --ai-review \
  --ai-dry-run

AI can provide additional review notes, but it doesn't control the source code rewrite. The command above previews the AI review request without contacting a provider.

Interestingly, this is also how I want to work with AI in my own development.

Automate the tedious work without taking architectural decisions away from developers.

That's the philosophy behind type-tune.

💚 Give Your TypeScript Types a Better Home!

You can start by simply scanning your project.

npx type-tune scan --project tsconfig.json

No need to move anything yet. Just see what you find! 😸

necoz-oss / type-tune
