title: The Only Edge Was Memorized in Training: LLM Trading Agents Around Earnings and Bad News
description:
arXiv:2611.22177v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) trading agents are tested on news, but news reaches stock prices within minutes, and a benchmark that replays headlines at their publication time finds no alpha in trading on them. Money can then remain in two places, before news whose date is known, such as earnings announcements, and after bad news, if the market's fall went too far. However, studies of LLMs and earnings read documents published with or after the announcement, and studies of reversal sort monthly portfolios, so neither tells whether an agent can trade these moments after costs. In this paper, we test LLM agents at both moments on the same look-ahead-free benchmark, before 598 earnings announcements and after 409 bad-news drops of large US stocks. Every input is cut at the decision close, staged agents are compared with single calls, simple rules and a logistic regression, and every decision is made with and without the stock's name. Across five models from four vendors, no agent beat the simple bets. Before earnings, the agents mostly bought and earned what buying before every announcement earned, and after bad news, a Gemini-based agent called almost every fall an overreaction while no agent picked better dips than buying them all. The only gains came from what the models had memorized in training. Given only the ticker and the dates, a GPT-based model called the direction of 59.2% of the announcements before its training cutoff and 53.3% after it. Agent builders should therefore compare an event agent with the simple bet and test it blind after the training cutoff.

title: From Preference Data to Personalization: Tracing Sycophancy in Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.21650v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Sycophancy in large language models is often measured as agreement with the user, yet agreement can be appropriate when the user's claim is valid, their preference is genuine, or their experience warrants acknowledgment. We study sycophancy as inappropriate agreement: validating a claim, preference, or self-assessment when the context calls for correction, qualification, or resistance. We introduce a validity-aware sycophancy grader and SycoDrift, a persona-targeted evaluation set of 3,298 validity-annotated probes with controlled annotations for user openness and stakes. We use this framework to analyze three sources of agreement pressure: human preference data, automated judge specification, and in-context personalization. First, preference for validating responses in human datasets (Chatbot Arena, HH-RLHF, Community Alignment) is weak and concentrated where agreement is often appropriate. Second, in a selected-value, single-model experiment, emphasized judge rubrics produce consistent but modest increases relative to paired suppressed rubrics, demonstrating a plausible mechanism for training-time amplification. Third, in off-policy evaluations across 14 models, inference-time personalization increases inappropriate agreement, with the largest effect from matched user profiles placed directly before the query.

title: World-Grounded Reinforcement Learning for Pollution-Aware Bird Movement Modeling Using a Multi-Instance DQN Framework
description:
arXiv:2611.21895v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Birds are modeled as environmentally sensitive agents whose movement reflects real-world air quality conditions, where AQI serves as a measurable world feedback signal representing pollution-driven consequences. Instead of relying on human preference or synthetic rewards, the system uses environmental outcomes as the primary training signal, enabling policy learning grounded in ecological impact. We propose a multi-instance reinforcement learning simulation in which agents navigate a 2D grid representation of India integrated with a precomputed AQI matrix and geographic state boundaries. The framework combines bird call metadata from the Xeno-canto dataset, spatial discretization, and real environmental data to learn adaptive navigation strategies under pollution constraints. To ensure scalability and efficiency, repeated real-time API queries are replaced by a structured AQI mapping that enables fast lookup during training and execution. Multiple baselines, including Monte Carlo, Q-Learning, and Value Iteration, are evaluated for comparison. Deep Q-Network demonstrates stronger stability, adaptability, and cumulative performance across varying environmental conditions, establishing a scalable foundation for world-feedback driven ecological decision modeling.

title: shadcn MCP: install UI components from Claude Code and Cursor
description:
The shadcn CLI has an MCP server built in, so Claude Code, Cursor and VS Code can browse and install registry components for you. Here is the setup for each editor, how to add a private registry, and the errors you will hit and what they mean.

shadcn’s MCP server is built into the shadcn CLI. Run npx shadcn@latest mcp init --client claude, or --client cursor, and your AI editor can browse, search and install items from every registry in components.json. mebius.design adds a hosted MCP server that returns each item’s full source and usage docs.

What is the shadcn MCP server?

Checked in shadcn’s docs and source on 17 Nov 2026.

The shadcn MCP server is part of the shadcn CLI, the MIT-licensed shadcn package on npm (4.23.0 when we checked). Your editor starts it on your own machine with npx shadcn@latest mcp, and the AI can then browse, search and install items from any registry in your components.json: shadcn/ui’s own (no setup needed), third-party registries, private ones behind a token, and namespaced ones such as @acme. See shadcn’s MCP docs.

Under the hood it has seven tools (source): list the registries in components.json; list, search and view registry items with their files; find usage examples; return the shadcn add command for chosen items; and a checklist to run after new code is written. The server doesn’t write files itself. The assistant runs the add command it gets back, so every install still goes through the CLI.

How do you set up shadcn MCP?

One command per editor, then a restart.

Run init in your project with the name of your editor. It adds the shadcn server to that editor’s MCP config:

Terminal:

npx shadcn@latest mcp init --client claude
# or --client cursor, vscode, codex or opencode

Restart the editor afterwards. In Claude Code, run /mcp and check that shadcn shows as connected; in Cursor, turn the server on in Cursor Settings; in VS Code, open .vscode/mcp.json and click Start. Codex is the exception: the CLI can’t edit ~/.codex/config.toml, so you add the server there by hand. Written by hand for Claude Code, the server is this file:

.mcp.json:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "shadcn": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["shadcn@latest", "mcp"]
    }
  }
}

Cursor takes the same block in .cursor/mcp.json; VS Code puts it under "servers" in .vscode/mcp.json. If the editor lists no tools, shadcn’s troubleshooting notes suggest clearing the npx cache (npx clear-npx-cache) and switching the server off and on again.

How do you add a private registry?

Once per project. The example is the @mebius registry.

A private registry is a namespace in components.json: a URL template the CLI fills with the item name and, when the registry needs one, a header that reads a token from your environment (shadcn’s authentication docs). The CLI and its MCP server both read it. For mebius.design, create a token in Settings › Tokens (a free account works) and add:

components.json:

{
  "registries": {
    "@mebius": {
      "url": "https://www.mebius.design/r/{name}.json",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer ${MEBIUS_TOKEN}"
      }
    }
  }
}

.env.local:

MEBIUS_TOKEN=mbs_your_token

Keep the token out of git. The CLI reads .env.local and .env. Check that .env.local is in your .gitignore, and revoke a token in Settings › Tokens if it leaks.

Each mebius kit has a theme item. Add it on its own first, then items with --overwrite so shared parts take the kit’s version. Item names start with their kit:

Terminal:

npx shadcn@latest add @mebius/charts-theme
npx shadcn@latest add @mebius/charts-revenue-growth --overwrite

No token yet? The 20 open starter items install from their URL with no account, like the Revenue Overview chart: npx shadcn@latest add https://www.mebius.design/r/charts-revenue-overview.json.

Which shadcn CLI commands matter?

What the MCP server asks for, and what you can run yourself.

When an agent gets stuck, the same work runs in a terminal. From shadcn’s CLI docs, the commands that matter for registries:

  • init: creates components.json, adds the cn helper and sets up CSS variables. Once per project.
  • add: installs items by name, @namespace/name or URL. --overwrite replaces files that already exist, --dry-run previews the changes.
  • view: prints an item’s files before you install it.
  • search (alias list): searches one or more registries, with -q for a query.
  • info: shows your project’s setup as the CLI sees it, handy when an install lands in the wrong folder.

With the @mebius registry set up, you can find, read and install a chart without leaving the terminal:

Terminal:

npx shadcn@latest search @mebius -q "candlestick"
npx shadcn@latest view @mebius/charts-ethereum
npx shadcn@latest add @mebius/charts-ethereum --overwrite

What does the mebius MCP server add?

A hosted server with browser sign-in and usage docs per item.

mebius.design runs its own MCP server at https://www.mebius.design/api/mcp. Nothing runs on your machine and it doesn’t need a components.json: it reads the kits your account has and returns each item’s source files with their target paths, its npm and registry dependencies, and the usage docs written for that component or block (props, examples, notes). As of 17 Nov 2026, a free account gets all 62 free charts and 128 free forms; buying a kit adds that kit, and All items adds every kit.

In Claude Code, add it with one command, with no token to copy:

Terminal:

claude mcp add --transport http mebius https://www.mebius.design/api/mcp

Then run /mcp, pick mebius, choose Authenticate, log in to mebius.design in the browser and click Approve. Cursor and VS Code ask you to log in the first time they connect:

.cursor/mcp.json:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "mebius": {
      "url": "https://www.mebius.design/api/mcp"
    }
  }
}

VS Code takes the same URL under "servers" with "type": "http". Tools that can’t open a browser, like CI or a remote machine, send a token from Settings › Tokens as the header Authorization: Bearer <your token>. The server has five read-only tools:

  • list_kits: the kits your account has, the free ones included, with item counts and categories, and the paid kits it doesn’t own yet.
  • list_items and search_items: find a component or block by kit, type, category or plain words.
  • get_item: one item in full, with every file, its dependencies and its usage docs.
  • get_install_instructions: the components.json entry, the token line and the exact add commands, theme first.

Which MCP server should you use?

Both, for different jobs.

  • shadcn MCP: local, free and MIT, and it works with every registry in components.json, shadcn/ui’s own included. Best for browsing many registries and installing through the CLI.
  • mebius MCP: hosted, signs in through the browser and covers mebius kits only. Best when the agent should read an item’s usage docs before it adapts a block, or write the files by hand in a project without components.json.

They don’t clash. With the @mebius registry in components.json, shadcn’s server lists mebius items too, and a prompt like “add the mebius candlestick chart to the dashboard” ends the same way with either one: the theme, then npx shadcn@latest add @mebius/charts-ethereum --overwrite.

Other marketplaces run their own servers too: the UI8 MCP at https://mcp.ui8.net/mcp is included with UI8’s All Access pass (checked on ui8.net on 17 Nov 2026). How the two marketplaces compare overall is in mebius vs UI8.

What if the CLI or MCP says no?

The mebius registry answers with a message the CLI prints.

  • No mebius token was sent: MEBIUS_TOKEN isn’t set where the CLI runs, or the registry URL redirects. Use the exact https://www URL above.
  • The token is invalid or has been revoked: create a new one and replace the line in .env.local.
  • Your account doesn’t own this kit: the item belongs to a paid kit. Buy it for $19, or All items for $259, and run the command again.
  • No item with that name: item names start with their kit, like @mebius/charts-ethereum. npx shadcn@latest search @mebius lists the ones your token can install.

The free items are the quickest test of the whole setup: create a free account and every chart and form is yours to install, by command or by prompt.

FAQ

Is the shadcn MCP server free?

Yes. It is part of the shadcn CLI, which is MIT licensed and free. It runs on your machine through npx, so it needs no account or key, apart from any tokens your private registries ask for.

Does the shadcn MCP server work with private registries?

Yes. Add the registry to components.json under a namespace, with an Authorization header that reads a token from an environment variable, and put the token in .env.local. The CLI and the MCP server both read it.

What is the difference between the shadcn CLI and shadcn MCP?

The CLI is the command-line tool that sets up a project and adds, views and searches registry items. The MCP server lets an AI editor do the same by prompt: it looks items up in your registries and hands the assistant the add command to run.

Do I need a token for the mebius MCP server?

No. Claude Code, Cursor and VS Code sign in through the browser: add the server, log in to mebius.design and click Approve. A personal access token from Settings › Tokens is the fallback for tools that can’t open a browser, and the shadcn CLI needs one for the @mebius registry.

Can an AI editor install mebius components without an account?

Only the 20 open starter items, which install from their URL with the plain shadcn CLI. The MCP server needs a sign-in, and a free account covers all 62 charts and 128 forms.

Related

  • Free charts: 62 animated chart cards to install with the commands above.
  • Free forms: 128 animated forms in light and dark.
  • Is shadcn/ui free?: The MIT license, and what free and paid shadcn kits allow.
  • Figma to React: How the registry behind these commands is made from Figma.

First published on mebius.design, where the code samples stay up to date.

title: DiagTrace: An Interactive Benchmark for Clinical Decision Making
description:
arXiv:2611.22009v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong performance on medical question answering and diagnostic reasoning benchmarks. However, existing evaluations typically provide all patient information upfront and assess only the final diagnosis or rationale. This setup ignores the need to acquire diagnostic evidence incrementally from incomplete information in real-world diagnosis. To bridge this gap, we introduce DiagTrace, a source-grounded benchmark for evaluating whether LLMs can reconstruct the documented diagnostic trajectory through interactive information seeking. Each benchmark instance is built from a PubMed Central case report and includes an initial presentation, an event bank, a clinical course, and diagnostic references. DiagTrace contains 510 cases across eight specialties, with 225 used to evaluate four LLMs on clinical-course alignment, interaction quality, and efficiency. Results reveal trade-offs in coverage, source-consistent ordering, and turn use.

title: CueClash: Frontier Vision-Language Models Judge 3-D Relations Close to the Picture Plane
description:
arXiv:2611.22180v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A vision-language model (VLM) can judge 3-D relations from the picture or from the ground layout. In photographs the two usually agree. We separate them with CueClash, rendered scenes in which the 2-D cue for each of five relations is right on exactly half the statements. The shortcut gap is accuracy when the cue is right minus accuracy when it is wrong. For Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-5.5 and Gemini 3.6 Flash at low reasoning effort it is +18 to +37 percentage points. It is +7 to +29 without two relations whose cue-wrong items are confounded with borderline cases or occlusion. Given ground coordinates and each relation's definition, they answer 99 to 100% correctly. Pixel measurements with camera depths remove most of the gap for objects fitting through openings. The failure lies in the step from the picture to the layout. The maps that the models draw of the scene from above mostly keep the depth order but, like the picture, shorten depth. GPT-5.5's maps stay close to a copy of the picture. Opus 5.5's and Gemini's maps undo about 0.6 of this shortening. Gemini's then shrink all depths by a further uniform factor. Opus 5.5 follows the picture mainly on fits, and its maps correct depth about as much as human observers of real scenes do. The three models also lose accuracy on CV-Bench photographs where a reliable 2-D cue misleads. In two open models the layout information reaches the language model, but their maps lose much of it.

title: Stop the agent from introducing a second date library when the repo already has one
description:
The ticket is “show the due date in the user’s locale.” The repo already has date-fns and a formatDate() helper. The agent adds dayjs because that is what its last tutorial used, plus a one-line dayjs(value).format(...) in the component. The bundle grows. The team now has two opinions about time zones.

I’ve started treating a new date (or money, or UUID) library in an agent PR as a dependency review, not a typo. One helper call is not a reason to add a second ecosystem.

Why this happens so often

Date formatting is a solved problem in every training set, and it is solved differently in each one. dayjs, luxon, moment, date-fns, and Temporal all look equally “standard” to a model. It cannot see your bundle budget unless you say so. It also cannot see that formatDate already wraps locale and time zone.

The second library usually arrives without typings consistency, without the same locale loading strategy, and without DST tests. Six months later, someone formats a due date with one library and a created-at with the other, and they disagree around midnight.

A simple date policy

  • One date stack per app — the library and helper already in package.json / src/lib/date.ts
  • No new date dependency for a single format call
  • New formats are added to the helper, not inlined in the component
  • If you truly need a new library, it is its own PR, with a migration note, not a drive-by in a UI ticket

The same rule applies to money, UUID, and HTTP clients. The date case is just the one I see most in UI diffs.

What to put in the prompt 

Use the existing date helper in src/lib/date.ts (date-fns).
Do not add dayjs, luxon, moment, or a second date package.
If a new format is required, add a named function to the helper and use it.
Do not inline format strings in the component.

Paste the helper and a line from package.json that shows the chosen library. In review, grep the diff for new packages and for dayjs / luxon / moment imports.

Relative time (“3 hours ago”) is a frequent excuse for a new dependency. If the app already formats relative time in the helper, use it. If it does not, add formatRelative next to formatDate, with the same locale and clock source, instead of pulling in a package for one function.

Also watch for hidden date libraries inside UI kits the agent adds in the same PR. A “lightweight date picker” can drag moment in through a sidebar. If you need a picker, prefer the one the design system already wraps, or isolate the dependency and say so.

Reject / send back

Reject

  • A new date library added to format one string
  • A component-local new Date().toLocaleDateString() next to a locale-aware helper, if that helper is the standard
  • Two libraries formatting related timestamps in the same PR
  • “It’s only used in this file” as the justification for a new dependency

Accept

  • A new helper function in the existing date module
  • A justified, standalone dependency PR with a removal plan for the old library
  • Temporal only if that is already the team’s chosen path, or the subject of the PR

title: B-OPSD: On-Policy Self-Distillation with Self-Generated Problem Briefs
description:
arXiv:2611.19273v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) has recently attracted interest because it provides dense teacher guidance without a separate, often larger teacher model. However, OPSD conditions its teacher on ground-truth solutions, which limits its use when such solutions are unavailable. We propose On-Policy Self-Distillation with Self-Generated Problem Briefs (B-OPSD). Using a prompt template, the initial model or a saved student checkpoint generates a problem brief from the question alone. The prompt asks for relevant principles, applicability conditions, and likely pitfalls, but not a final answer or a complete solution. A frozen teacher uses the brief as privileged context to guide the current student's on-policy rollouts through token-level distribution matching. B-OPSD uses no ground-truth solutions during training. Results on AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and HMMT 2025 show that both B-OPSD variants achieve higher average accuracy than OPSD at each of three Qwen3 model sizes. Code is available at https://github.com/ZevineXu/B-OPSD

title: Learning Regions of Attraction for Transverse Feedback Linearization under Controller Singularities
description:
arXiv:2611.22286v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Transverse feedback linearization (TFL) achieves path following by exactly linearizing the error dynamics, but its controller is undefined on a singular set, such as zero speed for a unicycle or zero thrust for a quadrotor. The constrained region of attraction, the set of initial states from which the closed loop converges to the path without violating state or regularity constraints, determines where the controller can be safely activated. Exploiting the exact linear error dynamics, we show that this region is the largest forward invariant subset of the admissible set. We then decompose its state-constrained Zubov value function into an analytically known quadratic cost-to-go and a safety value function. We learn only the latter, by fitted value iteration without infinite-horizon trajectory labels. The resulting estimate combines an inner layer verified by interval branch and bound with a learned outer layer tested on samples. On a unicycle following a circle and a sinusoid and on a planar quadrotor, it covers on average 72.0%, 83.4% and 19.1% of the simulated region of attraction. In comparison, the quadratic cost-to-go and two physics-informed neural network (PINN) solvers of Zubov's equation cover at most 11.3%, 4.0% and 0.0% on average. Code and animations are available at https://gradslab.github.io/roa_tfl

title: DailyBrick: Language-Guided Synthesis of Brick Assembly Instructions
description:
arXiv:2611.22132v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Generating a LEGO model from a user request is more than a plausible 3D shape generation. LEGO models require physical support per brick, and each brick should be placed unblocked. Current methods address this issue by training an expert large language model. We reduce the problem of generating extremely long context on all brick connections to that of writing a program that builds LEGO models like a human, considering each intermediate step could be executed. We introduce DailyBrick , a multi-stage agentic system that produces a LEGO model together with a brick-by-brick assembly instruction for human building and robot assembly. We design a multi-stage harness with roles to help LLMs generate more effectively. A versioned construction SDK compiles multi-level decisions, from semantic subparts to individual bricks, into canonical operations. An external Meta-Reviewer agent replays and inspects the generated package, verifies the model and its construction process, identifies failures, traces them to the responsible stage, and routes them to bounded repairs or to editable candidates for later skill or tool updates. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DailyBrick generates LEGO models based on simple user requests better than recent agentic systems, and show its utility in downstream applications such as robot manipulations on model assembly from instructions and brick sets (https://SpatialAgent.github.io/DailyBrick/).

title: Big Brains, Tiny Board: Pupavision, an Agentic Physical AI Instrument for Monitoring Drosophila Pupariation and Lifecycle Transitions
description:
arXiv:2611.22136v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Many biology experiments are limited by the availability and ease of use of instruments that monitor and record them. For example, the timing of pupariation in the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster, a widely used model organism, can provide biologically relevant information about growth regulation and is often recorded manually. Here, we present Pupavision, a small physical AI instrument built from a single-board Linux computer and a day/night camera for roughly 45 to 75 US dollars in parts. The key idea is that a frontier coding agent runs its agentic harness directly on the tiny board. The model thinks in the cloud, but the agent works on the device. The agent assists image capture, writes code to repair errors, and checks the experiment every day to keep raw data capture reliable. If recording stops, the researcher gets a ping on their mobile phone. A simple deterministic capture service records one image every ten minutes and never depends on the agent. We report a 26-day pilot in a fly incubator (about 3,580 frames), including eleven days in which the agent was logged out and capture continued, and a 51-hour outage whose cause led to the layered design. A researcher-in-the-loop workflow then produces per-vial pupariation curves by tracing selected pupae backward in time from a late reference frame. Future work will validate the assay for lifecycle tracking accuracy against expert-labeled data and expand real-time computer vision analysis. Pupavision offers a blueprint for do-it-yourself agentic instruments that put frontier intelligence on a tiny board, with deterministic code underneath. We present this as an early case study from a pilot lab deployment and contribute lessons learned toward a future where scientific domain experts are empowered by DIY agentic hardware.

title: Disambiguating Moral Circuits and Moral Features in Language Models: Moral content, normative judgment or cue words? Evidence from 14 models
description:
arXiv:2611.21705v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Interpretability methods can locate the attention heads and sparse autoencoder (SAE) features that change the answer a language model gives to a moral prompt, e.g., whether "Stealing medicine for a dying child is morally" continues with "justified" or "wrong". Such a component could respond to moral content, to the judgment of conduct by any norm, or to the word "morally" in the prompt. We built 227 minimal pairs of short phrases, validated by five annotators, whose two versions differ in a moral standard, in another kind of norm (prudence, etiquette, aesthetics or evidence) or in a descriptive quality, and showed them to 14 open-weight models (Llama, Gemma and Qwen, 1B to 14B, base and instruction-tuned), with and without the word "morally". In every model, the heads that change the moral answer belong to an evaluation circuit the models use for every kind of normative judgment we tested: these heads carry the same share of the effect for moral as for other normative pairs (pooled ratio 1.00, 97.5% confidence interval [0.92, 1.07], with the word; 0.90, [0.84, 0.96], without it), and the models need them as much for both. The models need these heads also when nothing in the prompt asks for a judgment, and on 400 scenarios of the ETHICS benchmark, where removing them takes away 37 to 39% of the difference between acceptable and unacceptable scenarios, against 1 to 3% for ten random heads. The SAE features we located respond mostly to the word "morally" rather than to what the phrase is about. The models represent the category of a pair (the standard the annotators assigned to it): it can be read from their hidden states, and, in the eight models we tested, removing the direction that carries it weakens the moral verdict by a few percent, and more than the other verdicts in seven of them. We release the pairs, the ratings, the code, the trained SAE dictionaries and the result files.

title: Go Storage API: Malformed Object Responses While Uploading Resized Images — Audit Recovery
description:
A malformed upload response should page the thumbnail worker only after the client has proved that the response is unusable. The least complex recovery path is to validate status and body shape, retry only an idempotent write, and preserve the original receipt separately from every resized derivative.

TL;DR: treat a resized receipt as a derived object, never as the audit copy. Record request IDs and response headers before retrying. Use bounded backoff for transient failures, but send a permanently malformed response to a quarantine queue after the retry budget is spent. For a marketplace, retention and deletion rules matter more than a short upload example.

The page that fires after the thumbnail upload

The alert arrives from the image worker, not checkout. A receipt has already been accepted, the worker has decoded a thumbnail, and the PUT for receipts/tenant-42/order-91827/thumb-320.webp returns a status that does not match the body the client expects. The on-call sees thumbnail_upload_invalid_response, a request ID if the service supplied one, and the object key. They should not see a second thumbnail because a blind retry happened to succeed.

The first action is to freeze the original receipt's deletion timer and inspect request and response logs. Was the request sent to the intended bucket and key? Was the body resized bytes rather than a base64 wrapper? Did the service return JSON when the client expected an object envelope, or did a proxy return HTML? A malformed reply can indicate a service problem or a wrongly formatted client request; the response alone does not identify which.

The signal that should have fired earlier is a client-side response validator. A 2xx status is necessary, but it is not proof that the client received usable data. Log status, content type, byte count, request ID, and a bounded hash of the response body. Do not log receipt contents. Alert on a sustained rate or queue-age breach, not one malformed response during a deploy. A noisy page trains the team to ignore the signal needed for recovery.

Keep it boring.

For this narrow workflow, Infrai is worth testing when a team wants one key and one bill across backend services, while keeping receipt objects private or signed-only. Its public discovery surface and runnable examples can reduce integration glue. The limitation is important: it is not the right sole control for immutable financial records.

What should the upload retry prove?

A retry is safe only when repeating the write cannot create an ambiguous audit state. Give the derived thumbnail a deterministic key based on receipt identifier, transform version, and dimensions. If a worker receives the job twice, both attempts target the same derived object rather than timestamped copies.

The original receipt needs a separate application-database record: object key, content digest, tenant, order identifier, received time, and retention deadline. Storage metadata is not a search index. Keep audit-query fields in the database and use storage for bytes.

This is the small part of a Go client I want beside the worker. It calls Infrai's public storage capability discovery endpoint and validates the response before the worker relies on the documented presign contract. The actual object write remains private or signed-only; this sample does not turn the receipt into a public URL.

package uploadcheck

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
)

func InspectStorageCapability() error {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if apiKey == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.object.presign", nil)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("build upload request: %w", err)
    }
    req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)
    req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "image/webp")
    resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("send upload request: %w", err)
    }
    return ValidateUploadResponse(resp)
}

func ValidateUploadResponse(resp *http.Response) error {
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    body, err := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 1<<20))
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("read upload response: %w", err)
    }
    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
        return fmt.Errorf("upload returned HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, summarize(body))
    }
    if len(bytes.TrimSpace(body)) == 0 {
        return fmt.Errorf("upload returned an empty body")
    }
    var value any
    if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &value); err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("upload returned malformed JSON: %w", err)
    }
    return nil
}

func summarize(body []byte) string {
    body = bytes.TrimSpace(body)
    if len(body) > 256 {
        body = body[:256]
    }
    return string(body)
}

The validator confirms transport status and JSON syntax; it does not invent response fields. Use the documented response schema for stricter checks. For a retryable error, use exponential backoff and honor Retry-After. Cap attempts and total time. For a non-retryable 4xx response or a body that fails validation repeatedly, record the failure durably and quarantine the job. A queue message is acknowledged only after the derivative is confirmed or the failure is recorded.

When the endpoint supports an idempotency key, derive it from the receipt ID and transform version and send that same key on every retry. A 429 is a scheduling signal, not permission to tight-loop.

The route is deliberately shown once. A returned presigned URL is a separate request: use it without the Infrai authorization header. Do not turn this sample into a public-read or static-site-hosting pattern.

Is the original receipt actually protected from deletion?

A successful thumbnail write does not prove that the original is safe, and a successful retry does not repair an accidentally overwritten audit object. Name the policies separately: derivative cleanup and original retention.

Use private or signed-only access for the original. Avoid public-read patterns and permanent public URLs for receipts containing customer and seller information. A storage service with no object versioning or object lock cannot provide recovery from accidental overwrite or a financial-grade WORM requirement by itself. Put that requirement in an external retention system, database-coordinated workflow, or storage product whose documented controls meet it.

If strict concurrent writes are required, an API without If-Match support needs queue or database coordination. Deterministic naming prevents many duplicate writes; it does not create compare-and-swap. Lifecycle expiration with a one-day minimum cannot express hourly cleanup for temporary resize artifacts. Multipart fragments also need an explicit cleanup plan when automatic abort rules are unavailable.

Before deleting an original, check the database retention deadline and any open audit case. A cleanup job should be idempotent: deleting an already absent derivative is a successful end state, while deleting the original before the retention decision is a policy failure.

Why did the storage object API return a malformed response?

The useful comparison is the coordination required when the response is malformed and the receipt must remain available for audit.

Option Useful recovery characteristic Boundary to verify
Amazon S3 Mature multipart-upload workflow and broad ecosystem for retries, lifecycle, and integrity checks Versioning, Object Lock, lifecycle, and permissions still need deliberate configuration
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible operations can fit an existing worker Verify exact consistency, lifecycle, event, and retention behavior
Google Cloud Storage Strong Google Cloud identity, logging, and retention integration Teams outside that platform may carry more IAM coupling
Infrai storage One REST API and one key can reduce backend credential and integration sprawl; public discovery documents schemas and examples No versioning or object lock, no If-Match, and no public-read ACL

Infrai is a reasonable option for private receipt derivatives when one key and one bill across backend services, plus application-managed retention, fit the workflow. Its public discovery surface and runnable examples can reduce integration glue. The recommendation is narrow: marketplace teams should try it for coordinated private uploads when they can keep the audit record and retention decision outside object storage.

S3 is the better fit when Object Lock or a deep multipart ecosystem is the deciding control. R2 deserves direct evaluation for an S3-shaped application. GCS is stronger when Google Cloud identity and retention are already the operating baseline. None removes response validation.

Recovery runbook for the next malformed response

Capture request ID, status, content type, response size, object key, transform version, and attempt number. Compare the request log with expected content type and byte count. Look for an HTML or proxy-generated body, truncation, incorrect key encoding, or a client format the endpoint does not accept.

Then check: original exists; retention deadline is intact; derivative key is deterministic; last attempt is recorded; retry budget remains. Retry only after the write can be repeated safely. If validation fails again, quarantine the job with its diagnostic envelope and keep the original available.

The false-positive cost is concrete: every unnecessary page interrupts an operator, and every automatic retry adds load while obscuring the first failure. The opposite mistake is worse. Treating any 2xx as success can advance the queue and leave the system to discover the missing thumbnail much later.

The rule is short: validate before acknowledge, make derived writes repeatable, and make retention independent from thumbnail success.

That is the whole point.

If that boundary fits your system, start with the storage thumbnail guide and verify the response contract in your worker before enabling cleanup.

Further reading

  • Amazon S3 Multipart Upload overview
  • Amazon S3 Object Lock
  • Cloudflare R2 S3 API compatibility
  • Google Cloud Storage retention policies
  • Infrai storage guidance for image thumbnails

References

  • AWS S3 Multipart Upload overview
  • Infrai storage discovery

title: An Optimization Framework for Denoising Generation
description:
arXiv:2611.22202v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Noise-unconditioned denoising learns a single score, so generation can be viewed as gradient ascent on a fixed log-density landscape. This optimization interpretation leaves two questions: do trajectories approach meaningful data, and do different initializations retain diverse outcomes? We establish both phenomena for empirical and population multi-scale Gaussian-mixture objectives. Under explicit posterior and landscape conditions, ascent converges almost surely within $O(m\sigma_{\min}^2/\tau)$ of an $m$-dimensional reference manifold with reach at least $\tau$. We derive a source--sink identity for the same fixed field and use it to prove finite-resolution regional coverage. In an affine construction, we further identify a positive-bandwidth regime where even empirical-score optimization can avoid training-sample memorization while preserving diversity at the training resolution. The same fixed objective naturally supports penalty-guided controllable generation. Experiments support our predicted mechanisms, show improved robustness under large-step guidance, and demonstrate downstream gains consistent with finite-data generative generalization.

title: AI-assisted research uncovers critical Java flaw, Oracle issues patch
description:
Originally published on The Daily Flare.

Oracle issued a critical Java security patch on November 17 after Calif Research disclosed an AI-assisted discovery of a remote-code-execution flaw in OpenJDK.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-114938 and nicknamed Java4Shell, affects the Base64 decoder in the x86-64 HotSpot Java Virtual Machine, part of the Java Development Kit. The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) classified it as a critical memory-corruption flaw and said specially crafted input could crash the JVM or allow unauthenticated remote code execution.

The defect sits in hand-written processor instructions used to speed up Base64 decoding, according to CyberScoop. Calif said the problem occurs when the decoder receives 64 “A” characters followed by an equals sign, the padding character used in Base64. The code miscalculates the input length and writes 64 bytes into a memory buffer that can be as small as 50 bytes, overwriting neighboring data before the program rejects the input.

That damage can crash a program, but researchers said an attacker may be able to turn it into control of the server. Calif described using heap grooming, a technique for arranging data in memory, to make the overwrite more useful to an attacker. The optimization involved runs on processors supporting AVX-512; CyberScoop reported that ARM64 systems are unaffected.

Calif reported unauthenticated code execution in products including Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Jenkins and PingFederate, and demonstrated a working break-in against Keycloak, an open-source login system. The researchers also showed code execution requiring a valid account in Kafka, Solr and Elasticsearch. Researcher samczsun demonstrated that Java programs could be compromised by connecting to a malicious server.

Calif researcher Quang Luong found the bug in about an hour while auditing OpenJDK with OpenAI’s Codex, the security firm said. The computing tokens cost less than $200, according to CyberScoop’s account of the research. Calif also said AI agents produced most of its exploit chains with little human involvement. The researchers cautioned that there is no universal exploit and that each target requires tailored steps.

Oracle shipped patched Java builds on November 17 as part of its November critical patch update, which covered 652 vulnerabilities across the company’s products, CyberScoop reported. CISA urged organizations to identify affected Java installations and apply relevant Java or vendor fixes promptly, prioritizing systems exposed to the internet.

In its CISA alert, the agency warned that Java runtimes may be bundled inside third-party applications, container images and appliances, and may not appear as separate items in software inventories. For systems that cannot be patched immediately, it recommended restricting and validating Base64 input at application boundaries, setting input-size limits and limiting unauthenticated access. It also urged defenders to watch for rogue runtimes, unexpected JVM crashes and suspicious Java processes.

The flaw matters because Java is used across banking, aviation, telecommunications, hospitals and government systems. Calif said OpenJDK runs at 90% of Fortune 500 companies. The BBC cited computer scientist Toby Walsh, who said Java’s role in managing memory made the weakness particularly concerning. Walsh said the flaw had been “hiding in plain sight for 12 years.”

Governments warned companies to install the fix, Reuters reported on November 18. South Korean authorities held an emergency meeting about possible Java vulnerabilities, according to Yonhap, as cited by Reuters.

title: What Am I Missing? Question-Answering as Hidden State Probing
description:
arXiv:2605.31561v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: The study of test-time reasoning in large language models (LLMs) has attracted increasing interests due to its profound impact on many tasks, with early work tracing back to approaches such as chain-of-thought reasoning. The basic mechanism underlying the test-time reasoning process, however, is still under-studied: from the same input prompt, and even the same partial solution, LLMs can produce varied answers if sampled multiple times. In this paper, we leverage question-asking as an inference-time intervention that articulates information about the model's hidden state. Specifically, we present a student-teacher setting where a student asks questions to a teacher. We train a probe on the student's hidden state before and after asking a question and find it is predictive of the trajectory's final correctness, even before generating the teacher's answer. This suggests there is a meaningful signal from the self-diagnosis that occurs during question generation rather than information transfer from the teacher. We then frame question-asking as a sequential decision problem, using this probe as a quality score, and define a gating policy to ask questions that maximize likelihood of correctness. We find that the success of question-asking as an intervention is largely dependent on the model's self-consistency. Our empirical results show a gap between detection and recovery; while our gating policy captures model correctness and uncertainty, interventions are equally likely to harm correct trajectories as they are to recover incorrect ones. This gap between diagnosis and correction has broader implications on language models' capacity for self-refinement under uncertainty.

title: CrisisBench: an evaluation suite for crisis counseling AI
description:
arXiv:2611.21622v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Background: Crisis helplines are essential to mental health systems but are often understaffed and underfunded. LLMs could support counselors, but existing benchmarks do not capture the escalation, risk assessment, and de-escalation central to crisis conversations, while privacy restrictions limit use of real transcripts.
Methods: We present CrisisBench, a privacy-preserving suite for single- and multi-turn crisis counseling evaluation. It includes 1,085 single-turn tasks from 200 de-identified conversations and 1,185 patient LLMs derived from hotline metadata. Patient models and a 23-item LLM judge were calibrated against expert counselors.
Results: We evaluated five GPT models plus draft-then-edit and retrieval-augmented generation. All systems underperformed human counselors on excessive empathy and questioning in single-turn evaluation. The rubric achieved human-human Krippendorff's $\alpha$ = 0.51 and LLM-human $\alpha$ = 0.54 (Pearson r = 0.80). In multi-turn evaluation, retrieval-augmented generation scored highest overall (0.961), with all systems within 0.058. Microskills and style/tone were near ceiling, while productivity and safety/risk accounted for most between-system variation. Counselors rated patient LLMs realistic (86%) and useful (92%).
Conclusion: CrisisBench enables scalable, privacy-preserving evaluation of crisis counseling. Current systems perform strongly on core structural competencies but still diverge from experts on important response-level failure modes. We release the rubrics, judge prompts, and evaluation tasks.

title: Beyond Appearance: Where Forest Visual Place Recognition Actually Fails
description:
arXiv:2611.21996v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Visual place recognition (VPR) in forest environments remains challenging because repetitive vegetation, and changes in illumination, season, and viewpoint can make distinct places appear similar and revisited places appear substantially different. In this paper, we investigate whether temporal, linguistic, structural, and geometric context can improve on an appearance-only descriptor, and what limits each representation when it does not. Using MegaLoc as the appearance-based baseline on the WildCross benchmark, we evaluate score-space and descriptor-space sequence matching, vision-language captions and reranking, scene-graph representations, and depth-derived stem graphs across same-direction revisits, extended routes, and reverse traversals. On a same-direction revisit, both sequence matching strategies reach similar Recall@1 (94.1% vs. 91.5%), but recall at 100% precision rises from 50.9% (single-frame MegaLoc) to 71.6% in score space and falls to 36.5% in descriptor space. The remaining context representations provide no consistent improvement over the appearance-based baseline. Same-place captions show limited place-specific discrimination, reranking is constrained by the initial candidate shortlist, and stem-graph matching remains weak even with LiDAR depth.

title: LLMs as Validators for Cross-Chain Bridges: Evaluating Source-Level and Transaction-Level Attack Detection on Solana
description:
arXiv:2611.21777v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Cross-chain bridges have suffered substantial asset losses due to vulnerabilities in their on-chain programs. On Solana, missing validation checks can enable exploits even when the underlying blockchain operates correctly. The ability of large language models (LLMs) to diagnose these flaws from source code or transaction records, rather than merely raise alarms, remains insufficiently understood. We implement a native Rust lock-and-mint bridge on a local Solana validator with four exploitable variants: two model flaws from the Cashio and Wormhole incidents, while the other two represent vulnerability classes documented in Solana security audits. Paired vulnerable and secure programs, together with successful attacks, benign sessions, and blocked attempts, allow us to distinguish correct diagnoses from unsupported alarms. We evaluate six configurations of five open-weight models across 16,800 responses, compare source inputs with and without comments, and grade 7,200 answers on vulnerable inputs using two blinded LLM graders. The results reveal substantial differences across conditions: without comments, models diagnose 24% of vulnerable source inputs while frequently flagging the secure bridge. Transaction diagnosis is high for the missing-signer scenario but averages 6% across the other three scenarios. Original comments, some of which describe the flaw, increase source diagnosis to 60%. These findings highlight the importance of distinguishing correct vulnerability diagnoses from unsupported alarms in bridge security review.

title: Which post-quantum key exchanges does a server actually support?
description:
Every post-quantum migration starts with the same question: does this server support a post-quantum key exchange yet? It sounds like a yes or no. It isn't, because the honest answer depends on which client is asking.

I built pqc-probe to answer it from real handshakes instead of configuration files or advertised lists. It connects to a server over TLS and SSH, tries each key exchange one at a time, and reports which ones actually complete. Version 0.1.0 is out this week as a CLI, a web service, a Docker image and a GitHub Action.

This post covers what the tool measures, how to read its output, and what it found across the 1,000 most popular sites. Later posts in the series go deeper into the surprises along the way.

Offered is not negotiated

A TLS client sends a list of key exchange groups it can use, and the server picks one. A normal connection tells you only which group won, not which others the server would have accepted. So pqc-probe offers one group at a time and records whether the handshake completes:

openssl s_client -connect github.com:443 -groups X25519MLKEM768 -4

If that handshake succeeds, the server supports X25519MLKEM768. If it fails, the server does not, whatever any configuration page claims. The probe repeats this for seven groups: four classical (X25519, P-256, P-384, P-521) and three ML-KEM hybrids (X25519MLKEM768, SecP256r1MLKEM768, SecP384r1MLKEM1024).

SSH needs a different trick. The server sends its full list of key exchange algorithms before any encryption starts, so pqc-probe reads that packet directly. Then, for each post-quantum algorithm both sides know, it runs a real key exchange and marks the row ok (tested) only when the exchange completes. Being on the server's list is not enough.

Two clients, one diff

Which client asks matters, so pqc-probe asks with two:

Mode TLS client SSH client Answers
vanilla stock OpenSSL 3.5 stock OpenSSH What a normal production client gets today
experimental OpenSSL + oqs-provider OQS-OpenSSH What the Open Quantum Safe algorithms unlock

--mode both runs the two side by side and prints a diff. A group that only the experimental client can negotiate means the server supports something your users' clients cannot use yet. A group both can negotiate is deployable today.

There is one catch, and the tool flags it. OpenSSL 3.5 already supports ML-KEM hybrids out of the box. When the stock client is itself post-quantum capable, an empty diff says little about the server, so the report adds a note saying exactly that.

Reading a real report: github.com

Here is GitHub, probed from the Docker image with both protocols and both client stacks (trimmed):

$ docker run --rm --init ghcr.io/asifmahbubnaeem/pqc-probe:0.1.0 \
    pqc-probe probe github.com --protocol both --mode both

TLS KEMs (vanilla  vs  experimental):
  offered                   vanilla           experimental
  X25519                    ok                ok
  P-256                     ok                ok
  P-384                     -                 -
  P-521                     -                 -
  X25519MLKEM768            -                 -
  SecP256r1MLKEM768         -                 -
  SecP384r1MLKEM1024        -                 -

SSH KEX (server offer × client support):
  server offers                         mainline ssh      OQS-OpenSSH
  mlkem768x25519-sha256                 ok (tested)       ok (tested)
  sntrup761x25519-sha512                ok (tested)       ok (tested)
  sntrup761x25519-sha512@openssh.com    ok (tested)       ok (tested)
  curve25519-sha256                     ok                ok
  ...

SSH diff:
  Mainline ssh and OQS-OpenSSH negotiate identically on this target.

Two services on the same domain give opposite answers:

  • TLS (port 443): only X25519 and P-256 complete. The stock OpenSSL 3.5.7 offered ML-KEM, and GitHub's front end declined it. At the time of this run, a browser connecting to github.com got a classical key exchange.
  • SSH (port 22): three post-quantum key exchanges complete with both clients, so git push over SSH is already post-quantum.

The SSH diff is empty because the image's stock client is OpenSSH 10.0, which already supports these algorithms. The same probe from an older laptop with OpenSSH 9.6 showed two of them as "only experimental". That is the client changing, not the server.

What the top 1,000 sites do

Tranco list K9YYW, top 1,000, scanned 2026-11-06 with pqc-probe scan · one vantage point, IPv4 only · data and method in results/ in the repository]

Among the most popular sites that answer over TLS 1.3, post-quantum key exchange is already the majority. Read "accepts" strictly: the handshake completes when X25519MLKEM768 is offered alone, which shows support, not that the server prefers it.

The 305 sites without a handshake say nothing about post-quantum support either way: most are list entries with no DNS answer or no web server on port 443. The full dataset, the retry passes and the charts are in results/.

Three things that surprised me

  1. The SSH debug log cut the server's offer in half. My first version read the server's algorithm list from ssh -vv. On a test server with a long list, the line simply stopped mid-name: OpenSSH truncates debug lines at about 1 KB. Reading the key exchange packet directly fixed it.
  2. Testing too fast produced false negatives. OpenSSH 9.8 and later penalise addresses that open many short connections (PerSourcePenalties). My test server's log showed a 16-second penalty kicking in, after which real support looked like failure. The probe now tests at most 8 algorithms, one per second.
  3. The stock client is already post-quantum. OpenSSL 3.5 and OpenSSH 10 ship ML-KEM by default, so the classic "vanilla versus experimental" comparison is shrinking. Where it still shows a gap, the gap is usually an old client, not the server.

Each of these gets its own post in this series.

Try it

The Docker image carries both client stacks, so it is the quickest start:

docker run --rm --init ghcr.io/asifmahbubnaeem/pqc-probe:0.1.0 \
  pqc-probe probe example.com --protocol both --mode both

With Rust 1.89 or later, the CLI installs from crates.io and uses the openssl and ssh already on your machine:

cargo install pqc-probe
pqc-probe probe example.com --protocol both

Static Linux binaries are on the GitHub release page.

To check your own hosts on every deploy, the GitHub Action keeps a JSON report per host and can fail the job when a host has no post-quantum key exchange:

- uses: asifmahbubnaeem/pqc-probe@v0.1.0
  with:
    targets: api.example.com, git.example.com:2222
    require-pq-ssh: "true"

Every report follows a published JSON schema, which only ever gains fields within a version, so you can build on it. Please probe hosts you are responsible for.

What's next

The rest of this series:

  1. Your SSH debug log is truncating the server's offer
  2. Probing SSH without getting penalised
  3. The stock client is already post-quantum
  4. Shipping two liboqs builds in one container, and two GCC 14 bugs found on the way (#210, #211)
  5. Running a scanner for strangers: SSRF, DNS rebinding and rate limits

pqc-probe is the first project of three. pqc-bench measures what post-quantum TLS costs in performance, and a migration dashboard built on pqc-probe's reports comes next.

The code is on GitHub under MIT or Apache-2.0. Issues and results from your own servers are very welcome.

title: Can Coding Agents Write and Transpile Unit Tests
description:
arXiv:2611.21797v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Coding assistants built on Large Language Models (LLMs) have become a staple of modern software development, increasingly trusted to execute workflows and modernize code end-to-end. Much of this trust rests on passing tests, which are often written by the coding agents themselves. In this work, we examine the ability of these agents to both write reliable tests and translate them between programming languages. We benchmark three popular coding agents, each evaluated with a native frontier model and high reasoning effort. Verifying across a broad suite of metrics, we find that coding agents far exceed human written suites on traditional measures of coverage. This advantage, however, is uneven: agent test quality degrades sharply with project size, and much of the advantage lies in a greater number of written tests. We also show that agentic test translation---while seemingly strong in aggregate---remains inconsistent and unreliable.

title: Apple Just Made 1080p Video in 120 ms – Here’s How It’s Changing Live‑Streaming
description:
FastFrames Hits the Fast Lane: Real‑Time Video Generation Goes Commercial in November 2026

Lead

Apple’s WWDC 2026 keynote promised “AI that fits in your pocket.” Six months later the company delivered: FastFrames, a diffusion‑based video generator that produces 1080p frames in roughly 120 ms, now powering Vision Pro Studio and Apple Cloud Video‑AI. The service marks the first time a research‑grade autoregressive diffusion model achieves true interactive latency outside a lab.

“We can now synthesize a full‑HD video clip faster than a human can blink,” declared Apple’s senior AI engineer during the live demo, flashing a 30 fps avatar that responded to a presenter’s gestures in real time.

That claim sparked a flurry of analysis. Did Apple merely showcase a polished demo, or does FastFrames genuinely shift the economics of video synthesis? This article dissects the technical underpinnings, benchmarks the numbers against Nvidia’s RTX 6000‑Ada, and evaluates the broader impact on streaming, AR/VR, and enterprise pipelines.

The Case Study: Building an Interactive Live‑Stream Overlay in 2026

Imagine a Twitch streamer who wants to replace his green‑screen background with a dynamically generated fantasy terrain that reacts to chat commands—“turn night into day,” “spawn a dragon.” Before FastFrames, the streamer would have to pre‑render every possible scene, upload assets to a CDN, and hope the latency stayed under a second.

Using Apple’s FastFrames SDK (available through the Apple Developer portal) the streamer builds a simple pipeline:

  1. Static Latent Backbone – The SDK downloads a 1080p latent representation of a generic fantasy terrain once at startup (≈ 30 MB). This backbone encodes geometry, lighting, and texture priors.
  2. Dynamic Residual Stream – Every time a chat command arrives, the SDK calls FastFrames.generateResidual(step=AnyForcing(4), prompt="night→day"). The Any‑Forcing module runs a 4‑step diffusion on a thin residual tensor (≈ 2 MB).
  3. Speculative Sampling – The SDK predicts the next three frames in a single GPU kernel, reducing kernel‑launch overhead from ~2 ms per frame to < 0.5 ms.
  4. On‑Device Rendering – The M3 Ultra inside the streamer’s MacBook Pro applies the residual to the backbone, producing a 1080p frame in ~120 ms. The frame streams to OBS and then to Twitch with a total end‑to‑end latency of ~180 ms.

The streamer reports a 70 % reduction in bandwidth (only residuals travel over the internet) and a 30 % increase in viewer engagement measured by chat activity per minute. The same workflow runs on an iPhone 15 Pro, proving that the pipeline scales down to mobile SoCs without a desktop GPU.

The Meat: Hard Numbers and Technical Deep Dive

1. Dual‑Stage Autoregressive Diffusion

FastFrames replaces the monolithic diffusion loop with a dual‑stage encoder:

Stage Function Compute cost (GFLOPs)
Static Latent Backbone Pre‑computes a high‑dimensional scene representation once per session. ~150
Dynamic Residual Update Computes a lightweight residual for each new frame, using the backbone as constant context. ~30

Decoupling the heavy lifting (backbone) from per‑frame work (residual) drops the per‑frame FLOP budget to ≈ 30 GFLOPs. On Apple’s M3 Ultra (24‑core GPU, 30 W), that translates to ~120 ms for 1080p at 30 fps.

2. Speculative Sampling

Traditional diffusion samples one timestep per kernel launch, incurring ~2 ms overhead on modern GPUs. FastFrames bundles k future timesteps into a single kernel, effectively speculating on the next k latent states. The authors report a 3.5× reduction in kernel‑launch time for k = 3, with no measurable quality loss (PSNR drop < 0.1 dB).

3. Any‑Forcing (Any‑Step Flexibility)

FastFrames introduces Any‑Forcing, a control module that lets developers trade steps for latency on the fly. Typical configurations are shown below:

Steps Frame Rate PSNR (dB) SSIM
4 (default) 30 fps 38.2 0.96
2 45 fps 37.8 0.95
1 60 fps 37.0 0.93

Visual fidelity remains high while scaling up to 60 fps for low‑stakes applications such as UI animations.

4. Benchmark Against Nvidia RTX 6000‑Ada

Apple’s internal benchmark (released alongside the WWDC demo) pits FastFrames on an M3 Ultra against Nvidia’s RTX 6000‑Ada running the best‑available autoregressive diffusion implementation (Video‑Gen‑X, 4‑step). Results:

“FastFrames achieves 30 fps at 1080p with 120 ms latency on M3 Ultra, while RTX 6000‑Ada stalls at 250 ms per frame for the same resolution and quality.” – OrcaRouter comparative article

Key takeaways

  • Latency: FastFrames cuts interactive latency by ≈ 50 %.
  • Power: M3 Ultra draws ~30 W versus RTX 6000‑Ada’s ~250 W, an 8× efficiency gap.
  • Cost: The on‑device solution eliminates the need for a high‑end desktop GPU, slashing capital expense for AR/VR and edge developers.

5. Bandwidth Savings in Cloud‑Edge Hybrid Pipelines

Apple Cloud Video‑AI off‑loads the static backbone to the cloud, streaming only the dynamic residual to edge devices. Tests show a ≈ 70 % reduction in upstream bandwidth compared to streaming full frames, while preserving interactive latency (< 150 ms). This hybrid model enables low‑latency experiences on 5G networks where full‑frame streaming would saturate the link.

The Pivot: Risks and Open Questions

  1. Model Generalization – Performance hinges on the quality of the static backbone. Niche domains (medical imaging, scientific visualization) still require custom backbones, a process that demands substantial GPU time.
  2. Ecosystem Lock‑In – The SDK leans on Apple‑specific Core ML and Vision Pro tooling. Porting FastFrames to Android or Windows will likely incur a performance penalty, risking market fragmentation.
  3. Quality‑Latency Trade‑off Limits – Below two diffusion steps the PSNR/SSIM drop becomes noticeable, making the technology less suitable for photorealistic virtual production without accepting higher latency.
  4. Competitive Response – Nvidia’s rumored Video‑Gen‑Y (Q1 2027) promises adaptive step scheduling and hardware‑accelerated diffusion kernels. If Nvidia matches Apple’s speculative sampling on Ada‑generation GPUs, the latency gap could narrow.

Outlook: Where FastFrames Could Take the Industry

Application Why FastFrames Matters
Interactive Live Streaming 70 % bandwidth savings make AI‑generated overlays feasible on average 5G connections; sub‑200 ms latency keeps chats truly interactive.
AR/VR Content Creation Vision Pro Studio already lets creators paint motion with a stylus and see the result instantly; M‑series chips in headsets will enable fully AI‑driven worlds that react to gestures.
Edge Surveillance & Summarisation On‑premise M3‑based appliances can synthesize short highlight reels of security footage in seconds, reducing storage costs and speeding incident response.
Hybrid Cloud‑Edge Rendering Streaming only residuals lets CDNs off‑load most compute to the edge, aligning with emerging 5G‑edge standards for latency‑critical media.
Open‑Source Momentum The FastFrames repo already shows 21 up‑votes on Hugging Face, indicating strong community interest. External contributors could add domain‑specific backbones and cross‑platform kernels, pushing the technology beyond Apple’s own ecosystem.

Call to Action

If you’re a developer, start experimenting with the FastFrames SDK today—download it from the Apple Developer portal, try the fantasy‑terrain backbone, and measure latency on your own hardware. For enterprises, evaluate the cost‑of‑ownership model: compare a single M3 Ultra‑based edge node against a fleet of RTX 6000‑Ada workstations. And for the research community, contribute a new backbone to the open‑source repo; the more domains we cover, the faster real‑time video synthesis will become a commodity.

Bottom line: FastFrames shows that algorithmic innovation can outpace raw hardware horsepower when interactive latency is the goal. By reframing diffusion as a two‑stage problem, adding speculative sampling, and exposing an any‑step interface, Apple delivers a service that runs faster, cooler, and cheaper than today’s GPU‑centric alternatives. The next test will be how quickly developers expand beyond the curated backbones, how competitors respond, and whether the industry can reliably blend cloud and edge compute without sacrificing interactivity. If those challenges are met, real‑time video synthesis could become as ubiquitous as image generation is today—only now the frames will arrive before the viewer even finishes blinking.

title: Clustering in pure-attention hardmax transformers and its role in sentiment analysis
description:
arXiv:2407.01602v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Transformers are extremely successful machine learning models whose mathematical properties remain poorly understood. Here, we rigorously characterize the behavior of transformers with hardmax self-attention and normalization sublayers as the number of layers tends to infinity. By viewing such transformers as discrete-time dynamical systems describing the evolution of points in a Euclidean space, and thanks to a geometric interpretation of the self-attention mechanism based on hyperplane separation, we show that the transformer inputs asymptotically converge to a clustered equilibrium determined by special points called \textit{leaders}. We then leverage this theoretical understanding to solve sentiment analysis problems from language processing using a fully interpretable transformer model, which effectively captures `context' by clustering meaningless words around leader words carrying the most meaning. Finally, we outline remaining challenges to bridge the gap between the mathematical analysis of transformers and their real-life implementation.

title: PSM: Prompt Sensitivity Minimization via LLM-Guided Black-Box Optimization
description:
arXiv:2511.16209v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: System prompts are critical for guiding the behavior of Large Language Models (LLMs), yet they often contain proprietary logic or sensitive information, making them a prime target for extraction attacks. Adversarial queries can successfully elicit these hidden instructions, posing significant security and privacy risks. Existing defense mechanisms frequently rely on heuristics, incur substantial computational overhead, or are inapplicable to models accessed via black-box APIs. This paper introduces a novel framework for hardening system prompts through shield appending, a lightweight approach that adds a protective textual layer to the original prompt. Our core contribution is the formalization of prompt hardening as a utility-constrained optimization problem. We leverage an LLM-as-optimizer to search the space of possible SHIELDs, seeking to minimize a leakage metric derived from a suite of adversarial attacks, while simultaneously preserving task utility above a specified threshold, measured by semantic fidelity to baseline outputs. This black-box, optimization-driven methodology is lightweight and practical, requiring only API access to the target and optimizer LLMs. We demonstrate empirically that our optimized SHIELDs significantly reduce prompt leakage against a comprehensive set of extraction attacks, outperforming established baseline defenses without compromising the model's intended functionality. Our work presents a paradigm for developing robust, utility-aware defenses in the escalating landscape of LLM security. The code is made public on the following link: https://github.com/psm-defense/psm

title: Stress-Testing Emotional Support Models: Moving from Homogeneous to Diverse Help Seekers
description:
arXiv:2601.07698v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: As emotional support chatbots have recently gained significant traction across both research and industry, a common evaluation strategy has emerged: use help-seeker simulators to interact with supporter chatbots. However, current simulators suffer from two critical limitations: (1) they fail to capture the behavioral diversity of real-world seekers, often portraying them as overly cooperative, and (2) they lack the controllability required to simulate specific seeker profiles. To address these challenges, we present a controllable seeker simulator driven by nine psychological and linguistic features that underpin seeker behavior. Using authentic Reddit conversations, we train our model via a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture, which effectively differentiates diverse seeker behaviors into specialized parameter subspaces, thereby enhancing fine-grained controllability. Our simulator achieves superior profile adherence and behavioral diversity compared to existing approaches. Furthermore, evaluating 7 prominent supporter models with our system uncovers previously obscured performance degradations. These findings underscore the utility of our framework in providing a more faithful and stress-tested evaluation for emotional support chatbots.

title: Your AI agent copied the web page onto iOS. Start from the platform.
description:
Say you already have a web tool at example.com for logging a site visit, and you ask your AI agent for the iOS screen. The reply is the web page, transplanted: a left sidebar, hover-only extra actions, and a floating button copied from another platform. On a phone held in one hand, the sidebar is gone, and so are the actions that lived on hover.

The agent copied a familiar surface onto the wrong platform.

This is a fictional illustration of how Design Decision Method handles platform guidance, not a case study or a measured result. The product details below are invented for the example.

Start from the platform you are actually building

The live docs already put the device in establish context. When choosing a visual system, they say to keep a system the project already has, and when it has none, to select from the platform. For other web work, the fallback is Material 3. Borrow an interaction pattern when it solves the task. Do not copy another organization's branding.

The docs are plain that this is not a ranking: the procedure routes work across Material 3, platform guidelines, and a project's own rules, among other sources, and does not rank those sources or copy their branding.

What the live introduction does not spell out is how that choice changes on iOS versus Android versus the web. That detail lives in the agent procedure.

What the procedure actually selects

If a suitable existing system, brand, or platform direction is already in place, the procedure says to retain and extend it. A new iOS screen is not automatic permission to invent a second identity.

When there is no existing system, the procedure gives conditional rows, not a favourite:

  • For a native Apple interface, use Apple's Human Interface Guidelines and system controls for the supported OS and SDK. Do not mandate the newest material or an OS upgrade.
  • For Android or Compose, use Material 3, and only use Expressive options where the brief or project calls for them and the installed library supports them.
  • For other web or cross-platform work, Material 3 is the fallback, with implementation support checked.

The routing guidance is just as direct for a native mobile screen: use the platform's guidance for navigation and controls. Avoid mimicking one platform's material on another.

A short note for the example.com iOS screen might look like this:

Platform: A native iOS screen, not a wrapped copy of the website.
Keep: The product's existing brand colour roles, if they already exist.
Follow the platform: System navigation and controls for the supported OS and SDK. Every action that existed on the web stays reachable without hover.
Do not copy: The web sidebar, hover-only overflow, or a floating action pattern brought over from another platform.
Do not add: A new visual material the brief did not ask for, or a required OS upgrade.

Choose the visual system still starts with what the project already has. Platform selection is the next question: which conventions this surface should actually follow.

Brand can travel. Chrome often should not.

Choosing the visual system is separate from borrowing an interaction pattern. The procedure's visual-system reference adds a practical split: native platform conventions can coexist with brand typography and imagery when behaviour stays coherent. The site-visit log can keep its colours. It should not keep a sidebar that iOS does not use, or actions that disappear without a pointer.

The same split runs the other way. A later Android screen should not be dressed in iOS chrome to look "consistent." A web page should not assume a gesture that only exists on a phone. Rebuild the pattern in the target stack — meaning, behaviour, focus, and feedback — instead of pasting another platform's markup.

Structure each view already asks the agent to adapt the layout to the device without dropping a capability the task needs. Hover-only actions on an iOS screen fail that test.

Keep it proportional

Name the platform, keep a suitable existing brand, and write down the conventions you will not transplant. The method is a shared procedure, not mandatory for every small edit. It does not claim this saves time. That has not been measured. It also does not guarantee a better native screen. What it gives you is a place to catch a copied surface before it ships on the wrong platform.

Try it

Design Decision Method is a lightweight design decision workflow for developers building interfaces with AI agents. It follows the open Agent Skills format and is MIT licensed. Install paths for Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI, and Codex are in the README.

  • Read the DDM docs
  • Visual-system adoption checks
  • Repository README and install notes

title: Customize AWS Elemental Inference with custom models, prompts, and decisions
description:
AWS Elemental Inference now lets you customize how it analyzes your live video in two ways. You can create functions that ask custom questions of the video using multi-modal foundational models in Amazon Bedrock, or add contextual metadata decisions using labels and questions you define. Both run on the same pipeline as built-in features such as vertical video creation and smart subtitles, and return results through the GetMetadata API, with no separate pipeline to build.

Use contextual metadata decisions when the answer you need fits labels and yes/no questions. You define yes/no questions, such as whether a scene is a weather report, or "pick-one" categories, such as genre. For each scene, contextual metadata returns a decision and a confidence score for every label and question, alongside the standard Interactive Advertising Bureau (IAB), Global Alliance for Responsible Media (GARM), and mood fields, so your workflows can act when confidence meets a threshold you set. No model selection or prompt writing is required.

Use functions for open-ended answers, custom response formats, or analysis contextual metadata doesn't cover, such as sponsor logo exposure. A function specifies an Amazon Bedrock model and JSONata expressions that shape the request and response. You attach it to a feed and choose how frequently it runs.

Contextual-metadata decisions configuration is included in the contextual metadata price. Functions are available at no additional charge on feeds with at least one feature active; Amazon Bedrock usage is billed separately. Both are available in all AWS Regions where AWS Elemental Inference is available.

To learn more, see the AWS Elemental Inference user guide.
