title: Best animation library for Unity UI Toolkit: Cascade vs PrimeTween vs LitMotion
description:
If you search for a way to animate Unity UI Toolkit, three libraries come up: PrimeTween, LitMotion and Cascade. All three can fade and move a VisualElement. They were built for different jobs, and that shows once your UI gets bigger than one button.

Disclosure: I make Cascade. I've tried to be fair to the other two. Every claim about PrimeTween and LitMotion below comes from their source code and docs (PrimeTween 1.5.2, LitMotion 2.0.2, checked November 2026). The Cascade version is 1.2. Every code sample here was compiled and run in one Unity 6000.4 project with all three libraries installed, and checked against what the text says it does. If something is wrong or out of date, tell me and I'll fix the page.

The short answer

  • Your project already uses PrimeTween or LitMotion for gameplay: use the same library for simple UI Toolkit tweens. One tween library is easier than two.
  • You need the fastest possible tweens for thousands of objects: LitMotion (Burst and the Job System) or PrimeTween. In my UI Toolkit benchmark below, LitMotion was the fastest, Cascade second and PrimeTween third.
  • Your UI is built in UI Toolkit and has a lot of motion (screens that come and go, lists, interruptible buttons, springs): Cascade was written for exactly that.
  • You write most of your UI code with an AI assistant: Cascade is the only one of the three with official assistant support. See AI coding assistants.
  • You're on Unity 2022 or older: Cascade needs Unity 6, so pick PrimeTween or LitMotion.

At a glance

PrimeTween LitMotion Cascade
Built for Transforms, materials, uGUI, also UI Toolkit Any value, very fast (DOTS) UI Toolkit only
Price free (PRO edition $32.99 adds Inspector animations) free Lite free; Pro paid
License custom (free for commercial use) MIT Lite MIT; Pro Asset Store EULA
Unity 2018.4+ (per its package) 2021.3+ 6000.0+
Dependencies none Burst, Collections, Mathematics none
UI Toolkit tweens built in opacity, color, background color, translate/rotate/scale, left/top/width/height opacity, colors, translate, scale, rotate, transform-origin, left/right/top/bottom, width/height, font size, text, progress bar opacity, translate, scale, rotate, colors, width/height, left/top/right/bottom, border radius/width/color, font size, padding, background-image tint, slide-in from an edge, any float
Other styles Tween.Custom Bind Value
Sequencing yes (Sequence) yes (LSequence, since 2.0) yes (Then(), At(seconds))
Await yes yes yes
Physics springs no (elastic/overshoot easing) no (elastic easing) Pro
Stagger helper no (use delays) no (use delays) Pro
Shake / punch Transform only yes (float/Vector values, bind to any style) yes: Shake, Punch (Lite); PunchScale, PunchRotate, Pulse, Wiggle, Pop (Pro). Additive, always end at rest
Stops when the element leaves the panel no (measured: keeps writing to it) no (measured: keeps writing to it) yes
Reduced motion setting no no yes (Lite and Pro)
AI coding assistant support no official support (community-made agent skills exist) no official support (community-made agent skills exist) official agent skill, AI guide in the package, compile-time code checks; Pro: validated JSON animations
Screen transitions, hover/press, no-code component no no (the Inspector component has no UI Toolkit tracks) Pro

The same animation in all three

A panel fades in while it slides up 40 px, a common way to show a window.

PrimeTween 

using PrimeTween;

Tween.VisualElementOpacity(panel, startValue: 0f, endValue: 1f, duration: 0.3f, ease: Ease.OutCubic);
Tween.Position(panel, startValue: new Vector3(0, 40, 0), endValue: Vector3.zero, duration: 0.3f, ease: Ease.OutCubic);

Tween.Position, Rotation and Scale accept a VisualElement and write style.translate, rotate and scale on Unity 6.2 and newer.

LitMotion 

using LitMotion;
using LitMotion.Extensions;

LMotion.Create(0f, 1f, 0.3f).WithEase(Ease.OutCubic).BindToStyleOpacity(panel);
LMotion.Create(new Vector2(0, 40), Vector2.zero, 0.3f).WithEase(Ease.OutCubic).BindToStyleTranslate(panel);

Every motion takes an explicit start value. LitMotion has the widest set of built-in style bindings of the three.

Cascade 

using Cascade;

panel.Animate()
     .Fade(1f, 0.3f).From(0f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic)
     .MoveY(0f, 0.3f).From(40f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic);

Without From(), Cascade starts from the value the element has on the frame the animation begins, including values that come from USS.

A sequence: fade in, then pop

PrimeTween 

Sequence.Create()
    .Chain(Tween.VisualElementOpacity(panel, startValue: 0f, endValue: 1f, duration: 0.2f))
    .Chain(Tween.Scale(panel, endValue: new Vector3(1.1f, 1.1f, 1f), duration: 0.2f, ease: Ease.OutBack))
    .ChainCallback(() => Debug.Log("done"));

LitMotion 

LSequence.Create()
    .Append(LMotion.Create(0f, 1f, 0.2f).BindToStyleOpacity(panel))
    .Append(LMotion.Create(Vector3.one, new Vector3(1.1f, 1.1f, 1f), 0.2f).WithEase(Ease.OutBack).BindToStyleScale(panel))
    .Run(b => b.WithOnComplete(() => Debug.Log("done")));

Cascade 

panel.Animate()
     .Fade(1f, 0.2f).From(0f)
     .Then()
     .ScaleTo(1.1f, 0.2f).Ease(Ease.OutBack)
     .OnComplete(() => Debug.Log("done"));

All three read well. All three can also place a tween at an exact time inside a sequence: PrimeTween and LitMotion with Insert, Cascade with At(seconds).

Where the differences show up

When the element leaves the screen

PrimeTween stops a tween when its target is a destroyed UnityEngine.Object, and LitMotion links motions to a GameObject with AddTo. A VisualElement isn't a Unity object, so neither check applies. Neither library listens for an element being removed from its panel, so when a screen closes or a list row is recycled mid-tween, stop it yourself. I measured it: a 2-second fade, with the element removed after 0.3 s, keeps changing the removed element's opacity in both libraries.

// PrimeTween
panel.RegisterCallback<DetachFromPanelEvent>(_ => Tween.StopAll(onTarget: panel));

// LitMotion: keep the handles and cancel them
panel.RegisterCallback<DetachFromPanelEvent>(_ => handle.TryCancel());

Cascade cancels an animation when its element leaves the panel and never writes to an element that isn't displayed. In a UI with many screens, that's the bug class I most wanted to remove.

Interrupting an animation

Buttons and drawers get interrupted all the time: hover out before the hover-in finishes, close a drawer while it's opening. With PrimeTween or LitMotion you stop the old tween and start a new one, usually from the current value. The new tween starts from rest, so the motion visibly loses its momentum.

Cascade Pro has physics springs. A spring that gets a new target keeps its current velocity, so the motion bends toward the new target instead of restarting:

drawer.Animate().MoveX(open ? 0f : -320f, 0f).Spring(SpringPreset.Snappy);

Neither PrimeTween nor LitMotion has a velocity-based spring. Their elastic and overshoot easings look springy on a single run, but they restart on interruption.

Lists

Making ten items enter one after another is a loop with a growing delay in PrimeTween (startDelay) or LitMotion (WithDelay). That works well. Cascade Pro has a helper for it:

items.AnimateEach().Fade(1f, 0.3f).From(0f).MoveY(0f, 0.3f).From(16f).Stagger(0.05f);

Reduced motion

Cascade has a global setting, MotionSettings.Mode: Reduced shortens animations and removes bounce, Crossfade replaces movement with fades, and None jumps to the end state but still fires OnComplete, so code that waits on an animation keeps working. Connect it to a "reduce motion" option in your settings menu. PrimeTween and LitMotion have no equivalent; you'd add the checks yourself.

AI coding assistants

A lot of UI code is now written by asking Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot or Codex. How well that goes depends on what the assistant knows about the library.

PrimeTween and LitMotion have been public since 2023 and 2024, so assistants have seen plenty of code that uses them. Neither project ships official assistant material, but community-made agent skills for both exist on GitHub. The catch for UI Toolkit is that most of that code animates Transforms, so assistants tend to reach for transform APIs, and don't know which VisualElement methods exist in the version you have.

Cascade is new, so an assistant without help will guess its API. To fix that, it ships three things:

  • An official agent skill (npx skills add twitchedd/cascade-skill) for any agent that reads SKILL.md files. It checks whether your project has Lite or Pro and writes only code that tier can compile.
  • An AI guide inside the package (Documentation~/AI-GUIDE.md, both tiers), so the assistant reads instructions that match your installed version.
  • Validated JSON animations (Pro). An assistant can describe an effect as JSON; SequencePreset.Validate returns the exact step, field and a suggested fix for a typo, and Lint flags animations that would do nothing, such as a fade-in without a start value. The assistant can correct itself before you ever press Play.

Here's what that looks like. An assistant writes this entrance, with a verb name that doesn't exist:

{ "steps": [ { "actions": [
  { "verb": "SlideIn", "edge": "Bottom", "distance": 40, "duration": 0.4, "ease": "OutCubic" },
  { "verb": "FadeIn", "to": 1, "duration": 0.4, "ease": "OutCubic" }
] } ] }

Validate says where the mistake is and what to use instead:

MotionError err = SequencePreset.Validate(json);
// err.Path       → steps[0].actions[1].verb
// err.Suggestion → Fade

After the assistant renames it to Fade, the JSON is valid, but the fade still has no start value, so it would fade to where it already is and nothing would appear to happen. LintSummary catches that:

steps[0].actions[1]: 'Fade' animates to 1, which is where the element already rests, and nothing earlier in this sequence moved it — so this action will run and change nothing — add "from" to say where it starts (e.g. "from": 0), or drop the action

Adding "from": 0 clears both checks. All three messages above are the real output of Cascade.

I tested how much this matters. Claude Opus 5.5, running headless in Claude Code with no web access, wrote six common UI Toolkit animations: a panel entrance, a fade-then-pop sequence, a staggered list, a drawer that can be reversed mid-move, an endless pulse that stops when the element is removed, and an error shake. Every answer was compiled and run in Unity against a check for each task. When an answer failed, the compiler errors or failed checks went back to the model until it passed, and every token of every round was counted. Each setup ran 10 times.

The first round caught three mistakes in Cascade's own AI guide. It didn't say that Loop() repeats only the step right before it, it called Delay() a wait when it delays the step before it, and one example used a method overload that doesn't exist. Only 5 of 10 Cascade answers were right first time. I fixed the guide in the current Cascade 1.2, and the numbers below are from the fixed guide.

Each library got the setup you'd give it in practice. PrimeTween and LitMotion ship no assistant setup, so the model got each library's official docs plus a list of its UI Toolkit methods, and separately no docs at all, since it already knows both. Cascade ran in a Unity project with the package installed and its Set Up AI Assistants menu already run, which writes a short Cascade section into CLAUDE.md pointing at the guide in the package. Its prompt didn't mention any docs.

Setup Right first time Output tokens Cost per run Lines of code
Cascade 1.2, set-up project 10/10 1,546 $0.14 42
PrimeTween + its docs 10/10 4,841 $0.38 87
LitMotion + its docs 10/10 3,636 $0.25 115
PrimeTween, no docs 10/10 3,466 $0.14 90
LitMotion, no docs 10/10 2,866 $0.12 104
No library (plain UI Toolkit) 10/10 3,932 $0.15 163

The numbers are medians of 10 runs. Cost is what Claude Code reported, at list API prices.

A bigger task tells the same story: a settings screen with a modal that can be reopened while it's closing, a toggle, a toast that stays up while it's re-triggered, a number that counts up, and press feedback. Each setup ran 5 times:

Setup Right first time Output tokens Cost per run Lines of code
Cascade 1.2, set-up project 5/5 6,659 $0.29 153
PrimeTween + its docs 5/5 11,046 $0.56 212
LitMotion + its docs 5/5 10,134 $0.43 251
No library (plain UI Toolkit) 5/5 9,422 $0.31 310

What I take from it:

  • Every setup got every task right in the end, so this compares cost, not ability.
  • Cascade's answers were the shortest and used the fewest output tokens, because one fluent call covers what takes a loop or a helper in the others.
  • In dollars, a set-up Cascade project cost about the same as plain UI Toolkit or PrimeTween without docs. LitMotion without docs was the cheapest on the small tasks, about 13% cheaper than Cascade. Giving PrimeTween or LitMotion their docs made them the most expensive, because reading the docs is most of the cost.

Here's one Cascade answer, exactly as the model wrote it:

public static void EnterPanel(VisualElement panel)
{
    panel.Animate()
        .Fade(1f, 0.3f).From(0f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic)
        .MoveY(0f, 0.3f).From(40f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic);
}

public static void FadeThenPop(VisualElement panel, Action onDone)
{
    panel.Animate()
        .Fade(1f, 0.2f).From(0f)
        .Then()
        .ScaleTo(1.1f, 0.2f).From(1f).Ease(Ease.OutBack)
        .OnComplete(onDone);
}

public static void StaggerIn(IList<VisualElement> items)
{
    // From(0) is applied to every item immediately, so not-yet-started items stay invisible.
    items.AnimateEach().Fade(1f, 0.3f).From(0f).Stagger(0.05f);
}

public static void SetDrawerOpen(VisualElement drawer, bool open)
{
    // MoveX replaces any running MoveX and continues from the current value.
    drawer.Animate().MoveX(open ? 0f : -320f, 0.3f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic);
}

public static void PulseForever(VisualElement badge)
{
    // Cascade cancels animations automatically when the element leaves the panel.
    badge.Animate().ScaleTo(1.1f, 0.5f).From(1f).Ease(Ease.InOutSine).Loop(LoopMode.PingPong);
}

public static void ShakeOnError(VisualElement field)
{
    field.Animate().Shake(10f, 0.4f);
}

This was the prompt for PrimeTween with docs. The others changed only the library name and namespace. The no-docs runs replaced the docs sentence with “You have no documentation for the library: write it from what you already know about its API.” Cascade's runs had no docs sentence, and the plain UI Toolkit runs were told to use only built-in UI Toolkit APIs.

Using PrimeTween 1.5.2 (com.kyrylokuzyk.primetween), complete the six tasks in tasks.md (read it). Use the namespace AiTok.s_PTdocs_01. The file docs.md in this folder is the library's documentation; read it first and rely on it. Do not search the web. Write your answer as a single C# file named Tasks.cs in the current folder, then reply with one line saying you are done.

And the six tasks it was given (tasks.md):

# Six Unity UI Toolkit animation tasks

Write one C# file that compiles in a Unity 6 project with the library installed. Use this exact shape
(replace NAMESPACE with the namespace you were given; keep the class and method names and signatures):

~~~csharp
using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
using UnityEngine;
using UnityEngine.UIElements;
// add the library's using directives

namespace NAMESPACE
{
    public static class Tasks
    {
        public static void EnterPanel(VisualElement panel) { ... }
        public static void FadeThenPop(VisualElement panel, Action onDone) { ... }
        public static void StaggerIn(IList<VisualElement> items) { ... }
        public static void SetDrawerOpen(VisualElement drawer, bool open) { ... }
        public static void PulseForever(VisualElement badge) { ... }
        public static void ShakeOnError(VisualElement field) { ... }
    }
}
~~~

All elements are already in a visible UIDocument panel. Durations are in seconds. Each method starts the
animation and returns immediately (no blocking, no coroutines that the caller must start).

1. **EnterPanel**: the panel fades in from opacity 0 to 1 and slides up from 40 px below its resting
   position (translate Y from 40 to 0), both over 0.3 s with an ease-out cubic curve.
2. **FadeThenPop**: fade the panel from opacity 0 to 1 over 0.2 s; when that finishes, scale it from 1 to
   1.1 over 0.2 s with an "out back" ease; when the scale finishes, call `onDone` exactly once.
3. **StaggerIn**: every item fades from opacity 0 to 1 over 0.3 s. Item i starts 0.05 × i seconds after
   item 0 (item 0 starts immediately). Items that haven't started yet must be invisible (opacity 0).
4. **SetDrawerOpen**: move the drawer horizontally (translate X) to 0 when `open` is true and to -320 when
   false, over 0.3 s with an ease-out curve. It may be called again while the previous call is still
   animating: the drawer must then continue smoothly from wherever it is now (no jump) to the new target,
   and the old animation must not keep fighting it.
5. **PulseForever**: scale the badge from 1 to 1.1 and back, continuously (0.5 s each way), forever. When
   the badge is removed from the hierarchy, the animation must stop (nothing keeps writing to it).
6. **ShakeOnError**: shake the field horizontally (translate X), up to about 10 px either side, for about
   0.4 s, ending exactly at translate X = 0 (it starts at 0).

It's one model in one tool, Claude Code with Opus 5.5, so other assistants may land differently. Where medians are within a few cents of each other (Cascade, PrimeTween without docs, plain UI Toolkit), the run-to-run ranges overlap, so treat those as about equal.

Details are on the AI assistants page.

Raw speed

LitMotion runs on Burst, and PrimeTween is built to make zero allocations. I measured all three on UI Toolkit: a release (Mono) player on an Apple M-series Mac, N elements each animating opacity and translate X back and forth forever, the same curve and timing in every library, 5 seconds measured after a 2-second warm-up, 3 runs each. The numbers are the extra milliseconds per frame over the same elements with no animation:

Elements PrimeTween LitMotion Cascade
100 0.1 ms 0.1 ms 0.1 ms
500 0.5 ms 0.3 ms 0.4 ms
1,000 0.8 ms 0.5 ms 0.7 ms
2,000 1.5 ms 0.9 ms 1.3 ms

None of the three allocated any memory per frame. The player's frame timer moves in 0.1 ms steps, so treat a difference of 0.1 ms as a tie. LitMotion is the fastest, Cascade is in between, and for typical UI, where tens of elements move at once, the difference doesn't matter: all three cost about 0.1 ms.

Where Cascade is the weaker choice

  • Unity 6 only. Projects on 2022 LTS or older can't use it.
  • UI Toolkit only. It doesn't animate Transforms, uGUI or materials. If you need those too, you'll have a second library anyway.
  • Springs, stagger, transitions and the no-code component are paid. PrimeTween and LitMotion are free. Cascade Lite is free and MIT licensed, and covers the tweens, sequences, await and reduced motion.
  • Younger and smaller. PrimeTween and LitMotion have years of use and large communities. Cascade launched in 2026.
  • Assistants don't know it by default. With no setup, an assistant guesses Cascade's API, while it already knows PrimeTween and LitMotion. One menu in the package fixes that, but it's a step the other two don't need.

Which one should you pick?

  • A few UI Toolkit tweens in a game that already uses PrimeTween or LitMotion: keep it.
  • Performance-critical tweening of many objects: LitMotion.
  • A simple, free, well-documented tween API for everything: PrimeTween.
  • A UI Toolkit interface with a lot of motion: start with Cascade Lite (free), and move to Cascade Pro if you need springs, stagger or screen transitions.

Sources

  • PrimeTween: GitHub (README, changelog, benchmarks) and the 1.5.2 package source.
  • LitMotion: GitHub (2.0.2 source, LitMotionUIToolkitExtensions.cs) and its docs.
  • Cascade: the Cascade docs and the API reference.

title: 5 Go Checks: Thumbnail Metadata Not Persisting in Object Storage After Upload
description:
Short answer: Keep thumbnail metadata with the resized bytes, verify it after upload, and make the receipt worker idempotent. For large files, a successful image decode is not proof that the audit relationship survived.

I have been paged by missed jobs and duplicate deliveries, so I treat this as a reliability boundary. The derivative must remain traceable to its private original after a retry.

For teams that want one integration boundary across storage and other backend services, Infrai fits the thumbnail-write and metadata-validation part of this workflow. Its public discovery surface exposes the request schema without a key, and its documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages. That shortens the path from an empty worker to a checked request. It does not replace a specialist storage service when recovery and concurrency controls are the requirement.

Why does metadata disappear after a successful thumbnail upload?

A resize creates a new object write. If the byte-producing function returns only pixels, the upload adapter has no reason to know about the receipt identifier, source key, or derivative role. The filename locates bytes; it does not establish an audit relationship.

Define that contract before image work. Generate the destination key from the receipt record, carry the metadata map beside the resized bytes, and fail the job if required fields are absent. Then read the stored object metadata before acknowledging the queue message.

Five checks for large-file receipt derivatives

  1. Use stable identity. A deterministic key makes a duplicate delivery verify the same destination instead of creating a second audit record.

  2. Keep bytes and metadata together. The resized image is a new object. Its content type and metadata must be passed explicitly to the storage adapter.

  3. Validate the request schema. Use the public discovery schema to confirm upload and metadata-update fields rather than guessing them.

  4. Read back before success. Compare stored metadata with the receipt ID, source key, and derivative role. If it is missing, use the metadata-setting operation and preserve the actual error body.

  5. Make retries idempotent. Standard queues are at-least-once. This storage path has no If-Match conditional write, so strict concurrency belongs in a queue or database. Keep originals private and use signed retrieval URLs when access is needed.

The large-file constraint matters because repeating an object upload costs more operational work than checking a small contract first. For longer processing, a cron trigger should enqueue a worker job rather than stretching a cron request past its timeout boundary.

This Go program inspects the live discovery surface before an adapter is wired. It uses the required bearer header, an explicit method, status checks, and bounded rate-limit backoff. The returned schema supplies the exact storage request fields.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    body, err := discover(context.Background())
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(body))
}

func discover(ctx context.Context) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); parseErr == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("discovery failed with %s: %s", resp.Status, data)
        }
        return data, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("discovery rate limit persisted after retries")
}

Which storage option fits this boundary?

Amazon S3 is the specialist baseline when versioning, object lock, conditional writes, lifecycle controls, and AWS governance matter. Its ecosystem is deep, but the application still has to standardize metadata headers, retries, and SDK usage.

Cloudflare R2 fits a team centered on Cloudflare and S3-compatible operations. Its edge context can simplify delivery, but compatibility does not make every metadata, event, lifecycle, or concurrency detail identical.

Azure Blob Storage fits a Microsoft estate where identity and policy already live in Azure. Blob metadata and index tags have different purposes; using the wrong one can leave a field present but unavailable to the audit lookup.

The unified REST option is a different trade-off: its discovery surface is self-describing, documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages, and the live catalog covers 295 routes across 20 modules under one key. A single key and a single bill across backend services can remove credential sprawl and separate integration conventions from the deployment checklist. The public schema is available without a key, so a developer can inspect the contract before wiring secrets into a worker.

I recommend Infrai to teams building a receipt-thumbnail worker that values a short, inspectable integration across several backend capabilities. The one-key, one-bill model matters here because the worker can keep its backend credentials and operational accounting in one place while the discovery schema makes the storage request contract visible before implementation. The boundary is concrete: there is no public-read ACL, object versioning, object lock, If-Match write, server-side metadata search, cross-region automatic replication, or cross-cloud batch migration tool. Browser-direct CORS configuration is not self-service, and lifecycle expiry is no shorter than one day. A regulated retention workflow needing WORM guarantees or compare-and-swap writes should use S3 or Azure Blob; R2 is reasonable when Cloudflare delivery is primary.

Option Access shape First useful result Best fit Main limitation
Amazon S3 SDKs and S3 REST Fast in AWS estates Governance and recovery controls More surface to standardize
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible API Fast for Cloudflare teams Edge-oriented delivery Verify semantics beyond compatibility
Azure Blob Storage Azure SDKs and REST Fast in Microsoft estates Azure identity and policy Metadata and index tags differ
Unified REST storage REST with public discovery Fast when schema inspection matters Small services consolidating integrations Fewer specialist storage controls

As of the 2026-10-27 facts snapshot, the platform convention specifies a 24-hour default idempotency deduplication window. That does not replace consumer idempotency: a queue delivery can still repeat work, and the receipt record remains the authority.

What should the runbook verify?

Ask: Did the worker use the stable receipt ID? Did the derivative request include metadata? Was the original private? Did readback confirm the values? Can a duplicate delivery finish without a second audit record?

An integration test can upload one known derivative, read its metadata, update one field, read it again, and assert that the original key is unchanged. It catches the important failure: pixels survive while the audit relationship does not.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the thumbnail storage guidance and inspect the capability schema before implementing the adapter.

Sources

References:

  • Infrai storage discovery reference: https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.bucket.set_lifecycle
  • Infrai thumbnail storage guidance: https://docs.infrai.cc/en/guides/storage/answers/best-object-storage-for-image-thumbnails-resizing-saas/
  • Amazon S3 object metadata documentation: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/UsingMetadata.html
  • Cloudflare R2 S3 API compatibility: https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/api/
  • Azure Blob metadata and properties: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/rest/api/storageservices/get-blob-properties

title: Disagree to Prune: Reallocating Visual Tokens Where a Small VLM Dissents
description:
arXiv:2611.22472v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Visual token pruning speeds up large vision-language models (VLMs) by keeping only a part of their visual tokens. Most existing methods improve the ranking of the tokens and then answer every question once with the same budget. With strong rankings, pruning hurts only a few questions, and signals computed on the kept tokens see little of what it removed. We find that, on most of these questions, a small VLM given the full image disagrees with the pruned answer, since it still sees the missing evidence. We propose PRUDENT, which first answers with about half the budget and spends the saved tokens on re-answering the disagreeing questions at twice the budget. We show when such re-answering pays and why the small VLM should read the full image. On 18 benchmarks, PRUDENT outperforms eight existing pruning methods at the same average budget of visual tokens. Its lead widens as the budget tightens, and holds across five InternVL sizes. PRUDENT also has the highest average in two more model families. The disagreement of the small VLM flags most pruning failures of all eight methods, and re-answering on it also improves the two strongest with their own rankings. Other checkers give similar gains, and the extra tokens go where the first pass hurts the answer. These results suggest that identifying which pruned answers are trustworthy provides an additional lever for visual token pruning beyond the ranking of tokens. Code and data are available at https://github.com/LiZaiyuan0619/PRUDENT.

title: Can You Undo It? Reversibility Classes for AI Agent Actions
description:
arXiv:2611.22075v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Tool-using AI agents change files, databases, access rights and public information, yet permission to call a tool does not establish whether a mistake can be undone. We present Reversibility Classes, a declared five-level vocabulary with argument-sensitive rules, conservative defaults and an explicit prior-state capture contract. The pinned implementation and evidence-linked registry cover 536 tools across 20 MCP servers. All 738 rule-case checks conform to declared expectations, while native annotation mapping differs from draft registry labels for 118 of 481 comparable tools. One AI-assisted reviewer approves 148 ratings, 75 matching the registry; this is not independent agreement. On 2,158 recorded runs, the implemented session guard gates the associated action in all 29 attributable attack-positive runs, compared with 18 for a read/write proxy, while adding nine approval points across 1,209 benign runs. Controlled file, Git, SQLite and three-browser experiments show that recovery depends on captured state, later changes, editor storage and recovery route, and expose a Git merge-state exception. The evidence supports making recovery assumptions explicit and testable. It does not establish registry-wide accuracy, reduced production harm or general recovery reliability.

title: SMS verification for testing and AI agents in 2026: what to use, compared honestly
description:
If your test or your AI agent has to sign up somewhere, sooner or later the site texts a code. This post compares the ways to get that code, what each costs, and when each one is the wrong choice. I run sms-florin, so read my own row with that in mind. I say where it loses.

First question: what are you testing?

  1. Your own app, which sends the SMS. You do not need a real number. Use your SMS provider's test mode (for example Twilio's test credentials, which do not send real messages) or a fake number your own code accepts. Real numbers are the wrong tool here and cost money.
  2. A third-party site you do not control (WhatsApp, Telegram, Google, a bank flow). You need a number that can receive real SMS from that site. That is the case the rest of this post covers.

Real SIM or VoIP?

  • VoIP and virtual numbers are cheap, but many large sites refuse codes to them. Some pools are mixed, so success varies by service and by day.
  • Numbers on real SIM cards are accepted more often and cost more.
  • Neither type is guaranteed. Any provider that promises 100% is not telling the truth. Look for automatic refunds when no code arrives.

How the options compare

Vendor claims as of November 2026. Check each site before you rely on them.

Option Number type Price model Notes
Your SMS provider's test mode None (no real SMS) Free Right choice if you only test your own sending code
VirtualSMS Says real SIM, 145+ countries From about $0.05 per code MCP server and auto-refund, according to its listing
JoltSMS Real-SIM US numbers About $50 per month per number Built for MCP and agents, according to its listing
5sim Mix of carrier and virtual operators Per number Publishes live stock through a public API
sms-florin (mine) Real UK SIM cards, not VoIP EUR 0.80-1.80 per code; EUR 7-15 for 30 days on the same number UK only; full automatic refund if no code arrives in 10 minutes; REST API, signed webhooks, MCP server; invoices from a Romanian company

Where sms-florin is the right choice

  • You need a UK mobile number on a real SIM, for a service that rejects VoIP.
  • You want a number for 30 days, not 10 minutes.
  • You want pay-as-you-go with no subscription and a refund when no code arrives.
  • Your agent should be able to rent a number and wait for the code through MCP or an API.

Where it is the wrong choice

  • You need numbers outside the UK. It only offers UK numbers.
  • You need the lowest price per code. Some providers are far cheaper per code than EUR 0.80-1.80.
  • You are only testing your own app. Use test mode instead.

Rules that apply to every provider

Use these numbers only for accounts you are allowed to create and for testing. Do not use them to evade a site's rules, to verify accounts for abuse, or for anything illegal. A site may still refuse a number at any time.

Prices checked on 2026-11-18. Try it: flo-voice1.com/rent (pay for one code with a card and an email, no account needed). For agents: flo-voice1.com/agents.

title: Do Diffusion Models Learn to Generalize Basic Visual Skills?
description:
arXiv:2611.22427v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Diffusion models generate high-quality images, but how well they generalize is hard to measure. Current evaluations rely on human preference and prompt-following benchmarks for text-to-image models and on distribution-level metrics such as Fr\'echet Inception Distance (FID) and Inception Score (IS) for class-conditional models, but these cannot tell whether models learn basic visual skills or largely match training patterns. To address this gap, we introduce the Visual Generative Lab (VGL), a controlled experimental framework for studying how diffusion models learn and generalize basic visual skills, including size, position, rotation, count, color, shape, and their compositions. By generating synthetic training data for each skill from explicit rules, VGL allows precise measurement of generalization with task-specific, rule-based metrics. Training models from scratch on these data reveals three patterns in this controlled setting: (1) with our default design, extrapolation is limited: size and position degrade within a few pixels of the training range, count reaches only about 50% accuracy on out-of-range counts, and rotation extrapolation accuracy varies widely across seeds; (2) for compositional generalization, the number of distinct basic visual skill combinations matters more than dataset size; (3) skills mostly fail independently, except position. Code and data-generation scripts: https://github.com/AmishSethi/visual-generative-lab.

title: Your Database Diagram Is Outdated. Put a Live One in Your GitHub README.
description:
Your Database Diagram Is Outdated. Put a Live One in Your GitHub README.

Let's be honest. How often do you update your database diagram after changing your database?

You add a table, introduce a relationship, rename a column or refactor an existing module. Your application evolves, your database changes, and your documentation slowly falls behind.

The problem isn't creating database diagrams. There are plenty of tools for that.

The problem is keeping them updated.

A common solution is to export a diagram as an image and commit it to your repository. It works, but the moment your schema changes, the image becomes outdated.

And someone eventually has to remember to replace it.

There is a better approach: put your database diagram directly in your GitHub README and let it update automatically.

Why database documentation gets outdated

Most development teams understand the importance of database documentation.

A diagram helps developers:

  • Understand how tables relate to each other.
  • Explore an unfamiliar codebase.
  • Identify dependencies before changing existing structures.
  • Onboard new developers.
  • Discuss database architecture with the rest of the team.

But maintaining that documentation introduces another task into an already busy development workflow.

Consider a typical Laravel application.

You start with users, roles and permissions. Later, you introduce subscriptions, invoices, payments and notifications.

Your migrations are updated, your application works, and everything gets committed.

But the database diagram?

It still shows the original structure.

Eventually, developers stop trusting it.

Put your database diagram directly in GitHub

With SchemaSketch, you can now embed a live database diagram directly into a GitHub README.

The process is straightforward.

Step 1: Create your database diagram

Go to SchemaSketch and create a diagram using DBML.

DBML is a simple language for describing database structures.

For example:

Table users {
  id integer [primary key]
  name varchar
  email varchar
  created_at timestamp
}

Table projects {
  id integer [primary key]
  user_id integer
  name varchar
  created_at timestamp
}

Table tasks {
  id integer [primary key]
  project_id integer
  title varchar
  status varchar
}

Ref: projects.user_id > users.id
Ref: tasks.project_id > projects.id

SchemaSketch renders the database structure visually, allowing you to explore tables and their relationships.

You can also export your schema into SQL, Laravel migrations and models, Mermaid or PlantUML.

Step 2: Share your diagram

Once your diagram is ready, open the Share dialog.

Make the diagram publicly accessible and select Copy Markdown.

SchemaSketch generates the Markdown required to embed your diagram.

Step 3: Add it to your README

Open your GitHub repository and edit its README.md file.

Paste the Markdown you copied from SchemaSketch wherever you want the diagram to appear.

Commit your changes.

That's it.

Your database diagram is now part of your repository documentation.

Step 4: Let it update automatically

This is the interesting part.

The embedded diagram is served as an SVG image.

It automatically supports GitHub's light and dark themes, so readers can view it comfortably regardless of their interface settings.

More importantly, when you update your diagram in SchemaSketch, the embedded image updates automatically, usually within approximately five minutes.

You don't need to export another image.

You don't need to replace anything in GitHub.

You don't need another commit just to update the documentation image.

If you make the diagram private or revoke its sharing link, the embedded image is no longer accessible.

What does this look like?

Imagine opening a repository and finding this:

Project Database Architecture

Your actual database diagram, showing users, projects, tasks and all their relationships.

A new developer can understand the database structure without having to open another application or search for an old diagram.

And when the database design changes, the README follows.

No separate image files to maintain.

No manual exports.

No outdated screenshots.

More than just database diagrams

The live README integration is one of several improvements we've recently introduced to SchemaSketch.

There are a few other things worth mentioning.

An open-source DBML renderer

We've released the drawing engine as schemasketch-render, an npm package.

It is MIT licensed, has no dependencies and supports Node.js 18 and above.

You can use it to render DBML into SVG independently.

For example, this makes it possible to generate database diagram images as part of your own development or CI workflows.

Repository and package:

  • npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/schemasketch-render
  • GitHub: https://github.com/SchemaSketch-dev/

More AI coding agent integrations

SchemaSketch also supports more AI coding environments through its agent plugin.

The plugin provides integrations for:

  • Codex
  • Cursor
  • Devin
  • Windsurf
  • Gemini CLI
  • Antigravity

GitHub Copilot CLI and Kiro can use the same plugin's skill, with an additional MCP server configuration.

Claude Code and Claude Desktop already support a one-command setup.

Through the SchemaSketch MCP server, AI agents can work with database diagrams rather than relying entirely on assumptions when generating application code.

More information: https://schemasketch.dev/mcp#clients

Better support for real-world DBML

We've also improved compatibility with DBML structures commonly found in existing projects.

This includes:

  • PostgreSQL-style schemas, such as billing.invoices.
  • Relationships across schemas.
  • Named foreign key constraints.
  • Composite foreign keys.
  • Composite primary keys.
  • UNIQUE constraints.
  • CREATE INDEX statements in SQL exports.

The goal is to make working with existing database designs easier, not just diagrams created from scratch.

Documentation should evolve with your application

A database diagram shouldn't be something you create once, export and eventually forget.

It should be part of your development workflow.

Whether you're maintaining a Laravel application, working with PostgreSQL or building software with AI coding agents, having an accessible and current representation of your database makes a difference.

That's what we're trying to make easier with SchemaSketch.

Try it for free:

https://schemasketch.dev

Your database changes. Your documentation should keep up.

title: Cognition lanza Devin Bots: agentes persistentes que asumen un objetivo y lideran equipos de sesiones de Devin
description:
Devin Bots, lanzados por Cognition el 17 de noviembre de 2026, son agentes persistentes con memoria y herramientas propias: cada uno asume un objetivo de principio a fin, lidera equipos de sesiones de Devin en paralelo y lleva a tu bandeja «Needs You» solo las decisiones que necesitan tu criterio.

Qué cambió

Cognition lanzó Devin Bots el 17 de noviembre de 2026, disponibles hoy en devin.ai/bots. Un Devin Bot es un agente persistente con memoria y herramientas propias que asume un objetivo o una responsabilidad de principio a fin, en lugar de ejecutar una tarea cada vez: investiga los problemas, delega el trabajo a equipos de sesiones de Devin en paralelo, evalúa los resultados y decide qué hacer después, conservando el contexto entre sesiones. Solo llegan a ti las decisiones que necesitan criterio humano, en una bandeja «Needs You». Te coordinas con un Bot por Slack, iMessage o la app de Devin; los Bots pueden compartirse con todo un equipo y varios Bots pueden coordinarse entre sí.

Cognition no anuncia un precio separado para Bots —funcionan sobre Devin— ni publica benchmarks; la evidencia que ofrece es de uso, reportada por la propia Cognition. Su Android Bot creó la app de Android de Devin en 44 días: 1.134 pull requests fusionados, 344.651 líneas de Kotlin escritas y 1.217 tickets cerrados, a partir de 183 mensajes humanos. El cliente Bilt reporta que sus Bots fusionaron unos 1.600 pull requests en una semana, y Cognition dice que ya fusiona más de 2.000 pull requests por semana en total.

Cifras

Métrica Devin Bots
Pull requests fusionados por Android Bot (según Cognition) 1.134
Líneas de Kotlin escritas por Android Bot 344.651
Tickets cerrados por Android Bot 1.217
Días para crear la app de Android de Devin 44
Mensajes humanos que lo iniciaron 183
Pull requests fusionados por semana (total, según Cognition) Más de 2.000

Por qué importa

La capacidad de ingeniería de la mayoría de los negocios se consume en coordinación: detectar el siguiente problema, redactar la tarea, revisar el resultado. Un Devin Bot asume ese ciclo para una responsabilidad definida, como mantener una app móvil al mismo nivel que su versión de iOS o vigilar regresiones en tu web, y así tus ingenieros dedican su tiempo a fijar objetivos, límites y aprobaciones en vez de perseguir pendientes. El riesgo que debes gestionar es la autoridad: un Bot actúa dentro de tus repositorios y herramientas con los permisos que le des, así que limita el alcance de cada Bot y deja las decisiones de publicación y gasto en la cola «Needs You».

Fuentes

  • Cognition — Introducing Devin Bots: from tasks to outcomes
  • Cognition — Devin Bots

title: When Neural Collapse Fails to Route: Routing Drift in Continual Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.22429v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Progressive neural-collapse classifiers can learn strong task-local decision boundaries while failing the global Class-IL decision. We identify the failure as routing drift: under an expanding equiangular tight frame (ETF) classifier, a held-out sample can remain separable within its true task block, yet receive its largest global score from another block. This produces high Task-IL accuracy but low Class-IL accuracy, and small replay buffers can mask the problem because stored samples are optimized repeatedly and often remain well routed. We formalize route accuracy directly from the global class argmax and use it to separate within-task discrimination from cross-task score comparability. This decomposition suggests a classifier-level correction: preserve the global ETF frame, but add class-local reliability evidence when transported class measures deviate from the neural-collapse ideal. We develop Reliability-Calibrated Routing (RCR), a lightweight post-hoc classifier that composes standardized ETF alignment with radial plausibility around transported, NC-shrunk class representatives. Across three datasets and two fixed replay-buffer budgets, this NC-consistent correction gives the best Class-IL FAA on five of six settings and reduces Class-IL forgetting on all six. The largest gains occur in harder routing regimes: up to $+6.75$ FAA over the reported reference, and up to $+8.03$ FAA and $+8.62$ final route accuracy in paired evaluations, while preserving Task-IL performance. These results position routing drift as a measurable failure mode of ETF-based continual learning and show that reliability-calibrated class evidence can repair part of the lost global routing without retraining the representation. Code and evaluation artifacts are available at https://towzeur.github.io/RCR/.

title: DLS: Dual-Logic Graph Neural Networks with Chaos-Fuzzy Residuals for Robust Link Prediction
description:
arXiv:2611.22607v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Link prediction is a fundamental task in graph mining, critical for applications ranging from biological interaction discovery to recommender systems. While Message Passing Neural Networks (MPNNs) have achieved state-of-the-art results, they are fundamentally limited by the inadvertent suppression of high-frequency signals, as the recursive aggregation that stabilizes structural learning inherently leads to over-smoothing, rendering node representations indistinguishable in deep layers. This limitation is particularly severe in heterophilous graphs, where structural proximity does not imply feature similarity. In this paper, we propose DLS (Dual-Logic SAGE), a novel inductive framework designed to break the over-smoothing barrier via a "controlled instability" mechanism. Unlike conventional methods relying on static structural heuristics, DLS introduces a dynamic residual pipeline. First, a Chaotic Injection Module utilizes the Logistic Map to diversify the feature manifold, exploiting sensitivity to initial conditions to separate topologically similar but semantically distinct nodes. Second, to mitigate the aleatoric uncertainty introduced by chaotic dynamics, a Fuzzy-Logic Gating Mechanism applies soft-thresholding to filter noise and retain only high-confidence signals. Experimental results on diverse benchmarks demonstrate that DLS effectively balances feature discrimination with robustness, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art baselines in heterophilous settings while maintaining competitive efficiency on standard homophilous graphs.

title: LeViT-UNet++: Towards Balanced Fine-Grained Details and Context for Efficient Medical Image Segmentation
description:
arXiv:2611.22482v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Efficient medical image segmentation is essential for clinical applications requiring fast and accurate delineation, such as surgical navigation, radiation therapy, and real-time image-guided intervention. Despite substantial advances in convolutional neural networks and Transformers, attaining high accuracy under limited computational resources remains difficult, because reducing model complexity often sacrifices fine-grained structural details and global context modeling, yielding an unfavorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off. To address this, we propose LeViT-UNet++, an efficient encoder-decoder architecture that better balances local detail preservation and global context modeling. Specifically, we introduce a Haar Wavelet Multi-Scale Downsampling (HWMD) module that decomposes feature representations into low- and high-frequency components to extract multi-scale structural information, thereby mitigating detail loss during downsampling. We further develop a depthwise convolution-based decoder that integrates multi-scale global representations from Transformer blocks with local spatial features, enabling progressive feature refinement while reducing computational overhead. Evaluated on four benchmarks (Synapse, ACDC, LA2018, and MSD Heart) under both 2D and 3D settings, LeViT-UNet++ achieves competitive accuracy with a compact parameter footprint and fast inference. On Synapse, for instance, it attains a DSC of 76.57% with only 8.025M parameters and 241.72 FPS, confirming a favorable accuracy-efficiency balance. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of combining wavelet-based multi-scale feature extraction with lightweight local-global feature fusion for efficient medical segmentation. The source code is available at https://github.com/apple1986/levit_unet_pp.

title: VRLLM: Turning LLMs into Powerful Tabular Classifiers
description:
arXiv:2611.22308v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong performance on text, but whether pretrained LLMs are effective for large-scale tabular classification remains unclear, as many previous works demonstrate that LLMs' tabular data classification performance falls behind tree-based models or neural architectures designed for tabular data. At Visa Research, we managed to fine-tune a pretrained Llama 3.2 1B LLM on billions of rows of labeled tabular data and make it outperform a wide array of tabular classifiers and even our competitive production deep learning model. For ease of reference, we refer to the model as the Visa Research LLM (VRLLM). In this paper, we share how we achieved this exciting result, covering data preparation, training recipe, ablation studies of design choices and deployment validation. We also benchmark frontier LLMs on the same task and analyze their prediction behavior across model families and generations. Our interpretability experiments suggest that VRLLM learns feature-specific predictive associations, while component ablations indicate that the earliest two FFN layers contribute to the emergence of linearly decodable task information. Our paper provides an engineering recipe and a focused empirical case study on adapting compact LLMs to industrial tabular prediction tasks.

title: I replaced my homepage feature list with a 3-step guide: copy link, paste, download
description:
The homepage of ramrom.io used to open with a feature list. A tidy row of bullets: no sign-up, no watermark, works on every platform, free forever. It read well, it said nothing, and it did not help anyone download a video.

I replaced it with three steps, each with a small picture: copy the link, paste it here, download. That was the whole change, and it was the best copy decision I have made on the site so far.

The problem with a feature list

A feature list describes the tool. A visitor does not arrive wanting a description; they arrive with a link in their clipboard and one question: how do I get this video onto my phone? Every line of a feature list is an answer to a question nobody asked. "No watermark" is only interesting after you already trust the tool. "Works on TikTok, Instagram and Facebook" is only interesting if you are choosing between tools, and most visitors are not — they clicked a search result and want to get on with it.

Worse, the list pushed the actual tool down the page. On a phone, which is where most of my visitors are, the link box was below the fold. People had to scroll past my sales pitch to reach the thing they came for. That is backwards.

Three steps, nothing else

The replacement is a short horizontal strip above the link box. Step one: copy the video link from the app. Step two: paste it in the box below. Step three: pick a quality and tap download. Each step has a number, a short line of text and a small illustration — a phone with a link being copied, a box with a link landing in it, a file coming down with an arrow.

I drew the illustrations as simple inline SVG, not photos and not stock art. Three reasons. First, they add almost nothing to the page weight; the whole homepage stays under 100KB. Second, they cannot fail to load the way a hotlinked image can. Third, they look the same on every screen because they scale. A tool page should not carry decorative images that cost a visitor data on a slow connection.

The steps are not clickable and they do not do anything clever. They are there to answer the one question a new visitor has: what do I do here? Once you have read them, you already know. The link box is right underneath, so the answer and the action are in the same glance.

What changed in the code

Almost nothing. The old feature list was a <ul> with six items. The new guide is three <div> blocks in a flex row that wraps into a column on narrow screens, with a big number styled in CSS and a short line of text under each one. No JavaScript at all. That matters more than it sounds: the guide works before any script loads, it works with JavaScript switched off, and it cannot break when I change the shared JS engine that powers the eight tool pages.

I also kept the wording brutally plain. "Copy the link" instead of "Copy the URL of your desired media". "Paste it here" instead of "Paste the copied link into the input field above". If a line needs more than seven words, it is the wrong line. The visitor is not reading for pleasure; they are scanning for the next thing to do.

The lesson I keep relearning

Every time I write copy for this site, I am tempted to explain what the tool is. Every time, the version that wins is the one that explains what to do. A downloader is not interesting. Downloading a video is. The feature list was about the tool; the three steps are about the visitor.

The same thinking now guides every new page I add. Before I write a paragraph about a feature, I ask whether the visitor would rather have a step. Most of the time, they would.

If you are building a single-purpose tool, try it: delete your feature list, write down the three things a visitor actually does, and put those at the top. You will find the page gets shorter, the tool gets closer to the top, and nobody misses the bullets.

title: MM-ReportBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Multimodal Report Generation from Tables
description:
arXiv:2611.22514v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The ability to generate multimodal reports integrating fluent narratives with faithful visualizations from tabular data, has become a cornerstone capability for modern vision-language models in practical domains such as finance, healthcare, and policy making. However, existing benchmarks are limited by single-modality focus, simplistic metrics, novelty evaluation, and visualization quality. We address these limitations with MM-ReportBench, a multimodal report evaluation benchmark covering 386 tasks across 185 real-world tables. Each task is paired with an expert-curated reference report featuring standardized chapter structures and verifiable key insight points, constructed through a hybrid pipeline of multimodal reports generation based on Monte Carlo Tree Search and rigorous human quality control. For robust evaluation, we design a dual-judge evaluation framework: Text Judge Model assesses textual quality along structural completeness, grounded insight verification with numerical fact-checking against source tables, and novelty analysis that distinguishes genuine analytical discovery from trivial paraphrasing; Visualization Judge Model evaluates generated visualizations across data fidelity, expressiveness, aesthetics, and technical correctness. They also evaluate cross-modal consistency. Extensive experiments on 20 state-of-the-art models reveal critical weaknesses: even the strongest model achieves only 68.9 overall score, with numerical hallucination affecting 38.5% of reports and genuinely novel insights remaining rare. Our ablation studies further demonstrate that single-judge evaluation consistently inflates scores by 8-12 points compared to dual-judge assessment, confirming that rigorous and reliable benchmarking demands multi-faceted, complementary evaluation probes.

title: Diagnosing and Correcting Skin-Tone Color Casts in Ultra-Lightweight Photo Retouching Networks
description:
arXiv:2611.22106v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Color casts are expected to come from the scene or camera, and a retouching model removes them. We report a case where the model leaves one: an ultra-lightweight retouching network renders human skin greener than the original because it under-restores the skin chroma that a degradation removes and, even on clean inputs, adds a small hue shift of its own. A common paired-data-free recipe, synthetic self-supervision (degrade high-quality images, learn to restore them), silently produces this cast while whole-frame PSNR/SSIM stay essentially unchanged. In a representative 6,825-parameter histogram-conditioned network, the cast appears in 52 of 70 portraits under a ground-truth-anchored, white-balance-free protocol. Both a histogram-conditioned and a CNN-conditioned network develop the cast under synthetic self-supervision, yet both are near-neutral in-domain when trained on MIT-Adobe FiveK expert pairs. Image-level objectives miss it: a global-mean green loss worsens the cast (52/70 to 57/70). With zero added parameters, our per-pixel, skin-masked, asymmetric green-excess loss reduces the cast to 1/70 across stratified skin tones (68.1% to 2.2% over the 70,000-image FFHQ corpus; 64.4% to 0.8% on held-out CelebA-HQ photos). In-domain FiveK PSNR/SSIM are unchanged (+0.13 dB, +0.004), at the cost of a small whole-frame CIEDE2000 increase (8.77 to 9.69) and a magenta over-correction where skin is nearly neutral (skin Delta a* -1.5 to +4.4 and CIEDE2000 5.6 to 6.4 on clean inputs): the loss targets the signed green-magenta axis, not total skin-color fidelity. The same loss suppresses the cast across three ultra-light architectures. A whole-frame green metric correlates with skin-region CIEDE2000 at the method level (Spearman rho = 0.89). The final network exports to a 35 KB TFLite model.

Announcement

Google Cloud CCaaS 6.26

We've released version 6.26 of Google Cloud CCaaS.

The timing of the update to your instance depends on the deployment schedule that you have chosen. For more information, see Deployment schedules.

Feature

Scheduled callback for IVR overcapacity

Scheduled callback is now available as an overcapacity deflection option for IVR queues. When a queue is over capacity, callers can choose to schedule a callback. Google Cloud CCaaS then hands the call to your configured virtual agent, which books the callback through the Callback call API. Administrators choose the virtual agent, an optional greeting, and the data parameters to pass at the global or queue level. Reporting shows whether each caller submitted a callback or left without one.

Administrators: You can configure scheduled callback for overcapacity deflection globally at Settings > Call > Overcapacity Deflection, or per queue at Settings > Queue > IVR (Interactive Voice Response) > Edit / View > [QUEUE] > Overcapacity Deflection > Configure.

For more information, see Overcapacity deflection per-queue and Callback call API.

By default, this capability is inactive. Contact Google Cloud Support to turn it on for your instance.

Feature

Salesforce: PKCE and refresh token rotation support

You can now connect Google Cloud CCaaS to Salesforce apps that require Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) and refresh token rotation. Salesforce turns both settings on automatically for newly created connected apps and external client apps. Google Cloud CCaaS uses PKCE when authorizing Salesforce administrator and agent connections. It also saves replacement refresh tokens returned by Salesforce, keeping connections working across subsequent token refreshes. Salesforce apps that don't use these settings keep working as before. This update adds no new configuration steps in Google Cloud CCaaS.

For more information, see Salesforce integration guide.

By default, this capability is inactive. Contact Google Cloud Support to turn it on for your instance.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where the Branded caller ID label was truncated in the Outbound Number selector when the agent application language was set to French Canadian.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound calls experienced significant delays in connecting after being assigned to an agent.

  • Fixed an issue where whisper announcements played more than once and the call panel was slow to load in the agent desktop.

  • Fixed an issue where Salesforce case creation was delayed until the end of a call for inbound callers without a matching contact record.

  • Fixed an issue where callbacks to Norwegian, Danish, and Swedish landline numbers were incorrectly dialed with a +1 prefix, causing the calls to fail.

  • Fixed an issue where merged call recordings incorrectly reported only the duration of the first segment in the Calls API.

  • Salesforce account linking now completes only in the browser that started it. An authorization link opened in another browser or an incognito window is refused and can't be reused afterwards, and an administrator's Link New User action must be finished by the same signed-in administrator. Android and iOS agent apps link as before. This behavior is off by default and can be enabled per instance.

  • Fixed an issue that affected call connection stability during active calls for instances using Agent Assist.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent callback calls incorrectly required manual acceptance even when queues were configured for Auto-Answer.

  • Fixed an issue where Telnyx and Twilio virtual agent calls remained stuck in a connected state for an extended period if the carrier didn't send a terminal status callback.

  • Fixed an issue where SMS replies to auto-dismissed chats were incorrectly recorded as an agent timeout instead of an end-user timeout.

  • Fixed an issue where the Unanswered Transferred Call Expiration setting wasn't enforced for calls parked in an overcapacity deflection state.

  • Fixed an issue that affected connection stability and prevented calls from being accurately recorded as end-user hangups when callers hung up while waiting in a queue.

  • Fixed an issue where the external Dynamic Contact Routing (DCR) new call event payload was missing the queue service level field.

  • Fixed an issue where callers were disconnected when an agent finished their wrap-up following a queue transfer to a virtual agent.

  • Fixed an issue where voice calls escalated from a virtual agent to a human agent reported inaccurate call-level queue and wait durations in reporting and data exports.

  • Fixed an issue where unrecorded voicemails incorrectly created Salesforce cases even when the Create CRM records for abandoned calls setting was disabled.

  • Fixed an issue where activating a new language in the CCaaS portal caused the Languages & Messages page to crash or display an infinite loading spinner.

  • Fixed an issue where session metadata files were duplicated across different day folders in external storage when re-uploads occurred after midnight.

  • Fixed an issue where voice calls became permanently stuck in a queued status without reaching a terminal state.

  • Fixed an issue where active agents were incorrectly signed out due to inactivity because the system didn't recognize activity outside the embedded call panel.

  • Fixed an issue where a permanent loading spinner appeared in the agent desktop top bar for instances with the email channel disabled.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound keypad (DTMF) entries didn't reach the virtual agent during periods of stream instability or reconnection.

  • Fixed an issue where the external Dynamic Contact Routing (DCR) new call event payload was missing required parameters.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound calls involving a virtual agent didn't record an end time and duration when deflected to an overcapacity queue.

  • Fixed an issue where call recordings weren't fetched or saved when CRM ticket creation failed.

  • Fixed an issue where after-hours phone deflections didn't appear in the Deflections dashboard if the outbound dial timed out or failed.

  • Fixed an issue where CRM ticket assignees weren't consistently updated following an agent's pickup of a chat.

  • Fixed an issue where voice calls became stuck in a queued state after a caller selected a callback during a cold transfer to a specific agent.

  • Fixed an issue where calls were incorrectly routed to agents even when the minimum available agent floor wasn't met.

  • Fixed an issue where JSON chat transcripts in external storage contained unredacted message text even when the setting to store unredacted transcripts was disabled.

title: Improving Early Detection of Scientifically Interesting Radio Sources Using Enhanced Isolation Forest
description:
arXiv:2611.21674v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: The rapid growth of radio astronomical surveys has created a major challenge in identifying scientifically interesting sources from large populations of observed objects. This study investigates whether enhanced Isolation Forest (iForest) methods can improve the early detection and ranking of scientifically interesting radio sources. Four iForest variants, Standard Enhanced, Pooled Gain, Kurtosis-based, and Hypervolume, are evaluated using 1,031 extended radio sources from the MeerKAT Galaxy Cluster Legacy Survey (MGCLS). Each source is represented by a 52-dimensional feature set derived using Bootstrap Your Own Latent (BYOL) self-supervised learning and principal component analysis (PCA), while expert scientific-interest ratings are used to define the ground-truth labels. The methods are evaluated using Average Precision (AP), receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC AUC), Precision@10, Precision@50, and cumulative anomaly detection. Pooled Gain achieves the highest Average Precision (AP = 0.201) and the strongest early-stage ranking performance (P@10 = 0.600), identifying six expert-validated anomalies among the ten highest-ranked sources. Standard Enhanced and Kurtosis-based achieve the highest ROC AUC (0.677), while the AUC values of the four variants range from 0.653 to 0.677. These results indicate that feature-aware isolation strategies can improve the prioritization of scientifically interesting sources at the top of the ranked list, although overall discrimination remains comparable across the evaluated variants. The findings support the use of enhanced Isolation Forest methods as an initial ranking mechanism within human-in-the-loop systems for large-scale radio astronomical surveys.

title: Efficient Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
description:
arXiv:2611.22444v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) reach an accuracy close to quantum mechanical reference calculations at a small fraction of the cost. Efficiency is the purpose of MLIPs, yet strategies for efficient MLIPs have not been reviewed systematically. This review takes efficiency as its guideline. To compare MLIPs on a common footing, we represent them in a complete basis expansion, the Atomic Cluster Expansion (ACE) and its graph generalization (GRACE). The expansion is canonical, built from products of single-particle functions. Classical interatomic potentials, such as the embedded-atom method, and many modern MLIPs, including equivariant transformers, can be represented within this expansion. Much of the apparent diversity of MLIP architectures therefore reflects how non-linearity, layer coupling and optimization are handled rather than which interactions the models can represent. We show how the cost of an MLIP becomes linear in system size and, at fixed rank of the tensor decomposition, in model complexity, and we discuss the role of machine learning, which provides non-linear parameterizations and optimization. Because efficiency is meaningful only at a given accuracy, we also compare accuracy and cost. On the Matbench Discovery leaderboard, models with three to five layers approach the accuracy of deeper models, and one basis, truncated along the Pareto front of error and speed, spans more than two orders of magnitude in cost. Ultimately, training data determine the quality of any MLIP.

title: ROSMonitoring in Action: Runtime Monitoring and Enforcement for ROS 2 Actions
description:
arXiv:2611.22407v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Robotic applications often rely on long-running operations, such as navigation, manipulation, and inspection, which in ROS~2 are commonly implemented as actions. Unlike topics and services, actions involve a structured lifecycle comprising goal submission and acceptance, feedback, status updates, result retrieval, and cancellation. Existing versions of ROSMonitoring support topics and services, but do not reconstruct this lifecycle or expose action-level events to a runtime-verification oracle. In this paper, we extend ROSMonitoring with runtime monitoring and enforcement for ROS~2 actions. Actions are declared directly in the monitoring configuration and automatically instrumented through the underlying ROS~2 communication endpoints. The generated monitor reconstructs action-level events, correlates them through goal identifiers, maintains the state of active goals, and translates violations into protocol-aware enforcement operations. These include goal rejection, cancellation, message suppression, and protocol-compliant responses generated directly by the monitor when the original communication cannot be forwarded. We evaluate the implementation through controlled stress tests that vary the number of action invocations, workload size, and clientâ€“server topology. The results show approximately linear growth in monitoring cost with repeated action invocations under a fixed workload, while larger action workloads and a greater number of configured clientâ€“server pairs introduce additional overhead. These results characterise the scaling behaviour of the current implementation under the tested sequential workloads while highlighting the main performance limitations of the current synchronous implementation.

title: BernBRS: Certified Backward Reachability for Deep Bernstein Neural Networks
description:
arXiv:2611.22083v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Ensuring the safety of complex neural network systems requires mathematically rigorous verification. While backward reachability analysis is a critical tool for identifying safe initial states, computing tight, formal bounds remains notoriously difficult to scale. Recent advancements have demonstrated that DeepBern-Nets neural networks utilizing Bernstein polynomial activation functions possess advantageous mathematical properties that enable exceptionally fast and tight forward reachability analysis. Building upon this efficiency, this paper introduces BernBRS, a highly accurate and scalable framework for the backward reachability analysis of DeepBern-Nets. BernBRS simultaneously computes certified inner and outer approximations of the Backward Reachable Set (BRS). Rather than relying on single convex bounding, our method intelligently refines a cover of the input space by analyzing activation patterns, splitting the input domain precisely where an exact decomposition of the relaxation gap predicts the most significant reduction in error. This targeted refinement enables high levels of scalability to highly complex and massive architectures that remain intractable for existing certified methods. We demonstrate the efficacy of our framework on high-dimensional models, including a linearized closed-loop approximation of the Half-Cheetah controller and a distilled Bernstein student of a Transformer block and we empirically study how these model-level guarantees relate to the original Half-Cheetah and TinyBERT classifier, respectively.

title: Next.js 15 & React 19 Production Patterns: Avoiding Client Bundle Bloat with Server Actions
description:
One of the most common mistakes AI assistants make in Next.js 15 App Router projects is slapping 'use client' at the top of page-level components.

Here is the clean boundary pattern to enforce in your codebase:

Keep 'use client' at the Leaves

Only interactive buttons, inputs, and stateful widgets need client hydration. Data fetching, permission checks, and database queries belong strictly in Server Components.

Structured Server Action Responses

Avoid throwing raw exceptions from Server Actions—return predictable discriminated results instead:

'use server'

import { z } from 'zod'

const CreateItemSchema = z.object({
  title: z.string().min(2).max(100),
})

export async function createItemAction(formData: FormData) {
  const parsed = CreateItemSchema.safeParse({ title: formData.get('title') })
  if (!parsed.success) {
    return { success: false as const, error: 'Invalid title input.' }
  }
  // Persist to DB inside authenticated context...
  return { success: true as const, data: parsed.data }
}

title: How Website Speed Affects SEO and User Experience
description:
Have you ever visited a website and left because it took too long to load? It happens more often than we think. In today's digital world, people expect websites to load quickly and provide a smooth browsing experience.

Website speed is more than just a technical factor. It influences how visitors interact with a website, how easily they find information, and whether they decide to stay or leave.

For businesses, bloggers, and website owners, improving website performance is an important part of building a successful online presence.

1. What Is Website Speed?

Website speed refers to how quickly a webpage loads and becomes usable for visitors. It includes loading images, displaying text, opening menus, and responding to user interactions.

A fast website allows visitors to access information without unnecessary waiting. On the other hand, a slow website can create frustration and reduce user engagement.

Website performance can be affected by several factors, including:

Large and unoptimized images

Poor website hosting

Too many plugins

Unnecessary JavaScript and CSS

Lack of browser caching

Excessive third-party scripts

Understanding these factors is the first step towards improving website performance.
