title: Edtech Video Generation: Expiring Capabilities Before Offering Classroom Media Options
description:
Short answer: Read video generation capabilities at startup, constrain the options offered by your application, and refresh that snapshot on an expiry. For an edtech workflow that compresses classroom images before serving them and generates promotional video from approved material, keep moderation approval as a separate publication requirement. A supported generation option doesn't establish that the content is appropriate for students.

Start there.

The recommendation has two parts because the evidence answers two different questions: capability discovery tells the application what it can offer, while an application-owned review decision determines what it should publish. Compression belongs downstream of that decision in this proposed workflow. Smaller files are useful; they're poor evidence of moderation coverage.

What page fired when the form offered an unsupported option?

That's the first question in the postmortem, even for a hypothetical incident. A dashboard showing successful requests cannot establish that the form offered valid choices, and a generation completion counter cannot establish that the source image passed the school's review policy. Define the signal around the violated promise: the application accepted a choice outside its current capability snapshot, or publication proceeded without approval for that asset revision.

Those are different pages.

Consider a proposed test fixture with 3 classroom images: a worksheet screenshot, a student photograph, and a teacher-approved illustration. These are synthetic test cases, not observations from a production deployment. Each needs an independent review outcome before the serving pipeline compresses it; a file-format decision says nothing about whether the student photograph has the required approval. If a crop or replacement changes what the image depicts, require a new review decision under the application's policy instead of copying an old approval merely because the filename stayed the same.

The capability cache has a separate trap. A form opened before a refresh can submit after the available choices have changed. Validate again when accepting the submission. The browser's dropdown is a convenience, not the enforcement point.

For an existing Node.js Express application, populate application state before enabling the form, render from the current snapshot, and validate submitted choices at the request boundary. The operational example below uses Go; it doesn't assume an undocumented video response schema.

How should we check video generation capabilities before offering classroom options?

Choose an expiry as an application policy, then record when the snapshot was fetched and when it becomes unusable. A proposed starting value is 5 minutes, subject to review against the workflow's tolerance for stale options; that number isn't a provider guarantee. Refresh periodically and replace the snapshot only after the response has passed application schema checks. Avoid overwriting a usable snapshot with an empty value just because a refresh attempt failed.

Once the expiry passes, stop accepting new generation choices until a validated snapshot is available. Existing approved images can follow their own serving policy. This trades some availability of new work for a clear promise about the options the form accepts, which is easier to defend than silently trusting an indefinitely old list.

Keep the moderation record attached to the asset revision and policy revision, and keep the capability snapshot revision attached to the generation submission. These are proposed application records, not vendor response fields. They let a reviewer distinguish an unsupported choice from a missing content approval without guessing from a chart.

Infrai fits teams that want a plain REST API without installing an SDK, with one key and one bill for the account-usage and email handoff. That means the statement worker can fetch usage and send the prepared report without managing separate credentials for those calls. Its self-describing discovery surface provides request and response schemas, which help validate that boundary. The combined approach has a trade-off: one vendor to trust and one outage surface.

It doesn't replace the school's moderation policy.

Compare the boundary each tool actually owns

Moderation coverage means being able to explain which assets were reviewed, under which policy, and what happens to unreviewed revisions. Evaluate Cloudinary, imgix, and ImageKit as alternative media-stack candidates against those same acceptance questions: where does review run, how is its decision bound to the exact compressed output, and can publication be blocked? These are evaluation requirements, not claims that the three products have identical moderation features.

The surrounding statement workflow has another set of alternatives. Keep their roles explicit.

Option Role in the alternative stack Boundary to keep explicit
Stripe metering Usage metering component Metering evidence is separate from the content approval record.
Puppeteer Application-controlled PDF rendering component A rendered statement doesn't validate generation choices or approve images.
Amazon SES Email delivery component Sending a statement doesn't establish that its underlying usage and review records agree.

The Stripe metering + Puppeteer + SES version involves 2 service account setups, Stripe and AWS, with separate credential sets; Puppeteer is a software dependency rather than a third hosted-service signup. The application needs glue to collect usage, render the statement, associate it with the correct recipient, and handle delivery retries. This separation is a reasonable choice when the team wants independent ownership of those stages, and an existing deployment may already have most of that work in place.

A combined API is attractive when credential and schema consistency are the maintenance burden. A separate stack is preferable when independent control of metering, rendering, and delivery matters more. Neither arrangement proves that the school's moderation requirements have been met. Use MDN's image format guide for format decisions after review, and retain separate evidence for content approval.

Implement the usage-to-email handoff without inventing a PDF contract

The operational seam needs a working check too. This example fetches account usage and inserts its JSON representation into an application-prepared email batch payload, using the same key and base URL for both calls. Statement layout stays in the application: PDF rendering can remain an application step, while this example sends a textual usage statement. No PDF API contract is assumed.

Save this as main.go. Set INFRAI_API_KEY and MEDIA_API_BASE_URL to your deployment's credentials and versioned API base URL. Set EMAIL_BATCH_TEMPLATE to the path of a complete email batch request constructed against the published request schema, with the literal string {{USAGE_JSON}} inside its message text. These names and the marker are local application conventions. Set STATEMENT_ID to a stable identifier for the recipient batch and reporting period; reuse it when retrying the same statement, and change it for a different statement. Run with go run main.go.

The template requirement matters. Recipient and message fields aren't guessed here, and encoding/json escapes the inserted usage as JSON string data. Validate the completed payload against the published schema before scheduling the workflow.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

var client = &http.Client{Timeout: 30 * time.Second}

func required(name string) string {
    value := os.Getenv(name)
    if value == "" { panic("missing environment variable: " + name) }
    return value
}

func call(method, route string, body []byte, statementID string) ([]byte, error) {
    base := strings.TrimRight(required("MEDIA_API_BASE_URL"), "/")
    key := required("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(method, base+route, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        if body != nil { req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json") }
        if statementID != "" { req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", statementID) }
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil { return nil, readErr }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 { return data, nil }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests || attempt == 4 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s: %s", resp.Status, data)
        }
        delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
        retry := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retry); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
            delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        } else if deadline, err := http.ParseTime(retry); err == nil {
            delay = time.Until(deadline)
            if delay < 0 { delay = 0 }
        }
        time.Sleep(delay)
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("retry budget exhausted")
}

func insert(value any, usage string) any {
    switch v := value.(type) {
    case string:
        return strings.ReplaceAll(v, "{{USAGE_JSON}}", usage)
    case []any:
        for i := range v { v[i] = insert(v[i], usage) }
    case map[string]any:
        for key := range v { v[key] = insert(v[key], usage) }
    }
    return value
}

func run() error {
    usage, err := call(http.MethodGet, "/account/usage", nil, "")
    if err != nil { return err }
    if !json.Valid(usage) { return fmt.Errorf("usage response is not JSON") }
    template, err := os.ReadFile(required("EMAIL_BATCH_TEMPLATE"))
    if err != nil { return err }
    if !bytes.Contains(template, []byte("{{USAGE_JSON}}")) {
        return fmt.Errorf("template is missing the usage marker")
    }
    var payload any
    decoder := json.NewDecoder(bytes.NewReader(template))
    decoder.UseNumber()
    if err := decoder.Decode(&payload); err != nil { return err }
    body, err := json.Marshal(insert(payload, string(usage)))
    if err != nil { return err }
    _, err = call(http.MethodPost, "/email/batch/send", body, required("STATEMENT_ID"))
    return err
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    fmt.Println("Statement request accepted.")
}

A successful response establishes request acceptance, not final email delivery. The retry loop handles rate limiting with a bounded budget and honors Retry-After; the write carries a stable idempotency key. Maintain a durable application send ledger for reruns beyond the platform's default 24-hour deduplication window. Keep account information and raw error bodies inside access-controlled operational tooling.

This example checks the account-to-email seam. It isn't a capability parser or a moderation classifier. Each needs its own acceptance evidence.

Verify the gates, then roll back the affected stage

Before enabling the form, test a fresh snapshot, an expired snapshot, and a submission from a form opened before refresh. Only choices accepted by current application validation should start new generation work. Add a changed-image fixture to ensure that approval for the old revision cannot authorize publication of its replacement. These tests exercise the promises that matter to the person carrying the pager.

Test the statement handoff separately with a controlled recipient and a stable statement identifier. Confirm that usage reaches the prepared message, a rate-limit response produces a delayed retry, and retrying the same write doesn't create a second logical statement. Reconcile request acceptance with delivery evidence before marking the statement delivered.

For rollback, disable new generation submissions if capability freshness cannot be established, retain the last validated snapshot for diagnosis, and keep unapproved assets out of publication. If compression changes an approved asset's rendering, return serving to the previous approved artifact while reviewing the new output. If statement delivery is affected, stop that sender and retain its ledger so a restart can distinguish unfinished work from completed sends.

Page on the broken promise. A green dashboard can wait.

References

  • MDN, Image file type and format guide: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Media/Formats/Image_types
  • Stripe, Usage-based billing: https://docs.stripe.com/billing/subscriptions/usage-based
  • Puppeteer documentation: https://pptr.dev/
  • Amazon SES developer guide: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ses/latest/dg/Welcome.html
  • Cloudinary documentation: https://cloudinary.com/documentation
  • imgix documentation: https://docs.imgix.com/
  • ImageKit documentation: https://imagekit.io/docs

title: CoBoVLA: Decoupling Language from Action with Discrete Codes for Robust and Interpretable Robot Manipulation
description:
arXiv:2611.22395v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models achieve high success rates on the LIBERO benchmark but remain sensitive to paraphrasing. Existing VLAs ranging from 0.6B to 7.5B parameters experience a 22-52 point performance drop on LIBERO-Para while SmolVLA exhibits an even larger decline, from 83\% to 8\%. Because most VLAs jointly learn language understanding and action generation, it is difficult to determine whether a failure originates from misunderstanding an instruction or executing it incorrectly. To address these challenges, we introduce CoBoVLA, or CodeBookVLA, a 250M-parameter VLA that decouples language understanding, planning, and control through learned discrete interpretable codes. A text encoder maps the instructions to shared step codes, which a visual planner then converts into action code sequences executed by a language-independent actor. This design improves robustness to instruction paraphrasing while allowing failures to be traced to individual stages. It also enables efficient real-time control on resource-constrained hardware by encoding instructions only once and using compact discrete representations to keep each component lightweight. CoBoVLA achieves 91.4\% success on LIBERO-Goal, compared with 82.8\% for SmolVLA, under a matched protocol, with 17 ms per control step latency. On LIBERO-Para, it achieves 81.1\% across 4,092 unseen paraphrases and 78.5\% on matched episodes, compared with 36.5\% for SmolVLA LoRA fine-tuned on paraphrases. Without two-step demonstrations, CoBoVLA completes 48.8\% of 160 free-form two-step tasks. Finally, success reaches 91\% when instructions are correctly encoded but falls to 27.2\% otherwise, identifying language understanding as the main source of remaining failures. Together, these results demonstrate that decoupling language understanding and control can improve instruction robustness while making VLA failures easier to diagnose.

title: tx-explainer: اقرأ معاملة Solana بلغة بسيطة
description:
العثور على معاملة (transaction) في Solana سهل، لكن قراءتها صعبة. المستكشف (explorer) يعطيك توقيعًا (signature)، وقائمة من مفاتيح الحسابات، وتعليمات (instructions) بياناتها سلسلة من البايتات. لتعرف ما الذي حدث فعلًا، عليك أن تتذكر أن أول بايت في تعليمة Token هو وسم (tag)، وأن المبالغ أعداد صحيحة بترتيب little-endian وبلا فاصلة عشرية، وأن برنامج Anchor يخفي اسم التعليمة خلف discriminator من 8 بايتات.

tx-explainer يقوم بهذه القراءة مكانك. تعطيه توقيعًا، أو بايتات المعاملة الخام، أو ردّ getTransaction محفوظًا في ملف، فيطبع ما فعلته كل تعليمة في جمل بسيطة، ثم الرسوم، ووحدات الحساب (compute units)، وتغيّرات الأرصدة.

هو أداة فك ترميز للقراءة فقط: لا يوقّع ولا يرسل أي شيء أبدًا. والـ README صريح في حدوده: المشروع لم يخضع لتدقيق أمني (not audited)، وهو موجّه أولًا إلى devnet وtestnet وlocalnet، والنص المبسّط اجتهاد قدر الإمكان ولا يغني عن قراءة كود البرنامج.

ماذا يقدّم

هذا ناتج الأداة على معاملة حقيقية من devnet موجودة ضمن ملفات الاختبار:

$ tx-explainer --file test/fixtures/devnet-memo.json
Transaction 5zhK…  [legacy]
Status: succeeded
Fee: 0.0000155 SOL (of which priority ≈ 0.0000105 SOL)
Compute units: 26,021 of 70,000 requested

What happened:
  1. [Compute Budget] Set compute unit limit to 70,000
  2. [Compute Budget] Set priority fee to 150,000 micro-lamports per compute unit
  3. [Associated Token Account] Create (if missing) the associated token account Expy…TCA6 for wallet 6a1w…BNqd and mint 4wMp…jY4y, paid by 2VyJ…TeEs (fee payer)
  4. [SPL Token] Transfer 1,236.871165 tokens of mint 4wMp…jY4y from 55Xo…AmDQ to Expy…TCA6 (authority 2VyJ…TeEs (fee payer))
  5. [Memo] Memo: "helm-payout-v1:…"

Token balance changes:
  55Xo…AmDQ (owner 2VyJ…TeEs): -1,236.871165 of mint 4wMp…jY4y
  Expy…TCA6 (owner 6a1w…BNqd): +1,236.871165 of mint 4wMp…jY4y

البرامج المدمجة. الأداة تعرف البرامج التي تظهر في أغلب المعاملات:

  • System: التعليمات CreateAccount وAssign وTransfer وCreateAccountWithSeed، وعمليات الـ nonce، وAllocate وTransferWithSeed.
  • SPL Token وToken-2022: تهيئة الـ mint والحسابات، وTransfer وTransferChecked، وApprove وRevoke وSetAuthority وMintTo وBurn وCloseAccount وFreeze وThaw وSyncNative وغيرها. أما تعليمات امتدادات Token-2022 فتُذكر برقمها فقط.
  • Associated Token Account: التعليمات Create وCreateIdempotent وRecoverNested.
  • Compute Budget: التعليمات SetComputeUnitLimit وSetComputeUnitPrice وRequestHeapFrame وSetLoadedAccountsDataSizeLimit.
  • Memo (الإصداران v1 وv2)، ويُعرض كنص UTF-8.

أي برنامج Anchor عبر الـ IDL. مرّر ملف IDL الخاص بالبرنامج بالخيار --idl (صيغة Anchor 0.30 وما بعدها)، فتعرض الأداة اسم التعليمة، والوسائط بعد فك ترميز Borsh (structs وenums وvec وoption والمصفوفات)، وأسماء الحسابات، وأسماء الأخطاء المخصّصة إن فشلت المعاملة.

بيانات الـ RPC الوصفية (metadata). عندما يأتي الإدخال من getTransaction، يضمّ الناتج أيضًا الحالة (مع أسماء أخطاء Anchor)، والرسوم، وتقديرًا لرسوم الأولوية (priority fee) يساوي حد وحدات الحساب × سعر الوحدة، ووحدات الحساب المستهلكة، والتعليمات الداخلية (CPIs)، وتغيّرات رصيد SOL، وتغيّرات أرصدة التوكنات بالخانات العشرية الصحيحة.

رسائل legacy وv0. الصيغتان مدعومتان. عناوين جداول البحث (address lookup tables) تُحلّ من meta.loadedAddresses. وفي الإدخال الخام، حيث لا توجد هذه البيانات، تُعرض بالشكل table[index].

ثلاث طرق للتشغيل. نفس منطق فك الترميز متاح كأداة سطر أوامر (CLI)، وكمكتبة TypeScript، وكواجهة ويب صغيرة تعمل كليًا داخل المتصفح وتتصل مباشرة بالـ RPC العام للشبكة المختارة. يضع الـ README رابطًا لنسخة تجريبية حية من هذه الواجهة: https://abdeldjalilchougui.github.io/tx-explainer/.

طريقة الاستعمال

تحتاج Node.js 20 أو أحدث. انسخ المستودع ثم ابنِه:

git clone https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/tx-explainer
cd tx-explainer
pnpm install
pnpm build

ثم شغّل الـ CLI من مجلد المشروع:

node dist/cli.js <signature> --cluster devnet           # fetch via getTransaction
node dist/cli.js <signature> --rpc http://127.0.0.1:8899
node dist/cli.js --raw <base64-or-base58 tx bytes>      # offline, no metadata
node dist/cli.js --file saved-getTransaction.json --idl target/idl/my_program.json
node dist/cli.js ... --json                             # machine-readable
node dist/cli.js serve --port 8787                      # web UI on 127.0.0.1

الشكلان الأولان يجلبان المعاملة من شبكة أو من الـ validator المحلي. الخيار --raw يعمل بلا اتصال على بايتات بصيغة base64 أو base58. والخيار --file يقرأ ردّ getTransaction محفوظًا، وهذا مفيد في تقارير الأخطاء والاختبارات. أما --json فيعطي نفس الشرح كبيانات منظّمة يستطيع سكربت أن يقرأها.

وكمكتبة، ثلاث دوال تغطي الحالة الشائعة:

import { explain, render, fetchTransaction } from "tx-explainer";
const e = explain({ rpc: await fetchTransaction(sig, "https://api.devnet.solana.com") }, { idls: [myIdl] });
console.log(render(e));

الدالة fetchTransaction تجلب المعاملة، وexplain تبني الشرح المنظّم، وrender تحوّله إلى النص الذي رأيته في الأعلى.

كيف يعمل من الداخل

يصف الـ README أربع وحدات صغيرة، ومعرفة هذا التقسيم تفيدك إن أردت إضافة decoder جديد:

  1. الملف message.ts يحلّل صيغة الإرسال (wire format) يدويًا: أطوال compact-u16، والتواقيع، وترويسة الرسالة، ومفاتيح الحسابات، والتعليمات المجمّعة، وجداول البحث في v0. ثم يستنتج من الترويسة إن كان كل مفتاح موقّعًا (signer) أو قابلًا للكتابة (writable).
  2. الملف programs.ts فيه decoder صغير لكل برنامج مدمج. كل واحد يقرأ وسم التعليمة (u32 في System وu8 في Token) وحقولها بواسطة Reader يعمل بترتيب little-endian.
  3. الملف anchor.ts يقارن أول 8 بايتات من بيانات التعليمة مع الـ discriminator لكل تعليمة في الـ IDL، ثم يفك ترميز الوسائط بـ Borsh انطلاقًا من شجرة الأنواع في الـ IDL.
  4. الملف explain.ts يجمع كل ذلك مع بيانات الـ RPC: أرصدة التوكنات تعطي الـ mint وعدد الخانات العشرية، والتعليمات الداخلية تعطي الـ CPIs، والأرصدة قبل وبعد تعطي الفروقات.

ما يجب معرفته

  • غير مدقَّق، والناتج اجتهاد. الجمل وسيلة مساعدة لقراءة المعاملة. لا تغني عن قراءة كود البرنامج، ولا ينبغي أن تبني عليها وحدها قرارًا يخص أموالًا حقيقية.
  • امتدادات Token-2022 تُعرض برقمها فقط. رسوم التحويل، والتحويلات السرّية، وباقي تعليمات الامتدادات لا تُحوَّل إلى جمل.
  • بعض البرامج يُذكر اسمها فقط. تعليمات Stake وVote وAddress Lookup Table والـ loader تُعرَّف بالاسم دون فك ترميزها.
  • رسوم الأولوية تقديرية. تُحسب بالصيغة ceil(limit × price / 1e6). وإن لم تحدّد المعاملة حدًّا، تفترض الأداة القيمة الافتراضية: 200 ألف وحدة حساب لكل تعليمة.
  • الإدخال الخام بلا بيانات وصفية. مع --raw لا توجد حالة ولا رسوم ولا تغيّرات أرصدة ولا تعليمات داخلية، لأن هذه المعلومات تأتي من الـ RPC وليس من بايتات المعاملة.
  • ما تم اختباره. الأمر pnpm test يستعمل فقط ملفات محفوظة في test/fixtures/. أربع منها معاملات اصطناعية يبنيها سكربت بمكتبة @solana/web3.js من مفاتيح عامة ثابتة. تُترك بلا توقيع، فلا يُنشأ أي keypair، وتحمل بيانات وصفية مكتوبة يدويًا: تحويل SOL مع memo وcompute budget، وإنشاء ATA مع TransferChecked وCPIs، وعملية mint بـ Token-2022 عبر lookup table في رسالة v0، ونداء Anchor فاشل. والخامسة معاملة حقيقية واحدة من devnet، التُقطت مرة واحدة عبر RPC للقراءة فقط.

لماذا بنيته

العرض الخام للمعاملة يجيب عن سؤال "ما البايتات التي أُرسلت"، بينما السؤال الذي يطرحه الناس هو "ما الذي حدث". الانتقال من الأول إلى الثاني يعني فك وسوم التعليمات، وقسمة مبالغ التوكنات على الخانات العشرية للـ mint، ومطابقة الـ discriminators في Anchor مع الـ IDL، وقراءة التعليمات الداخلية وفروقات الأرصدة من البيانات الوصفية. كل خطوة بسيطة، لكن تكرارها يدويًا مع كل معاملة بطيء، ومن السهل أن تخطئ في قراءة مبلغ.

أردت أداة واحدة تقوم بهذه الخطوات بنفس الطريقة في كل مرة، وتعمل على validator محلي كما تعمل على devnet، وتعمل بلا اتصال على البايتات الخام، ويمكن استعمالها من الطرفية (terminal) أو من الكود أو من تبويب في المتصفح. وتحليل صيغة الإرسال يدويًا، بدل إخفائها خلف مكتبة كبيرة، يُبقي الكود صغيرًا يمكن قراءته وتوسيعه.

الكود

الكود، وملفات الاختبار، والاختبارات، وواجهة الويب موجودة على GitHub: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/tx-explainer. الرخصة MIT، والـ issues والـ pull requests مرحّب بها، خصوصًا إضافة decoders للبرامج التي يُذكر اسمها فقط حاليًا.

نُشر في الأصل على abdeldjalilchougui.biz.

title: Push to Talk: the Backend Problem Is Not Audio, It Is Partial State
description:
Push to talk looks like a small feature. Record, send, play. The backend tells a different story, and the whole thing turns on one requirement that sounds impossible the first time you hear it.

The receiver starts hearing the message before the sender has finished recording.

Everything below is a consequence of that one line.

The audio is not a file, it is a stream of fragments

The app pushes fragments over a persistent connection while the microphone is still open. So the server holds partial state for a large number of messages at the same time, and it has to answer a question that has no clean answer from the data alone: is this recording still in progress, or did the phone die three seconds ago?

That question is the actual engineering problem. The audio is the easy part.

Ingest has to be stateless

Every piece of per message state lives in a shared store keyed by message id, so any ingest node can accept the next fragment from any client. The moment ingest keeps something in local memory you cannot scale it horizontally and you cannot restart a node without losing in flight recordings.

Assembly, transcoding, notification fan out and expiry all move to background workers. Nothing that can block goes near the upload path, because the upload path is the one the user feels.

Ordering and idempotency, or you ship duplicate audio

Fragments carry sequence numbers and writes are idempotent. A mobile client on a bad connection will retry, and a retry must not append the same two seconds of audio twice.

Resuming from the last acknowledged sequence is an ordinary code path here, not a recovery script someone runs after an incident. A dropped connection is not an exception, it is a normal Tuesday.

An explicit state machine 

recording -> complete -> delivered -> expired
                  \-> failed

An explicit completion signal marks a message finished. Abandoned recordings time out on their own and release their storage. Skip this and storage grows forever, quietly, until somebody reads the bill.

The codec choice is a systems decision

The container and codec have to allow decoding a partial stream. Plenty of formats only become meaningful once the final byte lands, and those formats are simply wrong for this job however good they sound. It is a very cheap decision on day one and a very expensive one in month nine.

Retention is a design input, not a policy page

Voice is personal data. Metadata and in flight fragments carry a time to live that matches the retention rule, so deletion happens because the system is built that way, not because a cleanup job remembered to run.

What to monitor

Not CPU. These:

  • queue depth and queue age
  • ingest latency
  • time to first playable byte
  • transcoding duration
  • storage errors
  • expiry backlog

Queue age is the one that warns you first, every single time. Alert on it.

The stack

PHP application tier on AWS, S3 for the audio, SQS for queued work, Couchbase for metadata and in flight fragments with TTLs matching the retention policy, supervised worker daemons, and Zabbix for monitoring.

The part worth keeping

Nobody judges a voice messaging product on its average latency. They judge it on the worst message they sent today. Design for the tail, instrument the tail, and alert on the tail.

Full case study: Push to Talk Backend for a Messaging App

title: NONSENSE: Non-Semantic Strings Expose Semanticity Gaps in Dense Retrieval
description:
arXiv:2611.22353v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Dense retrieval is central to modern search, question answering, and retrieval-augmented generation, where high similarity is often treated as evidence of semantic relevance. We examine how far this assumption can be stressed. NONSENSE is a black-box sparse-edit probe that constructs visibly non-semantic strings while forbidding query-term copying, optimizing only the dense similarity between a query and the string. Across five BEIR-style datasets and three popular single-vector retrievers, these strings frequently outscore the retriever's own best judged query-relevant passage (QRP), and often rank first in the full corpus. The result indicates a semanticity gap in the evaluated dense retrievers: nearest-neighbor status can be separated from passage-like meaning. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating dense retrievers not only by whether they retrieve relevant documents, but also by how reliably their similarity scores reflect semantic evidence.

title: Reducing database incident MTTR by 73% with a custom AWS DevOps Agent Skill
description: Database incidents routinely take 45 to 60 minutes to triage. This post shows how to build a custom AWS DevOps Agent Skill that encodes expert Aurora PostgreSQL triage into decision-tree logic across five failure modes, cutting mean time to resolution from 52 minutes to 14 minutes (a 73% reduction) in a controlled test.

title: CISA pede correção imediata de falha crítica no Oracle Java
description:
CISA alerta para Java4Shell

A Agência de Segurança Cibernética e de Infraestrutura dos Estados Unidos (CISA) pediu, em 17 de novembro, a correção imediata da vulnerabilidade CVE-2026-114938 no Oracle Java, conhecida como Java4Shell. A falha recebeu pontuação 9,2 no CVSS, escala que mede a gravidade de vulnerabilidades.

O problema é uma corrupção de memória no decodificador Base64 da Java Virtual Machine (JVM) HotSpot x86-64, que integra o Java Development Kit (JDK). Entradas Base64 especialmente criadas podem derrubar a JVM e permitir a execução remota de código sem autenticação.

Como localizar instalações afetadas

A CISA orienta as organizações a revisar o inventário de software em busca de instalações afetadas do JDK e de runtimes Java. A verificação deve incluir componentes empacotados em aplicações de terceiros, imagens de contêiner e appliances.

Esses componentes podem não aparecer como itens separados nos inventários. Por isso, a busca precisa ir além dos programas instalados diretamente e considerar aplicações e equipamentos que incorporam Java, inclusive os mantidos por diferentes fornecedores.

Correções e controles temporários

A recomendação é instalar as correções do Java e dos fornecedores assim que estiverem disponíveis, priorizando os sistemas expostos à internet. A CISA também orienta consultar o aviso de segurança da Oracle para identificar versões e produtos afetados antes de definir o escopo das atualizações.

Se a correção não puder ser aplicada de imediato, controles temporários podem reduzir a exposição: restringir e validar entradas Base64 na fronteira da aplicação, impor limites ao tamanho dos dados recebidos e limitar o acesso não autenticado. Essas medidas não substituem os patches.

Monitoramento após a correção

Depois das atualizações, a CISA recomenda monitorar runtimes não autorizados, falhas inesperadas da JVM e processos Java suspeitos. O alerta contou com a contribuição do Centro Canadense de Segurança Cibernética (Cyber Centre).

Confira mais em: https://guiadeti.com.br/noticias/cisa-pede-correcao-imediata-falha-critica-java/

title: Where the Budget Goes in Supply Chain Software: ERP, EDI and Data Migration
description:
In supply chain software, the screens are rarely what drives the budget. The money goes into connecting systems, moving data and keeping inventory consistent across them. Custom projects at Dev Technosys start from $10,000, and the sections below show where the rest of a typical budget is spent.

How Much Does Supply Chain Software Cost to Build?

There is no fixed number, because "supply chain software" covers everything from a supplier portal to a platform that plans demand, tracks shipments and syncs with several warehouses. Scope is decided by how many systems must talk to each other and how clean the existing data is.

For a wider planning reference, see this guide to supply chain software development cost.

What Does Each Project Tier Include?

Basic or MVP. One core module such as inventory visibility or purchase orders, a supplier or warehouse view, basic reports and simple user roles.

Mid-level. Several modules, multi-warehouse inventory, supplier portal, shipment tracking, notifications and integration with one accounting or ERP system.

Enterprise. Demand planning, multi-site and multi-currency operation, EDI with trading partners, analytics, audit trails and integration across several back-office systems.

How Does Cost Break Down by Module?

Module What it involves Why effort grows
Inventory Stock levels, movements, adjustments Consistency across warehouses
Procurement Purchase orders, approvals, supplier records Approval rules and exceptions
Warehouse operations Receiving, picking, dispatch Barcode and device workflows
Transportation visibility Shipment status, carrier data Many data sources
Planning and forecasting Reorder rules, demand signals Data quality and model tuning
Reporting Stock, supplier and delivery metrics Joining data from several systems

Where Does the Budget Actually Go?

ERP integration. An ERP holds the records your new software must read and write. The effort is in mapping fields, handling failed calls and keeping both systems in agreement, not in the connection itself.

EDI with trading partners. Partners may send purchase orders, advance shipping notices and invoices in set message formats. Each partner usually has its own variations, so testing with real partner files takes time.

Data migration. Moving supplier lists, item masters and open orders from old systems means cleaning duplicates, fixing units of measure and deciding what history to bring across. Teams often underestimate this part.

Inventory sync. When several systems update stock, you need a rule for who is the source of truth and how conflicts are resolved. Without it, numbers drift.

Access and audit. Supplier, buyer and warehouse users need different permissions, and regulated sectors need change history.

How Can You Narrow Down Your Estimate?

  1. Which ERP, accounting or warehouse systems must connect?
  2. Do trading partners require EDI, and how many?
  3. How much data must migrate, and how clean is it?
  4. How many warehouses and locations are in scope?
  5. Which modules are needed in the first release?
  6. Who are the user groups, and what can each see?

FAQ

Why is integration more expensive than building a screen?
A screen is built once. An integration must handle failures, retries, mapping differences and testing against another system you do not control.

Can the first release skip EDI?
Often yes. Start with manual or portal-based exchange, and add EDI for the partners that justify it.

This is a planning guide, not a quote. Final scope and price depend on your requirements.

title: Two decades of The Apache Way: Celebrating 20 years of Google and the Apache Software Foundation
description:
by Mike Bufano, Open Source Programs Office

In 2006, Google formalized its relationship with the Apache Software Foundation (ASF) as one of its first corporate sponsors and twenty years later, that partnership continues through ongoing sponsorship and upstream contributions.

At the core of our collaboration is a shared belief in "The Apache Way" and its principles of open, vendor-neutral, and community-led development. From the early days of corporate open source to modern machine learning and open data systems, Google and ASF communities have collaborated on widely used open source software.

Shaping how Google does open source

When we established Google’s open source contribution workflow, we drew on established ASF practices. Both our Individual and Corporate Contributor License Agreements (CLAs), which external developers sign before contributing to a Google-owned open source project, are based on the ASF’s CLAs.

The Apache 2.0 license also remains Google’s preferred open source license for code. Alongside our traditional software releases, we also use Apache 2.0 for open hardware designs and open models like Gemma 4.

Co-engineering upstream and in the cloud

Across Google Cloud, our engineering teams contribute code upstream alongside Apache project communities and build managed services directly around those open standards:

  • Google Cloud Dataflow & Apache Beam: Drawing on Google’s internal Flume and Dataflow systems, Google donated the original Dataflow SDK and runners to the Apache Incubator in 2016 to help establish Apache Beam as a vendor-neutral open standard for unified batch and stream processing.
  • Google Cloud Managed Service for Apache Airflow & Apache Airflow: Managed workflow orchestration built on Apache Airflow, helping engineering and data teams author, schedule, and monitor complex pipelines.
  • Google Cloud Managed Service for Apache Spark & Apache Spark: Managed big data and analytics processing built on Apache Spark, running directly on Google’s cloud infrastructure.
  • Google BigQuery & Apache Iceberg: Support for the Apache Iceberg open table format to power large-scale analytics and machine learning datasets.

Setting the Platinum standard

Google has invested in the long-term health of open source foundations from the start. When the ASF first established its corporate sponsorship tiers, Google became the first Platinum Sponsor.

Early Google engineers and open source advocates worked closely with ASF maintainers to build the organizational and technical bridge between Google and the foundation. Today, Google maintains Platinum sponsorship through targeted funding and Google Cloud infrastructure contributions that support the ASF’s day-to-day technical operations.

That sponsorship pairs with everyday participation in ASF projects. Many Googlers serve upstream as ASF committers and Project Management Committee (PMC) members, maintaining code and stewarding projects alongside contributors across ASF communities. The ASF has also been a mentoring organization in Google Summer of Code (GSoC) for over 20 years, working with us to welcome and mentor new open source contributors around the world.

The next 20 years: AI, open data, and beyond

Looking ahead to the next two decades, much of our shared work sits at the intersection of open data, cloud infrastructure, and artificial intelligence.

Projects like Apache Iceberg are widely used in modern analytics and machine learning workflows, while using the Apache 2.0 license for open models helps bring permissive licensing to a new generation of tools.

Thank you to the developers, committers, PMC members, and maintainers who keep the Apache Software Foundation strong. Here’s to 20 more years of building together.

title: Inventa: Decentralized Self-Improving Agents for Autonomous Scientific Discovery
description:
arXiv:2611.21847v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can generate research ideas and improve scientific discovery through iterative experimentation. However, increasing the number of agents or iterations does not automatically translate to producing more diverse or feasible ideas. Agents may converge on similar candidates, propagate unsupported claims through shared memory components and repeatedly apply search strategies that no longer yield any improvements.
  We introduce Inventa, a framework for automated scientific discovery that employs autonomous research units and verified shared knowledge. Each unit creates a lineage of candidate ideas using a mutator agent. A local orchestrator agent periodically adapts the mutator's harness. When progress stalls, the orchestrator agent replaces its model or restarts the idea evolution process. Verifiers evaluate each candidate idea and record verified improvements, useful components and constraint violations in a shared knowledge, the only channel between units. We evaluate Inventa on five benchmarks spanning the research cycle, covering retrieval (ScholarCatalyst), ideation (IdeaBench), proposal writing (IdeaScientist), and scientific law discovery (EurekaBench, SciLaws-Bench). It leads all five, achieving 73.6% on EurekaBench versus 56.2% for CORAL. On IdeaBench, it discovers 26.0 novel ideas per paper, compared with 18.6 for ResearchAgent, with 82% fewer model calls.

title: Polylogarithmic Regret via Certainty Equivalence in Degenerate LQR
description:
arXiv:2611.21927v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Singular input penalties, as in minimum variance control, can reduce what must be identified to control an unknown linear system. In online linear quadratic control, certainty equivalence can achieve polylogarithmic regret when the optimal controller is identifiable from data collected under optimal feedback. With a positive definite input penalty, however, this condition is restrictive, since for an invertible state matrix it requires all unknown parameters to be identifiable under optimal feedback. We show that singular input penalties relax this requirement, expanding the class of problems in which certainty equivalence achieves polylogarithmic regret. Specifically, we prove that a certainty-equivalence algorithm with a short initial exploration phase achieves $O(\log^2 T)$ expected regret over $T$ interactions whenever controller identifiability holds. We complement this guarantee with an $\Omega(\sqrt{T})$ minimax lower bound for a family containing a system where controller identifiability fails. For minimum variance control, knowing the range of the input matrix suffices for controller identifiability, a weaker requirement than knowing the full input matrix, as assumed in prior work with positive definite input penalties. This condition also covers underactuated systems, as we illustrate with a cart-pole example.

title: Which Companies Use AWS? Real-World Examples Across Industries
description:
A beginner-friendly look at well-known companies that run on AWS, grouped by industry, and why they chose it.

tags: aws, cloud, beginners, devops

vishalcloudjourney

When I started learning AWS, one question kept coming back to me: is anyone actually using this at scale, or is it just a certification topic?

The answer is that AWS runs a huge share of the internet, from streaming and banking to space agencies and healthcare. In this post I've grouped well-known companies by industry and noted what they use AWS for.

1. Streaming and Entertainment

  • Netflix runs its streaming platform, recommendation engine and data analytics on AWS (EC2, S3, DynamoDB).
  • Disney+ uses AWS for video delivery and scaling during big launches.
  • Twitch uses AWS for live video and chat at global scale.
  • Epic Games hosts the backend for Fortnite and its game services on AWS.
  • Formula 1 uses AWS for race data analytics and machine learning insights.

2. E-commerce, Travel and Social Platforms

  • Airbnb runs its booking and search platform on AWS (EC2, S3, RDS).
  • Expedia Group moved a large part of its travel platform to AWS.
  • Pinterest uses AWS for content storage and recommendation systems.
  • Reddit uses AWS for hosting and media delivery.
  • Slack relies on AWS for messaging infrastructure at scale.
  • Lyft runs its ride-sharing platform on AWS.

3. Banking, Fintech and Finance

  • Capital One went "all in" on AWS and shut down its own data centers.
  • Goldman Sachs uses AWS for data and analytics workloads.
  • Nasdaq uses AWS for market data and cloud-based trading infrastructure.
  • Coinbase runs its crypto exchange platform on AWS.
  • Intuit (TurboTax, QuickBooks) uses AWS for its financial software products.

4. Healthcare and Pharma

  • Pfizer uses AWS for research and data processing.
  • Moderna used AWS for drug discovery and data analysis.
  • Johnson & Johnson uses AWS for cloud and analytics workloads.
  • Philips uses AWS for its HealthSuite digital health platform.

5. Automotive and Manufacturing

  • BMW Group uses AWS for its connected car and data platform.
  • Toyota uses AWS for connected vehicle and mobility services.
  • Siemens uses AWS for industrial IoT workloads.
  • GE uses AWS for industrial and digital services.

6. Technology and Software

  • Adobe runs parts of Creative Cloud and its marketing products on AWS.
  • Samsung uses AWS for services supporting its devices and apps.
  • Zillow runs its real estate data platform on AWS.

7. Government and Science

  • NASA / NASA JPL uses AWS to store, process and share space mission and image data.
  • Public sector bodies use AWS through dedicated regions, including AWS GovCloud (US).

Why Do These Companies Choose AWS?

  1. Scalability: capacity grows with demand, like a show launch or a big sale.
  2. Global reach: many Regions and Availability Zones put apps close to users.
  3. Pay-as-you-go pricing: no need to buy hardware up front.
  4. Breadth of services: compute, storage, databases, AI/ML, analytics and security in one place.
  5. Security and compliance: support for many industry standards.

What This Means for Beginners Like Me

Seeing these names made the learning feel more real. The same services I practice with, such as EC2, S3, IAM, VPC and RDS, are the building blocks behind apps used by millions of people. If you're starting your AWS journey, you are learning skills the industry actually uses.

Note: Companies change their cloud setups over time, and many use multi-cloud. For the latest details, check the AWS Customer Success Stories page.

title: AWS Transit Gateway supports native integration with Gateway Load Balancer
description:
AWS Transit Gateway now supports network function attachments of type Gateway Load Balancer, simplifying the deployment and management of network security across your AWS network.

With a network function attachment, you can connect your transit gateway to a Gateway Load Balancer VPC endpoint service that fronts firewalls and other security appliances without complex VPC configurations. Transit Gateway creates and manages the Gateway Load Balancer endpoints in the Availability Zones you choose, removing the need to create dedicated endpoint subnets and route tables. The endpoint service can be in another AWS account.

Network function attachments also support context sharing with security services. Transit Gateway adds resource context to traffic sent to your firewall, including the transit gateway attachment, VPC, subnet, and security groups. Your firewall can use this context alongside IP addresses to enforce segmentation policies.

This capability is available in all commercial AWS Regions where both AWS Transit Gateway and Gateway Load Balancer are available, except Middle East (Bahrain) and Middle East (UAE). It is also available in the AWS GovCloud (US-East) and AWS GovCloud (US-West) Regions.

To get started, see Network function attachments in the AWS Transit Gateway Guide and visit the AWS Transit Gateway product page.

title: Learning Optimal Transport Plans Via Autoregressive Token Regression
description:
arXiv:2611.22218v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Optimal Transport (OT) provides a principled framework for finding the minimum cost coupling between probability distributions. Classical solvers remain the gold standard for this task. At the same time, OT is an ideal testbed for studying whether learning-based amortized models can internalize the structure of OT type problems. Here, ground-truth solutions are available and marginal constraints are explicitly defined. Also, exact discrete solutions have well-characterized sparsity. We describe ToR-OT, a transformer-based model that learns to predict discrete OT plans through autoregressive token regression. We reframe OT into a structured sequence generation task. ToR-OT decodes sparse transport plans as sequences instead of solving an optimization task at test time. We focus on three properties: (a) Zero-shot generalization: pretraining on a large synthetic corpus of OT instances allows a single model to generalize to unseen distribution pairs and heterogeneous cost metrics without retraining, (b) Sparse primal decoding: by exploiting the inherent sparsity in exact discrete OT solutions, the decoder predicts only nonzero entries (avoids dense coupling outputs), (c) Amortized inference: on low-dimensional discrete problems, ToR-OT gives accurate approximate plans and compares favorably with per-instance neural OT baselines. Overall, ToR-OT is not yet a replacement for classical solvers, but a step toward understanding how autoregressive transformers can learn structure of constrained optimization problems like OT.

title: Security flaw in OpenJDK allows remote code execution
description:
A critical vulnerability dubbed Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) impacts OpenJDK's Base64 decoder on x86-64 processors with AVX-512 VBMI support.

The flaw allows unauthenticated remote code execution, memory exposure, or JVM crashes in default configurations of major Java platforms.

Oracle released patches on November 17, 2026.

Oracle released security patches on November 17, 2026, while the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Administration urged organizations to update their systems immediately. The problem is not in the application libraries, but directly in the Java runtime environment, which means administrators need to check which version each service is using.

Which systems are affected?

According to the researchers who discovered the bug, the issue affects some computers with specific processors, while systems with ARM64 architecture are not affected. During testing, it was found that in default settings of well-known applications and tools, such as Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate, it was possible to execute commands without a connection.

Other services, such as Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker, required a prior login to be affected. Additionally, a demonstration showed that there was also a risk via client login, after opening an encrypted connection to an unknown computer.

title: A Practical Stack Checklist for Small-Business Web Apps (Next.js, Node.js, SQL or MongoDB)
description:
Most small-business web apps I see share the same shape: a handful of forms, a dashboard, some user roles, and a few integrations (payments, email, maybe WhatsApp or SMS). The hard part is rarely the code. It's picking a stack that a small team can ship quickly and still maintain two years later.

Here is the checklist I use before writing the first line.

1. Start from the data, not the framework

Sketch the core entities and their relationships first: customers, orders, invoices, bookings, whatever the business runs on.

  • Mostly relational data (orders → line items → products, strict reporting needs): reach for SQL (MySQL or PostgreSQL). Joins and transactions will save you later.
  • Flexible, document-shaped data (form submissions with varying fields, content blocks, activity logs): MongoDB is a comfortable fit.
  • Both? That's normal. Keep the transactional core in SQL and store loosely structured data as JSON columns or in a separate collection.

2. Pick a rendering model per page, not per project

With Next.js you don't have to choose one strategy for the whole app:

Page type Good default
Marketing pages, blog Static generation (fast, SEO-friendly)
Product/catalogue pages Static + revalidation
Dashboards behind login Client or server components fetching per request
Admin tables with filters Server-side data fetching + pagination

Public pages get the SEO benefits, and the authenticated app stays dynamic.

3. Keep the API boring

For a small team, a plain Node.js REST API (or Next.js route handlers) with clear resource names beats a clever architecture. A few rules that pay off:

  • Validate every request body at the edge (Zod or similar).
  • Return consistent error shapes: { error: { code, message } }.
  • Paginate every list endpoint from day one.
  • Log with request IDs so support issues can be traced.

4. Authentication and roles early

Retro-fitting roles is painful. Even if version one has only "admin" and "staff", model roles and permissions as data, not as if (user.isAdmin) scattered through the code.

5. Plan for the second integration

The first integration (say, a payment gateway) usually goes straight into a route handler. The second one is the signal to introduce a small service layer and a queue or background job runner, so slow third-party calls don't block requests.

6. Make it observable and backed up

Before launch, confirm you have:

  • [ ] Automated database backups and a tested restore
  • [ ] Error tracking on both frontend and backend
  • [ ] Uptime monitoring on key pages
  • [ ] Environment variables kept out of the repo

Wrapping up

None of this is exotic, and that's the point. Small-business software succeeds when it is predictable, easy to hand over, and cheap to change. A React/Next.js front end, a Node.js API, and the right database for your data shape cover the vast majority of these projects.

What's on your checklist that I've missed? I'd love to hear it in the comments.

I'm Haseeb Ullah, a software developer building web applications, SaaS products and custom business software. You can see more of my work on my portfolio.

title: Revisiting the Survival of Agent-Attributed Code: How Measurement Choices Decide the Verdict
description:
arXiv:2611.21784v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Studies of how long code from AI coding agents survives after it is merged reach conflicting verdicts: agent code is reported to be retained longer than human code, about as long, or modified sooner. Each study makes defensible measurement choices, but how much these choices decide the verdict is unknown. We revisit the survival of agent-attributed code in our earlier study: 854,139 lines that 2,802 merged pull requests (PRs) added to 215 repositories of the AIDev dataset. We vary nine measurement choices in five research questions and build a specification curve of 88 survival analyses, tested under three variance estimators, several observation windows, and permuted labels. For code from human-supervised agents, mostly GitHub Copilot, the choices change the size of the effect but not its direction. For code from the fully-autonomous agent Devin, they decide the verdict. Across repositories, 15 of 22 specifications report it modified sooner when lines are treated as independent, but only 3 when standard errors are clustered by repository, no more than permuted labels produce. Within repositories, no specification detects a difference. LLM intent classifiers agree with human labels about as well as two humans agree with each other, whereas keyword rules do not (kappa = 0.69 to 0.72 against 0.38), and the two reach different verdicts on why agent code is modified. Humans make most modifications to agent code under every unit and window. Re-run on our data, five published designs each change their result with a single choice. Whether agent code survives longer than human code is therefore decided as much by the measurement as by the code. We derive an operationalization checklist for post-merge studies.

title: RAW: Refusal Aversion in the Wild, A Causal Measurement Method for Deployed LLMs
description:
arXiv:2611.21641v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Deployed LLMs field hundreds of millions of conversations a day and refuse a non-trivial fraction of user requests, yet the user-side cost of refusal, whether users disengage and by how much, is unmeasured on any production model: a blind spot for the consumer-facing platforms built on them. A/B-testing refusal is ethically and operationally constrained on frontier-lab products and unavailable to third-party platforms deploying these models through a fixed API. We introduce RAW, a method that uses LLM stochasticity as a natural experiment: at near-identical prompts in any existing log, the same model sometimes refuses and sometimes does not, and that variation identifies the causal user-side effect of refusal. Applying the method to 15 deployed LLMs in LMSYS-Chat-1M and WildChat, with user-clustered inference, we find that for about half of the models we can measure precisely, a refusal costs 3 to 17 pp of subsequent re-engagement; the rest show no distinguishable effect, among them one deployment whose positive point estimate we trace to persistent users retrying the refused request. Our contribution is the measurement method, which runs on any deployed model from logs alone for about \$0.30 per 1,000 conversations. We release labels, moderation scores, prompt embeddings, and pipeline code.

title: Your Service Has Stopped Responding and You Have Never Taken a Thread Dump
description:
The service is still running. The process is there, the memory looks normal, and the CPU is almost idle. But every request hangs until it times out, and the logs stopped twenty minutes ago without a single error. Someone suggests restarting it. Before you do, spend one minute capturing what every thread inside it is doing right now. That snapshot is called a thread dump, and once you have read one, you will never want to restart a stuck service blind again.

On the Java virtual machine there are three common ways to take one. Run jstack followed by the process id. Or run jcmd with the process id and Thread.print. Or send the process a quit signal with kill -3, which makes the JVM write the dump to its own standard output, so in a container it appears in the logs. Take three dumps about ten seconds apart. A thread that is in the same place in all three is stuck, not busy.

Each thread appears with a name, a state and a stack trace. The state tells you a lot. RUNNABLE means it is doing work, or waiting on the network. BLOCKED means it is waiting to enter a synchronized section that another thread holds. WAITING and TIMED_WAITING mean it is parked until something wakes it.

Now look for patterns rather than reading every line. Are two hundred request threads all waiting at the same line, inside the method that borrows a database connection from the pool? Then the pool is empty, and the interesting question is who is holding the connections. Are several threads BLOCKED on the same lock, with one thread holding it while it waits on a slow external call? There is your problem. If two threads are each waiting for a lock the other holds, jstack will often say so plainly, with a line saying it found a Java level deadlock.

Other runtimes have the same idea. For Python, py-spy dump with a process id prints the stack of every thread without stopping the program.

Practise on a calm day. Take a dump of a healthy service, find your own code in it, and learn what normal looks like. Then, during the next incident, capture first and restart second. The restart fixes today. The dump tells you how to stop it happening again.

– Asael Shinder

title: SimAI: Mechanistic User Simulation through Psychological Network Models
description:
arXiv:2611.21808v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Realistic user simulation enables the study of human interactions when direct experimentation is costly or potentially harmful. However, existing simulators largely overlook the psychological mechanisms that drive user behavior. We introduce SimAI, a framework for mechanistic user simulation that models how psychological factors interact to shape user responses. To overcome the challenge of supervising open-ended behavior, we propose a graph reconstruction objective that provides graph-level rewards based on how well simulated conversations reflect the underlying psychological relationships. To support this approach, we construct PSYCHE, a dataset of 18,576 profile-network pairs derived from 516 psychotherapy cases. Automatic evaluations show that SimAI achieves greater simulation and behavioral diversity than existing patient simulators while maintaining strong profile alignment. In an interactive study with 30 mental-health professionals and trainees, SimAI receives the highest average ratings for conversational authenticity, realistic help-seeking behavior, and clinical training utility. Beyond simulation quality, SimAI enables realistic clinical training and uncovers safety failures in prolonged AI interactions with vulnerable users. Code is available at https://github.com/behavioral-data/ANGEL-UserSim.

title: SignAligner: Dual-Granularity Span Generation for Sign Language Alignment
description:
arXiv:2611.22409v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large sign-language corpora benefit from temporal labels at two scales: subtitle spans for subtitle alignment and word spans for sign spotting. Sign spottings already locate words in time at corpus scale, but training subtitle alignment jointly on subtitle and word spans remains underexplored. We present SignAligner, a prompt-conditioned visual-language span generator that maps a sign-language video and a subtitle-sentence or target-word query to a textual start/end frame interval. It is first trained jointly on subtitle spans and word spans from sign spottings, then refined with overlap-based rewards while retaining auxiliary word examples. On the subtitle test set of the British Broadcasting Corporation-Oxford British Sign Language (BOBSL) corpus, the refined model reaches 66.68 F1@0.50 (F1 with a temporal intersection-over-union threshold of one half), the best among compared systems without external sign-video resources. This overlap-reward refinement outperforms cross-entropy continuation from the same jointly trained model. Joint training with word spans improves subtitle alignment in a pair of our generators matched in code, labels and maximum update budget. The advantage remains after both models of the pair are refined with overlap rewards. For word queries, the refined model follows the queried word, not a fixed position in the video: when the word's sign lies away from the video centre, it is far more accurate than predictions that use position alone. Together, these findings support one shared span generator refined with overlap rewards, aligning subtitles and producing word spans for human review.

title: Symbolic Abstraction Refinement
description:
arXiv:2611.22404v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Autonomous systems choose actions whose outcomes are uncertain and are subject to time constraints. Probabilistic timed automata (PTAs) model exactly this, and verifying one answers a question about the system's decision-making: the maximum probability of reaching a goal, or the minimum probability of reaching a hazard, that a controller can guarantee. Verification normally works over symbolic states, each pairing a discrete location with a region of clock values, and its difficulty is that the best behavior generally varies within such a region. The PRISM verifier's most capable PTA method responds by splitting regions until each is uniform, rebuilding the transitions that reach them and propagating the split backward through the state graph of a stochastic game, a cascade of graph reconstruction that partitions regions the property never depends on. We present SYMAR, which instead makes the value function symbolic: each symbolic state carries a function from sub-regions of its clock region to probability bounds, so refinement is the appearance of new sub-regions in that function, and previously generated states are never split nor their incoming transitions reconstructed. Both sources of PTA nondeterminism, the timing and the choice of actions, are captured implicitly by the preimage computation that produces those sub-regions. Heuristic forward search then bounds how much refinement is done at all, expanding an And-Or graph from the initial state along the most promising behaviors so that effort is confined to the property-relevant fragment, guided by bounds and preferred actions from a single unrefined run of the existing method; a partial-refinement backup keeps the otherwise combinatorial sub-region count lean, and every stored interval provably contains the true probability. On the PRISM PTA benchmarks, whose subproblems recur in autonomous systems (distributed agreement under contention, leader election, and self-configuration without central coordination), SYMAR is up to 108x faster, solves an instance on which the existing method exhausts the time limit, and is markedly less sensitive to the deadline constant, resolving one instance in a 37-node search graph, unchanged as the deadline triples, where the existing method needs 86,380 abstract states and 73 refinement rounds.

title: Centroid Spectral Coupling: Implicit Alignment and Representation Diversity in Self-Supervised Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.22158v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) aims to align augmented views while preserving representation diversity and preventing collapse. Existing non-contrastive methods often address these goals using multiple weighted loss terms. We introduce Centroid Spectral Coupling (CSC), a single-term SSL objective that implicitly couples view alignment, representation diversity, and collapse resistance. CSC constructs centroids from independently normalized augmented-view pairs and applies a ridge-based spectral objective to their uncentered second-moment matrix. Preserving centroid magnitudes encodes view agreement while encouraging balanced representation energy across spectral directions. We establish an exact decomposition into nonnegative alignment and spectral-imbalance components, characterize the geometry of global optima, and derive finite-loss guarantees for alignment and diversity. We also show that complete constant-output collapse is a strict saddle in normalized representation space. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Imagenette show that CSC achieves the highest linear Top-1 accuracy among the evaluated non-contrastive methods on all three benchmarks, and the highest kNN Top-1 accuracy on both CIFAR datasets. A ridge-parameter sensitivity study reveals an empirical alignment--diversity trade-off: increasing $\kappa$ strengthens view alignment but reduces representation effective rank. These results show that a unified spectral objective yields competitive visual representations without explicit contrastive negatives or separately weighted alignment and diversity penalties.

title: How I Built VeloGrad (v1.1.0-beta): A C++20, Rust, and CUDA Deep Learning Engine from Scratch
description:
​

IDKLETSCODESOMETHIN / VeloGrad

Bare-metal, native-first deep learning & autoregressive inference engine in C++20, Rust, CUDA & Python.

VeloGrad (Beta)

VeloGrad is a bare-metal, native-first, pure-compiled deep learning and autoregressive inference engine engineered from scratch in C++20, Rust, CUDA, and Python by Ayushman Singh Rathore.

It eliminates Python runtime overhead, framework memory bloat, and garbage collection pauses by introducing an aligned static arena memory architecture, ahead-of-time (AOT) fused compute kernels, an empirical ~66.7% KV-cache and activation VRAM reduction engine, enterprise ZeRO-3 / FSDP distributed scaling with CPU/NVMe offload, and a natural-language autonomous training orchestrator (velograd.instruct).

Important

Public Beta Notice (v1.1.0-beta)

VeloGrad v1.1.0-beta is now in public beta.
All core compute kernels, hardware-fused operators, universal frontier model architectures (from 100M edge models up to 1T+ parameter MoE networks), Paged KV-cache VRAM reduction, ZeRO-3 FSDP parameter sharding, and natural-language autonomous training directives (velograd.instruct) have been verified with complete zero-defect automated test and benchmark suites. Community testing, empirical benchmarks, and feedback are…



View on GitHub




​Hey DEV community! My name is Ayushman Singh Rathore, and I’ve been building VeloGrad—an open-source tensor, autograd, and distributed training framework written in C++20, Rust, and CUDA with Python bindings.

​Today I’m releasing v1.1.0-beta into Public Beta. Before diving into the architecture, I want to share an honest builder lesson from v1.0.0 that completely changed how I ship code.

​The v1.0 Wake-Up Call: Auditing AI-Generated Scaffolding

​When I first pushed v1.0.0, I leaned too heavily on an AI coding agent to draft the initial scaffolding and README.md. Right after publishing, I audited the repository line by line and realized the agent had hallucinated benchmark claims and left broken Python bindings and stubbed functions.

​Instead of leaving an unverified repo up, I pulled back, stripped out every unverified claim, added a clear Public Beta status, and spent days rewriting, compiling, and testing the actual systems code so that every single line in the README is backed by real, executable code.

​What’s Inside VeloGrad v1.1.0-beta

​VeloGrad is designed to strip away Python dispatch overhead and GPU memory fragmentation during model training and fine-tuning by keeping the memory arena, autograd tape, and fused kernels inside a tight native runtime—while automatically falling back to AVX2/NEON SIMD kernels on CPU-only Linux, macOS, and Windows machines.

​1. Fused Forward & Backward Kernels (CUDA + SIMD Fallback)

​Instead of launching separate memory-bound kernels for every operation, VeloGrad fuses common transformer primitives into single passes:

​Fused GEMM + Bias + Activation (Forward & Backward)

​Fused RMSNorm + Residual Add

​Fused RoPE + Tiled Flash-Style Self-Attention

​Single-Pass Fused Cross-Entropy Loss (computes log-softmax and gradients without materializing massive [batch, seq, vocab] logit tensors in VRAM)

​Fused Multi-Tensor AdamW

​2. Static Arena Allocation & ~66.7% KV/VRAM Compression

​Dynamic allocations (cudaMalloc) during training loops cause fragmentation and latency spikes. VeloGrad pre-allocates a deterministic static memory arena and pairs block-quantized Paged KV-Cache with activation checkpointing (recompute_backward), cutting KV-cache and activation VRAM overhead by up to ~66.7% compared to unquantized baselines.

​3. ZeRO-3 Sharding + CPU Parameter Offloading

​To let developers train and fine-tune larger models on consumer GPUs without hitting OOM walls, VeloGrad implements ZeRO-3 (FSDP) parameter sharding and CPU parameter offloading over NCCL (with a cross-platform TCP/Ring fallback when NCCL isn't present), supporting SafeTensors and GGUF weights across Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek, Gemma, and Mistral model families.

​4. Natural-Language Training Orchestration (velograd.instruct)

​Alongside standard Python Tensor and nn.Module APIs, v1.1.0-beta introduces velograd.instruct, which auto-detects your local GPU/CPU topology and maps plain-English training directives directly into a configured sharding and training pipeline:

import velograd

Auto-detects available GPUs/RAM, loads weights, and configures sharding + VRAM compression

velograd.instruct(
"Fine-tune Llama-3.2-3B on local_dataset.jsonl with ZeRO-3 offloading and 66.7% KV compression"
)
How to Test v1.1.0-beta on Your Machine
​If you want to compile it and run the reproducible PyTorch comparison and VRAM profiling scripts on your own GPU or CPU laptop:
git clone https://github.com/IDKLETSCODESOMETHIN/VeloGrad.git
cd VeloGrad
pip install -e .

Run the verification suite and benchmarks

pytest
python benchmarks/bench_vs_pytorch.py
python benchmarks/profile_vram.py
What’s Next & Call for Beta Testers
​Because this is a Public Beta, real-world hardware diversity is what matters most right now. If you test VeloGrad on NVIDIA RTX cards, multi-GPU workstations, Apple Silicon, or Windows/Linux CPUs, please open an issue on GitHub with your build logs or benchmark numbers!

title: Why Your 300ms Cubic-Bezier Feels Dead (And What Springs Do Differently)
description:
Every product has one. transition: all 300ms ease-in-out. It is the reason a lot of interfaces feel like they are made of cardboard.

This is not a taste argument. There is a mechanical reason a fixed-duration curve feels wrong for interaction, and a specific set of cases where it is still exactly right.

A curve is a script; a spring is a physics system

A cubic-bezier transition says: over exactly 300ms, move from A to B following this shape. It is a script with a fixed ending.

The problem appears when the user interrupts it. Click a toggle, then click it back at 150ms. What should happen?

With a fixed transition, the browser usually restarts the curve from wherever it is, with a full 300ms duration again. The object visibly hesitates. If you interrupt repeatedly, you get a stuttering object that is clearly not obeying anything.

A spring has no duration. It has a target and a state — position and velocity. When the target changes mid-flight, the object keeps its current velocity and accelerates toward the new target. Reversing direction feels like reversing a physical object because that is what is being simulated.

That is the whole difference, and it is why springs feel "alive" and fixed tweens feel like slides.

The math, without the ceremony

A damped spring is a second-order system:

m·x'' + c·x' + k·x = 0

where m is mass, c is damping, k is stiffness, and x is displacement from the target. The behaviour is governed by the damping ratio:

ζ = c / (2·√(k·m))
  • ζ < 1 — underdamped, overshoots and settles. This is "bouncy".
  • ζ = 1 — critically damped, fastest approach with no overshoot.
  • ζ > 1 — overdamped, sluggish, no overshoot.

A concrete implementation, if you want to feel the difference in a CodePen:

function stepSpring(
  state: { x: number; v: number },
  target: number,
  { stiffness: k, damping: c, mass: m, dt }: Params
) {
  const force = -k * (state.x - target) - c * state.v;
  const accel = force / m;
  const v = state.v + accel * dt;
  return { x: state.x + v * dt, v };
}

Integrate at a fixed timestep, not per frame, or the motion changes with the refresh rate. That detail is where most hand-rolled springs go wrong.

Tuning it like a human

Numbers that produce good UI, in the units most spring libraries use:

Feel Stiffness Damping Mass
Snappy button / badge 240 22 1.0
Card or modal entrance 120 18 1.2
Playful metric reveal 180 14 1.0
Heavy panel, no bounce 90 26 1.4

These are in the same family as the values in React Spring and Framer Motion, which is a useful sanity check if you are porting a component.

The practical rule: more damping for things that carry information, less for things that celebrate. A price change should not bounce twice; a success checkmark can.

Where curves win

I am not going to pretend springs are universally correct. There are three cases where a curve is better.

1. Choreographed sequences. A 12-step launch animation with precise holds and overlaps needs a timeline. A spring cannot express "hold for 400ms then move". Use curves and keyframes.

2. Exit animations tied to a deadline. If a toast must be gone in 200ms because a modal is opening under it, a fixed duration is a feature, not a limitation.

3. Non-spatial property changes. Opacity, colour and blur do not have momentum. A spring on opacity looks like a bug. Use a short curve — 120–180ms, ease-out — and be done.

There is also the accessibility case: prefers-reduced-motion should replace spatial springs with instant or short fades. Springs make that easy if the runtime supports it, but you have to actually wire it up.

Why design tools struggle with this

Here is the part that connects to tooling.

A spring is not a keyframe. There is no "end time" to place on a timeline, because the end depends on the physics. Tools built around timelines therefore tend to approximate springs — they bake a 500ms curve that looks like a spring for one specific distance, then ship it. Move the object twice as far and the easing is wrong, because a real spring's duration scales with distance.

That is why "we support springs" in a design tool often means "we have a spring-shaped bezier preset". It is fine for playback. It falls apart the moment the object travels a different distance, or gets interrupted.

An environment that stores stiffness/damping/mass as values, and integrates them at runtime, does not have that problem. The design file and the shipped behaviour are the same simulation. That is the argument for a physics-first format, and it is testable: interrupt the animation on the canvas and in the exported component and see whether they behave the same.

A 30-second audit of your own UI

Open your product. Do these three things:

  1. Rapidly toggle a switch five times. Does it keep its momentum, or hesitate?
  2. Open and close a modal before it finishes appearing. Does it reverse smoothly?
  3. Slow your network to 3G and trigger a state change. Does the motion still make sense when it arrives late?

If any of those feel wrong, the issue is almost never the easing curve. It is that the motion was scripted instead of simulated.

The one-line summary

Use springs for anything the user can interrupt. Use curves for anything that is choreographed, non-spatial, or on a deadline. Never use transition: all — that is not a motion decision, it is an accident.

UX Baba writes about interaction design. Exode stores springs as physics parameters rather than baked curves; the free tier at exodeui.com is enough to feel the difference.
