title: Regularized Score Centering
description:
arXiv:2611.21791v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Asynchronous reinforcement learning increases training throughput, but data from stale policies and numerical mismatch between training and inference can destabilize learning. To stabilize off-policy learning, score centering (SC) removes the effect of reward baselines on the expected update. Our gradient diagnostics show less extreme gradients with SC than with importance sampling (IS), but SC can still fail when the learner moves far from the behavior policy that generated the data. To limit this policy mismatch, we introduce Regularized Score Centering (RSC), which adds a reverse Kullback-Leibler (KL) penalty to encourage the learner's next-token distribution to stay close to the behavior policy's next-token distribution. RSC works with or without truncated importance sampling (TIS), which caps token importance weights. Our theoretical analysis supports this approach, showing that KL regularization improves convergence guarantees. We evaluate dense and mixture-of-experts models on mathematical reasoning and agentic tasks, including online shopping, tool use, games, and fully asynchronous software engineering. RSC with TIS substantially improves sample efficiency across all agentic benchmarks, attaining higher training rewards with the same number of sampled responses. In final evaluations, it achieves top performance across all six agentic tasks, improving by 14.3% on AppWorld and reaching 9.9 times the strongest baseline's score on BabyAI.

title: Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938): An AI Found a Critical RCE in Java's Base64 Decoder — Patch Now
description:
A 65-byte string can take over your Java server. That is the short version of Java4Shell, the critical vulnerability disclosed on Tuesday, November 17, 2026. The longer version is the one that should change how every Java team thinks about security: the flaw was found by a researcher working with OpenAI's Codex, in about an hour, for under $200 in tokens.

Oracle patched it the same day. If you run Java on x86-64 servers, the patch is the job. Everything else in this article is context for why it matters and what to do first.

Every fact below comes from the disclosure by security firm Calif, Oracle's November 2026 Critical Patch Update, and CISA's alert of November 17, 2026, as reported by CyberScoop, Qualys, Orca and CISA coverage. Severity scores and affected-version lists are the vendors' own. I have not tested the exploit — this is researched analysis, not hands-on testing.

What Java4Shell actually is

Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) is a heap out-of-bounds write in the Java runtime itself — not in your application, not in a library, but in the JDK's own Base64 decoder.

The bug sits in hand-written x86-64 assembly that the HotSpot JVM uses to speed up Base64 decoding with AVX-512 VBMI instructions. A specially crafted Base64 input — reportedly as simple as 64 letter "A" characters followed by a single equals sign — makes the decoder write past the end of its heap buffer, about 62 bytes past it. From there, Calif (the firm that found it) turned a memory overwrite into full remote code execution.

Two things make this worse than the average critical CVE:

  • No login needed. Calif demonstrated unauthenticated RCE — code execution without any credentials — against default configurations of Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate. It also demonstrated post-authentication RCE (a login first) against Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker.
  • It is in the standard library. Any Java service that decodes Base64 — which is to say, almost every Java service that handles tokens, basic auth headers, file uploads or API payloads — runs this code path, provided the hardware matches.

Who is affected

The conditions are specific, and that is the only good news:

  • Software: OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later, including Java 21, 25 and 27, plus Oracle's Java 8 Enterprise Performance Pack. The vulnerable AVX-512 decoder reached the Java 17 line with 17.0.6 in January 2023. Downstream builds are affected too — Amazon Corretto, Eclipse Temurin, Red Hat, Azul and Microsoft builds.
  • Hardware: x86-64 processors with AVX-512 VBMI support — Intel Xeon from Ice Lake onward (including Sapphire Rapids, Emerald Rapids and Granite Rapids) and AMD EPYC and Ryzen from Zen 4 onward.
  • Not affected: ARM64 servers. Graviton and Ampere machines never take this code path.

Check your JDK version against Oracle's advisory before assuming anything — the version line and the CPU both matter. If you run Java 17 or newer on a recent Intel or AMD server, assume you are exposed until the patch is in.

The scores, and why they disagree

Calif rates the flaw 9.2 (Critical) under CVSS 4.0. Oracle rates it 8.1 (High) under CVSS 3.1, and Red Hat published a preliminary 9.8. The disagreement is about scoring methodology, not about the bug — everyone agrees a pre-auth RCE in the JDK is about as bad as it gets.

As of November 17, no exploitation in the wild had been reported, and CISA had not added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue when checked at 00:05 UTC on November 18. That window is the point: the patch exists, the trigger is public, and the race is now between defenders patching and attackers repeating the discovery.

What to do right now

1. Patch the runtime. Oracle's fixed builds are 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1 and 27.0.1.1, shipped in the November 17 Critical Patch Update (which contains 655 fixes in total). Amazon had Corretto 17.0.21.1.2 out on day one, and Azul shipped fixed builds too. Red Hat had not yet shipped fixes for RHEL 8, 9 and 10 at the time of writing — if you are on Red Hat builds, watch their bulletin and use the workaround below meanwhile.

2. Restart every JVM. A patched JDK does nothing until every JVM using it has been restarted. This is the step teams most often miss: the new runtime sits on disk while the old, vulnerable one keeps serving traffic. Restart everything — app servers, CI runners, message brokers, the lot.

3. If you cannot patch yet, disable the fast path. Launch with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics, which switches off the hardware-accelerated Base64 decoder at some throughput cost. That is the workaround Qualys and Orca recommend. (An alternative flag, -XX:UseAVX=2, disables AVX-512 entirely, but Orca warns it is not dependable on Java 21 and later, where the intrinsic stays live through its AVX2 path — prefer -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics.)

4. Audit what you actually run. List every JVM in your fleet — the forgotten Jenkins controller, the Keycloak instance someone stood up two years ago, the Confluence server, the Kafka broker. Calif's demo list reads like a standard enterprise stack, and the vulnerable ones are exactly the services that sit on the network edge decoding Base64 all day.

The Codex angle — and why it matters more than the CVE

Here is the part that will outlive this patch cycle. Calif researcher Quang Luong found the flaw while auditing OpenJDK's JIT compiler, intrinsics and cryptography code with OpenAI's Codex. Codex surfaced the Base64 bug after about 20 minutes of prompting past false positives. Luong spent about an hour on discovery and two more hours building the first working exploit, at a total AI token cost of under $200. Calif says AI agents built most of its exploit chains.

Read that again: a critical RCE in the Java standard library, found by one researcher with a coding agent, in an hour, for less than a nice dinner.

That changes the threat model in two directions at once:

  • Defenders get the same tool. The same Codex-style auditing that found this bug can be pointed at your own codebase, your dependencies, your fork of an open-source project. Security auditing by AI agent is no longer a research demo — it just produced a 9.2.
  • Attackers get the same tool, cheaper. The barrier to finding the next Java4Shell is no longer a team of specialists with months of time. It is an afternoon and a token budget. The disclosure details leaked before the coordinated release, and Calif has published a safe trigger plus its general exploitation technique. The weaponised chains for specific products are not public — but the path to rebuilding them is now visible to anyone with the same tools.

The practical consequence is boring and urgent at the same time: patch windows shrink. Vulnerabilities that used to take months to find will be found in hours, by either side. The teams that survive that shift are the ones whose patching is already fast and boring — automated runtime updates, a full JVM inventory, restarts that actually happen.

The honest limits

  • No observed exploitation yet. As of November 17, nobody had reported Java4Shell being used in real attacks, and CISA had not listed it as exploited. That is a snapshot, not a guarantee — it can change overnight.
  • Red Hat users are waiting. Fixed builds were not out for RHEL/OpenJDK at the time of writing. The workaround flag is your cover until they land.
  • The trigger is public; the weaponised chains are not. Calif published a safe trigger and its technique, not the full exploit chains for Jira, Jenkins and the rest. Do not mistake that for safety — it is a head start, and it is short.
  • Patching is the only complete fix. The JVM flag is a stopgap with a throughput cost. It buys time; it does not close the hole permanently.

The bottom line

Patch your JDKs today, restart every JVM, and check the stragglers — Jenkins, Keycloak, Confluence, the services nobody remembers. Then look at the bigger lesson: an AI coding agent found a critical RCE in Java's standard library in about an hour for under $200. The next one will be found the same way, by someone. The only question is whether your runtime is patched before they try it on you.

Sources: Calif disclosure via CyberScoop and CyberKendra, November 17–18, 2026; Oracle November 2026 Critical Patch Update (fixed builds 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1, 27.0.1.1); CISA alert, November 17, 2026; Qualys and Orca analysis of affected versions and the -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics workaround; SQ Magazine and HWBusters reporting on the Codex discovery detail and Red Hat status. Severity scores are Calif's (9.2, CVSS 4.0) and Oracle's (8.1, CVSS 3.1) own ratings. No hands-on testing was performed — where a fact is a vendor's claim, we say so. Full version with FAQ on ToolsDig.

Are your Java services patched yet — and do you actually know every JVM running in your fleet? That inventory question is the one most teams can't answer honestly.

title: Right Labels, Wrong Reasons: Signed Feature Attribution for Multi-Label Explainability
description:
arXiv:2611.22515v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When a multi-label classifier assigns the right labels, it may do so for the wrong reasons. Diffuse feature combinations may vary across classifier families and lack a dominant feature. This paper proposes FLEX (Fisher LDA Explainer), a global surrogate that fits a single direct multi-label Fisher LDA over the full binary label matrix, producing signed feature attribution lists for each label in a single coherent coordinate system. Across the evaluated benchmarks and classifier families, FLEX reproduces the black box's predictions with consistently high fidelity. Pooling covariance across labels outperforms a per-label alternative on most datasets, with the advantage growing largest where labels are numerous and positive examples are scarce. FLEX's fidelity-complexity Pareto curve is monotonically increasing, giving practitioners a predictable path to higher-fidelity explanations as more features are used, and its in-sample fidelity matches or leads Binary Relevance alternatives once a modest feature budget is allowed. The magnitude of each discriminant weight vector bounds its label's separability, flagging labels that may be predicted correctly for the wrong reasons. The evaluated classifiers largely agree on which predictions to make, but reach those decisions through different feature subsets when no single feature dominates.

title: Don't ask the model to be brief. Cut it in code, and count what you cut.
description:
DevReview, the AI code reviewer I'm building, never posts more than eight comments on a pull request [src:facts]. That limit isn't something the model is asked to respect. It's a constant in the application code, applied after the model has finished talking.

I've mentioned that design before, in one line: a prompt is a request, a slice() isn't. This post is the longer version of that line, because when I actually wrote down why, the reasons turned out to be more specific than "models don't always follow instructions." There is also one consequence I didn't expect: once the limit lives in code, the prompt has to say the opposite of what you'd normally write.

The obvious version, and why I didn't ship it

If you want an AI reviewer that doesn't bury a pull request in comments, the first thing you reach for is the prompt:

Only report the most important issues. Keep it to a handful of comments.

That works in the sense that the output usually gets shorter. For a demo, that's enough. I didn't keep it, and not because I measured it failing. I haven't measured how often a prompt-only limit gets ignored, and I don't want to invent a number for it. I dropped it because of what the limit is when it lives in the prompt, regardless of how well the model follows it.

There are four problems with it. Only the first one is about compliance.

1. A request has no failure mode you can see

When the limit is a sentence in the prompt, "the model followed it" and "the model mostly followed it" look the same until someone counts. If a review comes back with too many comments, nothing in the system notices. There's no exception, no log line, no failing check. You find out when a user complains that the tool is noisy, which is the exact complaint the limit was supposed to prevent.

It also drifts. A prompt that produces short output with one model, one set of sampling settings and one style of diff may not do the same after any of those change. You can re-test after every change, but what you're re-testing is a tendency, not a rule.

A limit in code has an obvious failure mode: the number of comments posted is greater than the constant. That can be asserted, and an assertion either passes or it doesn't.

2. The model chooses what to drop before anything is ranked

This is the one that actually decided it for me.

If the model is told to keep the list short, it does the trimming while it writes. Whatever it decided not to say never makes it into the output. So the selection, the most important decision in the whole review, happens inside the generation, in an order I don't control and can't inspect.

What I wanted instead was a fixed rule that I can read:

  1. Collect every finding.
  2. Sort by severity: BUG, then WARN, then NIT, then PRAISE [src:facts].
  3. Within the same severity, keep the order the model produced them in.
  4. Keep the top of the list up to the cap. Count the rest.

The rule isn't clever. Its value is that it's the same rule on every review, and when someone asks "why was this comment cut and that one kept?", the answer is a sentence, not a guess about what the model was weighing at the time.

A side effect is that the ranking is across the whole pull request, not per file. When you ask a model to be brief, you have no idea whether it's being brief across the PR or per file, or front-loading whatever it saw first. With a sort over the full list, a bug in the last file outranks a nit in the first one by construction.

3. You can't disclose what was never written

When DevReview cuts comments, it says so in the review: how many remarks were suppressed to keep the review focused, and (since a change I'll get to below) what severities they were. I call that the Noise Report.

That disclosure is only possible because the cut happens in code. The code has the full list and the shortened list, and the difference between their lengths is a number it can print.

If the model trims itself, there's no full list. The things it chose not to say don't exist anywhere. You can't count them, you can't show them, you can't tell the reader "there was more, and here's roughly what kind." A quiet review and a review that missed something look identical from the outside, and a prompt-side limit makes it impossible to tell them apart even in principle.

This is also why I don't describe DevReview as having nits "off by default." It doesn't. NITs are generated and kept like any other finding, and they're shown if they fit under the cap [src:facts]. They're just the first thing to go when the list is long, and when they go, they're counted.

4. The pull request is in the same context as your instruction

An AI reviewer reads text written by the PR author: the title, the description, the diff. All of that lands in the same context window as the instructions. If the limit is an instruction, then "keep it short" is one sentence competing with whatever else is in that window, including text written by someone you don't control.

I don't want to overstate this. The prompt tells the model to treat PR content as material to review, not as instructions, and that's the main defense. But for the specific question of "how many comments can end up on this PR," I'd rather the answer not depend on that defense holding. With the cap in code, the most any text in the PR can do to the count is fill it.

The part I didn't expect: the prompt has to say the opposite

Once the cap was in code, I had a prompt that still asked the model to be selective. That's two limits stacked on top of each other, and the combination is worse than either one alone.

Walk through it. The model trims itself to a short list, silently. The code then sees a list that's already under the cap, cuts nothing, and reports that nothing was suppressed. The review looks complete and disclosed, but the selection happened in the one place that can't be counted. The Noise Report says zero while the model has quietly dropped things. The code-side limit is still enforced, but the honesty it was supposed to buy is gone.

So the prompt now says the reverse. The relevant rule tells the model to report every genuine finding, and then:

DevReview enforces the comment budget in code — do not self-limit, but do not pad the list either. Only real findings.

Both halves matter. "Do not self-limit" is there so the code gets the full list and the count means something. "Do not pad" is there because the obvious way for "report everything" to go wrong is a model inventing filler to look thorough. The rest of the prompt pushes in the same direction: a list of common false positives to avoid, and an instruction to downgrade or skip anything it's not sure is a bug.

The split of responsibilities ends up clean:

  • The model decides what is a real finding and how severe it is.
  • The code decides how many get posted, in what order, and reports what it cut.

The model is good at the first job and has no reason to be trusted with the second.

What the code-side limit doesn't fix

Putting the limit in code moves the problem. It doesn't remove it. These are the costs and gaps I know about.

The ranking trusts the model's severity labels. The sort is deterministic, but the input to it isn't. If the model labels a real bug as a NIT, the code will faithfully rank it with the NITs and, on a long review, cut it. The code enforces the count, not the judgment. The best it can do is make the cut visible, so a reader who sees "suppressed: some NITs" at least knows there's something to expand.

The cap can cut a bug. If a pull request has more genuine bugs than the cap, some of them don't get posted. Sorting puts bugs first, so you see the worst of it, but "the cap never hides a real bug" is not something I can claim. I used to describe the suppressed comments as "lower-priority," and I removed that word for exactly this reason: when the list is all bugs, what gets cut is also a bug. The note now lists what severities were cut instead of characterizing them.

The order of filters decides what the count means. Counting suppressed comments is only honest if everything that removes a finding is counted, and if invalid findings don't compete for slots with valid ones. I got that wrong once: findings that pointed at files not in the PR were filtered after the cap, so they could take slots and then disappear, and in the worst case the review showed a green check. I wrote that up separately in When a Code Review Says "No Issues" but Found Bugs. The short version: the path check now runs before the cap, and discarded findings are counted too. A code-side limit doesn't make the pipeline honest by itself. It makes it possible to be honest, and then you have to check every filter.

You pay for findings you throw away. If the model reports everything and the code keeps a fraction, the tokens spent on the rest are spent for a number in the Noise Report. I think that's the right trade, since the count is part of what makes the review trustworthy, but it's a real cost and it grows with the size of the PR.

Why the cap is eight [src:facts] is a separate question. This post is about where the limit is enforced, not about its value. I don't have measured data on the value to share yet, so I'm not going to argue for it here.

Because it's code, it can be tested like code

The practical payoff of all this is that the limit stops being a behavior you evaluate and becomes a property you assert.

Testing a prompt-side limit means running the real model on a set of PRs and looking at the distribution of comment counts. That's useful, but it's an evaluation: it tells you how the model tended to behave on those inputs at that time.

Testing a code-side limit means faking the model's response and checking what the pipeline does with it. The model is out of the loop, so the result is the same every run. This is roughly the shape of the test (the helper name here is illustrative, not a file you'll find in the repo):

test("cap is enforced in code and overflow is counted", async () => {
  // Fake model output: more findings than the cap, severities mixed and
  // deliberately out of order, all pointing at files that exist in the PR.
  const findings = [
    ...Array.from({ length: MAX_COMMENTS }, (_, i) => nit(`a.ts`, i + 1)),
    bug("b.ts", 10),
    warn("b.ts", 20),
    praise("a.ts", 30),
  ];

  const result = await reviewWithFakeModel({ comments: findings });

  // 1. Never more than the constant.
  expect(result.comments.length).toBeLessThanOrEqual(MAX_COMMENTS);

  // 2. Severity order wins over model order: the bug and the warning
  //    the model listed last are posted first.
  expect(result.comments[0].severity).toBe("BUG");
  expect(result.comments[1].severity).toBe("WARN");

  // 3. Nothing disappears without being counted.
  expect(result.comments.length + result.suppressedCount).toBe(findings.length);
});

Three assertions, and each maps to one of the reasons above:

  1. The count is a rule, not a tendency.
  2. Selection follows a fixed order that I wrote down, not one the model chose while generating.
  3. Everything that was cut is disclosed. If a future change adds a filter that drops findings without counting them, the third assertion is the one that should catch it.

The third one is the assertion I care about most, and it's the one a prompt-side limit can't have at all, because there's no "findings.length" to compare against when the model never wrote them.

Since the change I described in the post on the false green check, the review function has been tested end to end with faked responses from the model and from GitHub. The block above shows the idea, not a copy of that suite. The budget itself is also pinned by a plain unit test that feeds generated findings straight into the pure rank-and-slice function, so the cap, the order and the suppressed count don't depend on any model call at all. Before that, I relied on a demo pull request with an expected review written down before running it. One of its pass conditions was that the suppressed count equals the number of generated findings minus the cap. That's the same invariant as the third assertion, just checked by hand.

When a prompt-side limit is fine

None of this means "never put limits in prompts." I'd still use one when:

  • Nobody downstream relies on the limit. If longer output is just a bit annoying and nothing breaks, a prompt instruction is the cheapest thing that mostly works.
  • There's no list to cut. Free-form prose doesn't have a natural unit to slice. Truncating a paragraph in code is worse than asking for a shorter one.
  • You don't need to tell anyone what was left out. If there's no equivalent of the Noise Report, the strongest argument for doing it in code goes away.

For a code reviewer, none of those apply. The output is a list, the reader relies on it being short, and the reader also needs to know whether short means "nothing else" or "more, cut on purpose." That's what pushed the limit out of the prompt.

The rule I'd keep

If an LLM produces a list and something about that list has to be true every time (a maximum length, an order, a guarantee that nothing vanishes without a count), enforce it in code after generation and test it with a faked response. Use the prompt for the part only the model can do: deciding what goes on the list. Then make sure the prompt isn't quietly enforcing the same limit too, because a limit nobody can count is the one you were trying to get rid of.

I'm building DevReview at getdevreview.com. It's a GitHub App that ranks review comments by severity and caps them in code, and there's a free tier if you want to see what a capped review looks like on your own PRs. If you've solved the "the model trims itself before your code can count" problem differently, I'd like to hear how.

Bug ID Description

562964081 The sgpUserIntentMatchingMode verdict-log field is now always present, including on dry-run policy records, and shows the mode used for the evaluation, including when sgpUserIntentMatching isn't set (CONSTRAINTS_AND_INTENT, or INTENT_ONLY when no policies match the tool call).
524115876 Fix an intermittent HTTP 400 error in the OASValidation policy's strict parameter validation that rejected valid requests.
572025634 Responses with a compressed text/event-stream body to a proxy with an EventFlow now skip EventFlow processing and pass through intact instead of returning a corrupted body.
549078690 If no SGP policy is attributed for a denial, a customer sees the generic fallback message. This fix short-circuits to show the rationale instead when no matched policy has a configured denial message.
492041991 VerifyAPIKey and VerifyAccessToken now set the apiproduct.operation.llmTokenQuota.* flow variables only from the LLM operation(s) that matched the request; they are no longer set from unmatched LLM operations or for requests that match no LLM operation.
567244615 Semantic Governance now evaluates LLM requests it previously skipped, such as OpenAI requests whose message content is an array of parts, which can produce new denials and judge-model usage. It considers every system message rather than only the last, and a non-streaming OpenAI or an Ollama tool call whose arguments are not valid JSON is now an evaluation error.
567244615 Semantic Governance no longer evaluates a request or response with a field it cannot read when a tool call is involved. It records verdict ERROR naming the field, with status MODEL_ERROR. The inline SemanticGovernance policy instead raises GovernedLLMResponseParseError or GovernedLLMProviderDetectionFailed (HTTP 500), in DRY_RUN too unless continueOnError is true. It also reads every text part of a Gemini system instruction and Gemini tool parameters given as parametersJsonSchema, and no longer loses the rest of a Claude or Gemini request when one field has an unexpected shape.
560272924 Added continuous-scan bidirectional gRPC streaming support for the SanitizeModelResponse policy over Server-Sent Events (SSE) streams, preserving native LLM provider SSE JSON envelopes and event framing.
555332621 Model Armor policies now honor HTTPClient.managementplane.skip.proxy: with it set, Model Armor callouts bypass the forward proxy like other googleapis traffic. Streaming (ContinuousScan) Model Armor traffic uses the forward proxy.
158204922 VerifyJWT now rejects a JWT whose header contains "b64":false, with fault steps.jwt.InvalidToken, as RFC 7797 section 7 requires. Previously, such a token could be accepted if KnownHeaders listed b64, IgnoreCriticalHeaders was true, or the header had no crit.
158204922 GenerateJWS supports RFC 7797 unencoded payloads. GenerateJWS now raises MissingPayload, InvalidPayload or FailedToResolveVariable for payload errors, where it previously raised GenerationFailed. KnownHeaders and CriticalHeaders in the JWS and JWT policies accept names separated by whitespace, such as one per line. A b64 header supplied through AdditionalHeaders is now rejected, with steps.jws.InvalidNameForAdditionalHeader for GenerateJWS and steps.jwt.InvalidNameForAdditionalHeader for GenerateJWT. A proxy that set b64 through an AdditionalHeaders variable produced an RFC 7797 JWS before this change, and must move to UnencodedPayload, with DetachContent for the detached form.
158204922 VerifyJWS verifies RFC 7797 unencoded-payload JWS (b64:false), attached or detached. b64 in crit no longer needs a KnownHeaders entry. VerifyJWS rejects b64:false unless crit lists b64, with the new fault steps.jws.UnencodedPayloadNotCritical; IgnoreCriticalHeaders does not change that. DecodeJWS reports the raw payload of such a JWS.
559228730 ext_proc: ImmediateResponse now carries any Content-Type (raw body bytes + preserved Content-Type); replies too large to buffer use StreamedImmediateResponse.
544751120 Semantic Governance Policies marked as dry run are now evaluated and logged without blocking the request. Each dry-run policy adds a second judge evaluation per tool-calling response, whose tokens are billed. Dry-run verdicts are written to the semantic-governance-policy log as separate records flagged sgpDryRunPolicyEvaluation=true; queries that count verdicts should add sgpDryRunPolicyEvaluation != true to exclude them.
554114419 Fixed: an AssignMessage/HTTPModifier/RaiseFault policy that creates a new request (createNew="true") in an HTTP/2 flow can now set the :path and :authority pseudo-headers instead of failing with an invalid-header error.
567812025 FILESYSTEM persistence mode makes the synchronizer skip Cassandra entirely (no connections, reads, writes, or datastore health probes).
559009293 Fixed elevated OAuth latency and Cassandra read load for AppGroup apps, including access token verification and token and authorization-code generation, by caching AppGroup lookups in the message processor runtime, matching Developer behavior.
568860869 Fixed RegularExpressionProtection patterns of the form "...." whose middle section contains regular expression syntax (for example, ".?Exception in thread." or "(?i).<script.>.*") being matched as literal text instead of as regular expressions. Such patterns now raise steps.regexprotection.ThreatDetected for all matching input.
564945600 Enhance VerifyAPIKey policy to better handle leading spaces.
502231886 Fixed the default source templates for SanitizeUserPrompt and SanitizeModelResponse so a policy that omits the source element extracts content correctly when IgnoreUnresolvedVariables is false.
562964081 Semantic Governance now honors the sgpUserIntentMatching AuthzExtension metadata key (ENABLED or DISABLED) to toggle user-intent matching in policy evaluation; DISABLED evaluates against constraints only.
565004219 Fixed Semantic Governance Policy skipping evaluation for Anthropic requests that send system as a content-block array (the form ADK and LiteLlm emit). Affected agents are now evaluated, which may produce new denials and new judge-model usage on the consumer project.
527517087 SGP policy logs written to your project now identify their originating region. resource.type changes from "global" to "generic_node" and the region appears in resource.labels.location. Anything selecting these entries by resource.type="global" must be updated -- including log-based metrics, sinks, exclusion filters and alerts, which stop matching silently rather than erroring.
575439485 JavaCallout policies that run remotely (per-contract offload) can now pass every value type allowed by the GCP-2025-023 setVariable restriction between policies (collections, maps, arrays, primitive wrappers including Character, Date, BigDecimal, UUID, java.time, atomics, JDK enums, Optional), with their types preserved, instead of failing with steps.remotepolicy.NonSerializableVariable.
575439485 Remotely executed (per-contract offload) JavaCallout policies with continueOnError="true" now continue the flow when the callout faults, instead of returning HTTP 500.
567244901 In enforce mode, Semantic Governance now blocks a tool call when the governance check cannot be completed, instead of letting it through.
573622417 Fixed an issue where istio-ingressgateway forwarded the x-envoy-decorator-operation header to upstream runtime and target backends.
571679067 removes old version of ApigeeTelemetry CRD.
571378258 The Apigee Redis container is now built from the Valkey engine (BSD-3-Clause, Linux Foundation) at version 8.1.10. Wire protocol is unchanged (RESP2) and the redis-server/redis-cli binary names are preserved.

title: Deciding Without Pointing: A Case Study of Whether a Decision Model Localizes the Anomalies It Detects
description:
arXiv:2611.21995v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Decision models can answer a typed question about an image with a probability per option, without generating text. In our case study of Clef-flash (post-trained Qwen3.5-9B backbone) on industrial inspection benchmarks, we ask whether it localizes the anomalies it detects. We obtained uneven results with zero-shot detection: per-category image AUROC 0.924 on MVTec AD and 0.668 on MVTec AD 2. On the former, the decision head's routing attention produces 0.391 mean per-image pixel AUROC, and hiding the image tokens from it leaves detection unchanged. The multimodal LLM's backbone attention does point at the defect, however it falls below a center prior when we change question. It falls below chance if we remove textual context in the question, partly due to backbone attention leaving the object, while the head's map hardly changes. The backbone's states carry the location when probed with normal images, on the test-split images, however, the decision depends on the defect region. A larger model, Clef, that comes with a post-trained Qwen3.8-27B backbone, gives no useful map in the decision head either. We found that it's possible to recover anomaly location by asking question specifically on an image region, retraining the head or reading the backbone, but none matches dedicated few-shot localizers.

title: COTTI: Contrastive Training and Time-Aware Inference for Robust Industrial Recommendation under Promotional Drift
description:
arXiv:2611.22597v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Promotional events shift traffic composition, purchase behavior, and the scale of conversion probabilities on different time horizons. We present \textbf{COTTI} (\textbf{CO}ntrastive \textbf{T}raining and \textbf{T}ime-aware \textbf{I}nference), an industrial recommendation framework that separates historical representation learning from event-time score adjustment. Cross-Period Contrastive Alignment (CPC) regularizes paired histories of the same user with adaptive consistency weights. Active Re-weighting (RW) controls the influence of promotional examples through historical-interest distance. Adaptive Boundary Alignment (ABA) combines stochastic prediction variability with a temporal event kernel to adjust logits while keeping predictor parameters fixed. We analyze the weighted objective and bound ABA-induced probability and ranking changes. On Fliggy data, COTTI attains an offline AUC of 0.8127, compared with 0.8101 for TEN and 0.8123 for TEN with ABA. Cross-category analysis reveals improved discrimination alongside declines in paid-item recall for novel categories. End-to-end measurements give a p99 latency of 38.9\,ms and throughput of 14,700 requests/s; enabling ABA adds 2.2\,ms to p99. A ten-day online experiment against the serving HDR model yields relative gains of 3.14\% in conversion rate and 2.68\% in revenue per mille. Together, these results characterize the trade-off between aggregate prediction, novel-category discovery, and serving cost in promotional recommendation.

title: Every Measurement, Every Direction, All at Once: Multimodal Flow Matching for Molecules and Spectra
description:
arXiv:2611.22098v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generative modeling in science is often data-limited, where experiments are expensive. However, each experiment may yield several coupled measurements of the same physical entity. Standard generative models often train only on a single direction, discarding supervision from the rest. We argue that each experiment contains more training signal than this asymmetry allows the model to exploit: random masking enables measurements to serve as either conditioning inputs or prediction targets, yielding multiple supervised denoising tasks from a single experiment. We investigate this premise with MOSAIC, a multimodal flow matching transformer over molecular 3D structure and UV, IR, and Raman spectra. MOSAIC is a single model that is capable of any-to-any generation: generating any subset of modalities from any disjoint subset of the others. On QM9S, MOSAIC achieves 88.8% molecular graph recovery, outperforming the strongest spectra-to-structure baseline by 23.2% in structure generation, while simultaneously outperforming a structure-to-spectra specialist model in spectral generation. Ablations show that the any-to-any objective improves structure generation over structure-only training across model sizes. Furthermore, MOSAIC supports arbitrary subsets of available measurements and enables molecular identification by matching generated spectra to experimental references.

title: Building Type-Safe Presentation Components in Vue 3: Converting ContributorSocialLinks to TypeScript
description:
In frontend design systems, presentation components-small, focused components responsible solely for displaying data—are the building blocks of clean UI architecture. However, when these components accept raw arrays without strict contracts, optional fields like social links, profile URLs, and handles can easily lead to template errors or broken links.

In my recent contribution to GitLab's Contributors Platform (MR !3194), I migrated the ContributorSocialLinks component and its test suite to strict TypeScript.

Here is a quick breakdown of how typing lightweight presentation components improves maintainability and test reliability.

1. The Challenge: Loose Array Props

Originally, ContributorSocialLinks.vue accepted contributors through standard runtime prop validation:

<!-- Before (JavaScript) -->
<script setup>
const props = defineProps({
  contributors: {
    type: Array,
    required: true,
  },
});

const contributorsWithSocials = props.contributors.filter(
  contributor => contributor.discord || contributor.linkedIn
);
</script>

Why was this problematic?

  1. Missing Shape Contract: The compiler had no knowledge of what attributes a "contributor" held. A parent passing an object with linkedin (lowercase 'i') or discord_handle would fail silently.
  2. Untyped Filter Results: contributorsWithSocials held elements of type any, preventing type checking across the component template (such as icon rendering or URL generation).

2. Strong Type Contracts with interface

By adding lang="ts" and exporting a discrete Contributor interface, we created a clear contract for both the component and its consumers:

<!-- After (TypeScript) -->
<script setup lang="ts">
export interface Contributor {
  name: string;
  gitlabUsername?: string;
  linkedIn?: string;
  discord?: string;
}

const props = defineProps<{
  contributors: Contributor[];
}>();

const contributorsWithSocials = props.contributors.filter(
  contributor => contributor.discord || contributor.linkedIn
);
</script>

Advantages:

  • Type-Only defineProps: Eliminates verbose runtime object definitions. Vue 3 automatically validates props at compile time based on the TypeScript definition.
  • Reusable Interface: Parent components (e.g., contributor lists, award cards) can import type { Contributor } directly to ensure prop compatibility.
  • Safe Filtering: TypeScript's type checker now verifies that .discord and .linkedIn exist on the Contributor model.

3. Strict Type Safety in Unit Tests

In ContributorSocialLinks.spec.ts, untyped factory helpers were replaced with typed parameters using the exported interface:

import { shallowMount } from '@vue/test-utils';
import type { Contributor } from './ContributorSocialLinks.vue';
import ContributorSocialLinks from './ContributorSocialLinks.vue';

describe('ContributorSocialLinks', () => {
  const createWrapper = (contributors: Contributor[]) =>
    shallowMount(ContributorSocialLinks, {
      props: { contributors },
    });

  it('does not render when no contributors have socials', () => {
    const wrapper = createWrapper([
      { name: 'Test User' }, // Fully conforms to Contributor interface
    ]);

    expect(wrapper.find('p').exists()).toBe(false);
  });
});

Spec assertions are now resilient against future schema changes, ensuring that mock objects always mirror realistic application data.

Key Takeaways

  1. Export Component Prop Interfaces: When a component receives structured domain data (like a user, contributor, or product), export its interface so parent views and test suites remain in sync.
  2. Favor Type-Only defineProps: defineProps<{ data: T }>() is cleaner and offers better IDE autocompletion compared to JavaScript options-based prop validators.
  3. Keep Spec Helpers Strongly Typed: Passing typed parameters into helper functions like createWrapper prevents accidental drift between test fixtures and production models.

Author: Manish Kumar

title: DACE: Diversity-Driven Adversarial Co-Evolution for Robust LLM Safety Alignment
description:
arXiv:2611.22278v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Ensuring robust safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) is increasingly difficult as adversarial attacks evolve and outpace alignment pipelines built on pre-collected data. Existing co-evolutionary frameworks let the defender chase a moving attacker, yet their training dynamics expose two compounding pathologies: \emph{attack strategy collapse}, where the attacker overfits to a narrow set of high-reward rewrites, and \emph{defense adversarial forgetting}, where the defender loses competence against earlier attacks as the attack distribution drifts. Existing remedies are partial: attacker-side diversity rewards score textual novelty rather than strategy novelty, and defender-side replay relies on discrete judge scores that ignore estimation uncertainty, response stochasticity, and defender non-stationarity. We introduce \textbf{\method}, a diversity-driven adversarial co-evolution framework that targets both pathologies jointly. On the attacker side, \method couples an explicit two-dimensional strategy space (risk category $\times$ attack style) with a \emph{normalized marginal coverage gain} reward, providing a bounded, non-vanishing exploration signal at the strategy layer. On the defender side, \method maintains a unified \emph{Bayesian adversarial replay pool} whose Beta--Bernoulli threat posteriors are refreshed by time decay and sampled via Thompson sampling, anchoring defender training to an evolving threat landscape. Across standard safety, automated-attacker, and general-capability benchmarks, \method improves robustness to out-of-distribution attacks while preserving general capabilities, and yields broader attacker strategy coverage.

title: Google showed an AI Overview on all 40 email-marketing searches. YouTube was its top source
description:
If you market an email tool, assume your buyers will see Google's AI Overview before your ranking. It appeared on all 40 US searches in this test, covering how-to questions, best-of lists and brand comparisons. The source it cited most often was YouTube, in 31 of the 40 Overviews. YouTube ranked among the regular results on only 4 of the 40 pages. Of the domains cited in an Overview, only 62 of 283 also appeared in the regular results on the same page.

What the Overviews cited

I ran 40 email-marketing searches through automatic/google-search-results-scraper on November 18, 2026 UTC, in English with the country set to us. Each search read one results page. The Actor reports the Overview's status and its cited links on that page. All 40 rows came back present. The 40 Overviews held 308 cited links from 139 distinct domains. One Overview, for "best email service provider for developers", had no cited links.

Domain Overviews citing it Cited links Pages where it ranked in regular results
youtube.com 31 49 4
reddit.com 24 24 16
zapier.com 13 13 3
mailchimp.com 11 14 4
campaignmonitor.com 7 7 4

Domains are hostnames without www., so help.klaviyo.com counts separately from klaviyo.com. Regular results are the page's organic list, with roughly 7 to 10 links per page. Some Overviews cited several YouTube videos, giving 49 YouTube links across 31 Overviews. Reddit was closer to its regular ranking. It ranked among the regular results on 16 pages and was cited in 24 Overviews.

Does the type of search matter?

I wrote 14 how-to questions, 13 best-of or tool searches and 13 searches that name a brand. The full list is in the snapshot.

Search type Searches With an Overview Citing YouTube Citing Reddit
Question or how-to 14 14 12 8
Best-of or tool search 13 13 9 8
Brand, pricing or comparison 13 13 10 8

Questions leaned most on video. Brand searches still sent readers toward the brands. In all 12 brand searches that named a vendor, the Overview cited at least one named vendor's own site. "Mailchimp pricing", "sendgrid vs mailgun" and "brevo review" were among them. I counted twilio.com as SendGrid's site. I left out "substack alternatives" because it asks for rivals.

For an email product, I'd put a short video and an honest Reddit answer on my content list next to the blog post. On these pages, they were the two most-cited sources. Keep your own pricing and comparison pages current, too, because Overviews for brand searches cited them.

Limits

This is a single collection from one country, in English, without a signed-in Google account. AI Overviews change between runs and between users, so repeat the searches before relying on one count. I chose the 40 searches. They indicate patterns for this niche and do not measure all of Google. The regular results include a YouTube link only when Google ranks it among the organic links. A separate row of videos elsewhere on the page might not be counted. Nine organic links could not be resolved, and the script skips them. The first run reached its 300-second limit after 18 searches. I split the remaining 22 into two more runs with the same country and language. Every search has exactly one results page in the snapshot.

Reproduce the tables

Download the captured analysis fields as overviews.json. The snapshot preserves the returned order. It keeps the cited and organic URLs and omits answer text. Save the code as overviews.py and run python3 overviews.py overviews.json.

import json
import sys
from collections import Counter
from pathlib import Path
from urllib.parse import urlparse

runs = json.loads(Path(sys.argv[1]).read_text())["runs"]
pages = [page for run in runs for page in run["items"]]
order = runs[0]["input"]["queries"]  # all 40; runs 2 and 3 finish the rest
groups = {"Question or how-to": order[:14], "Best-of or tool search": order[14:27],
          "Brand, pricing or comparison": order[27:]}

def domain(url):
    return (urlparse(url).hostname or "").removeprefix("www.") if url else None

by_term = {page["term"]: page for page in pages}
assert sorted(by_term) == sorted(order)
present = [p for p in pages if p["aiOverviewStatus"] == "present"]
print("Searches", len(pages), "with an AI Overview", len(present))

cited_in = Counter()
links = Counter()
for page in present:
    domains = [domain(url) for url in page["aiOverviewSources"]]
    links.update(domains)
    cited_in.update(set(domains))
print("Cited links", sum(links.values()), "distinct domains", len(links))
print("Overviews with no cited links", sum(not p["aiOverviewSources"] for p in present))

def in_organic(page, site):
    return site in {domain(url) for url in page["organicUrls"]}

for site, overviews in cited_in.most_common(5):
    organic = sum(in_organic(page, site) for page in pages)
    print(f"{site}: cited in {overviews} overviews ({links[site]} links), "
          f"organic results on {organic} pages")

for name, terms in groups.items():
    group = [by_term[t] for t in terms]
    print(name, len(group),
          "overviews", sum(p["aiOverviewStatus"] == "present" for p in group),
          "youtube", sum("youtube.com" in map(domain, p["aiOverviewSources"]) for p in group),
          "reddit", sum("reddit.com" in map(domain, p["aiOverviewSources"]) for p in group))

pairs = shared = 0
for page in present:
    cited = {domain(url) for url in page["aiOverviewSources"]}
    organic = {domain(url) for url in page["organicUrls"] if url}
    pairs += len(cited)
    shared += len(cited & organic)
print(f"Cited domains also in the same page's organic results: {shared} of {pairs}")

vendors = {"mailchimp": {"mailchimp.com"}, "klaviyo": {"klaviyo.com", "help.klaviyo.com"},
           "beehiiv": {"beehiiv.com"}, "substack": {"substack.com"}, "kit": {"kit.com"},
           "sendgrid": {"sendgrid.com", "twilio.com"}, "mailgun": {"mailgun.com"},
           "brevo": {"brevo.com"}, "mailerlite": {"mailerlite.com"},
           "activecampaign": {"activecampaign.com"}, "hubspot": {"hubspot.com"},
           "postmark": {"postmarkapp.com"}, "constant contact": {"constantcontact.com"}}
named = own_site = 0
for term in groups["Brand, pricing or comparison"]:
    if term.endswith("alternatives"):
        continue  # names one brand but asks for its rivals
    sites = set().union(*(v for k, v in vendors.items() if f" {k} " in f" {term} "))
    named += 1
    own_site += bool(sites & {domain(u) for u in by_term[term]["aiOverviewSources"]})
print(f"Brand searches citing a named vendor's own site: {own_site} of {named}")

To run a fresh check in your own niche, put your searches in queries and use the saved first input object as the body for POST https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/automatic~google-search-results-scraper/runs?maxTotalChargeUsd=0.15&timeout=600 with an Apify bearer token. When the run finishes, read defaultDatasetId from the run record, then fetch GET https://api.apify.com/v2/datasets/{datasetId}/items?format=json. Each row's aiOverview has status, text and sources. Use the 600-second timeout above for 40 searches, or split them across runs as I did.

On November 18, 2026 UTC, the run records listed customer prices of $0.0015 per results page and $0.005 per GB of memory per run start. At the default 2 GB, that's $0.01 per start. The Actor's README says the page price becomes $0.002 on November 23, 2026. At the November 18 prices, these three runs would have cost a customer about $0.09 for 40 pages. On the publisher account, they used $0.067 of platform usage.

title: Cloudflare Turns a Spending Cap Into a Runtime Decision
description:
TL;DR

  • Spend Management is a billing control in Cloudflare that sets a dollar limit on usage-based products and pauses the product when the limit is reached; it entered Beta on 13 November 2026 for pay-as-you-go accounts, starting with Workers and Durable Objects.
  • The configuration is small: a spending limit, a recipient email and one or more alert thresholds, set in the dashboard under Manage Account, Billing, Spend limits, or through the REST API and the cf CLI with a spend policy that carries threshold_cents and an action of usage_block.
  • Cloudflare built the control on a two-stage metering pipeline: parsers bucket raw events into one-minute windows, a second service merges those partial aggregates over five-minute windows, and the consolidated data is archived before the Usage Engine reads it.
  • The Usage Engine partitions processing by account, keeping each account's usage and subscription state together with local state and a durable write-ahead log, so pricing runs in parallel across accounts and survives a failed processor.
  • The Rating Engine combines usage records, subscription information and pricing rules, holds usage as pending when subscription data arrives late, applies included allowances and prices accumulated usage.
  • Enforcement travels through Quicksilver, Cloudflare's internal key-value store for global replication: the runtime picks the cap up on its periodic refresh and rejects capped invocations from local state, which keeps rating out of the request path.
  • A pause stops the invocations that incur cost. In Workers, Cron Triggers and Queue consumers stop. Static assets remain available. The block clears when the limit is raised, the policy is disabled or the next billing cycle starts.

Cloudflare's own screenshot of the Workers configuration: block usage at the limit, a 10 dollar cap, a recipient address and two alert thresholds. Source: blog.cloudflare.com/spend-management, retrieved 15 November 2026.

What Spend Management turns on in the dashboard

The launch post opens with the demand behind the feature: spend controls had been the most requested item from developers on the platform, and Cloudflare counts more than 10 million developers building on it. Usage notifications and budget alerts already existed for paid plans, and the billing documentation describes them as emails sent when account-wide usage-based spend crosses a dollar threshold. The new part is a limit that stops the product.

The configuration sits behind that sentence. A pay-as-you-go account enables controls on a product, sets a spending limit, names a recipient for notifications and picks one or more alert thresholds. The API call in the post carries the same fields as JSON: a name, a product identifier, an enabled flag, threshold_cents set to 10000, an action of usage_block and a notification address. The cf CLI exposes the same objects with list, create, get, update, delete and two audit commands.

Cloudflare's usage-based billing documentation lists the supported products, the included allowances and the notification options behind Spend Management. Source: developers.cloudflare.com/billing/understand/usage-based-billing, retrieved 15 November 2026.

One detail in the post is easy to miss and matters at month end: the billing cycle starts when the paid subscription begins, so a subscription that starts on 10 October gives a cycle from 10 October to 10 November. A team that sets a cap mid-cycle is measuring against a billing window that has already begun.

Two metering stages aggregate usage close to the source

Every invocation produces measurements, and the post names them: requests, CPU time, execution duration or storage operations, depending on the product. Shipping that volume intact to a rating engine would not scale, so Cloudflare aggregates close to the source in two stages.

The first stage runs next to parsing. Each metering parser converts raw events into usage measurements and combines matching ones into buckets that typically cover one minute, and the post is candid that several records can still describe the same account and time window. The second stage is a separate service that merges those partial aggregates with the same grouping rules over windows that typically cover five minutes, then archives the consolidated result as a durable dataset for analytics and reconciliation.

Cloudflare's diagram of the metering pipeline: parse, one-minute buckets, a merge over five-minute windows, then the Usage Engine and Rating Engine. Source: blog.cloudflare.com/spend-management, retrieved 15 November 2026.

The ordering is the interesting engineering decision. Volume falls before the expensive systems see it, so the Usage Engine and the Rating Engine only handle accumulated usage. For an operator reading this from outside, the lesson transfers to any internal metering work: the cost of a billing pipeline is dominated by the volume carried forward at raw resolution.

The Usage Engine keeps each account in one partition

The Usage Engine turns aggregated measurements into usage records, the standardized shape that carries an account identifier, a usage window, a usage metric, a measured quantity and the relevant product dimensions. Its other job is to map each product-specific meter onto the standardized usage metrics that the billing system supports.

Cloudflare's flow for one capped billable event: usage reports, the Usage Engine, the Rating Engine, policy evaluation, notifications, and the cap propagated to every node. Source: blog.cloudflare.com/spend-management, retrieved 15 November 2026.

Cloudflare partitions that processing by account, so an account's usage and subscription information meet in the same place and its accumulated usage plus included allowances can be maintained without coordinating with other pricing processors on every update. Each partition holds local state for fast access and a durable write-ahead log on disk, which the post credits with four properties: less cross-partition coordination, consistent pricing, parallel processing and recoverability after a failure.

The Rating Engine prices accumulated usage against allowances

The Rating Engine answers one question: given what the account has consumed, its subscription and its pricing, how much has it spent so far. It brings together usage records, subscription information and pricing rules covering rates, included allowances and billing rounding.

Cloudflare's pause notification: Workers reached a 10 dollar limit, the block is dated, and the notice states what a pause means. Source: blog.cloudflare.com/spend-management, retrieved 15 November 2026.

Usage and subscription data arrive as independent streams, so the two streams carry no ordering guarantee. The post describes the consequence directly: when usage arrives before the subscription information needed to price it, the engine retains it as pending and revisits it after the subscription information arrives, which tolerates a delayed webhook while retaining that usage for later pricing. The engine also applies the included allowance before pricing any excess, and it prices accumulated usage, with rounding applied to the total.

Two outputs follow. Policy evaluation decides whether a warning or blocking threshold has been reached, and reporting pushes estimated charges to the dashboard and sends the email alerts.

Enforcement runs on local state that Quicksilver propagates

Cloudflare's audit log for spend policies, listing the change, the member and the new limit. Source: blog.cloudflare.com/spend-management, retrieved 15 November 2026.

The rating engine stays out of the request path. When a policy blocks, the policy service sends the cap to the runtime configuration service and to Quicksilver, the internal key-value store Cloudflare built for fast global replication and low-latency access, and the cap propagates to all nodes asynchronously. Each runtime picks it up during its periodic refresh and starts rejecting capped invocations or operations.

The post states the property that makes this work: enforcement uses local state, so a request never waits on the Rating Engine. The architectural point for anyone designing a similar control is the split between where the decision is computed and where it is applied. The trade-off is a cap with a distributed enforcement delay: after policy evaluation, asynchronous propagation and periodic refresh leave an interval in which some runtimes may still accept billable invocations, so the configured amount cannot guarantee the final spend.

Runtime effects of the pause

A cap that lands rejects new invocations of the product, with one qualification the post states plainly: Cloudflare pauses the customer-code invocations that incur cost. In Workers, Cron Triggers and Queue consumer invocations stop. Static assets continue to be served.

Netics visual, 15 November 2026: the five stages a capped invocation passes through, as the post describes them.

That behaviour decides how a cap should be sized. A site whose traffic is mostly cached assets keeps answering requests. Scheduled jobs and queue consumers behind background work stop. An operator planning a cap around a public launch should expect the visible page to remain available. Asynchronous work accumulates unprocessed until the limit is raised, the policy is disabled or the next cycle begins.

The dashboard adds two facts an operator needs for the same discussion. Costs for each supported product appear in near real time, under 10 minutes, and an audit log records who changed a limit and when a cap was reached. Both feed the same operational question: how much spend can accumulate between the moment a threshold trips and the moment the block is picked up across the network.

Cloudflare is explicit that this is a first step. More products will follow, the team wants the gap between measurement and enforcement down toward a minute, and the post describes a future where calls are tagged so spend can be attributed to an application or an agentic task and paused across products. For now the control covers Workers and Durable Objects, and the cloud infrastructure and cost control work that teams already run at the account level gains a runtime counterpart.

Netics visual, 15 November 2026: what the pause covers in Workers, and how the block clears.

Originally published on the Netics blog.

title: Lost in Read-out: Locating the Image Quality Gap in Vision-Language Models with a Closed-Form Edit
description:
arXiv:2611.22564v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are widely used as zero-shot image quality assessors, yet their good-vs-poor answers agree only moderately with human opinion. We ask whether these models fail to see quality or fail to say it. Layer-wise probes on five VLMs point to the second: quality is linearly decodable from the vision encoder and still from the last language layer, far better than the answer reveals, and about a hundred labels recover most of it. The loss lies mainly in the final read-out, which partly reads something else: relative to human opinion, it over-rewards colorfulness and under-rewards sharpness on all five models. We test this by intervention: if the read-out is at fault, a closed-form edit of a single last-layer neuron, fitted to many prompts at once, should close the gap and no more. Both hold. Under prompts never used for fitting, the edit recovers 86--100\% of what a ridge head on the last-layer state, fitted under the same prompts, finds beyond the answer on KonIQ. Where that gap is small, it gains little, too little for our transfer criterion on the two largest models; where the head itself is below the answer, it lowers the score; and it works only when written from the middle of the language model on. Unlike unconstrained fine-tuning, the edit leaves perception question answering intact. It does not carry over to yes-or-no or rating questions, and it reverses the good--poor contrast after sentiment-laden sentences. Code will be made available.

title: Breaking Visual Conventions: Spectrally Coupled Weight Perturbation for Creative Image Generation
description:
arXiv:2611.22318v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) models often produce high-quality images that follow familiar visual conventions, even in response to open-ended prompts such as ``a creative [CLS]''. Existing methods encourage novelty by exploring semantic conditions or modifying features and guidance during denoising. Pretrained weights offer a complementary source of creative variation, but unstructured perturbations can have little visual effect or degrade image quality. We introduce Coupled Spectral Perturbation (CosPert), a training-free method that targets attention projections in layers identified by a one-time sensitivity analysis. For each projection, CosPert uses a shared random transformation and its transpose to couple updates to the singular-vector factors while perturbing the spectral gains. A common relative budget calibrates the magnitude of weight changes across projections, and a sigmoid schedule concentrates their influence in early denoising and gradually attenuates them during refinement. CosPert provides plug-and-play creativity enhancement at inference time. Once the perturbations are prepared, sampling requires no auxiliary networks or additional model evaluations. On both FLUX.1 and Stable Diffusion 3.5, CosPert enhances visual creativity, producing more varied object structures while preserving category identity. Across 50 object categories, CosPert achieves the highest mean CREward among the evaluated methods while maintaining strong prompt alignment.

title: The Language-Energy Divide: Measuring Energy Costs of Multilingual LLM Inference
description:
arXiv:2606.21869v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in multilingual settings, yet the energy costs of serving these models across different languages remain poorly understood. We present a systematic study of inference energy consumption across languages with ML.Energy framework (Chung et al., 2026). We find striking disparities: energy consumption per output token varies by up to 8.3 times across languages, while total energy for a fixed set of requests varies by up to 179 times between the cheapest (English, 17.6 kJ) and the most expensive (Pashto, 3,147 kJ) languages. Our analysis shows that this disparity is driven by two compounding factors: (1) higher per-token energy costs for languages using complex or rare scripts, and (2) more tokens generated for low-resource languages. Moreover, we find a double cost + performance penalty: languages with the highest energy footprints also tend to achieve the lowest task accuracy. We reveal that the energy divide persists across models, hardware, and tasks, suggesting a systemic energy inequity in multilingual LLM deployment. Finally, we recommend that the community treat energy as a first-class evaluation axis, extend reporting checklists and model cards to include it, and adopt deployment-side mitigations for better energy efficiency.
