title: What 247 Million Power Outage Records Can Actually Tell Us
description:
The U.S. outage records for 2025 add up to 52.8% fewer reported customer-hours than the records for 2024. How much of that gap comes from a handful of severe days? Drop each year’s ten highest-burden days and the difference is still 41.3%.

That check took a few lines of Python. Deciding what to sum took more care. The data behind this comparison cover 11 calendar years, 2015–2025, and about 247.6 million source rows. Each row is a county-level observation, with a timestamp and a count of customers reported out at that moment.

What a snapshot can measure

Suppose a county reports 400 customers out at 08:00 UTC and 600 at 08:15. At the source’s nominal 15-minute cadence, those samples contribute (400 + 600) × 0.25 = 250 customer-hours. The second snapshot can represent a different set of customers. The data lack the customer IDs needed to reconstruct individual outage durations.

An earlier version of the analysis stitched county snapshots together when gaps were short. That could turn a moving set of small outages into one apparently long event. It could also put an entire event into the year it started. The revised pipeline assigns every valid snapshot to its own UTC day and year. It sums positive integer counts, uses 0.25 hours as a nominal weight, and leaves collection gaps unfilled. The manifest tracks off-grid timestamps and input hashes. A missing row leaves coverage unknown.

The build reads each CSV in 500,000-row chunks and writes daily and county-year summaries. When validating a published number, the small annual CSV is enough. Use the source archive and manifest if you need to audit the raw inputs.

How much does the 2024–2025 comparison move?

Calculation 2024 customer-hours 2025 customer-hours Change
All valid snapshots 1,891.7 million 892.7 million −52.8%
Exclude snapshots above the modeled county customer count where a match exists 1,664.9 million 859.6 million −48.4%
Counties with positive records in all 11 years 1,606.7 million 687.3 million −57.2%
Exclude each year’s 10 highest-burden days 1,311.6 million 770.4 million −41.3%

The top ten days account for 30.7% of the recorded total in 2024 and 13.7% in 2025. Removing them narrows the gap. The county screen is another sensitivity check. Its denominator is a modeled 2022 customer count, so a flagged row merits inspection. The 2,311-county subset checks whether the result holds within the same group of counties across years. A positive record in every year still leaves coverage within each year uncertain.

Reproduce the table with Python

Download the annual CSV beside your script and run it with Python 3. The numbers below come from the published aggregates.

import csv
from decimal import Decimal

with open("annual.csv", encoding="utf-8-sig", newline="") as source:
    rows = {int(row["year"]): row for row in csv.DictReader(source)}


def amount(year, column):
    return Decimal(rows[year][column])


def compare(label, before, after):
    change = 100 * (after / before - 1)
    print(f"{label}: {before:,.0f} -> {after:,.0f} ({change:+.1f}%)")


for column, label in (
    ("ch", "All valid snapshots"),
    ("screen1", "County customer screen"),
    ("common_ch", "Counties with records every year"),
):
    compare(label, amount(2024, column), amount(2025, column))


def without_top_days(year):
    return amount(year, "ch") - amount(year, "top10_ch")


compare("Without the top ten days", without_top_days(2024), without_top_days(2025))

All four comparisons point in the same direction. The size of the decline depends on how you handle coverage, high observations and concentrated days. A reliability claim would need consistent reporting coverage or an independent benchmark. The most useful thing to publish alongside the headline is the rule for turning a single row into a number a reader can reproduce.

Data and methods. I publish the WattSizer outage methods and source manifest. The EAGLE-I data descriptor covers 2014–2022. The later files are listed separately in the manifest. AI was used to draft this write-up from the published analysis and check the reproducible example.

title: WAL-G 3.0.10 released
description:
The WAL-G team is pleased to announce the release of WAL-G 3.0.10.

WAL-G is an open-source backup and recovery tool for PostgreSQL, Apache Cloudberry, MySQL/MariaDB, MongoDB, Redis, and other databases.

The main new PostgreSQL feature is wal-send. It serves archived WAL over PostgreSQL's streaming replication protocol, allowing standbys and pg_receivewal to read WAL directly from object storage and follow new segments as they arrive.

Other PostgreSQL improvements include:

  • Continuous WAL archival in daemon mode: the pipeline keeps working between requests, and retained lookahead reduces directory scanning (#2697, #2698).
  • Optional backup-push --wait-for-archive: WAL-G waits for all WAL segments required by the backup to reach the selected backup storage before publishing the backup as complete (#2722).
  • Backup-name reservation before upload, protecting against concurrent reuse of the same name (#2707).
  • WAL prefetch files are published only after a successful download (#2696), and WAL source files are closed after upload failures (#2695).
  • Standard X/X LSN notation in catchup-push --from-lsn (#2643).

S3 support now uses AWS SDK v2 and adds configurable request timeouts, retryable error codes, and checksum settings. Backup copying can use server-side S3 copy and configurable transfer concurrency.

Greenplum and Cloudberry improvements include per-backup accounting for shared AO/AOCS/PAX storage and fixes to segment backup, restore, and copy operations.

One behavior change to note: permanent backups remain protected from retention-based deletion, but an explicit delete target can now remove them (#2808).

WAL-G v3.0.10 is available for download, along with the full release notes, on our GitHub releases page.

Have a nice day!

title: Stablecoin Payments Backend: Dual-Ledger Spring Boot
description:
Short version of the design: keep an internal double-entry ledger, treat the blockchain as a second, slower source of truth, only release value after a per-chain finality depth, and run a job whose only purpose is to prove the two agree. In Spring Boot that is a ledger service, a confirmation state machine, idempotent Kafka consumers and a scheduled drift check.

Toss, the Korean fintech super-app, has reportedly started offering its users a wallet built around dollar stablecoins, and Kakao attempted something comparable before without gaining much traction. I have not seen any public detail about either company's backend, so I am not going to claim to know why one worked and the other did not. Distribution, licensing, KYC approval and FX pricing probably explain most of it. What interested me is narrower: whichever app wins users, its balances still have to be correct, and that part is plain engineering that any team can get wrong. This post is about that part.

I have worked on payment backends for years, including Open Banking PSD2 integrations, and the mistakes below are the ones I keep seeing in review. Where I describe a failure, treat it as a scenario to design against, not a war story with invented numbers.

Part 1: Why "sent" and "final" are different states

Quick glossary, only what the rest of the post needs. A stablecoin (USDT, USDC) is a token that tracks a fiat currency. The chain is the public ledger that records who holds how many tokens. Settlement, for our purposes, is the point after which you would be willing to bet money the transfer will not be reversed.

When a user taps "send 50 USDC", three separate things happen on different clocks:

  1. Your database records the debit. Immediate, and only your company's claim.
  2. Your service signs a transaction and submits it to the network's mempool, where it waits for a block producer to pick it up. A low fee or a bad nonce can leave it sitting there for a long time.
  3. A block includes it, and later blocks stack on top. Each extra block makes a rollback less likely. At some chain-specific depth you stop worrying.

So for a stretch of seconds to minutes, your DB and the chain disagree on purpose. The backend's job is to know, for every transfer, which of "submitted" or "settled" is currently true, and to say only that to the customer.

Part 2: Where custody ledgers actually break

The three generic failures (crediting too early, double-processing, silent drift) are real, but the ones that cost time in practice are more specific. This is the checklist I would run any design against.

Crediting before finality. The watcher sees a deposit in a block and credits immediately. A reorg drops that block, and the customer has already spent the credit. The fix is the state machine in Part 5.

Duplicate events. Kafka and every other broker deliver at least once. A restart replays the last batch, and the deposit is credited twice unless the consumer can recognise a repeat.

Decimals. USDC on Ethereum uses 6 decimals. USDT on BNB Chain uses 18, and the same ticker elsewhere may use 6. If you store a single decimals constant per asset instead of per asset-per-network, you will eventually mis-scale a transfer by a factor of a trillion. Store base units as integers and keep decimals in network config.

Nonce management. On account-model chains, every outgoing transaction from a hot wallet carries a sequential nonce. If transaction 41 is stuck on a low fee, 42 and 43 queue behind it. You need a single owner for nonce assignment, a policy for replacing a stuck transaction with a higher-fee one at the same nonce, and a way to tell the ledger that the original hash is dead and the replacement is the real one.

Gas funding. Sending an ERC-20 token costs the chain's native coin, not the token. A hot wallet full of USDC and out of ETH cannot move anything. Native-coin balance of every signer needs its own alarm.

Wrong-chain and wrong-token deposits. Users send USDT to a USDC address, or a Tron-network token to an Ethereum-format address. Some of these are recoverable by hand. The ledger must not auto-credit anything it did not expect, and unknown arrivals need a quarantine account.

Issuer freezes. Tether and Circle can blacklist addresses. A frozen omnibus address means your on-chain balance can stop moving while the ledger still shows funds. Reconciliation should flag a balance that stays unchanged while pending withdrawals pile up.

Sweeping and rebalancing. Many custodial designs give each customer a deposit address and sweep funds to an omnibus hot wallet, with a rebalance to cold storage past a threshold. Every sweep is itself a chain transaction with fees, and it moves value between your own addresses. Those internal moves must be ledger postings too, or the totals drift by exactly the sweep fees.

Travel-rule and sanctions screening. In many jurisdictions a withdrawal to an external address needs screening before broadcast. That is one more state before APPROVED, and it can reject a transfer after the customer has already seen the button turn green.

UTXO chains differ from account chains here: there are no nonces, but you manage coin selection and change outputs, and one deposit may arrive as several inputs. The state machine below still applies; only the watcher and the signer change.

Part 3: The shape of the system

The company side is fast and fully yours. The chain side is slow and outside anyone's control. The interesting engineering sits in between.

Components:

  • Internal double-entry ledger. The authoritative record of who is owed what.
  • Broadcast path. Turns an approved transfer into a signed chain transaction.
  • Confirmation tracker. Follows the chain and walks each transfer through explicit states.
  • Reconciliation job. Periodically proves ledger and chain agree.

Each of these has a real alternative, so the trade-offs deserve a word.

Broadcast path. I use a transactional outbox: the ledger posting and the "please broadcast" row commit in one DB transaction, and a poller publishes them. Change-data-capture with Debezium reads the same table from the WAL instead, which gives lower latency and no polling load, but adds Kafka Connect as a component to operate and monitor. For a wallet doing modest volume, polling every second or two is simpler and easier to reason about during an incident. For high volume, CDC pays for itself. Delivery mechanics are in my transactional outbox post.

Watcher. Polling eth_getLogs per block is easy and restartable from a stored height. Subscribing over WebSocket is quicker but drops events on disconnect, so you still need the polling backfill. I would build the poller first and treat subscriptions as an optimisation.

Failure analysis. If the broadcaster dies after signing but before recording the hash, you can resubmit the same signed bytes (same nonce, same hash) safely. If the watcher dies, it resumes from its last stored height and re-emits observations, which the idempotent consumer absorbs. If the reconciler dies, nothing breaks, but you lose detection, so its own freshness needs an alert.

Part 4: The internal ledger

A double-entry ledger writes every movement as two or more lines that sum to zero. Value is never created or destroyed inside it, only moved. That gives you a cheap invariant: if the global sum is not zero, something is wrong, and a query tells you before a customer does.

Accounts for a custodial stablecoin wallet:

  • CUSTOMER:{id}:USDC for each customer's spendable balance.
  • CUSTOMER:{id}:USDC:HELD for amounts reserved while a withdrawal is in flight.
  • OMNIBUS:USDC which mirrors the pooled on-chain address the company controls.
  • FEES:USDC and NETWORK_FEE:USDC for revenue and costs.
  • IN_FLIGHT:USDC for value that has left the customer but not yet been proven final on chain.
  • QUARANTINE:USDC for arrivals nobody expected (wrong token, unknown sender).

IN_FLIGHT earns its place. Without it, a withdrawal jumps from "customer has 50" to "customer has 0" and you can no longer express that the transfer is unfinished. With it, each lifecycle step is a posting that mirrors a real-world fact.

Amounts are integer base units, never floating point.

@Service
public class LedgerService {

    private final JournalRepository journals;

    public LedgerService(JournalRepository journals) {
        this.journals = journals;
    }

    /** Move funds from the customer into IN_FLIGHT when a withdrawal is approved. */
    @Transactional
    public Journal reserveWithdrawal(UUID transferId, String customerAcct,
                                     long amountMicros, long feeMicros) {

        // Idempotency: the same transferId can only ever post once.
        return journals.findByBusinessKey("WD-RESERVE-" + transferId)
            .orElseGet(() -> {
                long available = journals.balanceOf(customerAcct);
                if (available < amountMicros + feeMicros) {
                    throw new InsufficientFundsException(customerAcct);
                }
                Journal j = Journal.open("WD-RESERVE-" + transferId)
                    .debit(customerAcct, amountMicros + feeMicros)
                    .credit("IN_FLIGHT:USDC", amountMicros)
                    .credit("FEES:USDC", feeMicros)
                    .build();           // throws if debits != credits
                return journals.save(j);
            });
    }
}

Two details. The business_key column carries a unique constraint, so if two threads race, the database rejects the second insert; idempotency lives in the data. And build() refuses to create an unbalanced journal, so a whole class of bugs becomes a test failure rather than silent drift. Adding that constraint to a table that already holds live postings is its own risk; I cover the safe sequence in my zero-downtime database migrations guide.

One caveat on the balance read: in production take a row lock on the customer's account record (or use an optimistic version column) so two concurrent withdrawals cannot both pass the check. A double-spent mandate in Commercial VRP mandate payments is a regulatory issue, not merely a bug, and the same append-only habit carries into IBAN-name verification and fraud-liability decisions under PSD3, where every decision has to be reproducible later.

Part 5: Confirmation as a state machine

Most first versions model a chain transfer as a boolean confirmed. That flag is where reorg bugs are born. A transfer has a lifecycle, and each state should map to one ledger effect and one sentence you are allowed to show the customer.

State Meaning Customer sees Ledger effect
APPROVED Passed risk and balance checks "Processing" Funds moved to IN_FLIGHT
BROADCAST Signed and sent to the network "Sent, waiting for network" None
SEEN Found in a block, few confirmations "On the network" None
CONFIRMING Buried under N blocks, below final threshold "Almost done" None
FINAL Reached the chain's finality depth "Completed" IN_FLIGHT released to omnibus
REORGED Block it lived in was replaced "Delayed, re-checking" None, state rolled back
FAILED Rejected or dropped permanently "Failed, refunded" IN_FLIGHT returned to customer

Rules I do not bend:

  1. Only FINAL moves value out of IN_FLIGHT. Seeing a transaction is a hint; finality is the fact.
  2. A state may move backwards only through REORGED. Everything else is forward-only, so illegal histories cannot be represented.
  3. Finality depth is per-network configuration. Ethereum-style chains, Tron and layer-2s settle at different depths, and a single global "6 confirmations" is a bug waiting to be copied into the wrong place. Some L2s also have a gap between sequencer confirmation and L1 finality, which your config must be able to express.

Deposits mirror this, with a stricter rule: never credit spendable balance on SEEN. Show a pending line in the UI if you like, but post the spendable credit on FINAL.

A replaced transaction (the nonce-bump case from Part 2) fits as well: the original hash moves to FAILED-superseded and the replacement hash becomes the tracked one, with the ledger untouched because the reservation is keyed on the transfer, not the hash.

Part 6: Idempotent confirmation handling with Kafka

The watcher emits observations: "transaction X is in block B at height H", "block B was replaced", "tip is now H+12". I key them by transfer id so one transfer's events land on one partition in order, and the consumer advances the state machine.

The consumer has to survive duplicates, out-of-order events after a rebalance, and reorg events that contradict earlier ones. Each handler is a function of stored state plus the event, guarded by a sequence number.

@Component
public class ConfirmationConsumer {

    private final TransferRepository transfers;
    private final LedgerService ledger;
    private final ChainProperties chains;

    // ... constructor omitted

    @KafkaListener(topics = "chain.observations", groupId = "confirmation-tracker")
    @Transactional
    public void on(ChainObservation obs) {
        Transfer t = transfers.findByIdForUpdate(obs.transferId());

        // Idempotency: ignore anything not newer than what we already applied.
        if (obs.observedSeq() <= t.getLastAppliedSeq()) {
            return;
        }

        long depth = obs.chainHeight() - obs.blockHeight() + 1;
        long finality = chains.finalityDepth(t.getNetwork());

        switch (obs.kind()) {
            case INCLUDED -> t.moveTo(depth >= finality ? State.FINAL : State.CONFIRMING,
                                      obs.blockHash());
            case BLOCK_REPLACED -> {
                if (t.getState() == State.FINAL) {
                    // Finality violated: page a human, never auto-heal money.
                    throw new FinalityBreachException(t.getId(), obs);
                }
                t.moveTo(State.REORGED, null);
            }
            case DROPPED -> t.moveTo(State.FAILED, null);
        }

        if (t.getState() == State.FINAL && !t.isSettledInLedger()) {
            ledger.releaseInFlight(t.getId());   // idempotent by business key
            t.markSettledInLedger();
        }
        if (t.getState() == State.FAILED && !t.isRefunded()) {
            ledger.refundWithdrawal(t.getId());
            t.markRefunded();
        }

        t.setLastAppliedSeq(obs.observedSeq());
        transfers.save(t);
    }
}

What the code deliberately avoids: it does not trust Kafka to deliver once, because observedSeq plus the row lock make replays harmless. It does not quietly repair a FINAL transfer that gets reorged; that throws and pages someone, since a finality breach means an assumption in the model was wrong and money decisions made on a broken assumption should be human ones. And the ledger calls are idempotent by business key, so a crash between the ledger write and the state update just re-runs.

For retry topics, dead-letter handling and poison messages, the patterns in the outbox and idempotent consumer write-up apply unchanged. Share groups in Kafka are interesting for queue-style scaling, but they give up the strict per-key ordering this design depends on, so test carefully before adopting them here.

Part 7: Reconciliation

The earlier parts make drift unlikely. Reconciliation makes it visible. I treat it as a product feature with its own owner, not a nightly script nobody reads.

For a custodial wallet, the ledger's total of customer balances plus fees plus in-flight value must equal what the company's addresses hold on chain, after adjusting for known pending items. Each run does three comparisons:

  1. Total check. OMNIBUS:USDC ledger balance against the real on-chain token balance of the controlled addresses, read at a specific block height (not "latest", which keeps moving).
  2. Transfer check. Every journal tied to a FINAL transfer has a matching chain transaction, and every chain transaction touching our addresses has a matching journal. The second direction is what catches deposits we never noticed, and wrong-token arrivals.
  3. Stuck-state check. Any transfer sitting in BROADCAST, SEEN, CONFIRMING or REORGED past an agreed limit is listed for a person. Stuck BROADCAST is usually a nonce or gas problem from Part 2.

The total check query is intentionally dull:

-- Run against a ledger snapshot taken at the same moment as the chain block read
SELECT
  l.omnibus_micros                         AS ledger_omnibus,
  :chain_balance_micros                    AS chain_balance,
  l.omnibus_micros - :chain_balance_micros AS drift,
  l.in_flight_micros                       AS pending_outbound
FROM (
  SELECT
    COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN account = 'OMNIBUS:USDC'   THEN signed_amount END), 0) AS omnibus_micros,
    COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN account = 'IN_FLIGHT:USDC' THEN signed_amount END), 0) AS in_flight_micros
  FROM journal_line
  WHERE posted_at <= :snapshot_ts
) l;

Time alignment is the subtle part. The ledger runs on wall-clock time and the chain on block heights. I record the height I read and compare against postings up to that block's timestamp, with a small margin. Skip this and every transfer that lands mid-run produces a phantom discrepancy, the team learns to ignore the alert, and an ignored alert is worse than none.

On a mismatch the job never edits balances. It opens a ticket carrying the block height, both numbers, the diff and the candidate transfers. Corrections go in as new journal entries with a reason and an approver. The ledger is append-only.

The same habit shows up in my deterministic replay post: if you cannot re-derive a number from recorded history, you cannot defend it.

Part 8: Observability and operational edges

Signals I would have on a dashboard from the first deployment:

  • Count and age of transfers in each state, per network.
  • Reconciliation drift in base units, with an expected value of exactly zero.
  • Reorg events per day, per chain, plus maximum depth seen.
  • Consumer lag on the observations topic.
  • Native-coin (gas) balance of each signer.
  • Hot-wallet versus cold-storage balance ratio.

Trace IDs should follow a transfer from the API call through the ledger posting, the broadcast and each confirmation event; my distributed tracing guide for Spring Boot covers the setup. When support gets "my money has not arrived", one trace should tell the whole story.

Part 9: The Korean won angle and regulation

Reports suggest Korea's large platforms are all positioning for won-denominated stablecoins: Toss linked to a chain built on the OP Stack, Naver tied to the exchange operator Dunamu, and Kakao with its own plans after the earlier wallet struggled. This is moving quickly and I cannot verify commercial terms, so read those specifics as reported rather than confirmed.

The engineering consequence is clearer. A won token on a layer-2 has different finality behaviour from USDT on Tron or USDC on Ethereum, which is the reason finality depth lives in configuration. Regulated issuance also tends to demand reserve reporting, meaning you must show tokens outstanding against reserves held. A proper double-entry ledger gives you that nearly for free; mutable balance columns do not.

Two regulatory threads make this skill set marketable:

  • MiCA, the EU's Markets in Crypto-Assets regulation, sets expectations on safeguarding client assets, record-keeping and complaints for stablecoin issuers and service providers. A custodial wallet serving EU users needs demonstrable asset segregation and auditable records, which are ledger and reconciliation features.
  • ASEAN cross-border payments are linking national QR and instant schemes, and stablecoins compete for the same corridors. I covered the QR side in my piece on EMVCo-based ASEAN QR routing. A ledger that sits cleanly between a QR scheme and a token rail is a useful thing to be able to design.

Some compliance evidence can be generated automatically; policy-as-code for DORA and NIS2 shows how I produce audit artefacts from the deployment pipeline.

What I would do differently from a first draft

  • Make finality a per-network config object from the first commit, with a test that fails when a network is added without one.
  • Never let a human edit a balance. Allow only a new, signed, reasoned journal entry.
  • Reconcile from day one, even against fake money in staging. It is cheapest to build before anything depends on it.
  • Treat "FINAL breached" as an incident, not an exception to retry.
  • Keep the customer-facing vocabulary smaller than the internal one. Nobody needs to see CONFIRMING; "Almost done" is enough.

None of this is glamorous. Whether any wallet keeps user trust through a bad day on the network will depend more on this layer than on which token it moves. Customers tolerate slow; they do not tolerate wrong.

Work with me

If you are building or rescuing a payments backend, ledger or reconciliation pipeline, you can see the systems I have shipped in my projects and reach me through the contact section. Send a short description of your transfer flow and the failure you fear most, and I will reply with a first-pass state model for it.

Related Articles

  • Transactional Outbox and Idempotent Consumers in Spring Boot Payment Systems
  • Open Banking PSD2 API Development
  • ASEAN Cross-Border QR Payments: EMVCo Router with PayNow, DuitNow, PromptPay and QRIS in Spring Boot

FAQ

What is a stablecoin?

A token pegged to a fiat currency, most often the US dollar. USDT and USDC are the big dollar ones, and they travel over public blockchains rather than bank payment rails.

Is a stablecoin transfer instant?

Not in the sense a backend cares about. An app can show "sent" within a second, but the payment is only safe to treat as done once enough later blocks sit on top of it, and that depth differs per chain.

What is a double-entry ledger?

A ledger where each posting touches at least two accounts and the amounts net to zero. If a posting is lost or applied twice, the totals stop balancing and the bug shows up in a query instead of in a customer complaint.

Why does a wallet app need reconciliation?

Because the app's database and the chain are two independent records that can drift apart through missed events, manual fixes or fees nobody posted. A scheduled comparison surfaces the gap on your schedule, not the customer's.

title: Coordination of Heterogeneous Teams with Uncertain Task Requirements
description:
arXiv:2611.21828v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Coordinating a team of heterogeneous agents to complete tasks with unknown requirements is a challenging multi-agent planning problem. Agents differ in their ability to discover task requirements and in their ability to engage tasks, so the planner must coordinate task discovery, execution, and staging. This paper introduces a hierarchical planner that uses a graph neural network policy to assign actions to agents, then finds a path to the action's location using a shortest-path algorithm. The central part of our approach is the CAAT graph, which is a graph representation of the planning context consisting of the agents, tasks, capabilities, and actions. We demonstrate that our learned planner can jointly coordinate a heterogeneous team to simultaneously discover task requirements and complete tasks in a shorter time compared to baselines that optimize task discovery and task engagement independently. Furthermore, we show that our policy can zero-shot plan on out-of-distribution settings by training only on an outdoor map then transferring without finetuning to an indoor map with more agents, tasks, and capabilities than seen during training.

title: Estados de email accesibles en React
description:
Un formulario de registro puede parecer terminado cuando el usuario pulsa “Crear cuenta”. En realidad, ahí empieza una parte delicada: enviar el email, esperar la respuesta, mostrar el resultado y permitir que la persona continúe sin adivinar qué ocurrió.

En proyectos React he encontrado que este flujo se trata aveces como un detalle visual. Un spinner aparece, el botón se desactiva y, si todo va bien, llega un mensaje verde. Ese enfoque falla cuando el correo tarda, cuando el usuario navega con teclado o cuando un lector de pantalla no recibe el cambio. La interfaz necesita un modelo de estados explícito, no solo una animación.

El problema: verificar no es solo mostrar un spinner

Un estado de email tiene al menos cinco momentos útiles:

  1. Inicial: todavía no se ha enviado nada.
  2. Enviando: la petición está en curso y no debe duplicarse.
  3. Esperando: el servidor aceptó la solicitud, pero el mensaje aún no ha sido confirmado.
  4. Verificado: el enlace fue aceptado y el flujo puede continuar.
  5. Error: la persona necesita una explicación y una acción posible.

Separar “enviando” de “esperando” mejora la experiencia. El primer estado responde a la petición HTTP; el segundo describe una espera real del usuario. Mezclarlos en un único loading hace más dificil decidir qué texto anunciar, cuándo habilitar un reenvío y qué parte del formulario debe conservar el foco.

Para probar el flujo sin tocar buzones personales, un generador de correo temporal puede servir como fixture de desarrollo o QA. La regla importante es aislar cada prueba y no usar esos datos para cuentas reales.

Un pequeño modelo de estados para React

Un useState con varios booleanos suele producir combinaciones imposibles: isSending y isVerified activos a la vez, o un error visible después de un reenvío exitoso. Prefiero un único estado discriminado:

type EmailState =
  | { kind: "idle" }
  | { kind: "sending" }
  | { kind: "waiting"; address: string }
  | { kind: "verified" }
  | { kind: "error"; message: string };

const [emailState, setEmailState] = useState<EmailState>({ kind: "idle" });

El render puede decidir qué mostrar a partir de kind, sin depender de una colección de flags que se contradicen. También facilita las pruebas: cada acción tiene una transición visible y es más facil comprobar que un reintento no aparece antes de tiempo.

Para un reenvío, conservaría un contador local o una marca de tiempo de la última petición. El objetivo no es castigar al usuario, sino evitar que varios clics creen mensajes difíciles de distinguir. Si el servidor responde con un error temporal, el mensaje debe explicar qué puede hacer la persona ahora, por que el siguiente intento está disponible y si el email anterior sigue siendo válido.

Accesibilidad: foco, mensajes y semántica

El texto de estado debe existir en el DOM, no solo cambiar el color del botón. Un contenedor role="status" con aria-live="polite" puede anunciar que el mensaje fue enviado sin interrumpir una tarea actual. Para un fallo que requiere atención inmediata, role="alert" es más apropiado, pero no conviene usarlo para cada cambio pequeño.

Cuando aparece un error debajo del campo, relaciónalo con el input mediante aria-describedby. Si la validación impide avanzar, el foco debe ir al primer control con un problema, no a un banner lejano. La validación y el foco visual debe mantenerse consistente tanto con teclado como con ratón.

El estado de espera necesita una salida clara. Un enlace “Cambiar dirección” o “Reenviar email” debe tener un nombre comprensible fuera de contexto. “Haz clic aquí” no explica nada en una lista de enlaces de un lector de pantalla.

También revisaría el contraste, el indicador de foco y el movimiento. prefers-reduced-motion permite eliminar una animación innecesaria, mientras que un icono no debe ser la única señal de éxito. Un pequeño checklist de calidad antes del email ayuda a revisar estos detalles junto con el resto del onboarding.

CSS y rendimiento sin perder claridad

Los estados visuales no necesitan una biblioteca grande. Una clase por estado, una transición corta y una estructura estable suelen bastar:

.email-status {
  min-height: 1.5rem;
}

.email-status[data-state="error"] {
  color: var(--color-error);
}

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .email-status,
  .email-status * {
    transition: none;
    animation: none;
  }
}

Mantener una altura mínima evita que el formulario salte cuando entra el mensaje. Ese cambio pequeño reduce ruido visual y hace que el foco no parezca moverse. Para medir el resultado, observaría el tiempo hasta el primer mensaje útil, los reintentos duplicados y los errores de validación, no solo el tiempo de carga inicial.

En la práctica, el frontend también debe tolerar respuestas lentas. Una señal como “Estamos esperando el email” es mejor que un spinner infinito. Si el backend finalmente deja de reintentar, la interfaz debe reflejar la misma decisión; este principio de decidir cuándo dejar de reintentar un email evita prometer una recuperación que ya no existe.

Checklist para revisar el flujo

  • ¿Cada transición tiene un texto visible y entendible?
  • ¿El botón evita peticiones duplicadas mientras se envía?
  • ¿El lector de pantalla recibe los cambios mediante una región viva?
  • ¿El foco llega al campo correcto cuando hay un error?
  • ¿El color no es la única diferencia entre éxito, espera y fallo?
  • ¿Existe una acción para corregir la dirección o reenviar el email?
  • ¿La prueba usa un buzón aislado, como tamp mail com, y limpia sus datos después?
  • ¿Los estados funcionan sin animación y con una conexión lenta?

Diseñar esta frontera con cuidado produce una interfaz más tranquila y más fácil de probar. React aporta la estructura, CSS comunica el estado y las reglas de accesibilidad convierten una espera incierta en una secuencia que el usuario puede entender.

title: AI couldn't see the bug. Working examples from Clay UI changed that
description:
Originally published on LinkedIn.

I wanted readers to turn the pages of The Art of AI like a real book. On my laptop the animation looked right. On my phone, parts of the page flashed black.

Several attempts to fix it with Claude Opus 5.5 failed. Working examples found through Clay UI pointed to a better approach, which we proved in an Android emulator and checked on my phone. Opus built the first working prototype, and Fable 5.2 settled it and brought it to the version that is live today.

This article is about how we got from plausible fixes to a page turn that works, and what made the difference.

A book that should turn like paper

The Art of AI is an illustrated book of short reflections on artificial intelligence, published as a website. I prepared the code for the page turn myself, so that a page lifts at the corner, curls softly and settles on the next one. When it broke on my phone, I asked Claude Opus 5.5 to help me fix it.

What I saw on the phone

During a turn, parts of the page went black. Often the whole lower half vanished behind a straight edge under the illustration, and sometimes stripes ran across the paper. A few frames later the page was fine again, so it looked like a flicker. On a computer none of this happened.

This is a screenshot I took on my phone in the middle of a turn. The text is cut off and the left half of the page is simply missing.

Why the AI kept failing

The AI failed several times before it got anywhere. Its first report said: "I couldn't find a single flash frame." It had checked in a desktop browser set to a phone's screen size. That copies the size of a phone, but not its small graphics memory, and that is where the fault lived. Reading the code did not reveal the cause.

My own assumption didn't help. I said it had not flickered before, but the older version broke the same way in an Android emulator. There was no recent change to blame.

The older version in the Android emulator. Stripes and broken paper run across both pages, with the same library and the same pages as before.

The emulator gave shaky answers too: the same unchanged build broke in 17%, 27% and 53% of frames on three runs. So the AI guessed and tested one suspect after another, from shadows and the paper texture to the illustrations and browser hints. None of them fixed it.

Frames from one emulator recording of the live site. Black lower halves, half-drawn pages and stripes appear in different frames of the same turns.

The way out: working examples from Clay UI

The AI failed again and again; the way out came from the patterns in Clay UI, which is open source on GitHub. Clay UI searches catalogs of ready-made interface components and downloads their source code. For a page-flip book it found two working examples: page-flip from Kokonut UI and book-flip from Avara.

What Clay UI does, in under 40 seconds of clay: proven components from real libraries, shaped to your style. Watch the film.

They paid off first on the buttons. Ours switched off during every turn and faded to 42% opacity. Kokonut keeps its buttons on and ignores extra clicks in code, and we did the same.

The controls frame by frame during page turns. In the left column, before the fix, Previous and Next fade out on every turn.

On the pages, the examples changed the question. It stopped being "what is wrong with my page" and became "what do working page turns do differently". In plain words: my version made the phone redraw the whole page again and again during a turn. The working examples draw the page once and then only move that finished image.

For developers: Avara turns a page with a 3D rotation, which the graphics chip can apply to an already painted layer. My library cut the page to a new shape in every frame, so the browser had to repaint it 60 times a second. With a paper texture and a large illustration on every page, the phone ran out of graphics memory, and each missing tile showed as black.

A quick copy of Avara's approach, with rigid pages, removed the black halves, but the page turned like a board. I wanted the soft curl. The patterns gave us the direction; proving it and building it were still ahead.

The key: patterns plus emulation and tests

The patterns inspired a much stricter process. Opus 5.5 limited Chrome's graphics memory in the emulator to 96 MB, a deliberately low setting that imitates a phone under pressure. From then on the bug appeared every time, just as on my phone. Then it ran a control: the same library with plain pages, under the same limit, turned 65 frames without a broken one.

The control run: the same library with plain pages, recorded frame by frame. Every turn draws cleanly.

So in this test the library alone held up. The difference was my heavy pages, painted again in every frame. A memory reading showed that my page held 118 MB of graphics memory even at rest.

The drawing below shows the difference in what the phone has to do in every frame of a turn.

The tests also showed why guessing never worked. Removing one ingredient made the page lighter, but it was still painted again in every frame.

Fable 5.2 settles it

Opus 5.5, guided by the Clay UI patterns, found the direction and built a first prototype: the turn drawn from finished pictures of the pages. In the emulator, under the same low memory limit, we checked 949 animation frames in a row and found no broken one. Fable 5.2 settled the matter and brought it to the version that is live today.

Fable measured the graphics memory and wrote its own page-curl engine on a canvas, a drawing surface inside the browser. A script photographs each of the 86 pages in a fixed phone layout. During a turn the canvas finds the fold line, keeps the front of the page flat and mirrors the back of the paper over the fold, so nothing on the page is painted again. When I opened it on my phone, I wrote back: "It looks very good, I can't see anything breaking."

The comparison below comes from the emulator with the 96 MB limit. The top two rows are the old version and the bottom two the canvas version, turning the same pages.

The last details

The first version showed a picture of the page during a turn and switched back to live text when the turn ended. Every small difference between the two showed as a jump. Fable 5.2 fixed them one by one:

  • The chapter 9 title sat on three lines during a turn and on two after it. The line breaks are now recorded with the pictures and forced on the live page.
  • After each turn the text got a little thinner and the illustration twitched. The pictures had been taken on a Mac, which draws text bolder than a phone. They are now taken without that, and the picture stays on screen after the turn too, so there is no switch to see.
  • A zoomed illustration jumped at the end of closing. It now lands on the picture's exact spot, with matching corners and shadow.
  • A page now has to finish turning before the next turn can start.

What made the difference

On its own, AI kept failing on this. Working patterns from Clay UI showed what good page turns do differently, and a detailed process of emulation and tests turned that idea into proof. Opus 5.5 found the direction with them, and Fable 5.2 finished the job. The Clay UI source is on GitHub.

The last part was mine. Our automated checks missed a title that changes lines and text that gets a little thinner. I caught them by reading my own book on my own phone. You can turn its pages at theartofai.behavio.one.

About the author: Marcin Tabędzki, author of The Art of AI, builds Clay UI and AI tools at Behavio One. Find me on LinkedIn: linkedin.com/in/marcin-tabedzki

title: Amazon EVS launches support for r7i.metal instances, external principal storage, and an Agent Skill
description:
Today, we are announcing that Amazon Elastic VMware Service (Amazon EVS) now supports the r7i.metal-24xl and r7i.metal-48xl Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2) bare metal instance types for VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) 9.x deployments. EC2 r7i instances are memory optimized, with custom 4th Generation Intel Xeon Scalable (Sapphire Rapids) processors, and designed to be used with external storage. With these instances possessing no local NVMe disks, Amazon EVS now supports VCF external principal storage with solutions such as Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP. With this launch, you can use the Amazon EVS Deployment Orchestrator (EDO) within the Solutions for EVS GitHub repository to fully automate the end-to-end deployment and configuration of your VCF 9.x environment on EVS.

With this release, you now have more options for running VMware-based Virtual Machines (VM) in your Amazon VPC - while keeping the same tools, skills, and operational processes, and full control of your architecture, configuration, and lifecycle of your environment. 

We are also launching a new Amazon EVS Agent Skill, which gives your AI Agents context to help you plan, deploy, and operate your Amazon EVS environments - from answering questions and recommending designs to generating blueprints and driving deployments with EDO. To get started, point the AI agent of your choice to the EVS Agent Skill file in the latest release of the EVS GitHub repository.  

This release is available in all regions where Amazon EVS is offered. To learn more about Amazon EVS, visit the product detail page and the user guide.

title: Amazon DynamoDB caching is now available with Amazon ElastiCache Serverless for Valkey
description:
Today, AWS announces the general availability of DynamoDB caching with Amazon ElastiCache Serverless for Valkey, a serverless alternative to Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) that delivers sub-millisecond read latency for frequently accessed DynamoDB data. Previously, if you needed faster reads than the single-digit millisecond latency of DynamoDB, you had to provision and scale DAX nodes or run your own cache and keep it in sync with DynamoDB. Now you can access DynamoDB table data from a write-through cache that updates as data changes and scales automatically to meet changing workload demands, with no clusters or nodes to manage.

DynamoDB caching requires no application logic changes and minimal configuration. You choose which DynamoDB tables and APIs to cache and how long to retain cached data. Your application's IAM credentials are used to access DynamoDB, so existing access control policies are automatically applied.

DynamoDB caching is available in all commercial and AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. DynamoDB caching is offered at no additional cost, so you pay only for the ElastiCache Serverless and DynamoDB resources your applications use. To get started, see the ElastiCache Developer Guide.

title: Domain-Tuned Diffusion Super-Resolution for 4K Facial Asset Maps
description:
arXiv:2611.21890v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Physically based facial assets require 4K albedo and displacement maps for cinematic close-ups, yet generative pipelines commonly produce them at only 1K. Naively applying photographic super-resolution is a poor fit: facial UV maps have domain-specific statistics, and displacement is a scalar height field whose errors directly distort geometry. We present a domain-tuned diffusion upscaler for 4x (1024 to 4096) facial asset super-resolution. Starting from a bilinearly upsampled map, we adapt a frozen SDXL backbone per modality with lightweight LoRA modules, while a Tile ControlNet preserves input structure as the diffusion prior restores pore- and wrinkle-scale detail. On held-out maps, our method produces sharper, more faithful detail than bilinear and off-the-shelf GAN and diffusion super-resolvers, reducing albedo LPIPS from 0.21 to 0.08 while avoiding misplaced or excessive displacement relief. These results show that lightweight domain adaptation can produce render-ready 4K facial asset maps without a custom super-resolution architecture.

title: The Fragility of Reasoning-Importance Attribution for Pruning Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.22234v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Attribution-guided pruning scores components by their causal contribution and protects the important ones, and it is increasingly applied to compress reasoning language models without destroying their chain of thought. Its reliability rests on an unexamined assumption: that reasoning importance can be faithfully measured. Across four small reasoning models, we show this measurement is fragile in three ways, each of which changes pruning decisions. First, scoring final-answer tokens, the natural choice, saturates in every chain-of-thought model we test (answer-token negative log-likelihood, NLL, of $10^{-4}$--$10^{-3}$) because the model states its answer inside its own reasoning; guiding head pruning with this target costs 27.6 and 32.2 accuracy points relative to scoring reasoning tokens on the two models we power with five seeds, while perplexity barely moves and even reverses sign at 7B. Second, causal importance is not localizable to single units: single-neuron effects sit at the measurement floor, their cross-split ranking is noise, and they cancel: a group's ablation effect disagrees in sign with the summed effects of its members in 90\% of groups. Reproducible importance emerges only at groups of $\sim 100$ neurons. Third, contrastively isolated ``reasoning-specific'' importance is not separable from generic importance, and protecting it is worse than protecting raw importance. We additionally pre-registered the hypothesis that distillation-induced concentration of importance predicts the pruning cost; it is not supported, and since our grid confounds concentration with scale, we report it as unresolved rather than reversed. The result is a short set of measurement rules: score reasoning tokens, attribute at coarse granularity, and evaluate with accuracy rather than perplexity.

title: Typing Untyped Vue 3 Libraries and Named defineModel in TypeScript: The ProjectFilter Migration
description:
When converting legacy Vue applications to TypeScript, third-party component libraries often become a stumbling block. Some popular ecosystem packages still lack first-party TypeScript definitions or ship incomplete @types packages, resulting in TS7016: Could not find a declaration file for module errors during build time.

In my recent contribution to GitLab's Contributors Platform (MR !3199), I converted the ProjectFilter component to strict TypeScript.

Here is how we handled untyped third-party dependencies with ambient declarations, implemented Vue 3.4's named defineModel macro, and tested scoped slot rendering.

1. Handling Untyped Libraries with Ambient Declarations (.d.ts)

The ProjectFilter component integrates the popular vue-select dropdown package to allow contributors to filter community issues across dozens of GitLab projects.

Because vue-select does not ship built-in type definitions, importing it in a TypeScript SFC produces compiler errors:

import VueSelect from 'vue-select'; // ❌ TS7016: Could not find declaration file

Instead of bypassing type checking with // @ts-ignore, the idiomatic TypeScript solution is creating an ambient module declaration in the project's source root (app/javascript/vue-select.d.ts):

declare module 'vue-select' {
  import type { DefineComponent } from 'vue';

  const component: DefineComponent<Record<string, unknown>>;
  export default component;
}

Why this approach works:

  • Zero Suppression Comments: The compiler recognizes vue-select as a valid Vue component without polluting component files with suppressions.
  • Global Availability: vue-tsc picks up all *.d.ts files included in tsconfig.json, enabling any other component across the codebase to import vue-select safely.

2. Implementing Named Two-Way Binding: defineModel('selectedProjects')

In Vue 3.4+, components can bind multiple models or use custom model names using the first argument of defineModel().

In ProjectFilter.vue:

<!-- After (TypeScript) -->
<script setup lang="ts">
import { BFormGroup } from 'bootstrap-vue-next';
import VueSelect from 'vue-select';
import 'vue-select/dist/vue-select.css';

defineProps<{
  availableProjects: string[];
}>();

// Strongly typed named model with required flag
const selectedProjects = defineModel<string[]>('selectedProjects', { 
  required: true 
});
</script>

<template>
  <BFormGroup label="Project">
    <VueSelect
      v-model="selectedProjects"
      multiple
      :options="availableProjects"
    >
      <template #no-options="{ search, searching }">
        <template v-if="searching">
          No projects matching "{{ search }}"
        </template>
        <template v-else>
          No projects available
        </template>
      </template>
    </VueSelect>
  </BFormGroup>
</template>

Improvements:

  • defineModel<string[]>('selectedProjects', { required: true }) automatically types both props.selectedProjects and emits update:selectedProjects with a payload of string[].
  • Prop validation for availableProjects is enforced at compile time without verbose runtime type objects.

3. Testing Scoped Slots in Vue Test Utils

A unique testing pattern in ProjectFilter.spec.ts is verifying custom template slots like #no-options="{ search, searching }".

In TypeScript, accessing $slots on a child component's vm requires proper typing and optional chaining:

import type { VueWrapper } from '@vue/test-utils';
import { shallowMount } from '@vue/test-utils';
import VueSelect from 'vue-select';
import ProjectFilter from './ProjectFilter.vue';

describe('ProjectFilter', () => {
  let wrapper: VueWrapper;
  const findSelect = () => wrapper.findComponent(VueSelect);

  // Type-safe slot helper rendering the child's scoped slot
  const findNoOptions = (slotProps: Record<string, unknown>) =>
    shallowMount({
      render: () => findSelect().vm.$slots['no-options']?.(slotProps),
    });

  it('emits updated projects when selection changes', async () => {
    createWrapper();

    await findSelect().vm.$emit('update:modelValue', ['gitlab']);

    // Emits are typed as Array of argument arrays
    expect(wrapper.emitted('update:selectedProjects')).toEqual([[['gitlab']]]);
  });

  it('renders matching text when search has no results', () => {
    createWrapper();

    const noOptionsWrapper = findNoOptions({ search: 'non-existent', searching: true });
    expect(noOptionsWrapper.text()).toContain('No projects matching "non-existent"');
  });
});

Using optional chaining findSelect().vm.$slots['no-options']?.(slotProps) prevents runtime TypeError when a component's slot is undefined during mounting.

Key Takeaways

  1. Ambient Declarations for Untyped Packages: Create clean .d.ts declaration files instead of relying on @ts-ignore when working with untyped npm packages.
  2. Named defineModel<T>('name'): Leverages Vue 3.4's macro to type non-default model bindings cleanly and succinctly.
  3. Safe Scoped Slot Testing: Use typed inline render helpers with optional chaining to mount and assert custom slot templates in Vue Test Utils.

title: FastAPI vs Laravel for AI Backends: When to Use Which
description:
When full-stack software developers and engineering teams start building AI-powered features into commercial products, they hit an immediate architectural crossroads: Should we build AI features directly inside our existing Laravel application, or should we introduce a separate Python FastAPI microservice?

Both frameworks are exceptionally capable, battle-tested in production, and widely adopted across the software industry. However, choosing the wrong architecture for your specific business stage can introduce months of unnecessary infrastructure complexity — or force a painful codebase migration down the road. This comprehensive guide provides technical founders, software architects, and backend engineers with a concrete decision framework based on real-world production setups.

1. Understanding the Core Framework Philosophies

Laravel and FastAPI serve fundamentally different roles in the modern web development ecosystem:

Laravel (PHP): A full-stack web application framework designed around developer productivity, convention over configuration, and a massive batteries-included ecosystem. It provides first-party solutions for database migrations, Eloquent ORM, background queues via Laravel Horizon, session authentication, API token management via Sanctum, task scheduling, live reactive views via Livewire, and administrative dashboards. It excels at managing complex domain business logic, relational databases, user authorization roles, billing integrations, and rich user web interfaces.

FastAPI (Python): A lightweight, ultra-high-performance asynchronous micro-framework built around Python 3.8+ type hints, automatic Pydantic data validation, and OpenAPI documentation generation. It is designed specifically for asynchronous computational workloads, high-throughput microservices, data processing pipelines, and RESTful API endpoints.

The primary reason this framework debate arises is that 95% of the machine learning and artificial intelligence ecosystem — PyTorch, Hugging Face transformers, LangChain, LangGraph, sentence-transformers, scikit-learn, OpenCV, SciPy — is written natively in Python. The architectural question is not which framework is inherently "better," but rather how much native Python machine learning execution your product genuinely requires in order to deliver its core value proposition.

2. Detailed Architectural Comparison

Here is how Laravel and FastAPI compare across core application engineering requirements in an AI-first product:

Evaluation DimensionLaravel Direct IntegrationFastAPI Dedicated Service Primary AI Use CaseHosted LLM API Orchestration (OpenAI, Claude, Gemini)Local ML Models, Custom Embeddings, LangGraph Agents Database & Auth IntegrationNative Eloquent ORM, Session/Sanctum Auth, MigrationsRequires SQLAlchemy setup & JWT handling ML Library AccessRestricted to REST API wrappersNative access to PyTorch, Hugging Face, SciPy Concurrency ModelPHP-FPM worker pool / Octane (Swoole)Native asyncio event loop (High concurrency) Operational OverheadSingle codebase, simple deploymentRequires separate Docker container & CI/CD pipeline ## 3. When to Use Laravel Directly (The Monolithic Advantage)

If your AI feature relies primarily on hosted cloud LLM APIs (such as OpenAI's GPT-4o, Anthropic Claude 3.5, or Google Gemini Pro), you do not need Python in your stack at all. Laravel can orchestrate these API calls with extreme efficiency and unmatched developer speed.

Building inside Laravel allows software developers to leverage existing application infrastructure directly. You do not need to create secondary database connections, replicate user authentication schemas, or configure cross-service authentication headers. Everything executes within your established transactional boundaries.

Choose Laravel Direct Integration when:

  1. You are orchestrating cloud APIs only: Calling OpenAI's REST API or sending prompt payloads via HTTP clients is fundamentally a network I/O task. PHP handles REST HTTP requests just as easily and fast as Python.
  2. Your logic is prompt-driven: If the intelligence lives inside the cloud model and your backend's job is formatting prompt templates, storing user inputs, and saving JSON responses to MySQL/PostgreSQL, Eloquent handles this seamlessly without needing an extra service layer.
  3. You need deep transactional database logic: If an AI action must read user permissions, update database records inside a SQL transaction, and dispatch queued background notifications (via Laravel Horizon), keeping this logic inside a single Laravel codebase avoids cross-service network latency and distributed data inconsistencies.
  4. Your team is Laravel-first: Introducing Python microservices into a PHP-focused engineering team introduces separate Dockerfiles, dependency management tooling (Poetry/uv), separate monitoring pipelines, and mental context-switching overhead. 
// Example: Safe AI processing inside a Laravel Job
class ProcessAiDraftJob implements ShouldQueue
{
    use Dispatchable, InteractsWithQueue, Queueable, SerializesModels;

    public function __construct(public Ticket $ticket) {}

    public function handle(OpenAiService $ai): void
    {
        // 1. Fetch data via Eloquent
        $context = $this->ticket->getFormattedHistory();

        // 2. Execute OpenAI REST API call
        $draft = $ai->generateResponseDraft($context);

        // 3. Save directly within database transaction
        $this->ticket->update(['ai_draft_reply' => $draft]);
    }
}

4. When to Use FastAPI (The Python ML Path)

You should introduce a dedicated Python FastAPI service when your product requires features that depend directly on the native Python machine learning ecosystem.

FastAPI provides an asynchronous non-blocking event loop that excels at streaming responses to frontend user interfaces. Furthermore, FastAPI integrates natively with Pydantic, enabling strict input data validation and automatic OpenAPI client generation.

Choose FastAPI when:

  1. You are running open-source or local models: If you run local embedding models (e.g. sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2), Hugging Face transformers, PyTorch inference, or local OCR models (Tesseract, PaddleOCR), you require Python.
  2. You need LangChain or LangGraph agent state machines: Building multi-agent workflows with state checkpoints, conditional branching loops, and tool execution is best achieved using Python agent frameworks.
  3. You are building custom vector retrieval pipelines: If document chunking, semantic re-ranking, and vector mathematical transformations happen in-memory before vector database upsert, Python provides superior tooling and native matrix execution speed.
  4. You require high-throughput streaming concurrency: FastAPI's native asyncio event loop handles thousands of concurrent Server-Sent Events (SSE) streaming connections efficiently for real-time AI chat interfaces. 
# Example: FastAPI microservice for local document embeddings
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

app = FastAPI()
model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")

class EmbeddingRequest(BaseModel):
    texts: list[str]

@app.post("/api/v1/embed")
async def generate_embeddings(payload: EmbeddingRequest):
    # Generates 384-dimensional vector embeddings locally
    vectors = model.encode(payload.texts).tolist()
    return {"vectors": vectors}

5. The Pragmatic Hybrid Architecture

For growing mid-size SaaS products, the most popular production architecture is Hybrid: Use Laravel as your primary web monolith (handling user authentication, billing, database persistence, and UI rendering), and extract a focused FastAPI microservice specifically for heavy AI/ML pipelines.

Communication between Laravel and FastAPI happens asynchronously via queue jobs and HTTP/REST webhooks, keeping your web application responsive while letting Python execute complex AI operations.

For example, when a user uploads a PDF document in Laravel: Laravel stores the file in AWS S3 and dispatches a background job. The job sends an HTTP request to FastAPI containing the document URL. FastAPI downloads the file, chunks the text, computes PyTorch embeddings, upserts vectors into pgvector, and sends an HTTP webhook back to Laravel notifying that processing is complete. This architecture preserves Laravel's rapid web development speed while unlocking Python's advanced AI capabilities.

6. Infrastructure & Deployment Trade-offs in Production

Deploying a dual-framework hybrid architecture introduces specific operational trade-offs that software architects must evaluate carefully. Operating a monolithic Laravel application on traditional cloud infrastructure (such as AWS Elastic Beanstalk or Laravel Forge) requires managing web server worker pools, database connection pools, and Redis queue workers. Introducing a secondary Python FastAPI microservice expands your DevOps scope to include separate Docker container registries, Kubernetes deployment manifests or ECS task definitions, cross-service secret management, and distributed tracing instrumentation.

Furthermore, cross-service networking latency must be minimized using low-latency internal cloud networks or asynchronous queue messaging systems. Passing large payloads (such as high-resolution images or large document buffers) across network boundaries introduces bandwidth overhead. Modern hybrid setups optimize performance by storing large media artifacts in shared S3 bucket object stores, passing lightweight object URLs between Laravel and FastAPI microservices rather than transferring raw binary streams across HTTP endpoints.

7. Performance & Scale Considerations

When comparing raw HTTP throughput, FastAPI running on Uvicorn with asyncio can process high numbers of concurrent idle connections (such as streaming LLM responses). On the other hand, Laravel running on Laravel Octane (powered by Swoole or RoadRunner) keeps the application in memory, bringing PHP performance remarkably close to compiled languages. Therefore, raw performance alone is rarely a reason to avoid Laravel unless you specifically require Python-native CUDA computational bindings.

8. Managing Cross-Service Authentication & Security Tokens

When implementing a hybrid architecture where a PHP Laravel web monolith delegates machine learning tasks to a Python FastAPI microservice, securing cross-service network communication is paramount. Unprotected microservice HTTP endpoints expose private data pipelines to unauthorized internal network traffic or external injection attacks.

The standard enterprise pattern uses Asymmetric JWT (JSON Web Tokens) or Shared HMAC Signature Verification. When Laravel dispatches an HTTP request to FastAPI, it attaches a cryptographically signed HMAC header generated using a shared secret key and a timestamp payload. The FastAPI middleware inspects the request signature, validates the timestamp within a 60-second execution window to prevent replay attacks, and verifies that the requesting service is authenticated.

9. Handling Distributed Queue Jobs and Webhook Callbacks

Because artificial intelligence processing can take anywhere from 3 seconds to 2 minutes, synchronously blocking HTTP web worker threads during microservice calls degrades web application throughput. In production setups, decouple service execution using asynchronous queues.

Conclusion

Do not over-engineer early. If your product uses hosted cloud LLM APIs, start monolithic inside Laravel. When your feature set demands local models, LangGraph agents, or PyTorch inference, extract a modular FastAPI service.

title: Retrieval Architecture for Travel Itinerary Planners: Access Rules (and Freshness)
description:
Short answer: use staged retrieval with explicit collections, bounded queries, and source context that survives all the way into the answer. For a travel itinerary planner, access rules and freshness belong in the retrieval contract, not in a last-minute prompt filter.

Here is the decision rule I use: keep fast-changing public facts (opening hours, advisories, transit changes) in a web-search stage, keep approved itinerary records in a filtered vector stage, and reject a result when its scope or freshness cannot be explained. This makes retries and recovery boring, which is exactly what production retrieval should be.

Option Good fit Operational trade-off
Elasticsearch Teams already operating text search, filters, and observability More tuning and cluster ownership for semantic retrieval
Pinecone A managed vector-first workflow with a small platform surface Search and policy metadata still need application glue
Weaviate A vector database with schema and hybrid-search features More schema decisions before the first useful query
Infrai A mixed web-plus-vector pipeline where plain HTTP and one credential matter You still own collection policy, labels, and evaluation

I would try Infrai for the retrieval calls when the team wants one REST API, no SDK installation, and the same bearer credential across backend capabilities. That removes a layer of client-version and key-management glue; it does not decide which traveler may see a document. Keep that boundary explicit.

How should retrieval architecture enforce access rules for a travel itinerary planner?

Start with a retrieval unit. “Paris tips” is not a unit. A unit is a dated, source-linked fact such as museum:opening-hours:2026-06-14, with tenant_id, trip_id, locale, valid_from, valid_until, and source_url metadata. The answer generator receives the unit and its provenance together.

Access checks happen before ranking. A query for one user's itinerary should include the tenant and trip scope in the filter, and public web results should be tagged as public rather than mixed into a private collection. Never fetch a broad top-k set and hope the prompt hides a private record. That is an authorization bug wearing a relevance costume.

Bound the query as well. Set a small candidate count per stage, cap the total fetched text, and carry a request ID through ingestion, query, and citation. A bounded request is easier to retry after a 429 and easier to inspect when a planner produces a stale suggestion.

Small is good.

The two-stage shape maps cleanly to the available Infrai surfaces: /v1/web/search for current web-backed context and /v1/vector/query for embeddings plus metadata filters. The API is ordinary HTTPS, so a TypeScript CLI can call it without adopting a vendor SDK. I am not claiming that a route supplies your policy; the policy remains in the collection metadata and the calling service.

What should freshness and retries look like in the retrieval contract?

Freshness is a field, not a feeling. Give every record a deadline appropriate to its domain: a transit disruption may expire in hours, while a trail description can last months. At query time, filter expired records, then record the newest accepted timestamp in the trace. If no source meets the deadline, return a visible “needs verification” state instead of silently stretching the window.

Retries need the same discipline. Search and query are reads, but your ingestion path can be retried after a timeout, so each upsert needs a deterministic record key. A retry must replace the same unit, not create a second copy that wins by accident. On 429, honor Retry-After when present and back off exponentially; log the attempt, status, and request ID. Three retries is a policy choice, not a universal truth.

This small TypeScript contract keeps access and freshness decisions testable before any network call:

type RetrievalUnit = {
  id: string;
  tenantId: string;
  tripId: string;
  visibility: "private" | "public";
  validUntil: string;
  sourceUrl: string;
  text: string;
};

export function eligible(
  unit: RetrievalUnit,
  request: { tenantId: string; tripId: string; now: Date },
): boolean {
  const scopeOk =
    unit.visibility === "public" ||
    (unit.tenantId === request.tenantId && unit.tripId === request.tripId);
  return scopeOk && new Date(unit.validUntil).getTime() >= request.now.getTime();
}

Here is the network edge I put around the vector stage. The payload is deliberately supplied by the caller because the collection schema is application-specific; the wrapper owns the parts that must be consistent: the base URL, bearer token, explicit method, bounded retries, and useful error text.

const baseUrl = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";

export async function vectorQuery(payload: unknown): Promise<unknown> {
  const key = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
  if (!key) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/vector/query`, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${key}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
      },
      body: JSON.stringify(payload),
    });

    if (response.ok) return response.json();
    if (response.status !== 429 || attempt === 3) {
      const detail = await response.text();
      throw new Error(`Infrai vector query failed (${response.status}): ${detail}`);
    }

    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
    const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
      ? retryAfter * 1000
      : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
  }

  throw new Error("unreachable");
}

The function is intentionally dull. That is useful. Unit-test it with an expired train notice, a different tenant, and a public museum page before wiring it to a retriever. Then add an evaluation set with labeled relevant and irrelevant units; a dozen carefully chosen trips can reveal a filter mistake long before production traffic does.

Where does observability fit when a result is wrong?

Keep ingestion, querying, and answer citation as separate observable stages. Each stage should emit the collection name, filter summary, candidate IDs, freshness decision, latency, and request ID. Store the final cited source beside the generated itinerary so a support engineer can replay the decision without guessing which top-k list the model saw.

I measure two things first: access violations (the count must be zero) and citation coverage (the share of claims with an accepted source). Relevance metrics come next. This ordering matters because a highly relevant private booking is still a security failure.

Trace it twice.

Infrai's discovery surface is public and describes capabilities, schemas, billing, and runnable examples, while the search-rag group exposes the web and vector routes used above. That self-describing surface is handy for a CLI that checks its configuration at startup. It is a supporting convenience, not evidence that retrieval quality is solved for your data.

When should you choose a different retrieval stack?

The catch is ownership. If your organization already has Elasticsearch clusters, mature analyzers, and on-call expertise, adding semantic fields there may be safer than introducing another control plane. Choose Pinecone when a managed vector service is the primary requirement and your team accepts application-side policy glue. Choose Weaviate when its schema and hybrid-search model match your data better than a thin HTTP contract.

Infrai is a fit when the valuable constraint is integration surface: one REST API and one key can cover both web context and vector queries, so a small tool can keep fewer SDKs and credentials in its dependency graph. It is not suitable when you need a search specialist's deeply customized ranking stack or an existing cluster's operational guarantees. Your mileage may vary; the right answer depends on the labels and freshness windows you can actually maintain.

Before launch, replay the labeled set after every chunking change. A chunk that is too large hides the access boundary; one that is too small loses the date and source needed for a citation. When a retry lands after a worker restart, compare the deterministic unit ID and request trace before accepting the result, then check the freshness deadline again. That extra inspection feels slow during a demo, but it prevents a plausible, expired train notice from becoming a confident itinerary. The architecture is staged, but the contract is one thing: scope, freshness, bounded retrieval, and traceable evidence.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the vector retrieval guide.

title: How I verify AI-generated work: 1,375 rows, 761 candidates, and a lot of counting
description:
Introduction

I run a parking database for Sendai, Japan, as a solo project, with a personal AI agent (Muse) as my working partner. The database lists parking lots with prices checked against official sources, and anything unverified is labeled as such.

In November 2026 I ran a full sweep of the database: for all 1,375 rows, I wanted two things — candidate coordinates for each facility's real location, and signals of closures or operator changes hiding among the unverified rows.

How the work was split

  • The agent side worked in units of 20 rows, searching by facility name and recording: candidate coordinates (only when the source page itself shows the spot's coordinates), plus a business-status signal for every row, with the source and date.
  • My side (well, the coordinating agent) verified every unit mechanically before accepting it: row counts match, the original columns are untouched (diff = 0), and the candidate counts are recalculated from the final files.

Result: status signals for all 1,375 rows and 761 coordinate candidates.

Rules that made it work

  • "Not found" is not evidence. A facility was never written off as closed or non-existent just because a search missed it. The record had to say "not found in (search scope: ...)".
  • Absence claims need positive confirmation. A closure was only treated as real when an operator-side source said so.
  • Normalize before matching. Full-width vs half-width digits and address notation differences were normalized first, or the same facility looks like two different ones.
  • Counts come from the final file, not from progress reports. Intermediate numbers drift; the delivered file is the only source of truth.

What I don't delegate

Final judgment on the data, anything involving money, and publication decisions stay with me. The agent drafts, searches, counts, and cross-checks — and shows its work so I can verify rather than trust.

The project site: https://sendai-parking-db.pages.dev/
