title: Think Once, Act Fast: Cost-Effective Recursive Self-Improvement for Decision Model Harness
description:
arXiv:2611.22432v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Fast System-1 models enable responsive actions but struggle with complex or unfamiliar tasks. Large language model (LLM)-based System-2 provides strong reasoning capabilities, yet repeated invocation incurs substantial latency and computational costs. To bridge this gap, we propose JevRSI, a System-1/System-2 collaboration framework that transforms LLM reasoning into transferable decision support through recursive harness improvement. A Jev-style System-1 model enables low-latency action selection, while an asynchronous System-2 LLM develops a modular harness. The harness integrates procedures, state memory, and world models to provide decision contexts spanning the past, present, and future. Utility-driven retrieval selects modules based on both contextual relevance and their utility on previous tasks. Environmental feedback guides targeted revisions and enables recursive self-improvement. Experiments across three datasets show that JevRSI consistently improves decision quality, matching or surpassing LLM agents in several settings. It preserves low-latency execution with favorable performance-cost trade-offs. Moreover, System-2 development interventions decrease as the harness evolves, amortizing System-2 costs through continuous improvement. Our project is available at https://github.com/usail-hkust/JevRSI.

title: Fine-Grained Japanese Clinical Named Entity Recognition: A Controlled Comparison of BERT and Open-Weight Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.22219v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Background: Generative large language models (LLMs) offer an alternative to encoder-based clinical named entity recognition (NER), but their performance on fine-grained Japanese extraction tasks and sensitivity to generation settings remain uncertain. Methods: We compared two fine-tuned BERT-CRF baselines with nine open-weight LLMs on iCorpus, which defines 113 entity categories. The evaluation used 433 sentences from 36 test documents; 1,672 sentences were used for training. LLMs were evaluated using zero-shot prompting with and without JSON Schema constraints and three-seed QLoRA fine-tuning. Fine-tuned models were assessed under different output-token limits, including 900 and larger model-specific limits of 2,600 or 4,096 tokens. Performance was measured using sentence-level label-surface matching with relaxed and exact-surface F1. Results: The highest zero-shot relaxed F1 was 0.337, compared with 0.836-0.841 for the BERT baselines. At the larger output limits, all eight fine-tuned LLMs with at least 13B total parameters exceeded both BERT baselines (relaxed F1, 0.882-0.914; exact-surface F1, 0.840-0.880). Across three-seed means, increasing the output limit improved relaxed F1 by 0.052-0.085, alongside higher recall and fewer length-limited outputs. JSON Schema constraints changed relaxed F1 by -0.014 to +0.008 among seven models outside the two reasoning-oriented configurations, while medical-general model pairs showed no consistent advantage for medical specialization. Conclusions: On this historical Japanese case-report benchmark, task-specific fine-tuning combined with adequate generation capacity was associated with stronger LLM extraction performance. Output-token limits materially affected comparisons with BERT, whereas enforcing output structure alone did not overcome low zero-shot accuracy.

title: Fixing Session Leaks in Axion's MongoDB Transactions
description:
Hey friends! 👋🏻

I wanted to share another cool backend fix I implemented in my microforum, Axion. This time, it involves MongoDB transactions, session management, and taking advantage of Express 5's upgraded error handling to keep my code clean.

Why Use Transactions in the First Place? When you're building a platform like Axion, some actions require multiple database operations to happen together. For example, in the post-deletion route, I need to remove related documents like bookmarks, likes, and comments all at once.

Transactions act as a way to execute a set of database operations where if a single operation fails, everything rolls back and no operations execute afterwards. This guarantees data consistency.

The Bug I Encountered: Session Leaks. When running a transaction in MongoDB, you must start a client session and end it when you are finished. My code was written sequentially, assuming it would always reach the cleanup phase at the bottom. But if my withTransaction block crashed early, session.endSession() wouldn't get called. This left some sessions running in the background, which slowly drained resources and caused memory leaks.

My Solution: Using try/finally in Express 5. The fix was straightforward, but I wanted to implement it without adding unnecessary boilerplate code. I wrapped the session management inside a try/finally block:

const session = await mongoose.startSession();
try {
  await session.withTransaction(async () => {
    // My atomic database operations...
  });
} finally {
  await session.endSession();
}

The beauty of the finally block is its absolute guarantee: no matter what happens inside the try block, the code inside finally is always executed. This ensures session.endSession() runs every time, eliminating the session leak problem.

Oh, yeah, and since I'm using Express 5, any exception thrown inside an async route is automatically caught by Express and routed to my global error-handling middleware. I no longer need those repetitive catch blocks!

Thanks for hanging out and reading through! How do you structure your database transactions to keep them clean and leak-free? Let's talk in the comments below. See you next time! 🌟

title: Fan-Out Shipment Updates in Node.js: Retry Backoff for Delayed Messages
description:
A shipment update sent to thousands of game players is not one job. It is a set of independently failing deliveries, and that distinction changes the retry design.

Short answer: persist one delivery intent per subscriber and channel, schedule retryable failures as delayed queue messages with capped exponential backoff and full jitter, and make the delivery effect idempotent. Acknowledge only after the next state is durable; route exhausted or permanent failures to a dead-letter state.

This is an exactly-once mindset applied to an at-least-once transport. A queue can redeliver. The application must make redelivery harmless.

What does a shipment fan-out need to preserve?

Consider shipment SHIP-4821 for a newly purchased game item. The update goes to a player inbox, mobile push, a guild feed, and an analytics consumer. Each subscriber has a separate latency budget and failure mode. If all recipients share one message, one slow push provider controls the fate of the whole batch, while reconciliation cannot explain which recipient was actually delivered.

The durable unit should be a delivery intent identified by (shipment_id, subscriber_id, channel). Store its status, attempt count, next due time, last failure classification, and an idempotency key in a database. Keep the shipment event immutable. The delivery row describes what the system intended and what happened; the queue schedules work but should not become the system of record.

The invariants are more important than the delay curve:

  • A subscriber receives at most one business effect for one shipment and channel, even after redelivery.
  • Every retry has a durable due time and a finite attempt budget.
  • A transient failure can be retried without holding unrelated subscribers.
  • A permanent failure remains inspectable instead of consuming infinite capacity.
  • Acknowledgement follows durable business state.

The uncomfortable boundary is the external call followed by the local commit. If a push provider accepts the request and the worker exits before recording success, the next attempt must reuse the same provider-facing idempotency key or query the provider. If the database commits but acknowledgement is lost, redelivery is expected; a unique delivery key turns the second application into a no-op. Those are ordinary states in an at-least-once design, not exotic edge cases.

How should failed jobs use exponential backoff in a delayed queue?

Treat backoff as load shaping. For attempt n, calculate upper = min(cap, base * 2^n) and choose a random delay from zero through upper. Full jitter keeps a shared outage from waking every worker at the same instant. The cap prevents an old shipment from acquiring an unbounded tail, while the attempt budget defines when the system stops trying.

Classification comes before scheduling. A timeout, temporary network failure, or rate limit is usually retryable. An invalid player identifier, revoked consent, or permanently rejected payload should go straight to a dead-letter state. Record the classification with the retry decision; a count without a reason is poor evidence during reconciliation.

The reader may implement the worker in Node.js, but the critical transition below is Go so the state changes are explicit and dependency-free. Scheduler stands for the queue adapter. Its contract is deliberately generic, which keeps the retry policy independent of a commercial client library.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "math/rand"
    "time"
)

type Delivery struct {
    ShipmentID  string
    Subscriber  string
    Channel     string
    Attempt     int
    MaxAttempts int
}

type Scheduler interface {
    Publish(ctx context.Context, queue string, body Delivery, delay time.Duration, key string) error
}

func fullJitter(attempt, base, capSeconds int, r *rand.Rand) time.Duration {
    upper := base
    for i := 0; i < attempt && upper < capSeconds; i++ {
        upper *= 2
    }
    if upper > capSeconds {
        upper = capSeconds
    }
    return time.Duration(r.Intn(upper+1)) * time.Second
}

func scheduleRetry(ctx context.Context, q Scheduler, d Delivery, r *rand.Rand) error {
    d.Attempt++
    key := fmt.Sprintf("%s:%s:%s", d.ShipmentID, d.Subscriber, d.Channel)
    if d.Attempt >= d.MaxAttempts {
        return q.Publish(ctx, "shipment-dead-letter", d, 0, key)
    }
    wait := fullJitter(d.Attempt, 5, 3600, r)
    return q.Publish(ctx, "shipment-delivery", d, wait, key)
}

The key is stable for the logical delivery, not freshly generated for each attempt. The queue adapter may receive the same publish request again after a worker restart; its idempotency behavior, or an outbox publisher in front of it, must prevent duplicate scheduling from becoming duplicate business effects.

Do not sleep inside the worker for the whole delay. A short local retry can be reasonable within a request deadline, but a delayed queue message makes pending work visible and lets the worker process other deliveries. That difference matters during a deploy, when in-memory timers disappear or compete with shutdown.

Which retry boundary is easiest to reconcile?

There are several valid boundaries, and they should not be confused:

Boundary Useful for Main limitation
In-worker timer A short operation inside one request budget Uses a worker slot and is fragile across restart
Delayed queue message An independent, reconstructible delivery attempt Requires duplicate handling and attempt metadata
Database due-time scan Long schedules driven by business state Requires polling, leases, and lock discipline
Workflow history Multi-step work with timers and compensation More operational state than one delivery needs

The practical choice is determined by the failure you need to explain. If the question is “why has this player not received the shipment?”, a delivery table with an audit trail is more useful than a queue dashboard. If the question is “which independent attempt should run next?”, a delayed message is a good scheduling boundary. If several steps must agree before the process advances, a workflow record is a better model.

A transactional outbox is useful when writing the delivery row and publishing its first message must be coordinated. Commit the business change and an outbox row together; a publisher can retry the outbox operation using the same logical key. This still does not make the external provider call magically atomic with the database. It makes the recovery evidence durable.

How do Node.js workers prove that retries are safe?

Observability should show more than queue depth. Track ready messages, delayed messages, oldest delivery age, retry counts by failure class, dead-letter growth, and shipment-to-acknowledgement latency. Segment those measures by channel so a mobile provider's rate limit does not hide a healthy in-game inbox consumer.

Each state change should record the shipment ID, subscriber ID, channel, attempt, idempotency key, classification, chosen delay, worker version, and timestamps. Logs are not enough: retention, sampling, and concurrent retries can erase the causal sequence needed for an audit trail.

Test the gaps deliberately: provider acceptance followed by a worker crash, duplicate delivery after a committed transaction, a rate limit with and without a retry hint, malformed payloads, clock skew near a due time, and dead-letter replay. Property tests can assert that the delay never exceeds its cap and that one delivery key cannot produce two successful business transitions.

Three words: make it replayable.

I am not sure one backoff curve can suit a provider with second-scale recovery and another with hour-scale recovery; your mileage will vary with provider behavior and the business deadline. The invariant is stable even when the curve changes: no unbounded retries, no early acknowledgement, and no delivery effect without an auditable idempotency decision.

When are delayed messages the wrong choice?

Delayed delivery fits when each attempt is independent, the payload can be rebuilt, and the deadline fits the queue's retention and delay limits. It is not suitable when the operation needs a long queryable schedule, human approval, compensation across several systems, or coordinated progress among many steps. Persist the workflow state and choose a scheduler or workflow engine whose history matches that business process.

There is a second trade-off. A high-value shipment may justify an outbox, reconciliation job, and manual review even when the queue supports delayed delivery. A low-value cosmetic notification may accept a shorter retention period and a smaller retry budget. The right abstraction follows the consequence of duplication and loss, not the convenience of the queue API.

References

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-fifo-queues.html
  • https://microservices.io/patterns/data/transactional-outbox.html
  • https://docs.bullmq.io/guide/retrying-failing-jobs
  • https://cloud.google.com/tasks/docs/dual-overview
  • https://docs.temporal.io/encyclopedia/retry-policies

title: Goldcrest: Conversational State to Monte Carlo Parameters
description:
Goldcrest is a household financial planning tool that replaces spreadsheet forms with a conversational interface. You answer short questions in a chat. The agent extracts income, expenses, asset values, and timeline assumptions, then feeds them into a Monte Carlo simulation that projects your financial trajectory across thousands of market paths.

The interesting plumbing is the boundary between the LLM-driven conversation layer and the deterministic financial engine. The agent must maintain dialogue state across multiple turns, validate inputs, resolve ambiguity, and serialize a complete parameter set without letting the LLM touch arithmetic or generate advice.

Architecture: Conversation State to Simulation Parameters

The system splits into three layers:

  1. Conversational agent: Asks questions, parses natural language responses, maintains dialogue context.
  2. Parameter store: Holds structured financial data (income streams, expense categories, asset balances, tax rates) on the server.
  3. Monte Carlo engine: Runs deterministic simulations using the parameter store as input.

The agent never performs calculations. It extracts values and categories from user responses, writes them to the parameter store, and hands off to the engine. The engine produces every number in the projection.

Data Flow 

User input (natural language)
    ↓
LLM extracts structured fields
    ↓
Validation layer (type checks, range constraints, consistency rules)
    ↓
Parameter store (server-side, pseudonymized for LLM calls)
    ↓
Monte Carlo engine (deterministic, no LLM involvement)
    ↓
Year-by-year projections + probability distributions

The LLM sees pseudonymized data when it needs context for follow-up questions. Actual dollar amounts and identifiable details stay on the server. The model receives tokens like <income_source_1> or <expense_category_2> instead of "salary from Acme Corp" or "mortgage payment."

Dialogue State Management

The agent tracks which parameters it has collected and which are still missing. A typical rent-vs-buy scenario requires:

  • Current income (gross, net, frequency)
  • Expected income changes (raises, bonuses, career shifts)
  • Monthly expenses (housing, utilities, groceries, discretionary)
  • Savings and investment balances
  • Debt obligations (student loans, car payments)
  • Home purchase details (price, down payment, mortgage rate, closing costs)
  • Rental costs (monthly rent, expected increases)
  • Timeline (years until retirement, life expectancy assumptions)
  • Risk tolerance (asset allocation, withdrawal strategy)

The agent maintains a checklist. After each user response, it updates the parameter store and decides whether to ask a clarifying question, move to the next category, or declare the parameter set complete.

Handling Ambiguity

When a user says "I make around 80k," the agent must resolve:

  • Gross or net?
  • Annual, monthly, or biweekly?
  • Single income or household total?
  • Expected to change?

The system uses a two-pass approach. First pass: extract the stated value and write it to the parameter store with a confidence flag. Second pass: ask targeted follow-up questions only for low-confidence fields. This avoids the "20 questions" problem where every input triggers a cascade of clarifications.

If the user provides conflicting information across turns (e.g., "I spend $3k a month" followed later by "my rent is $2k and other expenses are $1.5k"), the agent flags the inconsistency and asks which figure to trust.

Validation and Constraint Logic

The parameter store enforces constraints before allowing a simulation run:

  • Income must be positive.
  • Expenses cannot exceed income by more than available savings.
  • Asset allocations must sum to 100%.
  • Mortgage terms must match standard products (15, 20, 30 years).
  • Tax rates must fall within plausible ranges for the jurisdiction.

The validation layer runs after each parameter update. If a constraint fails, the agent asks a corrective question rather than proceeding with invalid inputs.

Example Validation Table

Parameter Constraint Failure Behavior
Annual income > 0, < $10M Reject, ask for correction
Monthly expenses > 0, < income + savings drawdown Warn, allow override
Down payment 0-100% of home price Reject if outside range
Mortgage rate 0.1%-20% Reject, flag as likely error
Asset allocation Sum to 100% ± 0.01% Reject, show current total
Retirement age 50-80 Warn if < 60 or > 75

The system allows overrides for warnings but hard-blocks on constraint violations that would break the simulation.

Serialization and Handoff to the Engine

Once the parameter set passes validation, the system serializes it into a JSON structure:

{
  "income_streams": [
    {"source": "salary", "amount": 80000, "frequency": "annual", "growth_rate": 0.03}
  ],
  "expenses": [
    {"category": "housing", "amount": 2000, "frequency": "monthly", "inflation_adjust": true},
    {"category": "discretionary", "amount": 1500, "frequency": "monthly", "inflation_adjust": true}
  ],
  "assets": [
    {"type": "checking", "balance": 15000},
    {"type": "retirement", "balance": 120000, "allocation": {"stocks": 0.7, "bonds": 0.3}}
  ],
  "scenarios": [
    {"name": "rent", "housing_cost": 2000, "housing_type": "rent"},
    {"name": "buy", "housing_cost": 2500, "housing_type": "own", "home_price": 500000, "down_payment": 100000, "mortgage_rate": 0.065, "term_years": 30}
  ],
  "timeline": {"current_age": 32, "retirement_age": 65, "life_expectancy": 90},
  "simulation_params": {"iterations": 10000, "inflation_mean": 0.025, "market_return_mean": 0.07, "market_volatility": 0.15}
}

The Monte Carlo engine reads this JSON, runs 10,000 iterations with randomized market returns and inflation rates, and produces:

  • Year-by-year net worth projections (median, 25th percentile, 75th percentile)
  • Probability of meeting retirement goals
  • Sensitivity analysis (which parameters have the largest impact)

The engine writes results back to the parameter store. The frontend fetches them and renders charts.

Security and Data Handling

The system pseudonymizes data before sending context to the LLM. The LLM never sees:

  • Actual dollar amounts
  • Account numbers
  • Employer names
  • Addresses

Instead, it receives abstract tokens and category labels. When the LLM generates a follow-up question, the server substitutes real values back in before displaying to the user.

This limits exposure if the LLM provider logs requests or if a prompt injection attack tries to exfiltrate data. The worst an attacker can extract is the structure of the conversation, not the financial details.

Prompt Injection Mitigation

The agent uses a strict output schema. Every LLM response must be valid JSON with predefined fields:

{
  "next_question": "string",
  "extracted_values": {"field_name": "value"},
  "confidence": "high | medium | low",
  "needs_clarification": ["field_name"]
}

If the LLM returns anything outside this schema, the system rejects it and retries with a stricter prompt. This prevents the LLM from injecting arbitrary text or attempting to execute commands.

Failure Modes

Incomplete parameter sets: If the user abandons the conversation halfway through, the parameter store is incomplete. The system blocks simulation runs until all required fields are populated. The agent can resume from the last saved state.

Garbage inputs: If the user provides nonsensical values ("I make negative $50k a year"), the validation layer catches it. But if they provide plausible but wrong values ("I spend $500 a month" when they actually spend $5000), the simulation runs with bad data. The system relies on the user to review and correct extracted values before finalizing.

LLM hallucination: The LLM might misinterpret a response and extract the wrong value. The system shows every extracted parameter to the user for confirmation. The user can edit any field before the simulation runs.

Market assumption drift: The Monte Carlo engine uses historical return and volatility distributions. If future market behavior diverges significantly, projections will be wrong. This is a modeling limitation, not a plumbing failure.

Technical Verdict

Use Goldcrest's pattern when:

  • You need to gather structured data from users who hate forms.
  • The downstream process (simulation, calculation, workflow) requires deterministic inputs.
  • You can clearly separate the conversational layer from the execution layer.
  • You have well-defined validation rules and can enforce them before handoff.

Avoid this pattern when:

  • The parameter space is too large or too ambiguous for multi-turn dialogue.
  • Users need to see all fields at once to understand dependencies.
  • Real-time feedback on intermediate results is critical (forms with live calculations work better).
  • You cannot tolerate the latency of LLM calls for every user input.

The key insight is treating the LLM as a data extraction tool, not a reasoning engine. The agent asks questions and parses answers. The deterministic engine does the math. This keeps the system auditable and prevents the LLM from generating financial advice or performing calculations it will get wrong.

title: FrameSeg3D: Learned Local Frames for Segmenting Small Parts on High-Resolution 3D Scans
description:
arXiv:2611.22124v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Segmenting small parts on high-resolution 3D scans, such as nails on hand scans and teeth on intraoral scans, poses three challenges: 1) each part covers a tiny fraction of the scan, 2) its boundary is only a subtle change of height and curvature, and 3) it faces its own direction. Existing methods fall into two groups, and both fall short. The first group processes the whole scan at once and sees each part too coarsely. Point and mesh networks must shrink the scan to fit in memory, so a small part keeps only a few of its points. Multi-view methods render images of the whole object, so each part fills only a few pixels and a tilted part is seen from the side. The second group first finds each part and then segments it up close. But these methods find the parts with knowledge about one kind of part, for example the shape of the dental arch for teeth. Such knowledge does not carry over to other kinds of parts. We find that accuracy is limited by how a part is seen, from which direction and at what scale, not by how many points land on it. We therefore present FrameSeg3D. It first predicts a local frame for every part, its center and the direction it faces, from a low-resolution view of the whole scan. It then segments the part in views around its frame normal at the scanner's resolution, so covering the whole scan no longer costs resolution. Because every part arrives centered, facing the camera, and at a fixed scale, one segmentation network can serve different kinds of parts and learn from few labeled masks. We test FrameSeg3D on two kinds of parts, nails and teeth. It outperforms state-of-the-art methods on hand scans (mean Dice 0.970 on nails) and on the Teeth3DS+ test fold (per-tooth IoU 96.5), with the most accurate tooth boundaries (boundary IoU 70.5).

Action is required: if your organization uses a firewall, proxy, or secure web gateway that allows access to Gemini Notebook by a specific URL path. If this applies to you, Google recommends that you add the following URLs to your allowlist:

  1. Allowlist notebooklm.cloud.google.com/* and notebook.cloud.google.com/*

  2. If you use Workforce Identity Federation, allowlist notebooklm.cloud.google/* and notebook.cloud.google/*

  3. If you use Gemini Notebook within Gemini Enterprise, allowlist vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/notebooklm/*.

Google recommends allowing entire domains (/*) so that future path changes don't require additional updates.

If you don't allow /*, you must allow both /REGION and /go/REGION, where REGION is your location value: global, us, eu, asia-northeast1, au, ca, de, europe-west2, in, kr, or sg. For example, notebooklm.cloud.google.com/us/ and notebooklm.cloud.google.com/go/us/

Temporary workaround: If your firewall blocks users before you update your allowlist, users themselves can access the original URLs by removing /go from the URL and adding version=legacy. title: AWS Workload Credentials Provider adds container support for ACM certificates
description:
The open source AWS Workload Credentials Provider can now export AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) certificates to applications running in containers on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), including AWS Fargate, Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), and Docker on Amazon EC2. You can now automate certificate deployment and renewal for containerized TLS workloads the same way you do on EC2 instances, on both Linux and Windows.

The provider runs as a sidecar in your ECS task or EKS pod. It exports each certificate and private key to a shared volume and writes the renewed files when ACM rotates the certificate. For TLS servers that don't reload certificate files on their own, such as NGINX, Apache, HAProxy, or IIS, a companion watcher in the TLS container runs your reload command after each renewal. The watcher needs no AWS credentials. TLS servers that reload automatically, such as Envoy, Traefik, and Caddy, need only the shared volume. Access is controlled through IAM: the sidecar assumes a per-workload role that is allowed to export only that workload's certificates.

To get started, download the provider and watcher binaries for Linux (x86_64 and Arm64) or Windows, and follow the setup steps and ECS and EKS examples in the AWS Workload Credentials Provider README on GitHub. The provider is available at no additional charge, and standard ACM charges apply to exported certificates. To learn more, see the AWS Certificate Manager documentation.

title: From Top to Bottom: Quark Mass Hierarchies in Heterotic String Theory
description:
arXiv:2611.21751v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Standard Model fermion masses exhibit large hierarchies, spanning more than five orders of magnitude in the quark sector alone. In this paper, we study whether these hierarchies can be generated perturbatively at tree level in smooth heterotic Calabi-Yau compactifications, where the supergravity approximation remains under computational control. In such backgrounds, physical Yukawa couplings combine holomorphic superpotential integrals with matter field Kahler metrics. The former can be computed algebraically, while the latter require solving a coupled system of partial differential equations for the Ricci-flat metric, Hermitian Yang-Mills connections, and harmonic bundle-valued forms. Within this framework, we identify two new tree-level mechanisms by which complex structure moduli can generate fermion mass hierarchies and show analytically and numerically that both mechanisms are obstructed for previously studied tetra-quadric models. Motivated by these obstructions, we scan the existing databases of tens of thousands of complete intersection Calabi-Yau line bundle models and find a unique smooth quotient admitting a rank-three up-quark Yukawa matrix at tree level. Evaluating the physical couplings on this manifold and evolving them under the renormalization group, we obtain realistic mass hierarchies for the top, charm, up, and bottom quarks in the smooth supergravity regime.

title: Calif Says AI Found Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) in an Hour for Under $200
description:
Calif Says AI Found Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) in an Hour for Under $200

Buried in the Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) coverage is a line most people scrolled past. The researchers at Calif say they found the bug with AI help in about an hour. They say a first working exploit took about two hours after that. And they say the whole thing cost under $200 in AI token costs.

Qualys repeats those numbers and attributes them to the researchers, and Upwind reports the one-hour and two-hour parts. Nobody has independently checked them. Treat them as a claim. But look at what happens if they are even roughly true.

TL;DR

Claim Source Checked by others
Bug found with AI help in about an hour Calif, via Upwind and Qualys No
First working exploit about two hours later Calif, via Upwind and Qualys No
Under $200 in AI token costs Calif, via Qualys No
Fix committed under embargo October 14, 2026 Endor Labs Single source
Public disclosure and Oracle fixes November 17, 2026 Qualys, Upwind, Endor Labs Four sources
Bug leaked before its patch Calif, via Upwind and Endor Labs No

Do the arithmetic on the defender side

Put the two clocks next to each other.

The discovery side, per Calif: about three hours of work from nothing to a working exploit, for a bill that fits on a corporate card without sign-off.

The defender side, from public dates: the fix landed on October 14, 2026 and the public advisory and vendor builds landed on November 17. That is 34 days between a committed fix and a public one. Endor Labs adds that on November 17 the public jdk17u, jdk21u and jdk25u repositories did not yet carry the fix, and that a South Korean advisory flagged an unauthenticated Java RCE a day earlier.

After the build exists, you still have to find every JVM, rebuild images and restart processes. The runbook in my earlier post covers that. That part is slow, and your change windows set its pace, not the clock.

I am not saying attackers will win that race. I am saying the race is now one where one side's cost fell through the floor, while the other side's cost is the same human approval chain it always was.

What the broader numbers say

I did not read the full reports, only the headlines, so take these as pointers and not evidence for this CVE.

The headline of Rapid7's 2026 annual threat report says exploited high and critical severity vulnerabilities surged 105 percent as attack timelines collapsed. A separate Rapid7 Q2 2026 release says nearly two thirds of exploited vulnerabilities needed no user interaction. A news summary of that quarter says newly exploited vulnerabilities jumped from 8 percent to 40 percent.

None of that proves AI is the cause. That fits a world where finding bugs got cheaper, and Java4Shell is a vivid example, if Calif's numbers hold.

The Token Tab, from the other side

I have written before about the bill AI tools quietly send you. This is the reverse entry. Someone else's tokens are now a line item on your risk register. By Calif's account, the discovery took one engineer, some prompts and an afternoon.

The honest caveats matter here. Calif says it holds back its product-specific exploits and there is no universal one. The sources I read show no public proof-of-concept shell. Equixly calls code execution unproven and a crash the realistic outcome. A cheap discovery does not mean a cheap, reliable exploit against your particular deployment.

What I would change in my own process

Three policy changes follow from a cheap-discovery world, and none of them need a new product.

First, measure your restart latency. Patching a file does not fix a running JVM. How long does it take your slowest service to go from "fixed build available" to "process restarted on the fixed build"? If you cannot answer, that is your real patch window.

Second, tie your deadline to exposure instead of a flat number. Qualys orders its priorities as internet-facing identity providers first, then Jira, Confluence, Jenkins and Artifactory, then other internet-facing Java services, then internal data systems.

Third, keep a runtime inventory that is always on. The Java4Shell exposure depends on the JDK build and the CPU feature, and neither shows up in a dependency scan.

A triage script

This script takes the inventory output from the runbook, one line per JVM (pid, path, version), plus an AVX-512 flag, and sorts each into patched, exposed or not affected using the version ranges Qualys and Upwind list. It does not check for vendor-specific builds, so a version number that passes is not a promise. Confirm against the vendor advisory.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""java4shell_triage.py: classify JVM versions against the published ranges.

Input: lines of "pid<TAB>path<TAB>version" on stdin, e.g. 17.0.19, 21.0.13.
Usage: python3 java4shell_triage.py --avx512 < inventory.tsv
"""
import argparse
import re
import sys

# line -> first affected, first fixed (Qualys and Upwind, November 17, 2026)
RANGES = {
    17: ((17, 0, 6), (17, 0, 21, 1)),
    21: ((21, 0, 0), (21, 0, 13, 1)),
    25: ((25, 0, 0), (25, 0, 5, 1)),
    27: ((27, 0, 0), (27, 0, 1, 1)),
}


def parse(version: str) -> tuple:
    nums = [int(n) for n in re.findall(r"\d+", version)[:5]]
    return tuple(nums)


def pad(t: tuple, n: int = 5) -> tuple:
    return t + (0,) * (n - len(t))


def classify(version: str, avx512: bool) -> str:
    v = parse(version)
    if not v or v[0] not in RANGES:
        return "not-affected-or-unknown"
    first_bad, first_fixed = RANGES[v[0]]
    if pad(v) < pad(first_bad) or pad(v) >= pad(first_fixed):
        return "not-affected-or-fixed"
    return "EXPOSED" if avx512 else "vulnerable-code-no-avx512"


def main() -> None:
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--avx512", action="store_true", help="host has all four AVX-512 flags")
    args = ap.parse_args()
    for line in sys.stdin:
        parts = line.rstrip("\n").split("\t")
        if len(parts) < 3:
            continue
        pid, path, version = parts[0], parts[1], parts[2]
        print(f"{classify(version, args.avx512):28} pid={pid} {version} {path}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The middle state matters. A host without AVX-512 VBMI runs vulnerable code that cannot reach the bad path today. Qualys warns that a resize or instance change can move a workload onto an affected CPU later, so that state deserves a ticket, not a shrug.

The bottom line

The part of Java4Shell that will age best is not the 62-byte overflow. It is a line in a vendor blog post saying someone did the discovery work in an afternoon with a model. Even if those exact numbers fail scrutiny, plan your patch process for the version of the world where they do.

If a bug like this took three hours and under $200 to find, how long does your slowest service take to restart?

GDS K S · thegdsks.com · building Glincker · follow on X @thegdsks

Cheap discovery moves the bottleneck to your restart window.

Sources: Qualys, Upwind, Endor Labs, Equixly, Rapid7 Q2 2026 release.

title: My keyword filter read "tomografia computadorizada" as a computer purchase
description:
I follow the small municipalities around my region in Brazil. Everything they buy is published as a text description in a national procurement API, and a share of those purchases is IT work I can bid on: maintenance contracts, network cabling, software licenses, toner, a hosted portal. The API has no full text search worth using, so I wrote a filter over the object description. Last run made 424 requests across four procurement modalities, found 165 objects containing an IT term, and marked 12 of them as billable under the MEI occupations I hold today.

The filter is a keyword classifier. It has two ways to be wrong, and they cost very different things. A false positive costs me a minute of reading. A false negative costs the opportunity and leaves no trace in the run. Everything below came from a real object that fooled it.

Accents first, because the source is Portuguese

Object descriptions arrive in uppercase, with and without accents, and often carry a platform prefix like [Portal de Compras Publicas] -. Both get normalized before any matching:

def sem_acento(txt):
    n = unicodedata.normalize('NFKD', txt or '')
    return ''.join(c for c in n if not unicodedata.combining(c)).lower()

def limpa_objeto(txt):
    """Remove prefixos de plataforma tipo '[Portal de Compras Publicas] - '."""
    t = re.sub(r'^\s*\[[^\]]{0,60}\]\s*-?\s*', '', (txt or '').strip())
    return re.sub(r'\s+', ' ', t).strip()

NFKD decomposition plus a filter on combining characters turns Manutenção into manutencao. Without it, half my keyword list never matches, and the failure is invisible because a filter that finds nothing looks like a quiet week.

Short terms need a word boundary

Seventy-four terms make up the strong list. Most are long enough that a plain substring test is correct: computador should match computadores, and that inflection is the normal case in Portuguese. Short terms behave differently, because they live inside other words.

    for termo in FORTES:
        if len(termo) <= 3:
            if re.search(r'\b' + re.escape(termo) + r'\b', t):
                achados.append(termo)
        elif termo in t:
            achados.append(termo)

One term in the list is short enough to need it: ti. A plain substring test on those two letters fires on licitacao, noticia and importante, which appear in most of a procurement feed. Everything longer stays on the substring test, rack included, because computador has to match computadores and that inflection is the rule rather than the exception.

Ambiguous words need a companion in the same sentence

Four terms are real IT vocabulary and also everyday Portuguese: servidor (server, or civil servant), suporte tecnico (IT support, or support for anything), cartucho (printer cartridge, or respirator cartridge), licenca (software license, or a professional registration fee). Those four never classify an object on their own:

    if all(a in TERMOS_FRACOS for a in achados):
        if not any(c in t for c in COMPANHIA_IT):
            return achados, 'termo ambiguo sem companhia de TI'

The companion list has 53 entries, from impressora to cabeamento. The rule was added after a measurement on 19/10/2026 over 173 findings: without it, 15 objects entered by mistake, among them medical expert examinations, uniforms, a marmitex lunch contract, a water cooler, an LED panel rental, and two consultancy contracts in social assistance and public transparency. No legitimate object was lost by adding it.

That measurement is the reason I trust the rule. Fifteen wrong entries in 173 was enough to act on, and losing no legitimate object is what made the rule safe to keep.

The reject list is a log with dates

Eighty-three entries exist to kill a match even when a strong term is present. Each one came from a specific sentence:

  • tomografia computadorizada matched computador.
  • filmes radiologicos para impressora de imagens medicas matched impressora.
  • leite integral UHT para pacientes, acompanhantes e servidores da Fundacao matched servidor.
  • independente de transcricao is boilerplate at the end of a metalwork contract and matched transcricao.
  • licenca anual de Anotacao de Responsabilidade Tecnica matched licenca.
  • linha fixa for a telephone line matched telephony, which is not an occupation of mine.

The comments in the file carry the date of the scan that produced each group. That turns the reject list into a record of what the source actually contains, and the next person editing it can see why a line exists instead of deleting it as noise.

One reject entry nearly killed a real opportunity

Civil servants are everywhere in this feed. A notice for a basic computing course aimed at municipal employees is a legitimate purchase I can invoice, and it contains the word servidor in its most common sense. The reject rule therefore has an exception:

    for r in RUIDO:
        if r in t:
            if r in RUIDO_SERVIDOR and any(f in t for f in SERVICO_DE_MEI):
                continue
            return achados, r

If the noise belongs to the group about people, and the same object also matches a service I actually sell, the object survives. Without those two lists, curso de informatica para os servidores municipais would be dropped by my own filter, silently, and it is one of the few things I can invoice.

The tests are a list of inputs that must be rejected

The test file holds 15 positive cases and 24 negative ones, and it fails the run when any of them misses. A negative case passes when the classifier finds no term at all, or when it finds terms and returns a reason to discard:

for nome, txt in negativo:
    a, m = v.classifica(txt)
    ok = (not a) or bool(m)
    falhas += 0 if ok else 1

The negative list is the valuable half, because I wrote it by pasting objects that had already fooled the filter. AQUISICAO DE FILMES RADIOLOGICOS DRY FILM PARA IMPRESSORA DE IMAGENS MEDICAS is in there. So is a car rental that mentions computer maintenance, and a school lunch contract that mentions IT equipment.

One case checks the reason, not the outcome. A bank accreditation notice matches digitacao and would be labeled with my data entry occupation. The correct behavior is a discard by a specific noise entry, so the assertion names the entry:

achados, ruido = v.classifica(txt_banco)
ok = bool(achados) and ruido in ('instituicoes financeiras', 'arrecadacao de tributos',
                                 'documento de arrecadacao municipal')

Written as "no profile, therefore fine", that test would pass for any future reason, including a rule that drops legitimate notices. The same notice, from Senador Modestino, had already been published as billable before the fix.

Recall fails without a message

On 16/11/2026 a Diamantina notice for aquisicao de computadores was marked as outside my MEI, which was wrong, since buying computers falls under a commerce occupation I can use. The fix added four phrases that name the purchase explicitly: aquisicao de computadores, fornecimento de computadores, aquisicao de microcomputadores, aquisicao de computadores e perifericos.

I did not add computador alone to that list, even though it would have caught the case. It would also match spare parts, maintenance and rental, and those are different occupations. The narrower fix costs a future miss and keeps the report honest.

That is the asymmetry I plan around. Precision errors show up in the output and get fixed in a minute. Recall errors do not show up at all, which is why the report is read every week instead of trusted. The test suite catches what I thought of. Reading the notices catches what I did not.

Today the filter has 74 strong terms, 53 companion terms and 83 noise entries. Run against the current snapshot of 164 objects, none of them would be dropped by the rules as they stand, and the control suite finishes with zero failures. None of that says the next municipality uses a phrase I have not seen.

Se você mantém algum filtro de palavra-chave em cima de texto de terceiro, comenta qual foi o primeiro falso positivo que te obrigou a escrever um teste. Eu respondo em português aqui embaixo.

title: Reliability-Driven Feature Correction for Hyperspectral and LiDAR Classification
description:
arXiv:2611.22508v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Hyperspectral image (HSI) and LiDAR data provide complementary spectral and elevation information for land-cover classification. However, the spatially varying class-discriminative reliability of modality features is rarely modeled explicitly, allowing weak or ambiguous features to adversely affect cross-modal interaction and fusion. To address this issue, we propose ReDF, a reliability-driven framework that quantifies the reliability of each modality's features at each spatial location through the strength of class-related evidence they provide, and uses it to guide feature correction and fusion. Specifically, a Reliability-Guided Feature Correction module introduces a class prototype bank for each modality and converts feature-prototype similarities into class evidence for reliability estimation. The estimated reliabilities are used to construct a reliability-weighted shared representation and to guide bidirectional cross-modal feature correction based on neighborhood agreement, refining modality features with weak class evidence through information from the other modality. Building on these outputs, a Reliability-Guided Feature Reweighting module conditions a low-rank modulation on the estimated reliabilities and the cross-modal disagreement, and applies it to the corrected modality-specific descriptors to adaptively rescale each modality's contribution to the fused representation used for final classification. Experiments on three public HSI-LiDAR datasets show higher mean overall accuracy and Kappa than the compared methods.

title: Saga in microservices: orchestration or choreography?
description:
Most of you have probably heard of the Saga pattern in microservice architectures. It helps coordinate a business process that spans multiple services and cannot be handled by a single transaction.

Each participant in a Saga commits a local change. If a later step fails, the system runs compensating actions to bring the process back to an acceptable state. But who should manage the sequence of steps: the services themselves, or a dedicated coordinator?

Orchestration or choreography?

With choreography, services react to one another’s events, and there is no central coordinator. With orchestration, a dedicated coordinator defines the order of actions, tracks the process state, and decides what to do when something fails.

The choice depends on the complexity of the business process and the level of control it requires. Let’s compare both approaches using the same example.

Example: placing an order

Choreography: services react to events

Consider an order workflow. The Order service publishes an OrderPlaced event. The Inventory service checks availability and attempts to reserve the items. It then publishes either StockReserved or StockUnavailable.

After receiving StockReserved, the Payment service processes the payment and publishes either PaymentCompleted or PaymentFailed. Once payment succeeds, the Shipping service creates a shipment.

No single service owns the entire workflow: each participant reacts to the events it needs. The services remain independent, but the order’s state is spread across their handlers. When something goes wrong, understanding what happened may require tracing a chain of events across several services.

For example, if payment fails, the Inventory service needs to receive a failure event and release the reservation. If a shipment cannot be created after payment succeeds, the system needs a recovery step: retry, cancel the payment, or route the order for manual handling.

Choreography is easy to follow while the process is short and reactions are simple. As branches and recovery paths accumulate, it becomes harder to understand.

Orchestration: one component coordinates the steps

An Order Saga can manage the workflow instead:

  1. Ask the Inventory service to reserve the items.
  2. Start payment after the reservation is confirmed.
  3. Request shipment creation after payment succeeds.
  4. If payment fails, ask Inventory to release the reservation.
  5. If shipment creation fails, retry or run the agreed recovery flow.

The orchestrator tracks the order’s state and decides what to do when a step fails or times out. The process is easier to observe, but the coordinator itself must be operated and maintained. Its role is to manage the sequence of steps, not to take business logic or data ownership away from the services.

How to choose

Choreography Orchestration
Process Short and mostly linear Long-running or branching
Process state Reconstructed from events Tracked by the coordinator
Failure handling Distributed across participants Defined in the workflow logic
Main cost Harder to trace as the process grows An additional component to operate

If the steps are simple and services can react to events independently, choreography may be enough. If the team needs to track the state of each order, handle timeouts, and manage several failure paths, orchestration gives the process an explicit owner.

One thing remains true in either approach: compensation is not a transaction rollback. Releasing reserved stock or cancelling a payment is a new action, and that action can fail too. Handlers need to be idempotent; retries, timeouts, stuck orders, and manual recovery should be planned for in advance.

title: Your Claude Code skills are going blank. Three settings that fix it.
description:
Last week I wrote about measuring what my Claude Code setup costs on every request. The short version: 68.5k tokens before I typed a word, and 220 of my 283 skills listed with no description at all.

The obvious follow-up question was: what do you actually do about it? Uninstalling everything you didn't use this week is a blunt answer. It turns out Claude Code has settings for exactly this, and I hadn't heard of any of them.

Why skills lose their descriptions

Every session starts with a listing of your skills: a name and a description for each. Claude reads the descriptions to decide when a skill applies.

That listing has a budget. According to the docs it scales at 1% of the model's context window. On a 1M-token model that came out at 29,997 characters in my transcripts. When the listing overflows, Claude Code keeps every name but drops descriptions, starting with the skills you invoke least.

That matches what I saw. All 13 skills I'd used in the last month kept their descriptions. The 220 that went blank were all skills I hadn't touched. The catch is that a skill you just installed has zero invocations too, so it's first in line to go blank, and Claude can't reach for it on its own because all it sees is a name.

The three settings

skillOverrides

Decides how each skill shows up:

{
  "skillOverrides": {
    "old-report-skill": "user-invocable-only",
    "deploy": "name-only"
  }
}
value Claude sees in the / menu
"on" (default) name + description yes
"name-only" name only yes
"user-invocable-only" nothing yes
"off" nothing no

user-invocable-only is the useful one. The skill disappears from what the model sees, but you can still run it yourself with /name. For a skill you haven't used in a month, that's usually what you want.

One catch: plugin skills aren't affected by skillOverrides. For those, the only option is disabling the plugin.

skillListingBudgetFraction

This is the 1% itself. 0.02 doubles the room. It isn't free, though: my listing is about 30k characters, so doubling it can cost up to ~8k more tokens on every request once it fills up. Hiding the skills you don't use is the cheaper way to get room back.

disableClaudeAiConnectors

If you've connected services on claude.ai, Claude Code loads their tool names and instructions in every session. Setting this to true stops Claude Code from fetching them. They stay connected on claude.ai. If you use some connectors but not others, toggle the unused ones off in /mcp instead (that's stored per project).

Doing it from your actual usage

Choosing what to hide by hand isn't fun with 283 skills, so I added it to deadweight, the tool from the last post. It already reads the transcripts in ~/.claude/projects to see what you used in the last 30 days. Version 0.3.0 uses the settings above:

cargo install deadweight
deadweight fix --dry-run

Disable these plugins (settings.json → enabledPlugins: false)
  ...
Hide these skills from Claude (settings.json → skillOverrides: "user-invocable-only"; /name still works)
  ...
Turn off claude.ai connectors in Claude Code (settings.json → disableClaudeAiConnectors: true)
  ...
Saves ~5.3k tokens per request. Undo any time with deadweight undo.

On my machine that's 17 unused plugins, 30 unused skills and one connector. The previous version moved skill folders into a backup. Now nothing on disk moves: it's a few keys in settings.json, and deadweight undo puts back exactly what was there before, including overrides you had already set yourself. --park-skills keeps the old behaviour if you prefer it.

When descriptions are being dropped, the report also does the budget math for you:

✗ 220 of 283 skills are listed without a description: the skill listing is full
    (~30.0k characters). Claude sees only their names, so it can't tell when to use them.
    Make room: hide what you don't use (deadweight fix), or set "skillListingBudgetFraction": 0.02 in settings.json
    (default 0.01; the extra room costs up to ~8.3k tokens per request).

What I'd still check by hand

  • Plugins that run hooks. deadweight won't disable them unless you pass --include-hooked, because a hook can do useful work that never shows up as a tool call. On my machine that's a memory plugin I'd rather keep.
  • Skills you use rarely. Claude Code deletes transcripts after 30 days by default (cleanupPeriodDays), so a skill you use once a quarter looks unused. --keep NAME protects it.
  • Servers you never signed in to. I had 36 of them still listing authenticate tools in every session. They all came from plugins, so disabling the plugin is what removes them.

A lot of this was worked out by people measuring their own listings in anthropics/claude-code#81081. It's worth a read if you want the details of the drop order.

If deadweight gets something wrong on your setup, run deadweight --json and open an issue. Those reports are the most useful thing anyone can send me.

title: RehearsalBench: Can AI Predict What Happens When You Change a Company?
description:
arXiv:2611.22480v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Organizations increasingly ask AI systems what will happen if they change how they operate: which work to automate, which team to resize, what a voice agent will do to waiting times. We introduce RehearsalBench, a benchmark that measures whether AI models can diagnose an operation, choose an intervention, and forecast its consequences. Each model is placed in a simulated bank contact center fitted to real call-level records, sees only what a manager would see, and submits a plan and forecasts that are then played out across 200 seeded futures and three plausible versions of the organization. Decisions are scored in dollars at the stakeholders' stated valuations; forecasts are scored on the effect of each change relative to doing nothing. Ten models made 280 attempts across 14 organizations. The best model, GPT-6 Astra, improved on doing nothing by 6.8% of the no-change cost and made 77% less forecast error than a forecaster who always predicts no effect. On average, every model forecast the direction of every specified effect correctly, but models erred on the size of the same effects in the same direction, overstating a voice agent's effect on repeat contacts about five-fold. No model ever recommended holding off when doing nothing was the right choice. To test external validity, twelve models forecast 33 real organizational changes with known outcomes. Under verdict rules fixed in advance, the benchmark's forecast ranking agreed with the real-world ranking (Spearman $\rho = 0.92$, 95% lower bound 0.50). We report the result alongside an inconclusive first test, the analysis choices made after outcomes were seen, and evidence that part of the agreement reflects how well models size their uncertainty.

title: The event loop: the mental model that changes everything
description:
There's a bug that turns up in every Node service sooner or later, and it almost always gets diagnosed wrong. The app serves fine, the logs are clean, the process is alive… and then it stops answering for a few seconds. htop shows one core at 100% and the other eleven watching, bored.

It isn't the database. It isn't the network. It's that somebody put CPU work on the only thread allowed to take requests.

To understand why that freezes everything, and why setTimeout(fn, 0) doesn't mean "now", you have to open the box. This lesson is the box.

One thread, and concurrent anyway

JavaScript runs on a single thread: one call stack, one instruction after another. Two lines of your code never run at the same time. Ever.

So how does Node serve thousands of connections? Because it doesn't serve them at once: it accepts them all and refuses to wait for any of them.

The difference is in what you do while waiting. In the classic thread-per-connection model, each request reserves a thread and leaves it staring at the ceiling until the database answers. Thousands of connections are thousands of threads, nearly all asleep. In Node, when an operation has to wait — reading a file, talking to the network, resolving DNS — you hand it off and move on. When the result is ready, someone tells you.

That "someone tells you" is literal: the operating system knows when a socket has data and notifies the process. libuv, which you met in the first lesson, translates those notifications from epoll, kqueue or Windows completion ports into something Node understands. And for the work the OS can't background on its own — some disk operations, DNS, cryptography — libuv keeps a thread pool of its own.

The concurrency is real. What doesn't exist is your code running twice at once.

If you come from Python, the comparison clears the ground: the GIL and the event loop are two answers to the same question. Python lets you write threads and then serialises them; Node doesn't let you write them and forces you to think in terms of waiting. Neither is better. They're two ways of saying "don't block".

The loop, from the inside

One moving part explains nothing. There are four, and all of them matter:

  • The call stack: where your code runs. One function on top of another. When it's empty, there's nothing to do right now.
  • libuv: where the operations waiting on something external live.
  • The macrotask queue: setTimeout callbacks, network events, disk reads. Things waiting their turn.
  • The microtask queue: promise continuations, and whatever you enqueue with queueMicrotask.

The loop does the same thing every time, in this order: if the stack is empty, drain the microtask queue completely, and only then take one macrotask. When that one finishes, drain microtasks again, and on it goes.

The asymmetry is the whole point: microtasks are drained entirely before moving to the next macrotask. If a microtask enqueues another microtask, that one goes into the same turn. That's where half the surprises come from.

It's easier to run than to describe:

console.log("1");
setTimeout(() => console.log("2"), 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("3"));
queueMicrotask(() => console.log("4"));
console.log("5");

1
5
3
4
2

Line by line: 1 is synchronous and leaves immediately. setTimeout runs nothing, it queues a macrotask. The promise and queueMicrotask queue microtasks. 5 comes out before any of them because the script is still running. When the module ends, the stack empties and the loop drains the microtasks in order: 3, then 4. Only then does the macrotask get its turn: 2.

3 before 4 isn't magic: it was queued first.

setImmediate is not setTimeout(0)

Node has a third way to ask for a turn, and the name lies: setImmediate doesn't run immediately, it runs in a phase of its own — the check phase — right after the poll phase.

setTimeout(() => console.log("timeout"), 0);
setImmediate(() => console.log("immediate"));

immediate
timeout

At the top level setImmediate comes first, and not by accident: a timer needs at least a millisecond, and the loop reaches the check phase before that. Don't turn it into law, though, because it depends on how long the process takes to start; on another machine you can see the opposite order.

Where it is deterministic is inside an I/O callback:

import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";

readFile("./package.json", "utf8").then(() => {
  setTimeout(() => console.log("timeout"), 0);
  setImmediate(() => console.log("immediate"));
});

immediate
timeout

There setImmediate always wins, because the check phase runs in the same turn of the loop, before the timers look at the clock again. If you read documentation promising a fixed order at the top level, be suspicious: it's the one point in the loop where the answer is arguable.

The queue Node adds on the side

Node also has process.nextTick, which is neither a promise nor a timer and has a queue of its own. It does what the name promises — it runs very soon — but its exact priority depends on where you enqueue it: at the top level it runs after promises, and inside a timer callback it runs before them.

Don't put it into the two-queue model, because it doesn't fit, and be suspicious of any tutorial that sells it as "the microtask that goes first" and stops there. Recognise it when you meet it in someone else's code and move on. What you do need to know is that it isn't a promise, and mixing them produces orderings you didn't write.

What this means in practice

Never block the loop

The call stack has one lane. If a synchronous task takes three hundred milliseconds, then for three hundred milliseconds nothing else runs: no callbacks, no promises, no new requests.

You don't have to take my word for it. Schedule a zero timer and block it on purpose:

const t0 = performance.now();
setTimeout(() => {
  console.log("setTimeout(0) delay:", (performance.now() - t0).toFixed(1), "ms");
}, 0);

const start = Date.now();
while (Date.now() < start + 300) {}

console.log("the blocking ended after", Date.now() - start, "ms");

the blocking ended after 300 ms
setTimeout(0) delay: 308.1 ms

The timer asked for a slot at zero milliseconds. It ran at 308.1, because the thread was busy. Your exact numbers will differ; the order of magnitude won't.

On a server that isn't an impatient timer: it's every request queueing behind whoever decided to parse a whole CSV in memory.

You can block it without a for

The example above is obvious: a three-hundred-millisecond synchronous loop. The case nobody spots produces the same effect with no long loop at all, just by keeping the microtask queue permanently full:

const start = Date.now();
setTimeout(() => console.log("the timer ran after", Date.now() - start, "ms"), 0);

let n = 0;
function step() {
  let x = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < 1e6; i++) x += i;
  n++;
  if (n < 50) Promise.resolve().then(step);
}
Promise.resolve().then(step);

the timer ran after 448 ms

Fifty chained microtasks, each with a small piece of synchronous work. The timer asked for a turn at zero milliseconds and ran at 448. There's no big while anywhere: there's a queue that never empties, and the loop won't take the next macrotask until it does.

That's the dark side of the rule you just learned. A .then that re-enqueues itself leaves the server unattended just as thoroughly as a two-hundred-megabyte JSON.parse.

setTimeout(fn, 0) isn't zero

Same thing, with no blocking involved: a zero timer takes about a millisecond, not zero.

const measure = (n) => {
  const t0 = performance.now();
  setTimeout(() => {
    console.log("round", n, (performance.now() - t0).toFixed(2), "ms");
    if (n < 3) measure(n + 1);
  }, 0);
};
measure(1);

round 1 1.26 ms
round 2 0.18 ms
round 3 1.14 ms

0 doesn't mean "immediately", it means "as soon as you can, and not before zero". The system has a clock resolution, the loop has to reach the timer phase, and there's work ahead in the queue. It's a few milliseconds that become a real problem the moment somebody treats setTimeout as a precision sleep.

The timer that won't let the process exit

One oddity that produces some of the best "why won't my script end?" moments: a pending timer keeps the process alive, and you can opt out.

setTimeout(() => console.log("this never runs"), 5000).unref();
setTimeout(() => console.log("this one does"), 0);
console.log("script ends");

script ends
this one does

The process finishes in hundredths of a second, not five seconds. unref() means "don't count on me to keep the process running": if it's the only thing pending, Node exits. It's used for cleanup timers, caches and keepalives that shouldn't stop the program from finishing.

Chunk it before you delegate it

Before shipping the work to another thread there's a cheaper option: cut it into chunks and let the loop serve between one and the next. The request takes the same total time, but the server keeps answering.

With one trap that costs an afternoon: the yield has to be a macrotask. Chaining promises doesn't release the loop, because microtasks are drained in full before the next macrotask is even considered.

const start = Date.now();
setTimeout(() => console.log("the timer ran after", Date.now() - start, "ms"), 0);

const chunks = (n) => {
  if (n === 0) return Promise.resolve();
  let x = 0;
  for (let j = 0; j < 1e6; j++) x += j;
  return Promise.resolve().then(() => chunks(n - 1));
};

chunks(100).then(() => console.log("the work finished after", Date.now() - start, "ms"));

the work finished after 892 ms
the timer ran after 898 ms

A hundred rounds chained with .then and the timer still runs after all the work. Chaining microtasks hands the turn to other microtasks, not to I/O.

Change that one line for a macrotask and the story changes. Node has a module for this, node:timers/promises, which exports setTimeout, setInterval, setImmediate and scheduler in promise form so you don't wrap callbacks by hand:

import { scheduler } from "node:timers/promises";

const start = Date.now();
setTimeout(() => console.log("the timer ran after", Date.now() - start, "ms"), 0);

const chunks = (n) => {
  if (n === 0) return Promise.resolve();
  let x = 0;
  for (let j = 0; j < 1e6; j++) x += j;
  return scheduler.yield().then(() => chunks(n - 1));
};

chunks(100).then(() => console.log("the work finished after", Date.now() - start, "ms"));

the timer ran after 6 ms
the work finished after 796 ms

scheduler.yield() does exactly what the name says: it hands control back to the loop and gives it back to you afterwards. Older Node versions don't have it; the equivalent is setImmediate from the same module, or setTimeout(resolve, 0) if you're working with callbacks.

And look at what doesn't change: the total work is the same, 892 ms in one case and 796 in the other. Yielding neither gives nor takes away speed in any meaningful way; what changes is whether the timer runs at 898 milliseconds or at 6. The difference isn't performance, it's whether the server answers while it works.

Pick the chunk big enough that the round trip doesn't dominate, and small enough that the worst wait for a request stays acceptable.

Two clarifications that save confusion:

  • This is not parallelism. Same core, same work, same total time, just spread out. It stops the server going mute; it doesn't make it faster.
  • A generator's yield doesn't do this. It pauses the function, not the loop: whatever drives the generator still needs a macrotask between steps. It's the same trap with a syntax layer on top, and generators are a different story this course doesn't cover.

The emergency exit

When the work can't be chunked — or when chunking isn't enough — the answer isn't "optimise the loop": it's getting it off the thread. worker_threads gives you real threads and cluster gives you processes. Neither is a silver bullet: both cost startup, both force you to move data between contexts, both add failure surface.

That has its own section later in the course. Here, the rule is enough: the loop doesn't get blocked, the work gets moved.

Predict the order before you run it

This is the lesson's exam. Read it, write the order down, then run it:

console.log("A");
setTimeout(() => console.log("B"), 0);
Promise.resolve()
  .then(() => console.log("C"))
  .then(() => console.log("D"));
queueMicrotask(() => console.log("E"));
console.log("F");

A
F
C
E
D
B

If you got D and E wrong, that's fine: it's the detail almost everyone misses. C is the first microtask and it enqueues D at the end of the queue, behind E, which was already waiting. The order doesn't depend on when the promise was created, but on when each continuation was queued.

If you got B wrong, go back to the loop section. And if you got everything right, you already have the model most people writing Node don't have.

Common problems

The server stops responding for a few seconds, then recovers

CPU work on the main thread: JSON.parse on a huge response, a for over a million items, a regular expression that runs away, a readFileSync on a request path. All of it blocks the loop exactly like the while above.

setTimeout(fn, 0) is delayed far more than expected

Either there's synchronous work ahead, or there are many macrotasks queued. The timer isn't broken: the loop is getting there when it can.

The interval overlaps itself

setInterval doesn't wait for your callback to finish: it schedules the next turn anyway. With a callback taking 250 ms and an interval of 100, you end up with three executions at once.

let n = 0;
let running = 0;
const id = setInterval(() => {
  running++;
  console.log("tick", ++n, "· running:", running);
  setTimeout(() => {
    running--;
  }, 250);
  if (n === 3) clearInterval(id);
}, 100);

tick 1 · running: 1
tick 2 · running: 2
tick 3 · running: 3

If you don't want that, don't use setInterval: chain a setTimeout at the end of the work, so the next turn is scheduled once the previous one finished. And when the callback is synchronous but slow, the interval doesn't catch up either: gaps go from 100 to 250 ms and continue at 100.

One detail the example takes for granted: setInterval returns an identifier you cancel with clearInterval, and setTimeout with clearTimeout. Without that, the timer stays alive as long as the process does.

A huge delay fires immediately

A timer's delay is a signed 32-bit integer. Ask for more and it doesn't wait: it warns you and sets it to 1 millisecond.

setTimeout(() => console.log("fired"), 2147483648);

TimeoutOverflowWarning: 2147483648 does not fit into a 32-bit signed integer.
Timeout duration was set to 1.
fired

The first line arrives prefixed with (node:PID), which changes on every run. It's the kind of bug that shows up when somebody configures a "one day" timeout from a computed number: the maximum is 2,147,483,647 ms, about 24.8 days, and above that the timer becomes immediate. The exact opposite of what was asked for.

A promise that should run first runs later

Check whether a new microtask is in the way, and whether process.nextTick is in the mix. The order follows a rule, but not the one the code's shape suggests.

A long job seems to freeze the server

If the work is CPU, no timer fixes it: the thread is busy and everything else waits. Chunking and yielding eases it; moving it off the thread solves it.

What you take from this lesson

  • JavaScript runs on one thread. The concurrency is in the waiting, not in the code.
  • libuv hands the waiting to the operating system and reports back when there's a result.
  • The loop drains all microtasks before taking another macrotask.
  • Promises and queueMicrotask are microtasks; timers and I/O callbacks are macrotasks.
  • process.nextTick exists, isn't a promise, and doesn't fit the two-queue model.
  • setTimeout(fn, 0) takes about a millisecond, and much longer when the thread is busy.
  • Blocking the thread doesn't slow the server down: it stops it.
  • CPU work gets moved off the thread, not optimised inside it.

With this you can read any interleaved log without assuming the order is the one it looks like. Which helps, because the next lesson is about promises: the mechanism that creates the microtasks you just learned to order.

Never stop coding!

title: Sub-Meter Canopy Height Synthesis from Sentinel-2 via Anchored Residual Flow
description:
arXiv:2611.22636v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Canopy height models (CHMs) - per-pixel maps of vegetation top height - are essential for forest carbon accounting, wildfire fuel mapping, and tree-level ecology, yet sub-meter CHMs require airborne LiDAR refreshed on multi-year national cycles. We produce 0.5 m CHMs from free 10 m Sentinel-2 imagery, a 20$\times$ cross-modal super-resolution task where optical reflectance must predict geometric height it does not directly observe. Motivated by the perception-distortion trade-off, we derive two operating points with shared conditioning. A deterministic regressor (Anchor) targets low distortion; a conditional flow matching model, trained on the Anchor's residual in a learned CHM latent space (AR-flow), targets perceptual fidelity. Trained on 197k LiDAR-paired tiles spanning 69 ecoregions across the contiguous United States and evaluated on 2,530 held-out tiles against eight baselines, the Anchor achieves 2.83 m MAE using only free satellite input. The AR-flow reduces sliced Wasserstein distance from the Anchor's 1.13 to 0.208, at a higher MAE of 3.68 m. Crown-scale statistics improve, but strict individual-tree detection remains weak: generated sub-pixel detail represents plausible structure rather than measured individual trees. Quarterly continental refresh becomes tractable, letting satellite monitoring inform timing and extent for more expensive data acquisitions.

title: How Agent Anomaly Detection scores on benchmarks we didn't write
description: Agent Anomaly Detection (AAD) provides asynchronous, low-latency monitoring for AI agents by analyzing OpenTelemetry traces and logs to flag goal hijacks and tool misuse. Tested across five public security benchmarks, AAD successfully caught 87% of harmful instructions carried out by agents without adding runtime latency. Developers can integrate AAD alongside semantic governance and strict tool limits as part of a defense-in-depth strategy to secure agentic applications.

title: Video recordings and play behaviour annotations of group-housed dairy calves on two Dutch farms
description:
arXiv:2611.21706v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Play is used as an indicator of positive welfare in dairy calves, but openly available video of group-housed calves with individual behaviour annotations is scarce. We describe video from four camera deployments of about one week each in group pens of dairy calves on two farms in the Netherlands: a research and teaching dairy farm (2024 and 2025) and a commercial dairy farm (2024). The recordings comprise 1,173 video files spanning 651 h. For eight observation days, trained observers coded calf behaviour continuously in Noldus The Observer XT with an 18-item ethogram of play and other behaviours, covering 104 h of video, 90 h of which have every calf in the pen coded. The release also contains 1.1 million decoded frames from seven annotated sessions, a per-frame timestamp read by optical character recognition from the camera clock burned into each frame, per-calf segmentation tracks and per-calf frame-level play labels. The data support studies of calf behaviour and welfare and the development and evaluation of automated behaviour recognition.

title: Docusaurus for Beginners: Turn Markdown Into a Beautiful Documentation Site
description:
Docusaurus is Meta's open-source tool for building documentation websites, and it is the default choice for an enormous number of open-source projects. You write Markdown, and Docusaurus turns it into a fast, searchable, versioned docs site with navigation, dark mode, and a blog — all with almost no configuration.

The reason so many projects use it is simple: docs live next to the code, in Markdown, and the site builds itself. You do not design a docs site; you write docs, and Docusaurus handles the rest.

npx create-docusaurus@latest my-docs classic
cd my-docs
npm start

A doc page is just Markdown with front matter:

---
title: "Getting Started"
sidebar_position: 1
---

# Getting Started

Install the package, then run the command below.


bash
npm install my-package

Docusaurus is a great fit for project documentation, API guides, tutorials, and any site where content is mostly Markdown. Versioning lets you keep docs for v1 and v2 side by side, and the built-in search works without a server.

The limits are narrow. Docusaurus is a docs site generator, not a general app framework — if you need custom interactivity everywhere, you will fight it. Heavy customization of the theme takes real React work. And for a simple blog, a lighter tool may be enough.

But if you maintain an open-source project or a product with real documentation, start with Docusaurus. Your users will thank you, and your docs will finally stay up to date.
