title: EgoLink: Egocentric Language-Vision Interactive Network Knowledge Challenge Summary
description:
arXiv:2611.21690v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The EgoLink Challenge at ACM Multimedia 2026 benchmarks egocentric multimodal intelligence linking first-person perception, social reasoning, and interactive action. Unlike benchmarks centered on visible objects and activities, EgoLink evaluates whether models can interpret emotional and social cues, resolve visually grounded references, and convert user requests into verified tool-mediated actions. Its two tracks cover social reasoning in egocentric video and interactive agents that complete service tasks through dialogue, tool use, and closed-loop execution. Together, they test whether perception, reasoning, and decision-making remain coupled under both offline question answering and state-changing interaction. We highlight a multi-stage Track 1 data pipeline for multiple-choice question (MCQ) generation, chain-of-thought generation, automatic quality grading, and video-contribution filtering. We summarize the task design, evaluation metrics, rules, leaderboards, and representative solutions. The benchmark combines objective answer scoring with process- and result-based evaluation, enabling analysis of both final correctness and execution quality. The best Track 1 system achieved 0.9263 accuracy, while the best Track 2 system achieved 0.844 joint success and 0.916 micro accuracy. Participant reports reveal a shared principle: strong systems make intermediate evidence explicit through candidate verification, option-robust reasoning, scenario-aware planning, tool canonicalization, and state-aware correction before answering or acting. These findings highlight the importance of process verification and evidence-grounded reasoning for reliable egocentric multimodal intelligence.

title: FCP: Formal Context Protocol for Verifying LLM-Generated Artifacts
description:
arXiv:2611.21679v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: When a language model writes both an artifact and the tests meant to check it, a passing test is weak evidence: one misreading of the request yields a faulty artifact and a check that accepts it. We present the Formal Context Protocol (FCP), which checks AI-generated artifacts against the request itself. FCP separates conformance (does the artifact satisfy a formal reading of a requirement?), which model checkers and SMT solvers decide, from fidelity (does the reading mean what the prose means?), which has no decision procedure but is refutable by a concrete witness. Eight ways a proof can falsely certify a requirement each become a mechanical check that returns a witness, and what no machine can settle becomes concrete questions for the request's author. Adapters place hardware, text, agents and code on the same engines. On four hardware designs, trusting AI-written assertions certified 23% of violated requirements, and FCP certified none. On ten code tasks, code from three language models passed its own tests and violated the request every time. Trusting the tests certified all 33 violations, and FCP certified three. Agreement among models, readings or tests did not imply correctness.

title: Charge only for successful results in a pay-per-event Apify Actor (and test it locally)
description:
If you sell an Apify Actor with pay-per-event (PPE) pricing, the most important line of code is the one that decides when a user gets charged. Get it wrong and users pay for timeouts, 404s and empty pages, and they leave a one-star review. Get it right and the pricing sells itself: "you only pay for results you actually got".

This post shows the pattern in about 30 lines of Node.js, and, more usefully, how to test the charging locally before you publish, using two SDK environment variables that are easy to miss.

Everything below was run today with apify 3.8.0 on Node 22.

The rule

  • Success: save the row and charge one event, in the same call.
  • Failure: still save the row (so the user can see what went wrong), but don't charge.
  • Budget hit: if the user's "max cost per run" is reached, stop cleanly instead of doing work nobody pays for.

In current 3.x versions of the SDK, Actor.pushData() takes an optional event name as its second argument. That one call stores the item and charges the event, and the result tells you whether the user's budget is used up.

The code

package.json:

{
  "name": "ppe-demo",
  "type": "module",
  "private": true,
  "scripts": { "start": "node src/main.js" },
  "dependencies": { "apify": "^3.7.2" }
}

src/main.js, an Actor that fetches each URL and returns its <title>:

import { Actor, log } from 'apify';

const CHARGE_EVENT = 'result'; // must match the event name in your PPE pricing

await Actor.init();
const { urls = [], timeoutSecs = 20 } = (await Actor.getInput()) ?? {};
if (!urls.length) await Actor.fail('Input "urls" must be a non-empty list.');

let charged = 0;
for (const url of urls) {
  const base = { url, fetchedAt: new Date().toISOString() };
  try {
    const res = await fetch(new URL(url), { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(timeoutSecs * 1000) });
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
    const html = await res.text();
    const title = html.match(/<title[^>]*>([\s\S]*?)<\/title>/i)?.[1]?.trim() ?? null;

    // Success: save the row AND charge one event, in one call.
    const { eventChargeLimitReached } = await Actor.pushData({ ...base, status: 'ok', title }, CHARGE_EVENT);
    charged += 1;
    if (eventChargeLimitReached) { log.info('User budget reached, stopping.'); break; }
  } catch (err) {
    // Failure: save the row so the user can see why, but don't charge.
    await Actor.pushData({ ...base, status: 'failed', title: null, error: String(err.message ?? err) });
  }
}
log.info(`Charged ${charged} of ${urls.length} URL(s).`);
await Actor.exit();

A few details worth copying:

  • new URL(url) throws on garbage input ("not a url"), so invalid input falls into the free catch branch automatically.
  • AbortSignal.timeout() turns slow sites into a clean, uncharged failure instead of a hung run.
  • Actor.fail() on empty input happens before any billable work.
  • Failed rows have the same shape as good ones (title: null plus an error), so the user's table view and exports don't break.

Testing the charging locally

Create the input file at storage/key_value_stores/default/INPUT.json:

{ "urls": ["https://example.com", "https://httpbin.org/status/404", "not a url", "https://www.iana.org/help/example-domains"] }

Then run with two environment variables:

npm install
ACTOR_TEST_PAY_PER_EVENT=true ACTOR_USE_CHARGING_LOG_DATASET=true npm start
  • ACTOR_TEST_PAY_PER_EVENT=true makes the SDK behave as if the Actor had PPE pricing (local runs only; the SDK refuses it on the platform).
  • ACTOR_USE_CHARGING_LOG_DATASET=true writes every charge to a local dataset named charging_log, so you can see exactly what would have been billed.

Output from my run:

INFO  Charged 2 of 4 URL(s).

storage/datasets/default/ holds all four rows:

{"url": "https://example.com", "status": "ok", "title": "Example Domain"}
{"url": "https://httpbin.org/status/404", "status": "failed", "title": null, "error": "HTTP 404"}
{"url": "not a url", "status": "failed", "title": null, "error": "Invalid URL"}
{"url": "https://www.iana.org/help/example-domains", "status": "ok", "title": "Example Domains"}

(fetchedAt removed for brevity.) And storage/datasets/charging_log/ holds exactly two entries, one per successful row:

{"eventName": "result", "eventTitle": "Unknown event 'result'", "eventPriceUsd": 1, "chargedCount": 1, "timestamp": "..."}
{"eventName": "result", "eventTitle": "Unknown event 'result'", "eventPriceUsd": 1, "chargedCount": 1, "timestamp": "..."}

The 404 and the invalid URL are in the dataset but not in the charging log. That's the whole point.

Locally the SDK doesn't know your real prices, so an unconfigured event shows up as "Unknown event" at a placeholder $1. Only the count matters here.

Testing the budget stop

Users can set a maximum cost per run. Simulate it with ACTOR_MAX_TOTAL_CHARGE_USD. With the placeholder $1 per event, a $1 cap allows exactly one charge:

rm -rf storage/datasets
ACTOR_TEST_PAY_PER_EVENT=true ACTOR_USE_CHARGING_LOG_DATASET=true ACTOR_MAX_TOTAL_CHARGE_USD=1 npm start

INFO  User budget reached, stopping.
INFO  Charged 1 of 4 URL(s).

The run stops right after the first paid result instead of fetching the remaining pages for free.

Before you publish

  1. In Console, open Publication > Monetization > Pay per event and create an event whose name exactly matches CHARGE_EVENT (result here). A typo means nothing gets charged.
  2. Say in your README what counts as a chargeable result and what's free. Users read it, and it's the honest thing to do.
  3. Check the price of the synthetic Actor-start event in the same screen. Keep it tiny (or zero) if your promise is "pay only for results", otherwise every empty run still costs the user something.

Want the full template?

The snippet above is all you need to get the pattern right. If you'd rather start from a complete project (input/dataset/output schemas that the Store accepts, a Dockerfile, unit tests and a README skeleton), we packaged ours as the Pay-Per-Event Actor Starter Kit (MIT, $9 one-time): details · buy.

It's the same pattern we use in our own Actors at apify.com/siftwright. If you're choosing between per-result and subscription pricing for a data API, we wrote up the break-even maths with real numbers.

Questions or corrections: support@siftwright.com.

title: How to design agentic tools for work
description: The Gemini Enterprise team shares their approach to making complex, multi-agent workflows feel simple, intuitive, and trustworthy.

title: From Constraints to Causality: Petri net Encodings for Explaining Binary Neural Network Inference
description:
arXiv:2611.22396v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Binary Neural Networks (BNNs) are attractive for resource-constrained hardware and on-device components in autonomous systems. However, their discrete, non-linear behaviour makes them difficult to analyse and trust in safety-relevant settings. Existing approaches based on SAT and Satisfiability Modulo Theories can verify a BNN's input-output properties, but treat it as a monolithic constraint system, which reveal only whether a property holds and not how the computation reaches its result. In this paper, we present an early work that provides a complementary, discrete-event view. We give a compositional translation from the inference semantics of a fixed, trained BNN to a 1-safe Petri net (PN), where each computation step is an explicit transition, so that a firing sequence is a causal trace of the BNN's decision. On a worked example, we establish faithfulness via exhaustive input-output equivalence against a reference implementation, and show how contrasting firing sequences localises where a single-feature change alters the prediction. Finally, we outline two directions this opens: a correctness-of-translation theorem, and a causal-trace analysis of where two trained BNNs diverge in their decisions, a structural question that constraint-based verifiers cannot express.

title: DeltaHarness: Self-Evolving Harnesses for Resource-Adaptive Tool Execution
description:
arXiv:2611.21688v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Tool-using agents rely on execution harnesses to organize and schedule tool operations. The same task and resource description can conceal runtime conditions that reverse the latency ordering of valid execution plans. Resolving this uncertainty requires firsthand execution in the target setting. We introduce DeltaHarness, an execution-guided policy-search method that adapts agent harnesses from cold-start measurements. Its QHI loop uses the observed response to update runtime dispatch, revise physical plans, and select experiments for later proposals. An independent confirmation panel controls policy replacement. With fixed dispatch, a revised materialization policy reduces complete-delivery latency by 30.0% on one video-editing task across three fresh pairs. On held-out tasks, the evolved policies reduce latency by 8.2% relative to the best fixed plan in one seed and by 4.6% relative to the initial proposal in another.

title: OAK-Mind: Zero-Training Mental Health Change Inference from Passive Sensing via Knowledge-Grounded Multi-Agent LLMs
description:
arXiv:2611.22248v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Wearable and smartphone sensors capture behavioral signals associated with mental health, yet inferring mental health outcomes from these signals has traditionally relied on supervised models requiring labeled data and offering limited insight into their predictions. Large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities to reason over behavioral evidence, but existing LLM-based approaches to passive sensing have largely continued to rely on task-specific fine-tuning or sensor-specific pretraining. In this paper, we introduce \textbf{OAK-Mind}, a zer\textbf{O}-training, multi-\textbf{A}gent, \textbf{K}nowledge-grounded LLM pipeline for inferring mental health changes from passive sensing data. The pipeline organizes sensing data into behavioral dimensions including sleep, physical activity, location mobility, and smartphone use, and orchestrates specialized agents grounded in mental health literature to interpret longitudinal behavioral changes. It synthesizes their assessments and applies questionnaire-based symptom rating to infer changes relative to an individual's baseline assessment with human-readable rationale grounded in observed behavioral patterns and domain knowledge. Across datasets and prediction tasks, while without task-specific training, OAK-Mind achieves comparable or better performance than the most predictive supervised baselines trained on additional labeled samples. It also demonstrate consistent improvement upon direct prompting across four tested LLM backbones. Ablation analyses support the benefits of combining behavioral interpretation with symptom rating, distributing analysis across domain-specific agents, and incorporating domain knowledge. Our findings highlight the potential of knowledge-grounded, multi-agent LLMs for training-free inference of mental health changes from passive sensing data.

title: How to deploy an AI agent using Google ADK in Agent Runtime and register it in Gemini Enterprise
description:
John BullaFollow

💼 Sr. Cloud Solutions Architect - Cloud, Data & AI | Pre-Sales Architect | Cloud Evangelist 🏆 Google Developer Expert | AWS Community Builder | Alibaba Cloud MVP | Ex-Microsoft MVP

✋ Note: This article was originally published on my blog Wiki Cloud.

Introduction

The development of artificial intelligence agents is changing how organizations access information, automate tasks, and improve their business processes. However, building an agent is only the first step. To make the most of its potential, we need an environment where it can run continuously, serve different users, and support important requirements such as security, scalability, and monitoring.

In this context, deploying AI agents to the cloud allows us to move from a solution developed locally to an enterprise application capable of supporting an organization's needs.

In the previous article, we built a Corporate Policies Assistant using Google ADK, Gemini, Google Drive, and Streamlit. We learned how to query corporate documents using an in-memory lexical RAG system and generate natural-language answers with references to their original sources.

Now we'll take the next step: deploy our agent to Google Cloud Agent Runtime, a managed service that allows us to run it in the cloud without relying on our local computer, and then integrate it with Gemini Enterprise so users can access the assistant through an enterprise platform.

We won't rebuild the application or the tools developed previously. Instead, we'll focus on preparing the agent for deployment, validating its operation in the cloud, and publishing it in Gemini Enterprise.

For this hands-on exercise, we'll continue using Windows, PowerShell, Python 3.12, and the same project repository. Both Spanish and English versions of the project are available in the repository.

Solution objectives and architecture

The goal of this exercise is to continue developing our Corporate Policies Assistant by reusing the agent built with Google ADK, deploying it to Google Cloud Agent Runtime, and then integrating it with Gemini Enterprise.

To achieve this, we'll package the agent as an installable Python distribution so that its logic and dependencies can run in a managed cloud environment. Google Drive will remain our document repository, while Gemini, through Vertex AI, will interpret queries and generate responses.


Figure 1 – Target architecture of the Corporate Policies Assistant.

In the previous article, we tested the assistant locally in three ways: Streamlit, through a custom web interface; ADK Web, which allowed us to interact with the agent and observe how its tools were executed; and ADK CLI, which we used to submit queries directly from the command line.

These tests helped us validate the integration between the different components and confirm that the agent could retrieve information from corporate policies through RAG, generate natural-language answers, and provide references to the documents it consulted.

In this second part, we'll evolve the architecture without changing its core functionality. Google Cloud Agent Runtime will host the agent in a managed environment that supports availability, scalability, and monitoring. Gemini Enterprise will add a new access layer for business users, allowing them to interact with the assistant without using development tools directly.

In this way, we'll preserve the solution built previously while making it available to more users across the organization.

Google ADK will continue to coordinate the conversation and execute the policy search tool, while our RAG system will retrieve relevant information from documents stored in Google Drive. Gemini will use that content as context to produce grounded responses. This integration takes us from an agent validated on a local computer to a solution accessible through Gemini Enterprise.

Architecture note: Connecting Streamlit to the remote agent is presented as a possible future enhancement. The Streamlit integration developed in the previous article ran the agent locally.

Implementation phases

To deploy our Corporate Policies Assistant to Google Cloud and integrate it with Gemini Enterprise, we'll follow seven stages. As shown below, we'll first prepare the environment and package the agent, then deploy it to Agent Runtime, validate it with remote tests, and finally publish it in Gemini Enterprise for authorized users within the organization.


Figure 2 – Agent implementation and deployment phases.

Prerequisites

Before continuing, we'll assume that the local application is already responding correctly, that the policy documents are stored in an authorized Google Drive folder, and that the project's virtual environment has the dependencies listed in requirements.txt installed.

For deployment, we'll need a Google Cloud project with billing enabled, Google Cloud CLI, permissions to create Agent Runtime resources, a service account for runtime execution, and a Cloud Storage bucket for temporary artifacts. The user performing the deployment must also have permission to use the service account.

Variable configuration

Before configuring the Google Cloud resources, we'll define a few PowerShell variables to use throughout the deployment. These variables identify our project, region, storage bucket, service account, and Google Cloud user. This makes the commands easier to run without repeatedly entering the same values.

Simply replace the placeholders with the values for your Google Cloud environment.

# Google Cloud project
$PROJECT_ID = "YOUR_PROJECT_ID"

# Deployment region
$REGION = "europe-west1"

# Cloud Storage bucket
$BUCKET_NAME = "YOUR_STAGING_BUCKET_NAME"

# Agent service account
$SA_NAME = "YOUR_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_NAME"
$SA_EMAIL = "$SA_NAME@$PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com"

# Staging bucket URI
$STAGING_BUCKET = "gs://$BUCKET_NAME"

# Google Cloud user
$USER_EMAIL = "YOUR_USER@YOUR_DOMAIN.com"

Select the GCP project and configure ADC

Before deploying our agent, we need to configure access to the Google Cloud project we'll be using. Open a PowerShell terminal in Visual Studio Code and run the following commands to verify the Google Cloud CLI installation, sign in, and select the project.

gcloud --version
gcloud auth login
gcloud config set project $PROJECT_ID
gcloud auth application-default login
gcloud auth application-default set-quota-project $PROJECT_ID

We'll use Application Default Credentials (ADC), a Google Cloud authentication mechanism that allows Python applications and libraries to obtain credentials automatically when accessing Google services.

The two sign-in commands serve different purposes: gcloud auth login authenticates the Google Cloud CLI, while gcloud auth application-default login configures the ADC credentials used by our deployment script. Finally, setting the quota project associates API usage with the selected project and helps avoid warnings about user credentials without an associated quota project, provided we have the necessary permissions.

Enable APIs

Once access to the project is configured, we'll enable the APIs needed to deploy and run the agent on Agent Runtime and integrate it with Gemini Enterprise. These APIs provide access to the AI, storage, authentication, and enterprise resources used by our solution.

Run the following command from PowerShell:

gcloud services enable `
  aiplatform.googleapis.com `
  storage.googleapis.com `
  cloudresourcemanager.googleapis.com `
  iam.googleapis.com `
  iamcredentials.googleapis.com `
  drive.googleapis.com `
  discoveryengine.googleapis.com `
  logging.googleapis.com `
  --project=$PROJECT_ID

This command enables the services required for Vertex AI and Agent Runtime, storing deployment artifacts in Cloud Storage, managing identities and permissions with IAM, reading documents from Google Drive, and integrating our agent with Gemini Enterprise. We also enable Cloud Logging so we can review execution logs.

Keep in mind that enabling APIs does not automatically grant access permissions. We'll configure those separately using the appropriate IAM roles.

Create the staging bucket in Cloud Storage

Next, we'll create a Google Cloud Storage bucket to serve as temporary storage during the deployment to Agent Runtime. It will hold the Python packages and artifacts needed to prepare and deploy our agent.

gcloud storage buckets create $STAGING_BUCKET `
  --project=$PROJECT_ID `
  --location=$REGION `
  --uniform-bucket-level-access

In this example, we'll use europe-west1 and enable uniform bucket-level access, which allows access permissions to be managed through IAM. Replace the example bucket name with a globally unique name and the project placeholder with your actual project ID.

If the bucket already exists, there's no need to create it again. We only need to confirm that we have the permissions required to use it during deployment.

Create and configure the service account

With storage ready, we'll create a service account for our Corporate Policies Assistant to use when it runs on Google Cloud Agent Runtime. This gives the agent its own identity for accessing authorized Google Cloud services without relying on the developer's personal credentials.

Create the service account

Run the following PowerShell command using the variables defined earlier:

gcloud iam service-accounts create $SA_NAME `
  --display-name="Corporate Policies Agent Runtime" `
  --project=$PROJECT_ID

This creates the service account used by the deployed agent. Its email address follows this pattern: YOUR_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_NAME@YOUR_PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com.

Next, we'll grant the roles/aiplatform.user role so the agent can use the Vertex AI services required to interact with Gemini.

gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding $PROJECT_ID `
  --member="serviceAccount:$SA_EMAIL" `
  --role="roles/aiplatform.user"

We use this role in the demo to simplify execution. For production environments, we should evaluate more specific permissions and follow the principle of least privilege.

Configure Google Drive access

Besides interacting with Gemini, our agent needs to read the documents stored in Google Drive. To enable this, share the corporate policies folder with the service account's email address and grant Viewer access, provided that your Google Workspace policies allow it.

Remember that Google Drive permissions are managed separately from Google Cloud IAM roles. Assigning roles/aiplatform.user does not automatically grant access to documents.

In the previous article, we used a JSON credentials file to run the agent locally. This time, we'll use the identity attached to Agent Runtime and Application Default Credentials (ADC), avoiding private keys in the deployment package.

This gives our agent a dedicated identity for accessing authorized services and running more securely in Google Cloud.

Configure IAM permissions for the Google Cloud user

After configuring the service account, we need to ensure that our Google Cloud user has permission to deploy the agent and run tests from PowerShell.

It's important to distinguish these identities: the service account is used when the agent runs, while our user prepares the deployment, creates the Agent Runtime resource, and verifies that it works.

For this lab, we'll use the following roles:

IAM role Description
roles/aiplatform.user Allows the user to access Vertex AI and Agent Runtime services, interact with Gemini models, and send queries to deployed agents.
roles/aiplatform.sessionUser Allows the user to create and manage conversation sessions with agents deployed on Agent Runtime.

Run these commands from PowerShell:

gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding $PROJECT_ID `
  --member="user:$USER_EMAIL" `
  --role="roles/aiplatform.user"

gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding $PROJECT_ID `
  --member="user:$USER_EMAIL" `
  --role="roles/aiplatform.sessionUser"

Project structure and deployment-specific files

Before moving on to deployment in Google Cloud Agent Runtime, let's briefly review the project structure and identify the files we'll need for this stage. Since we already developed the agent and its main components in the previous article, we don't need to change its architecture or rebuild its functionality.

We'll focus on the files responsible for creating the Python package, deploying the agent, and checking that it works once it's running in the cloud.

To make the process easier to follow, here's a simplified view of the repository highlighting the deployment and test files.

google-adk-gemini-corporate-policies-agent/
├── requirements.txt
├── sources_en/
│   ├── .env
│   ├── corporate_agent/          # Previously developed agent code
│   ├── pyproject.toml            # Wheel package metadata
│   ├── deployment/
│   │   ├── deploy_agent.py
│   │   └── runtime_resource.txt  # Created after deployment
│   └── test/
│       └── test_runtime.py
└── sources_es/                   # Equivalent Spanish version
File Description
sources_en/pyproject.toml Defines the installable corporate-policies-agent package and specifies that corporate_agent must be included.
sources_en/deployment/deploy_agent.py Validates the environment, builds the wheel, deploys AdkApp, and saves the remote resource path.
sources_en/deployment/runtime_resource.txt Output file containing the full path of the created resource.
sources_es/test/test_runtime.py Retrieves the remote resource reference, connects to Agent Runtime, and sends test queries.
requirements.txt Contains the project's dependencies; the script also specifies those required by the runtime.

Environment variables specific to this stage

With our project ready, the next step is to review the environment variables used to deploy the agent to Google Cloud Agent Runtime and verify that it works. These settings identify the project and region where the agent will run, the resources it needs, and how it will authenticate to Google Cloud services.

Since we configured the variables for local development in the previous article, we'll focus only on those related to cloud deployment and testing.

Variable Description
GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT Identifies the Google Cloud project where we'll deploy our agent.
AGENT_RUNTIME_LOCATION Defines the Google Cloud region where the agent will run. In this demo, we'll use europe-west1.
AGENT_RUNTIME_STAGING_BUCKET Specifies the Cloud Storage bucket used to temporarily store deployment files. Its format is gs://YOUR_STAGING_BUCKET.
AGENT_RUNTIME_SERVICE_ACCOUNT Contains the email address of the service account the agent will use to access authorized Google Cloud resources.
GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_VERTEXAI Indicates that the agent will connect to Gemini through Vertex AI. We'll set it to TRUE in Agent Runtime.
GEMINI_MODEL Specifies the Gemini model used to process queries and generate answers. Our project uses gemini-3.5-flash-lite as its default, provided the model is available to the project.
GEMINI_VERTEX_LOCATION Specifies the location used for Gemini model inference. In this example, we'll use global, which can differ from the Agent Runtime deployment region.
DRIVE_AUTH_MODE Controls how the agent authenticates to Google Drive. We'll use adc to rely on the runtime's identity without including a JSON credentials file.
AGENT_RUNTIME_RESOURCE Optionally specifies the deployed agent resource for remote tests. If omitted, test_runtime.py can also read it from deployment/runtime_resource.txt.

We'll also retain GOOGLE_DRIVE_FOLDER_ID and RAG_REFRESH_INTERVAL_SECONDS, which were introduced in the previous article. The first identifies the Google Drive folder containing our corporate policies, while the second sets the refresh interval for the agent's RAG index.

Packaging the agent with pyproject.toml

Before deploying our Corporate Policies Assistant to Google Cloud Agent Runtime, we need to prepare its code so it can be installed and run in the cloud. To do that, we'll use a wheel package (.whl), a Python distribution format that bundles an application's code and metadata into an installable file.

Wheel packages make it easier to distribute and install Python applications because they contain the files the target environment needs to recognize and import their modules. In our project, this mechanism will let us deploy the corporate_agent code to Agent Runtime and ensure its components can be imported correctly during execution.

To build the wheel, we'll use pyproject.toml, located in both the sources_en/ and sources_es/ directories. This file contains the configuration needed to build and distribute our agent as a Python package.

It defines setuptools as the build tool, sets the package name to corporate-policies-agent, and specifies that the corporate_agent module must be included, along with its main files such as __init__.py, agent.py, and drive_rag.py.

This allows Python to recognize and install our agent in the remote environment without manually copying files or changing the imports implemented earlier.

Prepare the packaging tools

Before deployment, let's make sure our virtual environment has the tools required to build the wheel package.

From the Visual Studio Code PowerShell terminal, run:

cd C:\Projects\google-adk-gemini-corporate-policies-agent
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
python -m pip install --upgrade setuptools wheel
python -m pip check

These commands activate the virtual environment, install or update the packaging tools, and check for dependency conflicts.

Generate the wheel during deployment

We won't need to build the wheel manually, because deployment/deploy_agent.py already handles this task, as we'll see in the next section.

When executed, the script temporarily builds the .whl file, verifies that it includes the agent's main files, and adds it to the dependencies installed in Agent Runtime.

This also helps ensure compatibility between our Windows development environment and the Linux environment used by Agent Runtime, avoiding absolute local paths that won't exist in the cloud.

With this approach, our agent's code will be ready for installation in Agent Runtime while retaining its original structure and without having to rebuild the components developed in the previous article.

Deploying to Google Cloud Agent Runtime

Now that we've prepared the Google Cloud resources and configured the agent's packaging process, we're ready to deploy it to Agent Runtime. We'll use deploy_agent.py to perform the necessary checks, prepare the code and its dependencies, and create the agent in Google Cloud's managed environment.

Structure and operation of deploy_agent.py

This file is located at sources_en/deployment/deploy_agent.py (English version) or sources_es/deployment/deploy_agent.py (Spanish version). It is organized into nine main blocks, summarized below.

Block Description
1. Imports and project environment variables Imports the libraries required for deployment and loads configuration variables from .env. It also identifies reserved variables managed automatically by Agent Runtime that should not be passed into the remote agent configuration.
2. Configuration loading and validation Checks that all required information is available, including the project ID, staging bucket, service account, and Google Drive folder. These checks help catch incomplete settings before creating cloud resources.
3. Authentication environment preparation prepare_deployment_environment() configures the use of Vertex AI and prepares ADC authentication. It also prevents accidental use of an API key or local JSON credentials.
4. Credentials and Cloud Storage access checks verify_deployment_credentials() verifies that valid ADC credentials are available and confirms access to the staging bucket.
5. Remote agent environment variables build_runtime_env() prepares the Gemini model settings, ADC authentication, Google Drive document location, and RAG index refresh interval.
6. Wheel package generation build_agent_wheel() builds the installable agent package, verifies that the main files are included, and prepares its paths for the remote environment.
7. Agent Runtime resource creation AdkApp prepares the ADK agent, and client.agent_engines.create() creates the managed resource with its dependencies, wheel, bucket, service account, and environment variables.
8. Deployed resource identifier recording The script retrieves the full resource identifier and saves it to deployment/runtime_resource.txt for testing and later registration in Gemini Enterprise.
9. Deployment entry point Runs main() when the file is invoked as a Python module and coordinates the preceding stages.

Run the agent deployment

Now that we understand what deploy_agent.py does, we can run the deployment. Open the PowerShell terminal in Visual Studio Code, navigate to the repository root, and make sure the virtual environment is active.

For the English version:

$env:PYTHONPATH = "$PWD\sources_en"
python -m sources_en.deployment.deploy_agent

For the Spanish version, use the corresponding package:

$env:PYTHONPATH = "$PWD\sources_es"
python -m sources_es.deployment.deploy_agent

This command starts the deployment using the configuration prepared earlier. During execution, the script verifies credentials, checks access to the Cloud Storage bucket, builds the wheel package, and sends the required components to Google Cloud Agent Runtime.

If everything succeeds, we'll see a message confirming that the agent was created, along with an identifier similar to the following:

Resource created:
projects/YOUR_PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/europe-west1/reasoningEngines/RESOURCE_ID

This identifier refers to the resource created in Agent Runtime and is saved in deployment/runtime_resource.txt, so we won't need to copy it manually for the following tests.

Keep in mind that deployment may incur Google Cloud charges and that a successful deployment doesn't necessarily mean the agent can answer queries. That's why we'll test it remotely before integrating it with Gemini Enterprise.


Figure 3 – Agent deployment in Agent Runtime.

Validating the agent with test_runtime.py

After deploying our Corporate Policies Assistant, we need to verify that it runs correctly in Google Cloud and can still access the documents stored in Google Drive.

We'll use sources_en/test/test_runtime.py (English version) or sources_es/test/test_runtime.py (Spanish version) to connect to the deployed agent and submit questions from the PowerShell terminal.

Unlike the tests in the previous article, these queries won't run against our local agent. They'll be sent to the resource we created in Google Cloud Agent Runtime.

Run the remote agent tests

From the repository root, with the virtual environment active, run the English version:

python -m sources_en.test.test_runtime

For the Spanish version:

python -m sources_es.test.test_runtime

The script automatically retrieves the deployed agent's identifier and connects to Agent Runtime. If the connection is successful, the output will look similar to this:

Proyecto: YOUR_PROJECT_ID
Región: europe-west1
Agente: projects/YOUR_PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/europe-west1/reasoningEngines/RESOURCE_ID
Conexión con Agent Runtime establecida.

The script will then submit several test queries, such as:

  • Hi, can you introduce yourself and explain what you do?
  • What is the corporate vacation policy?
  • How many vacation days do employees receive?
  • What is the company's remote work policy?
  • Which corporate policies can you help me with?

During these tests, we need to confirm that the agent responds correctly, uses search_corporate_policies when it needs to retrieve information, and generates answers grounded in the documents available in Google Drive.

It's also important to inspect the events returned by Agent Runtime. A successful connection does not necessarily mean that the Gemini model request completed successfully.

Once we've completed the tests and confirmed that the agent works correctly in the cloud, we'll be ready to integrate it with Gemini Enterprise and make it available to authorized users.

Registering the agent in Gemini Enterprise

Once we've deployed our Corporate Policies Assistant and confirmed that it works in Google Cloud Agent Runtime, the next step is to integrate it with Gemini Enterprise. This platform allows users across the organization to interact with our agent through a conversational interface, without having to use development tools such as Streamlit, ADK Web, or the command line.

We'll create an application in Gemini Enterprise and register the agent already deployed to Google Cloud, reusing its logic, tools, and connection to the documents stored in Google Drive.

Create an application in Gemini Enterprise

First, we'll create a new application in Gemini Enterprise that will serve as the entry point for our Corporate Policies Assistant.

From the Google Cloud Console, follow these steps:

  1. Open Gemini Enterprise and select your Google Cloud project.
  2. In the navigation menu, go to Apps.
  3. Click Create app to begin setup.
  4. Enter an application name, such as Corporate Policies Assistant, and complete the required fields.
  5. Choose the application location and any options available for your Gemini Enterprise edition. In this example, we'll select global.
  6. Review the settings and finish by clicking Create.

During application creation, make sure your project has the permissions and licenses required to use Gemini Enterprise. Also note that the application's location can differ from the region where Agent Runtime is deployed, as long as the configuration is supported.


Figure 4 – Creating an application in Gemini Enterprise.

Once created, the enterprise application will be ready for us to add the agent developed with Google ADK.

Register the custom agent

With the application created, we'll register the Corporate Policies Assistant we previously deployed to Google Cloud Agent Runtime.

Open the settings for our Corporate Policies Assistant application in Gemini Enterprise and follow these steps:

  1. Open the Agents section.
  2. Select Custom agent via Agent Runtime to register our custom agent.
  3. In the first step, which covers authorizations, we'll keep the default configuration for this demo.
  4. In the configuration step, fill in the agent details.
  5. Enter the name, description, and deployed resource identifier using the following example values:
Field Example value
Name Corporate Policies Assistant
Description An agent that consults internal policies—covering Human Resources, Finance, Legal, Security, and other areas—based on authorized documents stored in Google Drive.
Resource path projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/europe-west1/reasoningEngines/RESOURCE_ID
  1. Review the settings and confirm the agent registration.

The description helps identify the agent's purpose and the types of questions it can answer. The resource path establishes the connection to the agent running in Agent Runtime. It's the same identifier we obtained during deployment and saved in deployment/runtime_resource.txt.


Figure 5 – Registering the agent in Gemini Enterprise.

Once the agent is registered, we'll configure its availability so authorized users or groups can access it through Gemini Enterprise.

We also need to confirm that the application has permission to invoke the agent. If Gemini Enterprise and Agent Runtime are in different Google Cloud projects, we must configure cross-project access permissions.

Validate the agent in Gemini Enterprise

After registration, we can open our Gemini Enterprise application and interact with the Corporate Policies Assistant through its conversational interface.

To verify that the integration works correctly, we'll repeat some of the questions used during our PowerShell tests, such as asking about vacation days, remote work conditions, or reimbursement procedures.

During these tests, we should check that the agent provides coherent answers, retrieves information from documents stored in Google Drive, and includes source references when available.

We should also confirm that authorized users can access the agent and that its answers reflect the available corporate policies.

In our implementation, the agent accesses Google Drive using a service account. This means employees' individual document permissions are not automatically applied. If we later need to use confidential or department-restricted information, we'll need additional authorization and access-control mechanisms.

With these checks complete, we'll have integrated our Corporate Policies Assistant with Gemini Enterprise, allowing users to access the Google ADK agent from an enterprise platform while it continues to run in a managed Google Cloud Agent Runtime environment.


Figure 6 – Corporate Policies Assistant in action in Gemini Enterprise.
View animated GIF

Security, observability, and operations

Once our agent is deployed in Google Cloud Agent Runtime, we need to consider how to keep it secure and reliable. This means following the principle of least privilege, keeping sensitive credentials out of deployment artifacts, and controlling who can access the agent and corporate information.

Agent Runtime also provides observability capabilities that help us monitor execution and identify problems. During this demo, we can review Google Cloud logs and metrics to examine response times, query volume, execution errors, Gemini usage, and authentication issues.

We should also remember that our RAG index is stored in memory and refreshed on demand, so changes made to Google Drive might not become available immediately across all runtime instances.

If we decide to move this solution into production, we should strengthen security controls, review document access permissions, and evaluate persistent storage, monitoring, and scaling strategies that fit the organization's requirements.

Conclusions

Throughout this second part, we've taken an important step forward with our Corporate Policies Assistant, moving from an application developed and tested locally to a solution deployed on Google Cloud Agent Runtime and integrated with Gemini Enterprise.

We reused the agent built earlier with Google ADK, Gemini, and Google Drive, showing that we can move its existing components into a managed cloud environment without rebuilding the entire solution.

This hands-on exercise also showed why proper packaging, authentication, permissions, and post-deployment validation matter. The tests helped us identify and resolve potential issues related to dependencies, access to Google Cloud services, and Gemini model availability—all essential for a reliable integration.

Deploying AI agents to the cloud creates new opportunities for organizations by making solutions developed by technical teams available to more users through platforms such as Gemini Enterprise. To realize that potential, however, we also need to consider security, scalability, observability, and agent governance.

With this implementation, we've established a practical foundation for evolving our assistant into a more robust enterprise solution capable of integrating information, tools, and business processes securely and efficiently.

Resources

To explore the concepts and procedures covered in this hands-on exercise, here are some additional resources. You'll find the demo's source code, the previous article in this series, and official Google Cloud documentation for learning more about deploying, configuring, and integrating AI agents with Agent Runtime and Gemini Enterprise:

  • Demo project: Google ADK + Gemini Corporate Policies Agent
  • Previous article: How to Build an AI Agent with Google ADK
  • Agent Runtime quickstart with Google ADK: Official documentation
  • Deploy an agent to Agent Runtime: Official documentation
  • Register ADK agents in Gemini Enterprise: Official documentation
  • Model versions and lifecycle: Official documentation
  • Deployment troubleshooting: Official documentation
  • Cross-project access: Official documentation

title: Bookkeeping Is Not Judgement: EJBench, an Engineering Judgement Benchmark Built from a Conjugate Heat Transfer Design Campaign
description:
arXiv:2611.21707v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: We introduce EJBench, a benchmark of engineering judgement: whether a model can predict how a design behaves at new conditions from a few earlier results, and decide on it. Unlike engineering benchmarks that test whether an agent can operate simulation or CAD software, EJBench is software-agnostic and asks what an engineer would conclude without running a simulation. Its tasks come from a conjugate heat transfer design campaign for battery cold plates, in three families: matching unlabelled test results to their operating points, choosing which stored runs to reveal before signing off a design, and ranking new duties by peak cell temperature. Every answer is taken from a converged simulation, not from an LLM judge. The best of ten frontier models, GPT-6 Astra, scores 0.71, and models state almost the same confidence on tasks they get wrong as on tasks they get right. We also post-train Qwen3.5-9B with LoRA and reinforcement learning, rewarded by the share of answer criteria the simulation results confirm; on the held-out test split its score rises from 0.071 to 0.106. We release the train, validation and test splits, the evaluation harness and the leaderboard.

title: Internal Links Between Tool Pages and Guides: The Boring SEO That Compounds
description:
When I built ramrom.io, I spent the first weeks thinking about the downloader itself: the resolve endpoint, the proxy, the quality dropdown. Internal links were an afterthought. Every page had the same navigation menu, and I assumed that was enough. It was not.

The problem with a tool site is that visitors arrive with one job in mind. They land on the TikTok downloader, paste a link, download, and leave. They never see the guide that explains why a TikTok photo post has no video file. Search engines have the same blind spot: a crawler follows the links on a page, and if the only links are the menu and the footer, it learns that every page is equally isolated.

So I started linking pages to each other inside the content itself, where a real reader might actually click. The rule I settled on is simple: every tool page links to the guides that explain its limits, and every guide links back to the tool it describes. The TikTok downloader page links to the guide about TikTok photo posts, because that is the exact moment a visitor discovers a carousel has no video file. The Instagram guide links to the Instagram downloader, because someone reading about how reels resolve is probably one click away from wanting to try it. The YouTube guide links to the downloader page, and the downloader page links back to the guide that explains why audio comes down as M4A rather than MP3.

The links are plain anchor tags in the page copy, written as sentences, not dumped in a list at the bottom. A list of links at the bottom of a page is a sitemap wearing a disguise; nobody reads it. A link inside a sentence that answers the question the visitor is already asking gets clicked, and that is the whole point.

I also stopped linking everything to everything. A "related pages" block with eight links dilutes the signal: if a page links to eight others, a crawler treats all eight as mildly relevant. If it links to two, it treats those two as genuinely connected. I now aim for two or three contextual links per page, and only where the connection is real. The Facebook downloader does not link to the TikTok guide. It links to the Facebook guide and to the tools hub, the one page that explains what the site actually does.

The effect is slow and compounding, which is why I call it boring. No single internal link moves anything. But over weeks, guides that were orphaned start getting crawled more often, tool pages stop being dead ends, and visitors who came for one download stay for a second one.

There are a few practical rules I follow now, and they are all unglamorous:

  • Link from the page where the question arises to the page that answers it, in the sentence where it arises.
  • Use the real words a visitor would use as the anchor text, not "click here".
  • Keep it to two or three links per page, and only to pages that genuinely connect.
  • When I publish a new guide, I go back and add a link to it from the tool page it belongs to. A page with no incoming links from my own site is a page I have forgotten to finish.
  • Never link to a page that does not exist yet. A "coming soon" link is a promise I will forget to keep.

That last rule matters more than it sounds. I used to leave placeholder links for pages I planned to write, and the result was a site full of dead ends. Now the link goes in on the same day the page goes live, and the new page links back.

Internal linking will not save a site with thin content, and it will not rescue pages nobody wants. What it does is make sure the good pages you already have are actually connected — to each other, to your visitors, and to the crawlers that decide whether anyone finds them. It is the least exciting work on the site, and it keeps paying after everything else is done.

title: JET: Just-Enough Exploration Tuning for Efficient Tool-Calling Agents in Repository-Level Question Answering
description:
arXiv:2611.22539v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In repository-level question answering (QA), an agent explores a code repository with tools and should answer a question once enough information is gathered. Nevertheless, we find that LLM agents often continue to invoke tools even after the gathered information is already sufficient to answer. We call this phenomenon over-exploration. Moreover, even though existing methods improve task performance through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on expert trajectories, SFT also propagates the over-exploration in the trajectories to the agent. To mitigate over-exploration, we propose Just-Enough Exploration Tuning (JET), a fine-tuning method that trains the agent to answer once the gathered information is sufficient. JET truncates each training trajectory at the step where the gathered information becomes sufficient, inserts a rationale that explains why the agent can answer at that step, and fine-tunes the agent with a higher loss weight on the rationale. Experiments on two repository-level QA benchmarks with two open-weight 8B models demonstrate that JET reduces tool calls by 11 to 33% on self-generated trajectories while largely preserving the score. On expert trajectories, JET makes 18 to 28% fewer tool calls than SFT while retaining most of the score gain of SFT. In both cases, JET also lowers the inference cost.

title: What changed in wallet sign-ups this month
description:
I re-shoot these sign-up screens every week. The site is KYC Flows. It has side-by-side screenshots of Privy, Dynamic, thirdweb, MetaMask Embedded, Crossmint, and one KYC vendor, Didit. I use test accounts. I do not submit real IDs.

November had three weekly passes, on the 2nd, the 9th, and the 16th. The wallet login screens did not change. Didit redesigned its intro and added a required consent screen. Dynamic's public pricing moved to Fireblocks and dropped a free plan. Two weeks later the FAQ matched the price card.

Didit added a consent screen

Didit's intro changed on November 9. The new layout lists two steps, scan an ID and take a selfie, plus a control to continue on another device. It says the check takes about a minute. That is their claim, not a time I measured.

A new required screen now sits after that intro. The title is "Before we take your selfie."

The screen says face geometry comes from the selfie and the ID photo, plus a short liveness video. It says KYC Flows and Didit have that data, it is not sold, and it is deleted when no longer needed, never later than 12 months after the last verification. The checkbox is required before "Agree and continue."

The document screens after that are still the November 2 captures. The face steps are not on the site, because they need a real ID. Nine of twelve listed screens are captured. Didit and Crossmint were not re-shot on November 16.

Crossmint's wallet price, as of November 9

Crossmint's login screens did not change. Its public wallet price, recorded on November 9 from Crossmint's pricing page, is free for 5,000 monthly active wallets, then $0.01 per wallet. Custom pricing starts at $0.01. Those numbers were still on that page when I wrote this.

Onramps and checkout are listed as separate, per-transaction products. They are not part of the login price.

Dynamic's pricing page moved

Dynamic's pricing now lives on Fireblocks. That move showed up in the November 2 pass. dynamic.xyz/pricing redirects there. The free Launch plan is gone. Self-serve live mode starts on the Growth plan. The card lists Growth at $249 a month for up to 5,000 monthly active users.

On November 2 the Growth card already said $0.05 per extra monthly active user, and the FAQ on that page said $0.005. On November 16 both the card and the FAQ say $0.05. I also checked Fireblocks' Dynamic pricing page. It still bills each monthly active user past 5,000 at $0.05.

A Dynamic MAU is someone who logs in that month, or for whom an embedded or pregenerated wallet is created. The sandbox is still free to build and test. These are snapshots of public pages, not quotes.

The other logins did not change

The other wallet logins were unchanged. Privy, MetaMask Embedded, and thirdweb were recaptured on November 2, 9, and 16. Dynamic's login screens were unchanged too. The dated pictures on the site are still from November 2.

I have not timed any of these paths. The compare pages still say "Not measured yet" for time to a first wallet.

What I would take from this

Check the card and the FAQ on the live page. On Dynamic, those two lines disagreed for two weeks. Dynamic no longer has a free live plan. Growth is $249 a month for 5,000 MAU, then $0.05. Crossmint's public wallet offer is 5,000 monthly active wallets free, then $0.01. Those two pages bill differently, and either one can move.

The first screen is still a configuration. A sandbox that shows wallets up front is not a promise about your app. A KYC path can add a consent step even when the wallet login itself stays the same.

The screens, the public prices, and the weekly changelog are on kycflows.com. I run KYC Flows. Updates also go out in the newsletter.

title: ToolFlood: Beyond Selection -- Hiding Valid Tools from LLM Agents via Semantic Covering
description:
arXiv:2603.13950v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents increasingly use external tools for complex tasks and rely on embedding-based retrieval to select a small top-$k$ subset for reasoning. Prior work on attacking these systems competes for tool selection, assuming benign tools remain in the retrieved set; the robustness of the retrieval stage that produces this set is underexplored. This paper introduces ToolFlood, a retrieval-layer attack on tool-augmented LLM agents. Rather than altering which tool is chosen after retrieval, ToolFlood attacks retrieval itself: it injects a few attacker-controlled tools whose metadata is positioned to exploit the geometry of embedding space, so that these tools semantically span many user queries, dominate the top-k results, and push all benign tools out of the agent's context.
  ToolFlood uses a two-phase adversarial tool generation strategy. It first samples subsets of target queries and uses an LLM to iteratively generate diverse tool names and descriptions. It then runs an iterative greedy selection that chooses tools maximizing coverage of remaining queries in embedding space under a cosine-distance threshold, stopping when all queries are covered or a budget is reached. We provide theoretical intuition of retrieval saturation and show on a large catalog (ToolBench) that ToolFlood achieves up to a 95\% attack success rate with a ~1\% injection rate. The code is available at: https://github.com/as1-prog/ToolFlood

title: Multi-Estimate Elicitation Does Not Uniformly Debias Language Model Judgments
description:
arXiv:2611.00597v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Multi-Candidate Verbalization (MCV) is a task- and model-dependent output protocol: repairing format does not guarantee better posterior accuracy, and requesting weights differs from reweighting an already generated candidate set. Across 31,672 planned/admitted evaluation units and 32,184 planned/admitted calls (excluding retries), we connect a frozen six-configuration cohort to exploratory scale/organization experiments and two independently preregistered post-cohort formal suites. Stage 1 retains 11 directional confirmations among 45 frozen tests; only increased post-outcome confirmation error on gpt-oss-120b exceeds its SESOI. P1 completes 1,920 terminal units: smaller response scales sharply lower operational string-match rates but increase Bayesian error. P2 completes 2,560 calls and 2,048 units: eliciting weights raises three errors by +2.75 / +2.05 / +3.88 pp, while within-generation weighting changes them by only -0.052 / -0.049 / -0.067 pp, a 42x-58x magnitude difference. Unconstrained joint generation with post-hoc normalization offers a local normalized-error improvement for three exhaustive options, without confirmed accuracy improvement. These results distinguish format validity, numerical accuracy and psychological susceptibility; a descriptive three-class behavioral spectrum organizes heterogeneity without identifying internal causes. Materials: https://github.com/asj252/llm-judgment-studies

title: EfficientVPR: Toward Efficient Visual Place Recognition via Scene-Aware Prompt Tuning and Adaptive Feature Enhancement
description:
arXiv:2611.22506v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Visual place recognition (VPR) faces critical challenges in handling extreme environmental variations while meeting the computational constraints of practical applications. Current methods predominantly address these challenges by either scaling up model capacity or employing computationally intensive reranking stages, creating a significant efficiency bottleneck. To overcome this limitation, we propose EfficientVPR, a lightweight one-stage framework that achieves speed-accuracy trade-offs through two key innovations: i) a scene-aware visual prompt tuning method which adapts pretrained features with less parameters while dynamically adjusting to sample-specific characteristics, and ii) an instance-dependent key local feature enhancement module that further reinforces discriminative regions. Comprehensive evaluations on Pitts250k, MSLS, Eynsham, AmsterTime and SVOX demonstrate that our method establishes a new SOTA for DINOv2-small models by outperforming all same-scale competitors, and delivers a $73\times$ speedup with 60\% lower-dimensional features while maintaining competitive (within 2.5% average R@1 gap) against the SOTA DINOv2-large-based two-stage method. Our code will be available at https://github.com/WiniTang/EfficientVPR.

title: Lost in a Few Heads: Diagnosing and Repairing Block Selection in Sparse Attention
description:
arXiv:2611.21917v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Sparse attention models read a few blocks of keys for every query at a fixed budget and can lose much of their long-context retrieval accuracy at that budget. We ask where this loss is made. Using exact attention mass selection at the shipped budget as an oracle, we show that the selector under-ranks the needle rather than running out of budget. We find attention heads that miss the needle by running a calibration probe that teacher-forces the answer and reads two quantities in every head. The first is the needle attention that the selector forfeits, and the second is the share of the answer's log-probability that fixing the head's selection restores, integrated along the path from the shipped selector to full attention. Four checkpoints of the InfLLM-V2 family and NOSA-8B lose multi-key retrieval in the same three blind heads, which attend to the needle while a mean-pooled key summary dilutes its single decisive token. Full attention in those heads or a 4-bit scorer that keeps the shipped budget recovers most of the loss without training. On MiniCPM4.1-8B at 64K, either fix lifts multi-key retrieval accuracy from 54.1 to 97.5%, level with full attention in every head. In production serving engines, full attention in those heads keeps 84 to 89% of the time to first token (TTFT) that sparse attention saves at 32K to 128K context length. Beyond the InfLLM-V2 selector lineage, one unified rule flags attention heads above a threshold swept on each checkpoint until they close most of the gap to full attention on calibration prompts. A similar small set of blind attention heads carry the loss for the SeerAttention-R gates, NSA, and DashAttention, whereas many such heads exist in MoBA. On Qwen3-8B with the SeerAttention-R gates, full attention in 18 of 288 key-value heads lifts multi-key retrieval accuracy from 29.8 to 97.7%.

title: Why Small IT Teams Get Stuck Between Free VPNs and Netskope or Proofpoint
description:
Big-company security usually means two products: Netskope to filter what your team does on the web, and Proofpoint to catch sensitive data leaving. Both are built for large companies, with big seat minimums and long sales cycles. If you run IT for a small team, a clinic, or a handful of client offices, that is a hard fit.

I built Arx Cloud to cover the same ground for smaller teams. The full side-by-side is on the original page, and here is the short version.

Where the big tools make sense

If you have thousands of employees, a dedicated security team, and a need for every enterprise integration, Netskope and Proofpoint are proven and you should look at them first.

Where small teams get stuck

  • Free VPN tools only connect computers. They are great at that, but they do nothing about phishing sites or someone pasting a customer list into ChatGPT.
  • The enterprise tools want hundreds of seats. Most need a sales call before you can even try them.
  • You end up with several tools. One for web filtering, one for data leaks, one for remote access, each with its own console.

What Arx Cloud does in one app

  • Blocks known bad and phishing websites.
  • Checks what gets pasted or uploaded into AI tools like ChatGPT and stops real customer or patient records.
  • Gives staff private access to office apps without opening anything on your firewall.
  • Puts an approval step in front of AI coding assistants so they cannot change things on their own.
  • Starts at 5 users, sets up in minutes on your own, and includes a 30-day free trial.

The detailed comparison, including what each product covers, is on the original page.

Originally published at https://arxcloud.io/vs/netskope-proofpoint/. Side-by-side breakdowns: Arx Cloud vs. Netskope & Proofpoint and Arx Cloud vs. Tailscale & NordVPN.

title: Server-Side Pagination Looked Easy. It Took Me Longer Than Any React Concept Yet.
description:
This week I learnt server-side pagination, and omo, it humbled me.

On paper it's simple: instead of fetching every product and using .slice() like in client-side pagination, you ask the server for only the page you need. In practice I hit 13 bugs, and this is the longest I've ever spent on one concept.

I was building with dummyjson.com and the plan grew in stages: pagination, then search, then debouncing, then putting everything in the URL. Here are the bugs that taught me the most.

The core idea

For page 4 with 10 products per page:

const skip = (currentPage - 1) * productsPerPage; // (4 - 1) * 10 = 30

https://dummyjson.com/products?limit=10&skip=30

The server also sends back total, so the number of pages is derived, not stored:

const totalPages = Math.ceil(total / productsPerPage);

Bug 1: The URL rule I didn't know existed

When I added search, I found a URL online that looked like https://dummyjson.com/products?laptop. I used it and got a bad request. I changed it to ?search=laptop and it still didn't work the way I expected.

After a lot of back and forth, I learnt that every API has its own request structure, and DummyJSON's search lives on a different endpoint:

https://dummyjson.com/products/search?q=laptop

The Network tab showed 200 OK, yet my products weren't changing. A 200 only means the server handled the request. It doesn't mean it did what I meant. Now I check both the Request URL and the Response body in DevTools, and I read the docs before copying a URL from somewhere.

(Also: user input goes through encodeURIComponent() before it goes into a URL.)

Bug 2: Search only worked after I deleted a letter

This one stressed me, and I'm proud of how I found it. I noticed that when I typed a product name quickly, nothing updated. But when I deleted one letter, the search suddenly ran.

My fetching effect looked like this:

useEffect(() => {
  // fetching logic
}, [currentPage, searchTerm]);

But the URL inside it was built from debouncedSearchTerm. So:

  1. I type "phone" and searchTerm updates.
  2. The effect runs immediately, using the old debouncedSearchTerm.
  3. 500ms later debouncedSearchTerm becomes "phone".
  4. The effect doesn't run again, because debouncedSearchTerm isn't in its dependencies.
  5. I delete a letter, searchTerm changes, and finally a request fires.

The fix:

}, [currentPage, debouncedSearchTerm]);

Lesson: the values that decide what a side effect does must be in that effect's dependencies.

Bug 3: controller.abort vs controller.abort()

To avoid race conditions (an old request finishing after a newer one and showing wrong results), I used AbortController. My cleanup looked fine:

return () => {
  controller.abort;
};

It cancelled nothing. I never called the function. That's a JavaScript problem, not a React one: a function reference is not a function call. I wasn't paying attention to detail, and it cost me time.

The part I loved: URL search parameters

Moving page and search into the URL with useSearchParams was the most practical thing I learnt this week.

I expected refresh to reset to page 1, like it did with useState. Instead the page survived refresh, and I can now share a link like localhost:5173/?page=3&search=phone and the other person lands on exactly what I was looking at.

My final design:

  • Local state: searchTerm, for instant typing feedback
  • 500ms debounce: wait until typing stops
  • URL: the committed search and page
  • Fetching effect: requests products using the URL values

Once the URL became the source of truth, debouncedSearchTerm no longer needed its own state. That was my own call, and I'm getting better at asking "does this value really need to exist on its own?" before adding more state.

Stage 7 was the most frustrating, and Bug 13 stressed me the most

Combining the URL, debouncing and pagination broke things in ways I didn't expect: updating one parameter wiped another, every keystroke reset the page, Back created junk history entries, and shared links reset themselves to page 1 after 500ms.

Bug 13 was the worst. I'm on ?search=laptop, press Back, and the URL returns to ?search=phone, but the input still says "laptop". My debounce effect sees the mismatch, thinks it's a new search, and overwrites the URL with "laptop" again.

The fix I settled on is to sync the input whenever the URL changes:

useEffect(() => {
  setSearchTerm(urlSearchTerm);
}, [urlSearchTerm]);

Honest note: I haven't tested every Back/Forward case with this fix yet. I'd already spent too long on one concept, so I moved on. I'm sharing it as "reasonable, not verified", and it's on my list to test.

What this week taught me

  • Trace your code's execution properly. Almost every bug here (stale dependencies, effects firing on mount, mismatched state) was found by walking through what runs, in what order, with which values. This can't be over-emphasized.
  • Finding the bug is half the work, and the fix needs real reasoning too. The first fix that comes to mind often creates the next bug.
  • React is getting past syntax. I'm entering the stage where you have to think and think. I even got tired at some point.
  • Wondering aloud: I kept thinking about developers who learnt this without AI and wondering how deeply they must have reasoned. I can't prove they were sharper, but it made me want to make sure that, with AI around, I'm still doing the tracing myself.

What I'd do next

Test Back/Forward properly, then think about how to get rid of the useEffect that syncs input from the URL.

If you've handled debounced search plus URL state in a cleaner way, I'd love to hear how.

title: CADMAGEDDON: High-Fidelity CAD Reconstruction with Local Inference
description:
arXiv:2611.22563v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: CAD practitioners often work with proprietary parts that they are unwilling to share with external services. For individuals and small companies, bringing this work in-house also requires computational resources they can afford. We introduce CADMAGEDDON, an open-source agent that reconstructs editable CAD from meshes and can run locally on single-GPU systems and current-generation laptops. The method decomposes this complex task into a chain of simple visual decisions about what to construct and what to correct. Geometric tools support precise construction, allowing the agent to focus on visual reasoning. Using the mid-sized Qwen3.8-27B model, CADMAGEDDON outperforms prior approaches, including systems based on frontier models, in reconstruction quality on all the main benchmarks. CADMAGEDDON integrates with FreeCAD, bringing its reconstructions into practitioners' existing CAD workflows. Code: https://github.com/kulibinai/cadmageddon
