title: Go Application Logs API: Preserving Fintech Cohort Evidence Across Provider Changes
description:
A basic logging API is useful only if the evidence survives a provider change: keep the event contract in the application, and put provider-specific translation behind one adapter. TL;DR: for a small fintech application comparing an experiment across tenant cohorts, centralized ingestion and basic queries can support incident reconstruction; choose a specialist when the investigation requires trace trees, automated paging, or a durable export pipeline. A search box cannot repair missing cohort evidence.

The search for the best free API for centralized application logs with simple query support should start there. A free allowance is an evaluation constraint, not evidence that a service meets an incident's requirements.

Can an application logs API explain differences between tenant cohorts?

Consider a bounded design exercise: a Go payment service assigns tenants to control and treatment cohorts, and the team needs to reconstruct which application decisions accompanied a suspected treatment regression. Start with three synthetic records: tenant-a in control completes an authorization, tenant-b in treatment receives a decline, and tenant-b in treatment retries successfully. These are proposed test fixtures, not a production incident or a measured experiment.

One decline proves little.

To compare those records usefully, the application needs an opaque tenant reference, the cohort assigned at the time of the decision, an experiment revision, an operation reference, an attempt number, an outcome, and an event timestamp. These are application design choices, not a vendor's request schema. Avoid payment credentials and raw customer details; reconstruction needs the relationship between decisions, not their sensitive payloads.

The trap is reconstructing yesterday's cohort from today's assignment. If an assignment changes during an investigation, joining historical outcomes against the current configuration can tell a different story, even though every log line arrived correctly. Recording the assignment with the event preserves the decision context. It doesn't establish that the treatment caused the decline.

That distinction determines the boundary. The application owns an event's meaning and identity; an adapter translates it for ingestion; the logging service stores and retrieves it; the investigator compares the retrieved evidence. Trace identifiers can help correlate records, but correlation alone does not produce a distributed trace or a span tree.

For an early-stage team with small US/EU application workloads, the recommendation is to try Infrai for centralized event ingestion and basic log queries: its unified REST API keeps the capability contract stable when the provider behind it changes, so application call sites don't need a vendor-specific rewrite. Plain HTTP means no SDK to install: the Go adapter and a separate investigation tool can call the same interface without maintaining separate vendor SDK integrations. This removes a concrete handoff cost when application owners and the platform team use different runtimes.

Infrai provides one REST API with no SDK required: any language or runtime that can send HTTP requests can use it. For this workflow, that lets a Go service and an investigation tool share the interface without separate SDK dependencies. Infrai's one key, one bill model reduces credential handoffs and invoice reconciliation for the platform owner: a single API key replaces separate credentials for the backend capabilities the team adopts.

Infrai's public, self-describing discovery surface supplies another practical benefit: engineers can inspect request and response schemas without a key before wiring the adapter. Runnable examples in 10 languages help both teams implement the same boundary. Infrai's broad capability surface has a simple interface: 295 routes across 20 modules follow unified conventions, and swapping providers behind a capability doesn't change application code. For the cohort investigation, that means keeping the event validation path while changing the implementation behind the handoff. Breadth is useful only where adopting an adjacent capability avoids another integration; it isn't a reason to expand the incident stack.

Preserve the evidence before selecting the backend

The useful invariant is small: every admitted experiment event carries the assignment that governed that attempt. Put that check before the provider boundary, where it can be tested independently of a hosted service, and version the application contract so a later adapter change doesn't silently redefine a cohort.

There are two different measures here. The payment SLO concerns customer outcomes; a proposed telemetry completeness SLI concerns whether expected experiment events carry the fields needed to investigate those outcomes. A team might choose a 99.9% completeness target as an internal design objective, but that number is illustrative and makes no claim about any vendor's uptime. Count missing or rejected evidence separately. Otherwise, a clean-looking cohort comparison may describe only the requests that were easiest to observe.

Capacity needs the same skepticism. For an illustrative planning envelope of 20 application requests per second, three events per request, and an average serialized size of 600 bytes, ingestion is 36,000 bytes per second, or about 3.11 GB per day before transport overhead, indexes, or replication. None of those inputs is a measured workload or an Infrai limit. They are assumptions to replace with measurements.

Small applications generate volume.

If a separate sender buffers events, specify a bounded queue, a maximum event age, and an observable overflow policy. Decide what happens when telemetry delivery is unavailable without accidentally redefining payment availability; silently losing the treatment cohort during a burst is particularly damaging to this investigation. A local encoding success is also not an ingestion acknowledgment. Those boundaries need different failure counters.

Provider interchangeability has a limit. A stable capability contract can keep application call sites steady while its implementation changes, but it doesn't guarantee identical retention, query semantics, historical migration, or investigation results. The adapter's acceptance test should retrieve the synthetic control and treatment records and verify the evidence the team actually needs.

Buy the investigation depth you need

The buy-versus-build decision should follow the missing evidence, not the length of a feature list. These alternatives represent different operational commitments; suitability still depends on an acceptance test against the team's data and deployment requirements.

Option What the team buys or builds Incident-reconstruction trade-off
Infrai Use a common REST capability for centralized ingestion and basic queries; build the application's evidence contract and adapter. Fits a small workload with straightforward lookup needs. Choose a specialist for advanced distributed tracing or log export.
Grafana Loki Adopt a logging stack organized around labels and LogQL; decide who operates it. A candidate when label selection and log-query workflows fit the platform. Owning the deployment means owning capacity and on-call work.
Elasticsearch Build or adopt an indexed search workflow around its query interface. Consider it when richer search requirements justify an indexing and operations decision; test mappings and queries against the cohort fixtures.
Better Stack Evaluate managed logging as an alternative to operating the backend yourself. A candidate when reducing backend operations drives the purchase. Validate ingestion, retrieval, retention, and incident workflow before committing.

These are real alternatives, not interchangeable adapters by default. Loki's label model and Elasticsearch's indexed search model make different demands on the representation of evidence. Better Stack belongs in the managed-service evaluation. An HTTP interface alone doesn't erase those differences.

Infrai's scope here remains centralized ingestion and basic filtering. Build the choice around that scope. For paging rules and notification delivery, use a dedicated alerting system; for missed scheduled work, evaluate a heartbeat service such as Healthchecks. An investigator who needs source-map resolution, crash symbolication, or session replay should evaluate a specialist for those artifacts.

Retention policy, selective user-data deletion, bulk export, and subscriptions need a separate acceptance decision. Don't assume the basic logging boundary supplies those workflows, or treat an application log store as the sole compliance archive. Similarly, capture experiment assignments in the event itself rather than relying on a flag service to supply a historical change audit, evaluation statistics, or dependency history.

The recommendation becomes narrower, and more useful: buy a basic log capability when the question is which recorded application decisions differed between cohorts; buy deeper observability or a separate evidence system when the question requires artifacts outside those records.

A Go check at the query boundary

The preventative path has two acceptance checks: verify the event's decision context before ingestion, then verify retrieval through the selected adapter. For the three synthetic fixtures, reject a missing cohort or experiment revision before emitting a record. During retrieval, distinguish the two attempts for the same operation rather than counting the successful retry as an independent payment.

The following standalone program checks the HTTP side of retrieval. Save it as main.go, set INFRAI_API_KEY in the environment, and run it with Go. It uses only the standard library, sends an explicit GET, checks status, and bounds both retries and response size. It prints the returned response without assuming a response schema or adding filter parameters.

This is the query-boundary check; the application still owns the cohort comparison.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func retryDelay(value string, attempt int) time.Duration {
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(value); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        if seconds > 90 {
            return 91 * time.Second
        }
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    if date, err := http.ParseTime(value); err == nil {
        delay := time.Until(date)
        if delay < 0 {
            return 0
        }
        return delay
    }
    return time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
}

func run() error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set INFRAI_API_KEY")
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 90*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 15 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, "GET", "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/logs/search", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, (1<<20)+1))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if len(body) > 1<<20 {
            return fmt.Errorf("response exceeds local 1 MiB limit")
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            delay := retryDelay(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"), attempt)
            select {
            case <-time.After(delay):
                continue
            case <-ctx.Done():
                return ctx.Err()
            }
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("query returned HTTP %d: %s",
                resp.StatusCode, strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
        }
        _, err = os.Stdout.Write(body)
        return err
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The retry budget is deliberately finite. If Retry-After exceeds the overall waiting budget, the context expires and ends the operation rather than retrying before the server's requested delay. This read-only example needs no write deduplication; a production sender should separately verify the ingest contract's idempotency behavior before enabling write retries.

An HTTP success establishes that a response arrived. It does not establish cohort completeness. Retrieve the fixtures through the chosen contract, check their experiment revisions and attempt identities, and keep the payment SLO separate from the evidence SLI. If the investigation needs end-to-end span timing or a compliance archive, select that capability explicitly instead of stretching a basic log query into a promise it cannot support.

Sources

References for the logging concepts and the alternatives in the buy-versus-build decision:

  • OpenTelemetry logs concepts
  • Grafana Loki documentation
  • Elasticsearch documentation
  • Better Stack logging documentation
  • Healthchecks documentation

If this boundary fits your system, start with the request contracts and runnable examples in the Infrai documentation, then use the same cohort fixtures to evaluate the alternatives.

title: Checking an uploaded resume PDF before anyone reads it
description:
If your job board, career-services portal or review queue accepts resume PDFs, about 30 lines of Node.js can flag files with little extractable text, or with nothing that looks like an email address or phone number. Parsers work from the text they can pull out of the file, and that text can be missing things the page shows.

The failure that convinced me to check for this comes from a ReadableResume parsing test where a sample resume had its name and contact details in a Google Docs text box. Google Docs exported the box as a picture. The page looked complete, but the PDF's text had no name, email or phone, and the open-source parser in the test took the first heading, "EDUCATION", as the person's name. It got 34 of 46 fields right.

The check

This uses pdf.js in Node to pull the text out the way a parser would start, then runs three checks: fewer than 200 non-whitespace characters, no email match and no phone match.

// check-resume.mjs — usage: node check-resume.mjs resume.pdf
import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";
import { getDocument } from "pdfjs-dist/legacy/build/pdf.mjs";

const EMAIL = /[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+(\.[\w-]+)+/;
const PHONE = /\+?\d[\d\s().-]{7,}\d/;

async function checkResume(path) {
  const data = new Uint8Array(await readFile(path));
  const pdf = await getDocument({ data }).promise;
  const pages = [];
  for (let number = 1; number <= pdf.numPages; number++) {
    const page = await pdf.getPage(number);
    const content = await page.getTextContent();
    // Rebuild lines from text items; hasEOL marks the end of a line in pdf.js
    let text = "";
    for (const item of content.items) text += item.str + (item.hasEOL ? "\n" : "");
    pages.push(text);
  }
  const text = pages.join("\n");
  const firstLine = text.split("\n").map((line) => line.trim()).find(Boolean) ?? "";
  const problems = [];
  if (text.replace(/\s/g, "").length < 200) problems.push("fewer than 200 non-whitespace characters: possibly a scan or an image saved as PDF");
  if (!EMAIL.test(text)) problems.push("no text matched the email pattern");
  if (!PHONE.test(text)) problems.push("no text matched the phone pattern");
  return { pages: pdf.numPages, characters: text.length, firstLine, problems };
}

console.log(await checkResume(process.argv[2]));

I ran it on a one-page sample resume exported from Google Docs, then on the same file after turning it into an image-only PDF with ImageMagick (magick -density 150 sample.pdf scanned.pdf), which is roughly what a scan or a "print to image" gives you:

$ node check-resume.mjs sample.pdf
{ pages: 1, characters: 1494, firstLine: 'Grace Liu', problems: [] }

$ node check-resume.mjs scanned.pdf
{
  pages: 1,
  characters: 0,
  firstLine: '',
  problems: [
    'fewer than 200 non-whitespace characters: possibly a scan or an image saved as PDF',
    'no text matched the email pattern',
    'no text matched the phone pattern'
  ]
}

Both files look the same on screen. The script pulled 1,494 characters from the original and none from the image-only copy.

What to do with the result

  • No text at all. Ask for a fresh export from the original document instead of rejecting the upload outright. A scan or an image saved as PDF has no text until something runs OCR on it.
  • No email or phone match. Paste the PDF's text into a plain editor and look for the contact details. If they're missing there but visible on the page, in a text box or an image, ask the person to move them into the body of the document and export again.
  • Show the first line the script extracted. "Your PDF's text starts with 'EDUCATION'" lets the uploader compare it with the page and see whether their name made it into the text.

What this doesn't catch

A PDF can pass all three checks and still read badly. The script can't tell whether the words come out in the right order, whether a two-column layout mixed lines together, or whether a job's dates wrapped onto a second line in a narrow table column. That last one cost 6 fields in the same test: the parser read the year on the second line as the company. To check by hand, paste the text into a plain editor and read it top to bottom, checking that each job's dates still sit with the right entry; this guide on what to look for in the pasted text goes through the other cases. A free ATS resume checker shows what the same open-source parser put in each field and every line of text it read from the first three pages of a PDF; the file stays in your browser.

The phone pattern is loose on purpose so it accepts numbers with country codes, and it's too loose in one way: it also matches a date range like 2023 - 2024, so this check can miss a missing phone number. The parser in that test only recognised US-style numbers.

A form for review requests

If you review resumes by hand, ask people to upload the PDF or Word file they plan to submit. A resume review request template on Tally collects that file along with the role they're applying for, their career stage and when they need feedback. The job posting link is optional.

I work on ReadableResume, which ran the parsing test and makes the checker mentioned above.

I used AI to help draft this post.

title: MIRAGE: Motion Identity Reduction via Autoregressive Generative Encoding for Privacy-Preserving Skeleton-based Motion Data
description:
arXiv:2611.22200v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Skeleton motion identifies people through body proportions and movement style, and skeleton streams are increasingly passed to third-party analytics that run action classifiers trained on raw data. A prior adversarial anonymizer adds a per-frame residual in the raw coordinate space but sees one frame at a time; motion retargeting needs a target skeleton and complete sequences, which rules out online use. We present MIRAGE, a target-free, causal anonymizer that adds an identity-reducing residual to each incoming frame in the raw coordinate space, computed by attention over past frames. One causal, optionally windowed mask governs every attention in a rotary-position encoder-decoder, and key/value caches let the trained function run frame by frame; on all 56,578 NTU 60 sequences, batched and streaming outputs differ by at most 7.2e-6 m. Reported results use an unbounded window, so per-stream state grows with stream length. We evaluate against a passive adversary that applies raw-trained identity models and an adaptive adversary that trains on the anonymizer's output, treating the adaptive adversary as the headline, on NTU RGB+D 60 over five generator seeds, alongside the per-frame residual anonymizer of Moon et al. trained identically. When consumers retrain on the released data, MIRAGE keeps 83.9% action recognition (raw 89.1%; Moon et al. 88.7%) while a retrained identity classifier reaches 43.4% re-identification (RI) over 40 subjects, against 69.4% for Moon et al. and 75.4% on raw data. The strongest adaptive attacker still reaches 49.3% (chance 2.5%), so MIRAGE reduces identity leakage; it does not anonymize. Against raw-trained (frozen) classifiers, MIRAGE lowers RI below the strongest retargeting baseline (10.36% vs. 22.09%), but frozen action recognition falls to 37.04% (vs. 75.82%), so at full residual scale it is not a drop-in replacement for raw input to existing frozen models.

title: How to Collect Customer Feedback From Your Website
description:
Your website can ask your customers what they think, and most small business sites never do. A short form, a one-question survey or a small feedback button can tell you why visitors leave, what confuses them and what would make them buy. This guide covers the practical methods, where to place them, and how to wire them up without annoying your visitors.

Why Your Website Is Your Best Feedback Channel

Customers already tell you things in other places, but those messages arrive scattered, and the quiet visitors never say anything at all. Your website reaches every visitor, including the ones who leave without contacting you.

Feedback from your own site is specific. A visitor can point at the exact page, the exact form, the exact step where they got stuck. When someone writes "I could not find your delivery charges on the checkout page," you know exactly what to fix.

We see this pattern in our own client work. The businesses that learn fastest are the ones that read their form messages and chat transcripts every week. Three weeks of real visitor comments usually teach more than a year of guessing what customers want.

7 Ways to Collect Feedback Through Your Website

You do not need all seven. Start with one or two, and add more once you have a habit of reading the answers.

1. A Simple Feedback Form

A feedback form is a small form with a message box and two or three fields: name, phone or email, and the message itself. Keep it short. Every extra required field costs you submissions.

Test it the way a customer would. Fill it in on your own phone, press submit, and check that the message actually arrives. At aimEncoders, we test every form on real phones before a site goes live, because a form that silently fails is worse than no form at all.

2. A One-Question On-Site Survey

A short survey that appears while someone browses can catch the people who would never open a contact page. One question is enough. "Did you find what you were looking for?" works on almost any page. A clothing store can ask whether visitors found the right size. A clinic can ask whether patients found the appointment information easily.

Keep it to one to three questions and let people close it without answering. Show it after the visitor has had time to look around.

3. A Floating Feedback Button

A feedback widget is a small button that sits at the edge of the screen. Visitors click it when they have something to say, and it stays out of the way the rest of the time. It suits restaurants collecting comments about an online menu, service businesses hearing that a page is unclear, and stores learning that a product detail is missing.

Place it along the side or bottom corner, and check it on a phone. A button that covers the checkout button on mobile will cost you more than the feedback is worth.

4. NPS and Satisfaction Scores

Two short scores cover most of what you need. Net Promoter Score asks one question: on a scale of 0 to 10, how likely are you to recommend our business to a friend? Customer Satisfaction Score asks how happy someone is with a single purchase or interaction.

NPS fits follow-up emails and customer account pages. CSAT fits order confirmation pages, after a support chat, or after an appointment. Track the numbers over time instead of reading one survey in isolation. And read the written comments. They usually explain the score.

5. Post-Purchase and Post-Service Forms

The most useful feedback comes after the customer has actually bought something. Ask while the experience is fresh: how was the product quality, was delivery on time, what could we improve next time?

Send the form on the order confirmation page or in a short follow-up message a day or two after delivery. Keep it mobile friendly. Most of your customers will open it on a phone.

6. Live Chat Transcripts

If your site has live chat, your transcripts are a feedback source you already own. Look for repeats. A Pakistani ecommerce store often finds the same three questions: Cash on Delivery, delivery charges, exchange policy.

Every repeated question is a page that needs fixing. Turn the common answers into an FAQ section so the next visitor finds them without asking.

7. Review Prompts

Ask happy customers to leave a review on Google or in your testimonial section. Ask everyone. A short prompt on the thank-you page or in a follow-up message is enough: what did you like most, would you recommend us, what could we improve?

Never pay for positive ratings and never offer a reward in exchange for a good review. Honest reviews build trust, and they give you the same feedback a private form would.

What Visitors Do Not Say Out Loud

Not all feedback arrives as words. Your analytics show behaviour too. Watch four signals: pages people leave from, terms they type in your site search, forms they start but never submit, and pages where they spend a long time without acting.

If visitors keep leaving your checkout page, the delivery charges or payment options may be unclear. Treat these as clues, not proof. Pair them with a survey or a few customer conversations before you rebuild anything.

What Questions Should You Ask?

Good questions are short, specific and tied to the page the visitor is on.

On the homepage, ask whether visitors found what they came for and what is missing. On product and service pages, ask about the information they need to decide: price, sizes, delivery time, what is included. After a purchase, ask about the product, the delivery and the overall experience.

Avoid long questionnaires. Five questions get fewer answers than two. One open text box often tells you more than ten multiple-choice questions, because customers describe the problem in their own words.

Where to Place Feedback Without Annoying Visitors

Timing matters more than the tool you choose. A survey that pops up the moment someone arrives will be closed without reading. Wait until they have browsed a product, finished a purchase, or spent a minute on the page.

Show the same survey sparingly. A returning visitor should not see it on every visit. On mobile, keep every form short and every button thumb friendly. A form that is awkward on a small screen will simply be abandoned.

What to Do With the Answers

Collecting feedback is the easy half. The value comes from acting on it.

First, sort the answers into groups: navigation, product information, checkout, delivery, support. Patterns appear quickly. One complaint is an anecdote. Ten complaints about the same page are a job to do.

Second, fix the quick wins first. A missing size guide, a hidden delivery charge, a booking form with too many fields. These are small changes that affect every visitor.

Third, close the loop. Thank the people who wrote in, and tell them when their suggestion ships.

Fourth, compare before and after. Check whether size questions drop after you add the guide, or whether completed bookings rise after you simplify the form. If nothing moves, the fix missed the real problem.

How We Build Feedback Into Client Websites

Adding feedback to an existing site is usually a small job, not a rebuild. At aimEncoders, we add feedback forms, survey widgets and post-purchase emails to the sites we build, and we wire them to email or WhatsApp so nothing sits unread. For larger setups we build custom web applications with a feedback dashboard.

Every form goes through our QA pass before launch. We submit it on real phones, check the message arrives, and confirm the thank-you page and notifications work. A feedback form that drops messages is a broken promise, and we treat it like any other bug.

If your site needs feedback features, or your current forms are not bringing anything back, talk to us about custom websites and web apps built around how your customers actually behave. And if most of your customers find you through local search, reviews pull double duty as feedback and as ranking signals, which is why our local SEO playbook treats Google reviews as part of the website, not an afterthought.

A Quick Note for Developers

If you are the one building the form, keep the implementation boring: a plain HTML form posting to your backend or a form service, server-side validation, and a confirmation page. Store each response with the page URL and a timestamp so the business can see which page generated each comment. Test the submission on a real phone over mobile data before you ship it, and check the notification actually arrives. Most feedback forms fail silently, and nobody notices until a customer complains.

Frequently Asked Questions

How do I collect feedback without using pop-ups?

Use a floating feedback button or a link in your footer. Both stay available without interrupting anyone, and visitors click them when they are ready to talk.

How many questions should a feedback form have?

Two or three at most, plus one open text box. Short forms get far more replies than long ones, and the open box usually holds the most useful answer.

When is the best time to ask for feedback?

After the visitor has done something: browsed a product, completed a purchase, or used a service. Feedback asked too early is guesswork. Feedback asked after the experience is specific.

Do I need paid tools to collect customer feedback?

No. A simple form, a one-question survey and a review prompt cover most small businesses. Paid tools help when you have high traffic and need dashboards.

About the Author

Muhammad Asad Ullah is the founder of aimEncoders, a website development agency in Faisalabad. His team builds custom websites, web apps and ecommerce stores, and tests every form on real phones before launch.

title: Fast and Strong Image Protection against Diffusion Personalization
description:
arXiv:2611.22494v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Personalized text-to-image diffusion models can reproduce a person from a handful of photographs. Image protection perturbs each image before publication so that fine-tuning on it fails, but it optimizes every perturbation from scratch, so its cost grows with the number of images. We present the protective diffusion model (PDM), which is trained once and samples the perturbation of a new image over many denoising steps. PDM distills an iterative teacher and is then post-trained with the target residual projection (TRP) loss as a reward, a stronger objective than existing ones. PDM outperforms nine baselines on faces and artworks and nearly matches its teacher at a tenth of the cost.

title: How to Read Code You Didn't Write: Run, Enter, Follow, Break
description:
The first time you open a repository that is not yours, the instinct is to start reading files. Top to bottom. It feels productive for about four minutes, and then you close the tab, because nothing sticks.

The problem is not the code. The problem is that reading a program is not reading a text. A text tells you what it means. A program tells you what it does right now, and everything else why it is shaped that way, what used to be there, which of these five similar-looking functions actually runs is not written anywhere in the file you have open.

Reading code is a skill, and like the rest of them it has a method. This is mine: run it, enter it, follow one path, break something.

Why this matters more than writing

You will spend more time reading code than writing it. That is not a motivational phrase; it is arithmetic. Every change you make starts with understanding the surrounding code, every bug starts with finding the code that lies, and every review is reading.

Writing is a small fraction of the job. And yet every course, every tutorial and every book teaches you to write, and almost nothing teaches you to read. So people improvise, and the improvisation is "open files until something clicks", which works, eventually, at the cost of days.

A junior who can read unfamiliar code has a superpower that requires no permission: any repository on Earth is available today, for free.

The method

Four steps, in this order. The order is the point.

1. Run it. Before reading a single line.\
2. Enter it. Find the door and look at nothing else.\
3. Follow one path. End to end, ignoring the other 95%.\
4. Break something. Change one value and watch what screams.

And a fifth that is not a step but a habit: ask the history.

I will use a real repository to show each one: serverctl, a Go TUI for administering Linux servers over SSH. 107 Go files under internal/, split across ui, core, collectors and actions, plus the entrypoint in cmd/. That is enough code to get lost in, which is exactly why it is a good example.

Step 1: Run it

Before you read the code, make the program work. Clone it, build it, execute it.

git clone https://github.com/felipecastillo-b/serverctl.git
cd serverctl
make build
./bin/serverctl

This sounds like a detour and it is the single highest-value step. A running program answers questions the source code cannot: it tells you which of these features are real, which screen opens first, what happens when a file is missing, and where the output comes from.

It also builds the vocabulary. In serverctl you press a key and see a dashboard with CPU, memory, load and uptime; you press tab and you are in processes; you press ? and a help overlay appears. Now you know what the words mean before you meet them in the code.

If the build fails, do not skip ahead. Fixing the build is the first real exercise in reading the project: the error names a version, a dependency, or a missing header, and that is the first true thing you have learned about how it is put together.

Step 2: Enter it

Every program has a door. In Go it is main, and by convention it lives in cmd/<binary-name>/.

Open exactly one file: cmd/serverctl/main.go. It is 72 lines, and those 72 lines describe the entire shape of the program:

  • flags: -version and -config
  • config.Load(path) to read YAML, with defaults when the file is missing
  • keys.DefaultGlobal() and global.ApplyOverrides(cfg.Keys) to apply your keybindings
  • screens.ValidateScreenKeys(cfg.ScreenKeys) to reject invalid ones
  • one line that starts everything: tea.NewProgram(app.New(cfg), tea.WithAltScreen())

That is a compressed map of the application. Config is loaded first, validated before the terminal takes over, and then handed to a single model that owns the interface.

Do not read the rest of the code yet. You now know where the program starts and what it needs to start. That is enough for step three.

Step 3: Follow one path

Now pick one thing the program does and trace it from the door to the kernel, ignoring everything else. One path. Not all of them.

Take the dashboard. From step two, you know it is created by app.New(cfg). Open internal/ui/app/app.go. The comment at the top says what you would have guessed by now: it hosts the sidebar, the active screen, the refresh ticker, the keymap, the mouse input, the help overlay and the command palette.

That is still too big. Go narrower. The dashboard needs CPU numbers. Where do they come from?

This is the moment the method pays for itself. In serverctl, internal/core/ports.go defines interfaces: UnitLister, JournalReader, StorageLister, ContainerLister and friends. The UI depends on those interfaces, not on /proc. The things that implement them live in internal/collectors/, and the things that change the system live in a separate package, internal/actions/.

So the path is: screen asks a port, a collector implements it, the collector reads /proc or D-Bus, the data comes back as a typed struct.

You have just learned the architecture from the outside in, by following one number, instead of memorizing a diagram. And now the interface names make sense, because you needed one of them.

This is also how you read a repository with 107 files: you do not read 107 files. You read five, and you learn that the other 102 follow the same shape.

Step 4: Break something

Change one thing and observe the failure. This is faster than reading the code that handles it.

In serverctl, the config file lives at ~/.config/serverctl/config.yaml and accepts a keys section. Do this:

keys:
  quit: ctrl+q

Then change quit to something invalid — quit: notakey — and start the program. It refuses to open the interface and prints a readable error, before it ever takes over your terminal. That tells you something no amount of reading would have made obvious: validation happens before the alternate screen starts, deliberately.

And the source says exactly that, in a comment right above the call, explaining that app.New trusts the values are valid so they must be checked first. You earned the comment by breaking the thing it protects. That is the difference between having read it and having learned it.

Break things on purpose. Delete a file the program expects. Pass a flag with a wrong value. Point it at a path that does not exist. Every failure is a free lesson about how the code is ordered, and order is the part of a codebase that documentation never captures.

The fifth habit: ask the history

The code tells you what exists. The history tells you what was tried and removed.

serverctl's README has one line that is a small essay on its own: version 0.5.0 shipped SMART disk health, and version 0.5.1 removed it, because SMART reads require root or a raw I/O capability, and the whole project refuses to escalate privileges.

Nobody reading the current source would find that. The feature is gone. The reason is gone with it. It survives in a changelog and in git log.

So when something looks strange — an empty function, a configuration option nobody uses, a TODO from two years ago — do not assume the author was careless. Ask:

git log --oneline -- path/to/the/strange/file
git blame path/to/the/strange/file

Nine times out of ten, the strange thing is a scar. The tenth time it is genuinely bad code, and now you have evidence instead of an opinion.

Draw five boxes

When you finish, close the editor and draw the program on paper. Five boxes, arrows between them, no detail.

For serverctl mine would be:

  • cmd/serverctl — flags and wiring
  • internal/ui — models, screens, sidebar, palette
  • internal/core — domain types and the ports the UI depends on
  • internal/collectors — read-only adapters over /proc, /sys, D-Bus
  • internal/actions — the only package allowed to change anything

If you cannot draw it, you did not understand it; you memorized it. And memorized code disappears in a week.

The repository already has this map in ARCHITECTURE.md, with a layer table and a module table. Using existing documentation is not cheating, it is the fastest legal move. But verify it against the code: documentation ages, and the one thing worse than no map is a map of a city that was demolished two releases ago.

Three ways to do this badly

Reading breadth-first. Opening thirty files in ten minutes feels like progress and produces nothing. Depth over coverage, one path at a time.

Reading without running. You are reading a description of a program, written in a language designed for machines. Run it, or you are doing literary criticism.

Judging before understanding. "This is badly written" almost always means "I do not know why it is like this yet". That line in main.go that ignores an error and discards it with _, _ = looks careless — until you read the comment explaining that the linter requires an explicit decision and there is no recovery if writing to stderr fails. Two lines of context change the verdict completely.

Try it this week

  1. Pick a repository you already use and have never read. Any size.
  2. Run it, enter it, follow one path, break one thing.
  3. Draw the five boxes.
  4. Write one paragraph: what would break if you deleted the file at the center of the path you followed.

That paragraph is worth more than ten tutorials, because it is the only proof that you actually understood something.

The last thing

Nobody is going to give you permission to read a codebase. There is no onboarding for the repository you are curious about, no ticket, no reviewer. It is just there, and you can open it.

That asymmetry is the best deal available to a junior: the most senior engineer in the world has exactly the same access to that source as you do, today, for free. Reading it is a skill you can start practising in the next five minutes.

I wrote about how programmers think before. This is the other half: thinking is what you do once you can read.

description:
Vercel Sandbox now creates snapshots up to 10x faster. Median time to snapshot is under 0.4 seconds, down from 4.4 seconds. Snapshot restore speed has also improved by 50% from 500ms to 250ms at p50.

Snapshots are now able to write and restore by re-using frames within the Vercel Hive Snapshot (VHS) format. VHS now indexes data in a more efficient way which means that more read and write operations can be done in parallel. Snapshots can now restore more of your Sandbox base image in parallel with user data, leading to overall faster operations.

Persistent sandboxes, the default, snapshot automatically when a session stops and resume from the latest snapshot. This applies to all new snapshots, with nothing to configure. Existing snapshots keep the previous format.

Learn more in the snapshots documentation.

title: Web Scraping with Scrapy: Building a Spider from Scratch
description:
A requests and BeautifulSoup script is the right way to start scraping. But as soon as a job grows, you find yourself writing the same plumbing again and again: a loop over pages, retries, delays, de-duplication, saving results. Soon your 30-line script is 300 lines and mostly not about the data.

Scrapy is a framework that supplies that plumbing. You describe what to extract in a small class called a spider, and Scrapy handles requests, concurrency, retries, throttling, robots.txt, logging, and exporting results.

In this guide you'll build a complete Scrapy project from scratch. It will crawl every page of a bookstore, follow each book to its detail page, clean the data in a pipeline, and export it to JSON or CSV, politely.

Version note: this guide targets Scrapy 2.20 (released November 2026), which requires Python 3.11 or newer. Scrapy has changed a lot recently, and many tutorials online are out of date. The biggest example: the old start_requests() method was removed in Scrapy 2.16, and spiders now use async def start(). If you copy a spider from an older tutorial and it crawls nothing, that's probably why.

Why Scrapy?

Here's what you get without writing it yourself:

Need In a script In Scrapy
Many requests at once Threads or asyncio by hand Built-in concurrency
Retrying failures Your own loop Built-in retry middleware
Being polite time.sleep() Download delay and AutoThrottle
Obeying robots.txt Extra code One setting, on by default
Skipping repeated URLs A set() you maintain Automatic de-duplication
Cleaning and saving data Mixed into the scraping code Item pipelines and feed exports
Knowing what happened print() Logs and crawl statistics

When not to use it. For a single page or a quick one-off, requests and BeautifulSoup are simpler. For sites that build their content with JavaScript, you need a browser: see our guide to scraping JavaScript-heavy sites with Playwright. Scrapy shines when you need to crawl many pages reliably.

Setting Up

Check that you have Python 3.11 or newer, then create a virtual environment and install Scrapy:

python --version                 # 3.11 or newer
python -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate         # On Windows: venv\Scripts\activate
pip install scrapy
scrapy version

Now create a project:

scrapy startproject bookscraper
cd bookscraper

You get this layout:

bookscraper/
├── scrapy.cfg                # project marker (run commands from this folder)
└── bookscraper/
    ├── items.py              # the shape of the data you extract
    ├── middlewares.py        # hooks into the request/response flow
    ├── pipelines.py          # clean, validate and store items
    ├── settings.py           # all configuration
    └── spiders/              # your spiders live here

Two things in the generated settings.py are worth noticing right away: ROBOTSTXT_OBEY = True, so Scrapy respects robots.txt by default, and a DOWNLOAD_DELAY of 1 second with one request at a time per domain. New projects start out polite.

Explore the Page with the Scrapy Shell

Before writing any spider, experiment on the live page. The shell downloads a URL and gives you a response object to play with:

scrapy shell "https://books.toscrape.com/"

We'll use the sandbox site books.toscrape.com, which exists for practicing scraping. Inside the shell, try:

>>> response.css("article.product_pod h3 a::attr(title)").get()
'A Light in the Attic'
>>> response.css("p.price_color::text").getall()[:3]
['£51.77', '£53.74', '£50.10']
>>> response.xpath("//li[@class='next']/a/@href").get()
'catalogue/page-2.html'

A few things to learn from this:

  • response.css() takes CSS selectors, extended with ::text (the text of an element) and ::attr(name) (an attribute's value).

  • response.xpath() does the same job with XPath, which is handy for odd cases.

  • .get() returns the first match, or None if there isn't one. .getall() returns a list of every match.

The shell is the fastest way to get selectors right, so use it constantly. Type exit() to leave.

Your First Spider

A spider is a class with a name, a place to start, and a parse method that turns a response into data. You can generate a skeleton with scrapy genspider books books.toscrape.com, but it's short enough to write by hand. Create bookscraper/spiders/books.py:

import scrapy

class BooksSpider(scrapy.Spider):
    name = "books"
    allowed_domains = ["books.toscrape.com"]
    start_urls = ["https://books.toscrape.com/"]

    def parse(self, response):
        for card in response.css("article.product_pod"):
            yield {
                "title": card.css("h3 a::attr(title)").get(),
                "price": card.css("p.price_color::text").get(),
                "url": response.urljoin(card.css("h3 a::attr(href)").get()),
            }

How it works:

  • name is how you run the spider.

  • allowed_domains stops the spider from wandering off to other sites.

  • start_urls lists the first pages to download. Scrapy requests each one and passes the response to parse.

  • yield hands each result back to Scrapy. A spider doesn't return a list: it yields items one at a time, and Scrapy streams them to wherever they're going.

Run it and export to a file:

scrapy crawl books -O books.json

-O (capital) overwrites the output file, so you always start fresh. Open books.json and you'll have the first page of books.

Watch out for -o. In projects created with Scrapy 2.20, the generated settings include FEED_MODE = "create". If the file already exists, lowercase -o then logs an error (Not writing ... because it already exists) and throws that run's items away, yet the command still exits normally, so it's easy to miss. In older setups, and outside a project, -o appends, and appending a second run to a JSON file leaves you with a corrupted file. Use -O while you're developing, or pick the behavior explicitly with the FEED_MODE setting.

If you just want to try a spider quickly without creating a project, scrapy runspider books.py -O books.json runs a single file.

About start_urls and start()

start_urls is the simplest way to say where to begin. When you need more control, such as generating a list of URLs or adding headers, write an async def start() method instead:

class BooksSpider(scrapy.Spider):
    name = "books"
    allowed_domains = ["books.toscrape.com"]

    async def start(self):
        for page in range(1, 4):
            url = f"https://books.toscrape.com/catalogue/page-{page}.html"
            yield scrapy.Request(url, callback=self.parse)

This replaces start_requests() from older tutorials. Note that async def and yield together make it an asynchronous generator, which Scrapy knows how to run. A leftover start_requests() isn't an error: the spider simply starts, reports Crawled 0 pages, and finishes without a word of complaint.

Following Pagination

Scraping one page isn't much of a crawler. Add this to the end of parse to follow the "Next" link:

next_page = response.css("li.next a::attr(href)").get()
        if next_page:
            yield response.follow(next_page, callback=self.parse)

response.follow() creates a new request for the link and sends its response back to parse. It handles relative URLs for you (no urljoin needed), and Scrapy automatically skips any URL it has already requested. When there's no Next link on the last page, get() returns None and the crawl ends.

Following Links to Detail Pages

The listing doesn't have everything: the description and product code live on each book's own page. So the spider needs two callbacks: one for listing pages and one for book pages. It will also pass the star rating (which we only read from the listing) along to the second callback.

First, define the shape of your data in bookscraper/items.py. Recent Scrapy templates use a plain dataclass:

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Book:
    title: str | None = None
    price: str | float | None = None
    rating: str | int | None = None
    availability: str | None = None
    description: str | None = None
    upc: str | None = None
    url: str | None = None

Now rewrite the spider:

import scrapy

from bookscraper.items import Book

class BooksSpider(scrapy.Spider):
    name = "books"
    allowed_domains = ["books.toscrape.com"]
    start_urls = ["https://books.toscrape.com/"]

    def parse(self, response):
        """Listing page: follow every book, then the Next link."""
        for card in response.css("article.product_pod"):
            rating = card.css("p.star-rating::attr(class)").get().split()[-1]   # "star-rating Three" -> "Three"
            yield response.follow(
                card.css("h3 a::attr(href)").get(),
                callback=self.parse_book,
                cb_kwargs={"rating": rating},
            )

        next_page = response.css("li.next a::attr(href)").get()
        if next_page:
            yield response.follow(next_page, callback=self.parse)

    def parse_book(self, response, rating):
        """Book page: build the item."""
        availability = "".join(response.css("p.availability::text").getall())
        yield Book(
            title=response.css("h1::text").get(),
            price=response.css("p.price_color::text").get(),
            rating=rating,
            availability=" ".join(availability.split()),
            description=response.css("#product_description ~ p::text").get(),
            upc=response.css("table tr:first-child td::text").get(),
            url=response.url,
        )

Notes on what's new:

  • Callbacks chain the crawl. parse yields requests for book pages, and each response goes to parse_book, which yields items. A callback can yield both requests and items.

  • cb_kwargs passes extra data to the next callback as keyword arguments. That's how rating travels from the listing page to the book page.

  • Whitespace cleanup. The availability text has line breaks and padding around it, so we collapse it with " ".join(text.split()).

  • Missing data. Some pages will lack a field, a description for instance. .get() returns None instead of crashing, and the dataclass defaults to None.

Cleaning Data with Pipelines

Right now price is a string like £51.77 and rating is a word like Three. Item pipelines are the right place to clean and validate items, keeping that logic out of the spider. Each pipeline is a class with a process_item method. Open bookscraper/pipelines.py:

import re

from itemadapter import ItemAdapter
from scrapy.exceptions import DropItem

RATINGS = {"One": 1, "Two": 2, "Three": 3, "Four": 4, "Five": 5}

class ValidateAndCleanPipeline:
    def process_item(self, item):
        adapter = ItemAdapter(item)

        if not adapter.get("title") or not adapter.get("price"):
            raise DropItem(f"Missing title or price: {adapter.get('url')}")

        adapter["price"] = float(re.sub(r"[^\d.]", "", adapter["price"]))   # "£51.77" -> 51.77
        adapter["rating"] = RATINGS.get(adapter["rating"])                   # "Three" -> 3
        return item

class DuplicatesPipeline:
    def __init__(self):
        self.seen = set()

    def process_item(self, item):
        upc = ItemAdapter(item)["upc"]
        if upc in self.seen:
            raise DropItem(f"Duplicate book: {upc}")
        self.seen.add(upc)
        return item

Key ideas:

  • ItemAdapter lets one pipeline work with dictionaries, dataclasses, or scrapy.Item objects through the same interface.

  • Return the item to pass it along, or raise DropItem to discard it. Dropped items are logged and counted but never exported.

  • The first pipeline drops incomplete items and converts the price and rating to numbers. The second drops repeats using the UPC, a unique product code, because the same book can appear under more than one URL.

  • Older tutorials write process_item(self, item, spider). That still runs in 2.20 but prints a deprecation warning, so drop the spider argument in new code.

Pipelines are off until you switch them on in settings.py. The numbers set the order, and lower runs first:

ITEM_PIPELINES = {
    "bookscraper.pipelines.ValidateAndCleanPipeline": 300,
    "bookscraper.pipelines.DuplicatesPipeline": 400,
}

Crawling Politely: Settings

Scrapy is fast, which is exactly why you must configure it carefully. Add these to settings.py:

# Tell site owners who you are and how to reach you
USER_AGENT = "BookScraperBot/1.0 (+https://example.com/bot; contact@example.com)"

# Adapt the delay to how quickly the server responds
AUTOTHROTTLE_ENABLED = True
AUTOTHROTTLE_START_DELAY = 1
AUTOTHROTTLE_MAX_DELAY = 10
AUTOTHROTTLE_TARGET_CONCURRENCY = 1.0

# Retry temporary failures a couple of times
RETRY_TIMES = 2

# During development only: cache responses on disk so repeat runs don't hit the site
HTTPCACHE_ENABLED = True

# Export automatically, without command-line flags
FEEDS = {
    "output/books.json": {"format": "json", "mode": "overwrite", "indent": 2},
}

What each does:

  • USER_AGENT replaces Scrapy's default. An honest, descriptive agent with contact details lets site owners reach you instead of blocking you.

  • AutoThrottle adjusts the delay between requests based on how fast the server responds, backing off when the site slows down. It never goes below the project's DOWNLOAD_DELAY of 1 second, so it can only make the crawl gentler than the default.

  • HTTPCACHE_ENABLED stores every response on disk. Re-running the spider while you tweak your selectors then costs the site nothing. Turn it off for real runs, or you'll scrape stale data.

  • FEEDS defines the output in settings, with "mode": "overwrite" replacing the file on each run.

Two more settings are handy while testing: CLOSESPIDER_PAGECOUNT and CLOSESPIDER_ITEMCOUNT stop the crawl after roughly that many pages or items (requests already in flight still finish). You can pass any setting on the command line with -s:

scrapy crawl books -s CLOSESPIDER_PAGECOUNT=10 -O sample.json

One catch: -O adds a second output on top of FEEDS, so this sample run also overwrites output/books.json with the partial result. Comment out FEEDS while you experiment if that bothers you.

The sandbox has 50 listing pages of 20 books each, so a full crawl is about 1,050 requests. With a delay of at least one second each, expect 20 minutes or more, so test with a small sample first.

Spider arguments

You can also pass arguments to a spider with -a. For example, to crawl one category instead of the whole site, accept a start URL:

class BooksSpider(scrapy.Spider):
    name = "books"
    allowed_domains = ["books.toscrape.com"]
    start_urls = ["https://books.toscrape.com/"]

    def __init__(self, start_url=None, *args, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        if start_url:
            self.start_urls = [start_url]

scrapy crawl books -a start_url=https://books.toscrape.com/catalogue/category/books/travel_2/index.html -O travel.json

Reading the Results

When a crawl finishes, Scrapy prints a statistics summary. These lines tell you most of what you need:

Stat Meaning
item_scraped_count Items that made it through the pipelines
item_dropped_count Items discarded with DropItem
downloader/response_status_count/200 Successful responses (look for 403, 404, 429 here too)
dupefilter/filtered Requests skipped because the URL had been seen
robotstxt/forbidden Requests blocked by robots.txt
finish_reason finished for a normal end, or the reason it stopped early

A stat that never happened isn't printed at all, so no robotstxt/forbidden line means nothing was blocked. Check these after every run. A crawl that "worked" but dropped half its items, or got a pile of 403 responses, is telling you something.

Running a Spider from a Script

Sometimes you want to run a crawl from your own Python code, for example from a scheduler. Put this in a file at the project root:

from scrapy.crawler import AsyncCrawlerProcess
from scrapy.utils.project import get_project_settings

process = AsyncCrawlerProcess(get_project_settings())
process.crawl("books")
process.start()          # blocks until the crawl is finished

Run it from the same folder as scrapy.cfg, so Scrapy finds your project settings.

Responsible Scraping with Scrapy

Because Scrapy can send many requests quickly, a few habits matter more here than in a script:

  • Leave ROBOTSTXT_OBEY = True. Turning it off to get at pages a site has asked crawlers to avoid is the wrong fix for a "Forbidden by robots.txt" message.

  • Keep the delay and the concurrency low. The generated defaults are conservative, and AutoThrottle helps. Don't raise concurrency against a small site.

  • Identify yourself with USER_AGENT, and respect 429 Too Many Requests and Retry-After by slowing down, not by retrying harder.

  • Read the terms of service, and avoid personal data unless you have a lawful reason to collect it. Our guide "Is Web Scraping Legal?" covers this in depth.

Troubleshooting

Symptom Likely cause What to try
Spider runs but crawls nothing (Crawled 0 pages) Code from an older tutorial defines start_requests(), which was removed in 2.16 Use start_urls or async def start()
Not writing ... already exists and an empty export -o on an existing file; projects from 2.20 set FEED_MODE = "create" Use -O, or set FEED_MODE explicitly
Empty or None fields Selector doesn't match Test it in scrapy shell
Filtered offsite request in the log The link is outside allowed_domains Check the domain, or leave it if it's intended
Forbidden by robots.txt The site disallows that path Respect it; don't disable ROBOTSTXT_OBEY
ModuleNotFoundError: bookscraper You're not in the project folder Run from the folder containing scrapy.cfg
Lots of 403 or 429 responses You're going too fast, or the site refuses your traffic Slow down; check the site's rules
Fewer items than expected Pipelines dropped some, or the duplicate filter skipped URLs Check item_dropped_count and dupefilter/filtered

For more detail while debugging, run with -s LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG.

Where to Go from Here

You now have the core of a real crawler: a spider, items, pipelines, polite settings, and exports. Natural next steps:

  • CrawlSpider rules let you describe which links to follow declaratively instead of writing the pagination code yourself.

  • JavaScript sites need a browser. Plugins such as scrapy-playwright connect Scrapy to Playwright, so you keep the framework's crawling and pipelines.

  • Storing results in a database is a matter of writing another pipeline, for example one that inserts into SQLite or PostgreSQL.

  • Scheduling a nightly crawl is easy once your spider runs from a script or a command.

The mental model to remember: spiders extract, pipelines clean, settings decide how politely you crawl, and Scrapy runs the machinery. Once you've written your first spider, the second takes minutes.

Happy scraping, and please do it politely!
