title: MAVE: Reconstructing Editable 3D Blockouts from Film Shots
description:
arXiv:2611.22464v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Animated 3D blockouts support previsualization and provide structural conditions for video generation, but manually reconstructing them from reference videos is costly. This limits both their use by creators and the production of paired training data. We introduce MAVEBench, a benchmark of 50 film shots and 416 keyframes for evaluating camera motion, spatial layout, and character blocking. We propose MAVE, a video-to-blockout framework combining Metric observation, Agentic modeling, and evidence-based VErification. It first recovers cameras, human motion, and geometric evidence in a shared metric coordinate system. An agent then constructs an editable environment under constraints from these observations, while programmatic checks report inconsistencies to guide refinement. The outputs are editable Blender scenes and frame-aligned blockout videos. On MAVEBench, MAVE improves overall scores by 27.5-41.1 points across three agents over their corresponding vanilla baselines. With DeepSeek-1017, it achieves a score of 73.2 at an average API cost of only USD 0.054 per shot, outperforming the strongest vanilla baseline while reducing total reconstruction time by 53%. We also construct MAVEData-3K, a dataset of 3,000 blockout-video pairs for model training, and will release it publicly. Creators can change viewpoints and character paths, then render the edited scenes to condition video generation. Code is available at https://github.com/yfChang-cv/MAVE.

title: Semantic-Guided Geometric Decoding for Token-Efficient Visual Grounding
description:
arXiv:2611.22577v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) provide a unified interface for language-conditioned visual perception. In pixel-to-sequence grounding, autoregressive coordinate generation requires multiple sequential decoding steps per box, increasing inference cost with the number of instances. Pixel-to-embedding methods reduce this overhead but lack explicit spatial encoding when using a shared special token. We introduce SemGeo, a token-efficient visual grounding framework that represents each instance with a single grid token for coarse localization. A geometric decoder reuses visual features and hidden states to recover precise discrete box coordinates in parallel. To train proposal generation and box localization together, we introduce Gaussian soft labels that encode coordinate distances during supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Reinforcement post-training further combines box-set rewards with coordinate supervision on model-generated proposals. This stage trains the language model and geometric decoder on their own predictions to mitigate the mismatch between teacher-forced training and inference. Across eight benchmarks spanning object detection, referring object detection, and document layout grounding, SemGeo achieves the highest F1@mIou among compared MLLMs on six benchmarks. It also delivers $2.07\times$ and $1.25\times$ the mean box-generation throughput of representative grounding baselines under vLLM and Transformers, respectively, while achieving higher accuracy in both comparisons.

title: MInfoVisQA: A Multilingual Benchmark for Information-Rich Visual Question Answering
description:
arXiv:2611.21644v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) excel in vision-language tasks; yet, whether they maintain consistent understanding of information-rich visuals (InfoVis) when the surface language changes remains unclear. To quantify this capability, we introduce MInfoVisQA, a parallel benchmark with 8,960 QA configurations derived from 128 seed instances across 24 languages. We construct seed-matched, language-parallel visuals and QA pairs by disentangling numerical-structural data from text and programmatically synchronizing translated labels. We evaluate 25 MLLMs under two settings: Language-Aligned QA (LQA, matching visual-text languages) and Cross-Language QA (XQA, fixed QA language with varying visual languages). The results show that aggregate accuracy masks substantial robustness gaps: two models with comparable mean LQA accuracy (80.4\%) exhibit performance spreads of 7.8 and 20.3 percentage points across languages. Moreover, all 25 models score lower with non-English visuals under fixed English QA, underscoring the need for cross-language sensitivity metrics.

title: Physical UX in Angular, from CSS springs to easter eggs on a CV site
description:
A CV site is a strange thing to over-engineer. Most visitors stay for under a minute. That is exactly why I spent so much time on how mine moves: in a short visit, the feel of the interface is part of the message. A button that gives under your finger and springs back, or a menu selection that glides instead of flickering, says "someone cared" faster than any paragraph.

My thesis: an interface should behave like a small physical world with one set of rules. One material, one gravity, one press, one spring. Those rules should be written down as tokens, checked by the build, and switched off as a set when the user asks for less motion.

This is how I did that on my CV site (live, source), a prerendered Angular 22 app with signals and no zone.js. It covers what research and platform guidelines say, what I took from them, where I deviated, the easter eggs I added on purpose, and the bugs that taught me the most.

TL;DR

  • One material. Every duration, curve, radius and state colour is a CSS custom property. A Node script fails the build when a component uses a raw number of milliseconds or a hand-mixed hover colour.
  • Springs without JavaScript. A damped spring is sampled into a CSS linear() easing. A little bounce for small things, a no-overshoot variant meant for size and layout, no bounce at all on exits.
  • Feedback timing follows the research. A press responds within 80 ms, tooltips wait 400 ms and then "warm up", exits are shorter than entrances, and a navigation jump glides once instead of hopping through every section.
  • Scroll-driven choreography in CSS. animation-timeline: view() with the easing inside the keyframe. One scroll-derived number, --p, drives three elements of the header hand-over.
  • Reduced motion removes movement as a set, because every movement duration token goes to zero. The figure, the confetti and the pointer effects are not mounted at all.
  • The easter eggs are deliberate. They form a discoverable second layer: never required, hidden from assistive tech, off under reduced motion, no data collected. The reasoning draws on the peak–end rule. It is design intent, not a measured result.
  • The engineering keeps it sustainable. Pure TypeScript logic at 100 % coverage, a thin rendering layer, 220 unit and 114 end-to-end tests, axe, a strict CSP with build-time script hashes, and a Lighthouse gate.

1. One material: tokens, and a build that enforces them

The first decision was to think in kinds of motion rather than milliseconds: a press, a short state change, a medium move, a ring spreading out, something big arriving, a playful flourish. Each kind gets one token:

// app/src/styles/_tokens.scss (trimmed)
// Spring: stiffness 220, damping 22, mass 1 (about 3 % overshoot), sampled for linear().
--ease-spring: linear(0, 0.049, 0.164, 0.308, 0.458, 0.597, 0.717, 0.815, 0.891, 0.947,
  0.985, 1.009, 1.023, 1.03, 1.031, 1.029, 1.025, 1.02, 1.016, 1.012, 1.008, 1.005, 1.003, 1.001, 1);
--ease-out: cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1);    /* entering */
--ease-in: cubic-bezier(0.3, 0, 0.8, 0.15);    /* leaving: the exit is quicker than the entrance */
--ease-in-out: cubic-bezier(0.2, 0, 0, 1);     /* a move across the screen, and loops */
--ease-spring-smooth: linear(0, 0.079, 0.236, /* … */ 0.998, 1); /* no overshoot: size, layout, big surfaces */
--dur-tap: 80ms;    /* a press goes in within a tenth of a second */
--dur-fade: 200ms;  /* opacity and colour only */
--press-scale: 0.96;
--tip-delay: 400ms;
--dur-press: 150ms;
--dur-short: 250ms;
--dur-med: 400ms;
--dur-ring: 600ms;
--dur-long: 700ms;
--dur-play: 900ms;

The curves are borrowed. --ease-in-out is Material 3's emphasized cubic-bezier(.2, 0, 0, 1) and --ease-in is its emphasized accelerate (.3, 0, .8, .15), from the material-web motion tokens. The durations sit on Material's 50 ms grid but use fewer steps: six are easy to choose between, sixteen are not.

Tokens only help if they are used, so scripts/check-design.mjs fails the build when:

  1. a corner radius above 6 px is not a token (or a full round),
  2. a transition duration is a number rather than a --dur-* token,
  3. an animation under one second is not a token (long and endless ones are allowed),
  4. a hover, pressed, selected or current state is painted with an on-the-spot color-mix() instead of a --tint-* token.

The transition rule is the interesting one. It has to tell a duration apart from a delay:

// app/scripts/check-design.mjs (trimmed)
for (const m of text.matchAll(/(?<![\w-])transition:\s*([^;}]*)/g)) {
  // each property's first time is its duration (a second one is a delay): it must be a token, not a number
  for (const item of m[1].split(/,(?![^(]*\))/)) {
    const first = item.match(/(\d*\.?\d+m?s)|var\(--(?:dur|lag|lead)[^)]*\)|calc\([^)]*\)/);
    if (first?.[1]) at(m.index, 'duration', `"transition: ${item.trim().slice(0, 60)}" … use a --dur-* token`);
  }
}

left var(--lag) var(--ease-spring) 90ms passes (the 90 ms is a delay) and opacity 200ms ease fails. It is a regex linter, not a CSS parser, and it has still caught me several times.

2. The physics

Springs in CSS with linear()

linear() takes a list of progress points and connects them with straight segments. MDN points out that with enough points it approximates any curve, and the values may go above 1, which is all an overshoot needs. I simulated a damped spring once (stiffness 220, damping 22, mass 1) and pasted 25 samples into the token.

The numbers behind it: the damping ratio is ζ = 22 / (2·√220) ≈ 0.74, and the overshoot of an underdamped spring with that ratio is about e^(−ζπ/√(1−ζ²)) ≈ 3 %. You can read that off the curve, which peaks at 1.031.

Is 3 % right? Apple's WWDC23 session Animate with springs describes a spring by duration (pacing) and bounce. Bounce 0 is the default ("a great general purpose spring"), around 15 % "doesn't feel very bouncy yet" but brisker, 30 % gives "noticeable bounciness", and above about 0.4 "may feel too exaggerated for a UI element". Apple's bounce is not my damping ratio, so I don't claim an exact mapping. My spring is gentle and reserved for small things: a press releasing, a chip label flipping, the menu pill, a commit dot growing. Anything that changes size or layout should get --ease-spring-smooth (no overshoot) or an ease-out, because bouncing layout makes text wobble. That is Apple's zero-bounce default where it matters.

linear() is a shape, not a time, so the duration is chosen per use: 250 ms for a press release, 400 ms for the menu pill. Pacing first, then bounce, as the talk suggests.

What CSS springs cannot do is keep velocity. Apple notes that a retargeted spring "uses the velocity it had when it was retargeted". A reversed CSS transition starts again from rest. That is acceptable for a menu pill, and it is one reason the figure in section 5 lives in TypeScript.

Press: in within 80 ms, out with a spring

NN/g's response-time limits (going back to Miller 1968 and Card et al. 1991) say that 0.1 s is "about the limit for having the user feel that the system is reacting instantaneously". NN/g's animation and attention article applies the same number to feedback: the effect "must begin within 0.1 seconds of the initial user action". So the press goes in within --dur-tap (80 ms) with an ease-out, and goes back over 250 ms with the spring:

// app/src/styles/_motion.scss
.chip, .btn {
  transition: scale var(--dur-short) var(--ease-spring),
    background-color var(--dur-short) var(--ease-out), box-shadow var(--dur-short) var(--ease-out);
}
.chip:active, .btn:active {
  scale: var(--press-scale);
  transition-duration: var(--dur-tap);
  transition-timing-function: var(--ease-out);
}

The trick is that the transition declared on the state you are going to wins. Going into :active, the 80 ms ease-out applies. Leaving it, the base rule's 250 ms spring applies. One property, two different physics, no script.

On iOS Safari none of this showed up at first. WebKit bug 138816, filed in 2014, documents that :active on touch only applies when the page has a touch event listener. The fix is one passive no-op listener in home.ts, with a comment explaining why it is there.

Exits are shorter than entrances

NN/g's animation duration guidance says most UI motion belongs in 100–500 ms, that entrances "usually need a subtly longer duration" than exits, that ease-out suits things arriving and ease-in things leaving, and that "completely linear motion looks weird". The role cards in the Experience section follow it with the native ::details-content pseudo-element and interpolate-size:

// app/src/app/sections/experience.ts (styles, trimmed)
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
  details { interpolate-size: allow-keywords; }
  details::details-content {            /* the state it goes to when closing */
    block-size: 0; opacity: 0; overflow: clip;
    transition: block-size var(--dur-short) var(--ease-in), opacity var(--dur-press) var(--ease-in),
      content-visibility var(--dur-short) allow-discrete;
  }
  details[open]::details-content {      /* the state it goes to when opening */
    block-size: auto; opacity: 1;
    transition: block-size var(--dur-med) var(--ease-spring), opacity var(--dur-short) var(--ease-out) 50ms,
      content-visibility var(--dur-med) allow-discrete;
  }
}

Opening takes 400 ms with the spring and a text fade that starts 50 ms late. Closing takes 250 ms with ease-in and no spring. content-visibility … allow-discrete keeps the content painted while it collapses (the MDN ::details-content page shows the same pattern). Browsers without these features simply open the card at once, which is a fine fallback.

Tooltips: a delay, then a warm-up

A tooltip that appears the instant the pointer crosses it turns a row of icons into flicker. NN/g's mega-menu guidance uses a 0.5 s rest before showing hover content. PatternFly defaults to a 300 ms entry delay. I picked 400 ms (--tip-delay). Keyboard focus shows the tip at once, because NN/g's tooltip guidelines warn that hover-only tooltips are inaccessible.

The delay becomes annoying once the reader is looking for tooltips, for example when running along the menu. So core/tips.ts adds a warm-up: once a tip has really been shown (it listens for the animationstart of tip-in), leaving it puts html.tips-warm on the page for 300 ms, and in that window the CSS sets animation-delay: 0s. Escape sets html.tips-off until the pointer or the focus moves. The script only toggles classes. The timing stays in CSS.

A selection pill that travels, stretches and waits

The desktop menu has one selection pill. It is a real element positioned with CSS anchor positioning on whichever link currently holds anchor-name: --nav-target. When the anchor changes, left and right transition. To make it feel like something with mass, the leading edge moves fast with an ease-out and the trailing edge follows with the spring, so the pill stretches in the direction of travel:

// app/src/app/shell/header.ts (styles, trimmed)
.links { --lead: calc(var(--dur-short) * 0.75); --lag: var(--dur-med); }
.links[data-dir='right'] .sel {
  transition: left var(--lag) var(--ease-spring) 90ms, right var(--lead) var(--ease-out) 90ms, …;
}
.links[data-dir='left'] .sel {
  transition: left var(--lead) var(--ease-out) 90ms, right var(--lag) var(--ease-spring) 90ms, …;
}
@media (hover: hover) {
  .links:has(a:hover) a[aria-current]:not(:hover) { anchor-name: none; }
  .links a:hover { anchor-name: --nav-target; }
  .links:has(a:hover) .sel { transition-delay: 0s; }
}

The 90 ms delay is a small piece of hover intent. It applies only on the way back to the current item, so a pointer that crosses the menu's edge for a moment does not send the pill away and back. Following the pointer is immediate. The only script involved sets data-dir.

A navigation jump glides once

Clicking "Contact" in the menu smooth-scrolls past four sections. In the first version the active-section tracker named each of them in turn, and the pill hopped across the whole menu. Accurate, and wrong. holdActive(id) in core/active.ts now names the destination at once and ignores everything in between until scrollend fires, or after 1.2 s if the page didn't have to scroll. The smooth scroll itself is scroll-behavior: smooth in CSS, which reduced motion turns off. No script animates a scroll.

Scroll-driven reveals, with the easing inside the keyframe

Section content settles in as it enters the viewport, using animation-timeline: view(). No IntersectionObserver and no script:

// app/src/styles/_motion.scss
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
  @supports (animation-timeline: view()) {
    .reveal { animation: reveal linear both; animation-timeline: view(); animation-range: entry 0% entry 40%; }
  }
}
@keyframes reveal {
  from { transform: translateY(18px); animation-timing-function: var(--ease-out); }
  to { transform: none; }
}

On a scroll timeline the animation's own linear is correct, since the element should track the scroll 1:1. But a linear ramp stops dead at the end of its range. An ease-out on the keyframe (it applies from that keyframe to the next) lets the element settle while still being driven by the scroll. It is transform-only, so a contrast audit never catches faded text mid-reveal.

One scroll number, three elements

As you scroll past the hero, the large portrait drains from the top, the header's avatar slot fills from the bottom like a progress bar, and the name is written out beside it. An earlier version flew a cloned image across the page, which meant layout reads every frame, a duplicate image and z-index fights with the glass header. The current version computes one number and lets CSS do the rest:

// app/src/app/shell/avatar-dock.ts (trimmed)
const distance = img.getBoundingClientRect().bottom + window.scrollY - slot.getBoundingClientRect().bottom;
const raw = distance > 0 ? clamp01(window.scrollY / distance) : 1;
const p = reduce.matches ? (raw >= 1 ? 1 : 0) : raw;
box?.style.setProperty('--p', p.toFixed(3));   // the hero portrait
brand.style.setProperty('--p', p.toFixed(3));  // the header avatar and the name

.portrait img { clip-path: inset(calc(var(--p, 0) * 100%) 0 0 0 round var(--radius)); }      /* drains */
.fill        { clip-path: inset(calc((1 - var(--p, 0)) * 100%) 0 0 0); }                     /* fills */
.mark        { --edge: calc(var(--p, 0) * 140%);                                              /* is written */
               mask-image: linear-gradient(90deg, #000 calc(var(--edge) - 40%), transparent var(--edge)); }

It runs backwards when you scroll back up. The header image reuses the hero's currentSrc (no second request), nothing reads layout at scrollY === 0, and under reduced motion p simply jumps from 0 to 1.

Time-based easing, not per-frame easing

The animated background draws contour lines with marching squares on a canvas. They drift with the scroll and bend around the pointer. Its first version eased with per-frame factors, t += (goal - t) * 0.12. On a 120 Hz display that runs twice as often and settles twice as fast. The fix is exponential easing with time constants:

// app/src/app/shell/backdrop.ts
const dt = Math.min(100, stamp ? now - stamp : 16.7);
stamp = now;
const ease = (ms: number): number => 1 - Math.exp(-dt / ms);
t += (g.t - t) * ease(130);   // 0.12 per frame at 60 Hz ≈ a 130 ms time constant
bump = { x: bump.x + (aim.x - bump.x) * ease(85), y: …, k: bump.k + (aim.k - bump.k) * ease(200) };

The constants come from the old factors (−16.7 / ln(1 − 0.12) ≈ 130 ms), so 60 Hz looks exactly as before. And the loop stops once everything has settled.

3. What the research says, and what I did with it

Most of these are guidelines or conventions, not controlled studies. The table says which is which.

Where I deviated:

  • I use bounce at all. Apple's default is zero. I use a little, on small, user-initiated things, where it reads as "this object has mass". I would not defend it on anything big.
  • Some motion is longer than 500 ms. --dur-ring (600), --dur-long (700) and --dur-play (900) exceed NN/g's range. They are used for one-off flourishes, never for something the user waits on.
  • I have no user research of my own. Everything above was verified by tests and by watching. Nothing was measured with real users.

4. Reduced motion, done as a set

Because every movement uses a token, reduced motion is mostly one rule:

// app/src/styles/_motion.scss
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  :root { --dur-tap: 0s; --dur-press: 0s; --dur-short: 0s; --dur-med: 0s; --dur-ring: 0s; --dur-long: 0s; --dur-play: 0s; }
  .chip:active, .btn:active { scale: none; }
  ::view-transition-group(*), ::view-transition-old(*), ::view-transition-new(*) { animation: none !important; }
}

Everything that uses a duration token becomes instant. States still change and nothing is left half-animated. On top of that:

  • Scroll-driven reveals sit inside prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference, so they never apply.
  • scroll-behavior goes back to auto, so menu jumps are instant.
  • The figure, the confetti, the pointer-lit surfaces and the portrait tilt are not started. Each checks matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)') and returns before attaching anything.
  • The background contour lines are drawn once and stay still. An end-to-end test scrolls and moves the mouse, then compares a checksum of the canvas pixels before and after.

The intent is to remove movement and keep fades: A List Apart treats "non-moving properties, like opacity, color, and blurs" as unlikely to cause trouble, and a fade still tells the user what changed. To be honest about the current state, the --dur-fade token that reduced motion leaves alone is not used by any component yet, so most fades become instant too (see the limits).

For WCAG 2.2.2, the only thing that moves on its own for more than five seconds is the aurora behind the hero. It pauses when the hero leaves the screen, runs two alternations (drift 70s … 2 alternate) and then rests, and it is off under reduced motion. WCAG 2.3.3 (AAA) is covered because all interaction-triggered motion goes through the same query.

5. Gamification as a deliberate technique

The site has a second layer that you don't need and might not find. It exists on purpose.

The mechanics:

  • The figure. A small Prince of Persia-style stick figure sits at the end of the soft-skills row. Rest the mouse on a tile and it pulls itself up and runs after the pointer: it jumps gaps, grabs and climbs ledges, drops down, and climbs a web line to tiles far above. Leave past the end of the row and it runs off the cliff. In about a quarter of falls it shoots a web line and swings back. Otherwise a small cross rises over a patch of swamp in the footer, on the side it fell from. On touch screens, taps act as the pointer.
  • The scratch card. The hero portrait has a coin cursor. Drag over it and the photo scratches off to reveal one of ten prizes per language (never the same twice in a row): familiar scams that give themselves away, plus a copy-address button. Clear about two fifths (a quarter on touch) and the rest falls away in confetti. The card stays for five seconds with a countdown line, and then the photo heals.
  • Shift ×3. A photo scene, then a "stats sheet" that reads the page's own numbers live from the browser's Performance APIs: requests, third-party requests, cookies, storage keys, bytes, LCP, CLS, plus the release, test counts and coverage written at build time. The easter egg is also evidence.
  • The career graph. Experience drawn as a contribution graph (one square per year per skill family) that you scrub with a pointer or a finger.
  • The header hand-over from section 2.

The intent, and what it is based on:

  • A peak and a clean ending. The peak–end rule (NN/g, based on Kahneman and Fredrickson's research) says that people judge an experience largely by its most intense moment and by its end. So there is one peak that is the visitor's own doing (scratching, or watching the figure fall) and a quiet, slightly funny ending: the footer, where the visitor's own play is still visible as crosses in the swamp.
  • A discoverable second layer. The coin cursor, a console line (stat → shift shift shift), the figure waiting on the end of the row. Hints, not instructions. I don't cite a curiosity study here because I didn't verify one I'd stand behind. This is design intent.
  • Variation. Injected randomness varies the figure's jumps and rescues, and the prize changes, so a second go isn't a replay.
  • Craft affects perceived quality. The aesthetic-usability effect (Kurosu & Kashimura, 1995) says people judge attractive products as easier to use. That is a reason to care about polish, and a warning that polish can hide problems. Hence the gates in section 6.

The guardrails, which matter more than the mechanics:

  • Never required, never in the way. All of the content is readable without touching any of it. The figure has pointer-events: none and never takes a click. The scratch card's prize is inert and aria-hidden until it has been won. Then it becomes a role="status" region.
  • Hidden from assistive tech. The figure, the graveyard, the confetti canvas and the career-graph drawing are aria-hidden. The roles list under the graph remains the readable source.
  • Off under reduced motion. The figure is not mounted, there is no confetti, and the hero tilt is off.
  • Keyboard-safe. Shift ×3 (within 700 ms) ignores held-key repeat and resets on any other key, so typing capital letters never triggers it. Escape always leaves the scene.
  • No data collected. The graveyard lives in a signal for the lifetime of the page and nowhere else. There are no analytics. The stats sheet counts third-party requests and shows "0".
  • It costs nothing up front. The figure is behind @defer (on viewport(row); prefetch on idle), and the scene, the sheet and the command palette are @defer blocks rendered only when opened (angular.dev on @defer).

What I can't claim: that any of this improves retention or recall. I have no analytics by choice and no study of my own. It is designed against recognised principles and checked for harm (accessibility, performance, privacy). Whether it works is anecdotal.

6. The engineering that keeps it sustainable

A pure logic layer and a thin renderer

core/buddy.ts (about 1,200 lines) is pure TypeScript with no DOM. Geometry and pointer go in, and a View comes out: position, facing, nine joint angles, spin, web line. Inside: a hip under one gravity (1200 px/s², about four times "real" for a 57 px figure, as old games did), two-bone inverse kinematics to planted feet, ballistic jump planning, ledge hangs with a damped sway, pull-ups, a web swing, sitting and falling. Randomness is injected (new Buddy(random = Math.random)).

sections/buddy.ts (about 260 lines) renders it as an inline SVG with nine <g> joints, setting style.rotate each frame. It is DOM rather than canvas because it must go behind or in front of real tiles that tilt on hover, inherit currentColor in both themes, and be clipped by the tile it hides behind.

Because the logic is pure, the tests check physics, not snapshots. The spec rebuilds the drawn figure with forward kinematics, independently of the IK, and asserts properties:

// app/src/app/core/buddy.spec.ts (trimmed)
it('never slides a foot that is on the ground, and never puts one into it', () => {
  const views = sprint();
  let planted = 0;
  for (let i = 1; i < views.length; i++) {
    const [a, c] = [feet(views[i - 1]!), feet(views[i]!)];
    for (const k of [0, 1]) {
      expect(c[k]!.y).toBeLessThan(LONG.fixed + 1e-6);
      if (Math.abs(a[k]!.y - LONG.fixed) < 1e-6 && Math.abs(c[k]!.y - LONG.fixed) < 1e-6) {
        planted++;
        expect(Math.abs(c[k]!.x - a[k]!.x)).toBeLessThan(1e-6);
      }
    }
  }
  expect(planted).toBeGreaterThan(100);
});

Other tests check that jumps follow a parabola of the one gravity, that joints move smoothly through every change of state (bounded second differences), and that the web rescue follows random(). The same split holds for core/contours.ts (marching squares), core/scratch.ts, graph/*, content/* and search/search.ts. Components are covered end to end instead.

Gates

npm run verify runs strict type-checking, ESLint, unit tests (220, with 100 % statement/branch/function/line coverage of the logic layer), a 7:1 contrast check, the design check, the build, a privacy check, a check that docs/ matches the committed sources, Playwright (114 tests, including axe over WCAG 2.2 AA tags, reduced-motion emulation and CSP-violation listeners) and Lighthouse on both pages, mobile and desktop. Accessibility, best practices and SEO must be exactly 100. Performance has a floor of 95 because it is a noisy lab metric. Desktop scores 100. Mobile simulation has ranged from the high 80s to the high 90s on my machine, so a mobile miss gets re-run and investigated.

Static, hydrated, almost silent

  • SSG + hydration. Both language pages are prerendered (RenderMode.Prerender) and hydrated with provideClientHydration(withEventReplay()). There is no router in the browser: the language switch is a signal plus history.pushState. There is no zone.js in the dependencies. The one place that needs an immediate render calls appRef.tick() explicitly.
  • Lazy work. @defer for the figure and the overlays, and content-visibility: auto on three below-the-fold sections. The built main bundle in docs/ is about 381 kB before compression, under a budget that warns at 400 kB and fails at 450 kB.
  • A strict CSP as a meta tag (GitHub Pages can't send headers). scripts/csp.mjs hashes every inline script in the prerendered HTML at build time and writes script-src 'self' 'sha256-…', with object-src 'none', base-uri 'self' and form-action 'none'. Styles keep 'unsafe-inline' because the prerendered HTML carries style attributes. That is a known compromise.
  • One documented outside request. connect-src allows exactly https://dev.to/api/articles. The research block fetches my article list when it comes within 300 px of the viewport, with credentials: 'omit', referrerPolicy: 'no-referrer', an 8-second AbortController timeout, a loader and an error notice. A failure keeps the list fetched at build time, so the section is never empty.

7. Five bugs worth sharing

1. The spring that never ran. The new role-card spring looked exactly like the old ease-out. Further down the same stylesheet sat an older disclosure block with the same selectors and an ease-out transition. Same specificity, later in the source, so it won silently. Fix: delete it and keep one owner per selector. Lesson: when a motion change "does nothing", search for the selector before tuning numbers.

2. Two @keyframes reveal. I found this one while writing the article. _layout.scss defines reveal as a fade-and-rise for section headings, and _motion.scss defines reveal as a transform-only rise. Both land in one global CSS file, and keyframes don't cascade: "the last one encountered by the parser is used". So the headings never fade. That is the safer outcome for contrast audits, but by luck, not design. Fix: distinct names, and a design-check rule against duplicate @keyframes. Lesson: animation names are global.

3. The language switch that vibrated. The switch ran inside a View Transition (a root cross-fade), and the changed texts had their own entrance animation. They played back to back and the page shuddered. Fix: no View Transition here. Render synchronously, then restart one class on the live DOM:

// app/src/app/core/lang.ts
private settle(): void {
  const root = this.doc.documentElement;
  root.classList.remove('swap');
  void root.offsetWidth;          // a layout in between, so every switch plays from the start
  root.classList.add('swap');
  clearTimeout(this.swapTimer);
  this.swapTimer = setTimeout(() => root.classList.remove('swap'), 600);
}

Lesson: a View Transition is a choreography of its own. Don't stack another on it. (The theme switch keeps one, a circle growing from the button, since nothing else animates there.)

4. CLS 0.123 in the hero. On desktop the text is vertically centred next to the portrait. Until the image arrived, the portrait's box had no height, the row was only as tall as the text, and then the text jumped down. Fix: reserve the row from the first frame with grid-template-rows: minmax(min(20rem, 38vw), auto). CLS went to 0 in a throttled local simulation. Lesson: width/height on the <img> doesn't help when the container's size depends on it.

5. content-visibility versus the target-size audit. I put content-visibility: auto on every below-the-fold section. Lighthouse then reported buttons in Projects and About as "obscured", measured against cards of a section that was still a placeholder. Fix: keep it on Experience, Skills and Contact only, with a comment saying why. Lesson: optimisations that change geometry can confuse geometry-based audits.

Bonus: the 120 Hz per-frame easing bug from section 2. A constant like 0.12 in an animation loop usually means it is there.

8. What I would do differently, and the limits

  • The spring is bouncy on tall cards. About 3 % overshoot is pleasant on a 44 px button and visible on a 500 px role card (around 15 px). The cards should use --ease-spring-smooth for block-size and keep the bouncy spring for small things, which is the rule I wrote down myself.
  • "Keep the fades" is not fully implemented. --dur-fade exists and is not used. Under reduced motion most fades become instant too. The right fix is to move opacity and colour transitions onto --dur-fade and let the check enforce it.
  • Exits are inconsistent. The command palette has a spring entrance and no exit animation: it just disappears. The role cards get exits right, but the palette does not.
  • CSS springs don't carry velocity. Interrupt the pill mid-flight and it starts again from rest. For real interruptible motion you need script, as the figure does.
  • The evidence for the gamification is intent, not measurement. I chose not to track visitors, so I can't tell you whether anyone remembers the swamp.
  • The design check is a regex. It is cheap and useful but blind to some patterns (it missed the duplicate keyframes).
  • Mobile Lighthouse performance is noisy enough that a hard 100 would be a flaky gate. I keep the floor and investigate misses.

9. A checklist you can copy

  • [ ] Durations and curves are tokens, organised by kind of motion, not by number.
  • [ ] The build fails on a raw duration, a raw radius or a hand-mixed state colour.
  • [ ] Press feedback starts within 100 ms. Release can be slower and springier.
  • [ ] Exits are shorter than entrances and use ease-in. Entrances use ease-out. Nothing linear except scroll-linked motion.
  • [ ] Springs: bounce only on small things, none on layout or size changes.
  • [ ] Tooltips wait (300–500 ms) on hover, appear instantly on focus, warm up after the first one, and close on Escape.
  • [ ] A programmatic scroll names its destination once and doesn't report every section it passes.
  • [ ] Scroll-driven animations: linear on the timeline, easing on the keyframe, transform-only where contrast matters.
  • [ ] One scroll-derived custom property can drive several elements. Avoid flying clones.
  • [ ] Any rAF easing uses 1 - Math.exp(-dt / tau), not a per-frame factor.
  • [ ] Reduced motion zeroes the movement tokens and doesn't mount decorative motion.
  • [ ] Nothing moves on its own for more than five seconds without a way to stop it.
  • [ ] iOS: a passive touchstart listener so :active works.
  • [ ] Easter eggs: never required, aria-hidden, off under reduced motion, no data collected, lazy-loaded.
  • [ ] Animation names are global, so search for duplicate @keyframes.

The site is at er2es.github.io and all of the code above is in github.com/er2es/er2es.github.io (MIT). Try resting the mouse on the soft-skills row, scratching the portrait, or pressing Shift three times. If you find a motion bug, I'd like to hear about it.

title: From UX Designer to AI App Builder: My Journey into Creating an AI-Powered Kids' Storytelling App
description:
I have watched several YouTube tutorials about creating kids' channels and animated videos, and I noticed how easily people are now creating animated content using AI tools. With just a prompt, these tools can take care of everything from storyboarding and scriptwriting to suggesting ideas and generating voiceovers.

I became curious about how this process actually works, so I decided to experiment with it myself and explore its pros and cons.

As a UX designer, I wanted to take this a step further. Instead of relying entirely on third-party tools, I decided to explore how I could build my own application to create animated videos. My goal is to understand the technology, experiment with AI capabilities, and build a customized tool that gives me more control over the entire video creation process.

In this article, I'll share my learning journey, the challenges I encountered, and my experience building an AI-powered animated video creation application.

What I discovered from my research?

After watching plenty of YouTube videos, I noticed that many creators are already using AI tools to produce animated videos, often as a way to generate additional income or build a side hustle. Many are creating multiple videos using simple AI tools and paying monthly subscriptions to increase their content production.

However, I also came across several videos where creators discussed how AI-generated content could affect YouTube monetization. Some mentioned that their videos were demonetized or that their channels faced monetization restrictions or rejection.

This made me curious to try the process myself. I decided to create an animated video using one of these AI tools to understand how it actually works.

What I discovered was that several AI video-generation platforms offer monthly subscriptions ranging from approximately $15–25, allowing creators to generate multiple videos depending on their subscription plan and usage limits.

I signed up for a trial and started experimenting. One thing I quickly noticed was the lack of visual consistency and customization. When generating multiple videos, the characters often followed very similar patterns. For example, the baby's facial features, body proportions, and overall animation style looked almost identical across different videos.

It made me realize that many creators might be using similar AI-generated characters and animation styles to produce large volumes of content.

This experiment helped me understand both the convenience and limitations of AI-powered video creation tools.

After experimenting with those tools, I realized that I needed a simple, beginner-friendly tool that would help me create videos based on my own ideas. So, I decided to try creating a video myself first.

As I started exploring the process, I began thinking more about the kind of video experience I actually wanted to create.

What I have noticed about kids' content?

One thing I noticed about kids' content is how easily children get drawn into watching one video after another. Once a video ends, another one starts playing, and this cycle can continue almost endlessly. Sometimes, children find it difficult to stop watching, and when parents turn off the videos, it can lead to frustration or crying because they want to keep watching more.

This made me think about the role of autoplay and continuous video recommendations in kids' content. I wanted to understand how this experience works and explore whether I could build something different: a customized video creation application where I have more control over the content, characters, stories, and overall viewing experience.

So, my first priority was not to create long videos that would keep children watching the screen for extended periods. Instead, I wanted to experiment with a different approach to children's content.

My initial idea:

My initial idea was to start with a short visual introduction, lasting anywhere from 10 seconds to 1 minute, where the characters would introduce the story using facial expressions and gestures. After that, the experience would transition into a full voice-based storytelling format, allowing children to focus more on listening rather than continuously watching the screen.

I wanted to create something similar to a podcast-style experience for kids, where engaging stories, characters, and voiceovers would encourage children to listen and use their imagination instead of spending too much time in front of a screen.

That's where my story began!

Implementing next steps with my Goal:

My ultimate goal is to build a customized application that encourages children to enjoy stories through listening while helping reduce their screen time.

Then I started exploring and experimenting with different options. One of the first things I looked into was how to make illustrated characters lip-sync with the voice, matching their facial movements, expressions, and emotions to the narration.

As I explored further, I realized that I needed an application that could bring together two important capabilities: converting text into voice and generating illustrated images based on my stories or poems for children.

My biggest Challenge:

One of the biggest challenges I faced was finding the right voice options for my videos. I didn't want to use or expose my original voice. Instead, I wanted children to feel as though another child or a friendly cartoon character was telling them the story.
I started thinking about different voice personalities that would make the experience more engaging and relatable for children. For example:

  • Young female voices: To represent friendly female cartoon characters.
  • Child voices: So children could feel as though another child, similar to their age, was telling the story.
  • Adult female voices: To create a warm, gentle, and comforting storytelling experience, similar to listening to a mother or a familiar adult reading a story.

My intention was to create a collection of voice options that would make storytelling feel more natural, friendly, and engaging for children.

That is why having multiple voice options became one of my key requirements when planning my application.

First, I explored several AI voice-generation applications that offered text-to-voice and voice-to-voice conversion. However, most of these platforms required paid subscriptions to access additional features, and their free trials did not give me enough flexibility to experiment with different voice options.
So, I decided to take a different approach and build my own voice-generation application.

Building my own voice-generation application:

When I started building it, I discovered that AI-powered coding tools were very helpful in creating the application's interface, functionality, and interactions. They allowed me to build a good user experience and make changes to the application whenever I wanted.

My first challenge on building my own application: However, I faced another challenge: generating natural, human-like voices. Most of the solutions I initially explored produced robotic-sounding voices or focused mainly on audio processing features such as noise reduction. They didn't provide the kind of natural voice-generation experience I was looking for.

I realized that AI coding tools are excellent for building application interfaces and functionality, but building a voice-generation application requires additional voice technologies and integrations.

Next, I explored AI animation tools. These platforms offered pre-designed characters that could be animated using recorded audio. I could record my own voice, upload it, and the selected character would automatically generate lip movements and facial expressions that matched the audio.

Although this was an interesting approach, it didn't completely solve my problem because I wanted to use different AI-generated voices instead of recording my original voice.

Then, I explored another category of AI tools that could generate better application interfaces, illustrations, and visual assets. These tools helped me explore the visual possibilities, but I was still looking for a way to bring everything together into one customized application.

My biggest learning was that creating an AI-powered video application is not just about building an interface. It requires bringing together multiple capabilities, including voice generation, illustration creation, character animation, and audio synchronization.

I'll share my next experience in the upcoming article.
If you're interested in following my application-building journey and learning how I approach challenges as a UX Researcher and Designer, feel free to follow me!

And if you've already experimented with building similar applications or explored other AI tools, I'd love to hear about your experiences. Please share them in the comments. I'm always happy to learn from others, too!

title: In an audit, a green test means the bug is real
description:
An audit report says "this route lets anyone find out which accounts exist". The team reads it, nods and moves on to the next ticket. A test shows the request and the response. Anyone can run it again on their own machine.

TL;DR: in an audit, I write tests that pass as long as the flaw exists. A green test proves the problem, with the exact request and response. Everything runs on an isolated test database, with made-up accounts, never touching production. Once the flaw is fixed, the test is flipped and becomes a regression test. The report keeps its paragraphs for what the tests do not prove.

This article is for developers and leads who order a security audit, or receive one. No security background needed.

The setup: a white-box audit of an API

In September, I ran a white-box audit of an API. Two questions drove the work. Can someone without an account find out who is registered? Can a logged-in user touch another account's data?

The core of the audit was five HTTP tests. An HTTP test sends a real request to the API and checks the response. The five held 21 assertions. An assertion is one precise check, like "the status code is 200".

All five tests were green. That was the bad news.

Here I cover the public routes, the ones that work without an account. The other tests targeted another account's IDs sent in the request body, the topic of a separate article.

An audit test passes when the flaw exists

Usually a green test means the code works. I have written before that a green test only proves what it actually checks. In an audit, I make it check the dangerous behavior on purpose.

Each test describes the flaw as if it were the expected behavior. For example, "with a wrong token, the API returns the profile". If the test passes, the flaw is real. If it fails, the flaw was not reproduced under these conditions. Check the fixtures, configuration and actual response before drawing a conclusion.

That is the big difference with a paragraph. A paragraph can be wrong and nobody notices. A test makes the evidence reproducible. Tests can be wrong too, so review their assertions.

The example: "forgot password" answers 200 or 422

Take the "forgot password" route. You send an email address, and the API sends a link to change the password. Nothing could be more ordinary.

In this API, the response depended on the address. A registered address got a 200 status code, which means "OK". An unknown address got a 422, which means "request rejected".

That difference is enough for account enumeration. Someone tries a list of addresses and keeps the ones that answer 200. They now know who has an account, without any password.

And the route had no explicit rate limit. Nothing slowed down mass attempts.

Here is the audit test, simplified for this article. The API was written in PHP with Laravel, but the idea works in any language.

// Audit test: green means the flaw exists.
public function test_forgot_password_reveals_which_emails_exist(): void
{
    User::factory()->create(['email' => 'known@example.test']);

    $this->postJson('/auth/forgot-password', ['email' => 'known@example.test'])
        ->assertStatus(200);

    $this->postJson('/auth/forgot-password', ['email' => 'unknown@example.test'])
        ->assertStatus(422);
}

The test creates a fake account, then sends two requests. It passes if the two status codes differ. Green means the flaw exists.

This is not a rare case. In 2026, several CVEs describe exactly the same flaw. Here are two, checked in the official registry.

  • CVE-2026-24468, in the open source project OpenAEV. The /api/reset route answered 400 for an unknown email and 200 for a valid one. It is fixed in version 2.0.13.
  • CVE-2026-58503, in the Frappe web framework. The enumeration went through the reset_password route. It is fixed in versions 15.106.0 and 16.16.0.

Everything happens far from production

An audit must not cause the incident it is looking for. So no test touched production. Not a single request went to it.

The tests ran in a temporary Docker environment. That environment had no access to the outside network. Even a mistake in a test could not reach a real server.

The database was an isolated MySQL test database. The accounts and records were synthetic. Synthetic means made up for the test. No real person is behind them.

During the audit, I did not change the project's code. The proof tests were not added to its repository.

This setup has one more benefit. Anyone on the team can replay the tests, with no production access and no real data.

The report says what the tests do not prove

A test proves one precise thing, and nothing else. The report has to say so. That is where paragraphs really earn their place.

Take the "verify email" route. For an active account, it returned the profile with any non-empty token. That profile also held the account's internal ID.

Combined with "forgot password", this made a chain. You test addresses, then you collect the IDs of the accounts you found. Yet the report states the limit. It works one address at a time, from a guessed list. The audit found no route that hands out every account at once.

The report also splits two lists. On one side, flaws confirmed by a test. On the other, leads seen in the code but not tested. A lead stays a lead until a test confirms it.

Finally, the tests cover the local code, not the deployed application. And the project already had a test checking that one account was denied access to another's data. It passed too. Its green said nothing about the routes my tests targeted.

Once the flaw is fixed, the test flips

The cycle has four steps: reproduce the flaw, fix the code, see the proof fail, then write the protective test.

Green proves the flaw, then the same test keeps it closed. During the audit, the test passes as long as the route answers 200 or 422 depending on the address. After the fix, it expects the same answer for both.

A green audit test is an alarm. It should not stay green. After the fix, it fails, and that is the signal you want.

You then rewrite it the other way around. It becomes a regression test that replays the same request on every code change. For "forgot password", both addresses must receive the expected generic response. Two identical errors are not enough.

// Regression test: green means the flaw stays closed.
public function test_forgot_password_answers_the_same_for_every_email(): void
{
    \Illuminate\Support\Facades\Notification::fake();
    $user = User::factory()->create(['email' => 'known@example.test']);

    $known = $this->postJson('/auth/forgot-password', ['email' => 'known@example.test']);
    $unknown = $this->postJson('/auth/forgot-password', ['email' => 'unknown@example.test']);

    // This example's API contract is 200 with this exact generic response.
    $expected = ['message' => 'If the account exists, a reset link will be sent.'];
    $known->assertStatus(200)->assertExactJson($expected);
    $unknown->assertStatus(200)->assertExactJson($expected);
    \Illuminate\Support\Facades\Notification::assertSentTo(
        $user, \Illuminate\Auth\Notifications\ResetPassword::class
    );
    \Illuminate\Support\Facades\Notification::assertCount(1);
}

This example uses Laravel’s standard notification, intercepted by Notification::fake(). Adapt the status, message and notification to your API. This test does not measure response time. OWASP also asks for a constant response time. Otherwise the delay gives the address away. The rate limit deserves its own test too.

I did this flip on the "verify email" route. After the fix, I added a test that sends a wrong token. It expects a 422 rejection, with no profile data in the response. A second test checks that an unknown account gets the same error.

Why a test beats a paragraph

A report gets read once. A test lives in CI and runs again on every change. It keeps working after the auditor has left.

The test establishes the observed behavior. Severity still depends on the exposed data, required permissions and deployed configuration.

Finally, it sets the expected result without dictating the fix. The team chooses how to fix it. The test only says when it is done.

The checklist

In an audit, every confirmed flaw gets its test. Once the flaw is fixed, that test flips and stays in CI.

  • [ ] Write each suspected flaw as a test that passes if the flaw exists
  • [ ] Run the tests on an isolated test database, never on production
  • [ ] Use only made-up accounts and data
  • [ ] Cut network access from the test environment
  • [ ] Keep flaws confirmed by a test apart from leads seen in the code
  • [ ] Write in the report what each test does not prove
  • [ ] On "forgot password", compare the status code and message for a known and an unknown email
  • [ ] Test response time and rate limiting separately
  • [ ] After the fix, flip each test and keep it in CI

The takeaway

In an audit, green changes meaning. It no longer says "it works". It says "the flaw is here, and here is how to replay it".

Then the same test switches sides. Flipped, it keeps the flaw closed, long after the audit.

Want an audit that delivers proof your team can replay? See my audit and hardening offer, or let's talk.

Sources: Laravel, testing notifications · CVE-2026-24468 (OpenAEV) · OpenAEV, advisory GHSA-v6rg-hf9w-f8ph · CVE-2026-58503 (Frappe) · OWASP, Forgot Password Cheat Sheet · OWASP WSTG, testing for account enumeration · CWE-204, Observable Response Discrepancy

title: SeasonRainBench: Global Seasonal Precipitation
description:
arXiv:2611.22281v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Accurate seasonal precipitation forecasts help societies prepare for drought, flooding, and crop failure months in advance. While data-driven methods have made rapid progress in weather and subseasonal forecasting, operational seasonal precipitation prediction still relies on numerical ensemble systems. These systems are computationally expensive and exhibit biases and drift that increase with lead time, motivating more efficient data-driven alternatives. Yet this transition faces three linked challenges: comparing data-driven forecasts with operational ones requires (1) a global benchmark that does not exist, scoring them requires (2) metrics that capture operational priorities beyond anomaly correlation (ACC) and RMSE, and training them must (3) rely on a single, short observational record. To address the first two challenges, we introduce \BenchName, the first such benchmark, covering monthly precipitation forecasts 1--5 months ahead. It pairs global $1^\circ$ satellite precipitation with oceanic and atmospheric predictors, includes seven operational centers, and provides 310,944 simulated months from 52 climate models for training. Beyond standard scores, we introduce two operationally motivated metrics for anomaly strength and monthly rain-belt position. To address the third challenge, we develop \MODEL, which learns from simulations what the record lacks and transfers it to Earth through three modules: SimForced aligns the climate background, SimMemory transfers a history encoder pretrained on simulations, and SimAnalog supplements Earth labels with simulated analog outcomes. Extensive experiments show that \MODEL{} improves ACC, CRPS, anomaly strength, and rain-belt position by 12.0\%, 3.6\%, 2.9\%, and 0.3\% over the strongest operational or data-driven model, opening a path from simulated worlds to Earth system prediction.

title: Selecting the Right Testing Tools
description:
Software testing tools can be extremely useful in ensuring reliable software in web applications, mobile applications, enterprise applications and cloud applications.

Selecting the Correct Tools

There are many options to consider for your testing needs. Different test automation tools, API testing tools, performance testing tools and security testing tools exist, and selecting the correct tools for your needs depends on what you want to achieve.

Rather than selecting tools based on popularity, you should consider what you want to test, what technology you are using, what technical knowledge you have within your team, and what long term maintenance you require.

1. Unit Testing Tools

Unit testing allows testing of individual units, functions and modules within the software to check for errors early on.

Popular unit testing tools include:

  • JUnit – Java applications

  • pytest – Python testing tool with lots of plugins.

  • Jest – JavaScript and TypeScript testing.

  • NUnit – .Net applications.

  • TestNG – Java testing with parallel and data driven testing.

Using unit testing tools allows developers to ensure code quality, and detect unexpected behaviour.

2. API Testing Tools

APIs allow communication between different services and applications. API testing ensures the communication works as expected, including correct handling of requests, authentication, responses and any errors.

Popular API Testing Tools include:

  • Postman – Easy way to create, manage and test API requests.

  • REST Assured – Java based test tool that can be used for testing REST APIs automatically.

  • SoapUI – Tool for testing SOAP and REST based web services.

Using API testing tools can be very useful as issues can be found within the back-end without testing the full application directly in the browser.

3. Browser Automation

Web applications often have interactive elements. These can include forms, navigation menus, log in systems, shopping baskets and payment methods.

By using browser automation testing tools it is possible to simulate user interaction in order to ensure that key features of the application work correctly.

Popular tools include:

  • Selenium

Selenium WebDriver allows testing in multiple languages and browsers. This makes it a good option for teams requiring flexible browser testing.

  • Playwright

Playwright allows testing in Chromium, Firefox and Webkit. The auto-waiting, parallel execution features, and debugging tools can make it ideal for modern web applications.

  • Cypress

Interactive testing tool. Popular within front-end teams.

The best tool for your project depends on the current tech stack, browsers required and level of automation knowledge within your team.

4. Mobile Application Testing Tools

Mobile applications need to be able to function on a variety of operating systems, screen sizes, devices and networks.

Appium is a popular open source tool for testing native, hybrid, and web mobile applications on both android and iOS.

Testing across a variety of real devices and browser configurations can be achieved using cloud based testing platforms such as BrowserStack and Sauce Labs. These reduce the need to maintain a large physical lab of devices.

5. Performance Testing

Performance testing can be used to see how your application behaves under varying loads. It can detect if issues occur under higher amounts of traffic.

Performance testing will allow you to see how quickly your application performs, the stability, scalability, and resource usage.

Popular performance testing tools include:

  • Apache JMeter – Performance and load testing tools for a variety of protocols.

  • k6 – User friendly performance testing tool using JavaScript.

  • Gatling – Performance testing tool with detailed reports. Can be useful for teams using JVM technologies.

Performance testing tools can help to detect performance issues before affecting the user experience.

6. Security Testing

Security within applications is a key consideration. Security testing can be used to find potential vulnerabilities within software.

Popular tools include:

  • SonarQube – Static code analysis to detect any bugs, poor code quality and potentially vulnerable code patterns.

  • OWASP ZAP – Identifies security vulnerabilities within live web applications.

Whilst automated tools can be very useful, manual testing and professional penetration testing should be used alongside automated tools.

7. Test Management Tools

As projects get larger, it becomes increasingly important to manage your test cases, results, defects and produce reporting.

Test management tools help to create an organised set of testing within a project.

Popular test management tools include:

  • TestRail – Organises test cases, tracks testing and creates reports.

  • qTest – Test management tool with reporting capabilities for larger developments.

  • Xray – Can be used with Jira to link test cases to requirements and development issues.

These tools are useful for projects with many testers, multiple development teams and complex releases.

8. Which Tools To Choose

Consider the following in order to choose the best tools for your project.

  • Requirements

What type of testing do you need? Functional testing, automated testing, performance testing, security testing or test management?

  • Compatibility

Ensure that the tool works with the programming languages, frameworks and platforms that your project is using.

  • Maintainability

Automated tests will require regular maintenance. Ensure that the tools selected can be maintained easily by your team.

  • Compatibility with Development

Ensure that the testing tools can be implemented well within your development environment, version control systems and CI/CD pipelines.

  • Scalability

Ensure that the testing tools used can scale with the application, more users and increasing test suites.

  • Cost & Resource

Many powerful open source tools exist. Commercial tools may give extra support, infrastructure and enterprise features.

9. When To Implement Testing Tools

Implementing testing across the software development lifecycle means testing is more efficient.

Ideally, a testing strategy can be formed as follows:

Run unit tests and static code analysis on commits.

Run API testing and key functional tests at integration.

Run browser and mobile automation to test key journeys in the application.

Schedule performance and security testing appropriately.

Analyse test results, fix defects and validate fixes before release.

This means that development teams can find issues earlier in development, reducing re-work and giving more confidence in releases.

Summary

It is very important to use testing tools in software to ensure reliable, secure, performant and functional software. However, no one tool will fit every testing need.

JUnit, pytest and Jest can be used for unit testing. Postman and REST Assured can be used to verify APIs. Playwright and Selenium can be used for browser testing. Performance testing can be done with JMeter and k6. Security and test management tools can add further coverage.

To get the best results from testing, select a set of testing tools that are appropriate to your project goals, technology and resources.

For further detail on popular testing tools and how to best use them, take a look at 4Labs Technologies guide: Top Software Testing Tools for Every Testing Need

Selecting the right combination of testing tools can help development teams to produce more reliable software, increase user satisfaction and maintain consistent quality as the application grows.

title: The Comparison Surface a Multi-Model Song Generator Has to Expose
description:
If you ship a generative feature with more than one model behind it, the hard interface problem is not "can we call an API." It is whether a user can tell what was held constant and what was allowed to change.

I am writing this as an interface-level design memo, not as a source-code review and not as a listening test. I have not inspected private architecture, latency budgets, or training data. The questions below can be asked of any public song-generation UI, including one that offers a single model with multiple takes. They become urgent as soon as a product asks a person to choose among models.

The job is comparability, not novelty

A multi-model music UI fails in a particular way. The user writes a prompt, picks a familiar model, gets a finished-sounding track, and then tries a second model with a slightly different prompt because the first take "wasn't quite right." At that point the product has not provided a comparison. It has provided two unrelated experiments.

That is a UX issue before it is a model-quality issue. If prompt text, lyrics, duration, vocal setting, and output intent can drift between runs without being visible, the interface is training people to confuse taste with noise.

A useful test is simple: can a careful user answer, after two runs, "these two files were produced from the same brief"? If the answer is "I think so," the comparison surface is too weak.

Questions to ask of the public UI

The following questions do not require access to internals. They only require a page that is honest about state.

Prompt identity. Is the exact prompt still visible after a run, and can it be reused without retyping? If the product shows sample songs with their prompts, can those prompts be inspected before they are reused? A prompt that disappears into a history card with no copy path will not survive a fair comparison.

Lyrics path. Are "describe a song and let the system write words," "paste my lyrics and sing them as written," and "instrumental, no vocal" first-class paths, or are they hidden in the same box? If section tags such as [Verse] and [Chorus] matter, does the UI explain them before the user spends a run? A comparison that silently lets one model invent lyrics while another is bound to a pasted chorus is not a model comparison.

Model metadata before spend. Can the user see, before confirming a run, the model name, how many takes come back, whether length is user-set or automatic, and how credits will be charged? A selector that only shows brand names forces people to learn those differences from a FAQ, or from regret.

Voice and language controls. Are male, female, automatic, and instrumental choices visible as controls, not only as adjectives inside the prompt? If the product claims multilingual singing, is the language an explicit setting or an implied side effect of the lyric text?

Comparison without losing context. After two or more takes exist, can they be played in one context with the shared prompt still on screen? A library of isolated tracks is not the same as a comparison surface.

Export and rights as product states. Are download formats and commercial-use conditions visible as plan or asset states, or only as marketing language? A user who cannot tell whether a file is for personal use or whether a commercial license applies is being asked to decide after the fact.

If you are building a similar system, write these questions into a test plan. Click through the UI as if you were trying to keep a brief constant, and note every place the interface makes that discipline harder.

A public example of a comparison surface

Public homepage view of the five-model comparison (Suno, Mureka, ElevenLabs, Lyria, MiniMax). Verified official screenshot, not a personal test result.

SongMaker is a useful public example because it sells the comparison as the product idea, not as an advanced setting. The homepage describes an AI song maker that runs Suno, Mureka, ElevenLabs, Lyria, and MiniMax in one place, and tells you to try one prompt on every model and keep the song you like best. That is a workflow promise, not a quality benchmark.

The public AI Song Generator page is more concrete about the surface itself. It shows sample tracks that reveal the prompt on hover, so a style can be inspected before it is reused. It separates a prompt-based path from a Custom mode in which you paste lyrics, mark sections with tags, and optionally set length. It lists five models with published run rules: Suno at five credits per run, two songs, length up to six minutes; Mureka from five credits per run, two takes; ElevenLabs at twelve credits per minute, length up to five minutes, described as instrumental; Lyria at six credits per run, one song, singing pasted lyrics in Custom mode; MiniMax at twelve credits per run, and it can write lyrics if the box is left empty. Vocal controls are presented as male, female, auto, or instrumental. Downloads are listed as MP3, WAV, or FLAC, and the FAQ states that a commercial license is included with annual plans, while free and monthly plans are for personal use.

Those published differences are the metadata a comparison surface should expose before spend. They also show why a naive A/B is easy to get wrong. If you paste lyrics for Lyria and leave the lyrics empty for MiniMax, you are no longer testing the same brief. If you judge ElevenLabs against Suno without noticing that the official description frames ElevenLabs as an instrumental, length-controlled option, you are comparing different jobs.

I am not inferring how the models are orchestrated or billed internally, and I am not ranking how they sound. I am only pointing at visible interface facts that make a fair comparison possible.

A compact test matrix

If you are specifying a similar UI, a first test matrix can stay this small:

Requirement What to verify in the UI Easy failure
Prompt invariance Same text is replayable across models Prompt edited accidentally between runs
Lyrics binding Custom lyrics stay identical, or both runs are set to generate words One run invents a chorus, the other sings a pasted one
Pre-spend metadata Takes, length control, and credit cost visible before confirm User learns the cost only from a receipt
Job control Instrumental or vocal is an explicit state Mix compared against a sung track by accident
License state Personal use vs commercial license is visible before distribution User assumes every paid file is cleared for commercial use

A team can add latency, error recovery, and accessibility later. If this matrix fails, richer engineering will not save the comparison.

Limits that belong in the same memo

Published credit examples go out of date, and they should be re-checked on the live page before anyone treats them as a specification. A start with ten free credits, as the topic page describes, is enough to think about the workflow; it is not evidence about output quality. License text should be read in its precise form: annual plans include a commercial license; free and monthly plans are described as personal use. Downstream platforms such as YouTube and Spotify have their own rules for AI-generated music.

Do not pretend a public marketing page is a system design document. Use it as a set of visible states and as a reminder of what users will try to compare. If your own product offers more than one model, the work is to make that comparison honest: same brief, visible differences, and no silent change in the job the model was asked to do.

title: Preserving Visual UI Stability with TypeScript Snapshot Testing in Vue 3: The LegacyCategoryLegend Component
description:
During large-scale frontend modernization efforts, teams frequently convert dozens of components from JavaScript to TypeScript. While stateful components require deep assertions on reactive state, mutations, and API calls, pure static presentation components—such as legends, badges, and informational tooltips—serve a different purpose: preserving visual markup and design token consistency.

In my recent contribution to GitLab's Contributors Platform (MR !3195), I converted the LegacyCategoryLegend component to TypeScript and established an automated snapshot test suite using Vitest.

Here is an architectural look at how lightweight snapshot testing protects visual UI elements during progressive migrations.

1. The Component: Historical Contributor Tier Badges

On the Top Annual Contributors leaderboard, the platform honors historical contribution milestones (prior to the current point-based scoring system).

LegacyCategoryLegend.vue displays color-coded badges mapping to historical recognition tiers:

  • SuperStar (Warning badge): More than 75 merged MRs
  • Star (Info badge): Between 11 and 75 merged MRs
  • Enthusiast (Secondary badge): Between 5 and 10 merged MRs 
<!-- LegacyCategoryLegend.vue -->
<script setup lang="ts">
import { BBadge } from 'bootstrap-vue-next';
</script>

<template>
  <div class="text-muted small mt-2">
    <span class="me-3">
      <BBadge variant="warning">SuperStar</BBadge> More than 75 merged MRs
    </span>
    <span class="me-3">
      <BBadge variant="info">Star</BBadge> Between 11 and 75 merged MRs
    </span>
    <span>
      <BBadge variant="secondary">Enthusiast</BBadge> Between 5 and 10 merged MRs
    </span>
  </div>
</template>

Adding <script setup lang="ts"> ensures typed integration with bootstrap-vue-next component exports without any runtime overhead.

2. Fast, Deterministic Snapshot Testing with Vitest

For static presentation components without props or reactive state, writing redundant DOM query assertions for every badge text can be unnecessarily verbose.

Instead, a deterministic snapshot test using shallowMount provides 100% coverage while locking down the exact HTML structure and CSS utility classes:

// LegacyCategoryLegend.spec.ts
import { shallowMount } from '@vue/test-utils';
import LegacyCategoryLegend from './LegacyCategoryLegend.vue';

const createWrapper = () =>
  shallowMount(LegacyCategoryLegend, {
    global: { renderStubDefaultSlot: true },
  });

it('matches the snapshot', () => {
  expect(createWrapper().html()).toMatchSnapshot();
});

Why this pattern works well:

  • Instant Regression Detection: Any unintentional change to Bootstrap badge variants (warning, info, secondary), spacing classes (me-3, mt-2), or milestone descriptions is immediately flagged by the Vitest snapshot runner.
  • Stub Slot Rendering: Using global: { renderStubDefaultSlot: true } ensures that child slot content (like "SuperStar") is preserved inside <b-badge-stub> rather than discarded.
  • Zero Boilerplate: The spec is concise, clean, and runs in milliseconds.

3. Snapshot Output Verification

When executed, Vitest records the rendered template in __snapshots__/LegacyCategoryLegend.spec.ts.snap:

// Vitest Snapshot v1
exports[`matches the snapshot 1`] = `
"<div class="text-muted small mt-2">
  <span class="me-3">
    <b-badge-stub variant="warning">SuperStar</b-badge-stub> More than 75 merged MRs
  </span>
  <span class="me-3">
    <b-badge-stub variant="info">Star</b-badge-stub> Between 11 and 75 merged MRs
  </span>
  <span>
    <b-badge-stub variant="secondary">Enthusiast</b-badge-stub> Between 5 and 10 merged MRs
  </span>
</div>"
`;

This guarantees visual and structural stability as the underlying UI library upgrades across minor and major versions.

Key Takeaways

  1. Use Snapshot Tests for Pure Presentational UI: When a component has no internal logic or conditional branching, snapshot testing offers high confidence with minimal test maintenance.
  2. Always Enable renderStubDefaultSlot: In Vue Test Utils, shallow mounting child components can hide slot text unless renderStubDefaultSlot: true is configured.
  3. Every Component Counts: Converting even small UI components to TypeScript ensures the whole codebase maintains 100% type coverage without gaps.

👉 GitLab Contributors MR !3195

Author: Manish Kumar
