title: Essential Programming Skills to Build a Career in Software Development
description:
Tutorials teach syntax. Jobs ask for something broader. Here is a practical checklist of programming skills for software developers, with small examples you can try today.

1. Read and Write One Language Well

Pick one programming language (Python, JavaScript, Java or similar) and go deep before collecting more. Understand functions, loops, collections, error handling and basic object-oriented concepts.

2. Data Structures and Problem Solving

You don't need to memories every algorithm. You do need to understand when to use different data structures, such as lists, dictionaries and sets.

For example, sets are useful when you need to check whether an item exists in a collection, especially when working with large amounts of data.

3. Git and Collaboration

Almost every development team uses version control. Practice the complete Git workflow until it feels natural.

Learn how to:

  • Create and switch between branches.
  • Stage and commit changes.
  • Push code to a remote repository.
  • Open pull requests.
  • Respond to code review comments politely and clearly.

4. Testing

Testing helps prove that your code works as expected.

Start by writing simple tests for your functions and checking whether they return the expected results. Learning a testing framework such as pytest, Jest or JUnit is time well spent.

5. Debugging

Learn to read error messages and stack traces, use a debugger, and reproduce a bug before fixing it.

Most of the job is understanding why code behaves the way it does.

6. Databases and APIs

Understand basic SQL operations such as SELECT, JOIN and WHERE, along with how an application communicates with an API.

Most real-world software applications interact with databases and APIs, making these essential skills for developers.

7. Communication

Clear commit messages, readable code and honest status updates are important professional skills.

They often matter as much as the code itself.

A Simple Practice Plan

  • Build a small project, such as a to-do API or inventory tracker.
  • Upload it to GitHub with a README file.
  • Add three tests to check its functionality.
  • Ask a peer to review your work.

Conclusion

No single list guarantees a career, but these skills form a solid foundation. Build them through small, completed projects, and keep learning from feedback.

What skill helped you most when you started? Share it in the comments.

title: Motion-Aware Reward Modeling for Instruction-Guided Video Editing
description:
arXiv:2611.22495v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reward models for instruction-guided video editing can favor temporal consistency at the expense of motion. We study this failure, termed \emph{motion collapse}, using controlled motion-suppression variants of real edits. On VE-Bench, the evaluated composite reward prefers a motion-suppressed candidate in $97\%$ of cases. Learned video rewards and a VLM judge also struggle with mild suppression, while latent optimization and reward-guided fine-tuning exploit this weakness to increase reward as motion declines. A linear probe of our base reward backbone performs near chance on mild suppression, motivating an explicit inter-frame dynamics input. We propose a motion-aware reward model that combines an RGB frame-difference stream with preference training against motion-suppressed and fabricated-motion negatives. A distillation anchor preserves alignment with human quality judgments. On the VE-Bench motion ladder, our model reduces the rate of selecting motion-suppressed candidates to $0\%$ while achieving a Spearman correlation of $0.57$ with human quality ratings. It also detects unseen suppression variants and preserves motion during reward-guided fine-tuning on two editing pipelines. These results support explicitly modeling motion in rewards for video editing.

title: What a short-link redirect costs: about 4 microseconds in Go
description:
A short-link redirect looks like the simplest thing a web service can do: take a slug, return a 301 or 302. It is also the one request every click on every link has to pass through, so we built it as its own service with a written latency budget.

This post walks through that service: the choices we made, the reasons recorded in our ADRs, a few trimmed excerpts from the code, and a benchmark of what one request costs in-process. The benchmark is local and narrow, and we will say exactly how narrow. The conclusion is a little anticlimactic.

Split by latency budget, not by domain

The first decision (ADR-0013) was to divide the system by how fast each part has to be, not by business area. A link service that handled both redirects and link CRUD would share one latency budget between two very different workloads.

So there are three tiers:

  • Hot path: edge-redirect only. Target p50 5 ms and p95 15 ms on a cache hit. Nothing synchronous beyond the cache lookup.
  • Warm path: api-core, analytics-api, billing. User-facing CRUD, ClickHouse queries, payments.
  • Cold path: async workers fed by the event bus, such as click-ingester, notifications and the URL scanner.

The 5 ms figure is a design target recorded in the ADR. It is not a measured production number, and we are not presenting it as one.

The rule this buys is easy to enforce in code review: if it is not a cache lookup, it does not belong in the redirect handler.

Why Go, and why fasthttp

ADR-0002 picks Go for the latency-sensitive services. The reasons are unglamorous: static binaries that deploy trivially, goroutines for concurrency, short and tunable GC pauses, and a team that already knew the language. Rust was considered and set aside because the development cost was not justified at our scale. The ADR names a trigger for revisiting it: if p99 on cache hits exceeds 50 ms sustained at 10K RPS, benchmark Rust for this one service.

ADR-0003 goes one level down and picks fasthttp over net/http for the HTTP layer of this single service. fasthttp pools its request and response objects, which cuts allocation and GC pressure at high request rates. The ADR is honest about the cost: it does not work with the net/http middleware ecosystem, and its ownership rules (you must not hold a RequestCtx after the handler returns) are an easy way to introduce bugs. Every other Go service in the repo stays on net/http and chi.

That ownership rule shows up in the code. When a click is recorded, the handler copies what it needs out of the context before handing work to a goroutine:

// services/edge-redirect/internal/handler/redirect.go (trimmed)
// Snapshot fields before the fasthttp ctx is recycled; the goroutine below
// outlives the request cycle.
fullIP, _ := netip.AddrFromSlice(clientIP(ctx))
acceptLang := string(ctx.Request.Header.Peek("Accept-Language"))
...
h.spawn(func() { h.finishClick(ev, fullIP.Unmap(), acceptLang) })

The lookup: L1, then Redis, then origin

ADR-0004 describes the cache. The source of truth is Postgres behind api-core, and a round trip there on every request would eat the whole budget. So the service asks three places in order.

 client
   |
   v
 Caddy (TLS) --> edge-redirect (Go, fasthttp)
                    |
                    |  1. L1: in-process LRU, TTL in seconds
                    |  2. L2: Redis, longer TTL
                    |  3. origin: api-core (gRPC Resolve, else HTTP)
                    |
                    +--> 301/302 back to the client
                    |
                    +--> goroutine: enrich click, Produce() ---> Redpanda
                                                                    |
                                                                    v
                                                           click-ingester
                                                                    |
                                                                    v
                                                              ClickHouse

The resolver that implements this is short enough to read in one go:

// services/edge-redirect/internal/resolver/resolver.go (trimmed)
func (r *Resolver) resolve(ctx context.Context, host, slug string) (*origin.Link, error) {
    key := cacheKey(host, slug)

    if v, ok := r.l1.Get(key); ok {
        return v, nil
    }
    if v, ok := r.l2.Get(ctx, key); ok {
        r.l1.Set(key, v)
        return v, nil
    }

    link, err := r.origin.Resolve(ctx, host, slug)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }

    r.l1.Set(key, link)
    r.l2.Set(ctx, key, link)
    return link, nil
}

L1 is hashicorp/golang-lru with expiry. A hit is a map lookup in the same process, with no network at all. The ADR's argument against Redis-only is that every request would pay a network round trip (it estimates 0.5 to 1 ms inside a datacenter) while an in-process hit costs about 50 ns. Redis then absorbs the long tail of less popular slugs so they do not all fall through to origin. The ADR also notes the system degrades sensibly: if Redis is down, L1 still serves recent hits.

The trade-off is that you now have two TTLs, and a short L1 TTL means a deleted link cannot be served forever by one node. That is stated in the LRU's doc comment, and it leads to invalidation.

Cache invalidation

TTLs alone would make edits feel slow. ADR-0004 adds explicit invalidation on link update and delete. What the code does today is this: after every link mutation, api-core deletes the Redis key and publishes the cache key on a Redis pub/sub channel. Each edge process subscribes and evicts its own L1 copy.

// services/edge-redirect/internal/cache/invalidate.go (trimmed)
// api-core already DELs the L2 key; this channel only exists to evict the
// per-process L1 copy so an edit is live in about a second instead of after
// the L1 TTL.
const InvalidateChannel = "elido:link:invalidate"

The subscriber runs in a background goroutine and is never on the request path. If Redis is unavailable, the only consequence is that L1 entries live out their TTL. Note that the ADR text mentions Redpanda for these events; the implementation we read uses Redis pub/sub, and the code is what we describe here.

Clicks: fire and forget

Analytics is the reason a redirect service has side effects at all, and side effects are where latency budgets go to die. The rule from ADR-0013 is that the response never waits for them.

The handler builds a click event from cheap header copies, then starts a goroutine. That goroutine does the expensive parts (IP classification, scanner flagging, truncating the IP, hashing the visitor) and publishes the event to Redpanda, which speaks the Kafka protocol, through a franz-go producer. A separate service, click-ingester, consumes the topic and writes to ClickHouse. The redirect service never talks to ClickHouse.

The consequence is the usual one for this design: a click can be lost if the process dies between the response and the produce call, and we accept that trade for a hot path that has no dependency on the analytics store being up.

What one request costs

Now the numbers. These come from Go's go test -bench . -benchmem on an Apple M3 laptop, run on 2026-11-18. They are in-process handler benchmarks. There is no network, no TLS and no real client, so they measure our code and nothing around it.

Benchmark ns/op B/op allocs/op
Redirect, L1 hit, full request including spawning click work 4032 4680 71
Redirect, L1 hit, request path only 3619 3728 52
Click enrichment (runs off the request path) 911 912 19
Redirect through the CTA overlay page 28781 36526 297
Blocklist check 44 0 0
Query-parameter forwarding (mixed case) 379 192 3

Read the first two rows together: The request path itself is about 3.6 microseconds, and starting the click work adds about 0.4 more. The click enrichment, at roughly 0.9 microseconds, happens after the response is already decided. The blocklist check allocates nothing, which is the kind of result you hope for from a check that runs on every request. The CTA overlay page costs about eight times a plain redirect, since it does more work per request.

The allocation profile

Fifty-two allocations for a redirect is more than a pooled HTTP library might lead you to expect. Profiling the request path shows where they come from:

  • fasthttp header and argument handling, which are the largest allocators.
  • A context.WithTimeout for the origin call, created on every request even when L1 answers and the origin is never called.
  • Client IP parsing with net.ParseIP, done more than once per request.

You can see the second one in the handler:

// services/edge-redirect/internal/handler/redirect.go (trimmed)
resolveCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, h.cfg.OriginTimeout)
defer cancel()
link, err := h.resolver.Resolve(resolveCtx, host, slug)

All three are fixable. Creating the timeout only once the resolver misses L1 is a small change, and parsing the client IP once instead of several times is another.

Why we have not fixed them

At about 3.6 microseconds, the request path uses less than 0.1% of the 5 ms target. If we removed every allocation in the list above and saved, say, a third of that, the user would see no difference. A real redirect spends its time on the TCP handshake, the TLS handshake, and the distance between the client and the server. Those are measured in milliseconds, and no amount of work on net.ParseIP changes them.

There is also a cost on the other side of the ledger. Hand-tuning a handler to shave allocations tends to make it harder to read, and this handler already has to deal with passwords, previews, agent-readable JSON responses and warning pages.

So the plan is deliberately boring: keep the benchmarks in the repo so a regression shows up, fix the cheap allocations when we are in that code anyway, and put effort where the time is. We run in production today as a single EU VPS behind Caddy, so network distance is the next thing we would look at, long before another microsecond of Go.

The benchmark does not tell us about p99 under load, GC behavior at sustained throughput, or cache hit rate on real traffic. It tells us our own code is not the problem. That is a narrower claim than "fast", and it is the one we can back up.

What we would repeat

Split services around the budget, because "only cache lookups on the hot path" cannot be enforced inside a shared service. Push slow work behind a queue. Measure in-process, then say what you did not measure.

Elido is a hosted URL shortener built EU-first with custom domains, QR codes and click analytics. The docs are at elido.app/docs.

title: Same Row Count, Missing Records: 4 Ways a Count Check Can Fool You
description:
A common check after a batch job is to compare two numbers: how many records went in, and how many came out. If they match, the job is marked healthy.

That check is useful as an alarm. But it is not proof. Two lists can have the same length and still hold different records.

A tiny made-up example

The run was supposed to deliver four orders:

  • Expected: A, B, C, D
  • Found in the destination: A, A, C, E

Count check: 4 expected, 4 found. Looks fine.

Compare by ID instead:

  • missing: B, D
  • duplicate: A (written twice)
  • unexpected: E (not part of this run)

Three problems, and the count hid all of them.

4 ways the count can match while records are missing

1. A retry wrote duplicates that cancel out a drop

One batch failed halfway and was retried. The retry wrote some rows a second time, while a different set of rows never made it. The extra copies fill the gap in the total.

2. Rows from outside the run filled in

Late rows from the previous window, or rows near a time zone boundary, landed in this run's scope. They add to the count, so real gaps in this run stay invisible.

3. The key changed shape on the way

The record arrived, but its ID did not survive intact: 00123 became 123, a trailing space was added, or letters changed case. The count is right, but a lookup for 00123 finds nothing. To anyone searching by ID, the record is missing.

4. A filter removed rows while another step added some

One step skipped records it should have kept. Another step added test rows, or brought back rows that had been deleted. Minus a few, plus a few, same total.

How to check by ID

First, build the list of IDs that this run was expected to deliver, from that run's input or a saved copy. Do not use today's version of the source.

Then check three lists separately. A plain SQL sketch (function names vary slightly between databases):

-- missing: expected, but not in the destination
SELECT e.id
FROM expected_ids e
LEFT JOIN destination d ON d.id = e.id
WHERE d.id IS NULL;

-- unexpected: in the destination, but not expected
SELECT d.id
FROM destination d
LEFT JOIN expected_ids e ON e.id = d.id
WHERE e.id IS NULL;

-- duplicates: the same ID written more than once
SELECT id, COUNT(*) AS copies
FROM destination
GROUP BY id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

Before trusting the result, look at the shape of the keys on both sides:

-- IDs with extra spaces
SELECT id FROM destination WHERE id <> TRIM(id);

-- how many IDs of each length (run on both sides and compare)
SELECT LENGTH(id) AS id_length, COUNT(*) AS ids
FROM destination
GROUP BY LENGTH(id);

If one side has IDs of length 5 and the other has length 3, leading zeros were probably dropped somewhere. Decide on one rule and write it down. Do not quietly clean the keys on one side only, or you can hide the very problem you are looking for.

If the destination has a known delay before new rows are visible, wait for it before you call anything missing.

Then follow one missing ID

Pick one missing ID and look for it at every stage. Another made-up example, for order B:

Stage Result Evidence
Input found in the saved input for this run
Filter found not excluded
Batch 2, first try absent batch failed with a timeout
Batch 2, retry absent retry log lists batch 3's rows, not batch 2's
Destination absent not in the export

First known gap: the retry picked up the wrong batch. That also explains the duplicates. If you have no evidence for a stage, write "unknown" instead of guessing.

So, are counts useless?

No. A count is a cheap first alarm, and a mismatch is always worth a look. Just do not stop there: a matching count means "nothing obviously broke," not "everything arrived."

Have you seen a count check pass while records were missing? I would like to hear what caused it.

This post was drafted with AI and checked by a human before publishing.

title: CueSplat: Learning to Schedule Sparse Deformation for Dynamic Gaussian Splatting on Edge Devices
description:
arXiv:2611.22095v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Deformation-based 4D Gaussian splatting (4DGS) enables dynamic scene rendering. However, evaluating deformation networks for all Gaussians at every frame is compute-intensive on edge devices. We find that Gaussian trajectories are often locally predictable, yet prediction reliability varies across Gaussians and time. Thus, we propose CueSplat, a post-training framework that exploits local temporal regularity while keeping the pretrained backbone frozen and retaining its Gaussian set. Specifically, CueSplat predicts Gaussian attributes from recent history and uses a lightweight learned router to select exact deformation updates within a scene-specific budget calibrated offline. Selection accounts for prediction reliability and rendering contribution. Selected indices are reused across nearby frames to reduce routing overhead, while selected Gaussians still receive exact updates each frame. To control accumulated prediction error, we use drift signals to schedule three consecutive full-deformation frames that rebuild the prediction history. Evaluated across four mainstream 4DGS algorithms, CueSplat achieves up to $6.74\times$ and $8.15\times$ speedups on Jetson AGX Orin and Orin NX, respectively, with a negligible quality drop (at most $0.16$ dB in dataset-average PSNR).

title: The path to AI FDE #16: Functions: reusable pieces of logic
description:
Originally published on my newsletter, The Path to AI FDE. Subscribe free to get each issue by email.

This is a “From Zero” issue. Last week your code learned to decide and repeat. Today you learn to name a piece of code and reuse it, so you write it once and call it whenever you need it.

That named piece of code is a function. You’ve already used other people’s functions: print(), len(), type(). Today you write your own. By the end you’ll have a small script that shares pizzas fairly between friends, built from two tiny functions.

Part A · Building a function

1. def defines a function; calling it runs it. Save this as greet.py in your sandbox folder:

def greet(name):
    print("Hello,", name)

greet("Asha")
greet("Ben")

Run it with python3 greet.py (Windows: python greet.py):

Hello, Asha
Hello, Ben

The first two lines are the definition. def starts it, greet is the function’s name, (name) lists its inputs, and the line ends with a colon. The indented lines under it are the function’s body, just like the blocks in last week’s if and for.

Defining a function doesn’t run it. Python just remembers it under the name greet. The body runs only when you call the function: its name followed by brackets, greet("Asha"). Two calls, two greetings. Python reads your file from top to bottom, so put the def above the first line that calls it.

2. Parameters are the input slots; arguments are the values you put in them. A function can take more than one input:

def area(width, height):
    print(width * height)

area(3, 4)
area(10, 2)

12
20

width and height are the parameters: the names in the definition. 3 and 4 are the arguments: the values you pass when you call it. Python matches them in order, so the first argument goes into the first parameter. Inside the body, width is 3 and height is 4.

Leave one out, with area(3), and Python stops with:

TypeError: area() missing 1 required positional argument: 'height'

The message names the slot you left empty. People mix up the two words all the time, and it rarely matters, but now you know which is which.

3. return sends a result back. Without it, you get None. Our area prints the answer, but the rest of your program can’t use it. Change print to return:

def area(width, height):
    return width * height

total = area(3, 4) + area(10, 2)
print(total)

32

return hands a value back to the line that called the function. You can picture area(3, 4) being replaced by 12, so the line becomes total = 12 + 20. That’s the difference: print shows a value to a human; return gives it to your code.

Forget return, and the function still runs but hands back None (Python’s “no value here” from issue #14):

def double(n):
    n * 2

result = double(5)
print(result)

None

The function worked out 10 and then threw it away. return also ends the function immediately: any lines after it in the same block never run.

Part B · Functions that are easy to use

4. Defaults and keyword arguments let callers skip or name inputs. Give a parameter a default value with = in the definition, and callers can leave it out:

def make_tea(cups, sugar=1, milk=True):
    return f"{cups} cup(s), {sugar} sugar, milk: {milk}"

print(make_tea(2))
print(make_tea(2, sugar=0))
print(make_tea(milk=False, cups=1))

2 cup(s), 1 sugar, milk: True
2 cup(s), 0 sugar, milk: True
1 cup(s), 1 sugar, milk: False

The first call uses both defaults. The second passes a keyword argument, sugar=0, which sets that one input by name. The third names every input, so the order no longer matters. Names make calls easier to read too: make_tea(2, sugar=0) says more than make_tea(2, 0). One rule: arguments without names come first. make_tea(sugar=0, 2) gives SyntaxError: positional argument follows keyword argument. Later in the series you’ll see the same shape in AI code, such as a function that splits text with a default size=500.

The one trap: never use a list as a default. The default is created once, when Python reads the def, and then shared by every call:

def add_item(item, basket=[]):
    basket.append(item)
    return basket

print(add_item("apple"))
print(add_item("pear"))

['apple']
['apple', 'pear']

The second call “remembers” the apple. (append adds an item to the end of a list; lists get their own issue tomorrow.) The fix is to default to None and make a fresh list inside:

def add_item(item, basket=None):
    if basket is None:
        basket = []
    basket.append(item)
    return basket

Now the two calls print ['apple'] and ['pear'].

5. Scope: names made inside a function exist only inside it. Each call gets its own private workspace. Names created there disappear when the function ends:

def bake():
    dough = 200
    print("inside:", dough)

bake()
print(dough)

inside: 200
NameError: name 'dough' is not defined

(Python prints a few more lines above the NameError, called a traceback. You’ll learn to read those in issue #19.) The part of a program where a name exists is its scope. dough is a local name: it belongs to bake.

The other direction is softer: a function can read a name defined outside it. With greeting = "Hi" at the top of the file, a function can use greeting. But if a function assigns to a name, Python treats that name as local for the whole function. So this fails:

count = 0

def bump():
    count = count + 1

bump()

UnboundLocalError: cannot access local variable 'count' where it is not associated with a value

The clean habit: pass values in as arguments and return results out.

def bump(n):
    return n + 1

count = 0
count = bump(count)
count = bump(count)
print(count)

This prints 2. (Python has a global keyword that lets a function change an outside name. You’ll rarely need it; passing in and returning out is easier to follow.)

6. Give each function one job, and a name that says what it is. Small functions are easier to read, test and reuse. Here, one function does the maths and another builds the sentence:

def to_fahrenheit(c):
    """Convert Celsius to Fahrenheit."""
    return c * 9 / 5 + 32

def describe(c):
    f = to_fahrenheit(c)
    return f"{c}°C is {f}°F"

print(describe(100))
print(describe(-40))
print(to_fahrenheit(0) == 32)

100°C is 212.0°F
-40°C is -40.0°F
True

Three habits are packed in here:

  • One job each. to_fahrenheit only converts. describe only words the answer, and it reuses to_fahrenheit instead of repeating the formula.
  • A quick check. to_fahrenheit(0) == 32 prints True, so you know the maths is right. Because the function returns a value instead of printing it, it’s easy to test. That’s where proper tests (lesson 4.6) start.
  • A docstring. The string in triple quotes on the first line of the body says what the function does. Many editors show it when you hover over the name.

Give functions names that say what they do, in snake_case, the Python style guide’s choice for function names: to_fahrenheit, make_tea, add_item. If you can’t name a function without using “and”, it’s probably doing two jobs.

Try it (15 minutes)

  1. In your sandbox folder, create pizza.py, for sharing made-up pizzas between friends: 
def slices_each(pizzas, people, per_pizza=8):
    """How many whole slices each person gets."""
    return (pizzas * per_pizza) // people

def leftover(pizzas, people, per_pizza=8):
    """How many slices are left after a fair share."""
    return (pizzas * per_pizza) % people

print(slices_each(3, 5), leftover(3, 5))
print(slices_each(2, 4, per_pizza=6), leftover(2, 4, per_pizza=6))
print(slices_each(people=7, pizzas=1))
  1. Run python3 pizza.py. You should see: 
4 4
3 0
1

Three pizzas of 8 slices is 24; shared by 5, that’s 4 each with 4 left over. (// and % are whole-number division and remainder, from issue #14.)

  1. Delete the word return in slices_each (keep the maths) and run it again. The first number on each line becomes None. Put it back.
  2. Add print(slices_each(3, 0)) at the end. Read the last line of the error: ZeroDivisionError: integer division or modulo by zero. You can’t share between nobody. (Handling errors like this properly is issue #19.) Remove the line.
  3. Write a third function, pizzas_needed(people, slices_each=3, per_pizza=8), that returns how many pizzas to order. Hint: -(-a // b) rounds a division up. With 10 people, it should return 4.

Check your understanding: (a) In def area(width, height):, are width and height parameters or arguments? (b) What does a function return if it has no return line? (c) Why did the second add_item("pear") call also show the apple?

Answer: (a) Parameters: the names in the definition. The values you pass in a call are the arguments. (b) None. (c) A list default is created once, when the def runs, and every call shares it. Use None as the default and make a new list inside.

Common beginner mistakes

  • Forgetting return, then wondering why the result is None.
  • Printing inside a function when the caller needs the value. Return it, and print outside.
  • Defining a function and never calling it (no brackets, no run).
  • Using a list or dictionary as a default (def f(x=[])). It’s shared between calls.
  • Trying to change an outside variable from inside a function. Pass it in and return the new value.

Takeaway

def names a block of code, and calling it runs it. Parameters are the input slots, and arguments are the values you put in. return hands a result back; without it you get None. Defaults and keyword arguments make calls short and clear. Names made inside a function stay inside. Keep each function to one job.

Where this fits in my roadmap: this is part of my on-ramp, the Python basics everything else sits on. Every AI app I build later is a stack of small functions: one to load text, one to call a model, one to check the answer. Tomorrow: lists and dictionaries, the two containers that hold almost all the data you’ll touch.

Over to you: what’s a task you’d turn into a function? Reply with its name and its inputs, like make_tea(cups, sugar=1).

Sources

  1. Python tutorial, “More Control Flow Tools”, Defining Functions (def, the body is indented, a function without return returns None; docstrings). https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/controlflow.html#defining-functions
  2. Python tutorial, “More Control Flow Tools”, More on Defining Functions (default argument values, “the default value is evaluated only once”, keyword arguments, positional arguments before keyword arguments). https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/controlflow.html#more-on-defining-functions
  3. Python glossary, “parameter” and “argument” (the difference between the two). https://docs.python.org/3/glossary.html#term-parameter
  4. Python reference, “Execution model”, Naming and binding (a name assigned inside a function is local to it). https://docs.python.org/3/reference/executionmodel.html#naming-and-binding
  5. Python FAQ, “Why am I getting an UnboundLocalError when the variable has a value?” and “Why are default values shared between objects?”. https://docs.python.org/3/faq/programming.html#why-am-i-getting-an-unboundlocalerror-when-the-variable-has-a-value
  6. PEP 8, “Style Guide for Python Code” (function names are lowercase, with words separated by underscores). https://peps.python.org/pep-0008/#function-and-variable-names
  7. PEP 257, “Docstring Conventions” (what a docstring is; triple double quotes). https://peps.python.org/pep-0257/
  8. Python docs, “Built-in Exceptions” (TypeError, NameError, UnboundLocalError, ZeroDivisionError). https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/exceptions.html

All examples are made up and were run with Python 3.13 on Nov 2, 2026. Error messages are from Python 3.13; other versions word some of them differently. Sources checked Nov 2, 2026.

title: Watermark Evidence under Open-Weight LLM Modification: Exact Bounds for Low-Rank Output Watermarks
description:
arXiv:2611.21702v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Open-weight language models can continue generating after their released weights are modified, while a watermark verifier still scores outputs against the original base and marked models. We study how such modifications change the evidence available to an OpenStamp-style verifier. At each shared prefix, we represent the modification as a residual in the next-token logits. We derive an exact finite-vocabulary lower bound on the expected log-likelihood-ratio evidence under a residual-span constraint, along with a sharp span-only deviation bound. We also characterize the first-order evidence shift through a covariance term with an explicit second-order remainder, and determine the residual span needed to reach a target evidence level. For sequence-level detection, we derive an exact conditional exponential-moment bound and combine it with a supermartingale argument and a distribution-free order-statistic tolerance bound. This yields a high-confidence upper bound on miss probability after attack selection on calibration data and evaluation on independent certification continuations. In experiments with OpenStamp on Llama-2-7B and Mistral-7B-v0.3, INT8 quantization and 30% pruning retain test true-positive rates of 85.6-94.8%, while 500-step LoRA fine-tuning lowers them to 28.8% and 11.6%. The covariance prediction tracks the measured mean LoRA evidence drift on both models, with no remainder-bound violations across 160,000 test prefixes. Additionally, we observe zero false positives among 500 base-model continuations per model. Through these theoretical and empirical results, the current research provides a better understanding of watermark robustness to model-editing/tuning attacks.

title: AWS PrivateLink Tunnel Endpoints Open a Whole CIDR Range to Another Account
description:
AWS has detailed tunnel endpoints, a PrivateLink endpoint type that gives a consumer VPC access to an entire network segment in another account rather than one resource at a time, over an overlapping address space and with consumer-initiated connections only. The consumer must wrap traffic in GENEVE; only TCP and DNS pass, and access logs cannot attribute traffic to a workload behind the endpoint.

By Steef-Jan Wiggers

title: Build a shopping-agent shortlist before adding checkout
description:
A useful first shopping-agent task is small: take one buyer request and return a product candidate the buyer can inspect. You do not need to start with checkout.

Consider: "Find a black six-roll PLA pack for Singapore, and tell me what I still need to check."

I work on WebAZ. This example reads its public catalog over HTTP. It is not a built-in ChatGPT, Claude, Muse or other client's integration, and it does not require a wallet, an API key or an account.

1. Keep the exact option

The listing describes six rolls with 6kg total net filament weight. The selected black option is labeled Wireless drive. That label is unresolved: do not turn it into a claim about electronics, spool inclusion or feeder compatibility.

We will use product prd_c3c1de2c171f2cf79d2c6e93584d7a2e and variant pv_487412209252413e922baef5d5e44c99.

At the November 18, 2026 public observation, that variant exposed 54.21 USDC, stock 20 and in_stock: true. These are changeable listing facts, not a binding quote or stock reservation. Product-level prices can describe other options; never replace the selected option with a cheaper one silently.

2. Run a complete read-only adapter

The following is the complete example. Put it in shortlist.mjs and run it with Node.js 22 or newer. It uses only built-in modules and one public GET.

import { pathToFileURL } from "node:url";

const PRODUCT = /^prd_[a-f0-9]{32}$/;
const VARIANT = /^pv_[a-f0-9]{32}$/;

function checkSelection({ productId, variantId, quantity }) {
  if (!PRODUCT.test(productId) || !VARIANT.test(variantId)) throw new Error("invalid_selection_id");
  if (!Number.isSafeInteger(quantity) || quantity < 1 || quantity > 99) throw new Error("invalid_quantity");
}

export function buildCandidate(product, selection, observedAt) {
  checkSelection(selection);
  if (product?.id !== selection.productId || typeof product.title !== "string") throw new Error("product_mismatch");
  if (product.currency !== "USDC") throw new Error("unsupported_currency");
  const matches = Array.isArray(product.variants)
    ? product.variants.filter((variant) => variant.id === selection.variantId) : [];
  if (matches.length !== 1) throw new Error("variant_not_unique");
  const variant = matches[0];
  if (variant.in_stock !== true || !Number.isSafeInteger(variant.stock) || variant.stock < selection.quantity) {
    throw new Error("stock_not_confirmed");
  }
  if (typeof variant.price_usdc !== "number" || !Number.isFinite(variant.price_usdc) || variant.price_usdc < 0) {
    throw new Error("listing_price_missing");
  }
  return {
    product_id: product.id,
    variant_id: variant.id,
    title: product.title,
    options: variant.options ?? {},
    quantity: selection.quantity,
    currency: "USDC",
    listing_unit_price: variant.price_usdc,
    listing_goods_subtotal: Number((variant.price_usdc * selection.quantity).toFixed(6)),
    stock_indication: variant.stock,
    observed_at: observedAt,
    source: `https://webaz.xyz/api/products/${product.id}`,
    product_page: `https://webaz.xyz/product/${product.id}`,
    seller_declared_regions: typeof product.ship_regions === "string" ? product.ship_regions : null,
    delivered_total: null,
    unresolved: ["destination_specific_shipping", "tax_and_duty", "exact_variant_fit"],
    binding_quote: false,
    stock_reserved: false,
    purchase_authorized: false,
    payment_enabled: false
  };
}

export async function readCandidate(selection, fetcher = fetch) {
  checkSelection(selection);
  const response = await fetcher(`https://webaz.xyz/api/products/${selection.productId}`, {
    method: "GET",
    headers: { Accept: "application/json", "Accept-Language": "en" },
    credentials: "omit",
    redirect: "error",
    signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10000)
  });
  if (response.status !== 200) throw new Error(`catalog_http_${response.status}`);
  return buildCandidate(await response.json(), selection, new Date().toISOString());
}

if (process.argv[1] && import.meta.url === pathToFileURL(process.argv[1]).href) {
  const [productId, variantId, quantity = "1"] = process.argv.slice(2);
  try {
    console.log(JSON.stringify(await readCandidate({ productId, variantId, quantity: Number(quantity) }), null, 2));
  } catch (error) {
    console.error(error.message);
    process.exitCode = 1;
  }
}

node shortlist.mjs prd_c3c1de2c171f2cf79d2c6e93584d7a2e pv_487412209252413e922baef5d5e44c99 1

The fixed origin and ID validation keep user input from becoming an arbitrary fetch target. A missing or duplicate variant, insufficient stock, invalid price, or unsupported currency stops the adapter. An HTTP 402 also stops: this example never signs, pays or retries a paid request.

Treat titles and option labels as untrusted source data, not instructions to the agent. The adapter returns a small field allowlist rather than the entire catalog response. It is a learning example, not a complete production security or money-arithmetic library.

3. Give the buyer a source-linked answer

The output preserves the selected IDs and option labels, listing price and currency, quantity, observation time, and links to the public API and product page. The important distinction is:

{
  "currency": "USDC",
  "listing_unit_price": 54.21,
  "delivered_total": null,
  "binding_quote": false,
  "stock_reserved": false,
  "purchase_authorized": false,
  "payment_enabled": false
}

This is an excerpt of the November 18 observation, not output guaranteed for your later run. The executable prints its own observation time.

A useful assistant answer might be:

One candidate is the six-roll PLA pack, black / Wireless drive, listed at 54.21 USDC when observed. Singapore is a seller-declared region, not a confirmed destination quote. Exact filament diameter, spool dimensions and what the option label means still need confirmation.

Attach the returned source and product-page links to that answer. Do not present the sample as a recommendation that already passed fit checks.

4. Leave the delivered total blank

At this observation, the product declared Singapore in ship_regions, but its comparison data had no delivered total and marked purchase-estimate fees incomplete. A sales region must not become "free shipping" or "tax included" in the assistant's answer.

Do not combine today's listing price with an older shipping preview. A destination-specific total needs a fresh, separate quote for the exact variant, quantity and destination. This tutorial does not call a quote, reservation, order or payment endpoint.

5. Test the adapter before giving it to an agent

I reran ten local offline checks for the companion implementation on November 18: selected-option price rather than parent minimum; missing and duplicate variants; product mismatch; unavailable quantity; invalid prices; currency mismatch; invalid inputs causing no network request; the single credential-free GET; and stop-on-error behavior including 402. All ten passed.

Those tests validate this adapter's behavior, not compatibility with every agent client, external adoption or a successful purchase.

The smallest trial is useful on its own: reproduce one selected candidate and its unanswered buying questions. Shopping-agent builders: what information would your agent need next to turn that candidate into a justified shortlist entry?

Sources: public product page, public JSON endpoint, and WebAZ OpenAPI.

Disclosure: this article and example were prepared with AI assistance and are labeled AI Generated. No order, customer record, wallet signature or payment was used for the demonstration.

title: Chain-of-Thought Controllability Can Reduce Chain-of-Thought Monitorability
description:
arXiv:2611.21799v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring is a promising tool for detecting hidden goals, off-task behavior, and other failures in AI agents. One risk is that models could deliberately shape their reasoning to make it opaque to monitors. We stress-test this risk through persona-control training: supervised fine-tuning on mathematical reasoning traces rewritten in the voices of diverse personas. This induces a broader ability to control CoT, even though training contains no monitor-evasion examples. In covert side-task evaluations, traces in which a gpt-oss-20b model organism completes the hidden side task contain less monitorable evidence than the base model's. Averaged across evaluations and CoT lengths, weighted by side-task-success counts, the CoT monitorability metric g-mean$^2$ falls from 0.94 for the base model to 0.68 for the model organism without a hiding instruction, and to 0.22 when explicitly instructed to hide. In intervention evaluations, explicit hiding often drives monitorability near zero. The effect extends to a Kimi-K2.6 model organism in agentic environments, though hidden objectives requiring extended reasoning or longer trajectories remain more monitorable than simple single-step side tasks. We further discover that targeted transparency prompts can substantially recover monitorability, sometimes surpassing the base model. These model organisms provide a testbed for studying monitorability failures and potential mitigations. Our code can be found on https://github.com/yongzx/cot-control-model-organism.

title: One Frozen Simulator Is Not Enough: Simulator Collapse in Multi-Agent RL
description:
arXiv:2608.12253v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) for human-AI interaction usually trains the agent against a single large language model (LLM) that simulates the user. We show that agents trained this way can systematically fail to generalize, and we trace the failure to simulator collapse: the simulator LLM is mode-collapsed, and a policy trained against it learns narrow strategies that exploit the simulator's mode behavior; these strategies transfer poorly to unseen simulators and to real users. We formalize the collapse and propose two solutions. Verbalized Sampling, applied at inference time, samples each simulator reply from a verbalized response distribution. Co-Training, applied during training similar to self-play, co-evolves the simulator as the policy, so the policy cannot exploit the mode behavior. A population variant samples the simulator for each rollout from a pool of recent checkpoints. We validate both solutions on three benchmarks: Persuasion for Good, tau^2-bench, and CooperBench. Verbalized Sampling improves held-out success by up to 9% over single-simulator RL, and Co-Training pushes gains further to 14%; the human study shows similar gain on real users. Both solutions also preserve the policy diversity that collapses under single-simulator RL. Overall, our findings on simulator collapse point to diverse simulators as a requirement for RL agents that serve real users. We release SCOPE, an open-source framework for Population Co-Training in multi-agent RL.

title: Not All Evidence Is Admissible: Evidence Governance for Tool-Augmented Medical Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.22169v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Tool-augmented medical agents treat whatever their tools return as evidence. We show that this default is costly: medical tools fail silently, and a frozen reasoner cannot ignore what enters its context, so many cases it would have answered correctly are flipped to wrong once tool outputs are added. We call this evidence hijacking. $\mathcal{V}$-information explains the phenomenon: the reasoner has lost the option to ignore, so a tool output can carry negative usable information, and moving the decision of what to keep outside the reasoner restores that option. The theory further shows that part of any filtering gain comes merely from letting the reasoner see less, and only selection by content lets it see better. Building on this, we recast tool-augmented reasoning as evidence governance, which separates deciding what counts as evidence from the reasoner that answers, and propose context-independent evidence governance (CIEG), the first medical agent framework that rules, after acquisition, on whether each individual tool output may enter as evidence. Every tool output is written as a card that can be checked against the raw input; an independent checker that sees only the input and the cards decides which cards become evidence; and the reasoner answers from the admitted cards alone, with no training anywhere. On medical question answering, fundus glaucoma screening, and chest X-ray pneumonia classification, it achieves the highest accuracy among models of comparable scale, and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art tool-using agents and multi-agent systems built on the same backbone at lower cost.

title: Segmentation-Guided Direct Capacity Estimation of Rooftop Photovoltaics from Aerial Imagery
description:
arXiv:2611.22076v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Distribution planners need installation-level inventories of rooftop photovoltaic (PV) capacity, but interconnection records may be incomplete or spatially aggregated. Conventional image-based estimators segment PV arrays, convert the mask to physical area, and multiply by an estimated power density, coupling capacity prediction to mask-derived area. We propose Direct Head, a segmentation-guided architecture that retains U-Net segmentation and soft-mask pooling while directly regressing nonnegative capacity from PV-region features and area descriptors. We evaluate three independent runs on 7,590 French rooftop installations under the original split and a department-based holdout. Relative to a parameter-matched area-density neural model, Direct Head reduces mean absolute error by 8.7% and 12.5%, and symmetric mean absolute percentage error by 14.0% and 20.7%, respectively. Comparisons with conventional estimators, controlled architecture variants, auxiliary-loss ablations, and representative cases show that segmentation provides useful spatial evidence without requiring capacity to be determined by an area-density product.

title: Our tests imported the repository and passed while the package we deployed was missing eleven templates
description:
Our label service is a Python package that turns a consignment into a carrier label. Every carrier zone has a JSON template, and the package ships them inside itself, under labels/templates. setup.py listed them with package_data and the pattern templates/*.json, which had been right since the first carrier.

In September we added the Highlands and Islands zones for a carrier that prices them separately, and the engineer put the eleven new templates in a subfolder, templates/zones. The tests for all eleven passed in CI. The pipeline built a wheel, the image installed it, and the first Highlands label in production failed with FileNotFoundError. Ninety two parcels for Inverness and Skye waited on the dock until the afternoon.

The pattern was easy to blame once we looked. templates/*.json matches files directly inside templates and nothing in a folder below it, so the wheel held every old template and none of the new ones. setup.py did exactly what it said.

The real question was why CI had been green. Our tests ran with python -m pytest from the root of the checkout, and that puts the current directory first on sys.path. import labels found the folder in the repository, holding every file anyone had committed, before it could find anything installed. For four years we had tested the source tree. The wheel that production ran had never been imported by a single test.

We moved the code under src/, so the package cannot be imported from the repository root at all and the tests have to use an installed copy. CI now builds the wheel once, installs it into a clean virtual environment, runs the suite against that, and puts the same file into the image. A short step lists every file under templates in the repository and fails the build if any of them is missing from the wheel. The package_data pattern now covers subfolders, but the check is what we trust.

A green run tells you about the code your tests imported. Ours imported the repository, and we shipped a package.

– Sergey Shinder

title: PageSift 1.6: From Scraping Pages to Compiling Context for LLMs
description:
The standard way to feed an LLM context today goes like this: scrape a few pages, truncate them, concatenate the pieces into one big string, and stuff it into the prompt.

That approach has three problems. First, no provenance — the model cites a number, and you have no idea which page, which paragraph, or which crawl it came from. Second, no sense of time — the page changed its price last week, you're still holding the old version, and when the old and new copies disagree, nobody tells you. Third, no incrementality — one digit changes and the whole pipeline reruns; and when the token budget runs out, you chop the tail off, which may well be the table header.

PageSift 1.6, codename "Context", is built at exactly those three problems. The one-sentence version: context shouldn't be a concatenated string; it should be a compiled artifact — with identity, lineage, a budget, and a manifest of sources.

Repo: https://github.com/YOLOW92/pagesift (single Rust binary, Apache-2.0)

First, give knowledge a stable identity

In 1.6, content is broken into KnowledgeUnits. Each unit records four separate things: who I am (unitId), what state I'm in (revisionId and a content hash), where I live (document, byte span, heading path), and where I came from (lineage: created, unchanged, merely relocated, rewritten, split from, merged from).

Take a product page. After a redesign, untouched paragraphs keep their unitId. A paragraph that only got pushed further down the page is marked relocated — it doesn't get to impersonate a content change. A price that actually changed gets a new revisionId. Downstream systems cite "this fact", not "paragraph 7 of Tuesday's crawl". Everything else in 1.6 stands on that.

When a page changes, only redo what the change touches

Above the units sits Delta, a persistent incremental log. When a document is re-crawled, only the derived assets affected by the change are recomputed (the lexical index, the semantic sketch, the structure index and the graph index each carry their own dependency stamps); the rest is reused. In the local benchmark — 60 resources, 720 derived assets, one document edited — incremental maintenance is 4.37× faster than a rebuild, with 98.6% of assets reused. A document that comes back 304 Not Modified reuses 100%.

The delta log has consumer checkpoints: it can be replayed and acknowledged, so external systems consume at their own pace and resume after a crash without losing or duplicating work. And the index reports exactly which store version it currently reflects. No hand-waving.

In search, the two kinds of time must not be mixed

Search runs several strategies together: keywords, exact symbol matching, heading boosts, plus a disableable semantic sketch. It deliberately separates two notions of time: the observation cutoff (what you knew at that moment) and the validity window (the period during which a fact actually held). "What did this cost last month?" and "What does it cost now?" travel along two different timelines — most freshness bugs come from collapsing the two into one.

When two sources disagree on a price, search doesn't crown a winner. It retrieves both sides of the conflict together and counts independent sources honestly (syndicated mirrors don't inflate the count). Scores are reported as six decoupled dimensions — relevance, support, freshness, source independence, coverage, calibrated confidence — so the caller does the weighing.

The output is compiled, not truncated

The final step is called Pack. Give it a question and a token budget, and it compiles a context for you: every segment carries a provenance header (which unit, which document, what status, under which heading), with a full provenance manifest attached.

Some things are MustKeep: a table's header and caption, the negations and qualifiers inside a sentence, both sides of an active conflict. They go in as a group or not at all. If even the MustKeep closure doesn't fit the budget, Pack returns budgetInsufficient: true. If it doesn't fit, it says so — it won't quietly amputate half the evidence and pretend the result is complete.

One layer up sits Action, the entry point meant for agents: answer straight from local context when it's still fresh, with zero network calls (context mode); demand at least two independent sources when verifying (verify mode); and before spending money on a new crawl, estimate the value of information and check whether coverage can be estimated at all. On a small or heavily skewed corpus it returns estimable: false — not a made-up number.

How to use it

Context ships on every surface at once: the CLI (pagesift context), HTTP (/v2/context), an MCP tool (pagesift_context), Python, Node.js, and a C ABI. Installation is the usual:

  • Python: pip install pagesift
  • Node: npm install pagesift
  • Rust: cargo add pagesift, or grab the single binary from GitHub Releases

This release also bumps the HTML extraction library, yolowhtml, to 0.1.2. The reason is a very typical bug: article mode was treating academic figures and their captions as page furniture and deleting them — the text still said "see Figure 1", but the figure was gone. Figures, captions, and table captions are all preserved now.

Closing

PageSift's through-line hasn't changed: turn expensive, repeated AI information work into engineering capability that accumulates, can be verified, and can be reused. 1.5 turned observations into claims with a history. 1.6 turns claims into compilable context.

What comes next stays on the same line: from context toward conclusions, from a single node toward collaboration, from retrieval toward computation. Details when it ships.

title: Rethinking Perceptual Similarity for Remote Sensing: Multi-Layer Attention Scoring and Human Preference Benchmarking
description:
arXiv:2611.21816v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Perceptual similarity metrics for natural images transfer poorly to remote sensing (RS), where severe geospatial and semantic failures can remain visually plausible while still being decisively wrong for downstream use. To address this, we develop a novel human-aligned perceptual quality metric for generated RS imagery and evaluate it across several generation tasks. We first conduct a controlled perturbation study where we progressively increase the severity of common synthetic perturbations. Using the layer-wise Aligned Attention Score (AAS) responses in RemoteCLIP, we find that different RS artifacts are best captured at different depths. Based on these findings, we introduce Remote Sensing Perceptual Distance (RSPD), a pairwise metric that averages seven independently calibrated layer distances without tuning on human-preference labels. To evaluate our metric on realistic RS generation tasks, we construct a blind, reference-conditioned two-alternative forced-choice (2AFC) benchmark with five 300-triplet subsets spanning synthetic artifacts, airborne and spaceborne super-resolution, SAR-to-optical translation, and timeseries controls. We also construct a 300-triplet ordered misregistration benchmark with deterministic labels. Using the same RemoteCLIP checkpoint, RSPD substantially outperforms simple cosine distance with the final global embedding and is competitive with the strongest generic baselines across the realistic RS generation tasks.
