title: Amazon EMR 8.2 is now available
description:
Amazon EMR 8.2 is now available with new features across Amazon EMR on EC2, Amazon EMR on EKS, and Amazon EMR Serverless. This release upgrades Apache Spark to 4.1.3, Apache Iceberg to 1.11.0, and Delta Lake to 4.2.0, and it is designated a Long Term Support (LTS) release. This release makes it easier to run secure, governed analytics at scale — you can now write to the same Delta Lake table on Amazon S3 from multiple clusters concurrently, refresh Iceberg materialized views incrementally, and propagate end-user identity from Spark jobs and interactive sessions all the way to AWS Lake Formation and Amazon S3 so access is authorized and audited as the original user.

Amazon EMR 8.2 expands governance and performance across all three deployment options. New features include concurrent Delta Lake writes using Amazon S3 conditional writes (no DynamoDB log store required), and Lake Formation fine-grained access control (FGAC) now covers materialized views, governed user-defined functions, more Iceberg operations, and a broader set of Spark SQL features. The release also adds OpenLineage-based lineage capture to the AWS Glue Data Catalog and trusted identity propagation for steps and sessions. With EMR 8.2, data engineers can now precompute each pipeline stage as an Iceberg materialized view in SQL. Each materialized view refreshes only the changes instead of recomputing the entire source table across projections, inner joins, filters and SUM, COUNT aggregations. Specific to EMR on EC2, this release adds Spark Connect support on multi-primary clusters, along with Secret Agent improvements that cut user-provisioning latency by up to 97% under high concurrency. On EMR Serverless, new scaling profiles for Spark (performance-optimized, balanced, or cost-optimized) let you tune how quickly executors scale, and applications can now run Lake Formation-governed Glue UDFs. On EMR on EKS, the Spark Operator is upgraded to version 2 (based on open-source Spark Operator 2.5.0).

Amazon EMR 8.2 is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon EMR is available. To learn more, see the Amazon EMR 8.2 Release Guide for EMR on EC2, the EMR Serverless release notes, and the EMR on EKS release notes, or get started by creating a cluster from the Amazon EMR console.

title: Teaching Language Models to Narrow Boolean Patent Searches from Search Feedback
description:
arXiv:2611.22270v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Patent prior-art searchers issue Boolean queries line by line, broadening to find relevant documents and narrowing until candidates can be screened. We distill 38,397 Japan Patent Office search reports into executable expert strategies, re-execute them, and evaluate generated strategies by citation recall and the smallest set containing each citation. Prompted models write valid, high-recall strategies but leave citations in sets too large to screen. We adapt a generator offline from scored rollouts in two forms: strategy-level learning from a screening-aware strategy score, and line-level learning from citation-preserving narrowing credit, which upweights the query lines keeping a found citation in a smaller set. On shared rollouts, line-level credit outperforms strategy-level scores on screening measures; iterated, it cuts the median citation-containing set from 768 to under 50 and places more citations in sets under 100 documents than experts, at lower recall. Strategy-level preference learning reaches near-complete recall; the two forms are complementary.

title: YouTube's transcript panel gives you the full transcript — I scrolled three videos to prove it
description:
I built a YouTube transcript exporter, and one design question kept coming back: when the timedtext endpoint won't cooperate, is the on-page transcript panel a real fallback — or does it only hold the rows currently on screen?

On 2026-11-15 I measured that YouTube's timedtext endpoint returns empty bodies from datacenter IPs (curl: HTTP 200 with 0 bytes, then 429; real browser: json3 through srv3 all empty, no challenge page). Real users on residential IPs should be fine, but my test environment could not verify that path. So the panel became the question that mattered. I originally wrote that the panel "only gives the currently rendered rows, not the full transcript." That was an untested assumption. I tested it properly this week, at three scales.

How I measured it

Headless Chrome 154 with a local CONNECT relay, loading the real youtube.com watch page. For each video I opened the transcript panel, counted the rows, then scrolled the panel container to the bottom twice and counted again. I also ran my extension's own YTE_GET_TRANSCRIPT (source: panel) before and after scrolling, so the panel DOM and the extension's reading of it were checked against each other.

Results

Video Length Rows before scrolling Rows after 2 scrolls Cues (extension) Characters
Rick Astley — Never Gonna Give You Up (dQw4w9WgXcQ) 3:33 24 24 24 2,066
TED — Do schools kill creativity? (iG9CE55wbtY) 20:03 163 163 163 17,412
Randy Pausch — The Last Lecture (ji5_MqicxSo) 76:27 713 713 713 65,510

First cue to last cue covered the whole video in each case (0:01–3:23, 0:27–19:19, 0:17–1:15:26). The panel container's scrollHeight was far larger than its clientHeight (e.g. 39,870 vs 299 on the 76-minute video), so there was real scrolling to do — the row count simply did not change. The extension's transcript was identical before and after scrolling in all three runs.

What changed in my design

The panel is now the default full-transcript source (verified up to 76 minutes / 713 cues). timedtext is demoted to a backup for when the panel is unavailable. The panel DOM itself also changed recently: the old ytd-transcript-segment-renderer selector returns zero rows now; the current rendering uses <transcript-segment-view-model> with timestamps in .ytwTranscriptSegmentViewModelTimestamp and text in span[role="text"]. My reader tries the new DOM first and falls back to the old one.

Honest caveats

  • I have not tested 2-hour-plus videos or 1,000+ cue transcripts. If a virtualization threshold exists, it can only be at a larger scale than 713 cues.
  • My DOM probe truncated each row to 80 characters, so its character totals (1,776 / 11,471 / 49,505) are lower than the extension's (2,066 / 17,412 / 65,510). That is a probe-method difference, not a data difference.
  • The 2026-11-15 claim that "the panel only gives the currently rendered rows" is overturned at all three scales tested. It was wrong because I had not scrolled before writing it.

Status

YouTube Transcript Export v0.1.0 is in review on Microsoft Edge Add-ons and cannot be installed yet. The Pro tier (planned ¥19.90 one-time, Afdian activation code) is not on sale. Privacy page: https://alapha888.github.io/yt-transcript-export-privacy/

title: ORA-04068 After a Deploy: The Retry Works. The Package State Is Gone.
description:
The release went fine. Every script ran, every package compiled, the smoke test passed. A minute later the application log fills with this:

ORA-04068: existing state of packages has been discarded
ORA-04061: existing state of package body "APP.PRICING" has been invalidated
ORA-04065: not executed, altered or dropped package body "APP.PRICING"

Then it stops. A few dozen errors, one per connection, and nothing after. Someone opens an incident, someone else suggests rolling back, and by the time anyone looks, the errors are gone.

The package isn't broken. It holds state, the deploy threw that state away, and Oracle told each session about it the first time it came back. The error is the visible part. The quieter part is that the retry works with the state reset, and not only for the package you deployed.

This post covers what the error means, which packages and which changes raise it (two of them look harmless), what a connection pool sees, and how to deploy PL/SQL without it. It ends with a lab that proves each step on Oracle Database Free 26ai.

What the error means

Each session that uses a package gets its own copy of the package's variables: its package state. A counter, a cached config row, a flag set at login, a lookup table loaded once. Oracle's PL/SQL Language Reference calls a package stateful if it declares at least one variable, constant or cursor, and stateless otherwise. That state lives for the whole session.

Except when the package body is recompiled. A deploy (CREATE OR REPLACE PACKAGE BODY), an explicit ALTER PACKAGE ... COMPILE, or an automatic recompile after something the package depends on changed. The state in every session was built by the old code, so it can't be kept. The next time a session calls the package, Oracle discards that state and raises ORA-04068. The two errors under it say which package, and why.

In the lab, a session called a package with one variable, a call counter, twice: 1, 2. The deploy replaced the package body. The session's next call failed with exactly the three errors above. The call after that worked, ran the new code, and returned 1. The counter started again from its initial value.

Two things the error does not do, both checked in the lab:

  • It doesn't roll back the session's transaction. The session had an uncommitted insert before the deploy. It was still there after the error.
  • It doesn't come back. It's raised once per session per recompile. The next call re-creates the package state from scratch and runs.

It's the state, not the change

Whether a deploy raises ORA-04068 doesn't depend on how big the change is. It depends on whether the package holds state when it's recompiled. In the lab, a session used each package, one change was deployed, and the session called the package again:

Package Change deployed Next call
no package variables new body no error, new code at once
no package variables new spec (a function added) and body no error, new code at once
only a literal constant (c_rate CONSTANT NUMBER := 5) new body no error, new code at once
a constant set at load (c_loaded CONSTANT DATE := SYSDATE) new body ORA-04068
one variable ALTER PACKAGE ... COMPILE BODY, no code change ORA-04068
a %ROWTYPE variable on ORDERS ALTER TABLE orders ADD a column ORA-04068
a variable, but the code names its columns the same ADD column no error

Three of these surprise people.

A constant isn't always a constant. Oracle treats a package as stateless if its state can't change for the life of a session, which is the case when every item is a compile-time constant. A literal is one. SYSDATE isn't: its value is set when the session first uses the package. So c_loaded CONSTANT DATE := SYSDATE makes the package stateful, and the deploy that changed nothing else raised ORA-04068.

A recompile with no change is enough. ALTER PACKAGE pricing COMPILE BODY, with the exact same code, raised it. So does any script that recompiles invalid objects after a release, for every stateful package it touches.

DDL on a table can do it, with no PL/SQL deploy at all. A package body with a variable declared as orders%ROWTYPE depends on the table's column list. ALTER TABLE orders ADD a column invalidated it, and the next call raised ORA-04068. A package that used the same table but named its columns stayed VALID and didn't raise it. So the ADD COLUMN that waited politely for its lock can still throw errors at the application once it runs.

The other direction also held. A package with no variables switched to the new code silently, even when its spec changed. In a hand run, a standalone function that called that package was invalidated by the spec change, recompiled itself on its next call, and also raised nothing.

It resets packages the release didn't touch

The documentation has one more sentence that's easy to read past: all of a session's package states can be lost if any of its instantiated packages is invalidated and revalidated.

The lab tested it. A session used two packages, PRICING and AUDIT_CTX, each with its own counter. The release recompiled only AUDIT_CTX.

PRICING   (not redeployed): 1, 2, 3        then, after AUDIT_CTX's error: 1
AUDIT_CTX (recompiled):     1, ORA-04068, 1

PRICING kept counting until the session called AUDIT_CTX and got ORA-04068. After that, PRICING was back to 1 too. Its code hadn't changed and nobody had deployed it, but its state was gone. (In a hand run, recompiling a package without variables didn't do this: the session's other packages kept their state.)

So "we only changed one package" doesn't limit the damage. Any session that hits ORA-04068 for any package starts again with every package's state at its initial value. If one of them caches a user's permissions, a tenant ID or a feature flag, the retry that "fixed" the error runs with the defaults.

A recompile of a stateful package doesn't fail the deploy. It fails the next call in every session that had used the package, once, and that session's retry starts with every package's state at its initial value. Packages without state, SERIALLY_REUSABLE packages and edition-based redefinition avoid the error.

What a connection pool sees

A connection pool turns one recompile into a burst. Each pooled connection is a session, so each one that had used the package raises ORA-04068 once.

The lab opened 8 sessions; 6 of them called the package, 2 didn't. After one deploy, every session called it twice:

first round after the deploy:  6 of 8 calls failed with ORA-04068
second round:                  0 of 8

The 2 sessions that had never used the package got the new code with no error. The 6 that had used it failed once each, even though the call they made after the deploy only read a version string and never touched the variable. What's discarded is the session's copy of the package, not one variable.

That's the shape to recognize in a log: a burst right after a deploy, about one error per connection, then nothing. A pool of 200 connections gives you up to 200 errors and 200 resets of the package state. Unless your code retries, each of those errors is a failed user request.

Find the stateful packages before you deploy

There's no column in the data dictionary that says "this package is stateful", but PL/Scope can tell you. Compile with identifier collection on, then list the declarations at package level:

ALTER SESSION SET plscope_settings = 'IDENTIFIERS:ALL';
ALTER PACKAGE pricing COMPILE;          -- for each package you want to check

SELECT object_name, object_type, name, type
FROM   user_identifiers
WHERE  object_type IN ('PACKAGE', 'PACKAGE BODY')
AND    usage = 'DECLARATION'
AND    type IN ('VARIABLE', 'CONSTANT', 'CURSOR')
AND    usage_context_id = 1               -- declared at package level, not inside a subprogram
ORDER  BY object_name, object_type;

In a hand run on 26ai it listed the counter variable, a package-level cursor, and both constants. It didn't list the packages without package-level declarations. Check the CONSTANT rows by eye: a literal (:= 5) is stateless, anything else (:= SYSDATE, a function call) isn't. Note that ALTER PACKAGE ... COMPILE is itself a recompile, so run this on a test database, not under a live application.

Deploy without it

There are four ways to deal with it. They're not equal.

1. Keep state out of packages. A package without variables has nothing to discard. In the lab it took the new code with no error every time, spec change included. If a value must survive across calls, keep it somewhere a recompile doesn't touch: a table, or an application context (SYS_CONTEXT), which belongs to the session rather than to a package. In a hand run, a tenant ID set in an application context was still there after ORA-04068 had reset the package counter in the same session. This is the real fix, and it means changing the code.

2. Retry once in the application. The second call works, so catching ORA-04068 and retrying the call makes the burst invisible to users. It's cheap, and many teams do it. But the retry runs with every package's state reset, including packages the deploy didn't touch. Only retry if the code re-creates any state it needs, for example by re-running its login initialization.

3. PRAGMA SERIALLY_REUSABLE. A serially reusable package keeps its state only for the duration of one server call. In the lab, the deploy raised no error and the very next call ran the new code. The cost is in the name: the counter was 1 on every call, before and after the deploy, because nothing survives between calls. And a serially reusable package can't be called from SQL at all: SELECT pricing.version FROM dual failed with ORA-06534: Cannot access Serially Reusable package. It suits packages that only use their variables within one call. It isn't a switch you can turn on for a package that relies on its state.

4. Edition-based redefinition (EBR). Editions let two versions of the same package exist at once. Each session sees the version in its own edition. The release is compiled in a new edition while running sessions keep using the old one:

-- once, as a DBA: enable editions for the schema owner (this can't be undone)
ALTER USER app ENABLE EDITIONS;

-- per release
CREATE EDITION rel2;
GRANT USE ON EDITION rel2 TO app;

-- the deploy, in a session switched to the new edition
ALTER SESSION SET EDITION = rel2;
CREATE OR REPLACE PACKAGE BODY pricing AS ... END;

-- when you're ready for new connections to get the release
ALTER DATABASE DEFAULT EDITION = rel2;

In the lab, a session in the old edition (ORA$BASE) called the package before and after the new body was compiled in REL2: 1, 2, 3. No error, no reset, still the old code. A new session also got the old code until ALTER DATABASE DEFAULT EDITION = REL2; after that, new sessions got the new code. A connection pool moves to the release as its connections are replaced, and none of them sees ORA-04068 on the way.

EBR is in every edition of the database, Free included. The catch is preparation: ENABLE EDITIONS is one-way, and tables aren't editioned, so changes to table structure need editioning views and crossedition triggers to fully avoid downtime. For PL/SQL-only releases, it does exactly what this error needs.

Prove it

The lab runs Oracle Database Free in a container. Each "user" session is a SQL*Plus session that calls the package, waits for the deploy, then calls it again:

drill    case                                                 result
error    package body replaced under a live session           ORA-04068 / 04061 / 04065 once; the retry works,
                                                              counter back to 1; uncommitted insert kept
collat   only AUDIT_CTX recompiled, session also uses PRICING PRICING reset to 1 too, after AUDIT_CTX's error
which    no variables (new body; new spec)                    no error, new code
         a literal constant                                   no error, new code
         CONSTANT DATE := SYSDATE                             ORA-04068
         ALTER PACKAGE ... COMPILE BODY, no code change       ORA-04068
         %ROWTYPE variable, then ALTER TABLE ... ADD          ORA-04068 (named columns: no error)
pool     8 sessions, 6 had used it, one deploy                6 errors, then 0
serial   PRAGMA SERIALLY_REUSABLE                             no error, new code at once; counter always 1;
                                                              ORA-06534 from SQL
edition  new body compiled in edition REL2                    live session: no error, 1, 2, 3 on the old code;
                                                              new sessions: new code after the default switch

Don't take my word for it — run it. The package-state lab asserts every row: the three-error stack and the counter starting again at 1 after the retry, with the uncommitted insert still there; the untouched package reset by another package's error; which packages and changes raise it and which don't; exactly 6 errors from the 6 pooled sessions that had used the package and none on the second round; the serially reusable package's missing error, missing state and ORA-06534; and the live session in the old edition counting on with no error. If any of that doesn't reproduce, the run fails. Proven on every CI push.

What teams get wrong

  • Rolling back a good release. The burst looks like a broken deploy. It's one error per connection, and it's over by the time anyone looks. Rolling back is another recompile, and another burst.
  • Assuming the retry is clean. It runs, but with every package's state reset, including packages the release didn't touch.
  • Thinking CONSTANT means stateless. Only compile-time constants do. := SYSDATE makes the package stateful.
  • Recompiling "just to be safe". A no-change COMPILE BODY raises it for every session that had used the package.
  • Forgetting that table DDL recompiles PL/SQL. An ADD column under a %ROWTYPE package variable raises it, with no PL/SQL in the release.
  • Adding SERIALLY_REUSABLE to make the error go away. It does, along with the state, and SQL can no longer call the package.

Frequently asked questions

What does ORA-04068 existing state of packages has been discarded mean?

A session had used a PL/SQL package that holds state (package-level variables, cursors, or constants that aren't compile-time constants), and the package body was recompiled since: by a deploy, an ALTER PACKAGE ... COMPILE, or an automatic recompile after a dependency changed. Oracle can't keep state built by the old code, so on the session's next call it discards the state and raises ORA-04068, with ORA-04061 and ORA-04065 naming the package. The next call re-creates the state from scratch and works.

Why does ORA-04068 go away when I run the call again?

Because the error is raised once per session per recompile. The failing call discards the session's package state; the next call re-instantiates the package with its initial values and runs the new code. In the companion lab the retry worked every time, but a counter the session had built up was back to 1. Any value the package had cached for the session is gone.

How do I prevent ORA-04068 after deploying a PL/SQL package?

Keep state out of packages you redeploy (a package with no variables, or only literal constants, switched to new code with no error in the companion lab), retry the call once in the application if your code can re-create the state it needs, use PRAGMA SERIALLY_REUSABLE for packages that only need state within one call, or deploy with edition-based redefinition so running sessions keep the old version. In the lab, a session in the old edition saw no error and kept its state while the new code was compiled in a new edition.

Can ORA-04068 happen for a package I didn't change?

Yes, in two ways. A package is recompiled automatically when something it depends on changes: in the companion lab, ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN invalidated a package with a %ROWTYPE variable on that table, and the next call raised ORA-04068. And once a session gets ORA-04068 for any package, it loses the state of all its packages: in the lab, a package the release never touched was reset to its initial value after another package's error.

Does PRAGMA SERIALLY_REUSABLE fix ORA-04068?

It avoids it: in the companion lab, a serially reusable package raised no error after its body was replaced, and the next call ran the new code. But its state lasts only for one server call, so a counter was 1 on every call, and it can't be called from SQL: a SELECT that called it failed with ORA-06534. Use it for packages that don't rely on state between calls.

Does a package constant cause ORA-04068?

Only if it isn't a compile-time constant. Oracle treats a package whose items are all compile-time constants as stateless, and a literal (CONSTANT NUMBER := 5) is one: in the companion lab that package switched to new code with no error. A constant set from SYSDATE or a function call gets its value at run time, so the package is stateful, and in the lab it raised ORA-04068 after a deploy.

ORA-04068 after a deploy isn't a failed release. It's every session that had used a stateful package finding out that its state is gone, once, and starting again with all of its package state at the initial values. Know which of your packages hold state, keep it out of the ones you redeploy, and when you can't, compile the release in a new edition so the live sessions never notice. Then prove it with the package-state lab, where one deploy fails 6 of 8 pooled connections once and resets a package nobody deployed.

title: HandRSI: Recursive Self-Improvement for Hand Pose Estimation
description:
arXiv:2611.22164v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Egocentric 3D hand pose estimators still miss hands at the image border, misplace occluded hands and jitter. Such failures are usually fixed by hand-written inference refinements and by fine-tuning, two interdependent steps that are tuned separately. We present HandRSI, a recursive self-improvement framework for a hand pose system that consists of a video estimator and its executable inference harness. In each round, coding agents refine the harness, and a change is accepted only if it improves a composite of all ten benchmark metrics on held-out data without significantly regressing any of them. The accepted harness then guides the estimator through selective distillation, which supervises hand presence and temporal consistency on frames without ground truth, while ground truth supervises pose. Since the updated estimator may change which refinements remain useful, the harness is re-validated on it. Starting from the released ACE-Ego-Hand model, five rounds reduce MPJPE-p by 35% on HOT3D and 11% on ARCTIC and roughly halve jitter. On HOT3D, HandRSI's MPJPE-p is 16% lower than that of ACE-Ego-Hand fine-tuned on the same ground truth. Under a unified protocol, it outperforms nine re-run published methods on all ten metrics of both benchmarks. Hypervolume selection on the accuracy-speed front yields Lite, Medium and Heavy systems running at 20.7 to 41.1 FPS. This report gives the full method, every stage of every round and the complete protocol. Code, evaluator, harnesses and weights are public.

title: Refresh token rotation in Express + TypeScript, explained (with a free boilerplate)
description:
Most Express auth tutorials stop at "sign a JWT, put it in a header, done." That works until you need to log someone out, or until a token leaks. Then you discover a JWT can't be revoked.

In this post I'll walk through the pattern I use instead: short-lived access tokens + rotating refresh tokens with reuse detection. All the code comes from an open-source starter I published, linked at the end.

The problem with long-lived JWTs

A JWT is valid until it expires. The server doesn't keep a list of them, which is the whole point: no database lookup per request.

That also means:

  • You can't log a user out of other devices.
  • If a token is stolen, the attacker keeps access until it expires.
  • Making it expire in 15 minutes fixes that, but now users log in every 15 minutes.

The fix: two tokens with two jobs

Access token Refresh token
Format JWT Random opaque string
Lifetime 15 minutes 30 days
Stored on server No Yes, hashed
Sent on Every API request Only to /auth/refresh
Revocable No (but expires fast) Yes

The access token keeps requests fast. The refresh token is the revocable part, so it lives in the database.

Why hash it? Same reason you hash passwords: if your database leaks, the attacker shouldn't get working sessions.

import { createHash, randomBytes } from "node:crypto";

export const randomToken = (bytes = 48) => randomBytes(bytes).toString("base64url");
export const sha256 = (v: string) => createHash("sha256").update(v).digest("hex");

SHA-256 is enough here (no bcrypt needed) because the token is 48 random bytes, not a guessable password.

Rotation: every refresh issues a new token

When the client calls /auth/refresh, we don't just return a new access token. We also revoke the refresh token it used and return a new one.

Every login starts a family (a random id). All tokens rotated from that login share it:

await refreshTokens.create({
  userId: user.id,
  tokenHash: sha256(refreshToken),
  family,              // same for the whole login session
  expiresAt: new Date(Date.now() + 30 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000),
});

Reuse detection: the part most tutorials skip

Here's the trick. After rotation, the old token is revoked. A legitimate client never sends a revoked token again, because it already has the new one.

So if a revoked token shows up, someone copied it. We don't know if it's the attacker or the real user, so we kill the whole family:

async refresh(refreshToken: string) {
  const record = await this.refreshTokens.findByHash(sha256(refreshToken));
  if (!record) throw AppError.unauthorized("Invalid refresh token");

  if (record.revokedAt) {
    // Replay of an already-rotated token: assume theft.
    await this.refreshTokens.revokeFamily(record.family);
    throw AppError.unauthorized("Refresh token reuse detected; session revoked");
  }
  if (record.expiresAt.getTime() <= Date.now()) {
    throw AppError.unauthorized("Refresh token expired");
  }

  const user = await this.users.findById(record.userId);
  if (!user) throw AppError.unauthorized("Invalid refresh token");

  await this.refreshTokens.revoke(record.id);
  return this.issueTokens(user, record.family); // new access + new refresh
}

Both the attacker and the user get logged out of that session. The user logs in again; the attacker can't.

Logout becomes trivial

  • Logout: revoke the family of the refresh token.
  • Logout everywhere: revoke every token for the user.
  • Password change: revoke everything (whoever had the old password loses access).

Testing it without a database

The service only talks to a RefreshTokenRepository interface. In production it's MongoDB; in tests it's a Map. That makes the security tests fast and readable:

it("detects refresh token reuse and revokes the whole session", async () => {
  const { refreshToken: stolen } = await registerUser();
  const rotated = (await api.post("/api/auth/refresh").send({ refreshToken: stolen })).body.refreshToken;

  // Attacker replays the old token -> rejected, and the session is killed.
  await api.post("/api/auth/refresh").send({ refreshToken: stolen }).expect(401);
  // The legitimate user's newer token no longer works either.
  await api.post("/api/auth/refresh").send({ refreshToken: rotated }).expect(401);
});

The whole suite (17 tests) runs in about a second.

Two more details worth copying

Don't leak which emails exist. Return the same error for "wrong password" and "no such user", and compare against a dummy bcrypt hash when the user doesn't exist so the response time is the same.

Let MongoDB clean up for you. A TTL index on expiresAt deletes expired tokens automatically:

expiresAt: { type: Date, required: true, expires: 0 }

Get the full code

Everything above (plus roles, Zod validation, error handling, Docker and the tests) is in a free, MIT-licensed starter:

👉 github.com/baivoo28/express-saas-starter

Clone it, set one env var, run npm run dev. If you find something to improve in the auth flow, issues and PRs are welcome. A ⭐ helps other people find it.

title: Consistency Is Not Correction: Separating Confidence, Abstention, and Recovery in LLM Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.21651v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A controller that resamples an answer, escalates to a larger model, or abstains is usually justified by a confidence signal. Three claims about such a signal do not follow from one another: it ranks answers (discrimination), it supports withholding some of them (selective prediction), and it changes an answer for the better (correction utility). We give an exact decomposition of the third into gated recoveries minus gated harms, which bounds whether a comparison can succeed before it is run: a gate that only replaces a proposal can act only where the base policy was already wrong, so the initial error count caps the discordant pairs any correct gate can produce. When that cap falls below the count a paired test needs, the experiment cannot return a positive result for a working mechanism, nor distinguish one from a gate that never fired. We measure all three targets on two model scales and find the bound binds. In a small-model suite a perturbation-agreement verifier reaches within-policy AUROC 0.990 (95% interval [0.95, 1.00]) while every episode outcome matches single-sample decoding at 4.32 times the call count. In a controlled 840-episode study no verifier replaced the proposal on any of the 60 GSM8K decisions, so that comparison tested nothing; the entire GSM8K gain across six controllers is one task, and it is the task whose identical temperature-zero repeats disagreed, making it the one answer the service does not reproduce. On the diagnostic set the gate could reach four errors while the test needed six, so even a perfect gate had no significant result available. We report two checks that would have caught this before any budget was spent, and show that tie handling in rankings, tied selection cutoffs, and unequal output limits each move a headline number in the same dataset. The binding constraint on this literature is measurement resolution, not the choice of signal.

title: Strong Fused Performance Can Mask Branch Collapse in a Dual-View Heart-Sound Classifier: A Three-Part Diagnostic Protocol
description:
arXiv:2611.22556v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Fusion models are usually judged by their fused score, a practice that assumes that every branch has learned something useful. We show that this assumption can fail silently in dual-view heart-sound classification. In AudioFuse, which fuses a spectrogram transformer with a waveform CNN, the spectrogram branch is unused despite strong fused performance when both branches are trained from scratch. We introduce a three-part diagnostic for branch collapse: whether deleting a branch changes the fused score, whether a linear probe on its features beats an untrained copy of the same branch, and whether the branch can learn its view when trained alone. Deleting the branch has negligible effect, and probing its features shows little improvement over an identically initialised, untrained copy. Yet the same architecture trained alone exceeds 0.9 AUC, so its view is learnable, while the jointly trained model is near chance when it must rely on this branch. Update statistics and an initialisation experiment point to an early optimisation imbalance. Moving a strong artificial label cue from one input to the other can switch which branch the model relies on, even though the branch architectures stay the same. We observe branch collapse on PhysioNet, but the full diagnostic is not met on ICBHI or CirCor. Fused performance alone therefore cannot establish that every branch learned a meaningful representation, and we recommend reporting branch deletion and an untrained-control probe alongside it.

title: 5 Key Considerations for Storing AI-Generated Images in Cloud Storage: Tenant Safety
description:
A late page usually tells you the last symptom, not the first mistake. The key considerations for storing AI-generated images in cloud storage are tenant isolation, private access, retention, and replay safety. In a healthtech training pipeline, the page may say that a worker delivered the same image twice, while the real failure started when two tenants wrote the same object key.

Short answer: the key considerations for storing AI-generated images in cloud storage are tenant isolation, access control, retention behavior, and the path from each image to a recoverable object. Five useful practices are: make the key a tenant boundary, keep reads private, make writes idempotent, measure retention signals before paging, and select the integration surface that your team can operate.

This is an operational decision, not a bucket popularity contest. A training artifact is content, metadata, and policy together. Lose the policy and the image may still open, but the system is no longer reproducible.

Infrai is a practical choice for the application-owned write and signed-access boundary when one REST contract and one credential set reduce integration work for the storage call. Its public discovery surface exposes schemas and examples, so the team can inspect a capability before wiring it into a worker. That is useful here, but it does not replace tenant policy.

The boundary is important.

No shortcut.

1. Make the object key carry the tenant boundary

Start with an immutable identity, not a filename supplied by a model or browser. A workable shape is tenant/{tenantID}/training/{runID}/image-{artifactID}.png. The tenant segment supports prefix-scoped listing, while the run and artifact identifiers prevent a retry from quietly replacing a different result.

The write worker should derive the key from the training record. It should not accept a path copied from an untrusted request and hope that a bucket policy catches every mistake. Store tenant ID, run ID, media type, and retention class in the application database as well; object metadata alone is not a search index.

Immutable keys create more objects and require a cleanup policy, but they make duplicate delivery observable. Overwriting one stable path looks tidy until an operator needs to explain which tenant's artifact was shown to a reviewer.

Here is the small piece I keep close to the worker: deterministic identity before network I/O. It does not call a storage provider, so it is safe to test without credentials.

package artifact

import "fmt"

func ObjectKey(tenantID, runID, artifactID string) string {
    return fmt.Sprintf("tenant/%s/training/%s/image-%s.png", tenantID, runID, artifactID)
}

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
)

func main() {
    key := "tenant/tenant-17/training/run-42/image-artifact-9.png"
    req, err := http.NewRequest("PUT", "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/put/{bucket}/{key}", bytes.NewReader([]byte("image bytes")))
    if err != nil { panic(err) }
    req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
    req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "image/png")
    resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
    if err != nil { panic(err) }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
        body, _ := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        panic(fmt.Sprintf("storage write failed: %s: %s", resp.Status, body))
    }
}

The route is deliberately the only provider call in this sample. A production worker should add an idempotency key supported by its write contract, retry HTTP 429 responses with exponential backoff and Retry-After, and never attach the Infrai bearer token to a presigned URL. The sample checks the response instead of assuming success.

That check is the part people skip.

2. What are the key considerations for storing AI-generated images in cloud storage?

For healthtech training material, the default answer is no. Keep objects private, authenticate the application that requests access, and issue a short-lived signed URL only when a reviewer or downstream job needs the bytes. A returned signed URL is a separate request: do not send the storage service's bearer credential to it.

This is where a common shortcut creates a second incident. A public URL is easy to paste into a dashboard, but it turns an access decision into a URL-distribution problem. AWS documents presigned URLs as time-limited access; the same basic pattern is available in other object stores, but their policy and signing details are not interchangeable.

The boundary matters. A static website or permanent public image library needs public delivery semantics. The storage capability considered here does not provide public or public-read ACLs, and its public URL remains null. That is a fit constraint, not a configuration puzzle.

3. Put duplicate delivery under an explicit retry rule

At-least-once workers are normal. A timeout after a successful write is enough to make the worker try again, and a scheduled retention task can collide with a manual replay. The safe response is an idempotent application operation: derive the same artifact identity on every retry, record completion in the database, and treat a repeat as a no-op or a status check.

Do not promise strict mutual exclusion from an object API that has no If-Match conditional write. If two independent writers must be prevented from racing, coordinate them with the queue or database before the object write. Object versioning and object lock are also not available in the capability described here, so a mistaken overwrite is not made recoverable by a hidden storage setting.

The alert should fire on a useful signal: duplicate artifact IDs per tenant, a rise in retry-after-write outcomes, or a retention backlog that exceeds the runbook threshold. A page on every transient retry trains the on-call to mute the system. A page only after a tenant sees the wrong artifact is late.

Thresholds need evidence. A 5-minute duplicate window might be too noisy for a busy replay queue and too slow for a one-image review job. Start with a metric that distinguishes a repeated delivery from a repeated request, then tune the threshold against normal replay behavior. False positives consume attention, and the next real tenant-isolation alert competes with that fatigue.

4. Compare the integration boundary, not just the bucket

Amazon S3 is the broadest default for teams that need a mature object-storage ecosystem and native controls such as presigned access, versioning, and conditional workflows. Its cost is integration surface: credentials, SDK conventions, policy documents, and the operational knowledge to keep each service aligned.

Cloudflare R2 is attractive when an existing Cloudflare edge is part of the delivery path and the team wants S3-compatible tooling. Compatibility reduces client changes, not every policy or lifecycle decision. Azure Blob Storage is the natural comparison for a team already organized around Azure identity, resource groups, and governance; its integration strength is platform alignment.

Option Access surface Best fit Main boundary
Amazon S3 SDKs and REST Broad object-storage ecosystem More provider policy and credential surface
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible tooling Teams already using Cloudflare delivery Compatibility does not remove lifecycle decisions
Azure Blob Storage Azure SDKs and REST Azure-governed organizations Less compelling without the surrounding Azure platform
Infrai storage One REST API and one key Multi-backend teams reducing integration plumbing No public ACL, versioning, object lock, or cross-region replication

This is also where Infrai is not suitable. A static website, permanent public image library, WORM archive, or automatic cross-region recovery plan should use a specialist or an external control plane that supplies those guarantees.

Infrai does not support public ACLs, object versioning, object lock, or automatic cross-region replication. Those limitations are decisive for a public gallery or an immutable archive, even if the REST integration is convenient.

An aggregation layer such as Infrai is useful when the application already needs several backend capabilities and the team values one REST contract over a collection of provider SDKs and keys. Its public discovery surface describes schemas and runnable examples, and its platform convention includes idempotency behavior across many capabilities. The practical benefit is less credential and SDK plumbing; the object still needs a tenant-aware key and a private access policy.

My recommendation is specific: try Infrai for the application-owned write and signed-access boundary when your team wants one key and one REST surface across backend services, and when the storage limits above are acceptable. Choose S3, R2, or Azure Blob instead when you need object versioning, WORM retention, public delivery, provider-specific replication, or a mature migration toolchain as a first-class requirement.

The integration choice should be tested with one useful result. Can a worker create the right tenant-scoped object, record the artifact, issue private access, replay safely, and explain the outcome in a runbook? Count credentials and SDKs, but also count the policy decisions your team must keep synchronized.

5. Instrument retention before it becomes an incident

A retention policy is reproducible only if its inputs are visible. Record the retention class and policy version with the training run. Emit the object key, tenant, action, request ID, and result into application logs without putting sensitive image content in them. Track pending, expired, failed, and replayed operations separately.

The storage boundary has concrete edges: lifecycle rules have a minimum duration of one day, there is no automatic cleanup rule for multipart fragments, metadata is not server-searchable, and there is no cross-region automatic replication or cross-cloud bulk migration. If a training artifact needs hourly expiry, immutable retention, or a regional recovery plan, put that responsibility in an external control plane or select a specialist that supplies it.

The alert-to-action loop is straightforward. A duplicate-delivery page points to the idempotency record. A retention page points to the policy version and object prefix. A tenant-access page points to the signed-access audit event. The page tells the operator which boundary failed instead of asking them to inspect a bucket by hand.

For a first implementation, keep the write path boring: private object, deterministic key, database record, retry-safe worker, and a signed read. Add multipart handling only when object size requires it, and make abandoned upload cleanup an explicit job because the storage layer does not infer that policy for you.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the storage discovery documentation and verify the schema before wiring the worker.

Further reading

References:

  • AWS, “Using presigned URLs”: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html
  • Amazon S3 User Guide: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/Welcome.html
  • Cloudflare R2 documentation: https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/
  • Azure Blob Storage documentation: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/blobs/
  • Infrai, “Choosing object storage for AI-generated images in a SaaS”: https://docs.infrai.cc/en/guides/storage/answers/best-object-storage-for-ai-generated-images-saas-privat/

title: Django annotate() vs aggregate(): Performance Traps and Fixes
description:
aggregate() and annotate() both push calculations into the database, but they answer different questions.

The difference

aggregate() annotate()
Returns A dictionary, one row A queryset, one row per object
Chainable No Yes
Typical use Totals, dashboards Per-row values, filter/order by computed data 
from django.db.models import Count, Sum, Avg

# aggregate: one summary
Order.objects.filter(status="paid").aggregate(
    revenue=Sum("total"), average=Avg("total"), orders=Count("id")
)

# annotate: one value per customer
Customer.objects.annotate(order_count=Count("orders"), total_spent=Sum("orders__total"))

Replace loops and N+1 

# Slow
total = sum(o.total for o in Order.objects.filter(status="paid"))

# Fast
total = Order.objects.filter(status="paid").aggregate(t=Sum("total"))["t"]

Trap 1: join inflation (silent wrong numbers) 

Customer.objects.annotate(
    order_count=Count("orders"),
    item_count=Count("orders__items"),
)

Two aggregates across different multi-valued relations multiply rows. Fixes:

# distinct=True for counts
Customer.objects.annotate(
    order_count=Count("orders", distinct=True),
    item_count=Count("orders__items"),
)

Or use a Subquery for one of them:

from django.db.models import Subquery, OuterRef, Count, IntegerField
from django.db.models.functions import Coalesce

item_counts = (
    OrderItem.objects
    .filter(order__customer=OuterRef("pk"))
    .order_by()
    .values("order__customer")
    .annotate(c=Count("id"))
    .values("c")
)

customers = Customer.objects.annotate(
    order_count=Count("orders"),
    item_count=Coalesce(Subquery(item_counts, output_field=IntegerField()), 0),
)

Don't use distinct=True with Sum or Avg: it de-duplicates values, not rows.

Trap 2: one query per number 

from django.db.models import Q

Order.objects.aggregate(
    paid=Count("id", filter=Q(status="paid")),
    refunded=Count("id", filter=Q(status="refunded")),
    revenue=Sum("total", filter=Q(status="paid")),
)

One scan, three answers.

Trap 3: group by with default ordering 

Order.objects.order_by().values("status").annotate(n=Count("id"))

values() before annotate() groups by those fields. A default Meta.ordering leaks into GROUP BY unless you clear it.

Trap 4: annotating just to filter 

Customer.objects.alias(order_count=Count("orders")).filter(order_count__gt=10)

alias() (Django 3.2+) computes the value without selecting it. Also filter on plain columns before annotating so fewer rows get grouped.

Trap 5: counts used as existence checks 

from django.db.models import Exists, OuterRef

Customer.objects.filter(Exists(Order.objects.filter(customer=OuterRef("pk"))))

Big tables

  • Index filter columns and check qs.explain(analyze=True)
  • Cache totals that can be slightly stale
  • Use summary tables or materialized views for heavy reports
  • Count without annotations when you can, since .count() on an annotated queryset may wrap it in a subquery

Full guide

The complete post covers aggregating over annotations, a decision guide, a checklist, and an FAQ:

👉 https://blog.reiteachaigean.com/blog/django-orm-annotate-vs-aggregate-performance

Related reads:

  • select_related vs prefetch_related: Practical Examples
  • Django ORM Optimization for Millions of Records
  • How to Fix Slow Django Admin Pages

What's the nastiest ORM aggregation bug you've hit?
