title: Benchmarking Deep Learning Models for Wheelchair Configuration Classification in Accessible Automated Vehicle Applications
description:
arXiv:2611.21945v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Making automated vehicles accessible requires consideration of vulnerable road users, including wheelchair users. To offer a more tailored experience that supports independence for this group, vehicle design needs to accommodate the wide range of wheelchair configurations. However, wheelchairs are individualized, varying in frame geometry, propulsion, and visual appearance. Moreover, occupants or accessories may obscure visual cues. Existing mobility-aid datasets only label the presence of a wheelchair, rather than describing its specific configuration. To fill this gap, this paper introduces the Wheelchair Configuration Image Dataset (WCID), comprising 467 face-blurred images across 192 capture groups solely for evaluation. Each image is annotated with (i) a two-class label of manual or powered, (ii) a chair subtype, (iii) occupancy, viewpoint, setting, lighting, occlusion, propulsion, and control, with a 273-image validation split and 194-image test split. Three convolutional neural network backbones and a frozen vision-language probe are trained on an external image dataset and evaluated on WCID to measure cross-dataset generalization, while also testing robustness using Gaussian blur. Convolutional models do well on clean images, but performance drops under strong blur, leaving a gap before deployment. Code, split assignments, labels, trained weights, and the face-blurred images is available at: https://github.com/Mi3-Lab/MAID

title: NonoDB in practice #1: expiring invite tokens without Redis or cron
description:
Every small product eventually grows the same little subsystem: one-time
invite links.

A teammate clicks "Invite", we generate a token, send a URL, and the link must
work exactly once and stop working after seven days. It also has to be
auditable — "who invited whom, and when was the link used?" — because support
will ask.

The classic stack for this is three moving parts:

  1. Redis with SETEX invite:<token> 604800 <payload> for the expiry.
  2. Postgres for the durable invite record and the audit trail.
  3. A cron job that deletes stale rows so the table does not grow forever.

That is a cache, a database, and a scheduler for a feature that stores maybe a
few thousand rows. On a 1 GB VM it is also three more things that can page you
at 2 a.m.

This post rebuilds the feature with one process: NonoDB, a single Rust
daemon that owns LMDB files and speaks HTTP/JSON. The whole thing fits in the
same mental model as SQLite, but with document semantics, TTL, and per-document
history built in.

The requirements, written down

Before choosing anything, I wrote the actual contract:

  • A token is a random 32-byte value, stored hashed.
  • Default lifetime: 7 days.
  • Some invites are shorter — a support re-invite should die after 1 hour.
  • A token can be consumed at most once, even if two requests race.
  • Consuming a token must be atomic with marking it used.
  • We keep the invite record for audit, but not forever.
  • The whole service must run on a 1 vCPU / 1 GB VM next to the app.

The important line is number four. Expiry is not authorization. A TTL is a
garbage collector, not a lock. If two requests arrive at the same time, "is it
expired?" followed by "mark it used" is a race unless the check and the write
happen in one transaction.

Run the daemon

NonoDB publishes Linux amd64/arm64 images. Pin an exact version in
production; latest should be a deliberate choice, not an accident.

export NONODB_AUTH_FILE="$PWD/nonodb-auth.json"
nonodb-cli auth init
export TOKEN=$(nonodb-cli auth token create admin)

docker volume create nonodb-data
docker run -d --name nonodb \
  -e NONODB_AUTH_FILE=/etc/nonodb/auth.json \
  -e NONODB_TCP=0.0.0.0:7878 \
  -p 127.0.0.1:7878:7878 \
  --group-add "$(id -g)" \
  -v "$NONODB_AUTH_FILE:/etc/nonodb/auth.json:ro" \
  -v nonodb-data:/var/lib/nonodb \
  ghcr.io/essmos/nonodb:0.26.0

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:7878/healthz

The daemon runs as an unprivileged user. TCP requires the auth registry; the
Unix socket is the trusted local channel. For a single-host app, mounting the
socket into the app container is even simpler, and there is no bearer token to
rotate.

Create the collection once

NonoDB collections can carry a default TTL and a history retention setting.
Both are opt-in.

from nonodb import NonoDB

db = NonoDB(base_url="http://127.0.0.1:7878", token=TOKEN)
invites = db.collection("invites")

db.create_collection(
    "invites",
    ttl_seconds=7 * 24 * 3600,   # default: 7 days
    ttl_purge_history=False,     # keep revisions for audit
)
db.set_collection_history("invites", 20)

Two details matter here:

  • The collection default applies to documents inserted after it is set. It does not rewrite existing documents.
  • ttl_purge_history=False means an expiry leaves a delete tombstone in history instead of erasing the revisions. For an audit trail, that is what we want, at the cost of some disk.

There is no cron entry and no cleanup container.

Insert an invite with a per-document override

The default is seven days, but the support workflow needs one hour. The reserved
top-level _ttl field overrides the collection default for that document:

import hashlib
import secrets
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

def bson_date(value: datetime) -> dict:
    """Wrap an instant in MongoDB Extended JSON for the HTTP API."""
    return {"$date": value.isoformat()}

def create_invite(team_id: str, email: str, ttl_seconds: int = 7 * 24 * 3600):
    raw = secrets.token_urlsafe(32)
    token_hash = hashlib.sha256(raw.encode()).hexdigest()
    now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)

    invites.insert({
        "_id": token_hash,          # lookup by hash, never store the raw token
        "team_id": team_id,
        "email": email.lower(),
        "used": False,
        "created_by": "dashboard",
        "expires_at": bson_date(now + timedelta(seconds=ttl_seconds)),
        "_ttl": ttl_seconds,        # cleanup window, not the auth check
    })
    return raw

# Support re-invite: valid for one hour.
raw_token = create_invite("team_42", "new@example.com", ttl_seconds=3600)

_ttl is metadata: it is stored outside the document and is not returned by
reads. An update that does not mention _ttl preserves the current expiry, so
"resend invite" can extend or shorten the window explicitly:

def extend_invite(token_hash: str, ttl_seconds: int = 7 * 24 * 3600):
    new_deadline = datetime.now(timezone.utc) + timedelta(seconds=ttl_seconds)
    invites.update(
        {"_id": token_hash},
        {"$set": {"_ttl": ttl_seconds, "expires_at": bson_date(new_deadline)}},
    )

Consume the invite exactly once

This is where the Redis-plus-Postgres version needed a transaction or a Lua
script. In NonoDB, find_and_modify selects one document, applies the update,
and returns the image — all inside the single writer transaction.

from datetime import datetime, timezone

def consume_invite(raw_token: str) -> dict | None:
    token_hash = hashlib.sha256(raw_token.encode()).hexdigest()
    now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)

    old = invites.find_and_modify(
        {"_id": token_hash, "used": False, "expires_at": {"$gt": bson_date(now)}},
        {"$set": {"used": True, "used_at": bson_date(now)}},
        new=False,
        projection={"_id": 1, "team_id": 1, "email": 1, "used": 1},
    )
    return old   # None means: unknown, already used, expired, or swept

Two concurrent requests cannot both receive the invite. The second one matches
nothing, because the first transaction already set used: true. There is no
read-modify-write gap in application code, and no distributed lock.

The Python client passes the Extended JSON object through unchanged. Over raw
HTTP, NonoDB also accepts numeric milliseconds and RFC 3339 strings with Z or
a numeric offset; naive local times are rejected as ambiguous.

TTL is cleanup, not the security boundary

This deserves its own section because it is the most common design mistake with
any TTL feature, including Redis.

NonoDB TTL is eventual. A document stays readable until the background
maintenance worker sweeps it, normally within a few seconds of expiry. That is
perfect for garbage collection and terrible as the only check for "is this link
still valid?"

So the application contract has two checks, and the find_and_modify filter
above already carries both:

  1. used == false — enforced atomically by the write transaction.
  2. expires_at > now — the hard deadline, independent of cleanup timing.

The TTL setting exists so that the collection does not grow forever, and so that
support does not see year-old invites in the GUI. It is not SETNX.

If a document somehow survives long past its deadline, the expires_at filter
still rejects it. TTL remains the janitor, not the bouncer.

The audit trail is already there

Because history is enabled on the collection, the insert and the consume are
recorded as revisions in the same LMDB transaction as the current document.
There is no second write path to forget.

revisions = invites.history(token_hash, limit=10, include_docs=True)
for rev in revisions:
    print(rev["rev"], rev["op"], rev["at"], rev.get("doc", {}).get("used"))

rev is a global monotonic revision ID. For one document, revisions are ordered
but not necessarily consecutive — another document's write can take a number in
between. get_version(token_hash, rev) returns one exact revision, or None if
retention has pruned it.

The retention setting caps revisions per document at 20. For invites that is
plenty: created, maybe extended once, consumed, expired.

A real audit export can then be a single aggregation over the collection or a
batch of reads, without joining two databases.

What about the "expired invites" dashboard?

Support wants a count of live invites per team. With a secondary index on
team_id this is a normal indexed query:

invites.create_index(field="team_id")

live = invites.count({"team_id": team_id, "used": False})

count({}) is O(1) in NonoDB; filtered counts use the index when the filter
matches it. For a grouped report:

list(invites.aggregate([
    {"$match": {"used": False}},
    {"$group": {"_id": "$team_id", "live": {"$sum": 1}}},
    {"$sort": {"live": -1}},
    {"$limit": 20},
]))

No separate analytics store, no nightly rollup.

What this costs

The feature now has:

  • one daemon,
  • one data volume,
  • one collection with a TTL default and history retention,
  • no cache server,
  • no cron job,
  • no cleanup Lambda.

On a small VM the idle daemon is in the single-digit-megabyte range, which is
the main reason I reached for it instead of adding another service. Backups are
a single LMDB directory, and the daemon supports native or restic backups with
encryption if the data ever leaves the box.

When I would not do this

Honesty is useful in a tutorial:

  • If the app already runs Postgres and the team knows it well, a partial unique index plus a scheduled DELETE is a perfectly good solution. NonoDB wins when you do not want to operate a second database server.
  • If you need cross-collection transactions across many entities, a relational database with real foreign keys is still the safer default.
  • If the token volume is in the tens of millions per day, measure first. NonoDB serializes writes through one writer thread, which is ideal for this workload but not a horizontally sharded write firehose.

For the actual shape of this problem — a few thousand short-lived records, one
small VM, one process, atomic consumption, and an audit trail — one binary is
easier to reason about than three services.

Try it 

docker run --rm -it \
  -e NONODB_AUTH_FILE=/etc/nonodb/auth.json \
  -e NONODB_TCP=0.0.0.0:7878 \
  -p 127.0.0.1:7878:7878 \
  -v "$PWD/nonodb-auth.json:/etc/nonodb/auth.json:ro" \
  -v nonodb-data:/var/lib/nonodb \
  ghcr.io/essmos/nonodb:0.26.0

The full API surface used here — create_collection, _ttl, find_and_modify,
history, aggregate — is in the NonoDB docs. If you want the next article in
this series, it will take the same daemon and build a job queue with leases and
retries, again without Redis.

NonoDB is MIT-licensed. I am writing this series while exploring it; the
examples above are run against the 0.26 release.

title: ATLAS-Finance: Benchmarking AI Agents in Realistic Banking Environments
description:
arXiv:2611.22085v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Professional work involves under-specified assignments, where relevant information is spread across workplace applications and may conflict or change over time. To evaluate how well frontier agents can perform economically valuable work in such settings, we introduce ATLAS-Finance, a benchmark of 100 end-to-end investment-banking tasks across 13 simulated firms. As in real banking workflows, agents must search email, chat, calendars, notes, and files to identify requirements, gather information, reconcile conflicts/updates, and then build complex financial models. Tasks were developed by experienced bankers based on their real deal work and take them 15-30 hours to complete. Agent deliverables are evaluated with expert-authored rubrics (median: 124.5 criteria) covering financial rationale and results, spreadsheet construction, completeness, and formatting. Despite completing substantial portions of the requested work, current agents rarely produce correct deliverables. Across today's frontier models, the best ones (Claude Opus and Fable) pass fewer than 11% of tasks.

title: TypeScript `Omit` vs `Pick` vs `Exclude` in 2026: Choosing the Right Utility Type Without Guessing
description:
TypeScript Omit vs Pick vs Exclude in 2026: Choosing the Right Utility Type Without Guessing

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

Developers reach for Omit when they need Pick, apply Exclude to object types that need Omit, and ship code that compiles cleanly but accepts any string literal as a property name. TypeScript provides six property-manipulation utilities that look similar but operate on fundamentally different input shapes. The confusion costs hours in debugging sessions where the compiler stays silent while the runtime produces undefined values.

The root problem is naming. Pick and Omit transform object types. Exclude and Extract filter union types. No visual or naming convention signals which category each utility belongs to, so developers test by trial until the compiler accepts the syntax. The correct approach groups utilities by input shape first, then checks whether the operation adds or removes members.

Key Takeaways

  • Pick and Omit operate on object types by selecting or removing properties; Exclude and Extract operate on union types by filtering members.
  • Omit accepts any string literal without checking if the property exists, allowing typos to compile successfully while producing incorrect types.
  • Decision framework: check the input shape (object vs union) before choosing the utility, then decide whether the operation should include or remove members.
  • Strict variants from type-zoo (PickStrict, OmitStrict) enforce property existence at compile time, catching typos and refactoring oversights.
  • Object utilities preserve structure and return new object types; union utilities return new unions with fewer or different members.

Pick vs Omit: Object Property Selection

Pick<Type, Keys> constructs a new type by selecting a subset of properties from an existing object type. The operation requires two inputs: the source object type and a string literal or union of string literals naming the properties to extract. TypeScript introduced Pick in version 2.1 alongside Partial, Readonly, and Record.

interface UserAccount {
  id: string;
  email: string;
  passwordHash: string;
  createdAt: Date;
  lastLogin: Date;
  preferences: Record<string, unknown>;
}

type PublicProfile = Pick<UserAccount, "id" | "email" | "createdAt">;

const profile: PublicProfile = {
  id: "usr_123",
  email: "user@example.com",
  createdAt: new Date("2026-01-15"),
};

The pattern fits API response types where the backend returns a subset of database columns. GraphQL resolvers often return fragments that match a Pick type exactly. The alternative approach requires duplicating property definitions across multiple interfaces, which creates maintenance burden when field types change.

Omit<Type, Keys> constructs a new type by removing specified properties from an existing object type. TypeScript added Omit in version 3.5 as the inverse of Pick. The operation accepts the same input types but produces the complement set of properties.

type UserUpdatePayload = Omit<UserAccount, "id" | "createdAt">;

function updateUser(userId: string, updates: UserUpdatePayload) {
  // Implementation accepts all fields except immutable ones
}

The comparison reveals a structural difference beyond inclusion versus exclusion. Pick forces developers to list exactly what the new type contains. Omit forces developers to list what the new type excludes. The cognitive load shifts based on whether the remaining properties or the excluded properties form a shorter list.

Utility Input type Operation Output Use case
Pick Object type Select named properties New object type with subset API responses, public interfaces
Omit Object type Remove named properties New object type without exclusions Update payloads, sensitive data removal

The decision between Pick and Omit depends on which list is shorter and which intent is clearer. A type that needs 2 properties from a 10-property interface uses Pick. A type that needs 8 properties from a 10-property interface uses Omit. Neither choice affects runtime behavior or compilation output, but the shorter list reduces maintenance surface area.

TypeScript utility types decision matrix

Exclude vs Extract: Union Type Filtering

Exclude<UnionType, ExcludedMembers> constructs a new union by removing all members from UnionType that are assignable to ExcludedMembers. TypeScript introduced Exclude in version 2.8 as part of a set of conditional type utilities. The operation works on union types exclusively and fails when applied to object types.

type HTTPMethod = "GET" | "POST" | "PUT" | "DELETE" | "PATCH";
type ReadOnlyMethod = Exclude<HTTPMethod, "POST" | "PUT" | "DELETE" | "PATCH">;

function fetchData(method: ReadOnlyMethod, url: string) {
  // Only GET requests compile
}

Extract<Type, Union> constructs a new union by selecting all members from Type that are assignable to Union. The operation inverts Exclude by keeping matching members instead of removing them. Both utilities appeared in the same TypeScript release as complementary tools.

type MutatingMethod = Extract<HTTPMethod, "POST" | "PUT" | "DELETE" | "PATCH">;

function modifyResource(method: MutatingMethod, url: string, body: unknown) {
  // GET fails to compile
}

The confusion between object utilities and union utilities stems from overlapping terminology. "Exclude" and "Omit" both remove things. "Extract" and "Pick" both select things. The critical distinction is input shape: object types have named properties, union types have discrete members. TypeScript enforces this boundary at compile time but provides no naming convention to signal the category.

The pattern fits discriminated unions where runtime logic branches on a subset of possible values. State machines often use Extract to constrain valid transitions from a given state. Event handlers use Exclude to prevent certain event types from reaching sensitive code paths.

Utility Input type Operation Output Use case
Exclude Union type Remove matching members New union without exclusions Restricting valid values, state machines
Extract Union type Keep matching members New union with only matches Filtering event types, permission checks

Real-World Code Examples: API Response Types

Backend services often return nested JSON structures where different endpoints expose different subsets of the same entity. TypeScript utility types model these variations without duplicating property definitions. Consider a user service that stores comprehensive account data but exposes sanitized versions through public APIs.

interface DatabaseUser {
  id: string;
  email: string;
  passwordHash: string;
  passwordSalt: string;
  totpSecret: string | null;
  createdAt: Date;
  updatedAt: Date;
  deletedAt: Date | null;
  emailVerified: boolean;
  roles: Array<"admin" | "moderator" | "user">;
  loginAttempts: number;
  lastLoginIp: string | null;
  preferences: {
    theme: "light" | "dark";
    notifications: boolean;
  };
}

type PublicUserProfile = Pick<
  DatabaseUser,
  "id" | "email" | "emailVerified" | "createdAt" | "preferences"
>;

type AdminUserView = Omit<DatabaseUser, "passwordHash" | "passwordSalt" | "totpSecret">;

type UserUpdateRequest = Partial<
  Pick<DatabaseUser, "email" | "preferences">
>;

type AuthenticationResponse = Pick<DatabaseUser, "id" | "email" | "roles"> & {
  token: string;
  expiresAt: Date;
};

The composition demonstrates layering: Pick extracts the base structure, Partial makes fields optional for update operations, and intersection types add authentication metadata. Each derived type maintains a single source of truth for property shapes while modeling different access patterns.

Role-based filtering uses union utilities to constrain valid permission sets. The backend defines an exhaustive permission list as a union type, then uses Extract to model role-specific capabilities.

type Permission =
  | "users:read"
  | "users:write"
  | "users:delete"
  | "posts:read"
  | "posts:write"
  | "posts:delete"
  | "analytics:read"
  | "settings:write";

type UserPermissions = Extract<Permission, `users:${string}`>;
type PostPermissions = Extract<Permission, `posts:${string}`>;
type ReadOnlyPermissions = Extract<Permission, `${string}:read`>;

function checkPermission(
  userRole: "admin" | "moderator" | "user",
  required: Permission
): boolean {
  const rolePermissions: Record<string, Permission[]> = {
    admin: [
      "users:read", "users:write", "users:delete",
      "posts:read", "posts:write", "posts:delete",
      "analytics:read", "settings:write"
    ],
    moderator: [
      "users:read", "posts:read", "posts:write", "posts:delete"
    ],
    user: ["posts:read"]
  };

  return rolePermissions[userRole].includes(required);
}

The pattern works because Extract with template literal types filters by pattern matching. The result maintains type safety while avoiding string manipulation at runtime. Frontend code uses these derived types to conditionally render UI elements based on user permissions.

TypeScript utility types in production code

The Silent Bug: Why Omit Doesn't Catch Typos

Omit accepts any string literal in its second type parameter without verifying that the property exists on the source type. TypeScript designed this behavior intentionally to support mapped types and conditional logic, but the permissiveness creates a maintenance hazard. A typo in the excluded property list compiles successfully and produces an incorrect output type.

interface ApiResponse {
  data: unknown;
  status: number;
  headers: Record<string, string>;
  timestamp: Date;
}

// Typo: "header" instead of "headers"
type CleanResponse = Omit<ApiResponse, "header">;

const response: CleanResponse = {
  data: { userId: 123 },
  status: 200,
  headers: { "content-type": "application/json" }, // Still required
  timestamp: new Date(),
};

The code compiles without warnings. CleanResponse still contains the headers property because Omit silently ignored the nonexistent header property. The bug surfaces only when downstream code expects headers to be absent and receives an unexpected value at runtime. The compiler provides no indication that the exclusion list contains an invalid property name.

Refactoring compounds the issue. When a property name changes in the source interface, Omit calls that reference the old name continue to compile. The type system cannot detect that an excluded property no longer exists because Omit treats the exclusion list as an open set of string literals rather than a constrained subset of known properties.

interface ApiResponse {
  data: unknown;
  status: number;
  responseHeaders: Record<string, string>; // Renamed from "headers"
  timestamp: Date;
}

// Stale reference compiles successfully
type CleanResponse = Omit<ApiResponse, "headers">;

const response: CleanResponse = {
  data: { userId: 123 },
  status: 200,
  responseHeaders: { "content-type": "application/json" },
  timestamp: new Date(),
};

The workaround requires strict variants that check property existence at compile time. The type-zoo package provides OmitStrict, PickStrict, and similar utilities that fail compilation when property names do not exist on the source type. These variants add a constraint that maps the exclusion list to actual keys.

import { OmitStrict } from "type-zoo";

interface ApiResponse {
  data: unknown;
  status: number;
  headers: Record<string, string>;
  timestamp: Date;
}

// Compilation error: "header" does not exist on ApiResponse
type CleanResponse = OmitStrict<ApiResponse, "header">;

The tradeoff is explicit. Standard Omit supports dynamic property exclusion and conditional types at the cost of safety. Strict variants enforce correctness but require all excluded properties to exist in the source type. Teams must choose between flexibility and type safety based on codebase size and refactoring frequency. For more on union filtering, see TypeScript Exclude vs Extract: Union Type Filters Explained.

Practical Decision Framework: Which Utility When

The selection process starts with input shape classification. Object types with named properties use Pick or Omit. Union types with discrete members use Exclude or Extract. Applying union utilities to object types produces compilation errors because union operations expect string literals, not property access patterns.

interface Config {
  apiKey: string;
  timeout: number;
}

// Error: Type 'Config' does not satisfy constraint 'string | number | symbol'
type InvalidExclusion = Exclude<Config, "apiKey">;

Once the input shape category is correct, the second decision is inclusion versus exclusion. Count the properties or union members in each set. If the desired output contains fewer members than the exclusions, use the inclusive utility (Pick or Extract). If the exclusions form a shorter list, use the exclusive utility (Omit or Exclude).

The third consideration is change frequency. Types that evolve frequently benefit from inclusion-based utilities because adding a new property to the source type does not automatically add it to derived types. Exclusion-based utilities require explicit updates when new properties should be excluded.

Error messages guide correction. TypeScript reports different errors for category mismatches versus property name issues. Union utilities applied to object types produce constraint violation errors. Pick applied with nonexistent property names produces "does not exist on type" errors, while Omit accepts any string literal without complaint.

Decision factor Pick/Extract Omit/Exclude
List length Desired output is shorter than source Exclusions are shorter than output
Change frequency New properties default to excluded New properties default to included
Type safety Pick enforces property existence Omit accepts any string literal
Maintenance Explicit about included members Explicit about excluded members

The framework applies recursively to composed types. A type that uses both Pick and Partial applies each utility in sequence: first extract the desired properties, then mark them optional. The order matters because Partial operates on whatever type it receives as input.

interface FormData {
  username: string;
  email: string;
  password: string;
  confirmPassword: string;
  agreedToTerms: boolean;
}

// Extract fields, then make them optional
type PartialUpdate = Partial<Pick<FormData, "email" | "password">>;

// Equivalent to:
type PartialUpdate = {
  email?: string;
  password?: string;
};

Strict Variants and Type-Zoo Alternatives

Production TypeScript often combines standard utility types with custom mapped types to enforce stricter constraints. The type-zoo package provides battle-tested implementations of strict variants that catch common errors at compile time. Teams can implement these patterns inline or install the package as a development dependency.

OmitStrict requires that all excluded properties exist on the source type. The implementation uses a mapped type to check each key against the source type's keys before performing the exclusion.

type OmitStrict<T, K extends keyof T> = Omit<T, K>;

interface User {
  id: string;
  email: string;
  passwordHash: string;
}

// Compilation error: "password" is not assignable to "id" | "email" | "passwordHash"
type InvalidOmit = OmitStrict<User, "password">;

// Compiles successfully
type ValidOmit = OmitStrict<User, "passwordHash">;

The constraint K extends keyof T forces TypeScript to verify that every property in K exists in T before allowing the type to compile. This catches typos immediately and fails compilation when refactoring renames properties without updating all Omit callsites.

PickStrict provides similar guarantees for property selection. The standard library's Pick already enforces key existence because it must access those properties to include them in the output type. The strict variant adds no additional constraint but maintains naming consistency with other strict utilities.

Union type filtering benefits from strict variants when the exclusion list might contain invalid members. ExcludeStrict enforces that all excluded members exist in the source union before performing the exclusion. The implementation requires a helper type that checks membership.

type ExcludeStrict<T, U extends T> = Exclude<T, U>;

type Status = "pending" | "approved" | "rejected";

// Compilation error: "cancelled" is not assignable to Status
type InvalidExclude = ExcludeStrict<Status, "cancelled">;

// Compiles successfully
type ValidExclude = ExcludeStrict<Status, "rejected">;

The constraint U extends T ensures that every member of the exclusion union U is also a member of the source union T. This prevents situations where exclusion lists accumulate stale values after refactoring removes union members.

Teams should adopt strict variants when the codebase meets two criteria. First, the type system must enforce correctness rather than providing flexibility for dynamic types. Second, compile-time checks must catch refactoring oversights before they reach production. Codebases that prioritize rapid prototyping over type safety may find standard utilities sufficient. For related patterns, see TypeScript Partial, Required, DeepPartial: Optional Properties That Scale.

The installation adds zero runtime overhead because all utility types disappear during compilation. The package provides TypeScript definitions only and contains no JavaScript code. Development teams can audit the implementation by reading the source code, which consists entirely of type aliases and mapped types. For a broader overview, see 10 TypeScript Utility Types That Catch Bugs Before Production.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happens if I use Exclude on an object type instead of a union?

TypeScript produces a compilation error stating that the type does not satisfy the constraint string | number | symbol. Exclude operates exclusively on union types and cannot remove properties from object shapes. Use Omit for object property removal.

Does Pick enforce that all specified properties exist on the source type?

Yes. Pick requires that every property name in the second type parameter exists as a key on the source type. TypeScript enforces this constraint with K extends keyof T, which means attempting to pick nonexistent properties produces a compilation error immediately.

Can Omit remove optional properties from an interface?

Yes. Omit removes any property regardless of whether it was required or optional in the source type. The operation works at the structural level and does not distinguish between required and optional properties when deciding what to exclude.

Why does OmitStrict exist when Pick already enforces key existence?

Pick enforces constraints on included properties because it must access them to construct the output type. Omit accepts any string literal as an exclusion without verification, allowing typos to compile successfully. OmitStrict adds the same constraint that Pick has natively, catching excluded property typos at compile time.

When should I use Extract instead of Pick?

Use Extract when filtering members from a union type. Use Pick when selecting properties from an object type. The operations are incompatible because unions contain discrete values while objects contain named properties. TypeScript enforces this distinction through different generic constraints on each utility.

Conclusion

TypeScript utility types operate on two distinct categories: object types with named properties and union types with discrete members. Pick and Omit transform objects. Exclude and Extract filter unions. The selection process checks input shape first, then counts members to decide between inclusion and exclusion utilities. Standard Omit accepts any string literal without verification, allowing typos and stale property names to compile successfully while producing incorrect types. Strict variants enforce property existence at compile time, trading flexibility for compile-time safety in codebases where refactoring frequency justifies the constraint. Teams that adopt this classification framework stop guessing which utility applies and start building type-safe transformations that catch errors before they reach production.

  • TypeScript: Playground Example - Built-in Utility Types

title: Building an Intelligent Assistant: My Architect's View of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
description:
Have you ever gone shopping for a dress for a special occasion?

You walk into a shop, explore different designs, try a few options, check the fitting and perhaps ask someone for a second opinion before making the final decision. Sometimes, you find what you want immediately. Other times, you need a few adjustments before everything comes together.

Now imagine having a personal shopping assistant who coordinates different specialists to help you. One understands your preferences, another checks availability, someone else verifies the details, and another helps you make the final decision.

I saw the similar concept unfolding when building a multi-agent application.

Recently, I worked on a GenAI use case for a customer where we designed and implemented a multi-agent architecture using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and various AWS services.

Rather than building one large assistant to handle everything, we designed multiple specialised agents, each responsible for a specific action. A central orchestrator coordinating them, while AWS services provide the supporting capabilities for memory, tool integration, validation, data storage and security.

Before going further, a quick clarification: the actual customer use case has nothing to do with dress shopping! I've used this analogy purely to make the architecture easier to understand. The customer's business scenario and specific details are confidential, so I've intentionally masked those aspects while sharing the technical approach and architectural decisions behind the implementation.

The architecture at a glance

Here is how we brought the different AWS services together.

Here is how I would explain the different components using our dress-shopping analogy.

1. The personal shopping assistant: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime and Strands

Imagine walking into a shopping mall. You know what you are looking for, but you don't want to visit every shop yourself. You explain your requirements to a personal shopping assistant, who coordinates the different people needed to help you. This is exactly the role of our main orchestrator.

We used Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime to host our orchestrator, built using the Strands Agents framework.

The user provides an event brief, and the orchestrator takes responsibility for understanding the request and deciding which specialised agents need to be involved. What I like about AgentCore Runtime is that it provides a managed environment to run agents without us having to manage all the underlying infrastructure ourselves.

Instead of creating one large application that handles every responsibility, we can separate the work into smaller agents and let the orchestrator manage the overall flow. For me, this is an important architectural decision. It gives us a more structured way to build and extend the solution as business requirements grow.

2. Different specialists: Multiple agents running on AgentCore Runtime

When shopping for a dress, you may need different people to help you. One person understands the design, another checks availability, and someone else verifies the details. We followed the same thinking in our implementation.

We designed four specialised agents, each responsible for an isolated action. These agents run on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime, while the main Strands orchestrator coordinates their activities. The benefit is that each agent has a defined responsibility instead of having one agent trying to handle everything.

From an architecture perspective, I prefer this Seperation of Concerns approach because it gives us better separation of responsibilities. We can work on individual agents without necessarily changing the entire application. It also gives us room to introduce additional agents as the customer requirements evolve.

3. Remembering your preferences: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Memory

Imagine visiting the same shop again. Wouldn't it be nice if the shopping assistant remembered your previous preferences? You don't have to explain everything all over again.

This is where Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Memory comes into our architecture.

We use it to retain conversation context and event or venue history, allowing the orchestrator to refer to relevant information from previous interactions. I see Memory as an important capability when building applications that involve ongoing conversations. Without it, every interaction can feel like starting from scratch. With the right context available, the assistant can provide more meaningful responses. Of course, what information is retained and how it is used needs to be considered carefully, especially in enterprise environments.

4. Connecting to different shops: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway

A shopping assistant cannot do everything independently. Sometimes they need to check with another shop, retrieve information or use an external service. Imagine the dress is not available in one branch but available in another branch store. Our agents also need access to different tools to complete their tasks.

We used Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway to expose tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP).

In our architecture, AWS Lambda functions are made available as tools through the Gateway, allowing agents to invoke the required operations. This is an important part of the design because we don't want every agent to build its own connection to every backend operation. AgentCore Gateway provides a common integration point for these tools. What I find interesting here is that the agent moves beyond simply generating an answer. It can interact with actual business operations and retrieve information needed to complete a task.

5. Checking the details: AWS Lambda and Amazon DynamoDB

Let's say you have found a dress you really like. Before making the purchase, you still need to check the size, colour, availability and whether it fits your budget. You wouldn't want the shopping assistant to simply guess these details. We followed the same principle in our architecture by separating reasoning from validation.

We used AWS Lambda to perform deterministic validation. This means important business checks are handled through predefined code rather than relying entirely on the model. In our actual customer implementation, Lambda performs exact lookups against a facts store maintained in Amazon DynamoDB. I think this separation is particularly important for enterprise applications.

We should not expect a foundation model to handle every operation. Let the model focus on reasoning and language, while AWS Lambda and DynamoDB handle the checks that require predictable results.

6. The personal stylist: Claude on Amazon Bedrock

When shopping, sometimes you need someone who understands your preferences and can help you make a decision.

In our architecture, Claude on Amazon Bedrock provides the reasoning and generation capability. We use Claude to help the agents understand the information they receive, reason through the request and generate relevant responses.

What matters here is how we use the model within the overall architecture. We are not asking Claude to perform every operation. It works alongside the specialised agents, AgentCore Gateway and the Lambda validation components.

For example, the model can interpret a request and generate a useful response, while Lambda performs the exact checks against DynamoDB. This is one of the architectural decisions I find most valuable: use the foundation model where it adds intelligence, and use the surrounding AWS services where we need controlled execution.

7. Keeping everything within the rules: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails

Even when you have a good shopping assistant, there are certain boundaries it needs to follow. The same applies to our application.

_We included Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to provide additional safety controls around model interactions. _

For me, security and responsible usage should not be something we consider only after the application is built. When developing enterprise GenAI applications, we need to think about how the model behaves, what information it can respond to and what boundaries need to be enforced.

8. Preparing the information: Amazon S3, AWS Lambda and Amazon DynamoDB

Imagine a shop receiving a new catalogue with updated product information. Before the shopping assistant can use it, someone needs to organise the information and make it available.

We designed a similar process for the customer's business data. We used Amazon S3 as the storage location for uploaded Excel files. An AWS Lambda function processes these files, extracts the rows and converts them into structured records with the required metadata. The processed information is then loaded into Amazon DynamoDB, which acts as the facts store used by the application.

I liked this approach because it gave us a clear data ingestion process. Similar to a traditional ETL process. Instead of mixing file processing with the agent's actual conversation flow, we handle data preparation separately. It also means the agents can retrieve structured information from DynamoDB rather than having to process raw Excel files every time a user makes a request.

My final thoughts

What I found most interesting about this customer implementation is how we brought different AWS services together to build something beyond a traditional chatbot.

By combining Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Strands, Claude, AWS Lambda, Amazon DynamoDB and Amazon S3, we designed a solution where specialised agents work together, each handling a specific responsibility. One key takeaway for me is that building a multi-agent application is not about having more agents or using more AWS services. It is about making the right architectural choices, giving each component a clear purpose, and ensuring everything works together to solve the business problem.

There is still plenty to explore as GenAI continues to evolve, but I believe this approach opens up interesting possibilities for enterprise applications. And coming back to my dress-shopping analogy, having all the right people in the shop doesn't guarantee the perfect dress. What matters is how well they work together to get the final result right.

Similarly, the success of a multi-agent application comes not from the number of agents we build, but from how effectively we bring them together to deliver a meaningful business outcome.

title: ATS: Anti-Aliased Triangle Splatting with Exact Per-Primitive Integrals
description:
arXiv:2611.22512v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Triangle Splatting represents scenes using semi-transparent triangles, but it evaluates each triangle at the pixel center and culls any triangle with an inradius smaller than one pixel. The former causes severe aliasing, while the latter culls most of the scene at lower resolutions. We show that the integral of the Triangle Splatting window over a pixel admits an exact closed-form solution. The angle bisectors split the triangle into three sub-triangles, in each of which the window is a power of the distance to one edge. Each piece therefore has a closed-form antiderivative, and Green's theorem reduces the integral and its gradients to one term per side of the sub-triangle clipped against the pixel. The integral over the whole triangle, which we show has a closed form, then allows conservative culling, removing only triangles that cannot meet the renderer's alpha cutoff at any pixel. This exact formulation anti-aliases existing models without retraining, exhibits less temporal aliasing than 2x2 supersampling, and enables multi-scale training, matching or outperforming supersampled training at reduced resolutions.

title: AutoE2E: Don't speak - Language free end-to-end autonomy A Real-Time Driving Model for L2++ ADAS and L4 Robotaxis
description:
arXiv:2611.22374v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AutoE2E is an open-source end-to-end driving model developed by the Autoware Foundation Robotaxi Working Group. It introduces a temporal bird's-eye-view (BEV) architecture that combines multi-camera perception, HD-map information and route conditioning to predict future vehicle motion. The evaluated model uses a pretrained camera-BEV backbone, temporal feature fusion and a lightweight recurrent trajectory planner. It contains approximately 79.9 million parameters, of which approximately 1.45 million are trainable in the evaluated configuration. The v1.0 release provides model checkpoints, training and evaluation code, and DataModelConsole, a dashboard for visualizing and inspecting model experiments. On the KITScenes validation benchmark, the fine-tuned checkpoint achieves an average displacement error (ADE) of 0.745 m and a final displacement error (FDE) of 2.020 m at a three-second prediction horizon. The paper also reports preliminary real-vehicle research conducted with the Technical University of Munich's EDGAR platform, alongside ongoing collaboration with the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology. AutoE2E v1.0 is an early open research release. Its quantitative evaluation is open-loop, and the model has not yet demonstrated validated closed-loop autonomous driving. The release is intended to provide the autonomous-driving community with an inspectable baseline for further research, experimentation and collaborative development.

title: Integrating Multi-Modal LLMs into Governed BPMN Pipelines
description:
Customer Onboarding and Know Your Customer (KYC) compliance represent one of the most operationally friction-heavy domains in enterprise banking. Processing a single retail or corporate onboarding application requires verifying heterogeneous, unstructured visual documents: government-issued passports, national identity cards, utility bills for proof of address, tax identity certificates, and corporate articles of incorporation.

Traditionally, banking systems addressed document processing using one of two unsatisfactory approaches:

  1. Legacy OCR Systems: Brittle, template-based Optical Character Recognition (OCR) engines that require rigid pixel-coordinate mapping. Minor layout shifts, scans with poor lighting, or folded document corners cause extraction pipelines to fail, sending up to 40% of documents to manual data-entry queues.
  2. Unconstrained AI Scripts: Standalone Python/AI scripts that send documents to Large Language Models (LLMs) and execute database writes directly. While highly flexible, unconstrained AI scripts lack operational governance, process visibility, regulatory audit trails, and stateful human escalation paths.

Under the Xenon Architecture Standards, modern core banking platforms resolve this dilemma by constructing Governed Multi-Modal BPMN Pipelines. By embedding Multi-Modal LLMs (capable of simultaneous vision and textual inference) directly inside Flowable BPMN 2.0 process engines, document intelligence is treated as a stateful, auditable step within a enterprise-grade business workflow.

💡 Explore the Xenon Architecture Standard For comprehensive architectural blueprints, BIAN service domain mappings, and dual-orchestration integration patterns, visit the official Xenon Architecture Guide. To inspect reference code, infrastructure templates, and open-source banking modules, explore the VecPay-Tech GitHub Organization.

BIAN Service Domain Mapping & Document Extraction Taxonomy

Within a Banking Industry Architecture Network (BIAN) alignment, onboarding document processing is divided across isolated service domains. Multi-modal vision models extract facts, while BPMN gateways enforce compliance state transitions.

BIAN Service Domain Document Category Multi-Modal Inspection Scope Extracted Fact Payload Flowable Gateway Rule Fallback Target
Identity Verification Government Passport / ID Photo validity, MRZ text parsing, hologram/tamper check ID Number, Full Name, DOB, Expiry Date Confidence score ≥0.92 AND Expiry > Today KYC Analyst User Task
Party Data Management Utility Bill / Bank Statement Address layout validation, issuing authority verification Resident Address, Issue Date, Account Holder Name Issue Date ≤90 Days AND Name Match Compliance Review Task
Customer Onboarding Articles of Incorporation Corporate entity structure, beneficial ownership parsing UBO Names, Registration Number, Tax ID All UBOs Identified AND Sanction Checked Senior Underwriter Task
Credit Assessment Tax Return / Financials Income table extraction, auditor seal verification Gross Annual Income, Net Tax Paid, Audit Status Income ≥ Min Loan Qualification Threshold Credit Exception Task

Mathematical Model: Multi-Modal KYC Confidence & Risk Scoring

To prevent flawed AI extractions from silently propagating into core customer databases, a multi-modal extraction step evaluates a composite Document Confidence Index Ckyc-total​ :

Ckyc-total​=wvision​⋅Cvision-quality​+wmrz​⋅Cmrz-match​+wfield​⋅Cfield-extract​

Where:

  • Cvision-quality​ is the multi-modal model's visual assessment of document integrity (detecting blur, glare, edge truncation, and digital manipulation).
  • Cmrz-match​ is a deterministic checksum algorithm evaluating Machine Readable Zone (MRZ) characters against extracted visual text fields.
  • Cfield-extract​ is the average log-probability confidence score across extracted key-value fields.
  • wvision​,wmrz​,wfield​ are normalized weighting factors such that ∑w=1.0 .

If Ckyc-total​<Θauto-approve​ (typically set to 0.92), the BPMN engine routes the extracted payload alongside visual bounding-box metadata directly to a human compliance officer for visual verification.

Architecture Topology: Governed Multi-Modal BPMN Pipeline

The architecture strictly isolates Stateless Multi-Modal AI Inference from Stateful Workflow Management (Flowable) and Core Customer Persistence.

                   GOVERNED MULTI-MODAL BPMN PIPELINE

  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
  | FLOWABLE BPMN 2.0 PROCESS ENGINE                                                |
  |                                                                                 |
  |  [ Start Onboarding ] ───► [ ServiceTask: MultiModalKycDelegate ]               |
  |                                           │                                     |
  |                                           v                                     |
  |                            Calls Vision Inference API                           |
  |                                           │                                     |
  |                                           v                                     |
  |  [ ExclusiveGateway: Evaluate Confidence & Compliance Rules ]                   |
  +-------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------+
                                              |
            ┌─────────────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────┐
            | Confidence >= 0.92 & Valid                                        | Confidence < 0.92 OR Expired
            v                                                                   v
  +-----------------------------------+                               +-----------------------------------+
  | AUTOMATED PARTY CREATION          |                               | FLOWABLE HUMAN KANBAN TASK        |
  |                                   |                               |                                   |
  | [ Call BIAN Party Service API ]   |                               | 1. Render Side-by-Side Image UI   |
  | [ Persist Verified Data ]         |                               | 2. Highlight Extracted Fields     |
  +-----------------------------------+                               | 3. Await Human Review Sign-Off    |
                                                                      +-----------------+-----------------+
                                                                                        |
                                                                               Human Officer Approves
                                                                                        |
                                                                                        v
                                                                      +-----------------------------------+
                                                                      | AUTOMATED PARTY CREATION          |
                                                                      | [ Call BIAN Party Service API ]   |
                                                                      +-----------------------------------+

Technical Implementation: Flowable BPMN 2.0 & Multi-Modal Java Delegate

1. Flowable Process Definition (kyc-onboarding-process.bpmn20.xml)

This BPMN 2.0 XML definition orchestrates document extraction via a custom Java Delegate, evaluates extraction confidence via an exclusive gateway, and routes to a human user task if validation criteria are unmet.

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<definitions xmlns="http://www.omg.org/spec/BPMN/20100524/MODEL"
             xmlns:flowable="http://flowable.org/bpmn"
             targetNamespace="BIAN/CustomerOnboarding">

  <process id="kycMultiModalOnboarding" name="Multi-Modal KYC Onboarding" isExecutable="true">

    <startEvent id="startEvent" name="Onboarding Document Uploaded" />
    <sequenceFlow sourceRef="startEvent" targetRef="extractDocumentTask" />

    <!-- Service Task executing Multi-Modal Vision AI Extraction -->
    <serviceTask id="extractDocumentTask" 
                 name="Extract ID Document via Multi-Modal AI" 
                 flowable:class="com.xenon.banking.kyc.delegate.MultiModalKycDelegate" />

    <sequenceFlow sourceRef="extractDocumentTask" targetRef="evaluateConfidenceGateway" />

    <!-- Exclusive Gateway evaluating Confidence & Expiry Boundaries -->
    <exclusiveGateway id="evaluateConfidenceGateway" name="Confidence & Validity Check" />

    <!-- Path 1: Automated Approval (High Confidence & Valid Document) -->
    <sequenceFlow sourceRef="evaluateConfidenceGateway" targetRef="createPartyAccountTask">
      <conditionExpression xsi:type="tFormalExpression">
        ${kycConfidenceScore >= 0.92 && !isDocumentExpired && isMrzValid}
      </conditionExpression>
    </sequenceFlow>

    <!-- Path 2: Human Compliance Escalation (Low Confidence or Data Anomaly) -->
    <sequenceFlow sourceRef="evaluateConfidenceGateway" targetRef="humanReviewUserTask">
      <conditionExpression xsi:type="tFormalExpression">
        ${kycConfidenceScore < 0.92 || isDocumentExpired || !isMrzValid}
      </conditionExpression>
    </sequenceFlow>

    <!-- Human Task for Manual Compliance Review -->
    <userTask id="humanReviewUserTask" 
              name="Human KYC Compliance Review" 
              flowable:candidateGroups="kyc_compliance_officers">
      <documentation>
        Review document extraction anomaly for Application: ${applicationId}. 
        Confidence Score: ${kycConfidenceScore}. Reason: ${extractionFailureReason}
      </documentation>
    </userTask>

    <sequenceFlow sourceRef="humanReviewUserTask" targetRef="checkHumanDecisionGateway" />

    <exclusiveGateway id="checkHumanDecisionGateway" name="Human Decision?" />
    <sequenceFlow sourceRef="checkHumanDecisionGateway" targetRef="createPartyAccountTask">
      <conditionExpression xsi:type="tFormalExpression">${humanDecision == 'APPROVED'}</conditionExpression>
    </sequenceFlow>
    <sequenceFlow sourceRef="checkHumanDecisionGateway" targetRef="rejectApplicationEnd">
      <conditionExpression xsi:type="tFormalExpression">${humanDecision == 'REJECTED'}</conditionExpression>
    </sequenceFlow>

    <serviceTask id="createPartyAccountTask" 
                 name="Persist Party Record in Core Database" 
                 flowable:delegateExpression="${createPartyRecordDelegate}" />

    <sequenceFlow sourceRef="createPartyAccountTask" targetRef="onboardingApprovedEnd" />

    <endEvent id="onboardingApprovedEnd" name="Onboarding Approved" />
    <endEvent id="rejectApplicationEnd" name="Onboarding Rejected" />

  </process>
</definitions>

2. Multi-Modal Vision Java Delegate Implementation (Java 21)

This Java Delegate transmits document image bytes to a multi-modal vision endpoint using Structured JSON Schema Outputs. It parses the response, computes checksum validations, and sets execution variables in Flowable's memory context.

package com.xenon.banking.kyc.delegate;

import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.JsonNode;
import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;
import org.flowable.engine.delegate.DelegateExecution;
import org.flowable.engine.delegate.JavaDelegate;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

import java.net.URI;
import java.net.http.HttpClient;
import java.net.http.HttpRequest;
import java.net.http.HttpResponse;
import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter;
import java.util.Base64;

@Component
public class MultiModalKycDelegate implements JavaDelegate {

    private final HttpClient httpClient = HttpClient.newHttpClient();
    private final ObjectMapper objectMapper = new ObjectMapper();

    @Override
    public void execute(DelegateExecution execution) {
        String applicationId = (String) execution.getVariable("applicationId");
        byte[] documentImageBytes = (byte[]) execution.getVariable("documentImageBytes");

        System.out.println("Executing Multi-Modal Vision Extraction for Application: " + applicationId);

        try {
            // 1. Convert Document Bytes to Base64 Data URI
            String base64Image = Base64.getEncoder().encodeToString(documentImageBytes);

            // 2. Construct Multi-Modal Prompt with Structured Schema Response Format
            String requestPayload = buildVisionApiPayload(base64Image);

            // 3. Invoke Multi-Modal Vision API Endpoint (Internal Enterprise Gateway)
            HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder()
                    .uri(URI.create("https://ai-gateway.internal.xenon/v1/chat/completions"))
                    .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
                    .header("Authorization", "Bearer " + System.getenv("AI_GATEWAY_KEY"))
                    .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(requestPayload))
                    .build();

            HttpResponse<String> response = httpClient.send(request, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString());

            // 4. Parse Extracted Facts & Confidence Metrics
            JsonNode resultNode = objectMapper.readTree(response.body());
            String rawJsonContent = resultNode.path("choices").get(0).path("message").path("content").asText();
            JsonNode extractedFields = objectMapper.readTree(rawJsonContent);

            String idNumber = extractedFields.path("idNumber").asText();
            String fullName = extractedFields.path("fullName").asText();
            String expirationDateStr = extractedFields.path("expirationDate").asText();
            String mrzCode = extractedFields.path("mrzCode").asText();
            double confidenceScore = extractedFields.path("overallConfidenceScore").asDouble();

            // 5. Evaluate Deterministic Business Logic Rules
            LocalDate expirationDate = LocalDate.parse(expirationDateStr, DateTimeFormatter.ISO_LOCAL_DATE);
            boolean isExpired = expirationDate.isBefore(LocalDate.now());
            boolean isMrzValid = validateMrzChecksum(idNumber, mrzCode);

            // 6. Set Flowable Execution Variables for Gateway Evaluation
            execution.setVariable("extractedIdNumber", idNumber);
            execution.setVariable("extractedFullName", fullName);
            execution.setVariable("kycConfidenceScore", confidenceScore);
            execution.setVariable("isDocumentExpired", isExpired);
            execution.setVariable("isMrzValid", isMrzValid);
            execution.setVariable("extractionFailureReason", 
                    isExpired ? "DOCUMENT_EXPIRED" : (!isMrzValid ? "MRZ_CHECKSUM_MISMATCH" : "NONE"));

        } catch (Exception e) {
            System.err.println("Multi-Modal Extraction Failed: " + e.getMessage());
            // Fallback: Force flow to Human Review Task by setting low confidence
            execution.setVariable("kycConfidenceScore", 0.0);
            execution.setVariable("isDocumentExpired", true);
            execution.setVariable("isMrzValid", false);
            execution.setVariable("extractionFailureReason", "VISION_API_EXECUTION_FAILURE");
        }
    }

    private String buildVisionApiPayload(String base64Image) {
        return """
            {
              "model": "xenon-vision-kyc-v1",
              "messages": [
                {
                  "role": "user",
                  "content": [
                    {"type": "text", "text": "Extract passport data matching JSON schema: idNumber, fullName, expirationDate (YYYY-MM-DD), mrzCode, overallConfidenceScore."},
                    {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": "data:image/jpeg;base64,%s"}}
                  ]
                }
              ],
              "response_format": {"type": "json_object"},
              "temperature": 0.0
            }
            """.formatted(base64Image);
    }

    private boolean validateMrzChecksum(String idNumber, String mrzCode) {
        // Deterministic check: Verify MRZ line 2 contains exact ID number string
        return mrzCode != null && !mrzCode.isEmpty() && mrzCode.contains(idNumber);
    }
}

Regulatory Auditability, Bounded Autonomy, and Privacy

Deploying AI document processing under financial regulatory frameworks (such as EBA ICT guidelines, OCC Bulletins, and GDPR) mandates strict auditability and data governance:

1. Side-by-Side Visual Review Interface

When an application routes to the humanReviewUserTask, the Flowable operational UI renders the raw document image alongside the extracted fields. Extracted text is highlighted with bounding-box coordinates returned by the vision model, allowing human compliance officers to verify facts in seconds.

+------------------------------------+------------------------------------+
| DOCUMENT SOURCE IMAGE (PASSPORT)   | EXTRACTED FACTS & CONFIDENCE METRICS|
|                                    |                                    |
| [ PHOTO ]  P<GBRSMITH<<JOHN<<<<<<  | Full Name:   John Smith  [99.8%]   |
|            1234567897GBR8501010... | ID Number:   123456789  [99.5%]   |
|                                    | Exp. Date:   2028-05-12 [98.1%]   |
| [!] MRZ Checksum Passed            | Overall Confidence: 99.1% (PASSED)  |
+------------------------------------+------------------------------------+

2. Immutable Audit Snapshot Logging

AI extractions must never overwrite historical compliance logs. For every document processed, the pipeline persists an immutable JSON audit snapshot to the central compliance data lake (Elasticsearch / S3 WORM storage), linking the raw document SHA-256 hash to the Flowable ProcessInstanceId:

{
  "auditId": "AUDIT-KYC-2026-881204",
  "flowableProcessInstanceId": "PROC-901283",
  "bianDomain": "IdentityVerification",
  "documentHash": "sha256:e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855",
  "aiModelId": "xenon-vision-kyc-v1",
  "extractedPayload": {
    "idNumber": "123456789",
    "fullName": "John Smith",
    "expirationDate": "2028-05-12",
    "mrzChecksumPassed": true
  },
  "confidenceScore": 0.991,
  "gatewayOutcome": "AUTOMATED_APPROVAL",
  "timestamp": "2026-09-16T12:45:00Z"
}

3. Zero Data Retention at LLM Inference Layer

To comply with GDPR and local data residency laws, calls to third-party or internal multi-modal LLM gateways must use Zero Data Retention (ZDR) endpoints. Document image payloads are processed in-memory during inference and immediately purged from model memory without training log retention.

Embedding Multi-Modal LLM vision intelligence directly into Flowable BPMN pipelines solves the dual challenge of manual KYC bottlenecks and unconstrained AI risk. By relegating multi-modal vision models to structured fact extraction and leveraging BPMN exclusive gateways for rule evaluation and human escalation, modern core banking architectures achieve high operational throughput, sub-second onboarding execution, and complete regulatory compliance across all BIAN service domains.

title: How I set up a JSON mock server for a frontend team in an afternoon
description:
Last spring our frontend team had a sprint planned around a new orders dashboard. The designs were done, the tickets were groomed, and the backend was nowhere close. The API contract existed as a shared doc with three open comments on it. Four frontend devs were about to spend two weeks building against TODO and hard-coded arrays.

I'd seen that movie before. Everyone writes their own fake data inside components, nobody's fake data matches anyone else's, and the week the real API lands you spend two days ripping out mocks and finding out the date format was different all along.

So I blocked off an afternoon and gave the team a shared mock server instead. Here's exactly what I did, what worked, and the one thing I'd do differently.

Start from the contract, not from the UI

The temptation is to look at the Figma file and invent data that makes the screens look good. Don't. Open the API contract (or whatever the backend team has written down, even a Slack thread) and copy the field names exactly. If they say created_at in snake case, your fake data says created_at in snake case, even if it annoys you.

I asked the backend lead for fifteen minutes and we agreed on three endpoints:

  • GET /orders returning a list
  • GET /orders/:id returning one order with line items
  • PATCH /orders/:id to update status

That was enough to unblock the whole dashboard.

The JSON file

I used json-server because it takes a single file and gives you REST routes for free. Install it as a dev dependency so it's pinned with the project:

npm install --save-dev json-server

Then a mock/db.json at the repo root:

{
  "orders": [
    {
      "id": 1001,
      "status": "pending",
      "customer_name": "Test Customer A",
      "total_cents": 4599,
      "currency": "USD",
      "created_at": "2026-03-02T09:14:00Z",
      "items": [
        { "sku": "SKU-RED-01", "qty": 2, "price_cents": 1500 },
        { "sku": "SKU-BLU-07", "qty": 1, "price_cents": 1599 }
      ]
    },
    {
      "id": 1002,
      "status": "shipped",
      "customer_name": "Test Customer B",
      "total_cents": 0,
      "currency": "USD",
      "created_at": "2026-03-01T22:40:00Z",
      "items": []
    }
  ]
}

Notice order 1002. Zero total, empty items. I put that in on purpose. Mock data that only has happy, fully populated records trains your UI to break on the first weird row in production.

Add a script:

"scripts": {
  "mock": "json-server --watch mock/db.json --port 4000"
}

Run npm run mock and you've got GET /orders, GET /orders/1001, PATCH /orders/1001 and friends, all backed by a file you can commit.

Point the app at it with one variable

The frontend already read its API base URL from an env var. I added a .env.mock:

VITE_API_URL=http://localhost:4000

and a script dev:mock that loaded it. That's the whole switch. No if (isMock) branches in components, no special fetch wrapper. When the real API shows up, you change the URL and nothing else.

Fake the slow and the broken too

Real APIs are slow sometimes and fail sometimes. A json mock server that always answers in 2ms hides every loading-state bug you have. json-server takes a --delay flag, so I added a second script:

"mock:slow": "json-server --watch mock/db.json --port 4000 --delay 1500"

For errors I wrote a tiny middleware file that returns a 500 whenever a request has ?fail=1 on it. Twelve lines. It caught two missing error states in the first week, which paid for the whole afternoon.

What I got wrong

I let the mock data drift. By week two people had added fields to db.json that weren't in the contract because "the UI needed it." Some of those were reasonable asks, but they never made it back to the backend team. When the real API landed, three fields we'd been rendering didn't exist.

The fix is boring. Any change to db.json goes in its own PR, and the backend lead is a required reviewer on that path. Mock data is a contract, and contracts need two signatures.

There's a deeper issue too, and it's the reason I don't think hand-written mocks should live forever. A file you wrote by hand only knows what you thought the API would do. Once a real backend exists, it's worth looking at approaches that capture real responses and replay them, so your fakes are grounded in actual traffic. If you want the bigger picture on how a json mock server fits next to recorded mocks and other options, that write-up covers the trade-offs well.

My opinion: keep it dumb

People asked if we should add GraphQL, auth simulation, random data generators, the works. I said no. The value of this setup was that anyone on the team could open one JSON file and understand what the "API" would return. The moment your mock needs its own documentation, it's become a second backend that nobody owns.

Faker-style random data is the one I'd push back on hardest. Random names are fine, but random structure makes bugs unreproducible. If a teammate says "the table breaks on order 1002," everyone should see the same order 1002.

How the sprint actually went

The frontend shipped the dashboard against the mock in nine working days. The real API landed on day eleven. Switching over took about half a day, most of it spent on those three drifted fields I mentioned. Not zero, but a lot better than four devs idling for a week.

A practical tip before you try this

Put the mock server in the repo, not on someone's laptop or a shared box. When it's a committed file plus an npm script, new hires get it on day one, CI can run against it, and nobody has to ask "is the mock up?" ever again.

What's the weirdest record you keep in your mock data on purpose?

title: FaceRiff: Data-Efficient Unified Text-to-3D Face Asset Synthesis via Geometric Conditioning
description:
arXiv:2611.21867v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: High-resolution facial datasets with consistent UV-mapped geometry, albedo, and physically based displacement are scarce, yet such assets are essential for photorealistic digital-human rendering. Existing 3D face generation methods are often slow, single-modality, or require large specialized datasets. Meanwhile, large image diffusion models encode strong facial priors but do not natively produce lighting-independent textures, pore-scale displacement, or UV-aligned geometry. We present FaceRiff, a unified, data- and parameter-efficient framework for generating complete 3D face assets (mesh, albedo, and displacement) directly from text in a shared UV space. FaceRiff adapts a pretrained SDXL backbone with task-specific LoRA adapters and uses UV normal maps as geometric conditioning: per-instance normals guide albedo and displacement synthesis, while a dataset-mean normal provides a canonical spatial anchor for mesh generation. Using only 2,049 scans from approximately 350 identities and training on a single GPU, FaceRiff updates less than 3% of the backbone parameters per task and produces render-ready 3D face assets without per-instance optimization. Compared with FaceG2E and DreamFace, FaceRiff produces greater per-prompt diversity while preserving prompt alignment and fixed-topology UV consistency, and additionally generates lighting-independent albedo suitable for PBR relighting and pore-scale displacement absent from prior text-driven baselines. A blind study with 45 industry professionals shows that FaceRiff achieves substantially higher perceived realism than DreamFace, approaching that of real captures. Overall, FaceRiff demonstrates that pretrained diffusion priors can be adapted to unified 3D face asset synthesis under limited data.

title: Conserved Verdicts, Drifting Commitments: Identifying Harmful Overthinking
description:
arXiv:2611.21946v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A reasoning model that has reached a correct answer can lose it by continuing to think. Deciding whether to stop means comparing two probabilities at the same point of a chain: that the answer the model would give if stopped now is correct (its commitment), and that the answer it will finish with is correct (its verdict). We show that the verdict alone, which is what final-correctness probes estimate, cannot make this comparison. As a forecast of a fixed outcome it has no predictable drift, whether continuing helps or hurts. The commitment-verdict gap equals the expected remaining change in answer quality and the accuracy gained by stopping. A second identity splits any accuracy-versus-budget curve into answer change within chains and change in which chains are still running. We measure both on MATH-500. At all 379 points where DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B holds a correct answer, selected without regard to how its chain ends, continuing loses 3.6 points on average (95% CI [2.2, 5.2]), and the loss concentrates in a few problems. In six reasoning models from three families, on MATH-500 and OlympiadBench and with budgets up to 16,384 tokens, declining accuracy curves come from which chains remain, while the chains still reasoning keep or improve their answers. An oracle stopping rule gains at most +1.8 and +2.5 points at 1.5B and 7B. The framework says what to measure before building a stopping rule.
