title: A server that almost never says no
description:
Most servers are taught to say no. Bad request? 400. Unknown shape? 422. You're strict, you're correct, and somewhere a client fixes its bug and tries again.

vitals-receiver almost never says no, because for this server "no" means "delete this forever". This post is the long version: how it's put together, why each piece is shaped the way it is, and the things that went wrong on the way to the public repo. There's real code below, copied from the repo with comments trimmed.

What it is

It's a small self-hosted receiver for Apple Health exports. An iPhone app of mine (not public yet) sends batches of HealthKit samples over the home network. The receiver stores them in SQLite, outside the repo, and serves two pages on the machine itself: a fitness page with activity rings, the week and a card per metric, and an ops page that tells you whether the pipe is still alive.

It's TypeScript on Node 22, with Fastify, better-sqlite3 and zod. MIT-licensed. You can try it without a phone:

npm ci && npm run demo

That seeds a synthetic store from a fixed seed in the system temp directory and serves it. npm run demo -- --groups=sleep shows one metric group, --groups= shows the empty state. Ctrl-C stops it cleanly. Every number you'll see there is generated. No real reading has ever been in the repo.

The one rule

The phone never reads our response body. What it does next depends only on the status code:

  • No answer, 408, 425, 429, any 5xx: the batch stays in an outbox on the device and is retried under the same exportId and batchSequence, backing off from 15 minutes to an hour, for up to seven days.
  • 400, 401, 403, 404, 422, a bare 413, any 3xx: the batch is dropped the moment we answer. Nothing on the phone ever tries it again.

So on this endpoint a 4xx isn't feedback. It's a delete button, and the server is the one pressing it. Everything else in the design follows from that.

Two doors, never connected

One process, two Fastify instances, one store:

const ingest = buildIngestServer({ config, store, token, log });
const read = buildReadServer({ store, config });

async function main(): Promise<void> {
  await ingest.listen({ host: config.ingestHost, port: config.ingestPort });
  await read.listen({ host: config.readHost, port: config.readPort });

Look at the arguments. The ingest door gets token. The read door doesn't, and that's on purpose. Ingest faces the LAN, accepts POST, and checks the phone's credential. The read door is bound to loopback, serves the pages, and has no way to reach the credential, because it was never handed one. It can't leak what it never holds.

The split exists so two credentials never meet. If you put a reverse proxy with its own login in front of the dashboard, the proxy only ever points at the read door. Then the proxy password can't be replayed into ingest, and the phone's token can't read the data back. The README is blunt about it: the day you route a proxy to ingest is the day both separations stop being true.

The read door also enforces "read-only" in code instead of just promising it:

  app.addHook("onRequest", async (req, reply) => {
    if (req.method !== "GET" && req.method !== "HEAD") {
      void reply.header("allow", "GET, HEAD");
      await reply.code(405).send({ ok: false, error: "read-only listener: GET and HEAD only" });
      return reply;
    }
    return undefined;
  });

The ingest door mirrors it: any non-POST gets a 404 that says "this port accepts POST only", and that request still gets a row in the delivery log.

The token

The credential is 32 random bytes, hex, written to a file with mode 600. npm run token:mint makes it and never prints the value. The server re-reads the file only when its mtime changes, so rotating the token needs no restart. If there's no token at startup, the server refuses to start: a LAN-facing listener with no credential is worse than no listener.

The comparison:

export function tokenMatches(expected: string | null, provided: unknown): boolean {
  if (expected === null || expected.length === 0) return false;
  const candidate = Array.isArray(provided) ? provided[0] : provided;
  if (typeof candidate !== "string" || candidate.length === 0) return false;
  const a = crypto.createHash("sha256").update(expected).digest();
  const b = crypto.createHash("sha256").update(candidate).digest();
  return crypto.timingSafeEqual(a, b);
}

timingSafeEqual throws if the two buffers differ in length, and a length check before it would itself leak the length. Hashing both sides first gives two 32-byte digests every time. The comparison is constant-time and the length can't be measured either.

The ingest path, step by step

The handler is a short ladder. Every rung that would normally be a 4xx is a 200 here.

First, Fastify's body parsing goes away. If the framework parses JSON, a broken body becomes Fastify's 400 before our code ever sees it, and the batch is lost. So the body is taken as a raw string, whatever the Content-Type says:

  app.removeAllContentTypeParsers();
  app.addContentTypeParser("*", { parseAs: "string" }, (_req, body, done) => done(null, body));

Then:

  1. Credential. A wrong or missing one gets a 401. This is one of the two errors the server allows itself, because it's a configuration mistake the owner has to see. That batch is lost, and the README says so in bold.
  2. JSON. Bytes we can't parse are still health data. They go to quarantine and the phone gets a 200.
  3. Schema version. The wire contract says "reject unknown versions". We don't. 
    let parsed: unknown;
    try {
      parsed = JSON.parse(ctx.raw);
    } catch (err) {
      quarantine(ctx, "unparseable-json", err instanceof Error ? err.message : String(err));
      return reply.code(200).send({ ok: true, stored: 0, quarantined: 1 });
    }

    const version = (parsed as { schemaVersion?: unknown } | null)?.schemaVersion;
    if (version !== SCHEMA_VERSION) {
      quarantine(ctx, "unknown-schema-version", `schemaVersion=${JSON.stringify(version)}`);
      return reply.code(200).send({ ok: true, stored: 0, quarantined: 1 });
    }
  1. Envelope shape. zod, with loose objects everywhere, because the contract only ever adds fields within version 1. A mismatch goes to quarantine with every zod issue written into detail.
  2. Probe. The app's "test connection" button sends connectivityTest: true with no samples. That gets a delivery row and nothing else. A probe that somehow carries samples is treated as an export. We never throw samples away over a flag.
  3. Samples, one at a time. The envelope's samples is typed unknown[] on purpose, and each sample is validated on its own. One malformed sample goes to quarantine instead of costing the 999 good ones beside it.

The only other error is 413, for a body over 2 MB. The phone caps a batch well under that, so if it ever fires, the fix is to raise the cap, not to shrug. And there's a 500 for real bugs. It's survivable because the phone retries a 5xx, but its body isn't kept, so the README calls it "a defect, not weather".

The store

Five tables in one SQLite file, WAL mode, migrations tracked by user_version:

  • samples: one row per HealthKit sample, keyed on its uuid, with the original JSON kept in raw.
  • runs and batches: one row per export run and per batch. Run aggregates are recomputed from batches on every ingest, so a re-delivered batch can't inflate them.
  • deliveries: every request that reached us, including the refused ones.
  • quarantine: the bytes we couldn't turn into samples. 
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS quarantine (
  id          INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
  received_at TEXT NOT NULL,
  remote_addr TEXT,
  reason      TEXT NOT NULL,
  detail      TEXT,
  headers     TEXT NOT NULL,
  body        TEXT NOT NULL,
  bytes       INTEGER NOT NULL,
  delivery_id INTEGER
);

The headers are stored minus the credential. The token appears nowhere in the database file. That was checked against the real database file of a running server, not by reading the code.

deliveries is the table I'd keep if I could keep only one. The sender can't hear us, so this is the only place our side of every conversation is written down: status, bytes, how many samples were stored, how many were duplicates, how many were rejected, and how long it took.

The pages

/ is the fitness page: three rings, a Monday-first week strip, a card per metric with data. It has no scripts and no images, plus a CSP that allows exactly one same-origin stylesheet. /pipe is the ops page: the delivery log, export runs with their real span, how fresh each data type is, and quarantine. /api/summary and /api/fitness serve the same models as JSON, through the same code path, so the page and anything reading it can't drift apart.

/healthz answers 200 or 503, and it's the one read route that writes. It upserts a probe row into the store, so dbWritable is proven on every call instead of assumed. It also reports startedAt, and I'll come back to why.

What went wrong

The rule above sounds tidy. Getting the code to actually keep it took longer. These are the real problems, in the order we hit them.

1. The receiver was counting wrong, quietly. The first store reported stored: N for every sample it was handed, whether it already had it or not. Its upsert on uuid let a re-delivered batch rewrite the provenance of rows that were already correct. Worse, HealthKit was observed re-minting the uuid for identical heart-rate content, about 12 rows per real reading. The fix: insert-once, plus a partial unique index for that one type only.

ON CONFLICT(uuid) DO NOTHING
ON CONFLICT(content_id) WHERE type = 'HKQuantityTypeIdentifierHeartRate' DO NOTHING

Why only that type? For the other types the content id collides by design. In one measurement, 720 real samples carried 195 distinct ids, and a global unique index would have kept 195 and thrown away 525. Stored, duplicate and rejected also became three separate counters. Before, "we already had it" and "we couldn't store it" were the same number, and they need opposite reactions.

2. The test suite was testing the calendar. Two days later, npm test gave 102 pass and 9 fail on a commit that had been green. The day before, the same command on the same commit gave 104 and 7. Nothing had changed but the date. The unit tests pinned a clock, but the HTTP server read the wall clock, so pages built from fixtures dated on the 19th correctly reported "these numbers are from the 19th, not today". The product was honest and the tests were wrong. The fix makes the clock a dependency:

  now?: () => Date;

  const now = deps.now ?? (() => new Date());

It's a function, not a Date: a server that outlives its requests would otherwise freeze "today" at boot. It's optional, so production passes nothing and doesn't notice the seam. The comment in the repo says it better than I can: a suite that reads the wall clock is a suite that tests the calendar, and the calendar always wins eventually.

3. Half the delivery log was crying wolf. The ops page flagged "run metadata drift" whenever a batch disagreed with its run's first batch on generatedAt or the time window. But for one export mode, the window is each batch's own bracket and differs by design. The real store showed 201 of 420 deliveries carrying a false drift note. The fix compares only what the contract says is identical across a run, and keeps the run's window as the real extent of its batches. Before that, /pipe showed a one-hour window for a run that actually spanned 190 hours.

4. An invariant with nothing behind it. The fitness model has a rule: today is partial, always, and never counts toward an average. It was enforced in four places, and only one of them, steps, was tested. For each of the other three, the reviewer flipped partial: day === today to partial: false and the suite still passed, 123 of 123. So each site got a test that fails if you flip it. The repo also had no CI at all. Now it has a workflow that runs typecheck and the suite on every push and pull request.

5. The founding rule was written wrong. The first commit said the phone "never retries", so any non-2xx at all was data loss. Reading the app's source showed otherwise. It retries no answer, 429 and 5xx from an outbox for seven days, and drops only the permanent codes. That changes the meaning of a 500 from "lost" to "retried". Four stale comments had to be rewritten, and a README truth pass checked every claim against the code. A good rule with a wrong reason is a bug waiting for someone to "simplify" it.

6. A silent day had two possible meanings. Some days had zero deliveries. Was the receiver down, or did the phone just not send? The store couldn't say, because it only records what arrives. The fix was one log line and one field:

  return `vitals: started ${new Date(startedAt).toISOString()} commit ${rev}`;

The same instant shows up as startedAt on /healthz. With it, a gap reads as a receiver gap (started after it) or a phone gap (up the whole time). The investigation that prompted it found the phone silent in all three gaps, except one 63-minute slice when the machine was simply powered off. A small silence:check script, meant to run hourly, asks /healthz from the outside and speaks only when the phone has gone quiet.

7. Shutdown that wouldn't shut down. The first shutdown closed both servers, checkpointed the WAL and exited. A probe showed the hole: a request that had sent headers and 11 of its 500 body bytes, then SIGTERM, and the process was still alive more than 25 seconds later. Even a finished request held it open, because its keep-alive socket wasn't idle when close() ran, and Node's default keep-alive is 72 seconds. Now the drain is capped at 10 seconds by default (VITALS_DRAIN_CAP_SECONDS). Because every store write is synchronous inside one transaction, a request cut by the cap is cut before its handler runs, so there's nothing half-written to roll back.

Where it is now

The first version landed in one day, in five slices, with 42 tests. A two-line mutation (dropping uuid normalisation, conflating claimed with stored counts) made two of them fail, so we knew the suite bites. By the time it went public it had a README written for strangers, a vendored copy of the payload contract so the fixture checks run on a clean clone, an identity scrub and an MIT licence. That was 126 tests. At the last count it was 216, all green, with typecheck in CI.

It's a monitor with a store attached, not an analytics product. If you need a boring, honest pipe from your phone to your own disk, and you'd rather it keep the weird bytes than refuse them, take it. The code is public on GitHub under the MIT licence.

title: A Colleague in Another Team Copies Your Manager Into Every Email to You
description:
It started with one request. A colleague in the finance systems team needed a field added to an export, and they copied your manager into the email. Since then, every message they send you has your manager on it. A question about a date format. A thank you. A reminder about something you had already done. It feels like being watched, and you are starting to dread their name in your inbox.

Before you decide it is a power move, consider the ordinary explanations. Some people copy managers into everything because that is how their department works. Some were burned once, when a request disappeared, and now copy the manager as insurance. Some are not sure who decides your priorities, so they keep the person who might in the loop. Very few are doing it to make you look bad.

So start with your manager, not with the colleague. Mention it briefly. You are copied into all of my threads with the finance team. Do you want to stay on those, or shall I handle them and summarise anything important? Many managers will be relieved to be taken off. Now you know where you stand, and you have their backing for the next step.

Then talk to the colleague, ideally on a short call rather than in writing. Keep it practical. I have noticed my manager is on all of our emails. I am happy to own these requests directly, and I will tell you straight away if something cannot be done by when you need it. Is there anything that made copying them feel necessary? Listen to the answer. If they say a request of theirs was once ignored, offer something better than an audience. A shared tracker, or a short weekly note on progress.

Make the new arrangement easy to trust. Reply quickly for the first few weeks. Give dates and keep them. If something slips, tell them before they have to ask. People stop copying managers when they stop feeling they need a witness.

And if it continues after all that, let it go. A copied manager who already knows your work is reliable is not an audience to fear. Do good work in the thread and let them read it.

– Asael Shinder

title: How we split a 5,000-line Express server.js with zero behavioral diffs
description:
Our Express server.js went from 5,121 lines to 1,402 across incremental PRs. The result we cared about was zero behavioral differences in the checks we ran after each move.

The useful part of that story is the method: six gates that make a large file smaller while keeping each change narrow enough to review. We've released a clean-room implementation of that approach as JS Modularization Gold Standard, a CommonJS CLI built at DrRx.

The production numbers describe the original project. The public repository contains a synthetic Express example and a reproducible probe test; it does not include the production source or its probe logs. “Zero behavioral diffs” means the observed checks matched, not a mathematical proof over every possible input.

Move one domain at a time

An Express monolith is more than a list of routes. Handlers share helpers, middleware order, caches, and mutable bindings. Moving a handler can preserve its text while changing what it closes over.

Consider a cache used by both billing and session routes:

let sessionCache = {};

app.post("/billing/reset", (req, res) => {
  sessionCache = {};
  res.json({ reset: true });
});

Passing sessionCache directly to another module copies the current object reference. If the parent later assigns a new object, the extracted module can keep reading the old one.

Our module boundary passes closures over the original binding:

require("./modules/billing").register(app, {
  hashId,
  PRICE_TABLE,
  getSessionCache: () => sessionCache,
  setSessionCache: (value) => { sessionCache = value; }
});

The generated billing handler calls setSessionCache({}). The session module uses getSessionCache(). The parent still owns the binding, so a billing reset remains visible to the session routes.

That boundary is deliberately small: register(app, kernel). The kernel object makes the dependencies visible in the diff. The extraction preserves the selected statements apart from indentation and the wiring needed at the boundary. Cleanup happens in a later commit.

The six gates

1. Parse every changed file. Run node --check on the parent and each module. It catches broken syntax quickly, before spending time on behavioral tests.

2. Compare registration counts. Record a baseline before the move. After extraction, count registrations in the parent and modules together. A matching count cannot establish correctness, but a changed count immediately deserves an explanation. The CLI's current counter is a textual heuristic and only enforces parity when expectedRoutes is configured.

3. Check the module boundary. Every extracted module exports register(app, kernel). The CLI checks that export shape. Application tests must also exercise registration and startup; a textual export check cannot tell you whether middleware runs in the right order.

4. Audit residual free variables. Parse the generated module and look for references it has not declared or received. This complements live probes: a request that stops at an authentication check cannot tell you whether the code behind that check still has access to its dependencies.

5. Replay requests against old and new. Start each version with comparable fixtures, run the same sequence, and compare status and body. Include state transitions. In the public demo, a session gets read twice, billing resets the cache, and the session gets read again. That sequence tests a relationship between two extracted modules that isolated endpoint checks could miss.

6. Keep the PR small. Extract one domain, show the wiring, attach the checks, review, and merge. Recalculate the next cut's line ranges afterward. Renaming helpers, redesigning error handling, or changing business logic belongs in a separate change with its own evidence.

The first four gates catch structural problems. The fifth checks observed behavior. The sixth keeps the evidence understandable to the person reviewing the change.

Reproduce the public example

The package is available on npm:

npx js-modularization-gold-standard --help

To run the full demo:

git clone https://github.com/drrx-ai/JS-Modularization-Gold-Standard.git
cd JS-Modularization-Gold-Standard
npm ci
npm test

The test extracts billing and session modules, runs the static gates, then compares nine HTTP requests against the original and extracted applications. Those requests cover five route handlers; the registration baseline also counts one middleware registration. The reset-then-read sequence is part of the test.

The CLI can also survey routes and shared symbols, analyze a proposed line range, preview an extraction, and audit an individual generated module. Use a clean branch and inspect extract --dry before applying a cut.

Where review still matters

The current tool targets CommonJS and app.method(...) registration. It does not convert ESM applications or generate your production test suite. Complex mutable expressions, shadowed identifiers, relative imports, and dependencies between extracted regions still need careful review. Keep assignments simple and do not assume a generated setter preserves the return value of an assignment or increment expression.

For a production application, add authenticated requests, startup checks, middleware-order checks, and assertions for external side effects. Passing the public fixture establishes what works in that fixture.

The method is useful even without this CLI: make dependencies explicit, preserve the original binding, separate moving from cleanup, and require evidence at each step.

Explore the code, example, and six gates on GitHub. If you have a small example of shared-state wiring that breaks during extraction, we'd welcome a reproducible issue.

Disclosure: This article was drafted by an AI assistant from the project’s code, test results, and maintainer-provided production context.

title: AR-WAM: efficient streaming world-action modeling for autonomous driving
description:
arXiv:2611.21851v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Autonomous driving requires anticipating how traffic will evolve while responding quickly to new observations. Video foundation models offer the first ability, but repeated history encoding and iterative video generation make them costly to use for driving. We present AR-WAM, an efficient streaming world-action model that combines autoregressive temporal modeling with single-pass future conditioning. Because its video backbone is causal, AR-WAM updates its visual context incrementally, reusing past computation and conditioning future prediction on observed motion. We further hypothesize that future features computed from recent observations can improve generalization in dynamic traffic without iterative video generation. AR-WAM therefore obtains these features in one forward pass and uses them to condition trajectory generation, and reinforcement learning then improves the policy through direct optimization of driving rewards. With a single front camera, AR-WAM achieves 91.5 PDMS after supervised training and 94.0 after reinforcement learning on NAVSIM-v1, outperforming the compared strong end-to-end world-action models. In a dynamic setting of continuous driving, supervised AR-WAM keeps its visual history across decisions and outperforms strong world-action baselines.

title: eve 1.0: el framework de agentes de código abierto de Vercel llega a disponibilidad general, con el harness bajo tu control
description:
eve 1.0, el framework de agentes de Vercel, llegó a disponibilidad general el 17 de noviembre de 2026, tras su vista previa de junio y más de 230 versiones: tú controlas el harness, los agentes se ejecutan de forma duradera con Workflow SDK y, según Vercel, la latencia mediana por turno bajó de 3,036 s a 414 ms.

Qué cambió

Vercel puso eve 1.0 a disposición general el 17 de noviembre de 2026. eve es el framework de agentes de código abierto de Vercel para crear agentes listos para producción: su harness —el bucle que llama a los modelos, ejecuta herramientas y delega trabajo a subagentes— lo controlas tú: eliges el modelo, cambias las herramientas y defines qué acciones necesitan aprobación. El framework se ejecuta sobre Workflow SDK, también de código abierto, con ejecución duradera: guarda el progreso mientras el agente trabaja, así una ejecución se reanuda desde su último paso completado tras un fallo. Para alojamiento gestionado, los agentes se despliegan en Vercel Workflows y Vercel Sandbox, y un agente y su sitio pueden publicarse como un solo proyecto de Vercel, con integraciones nativas para Next.js, Nuxt, SvelteKit, TanStack Start y Vite.

Las sesiones son multijugador y eve se conecta nativamente con Slack, Microsoft Teams, Discord, Telegram, GitHub, Linear, Twilio, Web Chat e iMessage; Chat SDK añade WhatsApp, Messenger, Google Chat y correo, y el modo ambiente de Slack deja que un agente escuche en los canales que elijas y hable solo cuando aporta. Un mismo despliegue atiende a muchos clientes con credenciales, memoria y políticas de aprobación por cliente; los agentes conservan memoria entre sesiones, y OpenTelemetry y el panel Agent Runs muestran cada ejecución. El framework es de código abierto; lo gestionado se factura por el uso de Vercel Workflows y Sandbox. Según Vercel, la latencia mediana por turno alojada bajó de 3,036 s en la beta de septiembre a 414 ms (633 ms p95) en la 1.0, y el coste estimado de una sesión de 50 turnos bajó de 5,4¢ a 1,3¢, un 76 % menos. Rillet y Clay ya lo usan en producción.

Cifras

Métrica eve 1.0
Latencia mediana por turno, alojado 414 ms (633 ms p95)
Latencia mediana por turno, beta de septiembre 3,036 s
Coste estimado de una sesión de 50 turnos 1,3¢ (antes 5,4¢, un 76 % menos)

Por qué importa

Si tu negocio crea agentes para clientes o para tus propias operaciones, eve te da la infraestructura de producción —ejecuciones duraderas, aprobaciones humanas, aislamiento por cliente y presencia en las apps de chat que tus clientes ya usan— sin entregar el control del comportamiento del agente a una plataforma. Como el framework es de código abierto y el harness es tuyo, puedes autoalojarlo, cambiar de modelo y auditar exactamente qué puede hacer un agente; y como el coste por turno baja en las sesiones largas, mantener un agente trabajando en una tarea larga es más fácil de justificar.

  • Vercel — eve is now generally available
  • Vercel — eve — the agent framework

title: How Many Persistent Features Does a Biometric Need? A Law Linking Equal Error Rate to Feature Count and Persistence
description:
arXiv:2611.21973v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A biometric designer controls the number of features and their temporal persistence. Earlier empirical work linked the equal error rate (EER) to persistence and to the required number of features by straight lines. We derive the law behind these regularities. For $N$ independent standardized Gaussian features with test-retest correlation $\rho$, scored by cosine similarity, Fisher's $z$-transform turns the genuine and impostor scores into two normals, giving $\mathrm{EER}=\Phi(-\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{N}\,\operatorname{atanh}\rho)$ and, inversely, $N=(2q/\operatorname{atanh}\rho)^2$ with $q=\Phi^{-1}(1-\mathrm{EER})$; intercorrelated features enter through an effective count $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$. The central extension lets persistence vary across comparisons with spread $\tau$ on Fisher's scale: $\mathrm{EER}=\Phi(-m/(\sqrt{\tau^2+v}+\sqrt{v}))$ with $v=1/(N_{\mathrm{eff}}-2)$, which for a normal spread has a floor $\Phi(-m/\tau)$ that no number of features can lower. With no fitted parameter the simple law reproduces published simulations and the EER-ICC line, and predicts the KCC-EER relation of eye-movement embeddings on GazeBase ($R^2=0.88$), though less well on GazeBaseVR ($0.63$). Read from the genuine and impostor scores, the general form matches the EER of eye movements, keystroke dynamics, the ECG and face embeddings over 101 conditions with $R^2=0.98$ and a median error of $0.6$ points, against $0.87$ and $1.9$ points for the simple law. The 61 eye-movement, keystroke and ECG conditions check consistency on the same scores; the 40 face conditions use held-out subjects, with the same accuracy. The product $\tau\sqrt{N_{\mathrm{eff}}-2}$ gives a design rule: adding or decorrelating features pays fully while it is well below one and little once it exceeds about three, where only higher or more uniform persistence helps.

title: Why Repetition, Not Productivity, Is Your Team’s Real Problem
description:
Most teams don't have a productivity problem. They have a repetition problem.

Every week, hours go into tasks that follow the same pattern: moving data between tools, sending routine follow-ups, compiling reports, triaging requests. None of it requires human judgment, yet all of it consumes human time.

Why I build with an open-source stack

As an automation developer, I work with an open-source stack that includes n8n, a workflow automation platform that connects apps, APIs, and AI models through a visual, low-code interface. What I value most:

  • Extensive integrations: 400+ apps and services, plus HTTP and custom code when a native node doesn't exist.
  • Data ownership: self-hosting gives full control over privacy, compliance, and cost.
  • AI-native capabilities: embed LLMs and build AI agents directly into business processes.
  • Scalability: works for a first automation and for complex, multi-step workflows.

Workflows I build most often

  • Lead routing from forms to CRM with instant follow-up
  • Scheduled reports delivered to Slack or email
  • AI-assisted customer support triage
  • Content and social media pipelines

The real return

It isn't just efficiency. It's what teams do with the time they get back: strategy, creativity, and client relationships.

If your team still relies on manual, repetitive processes, it's worth exploring what automation could unlock.

title: Urban Representation Learning for Identifying Potential Disparities in Crime Reporting
description:
arXiv:2611.21825v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Open crime data support urban safety analysis but reflect reported incidents rather than the complete distribution of criminal activity, potentially introducing spatial distortions in downstream analysis. We propose a self-supervised urban representation learning framework for identifying unusual reporting patterns relative to representation-similar peers using only georeferenced crime records. The method constructs complementary hourly, weekly, and static reporting profiles, learns scale-specific representations under geographic self-supervision, and integrates them into a unified latent space. Neighbor Profile Divergence (NPD) is then used to quantify disagreement between each region's reporting profile and those of its retrieved peers. Experiments on more than 1.8 million crime records from Mexico City, aggregated into 1,058 H3 regions, show that the proposed representation achieves a mean Silhouette score of 0.4052, compared with 0.2863 for Hex2Vec. NPD rankings remain highly stable across neighborhood sizes, with Spearman correlations from 0.9720 to 0.9951, while most high-divergence candidates persist across configurations. The retrieved peers also extend substantially beyond immediate geographic neighborhoods, indicating that the learned representation captures structure beyond local spatial proximity. High-divergence regions exhibit spatially organized patterns and, in several cases, differences in incident volume relative to peer expectations. These results support NPD as an internal auditing and prioritization mechanism for identifying regions that warrant further investigation, rather than as direct evidence of underreporting.

title: Amazon Cognito now supports authentication level and method token claims
description:
Amazon Cognito now supports authentication context class reference (ACR) and authentication methods reference (AMR), by adding ACR and AMR claims to access, ID, and refresh tokens. Your application can use the authentication level (ACR) to make authorization decisions, such as requiring additional factors for sensitive operations. It can also use completed methods (AMR), such as time-based one-time password (TOTP), for auditing and compliance.

Amazon Cognito defines four authentication levels based on the factors a user completes, from password-only (level 1) to a password with a TOTP (level 4). Each token reflects the level achieved during sign-in, so your application can make authorization decisions based on how a user authenticated. If your application requires a stronger level, you can request a target level in your application's sign-in flow or through managed login, and Amazon Cognito issues new tokens once the user completes the required factors. You can also customize ACR level URIs for your user pool. For federated users from an OpenID Connect (OIDC) provider, Amazon Cognito maps the provider's ACR and AMR values to your levels.

ACR and AMR token claims are available in all AWS Regions where Amazon Cognito is offered. Every user pool includes ACR and AMR token claims, regardless of feature plan. Requesting a target authentication level and configuring custom ACR level URIs are available with the Essentials or Plus feature plan. To get started, configure ACR and AMR using the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, or AWS SDKs. See developer guide for details.

title: Lost in the Funnel: Selection-Induced Miscalibration in Ranking and Decision Systems
description:
arXiv:2611.22595v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Modern ranking and decision systems combine components with divergent objectives, and scores calibrated at the model boundary are used as calibrated probabilities throughout the funnel, across filtering, reranking, business-rule enforcement, and auctions. Yet calibration is typically validated only where the score is produced, so its breakdown where the score is used is routinely overlooked. We ask when calibration survives this selection, how inherited error differs from selection effects, and what can fail for a perfectly calibrated score at a component boundary. We study these questions through a boundary-wise diagnostic framework of residual identities. We target rubric-judged relevance rather than presentation-dependent metrics such as CTR, so calibration is measurable at every funnel layer of interest. We first present an industry-wide case study that applies our diagnosis to settings where calibration deteriorates at decision time, tracing the degradation to selection rather than model error. This diagnosis motivates Funnel-Aware Recalibration (FAR): post-hoc, selection-policy-aware recalibration at the boundary where scores drive decisions. In a live two-region production A/B test, FAR cuts decision-time expected calibration error (ECE) by 60-80% and improves auction efficiency. We further adapt two public datasets to simulate industry settings, providing additional evidence for the mechanism. We plan to release the adapted datasets and their generation pipeline to support further research. Finally, we distill these findings into practical operating principles for calibrating multi-stage scoring systems.

title: Framework Artex acelera ataques cibernéticos com agentes de IA
description:
Framework coordena modelos de IA e ferramentas de invasão

Desde o fim de agosto, criminosos vêm usando ferramentas de teste de intrusão com inteligência artificial para atingir empresas, órgãos públicos e bancos em vários países. O framework Artex está entre os mais citados por pesquisadores. Ele coordena modelos de linguagem externos e ferramentas de segurança existentes para automatizar etapas de reconhecimento e invasão.

Escrito em Go, o Artex foi publicado no GitHub em julho por uma pessoa desenvolvedora que usava o pseudônimo Autumn-27. O sistema não é, por si só, um modelo de inteligência artificial: ele conecta modelos externos por APIs a processos e ferramentas de teste de intrusão. Operadores podem fornecer instruções em linguagem natural; agentes dividem o plano em tarefas, tentam executá-las e apresentam os resultados.

Pesquisadores afirmam que esses frameworks não criam novas técnicas de ataque nem são especialmente sofisticados. O efeito está na automação e na velocidade: operações que poderiam levar dias podem ser concluídas em horas, com pouca intervenção humana. A facilidade de uso também reduz a barreira para pessoas sem experiência em segurança tentarem atacar redes mal protegidas.

Campanhas atingem organizações de diversos setores

Em um alerta, o FBI relacionou o uso do Artex a campanhas contra organizações de serviços financeiros, governo, tecnologia, defesa, energia, saúde, manufatura, telecomunicações e outros setores. Pesquisadores também associaram as ferramentas ao roubo de dados pessoais de milhares de instituições financeiras sul-coreanas, a possíveis tentativas de roubo de criptomoedas e à busca por credenciais expostas no GitHub.

Em outubro, segundo a CrowdStrike, o grupo ligado à China conhecido como Vapor Panda usou o Artex contra mais de 200 organizações. Entre os alvos estavam centros de pesquisa, empresas de semicondutores e defesa nos Estados Unidos, além de ministérios de relações exteriores na Europa e em outras regiões. A Microsoft também observou o grupo Storm-0940 tentando acessar ambientes Microsoft 365 após um ataque à cadeia de suprimentos; hackers obtiveram acesso privilegiado em menos de três horas.

Remoção do GitHub não encerrou a circulação

Em 8 de outubro, a pessoa que publicou o Artex removeu o projeto do GitHub e afirmou não ter relação com os ataques, dizendo que a ferramenta havia sido criada para pesquisa e educação. Cópias do framework, porém, continuam em circulação e desenvolvimento, junto a alternativas que operam de forma semelhante.

A GitGuardian documentou 45 frameworks de ataque com IA. Entre os nomes citados por pesquisadores estão CyberstrikeAI, Hexstrike, CAIRN e PentAGI. As ferramentas têm capacidades técnicas distintas, mas compartilham a combinação de modelos de linguagem, instruções de operadores e ferramentas já disponíveis para testar ou atacar sistemas.

Ruído nos sistemas ajuda a detectar ataques

Uma oportunidade para as equipes de defesa é que essas ferramentas ainda não são discretas. Segundo pesquisadores, algumas geram milhares de sondagens em sequência; a plataforma de programação Dosu relatou que o Artex enviou 80 mil solicitações aos seus sistemas em apenas 90 minutos. Esse volume pode aparecer em registros de rede e alertas de segurança.

Medidas básicas ajudam a reduzir a exposição: aplicar atualizações, evitar credenciais padrão, não deixar segredos expostos e monitorar atividades incomuns na rede. A Censys e a Shadowserver Foundation encontraram milhares de instâncias dessas ferramentas expostas à internet, e pesquisadores também localizaram servidores Artex sem proteção, onde puderam observar operações.

Em dois servidores expostos analisados recentemente, pesquisadores viram operadores chineses mirando outras entidades chinesas. Um dos casos envolvia uma universidade atacada com tentativas repetidas de senhas; os pesquisadores avaliam que parte da atividade pode ser organizada e criminosa, enquanto outra pode refletir ações menos sofisticadas.

title: What Does Weight-Space Programming Add to Diffusion Editing? Program Construction versus Score-Guided Refinement
description:
arXiv:2611.22228v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Weight-space programming (WSP) lets a language model construct executable weight updates for another network. We study diffusion concept editing through an interface in which programs define training contexts, preservation constraints and update directions, while a shared numerical fitter selects their coefficients. We compare generated programs with published editors, a shared-panel hand-written baseline and budget-matched search over conventional edits on 24 TIMED test edits for Stable Diffusion 1.4. The preregistered rewrite pipeline shows no advantage over the strong baseline. In an exploratory comparison, one-shot Astra programs improve fresh-scene VLM joint success, which requires subject presence together with whole-image target matching, by +10.0 points over the shared-panel baseline, while CLIP relative match shows no detectable change. These programs organise adjustable directions around protected text-state subspaces. Probing and rewriting the Astra programs then raises CLIP by +6.2 points while joint success changes by -9.7. On a fixed 144-image sample, five additional evaluators give point estimates in the same directions under whole-image target matching; checks of subject-local change give less decisive differences. Together, these results identify useful behaviour in complete generated programs and show that score-guided revision need not preserve it: program construction and revision should be evaluated as distinct stages of a WSP pipeline.

title: CRA: Continuous Risk Assessment for Safety-critical Visual Navigation
description:
arXiv:2611.22080v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Traditional safety-critical control methods often rely on predefined constraints that separate states into safe and unsafe regions. While recent studies have extended geometric safety toward semantic safety, real-world safety is rarely purely binary. The risk associated with an object or human can vary continuously with its physical properties, like motion, and interaction context; for example, a person carrying a heavy object or a hot object moving at high speed may require a different safety response from an ordinary static obstacle. In this paper, we propose a vision-based continuous risk assessment framework for safety-critical visual navigation. Our method uses RGB and LiDAR observations to estimate four risk factors (kinetic, potential, contact-severity, and thermal) and combines them into a continuous risk score for each assessed object or person. These estimates are integrated into a Poisson safety function with a Laplace guidance field as a safety filter, enabling online monitoring and intervention in open-world robot navigation. We demonstrate the proposed method in a simulated restaurant scene.

title: Hello, Dev.to: the three S's of regulated software, and the backend I'm building
description:
In the 90s in England, my mates and I spent endless nights tearing apart computers and rebuilding them one component at a time. Twenty-five years later I'm still doing something similar, except the computers are backends and the components are the controls regulated customers ask for.

Hi, I'm Niyi. I'm a Nigerian-British deep-tech engineer, an optimist, and the founder of Kilimanjaro. I'm writing from Lagos, Nigeria, and a good part of what I care about is a better future for Nigeria. This is my first post here, so let me say who I am and what to expect.

The path here

I fell in love with tech in those nights of tearing computers apart, coding in Pascal, then C, C++ and Java. I earned my degree in Computer Science at the University of Bristol, and it has been an unending stream of languages, frameworks and security standards ever since.

My first startup was an ad-tech company. Then I built a software consultancy, and then a BaaS for some of the biggest regulated companies in Africa, architecting critical software for multi-billion dollar banks, pension funds, and asset managers, which is what led my meandering journey to Kilimanjaro.

The three S's

Over 25 years I've learned that, in regulated industries, three things rule: stability, security and standards. Your software must keep running, protect sensitive data and pass audits. Teams that ship a working prototype usually find out how much that costs when the first regulated customer sends a 100-line feature checklist, and the backend has to be rebuilt to answer it.

Kilimanjaro is my answer: a backend where those controls are part of the services from the first day, so you don't rebuild. You get a database, files, real-time streams, AI guardrails, serverless compute, encryption, access control and an audit trail as one set of services, with the rules about where data lives and who can touch it built in. If you want details, the docs have them.

What you'll find here

I'll try to post regularly, in two kinds.

The journey. What we decided, what we got wrong and what changed our minds. The names we corrected, the pages we hid until they were true, the questions customers ask that no tutorial prepares you for.

Fixes for hard problems. The strange ones. The bug that only appears under a particular region setting, the encryption question that sounds simple and is not, the business problem nobody warned us about. Each post says what the symptom looked like, why it was hard, what caused it and how we fixed it, so you can fix yours faster than we did.

Kilimanjaro's own blog, the Summit Log, is where the practical how-to material lives. Here I'll tell the stories behind it.

Over to you

If you're building enterprise apps, I might be able to chip in some advice on questions like:

  • How do I get through the dreaded 100-line feature checklist that procurement sends?
  • How do I implement field-level encryption ahead of a PCI DSS 4.0/4.0.1 audit?
  • How do I avoid GDPR violations by sharding per-user data across regions?
  • How do I talk to an HSM through PKCS#11 or KMIP?

Tell me in the comments. The best ones become posts.

Thanks for reading, and see you next Thursday.

Niyi

title: TetherMark: Instance-Level Watermark Authentication Against Cross-Instance Transplantation
description:
arXiv:2611.22345v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Robust watermarking is commonly verified by asking whether a hidden payload remains decodable after compression, geometric distortion, or generative editing. Localized and semantic extensions may additionally check whether an expected region or category is still present. These tests establish evidence validity or content consistency, but not whether the evidence still belongs to the particular visual instance registered by its owner. We expose cross-instance transplantation: an attacker extracts or estimates valid watermark evidence from one registered image and transfers it to a different image of the same category. The message can still decode, the expected content can remain present, and the result can look natural, even though the evidence has been reassigned to the wrong instance. To enable instance-level watermark authentication, we introduce TetherMark, a post-hoc watermark that combines two complementary checks. The message check verifies an edit-robust payload, while the relation check uses secret patch-pair selection, a registered response, natural correspondence transport, and enrollment normalization to test consistency with the registered instance. The verifier accepts only when both checks pass. Across 240 test subjects, TetherMark attains 92.08% legitimate true acceptance with 9.17% and 16.25% attack success under WmForger and WMCopier, respectively, yielding the highest instance-binding balanced accuracy under both attacks.

title: Evaluating the Evaluation of Music Generation Models with Generative Psychometrics
description:
arXiv:2611.21809v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Subjective user studies are one of the major methods for evaluating music generation models. However, subjective evaluation protocols vary widely and are rarely specified in enough detail to be reproduced, hindering comparison across studies. In this paper, we map subjective evaluation methods in ISMIR music generation papers from 2020-2025 and apply generative psychometrics to assess the stability of their items. We extract 284 items from the papers' methodological descriptions, using an LLM and manual validation to standardize them. We represent these items as contextual embeddings and apply Unique Variable Analysis to remove redundant, locally dependent items and Bootstrap Exploratory Graph Analysis to estimate their latent dimensions. Results show the network converges onto a taxonomy of six stable quality dimensions: Rhythm, Melody, Audio, Composition, Structure, and Lyrics, pointing to a unified methodology for conducting user studies to evaluate music generation models.

title: 347,617 Zoom fingerprints do not mean 347,617 vulnerable clients
description:
347,617 Zoom fingerprints do not mean 347,617 vulnerable clients

Exposure counts are easy to repeat and easy to misinterpret. A ZoomEye query for app="Zoom" returned 347,617 product fingerprints while researching CVE-2026-108184. The exact CVE Filter returned 0. Neither number proves how many Windows clients are vulnerable. The first is a broad product observation, and the second reflects the current CVE index rather than a clean scan. A defensible response treats both as discovery inputs and uses endpoint inventory to decide which Zoom products need patching.

Vulnerability overview

CVE-2026-108184 is a high-severity certificate validation flaw in certain Zoom clients for Windows. Zoom published the issue as ZSB-26021 on October 13, 2026. The CVSS 3.1 score is 7.4 with network access, high complexity, no privileges, and no user interaction. The description says an unauthenticated user may disclose information through network access.

The bulletin also gives confidentiality and integrity a high impact rating. It does not provide the technical detail needed to map that rating to a specific attack chain. Security teams should record the scored impact and the described outcome without adding claims of confirmed compromise.

Mechanism and exploitation conditions

Certificate validation allows a client to decide whether a remote peer is the expected service. A correct implementation checks identity and trust. Zoom says validation is improper in the affected Windows products, but it does not identify the exact field, chain condition, or protocol path that fails.

The supported exploitation condition is network access to a vulnerable client during a certificate-related exchange. Attack complexity is high. That means an exposed fingerprint or an internet connection is not enough to conclude that an attacker can exploit the host. The bulletin does not provide an exploit sample, so a scan for one malformed request would be unreliable.

Impact

The advertised effect is sensitive information disclosure. Zoom does not list the data involved. The possibility of integrity impact appears in the vector, but the prose is not specific. A risk assessment should consider the role of each client and the sensitivity of its connections.

A Workplace client may carry collaboration data. A VDI client may sit inside a virtual desktop that reaches enterprise applications. A Rooms system may handle room and service configuration. These are different investigation scopes even though they share a CVE.

Affected products and scope

The bulletin lists Zoom Workplace for Windows from 7.0.0 before 7.2.0, the 7.1.9 branch, Zoom Workplace VDI Client for Windows from 7.0.11 before 7.0.13, and Zoom Rooms for Windows from 7.0.0 before 7.1.7.

These ranges require product-aware queries. A broad Zoom inventory may mix the main client, VDI components, and room software. Store the product name beside the version so a later patch report can be reconciled with the vendor bulletin.

Exposure context

The Search count of 347,617 comes from a successful ZoomEye query on November 18, 2026. It represents product fingerprints observed by ZoomEye. The count does not reveal the operating system, installed release, branch, configuration, or whether the certificate path is reachable. The Filter count of 0 is also not evidence that no vulnerable clients exist.

Use the product count to find internet-visible Zoom services and room-related surfaces that need an owner. Use authenticated inventory to determine whether each asset is Zoom Workplace, VDI Client, or Rooms and which version is running. If an external result cannot be mapped to a managed asset, record it as an ownership gap.

Remediation and mitigations

Upgrade Zoom Workplace for Windows to 7.2.0 or later and apply the fixed 7.1.9 branch where that branch is in use. Upgrade VDI Client above 7.0.13 and Zoom Rooms above 7.1.7 to vendor-supported fixed releases. Confirm the version after the process restarts. In VDI, verify a new clone. In Rooms, verify the device itself.

Until the update is complete, limit access from affected clients to untrusted networks and review room or virtual desktop egress. These measures can reduce exposure to hostile peers, but they do not change the vulnerable certificate validation logic. Avoid describing the 347,617 product count as the number of vulnerable devices in an executive report.

A useful completion metric is product-specific: fixed Workplace clients, fixed VDI sessions, and fixed Rooms devices, with counts for outstanding exceptions. That evidence separates actual patch coverage from public product discovery and prevents the exposure number from becoming a misleading headline.

References

  • Zoom ZSB-26021: Zoom Clients for Windows - Improper Certificate Validation
  • CERT-In CIVN-2026-0530: Multiple Vulnerabilities in Zoom Workplace Clients

title: Why H2H Over API? Understanding the Difference in Banking Integrations
description:
1. Introduction: What is an API?
An API (Application Programming Interface) is an interface that allows two different software applications to communicate with each other and exchange information.

For example, suppose XYZ Company wants to make a payment from its bank account using ABC platform.

The process works like this:

1.XYZ Company initiates a payment through ABC.

2.ABC sends an API request to the bank.

3.The bank receives and processes the request.

4.The bank sends a response to ABC.

5.ABC displays the payment response or status

This communication generally happens through individual API requests and responses.

Example:

XYZ Company wants to pay ₹50,000 to a vendor.

1.ABC sends the payment request to the bank.

2.The bank processes the request.

3.The bank responds with a success, failure or pending status.

The same process can be repeated for other payments. Alternatively, a bank may provide APIs that support bulk payment submissions.

2. What is H2H (Host-to-Host)?
H2H stands for Host-to-Host. It is a method of establishing direct and secure communication between two systems, such as a company's software and a bank's system.

Unlike a typical individual API request, H2H commonly uses file-based communication to exchange information in bulk.

Let's understand with the same XYZ Company example.

Suppose XYZ Company needs to make 500 vendor payments.

Instead of sending 500 individual payment requests, the company can:

Prepare a payment file containing details of all 500 transactions.

Place the file in a designated secure folder or transfer it through SFTP (Secure File Transfer Protocol).

The bank receives the file.

The bank validates and processes the transactions according to its rules and approval requirements.

The bank shares a response or status file containing the results of the transactions.

This allows the company to submit multiple transactions together rather than initiating each one separately.

title: Bias-Reduced and Parallel Heavy-Tailed Stochastic Convex Optimization in $\ell_p$ Geometries
description:
arXiv:2611.21844v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: We consider the fundamental problem of parallel stochastic convex optimization (SCO), whose aim is to approximately minimize a convex objective when given the ability to query a moment-bounded stochastic gradient oracle multiple times in parallel per round. Whereas most previous results have focused on the variance-bounded Euclidean ($\ell_2$-norm) setting, meaning the objective is Lipschitz with respect to the $\ell_2$-norm over an $\ell_2$-bounded feasible set in $\mathbb{R}^d$, in this work we study parallel SCO in $\ell_p$ settings for $2 \le p < \infty$ under a heavy-tailed noise model. We begin by introducing a new class of $\ell_p$-optimal-distance-convergence (ODC$_p$) algorithms, drawing on prior stochastic bias-reduced techniques [ACJ+21], which combine with multilevel Monte Carlo methods to efficiently estimate the optimum of uniformly convex objectives. As a consequence of our ODC$_p$ algorithms, we first establish rates for projection-efficient $\ell_p$-Lipschitz optimization, composite convex minimization, and efficient $\ell_p$-proximal point estimation. Combining our ODC$_p$ algorithms with a new $\ell_p$-generalized Gaussian-based stochastic gradient estimator ($p$-GREG), we provide two efficient $\ell_p$ parallel algorithms, EpochDA and $\ell_p$-AC-SA, which achieve optimization error $\epsilon > 0$ with at most $\tilde{O}(d^{\frac{p}{2p + 2}} \epsilon^{-\frac{p}{p + 1}})$ query depth, improving upon the sequential heavy-tailed stochastic query depth of $O(\epsilon^{-p})$ for $\epsilon \leq \tilde{O}(d^{-1/(2p)})$. We also establish dimension-dependent lower bounds of $\Omega\bigl(\min\{\epsilon^{-p},d^{p/(3p-2)}\}\bigr)$ adaptive rounds for nonsmooth convex optimization over a subset of the unit $\ell_p$ ball. Our results improve upon the $\Omega(\min\{\epsilon^{-p},\epsilon^{2/3}d^{1/3}\})$ bounds of [DG19], when adapted to the same feasible set.

title: AWS Lambda now supports scale to and from zero for Lambda Managed Instances
description:
AWS Lambda now supports scale to and from zero for Event Functions running on Lambda Managed Instances (LMI). Lambda automatically scales execution environments for your function to zero during idle periods and scales them back up when requests arrive, without requiring you to provision minimum capacity. This makes LMI cost-effective for intermittent workloads such as asynchronous processing, development, and test environments.

Lambda Managed Instances lets you run Lambda functions on your Amazon EC2 instances while maintaining the operational simplicity of Lambda. With Lambda Managed Instances, you can access specialized compute configurations and drive cost efficiency through EC2 pricing advantages, without managing infrastructure. Previously, customers needed to keep a minimum number of execution environments running even when there was no traffic. With this launch, Lambda scales execution environments for your function to zero after a period with no activity, and provisions them again when requests arrive. This improves cost efficiency for workloads with periods of no traffic.

This feature is available today in all AWS commercial Regions where Lambda Managed Instances is available. To get started, set MinExecutionEnvironments to zero for your function using the Lambda console, AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, AWS CloudFormation, AWS SAM, or AWS CDK. To learn more, visit the AWS Lambda Developer Guide and AWS Lambda pricing.

title: Beyond Bilingual Transfer: Multilingual Code-Switching in Instruction Tuning
description:
arXiv:2605.29414v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Recent studies have shown that code-switching data (CSD), in which multiple languages are mixed within the same context, can improve cross-lingual transfer and multilingual alignment in large language models (LLMs). Recent studies on synthetic code-switching for LLMs have primarily focused on bilingual transfer between English and a target language, leaving instruction-tuning settings that jointly mix three or more languages within each example largely unexplored. In this work, we investigate multilingual code-switching instruction tuning across four languages: English, Japanese, Korean, and Chinese. We evaluate multilingual understanding on Belebele and MMLU. Our experiments show that simple sentence-level multilingual CSD consistently improves the four-language average accuracy across all bilingual, trilingual, and quadrilingual settings for Gemma-2-2B, indicating that multilingual code-switching can be effective beyond bilingual transfer settings.
